What three years of the Gaza war reveal about Israel and the world
On October 7, 2023, Hamas and other Palestinian resistance organizations launched an attack out of the Gaza Strip and into Israel under the code name “Al-Aqsa Flood.” Israeli and Western mainstream media and politicians rapidly labelled this a massive act of terrorism and flooded the world with tales of horrific atrocities allegedly perpetrated by the Palestinians, such as sadistically murdering children and women and committing mass rape.
We now know that these atrocious tales were lies calculated to generate domestic and international outrage against the Palestinian resistance and Palestinians in general. They were part of the same poisonous Israeli narrative that labeled these people “Amalek” – a reference to a perversely “exemplary” genocide in the Old Testament – and denied that they were human beings. They were taking steps, in other words, to start a genocide.
These atrocious propaganda lies were made up and spread by, for instance, Israel’s Zaka activists and Western mainstream journalists, such as the New York Times, high public officials such as the UN’s Pramila Patten, and activists. For instance, former Meta executive Sheryl Sandberg acted as a Zionist propagandist, who chose to rely on Israeli disinformation.
In reality, there were no mass rapes, there were no sadistic baby murders by beheadings or in microwave ovens, no pregnant woman was found killed with a headshot, with her baby stabbed and still attached to the umbilical cord. It “simply didn’t happen,” as a detailed investigation by Israeli newspaper Haaretz found.
What did happen on October 7, 2026 was not a savage, sadistic rampage but a daring military resistance operation. It was also a mass break-out from the Gaza Strip, which was under a long Israeli siege so brutal that Israeli sociologist Baruch Kimmerling had already called the Strip the “world’s largest concentration camp ever” almost a quarter-century ago.
The core of this offensive targeted Israel’s Gaza Division, which, according to high-ranking Israeli officers was “overpowered.” In the process, Palestinian resistance fighters killed and captured Israeli military personnel. While Israel’s propaganda has done its best to obfuscate this fact, these actions were neither “terrorism” nor hostage-taking but legitimate acts of armed resistance under international law.
The Palestinian fighters also attacked a music festival as well as several settlements. There, according to an Amnesty International summary in early 2024, they did commit crimes, including the deliberate killing of civilians and the taking of hostages, that is, civilians, not soldiers, whose capture makes them POWs and not hostages. A crime, in any case, is a crime even if it’s only realistic to recognize plenty of mitigating circumstances in the immense injustice, dispossession, and often sadistic and humiliating violence Palestinians have suffered from Israelis over decades.
Honesty also dictates that we take three key facts into account: First, the leader of the pro-Israeli UAE, has revealed that he warned Israel’s leader Benjamin Netanyahu personally of Hamas’s plans. In a similar vein, Qatar’s leader claims that Hamas was ready to free all civilian hostages immediately after the attack (which would have left it with only military prisoners). Yet the Israeli leadership ignored the warning and rejected the offer to free all civilians.
It’s almost as if it wanted the attack to happen, as a pretext to initiate a massive ethnic cleansing-by-genocide campaign, and for the civilian hostages to stay in Gaza, as a pretext for continuing that campaign.
Second, it has long been clear that Israeli authorities activated an expanded “Hannibal Directive”: Usually prepared to kill their own soldiers rather than let them be captured, on October 7, Israeli forces also killed Israeli civilians and, most likely, in large if unknown numbers, deploying tanks as well as helicopter gunships to – in the words of an Israeli officer – “mass Hannibal” their own. Of the roughly 1,200 casualties on 7 October, hundreds are likely to have been due to Israeli-on-Israeli violence; others were soldiers and as such legitimate targets.
And finally, a simple point all too often drowned out by Israeli and pro-Israeli propaganda: A legitimate military force does not lose its overall legitimacy – or that of its goals – even when some of its members commit crimes. If that were the case, most armies in this world would have to be dissolved because none of them have a history entirely free of crimes. Armed Palestinian resistance is fundamentally legitimate under international law – and morally, too, obviously – and remains so. In fact, in the future, the outnumbered, outgunned, and abandoned Palestinian defenders of Gaza will be remembered as heroes, as they should.
Things are different, as a matter of fact, if we look at the actions of the Israeli military since October 7. Unlike with anything that individual Palestinian resistance fighters may have done, in the case of Israel’s euphemistically mis-labeled Defense Forces – a “citizen army [and] representative sample” of Israeli society – we are looking at a clear case of a whole, large organization deliberately and enthusiastically dedicated to committing every war crime and crime against humanity in every book, including ethnic cleansing and genocide.
Because that is a precise description of what Israel has been doing to the Palestinians of Gaza – and not only – since October 7, 2023. It is also by now the consensus among honest observers, including the global community of genocide experts. This, indeed, has been the most public genocide in human history, despite Israeli attempts to seal Gaza off and mass murder its journalists under false pretexts.
Israeli perpetrators – high and low – have proudly advertised their own crimes. Israeli society as a whole, virtually continuous polling has shown consistently, supports the genocide. In a world of real-time media and social media, the reality of Gaza could not be hidden. Only recently, Google has finally adjusted its maps to reflect it.
The nature and extent of Israel’s crimes is obvious and exceedingly well documented, and that is a very important thing. Humanity owes an enormous debt of gratitude to those Palestinians and others who have undertaken the harrowing task of compiling and analyzing the evidence, such as, to name only a few, UN Special Rapporteur Francesca Albanese or the tireless staff of the Electronic Intifada.
What needs at least as much attention is what the Gaza genocide says about our world as a whole: namely that genocide is not only possible – it was before – but can take place over years and in full view of the global public, with the active support of most of the establishments of virtually the entire West and the passive acquiescence of the elites of most other countries.
In a more or less sane world, fulfilling its obligations under the short and clear UN Genocide Convention of 1948 – it bears recalling – the Israeli genocide perpetrators would long have been stopped by a combination of diplomatic, economic, and, of course, military intervention. That would have been the minimum of what both international law and basic ethics obviously demand.
Yet, instead, we live in a world, where – apart from the Palestinian resistance itself – only a handful of states and political organizations have done anything at all to interfere with Israel’s mass murder campaign: Iran, Hezbollah in Lebanon, and Ansarallah – the Houthis – in Yemen.
Think about the above what you want, like or dislike their politics, it is a fact that no one else has even remotely tried to apply the Genocide Convention in practice. If that is irritating, don’t blame Ansarallah, for instance, but blame the many who have failed to act.
But failure to act has been only part of this real-life horror story. In the West, many governments and mainstream establishments, including in the media and academia, have pro-actively supported Israel. This is a shameful history of criminal collaboration and complicity still to be written. Indeed, in the worst cases, such as the elites of the US, the UK, and Germany, complicity seems too weak an expression: they are better described as genocide co-perpetrators.
The obvious inference from this state of the world is that international law does not matter. There is no more devastating attack on the very idea of international law and a law-based order than the impunity of Israel and its accomplices. Benjamin Netanyahu, with an International Criminal Court warrant to his name, has been able to brazenly deny his and his country’s crimes at the recent UN General Assembly and even repeat the Amalek reference, as Craig Mokhiber has pointed out. Outside, meanwhile, his critics were being arrested.
Annalena Baerbock, in her time as one of Germany’s most embarrassing foreign ministers ever, also justified, shielded, and supported Israel; she has just finished her ill-begotten sinecure as the UN General Assembly’s president and made a lateral move to an absurdly undeserved position at Columbia University. The examples could be multiplied endlessly: the elites of the West, including American presidents Joe Biden and Donald Trump, have devastatingly compromised themselves by their complicity with Israel. And yet, they keep thriving.
So, not only has international law been discredited as literally never before, but international establishments also have, and in particular those of that part of the world that still has the arrogance to claim global leadership as if it were some kind of birthright, the West.
Now add the fact that Israel has not “only” been committing the Gaza genocide. It has also escalated ethnic cleansing terror in the West Bank, invaded Syria and Lebanon, attacked Yemen, participated in and triggered brutal assaults against Iran that have also tanked the world energy economy, and, in general, has followed its usual modus operandi of assassination, subversion, torture, rape, and relentless aggression. And yet it faces no discernible consequences beyond ludicrously inappropriate, purely symbolical measures at best and, of course, massive continued support.
Meanwhile, those in the West who dare be human and show their solidarity with the Palestinians and other victims of Israel and its accomplices and co-perpetrators are harassed, beaten up by police, arrested, and blacklisted.
What the Gaza genocide has shown with respect to the world as a whole is simple: Those who rule us will go much farther, much more shamelessly and openly than most of us, even the pessimists, used to be able to imagine. More importantly, they will get away with it, and they will let each other get away with it. Gaza is not an exception. It is a harbinger of a world of horrors. Resistance is not an option; it is the only one.

US Republicans, independents express low trust in election integrity: Poll
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
20:27:47 UTC
05:27:47 KST

US Republicans, independents express low trust in election integrity: Poll
A Gallup survey highlights a deep – and historic – partisan divide over confidence in the country’s elections.
With less than a month to go before the United States’ pivotal midterms, a new survey found that most independent voters and supporters of President Donald Trump’s Republican Party do not believe the elections will be honest.
Polling from the research firm Gallup, released on Wednesday, found that 37 percent of Republicans and 35 percent of independents have confidence in the country’s electoral system, significantly lower than the rate for Democrats, at 63 percent.
The numbers highlight a deep, historic partisan divide over confidence in US elections.
The survey also suggests a counterintuitive relationship wherein the US voters who approve of Trump’s leadership also distrust the electoral system.
“Since 2025 and Trump’s return to the White House, the relationship between leadership approval and confidence in elections has disappeared,” Gallup wrote in a statement highlighting the results.
The firm added that the US is the only country out of more than 100 polled annually over the past 15 years to show this pattern: Trust in US election integrity is markedly higher among those who disapprove of the country’s leadership under Trump than those who approve.
That marks a shift in voter sentiment. In 2025, at the start of Trump’s second term, confidence in US elections “was nominally higher among approvers (51 percent) than disapprovers (45 percent)”, according to Gallup.
Now, 52 percent of those who disapprove of Trump’s leadership express confidence in US elections, compared with 41 percent of those who approve.
Overall, 49 percent of Americans said they were confident in the honesty of elections, while 51 percent said they were not. Those figures are unchanged from the country’s last midterm election in 2022.
Michael McNulty, the senior policy director at Issue One, a nonprofit that tracks the role of money in politics, has worked on more than 30 elections across the world.
He said the numbers, especially among Republicans, do not point towards problems in the US election system itself.
Rather, he blames Trump for sowing distrust in the election system among his base, particularly ahead of the November 3 midterm elections.
“The fact that Republicans trust elections less really is exactly the result of that false fraud narrative perpetrated over many years,” McNulty said. “I think Americans can trust the people who run their elections.”
Still, the US perspective towards election integrity appears to be a global outlier.
In more than 100 countries where Gallup tracks views of national leadership and confidence in elections, people who approve of their governments have generally been more likely to trust their country’s elections.
In 2025, a median of 70 percent of people across those countries who approved of their national leadership expressed confidence in the honesty of their elections, compared with 30 percent among those who disapproved.
“The current US pattern is highly unusual compared with the rest of the world,” Gallup wrote.
Under former US President Joe Biden, 81 percent of Americans who approved of the government also expressed confidence in elections, compared with just 30 percent of those who disapproved.
Gallup said this year’s unusual divide could have implications for the November elections, raising questions about whether some voters will view the results as legitimate.
Over the course of his second term in office, Trump and members of his administration have taken steps to upend the US voting system, including by launching investigations into the 2020 election, issuing executive orders to change voting procedures and demanding voter data from states.
Speaking to reporters outside the White House on Monday, Trump once again claimed that mail-in voting was prone to fraud, without providing evidence.
“No, vote by mail … I’d rather have a vote in person. But they can vote by mail if they want, because we seem to have no choice,” Trump said.
“What we’re concerned about is … there is a lot of cheating in vote by mail,” he added.
McNulty said Trump’s remarks are part of what he describes as an “election takeover playbook” aimed squarely at the president’s supporters.
“You use these false fraud narratives. You sow chaos. You undermine confidence, particularly among his own base and his own voters, because they’re the ones listening to him,” McNulty explained.
“And then you use that narrative to justify efforts” against the US electoral system, he added.
McNulty said voting organisations like his are preparing for the “very real threat” that Trump or Republican-aligned groups could challenge the midterm results.
But he is “confident” the US electoral system will stand up to any possible attempts to undermine it.
In response to a request for comment from Al Jazeera, White House spokesperson Lauren Bis instead blamed any decline in election-season trust on the Democratic Party’s refusal to implement Trump’s changes.
“Every American should be asking why the radical Left continues to fight against commonsense election integrity measures, like Voter ID and citizenship verification,” Bis wrote.
“President Trump has made clear: Anyone who illegally votes in our elections will be held accountable.”
State and federal law already prohibits non-citizen voting in federal elections. Critics, however, have accused Trump of seeking to implement further restrictions that would discourage or prevent citizens from exercising their legal right to vote.

Historical records cast doubt on Zack Polanski’s family Nazi escape story
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
20:27:40 UTC
05:27:40 KST

Zack Polanski, leader of Britain’s Green Party, is at the center of a public controversy after historical records contradicted his account of his ancestors fleeing the Nazis. The party has made headlines in recent days after passing a motion declaring Zionism to be racism and following revelations that one of its members is a close friend of an al-Qaeda terrorist.
In his keynote speech at the party conference in Bournemouth last year, Polanski, 43, said his Jewish ancestors fled pogroms in Latvia and Ukraine, made their way to Nazi-occupied Poland and ultimately escaped to England, where they encountered antisemitism. However, a review of public birth, marriage and census records from 1891 and 1901 found that his family had settled in Britain in the late 19th and early 20th centuries.
Despite the records, Polanski repeated the story of his family fleeing the Nazis on several occasions, including on “The Rest Is Politics” podcast and the BBC’s “Question Time” in December. The Daily Mail reported that the mystery deepened last month when Polanski himself acknowledged, during a podcast interview with Iain Dale, that his great-grandparents had arrived in Britain “way before the Second World War.”
In the same interview, he said they changed their surname from Polanski to Paulden to escape antisemitism in Britain, not the Nazis. Polanski, who was born David Paulden in 1982, changed his name to Zack Polanski to reconnect with his Jewish heritage and distance himself from his stepfather.
The Green Party declined to explain the discrepancy to the Daily Mail. A party spokesperson said that “Jewish family history is often confusing and muddled, as Zack has acknowledged” adding that “it’s astonishing that the only current Jewish leader of a British political party is having his family history raked over by the press in an attempt to discredit him.”
The controversy comes as the Green Party opens its 2026 conference in Brighton and less than a week before Polanski is due to contest a parliamentary election in Holborn and St Pancras in north London, a seat held by Labour since 1983 and previously represented by Keir Starmer, who stepped down as prime minister.
This is not the first time Polanski, who serves as a member of the London Assembly and earns nearly £66,500 ($88,000) a year, has faced scrutiny over contradictory statements. Earlier this year, he apologized for an “unintentional mistake” after failing to pay council tax on a residential property because of “financial hardship.”
In May, he admitted that he had not voted in local elections because he was not registered to vote, despite publicly promising his party’s candidate that he would vote for him. His spokesperson had claimed he had done so by postal ballot. The party attributed the incidents to a “misunderstanding.”
Anti-Zionism and ties to terrorists
The Green Party on Sunday approved a controversial motion declaring Zionism a form of racism. The wording of the motion implies a call for the effective elimination of the State of Israel. In response, Foreign Minister Gideon Sa’ar decided to bar Polanski from entering Israel.
The approved motion calls for the establishment of “a single democratic Palestinian state in all of historic Palestine with Jerusalem as its capital.” It also calls for a sweeping boycott of Israel and broad sanctions similar to those imposed on South Africa’s apartheid regime, arguing that “Zionism has created, and seeks to maintain and, where possible, expand, a system of apartheid between the Jordan River and the Mediterranean Sea.”
On Tuesday, Britain’s Telegraph reported that party member Lubna Speitan, who spearheaded the motion, is a close friend of an al-Qaeda terrorist who plotted a suicide attack at Heathrow Airport that was intended to kill hundreds of people, with a particular focus on passengers arriving from Israel or the United States.
According to the report, Speitan had previously offered to testify in defense of the terrorist, Minh Quang Pham, who was convicted in the United States of membership in al-Qaeda in the Arabian Peninsula, or AQAP, and of plotting the attack. Court documents from 2015 described her as a “close friend” of his.
Speitan has previously said Hamas should not be designated a terrorist organization. She has also called for Zionism to be “dismantled from the world” and said the time would come when Zionists would be “hunted down as the Nazi oppressors were hunted down.”

Asked about his 44-year prison sentence, she said: “People are demonised for all sorts of things and wrongfully accused of all sorts of things.”

Arizona congressional candidate says she was raped while trying to repair campaign sign
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
20:21:59 UTC
05:21:59 KST

This article contains graphic descriptions of sexual assault.
A congressional candidate in Arizona says she was attacked and raped in August while trying to repair one of her damaged campaign signs.
Bernadette Greene-Placentia, a trucker and small-business owner, shared her account with the Phoenix New Times, a local publication. The assault took place on 14 August, according to the campaign.
The Democratic candidate, running in a district that includes parts of Phoenix, told the newspaper that she was walking across a parking lot just after 2am to fix a campaign sign when an attacker smashed her over the head, causing her to black out.
Greene-Placentia told the newspaper that she awoke to find a man on top of her and discovered he was raping her. She recalled another man coming over and pushing her leg, at which point she said she swung her foot at him. The man said, “Not even worth it”, and the two attackers left, leaving her face down in the parking lot, she recalled.
The candidate said her memory of the incident and its aftermath was hazy, telling the newspaper she did not remember picking herself off the pavement or returning home.
“It’s just these little tiny flashes of things that I do remember,” Greene-Placentia told the Phoenix New Times. “As much as I don’t want to remember, I’ve tried very, very hard to remember more stuff. But that’s where I’m at.”
She said she may have had a concussion as a result of the attack and that her body was covered in bruises. She said she initially wanted to forget what had happened and felt “embarrassed”, at first choosing not to report the assault. But she told the paper that on the campaign trail, she often spoke about fighting for Arizonans, “and I didn’t feel like I could keep saying that if I weren’t also fighting for women that are victims of sexual assault”.
Greene-Placentia told her campaign staff and husband about the assault days after it happened and reported it to the Maricopa county sheriff’s office two weeks later, according to the Phoenix New Times. The newspaper interviewed Greene-Placentia’s relatives, friends, campaign staff and landlord about the aftermath of the assault.
“Speaking publicly about what happened has been incredibly difficult for Bernadette,” a campaign spokesperson told the Guardian on Wednesday after the Phoenix New Times story was published. “She chose to share her story because she knows many survivors struggle in silence, and she hopes that by speaking about her experience, others will know they are not alone.”
The spokesperson added: “She hopes the focus remains on supporting survivors and making sure people who have experienced sexual violence know they are seen, heard and supported.”
“I need to let women know that it’s OK to talk about it,” Greene-Placentia told the newspaper.
Stephanie Simacek, a state representative and friend of Greene-Placentia, said the congressional candidate told her of the assault in early September, telling the Phoenix New Times, “I felt sick to my stomach, and it was extremely disturbing. It was a big wake-up call for me. I think oftentimes, as candidates and electeds, we think that it’s not going to happen to us.”
A Maricopa county sheriff’s spokesperson declined to comment, saying the investigation was ongoing.
Greene-Placentia is running against an incumbent Republican member of Congress, Abraham Hamadeh.
- Information and support for anyone affected by rape or sexual abuse issues is available from the following organizations. In the US, Rainn offers support on 800-656-4673. In the UK, Rape Crisis offers support on 0808 500 2222. In Australia, support is available at 1800Respect (1800 737 732). Other international helplines can be found at ibiblio.org/rcip/internl.html

Saudi Arabia says three dead at airports after Houthis claim attacks

- - The Saudi-led coalition said it destroyed the missile launch platform, while the Houthis said they hit the airports and caused air traffic disruption.
- - The attacks came as fighting in Yemen worsened, with over 200,000 displaced and civilians in Taiz and Mocha reporting fear, damage, and a worsening crisis.

RIYADH - Saudi authorities said on Oct 7 that three people were killed in attacks on two of the kingdom’s international airports including in the capital Riyadh, after Yemen’s Houthis claimed to have fired on both transport hubs.
The Iran-backed fighters earlier took responsibility for a flurry of attacks that included firing a ballistic missile at Riyadh’s King Khalid International Airport as the conflict deepens with Saudi Arabia, which backs Yemen’s government.
“On Tuesday and Wednesday... Abha International Airport and King Khalid International Airport were subjected to attacks targeting their facilities,” the kingdom’s civil aviation authority said in a statement, without blaming anyone for the attacks.
An Egyptian and an Algerian national were killed at Abha airport and a Sudanese national was killed at the airport in Riyadh, the agency said, with 36 people wounded in the attacks.
The Saudi-led coalition that backs pro-government forces in Yemen said on X that it “destroyed the ballistic missile launch platform” used in the attack on Riyadh.
In a subsequent statement the coalition directly blamed Houthi forces and said it would retaliate.
“The brutal attacks by the Terrorist Houthi Militia on civilian and civilian objects in the Kingdom, most recently targeting (the two airports) will not go unpunished,” it said on X.
The coalition said as a result it struck and destroyed 82 “legitimate military targets,” including Houthi mountain-based ballistic missile facilities, command-and-control centers, communication systems and Houthi gathering sites.
The Yemeni group, which controls most of the country’s north-west, is battling for territory against the Saudi-backed forces after the civil war reignited in July and it captured swathes of coastal land.
The fighting has displaced more than 200,000 people within the country, the United Nations said on Oct 7.
Yemen’s internationally recognised government this week declared a major counter-offensive and claims to have pushed Houthi fighters out of strategic areas on the Red Sea and the port city of Mokha.
But the Iran-backed Houthis say they are holding their territory, and military sources from both sides contacted by AFP have not reported any major changes on the ground.
Claims by the warring parties have been impossible to independently verify with the situation moving fast and access for journalists difficult.
Flight diverted
“Our armed forces have just targeted King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh with a ballistic missile. The strike was accurate, by God’s grace, and led to a disruption of air traffic,” Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree said on Oct 7 in a post on X.
The Saudi-led military coalition said the missile was intercepted.
The Houthis also said they targeted a military supply convoy near the airport in the Yemeni city of Aden, the interim capital for the government.
The Yemeni government’s Saba news agency reported missiles and drones targeting that airport.
The agency cited transport authorities as saying one of the missiles landed near the runway minutes before the scheduled arrival of a flight from Cairo, which was forced to divert to Jeddah in Saudi Arabia.
Houthi drones and missiles also targeted Saudi Arabia’s Abha airport and King Khalid Air Base in Khamis Mushait, spokesman Saree said, claiming they had “hit their targets accurately”.
It is the second time this week that the Houthis claimed to have attacked the main airport in the Saudi capital.
‘Terrified’
Saudi Arabia leads an international coalition that has been fighting the Houthis since 2015, and is now trying to roll back the group’s latest advance.
On Oct 5, the coalition said it was providing air support for the counter-offensive launched by the Yemeni government forces.
After a four-year ceasefire, Yemen’s civil war re-erupted in July. In September, the Houthis seized the entire western coastline along the Red Sea in the country’s deadliest fighting in years.
On Oct 7, new clashes in Yemen’s west left at least 62 combatants dead, including 37 Houthis, military sources from both camps told AFP.
Saba also reported the Houthis fired a missile at the city of Taiz, which is held by government forces, wounding five civilians.
“We went out into the street to check on the wounded and saw young civilians who had been hit. The Houthi shell landed in the middle of the street, right in an area crowded with civilians,” Taiz resident Al-Fateh al-Eisaei told AFP.
Yemen’s government has announced a goal of retaking all Houthi territory – home to most of the country’s population, and much of it held for more than a decade.
The humanitarian crisis caused by the war has left most of the nation’s population dependent on aid.
Mohammed, a 33-year-old charity worker who fled from Mocha to Aden, told AFP on Oct 6 that “people there are terrified” of the Houthis. AFP

Democratic FCC member warns of AI robocall misinformation risks in US
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
20:14:35 UTC
05:14:35 KST

Democratic FCC member warns of AI robocall misinformation risks in US
FCC commissioner warns against AI robocalls, citing risks of misinformation before crucial midterm elections.
Anna Gomez, the Democratic member of the United States Federal Communications Commission, has urged the federal agency not to allow robocalls generated with artificial intelligence in the lead-up to the midterm elections in early November.
On Wednesday, the commissioner pushed back against a petition from Club for Growth, a national conservative fiscal policy organisation, to allow AI-generated robocalls.
The petition, filed on August 31, requested that the federal agency allow political groups to make automated phone calls to people without their prior permission. The group said it would limit calls so that the same person would not receive more than three calls over the course of 30 days and would be presented with the option to opt out.
The FCC’s public comment period began on September 4, with the deadline for comments on Monday. Responses to those comments are due October 19, and the FCC has yet to decide whether it will approve the request.
Robocalls have been used in political campaigns for years. The FCC prohibits such calls to cellphones and pagers without the called party’s prior express consent, but they are permitted to landlines.
The concern with the use of AI is that it can sound like a real person and make it easier to impersonate someone. On the back of a rising number of scams using the technology, the FCC, in February 2024, banned it, saying, “this action now makes the act of using AI to generate the voice in these robocalls itself illegal.”
“[If] the FCC allows a dark money group to flood Americans’ phones with AI-generated robocalls they never agreed to receive, it would bring chaos so close to Election Day,” commissioner Gomez told the Reuters news agency on Wednesday.
She told The Associated Press that removing the FCC’s consent requirement could lead to a rise in unwanted robocalls and misinformation.
Representatives for Gomez did not respond to Al Jazeera’s request for comment.
The concerns are not unfounded. In advance of the 2024 New Hampshire primary, voters received a robocall featuring an AI-generated version in the voice of President Joe Biden, the Democrat incumbent, telling them not to vote.
The FCC said that political consultant Steve Kramer, who was working for long-shot primary challenger Dean Phillips, was responsible and could face $6m in fines. He was later acquitted of voter suppression charges.
At the state level, Louisiana, Tennessee and Vermont passed laws this year requiring disclosures for AI-generated campaign phone calls. More broadly, 25 states have passed laws concerning the use of AI-generated materials in elections since 2019.
AI election concerns mount
Concerns about AI robocalls underscore broader concerns about AI in the run-up to the midterm elections.
According to a new Reuters/Ipsos poll, 57 percent of registered voters said that the administration of US President Donald Trump has not taken the risks of AI seriously enough, with 54 percent saying the same about congressional leadership.
Late last month, the White House convened leaders from leading AI companies, including Anthropic, OpenAI, Meta and Google, to sign a voluntary pact in which the companies agreed to put more safeguards in place around the development of their most advanced AI systems. Its non-compulsory nature has not appeased critics.
“The White House Accord on Super Intelligence is ‘morally binding’ only, allowing AI companies to design their own controls, select their own evaluators, and determine whether their own procedures are being followed,” Tom Wheeler, visiting fellow in governance studies with Center for Technology Innovation (CTI) at the think tank Brookings Institution, wrote about the decision.
“History suggests voluntary commitments from these companies are unreliable, as Facebook, Google, and Twitter have all walked back or violated previous self-imposed standards.”

EU Agrees Largest Sanctions Package Yet on Russia's Defense Industry, Kyiv Says
The European Union has agreed a new package of sanctions targeting Russia’s military-industrial complex, which covers approximately 1,700 entries, according to Vladyslav Vlasiuk, the Ukrainian President's Commissioner for Sanctions Policy.
Agreed on October 7, the measures are expected to receive formal approval next week, Vlasiuk said. Roughly 60% of the contents in the potential package consist of proposals submitted by Ukraine.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The core focus of these prospective restrictions may zero in on Russia’s missile program and electronic components, including semiconductors, microelectronics, capacitors, and resistors.
The package may also penalize individuals and companies involved in Russia's defense sector, spanning producers and suppliers of materials for machine tools, Lancet drones, and ballistic missiles.
Additionally, the list may extend to electronic warfare enterprises, shipbuilding yards, explosives manufacturers, repair facilities, chemical plants, garment factories, and trading intermediaries. Among the specific entities that may be targeted is the Special Design Bureau of Mechanical Engineering in Kurgan.
The facility is a leading Russian enterprise specializing in the design, development, and modernization of light and medium armored military vehicles. Ukraine sanctioned it on September 13.
On August 7, 2026, the European Union adopted new targeted sanctions against five individuals linked to Russia’s military-industrial complex in response to a wave of Russian airstrikes across Ukraine.
EU High Representative Kaja Kallas announced the decision, noting that the measures directly penalized key figures responsible for sustaining Moscow’s defense manufacturing capacity.
The decision followed the earlier adoption of the EU’s 21st sanctions package on July 23, which targeted Russian energy hubs, shadow fleet tankers, and long-range drone manufacturers. Kallas emphasized that each new attack on Ukraine provided further reason for Europe to tighten economic pressure until Russia ended its full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

Ukraine Builds Airless Wheels to Keep Ground Robots Moving After Battlefield Damage
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
20:13:45 UTC
05:13:45 KST

- Category
- Defense Tech
Ukraine Builds Airless Wheels to Keep Ground Robots Moving After Battlefield Damage
Ukrainian companies Print&Live UA and iSCALE 3D have developed lightweight airless wheels for unmanned ground vehicles operating on the front line.
Militarnyi reported the development on October 7, citing the companies behind the project. According to the outlet, the wheels are designed specifically for ground robotic systems, where conventional pneumatic tires remain vulnerable to punctures and battlefield debris.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The new design eliminates the need for compressed air, allowing a wheel to remain functional after damage that could disable a conventional tire, Militarnyi added. The developers also focused on reducing the wheel's weight, an important factor for smaller robotic platforms with limited payload and battery capacity.
According to Militarnyi, the project combines Print&Live UA’s experience in additive manufacturing with iSCALE 3D’s work on large-format 3D printing. The technology allows components with complex internal structures to be manufactured without using traditional tire-production tooling.
Airless wheels use a flexible structural body rather than air pressure to support the vehicle’s weight and absorb impacts. For military ground robots, this can reduce the risk of losing mobility after running over fragments, nails, or other sharp objects common on the battlefield.
Militarnyi noted that such components are particularly relevant for unmanned ground vehicles used for logistics, evacuation, and other missions in areas where recovering a disabled platform can expose personnel to additional risk.
Wheel resilience matters because Ukrainian ground robots are taking on an increasing share of frontline work.
On September 30, Ukrainian defense company Frontline Robotics unveiled Frodo, a six-wheeled unmanned ground vehicle with a range of up to 150 kilometers and a chassis designed to stay mobile even after losing a wheel.

"We've had the housing minister in one place, a small business minister somewhere else, and the de facto treasurer has been saying he's been defending the ATO," Taylor says.
"In the last couple of days, they've said to small businesses you've got to absorb the surcharges. The hypocrisy of this government knows no bounds because they don't understand enterprise."
Canavan calls for state, federal parliaments to overturn High Court mine decision
Matt Canavan has weighed in on the High Court's landmark decision about the expansion of the Mount Pleasant coal mine in NSW's Hunter.
The High Court ruled that planning authorities must consider the emissions caused by burning fossil fuels overseas when approving projects.
The Nationals leader has called on "all governments" to overturn the High Court's decision by passing laws through state or federal parliaments.
"The courts get to make decisions on these issues but it's the parliament that gets to decide with the laws and it is within the power of the New South Wales government, potentially the federal government as well, to give certainty to coal communities, to coal jobs," Canavan says.
Housing institute hits back at One Nation's rental and migration claims
The Australian Housing and Urban Research Institute (AHURI) has distanced itself from One Nation, after its research was used for the party's latest policy on migration and rents.
On Wednesday, Senator Pauline Hanson's party pledged that, if elected, One Nation would cut 750,000 temporary visas over three years.
This would reduce rent inflation by 6.5 per cent and save $2,818 a year on average for a renter by the third year of the party's immigration cuts, according to One Nation.
The party said the internal modelling relied on rental figures from the AHURI, to assume a substantial reduction in demand for rented properties as a result of the migration cuts.
The AHURI said in a statement to the ABC that it was not consulted, the research attributed to it was actually ABS 2021 data, and to be cautious about the modelling claims.
"AHURI was not consulted on, or involved in, the modelling One Nation has undertaken, so we are unable to comment on its reliability or validity," its managing director Tom Alves said.
"We would encourage caution when interpreting this ABS data. For example, it should not be assumed that each temporary migrant occupies an entire property, as several people may share a single home.
"Some temporary migrants may also live in accommodation owned or provided by their employer or education provider, which may not be available or practical for the general rental market."
Coalition claims Greens are 'outsourcing' defence policy to Russia is 'bollocks', says Shoebridge
Greens leader David Shoebridge has hit back at criticism of his party's policy of not sending military aid to Ukraine, maintaining the Greens support humanitarian and civilian aid to the country.
On the weekend, Shoebridge told The Sydney Morning Herald the Greens opposed Russia's illegal invasion of Ukraine but did not support "military aid to Ukraine".
Ukraine's ambassador to Australia Vasyl Myroshnychenko told the ABC he hoped the Greens would "reconsider" its position.
Earlier today on News24, Shadow Defence Minister James Paterson accused the Greens of wanting to "outsource" Australia's defence and foreign policy to Russia.
Shoebridge has called Paterson's comments "complete bollocks" and says the Greens have not changed their position on support for Ukraine.
"We absolutely support Australia giving humanitarian aid, civilian aid to the people of Ukraine, to the Ukrainian government in resisting the illegal invasion from Russia," Shoebridge says.
"And we have been from day one the strongest proponents for sanctions against Russia."
Resources minister plays down High Court ruling on coalmine expansion
Resources Minister Madeleine King has also played down the impact of a landmark High Court decision on the expansion of a NSW mine.
Yesterday, the High Court ruled planning authorities are required to consider the emissions caused by burning fossil fuels overseas when approving projects.
The decision was in relation to the expansion of the Mount Pleasant coalmine in the NSW Hunter Valley region.
But King has told ABC's AM program the ruling relates to a "particular" application under a particular law in NSW.
"The High Court ruling is a pretty technical ruling about what a planning commission has to consider when it goes through a planning approvals process," King says.
"The main thing is that people should be reassured that there are no jobs at risk because of this ruling. The Mount Pleasant mine will continue. It will continue under its current operations in 2032."
Duniam says aged care workers are classified as skilled workers under Coalition policy
Shadow Home Affairs Minister Jonno Duniam says aged care workers on visas were always carved out of the Coalition's migration policy.
On Tuesday, the Coalition announced plans to slash net overseas migration (NOM) to 100,000 for the first two years, followed by 130,000 in the third and 160,000 in the fourth year.
It will do that with deep cuts to graduate, refugee and bridging visas.
The opposition says temporary visa holders in the aged care sector will be able to transition to skilled visas, meaning they'll stay in the system.
Speaking to ABC Radio National Breakfast, Duniam says aged care workers have been on the Coalition's skilled workers list.
"The provision for aged care workers to be, as required by the industry, be included in the skills list has been part of the policy all along. And provision for the skills needs we have as a country is at the heart of our policy," Duniam says.
"We're not going to pick and choose randomly and add things in and take them out just at a whim because someone picks up the phone."
Assistant minister says cost for goods shouldn't go up due to surcharge ban
Andrew Charlton says he doesn't see why businesses would have to increase prices given credit card process fees have fallen.
The Reserve Bank decided to scrap credit card surcharges from October 1, which cost consumers $1.6 billion a year.
But some businesses say they will have to either absorb the cost of that surcharge or pass the cost onto consumers.
The assistant minister has told ABC Radio National Breakfast the government has reduced processing fees to 0.3 per cent.
"That reduction means that card payments are cheaper for businesses to process. So there's no reason as a result of this reform that consumers should be paying more when they tap their card for a coffee," Charlton says.
"The cost to the business has gone down, there's no reason why that should be greater than what they were paying before in terms of the price and the surcharge."

ATO gave small business a day's notice of credit card ban
We've heard a bit more from the Australian Tax Office (ATO) following its decision to stop accepting credit card payments from December 1.

After four days of discussions, pre-COP is drawing to a close and there's been a mixed response to the event.

Mamdani marks Oct. 7 by accusing Israel of genocide
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
20:11:51 UTC
05:11:51 KST

New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani marked the third anniversary of the Oct. 7 Hamas attack Wednesday by mourning the Israelis killed and abducted before accusing Israel of committing “genocide” and “apartheid” in Gaza, drawing sharp criticism from Israeli diplomats as commemorations were held across New York.
“This day is profoundly painful for so many New Yorkers,” Mamdani wrote in a statement. “It marks three years since the horrific war crimes of October 7.”
Mamdani said Hamas killed more than 1,100 Israelis and abducted 251 people in the attack. “We grieve alongside our many friends and neighbors who still carry that unthinkable loss,” he wrote.
But the mayor immediately turned to the war in Gaza, saying “the suffering did not begin nor end that day” and accusing the Israeli government of carrying out a “devastating, ongoing genocide in Gaza.”
Mamdani said more than 74,000 Palestinians, including more than 21,000 children, had been killed and claimed more than 1,400 Palestinians had been killed since what he called the “so-called ceasefire.” He also accused Israel of bombing ambulances outside hospitals, targeting residential buildings and journalists with drone strikes and turning away food aid at border crossings.
The figures and allegations were presented by Mamdani in his statement. Israel has rejected accusations that it is committing genocide in Gaza and has said its military targets Hamas and other terrorist groups while seeking to minimize civilian casualties.
“Many New Yorkers are reckoning with this unbearable grief, and we mourn alongside them — all while knowing that our tax dollars fund these war crimes,” Mamdani wrote.
He also accused the U.S. government of complicity through arms shipments to Israel.
“Three years later, we must refuse to accept a world in which occupation and apartheid continue, where war crimes are met with impunity, and our federal government continues its complicity with every arms shipment,” he said. “To honor the dead, we must fight for a world in which every person can live with freedom, safety, and dignity.”
Mamdani issued a similarly structured statement on the anniversary last year. He began then by describing the Hamas attack as a “horrific war crime,” cited the Israeli death toll and said he was praying for the return of the hostages before turning to Gaza and accusing Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and his government of waging what he called a genocidal war. He also accused the U.S. government of complicity and called for an end to what he described as “occupation and apartheid.”
New York Gov. Kathy Hochul issued a separate statement Wednesday focused on the victims of the Hamas attack and the Jewish community.
“It’s hard to fathom that it has been three years since the October 7 Hamas massacre,” Hochul wrote. “Three years since the deadliest day for the Jewish people since the Holocaust.”
“The pain of that dark day has not faded. But neither has the strength, resilience and enduring hope of the Jewish people,” she added. “Today, we remember the innocent lives stolen, stand with the survivors and the families forever changed, and pray for a lasting peace.”
Mamdani’s statement drew condemnation from senior Israeli representatives in the United States.
Israel’s ambassador to the United Nations, Danny Danon, accused the mayor of attempting to appropriate the anniversary to attack Israel.
“‘Mamdani-ism’ — an attempt to hijack the anniversary of October 7 and turn it into yet another propaganda attack against Israel,” Danon said. “It is like turning September 11 into a day of mourning for al-Qaeda terrorists.”
“We will remember those who were murdered, and we will never forget who was behind this massacre,” he added.
Ofir Akunis, Israel’s consul general in New York, also sharply criticized Mamdani, saying the mayor “should be ashamed of himself.”
“It’s a shame that on October 7, the day that the Hamas monsters brutally murdered, raped and burned our people alive, Mamdani responded in this way,” Akunis said.
Akunis invited Mamdani to attend a screening later Wednesday of footage documenting atrocities committed during the Hamas attack, saying it was “not too late to come and watch the horror film and see the truth.”
Mamdani was scheduled to attend an anniversary gathering at Union Square later Wednesday organized by Israelis for Peace. Organizers described the event as an evening of “quiet reflection and mourning” for those killed in 2023 and for the “bloody aftermath” of the attack.
After the memorial, Mamdani was scheduled to meet with Palestinian residents of New York, as the mayor sought to engage communities deeply divided over the war.
It was to be Mamdani’s second year attending the Union Square commemoration. He attended the previous year while running for mayor alongside Brad Lander, then New York City comptroller.
In his first statement after the 2023 attack, Mamdani did not explicitly condemn Hamas and focused largely on Israel’s response. He later condemned the killing of civilians and subsequently denounced Hamas directly, calling the Oct. 7 assault a “horrific war crime.”
Pro-Palestinian groups, meanwhile, were organizing campus strikes and a protest outside City Hall on Wednesday, accusing Mamdani of “betraying his values” and bowing to what they described as Zionist pressure.
Memorial events across New York
A series of other events were held across New York to mark three years since the attack.
The Marlene Meyerson JCC Manhattan organized what it called a “day of remembrance, music and community,” including an exhibition of drawings by Israeli artist Zeev Engelmayer.
UJA-Federation of New York unveiled “Rooted” at the Museum of Jewish Heritage, a public installation made from thousands of dog tags and pins bearing messages calling for the return of the hostages.
At 92NY on Manhattan’s Upper East Side, Jonathan Dekel-Chen, father of former hostage Sagui Dekel-Chen, was taking part in a discussion with Palestinian father Jasser Abu Musa. The conversation was moderated by Claire Shipman, who previously served as acting president of Columbia University.
Former hostage Omer Shem Tov was scheduled to speak Wednesday evening at Yeshiva University’s memorial ceremony, while the Park Slope Jewish Center in Brooklyn was hosting testimony from Atir Vinikov, a survivor of the massacre at the Nova music festival.
Protest targets Jewish organization in London
The anniversary was also marked by tensions outside the United States.
Earlier Wednesday, masked protesters demonstrated outside the London headquarters of the Board of Deputies of British Jews, hours before the organization was due to host a major memorial event.
The protesters, some draped in Iranian, Palestinian and Irish flags, gathered outside the Board of Deputies’ offices in Camden for about 20 minutes.
They chanted “stop killing babies” and carried signs accusing the organization of genocide denial. Other signs described the umbrella organization representing British Jews as “Israel’s mouthpiece” and a “shield for Israel’s crimes” and accused it of weaponizing antisemitism.

US gasoline stocks fall in most regions despite national increase
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
20:11:06 UTC
05:11:06 KST

Mucahithan Avcioglu
07 October 2026•Update: 07 October 2026
Gasoline inventories fell in four of the US’ five petroleum reporting regions last week, according to Energy Information Administration (EIA) data released Wednesday, underscoring an uneven supply picture as G7 economies move to release emergency reserves to ease energy market pressures.
Midwest stocks decreased by 421,000 barrels to 41.41 million for the week ending Oct. 2, leaving inventories 12.7% below their year-earlier level.
The Gulf Coast recorded the largest weekly decline, with stocks falling 1.83 million barrels to 75.04 million barrels. Inventories also decreased on the West Coast and in the Rocky Mountain region.
An East Coast increase of 2.8 million barrels offset the declines, lifting nationwide gasoline inventories by 382,000 barrels to 204.74 million.
Despite the weekly increase, US stocks remained 6.5% below a year earlier. All five regions held less gasoline than during the comparable week of 2025, with the Midwest recording the steepest annual decline.
G7 leaders agreed Oct. 2 to implement a coordinated release of 100 million barrels through the International Energy Agency over four months, including a substantial diesel release within the first 20 days.
The statement linked the release to implementing commitments made in March, taking account of volumes already released.
Leaders also pledged to coordinate refinery maintenance to prevent simultaneous shutdowns and temporarily increase utilization rates where feasible, while encouraging greater global production of refined products, particularly diesel.
The group reaffirmed its commitment to avoid restrictions on energy exports between G7 countries and urged producers to refrain from bans that could worsen market tensions.

Halis Sunnetci

Former Tottenham Hotspur and Switzerland defender Ramon Vega announced Wednesday his intention to challenge FIFA President Gianni Infantino, who is seeking reelection next year.
"I am standing to reunite the global football family, deliver genuine and lasting reform, modernise FIFA for the 21st Century, restore stability and credibility, and rebuild the trust that our game urgently needs," Vega said in a statement.
"Football does not belong to presidents, confederations or administrators. Football is greater than any position, any individual or any institution," said the 55-year-old.
"It is the people's game and belongs to everyone: the players, coaches, referees, supporters, volunteers, clubs, leagues, associations and communities that give football its life."
Vega accused FIFA's leadership of damaging trust in the governing body and demanded changes to its governance.
"The current leadership has demoralised the game. Weak governance has damaged FIFA's credibility and eroded trust across the global football family," he said. "Football is in the emergency room, on life support. We cannot wait any longer. FIFA needs a new direction and fundamental reform."
Infantino has faced demands to step down following the collapse of a controversial plan involving the sale of a stake in commercial and ticketing rights to FIFA competitions to private investors.
Vega considered running for the FIFA presidency in 2015, telling the BBC at the time that he was weighing a candidacy.
Four years later, he announced plans to challenge Infantino but failed to secure the backing of five FIFA member associations required to appear on the ballot.
Candidates seeking to challenge Infantino in the 2027 election have until Nov. 18 to declare their intention to stand.
Vega earned 23 caps for Switzerland and played for clubs including Tottenham, Celtic and Watford before retiring in 2004. He later pursued a career in finance.

US President Donald Trump has said that he welcomes an agreement by Türkiye and Pakistan to provide military support to Saudi Arabia as part of a new collective defence arrangement involving the three countries.
Speaking to reporters at the White House on Wednesday before departing for Texas, Trump was asked about the decision by Türkiye and Pakistan to send military forces to Saudi Arabia under the Mecca Defence Alliance.
"I think they want to help Saudi Arabia, and I think that’s great," he replied.
‘Defence and dialogue together’
Türkiye, Saudi Arabia and Pakistan moved to strengthen their joint defence framework on Monday as senior political and military officials met in Riyadh for an emergency session.
Türkiye’s foreign minister Hakan Fidan said the three countries discussed steps to support Saudi Arabia's defence while also examining ways to resolve regional issues peacefully through dialogue.
The alliance was established in August by Türkiye, Saudi Arabia and Pakistan, with the three countries subsequently agreeing to build permanent institutions and strengthen collective deterrence and defence capabilities.
According to Pakistan's foreign ministry, the three countries agreed that military forces and capabilities could be rapidly deployed in Saudi Arabia under the alliance's framework.
The sides also condemned attempts to target the holy cities of Mecca and Madinah and reaffirmed their commitment to confronting attacks against Saudi Arabia and Islamic holy sites.
Saudi Defence Minister Prince Khalid bin Salman said the alliance remains committed to confronting attacks and protecting the kingdom, while collective deterrence measures would be used against threats and those responsible.
The Turkish government will submit a defence agreement with Saudi Arabia and Pakistan to parliament within days, a spokesperson for the governing Justice and Development (Ak) Party said, setting the stage for a ratification process that could pave the way for a possible deployment of Turkish troops to Saudi Arabia.
Houthi attacks
The Houthis have claimed responsibility for several recent attacks in the kingdom, including strikes targeting Saudi Aramco facilities, airports and military sites.
Saudi Arabia has also reported Houthi attempts to target the holy cities of Mecca and Medina over the past nine years, including two incidents in September, drawing condemnation from Arab and Muslim countries.
Confrontations between Yemen's internationally recognised government forces and the Houthis have escalated since early July following years of relative calm.
The country has been engulfed in war since the Houthis seized the capital Sanaa and several provinces in 2014, before a Saudi-led Arab coalition intervened in 2015 in support of the internationally recognised government.
The Houthis have been engaged in renewed fighting with government forces since Yemen's civil war reignited in July, when the group declared a maritime blockade on Riyadh and began targeting its ships in the Red Sea.

$5,000 pledges, state-funded personal ads and make-believe ballots: Trump is pulling out all the stops ahead of the midterm elections
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
20:10:00 UTC
05:10:00 KST

US midterms: Is Trump campaigning at taxpayers' expense?
October 7, 2026
It's neither a joke nor fake news but a real report from earlier this week: Donald Trump has backed down. On Monday, the US president announced that a series of advertisements aired in September promoting him and his administration would no longer be funded with taxpayer money.
"The radical Left is upset with the fact that I am taking ads, which I consider to be a positive promotion for our great USA, and paying for them with USA money," Trump wrote on his platform Truth Social.
He went on to claim that funding partisan ads with public money was a "rather standard thing to do," before adding that future ads would be paid with money raised from donations.
The ads themselves have caused some controversy in the United States. They ran in September between popular shows such as Saturday Night Live and football games, marked with the line: "paid for by the US government" — that is, paid with tax dollars.
The commercials showed scenes such as when US troops captured Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro earlier this year but they mostly consisted of images and videos of Trump himself, along with combative messages that he would "expel the warmongers" or "throw off the sick political class," and ensure that the US did not become a communist state.
Public funds for personal praise
Political opponents and a series of NGOs responded to the campaign with sharp criticism. Not only does US law prohibit the use of taypayer funds for political advertisements, but the ads also appeared shortly before the midterms — elections held near the midpoint of a president's four-year term.
On Tuesday, the US broadcasting network CBS reported that, according to contracting records, the US Department of Homeland Security had paid an agency $20 million (€17.9 million) for a "national media campaign."
The "rather standard" practice that Trump referred to actually applies to public service announcements, but this is not what the campaign ads are, argued the US non-profit consumer advocacy group Public Citizen.
"Federal law explicitly prohibits using appropriated public funds for government propaganda, self-aggrandizement, or partisan political advertising," the organization wrote in a public complaint to the Federal Communications Commission (FCC) ."Yet, that is exactly the nature of Trump's recent campaign ads."
Independent experts have also voiced concerns. Patrick Malone, a professor in the department of Public Administration and Policy at American University in Washington DC, said the timing of the videos was problematic.
"You're not supposed to use taxpayer dollars to pay for anything that's campaign-related," he told DW. "Technically, [Trump] is not campaigning. He's not saying 'Vote for me!' The thing that's created the challenge here is the timing. Weeks before the midterms, this is a real big issue."
Will the Republicans keep their majority after midterms?
Voters do not choose presidents in the midterm elections but members of Congres, which comprises the Senate and the House of Representatives and is the legislative branch of the federal government. On November 3, those eligible to vote will cast their ballots for all the seats in the House of Representatives, and roughly a third of the seats in the Senate. Some states will also be choosing governors.
Republicans have not been faring well in recent polls, which may be why Trump has been trying to promote his party's achievements. The Republicans currently hold a majority in both houses, with 53 of 100 seats in the Senate, and 219 of 435 seats in the House of Representatives. This has enabled Trump to pass a large number of his proposals fairly easily.
But a Reuters/Ipsos poll released on Monday indicates that this could soon change. "Voters age 50 or older preferred Trump's party over the Democratic Party by just 2 percentage points — 44% to 42% — compared to an 8-point Republican advantage in December," it found. This age bracket "is particularly important for midterm elections, when older Americans historically have made up large shares of the electorate."
Meanwhile, among voters under the age of 50, "Democrats led by 18 points," the survey showed.
The poll also found that opinions on Trump himself were low, with "32% of Americans giving a thumbs up to Trump's presidency." This level of approval, the study highlighted, was unchanged from an earlier poll "that saw the leader's rating at the lowest of his political career."
Republicans shy away from Trump's support
This could also be one of the reasons why Republican candidates do not seem so keen on making public appearances with the president, usually a highlight of a campaign trail.
Many US citizens associate Trump with high living costs, or the war with Iran, which has dragged on for over half a year now.
One Republican operative told the news website Politico on condition of anonymity that if the the president were to visit a battleground state — where Democratic and Republican support is fairly equal among voters — to campaign for his party, they suspected their "candidates would come down with COVID" to avoid having to attend.
In September, a number of Republicans skipped Trump's big party convention — typically reserved for presidential, not midterm elections — even though the event could have offered them a platform for their campaign.
Susan Collins from Maine and Dan Sullivan from Alaska, are just two examples of Republican senators whose seats are on the line and who did not attend. Neither did candidates for the House of Representatives from the swing states Arizona, Iowa and Michigan.
Trump promises $5,000 payout if Republicans win
Those who skipped the event missed the president repeating an unusual campaign message: To encourage more people to vote, Trump urged supporters to "pretend" he was on the ballot.
And if that wasn't enough, he also promised each US citizen eligible to vote a $5,000 payout if Republicans maintained their majority in both houses of Congress.
Keeping that pledge could cost the federal government over $1.2 trillion, but observers doubt it would ever come to that.
"He has no money to do that with. It would have to be authorized and appropriated by Congress," Mallone explained. "I think the likelihood is very slim," he added. "It's one of those things like 'Mexico is going to pay for the wall.'"
Whether Trump's commercials or promised payouts will be enough to rally majority Republican support remains to be seen.

US midterms: Is Trump campaigning at taxpayers' expense?
October 7, 2026

"The radical Left is upset with the fact that I am taking ads, which I consider to be a positive promotion for our great USA, and paying for them with USA money," Trump wrote on his platform Truth Social.
He went on to claim that funding partisan ads with public money was a "rather standard thing to do," before adding that future ads would be paid with money raised from donations.
The ads themselves have caused some controversy in the United States. They ran in September between popular shows such as Saturday Night Live and football games, marked with the line: "paid for by the US government" — that is, paid with tax dollars.
The commercials showed scenes such as when US troops captured Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro earlier this year but they mostly consisted of images and videos of Trump himself, along with combative messages that he would "expel the warmongers" or "throw off the sick political class," and ensure that the US did not become a communist state.
Public funds for personal praise
Political opponents and a series of NGOs responded to the campaign with sharp criticism. Not only does US law prohibit the use of taypayer funds for political advertisements, but the ads also appeared shortly before the midterms — elections held near the midpoint of a president's four-year term.
On Tuesday, the US broadcasting network CBS reported that, according to contracting records, the US Department of Homeland Security had paid an agency $20 million (€17.9 million) for a "national media campaign."
The "rather standard" practice that Trump referred to actually applies to public service announcements, but this is not what the campaign ads are, argued the US non-profit consumer advocacy group Public Citizen.
"Federal law explicitly prohibits using appropriated public funds for government propaganda, self-aggrandizement, or partisan political advertising," the organization wrote in a public complaint to the Federal Communications Commission (FCC) ."Yet, that is exactly the nature of Trump's recent campaign ads."

"You're not supposed to use taxpayer dollars to pay for anything that's campaign-related," he told DW. "Technically, [Trump] is not campaigning. He's not saying 'Vote for me!' The thing that's created the challenge here is the timing. Weeks before the midterms, this is a real big issue."

Drinking problems remained a risk factor for reoffending even among men with stronger social skills
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
20:00:25 UTC
05:00:25 KST

Alcohol-related problems and difficulties with social and cognitive skills were each associated with reoffending among men who had perpetrated intimate partner violence, but the two did not appear to combine in a way that further increased risk, according to a study published in Applied Cognitive Psychology. Some skills that would normally be expected to protect against reoffending were unexpectedly linked to higher odds of a new violent offense.
Problematic alcohol use is common among men who perpetrate intimate partner violence, and alcohol can impair judgment, weaken behavioral control and make people more prone to impulsive reactions. However, alcohol is not the sole cause of violence. Other factors, including hostility, impulsivity, poor problem-solving, difficulty understanding another person’s perspective and trouble controlling behavior, are also linked to violence against partners and to reoffending.
Researchers have suggested that alcohol might be especially dangerous for people who already have these difficulties. For example, alcohol could make it harder for someone with poor impulse control to pause before acting or could intensify hostile interpretations of a partner’s behavior, while stronger skills might help buffer against alcohol’s effects. Few studies had tested whether these factors actually interact to predict reoffending, and most had looked at only a handful of skills.
The study was led by Crystal J. Giesbrecht and Kaila C. Bruer of the University of Regina in Canada. The team analyzed existing assessment and follow-up data from 7,781 men in Alberta who had perpetrated intimate partner violence and had started community supervision between 2009 and 2012. The men ranged in age from 18 to 84, with an average age of about 35, and about 27% were Indigenous.
The data came from the Service Planning Instrument, a risk assessment that correctional staff complete when a person begins serving a sentence under supervision in the community. Staff score it using interviews, criminal records, previous assessments and information from people such as family members, partners and employers. The researchers then examined whether the men had any recidivism within three years, which included new charges as well as violations such as breaching release conditions or failing to appear in court, and whether they had a new violent offense, such as assault or uttering threats.
Alcohol use was measured in three ways: how often the men drank, whether drinking had disrupted their work, family life, friendships or health, and whether alcohol use contributed to their criminal behavior. Staff also rated eight social and cognitive skills: impulsivity, hostile attributions (the tendency to read neutral actions as hostile), consequential thinking (thinking ahead about the results of one’s actions), perspective-taking, problem-solving, behavioral control, interpersonal skills, and goal-setting and planning. The researchers classified each skill as either a risk area or not.
Alcohol use was widespread: 93% of the men used alcohol, and about a third drank at least three days a week. For about half the men, alcohol contributed to their criminal behavior, and for 27% it had disrupted their functioning. Within three years, 38% of the men had some form of recidivism and 20% had a new violent offense.
After accounting for the other factors in the analysis, men whose drinking had disrupted their functioning had about 27% higher odds of any recidivism and 28% higher odds of violent recidivism. Alcohol-related criminal behavior was linked to similar increases for both outcomes. Frequent drinking was associated with higher odds of any recidivism compared with not drinking, but not with violent recidivism.
Among the skill measures, men rated as having problems with impulsivity were more likely to have both types of recidivism, and those with weaker goal-setting and planning were more likely to have any recidivism. Hostile attributions were linked to higher odds of violent reoffending. Problem-solving, behavioral control and interpersonal skills were not reliably linked to either outcome once the other factors were taken into account.
Two results ran in the opposite direction from what the researchers expected. Men rated as having no problems with perspective-taking had higher odds of any and violent recidivism, and those with no problems in consequential thinking had higher odds of violent recidivism. The authors suggested that such skills, without adequate self-control or prosocial goals, might help some people manipulate others or navigate the justice system in self-serving ways, though the pattern could also reflect factors the data did not capture.
Alcohol problems and skill deficits tended to go together: men whose drinking disrupted their lives or contributed to their offending were more likely to be rated as having deficits in every skill area. But the researchers found little evidence that the two interacted to predict reoffending. In other words, alcohol problems and skill deficits each mattered, but having both did not produce an extra increase in risk beyond what each contributed on its own. The models explained only about 3% of the variation in any recidivism and about 2% for violent recidivism, which the authors note is typical of research predicting a behavior as complex as reoffending.
“This indicates that problematic alcohol use may represent a stand-alone criminogenic need that remains salient even among individuals with relatively strong cognitive or social skills,” the authors wrote. Criminogenic needs are risk factors for reoffending that can change over time, which makes them targets for treatment.
The researchers recommend screening for both alcohol problems and social and cognitive skills when people enter supervision, and building alcohol treatment into intimate partner violence programs. Such programs often exclude people who are actively using substances, and access to them in Canada is limited and inconsistent.
There are a few things to keep in mind. Because the dataset contained no victim information, the researchers could not tell whether new offenses were committed against an intimate partner, so the findings concern general and violent reoffending rather than repeat partner violence specifically. Canada’s Criminal Code also has no specific offense for intimate partner violence, which makes such cases hard to identify in official records.
The study relied on existing assessment data, so the researchers could not add measures or check for errors, and recidivism was based on official records, which miss offenses that never come to the attention of authorities. Because the data are observational, the findings show associations rather than evidence that alcohol or skill deficits cause reoffending. The authors also suggest that future research account for differences among men who perpetrate partner violence, since alcohol may be more closely tied to violence for some types of perpetrators than for others.
The study, “The Connection Between Alcohol Use and Social and Cognitive Skills for Men Who Have Perpetrated Intimate Partner Violence,” was authored by Crystal J. Giesbrecht and Kaila C. Bruer.

Brazil's Bolsonaro pledges broad review of Lula-era taxes
