Brazil's Bolsonaro pledges broad review of Lula-era taxes
BRASILIA, Oct 7 - Brazil presidential candidate Senator Flavio Bolsonaro said on Wednesday his team was studying constitutional amendments to revise parts of a planned consumption-tax reform — alongside other fiscal measures — arguing the current design would leave the country with an excessively high tax burden.
"There are several constitutional amendments that are possible," Bolsonaro told reporters, citing "aspects of the tax reform" among measures he would pursue if elected, alongside lowering the age of criminal responsibility, ending presidential reelection and implementing a political reform.
In 2023, leftist President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva approved the consumption-tax reform, a long-awaited overhaul of Brazil's tax system, set to begin taking effect next year, which will consolidate multiple levies into a dual value-added tax administered at the federal and regional levels.
"I support modernizing our tax system, which is genuinely too complex," Bolsonaro said.
The reformed consumption tax's effective VAT rate — estimated to be about 28% by economists but not yet finalized by the government - would be too high, Bolsonaro said.
Bolsonaro also said he wanted to reduce payroll taxes and ensure that "more of Brazilian workers' income stays with them rather than the government."
On Tuesday, the senator's top economic adviser, Daniella Marques, told local media that a Bolsonaro administration would review a broad range of tax measures enacted under Lula, including a dividend tax that took effect in January.
Marques served in the elder Bolsonaro's government. She said that administration had previously only proposed taxing dividends alongside a reduction in corporate income taxes.
Bolsonaro would also eliminate the 12% tax on crude oil exports introduced this year by Lula's government, Marques said, describing the levy as an "aberration."
Lula introduced the tax to help finance fuel-tax relief for Brazilians amid a global oil-price spike linked to the US-Israeli conflict on Iran.
Other tax measures on the chopping block include reversing increases to the Financial Transactions Tax (IOF) on corporate credit operations, foreign-exchange transactions, and certain private pension investments, Marques said.
By contrast, Lula's platform pledged to deepen efforts to promote "tax justice" and reduce inequality through the elimination of tax distortions and privileges, while implementing the consumption-tax overhaul approved during his administration.
Lula this year introduced a tax on dividends to help finance an tax exemption on higher income for middle-income earners, while his administration has argued for further cuts to tax exemptions and the elimination of what it views as inefficient tax incentives.
Bolsonaro, the eldest son of ex-President Jair Bolsonaro, outperformed expectations to finish ahead of leftist incumbent President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva in Sunday's first round. The rivals go head-to-head in an October 25 runoff.
DEBT RESTRUCTURING
Amid near-record levels of household debt in Brazil, Senator Bolsonaro also said his government would buy debt from over-indebted consumers and refinance it through state-owned lender Caixa Economica Federal.
Borrowers would also gain access to new credit lines to help finance small businesses, he said.
Lula, like Bolsonaro, has also pledged to purchase debt as part of a campaign promise.
The government said it will hold an auction in November to buy and restructure household debt, spending 15 billion reais to acquire up to 150 billion reais of delinquent loans at discounts of at least 90%. The program is expected to cover about half of the debt stock deemed eligible.
Households would then be able to clear overdue obligations at the discounted value, with the full benefit of the write-down passed through to borrowers. REUTERS

====================================================================================================

Most Americans Want to Stop Changing the Clocks. Here’s Why Senators Are Hesitating
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
19:59:00 UTC
04:59:00 KST

In less than a month, most of the U.S. will fall back an hour, continuing the cycle of biannual clock changes. Some lawmakers are trying to end that practice—but are facing pushback from others.
In July, the House passed a bill with bipartisan support that would instate Daylight Saving Time year-round across the U.S.—the latest step forward in a yearslong effort to eliminate the clock change. President Donald Trump has repeatedly urged Congress to pass the bill. But the legislation now faces an uncertain future in the upper chamber. Earlier this week, Senate Majority Leader John Thune told POLITICO that there is no “consensus” among his colleagues on whether to advance the measure.
“The President feels strongly on it like he does a lot of issues,” Thune said. “It’s something we’re having conversations about, but there’s no clear path forward or consensus on it yet.”
Here’s what the bill would do, why some senators are backing it, and why others aren’t.
What would the Sunshine Protection Act do?
Most of the country follows the practice of changing the clocks twice a year, jumping forward an hour every March when Daylight Saving Time begins and falling back every November when it ends to observe Standard Time.
The system is widely unpopular. Polling conducted by the Associated Press/NORC last year shows that more Americans oppose the current biannual clock change than those who support it—47% compared to just 12%.
Americans are a bit more divided on whether they would rather observe Daylight Saving Time or Standard Time year-round, though the former tends to garner more support. Fifty-six percent support permanent Daylight Saving Time, compared to 42% for Standard Time, according to last year's AP/NORC poll.
Currently, federal law allows states to forgo Daylight Saving Time and stay in Standard Time throughout the year; Hawaii and most of Arizona have chosen to do so. States aren’t allowed, though, to observe Daylight Saving Time permanently.
The legislation that passed the lower chamber over the summer, called the Sunshine Protection Act, would change that.
If the bill succeeds in the Senate and is signed into law by the President, it would make Daylight Saving Time permanent nationwide—though it would allow states to opt out if they choose.
Why are some senators supporting permanent Daylight Saving Time?
Senators who have expressed support for making Daylight Saving Time year-round in the past have argued that most Americans dislike the biannual clock changes, calling the practice “antiquated.”
They have also pointed out that remaining in Daylight Saving Time permanently would mean that the sun would appear to set later throughout the year, rather than just in the summer, which, they claim, would encourage people to engage in more outdoor activity.
Florida Republican Sen. Rick Scott is one of the most vocal backers of the Sunshine Protection Act. In a statement last year, when he introduced a version of the bill in the upper chamber, Scott said that he hears from constituents that “they are sick and tired of changing their clocks twice a year—it’s an unnecessary, decades-old practice that’s more of an annoyance to families than benefit to them.” He added that he believes this is a “common-sense change that will simplify and benefit the lives of American families.”
“For many Americans, an extra hour of daylight means more time to play outside with their kids, walk their dog, or spend time with neighbors,” he said in a post on X on Wednesday. “Americans work hard, and they deserve more free time to enjoy all the outdoors has to offer. It’s time to pass my Sunshine Protection Act [so] they can enjoy every ounce of sunshine.”
In July, Sen. Patty Murray, a Democrat from Washington, applauded the House for passing the bill, saying that the lower chamber “delivered on something Americans all across the country actually want: to never have to change their clocks again.”
“It’s not lost on me that Republicans still refuse to do literally anything to make life more affordable for families or to hold the Trump administration accountable for its daily abuse of power, but if Congress can enact permanent Daylight Saving Time, I will take this opportunity to make it happen,” she said in a statement.
She went on to say that, in her home state, it often gets dark around 4 p.m. in the winter months. Her constituents, she said, have “made it abundantly clear” that they want to observe Daylight Saving Time year-round.
When Scott introduced a version of the bill last year, other senators from both parties also expressed their support for the measure.
“The head-spinning ritual of falling back and springing forward has a very real impact on our economy, our health, and our happiness,” Sen. Ed Markey, a Democrat from Massachusetts, said in a statement at the time. “Let’s say goodbye to 4pm winter sunsets and pass the Sunshine Protection Act for permanent Daylight Saving Time—permanently springing forward for brighter evenings year-round.”
Why are some senators against permanent Daylight Saving Time?
While it’s true that permanent Daylight Saving Time would mean later sunsets year-round, what that would look like for Americans depends on where in the country they live.
Some places already experience sunrises and sunsets an hour or so after other places in the same time zone do, which means that some parts of the U.S. wouldn’t see daylight until much later in the morning than others. In Indianapolis, for instance, residents would only see the sunrise after 9 a.m. local time on Jan. 15, 2027, if Daylight Saving Time were made permanent, AccuWeather predicted, while other parts of the country would see the sunrise around 8 a.m. their time.
Because of that discrepancy, some senators have objected to legislation that would establish year-round Daylight Saving Time. The most vocal opponent of the Sunshine Protection Act in the upper chamber has been Sen. Tom Cotton, a Republican from Arkansas, who has previously said that observing permanent Daylight Saving Time would “again make winter a dark and dismal time for millions of Americans.”
Cotton has also pointed out that the U.S. has unsuccessfully tried this move before. In 1974, the U.S. began observing Daylight Saving Time year-round, but it was unpopular among Americans and Congress repealed the legislation that had instituted the change just months after it took effect.
“No one likes changing the clock, me included,” Cotton acknowledged in a social media post on Saturday. But he argued that permanent Daylight Saving Time would result in “absurdly late sunrises in the winter.”
“Arkansans don’t want their kids going to school in the pitch dark, and I’ll always put Arkansas first,” he continued.
Read More: Daylight Saving Time Is Bad For Your Health. This Canadian Province Just Made It Permanent
Sen. Roger Wicker, a Republican from Mississippi, told reporters on Monday that he was aware that some people have “safety concerns in the more northern and rural states where children get on the school bus in very early hours.”
Sleep experts have opposed the idea of year-round Daylight Saving Time because they argue that Standard Time aligns best with people’s circadian rhythms. Organizations such as the American Academy of Sleep Medicine, have pushed for making Standard Time permanent instead, arguing that it would be better for health and safety.

Former Catholic bishop sentenced for abusing indigenous men in Australia
The Catholic Church in Australia has been marred by abuse allegations in recent years.
A former Roman Catholic bishop has been sentenced to six and a half years in prison for sexually abusing two young indigenous men in Western Australia.
Seventy-six year old Christopher Saunders was sentenced by the District Court of Western Australia and showed no reaction during Wednesday’s sentencing hearing.
In August, a court found Saunders guilty of one count of sexual penetration without consent and 12 counts of indecent assault.
The offences took place between 2010 and 2019 when he was bishop of Broome, a remote diocese in northwestern Australia.
Archbishop Timothy Costelloe, president of the Australian Catholic Bishops Conference, issued a statement apologising for the pain and suffering Saunders inflicted on victims, saying their trust had been “profoundly betrayed by a leader of the Church”.
Saunders was ordained a priest in 1976 and initially worked at mission stations in outback regions from the 1970s onwards. In the 1990s, he was appointed bishop of Broome by Pope John Paul II.
Following the abuse allegations, Saunders suspended his duties in 2020 and in August 2021 Pope Francis accepted his resignation. The clergyman has consistently denied the allegations.
It was revealed in court that the bishop had groomed his victims.
He is said to have regularly invited young indigenous Aboriginal men and teenagers to a beach house or a Catholic Church residence, providing them with alcohol and cigarettes, and giving them money and mobile phones.
The assaults on the two young men reportedly took place while they were heavily intoxicated.
Royal Commission and history of abuse
In 2013, Australia’s government set up a Royal Commission, a high-level inquiry into institutional child sexual abuse, after a series of scandals involving the Catholic Church.
In 2017, the commission revealed that most of the abuse took place in churches, with seven percent of Catholic priests accused of abusing children in Australia between 1950 and 2010. It said allegations were almost never investigated.
It found that 4,444 alleged incidents of child sexual abuse had been reported to church authorities. In some dioceses, more than 15 percent of priests were perpetrators.
The commission also heard testimony from the Vatican’s former finance chief Cardinal George Pell, who was found guilty in 2018 of sexually abusing choirboys in Melbourne, Australia in the 1990s.
Pell – who had been Pope Francis’s anti-corruption tsar – was released from prison in 2020 after a court quashed his conviction. He died in Rome on January 10, 2023, at the age of 81 due to heart complications following hip surgery.

Oct. 7 terrorist trials face delays, Rothman calls to accelerate process for early 2027 indictments
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
19:49:48 UTC
04:49:48 KST

Implementing the law to prosecute perpetrators of the October 7 Hamas massacre has faced recent setbacks, with estimates suggesting indictments for terrorists could be delayed until 2028, though MK Simcha Rothman called on Wednesday for the process to be accelerated.
He called for the initial indictments against the perpetrators of the attacks to be filed in the first half of 2027.
“It is an attainable target, and I call on you to make every effort to achieve it,” Rothman said.
Rothman, who chairs the Knesset Constitution, Law and Justice Committee, where the discussion took place, made the remarks to a panel of lawmakers and representatives from the Defense Ministry, Israel Prison Service, and the State Attorney’s Office, who provided an update on the ongoing process of implementing the legislation.
The Knesset committee meeting was held on the third anniversary of the massacre.
There has not yet been a full accounting for the events of October 7 in a criminal courtroom. Special legislation has been passed for military tribunals that has not yet been implemented.
The Knesset passed a law in May to prosecute terrorists involved in the attacks, granting authority to impose the death penalty and conduct public trials for the perpetrators of the attacks at a Jerusalem military court.
Later, in June, the government approved a budget of over NIS 1 billion to carry out the military tribunals, as the law’s proposal consists of a broad framework for implementing the trials and building a full complex for them to take place.
Committee meeting vowed to resolve budget issues in prosecution
The committee meeting discussed delays in moving forward with the prosecutions, largely due to stalled budget issues.
MK Yulia Malinovsky (Yisrael Beytenu), who sponsored the bill with Rothman, vowed to resolve any existing issues holding back the legislation from being implemented.
“If there are problems, we will solve them, and if we need to bang on the table, we will, but we want results. The people of Israel deserve answers,” she told the panel.
“We did what we needed to do; we passed the law, and now every official needs to put personal whims and disagreements aside and rise to the occasion. Regardless of the election results and who sits in this chair, we will not let up. We owe this to the families,” she added.
Building infrastructure for October 7 military tribunal is underway
In June, Rothman said bulldozers had begun preparing the Atarot site in northern Jerusalem, where the dedicated military tribunal is slated to be built. The announcement marked the first public sign that the law had crossed into the implementation stage.
The infrastructure to be built for the trials includes the court complex, prosecution offices, and an IDF headquarters facility.
The legislation to prosecute the terrorists also includes ensuring that key moments of the trial for the military courts can be filmed and broadcast on a dedicated website.
It establishes provisions concerning judicial panels, public access to proceedings, audiovisual documentation of hearings, and the broadcasting of parts of the proceedings to the public.
The law further proposes establishing specific arrangements for appointing judges to the court, including sitting and retired judges.
It calls for establishing special arrangements regarding victims’ rights, legal representation for defendants, and the conduct of hearings via video conference.
Military tribunal likened to Eichmann trial
The legislation also proposes the creation of a special guard unit to secure the military court in Jerusalem.
It mandates administrative preparations for conducting the proceedings, periodic reporting to the Knesset, and the promulgation of regulations concerning the implementation of the death sentence.
Capital punishment has only been carried out twice in the history of the State of Israel. The last person to be executed by Israel was Nazi Holocaust architect Adolf Eichmann, who was hanged in 1962. He was the only person ever executed following a civilian trial in the Jewish state. (The other was the case of an IDF captain, Meir Tobianski, hastily court-martialed and executed by firing squad for treason in 1948 but posthumously exonerated by David Ben-Gurion and reburied with full military honors.)
Lawmakers, from both the coalition and opposition, who sponsored the bill likened it to the Eichmann trials in 1961, which broadcast live and recorded testimonies of Holocaust survivors throughout Israel and numerous other countries before Eichmann’s hanging took place.
During the October 7 massacre, Hamas terrorists brutally massacred over 1,200 people, mostly civilians, and kidnapped 251 hostages into Gaza. The attacks included sexual violence and rape.
Sarah Ben-Nun contributed to this report.

How Israel’s political parties plan to fix the public transportation crisis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
19:48:22 UTC
04:48:22 KST

Who will get us out of the traffic jam? In 20 days, Israelis will head to the polls as the daily reality on the country’s roads becomes increasingly unbearable. We examined how the parties plan to tackle the serious problems facing public transportation in Israel and which will continue to oppose buses and trains operating on Shabbat (Saturday). We also looked at what civil society organizations are urging politicians to do to genuinely address the difficult transportation challenges Israelis face every day.
Delays and rising costs
Transportation Minister Miri Regev’s tenure has been marked by a fare reform that drew criticism for favoring certain sectors, with further price increases expected. At the same time, numerous projects have been delayed, entire cities look like construction sites and political tensions, along with changes among the ministry’s professional staff, have held up critical initiatives.
While some parties did not address transportation at all in their platforms, those that addressed it are proposing different approaches to resolving the crisis. The Beyachad party has presented the most comprehensive and detailed plan, drafted by Keren Terner, a former director general of both the Transportation Ministry and Finance Ministry who is seeking to become transportation minister in the next government.
The key innovation in Beyachad’s plan is an overhaul of the way public transportation companies are compensated, based on the “Amsterdam model.” The state currently pays operators according to the number of kilometers traveled, a model that incentivizes the creation of long, winding routes that often run largely empty. The plan proposes shifting to compensation based on the actual number of passengers and strict service-quality metrics, including punctuality, cleanliness, seat availability and passenger satisfaction. It also calls for broad decentralization of authority to local governments and for the private sector to take over implementation of major infrastructure projects.
The Democrats have placed a sweeping budgetary and environmental commitment at the center of their transportation platform: allocating 80% of the Transportation Ministry’s budget to public transportation development, alongside a plan to acquire 4,000 new electric buses. The party is proposing a distinctive model for transitioning to clean, green transportation within cities, pledging to pass legislation establishing metropolitan transportation authorities and implement a national emergency plan to address the driver shortage, including direct pay raises and designating drivers as public employees.
Yisrael Beytenu is focusing on infrastructure solutions, connecting outlying areas and reducing travel times. At the heart of the party’s approach are more frequent train and bus service, dedicated public transportation lanes on major intercity and urban roads and the advancement of modern mass-transit projects.
The Yashar! party is placing regulatory and structural change at the center of its transportation platform. The party has pledged to immediately pass legislation establishing metropolitan transportation authorities, arguing that only by transferring management and planning powers to local and regional governments can public transportation routes be adapted to residents’ actual needs.
Likud continues to favor centralized government planning and management. Its platform focuses on “connectivity,” linking outlying areas with central Israel through the development of rail networks, high-speed trains and major national infrastructure projects while keeping management and budgetary authority in the hands of the central government.
The Shabbat issue
Public transportation on Shabbat also features prominently in some of the parties’ platforms. While parties including the Democrats, Yisrael Beytenu and Beyachad support allowing local governments to operate public transportation on weekends in accordance with the character of their communities, Likud opposes such a move in order to preserve the status quo.
In an appeal to all parties running in the election the Public Transportation Forum presented a firm position paper aimed directly at shaping the next coalition agreements. The organizations stressed that resolving the crisis will require more than additional funding and will instead demand fundamental changes to management, planning and compensation methods.
One of the forum’s main proposals is to break up the Transportation Ministry’s centralized control. The ministry in Jerusalem currently attempts to manage thousands of bus routes across the country, creating cumbersome bureaucracy, delays and services that do not adequately reflect local needs. The forum is calling for the establishment of metropolitan transportation authorities that would assume those powers.
The forum is also demanding a sweeping overhaul of public transportation tenders and a transition to a compensation system based on service quality and the actual number of passengers. Another critical solution at the center of the organizations’ proposals is a national emergency plan to address the severe shortage of some 5,000 bus drivers. The plan would include higher wages, upgrading drivers’ status to that of public employees, improving welfare facilities at route terminals and accelerated training programs.
Sivan Shmuelovitz, CEO of 15 Dakot, an Israeli advocacy organization dedicated to improving public transportation in Israel, said: “There are deep gaps in the system that ultimately affect our wallets, the cost of living and our quality of life. We are proposing practical solutions that can work for everyone, some of which can be implemented almost immediately.”
She emphasized the direct connection to the cost of living: “Good public transportation determines whether a person can get to a good job without owning a car, whether a family can live in the periphery and still have access to opportunities and whether we spend our lives sitting in traffic instead of spending time with our families.”
Even after the next government is formed and a new transportation minister is appointed, implementing the necessary reforms will not be simple. The main obstacle the incoming government is expected to face is structural and bureaucratic resistance within the Transportation Ministry itself, including concerns about relinquishing authority and budgets to local governments. In addition, the depth of the ministry’s management crisis, following an exodus of professional staff and senior officials in recent years, poses a significant obstacle to implementation.
According to Shmuelevitz, after the election, the real test for the next transportation minister will not be ceremonial declarations or campaign promises, but the ability to move immediately to implementation, mobilize professional officials and build a reliable, efficient and safe transportation system.
Shmuelevitz concluded: “There are deep gaps in the system that ultimately affect our wallets, the cost of living and our quality of life. We are proposing practical solutions that can work for everyone, some of which can be implemented almost immediately.”

The UN Interim Force in Lebanon (UNIFIL) said on Wednesday that several rounds of small arms fire struck its position near Kfar Shouba in southern Lebanon, hitting accommodation units and UN vehicles.
It occurred in the morning along the Blue Line in Sector East, the mission said in a statement on Telegram. The Blue Line is a temporary boundary that was established by the UN in 2000 to confirm the withdrawal of Israeli forces from southern Lebanon after a two-decade occupation.
All peacekeepers stationed at the position took shelter shortly after the first round of firing, and no one was injured.
Most rounds struck the perimeter wall, while some hit accommodation units and UN vehicles inside the base. Several were recorded at the post, said UNIFIL.
“It is unacceptable that firings continued towards a clearly marked UNIFIL position. Such deliberate attacks put the lives of peacekeepers at serious risk,” it said.
Possible war crime
UNIFIL said it launched an investigation to determine the circumstances of the incident. The statement did not identify who fired the shots.
“We strongly remind all actors of their obligations under international law to ensure the safety and security of UN personnel and properties at all times,” it said. “Any attack on UNIFIL peacekeepers constitutes a grave violation of international humanitarian law and of the Security Council Resolution 1701 and may amount to a war crime.”
The UN Security Council adopted Resolution 1701 in August 2006 following a 33-day war between Israel and Hezbollah.
The resolution calls for a complete cessation of hostilities between Lebanon and Israel and for an area between the Blue Line and the Litani River in southern Lebanon to be free of weapons and armed personnel, except those of the Lebanese army and UNIFIL.
Israeli attacks despite ceasefire agreement
The Israeli attacks have killed at least 4,386 people and wounded 12,407 others since March 2, according to Lebanese official figures.
On June 26, Lebanon and Israel signed a US-sponsored Framework Agreement in Washington providing for a gradual Israeli withdrawal from Lebanese territory and the deployment of the Lebanese army to areas vacated by Israeli forces.
Despite the agreement, Israel has continued to carry out attacks in southern Lebanon and maintains a military presence in parts of the south, including territory it has occupied for decades and other areas seized during more recent wars and military operations.

The original photo was modified using AI to make it appear the passengers were watching Trump TV. The post did not disclose that the image had been altered. Vedika Bahl explains in Truth or Fake.
The image, shared across the White House’s X, Facebook and Instagram accounts, appears to show a packed aeroplane cabin with passengers seemingly tuning in to the president’s new channel on their seat-back screens.
“It’s what everybody is watching,” the White House said in the post, promoting what it described as another “HUGE week” of administration events and directing viewers to Trump TV.
But the photograph is not an authentic image of passengers watching the White House stream.
An analysis using OpenAI’s image-verification technology detected a SynthID watermark in the image, indicating that it had been generated or modified using an AI tool. A reverse-image search also led to the original photograph, which was posted online three years ago in February 2023.
The original image shows passengers watching the NFL’s Super Bowl LVII during a flight. One passenger appears to be watching the 2005 romantic comedy “Hitch”, starring Will Smith, rather than the game, with the original user making light of this in the post.
The White House version retains the original scene but changes what appears on the passengers’ screens, creating the impression that the entire cabin is watching Trump TV.
The White House did not disclose in its social media posts that the photograph - taken from a personal social media post - had been altered using AI and repurposed.
The image was used to promote Trump TV, which launched in September as a 24-hour YouTube stream featuring footage of Trump and other White House and administration events. The launch came amid the administration’s feud with several major news organisations, after Trump banned CNN, Politico and MS Now from the White House.
The image also comes amid President Donald Trump’s recent comments about artificial intelligence. Trump has dismissed concerns about AI as a “hoax” and said on Truth Social that the "only control or 'guardrails' that AI needs is a strong and smart president."

Indian opposition leader Rahul Gandhi detained over election chief protest

Indian opposition leader Rahul Gandhi has been detained for the third time in two days during a protest demanding the resignation of the election chief over a controversial revision of voter lists.
Gandhi and other opposition lawmakers were apprehended by police on Wednesday as they marched towards Jantar Mantar, a designated protest site in India’s capital, New Delhi.
A live feed on the YouTube channel of Gandhi’s Congress Party showed police taking him into a vehicle and driving away. Authorities also detained several other opposition lawmakers and protesters.
Opposition parties, their student units and the “Cockroach” youth movement have been demanding the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar, accusing the poll body he heads of benefiting Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s ruling Bharatiya Janata Party.
India’s Election Commission has so far removed more than 130 million names from the voter lists, with millions appealing the removals. About 969 million people were eligible to vote in the 2024 election.
Protesters allege the changes disproportionately removed voters who support opposition parties while preserving or adding voters more likely to back Modi’s party.
The commission and government deny the allegations. They say the revision has no political motive but is aimed at removing duplicate and ineligible entries while ensuring eligible voters remain registered.
Opposition lawmakers led by Gandhi protested on Tuesday as well, before police broke up their gathering and briefly detained them.
Speaking before his detention on Wednesday, Gandhi said protesters showed up unannounced after Delhi police “stopped” their gathering the day before.
“We will go to the designated protest site, sit there, and tell the country that, for us, Gyanesh Kumar is not the legitimate commissioner,” he told reporters, referring to Jantar Mantar.
“The people who have done this [vote theft] are traitors … Gyanesh Kumar will have to resign,” he added.
There was no immediate comment from the police on the detentions.
The demonstrations present a new political challenge to Modi midway into his third term, just months after similar protests led by the Cockroach Janta Party youth movement forced the resignation of his education minister over exam paper leaks.
The “Cockroach” protests, one of the most visible signs of public dissent against Modi’s government in recent years, reflected growing anger over job scarcity, corruption and a lack of government accountability.

Ana Piquer, Amnesty International’s Americas Director.

EU drops sponsorship of disinformation conference at Trump officials’ request
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
19:38:24 UTC
04:38:24 KST

The Trump administration pressured multiple countries to withdraw their sponsorship of a leading European conference on disinformation, with Canada, Lithuania and the EU’s diplomatic service subsequently agreeing to do so, the Guardian understands.
The conference, #Disinfo2026, taking place Wednesday and Thursday, is the annual meetup of Europe’s counter-disinformation community and has drawn hundreds of researchers, journalists, technologists and policymakers to a hotel in Vilnius, Lithuania. It is run by an independent Brussels non-profit, EU Disinfo Lab.
Days before the conference, the logos of its main supporters – the Lithuanian ministry of foreign affairs, the European External Action Service (EEAS) and Global Affairs Canada, the country’s foreign ministry – were wiped off its website.
Photos of the event shared with the Guardian also show white stickers affixed over the logos of these organisations printed on official conference materials, appearing to indicate they were struck from the program in haste.
Three persons familiar with the matter, including European officials, confirmed that the US state department had been in touch with multiple governments over their support for the conference.
Internal state department documents seen by the Guardian also show US officials thanking Lithuania for “taking US concerns seriously”. The document says Washington was “grateful” Lithuania supposedly found a panel framing the US as a foreign information threat “reprehensible and surprising” and welcomed its decision to limit involvement in the conference.
That panel – called “USA as a FIMI threat: adapt, acknowledge, push back”, with the acronym FIMI referring to “foreign information manipulation and interference” – took place Wednesday. It explored how Europe’s disinformation community could rebuild resilience without Washington, and is the first time the conference appears to have entertained the idea that the US could be a disinformation actor in Europe. Sources and the internal document indicate the state department was explicitly focused on this panel, which included three American speakers, among them a former CIA officer.
According to one person familiar with the deliberations, other communications appeared to originate from the office of Sarah B Rogers, the US undersecretary of state for public diplomacy.
Nina Jankowicz, a former US official and disinformation expert who in 2022 briefly headed the Biden administration’s Disinformation Governance Board, which Republicans assailed as a vehicle for policing Americans’ speech, said she understood that Washington had pressured Lithuania and Canada to withdraw from the conference. The Guardian understands that France was contacted as well.
“What this amounts to is a purported defender of free speech at the state department using the enormous power of the US government to try to pressure Americans from criticizing their government,” said Jankowicz.
In statements, Lithuania, Canada and the EU said the program of the conference did not align with their official views on the US role in disinformation – although that program had been in place for months before they withdrew their support, since June.
“Lithuania has cancelled its participation in ‘Disinfo 2026’ as several parts of the conference programme differ from the official position of the Government,” Lithuania’s foreign ministry wrote in a statement.
Global Affairs Canada “carefully assesses participation in, and sponsorship of, external events on a case-by-case basis,” GAC spokesperson Samantha Lafleur said. “Following changes to the framing of several panel discussions, GAC decided to revise its participation in those sessions at the EU DisinfoLab 2026 conference.”
Canadian officials are still participating in the conference, Lafleur added.
An EU spokesperson confirmed that the European External Action Service had decided to withdraw its support from the conference because “the organisers chose to frame some of the discussions in a way which does not align with the official positions held by the EU.”
EU officials, the Guardian understands, did not agree with the characterisation of the US as a disinformation actor.
Despite withdrawing its branding as an official supporter, the EU continues to fund the conference.
In its latest report on foreign information manipulation and interference threats, published in March, the EU’s diplomatic service named Russia and China as “threat actors” without any negative reference to the US.
A diplomatic source at France’s foreign ministry said “there’s absolutely no reason for us to change our commitments” when it came to supporting the conference.
“We stick to supporting civil society. It’s not just principled, it’s operational,” she said, adding that the conference was a “laboratory” that helped Europe develop key policy around disinformation.
The US state department has taken an increasingly interventionist posture towards free speech and civil society in Europe over the past year. The Guardian has revealed that the state department is awarding millions of dollars in non-competitive grants to organisations across the continent supportive of Trump’s agenda.
Lithuania’s withdrawal comes just after the prime minister, Mindaugas Sinkevicius, said Lithuania would pay for a permanent US military base if the US agreed, a day after Trump said he would consider the request. Sinkevicius called a lasting American presence a critical guarantee of deterrence against Russia.
“They are great people, so we will certainly look at it,” the US president said on Monday.
Sinkevicius said he first proposed the idea in a meeting with Trump’s envoy John Coale, and called it a “critically important guarantee of deterrence and security.” Lithuania, a member of the EU and Nato, borders Russia and its close ally Belarus.
The US has kept a rotating armoured battalion of almost 1,000 troops in the country since 2019, the US Army has noted.

A suspected case of pneumonic plague is raising fears of an outbreak. Should you be worried?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
19:33:37 UTC
04:33:37 KST

World health experts are closely following a potential case of pneumonic plague—the most deadly form of the disease. Earlier this week Russian officials reported that an employee at a laboratory at an infectious disease research institute in Irkutsk Oblast in Siberia, had contracted pneumonia and died. The World Health Organization (WHO) is now working closely with the country’s health authorities to monitor and track the incident. But fears over whether the disease could spread are proliferating as officials move to isolate the woman’s contacts and bolster outbreak prevention efforts at local hospitals.
At a press conference on Tuesday, WHO spokesperson Christian Lindmeier said that the woman’s cause of death was still unconfirmed and that lab testing was in progress. But “according to the test results, no pathogens of dangerous infectious diseases were detected among any of the contacts” of the woman, Lindmeier told reporters.
Here’s what you need to know about the potential outbreak and what it means.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
What is plague?
What people commonly refer to as “plague” is an infectious disease caused by the bacterium Yersinia pestis. It is best known for causing the Black Death, which killed tens of millions of people across Europe, as well as Asia and North Africa, in the 1300s.
There are three main forms of plague—bubonic plague, septicemic plague and pneumonic plague. They are all caused by the same bacterium but differ in how the pathogen enters the body and where the infection manifests. Bubonic plague, which is the most common form, is usually spread by the bites of infected fleas or direct contact with infected animals. It affects the lymph nodes, where it causes swollen and painful blue-black sores, called buboes. Septicemic plague is spread in similar ways, but it affects the bloodstream and can lead to a systemic infection. Finally, pneumonic plague occurs when the bacterium infects the lungs—typically through inhalation of infectious droplets rather than flea bites.
How dangerous is plague?
The level of danger depends on what kind of plague is encountered and whether antibiotics are available. The 14th-century Black Death was particularly deadly because there were no antibiotics at the time and people lived in crowded cities, often with poor sanitation.
Today antibiotics are very effective against plague when they are used early in the infection. But even so, Y. pestis is still deadly. Once the disease reaches the bloodstream or lungs, which seems to be potentially what happened in the Russian case, it can quickly turn fatal.
“What we do worry about the most is pneumonic plague,” says Richard Martinello, a professor of infectious disease and pediatrics at the Yale School of Medicine. “People who are sick with pneumonia due to Y. pestis can produce droplets that contain the bacteria, and we know that they could be highly contagious and readily spread the Y. pestis to other people.”
In the case of pneumonic plague, antibiotics have to be given very early on in the infection for them to do any good, Martinello says. If they are given too late, they won’t stop the infection. Pneumonic plague’s mortality rate is almost 100 percent if untreated, but chances of survival are higher with rapid treatment.
Does plague pose a global threat?
Pneumonic plague can spread between people through respiratory droplets, and it can occur anywhere the plague bacteria exist. Martinello notes a recent report from the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention from earlier this month that describes a fatal case of pneumonic plague that occurred in Coconino County, Arizona, in July 2025. It was Arizona’s first pneumonic plague death since 2007.
But based on the information that is available right now about a single suspected case in Russia, Martinello is less concerned about global spread.
“It’s a concerning time because people are more indoors and they’re exposed to more people and thus exposed to their infectious respiratory droplets,” Martinello says. Still, he adds, “I don’t think we are going to see a great deal of spread by this.”
“If there was substantial and rapid growth, that would make me worried that there may be something else involved or something special about this strain of Yersinia pestis causing the infection—if it is, in fact, Yersinia pestis,” Martinello notes.
The WHO has been closely tracking the incident, and the White House is also monitoring the situation, according to Axios.
“Because this is so contagious and so deadly..., it really relies on that effective public health effort in a timely manner,” Martinello says.

As reported by Ukrinform, Volodymyr Zelensky stated in an evening address that 25 people were killed and 100 were wounded in the Russian combined strike on October 7.

Amid the rubble of a Ukrainian apartment building, locals have one wish for Putin’s birthday
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
19:30:35 UTC
04:30:35 KST

Amid the rubble of a Ukrainian apartment building, locals have one wish for Putin’s birthday
Local residents hug as they look at a multi-floor residential building destroyed following a Russian aerial strike in Pryluky on Oct. 7, 2026 Genya Savilov / AFP via Getty Images)
PRYLUKY, Chernihiv Oblast – Families stand outside the ruins of a five-story apartment building, watching rescuers dig through what remains of their homes.
Some sit wrapped in blankets, staring at the rescue operation, waiting to see who is pulled from the rubble next. Five so far are those of children, three of them only one year old.
They were among at least 20 people killed by a Russian cruise missile that struck a five-story residential building in Pryluky as part of a mass salvo that struck cities across Ukraine overnight on Oct. 7.
A date which also happens to be Russian President Vladimir Putin's birthday.
"As a Christian, you cannot wish death on someone," Olga, a 41-year-old resident of Pryluky, who asked that her surname not be published, tells the Kyiv Independent.
"But I wish that he could feel even the tiniest fraction of what our people and our children are feeling," she says. "I wish he could feel it, and that the people around him could feel what our children are feeling.”
"Let him feel what every person and every child in our country is feeling."
Others don't hold back.
"I hope he drops dead soon," says 75-year-old Volodymyr Ivashchenko.
As the search and rescue operation continues, people rush between buildings with relatives and neighbors, covering shattered windows and salvaging what they can from damaged apartments.
The roar of excavators fills the courtyard as emergency workers lift slabs of concrete from what had been apartments only hours earlier. Rescue workers standing on the exposed floors throw smaller pieces of wreckage below, stripping away ruined walls, furniture, and fragments of the lives that had been inside.
There is little to distinguish the neighborhood from countless other residential districts across Ukraine. Apartment blocks surround courtyards and children's playgrounds. Grocery stores and small businesses line the surrounding streets. Across the road stands the Children and Youth Creativity Center, one of the city's oldest institutions, where generations of children have gone to sing, dance, do gymnastics, and prepare for school.
Now the neighborhood is buried in dust.
Ivashchenko had woken at around 6 a.m. Before the explosions, the first thing he noticed was a humming noise outside.
"I said to my wife, 'Maybe the wind has picked up,'" he recalls.
Then the explosions began.
"The windows flew open, and the whole house shook. It shook very badly," Ivashchenko says.
He remembers several explosions in quick succession and a deafening sound overhead that made him think an aircraft was passing above his roof.
Hours later, his hands and legs are still shaking.
"I feel so sorry for those innocent people, especially those tiny children," he says. "A tiny child, one year old. A young mother who had her whole life ahead of her."
At 75, Ivashchenko says, he had already had the chance to live a long life. The children killed in the building had not.
"It's the 21st century. Is there really no one who can stop this one clown, or whatever you want to call him?" he says.
"How many more deaths can there be? How much more destruction?"
‘Let him feel what every child in our country is feeling’
For Olga, the sight of the destroyed building is inseparable from the children who filled the courtyards around it.
"There are actually so many children in our courtyard," she says.
On the morning of the attack, Olga and her family were asleep. Her children were in one room, she was in another, and her husband was sleeping in the living room.
After the first explosion, they rushed into the corridor and sheltered between two walls. A second explosion followed, and then, several minutes later, another.
When they eventually went outside, the neighboring building where her 7-year-old son regularly played with other children was partly destroyed.
The blast had blown out every window in Olga's apartment facing the courtyard. Her husband had been in the living room when a balcony door was thrown toward him, but he escaped serious injury.
"You can repair everything," she says of the damage to their home. "You can't bring back the lives of the people who lived there."
'Now I don't feel sorry for them anymore'
Tetiana Pinchuk, 69, has lived in the district since 1974. She had taken her dog outside early that morning and returned home to rest when the explosions began.
"There were several explosions. Bang, bang, bang," she said.
Every window in her apartment was blown out.
"All of them, literally every one," Pinchuk says.
Doors inside the apartment were damaged as well, including those leading to the kitchen and bedroom. Pinchuk was unhurt, but hours later, her dog was still terrified.
Looking at the damage around her, she keeps returning to the same question.
"I just can't understand why you would bomb ordinary people. Why?" she says.
It is not the first time she has seen strikes damage her part of Pryluky. She recalls previous attacks near the local Epicentr home-improvement store, the Nova Poshta delivery company, and elsewhere in the district.
"But none of the previous attacks were like this morning," she says.
When asked what she wished for Putin's birthday, Pinchuk does not hesitate.
"I wish his entire family would die."
Earlier in the war, she says, she had opposed strikes on homes inside Russia because she believed ordinary people should not be held responsible for the actions of their government.
"I thought you should only hit what needs to be hit, because I felt sorry for ordinary people," she says.
"Now I don't feel sorry for them anymore."
Pryluky, like many cities across Ukraine, has become home to families displaced from front-line regions. Pinchuk said some of those families had children who were playing in these same courtyards after already fleeing the war once.
"I wasn't born here, but I consider it my hometown," she says. "That's why this hurts so much."
Fifty-eight-year-old Ludmila was preparing for work at around 6:30 a.m. when she heard the explosions. Her mother lives directly opposite her, and Ludmila immediately began calling her before contacting her husband, who works in Kyiv.
"My old classmate was killed, her daughter, and her daughter's child," Ludmila says.
She tries to describe some of the others she knew who died, but can't get the words out. Instead, she looks back toward the destroyed building.
"Seeing the bodies, especially the bodies of children," she sighs. "That's very hard."

Eritrean troops enter Tigray as regional war fears grow
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
19:29:56 UTC
04:29:56 KST

Eritrean troops have deployed in Ethiopia's northern Tigray region, multiple sources said on Wednesday, threatening to turn an internal conflict into a wider regional war.
Fighting broke out between the rebel Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF) and Ethiopian federal forces on September 23, sparking fears of a return to the devastating 2020-2022 civil war.
Ethiopia accuses Eritrea of backing the rebels, and the two neighbours severed diplomatic ties last week.
The Ethiopian army has successfully pushed back the Tigrayan rebels with the help of local militias and entered the regional capital of Mekelle on the weekend without a fight as the TPLF abandoned the city.
Multiple sources told AFP that Eritrean troops have crossed the border and were positioned around Adigrat, some 115 kilometres (70 miles) north of Mekelle, and were pushing south.
Red Sea tensions rise
Eritrea fears landlocked Ethiopia plans to invade to seize direct access to the Red Sea, and analysts say it wants to prevent the war reaching its territory.
"The Eritrean army has entered Tigray in uniform, equipped with heavy weaponry," said Gebreigziabher Beyene, commander of the Tigray Peace Force, a pro-government militia that has fought alongside the Ethiopian army.
"This force is being struck by drones," he said, adding Eritrea was "deliberately deploying its forces so that the fighting takes place inside Tigray rather than spilling into Eritrea".
In a statement on X, Eritrea's Information Minister Yemane Meskel did not deny that troops had crossed the border, but said Ethiopia's government was creating "a fallacious narrative of 'self-defence' to rationalise and camouflage its war of aggression".
Residents voice concern
In Adigrat, two eyewitnesses told AFP they saw Eritrean soldiers on the streets, heading south in lorries with heavy weaponry.
A local official, speaking to AFP on condition of anonymity, said the troops had been there for days and "the population is very concerned".
Conflict monitor ACLED said Eritrean troops had crossed the border at Zelambesa on Wednesday. And it said Tigrayan rebel forces were "heavily present" around Wukro, a town along the same road that leads to the regional capital.
"Eritrean forces entered the war in Tigray to halt the Ethiopian government and allied forces from reaching the border and potentially fighting within Eritrea's territory," ACLED said in a briefing note.
Regional tensions
Eritrea gained independence from Ethiopia in 1993, and the two sides fought a brutal border war between 1998 and 2000.
Relations improved markedly with the rise of Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed in 2018, and Eritrea even fought alongside Ethiopia during the 2020-2022 civil war against the TPLF.
But the relationship soon deteriorated, particularly over Ethiopia's persistent claims that it has a right to sea access.
Earlier this month, Ethiopia expelled 10 Eritrean diplomats and shut its embassy in Asmara, while Eritrea responded that it would "sever all diplomatic ties".
Britain and the United States were among countries warning their citizens to avoid travelling in northern Ethiopia.

Russia’s post-election utility hikes push annual inflation above the central bank’s 2026 forecast range
Weekly inflation in Russia rose to 0.96% in the week of September 29 to October 5, while annual inflation reached 7.1%, according to Rosstat, Russia’s statistics agency.
Higher housing and utility rates that took effect on October 1 — shortly after the State Duma elections — drove the increase. The Economic Development Ministry estimated that the rate hikes contributed 0.75 percentage points to weekly inflation.
The Bell reported that annual inflation of 7.1% exceeds both the upper end of the Bank of Russia’s 2026 forecast (6–7%) and the Economic Development Ministry’s forecast (6.8%).
Russia raised utility rates as scheduled on October 1. Housing and utility bills increased by an average of 9.9% nationwide. The increases varied by region, with the largest rise in Stavropol Krai (22%). Residential gas and electricity prices rose by nationwide averages of 9.6% and 11.3%, respectively.
On September 24, immediately after the State Duma elections, the Economic Development Ministry said utility rates in Russia would rise by an average of 11% beginning July 1, 2027. The ministry had previously forecast an 8.7% increase in housing and utility rates next year.
The ministry said it revised its forecasts because of rising inflation and larger projected increases in gas and electricity rates.

"Anyone who lies, and whose sole ability is to delay decisions and flee from responsibility, is unworthy of the prices we have paid. They will not be able to repair things after the disaster. They are unworthy to lead Israel," said Eisenkot.
"Three years since the October 7 massacre - three years of a miserable attempt to escape responsibility. To make people forget the disaster. Eisenkot then called on the attorney-general to open a criminal investigation into "anyone who falsified documents and disrupted testimony" and hold them accountable. He also called for the establishment of a State Commission of Inquiry, vowing it would be the first order of business if he were to be elected prime minister.
Netanyahu's Likud message denies dire accusations
Netanyahu's October 7 message came in the face of a barrage of accusations from various directions regarding failure on his part, deliberate or otherwise, on the day of the massacre.
Accusations involve reports that the prime minister had received prior warnings of the event, which were subsequently ignored, as well as verifiable and consistent behavior, like his outright opposition to the establishment of a State Commission of Inquiry.
Accusations of prior warnings include, but are not limited to: An investigation by The Atlantic that revealed that Egyptian intelligence chief Abbas Kamel's visited Israel 11 days before the October 7 attack, in which he delivered a warning that Hamas was preparing for a significant attack; and an investigation published by Haaretz last month suggesting that UAE President Mohammed bin Zayed Al Nahyan warned Netanyahu that Hamas was planning a major operation against Israel in the days leading to the attack.
In the October 7 Likud message, Netanyahu took to the defense, saying "Sadly, on this painful day of all days, Channel 12 is broadcasting false political propaganda against Prime Minister Netanyahu and the Likud all day long, with the aim of toppling right-wing rule and paving the way for a left-wing government that will establish a Palestinian state."
Netanyahu released a 55-page document late in February that outlined answers he gave to State Comptroller Matanyahu Englman as part of the investigation into the October 7 Hamas attack.
The prime minister's answers point to failures among officials in the security establishment and appear to deflect his role in the outcome of the attacks.
Lapid: 'Sheer amount of lies leaves no choice' but to respond
Opposition leader and former prime minister Yair Lapid also took to X on Wednesday in response to the Likud message.
"The last thing I wanted was to start another argument with Netanyahu on this heartbreaking national day of mourning, but the sheer amount of lies leaves no choice," the message begins.
"If there was no intelligence warning, why did I convene a press conference on September 20 and warn of a security disaster based on the intelligence material that was also placed before Netanyahu?
"Why did he refuse on October 1, 2023, the proposals of the Shin Bet and the IDF to launch a preemptive strike in Gaza, claiming 'that it would harm peace with Saudi Arabia?'"
Lapid continued, asking, "Why did he ignore the fact that on July 24 the head of the Shin Bet told him: 'I am giving you a war warning right now.' Why on September 13 did the head of the Shin Bet convene the Intelligence Subcommittee to present it with the 'Perfect Storm' warning of a multi-arena flare-up, which Netanyahu was also aware of and also ignored?
"Why did he time and again ignore the warnings of the Shin Bet and Military Intelligence according to which the suitcases of Qatari cash were being used by Hamas's military wing to acquire weapons and munitions? Why did he say time and again that Hamas needs to be strengthened, instead of eliminating it as he promised?"
He concluded, saying, "Above all - why is he so afraid of a State Commission of Inquiry?... Netanyahu stood at the head of the system. The October 7 massacre happened. He is guilty. He is responsible."
Ofer Winter lays out plan for State Commission of Inquiry into October 7
Meanwhile, Ofer Winter's People of Israel party revealed its plan to establish a State Inquiry Commission into October 7 in a Monday statement.
"The fact that an inquiry commission has not been established to date is a shared disgrace for both the coalition and the opposition - both sides have an interest in avoiding an inquiry commission because they were part of the failure. We will lead an inquiry commission untainted by interests," the party said.
Under the proposed framework, an independent mechanism will be established outside the control of the government and political influence. The People of Israel party claims that the process will be based on principles of "truth, trust, and results."
They claim to aim the establish a commission undivided by political lines and uninfluenced by political entities that may obfuscate the "truth," a body that "possesses full investigative powers" and "operates without political restrictions on investigative directions," promising results within six months.
The People of Israel proposal involves a selection process in which the new Knesset will elect a chairperson and deputy chairperson in the manner of presidential elections, as well as a voting procedure via secret ballot, choosing from a list of retired judges proposed by Knesset members.
The party insists that the investigation team be composed of bereaved family members, hostage representatives, and individuals directly affected by October 7 - to take an active part in the commission.
"We owe this to the fallen and their families, to the wounded, and to our children, in order to ensure that such a thing never happens again. We can bring about a commission that investigates truthfully and is accepted by all parts of the nation. We will lead an inquiry commission untainted by interests," the party's statement concluded.
Keshet Neev contributed to this report.

"During the night, there were those who saw in real time all the warning signs and did nothing with them. They did not update Israel Police, the emergency response squads, the kibbutzim, the soldiers on the border fence, the people at the Nova music festival, or the prime minister," Likud said.
"If Netanyahu had been updated in real time, everything would have looked different. Netanyahu was the one who decided on the ground maneuver in Gaza and stood firmly against president Biden's pressure to make do with an aerial attack," Likud added.
"In the face of the heaviest pressures from home and abroad, including from all the 'former officials,' Netanyahu is the one who led the conquest of Gaza and Rafah, the tremendous success in releasing all of our hostages down to the last one, the pager operation [against Hezbollah] that stunned the world, the elimination of [Hezbollah leader Hassan] Nasrallah, [Hamas leaders, Yahya] Sinwar, and [Mohammed] Deif, the conquest of the Mount Hermon peak, the killing of [Iranian supreme leader Ayatollah Ali] Khamenei, the killing of the Iranian nuclear scientists, and above all, saving Israel from annihilation by Iran's atomic bombs," the party claimed.

The 'Post' revealed what happened among security leaders on October 7 in February exclusive report
Not one single IDF general was in the main operational command center underneath Tel Aviv's Kirya Headquarters, commonly referred to as "the pit," when the attack occured, the Post previously reported in February.
By 7:30 a.m., the IDF General Staff only knew about approximately 40% of the terror infiltrations, the previous report added.
The Israeli military's top commanders did not really start to manage the nation’s defense until about 1:00 p.m., which was also around the time Netanyahu's first video to the public came out, the Post wrote in February.
Then-defense minister Yoav Gallant is the only top official who can say that even his staff did not receive any warning prior to the 6:29 a.m. invasion, the Post reported.
Then-IDF chief of staff Herzi Halevi was woken up between 2 a.m. and 3 a.m. and received initial updates about a possible Hamas border threat, the Post wrote.
There were additional consultations between the IDF and Shin Bet (Israel Security Agency) between 4 a.m. and 5:15 a.m., with then-Shin Bet director Ronen Bar ordering his staff to update Netanyahu at 5:15, the Post reported.
However, Shin Bet staff only carried out Bar's order at 6:13 a.m. During those 16 minutes between Shin Bet's warning and the start of the infiltrations, Gil chose not to wake the prime minister, believing, along with the entire security apparatus, that no large-scale threat was imminent, the Post wrote in February.
Netanyahu consistently leaves out this fact when he discusses the timeline, trying to portray the defense establishment as intentionally leaving him in the dark, the Post noted.
Additionally, Netanyahu, Gallant, and Halevi did not speak until almost four hours into the war, the Post reported.

The US Treasury on Wednesday announced its first penalty under rules governing American investment in sensitive Chinese technologies, revealing a US$200,000 fine against the parent of Plug and Play Tech Centre for failing to report an investment in a Shanghai robotics AI company.

“This has no function whatsoever as an alternative to NATO, of which we are a member, or to other places,” said Celik. Instead, he said, it would have a "complementary role" in efforts to preserve regional and global peace.
Celik also said the defense arrangement could eventually be open to participation by other countries.
“These types of security agreements and alliances mature over time by engaging with other states within their own principles and frameworks,” he said.

Hungary Clears Path for Ukraine to Open Two More EU Accession Clusters
Hungary has agreed to allow Ukraine to advance in its EU accession negotiations and move toward opening negotiating clusters 2 and 3, European Pravda reported on October 7.

We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Hungary previously blocked approval of the screening results for the two clusters for several months, preventing Ukraine from moving to the next procedural stage. In September, Budapest was the only EU member state withholding consent for the process to advance.

Ukraine had already opened the first “Fundamentals” cluster in its EU accession negotiations in June, covering areas including democratic institutions, judicial independence, and the rule of law.

Judge orders officials to preserve all evidence tied to Christa Pike’s botched execution
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
19:22:25 UTC
04:22:25 KST

Christa Pike awoke “angry and confused” after surviving two lethal injections, her attorneys said on Wednesday, as a judge ordered Tennessee state officials to preserve all evidence related to the failed execution.
Pike, 50, was taken to hospital unconscious but alive from Tennessee’s execution chamber last Wednesday after two supposedly lethal doses of the barbiturate pentobarbital.
She was declared brain dead on Monday, her attorneys said, and her team was informed of plans to remove her from life support the next day. “But on Tuesday, to the shock of everyone … Christa woke up and began talking,” Randy Spivey, one of her lawyers, said at a press conference on Wednesday. He was told her first words were “Where am I?” and “Who are you?”
Pike remains hospitalized and shackled to her bed, despite pleas from medical staff for prison officials to remove her restraints, her lawyers said. She has pneumonia, a blood clot, and is unable to move either of her badly injured arms, they added.
“There’s still a lot of cognitive confusion, and so I will say that she has wanted to know what’s happened, and she’s asked about several people,” Spivey said. “She’s asked about her team. She’s asked about the victim’s family … I think she is angry and confused about everything right now.”
The update on Pike’s condition came after a contentious court hearing in Nashville, where judge I’Ashea Myles ordered the state to preserve “anything that was in the actual room” during the attempted execution a week ago.
Pike’s legal team accused Tennessee officials of “secreting away” evidence. Attorney Luke Ihnen said items from the attempted execution could be key to future legal challenges by Pike, should the state attempt to kill her again.
“The state has made no promises that Ms Pike will not be subject to a future execution, and the evidence that we are seeking to preserve now is relevant for any future challenge that she makes, because as we pled in January, the same thing is likely to happen,” Ihnen said.
Pike, believed to be the only person to survive a lethal injection, was injected withlarge doses of the sedative when Tennessee officials had attempted to put her to death, in a case that shocked many in the US and created headlines around the world.
At the press conference on Wednesday, Spivey said it was unclear “what if any function” Pike would regain in her arms. “Her hands look like if you were to blow up a surgical glove,” Spivey said.
Despite her condition, Pike was still being restrained, her team said, shackled to her hospital bed by her feet and right arm.
“Based on our understanding, medical staff have asked that the shackles be removed and have been denied that request [by the Tennessee correction department],” he told Myles earlier. He added: “We would also amend our request and ask for that relief.”
Witnesses to the attempted execution of Pike described how they heard her breathing raggedly after receiving the first injection. She was then hospitalized after a second dose failed to kill her and was declared to be in critical condition.
After the botched execution attempt, Spivey called the process “cruel and torturous”, adding that he had counted seven needles in Pike’s left arm, “one of which appeared to be bent when it was pulled from her”. Pike had lifted her head from the execution gurney to say her arms were burning as the drug was administered.
Her lawyers had warned before the execution that officials might struggle to locate veins and cause her suffering in the process, but the state had pushed to proceed and the US supreme court allowed the prison to move forward.
There is speculation from medical experts that perhaps some or a lot of the drug missed her vein and went into tissue, that one of her veins, which were problematic and this fact flagged by her lawyers months earlier – blew, or that the drug was faulty, or a combination.
Pike was 18 and her then boyfriend 17 at the time when they killed 19-year-old Colleen Slemmer, one of their classmates at Knoxville Job Corps, in Tennessee in 1995.
According to prosecutors, Pike was worried Slemmer was trying to take the boyfriend, Tadaryl Shipp, away from her. Together, they lured Slemmer into a wooded area, tortured and killed her.
Shipp was convicted of first-degree murder in 1997 and was given a life sentence with the possibility of parole. Pike has never denied her involvement in Slemmer’s killing. She was later diagnosed with bipolar disorder and post-traumatic stress disorder but, because she was 18, she was sentenced to death and has been on death row, isolated, for 30 years.

EXPLAINER - How a dispute over illegal Israeli settlements led to a Britain-Israel diplomatic crisis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
19:21:43 UTC
04:21:43 KST

Diplomatic tensions between Britain and Israel have escalated sharply over the past week as negotiations failed to resolve a dispute over the planned closure of the British Consulate General in occupied East Jerusalem.
Israel has ordered the mission to close by Oct. 8 and instructed its British diplomats to leave, prompting London to pursue private negotiations while reportedly warning it could retaliate by expelling Israeli diplomats.
The dispute represents one of the most serious confrontations between Britain and Israel in decades.
The confrontation began with Britain's decision under Prime Minister Andy Burnham's government to prohibit trade involving illegal Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank.
It has since expanded into a dispute involving Jerusalem's status, diplomatic representation to the Palestinians and relations between the two countries.
Since October 2023, British foreign policy toward Israel and Palestine has undergone significant changes.
What began under Rishi Sunak’s Conservative administration as strong diplomatic and military support for Tel Aviv has transformed into what some experts call one of the most significant pivots in modern British diplomacy.
The arrival of Prime Minister Andy Burnham and Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband this summer brought a sharper tone to Britain’s policy toward Israel, building on cautious changes introduced under Keir Starmer.
Britain, France and Canada announced measures on Sept. 8 targeting goods produced in illegal Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank.
The British measures include a ban on settlement goods and services and sanctions against individuals and companies accused of supporting, facilitating or profiting from settlement activity.
London said the measures were intended to protect the possibility of a two-state solution amid continued settlement construction and increasing violence against Palestinians in the occupied West Bank.
Miliband said London could no longer limit its response to statements of concern and accused Israel of carrying out "ethnic cleansing" in parts of the West Bank. He also called illegal occupiers "terrorists."
Israel rejected the allegations and disputed the British position that settlements are illegal under international law.
Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Saar described the measures as "morally distorted" and accused Britain's Labour government of interfering in Israel's domestic affairs ahead of its Oct. 27 general election.
Israel ordered Britain to close its consulate in occupied East Jerusalem within 30 days and required the diplomats working there to leave.
The order is scheduled to take effect Thursday.
Israel also removed British representatives from an international coordination center for Gaza in Kiryat Gat and ended British participation in training Palestinian Authority security forces in the occupied West Bank.
It also barred 12 British politicians and other nationals from entering Israel.
The Israeli measures were directed specifically at Britain, despite France and Canada joining the restrictions on settlement trade.
Israel said the British officials subjected to entry bans had been involved in antisemitic or anti-Israel activity or had denied Israel's right to exist.
Meanwhile, Israel's diplomatic mission in London has been operating without a permanent ambassador for more than a year.
The British Consulate General operates separately from the British Embassy to Israel in Tel Aviv.
It manages Britain's diplomatic relations with Palestinians in occupied East Jerusalem, the occupied West Bank and the Gaza Strip.
The mission also conducts political, economic and security work and provides consular services to Palestinians.
Located in occupied East Jerusalem's Sheikh Jarrah neighborhood, the mission represents a British diplomatic presence in Jerusalem dating back nearly two centuries.
Its separate status reflects Britain's position that sovereignty over Jerusalem has not been finally determined and must be settled through negotiations.
Britain recognizes Israel's de facto authority in West Jerusalem but does not recognize Israeli sovereignty over Jerusalem as a whole. Palestinians seek occupied East Jerusalem as the capital of a future state.
The consulate's closure would affect Britain's ability to conduct direct diplomacy with Palestinians and challenge London's established position on Jerusalem's status.
British National Security Adviser Jonathan Powell reportedly made an undisclosed visit to Israel to seek an agreement preventing the consulate's closure.
He held discussions with Israeli officials, but the talks failed to produce a settlement.
Diplomatic contacts have continued, although Israel has publicly maintained that the mission will close as scheduled.
A spokesperson for Saar said the Oct. 8 deadline remained in force.
Britain has said it is seeking to keep the consulate open but has not disclosed details of the negotiations.
Local employees have reportedly been dismissed, while British diplomats have been preparing to leave if the order is implemented.
Israeli news outlet Ynet reported that British Ambassador to Israel Simon Walters warned Israeli officials that London could expel 27 diplomats from the Israeli Embassy if the consulate were forced to close.
Under the reported proposal, Britain would expel one Israeli diplomat for each of the 27 British diplomats affected by Israel's decision.
Such a measure could severely restrict the Israeli Embassy's operations because its diplomatic staff is only slightly larger than the number reportedly facing expulsion.
The British Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office, however, did not confirm the reported threat when approached by Anadolu.
"I would steer you away from rumors. We would not comment on speculation or live discussions," a spokesperson said Tuesday.
British officials have reportedly been particularly angered by Israel's decision to give London only 30 days to close the consulate.
The UK government has maintained that the consulate plays an important role in its engagement with Palestinians and that its closure would undermine longstanding diplomatic and humanitarian work.
Referring to the Israeli government's response to Britain's sanctions measures, Miliband said in September: "I regret what the Israeli government has announced, but I'm proud of what we did and it was the right thing to do."
He also previously rejected speculation about possible British retaliation over the consulate.
"I do not want to speculate on this, but we do not want this to happen. It would damage the very important work that we are doing, helping people in those communities," he said.
"The consulate has been there for nearly 200 years. And this is a long-standing position that we have had. And so, you know, this is a conversation we continue to have, but we do not want this to happen."
Experts say Britain could attempt to conduct its relations with Palestinians through another office, potentially in Ramallah.
However, they say such an arrangement would reduce its direct diplomatic presence in Jerusalem and could be seen as accepting an Israeli decision over the mission's status.
London could also proceed with the reported expulsion of Israeli diplomats, impose further sanctions or take other reciprocal measures.
Israel could respond with additional restrictions on British officials or institutions, creating a cycle of retaliation.
A compromise could involve delaying the closure, modifying the consulate's status or allowing its personnel to continue operating under a different diplomatic arrangement.
No such agreement had been announced ahead of the deadline.
