UN Interim Force says gunfire hit its position in southern Lebanon
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
19:20:48 UTC
04:20:48 KST

Rania Abushamala
07 October 2026•Update: 07 October 2026
- UNIFIL statement did not identify who fired shots
The UN Interim Force in Lebanon (UNIFIL) said Wednesday that several rounds of small arms fire struck its position near Kfar Shouba in southern Lebanon, hitting accommodation units and UN vehicles.
It occurred in the morning along the Blue Line in Sector East, the mission said in a statement on Telegram. The Blue Line is a temporary boundary that was established by the UN in 2000 to confirm the withdrawal of Israeli forces from southern Lebanon after a two-decade occupation.
All peacekeepers stationed at the position took shelter shortly after the first round of firing, and no one was injured.
Most rounds struck the perimeter wall, while some hit accommodation units and UN vehicles inside the base. Several were recorded at the post, said UNIFIL.
“It is unacceptable that firings continued towards a clearly marked UNIFIL position. Such deliberate attacks put the lives of peacekeepers at serious risk,” it said.
UNIFIL said it launched an investigation to determine the circumstances of the incident. The statement did not identify who fired the shots.
“We strongly remind all actors of their obligations under international law to ensure the safety and security of UN personnel and properties at all times,” it said. “Any attack on UNIFIL peacekeepers constitutes a grave violation of international humanitarian law and of the Security Council Resolution 1701 and may amount to a war crime.”
The UN Security Council adopted Resolution 1701 in August 2006 following a 33-day war between Israel and Hezbollah.
The resolution calls for a complete cessation of hostilities between Lebanon and Israel and for an area between the Blue Line and the Litani River in southern Lebanon to be free of weapons and armed personnel, except those of the Lebanese army and UNIFIL.
The Israeli attacks have killed at least 4,386 people and wounded 12,407 others since March 2, according to Lebanese official figures.
On June 26, Lebanon and Israel signed a US-sponsored Framework Agreement in Washington providing for a gradual Israeli withdrawal from Lebanese territory and the deployment of the Lebanese army to areas vacated by Israeli forces.
Despite the agreement, Israel has continued to carry out attacks in southern Lebanon and maintains a military presence in parts of the south, including territory it has occupied for decades and other areas seized during more recent wars and military operations.

Meet the Vendors Selling ‘Cornell Seven’ Merch
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
19:17:29 UTC
04:17:29 KST

Last weekend, the clothing brand Cherrykitten published an Instagram post promoting T-shirts, crop tops, and sports bras with the slogan “I Am Jane Doe” emblazoned on the front. “ALL OF US ARE UNTIL NONE OF US ARE,” the company wrote in the caption, adding that it would donate 5 percent of the net sales proceeds to the National Organization for Women.
A reference to the “Cornell Seven” case, in which an anonymous woman accused seven Cornell University fraternity members of sexual assault, among other counts, #IAmJaneDoe started going viral last week. Many sexual assault survivors used the hashtag in solidarity with the alleged victim after trolls attempted to dox her on social media. (All seven of those accused have denied wrongdoing, and none have been charged with a crime.)
The message, while powerful, may have been ill-suited for appropriation by Cherrykitten, a brand perhaps best known for selling tank tops and crop tops with slogans like “Pls do not give me a cigarette no matter what I say” and “AI cannot generate tits like these.” The company received immediate backlash on social media for selling the shirts, with many accusing it of tastelessly capitalizing off of a grisly sexual assault case. “Using the cornell seven sexual assault as a merch idea and then donating ONLY 5% to a womens charity.. oh cherrykitten.. you’re fucked,” one tweet with 2.2 million views read.
The brand removed the post, issuing an apology for “turning a real and deeply serious situation into a product,” according to a screengrab of a now-deleted Instagram post. (Cherrykitten did not respond to WIRED’s requests for comment.) But Cherrykitten is far from the only brand attempting to market apparel around the Cornell Seven case, which has garnered outrage around the world.
On Amazon, there are more than 6,000 results for “I Am Jane Doe” T-shirts; on platforms like Etsy and Redbubble, there are hundreds of sellers promoting such merch, including T-shirts, sweatshirts, hats, bracelets, mugs, and bumper stickers. The listings, which include keywords like “feminist,” “true crime,” “protest,” and (weirdly, on Redbubble) “lizzieborden,” often feature AI-generated photos of women with shiny hair and broad grins modeling the merch.
One such seller, who requested her name be withheld to protect her privacy given the sensitive nature of the case, is the owner of a three-year-old shop on Etsy which sells T-shirts with progressive slogans. Her “I Am Jane Doe” sweatshirts in shades like ash, dark chocolate, and purple cost between $19.53 and $27.93; she’s sold 21 since October 1.
An assault survivor herself, the seller tells WIRED via email she came across the Cornell Seven story on social media, and was “deeply moved” by the #IAmJaneDoe movement. “I wanted this shirt to be a small but visible way of saying: we see you, we believe you, and we stand with you,” she says.
“[When] I came across the Jane Doe story on social media, I saw yet another woman who had been failed by people and systems, and I felt really strongly about that. That we need to stand up for her. That she deserves justice ... For me, ‘I Am Jane Doe’ was not about turning anyone's pain into a trend,” she says. “It was my way of saying that I see her, I believe her, and I stand with her.”
It’s not uncommon for Etsy vendors to sell items inspired by current events. It happened after the murder of George Floyd in 2020 and during the 2022 Johnny Depp/Amber Heard defamation case, where much of the merch was pro-Depp and featured quotes from Depp on the stand. As WIRED has previously reported, the rise of mass-produced print-on-demand goods, as well as Etsy’s relatively lax policies toward AI-generated listings, allow vendors to rapidly create, design, promote, and sell such items in accordance with the news cycle.
Yet there are often ethical questions associated with commodifying social movements for a quick buck, and it can be difficult for consumers to vet the motives of those selling such products.
“If [people are] raising money to support survivors, that’s OK,” Simintha Esson, chief development officer for RAINN, the country’s largest anti-sexual-assault organization, tells WIRED when asked about the recent onslaught of Jane Doe merch. “We know the need is there—calls to RAINN’s National Sexual Assault Hotline are up 73 percent in the last week. But if it’s just exploiting Jane Doe’s name and case for profit, people are better off giving to an organization that is trying to make things better.”
Even those who purport to be financially supporting survivors are worthy of skepticism. The website I Am Jane Doe Merch, for instance, includes such bestselling items as an “I Am Jane Doe” baby tee, an “Educate Your Sons” crop top stenciled with a butterfly, and a “Dead Men Don’t Rape” T-shirt featuring the serial killer Aileen Wuornos. (According to website data, more than 700 Aileen Wuornos T-shirts have sold.)
The website, which was created on October 2, according to the domain reverse-search tool WhoIs, includes a description stating that an unspecified percentage of the proceeds will go directly to Jane Doe herself, “to help her legal expenses and related costs.” “Any contribution, no matter the amount, can help lessen that burden and support Jane in accessing support, advocacy, and/or justice and accountability,” the description reads.
When reached for comment, however, Thomas P. Giuffra, the attorney for Jane Doe, tells WIRED that there are no authorized fundraising sites for Jane Doe. While she has requested that all donations go to RAINN, other efforts such as I Am Jane Doe Merch are “not affiliated with us, and we urge the public to use caution before contributing to one,” he says in a statement. (Though WhoIs data has kept the identity of the owner of I Am Jane Doe Merch anonymous, WIRED has reached out to an email address associated with the website for comment.)
Some influencers selling “I Am Jane Doe” merchandise are donating all or most of the proceeds to organizations benefiting sexual survivors. Justin Kralemann, a content creator and activist who goes by the handle the Woke Ginger, says he was inspired to sell shirts after women flooded to his comments section to share their own experiences with sexual assault and trauma.
“Their stories broke my heart,” he says. “I’m a cisgender man and can’t directly speak to women’s lived experiences, but I wanted to do something beyond sharing news updates to help those fighting sexual violence against women.”
With EQNQ Studio, a company that makes “progressive apparel that celebrates equality, community, and the courage to speak up,” according to its website, Kralemann is selling “I Am Jane Doe” T-shirts in teal (the color associated with Sexual Assault Awareness Month) and dark heather for $24.95 a pop. He says approximately 67 percent of the proceeds will support the national organization End Rape on Campus, and approximately 33 percent will go to EQNQ Studio, the small business producing, hand-making, and shipping the shirts. Per EQNQ, they have sold 255 shirts thus far.
A few days after we started corresponding, the Etsy vendor selling sweatshirts provided an update: she had decided to stop selling the “I Am Jane Doe” sweatshirt and to donate the remainder of the profits to RAINN. She didn’t think that she or those who purchased the sweatshirt had bad intentions—“we all know how difficult it is to change things as individuals, [and] at the very least, we can show our support with a shirt,” she says. But she said that she has come to understand the potential ethical issues raised by “turning a story like this into something that is sold, even when the intention behind it is solidarity.”
“Even though we don't know who Jane Doe is, and we don't need to know, this is still her story,” she says. “I have decided that stepping back from this particular design is the right thing for me to do.”

Bangladesh's national carrier Biman Bangladesh Airlines on Wednesday signed an agreement to purchase 10 aircraft from European manufacturer Airbus, the airline said.
The agreement covers four Airbus A350-900 widebody aircraft for long-haul international operations and six A321neo single-aisle aircraft for regional operations, according to a Biman statement.
The aircraft are expected to join Biman's fleet from around 2033.
"It marks a significant milestone in Biman's fleet modernization and long-term growth strategy," the statement said.
The EU ambassador to Bangladesh described the agreement as a strategic step in Bangladesh's growing relations with Europe.
"We regard this agreement as a strategic step in Bangladesh's growing commercial and investment relations with Europe—relations built on international competitiveness, innovation and reliability," said Michael Miller.
The combination of the A350 and A321neo will create an effective fleet strategy for Biman, according to Airbus Executive Vice President for Sales Benoit de Saint-Exupery.
He said the aircraft would support Biman's expansion to new international destinations and help meet growing demand across its network.
Bangladesh Civil Aviation and Tourism Minister M Rashiduzzaman Millat said Biman's "fleet, route network and operational capabilities will be further strengthened."
None of Biman's 19 operational aircraft are currently manufactured by Airbus, according to the airline.
The national carrier last month ordered 11 more Boeing aircraft as the national flag carrier expands and renews its fleet, bringing its total Boeing orders this year to 25. The latest order comprises five 787-10 Dreamliners and six 737-8 jets, according to Boeing.

Three years since October 7: Israelis tell Meduza how the worst terrorist attack in their country’s history changed them and the world around them
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
19:11:50 UTC
04:11:50 KST

Three years since October 7: Israelis tell Meduza how the worst terrorist attack in their country’s history changed them and the world around them
The Hamas attack on October 7, 2023, was one of the most horrific events in recent world history. Ahead of its third anniversary, Meduza spoke with residents of Israel, where the terrorist attack touched everyone. Eight people from cities across the country described what happened to them in those days and how they and the world around them have changed since.
Warning: This article contains profanity.
Exactly three years ago, on October 7, 2023, some 3,000 militants from the Palestinian terrorist movement Hamas attacked Israel and took 251 people hostage. About 1,200 other civilians, including 38 children, were killed; more than 350 of them were at the Nova music festival. Some were tortured, others burned alive. The militants also raped a large number of women — Israeli human rights advocates believe this was a deliberate Hamas strategy.
In response to October 7, Israel launched an operation in the Gaza Strip. Tens of thousands of people have died. Hamas has been defeated but still exists. The operation has drawn international criticism and has been accompanied by a rise in anti-Israel and antisemitic sentiment. During the operation, Israel freed 166 hostages. Another 85 died.
Yeva Broyde-Zaitsev, 37, ceramics shop owner and Hebrew teacher, Tel Aviv
In Russia, I worked in the archives of an art college and played in a band. I left Russia 10 years ago through the repatriation program. Russia had already seized Crimea, things were looking ominous, and I wasn’t expecting anything good.
At first, I didn’t think I’d stay in Israel: I planned to get Israeli citizenship and a darkon — an Israeli passport. Then I saw how much more people value human life here, how they respect individual freedom. My friends in Russia started scattering around the world, and in the end, I had no reason left to go back.
Throughout Israel’s history, there’s always been some fucked-up shit happening, terrorist attacks every year. But that happened in Moscow too. Whenever people asked whether I was scared of being blown up, I’d always say that if you’re going to get blown up, it might as well happen by the sea. So moving to Israel didn’t scare me. I think you face far more dangers every day in Moscow than you do in Israel. Here, I’m not afraid that someone passing by will give me grief about how I look or get aggressive. People are much friendlier here.
Before October 7, I didn’t have a feeling that something bad was going to happen. Or rather, this is the Middle East — you can have that feeling every day.
I was looking forward to my birthday on October 12. My friends and I were planning to fly to London and have a fucking amazing celebration. We ended up having to celebrate in a bomb shelter. Lots of people came, even though getting to my place was dangerous. We kept getting bombed, and we got horribly drunk because there was so much stress and terror, and we needed to let it out.
My husband serves in the military’s medical corps. When the siren went off early on October 7, he didn’t even wake up. That morning, I told him this whole nightmare had begun, and he reassured me that if things were really bad, he’d have been called up.
That happened the next day.
Several of my friends died at the Nova festival, where Hamas massacred people and took hostages. I spent the first few days with a friend. We just sobbed.
Whenever I was home alone, I’d sit there with a knife. I thought that if a terrorist broke in, of course I wouldn’t be able to fight him off. The knife was so I wouldn’t be taken captive: I was prepared to kill myself. That would have been much more peaceful than the endless suffering of being a hostage.
From the start of the attack, I also had this strange feeling… Relief, in a way. When Russia attacked Ukraine, I felt guilty because I’m from Russia, and my country had attacked another country. Here, we weren’t the ones attacking — we were being attacked. Finally, we weren’t the bad guys. But then [after the war in the Gaza Strip began], Israelis faced even more hatred than Russians.
In November, a friend in Berlin invited me and a mutual friend to stay with him. He said: Come over, just take a breather. Here, you won’t have to run to a bomb shelter 10 times a day.
We flew to Berlin, walked around the city a lot, and kept coming across pro-Palestinian flyers everywhere. The most progressive neighborhoods in Berlin were plastered with Free Palestine imagery. On one wall, there were photographs of Israeli hostages, and every one of them had nasty things written and drawn all over it.
How is that possible? To me, it’s just the usual barbaric attitude. “We’re so good and innocent, and those Israelis are killing Palestinian babies and deserve to have Hamas take them all captive.” “We can afford to forget that we do terrible things ourselves.” Meduza itself writes a lot whenever Israelis destroy something in Gaza, but not when Hamas destroys something in Israel and people are killed.
Anyway, my friend and I stayed in Berlin for a week and left because it was emotionally hard.
Since October 7, almost every time I meet people in other countries, I have to watch what I say. Because plenty of people take pleasure in hating Israelis. It’s easy to feel virtuous when you say you support everything good and oppose everything evil.
If someone near me starts talking about Palestine, I jump right into the conversation. I feel responsible because there’s so much people don’t know. They don’t know that Hamas literally governs Gaza, that it really is under Sharia law, or how extensive Hamas’s network of tunnels beneath civilian sites in Gaza is. Or that if Hamas had let ordinary Gazans shelter in those tunnels, there would have been far fewer casualties.
I feel I need to share my experience and tell people about Israel. I try to do that without downplaying Palestinians’ suffering.
We have to remember that we’re all human, and you can’t hate someone simply because they belong to a particular social group.
But I want the world to know that rockets landed near my home, that my friends no longer have a home, that people I loved were killed at a music festival — and in this war in general. And how many of us have suffered? All of us — every single one.
Tatyana Konev, 59, marketing specialist, Karmiel
I’ve been in Israel for 30 years — my husband and I came here in 1995. We were born and raised in Donetsk.
The war after October 7 isn’t our first war in Israel. There was the Second Lebanon War in 2006. It was very frightening because we had two small children, and my husband kept getting called up for military training, though he wasn’t sent to the front.
On October 8, this new war reached the next generation: My son got a call-up notice. It came while he was at work, and I packed his backpack while he was on his way home. Then my husband drove him to his military unit.
A couple of hours later, they came back. It turned out that 20% more people had reported for duty than the unit needed because some had shown up without call-up notices. They let my son go because they didn’t need that many people, and he worked at an important medical equipment manufacturer.
I don’t know what would have happened if my son had stayed with the unit. Its soldiers cleared mines from tunnels in Gaza. So many of them died.
In Israel, war is always close by. There’s an old saying here that our children won’t have to fight. Meaning that any day now, the wars will end. But children and grandchildren have been fighting for generations.
October 7 was Shabbat and the holiday of Simchat Torah — “Rejoicing in the Torah.” Religious families had their phones and televisions, all their means of communication, switched off that day. They didn’t know what had happened. October 2023 also marked 50 years since the start of the Yom Kippur War. I kept saying that Israel’s enemies would want to mark the occasion.
I know a family whose kibbutz was invaded by militants. The family hid in a bomb shelter and stayed there for 28 hours. The militants took over their house. The Israeli army came to liberate the kibbutz, and the militants fired back from inside the family’s house. When the family came out of the bomb shelter, their house was covered in blood.
That day turned many Israelis’ worldview upside down. People in the kibbutzim in the south were mostly very left-wing. I often argued with them about left-wing ideas and told them about my life in the Soviet Union. Left-wing people here couldn’t believe things like that could happen under socialism — to them, it was the ideal.
A lot of people on the left thought that if we helped the people of Gaza, they’d warm to us. October 7 showed how badly that idea failed. A colleague of mine called herself a “proud leftist,” and after October 7, she wrote that she’d lost faith in her ideals.
Some people moved further right, others turned to religion. Israelis generally started looking at life differently. So many times before bed, I’ve thought: “Here I am, going to sleep in my own bed. Tomorrow I’ll get up and have coffee. What’s it like to be a hostage underground? To spend a year or two like that, with almost no food or water, under constant threat of violence?”
One of my colleagues served in the army in a role we call the “knock on the door.” When a soldier’s death is confirmed, someone assigned to that task goes to their family to tell them what happened. For two years after the war began, my colleague was hardly ever in the office. She had so many doors to knock on.
And even after all the hostages were released, my colleague was still making lots of visits to people’s homes. We asked her why. She said not all hostages and soldiers are mentally well when they return to civilian life. People can’t cope with what happened and take their own lives.
For example, last year, a young man whose girlfriend had been killed right in front of him at the Nova music festival took his own life.
Another colleague of mine lost his daughter. I’d drawn cards for her bat mitzvah, and then the girl was gone, killed in combat on October 7 or 8.
Now, every morning, I thank God that my house hasn’t been bombed and my children are alive.
Boris Voitsekhovsky, 53, artist, cook, and former journalist, Haifa
In November 2022, my wife and I moved from Moscow to Haifa through the repatriation program because of the mobilization. We’d never been to Israel before. When I left, I had a remote job as the managing editor of Moslenta, but I quit after moving. Now I write children’s books, cook food to order, and paint — a whole range of things.
There was a blizzard in Moscow that November. We were freezing at the airport, and then we arrived in Haifa: warmth, sunshine, palm trees. Beautiful. It was a strange contrast. For the first year, it felt like some kind of extended vacation. There was a forest near our apartment, and we could get to the sea in 20 minutes by bus. We really relaxed and didn’t feel any danger.
That’s pretty much how the whole year before October 7 went: meeting friends, grilling kebabs, drinking wine by the sea. In time, I realized Haifa reminded me of Sukhumi, the largest city in Abkhazia, where I used to spend vacations as a child. Even the smells are the same — the same flowers grow there.
Of course, we understood that terrorist attacks happen regularly in Israel: Someone shoots at a car somewhere, someone gets stabbed. But we saw them all as isolated incidents. There was no sense that trouble was brewing.
On October 7, I was alone in Haifa. My wife had flown to Moscow to see her parents. I was planning to go to a friend’s birthday party. I woke up and read the news. At first, I thought: All sorts of things happen in Israel. Give it a day or two, and it’ll be over. Then reports started coming in that huge numbers of people had been killed, both at the festival and in the kibbutzim…
It seemed like it wouldn’t affect us because Haifa is in northern Israel, and the main events happened in the south, on the border with Gaza. So I went to the birthday party, and my wife flew back the next day.
Toward nightfall, we started hearing explosions. It wasn’t clear exactly what was happening, but it was clearly nothing good.
We started getting daily warnings about the risk of rocket attacks. A special app sent us instructions on what to do if an alarm went off. First, you’re supposed to go into a mamad — a reinforced room in your apartment. But our building is old, and we don’t have one. The instructions say that if you don’t have a room like that, go to the basement; if there’s no basement, go to the stairwell; if there’s no stairwell, stay in a room without windows. We don’t have a basement. We live on the second floor of a two-story building, and the stairs lead straight from the street into our apartment. We even have windows in the bathroom. Basically, as unsafe as it gets.
So every time, my wife and I ran to the stairwell of the building next door. You get an alert, and you have a couple of minutes to get there. But when ballistic missiles started coming from Iran, it got harder because then you only have about a minute.
In 2024, my wife and I spent nights in a bomb shelter at a school. If an attack happens at night, it’s hard to get to the building next door in time. But being in the school’s bomb shelter was great. You get an alert, and you don’t have to go anywhere — you’re already there. We slept on a camping mat. We brought blankets and pillows from home. The concrete floors were cold, and the air was stuffy. My back hurt afterward — it was a concrete floor, after all.
I couldn’t count how many warnings we got, but Haifa itself wasn’t hit all that often. There were deaths, though: In the first few months, for example, a rocket hit an oil refinery outside the city, killing workers.
Some people in Israel are, let’s say, bloodthirsty. They say all of Gaza should be paved over because they’re all scum there. I don’t understand that. Just as I can’t accept the idea that all Russians are assholes because Russia attacked Ukraine. I know plenty of good people in Russia. My parents live there, after all.
But there are fewer bloodthirsty people now — that’s how it seems to me. Because people are exhausted. When the war began, it seemed like it would end quickly, and now it’s been going on for years. People want to make plans and live in peace.
It was impossible not to follow what was happening with the hostages. Everyone was writing and talking about it, and there were constant street protests. I didn’t take part because, of course, the hostages need to be brought back, but I don’t know how rallies could help with that. Is the army going to do more, or what?
But I cooked for soldiers. Jews came to Israel from all over the world to fight. People helped however they could: putting them up in their homes, feeding them, raising money for equipment and footwear.
I don’t know if you could say I have PTSD, but sudden noises bother me. When a car suddenly starts honking, for example, or a tire bursts. Or that bang-bang when a motorcycle goes by. A motorcycle sounds just like a drone. Exactly the same.
When we first arrived in Israel, people had so many plans: They were opening shops, galleries. Now it’s impossible to know how to make plans at all. What’s going to happen tomorrow? Maybe another war? Should we buy property here, start a business? Or maybe move to another country before the kids get called up?
Larisa Zimina, 52, HR specialist, Netanya
In August 2023, there was a hot-air balloon festival at the very spot where the music festival took place, or somewhere very close by. I went with my children. There were several thousand big Israeli families there, with very young children, tents, and dogs. There’s only one road in. It still terrifies me to think that we wouldn’t have gotten out if the attack had happened that day. If I’d felt there was a threat [of a terrorist attack], I wouldn’t have gone.
On the morning of October 7, I was talking to a friend in America. Her son was in Israel and wasn’t answering her calls. She said he’d gone to some event. I said: It’s seven in the morning. He’s been dancing and drinking and partying all night. He’s probably asleep, and maybe his phone’s dead. We joked that trees don’t have power outlets. The guy’s 23, he’s finished his military service. Why keep calling him?
Then I started reading the news and realized things were looking bad. My mother called from Beersheba and said the sirens were going off there. I also remember religious [Jews] stopping me in the street. They couldn’t read the news [on Shabbat] and were asking what was happening.
The boy whose mother I’d been talking to was killed. That boy used to babysit my child. His brother was my son’s best friend. His mother flew in from Chicago right away — on October 9, we were at the missing-persons center that had been set up near Ben Gurion Airport. People were sobbing, screaming, wailing.
October 7 profoundly changed how safe I feel in Israel. It always used to be a short war, a long break, then another, and another. Suddenly, the war turned out not to be short. The odds of losing our “lottery” got much higher.
[Before,] there were knife attacks and suicide bombings, but they didn’t stop me from working, taking buses, going to parties, or just living my life. I used to work in news in Russia, and I know that the chance of dying of any cause in Russia is much higher than the chance of being killed by a terrorist in Israel.
I live my life as I always have — but if I had a house, I’d build a bomb shelter. Many of my friends have gotten gun permits. Now I’d think twice about renting an apartment in Kfar Saba.
October 7 was an astonishing combination of a fuckup and Israel’s usual laid-back attitude. I used to spend a lot of time working on this conflict, working with left-wing organizations that support two states for two peoples. And I understand how complicated it all is — how nobody’s hands are clean. How many stupid things and mistakes both sides have made, Israel included…
But I’m Israeli, and I’m on the Israelis’ side. And it always matters who started it — with the attack from Gaza, that’s obvious.
Really, everyone should be ready for anything. You can start with the basics: stock up on food, water, portable gas stoves, and blankets at home. Be ready for everything to suddenly shut down and another endless war to begin. I teach my children to steer clear of crowds and watch who’s walking behind them.
And you’ve got to keep yourself sane any way you can: exercise, sex, sleep.
Grigory Nedayev, 31, software developer, Tel Aviv
I moved from Moscow to Israel in March 2022, shortly after [Russia invaded Ukraine]. I knew where I was going, so the possibility that one of Israel’s neighbors might fire a rocket at it, or that a terrorist attack might happen somewhere, didn’t surprise me. So I was prepared — and before October 7, I felt safe.
The Hamas attack happened the day after my wife and I got back from a vacation in France. We flew into Israel on October 6 — lovely weather, warm, peaceful. Around 6:30 a.m. the next day, an outdoor warning siren went off. I woke up and thought: Something’s happening.
But something’s always happening here. I went up to the roof of our building. The sky was clear, no rockets or explosions, just the siren. So I went back to sleep. I really underestimated the danger.
That morning, my wife and I started reading the news and realized it was serious. There wasn’t any panic, though. I’m not an anxious person. I thought: There were Hamas attacks in 2019 and 2021 too. And the Gaza Strip is 80 kilometers [about 50 miles] from us. That’s a ridiculously short distance by Russian standards, of course, but it’s still not right on our doorstep. It seemed like it would last a couple of days, so the next day I didn’t even read the news.
I work on Sundays, and at the morning meeting I saw how tense my colleagues were. We didn’t discuss work, just what was happening. Over the next few days, I followed the news closely. Rockets were coming toward Tel Aviv, and the Israeli army was intercepting them. I’d never seen anything like that before — at most, some smoke in the distance from an intercepted rocket. Now it was frightening: Things were exploding right over your head.
I’m pretty resilient, but even I struggled with all the reports of people being burned and brutally killed. You read it and absorb all that horror. You get depressed.
After the hostage deal fell through and Hamas killed six hostages, I was so shaken that I went to a rally. I wanted to, how do I put it, express my opinion.
Then I came across a post looking for volunteers in a Russian-language Telegram chat. I signed up — I wanted to help however I could. They took us somewhere, something like a military base, and we spent the whole day packing food, canned goods, and all sorts of little things for soldiers.
About a year ago, all the hostages came home. There was almost jubilation in the streets. People weren’t exactly walking around shouting “hooray!” but you could see from their faces that they were happy. I felt a kind of happiness too, real relief. Because that horror had dragged on for so long, deals kept falling through, politicians did nothing but argue — you just wanted it to end.
Over these years, I’ve started questioning whether I want to live in Israel, and I’ve become more pessimistic about the future. Even though none of this has affected me personally. I live in a building with a reinforced room — my bedroom is a bomb shelter, so I don’t have to run anywhere. A couple of months after the war began, our company switched to remote work, so I just sat and worked in that room to the sound of rockets exploding. In theory, if a rocket hit the wall of that room, I’d be stunned by the blast, but it wouldn’t kill me.
I haven’t changed. But I think the country has. This war has pretty much killed the idea of peaceful coexistence with Palestine. My impression is that many people who used to be left-wing or centrist have shifted to the right.
Zina Kapitovskaya, 74, retiree, Haifa
When I learned what was happening on October 7, I was overcome with horror, fear, hatred. And sorrow, like any normal person, over the deaths of completely innocent people, including children.
We knew about the balloons they sent from Gaza. We knew they hated us. But we never thought it could turn into such a horrific massacre.
Years ago, I happened to miss a bus that later exploded. For a while afterward, I couldn’t get on buses. Israel is a country where something can happen at any moment. But a massacre like October 7 was unimaginable.
I didn’t see a therapist after October 7: It turns out I’m pretty resilient, and I can cope on my own. Probably partly because October 7 didn’t affect anyone close to me. My grandchildren were in the army at the time, but they didn’t get caught up in that meat grinder. If they had, I’d probably have been losing my mind just like other parents and grandparents in that situation.
I can’t say my everyday routine has changed since October 7. My sense of safety hasn’t changed either. Nor has my attitude toward the Arabs who live near us: I’m not afraid of them.
The worst thing is that no state commission of inquiry into the October 7 attack has been set up. There’s a law specifying how a state commission of inquiry must be formed and who must sit on it. Commissions like that were set up after several wars. Three years have passed, and no one has been held responsible. Only a few people acknowledged responsibility and resigned on their own. Elections are coming up in Israel, and setting up a state commission of inquiry is at the top of the sensible parties’ platforms.
My attitude toward the government changed enormously [after the events of October 7]. I think they bear a lot of the blame, and they absolutely need to be replaced. [Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin] Netanyahu says one thing, but who knows what he really thinks.
Of course, the problem didn’t start on October 7. This has all been going on for a very long time. I’m not a politician. I don’t know how to fix it, but I’m sure war isn’t necessarily the answer.
Gavriel Feldman, 49, editor of Mir Torah (World of Torah), a publication about Judaism, Jerusalem
October 7 was Simchat Torah. I went to the synagogue for the very first minyan [communal prayer service]. Most people go to the other, longer minyan: They sing for hours, dance with the Torah scrolls, and socialize. I went to the first minyan because it’s very short, so I could get home to the children and take them back [to the synagogue] for the main celebration and dancing without rushing.
Large floor-standing air conditioners had been set up in the room for the dancing. They were humming, and we couldn’t hear the sirens. I realized something was happening when I got home during a lull in the sirens.
Then rockets started hitting. We had to decide whether to take the children [to the synagogue]. Something was clearly happening, but we didn’t know what. We decided to go for a little while. The lower hall in our synagogue doubles as a bomb shelter. When we arrived, it was clear that the dancing was winding down.
Rumors started circulating because people in our community were being called up to fight. Secular neighbors told us a few things. We knew militants had broken through and hostages had been taken. A picture was beginning to emerge, but nobody understood the scale of it, how many people had been killed or abducted.
Turning on a phone or television is a direct violation of Shabbat. You can do it if there’s an immediate threat to life, but there wasn’t one. Rocket attacks are fairly routine in Israel.
This [observing Shabbat] is a difficult issue: It’s a holiday, Simchat Torah. There are stories about our great teachers who, even in moments of immense personal grief, set it aside when a holiday began and fulfilled the commandments. After the holiday, a person like that returns to their deep mourning, but during the holiday they rejoice, and it isn’t an act.
But we’re ordinary people… [For us,] that’s quite difficult. The children and I left the synagogue and went home fairly quickly. After that, we started going to bomb shelters…
The next day, once Shabbat and the holiday were over, people started collecting supplies for soldiers. Because it had become clear that the state wasn’t prepared for anything. The army couldn’t provide reservists with what they needed. On the morning of October 8, I bought the most urgently requested items and took bags of them somewhere.
Not long before that, our son had been born, and he had some [health] complications. He was our sixth child. Even as experienced parents, we had to learn a lot of things all over again. We were really tied down [caring for the baby], while the war was going on in the background.
I coped with it fairly easily. It was harder for my wife. Anxiety, not knowing what would happen next, no sense of certainty or safety.
For many people in Israel, October 7 shattered their understanding of the world. For me, it didn’t. If you start from the belief that the Almighty governs the world, while the world’s progressives are trying to take it in the wrong direction, then you understand that stability and tranquility are something of an illusion, a way of fooling yourself. If everything’s okay for you today, you shouldn’t assume it necessarily always will be.
October 7 woke a great many people up. In that sense, some good came out of this horrific tragedy. For a while, you could see the unity in Israel that everyone loves to talk about.
Then, of course, that unity fell apart — turning to “mold and linden honey,” as the Russian song goes. But at least we knew unity was possible.
Vitaly Starov, 44, programmer, Acre
My wife and I left Russia because repression was growing, and we suspected I might be jailed. We understood that we were moving to a country where terrorist attacks could happen, a country that’s constantly at war.
We arrived in Israel about three months before October 7. Luckily, we managed to get all our paperwork done except for my driver’s license. We got identity cards, bus and commuter train passes, and joined a health insurance fund. After October 7, everything closed, then opened only intermittently. It took me six months to get my license.
On October 7, I woke up with an inflamed ear, apparently because I’d walked barefoot on the tile [in our apartment] the day before. My ear hurt, and the pain spread to a tooth. I thought I should probably see a doctor, but then I started reading the news and felt even worse.
The Hamas attack was shocking: a brutal massacre with large numbers of civilian casualties. The videos of hostages being dragged through crowds in Gaza, beaten and spat on, really hit me hard.
That same day, checkpoints were set up at the northern entrances to Acre, and armored vehicles with men carrying automatic weapons were brought in. The Lebanese border is 10 to 15 kilometers [about six to nine miles] north of the city. The thinking was that Hezbollah might break through the border and make it as far as Acre. But it limited itself to rocket attacks. There were fears that unrest would break out among Israeli Arabs, but that didn’t happen.
Hezbollah launched its first attacks from Lebanon a day or two later, and after that, there were air-raid sirens on many days. Almost all the rockets were shot down. Only a few got through. The bomb shelters in Acre, like those in many cities in northern Israel, were full of junk and partly flooded. I went to help clear them out as a volunteer.
My attitude toward Israel hasn’t changed since October 7, but my attitude toward the current Israeli government has. For the worse: They haven’t solved a single problem, only compounded them. No state commission of inquiry into the events of October 7 has been set up. The goals of the war Israel has become embroiled in are unclear, and there are serious questions about how it’s being fought.
I wouldn’t say I have PTSD, and I probably don’t need to see a therapist. But naturally, there’s nothing good about air-raid sirens either. Now, wherever you go, you automatically look around for the nearest bomb shelter. Still, I don’t feel threatened by Arabs — and there are a lot of them in Acre.
After October 7, it became much clearer why so many Israelis carry guns in public. It doesn’t surprise me to see people carrying automatic military rifles while buying groceries in a supermarket. And overall, the Israeli army and security services showed their strength and proved they could regroup even after a huge failure.
Acre is a small city, and we didn’t really have rallies calling for the hostages’ release. But my wife and I went to roadside protests with signs several times, handed out ribbons, and put up banners around the city. Relatives of hostages came to Acre, and we met with them. The main demand was for the government to agree to a deal to free the hostages.
We did all this with local Hebrew speakers. There were no Russian speakers there. There was very little information in Russian about the movement supporting the hostages. I posted in Acre’s Russian-language chats a few times, but nobody came to the protests.
Israel is a small country. Almost everyone who’s lived here a long time has relatives or acquaintances who were harmed [in the terrorist attack] — or at least knows someone who does. Most Israelis think their country upholds European standards. Seeing that brutality [during the terrorist attack] convinced them that barbarians had attacked, people they couldn’t negotiate with. That’s where all those statements come from about there being no innocent people in Gaza, about building a parking lot in its place. Those statements cast Israel in the worst possible light.
I definitely don’t want to go back to Moscow. Sometimes it all gets too much, and I want to move somewhere else [to a third country]. But we’re citizens here, and in another country we’d have to go through all the bureaucracy again. Learn another language, unless it’s English.
Israel’s actually not a bad country to live in. Apart from the wars and the rocket attacks.

Iran transfers $200 million to Hezbollah despite tightening US sanctions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
19:10:33 UTC
04:10:33 KST

Hezbollah has received $200 million from Iran to help Lebanese displaced by this year’s war with Israel, two people with direct knowledge of the transfer said, the first significant aid from the group to supporters who bore the brunt of the conflict.
Hezbollah received the cash last month despite a tightening U.S. economic chokehold on Iran and increasing difficulties in getting funds to Tehran's Lebanese ally, said the people.
Intermediaries who moved the money charged a 20% fee, reflecting the risks of dealing with the group, they said. One said this was four times the normal fee.
Asked for comment, a Hezbollah official said an amount had been secured and a plan for distributing it would be announced in the coming days, without elaborating on the source of the funds.
The Iranian foreign ministry, Iran's permanent mission in Geneva, the U.S. Treasury Department and the Lebanese government did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
Israel’s bombardment and invasion of Lebanon uprooted hundreds of thousands of Hezbollah’s Shi’ite Muslim constituents after the group entered the regional war in support of Iran on March 2.
But those displaced have so far received little to no assistance from Hezbollah, an armed group founded by Iran’s Revolutionary Guards in 1982 which has suffered heavy Israeli blows in two wars since 2024 and is designated a terrorist group by Washington.
Aiding 50,000 families
Hezbollah would use the funds to pay an initial $3,000 per family, and priority will go to those whose villages have been destroyed or are inaccessible due to Israeli occupation, the sources said. These number around 50,000 families, one of the sources said.
Iran has maintained financial support to Hezbollah through years of crippling U.S. sanctions: it transferred $1 billion to the group in the first 10 months of 2025, according to the U.S. Treasury Department.
Tehran has never acknowledged financing Hezbollah. Iran's policy of funding regional proxies has stirred domestic protester anger against the clerical rulers in the past and could prove particularly sensitive at a time of worsening hardship in Iran.
Iran had promised Hezbollah more funding after Tehran signed an interim deal with Washington in June that allowed Iran to sell its oil, Reuters reported at the time. That agreement collapsed in July.
Washington has since intensified economic pressure on Iran, tightening sanctions and imposing a naval blockade to block Iranian oil exports.
Hezbollah leader Naim Qassem said in a speech last month that the group would soon contribute to a project aimed at housing thousands of people displaced by the war, using “available resources and donations”, without elaborating.
Hezbollah's ability to fund local services and provide post-conflict aid has helped shore up its support in the past. Following a war with Israel in 2006, the group immediately handed out large cash payments to those impacted and moved swiftly to help rebuild Beirut's southern suburbs, a stronghold.
But this time there has been little sign of reconstruction. Lebanese Prime Minister Nawaf Salam said last month that the total reconstruction costs from the two wars since 2024 could exceed $27 billion.
A costly war
The two sources provided no details on how the money got to Lebanon.
One of them said it was increasingly difficult for Hezbollah to move funds via financial companies that once processed such transfers. Such firms based in Iraq and Dubai were no longer an option, and they were also now under pressure in Turkey, this source said.
Hezbollah’s foes believed money was currently the group’s “oxygen”, the source added. Despite the difficulties securing funding, the group had not stopped paying its fighters and the family members of those killed in combat, this source said.
In Lebanon, the war has inflicted a heavy price on the Shi’ite Muslim community from which Hezbollah draws support. Israel has razed villages across a swathe of territory it has seized in the south, saying it aims to shield northern Israel from Hezbollah attack.

With OCX Axed, Space Force Moves Forward with New GPS Ground Plan
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
19:09:34 UTC
04:09:34 KST

After scrapping a long-delayed program to build a next-generation GPS ground system earlier this year, the Space Force and prime contractor Lockheed Martin are pushing toward delivery of the capability in time to support the first launch of the newest GPS satellites, currently planned for 2028.
However, a new report from the Government Accountability Office raises concerns about that timeline. Further, the Space Force still lacks a plan to operationalize a key civilian signal installed in GPS satellites already on orbit. That signal, called L5, provides higher bandwidth and is more resistant to jamming and interference than other civilian GPS signals—which is important for aviation and maritime safety.
The Space Force announced in April it would cancel its long troubled Next-Generation GPS Operational Control Segment, or OCX. The system was meant to operate “Generation 3” satellites, to include the GPS III and GPS IIIF variants. But the effort, led by prime contractor RTX, failed to meet cost and schedule targets. By the time the Space Force pulled the plug, the program was 10 years late and its cost had nearly doubled from $3.7 billion to $6.27 billion.
Erin Carper, the acting portfolio acquisition executive for positioning, navigation, and timing and satellite communications, told reporters in September the decision to cancel OCX after more than 15 years and billions of dollars was driven primarily by two imperatives: the need to deliver the ground control elements for GPS IIIF satellites on time and to contain development risk along the way.
“Can we do it faster and not perturb the IIIF schedule? That was a significant driver,” Carper said Sept. 15 at AFA’s Air, Space & Cyber conference. “And then the other thing was, do we understand the risk remaining? The test campaign for OCX and the burn down of [deficiency reports] and some of the other things, that’s where we saw risk to the schedule for OCX.”
Rather than continue with OCX, the service opted instead to funnel resources toward a series of upgrades Lockheed Martin has been delivering for the legacy GPS ground segment, dubbed the Architecture Evolution Program, or AEP. The service first put Lockheed on contract for AEP in 2016, when OCX was delayed, to ensure the ground system could support GPS III launches and, eventually, command and control them once on orbit.
Since April, the Space Force has awarded Lockheed an additional $199 million to upgrade AEP to support launch and command and control for GPS IIIF satellites—an effort it’s calling AEP-M—and to begin a full technology refresh of the GPS ground segment hardware and software. That upgrade will lay the foundation for the next generation of the GPS ground system, known as Gen4. The service envisions that architecture as more modular and distributed, and it’s considering how it might leverage commercial antennas and other capabilities to support it.
Lockheed’s Vice President for Global Communications and Navigation Christina Mancinelli said that over the last 10 years, the company has completed more than 100 projects aimed at adding new capabilities to AEP, including a capability called M-Code Early Use, which allowed the ground system to task and monitor an advanced, secure signal called M-Code.
“We’ve been modernizing along the way,” Mancinelli said. “There have been some big upgrades we’ve made on the ground, but we have also been evolving it and doing projects to keep up with things for the last decade.”
Both Mancinelli and Carper said their teams are pushing to have AEP-M ready for the first GPS IIIF launch, though they noted that they’re still negotiating a formal schedule for the effort. A Space Systems Command spokesperson said the schedule is currently under review by the Pentagon’s Cost Assessment and Program Evaluation office. They declined to give an estimate of when the timeline might be solidified and wouldn’t provide a total cost estimate for the effort.
Meanwhile, GAO said in an Oct. 7 report that to support a 2028 launch, the ground control capability must be available by early 2027.
More broadly, Carper said she’s optimistic that Lockheed’s heritage on GPS ground and the program’s more incremental approach will help it avoid some of the pitfalls of OCX, which was attempting to pull off what she described as “a big bang delivery of capability.” In modern software development, incremental deliveries are favored because if there’s a glitch in an update, it’s easier to revert, or roll back, to a more stable version of the software to address it.
“There’s significant risk in cutting an entire constellation of operational satellites over to a brand new ground system, and that meant a level of test and oversight that was becoming very challenging,” she said. “With AEP-M, we’re able to roll out incremental capabilities, roll back more easily. … That’s not to say there aren’t inherent risks; there always will be. We will run into challenges, but we understand what some of those challenges are and are managing the risk.”
Modernization Delays
While the AEP-M contracts awarded to date cover the scope of what OCX would have provided for command and control and launch support, it doesn’t include modifications needed to operationalize the L5 signal. That signal is installed today on 21 spacecraft—some older GPS IIFs as well as all 10 GPS III satellites in orbit. However, due to OCX delays, the service hasn’t yet upgraded the ground system to monitor those signals.
SSC confirmed to Air & Space Forces Magazine that it has not yet awarded a contract for the L5 signal upgrades.
“The L5 effort was not included in the recently awarded control segment contracts to Lockheed,” a Space Systems Command spokesperson said. “The Space Force is focused on delivering capability incrementally as quickly as possible and is exploring all appropriate options for delivering modernized civil signals.”
SSC noted that it’s working with the Department of Transportation and the Federal Aviation Administration to finalize a plan for that work and expects to award contracts “in the near future.”
Amid a rise in GPS jamming and spoofing incidents in recent years, experts and commercial industry have been pushing for the U.S. government to operationalize the L5 signal—a move they say would make the aviation industry and commercial receivers more resilient. In 2024, the GPS Innovation Alliance recommended the Defense Department “increase the urgency and primacy” of upgrading the GPS ground system to support more robust civil signals.
“The more you can integrate multiple different types of signals into a receiver as well as combine that with specialized antennas … the better you are at resisting attempts to jam or spoof your receiver or device,” Lisa Dyer, the alliance’s executive director, told Air & Space Forces Magazine on Oct. 7. “We see today a need for that kind of capability, and L5 is one of those signals that we’d really like to see get integrated as soon as possible.”
There are other complicating factors beyond the ground system upgrade plans, including a requirement that at least 24 satellites be broadcasting the signal before it can be declared fully operational. Some commercial firms have already integrated L5 into their operations, but more regulated industries like aviation need the FAA to certify the signal as healthy before they can follow suit.
It’s possible the FAA could approve the signal before it hits the 24-satellite threshold, but one source familiar with the discussions said the agency is unlikely to change its position or permit waivers due to safety concerns. There has also been discussion around fielding the first GPS IIIF satellites on a faster timeline, but it’s unclear if there would be room on the launch manifest to accelerate the program due to current bottlenecks in the launch industry. And according to the GAO report, even if the Space Force and Lockheed were able to accelerate IIIF deliveries, there’s no certainty that the ground segment would be ready to support an earlier launch.

Evicted pensioner, 87, who sparked Spain housing protests dies, says tenant union
MADRID - An 87-year-old Madrid woman whose eviction triggered nationwide protests over Spain’s chronic housing crisis and a political debate that culminated in early elections died on Oct 7, a tenants’ union said.
“We are sorry to announce that Maricarmen passed away today,” the Madrid Tenants’ Union said in a statement about Maricarmen Abascal, adding that her cause marked “a turning point in the history of this country”.
Abascal became a symbol of Spain’s housing market on Sept 23 when she was evicted from her life-long Madrid home on a stretcher after the real estate firm that owned the apartment drastically hiked the rent.
Outrage at her eviction triggered national demonstrations, with hundreds of people camping in Madrid’s Puerta del Sol square in the most symbolic of the protests.
The movement piled pressure on the minority leftist government to present urgent housing measures, including more restrictions on evictions and the automatic renewal of tenant contracts.
But their rejection in parliament last week prompted Socialist Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez to call a snap election for Nov 29 in which housing will feature prominently.
“The housing debate is at the centre, but the cost to get here has been too high,” the tenants’ union said of the election, originally due in 2027.
Abascal had been hospitalised with exhaustion after her eviction, but a deal had been reached with the company that owned her flat allowing her to return home.
“This solution has come too late. A totally avoidable situation after a torturous process,” added the tenants’ union. AFP

Cooperation, therefore, must extend beyond individual regions, with regions working together for collective security and growth.

The European Union envoys approved on Wednesday 1,646 new designations under the bloc's sanctions regime for Russia, with the majority focused on the country's military industrial complex, three EU diplomats said.
More than half of the newly added entities and individuals are involved in the chain of production of Russia's ballistic missiles, such as the 9M723 Iskander-M, which can only be intercepted by US-made Patriot air defence systems.
Ukraine is facing a severe shortage of Patriot interceptors as the US diverts military resources to the Gulf, while Russia has intensified ballistic missile strikes.
Russian politicians also targated
The designations include a range of entities involved in missile testing and research as well as the production of solid fuels and rocket engines for Russia's Iskander system.
The EU is also targeting producers of specialised textiles and synthetic and carbon fibres used across a range of different missile systems, one of the sources specified.
In addition, the list has drone manufacturers, shipyards that service submarines and 77 Russian politicians who ran for parliamentary seats in Russian-occupied Ukrainian territories.
The sanctions will be formally adopted when EU foreign ministers meet on Monday.
Putin ties diesel exports to sanctions as global supply tightens
Russian President Vladimir Putin said last week Moscow would not resume diesel exports - currently banned until the end of October - to global markets until sanctions are lifted.
The global diesel market has tightened due to the US-Israel war on Iran, which, combined with the loss of Russian diesel after Ukrainian strikes on Russian refineries, triggered shortages in Russia.
The EU, concerned about strengthening links between Russia and North Korea, also added seven North Korean entities and individuals linked to Moscow's war effort.

Was pre-COP a flop? Questions loom over the Australian government
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
19:05:28 UTC
04:05:28 KST

analysis
Was pre-COP a flop? Questions loom over the government's high profile climate gathering in the Pacific
As the Fiji Airways flight carrying dignitaries to Tuvalu sat on the airport runway at the heart of its tiny capital, Funafuti, an official struggled with a broken umbrella in the driving rain.
A pile of sodden brollies lay next to him as locals prepared to ferry leaders, ministers and assorted bigwigs out of the plane, across the tarmac, through the downpour, and into a traditional welcome ceremony.
The rather forlorn image seemed to fit neatly with the headlines back home in Australia, which had already declared the pre-COP summit a farce and a failure, particularly as the government had only managed to coax two non-Pacific leaders to fly to Tuvalu to see the climate emergency up close.
On the face of it, this might seem a little unfair.
By all accounts, the vibe on the ground was not nearly so grim.
After all, Tuvalu — which remains one of the most isolated and hard to reach countries in the world — is hardly famous for hosting major diplomatic gatherings.
And yet here they all were.
Pacific leaders standing side by side with ministers from across the world, including from India, the United Arab Emirates, Türkiye and Nepal.
UN heavyweights and top multilateral officials who hold the keys to billions in climate financing. All listening in person to Tuvalu's story, and examining an extraordinary land reclamation project designed to hold back relentless rising seas.
The carping and outrage about the cost to Australian taxpayers was also, frankly, a bit over the top.
When the cameras caught Climate Minister Chris Bowen apparently struggling to resist nodding off, the Shadow Energy Minister Dan Tehan joked he was having a rest after a "big day … by the pool on the banana lounge sipping a few cocktails".
But anyone who has had even a passing interaction with the famously diligent minister would laugh-choke into their piña colada at the implausible image of Mr Bowen gleefully dodging work by the pool.
And while it is always good to scrutinise government spending, let's keep some perspective.
The rough cost of the whole enterprise of around $20 million (or so) is somewhere between loose change and a minor rounding error.
It would buy about one seventh of a single F-35 fighter jet, or fund the NDIS for approximately three hours.
So, does all this mean that pre-COP was a great success, and that the carping critics have got it wrong?
Nope.
Because even when you cast aside the exaggeration and cheap shots, there is still simply no way for the federal government to hide the yawning gap between what it promised, and what it has delivered.
'We wanted to bring the world to Tuvalu'
When the government struck its rather ungainly bargain with Türkiye, it spruiked the pre-COP meetings in Tuvalu and Fiji as a spur to global climate action, bringing the world's polluters to the Pacific to see the devastating impact of the catastrophe in person.
COP could not just be a "jamboree of the willing" Mr Bowen told the Guardian in January.
Anthony Albanese has rapidly built up a fairly impressive network among fellow world leaders, and government officials were not shy about spruiking his "exceptional" personal relationships across Asia and Europe, suggesting that the prime minister might be able to land some big fish for Tuvalu.
Sure, there was zero chance of bringing in an apex predator like Donald Trump or Xi Jinping, but hopes seemed high that some heavyweights — like Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney, Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi, or then UK prime minister Keir Starmer — might be coaxed into making the trip.
But as the months dragged on, and leader after leader quietly let it be known they would not be willing to make a long journey to the Pacific, the mood shifted, accompanied by the groaning sound of goalposts being dragged across the ground.
Ministers were allowed to sub in for leaders.
About a month ago Fiji revealed that a grand total of just five leaders from outside the Pacific had agreed to come to Tuvalu.
And then, earlier this week, that already modest number was whittled down further to just two: Mauritius and Timor Leste, which together contribute to perhaps 0.01 or 0.02 per cent of global emissions.
Mr Bowen was even denying that the government had promised to bring "world leaders" to Tuvalu at all on Wednesday morning.
"No, I said we wanted to bring the world to Tuvalu," he said.
"We said we wanted to focus and lift the world's attention on the issues of the Pacific, small island developing states in particular, and I think it ticked that box and achieved that."
To call this cute is being generous.
If the minister is seriously trying to suggest that he did not mean "world leaders" when he said he wanted to bring "the world" to a "special leaders event" in the Pacific, then he is pushing credulity beyond breaking point.
It would also be a revelation to Australian officials who spent months (before the inevitable backdown) telling foreign officials that Australia and the Pacific were absolutely set on leaders only meeting in Tuvalu, and who were adamant ministerial level representation would not be contemplated.
Can promises turn into cash for Pacific nations?
It is possible to feel a twinge of sympathy here.
One Australia government source, frustrated by the "relentless negativity" around pre-COP, complained a few weeks ago that they were caught in a bit of a bind.
"If we push for leaders we get hammered for being unrealistic," they told the ABC.
"And if we don't (get leaders) then we get hammered for f***ing it up."
Fair enough.
But surely it would be better for the government to simply admit that it tried its best and fell short rather than blindly insisting everything is just dandy.
It is also worth pointing out that it might take a bit of time before anyone can truly say whether this pre-COP was a proper flop, or merely a tad underwhelming.
Loading
The Australian government has spruiked the gathering as a priceless opportunity to extract more cash for the Pacific Resilience Facility — a new climate fund which has been set up to give Pacific nations much more rapid (and easier) access to desperately needed climate finance.
So far, the new contributions unveiled in Nadi have been — to put it gently — modest.
But Pacific officials have taken every opportunity in Fiji to push for more hefty contributions, and are clearly hoping to see those promises delivered as hard cash commitments at the main COP gathering next month in Türkiye.
None of this means that the pre-COP failures are a millstone which will be hung forever around this government's neck.
If you are in the Pacific, you are — infuriatingly — already well accustomed to being at the mercy of the decisions taken by much larger emitters, and the major fossil fuel exporters.
Pacific's battle at the heart of global negotiations
It is also worth noting that while the Australian government will have to wear some embarrassment, its diplomatic stocks in the Pacific have not seemed to suffer.
That really does matter at a time when Australia remains locked in a "permanent contest" in the region with China — which is both the world's largest single polluter and the engine room of the global clean energy revolution.
Multiple Pacific leaders and officials have made it clear that they were still glad to see the Pacific's battle with climate change put, once again, at the heart of global climate negotiations, whatever pre-COP's shortfalls.
As one Pacific official put it yesterday to the ABC: why should Australia be blamed for trying, just because other leaders could not be bothered showing up?
Even Vanuatu's Climate Minister Ralph Regenvanu, who is not shy of criticising Australia on climate policies, made it clear that he did not blame the Albanese government for the underwhelming turnout.
"We were hoping for more (leaders)," he told Reuters.
"It just reflects the lack of attention and priority given to what Pacific nations consider the greatest threat to their future."
Chris Bowen and Anthony Albanese might be in the cross hairs right now, but if pre-COP (and COP) fall hopelessly short once again, then there will be plenty of blame to go around.

Trump says he may ask FBI to look into Nolan Wells death

Spanish pensioner whose eviction sparked nationwide protests dies, union says
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
20:02:32 BST
04:02:32 KST

Spanish pensioner whose eviction sparked nationwide protests dies, union says
- Published
An elderly woman whose eviction sparked nationwide protests over Spain's housing crisis and a political row that triggered early elections has died, according to Madrid's tenants union.
Maricarmen Abascal, 87, was forcibly removed on a stretcher from her apartment of more than 70 years on 23 September after she was unable to afford rent increases.
The company that owned the flat later offered to allow her to return at a lower rate - but she was unable to sign an agreement as she had been admitted to hospital.
"We regret to announce that Maricarmen passed away today," the Madrid Tenants' Union said in a statement, adding her situation marked "a turning point in the history of this country".
Union spokesperson Alicia del Río said: "Speculation costs lives, and today rentierism has finished killing our colleague Maricarmen" but "her memory lives on with us".
A cause of death was not announced.
Abascal's death was received in Puerta del Sol with a big collective gasp, then followed by a minute of silence.
It is in this square in the centre of Madrid where thousands have been camping since Abascal's eviction last month to demand more affordable housing.
On Wednesday, it became the place to pay tribute to her.
People lit dozens of candles around the square in a small improvised vigil that glowed with a warm light on a dry and warm autumn night.
Other candles formed an altar to Abascal in front of the headquarters of the Community of Madrid government.
Messages on cardboard banners next to the candles read "it's not a death, it's a killing", "the fight will continue" and "Mari Carmen, the grandmother of the whole country", among others.
A few hundred people then took to the streets that connect Puerta del Sol with the Spanish Congress, just 500m away, in an improvised protest.
During the march people chanted: "We will not tolerate a single eviction more" and "the fight will continue, Mari Carmen is still alive". There were other chants against fascism and against the police.
The police had set up barriers to block the march. There was not a big police presence, and there was the tension that protests sometimes have.
Many protesters seemed to feel the police have been complicit in the evictions, as under court orders they have to remove tenants who have been served eviction notices.
After a couple of hours, the chants near Congress gave way to another minute of silence. Then, a big collective shout of "murderers".
Wednesday night's march has finished, but the camping, already on its 12th night, will continue "as long as necessary" one of the protesters told the BBC.
Abascal became a symbol for Spain's housing crisis following her eviction.
Her father first rented the property in 1956 and she continued as the tenant after her parents died, during which time there was a cap on the rent.
However, Urbagestión, which bought the property in 2018, increased the rent from €500 per month (£428; $572) to €2,650 (£2,280; $3,020).
The company later offered to reduce this to €1,650 - still €300 more than Abascal's monthly pension.
Three previous attempts to evict her were blocked by the courts and the case has received increasing media attention.
Anger over the situation grew, leading to protests and putting pressure on the coalition government to approve emergency housing legislation - but it was rejected in Congress last week.
That led to further protests, with tens of thousands of people taking to the streets in cities across the country over the weekend.
Referring to the rejected bills, the Madrid Tenants' Union said: "While a historic agreement was reached that would have allowed her to return to her home, this solution has come too late. An absolutely avoidable situation after a torturing process."
It said the events surrounding her eviction represented a turning point in the country's history, but added that the cost to get to this point had been "too high".
"Above all, we will fulfil what she always asked of us: 'fight, keep fighting for what is yours'," it said.
In a video recorded from her hospital bed following her eviction, Maricarmen said: "I haven't managed to defend my home, but I have fought so that others can learn to fight for what's theirs."
"All my love goes to Maricarmen's family and loved ones," Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez said. "A hug as well to everyone who today feels this loss as their own."
Opposition People's Party leader Alberto Núñez Feijóo also sent his condolences to Maricarmen's loved ones, as he said on X: "No campaign, no parties, no self-interested exploitation. No more stones in the wall.
"In the face of a person's death, only respect is in order," he added.
Earlier on Wednesday, unions had called a general strike to take place on 11 November, demanding housing reforms.
The public outcry over Abascal's situation has led to political turmoil in Spain.
On Monday Sánchez, who leads a leftist coalition that does not hold a majority in parliament, called an early election for 29 November. It followed his failure to get the emergency housing legislation through Congress.
The political right had argued that the government's attempt to intervene in the housing market would have led to fewer homes being rented and would have raised prices further.
Speaking on Monday, Sánchez said he needed "a broader progressive majority" that can "overcome the resistance of the elites" to push through reforms.
Other issues not relating to housing, such as numerous corruption scandals linked to his party, and pressures relating to the cost of living and immigration, have also caused him problems.
Most opinion polls suggest the conservatives are likely to emerge as the largest party in the next election. However, they would be expected to need the support of the hard-right Vox party to form a government.
Additional reporting by Tom McArthur

Pressure mounting on Cornell administration, president over handling of alleged gang rape
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

Pressure mounting on Cornell administration, president over handling of alleged gang rape
NEW YORK - Cornell University’s administration and president are facing mounting pressure over the school’s handling of an alleged 2024 gang rape that has thrust it into the national spotlight and set off a wave of outrage over sexual violence on college campuses.
Since Oct 5, the administration has faced student protests, a no-confidence resolution from faculty, and criticism by alumni. A seven-hour sit-in in support of the alleged victim was planned for Oct 7.
Representatives for university president Michael Kotlikoff and Cornell did not immediately respond to a request for comment. 
Kotlikoff released a video statement over the weekend in which he said “we must do better” and the school would take “a serious look at the role of fraternities and sororities in campus life”.
Still, calls have mounted among some demonstrators for the resignation of Kotlikoff and members of his administration, blaming their policies for what protesters have described as a “culture of rape” on campus.
The demonstrators also want an external inquiry into how Cornell’s administration has handled the matter, independent hearings and uniform minimum sanctions for all sexual assaults on campus, as well as better training for campus police in responding to complaints of sexual violence and harassment.
Alumnus calls for freeze on donations
The Cornell Faculty Senate, which represents faculty members in university governance, introduced a resolution this week calling for a no-confidence vote in the administration’s handling of the school’s “ongoing crisis of sexual assault”.
The resolution will be debated at the Senate’s Oct 14 meeting.
Alumni are also voicing concern. 
In an open letter to Kotlikoff and the university’s Board of Trustees, posted on the Cornell Daily Sun website, alumnus Marco Fuentes wrote that the president and trustees had “single-handedly degraded” the school’s reputation and “eroded the value of the degrees earned by tens of thousands of proud alumni” through their “administrative negligence and spineless handling” of the alleged assault.
Fuentes wrote that he will no longer bequeath half his estate to the school, and is contacting alumni and donor networks to advocate for a freeze on donations until leadership changes occur.
The outcry began last month with a lawsuit in which the alleged victim, referred to as “Jane Doe”, said she was plied with drugs and alcohol and sexually assaulted by several members of the campus chapter of the Chi Phi fraternity in October 2024 after she became incapacitated.
She reported the alleged assault to police several weeks after the fact, leading to an internal university investigation and a law enforcement probe, but the local prosecutor declined to bring criminal charges in the case.
Cornell, which has defended its response to the original report, shut down the Chi Phi chapter and imposed a range of discipline on the fraternity members involved, including expulsions and other sanctions.
The alleged victim’s lawsuit criticised the university for having offered some of the alleged perpetrators a chance to mitigate their penalties by writing essays.
The men all denied any wrongdoing, some saying the sexual activity was consensual and others disputing their participation, the New York Times has reported, citing Cornell documents.
Cornell said this week it hired a top former US Justice Department lawyer to conduct an independent review of how Cornell prevents and responds to sexual assault claims. REUTERS

Canada will not allow assisted suicide for those with only mental illness

Unknown Publisher
