Canada will not allow assisted suicide for those with only mental illness
The government is seeking to close debate on one of the country’s most controversial healthcare issues
Canada will not allow medically assisted suicide for people whose only condition is mental illness, the justice minister said on Wednesday, seeking to close debate on one of the country’s most controversial healthcare issues.
Canada legalised assisted dying for those at the end of life in 2016.
The right was extended to those suffering from serious and incurable illnesses in 2021, even if death was not “reasonably foreseeable”.
Initially, Canada was to allow assisted death regardless of condition by 2024, but that date was pushed back three years, with the government saying it wanted to make sure that the already overwhelmed mental health system was ready.

Former RBA board member says another rate hike this year 'plausible'
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
18:57:23 UTC
03:57:23 KST

Former RBA board member says November interest rate hike 'plausible'
In short:
A former RBA member says the board has typically had split votes on monetary policy about 30 per cent of the time over the past decade.
Ian Harper says none of the treasurers in power during his 10-year tenure ever tried to influence him on interest rate decisions.
What's next?
The market is pricing in a one-in-three possibility of a rate hike on the first Tuesday in November.
Another interest rate hike this year is "plausible", but not necessarily likely, according to former Reserve Bank of Australia (RBA) board member Ian Harper.
A distinguished economist, Professor Harper was on the RBA board for a decade, from 2016 until after the Monetary Policy Board's (MPB) August meeting, when interest rates were left on hold.
The cash rate was subsequently increased at the bank's September meeting to a 15-year high of 4.6 per cent.
Speaking at a Centre for Independent Studies lunchtime event in Sydney on Wednesday, Professor Harper declined to offer his view on where interest rates might settle over a five- or 10-year horizon, but did make this comment on the short-term prospects for the cash rate.
"The bank moving again before the end of the year is plausible, from what I can see of the circumstances," he told the audience.
"But, again, I don't have the [board meeting] papers in front of me."
In a subsequent one-on-one interview with David Taylor for The Business, Professor Harper declined to characterise the chances of a back-to-back rate hike in November as "likely", repeating his assessment that it was "plausible".
This matches market pricing, which has the chances of a hike on Melbourne Cup Day at about a third.
Loading...
Harper offers rare insight into RBA board processes
Much has changed since Professor Harper joined the RBA board in 2016, with a major governance overhaul sparked by a federal government-commissioned review of the bank resulting in a split between the MPB and a governance board, taking effect in March 2025.
However, Professor Harper indicated the biggest change to the interest rate decision-making process was that the meetings now ran over two days.
He explained that the board convened at 1pm on the Monday and mets until about 5:30pm, hearing briefings from RBA staff and having the opportunity to put questions to them.
He indicated the governor would often take something of an informal straw poll at the end of that first day about what people thought should be done with rates.
Sometimes the board members will go out to dinner together before "people go off and think about it overnight and come back the next day," Professor Harper explained.
"The meeting starts at 9[am] and you run through to 11:30.
"And in that process, of course, there's further discussion, the decision gets made, the statement gets drafted, the draft gets considered, discussed and agreed."
That decision and the accompanying statement get published at 2:30pm AEDT, before the Reserve Bank governor holds a press conference at 3:30pm, a practice also recommended by the RBA review.
RBA board had dissent prior to votes being published
Another change instituted by the review was the publication of how many board members voted in favour of each option considered for rates.
Since the board began publishing the vote tallies from its July 2025 meeting onwards, there have been eight unanimous decisions and three split votes.
Professor Harper told The Business that such a level of dissent was fairly typical prior to the period in which vote tallies were published.
"The Reserve Bank Act has always provided that each member of the board has a deliberative vote and the governor the casting vote if there happens to be someone missing," he explained.
"About 30 per cent of the time it was a split vote. 70 per cent of the time all the members are agreeing with whatever the [RBA staff] recommendation was."
When asked whether any RBA governor over the past decade had ever been on the losing side of a contested vote, Professor Harper said: "That's never happened."
"The reserve bank review made the point that the independent directors of the bank had never succeeded, if you like, in voting against where the bank was coming from," he continued.
"What the review didn't point out is that, nonetheless, there were often contested votes amongst all of the board members about whatever matter it was that was being discussed."
While there is constant speculation about whether the treasurer of the day is pressuring the RBA governor to make certain decisions on interest rates, Professor Harper categorically ruled out any attempt to influence him as a board member during his tenure at the bank.
He said he had heard directly from the treasurer on only three occasions: his appointment, his reappointment and via a thank-you note upon his retirement from the board.
"The notion that in some way the government directly influences, or the treasurer directly influences, the decision-making is just wrong," he told The Business.
"I was on the board for 10 years under governments of both political persuasions. Never happened, David."
Professor Harper said that did not mean that treasurers did not try to exert some influence in more public ways.
"You'd expect the treasurer to have a view," he said.
"But that's very different from saying the treasurer in some way calls up and says, 'This is what I want to happen.' That's never the case."

Ultra-Orthodox rabbi’s anti-Zionist remarks stir Israel election row
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
18:57:18 UTC
03:57:18 KST

Ultra-Orthodox rabbi’s anti-Zionist remarks stir Israel election row
Rabbi Dov Lando’s comments expose tensions over Zionism, conscription and Netanyahu’s ultra-Orthodox allies.
Comments by one of Israel’s most senior ultra-Orthodox rabbis postulating that Jews may have been better off without a state have prompted controversy in the country.
In footage broadcast by Channel 12 on Monday, the 96-year-old Rabbi Dov Lando, the spiritual leader of the Degel HaTorah party, also said that soldiers adhering to “Religious Zionism” killed in Israel’s wars were dying because of what their rabbis had taught them. The remarks, made at a closed meeting at his home in Bnei Brak, have set off a political storm three weeks before Israel’s October 27 parliamentary election.
“They are killed because their rabbis teach them a distorted Torah,” Lando said, adding that many military operations are carried out “not for saving lives, but for the honour of the state”.
Lando’s comment came in response to a question about admiration among some ultra-Orthodox Jewish men – who have traditionally refused the military draft – for religious Zionists who combine Torah study with military service.
His comments aren’t new – they were first published in February 2025. However, their reemergence this week comes amid an election campaign in which ultra-Orthodox military service has become one of the sharpest fault lines in Israeli politics.
The Israeli Supreme Court ruled in 2024 that there was no legal basis for ultra-Orthodox seminary students to have exemptions from military service, and the government has since not been able to pass legislation restoring the exemptions. The issue has led to large protests on both sides of the divide.
“The question is not what he said, but why this discourse has been placed at the heart of the Israeli debate three weeks before the election,” Ehab Jabareen, a researcher on Israeli affairs, told Al Jazeera.
Better ‘without a state’
Lando’s party is one of the two factions of the United Torah Judaism (UTJ) alliance, which won seven seats during the last election in 2022, and had been part of Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s government before its ministers resigned last year.
The bloc did continue to intermittently support the coalition government, however, and Netanyahu has been wary of removing the military exemption – despite widespread opposition to it from many in Israel – out of fear that the UTJ and similar parties would remove their support completely.
Along with his role within Degel HaTorah, Lando is also one of the spiritual leaders of Israel’s Lithuanian ultra-Orthodox community, which makes up roughly a third of the country’s estimated 1.45 million ultra-Orthodox Jews, also known as Haredim.
In May, he said he no longer trusted Netanyahu and called for parliament to be dissolved.
In the footage, he goes further. “It is possible to live well with the Arabs without a state,” he says, adding that international or Palestinian rule would have been “the best situation”.
Zionism, he argues, “caused the Arabs to hate us” and brought physical as well as spiritual disaster on the Jewish people. He describes secular Israelis as having built “a state of apostasy and heresy”.
The comments reflect non-Zionist and anti-Zionist positions that used to be dominant within ultra-Orthodox Judaism, but take on an overt reference to the possibility of living within a non-Zionist state, something that is even more controversial in Israel.
Ibrahim Khatib, a conflict studies scholar at the Doha Institute for Graduate Studies, said Lando’s remarks drew a line between Zionism and Judaism “from inside the Jewish community itself”, at a time when the official Israeli establishment “tries to bind them together”.
They also put to the test the narrative that Jewish communities in Arab societies were in danger and threatened, and that the Zionist movement came to “save them” at the formation of the state of Israel in 1948, he told Al Jazeera. However, Khatib cautioned that the ultra-Orthodox polity in Israel “is right-wing, its leaders hold right-wing positions, and some of them have made clearly offensive statements about Arabs and Palestinians”.
Political ammunition
Israeli opposition leaders moved quickly after the footage of Lando emerged this week, taking it as an opportunity to attack a figure from a party within Netanyahu’s electoral bloc.
Former Prime Minister Naftali Bennett – one of Netanyahu’s main challengers in the upcoming elections – called the remarks “anti-Semitic, anti-Zionist and anti-[Israeli military]”, but aimed his fire at Netanyahu and Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich, who he said “back [Lando] and funnel tens of billions of shekels to him and his friends”.
Gadi Eisenkot, another opposition leader whose Yashar party has campaigned on enforcing the military draft, urged every Zionist party to pledge not to sit with Lando’s party.
Netanyahu, who publicly rejected Lando’s remarks in July when the rabbi accused the Religious Zionism movement of “incitement to murder” for its support of the drafting of religious seminary students to the military, has not yet commented.
Yair Golan, leader of the Democrats, put it bluntly: “Netanyahu is silent because without Rabbi Lando and his emissaries, he has no government.”
Jabareen sees Netanyahu’s silence as “calculated”.
“If Netanyahu attacks Lando forcefully, he pays a price with the Haredim he needs to form a government,” he said. “If he stays silent, he hands his rivals material to tell right-wing voters that the man who speaks of Zionism and security depends on a religious leadership that doubts Zionism itself.”
Who fights and who dies
The military draft of the ultra-Orthodox, Jabareen added, has turned “from an old dispute over religion and state into a question about the Israeli [social] contract itself: Who fights? Who dies? And who gets the exemptions, the budgets and the political influence in return?”
Mohammad Abu Rumman, an academic adviser at the Politics and Society Institute in Amman, said the significance of Lando’s remarks lay in the question that prompted them. The example of a young religious man who combines Torah study with military service, he said, “raises a question inside the ultra-Orthodox world itself: Why don’t we do the same?”
“When Lando describes their teaching as a distorted Torah, he is trying to close the door on emulating them,” Abu Rumman told Al Jazeera. “His words are aimed at his own audience as much as at his opponents.”
But Jabareen argued that the row exposes a rift more dangerous for Netanyahu than the familiar clash between secular and religious Israelis, because it runs through the right itself. Religious Zionists have paid a heavy human price in the war, while the ultra-Orthodox leadership still rejects conscription. Caught between those who pay the price of war and those who refuse to, Netanyahu needs both, and cannot satisfy them at once.
Whether the outrage over Lando’s comments translates into votes is less clear. Abu Rumman expects the remarks to “reinforce existing positions more than change voters’ choices”. The space where they could matter, he said, lies among right-wing voters who serve in the army and resent Netanyahu’s protection of ultra-Orthodox demands.
“If Netanyahu needs these parties to build a majority, that need will not disappear because of a rabbi’s remarks, however shocking,” Abu Rumman said. Netanyahu is also not the UTJ’s only suitor: Channel 12 reported that, frustrated by his failure to secure a law exempting ultra-Orthodox men from military service, the party would not rule out or oppose a government led by Eisenkot.
“The Israeli right has managed to bring under one political roof two currents with almost contradictory visions of the Jewish state,” Jabareen said. “One sanctifies the state and the expansion of its sovereignty. In the other, one of its most important rabbis can say it might have been better had the state never been founded.”

President Donald Trump has said that the US does not believe a reported plague death in Russia is the result of a biological weapon and that officials are continuing to assess the situation.

“So, we hope it is very sophisticated and very smart, and they're saying it's very much under control,” he said. “So, we hope not.”
Trump reiterated that he has a phone call scheduled with Russian President Vladimir Putin on the issue but would not say when.
"Today is Vladimir Putin's birthday," Trump added.
Cause undetermined
Several countries and international health authorities pressed Russia for greater transparency over the reported death of a laboratory technician in Siberia, as Moscow insisted there is no evidence of an epidemic and said the cause of death remains undetermined.
The international response follows reports that a 28-year-old woman working at the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Research Institute died on October 2 after being hospitalised with severe pneumonia.
Russian authorities said she died of pneumonia and that the cause has not been established, while reports that she contracted pneumonic plague have not been independently confirmed.
Russia’s health agency said that there were “no epidemic risks” and rejected suggestions of a confirmed plague outbreak.
Earlier, the World Health Organization (WHO) said it is seeking additional information from Russia on the death of a laboratory worker from suspected pneumonic plague, as well as reports of a second employee with pneumonia of unknown cause.
WHO officials said Russia described the illness as “community-acquired severe pneumonia of unknown aetiology, which would indicate that authorities believe the infection did not originate in the laboratory.”

Scorched books from Kharkiv became an installation at the Frankfurt Book Fair
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
21:50:10 EEST
03:50:10 KST

Scorched books from Kharkiv became an installation at the Frankfurt Book Fair
Kyiv • UNN
Twenty-two books rescued after the attack on Kharkiv’s “Ranok” center were presented in the Born/Burn Alive installation. It tells the story of 400\r\nyears of the destruction of Ukrainian books.
The books that burned on August 1 at the "Ranok" logistics center in Kharkiv were brought to Frankfurt. The charred editions became the basis for the Born/Burn Alive installation, set up at Ukraine’s National Stand at the 2026 Frankfurt Book Fair. The installation was created by artist Valentyna Veremko. This is reported in an article by the "Ranok" publishing house, according to UNN.
Details
From October 7 to 11, while the Frankfurt Book Fair is open, an unusual glass display case will stand beside the booths showcasing bright new book releases. Inside it is a stack of 22 books with charred pages and traces of ash. These are not decorations or objects specially created for an art project. The books were salvaged after the Russian attack on the "Ranok" automated logistics center in Kharkiv on August 1, 2026.
That day, as a result of the strike and fire, around 8 million copies of books were destroyed, including more than 620,000 school textbooks. The Guardian also recently wrote about the scale of the destruction of Ukraine’s book infrastructure. Today, some of the books that survived the fire have ended up in Frankfurt as material evidence of the destruction of Ukraine’s book infrastructure.
"These books were meant to reach readers: schoolchildren, students, everyone who opens a page to learn something new. Instead, they passed through fire. Looking at this installation, I see how four centuries of history fit into a single glass display case. The red scale on the glass begins in 1626, when Ukrainian books were first burned. Since then, our language has been banned again and again, yet it remains alive because in every generation there have been people who printed and read it. We, the publishers, continue this work. Thank you, Valentyna Veremko, because thanks to you, the charred pages are telling their story precisely where they will be heard by the greatest number of readers," said Viktor Kruhlov, CEO of the "Ranok" publishing house.
Valentyna Veremko says that the idea for the project arose back in 2024 after the Russian strike on a Kharkiv printing house. However, it was only possible to realize it now.
One Book Tower and 400 Years of History
According to the artist’s concept, as noted by the publishing house, the charred books are arranged into a vertical tower and enclosed in a glass display case. A vertical scale with 12 dates is drawn in red on the glass. Exactly 400 years lie between the first and last dates. This scale connects the modern war crime with the centuries-long chronology of Ukraine’s linguicide and cultural genocide:
-  1626 — The Synod of the Moscow Church orders the removal of books in the old Ukrainian print tradition from Ukrainian churches;  
-  1627 – By decree of Tsar Mikhail and Patriarch Filaret, the print run of K. Stavrovetskyi’s “Teaching Gospel” is burned;  
-  1720 — Peter I’s decree prohibits the printing of new books in the Ukrainian language;  
-  1763 — Catherine I closes Ukrainian schools;  
-  1775 – The destruction of the Zaporozhian Sich, along with its printing house and library;   
-  1863 — The Valuev Circular prohibits the printing of educational and religious literature in Ukrainian;  
-  1876 – The Ems Ukaz prohibits the printing and import of Ukrainian books;  
-  1937 – The Executed Renaissance — the physical destruction of authors along with their texts;  
-  2014 — The removal of Ukrainian books from libraries in the occupied territories;  
-  2022 — The destruction of libraries and book collections during the full-scale invasion;  
-  2024 — A missile strike on the “Faktor-Druk” printing house in Kharkiv destroys 50,000 books;  
-  2026 – The current phase of the war: the removal of Ukrainian books in the occupied territories and the targeted destruction of Ukrainian libraries, printing houses, publishing companies, and warehouses.  
Why Born Alive Turns into Burn Alive
The installation’s title is built around changing just one letter. In the word Born, the letter o is crossed out, and a u appears above it. Thus, the “born” becomes the “burned.” Born Alive — “born alive.” Burn Alive — “burned alive.”
For the artist, this is a metaphor for Ukrainian culture and books that people are trying to physically destroy, but which remain evidence of what happened even after their destruction. That is why the work is based on genuine charred editions.
Will 2026 become the final date in the chronology of destruction?
The two final red lines without dates on the glass, which are visually positioned above 2026 and relate to books, are the installation’s most powerful detail. The artist deliberately left them blank; it is like one unspoken yet important thought: "A history that has not been stopped strives to repeat itself. The ending of this chronology is being decided right now."
The "Born/Burn Alive" installation speaks not only about the past. It poses a simple and uncomfortable question to visitors to the Frankfurt Book Fair: will 2026 become the final date in this chronology?
Overall, during the 78th Frankfurt Book Fair, the National Stand of Ukraine presents books from 44 Ukrainian publishers, along with scheduled discussions, presentations, and meetings with international publishers and literary agents.

Evicted Spanish woman who sparked housing protests has died

Maricarmen Abascal, the 87-year-old woman at the center of the nationwide protests in Spain due to her eviction from her Madrid home, has died, the local tenants' union said.
"We are sorry to announce that Maricarmen passed away today," the Madrid Tenants' Union said in a statement, adding that Abascal's cause marked "a turning point in the history of this country."
Who is Abascal and how did she spark Spain's protests?
Abascal was evicted from the home where she lived her whole life on a stretcher after the company owning the apartment drastically increased the rent.
She had been hospitalized after the eviction took place due to exhaustion as an agreement with her home's owners was reached.

Spain's unions call for general strike

The nationwide protests triggered by Abascal's eviction and lawmakers' rejection of housing reforms intended to help tenants led Sanchez to call for early elections on November 29.
Sanchez, of the Socialist Party, is looking for a shift in the public narrative after his government's handling of the migrant crisis in Ceuta, as well as alleged corruption among his party's ranks.

====================================================================================================

These Researchers Made AI Drive a Toyota Corolla to Get In-N-Out
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
18:45:00 UTC
03:45:00 KST

Aditya Ramabadran, Simon Mahns, and Tobias Gessler, three AI engineers at a startup called Axiom, recently fancied In-N-Out Burger for lunch.
They weren’t about to drive themselves, though. Sitting in a 2024 Toyota Corolla near the Bay Area restaurant’s drive-thru lane, they opened a laptop and asked OpenAI’s GPT-6 Astra to take the wheel. They linked a chat interface to a server, which was connected to several windscreen-mounted cameras and the car’s power steering system. A safety driver kept one foot above the brake, just in case.
The AI model, which is normally tasked with generating text, code, and the odd image, slowly but surely navigated the vehicle up to the take-out window so they could collect their food.
“Maybe AGI is here after all,” one of the engineers remarked, referring to artificial general intelligence, the much-ballyhooed idea of machines that can match human intelligence.
Self-driving cars are nothing new, of course, but they’re normally operated by algorithms specifically trained and engineered for the task. In this case, the operation came from a model designed to output text, and it happened on the fly, with no prior coaching by the trio. The fast-food stunt, as well as a number of other experiments, suggest that language-based AI models are starting to gain a rudimentary but useful understanding of the physical world.
Though nothing overtly alarming happened during the trio’s lunchtime jaunt, they admit that putting a general-purpose model in charge of a fast-moving, two-ton hunk of steel is a high-stakes undertaking. As physical understanding improves, we could see AI models reach into the real world in impressive—and perhaps dangerous—new ways.
Getting Physical
Today’s smartest models are incredibly good at answering complex questions and even performing some virtual tasks autonomously, but their skills tend to be limited to the world of computers and the internet. Take these models into the real world and they quickly become befuddled. Despite claims that AGI has arrived, AI companies evidently see physical reasoning as a yet-to-be-conquered frontier for AI.
Some researchers have left big companies to found startups focused on solving physical reasoning. Andrew Dai, the CEO of one such outfit, called Elorian AI, previously worked as a researcher at Google DeepMind. He says better visual reasoning will open up a lot of new applications for AI, like systems that understand whether diners are enjoying their meal in a restaurant or robots capable of functioning in a home. Dai says robotics is a crucial test case for physical reasoning skills. “It’s pretty essential for robotics,” he says. “You can’t really imagine home robotics without this.”
Elorian and Scale AI, a company that provides training data to big AI labs, recently developed a new benchmark, Humanity’s Sixth Sense, which measures models’ ability to understand physical scenes.
“Most visual AI research is about perception,” says Xingang Guo, a research scientist at Scale AI who was involved with developing the benchmark. “We wanted to ask what it would actually take for a model to understand a scene intuitively, the way a person does without thinking about it.”
For Ramabadran, Mahns, and Gessler, the goal with their In-N-Out project, done outside of their work at Axiom, was to measure how well models can operate in the messy real world.
They got the idea to test models’ driving skills while hanging out one weekend. They noticed that models like Astra were capable of building complex 3D simulations, and wondered if it might translate to an ability to navigate the real world.
“We all live in the Bay Area, and we’re exposed to Teslas and Waymos, so maybe that played a role,” Ramabadran tells me.
The engineers tried testing SpaceXAI’s Grok before experimenting with the latest models from OpenAI and Anthropic. At first, the models refused to take control of the vehicles—they spat back things like, “I can help interpret road images, but I can’t issue motion commands to a physical car.” But with a little careful prompting, they could be coaxed into going further. The three were stunned when models began driving.
The engineers say big AI companies seem to be focusing on improving the spatial reasoning capabilities of their latest models, but they doubt this means they’re actually training them to drive cars. The models’ vehicular talents likely materialized as part of training focused on 3D reasoning, they say. “This could be like an emergent capability of just scaling up the multimodality of the model,” Mahns tells me, referencing inputs like images, video, and 3D models that are now used to train models.
Still, a new vehicular benchmark from the trio, called DrivingBench, suggests that these models still have a long way to go before they could pass a driving test. The benchmark measures a model’s ability to drive around a simple course, set up in a parking lot. Only Astra is able to complete the course—and very slowly at that. Claude Fable 5.1 made it 45 percent of the way around, and Grok made it just 11 percent of the way.
Ramabadran says the latest models seem capable of adjusting to errors; they apparently adapted to the car's controls and improved their driving in real time. “The models really did seem to be adjusting or in-context learning based on their mistakes and learning how to better navigate the controls,” he says. GPT, take the wheel.

The oldest known land animal is 194. How did he get so ancient?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
18:44:13 UTC
03:44:13 KST

Jonathan, an Aldabra giant tortoise on the South Atlantic island of Saint Helena, appears fully grown in a photograph researchers say was taken around 1882. That means he’s survived to at least 194 years old, about a century past his species’ usual upper limit. In a new Science Advances study, scientists read his DNA to try and figure out why.
To get the tortoise’s DNA material, Jonathan’s veterinarian Joe Hollins pretended to feed him, wedged his mouth open with a hard glove and scraped cells from inside his cheek. “It was quite tricky and dangerous,” says study co-author Stephen Clark, a researcher at the Kallel Foundation, a longevity nonprofit in Nashville.
But it was worth the maneuver: the researchers found that, compared with other Aldabra tortoises, Jonathan has unique variants in 287 genes, some involved in DNA repair. The surprise finding, Clark explains, came from chemical tags on DNA called methyl groups that help switch genes on and off. With age and without constant maintenance, these tags drift. Young organisms tend to have consistent tags from cell to cell, so the switch will flip reliably. Over time, the tags fall off or attach chaotically, meaning tags are inconsistent between cells and genes start turning on unpredictably. Scientists measure this disorder as entropy. “If I had to define what aging is, it’s increasing entropy,” Clark says. The overall entropy in Jonathan’s tags was higher than in tortoises aged 12 and 90, as expected. But they were not higher everywhere.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
In 272 of Jonathan’s genes, many tied to the cells’ power-generating mitochondria, the switches’ chemical tags stayed as orderly as in a youngster. Because keeping order takes energy, which mitochondria supply, Clark suspects part of Jonathan’s longevity secret might be a feedback loop. “Mitochondria that make energy are being kept pristine, so they keep making energy that keeps them pristine,” he says.
“The authors identify new candidate genes associated with longevity,” says João Pedro de Magalhães, a comparative genomics researcher at the University of Birmingham in England, who was not involved in the study. “In the long term, perhaps we may find ways in which this knowledge could be applied to improve human health.” First, though, Clark and his colleagues have to make sure they’ve got their candidate genes right.
Cheek cells yield shorter, bacteria-contaminated genetic material, so gaps in Jonathan’s genome had to be filled in using a younger tortoise’s DNA. “The result is a Frankenstein sequence, roughly 95 percent Jonathan,” Clark says. If any of Jonathan’s unique variants were hiding in the borrowed stretches, he explains, they would have been missed. This problem, Clark argues, could have been solved by instead drawing a blood sample from the tortoise, but Saint Helena’s officials forbade it.
“Drawing blood from a tortoise may be tricky and in itself dangerous for an elderly individual,” says Joanna Bagniewska, a zoologist at the University of Oxford, who was not involved in the study. “Considering Jonathan’s iconic status on Saint Helena, were anything to happen to the tortoise, it could lead to resentment toward researchers in general.”
Clark notes that researchers can’t yet say whether unusual tidiness in Jonathan’s genes keeps him alive or is a by-product of something else entirely. “We can’t really put a flagpole in something and say, ‘Oh, this is why he lived this long,’” he says. “This work is just the first step.”

Witnesses spot Eritrean troops inside northern Ethiopia as tensions flare
Eritrea dismisses allegation as Ethiopia’s pretext for more war.
Eritrean soldiers have been seen driving through a northern town inside Ethiopia, witnesses tell the Reuters news agency, days after the neighbouring countries severed ties.
At least two witnesses told Reuters they saw “dozens” of Eritrean soldiers drive through Adigrat in two trucks on Wednesday. The town is located 25km (15 miles) south of the border with Eritrea.
The witnesses said they could identify the soldiers as Eritrean by their off-white camouflage uniforms.
Another Adigrat resident who was not in town at the time said family members had told him they had also seen Eritrean troops, according to Reuters, which could not independently verify their accounts.
“The Eritrean army has entered Tigray in uniform, equipped with heavy weaponry,” said Gebreigziabher Beyene, commander of the Tigray Peace Force, a pro-government militia that has fought alongside the federal army.
“This force is being struck by drones,” he said, adding Eritrea was “deliberately deploying its forces so that the fighting takes place inside Tigray rather than spilling into Eritrea”.
Last week, the chief administrator in Ethiopia’s northeastern Afar region said Eritrean troops were fighting in the area, but Reuters was unable to confirm the claim.
In a statement on X, Eritrea’s Information Minister Yemane Meskel did not deny that troops had crossed the border, but said Ethiopia’s government was creating “a fallacious narrative of ‘self-defense’ to rationalise and camouflage its war of aggression”.
If confirmed, it would mark the first time Eritrean forces have been seen inside Ethiopia since the renewal of fighting between Ethiopian forces and a seven-group armed alliance, including the Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF), on September 23.
Ethiopia has accused Eritrea, as well as Egypt and Sudan of backing the armed alliance which is fighting to remove the government. All three countries have denied involvement.
Eritrea announced it was severing ties with Ethiopia on Thursday after Addis Ababa announced it would close its embassy in Asmara and expel 10 Eritrean diplomats.
In a statement, Eritrea’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs said Ethiopia’s actions had left it with “no option but to reciprocate in kind and sever all diplomatic ties with Ethiopia”.
On Monday, Ethiopian forces captured Tigray’s regional capital Mekelle, days after the TPLF confirmed that it had withdrawn from the city and moved its regional administration “temporarily” to another location.
It happened as Ethiopia’s Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed was sworn in for another five-year term, during which he insisted that his landlocked country must have access to the Red Sea.
On the same day, Eritrea joined Somalia, Sudan and Egypt in issuing a joint declaration calling for a political and peaceful solution to the war in Ethiopia.
The declaration appeared to push back against several policies pursued by Ethiopia in recent years, highlighting widening rifts between Addis Ababa and its neighbours.

'Survived to Tell:' After Hamas captivity, Keith and Aviva Siegel share their story - and their struggle to learn to live again
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
18:33:54 UTC
03:33:54 KST

- i24NEWS
- Israel-Hamas war
- Survivor Testimonies
- Keith and Aviva Siegel: From captivity to freedom, gratitude and a long road to healing
Keith and Aviva Siegel: From captivity to freedom, gratitude and a long road to healing
Kidnapped together on October 7 and separated for more than a year, Keith and Aviva Siegel recount their captivity in Gaza and the ongoing struggle to rebuild their lives
After being kidnapped from Kibbutz Kfar Aza on October 7, Keith and Aviva Siegel endured captivity together before being separated for more than a year. Now reunited, they are sharing their story — and learning how to live again.
For Keith and Aviva Siegel, something as ordinary as stepping outside, breathing fresh air and taking a morning walk has taken on an entirely new meaning.
“To be able to open the door, go outside… to see natural sunlight, to see the sky, to hear birds,” Keith said, reflecting on freedoms that disappeared during his captivity in Gaza.
For Aviva, “I say to myself, I’ve got air, I can breathe, I can drink water whenever I like.”
This year’s Jewish High Holidays carried particular significance for the couple. It was their first holiday season together with no Israeli hostages remaining in Gaza — a milestone coming three years after the October 7, 2023 attack.
“Two years ago, Keith wasn’t here,” Aviva said. “It was a very, very difficult holiday for me. I didn’t want to do anything, and I didn’t want to even feel that there’s a holiday.”
Now, she says, everything feels different.
“For Keith, 100%, we’re very, very lucky to have him with us alive. I think this year, having all the hostages home and having Keith home, it was the first holiday that I could feel that I was happy.”
While in captivity, Keith tried desperately to keep track of time.
“It was very important for me to keep track of the day of the week and the date,” he said. But Jewish holidays were harder to follow. During Passover, he said Hamas captors told him what holiday it was while forcing him to participate in a propaganda video.
“They told us that it’s now Passover and that we should talk in the video about our memories of time with the family during the holiday,” Keith recalled. “That’s when I started to cry.”
The Siegels’ story began nearly half a century earlier.
Keith grew up in North Carolina and moved to Israel at 21. Aviva was born in South Africa and grew up in Israel. The two met when Aviva was just 18 at Kibbutz Gezer.
“The minute that I saw Keith and he opened his mouth and he was like, you know, so calm — everything about him was beautiful,” Aviva remembered. “I fell in love with him.”
They married and eventually raised four children at Kibbutz Kfar Aza, close to the Gaza border.
“Kfar Aza is a beautiful community, really, with lovely, lovely people,” Aviva said. “I was a teacher for little ones, and I loved my job. I used to walk to work barefoot. I just loved it so much. I loved the kids and everything about it.”
Life along the border, however, had long carried danger. Aviva remembers years of rocket fire, including a period before today’s warning and protection systems were in place.
“There were rockets on Kfar Aza for many, many, many years,” she said. “Every time, my body would shake for 24 hours a day. I was so scared that it’s just going to happen and somebody would be killed.”
Nothing prepared them for October 7.
Keith remembers realizing almost immediately that the attack unfolding around them was fundamentally different from the rocket attacks they had experienced before.
“The point in time where I realized this was totally different was when we were getting text messages from all sorts of people that would never text us when it was only just rocket attacks,” he said.
Then came a message on the kibbutz WhatsApp group: “There are terrorists in the kibbutz. Lock the doors and windows. And stay in your safe room.”
Keith initially believed only a small number of attackers had breached the border.
“And then at around 10:30 in the morning, they broke into our house, into our safe room.”
Aviva remembers standing up and screaming.
“We didn’t try to do anything or hit them or shoot them or anything. We just surrendered,” she said. “We didn’t present a threat to them. We didn’t try to resist in any way.”
Keith and Aviva were taken into Gaza and spent the first 50 days of captivity together.
Keith described violence, threats and abuse during his captivity.
“I was incredibly grateful when a day passed when I wasn’t kicked, spat on, or threatened to be killed,” he said. “Because those were things that happened to me. And I also witnessed other hostages — a woman being beaten and literally tortured.”
Both describe moments underground when they “Touched Death” by suffocating..
“All you feel is that maybe one explosion will fall on the entrance of the hole going down underneath the ground,” Aviva said. “And then you suffocate. You haven’t got any air to breathe… We were literally barely gasping for our breath,” Aviva says.
Keith described one of those moments as an encounter with the possibility of death.
“In that tunnel, I experienced one of the few extreme feelings of “death might be imminent — like it’s close.”
Aviva says, “we were threatened all the time. We could have been killed so many times. I was just trying to keep myself alive and trying to figure out, ‘What is it going to be like to feel dead? And what is it going to be like seeing Keith dead?’ And I just prayed all the time, ‘Just let me go first. Please. I don’t want to see Keith dead.’”
Aviva was released after 51 days. Keith remained in captivity a total of 484 days, until February 1, 2025, when he was released as part of a hostage-prisoner exchange.
During his long captivity, Keith says mindfulness, gratitude and a growing connection to Judaism and spirituality helped sustain him.
One of his greatest sources of pain was imagining what his family was going through without knowing whether he was alive.
“The thought of my family not knowing if I’m alive — and if I am alive, how I’m doing — it was very, very…” Keith recalled.
Asked whether that uncertainty could sometimes feel worse than facing death himself, Keith answered simply: “Yes."
He began trying to communicate with his family in his mind.
“I thought that maybe it’s possible that I can convey to my family, mentally, that I’m alive and that I’m okay.”
He would also speak to his mother in his imagination, unaware that she had died two months before his release.
“My mom passed away two months before I was released,” he said.
Even though everyone in Israel knew, Keith did not learn of her death until he returned home.
Since their reunion, Keith and Aviva have taken their story around the world, determined to preserve the memory of October 7 and what they say they experienced in captivity.
Aviva has also written about her ordeal in her memoir, Survived to Tell, describing the process of putting the experience on paper as part of her effort to confront what happened.
Yet coming home has not meant leaving the trauma behind.
“Both of us, we’ve still got a lot to do before we feel like we came back,” Aviva said. “Because, you know, the trauma — you have to deal with that. It’s sitting on us. It’s there, and it’s not that I can take it out of what happened and say, okay, I’m like everybody else. It’s there, and I feel it all the time, and it’s with me all the time.”
As they continue to rebuild their lives, both Keith and Aviva say they carry a profound sense of gratitude toward those who fought to find them and bring them home.
“I don’t know how to even find the words to say thank you to all the IDF soldiers who looked for us and looked for Keith while he was there,” Aviva said.
Keith echoed her gratitude.
“I want to join Aviva in thanking the IDF, the soldiers and all of the security people.“ They’re the reason that we are here and alive and able to sit here and talk to you.”
For Keith, that gratitude extends far beyond those directly involved in the rescue efforts.
“To all the Jews in Israel and all over the world, I just want to say thank you very, very much,” he said. “Your support and your engagement and commitment to me and to my family and to the State of Israel is incredible.”
And after everything he and Aviva endured, Keith ended with a hope that extends beyond his own family.
Aviva has hope for humanity and knows there is a reason she witnessed and survived this dark moment in history. She hopes Survived to Tell, which is available on Amazon, will be a time capsule for future generations.
“Let’s hope and wish that the world will be a better world for everybody — for the Jews and for everybody that lives in this world. Forever. Amen.”

Ukraine squeezes more defense out of Soviet-era stock, pairing Kub launcher and American RIM-7 interceptors to catch Russia’s jet-powered drones
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
18:33:42 UTC
03:33:42 KST

Kyiv is bolting two Soviet-era missile systems together to knock down Russia's fastest Geran-4 and Geran-5 drones. Ukraine's 156th Maksym Kryvonis Anti-Aircraft Missile Regiment has downed about 20 air targets using a Kub launcher firing under the radar and fire control of a Buk unit.
Russia has switched to jet-powered Gerans, faster drones that Ukraine's cheap interceptors struggle to catch, so more of them reach their targets. The damage from Russian strikes is set to reach up to $10 billion this year, according to Ukraine's Economy Ministry.
Meanwhile, Western resupply has thinned too. Deliveries of air defense missiles from partners fell threefold in the first half of 2026 against 2025, even though those partners hold the missiles, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy says.
So crews stretch what they have. In the Kub-Buk hybrid, a Kub launcher cannot aim on its own, lacking a radar to light up a target for its missile, according to Militarnyi. A Buk has that radar, so the two fire together, the Kub sending its 3M9 missile where the Buk points. The pairing is possible because both come from the same Soviet design line.
Western missiles in Soviet launchers
The same regiment reaches for a second workaround as Buk missiles run short. Its crews have rewired launchers to fire American RIM-7 interceptors, a Soviet-Western mongrel that troops nicknamed Frankenstein and the US calls FrankenSAM.
The patchwork earns its keep. One crew commander said some of these machines have more than 34 air kills each, and a single launcher has sent up RIM-7s 131 times, Ukrainian troops said.
A layered answer
The hybrids are one thread in a wider web. Ukraine is stitching together a layered defense against the jet-powered Gerans, leaning on electronic jamming, fighter jets, and a new class of homegrown interceptor drones. Each tool has limits, and the newest interceptors still bring down only the occasional jet drone.
The bet now is on numbers. Ukraine aims to build up to 400 interceptor drones a month by the end of October to chase the faster Gerans, Zelenskyy said on 2 October. Until that scale arrives, improvised launchers like the 156th Regiment keep filling the gap.

In war-torn Kyiv, Elkin-led Israeli delegation confronts familiar threats while marking Babyn Yar
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
18:32:07 UTC
03:32:07 KST

To the Israeli delegation visiting the Ukrainian capital this week, the sound of sirens warning of incoming drones or missiles was familiar. But one important difference: Ukraine has no Iron Dome, no multilayered Israeli-style air defense system that can provide the same sense of protection as back home. When the alerts sound, people simply head underground and wait.
That was how Tuesday night unfolded for former minister Kharkiv-born Ze'ev Elkin and members of an Israeli delegation visiting Kyiv this week.
As ballistic missiles and drones targeted the Ukrainian capital, the delegation eventually spent the night together in a makeshift shelter arranged by the Israeli Embassy at their hotel, sleeping on beds placed side-by-side inside the protected room.
Elkin and the delegation had arrived in Ukraine for the 85th anniversary of the Babyn Yar massacre, when Nazi forces and their collaborators murdered tens of thousands of Jews in a ravine outside Kyiv in September 1941.
Ukraine today is fighting a war that has entered another dangerous and uncertain phase. Russian forces continue to attack Ukrainian cities, while Ukrainian forces have demonstrated an increasing ability to strike targets deep inside Russia.
The deterioration in the security situation prompted several international delegations expected to attend the Babyn Yar commemorations to cancel their visits. Among the senior-level delegations that did arrive were those from Israel and Germany.
Elkin was part of Israeli delegation, including Yad Vashem officials, to attend Babyn Yar memorial
The Israeli delegation included Elkin, Yad Vashem Chairman Dani Dayan, Yad Vashem representatives, and senior officials involved in Israel’s relations with Ukraine.
The symbolism was striking: a ceremony dedicated to remembering one of the darkest chapters in European history taking place while the same continent is once again experiencing a major war.
The most significant political meeting came unexpectedly. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky invited Elkin and the delegation to meet with him after learning that the Israeli minister was in Kyiv. The two discussed the war, the regional situation, and the strategic calculations surrounding Israel, Ukraine, and the United States.
Zelensky was particularly interested in Israel’s assessment of developments involving Iran and the broader Middle East.
Ultimately, both Israel and Ukraine understand that, as cooperation between Russia and Iran grows, what happens in Kyiv can eventually reach Jerusalem.
According to multiple reports, Iranian and Russian facilities are operating jointly inside Russia, where the two countries are upgrading their drones – with Iran receiving some of the drones.
Zelensky warned the Israeli delegation that the drones Iran is developing together with Russia today, combined with the operational experience the two countries are gaining, could eventually become a threat Israel will have to confront.
Beyond his meeting with Zelensky, Elkin met with senior Ukrainian government officials, including the speaker of the parliament and the minister responsible for rebuilding the country’s infrastructure following the war – a role that parallels Elkin’s own responsibilities for the reconstruction of Israel’s North and South.
Elkin, Israeli delegation held memorial for October 7 victims
Together with the Jewish community in Ukraine and the Israeli Embassy, Elkin and the delegation also held a memorial ceremony for the victims of the October 7 massacre.
The message from the Ukrainians in their meetings was clear: They want to see improved relations.
The central question hanging over Kyiv is whether the war is moving toward a negotiated settlement or another escalation.
Ukrainian attacks have increasingly reached targets inside Russian territory, changing a dynamic in which the fighting was largely concentrated inside Ukraine. At the same time, Russian forces have struggled to achieve rapid breakthroughs along the front.
That combination creates a dangerous incentive for Moscow to search for a new way to alter the balance.
The most difficult issue in any potential negotiations remains the Donbas.
Russia wants Ukraine to withdraw from the remaining Ukrainian-held territory in Donetsk Oblast, effectively demanding that Kyiv abandon positions that Ukrainian forces have defended since the war that began in 2014.
For Ukraine, the problem is not simply political.
The Donbas contains a defensive system built over more than a decade. Ukrainian forces have spent years constructing fortifications and positions there, and Russia’s slow progress demonstrates how difficult those defenses are to overcome.
Giving them up would mean more than surrendering territory. It would mean moving the defensive line westward and creating a new strategic vulnerability.
That is why the issue has become one of the hardest obstacles to any potential agreement.
Elkin's visit carried unavoidable symbolism.
At Babyn Yar, Elkin delivered his remarks in Ukrainian – a gesture that attracted attention in a country where language and identity have themselves become part of the struggle with Russia.
During their meeting, Zelensky highlighted Elkin’s command of Ukrainian, joking that his grammar and pronunciation were better than those of some Ukrainian ministers.
The Babyn Yar ceremony was intended to remember a catastrophe that took place 85 years ago. Yet in today’s Kyiv, remembrance and reality are impossible to separate.

What the Cornell 7 Case Reveals About Consent and Bravery
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
18:31:42 UTC
03:31:42 KST

By now, most parents have likely read an article or two about the alleged assault involving a young woman and seven young men that took place at a fraternity on the Cornell campus in 2024.
Since the story broke, I’ve heard a lot of people ask, “How could this have happened?” I’ve also seen the national conversation focus almost entirely on consent education as the answer. Are we teaching consent early enough? Are we teaching it right?
Frankly, I think that’s an incomplete conversation.
Most parents I know have had the consent talk with their sons. I hear age-appropriate versions of it on the playground. Schools teach it. They should.
The issue is, in 2026, any man who commits sexual assault almost certainly knows what consent means and has simply decided it doesn't apply to him.
Our sons know about consent. The real question is: Do they know how to be brave? Knowing about consent is one thing—living by it is another.
Much of our collective outrage about this horrific case has been focused on the “Cornell 7,” but I lay awake at night thinking about the more than 50 other young men in that fraternity group chat. They reportedly received a message inviting them to join the assault, followed by replies that grew more depraved as the night went on.
We don't know what each of them saw or did, or why it took so long for anyone to step in. Some legal experts argue those members who didn’t can't be charged with a crime, because they had no legal duty to intervene.
I trust in my heart that my sons would never be one of the seven boys in that bedroom. And I would guess most boy moms share my confidence. Still, I’m terrified to admit that I cannot control whether they will ever receive messages like the ones that appeared in that group chat. Moms dedicated to raising boys to be good men share my fear. But we cannot shield them from the culture around them. And I simply don’t think we have done enough to address that culture.
Years ago, I gave a TED talk arguing that we raise our boys to be brave and our girls to be perfect. I wrote a book urging girls to take more risks. I assumed boys had bravery covered. “They’re good,” I’d say to myself.
Turns out we were teaching them the wrong kind of bravery.
Too often, we tell young boys that courage means physical risk: run faster, jump further, climb higher. The manosphere sells an even more dangerous version: that strength means brute force and a real man answers to no one. Neither of these stories leaves boys with a script for the moment when the hardest thing to do is use their voice.
Bravery doesn't always feel good. Bravery is saying the thing that will cost a friendship. It can feel like rejection. It sometimes sounds like tattling. There’s no dramatic music. Nobody claps. You may even question if the right thing to do was the wrong choice.
The masculinity crisis is real. And it’s a crisis of courage that we helped create. We spent years teaching young men what not to do, and too little time teaching them what to do when someone else is doing it.
We have to preach more than "don't hurt anyone." Our sons need to hear that if they see someone about to cause harm, we expect them to act. They need practice, too, because nobody finds their voice for the first time late at night in a group chat with their peers.
So practice at the dinner table. Ask your son what he would type in that chat, and who he would call. Tell him you know he is capable of being brave. Tell him you would rather he lose his friends than his character.
If we want them to learn bravery, we have to be brave, too.
If you are a mom and a survivor of sexual assault and feel ready to share your story, consider telling your sons, as well as your daughters. For generations, these conversations have focused on teaching girls what not to do. Our boys need to hear their mothers’ stories, too.
Dads, you also have stories to share. Tell your sons about the time you laughed along at something you knew was wrong, or stayed quiet when a friend crossed a line. Tell them how it felt and what you wish you'd done differently.
We can show them that bravery doesn't always feel good and speaking up can be hard, but both feel better than regret.
Student journalists at The Cornell Daily Sun, including a senior named Cereese Qusba who spent 23 months on her investigation, showed us what this looks like. They kept asking hard questions of their own university, knowing that the right path was the hard path. I want our boys to grow up knowing that’s usually the case.
Somewhere, a boy is about to read a message that turns his stomach. I want him to be brave enough to do more than turn his screen off.

Most Fed officials see need for another rate hike before end of 2026
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
18:31:42 UTC
03:31:42 KST

Mucahithan Avcioglu
07 October 2026•Update: 07 October 2026
Most Federal Reserve officials indicated that another interest rate hike would likely be appropriate before the end of 2026, according to minutes of the central bank’s September meeting that were released Wednesday.
All participants supported a quarter-point increase at the Sept. 15-16 meeting, which raised the federal funds rate target range between 3.75% and 4%.
Officials generally emphasized that inflation remained elevated, economic activity was expanding at a solid pace and the labor market appeared near full employment, with some signs of strengthening.
Almost all participants assessed that inflation risks were tilted to the upside, while risks to the labor market diminished and were broadly balanced.
Many considered a higher interest rate path prudent as insurance against inflation remaining persistently above the Fed’s 2% target because of stronger demand or further supply shocks.
Some warned that persistently elevated inflation could affect expectations and become more entrenched in wage- and price-setting decisions.
Energy costs, AI investment fuel inflation concerns
Officials noted that geopolitical developments had pushed up crude oil and refined fuel prices, while surging investment in artificial intelligence was also contributing to inflation pressures.
Many assessed that the longer energy prices remained elevated, the greater the risk that higher costs in individual sectors could spread into broader price pressures.
Some warned that the AI investment boom could cause overall demand to outpace supply in the medium term, putting upward pressure on inflation.
Officials generally expected AI investment to improve productivity and potential output in the coming years, but stressed substantial uncertainty about the size and timing of those gains.
Financial conditions remain supportive
Despite a recent rise in longer-term Treasury yields, many officials viewed financial conditions as supportive of economic growth, citing substantial stock market gains and narrow corporate bond spreads.
Several noted that credit remained broadly available. A few, however, said elevated mortgage rates continued to weigh on housing activity.
Participants stressed that they would approach each meeting with an open mind and base future decisions on incoming information, the economic outlook and the balance of risks.

Putin Pushes Russia’s 2026 War Spending to $200 Billion—Matching Next Year’s Record Budget
Russia is set to spend around 17 trillion rubles ($200 billion) on its war effort in 2026—nearly matching the record level Moscow had planned to reach only next year—after Vladimir Putin ordered a major increase in military expenditures, Bloomberg reported on October 7.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The new estimate is roughly 40% above the Russian government’s original 2026 spending plan and comes just days after Moscow unveiled a record $200 billion military allocation for 2027.
According to Bloomberg, Putin ordered the government to increase war-related spending by nearly $60 billion after the Kremlin concluded that negotiations involving US President Donald Trump were unlikely to end the war on terms acceptable to Moscow.
Putin had initially expected that talks with Trump could pressure Ukraine into an agreement and allow Russia to avoid another major increase in military spending, a person familiar with the matter told Bloomberg.
By January, however, the Kremlin had concluded that no breakthrough had been achieved. The government subsequently accelerated advance payments to Russia’s defense industry and increased other military expenditures throughout 2026.
As a result, spending is now expected to reach around 17 trillion rubles ($200 billion) by the end of the year, according to two people close to the Russian government cited by Bloomberg.
The figure effectively brings Russia’s 2026 war spending to the level Moscow had presented as a new record for 2027. Russia’s draft budget for next year allocates 17.1 trillion rubles ($201 billion) to defense-related spending, representing roughly 35% of total federal expenditure.
Russia had initially budgeted roughly 12.1 trillion rubles ($142 billion) for defense in 2026, although actual military expenditures are classified and additional war-related spending is distributed across other parts of the federal budget.
The acceleration was already visible during the first half of the year. According to calculations by Janis Kluge of the German Institute for International and Security Affairs cited by Bloomberg, Russia spent 10.687 trillion rubles ($126 billion) on the war during the first six months of 2026, approaching its original full-year target.
The surge is also adding pressure to Russia’s public finances. The federal budget deficit is now projected to exceed 7 trillion rubles ($82 billion) in 2026, compared with an earlier target of 3.8 trillion rubles ($45 billion).
Earlier, senior Russian financial officials warned Putin that the country’s war spending was becoming unsustainable, with the Finance Ministry and Central Bank raising concerns that rising military expenditures could further widen the federal budget deficit.

ST. PETERSBURG, October 7. /TASS/. Russia has achieved full technological sovereignty in hydropower, with domestic manufacturers capable of producing the equipment required for every stage of hydroelectric power plant construction and modernization, RusHydro First Deputy CEO and Chief Engineer Sergey Kondratyev told reporters on the sidelines of the 18th scientific and technical conference Hydropower. Hydraulic Engineering. New Developments and Technologies.
"Overall, I can say with confidence that we have 100% technological sovereignty in Russia’s hydropower sector. In other words, from the very beginning of developing a dam site and constructing the dam, we can fully provide both the equipment and all the control systems using the capabilities of Russian industry," he said.
Power Machines Deputy CEO and Head of the Hydropower Division Vladimir Demyanov previously told TASS, the company is capable of producing a full range of equipment for hydroelectric power plants annually, with production capacity of up to 10 equipment sets totaling up to 2 GW.
Russia’s General Scheme for the Development of Electric Power Facilities through 2042 envisages the commissioning of 6.7 GW of new hydropower generation capacity, comprising seven hydroelectric power plants and four pumped-storage power plants. A total of 37 hydropower units of various capacities will be required. According to the document, the nearest commissioning dates for such units are scheduled for 2031, when eight hydropower units are due to come online, and 2032, when 13 units are scheduled for commissioning.
RusHydro is Russia’s largest energy company by installed capacity, bringing together more than 600 generating facilities. The total installed capacity of the company’s power plants stands at 38.7 GW.
RusHydro’s largest shareholders are the Russian Federation with a 62.2% stake, VTB Bank with 12.37%, and En+ holding company with 9.61%.

Will you really get 'left behind' if you don't use AI?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
18:30:00 UTC
03:30:00 KST

Avoiding AI won't 'leave you behind', but ignoring it could
Whether it was from the mouth of a tech leader or celebrity, you've probably heard that "if you don't use AI, you'll be left behind".
I guess you'll find me somewhere in the dust then.
I've used ChatGPT a handful of times, mainly to see what the hype was about, and ask very important water-guzzling questions like: "What would I look like with curtain bangs?"
I worry generative AI is bad for our brains, creativity and the planet.
They're common concerns. Most Australians think the risks of AI outweigh the benefits, and almost two-thirds believe it's moving too fast.
But will avoiding AI really leave me or you behind? I asked three AI academics who shared their advice for avoiders like me.
They all agreed on one thing: you don't have to use it, but you do need to understand it.
Do you believe people who don't use AI will be left behind?
Professor Mirjalili: In my experience, most people who say they do not use AI already use it every day. They are just not aware of it.
AI filters their spam emails, suggests the fastest route on their maps, recommends their next show, and flags suspicious bank transactions.
The real question is not whether you use AI. You definitely do. It is whether you use it knowingly and well.
In many jobs, there is a real risk to not adopting AI. If others can use AI to complete certain tasks faster and improve their quality, someone doing things manually may find it harder to keep up.
But not using AI does not automatically make someone less capable or less valuable.
The impact depends on the work and whether AI actually improves it.
Producing more content is not necessarily the same as producing better work.
Dr Ciriello: The inevitability narrative is very much being pushed by big tech companies.
It's in their interest to make the case we must all use it otherwise we will get left behind.
If the goal is simply to maximise speed and productivity, then people who don't use generative AI may well be disadvantaged compared with those who do.
But the harder question is deciding where we actually want to be, and what we want to become better at, and that's not something we can easily automate.
What are we racing towards? Faster is not automatically better. And productivity is not an end to itself.
Historically, modern society has tended to optimise for efficiency and productivity without necessarily considering the consequences or whether those ends are legitimate.
Professor Shafiabady: To me, using AI is similar to driving. Some people do not learn to drive and do not want to drive or they are scared of driving.
If you don't drive you will survive of course, but you won't have the convenience of taking your car and going where you like. You have to take public transport, it will be slower.
But I think it's very important that every individual is aware and in control of the reason they are doing things.
For example, if I'm writing an article for a media outlet, I prefer to start writing with my own thoughts and not use AI for that.
If I'm doing research for the ease of some work, I use AI and I just say "find this for me" … to make my life easier in accessing information.
I think we all have to learn how to use it ethically and responsibly.
Are there positive consequences to not adopting AI?
Professor Mirjalili: Yes. Doing work yourself gives you opportunities to improve your skills, develop your own ideas, and build deeper knowledge.
In 2025, a study found that experienced doctors became noticeably worse at spotting early signs of bowel cancer on their own after only a few months of working with an AI assistant.
You can fall behind by refusing to learn about AI, but you can fall further behind by letting AI do all your learning for you.
Dr Ciriello: Technology has often been deployed to serve the interest of a privileged few, while imposing harms and costs on society as a whole.
The resistance can be a good thing because it forces decision-makers and governments to consider the collective will of the people.
If enough people come together and say: "We don't want this on these terms," … it can be a signal to teach people in power what the people are not ready to participate in, and therefore, they need to find a better way.
And so much content and writing is now looking the same.
By not using AI, you might actually be able to differentiate yourself as someone who has a unique style and niche.
Professor Shafiabady: I love programming and coding. I have spent my career coding and developing algorithms.
But at the same time, I am against computers. And if it was up to me, I would ban them because it's changing the way we live.
The way we are not thinking about the consequences of what we are doing is killing our planet.
What advice do you have for AI avoiders?
Professor Mirjalili: Start with curiosity rather than fear.
You can start experimenting to see where and how it increases your productivity.
I suggest starting with a small, low-risk task and assess the result. Did it save time? Did it improve the quality of your work? How much checking or correcting did it require?
If checking and fixing the output takes longer than doing the task yourself, it does not make you more productive.
My advice is to learn enough to make an informed choice.
Knowing where and when not to use AI is also part of AI literacy.
Dr Ciriello: There's a difference between saying: "I'm not going to use ChatGPT to write my articles," versus: "I'm not going to bother looking into this at all."
Learning about these tools safeguards against misconceptions.
If you want to learn about the ethical use of AI or what it means for society … you can read about what other critical thinkers in this space have said about AI.
If you want to play around with tools, there's many more than ChatGPT, Claude and Gemini. There are tools being developed by communities for communities without that strong commercial incentive behind them.
See if AI can help you, and if not, that's perfectly fine. You might be doing a service to society.
Professor Shafiabady: The best thing to do is think about the ways AI can help each of us ethically and responsibly, and keep an open mind on that.
Each of us have to think about what can help us in our lives, in what we want to be in our careers, in the person we want to become, the goals we want to achieve, how it can help us ethically and responsibly.
And then we start learning how to use it in those ways.

Aaron Sorkin takes on Facebook again, and this time he's furious
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
18:30:00 UTC
03:30:00 KST

Aaron Sorkin takes on Facebook again, and this time he's furious
Two statistics are outlined in Aaron Sorkin's The Social Reckoning, and they will follow you out of the cinema. The first: 64 per cent of people who joined extremist groups on Facebook were sent there by Facebook. The second: 32 per cent of teen girls said Instagram made them feel worse about their bodies.
2010's The Social Network won Aaron Sorkin an Oscar for screenwriting but David Fincher was in the director's chair. This time Sorkin does both, delivering a damning, journalistic drama about how Facebook whistleblower Frances Haugen (Mikey Madison) and Wall Street Journal reporter Jeff Horwitz (Jeremy Allen White) exposed what Mark Zuckerberg (Jeremy Strong) and his senior team knew.
As the film tells it, the platform was addictive and harmful, yet they tweaked the algorithm to boost content designed to make users angry, because angry content gets re-shared and re-shares keep people scrolling and on the platform. Madison (who won an Oscar for her role as Ani in Anora) presents a welcome change of register as Haugen, while White is mercifully off The Bear's boil, playing a composed reporter.
From a network to a reckoning
Comparisons to The Social Network are inevitable, but this film stands on its own, even if it satisfies fewer people. It holds your attention but it's better written than it's made. The film is not a sequel in that almost nobody has returned except for cinematographer Jeff Cronenweth, who keeps the dark tonality of the film consistent with the earlier film; while Trent Reznor's and Atticus Ross's score has given way to Alexandre Desplat's slightly less memorable version of synths and unsettling piano.
For the most part, this is a good thing. After all, we're in an unprecedented chapter of social media.
Jeremy Strong, who opted for method acting throughout production, replaces Jesse Eisenberg and nails Zuckerberg's mannerisms and voice. We are 16 years on from Sorkin's original portrayal of Zuckerberg — young, flawed and, at moments, vulnerable, maybe even potentially redeemable. Now, he's a shell of a person, even ridiculous (apparently he has a bulletproof couch in his office, to hide behind in an attack). The film presents him as a villain, even if Sorkin says he isn't.
Yet, Sorkin's real target is us. How do you shock an audience who have already scrolled past the evidence? You open with proof. The film's prologue, which is wryly titled White Girl Wasted, begins with an alt-right Karen meltdown: a drunk white woman recording a viral video and screaming at two police officials of colour, claiming she's being targeted for being a white woman. We soon learn she was recently a progressive and a friend of Haugen, but has now been radicalised by Facebook. Are you angry yet? It's a human example in place of a statistic that would slide off.
The film hops between 2019 and 2022, sometimes to jarring effect. Haugen, a data scientist in Facebook's now-disbanded civic integrity team and a true believer in its mission, begins to question what she sees after this video. Horwitz, a beat reporter covering Facebook, who isn't even on Facebook (a true millennial), emails every civic integrity team member, attempting to cultivate an ongoing credible source. Haugen is the only one to reply, and she starts feeding him information, then evidence, including the algorithm change, palatably named MSI (meaningful social interactions).
Facebook, IRL
The Social Reckoning is a film about Facebook, but we don't actually meet Zuckerberg until roughly 30 minutes in, during deposition preparation in a mock hearing room with his press team, led by Raya (played by Oscar-nominated Wunmi Mosaku) and his advisers, including Bill Burr's Charlie, who urges him to fact-check political ads.
Zuckerberg simply responds with "we respect our users" to make their own mind up about content presented. Sorkin's quips and rapid-fire dialogue come alive here, and anyone who misses The Newsroom series will feel at home with the back-and-forth banter as the camera bounces between speakers. In another scene, a fellow journalist tells Jeff he's joined the last two minutes of print journalism, earning a chuckle, but fewer lines land with as much conviction and satisfaction as they did in The Social Network.
To its credit, the film doesn't glamorise journalism, and there's no romance between its leads, a trope we're usually handed. The only remotely sexy moment is when Haugen turns up at Horwitz's hotel room dressed, supposedly in disguise, as if she's on a date; it feels like a thinly veiled excuse to see Madison in tight clothing. In a film about platforms engineered to hold our gaze, it's an odd moment to catch Sorkin engineering one.
During my viewing of the film, I was wondering if it might have been more effective with more real-life consequences on screen. Then it reached the events of January 6, 2021, which is, arguably, enough. In the war room, as the frightening riot rages on at the Capitol in Washington, DC, they're asking Zuckerberg to block the sitting president on the platform (Trump is never named) from inciting more violence. We watch in disbelief as he hesitates.
Another potent moment comes when Haugen has a scare, thinking she's been outed as the source, and for a split second questions whether what Facebook is doing with the algorithm is even really a big deal and who is she to be a whistleblower? Horwitz says he isn't angry about apps like Facebook seeping into mainstream news, or even threatening his own future as an investigative journalist; he's angry because they're doing his job so badly and, yes, it is a big deal. This Wild West lack of regulation and the feeding of misinformation are actions he can't abide, and we shouldn't either.
Where do we go from here?
Sorkin has said in recent interviews he wants the film to be evergreen, and his reverence for American institutions and the media still stands. That's hardly new for him, but the cynic in me leans towards distrust.
But as our protagonists take risks, believing in journalism's ability to "cause pain" for the right reasons (as Horwitz puts it) and hold people accountable, it gives hope that there may still be goodness in media reporting.
Interestingly, Sorkin withholds a real-life postscript. Since the events of the film, Meta (the name change came three weeks after the release of the Journal's "Facebook Files"), has agreed to make major changes to Facebook and Instagram, and to pay up to $US18 billion to settle claims from dozens of US states over teen addiction. Perhaps even Sorkin knows there's more work to be done.
The Social Reckoning is for the cynics and the numbed. See it, then put your phone away on the walk home.
The Social Reckoning is in cinemas now.
