====================================================================================================

War in Ukraine spreads across 3 different dimensions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
17:52:13 UTC
02:52:13 KST

War in Ukraine spreads across 3 different dimensions
Recruits, supervised by instructors, cover a distance on Day Zero of Basic Military Training at the 118th Separate Mechanized Brigade of the Ukrainian Armed Forces, April 5, 2026. (Dmytro Smolienko/ Ukrinform/Future Publishing via Getty Images)
Kateryna Lisunova
Ukrainian journalist
Any war is not that simple and has many angles, but Russia's war in Ukraine is becoming more difficult each day. And not only because of its constant intensity, but because of its complexity.
In the next few months, we will see three concrete, distinctive tracks of Russia's war in Ukraine developing separately and very differently from each other.
You will see a lot of different, mixed news that will be hard to put together into one picture, but we need to accept that the war is changing, and our perception and understanding of it should change as well.
Russia's war will unfold in three main dimensions: civilian cities, the front-line battlefield, and diplomatic negotiations.
First dimension — cities
First, we will see more disturbing and cold-blooded attacks on civilian cities, their infrastructure, and energy facilities.
Alongside the now-routine campaign to plunge millions of Ukrainians into darkness, Russia has revived a tactic of destroying bridges with a long and particularly violent history.
After Ukraine's brief period of independence in 1917–1921, the Soviet army set about demolishing the bridges connecting the two banks of the Dnipro, which cleaves Kyiv in two, seeking to sever one of the capital's most vital arteries and render movement across the city perilous or impossible.
The crossings on the river were blown up and destroyed several times during the retreats of different armies, but the most extensive destruction, which completely cut off the left bank, took place in June 1920.
This was a sad and unfortunate chapter of Ukrainian history, followed by the forced incorporation into the USSR, the artificial famine, or the Holodomor as we know it today, as well as the persecution of the Ukrainian people, language, and culture, until Ukraine once again regained its independence in 1991.
Unfortunately, Moscow has evolved little in either strategy or geopolitical goals. We are therefore likely to see another attempt to cut Kyiv off from its connections across the Dnipro River.
This track is especially important to the Kremlin because it is one of the main reasons why the Ukrainian government is calling for immediate anti-ballistic support, as well as licenses to manufacture such systems domestically.
The main goal of the Russians is to kill the morale of the Ukrainian people and destroy their resistance.
Yet, no matter how terrible it sounds, for the most part, destroying historical sites and attacking civilians is an act of agony and desperation from Russian President Vladimir Putin. Because while he still has the capacity to show his power against civilian women and children, the situation on the battlefield is completely different.
Second dimension — front line
And this is how we come to the second dimension of this war: the front-line battlefield.
On the front line, despite intense fighting, Putin is struggling to show significant gains, while Ukraine is introducing new technologies that are changing how the war is fought. For the first time since 2023, Russian forces are actively losing ground.
These days, we are seeing major Ukrainian achievements on the battlefield and new military innovations.
One example is the NC13 Unit's new "Gryphon" tactic, which combines heavy bomber drones with unmanned ground vehicles (UGVs), essentially ground robots. Since January 2026, the unit has carried out more than 100 successful missions, deploying kamikaze UGVs deep behind Russian lines to strike personnel, logistics, and staging areas.
The technology has become an important part of Operation Vivaldi, a headline-grabbing Ukrainian counteroffensive that has liberated more than 176 square kilometers (68 square miles) of territory.
According to the Presidential Office, Russian forces suffered more than 5,000 casualties during the first three stages of the operation. The Third Army Corps separately reported 2,000 Russian personnel casualties during the latest stage.
UGVs also carried out approximately 80% of logistics operations and 90% of wounded evacuations for Ukrainian troops during the operation.
Ukraine has also introduced and deployed its domestically produced FP-7 ballistic missile in combat for the first time. With a range of 200-250 km (155 to 250 miles) and a weight of 150-200 kg (330-440 pounds), it is designed for counterattacks against Russian missile launchers and military-industrial sites in occupied territories or near the border.
President Volodymyr Zelensky also recently stated that Ukraine is working on a satellite system similar to Starlink.
And this is not to mention the regular, almost routine Ukrainian strikes on Russian oil refineries, which are actively crippling Russia's economy and demonstrating the remarkable capabilities of Ukrainian technology, with drones and missiles able to reach targets across vast distances of Russian territory, from Moscow to Siberia.
Third dimension — peace talks
The so-called third dimension of the war is perhaps the most confusing, as it is becoming increasingly difficult to understand what motivates the participants in this branch of the conflict.
We are talking about negotiations.
From a moral perspective, from the standpoint of technological development, and based on basic democratic alignment, the Western world should have provided Ukraine with more military aid, greater intelligence sharing so Kyiv could strike the launch sites of Russian ballistic missiles, and more support of every kind a long time ago.
But at this point, Putin appears to be convincing at least the American administration that he will somehow win a war he has been unable to win since 2014, while also presenting himself as holding the stronger hand in negotiations.
For Europe, meanwhile, horrific attacks on civilians and open threats of further aggression against the Baltic states, for some reason, do not seem to be working as an alarm or a call to action, but rather as intimidation that causes fear.
Although we are seeing more action and something of a wake-up call across the European continent, European countries are also confronting another reality: after relying heavily on the United States for their security since World War II and giving up much of their own defense capacity and leverage, they now find themselves unable to manufacture enough military capabilities to ensure their own security and fully support a neighboring country that is under invasion.
Meanwhile, it is the U.S. that is currently leading and managing negotiations between Ukraine and Russia.
Unfortunately, the White House has not shown much decisiveness in response to Russian threats and appears instead to be emboldening Putin, first by inviting him to Alaska and now to Miami for the G20 summit.
The facts on the ground also demonstrate that the Kremlin has intensified its attacks on Ukraine since the beginning of the Trump administration.
Despite promises to end the war in one day, over the past 2 years, the war has grown more dangerous and aggressive, with incidents increasingly affecting neighboring NATO countries on land and at sea. Yet the world appears to have gradually become accustomed to this reality without a proportionate response.
The logic seems to be that if a strike was not deliberately aimed at Moldova or Poland, or if a civilian vessel in neutral waters carrying corn and owned by Turkey was struck, killing the captain and damaging the ship, then somehow it does not count because Russia supposedly did not do it on purpose.
At the same time, at least judging by public statements from the American side, it appears that Ukraine is being pressured to surrender despite all the evidence of how Ukrainian forces and society are prevailing in this war.
When President Donald Trump calls for "both sides to stop the war" and attributes the conflict partly to the negative personal relationship between Putin and Zelensky, we risk losing sight of the basic realities of this war: Russia is the aggressor, the war began in 2014, when Zelensky was not even president, and it was certainly not caused by the personalities of the two leaders.
Putin has publicly expressed ambitions to restore the USSR and regain control over former Soviet territories, and his interests extend beyond Ukraine to countries such as Poland and the Baltic states.
What all of this means for Ukraine and the war
We will see major Ukrainian achievements on the battlefield and deep inside Russian territory. We will see terrible losses among Ukrainian civilians because of Russian strikes, and we will see the inability of negotiations to stop the aggressor.
As so many times before, it will all come down to the indecisiveness of Ukraine's allies and their willingness to actually pressure Russia and provide Ukraine with the military support it needs.
Demands that Ukraine surrender territory, including some of its most heavily fortified positions in Donbas, contrast sharply with the situation on the battlefield. One conclusion we can draw is that the Kremlin has somehow managed to convince the White House of its claimed achievements despite the facts on the ground.
It looks like Moscow is essentially threatening that if Ukraine does not give up on the battlefield, Russia will destroy its civilian cities and kill as many civilians as possible.
This also appears to be part of Putin's argument with Trump: "If you do not pressure them to surrender, I will kill as many civilians as possible." And it seems that this manipulation and blackmail are working, at least in the U.S.
As a result, Ukraine is not receiving all of the military aid and anti-ballistic systems it needs to protect its people. President Trump has repeatedly presented himself as someone who does not want to bet on the losing side, yet the current approach appears to underestimate Ukraine's ability to continue resisting Russia.
Editor's note: The opinions expressed in the op-ed section are those of the authors and do not purport to reflect the views of the Kyiv Independent.

“Passing in Esfand” tells story of Minab school victims
TEHRAN- “Passing in Esfand,” a play written and directed by Hassan Sobhani Minabi, is currently on stage at the Ebrahim Zarei Theater in Minab, Hormozgan province, portraying the stories of martyrs Makan Nasiri and Mahmoud Gholamiani, two of the victims of the Shajareh Tayyebeh School tragedy.
The first performance of the play, which was held on October 1, was attended by the head of the Minab Department of Culture and Islamic Guidance, the office director of the city’s representative in the parliament, a group of teachers, artists and theater enthusiasts, as well as members of the family of martyr Mahmoud Gholamian. The opening performance was dedicated to the mother of Gholamiani.
“Passing in Esfand” offers a poetic account of the lives of martyrs Makan Nasiri and Mahmoud Gholamiani, while recounting part of the story of the victims of the Shajareh Tayyebeh School in Minab. The production draws on local cultural elements, rituals and traditions to tell the story of the victims and their families.
The idea for the play emerged from Sobhani Minabi’s concern over the victims of the school tragedy and his sense of responsibility toward preserving their stories through theater. The production was subsequently developed as an artistic work for the people of Minab, with Gholamiani and Nasiri among its central figures.
“Passing in Esfand” has been selected for the 20th International Resistance Theater Festival and will compete in the festival’s main competition section. The production is also representing Hormozgan province at the event.
The play will remain on stage until October 10, with the venue accommodating 74 spectators each night.
The play draws particular attention to the story of Makan Nasiri, one of the students killed in the attack on the Shajareh Tayyebeh School in Minab and Mahmoud Gholamiani, a 35-year-old Minab resident.
The Minab school tragedy took place on February 28, when a school building in the city was hit during a US-Israeli military strike. The incident resulted in the deaths of 168 students and other civilians and caused widespread grief in the local community. The tragedy also left families facing the loss of their children and, in Nasiri’s case, continued uncertainty over the return of his remains.
On that day, Gholamiani went into the rubble of the school following the strike, searching for children and helping rescue those trapped. He managed to save one child but returned to the site to help others. He was killed in a second strike along with some other people.
Through the story of Nasiri, Gholamiani and the other victims, “Passing in Esfand” seeks to preserve the memory of those affected while placing their experiences within the cultural and social context of Minab. By incorporating local traditions and elements of the region’s cultural life, the production presents the tragedy not only as an event of loss, but also as a story remembered by the community through art and theater.

AS Monaco Basket announced Wednesday that they will suspend operations as they filed for bankruptcy, bringing an abrupt halt to one of European basketball's most successful recent projects.

"The ultimate goal remains to see Monaco reclaim its rightful place," the club said, expressing hope that the professional team could eventually return to the highest level.

Six pillars of Resistance

Turning to field developments, Sheikh Qassem delivered an assessment of ongoing hostilities across the Lebanese front.

15 destinations to discover the soul of Iran
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
17:50:43 UTC
02:50:43 KST

15 destinations to discover the soul of Iran
TEHRAN - Iran is a country of striking contrasts. In one journey, travelers can move from bustling historic bazaars to quiet desert towns, from ancient archaeological sites to misty Caspian forests and from the mountains of the Zagros to the warm waters of the Persian Gulf.
Its landscapes are as varied as its history. Mud-brick houses and windcatchers define many towns on the central plateau, while lush rice fields and forests dominate the north. In the south, islands with colorful cliffs and unusual geological formations offer a very different side of the country.
For travelers interested in history and culture, Iran also offers an exceptional concentration of heritage. The country has currently 30 properties on UNESCO's World Heritage List, ranging from archaeological sites and historic cities to cultural landscapes, gardens and natural areas.
The following 15 destinations offer a journey through some of Iran's most distinctive landscapes, historical periods and living traditions. They are not presented as a formal ranking, but as a selection of places that together provide a broad picture of the country.
Tehran
Many travelers arrive in Tehran and immediately continue to another destination. Yet Iran's sprawling capital is worth exploring in its own right.
Set against the southern slopes of the Alborz Mountains, Tehran brings together the energy of a modern metropolis with reminders of Iran's royal and cultural past. Museums, palaces, traditional bazaars, galleries and old neighborhoods give the city a character that changes from one district to another.
At the heart of the city's historic heritage is Golestan Palace. With origins reaching back to the Safavid period, the complex became an important royal residence and the seat of Qajar power in the 19th century. Its buildings and decorative arts reflect an encounter between Persian traditions and European influences, and the palace is now a UNESCO World Heritage site.
The National Museum of Iran, Sa'dabad and Niavaran palace complexes and the Grand Bazaar add further layers to the city's history. For a change of scenery, Darband at the foot of the Alborz offers mountain air, walking trails and restaurants beside the stream.
Isfahan
Few Iranian cities capture the elegance of Persian architecture as vividly as Isfahan.
The city flourished as the capital of the Safavid Empire under Shah Abbas I in the 17th century, when it developed into a major center of architecture, art and commerce. Its grandest expression is Naqsh-e Jahan Square, also known as Meidan Imam.
The enormous square is framed by the Imam Mosque, Sheikh Lotfollah Mosque and Ali Qapu Palace, with the historic bazaar extending from one side. The ensemble has been a UNESCO World Heritage site since 1979.
But Isfahan is not simply a city of monumental buildings. The Jameh Mosque, Chehel Sotoun Palace and Vank Cathedral reveal different chapters of its history, while the Si-o-se-pol and Khaju bridges offer some of the city's most memorable views.
A walk through Isfahan often feels like moving through a living architectural museum, but one where people still shop, meet, pray and gather as they have for generations.
Shiraz
Shiraz is a city of gardens, poetry and old-world charm. It is closely associated with two of Iran's best-known poets, Hafez and Saadi, whose tombs remain popular places for visitors and residents alike.
The city itself offers plenty to explore. The Nasir al-Mulk Mosque, Eram Garden, Vakil Bazaar, Vakil Mosque and Vakil Bathhouse provide a glimpse into the architectural and cultural history of Shiraz.
Yet the city's greatest appeal for many travelers lies in what surrounds it. About 60 kilometers northeast stands Persepolis, founded by Darius I in 518 BC as the ceremonial center of the Achaemenid Empire. Its monumental stairways, reliefs, columns and palace remains offer an extraordinary encounter with ancient Persian civilization. UNESCO inscribed Persepolis as a World Heritage site in 1979.
Pasargadae, the first dynastic capital of the Achaemenids, and the royal tombs and reliefs of Naqsh-e Rostam can also be visited from Shiraz, making the city an ideal base for exploring the ancient heartland of Persia.
Yazd
Yazd rises from the dry landscape of central Iran as a remarkable example of how people learned to live with the desert.
Its old neighborhoods are a maze of mud-brick walls, narrow lanes, courtyards and traditional houses. Above the rooftops, windcatchers rise into the sky, while beneath the ground an ancient network of qanats once carried water from underground sources into the city.
This relationship between architecture, water and climate is central to Yazd's identity. UNESCO describes the historic city as an outstanding example of adaptation to a harsh environment, and the Historic City of Yazd was added to the World Heritage List in 2017.
Visitors can explore the Jameh Mosque, Amir Chakhmaq complex and Dowlat Abad Garden, as well as sites associated with Iran's Zoroastrian heritage.
Yazd is perhaps best experienced on foot, when the quiet lanes and earthen walls reveal the ingenuity behind this desert city.
Kashan
Kashan offers travelers an intimate look at traditional Persian life and architecture.
The city is particularly known for its historic houses. The Tabatabaei, Borujerdi and Ameri houses feature courtyards, elaborate plasterwork, stained glass and carefully planned spaces designed to cope with the changing seasons.
The Fin Garden, one of Iran's celebrated Persian gardens, provides another expression of this architectural tradition. Nearby, the archaeological site of Sialk takes the story much further back into antiquity, while the desert landscapes around Abu Zeydabad offer a different experience altogether.
Spring gives Kashan another attraction. The annual rose harvest and golabgiri, the traditional production of rosewater, fill the surrounding villages with the fragrance of freshly gathered roses.
Tabriz
For centuries, Tabriz has stood at the meeting point of different worlds. Its location in northwestern Iran helped make it an important crossroads connecting Iran with Anatolia and the Caucasus.
That history is particularly visible in the Tabriz Historic Bazaar Complex. Its interconnected brick corridors once accommodated commerce, religious activity, education and social life. UNESCO inscribed the bazaar as a World Heritage site in 2010 and describes it as one of the historic Silk Road's important commercial centers.
The Blue Mosque, Constitutional House, Azerbaijan Museum and El Goli park provide further reasons to spend time in the city.
Tabriz is also a gateway to East Azerbaijan province. Among the region's most unusual destinations is Kandovan, a village where homes have been carved into volcanic rock.
Mashhad
Mashhad is the spiritual heart of Iran for millions of pilgrims. At the center of the city stands the shrine complex of Imam Reza (AS), dedicated to the eighth Shi'a Imam.
The shrine is an immense architectural ensemble of courtyards, mosques, arcades, museums and richly decorated spaces. For visitors, it provides an opportunity to experience an important dimension of Iranian religious and cultural life.
Mashhad can also serve as a starting point for exploring Khorasan. Nearby Tus is associated with Ferdowsi, the great Persian epic poet, while the wider region contains historic settlements and landscapes that extend well beyond the city itself.
Kerman
Kerman is where history and desert scenery come together.
The city developed along routes linking central Iran with the southeast and retains important examples of traditional architecture. The Ganjali Khan complex, with its bathhouse, caravanserai, mosque and bazaar, offers a glimpse of urban life during the Safavid era.
Kerman is also a gateway to one of Iran's most extraordinary natural landscapes: the Kaluts of the Lut Desert. Wind and erosion have sculpted the desert into vast formations that can appear almost otherworldly.
The Lut Desert was inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List in 2016. The nearby Bam archaeological area, including the monumental Arg-e Bam citadel, adds another major heritage destination to the region.
Qeshm Island
Qeshm introduces travelers to a completely different Iran.
Situated in the Persian Gulf, Qeshm is the country's largest island and is known for dramatic geological formations, coastal landscapes and distinctive local communities.
The Qeshm Island UNESCO Global Geopark includes such remarkable features as Chahkuh Canyon and Namakdan Salt Cave. The island's traditional boatbuilding heritage, mangrove ecosystems and nearby Hengam Island add further dimensions to the experience.
For travelers interested in geology, marine environments, traditional architecture and island culture, Qeshm offers experiences rarely associated with Iran's better-known inland destinations.
Hormuz Island
Near Qeshm, the small island of Hormuz is famous for a landscape painted in striking shades of red, yellow and ochre.
Its unusual geology is one of its defining attractions. Travelers can explore colorful valleys, beaches, cliffs and coastal landscapes, often within a relatively short journey around the island.
The Portuguese Castle recalls another chapter in the history of the Persian Gulf, when Portugal established a presence in the region.
Hormuz is particularly attractive to photographers and artists, but its fragile environment also calls for careful and responsible travel. The island's appeal lies partly in its relatively intimate scale and the opportunity to experience its landscape at a slower pace.
Rasht and the Caspian region
Rasht offers a very different picture of Iran. Here, the dry landscapes of the central plateau give way to humid air, rice fields, orchards and lush vegetation.
As the capital of Gilan province, Rasht is a natural place to experience the region's food and culture. Local markets, traditional dishes and rural agricultural life are central to the character of southern Caspian Iran.
Beyond the city, the Hyrcanian forests stretch along the southern Caspian region. These ancient broad-leaved forests are home to rich biodiversity and extend through parts of Gilan, Mazandaran and Golestan provinces. They were inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List in 2019.
For travelers accustomed to Iran's deserts and historic cities, the green landscapes of the Caspian region can come as a pleasant surprise.
Ramsar
Ramsar brings together the Caspian Sea, the Alborz Mountains and the forests of northern Iran.
The town is known for its setting between the sea and mountains, while the surrounding area offers beaches, forested slopes, waterfalls and opportunities for mountain excursions.
The former Pahlavi-era Ramsar Palace and its gardens provide a glimpse into the region's more recent history. But much of Ramsar's appeal lies outdoors, where the landscape changes dramatically within a short distance.
For travelers seeking a greener side of Iran, Ramsar offers a striking contrast with the country's desert cities.
Kermanshah and Bisotun
In western Iran, Kermanshah provides a gateway to the mountains and heritage of the Zagros.
One of its best-known attractions is Taq-e Bostan, where Sasanian royal scenes and reliefs were carved into the mountainside.
East of the city lies Bisotun, an archaeological site positioned along an ancient route between the Iranian plateau and Mesopotamia. Its most famous monument is the enormous inscription and relief commissioned by Darius I in the 6th century BC.
The inscription, written in Old Persian, Elamite and Babylonian, played an important role in the study and understanding of ancient cuneiform texts. UNESCO inscribed Bisotun as a World Heritage site in 2006.
Hamadan
At the foot of Mount Alvand, Hamadan offers another journey deep into Iran's ancient past.
The modern city is associated with ancient Ecbatana, known in Iranian sources as Hegmataneh. Archaeological remains at Hegmataneh reflect successive periods of settlement, including the Median, Achaemenid, Seleucid, Parthian and Sasanian eras.
UNESCO added Hegmataneh to the World Heritage List in 2024.
Hamadan also has strong literary and intellectual associations. The tombs of Avicenna, the celebrated Persian polymath, and the poet Baba Taher are among the city's notable landmarks. Nearby Ganjnameh combines ancient inscriptions with a mountain setting.
Masuleh
Masuleh is one of the most recognizable mountain villages in Iran.
Built into a steep, forested slope in Gilan province, the village is known for its distinctive stepped architecture. Houses are arranged so that the roof of one building can serve as a path or open space for the building above it.
The result is a settlement that seems to rise naturally from the mountainside. Its architecture reflects the terrain and climate of the region and differs markedly from the enclosed courtyard houses common in central Iran.
Masuleh is currently on Iran's UNESCO Tentative List rather than the World Heritage List. It can be combined with a wider journey through Gilan's forests, villages and food traditions.

Dozens of soldiers, militants and miners killed in Nigeria attacks
MAIDUGURI, Nigeria, Oct 7 - Nigerian troops killed more than 25 Islamic State-aligned militants as they fought off an assault on a military position in northeastern Borno State, suffering an unknown number of casualties of their own, military sources and a member of the civilian defence force said on Wednesday.
In a separate, earlier incident, gunmen on motorbikes killed more than 25 soldiers and over 100 small-scale gold miners in Zamfara State, in the northwest, a military source, government official, and three residents said.
The attacks underscore the persistent threat posed by Islamist insurgents in northeastern Nigeria despite years of military campaigns against Boko Haram and its offshoot, known as Islamic State West Africa Province. Meanwhile, violence is spreading in the northwest, where bandits and Islamist groups also operate.
Insecurity is likely to be a key issue in Nigeria's election early next year.
SPECIAL FORCES UNDER ATTACK
In the incident in the northeast, troops of the 101 Special Forces Battalion came under attack on Tuesday night from four directions in Kukawa, near Lake Chad, but repelled the assault with air support, according to the military.
"Preliminary assessment indicates that over 25 terrorists were neutralised, with 14 bodies recovered so far," Captain Mohammed Goni, acting military information officer for Operation Hadin Kai, said in a statement. Troops seized six AK-47 rifles and ammunition during follow-up operations.
The military sources said some soldiers were killed in the fighting but did not provide details.
A member of the Civilian Joint Task Force, which supports military operations in the northeast, said more than three of its members were killed.
The military said it would continue joint operations to prevent militants from regrouping and launching further attacks.
GUNMEN ON MOTORBIKES
On October 5, heavily armed bandits on motorcycles attacked a military camp in Bindin, a community in Zamfara's Maru local government area, killing at least 25 troops, three eyewitnesses told Reuters.
Salisu Abdu, a resident of the nearby Bindin village, said he had counted the bodies of 25 dead soldiers.
A military source who participated in an operation to reinforce security in the community on Wednesday confirmed the attack, saying that he too saw 25 bodies. The gunmen looted the base after overrunning the soldiers, he said.
The gunmen then opened fire in a mining pit on Tuesday where about 1,000 people were digging for gold.
At least 100 people were killed, according to a village head and relatives of the victims.
Reuters could not confirm the casualty figures. Neither the Nigerian military nor the Zamfara State government responded to requests for comment. REUTERS

UN holds 5th straw poll in race to succeed Antonio Guterres
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
17:48:57 UTC
02:48:57 KST

Islam Dogru and Merve Aydogan
07 October 2026•Update: 07 October 2026
The UN Security Council held a fifth non-binding straw poll Wednesday as the race to succeed Secretary-General Antonio Guterres moves into the next stage.
Greek envoy to the UN Aglaia Balta, who is the term president of the Security Council for October, confirmed that the fifth round had been completed.
"The fifth round of straw polls has taken place. Each candidate will be informed of their results through their respective permanent representatives of nominating member states. The president of the General Assembly will also be informed that the straw poll has been conducted," Balta told reporters at a news conference at UN headquarters in New York.
Balta did not provide information on when the next straw poll would be held.
Costa Rican diplomat Rebeca Grynspan headed the race to become the next UN chief, according to initial information leaked from diplomatic sources.
Sources said Grynspan finished the straw poll with nine votes and six against.
Grynspan was followed by Rafael Grossi with six in favor, seven against and two abstentions. Carolyn Rodrigues came third with five in favor, nine against and one abstention.
Among the other candidates, former Senegalese President Macky Sall received five votes and 10 against; Ugandan politician Olara Otunnu received three in favor and 12 against; Ecuadorian diplomat Maria Fernanda Espinosa gained three votes in favor, nine against, and three abstentions; and Ecuadorian politician Ivonne Baki received no votes in favor but 14 against and one abstention.
The secret straw polls are designed to gauge support among the 15 Security Council members and potentially narrow the field before a formal recommendation is made to the General Assembly.
A candidate needs at least nine votes in the Security Council to secure the required support, while any of the five permanent members -- the US, China, France, Russia and the UK -- can block a candidate with a veto.
The eventual nominee must be appointed by the General Assembly, with that step generally considered a formality once the Security Council has reached agreement.
Guterres' term ends Dec. 31.

Europe is in revolt – its leaders are preparing for war
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
17:47:18 UTC
02:47:18 KST

Europe is in revolt – its leaders are preparing for war
Europe’s leaders have grand plans – spend more on weapons, prepare for war, and tighten citizens’ belts. The people have more immediate concerns however, like finding somewhere to live, keeping their jobs, and getting an education. Across France, Germany, Spain, and other EU states, the widening rift has started to spill into the streets.
Recent weeks have seen housing marches across Spain, student riots and public-sector strikes in France, and demonstrations against military recruitment and industrial job cuts in Germany. Immigration has added to the anger over housing and overstretched services, while the prospect of conscription has young Germans asking whose wars they are expected to fight.
The demands differ, but a recurring complaint unites them – aside from those simply looking for an excuse to wreak havoc: governments aren’t listening. Instead of putting domestic problems first, European leaders are telling their constituents to accept less and sacrifice more, while committing billions to preparations for a suicidal war with Russia. That’s despite Moscow and even Europe’s own intelligence services repeatedly saying there is no imminent threat.
Spain: Priced out and fed up
Spain’s housing crisis has pushed tens of thousands into the streets. After years of soaring rents, the eviction of an 87-year-old woman from her home of 70 years in Madrid last month turned into a rallying point for those sick of being priced out of their homes and the government’s failure to tackle the housing affordability crisis.
The eviction sparked demonstrations across Spain, followed by mass marches and a continuing protest camp in central Madrid. Parliament’s subsequent rejection of emergency tenant protections added even more fuel to the fire, bringing tens of thousands into the streets in around 50 cities last weekend.
Rents in Spain have almost doubled over the past decade as immigration-driven population growth has continued to outstrip housing construction. The population, excluding migration, has meanwhile only continued to decline.
The pressure is even more visible in Ceuta, Spain’s North African enclave, where around 72,000 people crossed from Morocco in late July into a territory with roughly 84,000 inhabitants. Although most returned, thousands remained, overwhelming accommodation and straining public services.
Residents have taken to the streets demanding stronger border controls and faster deportations, accusing Madrid of abandoning them. Protests have escalated into clashes with police, while angry locals have torn down makeshift migrant camps.
Government promises to restore order have done little to quell the frustration of communities left to absorb the consequences.
France: School’s out
France has also been gripped by overlapping protests over wages, spending cuts, public services, and school conditions. Teachers, healthcare workers, firefighters and transport staff have joined numerous strikes in recent weeks, while a growing student movement has added school blockades to the disruption.
The school protests began in mid-September, with students demanding more teachers, smaller classes, repairs to neglected buildings, and lighter schedules. Thousands of teaching posts have been eliminated this year, with further cuts planned for next year.
Around 266,000 people joined demonstrations nationwide on Tuesday. More than 6,500 have been arrested over three weeks, while hundreds of students and police officers have been injured, including a 15-year-old who lost his hand to a police grenade and a 16-year-old who reportedly lost sight in one eye after being hit by a rubber bullet.
As the movement has grown, violent groups have joined the protests, torching buses, attacking emergency workers, and damaging schools. Across France, 24 schools have been burned or ransacked.
Similar demonstrations have spread to neighboring Belgium, where students have opposed education reforms, higher transport costs, and rising tuition fees. In Liege, school blockades have been accompanied by vandalism, fires and arrests.
France: The cuts keep coming
The student demonstrations came on the heels of wider protests that have gripped France for weeks, with public-sector workers protesting a squeeze on wages and services, compounded by soaring fuel prices.
Since 2017, public-sector pay has risen by 5%, while cumulative inflation has reached 24%. The government’s proposed €54 billion ($60.4 billion) budget package, which includes spending cuts and freezes affecting pensions and benefits, has only deepened the anger.
Other demonstrations have also challenged continued funding for Ukraine, with protesters arguing that the money should go toward hospitals, education, and lower fuel taxes.
Separate rallies in more than 20 cities have also opposed a bill that could give police shootings the presumption of legality, which critics say would make officers harder to hold accountable.
Germany: Factories shrink, the military grows
In Germany, workers and students have taken to the streets as Berlin pursues a frenzied military buildup in the midst of a deepening industrial crisis with hundreds of thousands losing their livelihoods and young men facing the prospect of being drafted.
Around 45,000 students joined protests in some 100 cities and towns in late September, carrying banners reading ‘We won’t fight in your wars’ and ‘Education instead of bombs’.
The government meanwhile is pressing ahead with plans to expand the armed forces to more than 260,000 active troops and 200,000 reservists by 2035 to align with Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s fixation on creating “Europe’s strongest conventional army.”
Young men are already required to register for potential service, but politicians have been pushing for a return to conscription if voluntary recruitment fails to fill the ranks.
Aside from the thousands protesting such plans in the streets, resistance is also showing up in applications to avoid military service. More than 12,000 people sought conscientious objector status in the first eight months of this year – over three times the total for all of last year.
Tens of thousands of automotive workers have also protested sweeping job cuts and threats to factories. Volkswagen, for example, plans to shed 100,000 jobs across its brands, while other manufacturers are cutting production or moving it abroad.
Germany’s industrial woes have been further compounded by the loss of cheap Russian energy, which helped make its manufacturers competitive. Higher energy costs, US tariffs, and Chinese competition are now squeezing businesses and threatening jobs across the sector.
For arms manufacturers, however, Berlin’s priorities and its latest €108.2 billion defense budget have been good for business. While Volkswagen shares have fallen more than 75% from their 2021 peak, Rheinmetall’s have soared over 1,100% since early 2022. One Volkswagen factory is even set to shift toward producing military equipment for an Israeli arms company.
More guns and more fear
Even with streets burning and protesters demanding relief, European leaders have not let the turmoil distract them from their military ambitions.
In France, Macron marked Tuesday’s mass demonstrations by publicizing a nuclear missile test, posting a photograph of himself watching the launch with his back to the camera. While his constituents marched for better living conditions, his message was that France “must be feared to remain free.”
In Germany, Merz and NATO chief Mark Rutte smiled and waved through boos and chants of “murderers” and “blood on your hands” after the military bloc received the Westphalian Peace Prize last week. Inside the ceremony, officials praised military strength as the foundation of peace.
Those priorities are also taking shape in Brussels’ budget negotiations. Germany and five other EU states have demanded cuts to the bloc’s next budget, pushing to sacrifice funding for farmers and poorer regions in favor of ever-growing military spending.
The urgency is being justified by the supposed threat of a future Russian attack. However, Moscow has repeatedly denied any such plans, while even Finland’s president has admitted that his intelligence services see no imminent military threat.
Nevertheless, for European leaders, preparations for that hypothetical conflict, which they appear to almost count on, continue to take precedence over the mounting problems already bringing people out onto the streets.

BAIT turns G-SHOCK’s classic DW5600 into a perfectly ripe banana
dubbed 'yamagata’s finest,' BAIT covers the yellow body of this G-SHOCK DW5600 in the brown freckles of a perfect banana.
a G-SHOCK DW5600 for THE PRODUCE AISLE
A banana has a very small window when everything is right. Most would agree that it reaches its prime once the skin turns bright yellow, and a slight scattering of brown freckles begin to appear. BAIT turns that familiar bit of timing into the premise for its latest G-SHOCK collaboration, wrapping the classic DW5600 in the colors and spots of a banana ready to eat. Called Yamagata’s Finest, the watch covers its resin case and band in saturated yellow with scattered brown marks, giving one of G-SHOCK’s most recognizable silhouettes a strangely convincing new skin.
Ripeness comes down to timing, and BAIT takes that connection far enough to make the fruit theme feel built into the object. A pale gray face surrounds the digital display while the yellow resin extends around the square bezel and down the strap. Dark flecks appear at different angles across the band instead of settling into a repeated graphic pattern. From a distance, it reads as a bright yellow G-SHOCK. Up close, the bruises and sugar spots give away the idea.
‘YAMAGATA’S FINEST’ LOOKS BACK TO CASIO’S JAPANESE PRODUCTION LINE
The name pulls the story back toward Japan. Yamagata Prefecture is home to Casio’s Premium Production Line, and BAIT uses the collaboration as a playful tribute to the place behind some of the company’s most precisely produced watches. The connection gives the banana concept another layer beyond its color. ‘Yamagata’s Finest’ sounds like the label on a prized piece of produce, while referring directly to Casio’s manufacturing presence in the prefecture.
BAIT and G-SHOCK keep that produce branding moving through the smaller details. Their cartoon mascot, Shawty with Freckles, appears engraved on the caseback and flashes across the display when the LED backlight is activated. The character turns up again on the packaging, where the watch arrives inside a custom tin and outer box treated like something pulled from a fruit shipment. A nutrition-label-style graphic covers the tin, translating the familiar language of packaged food into watch information.
sweetening A FAMILIAR G-SHOCK BASE
Under its spotted yellow surface, Yamagata’s Finest keeps the standard toughness associated with the DW5600. The digital watch uses a shock-resistant structure and offers water resistance to 200 meters. Its familiar functions include a 1/100-second stopwatch and countdown timer, alongside an alarm and LED backlight. The square format stays largely intact, which helps the banana treatment land. BAIT has changed the personality of the object while leaving its recognizable foundation easy to read.
The collaboration also understands when to stop decorating. There is no sculpted banana case or oversized fruit hanging from the strap. Color, freckles and packaging do most of the work. It is a fairly ridiculous premise handled with enough restraint that the DW5600 still looks like a watch someone could actually wear.

Iran, Russia Deepen Strategic Coordination
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
17:45:21 UTC
02:45:21 KST

Iran, Russia Deepen Strategic Coordination
TEHRAN- Iran and Russia are moving to further strengthen their strategic coordination as Presidents Masoud Pezeshkian and Vladimir Putin prepare are set to meet in Turkmenistan, with Moscow expressing readiness to contribute to diplomatic efforts to reduce regional tensions and emphasizing the continuity of bilateral cooperation under their Comprehensive Strategic Partnership Treaty.
Pezeshkian and Putin held a telephone conversation on Wednesday, during which the Iranian president highlighted the positive and expanding trajectory of Tehran-Moscow relations and stressed the importance of maintaining and strengthening cooperation across various fields.
 
Putin, for his part, underscored the importance of continued close coordination between the two countries, saying cooperation under the Comprehensive Strategic Partnership Treaty remains in place despite developments and tensions in the region.
The conversation comes ahead of a planned meeting between the two presidents on the sidelines of a meeting of the Commonwealth of Independent States (CIS) in Turkmenistan. Yuri Ushakov, an aide to the Russian president, said Putin would meet Pezeshkian during the gathering, which is scheduled for October 8-9.
The Turkmenistan meeting will provide the two leaders with another opportunity to discuss bilateral relations as well as broader regional and international developments at a time when both Tehran and Moscow are seeking to expand cooperation in an increasingly multipolar international environment.
Diplomatic coordination on regional tensions
During the phone call, Putin said Russia welcomes diplomatic initiatives aimed at reducing regional tensions and assured Iran that Moscow is prepared to contribute to such efforts and provide assistance.
Putin also praised the Iranian people s resilience in the face of attacks, saying their resistance had attracted attention and admiration in many parts of the world.
Pezeshkian, meanwhile, emphasized the common interests underlying continued Iranian-Russian cooperation, signaling Tehran s intention to preserve the momentum of ties despite the difficult regional environment.
The two presidents latest exchange also reflects the increasingly frequent high-level contacts between Tehran and Moscow, which have become an important component of both countries foreign policy engagement
Convergence through regional organizations
The growing Iranian-Russian partnership extends beyond bilateral relations and is increasingly reinforced by their shared participation in major regional and international organizations.
Both countries are members of the Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO), providing a platform for coordination on security, counterterrorism, transport, energy, and regional economic cooperation. Iran also became a full member of the SCO in 2023, further strengthening its institutional links with Russia and other major Asian powers.
Tehran and Moscow are also members of BRICS, where they cooperate with other emerging economies on issues ranging from economic coordination and trade to financial mechanisms and the reform of international institutions.
Their participation in these organizations gives the two countries overlapping diplomatic and economic platforms through which they can pursue common interests and deepen coordination on international issues.
Iran and Russia are also connected through other regional mechanisms and projects, including efforts to develop transport corridors linking Iran, Russia and other Eurasian economies. The International North-South Transport Corridor (INSTC) remains a major area of strategic cooperation, offering an alternative trade route connecting the Persian Gulf and the Indian Ocean with Russia and northern Europe.
Shared experience of US sanctions
Another factor contributing to Tehran-Moscow convergence is their shared experience of extensive US sanctions.
Both Iran and Russia have been subjected to broad and sustained US sanctions targeting major sectors of their economies, financial transactions, energy industries and international trade. The pressure has encouraged both countries to seek alternative mechanisms for trade, investment, banking and transportation and to expand economic ties with partners outside Western financial and commercial systems.
Against this backdrop, cooperation between Tehran and Moscow has increasingly acquired an economic as well as strategic dimension. The two countries have worked to facilitate bilateral trade, strengthen transportation links, expand the use of national currencies and develop mechanisms that can reduce their exposure to restrictions imposed through Western financial channels.
Bilateral trade has also expanded across a range of sectors, including agricultural and food products, energy, industrial goods, machinery and transportation. The development of the INSTC and closer cooperation within the SCO and BRICS are expected to provide additional opportunities for expanding trade and investment between the two economies.
For Tehran and Moscow, such cooperation is not limited to overcoming sanctions-related obstacles. It is also part of a broader effort to strengthen regional connectivity and build more diversified economic partnerships in Eurasia.
Strategic partnership continues
The Comprehensive Strategic Partnership Treaty provides a broader framework for the expanding relationship. Putin s reference to the continuation of cooperation under the treaty during his conversation with Pezeshkian underscores Moscow s view that bilateral ties should continue to develop despite regional crises and geopolitical pressures.
The relationship has gradually expanded from traditional political and security cooperation into energy, transportation, trade, investment, technology and regional connectivity. Both sides have repeatedly stressed the importance of long-term projects that can create stronger economic interdependence.
The upcoming meeting in Turkmenistan is therefore significant beyond the immediate issue of regional tensions. It comes as Tehran and Moscow are consolidating cooperation through multiple overlapping frameworks, including the SCO, BRICS, the CIS-related regional environment and the INSTC.
For Iran, closer relations with Russia form part of a broader foreign-policy approach centered on strengthening ties with neighboring states, Asian powers and emerging economic centers. For Russia, Iran represents a strategically important partner linking Eurasian markets with the Persian Gulf and the wider Indian Ocean region.
The Pezeshkian-Putin meeting is expected to provide an opportunity to review this expanding agenda, including bilateral economic cooperation, regional security, diplomatic initiatives and the development of transportation and trade corridors.
As both countries navigate sustained pressure from the United States and a rapidly changing geopolitical landscape, their expanding cooperation reflects a shared interest in strengthening strategic autonomy, diversifying economic partnerships, and enhancing the role of Eurasian regional institutions in shaping the future regional order.
Western analysts assess the significance of Iran-Russia cooperation
Western analysts and former officials have offered assessments of the deepening Iran-Russia relationship, focusing on its military-technical dimensions and its implications for the broader geopolitical balance.
Matthew Tavares, a former Pentagon analyst, argues that the relationship has evolved beyond the strategic level to include operational and tactical cooperation. He notes that information shared between Moscow and Tehran is now being employed in ways that affect US partners and forces in the region, describing this as a departure from earlier patterns of engagement. Tavares also highlights the emergence of shared defense production, observing that Iranian and Russian drone systems contain components and designs that suggest a two-way supply chain relationship, making it difficult for Western intelligence to determine the direction of technology flows. He cautions that the proliferation of low-cost precision-strike capabilities resulting from this cooperation could undermine traditional Western military advantages over the coming years.

“Dnipro-Arena” put up for auction for the fourth time with a "discount"
Kyiv • UNN
The stadium and training base have been put up for auction with a starting price of UAH 118.3 million. The auction will take place on October 15, 2026.
PrivatBank has once again put one of Ukraine’s largest and newest sports arenas—the Dnipro-Arena—up for sale together with its training base, while reducing the lot’s price by more than UAH 20 million. This was reported by PrivatBank’s press service, according to UNN.
PrivatBank has put the Dnipro-Arena football stadium and a training base with an indoor field in the city of Dnipro up for open auction with a starting price of UAH 118,329,000
Auction date: October 15, 2026. You can participate in the auction and follow the bidding on the Prozorro.Sale website. The guarantee deposit for participation is 5% of the starting sale price of the property (UAH 5,916,450).
The sale of the Dnipro-Arena stadium and the football training base is being conducted as part of the Strategy and operational plan for managing distressed assets approved by PrivatBank’s Supervisory Board, through a transparent and open bidding procedure. The proceeds from the sale will be used to increase the bank’s financial result and, accordingly, increase the amount of taxes and dividends paid to the state budget
Additional information
"Dnipro-Arena" is a modern football stadium in the city of Dnipro, opened on September 14, 2008. The arena has a capacity of 31,003 seats. Construction of the facility lasted from 2005 to 2008 and was financed by FC Dnipro, which at the time belonged to businessman Ihor Kolomoiskyi, through PrivatBank, which is currently under investigation over a number of allegations.
Until 2015, the arena was owned by the club and was actively used for Ukrainian Premier League matches, the 2009 Ukrainian Cup final, as well as home games in the Europa League. However, after the club’s financial problems—including debts to players, UEFA, and for the stadium’s construction—legal proceedings began in 2016.
In December 2016, following the nationalization of PrivatBank, the stadium became state property as part of the assets transferred toward repayment of debts. FC Dnipro ceased to exist as a professional team.
PrivatBank has repeatedly attempted to sell the arena, but no buyers were found. The first such attempt took place in 2022.
As reported by UNN, on September 21, PrivatBank for the third time put one of Ukraine’s largest and newest sports arenas—the Dnipro-Arena—up for sale together with its training base at a starting price of UAH 140,701,416.

Peskov also said he had “no information” regarding a demarche – a formal diplomatic request for clarification – from Washington. He also denied reports in the US media that cited US President Donald Trump as saying he had scheduled a phone call with Russian President Vladimir Putin to discuss the matter.
TASS, citing the press service of Rospotrebnadzor – Russia’s sanitary watchdog – said a full review of biosafety requirements at the Institute had found them to be fully compliant with all legislative requirements.
It said that an expanded series of tests on samples taken from the dead woman had “found no microorganisms associated with her professional activities.”
It then added that testing of around 190 workers who had been in contact with Shipilova had identified two cases of COVID-19 and several cases of rhinovirus infection.
Despite Moscow’s assurances, the Wall Street Journal on Wednesday evening cited unnamed “disease experts” as saying that the incomplete and sometimes contradictory information provided by Russia’s health authorities makes it impossible to draw firm conclusions about the risk to the wider population and fears over the potential spread of an unknown illness continue to rise.

Mexican president signs decree restricting dual nationality for top elected offices
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
17:39:53 UTC
02:39:53 KST

Mariam Ashalem De Andres
07 October 2026•Update: 07 October 2026
Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum signed a constitutional reform Wednesday requiring candidates for the presidency, state governorships and the Mexico City mayor’s office to hold only Mexican nationality.
“Starting in 2028, anyone who wants to run for governor, head of government, president or president of the Republic can only be Mexican. That is what this decree is about,” said Sheinbaum.
The reform will take effect from 2028 and requires anyone seeking to register as a candidate for one of the positions to meet the nationality requirement before registering with the National Electoral Institute, or INE.
Candidates who hold dual nationality will have to renounce their other nationality and retain only Mexican nationality before completing their electoral registration.
The measure does not ban Mexicans from holding dual nationality. The requirement applies only to those seeking the presidency, state governorships or the Mexico City government.
The reform was approved by the required majorities in Congress and ratified by 22 state legislatures before being signed into law.
Sheinbaum has presented the measure as a way to strengthen Mexico’s sovereignty and ensure that people holding the highest elected offices have a single nationality.
The reform raised debate about the political rights of Mexicans with dual nationality, including those born abroad to Mexican parents.
Mexican law allows people born outside the country to Mexican parents to acquire Mexican nationality by birth. The new provision does not remove that right but adds a requirement for those seeking the offices covered by the reform.
The measure will not affect the 2027 elections.
The government has said the reform seeks to strengthen national sovereignty and establish a single-nationality requirement for those seeking key elected positions.

40% of the premises damaged: the National Academy of Sciences explained what will happen to the building after the Russian attack
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07

40% of the premises damaged: the National Academy of Sciences explained what will happen to the building after the Russian attack
Kyiv • UNN
A drone strike damaged around 40% of the building of the Presidium of the National Academy of Sciences in Kyiv. The structure is planned to be mothballed before the cold weather to prevent its collapse.
The building of the Presidium of the National Academy of Sciences after the drone strike on September 28 is to be conserved before the cold weather. This was reported by First Vice President of the National Academy of Sciences of Ukraine Viacheslav Bohdanov in an interview with Ukrainian media, UNN reports.
Details
According to Bohdanov, the consequences of the strike proved to be more extensive than the immediate area of destruction. While the fire was being extinguished, water entered the premises through the damaged roof.
It is currently known that almost 40% of the premises—900 square meters out of the building’s total area of 2,350 square meters—were damaged. Due to the consequences of extinguishing the fire, part of the rooms that survived also cannot currently be used.
The building is old, with wooden floors, lath, and plaster, so after getting wet, some structures began to collapse and peel away. Because of this, it is currently impossible to work even in some of the rooms that were not directly affected by the fire
He added that the Kyiv Emergency and Rescue Service is currently completing the dismantling of the most dangerous structures. NAS employees are also helping clear the premises. After the priority emergency work is completed, they plan to remove construction debris and damaged elements, and then begin conserving the surviving parts of the building.
The NAS emphasizes that this work must be carried out before the onset of cold weather in order to prevent further destruction of the structure due to precipitation and low temperatures. At the same time, the cost of the work, the contractor, and the exact timeframe for the building’s full restoration have not yet been announced.
Context
On September 28, at around 1:30 p.m., a Russian jet-powered drone struck the building of the Presidium of the National Academy of Sciences of Ukraine at 54 Volodymyrska Street in Kyiv. As a result of the attack, structures between the second and third floors were partially destroyed, after which a fire broke out over an area of approximately 900 square meters.
Two people were killed and seven others were injured in the strike. Among those killed was Natalia Bukalo, an employee of the NAS Presidium.
Despite the damage, the NAS Presidium held its regular meeting on September 30 and announced that it would continue its work.

Russia starts pouring more into war after Putin judged Alaska talks with US would bring no “acceptable” deal to end fighting — Bloomberg
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
17:39:08 UTC
02:39:08 KST

Russia is spending more on the war than at any point since it began. Russia's military funding is on track to hit a record this year after President Vladimir Putin added almost $60 billion to the outlays set in the budget, Bloomberg reports, citing people close to the government.
Defense spending is expected to approach about $199 billion by the end of 2026, roughly 40% above the plan Moscow announced in late 2025. That reverses the course of a year ago, when the Kremlin meant to slow military growth, narrow its deficit, and rebuild reserves drained by the war.
Alaska was the turning point
Putin ordered the shift late last year, after concluding that talks with the US in Alaska would not produce an acceptable deal to end the fighting, the report says.
By January, the Kremlin judged an agreement with Ukraine to be out of reach, and the government began accelerating advance payments to defense firms and raising other war-related spending.
"The government is finally budgeting for a prolonged war in Ukraine, but still understates its cost," Bloomberg Economics economist Ekaterina Vlasova said.
The deficit nearly doubles
Paying for the war has blown out the budget. The projected 2026 deficit has climbed to more than $81 billion, up from about $44 billion as first planned, and the government covered the extra spending through increased domestic borrowing and gold sales.
The budget plans years of war
The spending is not set to fall soon. Under the budget plans, Russia's military outlays reach about $200 billion in 2027, then ease to $194 billion in 2028 and about $191 billion in 2029, a signal that Moscow is planning for a long war.
Earlier, Euromaidan Press reported that Russia was raising 2027 defense spending by 27% to a record, even as its deficit widens and oil and gas revenues fall.

Iran sends Hezbollah $200M for Lebanon war aid
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
17:38:00 UTC
02:38:00 KST

Iran has provided Hezbollah with $200 million to support Lebanese families displaced by this year’s war with Israel, two people with direct knowledge of the transfer said, marking the group’s first major aid effort for supporters hit hardest by the conflict.
Hezbollah received the funds last month despite mounting U.S. economic pressure on Iran and growing obstacles to moving money to Tehran’s Lebanese ally, the sources said.
Intermediaries handling the transfer charged a 20% fee because of the risks involved in dealing with Hezbollah, according to the sources. One said the rate was four times the usual fee.
A Hezbollah official, asked for comment, confirmed that funds had been secured and said a distribution plan would be announced in the coming days, but did not identify the source of the money.
Iran’s Foreign Ministry, its permanent mission in Geneva, the U.S. Treasury Department and the Lebanese government did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
Israel’s bombardment and ground offensive in Lebanon displaced hundreds of thousands of people, many from Hezbollah’s Shiite support base, after the Iran-backed group entered the regional conflict on March 2.
Hezbollah, founded with support from Iran’s Revolutionary Guards in 1982, has suffered heavy Israeli blows during two wars since 2024. The United States designates the group as a terrorist organization.
Many of those displaced have received little or no assistance from Hezbollah so far.
Hezbollah plans to use the funds to provide an initial $3,000 payment to each eligible family, with priority given to people whose villages have been destroyed or remain inaccessible because of Israeli occupation, the sources said.
About 50,000 families fall into those categories, according to one of the sources.
Iran has continued supporting Hezbollah despite years of U.S. sanctions. Tehran transferred $1 billion to the group during the first 10 months of 2025, according to the U.S. Treasury Department.
Tehran has not publicly acknowledged financing Hezbollah. Iran’s support for allied armed groups across the region has previously fueled domestic criticism, making the issue particularly sensitive as economic hardship deepens inside the country.
Iran had pledged additional funding for Hezbollah after Tehran reached an interim agreement with Washington in June that allowed it to sell oil. The agreement collapsed in July.
Washington has since intensified economic pressure on Tehran, tightening sanctions and imposing a naval blockade aimed at restricting Iranian oil exports.
Hezbollah leader Naim Qassem said last month that the group would soon contribute to a project to house thousands of people displaced by the war, using “available resources and donations.” He did not provide further details.
Hezbollah’s ability to finance social services and postwar assistance has helped sustain support for the group in the past. After its 2006 war with Israel, Hezbollah quickly distributed cash to affected families and helped rebuild Beirut’s southern suburbs, one of its main strongholds.
This time, however, reconstruction has been slow. Lebanese Prime Minister Nawaf Salam said last month that rebuilding after the two wars since 2024 could cost more than $27 billion.
The two sources did not disclose how the $200 million reached Lebanon.
One said Hezbollah was finding it increasingly difficult to transfer funds through financial companies that had previously handled such transactions. Firms in Iraq and Dubai were no longer viable options, while similar channels in Türkiye were also coming under pressure, the source said.
Hezbollah’s opponents increasingly view its access to money as crucial to the group’s ability to operate, the source added.
Despite the funding difficulties, Hezbollah has continued paying its fighters and providing money to the families of members killed in combat, according to the same source.
The conflict has exacted a heavy toll on Lebanon’s Shiite community, from which Hezbollah draws much of its support. Israel has destroyed villages across areas it seized in southern Lebanon, saying its operations are intended to protect northern Israel from Hezbollah attacks.
Israeli attacks in Lebanon have killed more than 4,300 people since March 2, according to Lebanon’s Health Ministry. The ministry does not distinguish between civilians and combatants in its toll.
Hezbollah has not disclosed how many of its fighters have been killed. Reuters reported on May 4 that several thousand Hezbollah fighters had died in the conflict.

Latvia moves to declare Russian journalist Leonid Ragozin persona non grata, Baltic outlet Delfi reports
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
17:37:43 UTC
02:37:43 KST

Latvia has initiated the process of adding another Russian citizen to its list of people barred from entering the country, Foreign Minister Baiba Braže wrote on X. According to the local outlet Delfi, the person is Leonid Ragozin, a Russian journalist who lives in Latvia.
The Insider reviewed Ragozin’s recent writing, including an August column in which he argued that, given the “devastating prospect” of another harsh winter, “painful compromises at the negotiation table once again emerge as Ukraine’s only way out of national catastrophe.”
Braže said:
“Taking into account the information received today from the competent authorities, and after discussions with the Prime Minister and the Minister of the Interior, I have decided to initiate the process of adding another Russian citizen to Latvia's list of personae non gratae.”
Braže did not identify the person in her tweet. Delfi noted, however, that on Sept. 30, Latvian Interior Minister Jānis Dombrava had called on Braže to add Ragozin to the list, saying that for years the journalist had expressed views contrary to Latvia’s interests. Dombrava said Ragozin has blamed the West for Russia’s aggressive actions, criticized sanctions, justified Russian foreign policy, and discredited Ukraine. Delfi reported that, according to its information, Ragozin is the person targeted by the procedure.
Press.lv describes Ragozin as an “independent international affairs journalist” who has lived and worked permanently in Latvia since 2014.
Ragozin has indeed worked with a range of Russian and foreign media outlets. A biography on the BBC Russian Service website says he worked there for eight years before joining Russian Newsweek as a correspondent, later becoming its international editor. From 2015 to 2021, Ragozin published columns in Politico. He also wrote for The Guardian. In one 2014 article, he challenged Vladimir Putin’s claims that regular Russian army units were not present in the Donbas. From 2014 to 2016, he contributed to the Kyiv Post, and in 2019 The Moscow Times published an opinion piece in which he argued that “the Russian president’s ideological flexibility gives him the upper hand in the postmodern world.”
After 2022, the number of outlets Ragozin worked with appears to have narrowed. His columns continued to appear in the Qatar-based Al Jazeera, where he criticized Ukraine’s leadership and its European allies, praised U.S. President Donald Trump’s efforts to revive negotiations with Moscow, and argued that “the pro-war party simply wants any talks with Russia to be doomed, like they wanted the Istanbul talks to be doomed in the spring of 2022 and Minsk agreements to be ditched before that.” In an August column, Ragozin described Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky’s rhetoric as “defiant” and argued that, in light of the “devastating prospect” of the approaching winter meant that the time had come for Ukraine to negotiate its way out of a “national catastrophe.”

Mattarella grants three pardons, jeweler Guido Gianni among recipients
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
19:34:52 CEST
02:34:52 KST

President Sergio Mattarella on Wednesday granted three individual pardons including a jeweler who was convicted of killing two robbers following a heist at his store in 2008. 
The first individual pardon decree was issued for A.A. (born in 1972), who had been sentenced to a total of seven years in prison for drug-related offenses and other crimes. 
In granting the pardon for the remaining sentence to be served (five years, five months, and ten days), the President of the Republic took into account the favorable opinions of both competent judicial authorities and the convict's extremely serious and irreversible health condition—grounds upon which the postponement of the sentence's execution had previously been ordered. 
The other two pardon decrees—according to the presidential website—concerned Guido Gianni (born in 1960), who had been sentenced to twelve years and four months in prison for double homicide and attempted murder; these crimes were committed in 2008 during an attempted robbery of which he was the victim inside his own jewelry store. 
The Head of State granted a partial pardon, remitting three years and two months of the prison term, after considering the favorable opinion of the supervisory magistrate and the time already served (five years and three months). 
As a result of the partial pardon, the individual concerned will serve a remaining prison sentence of less than four years—a duration that allows the competent Supervisory Court to consider applying the measure of probation under social service supervision (pursuant to Article 47 of the Penitentiary Act). 
G.B., born in 1981, was sentenced to ten years of imprisonment for drug-related offenses committed between 2002 and 2009. 
In granting the partial pardon—which remitted one year and nine months of the outstanding prison term—the Head of State took into account the favorable opinion of the supervisory magistrate. 
This opinion acknowledged the convict's change in lifestyle—specifically, his initiation and consolidation of a process of social, professional, and familial reintegration—as well as the health condition of his minor daughter. 
In this instance, too, following the act of clemency, the remaining sentence falls within the limit that allows for the potential granting of the alternative measure of probation.

Oil sales policies being pursued as seriously as ever: acting oil minister
TEHRAN- According to Mehr News Agency, citing the Ministry of Oil, Hamid Bovard, on Tuesday, on the sidelines of his introduction ceremony as Acting Minister of Oil, said regarding the ministry’s most important plans: The industry’s current programs in production and development are continuing and are being pursued with greater speed and precision.
