The Acting Minister of Oil recalled regarding oil sales: Matters related to oil sales are being pursued as always, but I cannot disclose information in this area, and we continue to pursue our work in this field seriously.
The Acting Minister of Oil emphasized regarding energy management: I ask all dear people not to consume wastefully and to help in all areas of energy carriers so that this year we achieve stronger savings compared with previous years.
Bovard recalled regarding supplying fuel to industries in winter: Comprehensive decisions are made in the Fuel Committee in the government, and after a decision is made in the government, it is communicated to all agencies.
The Acting Minister of Oil, emphasizing the need for comprehensive management of fuel consumption and strengthening transmission infrastructure, stressed the importance of a macro-level view in oil industry decision-making.
According to Mehr News Agency, Hamid Bovard, on Tuesday, in a meeting with the managers of the National Iranian Oil Refining and Distribution Company at the company’s central building, in addition to expressing appreciation for the efforts and hard work of employees and managers, stressed the need to use a strategic, scientific, and comprehensive view in managing the issues of the oil industry, especially the refining and distribution of oil products.
Referring to his 35 years of activity in the oil industry, he added: In management meetings, to provide the possibility of more precise decision-making and a macro view of issues, information should be presented coherently and in the form of management summaries.
The Acting Minister of Oil, stating that in large organizations the high volume of activities sometimes causes main issues to be less visible amid details and daily challenges, announced: Looking from above and outside the organization’s daily atmosphere can help identify problems more precisely and find suitable solutions.
Bovard, emphasizing issues related to the gas and oil products sectors, stressed the need to adopt more precise decisions based on the country’s domestic capacities and stated: Given that a significant portion of the country’s needed resources is supplied domestically, instead of letting others make decisions for us, we must have plans and programs with an accurate understanding of the situation.
He considered the issue of fuel consumption management, especially gasoline and diesel, one of the country’s important issues and recalled: Measures regarding the smart fuel card are important, but special attention must be paid to threats and cyberattacks, and the security and stability of fuel-related systems must be guaranteed.
The Acting Minister of Oil emphasized: Managing consumption and implementing expert plans in the fuel sector can help gradually improve the country’s situation; however, the main goal should not be only managing current affairs, but we must move toward reforming the governance model and improving the way organizations are administered.
Bovard considered the use of universities and scientific centers essential for developing specialized training and training young forces, and continued: A foundation must be provided so that young forces, especially in their first years of service, are placed on the correct organizational path and their capacity and motivation are used effectively.
Referring to the importance of the main corridors for transferring and moving oil and oil products, he stressed the need to direct part of organizational activities and programs along these routes and said: Attention to these capacities can be effective in strengthening the oil industry’s infrastructure.
The Acting Minister of Oil also, referring to the country’s situation and the need to create hope in society, stated: In the current situation, effective and tangible measures must be taken to provide the ground for increasing people’s hope. Proper management of consumption and optimal use of resources are among these measures.
Bovard, likening this situation to a fish in water, added: Sometimes people within a large organization, due to their continuous presence in it, understand less the importance and real dimensions of the work being done. In difficult times, if the executive and expert groups of the oil industry had not been on the scene, the country’s problems could have become much broader.
Appreciating the performance of expert forces and the management team, he counted the existence of expertise, empathy, and cohesion among managers as strengths of the organization and expressed hope that, by strengthening the scientific, strategic, and coherent view, this capacity would develop in various oil industry companies.
Mohammad Sadeq Azimifar, CEO of the National Iranian Oil Refining and Distribution Company, also in this meeting, presenting a report to the Acting Minister of Oil, announced: The National Iranian Oil Refining and Distribution Company, under conditions of war, sanctions, and limited financial resources, by changing its management approach, has pursued four main axes: supply-demand balance, value chain development, human capital development, and data-driven governance.
He added: In this framework, six strategies were defined, including increasing and improving the quality of production, consumption management, infrastructure development, improving storage levels and fuel supply, human capital development, and research and digital transformation.
Azimifar recalled: In the production sector, with increased feedstock, implementation of key projects, and major overhauls, average gasoline production increased by about 17 percent; also, four quality improvement projects came into operation, and about three percent was added to product production.
The CEO of the National Iranian Oil Refining and Distribution Company said: In the consumption sector, the annual growth in gasoline consumption, which was about 6 percent, reached about zero through a set of management measures and became negative in Shahrivar. This year, gas oil consumption also decreased by about 2 to 3 percent. Price reforms, consumption management, and combating smuggling, in addition to reducing consumption, improved targeted subsidy resources.
He continued: CNG is one of the important capacities for consumption management, and after implementation of the third-price plan, consumption of this energy carrier increased by about 12 percent.
Azimifar noted: In the field of combating smuggling, about 66,000 active cases were organized, about 77,000 waybills were reviewed and corrected, and about 2,000 migrant fuel cards were identified and organized; at the same time, organizing about 600,000 fuel cards in various sectors is also underway.
The CEO of the National Iranian Oil Refining and Distribution Company said: The plan to assign identifiers to free cards at filling stations in Tehran is being implemented, and the cards will not be eliminated; rather, their use will be organized and misuse prevented.
He stated: In the infrastructure sector, in two years about one thousand kilometers have been added to the country’s pipeline network, and important projects are being completed and put into operation. In addition, for human capital development, a center has been launched where about 100 people have so far participated in its specialized courses.
Azimifar announced: The main goal is to curb consumption, increase production, strengthen storage, and reduce dependence on gasoline imports as much as possible. In the diesel sector, too, a plan has been drafted for reducing subsidies and managing consumption and exports, which can create considerable resources for the country.
The CEO of the National Iranian Oil Refining and Distribution Company emphasized: In various sectors, the company’s maximum capacity is being used to fulfill missions and increase revenue and productivity.
The Acting Minister of Oil considered the stability of energy supply, especially in the cold months of the year, to require full coordination in the gas production, transmission, and distribution chain.
According to Mehr News Agency, Hamid Bovard, on Tuesday, during a visit to the Dispatching Center of the National Iranian Gas Company, emphasizing the importance of this center’s role in managing the country’s gas network, stated: Stability of energy supply, especially in the cold months of the year, requires full coordination among the gas production, transmission, and distribution sectors, and dispatching has a key role in this regard.
During this visit, while hearing the issues and concerns of the managers of the National Iranian Gas Company, he stressed the need to follow up on and resolve existing challenges and to make maximum use of the gas industry’s capacities to maintain network stability.
The Acting Minister of Oil, appreciating the round-the-clock efforts of gas industry employees, emphasized: It is necessary to use modern technologies, upgrade monitoring systems, and increase operational readiness to face various conditions.
Saeed Tavakoli, CEO of the National Iranian Gas Company, also during this visit, explaining the measures taken to maximize gas supply, said: The company has used all its efforts to increase production, and for this purpose, part of the major overhauls has been carried out ahead of schedule.
Referring to the possibility of gas tension in some provinces of the country this winter, he added: Necessary scenarios have been defined for all provinces so that the company can plan for network management and gas supply according to the conditions of each region.
Managers and officials of the Gas Dispatching Center during this visit presented a report on the process of gas supply, transmission, and distribution, the network’s readiness for consumption management, and the plans foreseen to maintain the stability of gas flow. They also shared the most important issues and challenges in various sectors and their suggestions with the Acting Minister of Oil.
According to the Ministry of Oil, Hamid Bovard, Acting Minister of Oil, on Tuesday, visited the Dispatching Center of the National Iranian Gas Company and was informed of the latest status of monitoring, management, and control of the country’s nationwide gas network.

Saudi Arabia, Pakistan, Turkey: Could the Mecca defense pact become a game changer in the war against the Houthis in Yemen?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
17:33:00 UTC
02:33:00 KST

Pakistan, Turkey boost role in Yemen's Houthi-Saudi conflict
October 7, 2026
The latest iteration of Saudi Arabia's defense deal with Turkey and Pakistan, the Mecca Joint Defense Agreement, is taking shape amid the country's escalating conflict with Yemen's Houthi militia.
According to the trilateral defense commitment, which was signed by Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan and Pakistani Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif on August 7, 2026, an armed attack on any one of the three states involved should be regarded as an attack on them all.
Yet, despite ongoing Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia and Saudi attacks on Houthi militants in Yemen, neither Pakistan nor Turkey had joined Saudi Arabia's combat operations since the deal was signed, arguing that the command and operational structures were still being developed.
But since Monday, the situation has changed after an emergency meeting between Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Turkey's defense and foreign ministers and senior military chiefs in the Saudi capital Riyadh. According to a joint statement, Turkey and Pakistan decided to implement the collective defense commitments in practical terms immediately. This means providing military forces and capabilities and ensuring their rapid deployment in Saudi Arabia. The appointment of a retired Pakistani lieutenant general, Nauman Mahmood, as the alliance's first secretary-general was also announced. He will serve a three-year term.
"Ankara and Islamabad undoubtedly will seek to strengthen the Saudi kingdom's posture vis-a-vis the Houthi threat and demonstrate that the Mecca agreement can pass its first real test and show up as a game-changing alliance," Burcu Ozcelik, a senior research fellow for Middle East security at the London-based Royal United Services Institute, told DW.
"However, what the activation of the Mecca pact means operationally, including the specific capabilities deployed and the scope of their missions, has not been made public," she said, adding that this was "not unusual for such a military operation amid myriad sensitivities."
According to the 2026 Global Firepower military strength ranking, Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Turkey between them have about 1.4 million active personnel, some 3,400 military aircraft, 6,000 tanks and more than 340 naval assets.
On Wednesday, Saudi Arabia intercepted another ballistic missile north of Riyadh. Earlier this week, Saudi-backed Yemeni government forces had launched a large-scale offensive, to recapture territory along the Red Sea coast around the strategic Bab el-Mandeb Strait and the city of Mokha. Saudi Arabia launched airstrikes to support the offensive.
Turkey considers a solution through dialogue
The scope of a potential Turkish military deployment remains unclear. Turkey is a NATO member, which means that any military involvement on its part could carry broader implications for the entire military alliance.
Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan noted after the meeting in Riyadh on Monday that there were not only military options on the table. "We also discussed what could be done to resolve the problem peacefully and through dialogue,"
Turkey's involvement in the Mecca defense deal has been criticized by opposition parties in the country. Under Turkey's constitution, international agreements generally require approval by the Grand National Assembly of Turkey but this has not yet been granted.
"How can the so-called Mecca agreement on joint defense be valid and implemented without having been submitted to the Turkish parliament for approval?" Namik Tan, an Istanbul lawmaker from the social democratic Yeni Parti and a former Turkish ambassador to Israel and the United States, asked in a statement.
Yani Bagcioglu, a retired Turkish admiral, also warned that "the risk of Turkish forces and commercial vessels linked to Turkey becoming targets of Houthi attacks should not be overlooked."
Pakistan's tightrope walk amid the Iran war
The third signatory, Pakistan, is walking its own particular tightrope. On Monday, Defense Minister Khawaja Muhammad Asif told Pakistani television channel Geo News that Pakistan and Turkey were playing a "supportive role," with their forces involved in "reconnaissance and other things," while Saudi forces were engaged in combat.
"Pakistan's contribution to the defense of Saudi Arabia is nothing new," Imtiaz Gul, an independent Pakistani security analyst, told DW. "The arrangement has existed for six decades," he said, adding that "defense against the Houthis nevertheless represents a different kind of challenge because the group is considered an Iranian extension and by implication, Iran would consider this an attack on its regional interests."
A direct engagement in Yemen at Saudi Arabia's side would, therefore, risk not only ending Pakistan's apparent neutral status as a mediator in the US-Iran war, but also strain relations with Tehran, he said. He pointed out that Saudi Arabia was a close ally of the US, while the Houthis are backed by Iran.
Hisham Al-Omeisy, a Yemeni conflict analyst in Washington, told DW that "for years, a cornerstone of the Houthi narrative and rallying cry has been a fight against perceived external enemies." Accordingly, he added, foreign boots on the ground in Yemen would "not only backfire, it would solidify the Houthi local coalitions and fuel their recruitment drives."
Haroon Janjua in Islamabad contributed to this article.
Edited by: Anne Thomas

Over 100 arrested in Belgium student protests over education costs
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
17:28:56 UTC
02:28:56 KST

Over 100 arrested in Belgium student protests over education costs
Protesting students demand accessible education in French-speaking areas of the country.
Police in Belgium have detained more than 100 people after demonstrations in the city of Liege against the rising cost of education turned violent in some places, as similar protests grip neighbouring France.
Students rallied in the city on Tuesday and Wednesday against overcrowded classrooms and difficulty accessing resources in Belgium’s French-language education system.
Eighty people were detained during the protests, and 27 were formally arrested, the Belga news agency reported, citing the Liege police.
Some protesters damaged property and set fires, the police added.
Attendees insisted that shortcomings in the education system gave them no choice but to take to the streets.
“When we saw nothing was changing without protests, we decided we would start,” said Amelia Di Salve, a 19-year-old studying to become a teacher, who added that protests in “France did influence us a little”.
“We support each other because we’re facing pretty much the same issues,” Alfred, another 19-year-old student, told the Reuters news agency.
‘Peaceful way’
Authorities were attempting to defuse tensions and head off further unrest.
“Dialogue can be established,” Willy Demeyer, the mayor of the city of Liege, told Belgian broadcaster RTBF, adding that he hoped “young people can express their grievances in a peaceful way and if possible have those concerns heard”.
In Belgium, education is managed independently by the country’s linguistic communities, and there is no single national curriculum.
Instead, the Flemish population regulates education in Belgium’s Dutch-speaking Flanders region while French-speaking Wallonia oversees its own curriculum.
Parents can decide where to enrol children in the bilingual capital Brussels.
The protests in Liege follow sporadic violent demonstrations over the summer in Brussels against an increase in tuition fees for students in French-speaking areas from 835 euros ($930) to 1,194 euros ($1,340).
Belgium’s education budget has been under pressure as a result of a cost-of-living crisis and the spiralling cost of energy, issues that are helping fuel student protests in France as well.

Rubio in Athens urges Europe to shoulder more of its defence burden
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
17:28:53 UTC
02:28:53 KST

The US secretary of state held talks on energy, military cooperation and regional security, pointing to Greece as an example of higher defence spending. The agenda also included LNG, F-35s, the Eastern Mediterranean and the Strait of Hormuz.
At a time when the security and energy landscape in Europe and the Eastern Mediterranean is undergoing constant change, Athens and Washington are seeking to further expand the strategic scope of their relationship. US Secretary of State Marco Rubio’s visit to Athens, for the sixth round of the Greece-US Strategic Dialogue, brought defence, security, energy, technology, trade and investment to the forefront.
The talks took place against a particularly complex international backdrop, with Greece emerging as an important US partner in the region, both in security and in energy planning for Central and Eastern Europe.
Two-hour Gerapetritis-Rubio meeting
On Wednesday morning, Marco Rubio visited the Foreign Ministry, where he met his Greek counterpart Giorgos Gerapetritis. The bilateral meeting lasted around two hours and covered a broad range of issues concerning both bilateral relations and regional and international developments.
Following the meeting, Gerapetritis highlighted the high level of Greek-US relations and the shared willingness to deepen them further.
He said Athens and Washington share a commitment to strengthening cooperation and promoting regional and international security.
Energy: Greece as a hub for US LNG
Energy cooperation featured prominently in the talks. The Greek Foreign Minister referred to Greece’s role as a hub for transporting US liquefied natural gas to Central and Eastern Europe.
“Energy cooperation between the two countries has reached an unprecedented level,” Gerapetritis said, also pointing to the increased presence of US energy companies in Greece.
In the same context, he referred to investments being developed in sectors including energy, technology and shipyards, which he said are adding new dimensions to the economic relationship between the two countries.
Marco Rubio also emphasised energy cooperation, referring to the expansion of US LNG imports as well as the development of new gas and electricity interconnections.
He said these developments could strengthen regional energy security and expand Greece’s role in the European energy system.
Defence: Alexandroupolis, F-16s and F-35s
A significant part of the talks focused on defence cooperation between Greece and the United States.
Gerapetritis described the Mutual Defence Cooperation Agreement as a key bilateral treaty governing relations between the two countries, while also highlighting the strategic importance of Alexandroupolis.
In the same context, he referred to the upgrade of Greece’s F-16s and the integration of F-35 fighter jets into the Hellenic Air Force.
He noted that defence cooperation is not only about strengthening national defence, but is also more broadly linked to strategic cooperation and stability in the region.
At the opening of the Strategic Dialogue, Gerapetritis described Alexandroupolis as a prime example of Greek-US cooperation.
Rubio: ‘Greece is a source of stability’
Marco Rubio spoke in particularly positive terms about the strategic relationship between the two countries, highlighting the historical and political ties linking Greece and the United States.
“The United States and Greece share a long history of friendship, cooperation and alliance,” the US Secretary of State said, noting that the importance of the relationship is even more evident in today’s international environment.
“It is both historic and foundational, but it is also critical. It is a source of stability in an unstable world,” he said.
Rubio also stressed that Greece remains an important US ally and that the two countries share common views on a range of threats and challenges.
Call for greater European responsibility for defence
The US Secretary of State also placed particular emphasis on the need for European countries to shoulder a greater share of responsibility for Europe’s defence.
“The nations of Europe need to take on a greater share of the burden and defending their continent, and Greece is doing just that,” he said.
The statement comes amid a broader US debate over strengthening European defence capabilities and increasing the contribution of European allies to the continent’s security.
New dimension to military cooperation with Florida
During Rubio’s visit to Athens, a cooperation agreement was also signed between the Chief of the Hellenic National Defence General Staff and the Florida National Guard, in the presence of Defence Minister Nikos Dendias and the US Secretary of State.
Dendias said the agreement adds a new dimension to cooperation between the armed forces of the two countries and forms part of Greece’s “Agenda 2030”.
He said Greece is looking for best practices to strengthen the operational capabilities of its armed forces and reservists, with cooperation with the Florida National Guard offering opportunities for knowledge transfer, training and the exchange of experience.
Marco Rubio described the agreement as an expression of the depth of the historic alliance between Greece and the United States.
Referring to possible areas of cooperation, he noted that the Florida National Guard has gained significant experience in responding to natural disasters such as hurricanes, while it can also draw on Greek experience in dealing with earthquakes and wildfires.
He said the partnership creates opportunities for interoperability and mutual learning and represents another step in building the modern Greek-US alliance.
Border security and counterterrorism
A significant part of the US position also focused on border security.
Marco Rubio described Greece as a “very close strategic partner” of the United States in tackling irregular migration, human trafficking, transnational criminal organisations and terrorism.
He also announced a new Memorandum of Understanding aimed at strengthening information-sharing between the relevant agencies of the two countries in the field of counterterrorism.
The US Secretary of State stressed the need to address contemporary challenges affecting the security of the West.
Eastern Mediterranean and maritime security
The two ministers also discussed major international crises, from the Middle East and Ukraine to Africa and migration flows.
Maritime security featured prominently on the agenda, with Giorgos Gerapetritis stressing its importance for the protection of international supply chains.
“Maritime security is a non-negotiable condition,” he said.
The Greek Foreign Minister also referred to cooperation between Greece and the United States in ensuring stability in the Eastern Mediterranean and protecting religious communities.
“Our shared concern with the United States is to create and safeguard conditions of stability in the wider Eastern Mediterranean region and to protect Christian populations, as well as every other ethnic and religious community,” he said.
Turkey in the background of regional developments
Turkey remained in the background of discussions over regional balances, although Marco Rubio did not mention the country by name.
The US Secretary of State referred to energy projects linked to a “very sensitive situation” involving other countries.
The careful wording reflects the complex diplomatic equation in the Eastern Mediterranean, where energy projects, regional partnerships and security issues are increasingly interconnected.
Rubio backs Guilfoyle
During his meetings in Athens, Marco Rubio was asked to comment on a Wall Street Journal report concerning US Ambassador to Greece Kimberly Guilfoyle.
The US Secretary of State avoided addressing the substance of the allegations and limited his response to saying that the US embassy in Athens was doing an excellent job.
He also described Guilfoyle as a strong representative of US interests in Greece, publicly reaffirming his support for the ambassador.
The sixth Strategic Dialogue and Greece’s role
At the opening of the sixth Greece-US Strategic Dialogue, Giorgos Gerapetritis stressed the strategic importance of the bilateral relationship and the role Greece can play in the region.
He said the country’s history, regional relationships and the influence of Hellenism allow Greece to maintain a broad network of partnerships.
“This gives Greece a specific responsibility, as well as the practical ability to connect countries, facilitate dialogue and build understanding,” he said.
The Greek Foreign Minister stressed that cooperation with the United States strengthens Greece’s role and security in the region, while the Strategic Dialogue can translate into concrete and tangible action.
A relationship with an expanded strategic scope
The sixth Greece-US Strategic Dialogue reflects the breadth of a relationship that now extends beyond the traditional boundaries of defence cooperation.
Energy, technology, investment, trade, border security, cultural heritage and regional stability are now integral parts of the bilateral agenda.
For Athens, strengthening ties with Washington is linked to its goal of playing a more active role in the Eastern Mediterranean and Southeastern Europe. For Washington, Greece is an important ally in a region where security, energy, maritime routes and regional balances are becoming increasingly significant.
Against this backdrop, Rubio’s visit to Athens and the sixth Strategic Dialogue reflect efforts by both sides to turn the already high level of the Greek-US relationship into even more concrete forms of cooperation, with a focus on security, energy and stability across the wider region.

Government should allow cultivation of HTBt cotton, farmers need technology: Seed bodies
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
17:27:32 UTC
02:27:32 KST

FSII Chairman informed that 1.25 crore packets of HTBt seed are being sold, currently worth Rs 1,500 crore. The total size of the cotton seed market is 5.5 crore packets worth Rs 6,000 crore.
NEW DELHI: Seed industry bodies FSII and NSAI on Wednesday demanded that the government allow commercial cultivation of herbicide-tolerant Bt (HTBt) cotton at the earliest, as the crop variety is being grown illegally in some parts of the country, creating a Rs 1,500 crore informal seed market.The Federation of Seed Industry of India (FSII) and the National Seed Association of India (NSAI) stressed the need to introduce high-yielding varieties and new technologies to boost domestic cotton production and reduce imports.India's cotton production stands at around 29 million bales (of 170 kg each).A study, Unauthorised Cultivation of HTBt Cotton in India: Extent, Drivers and Implications, was conducted by the South Asia Biotechnology Centre (SABC) with the support of these two associations. It covered 16 districts across Maharashtra, Telangana, Andhra Pradesh and Rajasthan, combining farmer surveys, supply-chain assessment and ELISA-based gene testing."Unauthorised herbicide-tolerant Bt (HTBt) cotton was grown on 65-72 lakh acres in Kharif 2025-26, or 24-30 per cent of India's total cotton area, sustaining an informal seed market worth an estimated Rs 1,500 crore," FSII Chairman Ajai Rana told reporters.
He informed that 1.25 crore packets of HTBt seed are being sold, currently worth Rs 1,500 crore. The total size of the cotton seed market is 5.5 crore packets worth Rs 6,000 crore.Sales of legal Bt cotton seeds have declined."The government should fast-track the approval of HT Bt cotton," he said, adding that Mahyco has already made an application for this purpose in 2024.The association also demanded changes in glyphosate label claims. The product is used for weed management in the cotton crop."Farmers are not breaking the law out of choice. They are paying a black-market premium because the regulatory system has not given them the technology they need," Rana said.The study found that farmers are actively bypassing formal channels and paying a premium technology fee to the black market just to secure operational survival and crop insurance, the FSII said."Unchecked use of unapproved genes and unmonitored glyphosate spraying could breed resistant pests and weeds that devastate cotton productivity," said Dr C D Mayee, President, Indian Society for Cotton Improvement and President, South Asia Biotechnology Centre.
The study pointed out that labour shortages are driving the shift. Weed control with glyphosate costs Rs 750-850 an acre, against Rs 12,000-15,000 for manual weeding. Glyphosate use rose 26 per cent in a year, from 27,721 kilolitres in 2024-25 to 35,642 kilolitres in 2025-26."Due to a drop in productivity per acre, India has lost self-sufficiency in cotton production and become an importer of cotton. To regain self-sufficiency and revive the cotton economy, regulatory approval of herbicide-tolerant cotton and the pink bollworm trait should be a national priority," Rana said.

Kalashnikov, Russia’s biggest small-arms maker, says it fills its entire 2026 arms contract on time with batch of 7.62mm Dragunov sniper rifle
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
17:24:18 UTC
02:24:18 KST

Russia's Kalashnikov concern has met its annual arms contract. The top producer of small arms has announced it delivered a batch of classic 7.62mm Dragunov sniper rifles to a Russian Security Forces customer and fully met its 2026 contract on time
The delivery shows how little the sanctions regime slows Russia's arms maker. In February 2026, Ukraine's Defense Intelligence said that nearly half of Kalashnikov's plants were still not subject to sanctions by any coalition country. Eight months later, the concern reports a full year's order delivered on schedule.
"The items were shipped on the set deadline, the obligations under the 2026 contract fully met," the manufacturer said.
A rifle in service for six decades
The weapon in that batch is not new. Designed by Yevgeny Dragunov between 1958 and 1963, the Dragunov sniper rifle entered serial production at the Izhevsk machine-building plant in 1963, so in 2026, it has remained in serial production for more than 60 years.
The self-loading 7.62mm rifle is meant to hit personnel and unarmored targets at ranges up to 800 meters, the concern said. It uses gas-operated automatics with a short-stroke piston and a gas regulator, and can fire any 7.62x54R round, though sniper ammunition yields the best grouping, according to the maker.
Sanctions chase a moving network
The sniper rifles are only one line in Kalashnikov's output. Russia's defense industry has leaned heavily on refurbishing Soviet-era armor as newer reserves run low, with Ukraine's intelligence reporting in June 2025 that Russia had begun deploying 1960s-era T-62 tanks.
The restoration work was centered primarily at the 103rd Armored Repair Plant in Atamanovka, Trans-Baikal Territory of Siberia. Ukrainian intelligence documented the transfer of 21 T-62 tanks from the eastern region to the western part.
Small arms are a different line of production, built new rather than pulled from storage. That is why a 1963 design keeps rolling off the line while the sanctions net, as Ukraine's intelligence describes it, still has holes.

Northwestern University evacuates October 7 play performance after fire alarm was set off
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
17:23:48 UTC
02:23:48 KST

A performance of the verbatim play October 7 at Northwestern University’s Cahn Auditorium was abruptly disrupted and forced to evacuate when a fire alarm was set off on Tuesday.
The production, written by Irish journalists Phelim McAleer and Ann McElhinney, is built from word-for-word survivor testimonies detailing the Hamas terror attacks in Israel.
The touring play has been staged at various universities and venues across the United States to present firsthand accounts of the events, with upcoming performances scheduled at CUNY in Manhattan in December, Cornell University in December, and the Holocaust Museum in Los Angeles in January.
McElhinney posted video footage of the incident online, capturing the packed theater as the alarm blared and audience members stood up to exit the auditorium. Sharing the video on social media, McElhinney wrote, “Breaking. Right now at Northwestern, our play October 7 has been disrupted by someone setting off a fire alarm. The whole theater has to be evacuated. This hits even stronger because it’s already October 7 in Israel.”
McElhinney and McAleer later posted on social media in an update following initial online postings of the disruption said to have been set off by a student, that it was not yet confirmed whether a student was responsible for triggering the alarm.
The play is based on accounts from survivors of Oct. 7
McElhinney posted video footage of the incident online, capturing the packed theater as the alarm blared and audience members stood up to exit the auditorium. Sharing the video on social media, McElhinney wrote, “Breaking. Right now at Northwestern, our play October 7 has been disrupted by someone setting off a fire alarm. The whole theater has to be evacuated. This hits even stronger because it’s already October 7 in Israel.”
Speaking to The Jerusalem Post, co-creators McAleer and McElhinney explained that they weren’t present at the sold-out performance but were watching it live via Zoom while their production team was on site. McAleer told the Post that approximately a quarter of the way into the show, someone pulled the fire alarm, leaving audience members very scared.
Among those in attendance was Abby Polin, the aunt of murdered hostage Hersh Goldberg-Polin, along with Hersh’s grandmother. Polin told the Post, “In the midst of a packed theater in Evanston, Illinois, on the Northwestern University campus, watching a riveting verbatim performance of testimonies of October 7 survivors produced by non-Jewish Irish journalists, that an alleged Jew-hater pulled the fire alarm to interrupt a story about hatred is so beyond appalling.”
“An audience member, also not Jewish, said she felt in a way that it enhanced the performance because it must be what Israelis feel like hearing alarms and sirens so often. After the fire department gave the okay to go back in, the audience once again went through security to watch the last 20 minutes of the performance, which closed with a standing ovation,” Polin told the Post.
She added, “It was an audience of people of all ages and religions in attendance. It just reinforced to the audience how evil people in this world can be.”
The show must go on
Following the evacuation, police arrived at the scene. McAleer told the Post that about half of the full house of roughly 940 people chose to return after the police gave the all-clear, while others did not feel safe enough to re-enter.
Emphasizing that the show must go on, McAleer said that the cast and crew were deeply determined not to be shut down, noting that the actors were exceptionally passionate and that finishing the performance yielded a standing ovation. McAleer added that organizers intended to file a formal police report to ensure the incident is fully investigated.
In a statement to the Post, the play’s director, Jeff Gurner, dismissed the disruption as an insignificant protest, asserting with a message to whoever the perpetrator was that he “achieved exactly nothing. The actors and audience reconvened, the performance picked up where it left off, and the voices of those people whose stories were told in the play, along with the memory of those who were lost on October 7, were more powerful than ever.”
Gurner said it was an “absurd little act of imagined revolutionary activism” that amounted to nothing more than them having to wait out an investigation, their inevitable outing, and facing deserved consequences.” He added that the police and fire authorities both immediately responded to the scene, and campus security said there would be an internal investigation by the university.
Jacob Baim, an actor from the Chicago area and an alumnus of Northwestern, also spoke to The Jerusalem Post, stating, "I was ecstatic to be returning to my Alma Mater to perform on a stage that I performed on over 50 times. I was happy to share the campus with my castmates, and to be able to invite my friends and family from my hometown to come see this play about first-person accounts of October 7th."
Baim continued, "While we don't know how the fire alarm went off yet (though I hope we will soon); what I do know is what I saw: fear and terror in the audience. Many members of my family left the theatre and did not return; some were survivors of the attack in Highland Park on July 4th and were too upset to finish the show."
Baim added, "It boggles my mind that in America in the 21st century, Jewish people have to be in fear for their lives when watching a piece of theatre that honors the voices of people who experienced a massacre. There were family members of hostages, friends of people who did not survive, and people who were there in support; all of whom had to fear for their lives when the alarm went off, their minds jumping to the worst-case scenario."
Baim further stated, "This is not a piece of theatre about Israel, or about Palestine, or about war or hate; It's a first-hand account honoring people who went through a catastrophe. To have that interrupted is a shame, but it does not change our resolve to continue to share this show or our voices."
Baim concluded, "When we came back, about half the audience was there; which, while disappointing, is a reminder that no matter what is thrown at the Jewish people, we will persevere.”
Elad Strohmayer, Israel’s consul-general in Chicago, reacted to the incident on X/Twitter, writing, “Tonight at Northwestern, when it was already October 7 in Israel, a fire alarm interrupted a play based on the testimonies of October 7 survivors, forcing the audience to evacuate. The survivors’ stories deserve to be heard, and the audience and production deserve to be safe.
“I am glad to hear that Northwestern is taking this seriously and investigating. The investigation must promptly establish what triggered the alarm and whether it was deliberately set off to disrupt the performance. If that is confirmed, those responsible must be held accountable.
Strohmayer wrote, “It is unacceptable that the Jewish community cannot hold an event honoring October 7 survivors, or any event for that matter, without fearing for its safety.”
Northwestern did not respond to a request for comment by publication time.

Oct. 7 Gaza Envelope bomb shelters designated antiquities as safeguard against 'clean up' projects
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
17:23:42 UTC
02:23:42 KST

The Gaza Envelope bomb shelters have officially been designated “antiquities” under Israel’s Antiquities Law, in an unprecedented move by the Heritage Ministry marking the third anniversary of the October 7 massacre.
Although the Antiquities Law (1978) was originally intended to preserve finds created before the year 1,700, Section 1 of the law grants the relevant minister the authority to declare locations or artifacts an "antiquity" should it have a distinct national historical value.
Made following an appeal by dozens of bereaved families and former hostages and extensive staff work carried out by the ministry, it is intended to halt any bureaucratic initiatives to "clean up the area.”
These initiatives could include removing, repainting, and plastering over the structures that came under fire, which would erase historical evidence.
Even so, the shelters’ designation does not transfer direct ownership to the state, but rather grants the structures legal protection against being physically altered without approval from the Heritage Ministry and the IAA.
On Wednesday morning, Heritage Minister Amichai Eliyahu approached the Gaza Envelope regional council heads and the deputy director of the Israel Antiquities Authority (IAA) to finalize the decision.
What are the Gaza Envelope bomb shelters?
As sirens sounded across the south and Hamas began its invasion of the Gaza Envelope, dozens of Israelis took cover in the mobile, roadside bomb shelters. Among them were deceased hostages Hersh Goldberg-Polin, Aner Shapira, Eliya Cohen and Or Levy.
From within the shelter, Shapira managed to fend off seven grenades thrown by Hamas terrorists before he was killed. Goldberg-Polin, Cohen, and Levy were all taken hostage by Hamas.
Goldberg-Polin was executed in August 2024. Cohen and Levy were released in February 2025.
"The events of October 7 seared a deep wound into our flesh,” said Eliyahu, “but they also revealed fortitude, heroism, and mutual responsibility that will be remembered for generations. In the midst of the inferno, the shelters scattered across the Gaza Envelope became arenas of a struggle for survival, of blood and of immeasurable heroism.”
“Our duty to future generations is to ensure that the stories of heroism and loss are told from within the space itself, and do not disappear under bureaucratic considerations or a hasty desire to ‘clean up the area.’”
The directive has been passed to all necessary authorities in order to ensure that the shelters are preserved as testimony and remembrance sites for the events of the massacre.

Russia open to a Trump-Putin call as questions mount over plague lab death
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
17:22:59 UTC
02:22:59 KST

Russia says it's open to a Trump-Putin call as questions mount over plague lab death
Russia's government said Wednesday that it was open to "promptly" scheduling a phone call between Presidents Trump and Vladimir Putin to discuss the still-unexplained death of a plague research center employee, but that nothing had been scheduled yet.
Mr. Trump told reporters Tuesday night that he expected to speak with Putin "very soon" about the Oct. 2 death of the Siberian lab worker, after Secretary of State Marco Rubio called on Moscow to be more transparent about the incident and to "share more information with the world."
A State Department spokesperson later told CBS News the U.S. Embassy in Moscow had "engaged Russian authorities about the reported death" and "asked for additional information," which it encouraged Russia to share "quickly and transparently."
So far, Russian authorities have only offered "pneumonia of unknown origin" as the cause of Darya Shipilova's death. Shipilova, 28, worked at the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Institute, more than 2,500 miles east of Moscow, and initial Russian media reports - some of which were quickly taken down - suggested she had contracted the pneumonic plague after a lab accident and died of the disease.
The United Nations World Health Organization called Wednesday on Russia's national health watchdog agency, Rospotrebnadzor, to provide more information about Shipilova's death, and the Russian body said it had provided further details.
In a statement, Rospotrebnadzor said it was easing precautionary measures that were put in place in the Siberian region of Irkutsk, where the lab is located, after determining there was no risk of an epidemic connected to Shipilova's death. It said no cases of plague were detected among the 200 people screened after coming into contact with her, and that 90% of those who had been put under quarantine conditions for monitoring had been released.
The agency said it had conducted nearly 5,000 lab tests of those individuals and that none of them had detected dangerous pathogens.
Rospotrebnadzor's statement added that Shipilova had been vaccinated against the dangerous infections she worked with, so she had immunity to them.
But despite the reassurances from Russia's government, the lack of any clear explanation for Shiplova's death has left rumors to swirl about what might have killed her, and what work might be underway at the Russian research center.
According to its website, the Irkutsk anti-plague lab's work extends beyond research on the well-known bacteria, which is present in animal populations in the region, as it is in other parts of the world, to include planning and preparation on how to deal with incidents involving "potential agents of bioterrorism."
In other words, the center is involved in Russia's planning for how to respond to potential biological attacks. Reports in Chinese and Western media this week have noted collaboration between the facility's director - who has also visited U.S. research facilities - and Chinese authorities, including participation in a "joint emergency drill" to practice for a theoretical "cross-border infectious disease epidemic" in August.
Irkutsk lab was previously a "cover for a biological weapons facility"
Annie Jacobsen, an American journalist and author of "Biological War," a fictional story about a hypothetical engineered pathogen - a pneumonic plague - accidentally breaking out of a lab in Siberia that was published just a few months ago, said the scenario is what military experts are "most worried about."
When it comes to "the accidental release of a genetically modified pathogen from a high or maximum containment laboratory around the world," she told CBS News, "the number-one worry is Russia."
"During the 80s and before, Russia had a very robust, illegal biological weapons program," Jacobsen said. "The facility in Irkutsk, which is in question right now, was a dual use facility, meaning, yes, it was doing what it purportedly did - which was create medical countermeasures against dangerous pathogens - but it was also a cover for a biological weapons facility."
She told CBS News all the scrutiny Russia has drawn this week is due not only to the reports by independent media of Shipiova dying of a possible plague infection, but also to"the quarantine of some 200 people" under what she said were "draconian measures."
The real indicator, according to Jacobsen, of a serious problem in Irkutsk will be any confirmed secondary infections.
The WHO said Wednesday that it had requested more information after some media reports suggested a possible second infection in the area, but nothing has been confirmed so far.
Russians relaxed, but not their neighbors
Lyudi Baikala, an independent Russian news outlet that was among the first to break the news of Shipilova's death, and to say it could have been a plague infection, quoted a colleague of Shipilova's on Tuesday as saying her illness began with cold symptoms before worsening rapidly.
After she was hospitalized, about 200 colleagues were reportedly quarantined at the research institute for three days, and tested twice daily before being released.
Residents of her apartment building have told Russian media that a van arrived on the night she died. They said people who appeared to be from the national health agency, wearing gas masks and orange protective suits, sprayed the building's entrance with a substance residents assumed was antiseptic.
Tight controls on information in Russia make independent verification of events difficult, but reporters with the French news agency AFP visited Irkutsk on Tuesday and said residents were going about their lives, and those who agreed to be interviewed said they were not worried, "because they [authorities] said there haven't been any confirmed cases, and people who've been in contact with infected individuals have been isolated, and nothing's happened [to them]."
But until Russia offers more definitive answers about what killed Shipilova, Moscow is likely to continue facing questions - and its neighbors may not be as willing to accept its reassurances.
As of Wednesday, authorities in Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan and Uzbekistan had all confirmed the implementation of additional precautionary measures at their borders with Russia, to guard against the possible spread of infectious diseases.

About 28% of companies plan to relocate if winter is severe, 60% seek alternative logistics routes – survey
Ukraine

20:22:26 EEST
02:22:26 KST

About 28% of Ukrainian companies cite preparing alternative locations or relocation options as a priority measure to ensure business continuity before the start of the 2026-2027 winter season, while 34% of companies have not set aside reserves for unforeseen expenses due to potential winter disruptions.
This is evidenced by the results of a joint study by Deloitte Ukraine and the American Chamber of Commerce in Ukraine titled "Winter Readiness: Ukraine Business Resilience Index 2026."
According to the survey, the overall level of business resilience stands at 58%, which is in line with the average. The highest scores were recorded in the areas of cyber resilience (70%) and operational resilience (66%), while financial resilience remains the most vulnerable component at 43%. Most companies have the resources to ensure financial resilience for at least half a year: 62% can maintain critical operations without external financing, and 53% can pay salaries; however, 34% of companies have not set aside reserves for unforeseen expenses related to potential winter disruptions. Among companies that have set aside reserves for unforeseen expenses, the most common amount is 3-5% of total expenses.
Additionally, about 60% of companies have established or plan to develop alternative logistics routes within the next three months.
The survey results indicate that increased support for employees is focused on safety measures and providing additional flexibility to ensure business continuity (67% of companies cited each of these areas). Only 9% of companies consider the current level of support to be sufficient.
The main risk factors for business continuity remain power supply (62%), physical asset security (45%), and logistics and transportation (42%). Among other risks, respondents highlight staffing (29%), heating (28%), water supply (24%), and communications or telecommunications (22%). Business preparedness efforts are ongoing: 60% of planned initiatives are still being implemented, while 21% have already been completed.
To ensure business continuity, companies are focusing on strengthening backup power supplies (74%), supporting employees (47%), as well as alternative heating (27%) and logistics routes (27%). At the same time, business engagement with local communities remains limited: 70% of companies are not familiar with local sustainability plans, and only 10% of respondents have been involved in developing them.
The survey was conducted in September 2026 among 95 business leaders from the chamber's member companies, with 56% of respondents serving as CEOs.

‘Is he alive?’: Bereaved families recall the moment they learned their sons were gone
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
17:21:04 UTC
02:21:04 KST

The wounds will never heal
On the eve of Simchat Torah, Lt. Yoav Malayev had his hands full. Four tanks from the IDF’s 77th Battalion deployed along the Gaza border had developed computer-system failures. During the day, Yoav and his soldiers repaired two of them. After Shabbat eve dinner, he decided to head back out and fix the remaining two.
“One of his soldiers asked him, ‘Why now? It can wait until Sunday,’” recalled his father, Alex. “Yoav replied, ‘You never know what will happen tomorrow morning.’ They worked until 2 a.m., replaced the faulty computers and returned the tanks to operational readiness.”
A few hours later, at 6:29 a.m., his words took on devastating meaning. “People ask me whether Yoav sensed that something big was about to happen. I don’t think so,” Alex said. “But he was always meticulous about readiness and operational capability.”
“Yoav was the duty officer that morning. When the rocket fire from Gaza began, he remained calm, ordered two soldiers to guard the entrances to a roadside shelter where headquarters personnel had gathered and reassured a female soldier who was panicking. He told her, ‘You should be proud of those tanks you repaired with me. Do you know what four more tanks on the border mean right now? What kind of power that gives us?’”
About 30 terrorists stormed Camp Yiftah, which housed, among other units, the headquarters of the 7th Armored Brigade’s 77th Battalion. A small group of soldiers led by Yoav, the battalion’s deputy communications officer, fought them at the entrance and prevented the base from being overrun.
Six soldiers were killed there: Lt. Yoav  Malayev, Staff Sgt. Ido Harush, Staff Sgt. Yoval Ben Yakov, Sgt. Nathanel Young, Sgt. Ilay Bar Sadeh and Cpl. Naama Bonny.
During the subsequent rescue effort, evacuation of the wounded and clearing of the base, three more soldiers were killed: battalion intelligence officer Lt. Sahar Tal, religious affairs NCO Staff Sgt. Orel Moshe and Maj. Aryeh Ziering, a company commander in the IDF’s Oketz canine unit who had arrived with reinforcements.
Yoav’s last message
“In the last message Yoav sent us, he wrote, ‘I’m in the protected area and there’s purple rain over us,’” said Alex, a retired IDF colonel who had previously commanded the Merkava tank production facility.
“At first we thought he had been inside the shelter and was shot there. Then, on Sunday afternoon, the battalion communications officer called and said, ‘It is important to me that you know your son was a hero of Israel.’”
Three weeks after his death, Yoav’s parents received the notebook that had been in his pocket. Wounded and bleeding, his handwriting unsteady, he had written one final message: “The best 20 minutes of my life. We crawled all the way here. I’ve been wounded and there’s another barrage now. Thinking of you, and I’ll think of you throughout the journey. I love you.”
Seventeen officers and soldiers from the 77th Battalion were killed on Oct. 7. Six of their bodies were taken into Gaza. The battalion had once stopped Syrian forces in the Valley of Tears during the 1973 Yom Kippur War. Its soldiers would continue fighting on October 7 and throughout the wars in Gaza and Lebanon.
On April 6, 2026, Sgt. Idan Fooks was killed in southern Lebanon by an explosive Hezbollah drone. His partner, Yuval, an IDF lookout serving in the sector, witnessed the incident in real time. Idan’s mother, Meital, a kindergarten teacher, was at work when she received the news.
The head of the local education department asked her to come to his office. “I was sitting there when the door opened and two female officers and another officer walked in,” she recalled during a meeting with Malayev’s parents. “I told them, ‘You have the wrong room.’ But they just stood there.
“I said, ‘Just tell me how he was wounded and what condition he’s in.’ Then one of the officers came over, held my hand and said that terrible sentence. “I collapsed. After a while, I told her, ‘There must have been some confusion, but I forgive you. Check again and you’ll see it’s a mistake.’ She kept repeating the same terrible sentence until I understood that it wasn’t a mistake. Idan had fallen.”
In the difficult days of shiva, however, Meital found one source of comfort. “When we went downstairs to leave for the funeral, we saw that someone had organized a procession with flags from our building toward the cemetery,” she said.
“We never expected so many people. To see the beautiful side of Israel, people who had never known Idan coming to say thank you, to hug us, to help us, it moved me so deeply. Because that was Idan. He was a kid who always did good.”
More than a bereaved mother
Both Yoav and Idan were the eldest children in their families. Idan is survived by three brothers, Rani, Oz and Raz. Yoav is survived by his sister Talia and brothers Avner and Harel.
“At 9 p.m., we were told Yoav had been evacuated to Barzilai Medical Center in Ashkelon,” said his mother, Dr. Maya Cohen-Malayev, head of the educational counseling program at Bar-Ilan University. “We got there within an hour, and at 2 a.m. the hospital director, Prof. Hezi Levy, broke the news to us.
“Half an hour later, the commander of the military medical liaison unit sat beside me. She told me she was herself a bereaved sister and described how her mother had screamed at the funeral, asking why God had taken her son instead of her. She asked me not to do to my children what her mother had done to her.
“Suddenly I understood that I had a role. I had three other children at home who had just experienced something shattering and needed their mother. I am a bereaved mother, but I am also the mother of bereaved siblings. That is a role in itself.
“What that officer said saved me. I will always be Yoav’s mother, until my final day. But understanding that I am not only a bereaved mother gave me meaning and became a compass.”
Alex said he initially felt trapped in complete darkness. “When Yoav fell, I understood that I could never bring him back, that nothing could repair what happened,” he said. “And that’s true. But there are still many things we can do. One of our responsibilities as bereaved parents is to improve what we can, in society, education, values and at home.
“Yoav and his friends did not stand by, and we try not to stand by either. We try to do good. It helps us try to heal the open wounds.”
“Wounds that will never fully heal,” Maya added.
Meital nodded. “From the moment Idan fell, my husband Gilad and I took it upon ourselves to commemorate the goodness in him,” she said. “It became our life’s work. And it starts with small things. Every person can do one good deed a day.
“You get into an elevator and someone is there; smile at them. Say hello to the security guard at the entrance so he doesn’t feel invisible. That is the best way to commemorate those who fell.”
‘Don’t worry, Dad. You’ll have grandchildren from me’
On a scrap of cardboard cut from a cereal box, Maxim Entis wrote what would become one of his final messages.
Ahead of his mother Larisa’s birthday on April 2, 2026, Maxsim, a soldier in the Nahal Brigade’s reconnaissance unit, knew he would be serving in Lebanon and unable to come home. He asked his sister Zhenya to buy flowers in his name and gave a friend heading home a note with the message he wanted attached:
“Mom, happy birthday to 120. I wish you health, love, happiness and everything good in the world. I love you so, so much, even from Lebanon.”
Maxim was killed a day later in an encounter with terrorists.  “Maksim was killed on March 30, three days before my wife’s birthday,” his father, Leonid, said. “We were sitting in the mourning tent when suddenly Eddie and Zhenya, his brother and sister, called us outside.
“Everyone was standing in a circle around a birthday cake. They wished Larisa a happy birthday and gave her flowers, exactly as Maxim had asked in his letter. He wanted us to keep living. He wanted his mother to be happy.”
Larisa and Leonid entered the world of bereavement only months ago. Dvora and Elad Saadon have lived in it for three years.
Their eldest son, Staff Sgt. Hallel Saadon, was killed defending the Sufa military post on the morning of Oct. 7. He too served in the Nahal reconnaissance unit.
When the two couples met, one question hung over the conversation: Is joy still possible for bereaved parents?
“It has to be,” Dvora said. “Three months after Hallel was killed, our fourth son, Sahar, had his bar mitzvah. We debated what to do and ultimately celebrated as planned. We told him, ‘We will rejoice at your bar mitzvah, and we will also cry and talk about Hallel.’ The fact that we keep living well and find joy in our other children gives much more meaning to his sacrifice.
“I tell his friends that too. Why did he run forward? To protect you, so that you could keep living, fulfilling yourselves and being happy. Just this month, we attended two weddings of his high school friends. They mentioned Hallel under the chuppah, and it means so much to me to see that he is still part of their lives. They even send us pictures from trips around the world with stickers bearing his image.”
“Maxim’s friends do the same,” Larisa said. “They take flags and stickers with them everywhere. When I go to the cemetery, I tell him, ‘Maxim, you’ve already been all over the world.’”
A heroic defensive battle
Maxim, the son of longtime immigrants from Ukraine, grew up in Bat Yam.
Hallel grew up in Elazar and attended the Neve Sharya youth village in the Jordan Valley. “They opened a horse farm there, and Hallel began learning to ride. He fell in love with it,” his mother said. “He competed, learned horse training and became a riding instructor.
“After the army, he planned to go to a ranch in Texas, become a real cowboy and then come back to a ranch in the Golan Heights. He was a cowboy at heart.”
When he was killed, a cowboy bandanna was found in his pocket. After his death, his family launched a major project to renovate the farm, which is now named Hallel Farm in his memory.
Hallel enlisted in the Nahal reconnaissance unit in November 2021 and joined its anti-tank company. In August 2023, the unit began manning the southernmost sector of the Gaza border. “They complained that it was a boring deployment,” Dvora recalled. “‘All we do is guard sand and more sand. Nothing happens.’”
On the morning of Oct. 7, dozens of terrorists stormed the Sufa post. Hallel, his team commander and several other soldiers fought to hold them back. Eventually, Hamas Nukhba terrorists managed to penetrate the compound and the soldiers were ordered to barricade themselves inside the dining hall. At about 7:30 a.m., while defending the entrance area, Hallel was killed.
Sixteen soldiers from the Nahal reconnaissance unit were killed that day, including its commander, Lt. Col. Yehonatan “Barnash” Tzor, and Hallel’s company commander, Maj. Roey Chapell.
“As soon as we heard what was happening on the Gaza border, we called him,” his father, Elad, said. “He didn’t answer. In retrospect, we know he was already dead. On Sunday afternoon, one of the wounded soldiers called and told us Hallel had been killed.”
The official military notification team did not reach the Saadon home until Monday. “That friend did us an enormous kindness,” Dvora said. “He spared us another 24 hours of uncertainty.”
Hallel is survived by his parents, grandparents, great-grandparents, brothers Tamir, Nevo, Sahar and Orel, and his partner, Eliora. On June 29, 2025, Eliora herself became a bereaved sister when her brother, Sgt. Yisrael Natan Rosenfeld, was killed in combat in Jabaliya.
Forever 21
When Hallel was killed, Maxim had not yet enlisted.
He joined the Nahal reconnaissance unit in April 2024.
“The last time he was home, he told me they were about to enter Lebanon,” Leonid recalled, wearing his son’s military dog tag. “I told him, ‘Don’t be a hero. Take care of yourself.’ 
“He said, ‘Don’t worry, Dad. You think I don’t want a family and children? Don’t worry, you’ll have grandchildren from me.’”
On March 30, in the village of Beit Lif in western Lebanon, Maxim was killed while trying to rescue a wounded comrade. Also killed in the encounter were his team commander, Capt. Noam Madmoni, Staff Sgt. Gilad Harel and Staff Sgt. Ben Cohen.
It happened during the Iran war. “There was a siren and we all went down to the basement level,” Larisa recalled. “Then one of our neighbors looked at her phone and said there had been a mass-casualty incident in Lebanon. We went back upstairs, turned on the television, and there was nothing.
“From 6 p.m. until 11 p.m., we sat in front of the TV. We live on the ninth floor, and suddenly we heard the elevator coming up and stopping on our floor. 
“People got out. I could feel them standing outside our door. And after a minute...” She began to cry.
“They knocked,” Leonid continued.
“I told him, ‘Don’t open it,’” Larisa said. “They knocked again. He opened the door, and three officers were standing there. “Leonid told them, ‘Just tell me one thing: Is he alive?’”
“Then they told us Maxim had been killed,” Leonid said, his voice breaking.
Maksim was 21. So was Hallel.
“When Hallel was born, the umbilical cord strangled him and he wasn’t breathing,” Dvora said. “He was connected to a ventilator for many hours. It was almost a miracle that he lived. At the first memorial marking his death, I suddenly had the thought that perhaps he wasn’t supposed to survive at all.
“Maybe whoever decides these things chose to give him 21 years,” Dvora said. “So instead of thinking about everything we lost, I try to hold on to the fact that I had 21 years with him. That’s what keeps me going.”
‘You go from being a combat company commander to feeling like a wreck’
Around midday on Oct. 7, the first organized military force reached the Nova festival site. It consisted of the commander of the Givati Brigade’s Shaked Battalion, two company commanders and soldiers from their command teams, just 12 officers and soldiers who had been deployed in the West Bank at the time.
One of the company commanders was Maj. Avihai Mulla. His wife, Lili, was seven months pregnant. “If I don’t come back alive,” he wrote to her, “name the baby Liam.”
Mulla remembers almost every moment. He remembers reaching a disabled tank around which dozens of massacre survivors had gathered. He remembers moving from there toward the festival grounds, about 400 meters away, and encountering terrorists three times along the route.
“In the second encounter, we killed terrorists who were carrying the body of an Israeli and trying to abduct him,” Mulla said. “His hands were tied.”
He also remembers reaching a yellow garbage container where 17 people had hidden until a terrorist discovered them and fired inside. “When we opened it, 11 were already dead,” he said. “There was one young woman, Naama, who was critically wounded in a major artery. We had to stop the bleeding. Thank God, she survived.”
He remembers the portable toilets. “You open one and a couple who were shot dead fall onto you.” 
He remembers two bar areas that had become killing grounds. “At the second bar, which the terrorists hit with an RPG, there was an unbelievable pile of bodies. We managed to rescue two people who were still alive.”
And he remembers one intensely human moment that captured the helplessness of that day. “We rescued a guy who had been hiding beneath a production trailer,” Mulla said. “The second I pulled him out, he slapped me across the face and shouted, ‘Where were you until now?’
“I accepted it. I told him I was sorry. But it shook me. After I was wounded, he came to visit me in rehabilitation.”
The force commanded by battalion commander Yair Attias rescued many people, prevented additional abductions and killed about 15 terrorists. Yet Mulla remains tormented by the thought that they could have done more.
“The people in that container were murdered while we were fighting on the way from the tank to the festival area,” he said. “Had we arrived 15 minutes earlier, they would be alive today.”
Staff Sgt. S., from Kiryat Ekron, enlisted in the same battalion six months later. Hearing Mulla recount the battle, he said, “You’re giving me FOMO.”
“I studied in Haredi schools and wasn’t sure I would enlist at all,” he said. “I postponed my service for two years. If I hadn’t, I might have been there with you at Nova.”
On April 11, 2026, S. was wounded in a clash in Bint Jbeil. “I was supposed to go to officer training,” he said. “As they were evacuating me, I asked my company commander, ‘How am I supposed to get to Officer Training School like this?’
“He told me, ‘You’ll get there. It’ll be fine.’ At Rambam Hospital, surgeons opened my abdomen to repair the damage.”
He never made it to officer training, but is now looking for a career-army position that will allow him to return to service.
Mulla was discharged from the IDF this week after 11 years of service, in addition to three years at the military boarding school in Haifa. He underwent a grueling rehabilitation after being wounded by grenade shrapnel during fighting in Kibbutz Kissufim, where his force went after finishing its mission at Nova.
Beyond the shrapnel wounds, the blast destroyed his kidneys and he eventually underwent a kidney transplant. “The donor was a guy I didn’t know before,” Mulla said. “A reservist, religious, a real tough guy from Yitzhar.”
The transplant took place on the eve of Israel’s Memorial Day. “After surgery, you’re not supposed to stand for 24 hours,” he said. “I woke up the next morning and said, ‘No matter what, I am standing for the siren.’
“I asked someone to raise the flags of the Shaked support company, and when the siren began, I got out of bed, stood and saluted. People died. How could I not stand in their memory?”
Staff Sgt. S. pulled a sheet of A4 paper from his wallet. “I carry a list of every soldier from the battalion who has fallen since the war began,” he said. “The last name added is a soldier from my company who was killed in Lebanon on June 5.”
After his transplant, Mulla sank into a severe emotional crisis and was diagnosed with PTSD. “You go from being a combat company commander to feeling like wreckage,” he said. “I couldn’t even pick up Liam. Then add all my friends who were killed.”
His condition has since improved. But one sentence, he says, will remain with him forever: “Where were you until now?”

Rubio calls for "unapologetic pursuit of national power" in Acropolis speech
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
17:20:03 UTC
02:20:03 KST

Rubio calls for "unapologetic pursuit of national power," invoking ancient Greece in Acropolis speech
Athens — As the United States wages a costly war with Iran and Europe struggles with the grinding conflict in Ukraine, Secretary of State Marco Rubio stood before the Acropolis on Wednesday and reached back more than two millennia to argue that the answer to the West's current problems can be found, at least in part, in ancient Greece.
In a speech timed to the sunset from the Pnyx, where Athenians gathered for their democratic assembly, Rubio cast ancient Greece as the source not only of Western democracy and philosophy, but of what he described as the character that fueled the West's rise.
"Here, in Athens, we found the first full realization of all the essential traits that would come to define the West," Rubio said, citing "fierce individuality and relentless ambition," and "a yearning for discovery, for adventure, risk and glory."
He argued that those modern Western societies had allowed those qualities to erode.
"The ideal of many ideologies in our time has, frankly, become a world of perfect safety, a world devoid of risk or failure, where neither the glory of victory, nor the shame of defeat," Rubio said. "We hold the most exceptional things among us hostage to the average, the ordinary, the mediocre."
His remarks were delivered before roughly 250 invited guests, including senior Greek government officials, members of the diplomatic corps and representatives of the business, educational and cultural sectors, according to a senior State Department official.
The speech expanded on themes Rubio laid out at the Munich Security Conference in February, when he warned that Europe faced "civilizational erasure" and argued that the U.S. and Europe needed to recover a shared Western identity. Still, his conciliatory tone in Munich came as a relief to European officials after Vice President JD Vance had used the same stage a year earlier to sharply rebuke the continent's leaders.
In front of the Acropolis, Rubio traced the development of the West from ancient Greece through Rome, European Christianity and eventually the United States, citing Alexander the Great, Caesar, Charlemagne and Columbus along the way. He portrayed America's frontier expansion, industrial development and space program as later expressions of the same drive.
Rubio said the West now stands at a crossroads, "because the next decade and the decisions we make will write the story of the next century."
"The course we take will determine whether the West maintains its place at the head of the world or resigns itself to a future of atrophy and servitude and decline. We will either choose to act now or lose the choice to act at all," he said.
"Under President Trump, the United States has made its choice," Rubio continued. "We choose the unapologetic pursuit of national power, to take back control of our critical supply chains, to reindustrialize our economy, to rebuild our defense, to fight for dominance of the technologies and industries of the future."
The history Rubio presented was arguably selective. He spoke relatively little about democracy or political equality at a site closely associated with both, focusing instead on competition, national loyalty and the willingness to take risks. He argued that modern societies too often seek "perfect safety" and concern themselves more with "the comfort of the worst than the potential of the best."
"The men who made the Parthenon, they built upwards. They held that the highest and most noble aspiration in life was to surpass all others, to strive to be the best in all things," he said.
The highly produced speech came during a trip largely devoted to more immediate questions of American power: where U.S. forces can operate, how NATO allies can help counter Russia and Iran, and how American energy can displace Russian supplies in Europe.
Greece was the second stop on a three-country tour that began in Iceland and ends in Portugal on Thursday. In Iceland, amid growing U.S. attention to Arctic security, Rubio left open the possibility of an increased American military presence, saying, "We'd never do anything without cooperating with officials here about what's available. I think there is a willingness to do more together."
In Athens, Rubio met Greek Foreign Minister George Gerapetritis for the sixth U.S.-Greece Strategic Dialogue, focused on defense, energy and regional security. At a news conference Wednesday, Rubio called Greece a "strong and model NATO ally," while Gerapetritis said Greece could provide maritime assistance in the Strait of Hormuz if a viable peace process is established.
Rubio was also asked by CBS News whether he was confident U.S. Ambassador Kimberly Guilfoyle's tenure had complied with State Department ethics rules, amid congressional scrutiny over allegations that Guilfoyle used her diplomatic position to benefit private business interests in Greece.
"This is not the format where we're going to address this," Rubio said. "Suffice it to say our embassy has been doing a great job. Our ambassador has been a strong ambassador." Guilfoyle has denied wrongdoing.
Rubio's visit and Acropolis address come at a complex moment for the Trump administration.
The U.S. is seven months into its war with Iran and has yet to secure an agreement to end it. Vice President JD Vance said this week that Iran would need to make a "meaningful" reduction in its uranium enrichment capacity, raising questions about whether the administration was backing away from its earlier insistence on zero enrichment.
Asked Wednesday by CBS News to clarify the U.S. position, Rubio declined to say what level of enrichment, if any, Washington might accept.
"I don't understand what the confusion is about the nuclear program. Iran cannot have a nuclear weapon. Simple, period and end of story," he said. "I'm not going to go into, you know, into the details about what would be acceptable or not."
The war has also helped push oil and gasoline prices sharply higher, adding an economic and political cost at home as the midterm elections approach.
In his remarks before the Acropolis, Rubio directly raised Iran. After invoking the Spartans at Thermopylae and Achilles' pursuit of glory at Troy, he contrasted Western ideas of sacrifice with what he called a "cult of death" among Iran's "radical mullahs."
"Our heroes may be willing to die for their cause, but they do not worship death," he said.
The speech also comes as Rubio's own political future attracts increasing attention. President Trump has publicly raised both Rubio and Vice President Vance as possible future standard-bearers for his movement.
Rubio did not overtly mention his own ambitions Wednesday, but pointed to recent administration achievements, including the Greenland deal he helped broker last month.
"It is a vision we saw in action," Rubio said, arguing the agreement would "reshape the Arctic and bolster the security of all of NATO."
"We want to win together," he said. "We must win together."

Russia: WHO not able to 'fully' assess plague situation
