Russia: WHO not able to 'fully' assess plague situation
October 7, 2026
The World Health Organization (WHO) said it could not fully assess the situation of the suspected plague death of a laboratory employee in Russia.
"We don't yet have the full picture of this event and we're not able to conduct a full risk assessment," WHO chief Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus said.
Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov played down the reports as "false information," insisting only Russian authorities' official statements should be relied on.
What has Trump said about the suspected plague situation?
Peskov also said he had no information regarding a planned call between US President Donald Trump and Russian President Vladimir Putin about the situation, despite Trump announcing such a call was scheduled.
Trump said the death of the technician did not appear to be linked to a biological weapon.
"We're going to find out soon, but we don't think so," Trump told reporters, adding that Russia claimed the incident was under control.
The US did make a formal request for more information on the matter from Russia, the AFP news agency reported.
Second suspected case reported
This comes after a 28-year-old female technician employed at a plague research institute in the Irkutsk region of Siberia died of the disease, possibly contracting it from a broken test tube.
According to the WHO head, Russia should clarify reports of a "second employee with pneumonia of undetermined cause" at the institute.
While the United States, the European Union and the WHO have all called on Moscow to be transparent about the case, Russian authorities insist the population in the region is safe.
"There are no epidemic risks for the population," the country's health agency said, adding its investigations had resulted in "no emergencies" and emphasizing the plague research institute's compliance.
"More than 90% of contacts have completed medical observation," the agency added. "The results of almost 5,000 laboratory tests did not reveal any dangerous pathogenic microorganisms."
In response to the reports, Mongolia said it implemented "health surveillance and monitoring measures" at the border between the two countries.
Pneumonic plague is a highly contagious bacterial infection of the lungs which can pass from person to person through the air, for example, via coughing.

Sharaa visits Riyadh amid speculation about Syrian role in Yemen

Breadcrumb
Sharaa visit to Riyadh fuels speculation about possible Syrian role in Yemen war
Syrian President Ahmed Al-Sharaa met Saudi Crown Prince and de facto leader Mohammed Bin Salman on Tuesday in Riyadh amid speculation about a possible Syrian role in Yemen.
A statement from the Syrian presidency said that Al-Sharaa and bin Salman discussed relations between the two countries and ways to develop them, as well as the latest developments in the region.
Al-Sharaa was accompanied on the visit by Syrian Foreign Minister Asaad al-Shaibani.
The statement made no mention of Yemen or the Houthi rebels, which Saudi Arabia has been fighting since September.
However, the visit took place amid intense fighting in Yemen between Saudi-backed government forces and the Iran-backed Houthis, with attempts by government forces to take control of the Red Sea coast and the strategic Bab al-Mandeb waterway.
Saudi Arabia is also attempting to activate its Mecca defence agreement with Pakistan and Turkey amid reports that the latter two countries could offer military support to Riyadh in the war, but without directly fighting the Houthis.
Syria has close relations with both Saudi Arabia and Turkey, with the latter in particular seen as having influence on Sharaa’s government, due to its support for rebel forces prior to former dictator Bashar al-Assad’s fall in December 2024.
Saudi Arabia has previously called on a number of countries for help in the campaign against the Houthis, including the United States and Egypt as well as its Mecca Agreement allies. The US, however, has declined to become involved directly.
Earlier in the current flare-up of fighting in Yemen, a social media campaign, promoted by some figures close to the Syrian government, drew parallels between the Yemen war and the 2024 rebel victory over Assad.
The campaign supported alleged Yemeni government victories over the Houthis and featured AI-altered images of Syrian activists in traditional Yemeni dress.
There have been some unverified reports that Syrian fighters may be present in Yemen, assisting government forces.
Hiba Nasr, the US correspondent for Asharq Bloomberg, said in a post on X on Wednesday that “Syria may join the war in Yemen. No final decision has been made, but the idea is under discussion, according to multiple sources.”
During the Syrian civil war, Syrian fighters reportedly assisted forces of the Turkish-backed Government National Accord against Khalifa Haftar’s forces in Libya.
There are reports that Saudi Arabia may be interested in deploying Syrian fighters to Yemen because of their previous experience operating Turkish-made drones and weapons.
In addition, Saudi Arabia may view them as more reliable amid reports of internal divisions among Yemeni government forces.
"There are no Syrian troops in Yemen, and the Syrian government has not sent any. However, Sharaa’s visit to Saudi Arabia may have been to study possible arrangements regarding Yemen, including the sending of troops," the New Arab’s correspondent in Syria said.

Denmark Says Russia Has Conducted Sabotage Attacks Against Its Defense Firms
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
17:15:39 UTC
02:15:39 KST

Russia has begun sabotage operations against Danish companies supplying Ukraine after concluding that broader disruption efforts failed to curb Western military support for the country, a Danish intelligence official said on Wednesday.
The shift reflects a significant escalation in Moscow's hybrid warfare campaign, Josefine Christensen, lead analyst at the Danish national security and intelligence service (PET), told a homeland security conference in Copenhagen.
"What we saw in the spring was a lot of planning, but very little carried out; what we saw in early summer is that they started to carry out a lot more," Christensen said.
Russia concluded that its previous broad-spectrum targeting "did not have the effect of deterring the Western [military alliance] NATO from supporting Ukraine," she said.
Moscow maintains political control over operations, but operational boldness is growing, she said. Russia is now "trying to hit targets that have a direct impact on the front line. That means weapons production."
Moscow has repeatedly denied involvement in sabotage or hybrid warfare operations. The Russian Embassy in Copenhagen rejected the allegations on Wednesday, accusing Danish authorities of making unfounded accusations against Russia.
Christensen cited a Russian Defense Ministry list of alleged European drone and drone component manufacturers that Moscow said in April amounted to potential military targets, without elaborating further.
Russia is increasingly using untrained proxies — including homeless people and people addicted to drugs — recruited via Telegram and other social media platforms. Recruitment typically starts with low-threshold tasks such as reconnaissance or photography, then escalates toward actual sabotage operations, PET has said.
"It could be anyone just looking for quick money," Christensen said. "If the first person isn't successful, they'll throw another one at the problem until they succeed."
Denmark's defense intelligence service last month said Russia is likely to intensify hybrid attacks against the West in coming months, after Germany blamed Russia for an attempted drone attack at Leipzig/Halle Airport in August.
In September 2025, before Denmark hosted an EU summit, drones disrupted air traffic at six Danish airports, including at Copenhagen, the Nordic region's busiest, in what Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen called a hybrid attack on her nation.

Rahul was later released from Barakhamba Road police station, where he had been taken after police stopped opposition leaders from proceeding towards Jantar Mantar.Rahul Gandhi was among several opposition leaders and MPs detained as they attempted to reach the designated protest site to protest against chief election commissioner Gyanesh Kumar and the Election Commission's Special Intensive Revision (SIR) exercise. Burnham, take note: water shareholders have their uses – they can be squeezed for cash | Nils Pratley
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
17:14:17 UTC
02:14:17 KST

Water is “a service where the shareholders never lose and the public never win,” Andy Burnham, the prime minister, told the Labour party conference last week, reflecting the popular feeling towards the industry in England.
And, of course, his big-picture point is familiar: the £80bn, or thereabouts, that has been paid in dividends over the past 35 years represented over-the-top rewards for investors in many cases. It is easy to agree the public was taken for a ride.
But the idea that shareholders never lose is not correct – and has been out of date for a while. For starters, the current owners of Thames Water have been wiped out. Their shares are worthless whatever the outcome of the interminable talks over whether to put the company into administration or opt for a recapitalisation by the creditors (who will get a sharp haircut on their debt in all circumstances).
Meanwhile, the owners of Southern Water have been obliged to shove in cash on dilutive terms. Now comes something similar at Pennon Group. The owner of South West Water, Bristol Water and Bournemouth Water is tapping its shareholders for £550m via a rights issue to fund, in effect, the cost of clearing up past failures.
The new-ish Pennon chief executive, Keith Haslett, outlined an extra £1bn of capital investment on top of the existing £2.6bn in the current five-year period. Of the new £1bn, only £400m represents spending on new infrastructure that can be charged to bills (an extra £10 a year for South West customers if Ofwat gives a thumbs up). The other £600m hits shareholders directly and is the catch-up cost of fixing things that should not have gone wrong in the first place.
Reading between the lines, Haslett seems shocked by what he found. The rights issue document talked about sustained improvement requiring “a fundamental change in how we plan, deliver and maintain our assets” and how previous efforts have been “held back by the way accountability sits within the organisation and gaps in the capability”.
Mr Fixit is not saying it’s an overnight job. All the biggies of water companies’ performance – pollution, leaks and supply interruptions – got a mention as items in need of improvement. The plan is merely to reduce regulatory penalties by 50% in the current period. Haslett’s hope is that, come 2030, Pennon will be closer to earning a few rewards via Ofwat’s incentive mechanism.
The point is that none of this will feel like a case of “shareholders never losing” if you’re unfortunate enough to own Pennon’s shares. Anybody who bought at virtually any point in the past five years has lost a packet. The price was £13.30 in July 2021. Now it is 361p, down 20% on Wednesday with the rights issue to a 22-year low.
For good measure, the dividend is being cut by 30% on a per-share basis to reflect the new equity issuance. Reality has arrived at Pennon. Burnham might reflect that private investors can have their uses: the capital has to come from somewhere and shareholders can sometimes be forced to swallow some financial medicine.
One could take the view that those investors deserve something even sourer, such as outright nationalisation. It’s a point of view but, since Burnham has pretty much ruled it out for water as a blanket policy (we wait to see what happens at Thames), the argument feels academic at this point.
If Burnham, despite it all, is going to live with a privatised system, he could do everybody a favour at this point by hurrying up and deciding what he means by his “public control” overlay. Keir Starmer’s water bill, based on Sir Jon Cunliffe’s 2025 review of the water sector and including a stronger regulator, would have been published about now. Instead, we’ll get Burnham’s “strengthened” version some time next spring, according to the Westminster whisper.
Given that it could take 12 months to become law, that will be four years for the Labour government to reform the water sector. That is shockingly slow. As Pennon’s fundraising demonstrates, even the current rickety system is moving faster.

Votes blocking far-right from key jobs are final, says EP
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
17:12:13 UTC
02:12:13 KST

The French National Rally's Jordan Bardella, left, and Portugal's Chega party's André Ventura speak at a press conference in Porto, Portugal on April 22, 2026. | Jose Coelho/EPA
LUXEMBOURG — The European Parliament can’t review the secret ballot votes that blocked the far right from key positions, its lawyers told a court in Luxembourg today.
In court, the Parliament’s lawyer, Niklas Görlitz, said: “The results of the vote are definitive. There’s no mechanism in our rules to redo the vote.”
The EU’s General Court was hearing a case brought by the Patriots for Europe group, which is challenging the long-standing firewall set up by Europe’s centrist forces — the European People’s Party, the Socialists and Democrats, the liberals of Renew, and the Greens — to keep the far right away from decision-making.
Advertisement
Specifically, the Patriots are contesting elections in which the chairs and vice-chairs of parliamentary committees were selected after the 2024 EU election. Those jobs were filled through voting in secret ballots. The group is also questioning the composition of the Parliament’s international delegations, saying its lawmakers were kept away from key roles.
Lawyers for the Patriots — home of France’s National Rally, Spain’s Vox and Hungary’s Fidesz, among others — said its MEPs being kept from top committee jobs was a “categorical exclusion” and it was “not acceptable” for the Parliament’s third-largest party to be locked out of these positions.
The Patriots have 85 lawmakers in the 720-strong chamber. Top jobs in Parliament come up for grabs again in January 2027, giving the Patriots another chance to try to get into powerful positions.
Hungarian lawmaker Kinga Gál, the Patriots’ first vice-president, has previously called the mainstream parties’ actions “outrageous” and “against the rule of law.”
The Patriots’ lawyer, Azelio Fulmini, referred to the EU institution’s own description of representation.
“This proportional distribution of leadership positions within Parliament prevents the dominance of political life by just one or two large political groups, ensuring that smaller political groups also have a say in setting the political agenda,” he read.
Advertisement
“I don’t know if there’s a clearer declaration than that,” he said, adding that he was reading directly “from the European Parliament’s website.”
Görlitz told the court that all groups can nominate candidates for key jobs, adding: “Not getting the votes … doesn’t justify your tribunal getting involved in our affairs.”
The Patriots’ lawyer accused the Parliament of going beyond the neutral administration of committee elections, arguing that officials helped implement a political agreement designed to keep the group out of leadership posts.
EPP chief Manfred Weber told POLITICO in May 2025 that giving the far right access to executive posts was a red line. Over the past two years, his group has repeatedly passed legislation with the far right’s support.
The presiding judge, the court’s new president Savvas Papasavvas, did not give a date for the court’s decision.

Italian choreographer and dancer Benini makes his debut in Helsinki
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
19:08:22 CEST
02:08:22 KST

The star of the show in Helsinki is Italian choreographer and dancer Simone Lorenzo Benini, one of the performers in the new production “Ghosts of Rosegarden” by Finnish-Karelian choreographer, dancer, and musician Elina Pirinen.
                                    
The show made its world premiere last night, October 6, on the stage of the Helsinki Dance House (Tanssin Talo), located in the historic rope-making district of the capital’s harbor. A three-part performance, conceived as a “Rite of Spring” for the third millennium, blending the archaic and joyful peasant rituals of Karelia with a crescendo of violence against the dancers’ bodies, mediated only by cameras that broadcast live onto the stage the action taking place in the basement of the performance space.
                                    
The ritual dimension of the choreography intertwines with a powerful musical component. The original melodies by Finnish composer Ville Kabrell are performed live by the prestigious chamber ensemble Avanti!. Benini, who trained at the renowned SEAD (Salzburg Experimental Academy of Dance) in Salzburg and was selected by Pirinen for the production’s international cast, is part of this complex stage setup.
                                    
“We support contemporary Italian creativity in all its forms,” declared Nicola Todaro Marescotti, the Italian Ambassador to Helsinki, after the sold-out performance, “further proof of the vitality of the ties between the Italian and Finnish artistic communities within a truly European context.”
“Ghosts of Rosegarden” will be on stage at Tanssin Talo Helsinki on October 8, 9, and 10, before continuing its tour in Estonia and Sweden.

How Hungary’s richest man funneled millions into Orbán’s propaganda machine
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
17:07:27 UTC
02:07:27 KST

Europe
How Hungary’s richest man funneled millions into Orbán’s propaganda machine
Since 2022, companies belonging to Lőrinc Mészáros, who amassed a fortune from government contracts, donated more than $13 million to an online mouthpiece of the Fidesz party, a new Direkt36 investigation reveals.
Companies owned by Hungarian oligarch Lőrinc Mészáros — a longtime friend of former prime minister Viktor Orbán — donated heavily to a right-wing influence operation that peddled propaganda online for the ruling Fidesz party, according to a new investigation by ICIJ media partner Direkt36.
Confidential documents show that since at least 2022 the rail giant V-Híd Zrt. and other Mészáros Group construction firms transferred billions of forints, amounting to almost $13.5 million, to the Megafon Center, an organization that trained Orbán-friendly social media influencers.
Megafon was founded in 2020 to enlist “professional Facebook warriors” to spread conservative ideas, according to the independent media outlet Telex, which found that the organization later outspent both Fidesz and the Hungarian government on political advertising on the platform. Despite its advertising costs approaching $6 million in 2024, Megafon has never disclosed its donors and has claimed to receive no public funding.
Now, Direkt36 has identified payments from Mészáros firms to the organization over several years, accounting for an estimated third of its revenue in that period. The internal records obtained by Direkt36 and analyzed using ICIJ’s research platform Datashare contain previously undisclosed details about V-Híd’s operations.
The findings, which are part of the Mészáros Files investigation, are based on documents including donation agreements and receipts that show a nearly $1 million contribution by V-Híd to Megafon as early as 2022. A list of expenditures shows another Mészáros firm reportedly provided almost $300,000 to Megafon shortly before Hungary’s April 2022 parliamentary elections.
“On behalf of the entire Megafon team, I would like to once again thank you for your previous support,” wrote Megafon’s founder István Kovács in a February 2023 email to V-Híd’s CEO. Only a week later, the records show, the construction firm’s finance department transferred another $1.4 million to Megafon shortly after a request for donations. It sent another $1.1 million a few months later, Direkt36 found.
The donations continued into 2024, when V-Híd provided about $9 million to Megafon, according to internal emails — one of several proposed contributions to the organization and its staff that year.
Representatives for V-Híd and Megafon did not respond to Direkt36’s requests for comment.
During Orbán’s 16 years in power, Mészáros grew his business empire with the help of lucrative government contracts. He credited the former leader for some of his success in media interviews.
“God, luck, and Viktor Orbán certainly played a role in getting me to where I am today,” he told Heti Válasz magazine in 2014. “But … I earned everything through my work and my wits.”
V-Híd is one of Mészáros’ most profitable companies and has received substantial public funds through contracts to modernize railway infrastructure and expand highways. Its website lists no commercial projects yet the firm made more than $74 million in profit last year, Direkt36 reported.
Additional reporting by Direkt36 for the Mészáros Files reveals V-Híd spent lavishly on employee trips around Europe, to Dubai and the United Arab Emirates, and to Tajikistan’s picturesque Pamir Mountains, a popular destination for hunters. Its foreign travel spending topped $3.5 million in recent years, despite operating predominantly in Hungary, Direkt36 found. The records also show that a trust managing assets for Mészáros firms owned two private jets frequently used by the billionaire.
“It’s a vicious cycle,” executive director of Transparency International Hungary József Péter Martin told Direkt36. “Mészáros’s company wins the public procurement contract and gets rich as a result. He uses that money to fund a private company that works to keep Fidesz in power by spreading propaganda.”
Orbán’s tight control of the press was a central pillar of his regime as he turned public broadcasters into propaganda machines and folded favorable private media into a conglomerate controlled by wealthy Fidesz loyalists.
That media empire began to crumble following Prime Minister Péter Magyar’s landslide victory in Hungary’s April elections.
Megafon pledged to keep operating but shut down its website in August after mass layoffs. In a recent public appearance, one prominent staffer described the closure as “inevitable.”

The Atlantic hurricane season has been eerily quiet—Tropical Storm Isaias could change that
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
17:05:32 UTC
02:05:32 KST

Tropical Storm Isaias, a cyclone in the Gulf of Mexico, is expected to strengthen into a hurricane by Thursday, according to the U.S. National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration. If it does, Isaias would be the latest-forming first hurricane in the Atlantic season since reliable records began.
As of Wednesday morning, Isaias sat about 260 miles (420 kilometers) off the coast of Progreso, Mexico, and NOAA forecast that it is headed toward the U.S. Gulf Coast, including parts of Mississippi, Alabama and Florida.
Isaias’s winds are up to some 45 miles per hour (75 kilometers per hour) as of this writing. To be considered a hurricane, winds must hit or surpass 74 mph (119 kmh).
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
If Isaias makes landfall as expected, the storm will likely bring strong gusts and heavy rainfall, with the potential for flash flooding and dangerous storm surge, says Jennifer Tate, a meteorologist at NOAA’s Weather Prediction Center.
As Scientific American previously reported, hurricane activity in the Atlantic typically begins in June and peaks in September. But this year the region has been quiet—with no hurricanes all season. Soon-to-be Hurricane Isaias would mark a historically late arrival for the first hurricane of the season.
The quiet is in part linked to El Niño, meteorologists say. In an El Niño year, waters in the Pacific are unusually warm. This can drive global weather patterns, including in the Atlantic Ocean. There high vertical wind shear—changes in wind speed or direction with altitude—typically make it difficult for hurricanes to form during El Niño years.
“It is common during El Niño patterns for the Atlantic to be quieter in terms of hurricanes,” Tate says, “whereas the eastern Pacific, and the Pacific in general, is more active. And we have seen that this year.”
Indeed, in the Pacific, hurricanes have threatened Hawaii to an unusually high degree this season.
For those on the Gulf Coast, Tate recommends staying up to date on hurricane forecasts, getting prepared with food and supplies in the case of a power outage and following any local evacuation orders.

US mortgage rates hit their highest level in three years
Rising borrowing costs have pushed mortgage applications to lowest level since February 2025.
Mortgage rates in the United States have hit their highest level in nearly three years, as cost-of-living concerns weigh on Americans less than a month before the midterm elections.
The average cost for a 30-year fixed-rate mortgage jumped 19 basis points to 7.49 percent for the week ending October 2 , according to the Mortgage Bankers Association’s weekly report released on Wednesday.
Meanwhile, applications for mortgages tumbled 4.2 percent from the previous week, according to the report. Applications are at their lowest level since February 2025 and have fallen by almost half since the beginning of the year.
“Very few homeowners have an incentive to refinance at these rates, and the jump in borrowing costs has caused many potential borrowers to step back from the purchase market,” Joel Kan, vice president and deputy chief economist at the Mortgage Bankers Association, said in a press release.
Mortgage rates are closely tied to US 10-year Treasury notes. Earlier this week, those hit a 24-year high of 5.3 percent amid surging oil prices tied to ongoing tensions with Iran.
Meanwhile, the yield on 30-year Treasury bonds rose to its highest level since 2002, at 5.7 percent on Wednesday.
Mortgage rates have jumped since late February, when the US and Israel first struck Iran. Since the strikes, mortgage rates have climbed 1.4 percent. Inflation, which has risen by 3.4 percent from a year ago, is also putting pressure on mortgage rates.
It comes as the cost of living is top of mind for voters as they approach the congressional midterm elections that could decide the balance of power in Washington, DC. According to a Reuters/Ipsos poll in late August, 47 percent of voters said that the cost of living was the single most important issue ahead of the midterms.
In a separate Reuters/Ipsos poll in September, 17 percent of voters said they approved of US President Donald Trump’s handling of cost of living-related issues.

France suspends the use of stun grenades after student protester loses hand

France suspends the use of stun grenades after student protester loses hand
The French government said Wednesday it would suspend the use of stun grenades in its attempts to manage the student protests now roiling the country after a 15-year-old boy had his hand blown off during a clash with riot police.
French Interior Minister Laurent Nunez on Wednesday said he had ordered the suspension until there was more clarity around the events that took place in the northern city of Lens on Monday. Nunez said there was a “strong possibility” the firing of a non-lethal stun grenade had caused the teenager to lose his hand.
“I am suspending their use for the high school students’ movement until light has been shed on what happened in this case,” said the minister, who added that 18 investigations in total had been referred to the police inspectorate.
Rights groups, students and some political opponents have accused police in France of using disproportionate force during a more than two-week-old wave of student protests that has exposed deep-seated public anger ahead of elections next year.
Read more'We're fed up': Paris students rise up in a movement that shows no sign of slowing
Hundreds of schools closed
The high school students are angered over dilapidated infrastructure, teacher shortages, overloaded schedules and a lack of funding in education.
They blame the poor learning conditions for France’s worsening scores in the OECD’s Programme for International Student Assessment (PISA), which have fallen faster than the OECD average since 2015, according to the rankings.
In reading, French 15-year-olds, the age when high school begins, scored 43 points lower in 2025 than a decade earlier, the biggest drop in the OECD. Their math scores also dropped the most.
Protests showed no sign of easing on Wednesday, with more than 500 schools closed a day after demonstrations swept across the country. Unions called for another day of street marches later in the week.
French Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu has acknowledged the “legitimate” demands of France’s students but also described the unrest as the most violent student demonstrations in decades.
Far-right and far-left parties are the front-runners in the presidential race to replace President Emmanuel Macron six months ahead of the election.
Under pressure to tame public debt amid weak growth, the government has little spare cash to address student complaints of understaffing, a lack of investment in ageing school buildings and inequality between regions.
The left-wing CGT trade union, France’s second-largest, said it would rally behind the student union’s call for further street protests on Thursday.
“The CGT will continue to shoulder its responsibilities in supporting the young people who have mobilised and protecting them from violence and police repression,” a CGT statement said.
Protests spread in Europe
In a sign the protests in France might spur unrest elsewhere in Europe, where budgets have been under pressure as governments respond to successive cost-of-living and energy crises, students in parts of Belgium have launched copycat actions.
In the Belgian city of Liege in the southern French-speaking Wallonia region, at least 107 people have been arrested in connection with student protests this month, the Belga news agency reported.
Teachers are also on strike.
In Portugal, the main teachers’ union FENPROF launched an indefinite strike in mid-September against overtime, with teachers refusing to do any unpaid work beyond 35 hours a week mandated by law.
“The underlying causes of the [French] protests reflect problems familiar to teachers and students in other countries: deteriorating school conditions, teacher shortages, excessive workloads, and widening inequalities in access to education,” FENPROF said in a statement.
In Spain, teachers’ unions have been protesting conditions in state schools. Teachers in Madrid plan a strike on October 14 to press demands including a reduction in hours, smaller class sizes and higher salaries.

"Continuing to use missiles against Ukraine, against our people, our children, is an absolutely conscious choice of terror. This is what Moscow chooses despite all our efforts with partners to bring peace closer," Zelenskyy says.
He urges partners to increase pressure on Russia and bolster defense support for Ukraine, saying it is important that world leaders understand this and that the world not remain silent.
A pattern of strikes on Chernihiv Oblast
Pryluky, about 150 kilometers east of Kyiv, lies in a region Russia has hit repeatedly. The overnight barrage also damaged civilian and utility infrastructure across the Pryluky community, the city council said.
Ukraine had seen the attack. The day before, Zelenskyy warned that intelligence indicated a massive Russian strike was in preparation. Russia fired about 70 missiles overnight, killing two people each in the capital Kyiv and in the cities of Kremenchuk and Oleksandriia in addition to the Pryluky dead.

Budapest has gone its own way: Hungary will retain protection for Ukrainians liable for military service
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
20:04:16 EEST
02:04:16 KST

Budapest has gone its own way: Hungary will retain protection for Ukrainians liable for military service
Kyiv • UNN
Hungary informed the European Commission that it is maintaining broader protection for some Ukrainians liable for military service. The rules will remain in effect until March 4, 2028.
Hungary has officially informed the European Commission that it will continue to provide temporary protection to some Ukrainians who are subject to military obligations in Ukraine. At the same time, the European Commission emphasizes a common rule concerning newly arrived persons whom the Ukrainian authorities did not allow to leave the country because of their military obligations, UNN reports.
According to European Commission representative Markus Lammert, Hungary decided to make use of a provision of European law that allows EU countries to independently expand the list of people eligible for temporary protection. This concerns Article 7 of the EU Temporary Protection Directive. It allows member states to extend protection to categories of people not covered by the European Union’s general decision. Lammert confirmed that Budapest had officially informed the European Commission of this decision.
"As I have already said, member states have the possibility to exercise their discretion when it comes to applying the framework of the Council decision and the Temporary Protection Directive. This is provided for by Article 7 of the Temporary Protection Directive, and Hungary informed us in this regard that they are doing so," he said in response to questions from Ukrainian journalists.
At the same time, the European Commission did not clarify whether the separate approach would apply to ethnic Hungarians from Zakarpattia. Lammert noted that this question should be addressed directly to the Hungarian authorities.
Context
Earlier, the EU extended temporary protection for Ukrainians until March 4, 2028. However, new conditions were introduced for newly arrived Ukrainians. In particular, people who have military obligations in Ukraine must confirm that they are fulfilling them or have legal grounds to leave the country.
However, EU countries may independently decide to provide protection to a broader group of Ukrainians as well. To do so, they must officially notify the European institutions of their decision. Hungary has made use of this option. Government Resolution No. 145/2026 of September 4 states that Budapest did not support the EU Council’s decision to narrow the range of people eligible for temporary protection.
The Hungarian authorities also disagreed with refusing protection to people who cannot legally leave Ukraine because of their military obligations. Therefore, Hungary decided to retain the previous rules and continue providing temporary protection to a broader group of Ukrainians. The relevant documents will remain valid until March 4, 2028.
Reminder
Back in late June 2026, Hungarian Prime Minister Peter Magyar stated that the country would grant refugee status to men from Zakarpattia who evade conscription, even if the EU decides not to provide them with protection.

German court orders detention of former intelligence chief after spying arrest
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
17:03:53 UTC
02:03:53 KST

A formal arrest warrant has been issued against Germany’s former top spy, with a judge ordering him to be held in pre-trial detention, a day after he was arrested on suspicion of treason and spying on behalf of an overseas intelligence agency.
August Hanning, 80, is accused of buying secret documents from a former colleague and using them to advise a foreign intelligence service, according to the office of the federal prosecutor.
Hanning’s arrest on Tuesday, along with that of his former office head, referred to as Manfred D. It has sent shock waves through Germany’s political and intelligence community, with analysts calling it potentially the country’s biggest espionage scandal since the end of the cold war.
It has raised questions in Berlin over how Germany’s foreign intelligence service can uphold its reputation internationally, particularly at a time of heightened security concerns. Also under scrutiny is the sustainability of rules governing the conduct of retired senior officials and their ability to earn extra income based on their insider knowledge and professional networks.
Hanning was head of Germany’s foreign intelligence service (BND) between 1998 and 2005.
A lawyer for Hanning denied he had been involved in any wrongdoing on Wednesday, telling the conservative daily newspaper Die Welt: “While it is true that he was in possession of confidential documents, the allegation that he passed on information contained therein to the detriment of Germany, let alone for payment, is incorrect.”
Manfred D, who was also placed under formal arrest on Wednesday by the judge in Karlsruhe, has yet to respond to questions via his lawyer.
Hanning is alleged to have agreed in 2010 to pay for information from Manfred D, who allegedly then smuggled it out of the BND. Manfred D, 64, had worked under Hanning and went on to serve subsequent BND bosses after Hanning, before retiring in March this year.
Hanning is believed to have received about 2,000 documents from Manfred D until June 2022, some of which were classified, according to prosecutors. He is alleged to have used the information in his papers for his private consulting work.
Prosecutors were alerted to Hanning’s alleged criminal activities by investigators gathering evidence in a separate child kidnapping case involving a steakhouse restaurant dynasty, which the former spy chief is accused of participating in using his former contacts with Israeli intelligence. Christina Block, an heiress to the business, allegedly paid Hanning and a retired police officer more than €100,000 (£85,000) for their roles in the alleged abduction of her two children from her ex-husband.
A report in Der Spiegel on Wednesday said investigators were looking into a possible connection to the foreign intelligence service of Azerbaijan as one of the agencies Hanning may have been passing information to.
Azerbaijan’s media and broadcasting council denied any connection to Hanning or the investigation. “The malicious intent of the forces behind this disinformation operation is to damage Azerbaijan-Germany relations,” the council said in a statement.
The scandal has awakened memories of the Günter Guillaume affair, when an East German Stasi spy and his wife posing as refugees infiltrated the government of the then chancellor Willy Brandt, leading to Brandt’s resignation in 1974.
Marc Henrichmann, the head of the parliamentary committee overseeing the intelligence services, which has repeatedly raised questions about the post-career consulting activities of intelligence agency employees but has been told legal obstacles stood in the way of challenging them, said he was “fairly flabbergasted” by the affair, but stressed it was as yet unclear the breadth and extent of the alleged wrongdoing.
“As yet we don’t know exactly what happened,” he told the public broadcaster Deutschlandfunk, while acknowledging the need to “restore broken trust” in the BND.
On Wednesday, politicians and intelligence analysts called for stricter regulation around allowing former security employees to make use of their influence and knowledge after retiring.
The scandal comes at a time when Germany is attempting to make its intelligence agencies, including the BND and its domestic sibling, the BfV, more robust, efficient and independent from those of its allies, in particular boosting their powers of surveillance to more effectively tackle sabotage and hacking attacks, amid rising threats from external powers such as Russia and Iran.
The scandal is yet another blow to the BND’s reputation. Not only is it notoriously dependent on information from foreign agencies to foil terror attacks on German soil, but it has faced other cases of its staff allegedly spying for other countries.
It has also been reeling from the case of a department head, Carsten L, who was accused in December 2022 of spying for Russia. His trial is now being heard by Berlin’s higher regional court.
Sensitivities over the country’s past, when dictatorships misused their powers of surveillance to spy on their own people, have made reform of the agencies hard to pursue.
Hanning, the son of a brickyard owner, rose through the ranks of the intelligence service to become its head. After the attacks of 11 September 2001, he oversaw the investigation into some of the terrorists who had studied in Hamburg. He initiated wide-reaching reforms of the BND including bringing it closer to politics, becoming a close adviser to the then interior minister Wolfgang Schäuble. He spoke out against a “culture of leaks” and was deeply critical of the NSA whistleblower Edward Snowden, calling him an “internal offender”.
Once his civil service career was over, Hanning continued to hold a role as a respected behind-the-scenes negotiator, and frequently intervened in government security policy debates. At the same time he built up his consultant business, founding an agency with his wife, Ruth, called Hanning Consult, and worked for various other global consulting agencies. He even produced a “spy cookbook” with his wife, called “Top(f) Secret” (Topf being the German word for saucepan).

What Worries Experts About the Russia 'Plague' Incident
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
17:02:29 UTC
02:02:29 KST

A laboratory worker in a plague research institute in Siberia died last week after developing pneumonia. Since then, local reports suggesting that she broke a test tube containing plague bacteria have fueled speculation about how she became ill. Russian authorities disputed that account and told the World Health Organization (WHO) that plague had not been detected in her tests nor in those of her close contacts.
At the same time, Russian authorities have reportedly quarantined as many as 200 people, which public-health experts say would be an unusual response to an isolated case of pneumonia. On Tuesday evening, the WHO asked Russia for more information following media reports of a second case of pneumonia of unknown cause.
Researchers who work in public-health policy and infectious diseases have been watching this rapidly evolving and opaque situation with concern. Here’s what worries them.
This doesn’t look like the average lab accident
The pattern of events doesn’t fit neatly with the explanation that a lab accident with a known bacterium sickened the worker, says Jennifer Nuzzo, director of the Pandemic Center at the Brown University School of Public Health. In labs that study Yersinia pestis, the bacterium that causes plague, protocols are in place to deal with accidental exposure. Wearing personal protective equipment and working under a fume hood provides some protection. But if someone finds they’ve been exposed, they would take antibiotics, which is an effective treatment for naturally occurring plaque bacteria. “You’d be fine. You don't die, typically,” says Nuzzo. A lab exposure “would be a regrettable accident that sometimes occurs.”
That seems out of sync with the substantial response on the part of Russian authorities. “The magnitude and severity of that response is also worth looking at,” she says, referring to reports that up to 200 people are under observation and that local hospitals have been closed. “Now, that could just be bureaucratic reflexes. But I would feel more confident in what was going on if I knew specifically what she was tested for and what came back negative.” By this time, Nuzzo continues, “they should have a full sequence”—meaning the pathogen that killed the lab worker should be identified.
Much is unknown about the situation, and some experts have said it’s worth considering the possibility that an engineered pathogen, rather than a naturally occurring one, could be involved. Dr. Ashish K. Jha, who coordinated the White House’s COVID response under President Joe Biden, wrote on X on Oct. 4 that “an accidental release from a deliberate program” was a scenario he had long worried about. Russia has a long history of bioengineering pathogens. After the fall of the Soviet Union, that nation’s programs were officially shuttered, but the current situation is unclear.
“You can't help but worry that there is something more here than meets the eye,” Jha tells TIME. “What I will say from my conversations with friends in the [Trump] Administration is that they've been very worried about this…[But] they're not getting a lot of information and data.”
”I'm going to say something that's going to sound incredibly naive, but I'll say it: What I hope is that the Russians will be very forthcoming and transparent about what was going on in this lab, but one can imagine that they may not be,” Jha says.
“If it's plague, breathe a sigh of relief, because we know what to do about plague,” says Nuzzo. “We have a clear solution…The worry is it's not that, it is something different, something for which we don't have easy solutions.”
Are we prepared for an outbreak of a new pathogen?
No, Nuzzo and Jha agree. We are in a worse situation now compared to pre-COVID times, Nuzzo says. “The protections we had in 2019, early 2020–there are now fewer of them, and we are more vulnerable now than we were then,” Nuzzo says, pointing to reduced monitoring and less information flow between countries. “This is why countries need to fund and maintain overseas scientific engagements, because then they know the actors, they know their motivations, they know what's normal. It's also why you want to have a strong, capable, and relied-upon WHO, because sometimes they're the best entity to have the conversations to surface the information.”
Jha also flags the lack of monitoring: “The biggest weakness we have is we have almost no biodetection system in our own country.” If someone in Siberia was infected, got on a plane, and flew to New York City, “we would not know. We just need a much better global monitoring system on this.”
Jha and a colleague from the Biden White House, Nikki Romanik, have started a public benefit corporation to build a monitoring system that draws on search and social media information, clinical information from hospitals, and wastewater sequencing. Wastewater monitoring typically looks for hand-picked pathogens, such as RSV or COVID-19. “Our strategy is you flip it, you sequence everything in the wastewater and you look for anything that doesn't belong. That's how we would detect it,” he says. The system, called BioRadar, is currently being tested in Dallas.
It’s unlikely that the pathogen that caused the lab worker’s death—if it does turn out to be something new—would spread as effectively as COVID did, says Jha. Still, “a lot of the capabilities that I spearheaded building when I was at the White House for preparation for future outbreaks have been dismantled by U.S. Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy. A lot of stuff has been pulled back and taken away. We had put together a whole respiratory virus vaccine program called Project Next Gen that was taken down. We don't have mRNA vaccine platform funding anymore because of Secretary Kennedy. We are not nearly as ready as we need to be.”
What if it turns out to be nothing?
There is still the possibility that in the end, “this whole thing could be just a lot of coincidence and overreaction,” says Nuzzo. “And then people are going to be like, ‘You got us all whipped up about this thing.’ I am here to say, we have no idea. This could be nothing. But when your fire alarm goes off, you don't get mad at it for going off when nothing happened. You're glad nothing happened.” Ultimately, there could be real threats in our future, and the key is to be prepared, she says.
Jha views the situation as a wake-up call to Americans. “Continue to pay attention, because that is important. Secondly, push our political leaders to get much more proactive. Because the truth is, you don't want to get concerned after the outbreak has happened. You want to be concerned before, and build the systems you need to make sure that we are ready for the next one,” he says.
“Without sounding like an alarmist, look at what has happened in the last six months alone. There was the hantavirus outbreak on the cruise ship, and we're hearing from [AI company] Anthropic about all these people who are starting to use AI models to build biological weapons,” Jha says. “There's been this massive proliferation of high-risk labs around the world in the last five years, and so even if this one incident turns out to be not that big a deal, I am very worried we're going to see more and more things like this—and one of them will be a big deal.”

Beware rightwing economic myths such as ‘maxing out the nation’s credit card’ | Letters
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
17:01:00 UTC
02:01:00 KST

Larry Elliott’s column on the rightwing economic myths constraining Andy Burnham’s government should be required reading before John Healey’s budget (Rightwing economic myths could derail Burnham’s project – to destroy them, look to Keynes, 1 October).
I spent 20 years trading bonds, and agree that the household budget analogy bears no relation to how the UK state finances itself. Parliament votes on the spending, the Treasury instructs the Bank of England, and the Bank credits accounts in the private sector. Taxes withdraw money afterwards.
The same accounting exposes the “black hole”: every pound of government borrowing ends up as a financial asset held by households, firms and pension funds. That money hasn’t disappeared into any hole, black or otherwise.
The triple lock is debated as a question of whether Britain can afford its pensions, yet a government that issues sterling cannot run out of sterling to pay them. John Maynard Keynes and Clement Attlee understood this, and so did an unlikely ally. Asked in 2005 whether US pay-as-you-go pensions were secure, Alan Greenspan, then chair of the Federal Reserve, told Congress that there was “nothing to prevent the federal government from creating as much money as it wants and paying it to somebody”.
The same is true of sterling. The real question, he added, was whether the economy creates the real assets those pensions are used to buy. Deciding how to provide the care workers, homes and medicines is a political and moral question of the kind democracies exist to settle.
Elliott warns that Burnham risks becoming the prime minister who asked the right questions without finding the answers. Ending Treasury-Induced Decline, a report that I co-wrote, sets out the institutional reforms he needs. He could start by dropping the wrong question: “How will we pay for it?”
Vince Gomez
The 99% Organisation
Larry Elliott is right: Burnham’s government needs to challenge neoliberal ideas, “the nostrums of the past four decades”, like the one about the government being like a household, if it is to repair the damage done to our social services by the Tories. There are others which Elliott didn’t mention.
The Laffer curve cannot be accepted by a government when chronically underfunded public services are crumbling, and the richest 1% in the UK own 36.5% of all financial assets, with a value of £1.8tn. We must reject arguments against equalising capital gains and income tax and imposing wealth taxes – and of course increasing income tax when fiscal rules allow – which use this old and long-disproved Tory economic myth.
The same applies to the silly notion of trickle-down economics when tackling the excessive profits of banks and companies cashing in on the effects of war. That leads to the Bank of England’s inevitable blaming of wage increases for inflation, ignoring the relatively recent research in the US showing that that most price inflation comes from “companies seeking to maintain profit margins”.
Bernie Evans
Liverpool
 Grateful thanks to Larry Elliott for demolishing the conditioned belief that we must not “max out the nation’s credit card”. Producing and spending is fundamentally important to the ultimate revival of the UK economy and the restoration of industrialisation. My late husband always insisted that we could afford what we needed to and I didn’t believe him. I do now.
Val Bynner
London

Prime Minister Rumen Radev said after a Consultative Council for National Security meeting that Bulgaria currently has no evidence allowing it to definitively attribute the strikes on vessels in its exclusive economic zone to Russia.
Radev said the origin of the drones involved must be established through concrete evidence rather than assumptions.
"If we judge by the nature of the cargo and the ships' direction of travel, then the outcome, logically speaking, favors Russia. However, that does not mean we can claim the strike was carried out by Russia without having evidence. That is a hypothesis, and when discussing national security, we cannot operate based on hypotheses," Radev stated.
He said the government would seek to coordinate with Turkey and Romania and ask U.S. partners to support an examination of the area where the attacks took place.
Particular focus will be placed on the vessel Able, which was hit but did not sink. According to Radev, an inspection of its hull and debris could provide information needed to establish where the drones came from.
The prime minister also said Bulgaria had asked the European Maritime Safety Agency (EMSA) to carry out a free analysis of debris recovered from the sunken vessel.
"An examination of the sunken ship's wreckage should be conducted entirely free of charge, so we can see if any drone debris is found there as well," Radev said. He added: "Only then can we say what kind of drone it was and who carried out the attack,"
Responding to Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky's assertion that a joint effort with Bulgarian services had established that Russia was responsible, Radev said his priority was to determine the facts.
"My job is not to counter Zelensky, but to establish the truth," Radev said.
He said the CCNS meeting had included reports from the defense minister, the chief of defense and the heads of the security services.
"Here, at the Consultative Council, we received very clear reports from the Minister of Defenсe, the Chief of Defenсe, and the heads of the security services stating that there had been no communication with the Ukrainian side identifying the type of drone. As for what Zelensky said - that is his own responsibility," the prime minister said.
Radev stressed that Bulgaria currently faces no immediate threat to its national security, while acknowledging the existence of risks.
"I cannot say that there is an immediate threat to national security. Of course, there are risks. A war is being waged not far from us. As I said, it is expanding its geographical scope and has even reached the exclusive economic zone of the Republic of Bulgaria; however, at this moment, I can say there is no direct threat to the country's national security," he said.
The prime minister also called for stronger capabilities to defend against similar attacks, saying Bulgaria is acting within the resources available to it and its commitments to its allies.

Four companies have joined forces under a new banner called Forfield to bid for work managing the supply chains the Ministry of Defence depends on, according to Kuehne+Nagel, one of the partners.

Roger West, managing director for defence and government at TVS Supply Chain Solutions, said: “In an increasingly unpredictable environment, operational readiness depends on visibility, insight and agility across the supply chain. As demands evolve, organisations need supply chains that can adapt quickly, perform consistently and remain resilient in the face of disruption.”
The stated aim is improving the availability of equipment and materials for operations, with the partners offering a single point of contact rather than four separate relationships. Forfield says the demands on defence organisations continue to evolve, driven by global uncertainty, growing supply chain complexity, emerging technologies and the need to respond quickly when requirements change.

Plan to cut disability support will harm young people | Letters
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
17:00:33 UTC
02:00:33 KST

Reports that the government is considering removing the universal credit health element for disabled people under 25 will be alarming for families (Key disability benefit for young people may be axed under major welfare changes, 1 October). For many, it raises serious concerns about how they will keep disabled young people supported and able to participate in everyday life.
At Contact, we hear from families worried about universal credit and its impact on disabled family members. Some receiving the health element are studying, working part-time or volunteering; others have disabilities so significant that paid employment is impossible.
We recently joined more than 40 charities urging ministers not to take financial support away from disabled young people. We share the government’s ambition for young people to work and thrive, but we do not believe removing financial security will create those opportunities. Ministers have said that those with the most severe disabilities will be protected. But worried families still don’t know what criteria would apply or how hard it would be to prove eligibility.
Crucially, receiving the health element of universal credit does not mean a young person is not in education, employment or training (Neet). Before making such a fundamental change, ministers must publish the evidence. How many young people receiving the health element are actually Neet? And among those who are, how many cannot participate because of their disability or health condition?
Disabled young people need opportunity and security. One cannot safely be traded for the other.
Anna Bird
CEO, Contact
This proposal to cut support for disabled young people rather than provide equal access to welfare sends a message to them that they matter less to society. Far from improving their independence or opportunities for work, such cuts would harm their health and push more people into poverty. It is careless to assume that employment support could fill the gap.
Disability does not discriminate based on age; nor should the welfare system. A wheelchair, specialist equipment, transport or social care still costs the same whether you are 20 or 60. Young disabled people deserve a social security system that respects their human rights and dignity equally.
Rick Burgess
Chair, Amnesty International UK’s Disabled People’s Human Rights Network

Esther Rantzen’s Mama was a lifeline for new mums | Letters
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
17:00:28 UTC
02:00:28 KST

Esther Rantzen (Obituary, 1 October) is rightly remembered and honoured for her wide-ranging charity work, including establishing Childline and the Silver Line. One of the charities that she pioneered was the Meet-a-Mum Association (Mama), founded in 1979. Mama established a network of local groups offering friendship and support for new mothers.
In 1984, I was a young mum with a toddler and a two-week-old baby, and had just moved to Hertfordshire from South Yorkshire. Mama was a lifeline that helped me become part of the new community with access to support, and I joined the local Mama committee soon after.
Esther invited us to a meeting at the BBC studios in London to discuss the charity’s future. She was warm and a true inspiration, demonstrating how important being there for her own family was while she was also trying to make the world a better place. The meeting had to end promptly as she had to get to her daughter’s birthday party on time. I will always be grateful to Esther for establishing Mama and for the difference it made to my life and the lives of many others.
Fiona Lindop
Duffield, Derbyshire

‘I reside in Monaco’: billionaire said to have quit UK over potential wealth tax had already left
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
17:00:00 UTC
02:00:00 KST

When the Sunday Times broke the news that David Reuben, one of the richest men in the UK, had apparently fled to the tax haven of Monaco, there was much pearl clutching. Reuben had moved from his Holland Park house in London to live full-time in the principality.
Labour’s tax regime was blamed and there were said to be fears there would be a cascading effect across the economy, with wealth draining from the UK. It was reported that he had probably left because of potential taxes on wealth in the upcoming budget.
However, research by TaxWatch has found that Reuben, 88, has been a tax resident in Monaco since at least 2014.
A spokesperson for the Newcastle United shareholder, who with his brother Simon, 85, shares a combined estimated wealth of almost £28bn, confirmed this was the case.
Simon Reuben has lived in Monaco for 40 years since moving on health grounds while having cancer.
The principality is a popular place for those who do not wish to pay UK taxes as it does not impose income tax, capital gains tax or inheritance tax.
In July 2019, when David became a director of the Reuben foundation, the paperwork filed at the UK company registry stated he was “usually resident” in Monaco.
In 2024 he provided a signed declaration to a Los Angeles court stating: “I reside in Monaco. I have resided there for approximately 10 years.”
It was reported that the Reuben brothers were “non-doms”, which allowed them to pay UK tax only on income generated in the UK. The then chancellor Rachel Reeves axed this system in April last year, prompting a reported exodus of foreign super-rich individuals.
Asked whether Reuben would have been caught by changes to these rules if he had not decided to move out of his UK residence, a spokesperson said: “That’s an entirely hypothetical question to which it would be impossible to give an answer.”
Mike Lewis, the director of TaxWatch, told the Guardian: “When we started looking into this, we were surprised that publicly available documents completely contradicted a major news story. Sadly, these kinds of stories dominate the UK’s public and political conversation about our tax system.
“The autumn budget may see some of the biggest changes in years to how gains from wealth are taxed. Perhaps it’s time that our politicians, and our media, debate these changes based on public facts and verifiable numbers – not anecdotes and anonymous reports from billionaires and their spokespeople.”
The Labour MP Clive Lewis, who campaigns for a wealth tax, said: “If you want to live in this country, being British, having access to the culture of London, people want that, and there are lots of billionaires and millionaires who do stay because of that.
“It’s instructive that there is a grouping of commentators who put on the scare tactics to say the wealthy are leaving this country. We can see that many of these billionaires don’t reside here anyway, many of them do stay here, and those who want to go, we can’t stop them anyway. This has always been the case.”
Some of the super-rich are leaving. Analysis of Bloomberg’s Billionaires Index has found that super-rich UK residents worth a combined £121bn have either left or loosened ties with the UK since the Labour government came to power in 2024. This represents more than half of all billionaire wealth.
Among those who have left are the steel magnate Lakshmi Mittal, the Aston Villa co-owner Nassef Sawiris and the shipping magnate John Fredriksen.
Inheritance tax changes in Reeves’s budget were also blamed for pushing the wealthy out, and it is thought capital gains tax may be increased this autumn.
The Reuben brothers were born in Mumbai, moved to London in their teens, and went to a state school in Islington, leaving education aged 17 with no A-levels. They started businesses in metal trading and carpet importing. Since then, they have built a property empire.
They own prestigious locations including Mayfair’s chandelier-festooned Burlington Arcade, Admiralty Arch, which is being developed into a five-star hotel, and Millbank Tower in Westminster.

In 2024, Vladimir Putin lost a polling station in this Siberian science district. Last month, three local precincts bucked national voting trends again. Why?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
16:58:25 UTC
01:58:25 KST

In 2024, Vladimir Putin lost a polling station in this Siberian science district. Last month, three local precincts bucked national voting trends again. Why?
Yabloko’s State Duma candidate Dmitry Shabanov won the vote at three polling stations in Novosibirsk’s Akademgorodok in 2026, while United Russia failed to finish first in the party-list vote at those stations. During the 2024 presidential election, New People candidate Vladislav Davankov won at a polling station in a Novosibirsk State University (NSU) dormitory. The news outlet 7×7 visited Akademgorodok to ask voters at these polling stations — students, NSU faculty, and other residents — what they thought of the results. Meduza is translating the report in full.
Warning: This article contains profanity.
‘Fucking sick of the war and the crooks and thieves’
On the final day of voting, lines formed at the polling stations in the NSU dormitory and the university’s main administrative building. Some people who spoke to 7×7 said they waited two to two and a half hours to vote.
Kirill, an NSU student, arrived at the polling station in the administrative building on Sunday afternoon. He said:
There were lots of students around — they made up the vast majority of the line. Of course, there were other people too, but it was mostly students and NSU staff. People weren’t talking much about voting. They were mainly discussing science, exchanging contact information, or talking to people they knew at the other end of the line. Some were recording videos. Some waited patiently, and those who’d come without friends just looked around. I was in line with a friend.
Mark, a student at NSU’s Institute of Intelligent Robotics, also voted in the administrative building. He couldn’t choose between the Communist Party of the Russian Federation and New People in the party-list vote, so he flipped a coin. He ended up voting for New People and for Yabloko candidate Dmitry Shabanov in the single-member district race. He said:
There’s a sense of exhaustion with the special military operation, internet restrictions, and some other problems, but also a growing hope that our votes will make some people at the top realize that those willing to support the ruling party don’t make up a majority of the population.
Other students who spoke to 7×7 also said they voted as they did because they were tired of the war, distrusted the ruling party, and hoped their votes would be noticed. Ivan put his motivation bluntly: “I voted against them because I’m fucking sick of the war and the crooks and thieves.”
For Igor, an NSU student, it was important to vote “for peace.” He feared that Yabloko might “not survive” until the next election. He chose Dmitry Shabanov in the single-member district race and decided to spoil his party-list ballot:
A Yabloko candidate managed to win at three polling stations because people could see that Yabloko is the only party in Russia that stands for peace. As things stand, elections are the only legal way to express our political will, so students decided not to miss the chance to express their views at the ballot box.
‘It’s hard to expect them to vote just to go through the motions’
Shabanov won at the three polling stations but lost the district overall. Across District 139, the Yabloko candidate received just 7.31% of the vote, while the winner, Alexander Aksenenko of A Just Russia, received 45.79%. At the NSU dormitory polling station, however, Shabanov won 51.27% of the vote.
These polling stations also stood out in the party-list vote. United Russia came first in all 10 of Novosibirsk’s administrative districts, including Sovetsky District. But it did not finish first at the three Akademgorodok polling stations where Shabanov won.
Akademgorodok’s distinctive voting patterns date back to at least the early 2010s. According to the Higher School of Economics’ Laboratory for Regional Political Research, United Russia received 22.02% of the vote here in the 2011 State Duma election — its worst result in Novosibirsk — while the Communist Party received 39.16%.
Akademgorodok recorded similar results in later years. In 2020, a majority of voters at two local polling stations voted against amendments to the Constitution: 54.72% and 69.2%. In the 2024 presidential election, Vladislav Davankov received 42.5% of the vote at the NSU dormitory polling station, beating Vladimir Putin.
In the 2025 elections, Communist Party candidates won in three of Sovetsky District’s four city council constituencies. Across Novosibirsk, however, United Russia took 40 of the 50 seats. Ruling-party candidates also lost in two regional legislature constituencies that include parts of Sovetsky District: Communist Stanislav Lysenko won in Constituency 36, and Vladislav Plotnikov of A Just Russia won in Constituency 37.
People who spoke to 7×7 attributed the results to Akademgorodok’s distinctive character.
Akademgorodok was established in the late 1950s as a research center for the Siberian Branch of the USSR Academy of Sciences. It is home to research institutes and Novosibirsk State University, as well as scientists, students, and faculty.
Kirill, the NSU student, said:
Akademgorodok could be considered one of the last oases of democracy in Russia. There are several reasons for that: It’s far from the administrative center, it can develop its own elite and help them reach positions of authority, and our community has a strong desire to build connections among equals and help one another. There’s also a strong sense of continuity between generations.
He said the local culture had also been passed down to the new generations of students who came to Novosibirsk from across the country:
Students go to the same bars and restaurants as their professors, departments preserve student traditions that go back decades, and professors have the courage to stand by their views and discuss them. If you teach people to think for themselves, which is essential in science, it’s hard to expect them to vote just for show, just to go through the motions.
Oleg, a local resident, said voters’ ages might also have influenced the results at the three polling stations:
Most likely, the average voter is a little younger: These three polling stations serve the NSU dormitories and newer apartment buildings… where, 10 years ago, they were trying to house young scientists and their families.
‘My vote didn’t do much to change Russia’s future’
But even for those whose candidates won at individual polling stations, the election results were not an unqualified victory.
Mark said he felt “a deep sadness” for several days after voting: “I’m still aware that my vote didn’t do much to change Russia’s future, even if it helped Dmitry Shabanov win at the polling station where I voted.”
Mark still plans to vote in the next election: “I’ll keep showing that I’m one of those who still vote independently, even if I’m part of a 10% minority. And because I want a more peaceful life in Russia.”
After the election, Ivan felt “empty and disappointed.” He is not yet sure whether he will vote again:
Probably, if the opposition can agree on a common approach, then yes. But as long as it’s divided and our plan B is to spoil our ballots, there’s no point in elections. And I don’t see the point of standing in line for another two hours just to spread our votes across all the candidates.
By contrast, Anna, an English teacher who lives in Akademgorodok, was encouraged by the results at the three polling stations:
I was impressed that Shabanov came out on top at our polling stations. It’s really nice to see that kind of civic awareness among my neighbors. Of course I’ll vote again. I think, in our circumstances, it’s important to keep exercising our civic muscles however we can.

Betting on luxury and cutting costs - Porsche to restructure its business in preparation for an era of declining sales
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
19:56:46 EEST
01:56:46 KST

Betting on luxury and cutting costs - Porsche to restructure its business in preparation for an era of declining sales
Kyiv • UNN
Porsche is preparing for lower sales by betting on premium models and cutting costs. By 2035, the company plans to lay off 9,000 employees.
Sports car manufacturer Porsche said on Wednesday that it is restructuring its business in view of lower sales volumes in the future. The company is betting that a greater focus on premium models will help restore profitability despite subdued demand, UNN reports, citing Reuters.
The automaker, which—like its parent company Volkswagen—is undergoing a major restructuring to overcome the effects of sluggish sales and high costs, said in its business recovery plan that it would lower its break-even point to fewer than 200,000 vehicles. This is significantly below last year's figure, when total deliveries amounted to 279,449 units.
Porsche Becomes a Burden for Volkswagen Group — Media21.09.26, 22:15 • 8639 views
Porsche's global deliveries have already fallen by almost 10% compared with 2022—the period of the company's successful stock market debut. The decline was caused by falling demand in China and the introduction of tariffs by the United States, which negatively affected the brand's two most important markets.
At an investor event at the company's development center in Weissach, CEO Michael Leiters sought to convince attendees that a focus on high-end sports cars, such as the 911 model, would help the company regain its position; ambitious plans were also announced to raise prices on Porsche's 10,000 most expensive cars.
"We aim to strengthen Porsche's status as the world's most desirable sports car manufacturer," Leiters said, outlining a strategy of moving into the luxury segment to place the brand alongside manufacturers such as Ferrari.
In addition
The CEO, who took over the company at the beginning of the year with the task of carrying out a restructuring, said that for now his strategy would focus on cutting costs.
In the long term, Porsche plans to achieve an operating margin of 15% for the group, although, according to its medium-term forecast, a return to double-digit figures is expected only over the next five years.
Last year, Porsche's profitability fell sharply to 1.1%, well below the 17–19% levels recorded when the company went public four years ago under Oliver Blume, Leiters's predecessor, who now heads parent company Volkswagen. The updated strategy initially sent the shares up 5%, but the trend later reversed: as of 14:19 GMT, they were trading 1.2% lower.
Chief Financial Officer Jochen Breckner said that in the medium term, sales volumes are expected to remain at last year's level despite a sharp decline in performance in China.
This market, once the main driver of Porsche's growth, is expected to account for less than 10% of global sales in the coming years (by comparison, the figure reached 35% at the beginning of the decade).
"Regaining our position in China is not currently part of our plans," Leiters said.
Porsche plans to cut 9,000 jobs by 2035, reducing its total workforce by one-fifth, amid growing layoffs in Germany's automotive industry, which is under pressure from cheaper Chinese competitors.
In addition to existing workforce reduction programs and a plan to reduce the number of management positions by 40%, Leiters emphasized that lowering development and sales costs would make the company more resilient.
The company also aims to step up the practice of sharing platforms with the Audi brand (which is also part of the Volkswagen Group) in order to save costs.
