Two men serving indefinite jail sentences freed after two decades
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
16:56:06 UTC
01:56:06 KST

Two men jailed with indefinite sentences for public protection (IPPs) have been freed after each serving about two decades in custody despite receiving minimum terms of two years or less.
A high court judge and a magistrate hearing an appeal after a review by the Criminal Cases Review Commission (CCRC) told Luke Ings and Liam Bennett they would be freed, and also replaced an indeterminate sentence given to a third man, James Ward.
Ward, who was freed in 2017 after serving 10 years more than his one-year minimum and was later recalled to prison, was also in court, sitting in the public gallery to see his original sentence replaced.
Relatives of Ings and Bennett hugged in the public gallery at Wolverhampton crown court on Wednesday as Mr Justice Choudhury told them the IPPs had been “cancelled”.
Choudhury said Bennett would instead be sentenced to four years and 264 days, Ward to two years, and Ings to 42 months with a 30-month extended licence.
All three men’s original sentences were quashed and replaced after they argued that judges had wrongly found them to be dangerous or had not considered alternative sentences.
Choudhury, sitting with the magistrate Norma Grant, told the appellants: “You have already spent considerably longer than those [replacement] sentences in custody. The effect is that you, Mr Bennett, and you, Mr Ings, will be entitled to release without further supervision, and you, Mr Ward, will no longer be subject to supervision.”
The ruling came after the CCRC referred the cases of the three men back to the crown court to review minimum terms imposed on them by judges in Wolverhampton, Reading and Leicester respectively in 2006 and 2007.
Bennett and Ings, now both 38, were 17 when they committed offences that led to them being classed as dangerous offenders and given indeterminate sentences with respective minimum terms of 24 months and 21 months in 2007 and 2006.
Bennett was originally sentenced at Wolverhampton crown court in May 2007 after being found guilty of reckless arson for setting fire to items in the loft space of an empty council property, and admitting criminal damage and burglary.
Ings was sentenced to detention for public protection after appearing at East Berkshire youth court in March 2006 and admitting offences including a robbery in an underpass and an assault on a teenager in a fast food outlet.
Ward, now 41, was 21 when he was given a one-year minimum sentence in 2006 at Leicester crown court for arson and criminal damage. He admitted arson – after setting fire to items in his prison cell while serving time for assault – and was released in 2017, but was later recalled to prison and remained in custody until August this year.
Muin Boase, representing Bennett, successfully argued that the judge who sentenced him in 2007 did not give proper weight to his youth, lack of maturity and capacity to change after a difficult childhood.
In its ruling, the appeal court said there had been no proper basis for the original finding of dangerousness.
Detention for public protection and imprisonment for public protection (DPP and IPP) sentences were abolished in 2012, having been made available to tackle offenders considered a significant risk to the public in 2005.
The law was changed to stop courts handing out IPP sentences after warnings that they were being applied too widely, but the abolition was not retrospective, meaning many prisoners serving such sentences are still behind bars.
The government has faced calls to take action on IPP jail terms, with the former justice secretary Ken Clarke saying last month that ministers should not to be too cautious.
His comments came a week after the current justice secretary, Alex Norris, told MPs that the government planned to bring forward legislation to end IPP sentences “once and for all” by the end of this parliament.
More than 2,000 prisoners remain held indefinitely under IPP sentences, with 99% past their original tariff and 80% having served 10 years or more.

Mexico enacts reform barring dual citizens from presidency
MEXICO CITY, Oct 7 - Mexico's reform to block dual citizens from running for president will take effect on Wednesday, amid criticism that the ruling party designed the move to block opposition candidates.
The reform, which will also apply to state governors and the Mexico City mayor, was proposed in late August by President Claudia Sheinbaum, who defended it as a measure to prevent foreign interference.
Opponents say the move violates the rights of Mexicans who had migrated abroad and obtained citizenship in other countries, such as the United States, and note that Mexico's Constitution already establishes nationality requirements for top positions.
The reform, approved by a majority of lawmakers and senators from the ruling Morena party and its allies, will apply starting in 2028.
At that time, those with dual nationality must renounce any non-Mexican ties before running for any of the positions specified in the amendment.
Next year's midterm elections, in which some state governor positions will be on the ballot, will proceed without changes.
"Today we signed the decree ... No president or governor may hold dual citizenship," Sheinbaum said at her daily press conference. She said the official gazette would publish the bill later in the day.
Cuba, Nicaragua, and Venezuela also prohibit the president from holding another nationality.
The opposition PAN party said the reform is inconsistent with regulations for Congress, which allow lawmakers and senators to hold other nationalities.
Larry Rubin, president of the American Society of Mexico, who holds US and Mexican citizenship, criticized the reform.
"Loyalty to Mexico is not measured by how many passports a person has, but by their actions, their track record, and their respect for the Constitution," he said in a post on X. REUTERS

WHO says cannot conduct full risk assessment on Russia plague reports
- - WHO said it cannot make a full risk assessment on the suspected plague death in Russia because it still lacks the full picture and clear details from Moscow.
- - Tedros said the woman, a 28-year-old lab worker in Irkutsk, died after severe pneumonia, and WHO wants to know what infected her and how it happened.
- - WHO, the US and the EU have urged Russia to share timely, complete and transparent information, after reports of a possible second pneumonia case.
AI generated
GENEVA - The World Health Organisation said on Oct 7 it could not produce a full risk assessment as it did not have the whole picture from Russia on the suspected plague death of a laboratory technician.
The WHO, the United States and the European Union have urged Moscow to release more information after the death of the 28-year-old woman, who worked at the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Research Institute in Siberia.
“The lab worker died after being hospitalised with severe pneumonia. Initial media reports suggested pneumonic plague following an accidental lab exposure,” said WHO chief Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus.
“WHO is aware that the Russian government held a meeting on Oct 2 because they suspected a resident of the Irkutsk oblast (region) had contracted a dangerous infection,” he told a press conference.
Tedros said the WHO asked Moscow for more information on Oct 3, in accordance with the International Health Regulations (IHR).
The IHR provide a legally binding framework defining countries’ rights and obligations in handling public health events and emergencies that could cross borders – and countries are asked to respond within 24 hours.
Russia responded – on Oct 6 – saying no plague case had been reported in the Irkutsk region and that around 200 contacts had been quarantined.
The WHO has asked for more information on the lab tests conducted on the fatality, on the contacts, and details on their health status, said Tedros.
“We don’t yet have the full picture of this event and we’re not able to conduct a full risk assessment,” he stressed.
“Timely, complete and transparent information sharing under the international regulations is essential to clarify conflicting reports and enable an accurate assessment of potential public and risks.”
‘What did she die from?’
Maria Van Kerkhove, the WHO’s director of epidemic and pandemic management, added: “We don’t understand how she was infected.”
If pneumonic plague “is ruled out, what did she actually die from?” she said.
Van Kerkhove said the UN health agency wanted to know what tests were done, the specifics of the results, and what further analysis was being done if the cause of death was not yet known.
Furthermore, “what contacts were put under quarantine or under follow-up; what did that involve; if the quarantine period is over?”, she said.
As to whether Moscow should have provided more information, she said: “The simple answer is always: yes.”
‘Community-acquired’ infection
Silviu Ciobanu from the WHO Europe office’s public health intelligence alerts and reponse operations unit, said that “given the timeline given in IHR is 24 hours, obviously it’s not OK”.
“The sooner we get information, the better the outcome.”
Moscow has said the woman died from a community-acquired severe pneumonia of unknown origin, he added.
Van Kerkhove said there were people whose deaths were ascribed to unknown causes of pneumonia, but there were now laboratory methods that can determine the causative agent, such as PCR testing and genetic sequencing.
Community-acquired infection “would mean outside of the lab”, she added.
Russia warned on Oct 7 against “false” information as reports emerged of a second suspected case of plague, with its health agency saying it had determined there were “no epidemic risks for the population”.
Tedros said he wanted more clarification from Moscow following two media reports of “a second employee with pneumonia of undetermined cause”.
“We asked Russia to respond to that... because any reporting that comes, we cannot ignore it,” he said, adding “I hope we will get an answer to that, formally.”
Between 2019 and 2025, 10 countries reported suspected human plague cases to the WHO, six of which reported confirmed cases.
Overall, 3,847 suspected cases and 423 deaths were reported, giving case fatality rate of 11%. AFP

====================================================================================================

‘The loss is everywhere’: Nir Oz rebuilds three years after Oct. 7 catastrophe
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
16:52:23 UTC
01:52:23 KST

Three years after the Oct. 7 massacre, a woman walks along a path in Kibbutz Nir Oz. Leaving the local grocery store, she passes a construction site, a burned-out house, thick vegetation, a memorial and another building site before reaching home. She is carrying a shopping bag over one shoulder and another in her hand.
Telma Atzili returned to live in the kibbutz about four months ago. Her son, Aviv, was a member of the local community security squad and was killed in the fighting.
She captures the mood in a sentence: “Coming back is complicated. It’s not simple at all. On the one hand, there is good energy, growth, young people and a lot of green. At the same time, the loss is everywhere. The new construction makes me happy, but I also know it is happening in places where people were massacred.”
The kibbutz, which became a symbol of the failures surrounding the massacre, is now being rebuilt at extraordinary speed. Six residential complexes are going up at the same time, with enhanced protected areas and bullet-resistant doors added to new homes.
The old sewing workshop has become a temporary grocery store. The former boiler room is now a Pilates studio, the laundry has been converted into a dining hall, and beer barrels at the pub are emptied quickly.
But alongside the construction boom are far more difficult questions: How many residents will return? What should happen to the homes where people were murdered? What about those who have decided never to come back? And how do you rebuild a community in a place where nearly everyone was touched by the disaster?
It would be an exaggeration to say Nir Oz is bustling, but movement is clearly returning. About 120 people now sleep there every night, roughly a third of the population living in the kibbutz on the morning of Oct. 7. They include returning kibbutz members, participants in pre-military programs, volunteers, members of the Hashomer HaTzair youth movement and families who have come for varying periods to take part in the rebuilding.
Alongside the physical reconstruction, Nir Oz is also trying to create something no contractor can provide: routine.
“We are beginning to see life again, carefully and gradually, people riding bicycles, a pub drawing people from the whole area,” said Emi Palmor, Project Manager for the Nir Oz Rehabilitation. “All of that exists alongside burned houses that have not yet been demolished and all the construction. Veteran residents who have returned tell me, ‘You created everyday life here that makes it possible to come back.’ There is something to come back to, and that is far from obvious.”
It may be the clearest picture of Nir Oz today: new life taking shape inside a place that still carries signs of destruction almost everywhere.
‘My heart called me back’
On Oct. 7, Nir Oz had about 400 residents. Sixty-five were murdered and 76 were kidnapped. Roughly one in three residents was either killed or abducted. Terrorists entered more than 90% of the homes, and many buildings were severely damaged.
Most of the burned and destroyed houses have since been demolished, and the kibbutz is now undergoing a dramatic transformation.
Ron Bahat, who is responsible for the physical rehabilitation, is usually the first person people meet when they want to understand what is happening in Nir Oz. Walking through the kibbutz, he points out different areas and enthusiastically explains what will be built next.
A year ago, Bahat said: “By November, we’ll have 100 people in the kibbutz. By the end of 2026, more families will return, and by mid-2027 Nir Oz will be full again.” So far, the first two targets have been met. The third remains uncertain.
Bahat estimates that about 60% of the original residents will eventually return. The kibbutz plans to fill the remaining space with new families, initially by approaching people already connected to the community and later opening the process to entirely new candidates.
The construction itself is extensive. Six complexes are being built simultaneously. Seventy-six housing units are under construction, with another 106 larger units planned for the eastern side of the kibbutz on land where chicken coops once stood.
Eventually, Nir Oz is expected to have more than 220 housing units. “People talk to us about rehabilitation, but the story here is different,” Bahat said not long after the massacre. “Nir Oz has to be rebuilt.” Today, with construction fencing appearing every few meters, that statement has become tangible.
‘It feels great to see things being built’
Giora Zehavi, 82, and his partner Anne Marie returned in June. He welcomes visitors into his home wearing a shirt that reads “Nir Oz Garage.”
Zehavi lives directly across from former hostage Gadi Mozes. The two were members of the same Hashomer HaTzair founding group. “I’ve felt good from the moment I came back,” Zehavi said. “Why did I return? Where else would I go? I’ve been here since 1965.”
It is difficult to draw out any sense of hesitation from him. If anything, the construction around him makes him happy. “The building doesn’t bother me. The opposite. It feels great to see things being built and created,” he said calmly.
“The Philistines came here and wanted to destroy. They burned my house. This kibbutz will become a large kibbutz with more than 300 members. Right now there are only 23 kibbutz members living in Nir Oz, and I hope more will come. If not, we’ll bring in other good people.”
His age has not stopped him from continuing to work and help. “I provide some services at the kibbutz garage, help with sales, take cars for inspections and try to help however I can,” he said.
“I don’t want to travel abroad at all. I feel like I’m on vacation here, and the atmosphere is wonderful. We have no choice but to look forward. The only way to recover is to come here and be here. When I’m here, it gives strength to others who haven’t returned yet.”
Near his dining table is a painting by Eli Elgarat, brother of Itzik Elgarat, who was murdered. Eli, who died in 2017, had painted Zehavi’s children. A poem written by Zehavi’s son as a child was later added to the painting. One line reads: “Tall trees and some shorter ones, but still, the kibbutz and I are in love.” Zahavi smiles and says he agrees with every word.
Atzili was returning from the grocery store when we met her. She put down her bags and stopped to talk. “My heart called me back,” she said. “I wanted to feel at home. It wasn’t a decision that came from my head or from logic, and I knew I would be afraid. But I wanted to come and try.
“I have to return to this land even though it is soaked in blood. We had a very nice apartment in Carmei Gat, but it wasn’t home. I still have the option of going back there, but I’m here, and I see myself staying.”
Even as residents try to rebuild routine, no one in Nir Oz is truly forgetting Oct. 7. The new homes being built include additional security measures beyond standard Home Front Command requirements.
They include an extra bullet-resistant door, a protected bathroom connected to the reinforced safe room, a larger-than-standard safe room and electric shutters throughout the house that can also be operated from inside the protected space.
The additional door is designed to prevent terrorists from entering and allow residents to lock the protected area from within. The reinforced bathroom means residents can remain inside the protected space for long periods if necessary.
Palmor said the additional security measures are intended as much to restore a sense of safety as to provide physical protection. “No one understood how vulnerable safe-room doors were to gunfire,” she said.
“Since we’ve lost trust and there still hasn’t been a state inquiry commission, in many ways we feel we haven’t moved forward. Three years on, we should have been in a different place. We never imagined we would need to build this kind of protection into our homes.” She stressed that the added protection is being financed by the kibbutz itself.
Palmor said about 20 individuals and families have already registered to join the kibbutz. Some are families with children who lived in Nir Oz on Oct. 7 and have decided to return. Others are young people going through the membership process, including couples preparing to marry and single people seeking kibbutz membership.
Among them are Galia Tzur, 50, and Arnon Einhar, 53, a couple who know Nir Oz well. They lived in the kibbutz in the 1990s before eventually moving to New Zealand. After Oct. 7, they found it increasingly difficult to continue their old lives.
“We felt uncomfortable,” Einhar said. “It was like living two lives. You’re living somewhere where you don’t feel people understand you.”
Tzur described the feeling differently. “We were surrounded by some of the most beautiful scenery in the world. Everything was quiet, and everything we once enjoyed suddenly felt meaningless,” she said. “None of that beauty meant anything to us anymore.” She suggested they leave everything behind, get on a plane and help in Nir Oz. His answer was “Me too, but I didn’t want to pressure you.”
Einhar first came to Israel, Tzur later joined him and eventually the couple decided to sell their home in New Zealand and move to Nir Oz. Their 18-year-old daughter joined them, while their two other children, both university students, have remained in New Zealand for now.
The couple are now in the process of becoming full kibbutz members. Einhar works in high tech and is deputy head of the local community security squad. Tzur works in Nir Oz in several positions connected to the reconstruction, including the conversion of the old boiler room and sewing workshop.
“We sold the house and moved,” she said. “It sounds crazy, right? Friends told us, ‘Go get yourselves checked. Something is wrong with you.’ But to us, it felt morally and personally right.”
‘To choose life, we have to leave’
Despite the rapid construction, Nir Oz is making an effort to preserve its longstanding gardens and trees, which have been part of the kibbutz’s identity for decades.
Ran Pauker, 89, one of the kibbutz founders and its legendary gardener, has also returned to live there in recent months. 
About 45 families have decided not to return to Nir Oz and instead move to Kibbutz Beit Nir in the Beit Guvrin area. The organized group reached an agreement and will receive state benefits.
Families who want to leave independently and sever ties with the community, however, have yet to receive a solution.
One of them is the Maor family. Kibbutz member Yaron Maor survived the massacre after fighting terrorists who entered his home. He and his family decided that for their own recovery, they needed to leave the community and start again elsewhere. “To choose life, we have to get up and leave,” Maor said.
Since then, he has been fighting the state and the kibbutz for what he considers adequate financial compensation that would allow the family to begin again. “The national interest is to return residents to the Gaza border communities at any cost,” he said. “That is why, to this day, they don’t want to formulate a solution, because then people might decide not to return.”
Palmor said the community could not truly recover if some families were left without a way forward. “There can be no rehabilitation of the community if families are left by the wayside,” she said. The kibbutz is now pursuing legal action against the state over the issue, a dispute first reported by Ynet and Yedioth Ahronoth.
The memorial dilemma
The question of commemoration is another sensitive point. Most of the damaged homes have already been demolished, but several remain standing, including the Bibas family home.
A painful debate continues within the community over whether such homes should be demolished so residents are not forced to confront the disaster every day, or whether some should remain as testimony to what happened there.
A decision was expected earlier, but the vote was postponed. Kibbutz members concluded that trying to decide the issue before Oct. 7, the anniversary of the massacre, would only deepen existing divisions. It is now clear that no decision will be made before the sensitive date passes.
Meanwhile, opposite the destroyed home of the Kedem-Siman Tov family, who were murdered, stand the kibbutz’s old library and archive. The building has been transformed into a memorial space for those murdered and killed from Nir Oz.
The symbolic mailboxes that stood in the dining hall on Oct. 7 have been moved there, and visitors will be able to leave letters for those who were killed. Another space will document the campaign to free the hostages.
“We are trying to manage this sensitively and carefully without inflaming tensions that are already extremely difficult,” Palmor said. “The vote was postponed because the discussion is far more complicated than it first appears. There are enormous sensitivities involved.”
Alongside rebuilding its community, Nir Oz is also undergoing a process of privatization. The return is no longer an abstract idea. Residents shop at the grocery store, sit at the pub, eat in the dining hall, attend Pilates classes and are beginning to live again inside the kibbutz. Less than a month ago, Nir Oz even held its first wedding since Oct. 7.
More than 220 housing units are expected to be built. The question is no longer only who will live in them, but what kind of community will grow around them. For now, Nir Oz remains far from the kibbutz it once was.

Yemen war: Who are the Saudi-backed groups fighting the Houthis?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
16:51:55 UTC
01:51:55 KST

Breadcrumb
Yemen war: Who are the Saudi-backed factions fighting the Houthis?
The resumption of fierce fighting in Yemen has pitted the Iran-backed Houthi group against a kaleidoscope of different factions aligned with internationally recognised government and the Saudi-led coalition.
Non-state militias are playing a key role in pushing back against the Houthi advance in Taiz and are leading the counter-offensive to retake the Red Sea coast and the Bab al-Mandeb.
Here's a rundown of the key factions opposing the Houthi advance on the ground.
Yemeni armed forces
Commanded by Chief of Staff Saghir Hamud Aziz, the Yemeni armed forces are active mostly in the country's northern governorates, as well as the strategic Marib and Taiz provinces.
The size of the army is highly uncertain, with estimates varying wildly. Conflict data monitor ACLED estimates a troop count of 300,000-400,000 while others put the figure in the tens of thousands.
The government is trying to add thousands more to the army's ranks, with Rashad al-Alimi, the head of Yemen's Presidential Council, calling for a general mobilisation ahead of this week's counter-offensive.
Giants Brigades
The Giants Brigades are among the largest armed factions fighting with the Saudi-led coalition against the Houthis, with up to 30,000 fighters thought to be inside its ranks.
The militia is composed of tribal and Salafi elements and is commanded by Abdulrahman al-Mahrami, known by his kunya Abu Zaraa, who sits on the Presidential Leadership Council. The brigades were formerly backed by the UAE but have aligned with the Saudis after Emirati forces withdrew from the country earlier this year and have assumed responsibility for security in Aden.
The brigades are deployed throughout Yemen but are concentrated particularly in the Taiz, Lahej, and al-Dhale governorates. They are playing a leading role in the government's ongoing offensive to recapture the Red Sea from the Houthis and have been involved in fighting around the Bab al-Mandeb and the coastal town of Dhubab.
Nation's Shield Forces
The Nation's Shield Forces were established by al-Alimi in early 2023 and are Saudi Arabia's principal proxy force on the ground.
The group is thought to have between 30,000 and 45,000 tribal and Salafist fighters in its ranks, mainly from the eastern regions of Hadramawt and Al-Mahra. It was assembled by Saudi Arabia partly as a counter to the UAE-backed secessionist forces in the south. Since Emirati forces withdrew from the country, they have been deployed across the south, and recently to the northern Al-Jawf region.
The forces are commanded by Brigadier-General Bassam Mahdhar al-Sanabi.
National Resistance Forces
The National Resistance Forces (NRF) were first formed in 2017 and are led by Tareq Saleh, a member of the Presidential Leadership Council and nephew of the late former president Ali Abdullah Saleh.
The NRF suffered major setbacks during the Houthis' recent Red Sea offensive. Saleh reported that more than 500 of its fighters were killed and another 1,500 wounded as the Iran-backed group seized its stronghold in the port city of Mocha.
The group was originally backed by Abu Dhabi but is now fully aligned with the Saudi-backed government. It supports a unified Yemen but has avoided major clashes with southern secessionist forces also sponsored by the UAE.
Tihama Resistance Forces
The Tihama Resistance Forces originate from the eponymous coastal region, which stretches the length of Yemen's Red Sea coast from the Saudi border in the north to the Bab al-Mandeb in the south. It encompasses several key cities, including Hodeidah, which was seized by the Houthis in 2021, and Mocha.
The militia was first founded in 2014 to fight against Houthi control of Yemen's western region but was restructured as an affiliate of the NRF following the Iran-backed group's capture of Mocha. Announcing the reorganisation of the unit, Tareq Saleh said Tihama Resistance would be composed of fighters from the NRF's first and second battalions and would report directly to the Saudi-led coalition.
It is commanded by Major-General Zayed Mansir, a veteran Tihami military leader. The number of fighters in the group is unknown.

Israel’s olive harvest policy leaves Palestinian farmers shut out - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
16:49:32 UTC
01:49:32 KST

A map of the closure orders for the olive harvest season in the West Bank was published by the Israeli Civil Administration on September 29.
This set of orders, also known as the “coordination mechanism,” covers approximately 90,000 dunams this year – an area equivalent in size to the combined area of Tel Aviv-Jaffa, Ramat Gan, and Herzliya.
In these extensive areas, the military prevents Palestinian landowners from entering their privately owned land without “coordination.” What appears to be yet another routine set of orders issued by the military in territory occupied by Israel is, in fact, a draconian bureaucratic mechanism that completes the violent reality on the ground.
The olive harvest is a national and cultural Palestinian symbol, as well as a significant source of livelihood for tens of thousands of families in the West Bank who depend on it for their livelihood.
More than a decade ago, following the growing number of violent incidents by settlers against Palestinians, the military decided to establish a “coordination mechanism.”
Military coordination limits Palestinian's olive harvest
Under this mechanism, the military prevents Palestinian farmers from reaching their privately owned lands located near Israeli settlements and outposts, allowing them access only twice a year – to plow the land in the spring and to harvest the trees in the autumn.
The military is supposed to coordinate days on which soldiers will accompany the Palestinian farmers and protect them while they carry out the harvest and agricultural work.
However, past experience shows that when coordination is granted, it is usually too late (after settlers have already had time to steal a significant portion of the crop), with little advance notice, and for too short a time.
Moreover, not coincidentally, whenever and wherever Palestinians are coordinated to harvest, violent settlers also arrive at the site.
Then, instead of restricting the actions of settlers seeking to disrupt the harvesters, the military expels the Palestinian landowners and prevents them from harvesting their crops.
Thus, the “coordination mechanism” created by the military is ostensibly intended to protect Palestinians from settler violence, but in practice, it serves as a tool for preventing the olive harvest.
The total area covered this year by the closure orders that constitute the “coordination mechanism” has increased by approximately 10,000 dunams compared with last year.
This figure is not surprising. It results from the enormous proliferation of outposts in the West Bank. These outposts bring systematic violence against Palestinians with them.
The olive harvest season in the West Bank will officially begin only in mid-October. Meanwhile, since the first day of Sukkot, Yesh Din has already documented 107 incidents of settler violence related to the harvest in 73 different Palestinian villages, including attacks on Palestinian harvesters, expulsions from land, the cutting down of trees, and the theft of crops.
Settler violence, both during and beyond the harvest days, occurs under the surveillance of the military. In many of the violent incidents, soldiers were present and prevented Palestinians from reaching and harvesting their land; in other cases, they did not stop settlers who disrupted the harvest or attacked the harvesters.
For example, on Saturday morning, an armed settler summoned a military force to a Palestinian family from the village of Madama that was harvesting its private olive grove.
Armed soldiers arrived at the site, detained the family members, handcuffed them, and blindfolded them. “You are under arrest because you harvested olives,” the soldiers told them. “Tell the entire village that no one is allowed to come and harvest.”
The detainees were taken to a nearby military post and held on the ground in the open air. After more than six hours during which they remained handcuffed and blindfolded, without water or food, they were released without interrogation or charges, and without being able to harvest their trees.
This family’s plot in Madama is not even in an area requiring coordination. Still, the settler and the soldiers acted in line with the prevailing mood emanating from Jerusalem.
The combination of the “coordination mechanism,” settler violence, and the cooperation of the soldiers reveals the full picture.
In a vicious cycle, settlers use the military to drive Palestinians from their privately owned land; settlers then build an outpost on it; the military then issues an order prohibiting Palestinians from entering the area; and the cycle repeats itself – plot by plot, village by village.
The settlers serve the military, and the military serves the settlers. Both share a common goal: to prevent the harvesting and cultivation of agricultural land, economically harm Palestinians, push them off their land, and take control of it.
Not many years ago, the military boasted that it allowed Palestinians to harvest under the cynical slogan “until the last olive.” Today, the State of Israel – through its military orders, soldiers, and settlers – is effectively implementing a policy of preventing the olive harvest in the West Bank, starting with the very first olive.
The writer is the head of the research department at Yesh Din.

ILF launches dictionary to reclaim 'hijacked' terms related to October 7, Israel-Hamas war
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
16:49:04 UTC
01:49:04 KST

On the third anniversary of October 7, the International Legal Forum launched its ‘Dictionary of Terms,’ an online resource aimed at reclaiming terms it argues have been hijacked and inverted by anti-Israel activists.
The Israel-based ILF is a network of 4,000 lawyers led by CEO Michal Cotler-Wunsh.
Cotler-Wunsh took to social media today to announce the release of the Dictionary of Terms website (www.dictionaryofterms.org) with the hope that it will help “remember, reclaim, and renew the foundational principles of the law that have been systematically hijacked, redefined, inverted, and weaponized.”
“When terms such as “genocide,” “apartheid,” “war crimes,” and “crimes against humanity” are detached from their legal definitions and repurposed as weapons, the consequences extend far beyond the courtroom or classroom; the integrity of law itself risks collapse,” ILF said.
ILF describes a hijacked term as a word with a precise meaning in law or history that has been stripped of that meaning and repurposed as a political weapon.
The dictionary so far has nine terms, with six more in progress.
Users can submit terms to reclaim their original meanings
Under each term, a user can find the definition under international law, the background, examples, and a description of how the term has been weaponized and by whom.
There is also the option for users to submit a term.
“Three years of responses to the October 7 massacre and the multi-front war waged that day have exposed an additional existential warfront," said Cotler-Wunsh.
“This resource, which remembers the origins of these terms, reclaims their original meaning, and renews the shared pledge to uphold and protect them equally and consistently–is vital to fighting and winning this raging war that threatens humanity and freedom.
Alongside the website launch is a social media campaign featuring international experts from around the world who have joined ILF in its mission. The list of experts includes Irwin Cotler, Gerald Steinberg, and Natan Sharansky.
Cotler-Wunsh told the Post that the dictionary is not just a resource "for lawyers" but for the general public which "uses these terms in this war of words."
“The target demographic is actually all individuals across places and spaces.”

Israel is not Netanyahu: The Jewish case against political idolization - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
16:48:56 UTC
01:48:56 KST

Three years ago, Israel failed us. And here we are, still living with the consequences of October 7, 2023.
And in just 20 days, on October 27, Israelis will go to the polls. Benjamin Netanyahu is running for prime minister again.
Each election we say that it’s the most important. This one might actually be.
Because there are still Israelis praising “King Bibi” and preaching loyalty to the man who was in charge when thousands of our people were massacred.
That gives me cult energy.
And frankly, it isn’t Jewish.
Netanyahu has been in charge for way too long. He has spent roughly two decades altogether as prime minister.
During the years in which he was the prime minister, Hamas grew into a powerful terrorist organization in Gaza. Israel repeatedly chose policies of containment and deterrence toward Hamas rather than removing it from power.
Then, on October 7, 2023, Hamas infiltrated Israel by air, land, and sea, and our government failed to protect us.
That failure doesn’t belong to one person alone. The October 7 disaster involved failures across the political and security establishment, and those failures deserve accountability.
But Netanyahu was the prime minister.
That matters.
Three years ago, the worst massacre of Jews since the Holocaust happened on his watch.
That doesn’t automatically mean every decision made under his government caused October 7. It does mean that after such a catastrophic failure, Israelis are entitled to demand accountability from the people who were responsible for the country when it happened.
And this is where the Jewish part of this conversation matters.
The Torah says: “You shall not show partiality in judgment; you shall hear the small and the great alike” (Deuteronomy 1:17).
That’s the great and the small alike.
It is not: “Unless the great is your favorite politician.”
It is not: “Unless he has been prime minister for a very long time.”
And when the Torah talks about a king, it specifically warns that his heart should not become “lifted above his brethren” (Deuteronomy 17:20).
Judaism is profoundly suspicious of the human tendency to turn leaders into symbols larger than themselves.
Israel has no kings
Enough idolization of Netanyahu.
It’s weird, un-Jewish, and frankly, gross.
Developed democracies have term limits and other mechanisms limiting the concentration of political power for a reason. Israel is a young democracy, and we are still building some of the institutions and guardrails that older democracies have had much longer to develop.
But Netanyahu has been in power for a very, very long time.
And when one person becomes so synonymous with a country’s politics that criticism of him is treated as criticism of the country itself, something has gone seriously wrong.
Israel is not Netanyahu.
Netanyahu is not Israel.
Loving Israel does not require loving the person sitting in the prime minister’s chair.
Then there is the coalition.
In recent years, we have watched our government take a dangerous turn with extremist leaders such as National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir and Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich, who represent a minority of Israelis yet have Netanyahu under their thumb.
Without their parties, Netanyahu couldn’t have built his governing coalition after the last election.
How is that a democracy?
I’m not saying their voters don’t count. Of course they do. That’s a democracy.
But it is completely legitimate to question what happens when a prime minister becomes politically dependent on a small bloc whose priorities can determine the direction of an entire country.
And we saw how political and security priorities intersected even before October 7.
Two companies of IDF Commando Brigade troops – around 100 soldiers – that had been deployed to the Gaza border during the Jewish holiday season were sent to the West Bank just two days before October 7, amid heightened tensions there.
The troops were reserve forces used to bolster security in different regions, rather than the regular forces responsible for routine security along the Gaza border. The IDF said the General Staff made the decision based on a situational assessment and that it would be investigated.
That distinction matters.
So does the larger question.
Why were our security priorities what they were on that day?
Why did we miss so many warning signs?
Why was the country so catastrophically unprepared?
And who is responsible for answering those questions?
As a liberal Zionist Israeli content creator and activist, it gets harder to do my job when racist, extremist men who hold official positions in government say disgusting things on the world stage.
Things that, in my experience, do not represent the majority of Israeli society or the values I believe our country should stand for.
I spend my days explaining Israel to the world.
I talk about our democracy, our diversity, our creativity, our resilience, and our ability to argue with each other while still believing that this tiny country is worth fighting for.
Then I have to explain the people representing us.
And frankly, I’m tired of it.
But I am not giving up on Israel.
Quite the opposite.
I believe in an Israel that is strong enough to defend itself, confident enough to criticize itself, and democratic enough to hold its leaders accountable.
That is not anti-Israel.
That is Israel.
And perhaps the most important thing to remember going into this election is that we actually have choices.
Israel is not facing a binary between Netanyahu and chaos.
Experienced people have served this country in government, in the military, and in public life, people like Gadi Eisenkot, Yair Lapid, and Naftali Bennett.
They don’t agree on everything, and they shouldn’t.
That’s what a democracy is supposed to look like.
Different visions. Different priorities. Different leaders competing for the opportunity to lead.
We don’t have to agree on every policy to understand that Israel is bigger than one man – and that a healthy democracy requires the possibility of political change.
To criticize a Jewish leader is not a rejection of Jewish tradition.
In many ways, it is one of Judaism’s oldest traditions.
The Torah doesn’t sanitize its heroes.
Moses fails. David abuses his power. The prophet Nathan stands before the king and tells him: “You are the man” (The Book of Samuel 2:12:7).
Our tradition doesn’t demand that we pretend our leaders are perfect.
It demands that we tell the truth about them.
Three years after October 7, I think we owe ourselves that much.
No more kings.
No more saviors.
No more treating politicians like they are bigger than the country they serve.
We need leaders.
And we need to hold them accountable.
Because Israel is bigger than Netanyahu.
And our democracy should be, too.
The writer is an activist and content creator. A third-generation IDF veteran with over a decade in Israel advocacy, she has created and executed content for dozens of major organizations. She is an associate at the Tel Aviv Institute.

She also served as the minister of energy and mining from 2008 to 2011.

‘We are brothers’: After losing loved ones, an Israeli and a Palestinian join forces to show peace is possible
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
16:48:09 UTC
01:48:09 KST

- i24NEWS
- Israel-Hamas war
- Is peace possible after October 7? This Israeli and Palestinian think so
Is peace possible after October 7? This Israeli and Palestinian think so
"Two people who've lost family members who have every reason to hate each other. We're not just friends. We are brothers.”
In the early hours of October 7, 2023, Maoz Inon began receiving alarming messages from his parents, Bilha and Yakov Inon. They couple lived in Netiv Ha'asara, a moshav just steps away from the Gaza border.
Air sirens were wailing. There was some sort of escalation in the seemingly never-ending war between Israel and Hamas, and the elderly couple could hear shooting and shouting. Bilha and Yakov wrote to the family group chat that they were in the safe room of their home.
While rocketfire from Gaza was not unusual, Yakov wrote that this was no ordinary escalation. Something huge was happening.
Maoz phoned his parents. “I just told him, Daddy, I love you, tell mom that I love her… I will get ready for the day and I will call you in a few minutes.”
But the next time Maoz called, just a short while later, there was no answer.
The Inon siblings frantically called others in Netiv Ha'asara. It took them nearly nine hours to receive a reply. A neighbor of Bilha and Yakov delivered the devastating news to the family.
“He told us that my parents' house is burned to ashes, and there are two bodies inside,” Maoz said.
Bilha, 75, and Yakov, 78, were lifelong peace activists. Bilha was an artist, and painted mandalas daily in her turquoise-colored art studio. Yakov was an agronomist, and traveled the country consulting farmers.
While Yakov was initially listed among those murdered on October 7, it would take investigators around 10 months to identify the remains of Bilha. She was the last person said to be missing after the onslaught, and was finally declared dead in August 2024.
Through their pain, the surviving Inon family immediately decided to make a joint decision, one that would set Maoz on a new life path. That of a peacemaker.
“My young brother told us we must make a family decision. We must choose to reject revenge. He said that it will only escalate the cycle of fear, bloodshed, and trauma that we, Palestinians and Israelis, have been trapped within for a century. To memorialize my parents' legacy, and the way they raised and educated us, we must create an alternative path – a path to peace and reconciliation.”
Before the first IDF tanks would even roll into Gaza, the Inon siblings set off on a media blitz, taking to global news broadcasts armed with their message that peace was the only way forward. This, despite Maoz’s heartbreak at the loss of their parents, and fury with the Israeli government.
Even on October 7, while still awaiting news of his parents’ fate, Maoz had already begun posting on Facebook. “I already started sharing on my social media that the blood is on your hand. By your hand, I meant the Israeli government,” he said.
As the days went by, Maoz posted more, about his parents, and his devastation.
That’s when Maoz received a message of condolences from a Palestinian man from East Jerusalem, named Aziz Abu Sarah.
“I was literally drowning in the ocean of soul and pain,” Maoz said. “And when Aziz reached out to me, it was like a hand, reaching out and saving me from drowning.”
Aziz was a peace activist, and too had suffered great loss in the shadow of the Israeli-Palestinian conflict.
“I was not born as a peacemaker,” Aziz said. “If anything, I grew up opposed to it. I was shot at [for the] first time I think when I was 8-years-old.”
Aziz’s beloved older brother Tayseer died in 1990, following Israeli military detention for throwing stones. Aziz says his brother was severely abused while imprisoned, and shortly after his release, died from untreated trauma to his internal organs.
“I grew up very angry, very much feeling that vengeance is the only way,” Aziz said. But when he turned 18-years-old, things started to change.
Despite it being mandatory to learn Hebrew in his high school, Aziz had resisted learning it. “I refused to learn [Hebrew] because I saw it as the language of the enemy. [But] I realized that's a big mistake, because if you don't speak Hebrew in Jerusalem, the only job you really can get is a dishwasher or things like that.”
Aziz then made the unusual decision to study Hebrew in an Ulpan.
“I was the only Palestinian in that classroom,” Aziz said." And it was a very transformational experience because my Hebrew teacher just was an incredible person who went out of her way to make me feel welcome, and to treat me as an equal.”
Aziz went on to become a peace activist and author, and founded a tour company that provided dual-narrative tours, where stories were told from both the Israeli and Palestinian perspectives.
After Aziz reached out to Maoz, the two realized they had a shared vision for the future. One where there was peace and reconciliation between Israelis and Palestinians. They began speaking together publicly, and telling their stories.
The pair started to gain momentum, and it wasn’t long before they realized they had something special.
Since then, they’ve given a TED talk that has millions of views, have met two Popes, been guests on late-night shows and podcasts, and most recently, addressed the United Nations Security Council during the General Assembly in New York. They were also the first Israeli–Palestinian duo to serve as Peace Torchbearers for the Milano-Cortina 2026 Winter Olympic Games.
The pair also authored a book together, titled “The Future is Peace,” and are in the middle of an international book tour. The book is currently available in English, but will soon be released in both Hebrew and Arabic.
These days, the two are often by each other’s side, regularly address audiences of thousands of people, and tend to open their speeches with a hug.
“In the last few years, I am now very honored and proud to say that, yes, I lost my parents, I lost childhood friends. I lost people I knew my entire life, but I won Aziz as a brother,” said Maoz.
“The two of us doing this work provides people with an example,” said Aziz. “Two people who've lost family members who have every reason to hate each other. We're not just friends. We are brothers.”
But is a future of peace between Israelis and Palestinians possible, like Maoz and Aziz say?
A recent Pew survey finds a majority of Israelis and Palestinians say two-state coexistence is impossible. West Bank settler violence is escalating. And in the upcoming Israeli election, a two-state solution is not on the agenda for any leading candidate for prime minister.
Aziz and Maoz are well aware of these political realities.
That’s why they say their peace plan is not about a specific political framework. Plans already exist. But these deals sit idle, because they don’t have the political support to become reality.
So, instead of a specific plan that outlines borders, Maoz and Aziz are focused on generating the grassroots support that could one day make a peace deal politically possible.
“We are talking about a set of values that we will base and build our vision upon,” Maoz said. “And this set of values is equality and dignity, shared acknowledgement and recognition, reconciliation and healing, security and safety for both people, for all people.”
Once, on a flight, someone told Aziz that he was naive for his vision, because the pair hadn’t yet succeeded.
“It's interesting, if somebody next to you is working on cancer research, would you have told them they are naive because we still don't have a proper vaccination for cancer?” Aziz said.
“Even if you think our chances are low, treat us like you treat other people trying to solve problems in our world.”
Maoz and Aziz say that history proves that all conflicts end, and one day, so will the Israeli-Palestinian conflict. But how much loss must both sides experience until that day comes?
“The question we should ask ourselves, and this is the question Aziz and I ask everyone who is willing to listen to us is, what can we do in order to [ensure] this inevitable future happens soon, and to save many, many lives?”

Books Burned in Russian Attack on Kharkiv Become Art Installation at Frankfurt Book Fair
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
16:47:22 UTC
01:47:22 KST

- Category
- Culture
Books Burned in Russian Attack on Kharkiv Become Art Installation at Frankfurt Book Fair
Twenty-two books damaged in a Russian attack on the Ranok publishing house’s logistics center in Kharkiv have been brought to Germany and incorporated into an art installation at Ukraine’s National Stand at the 2026 Frankfurt Book Fair.
The installation, titled Born/Burn Alive, was created by Ukrainian artist Valentyna Veremko and features books recovered after the August 1 attack on Ranok’s automated logistics center. It will be displayed throughout the Frankfurt Book Fair from October 7 to 11.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The books, with burned pages and traces of ash, are arranged in a vertical tower inside a glass display case. They are among the surviving copies from the attack, which, according to the press release, destroyed approximately 8 million books, including more than 620,000 school textbooks.
“These books were supposed to reach readers: schoolchildren, students, everyone who opens a page to learn something new. Instead, they went through fire,” said Viktor Kruglov, CEO of Ranok publishing house.
“Looking at this installation, I see four centuries of history contained in a single glass display case,” he added. “The red scale on the glass begins in 1626, when Ukrainian books were first burned. Since then, our language has been banned again and again, yet it remains alive because in every generation there were people who printed and read it.”
According to the press release, the idea for the project emerged in 2024 following a Russian strike on a printing house in Kharkiv, but she was only able to realize it this year.
Alongside the damaged books, the glass case features a vertical red timeline marking 12 dates spanning exactly 400 years, from 1626 to 2026. According to the project’s concept, the chronology connects the destruction of Ukrainian books during the current war with earlier restrictions on Ukrainian-language publishing and episodes of destruction of Ukrainian cultural institutions and literature.
Among the events highlighted are the 1720 decree banning the publication of new books in Ukrainian, the 1863 Valuev Circular restricting Ukrainian-language educational and religious publications, and the 1876 Ems Ukaz banning the publication and import of Ukrainian books.
The timeline also marks the Executed Renaissance in 1937, the removal of Ukrainian books from libraries in occupied territories beginning in 2014, and the destruction of libraries and book collections following Russia’s full-scale invasion in 2022.
More recent entries include the 2024 missile strike on Kharkiv’s Factor-Druk printing house, which the press release says destroyed 50,000 books, and the continued removal of Ukrainian books from occupied territories and destruction of libraries, printing houses, publishing companies, and warehouses in 2026.
The installation’s title reflects the same theme. In the word Born, the letter “o” is crossed out and replaced with a “u,” transforming Born Alive into Burn Alive. According to the artist’s concept, the change symbolizes Ukrainian culture and books that face physical destruction but continue to serve as evidence of what happened.
Two additional red marks above the 2026 entry have deliberately been left without dates, raising the question of whether 2026 will be the final point in the installation’s chronology.
The installation also accompanies a discussion scheduled at Ukraine’s National Stand on October 7 titled “What Remains After an Attack? Ukrainian Publishers on Loss, Resilience, and Reconstruction,” featuring representatives of the Ranok and Zhorzh publishing houses.
The Frankfurt display follows further losses to Ukraine’s publishing sector in recent months. On August 28, more than 60,000 books were destroyed after a Russian drone struck a storage facility in the Kyiv region.
The strike hit a Nova Poshta sorting center, where a warehouse containing stock belonging to several major Ukrainian publishers and online booksellers was completely destroyed by fire.

Russia’s Algeria Military Air Bridge Runs Straight Through NATO Airspace
Algerian military transport aircraft are regularly flying to Russia through NATO airspace, including Poland, as part of an established logistics route linked to military cooperation between Algiers and Moscow, according to Defence24 on October 7.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The latest documented flight took place on October 6, when an Algerian Air Force Lockheed C-130H-30 Hercules flew from Boufarik Air Base in Algeria to Moscow’s Vnukovo Airport.
The aircraft crossed Italy, Croatia, Hungary and Slovakia before entering Polish airspace from the south. It then continued through Belarus before reaching Moscow.
According to Defence24, the flight was not an isolated case. In recent weeks, Il-76MD, C-130H/H-30 Hercules and LM-100J Super Hercules military transport aircraft have been recorded operating between Algeria and Russia, repeatedly using European airspace.
The exact cargo aboard the October 6 flight has not been publicly disclosed. Defence24 linked the regular traffic to broader military-technical cooperation between Algeria and Russia, including the transport of military equipment and personnel involved in servicing Russian-made systems operated by Algeria.
Algeria remains a major operator of Russian-made military equipment and has maintained extensive defense ties with Moscow. The country operates Russian aircraft and air defense systems and has continued purchasing Russian weapons, including additional combat aircraft.
Earlier, Algeria became the first foreign customer to receive Russia’s Su-57E fifth-generation fighter jet, with the aircraft spotted flying over Algerian territory in February 2026. Algeria has also signed contracts with Russia for Su-34ME and Su-35 fighter jets as part of its broader military cooperation with Moscow.

The Ministry of Transportation and Communications yesterday said more high-speed trains with non-reserved seating would run during the Double Ten National Day holiday.
The transport ministry is taking several measures to cushion ride conditions and seating capacity ahead of the holiday, officials said at a news conference at the ministry in Taipei.
Taiwan High Speed Rail Corp (THSRC) has sold 80 percent of its reserved seat tickets for the holiday, 10 percent more than the figure during the Mid-Autumn Festival, when overcrowded trains drew complaints, they said.
Photo : Wu Liang-yi, Taipei Times
Today, eight trains travelling from Taipei or Nangang to Taichung between 5pm and 9pm would each have eight carriages designated for non-reserved seating, Deputy Minister Wu Sheng-yuan (伍勝園) said.
The ministry is coordinating with Taiwan Railway Corp (TRC) and THSRC to boost transport capacity during the holiday period, he said.
Command centers at Taipei Railway Station and Taichung High Speed Rail Station would oversee train traffic and advise passengers on whether they should take the TRC or THSRC, he said.
Designating more cars for non-reserved seating allows each train to accommodate 1,600 to 2,200 people, which should help bleed off seating pressure, Wu said.
THSRC president Bob Chen (陳惠裕) said that extra seating would be featured in two trains per hour during rush hour, and that trains are to park on the platform for rapid cleaning so they can return to ready status.
Turnaround checks on the platform, carried out under the control center’s direction, would ready trains in 12 minutes, an improvement from the regularly 60 minute process, he said.
THSRC has crowd control measures in place to separate passengers heading to reserved and non-reserved cars, and is fielding additional staff members to maintain orderliness, Chen said.
Despite the increase in reserved-seat ticket sales, THSRC expects an overall decrease in passenger volume for the National Day holidays, he said.
The forecast is that 290,000 to 330,000 passengers would take the high-speed trains today, while no more than 340,000 people would use the high-speed rail to go back to work, Chen said.
However, people travelling south for vacation are expected to join commuters going home from work during rush hour, resulting in surges in crowds, he said.
TRC president Feng Hui-sheng (馮輝昇) said the railway company would run 123 additional trains to absorb demand during the holiday period.
Eighty-five of the extra trains would run on the east coast, and 38 in the west, he said. A firework festival in Taitung is the reason for the larger number of trains on the east coast, he said.
The public is urged to consider taking the TRC during the holidays, Feng said, adding that new EMU900 trains can reduce the travel time of Taichung-to-Taipei direct trains to two hours, 10 minutes.
TRC railway stations are closer to cities and towns than high-speed rail stations, he added.

Experts on how to get more comfortable with death
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
16:45:06 UTC
01:45:06 KST

For most people, death is not a standard conversation topic. Once, at lunch, a friend began talking about her mother’s death several years earlier. Her voice caught occasionally, but she spoke about it plainly — like a simple fact of life. As we talked, I noticed another friend was shifting uncomfortably in his seat; he didn’t say much.
Afterwards, I asked him what was wrong. “I really don’t like talking about death,” he said, his hands twitching anxiously. “I don’t even like thinking about it. It freaks me out.”
His discomfort struck me as silly — and also the most normal thing in the world. We are all going to die, and so is everyone we know. So why be terrified? And how can you not be terrified?
Photo: AFP
My friend is far from alone in his discomfort. “We live in grief-illiterate and grief-phobic societies,” says Lucy Hone, a resilience and grief researcher and author of the book How Will I Get Ever Through This?: A Practical Guide to Navigating Life’s Toughest Times.
Hone began researching grief over a decade ago, after the sudden death of her daughter, Abi. On our video call, she wears one of Abi’s old hats, an orange and white beanie with polka dots and a big orange pouf on top. It’s ridiculous, Hone says, but it makes her laugh.
For someone who has experienced such intense loss and spends so much of her time talking to people about their grief, Hone is remarkably cheerful and bubbly. This is in part because of her work, she argues. Hone and several other experts I spoke with said that thinking and being around death was “life-affirming”.
Below, experts share why so many of us are so scared of death, and how we can learn to get a little more comfortable with it.
WHY WE ARE UNCOMFORTABLE WITH DEATH
Death disrupts the usual orientation of our lives, argues Todd May, instructor of philosophy at Warren Wilson College.
“People in the west and elsewhere are forward-looking,” May says. We do not just exist in the moment — we engage in projects and relationships that we see unfolding over time. “The thought of our lives ending violates this future orientation we all have,” he explains.
The typically western, individualistic approach to life affects how we feel about death, says Sister Chan Tri Nghiem, an Australian-born Zen Buddhist nun. In the Judeo-Christian tradition, “there is a strongly shared belief that God created individuals separate from each other … we have a certain lifespan, and we die at a certain time”. This view causes fear and anxiety, argues Tri Nghiem.
In the Buddhist tradition, beginnings and endings are far less defined. Take a question as simple as when you first began to exist: was it when you were born? The nine months you were in your mother’s belly? When you were just a precursor cell within your unborn mother? “In Buddhism, we have always existed and there was no time when we didn’t exist,” says Tri Nghiem. Seen through this lens, death is less of an ending and more of a continuation.
The idea of finitude can bruise our fragile egos, says Alua Arthur, author and death doula. “We have no control at all, and that’s very disquieting,” she says. “We think we’re infallible, and death reminds us how small we are, and that’s uncomfortable.”
And the thought of death brings about big feelings that most people would prefer to avoid, says Luyi Kathy Zhang, a hospice and palliative care doctor.
“So many of us are ill-equipped to deal with uncomfortable emotions, and death is probably one of the peak uncomfortable experiences,” she says. “It is easier for us to say that death is an eventuality that we will deal with when it comes rather than to face the feelings now.”
Finally, dying increasingly happens out of sight, says Hone — in hospitals or care homes. But it wasn’t always this way.
“Throughout human history, we had death around us,” Hone says. “We’d care for the sick and dying at home, so we were forced to talk about it and think about it.”
This shift accelerated in the mid-20th century. “In Boston in 1912, about two-thirds of residents died at home,” the New York Times reported in 2019. “By the 1950s, the majority of Americans died in hospitals and by the 1970s, at least two-thirds did.”
Removed from our immediate surroundings, for many death became something more distant and abstract.

They paraded a lifestyle they hoped looked glamorous, appearing in public dressed in silk pajamas or with a woman in swimwear on each arm. Porn moguls like Hustler’s Larry Flynt or Playboy’s Hugh Hefner were household names. “Say what you want about these old perverts, who once set the tone of our sexual culture, but at least you knew who they were and what they were selling,” Patricia Nilsson writes in her new book, Guilty Pleasure: The Pornification

Book review: The quiet heroes who tried to stop Doge
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
16:45:06 UTC
01:45:06 KST

US President Donald Trump’s catastrophic errors get so much attention that his systemic ones can easily be missed. While the world looks on in dismay at his farcical war in Iran, the thuggery of Ice agents or clownish attacks on erstwhile allies like Canada and Denmark, the core functions of the American government are slowly disintegrating.
It is harder to get people to focus on the machinery of the state because the effects are often slow and hard to pin down. Outbreaks of disease — such as the recent wave of explosive diarrhea across the US — might have happened anyway, but were probably made worse by lay-offs at the Centers for Disease Control. Likewise, Trump is not directly responsible for natural disasters, but response times in the past year may have been hampered by mass redundancies at the National Weather Service. Cuts to tax collection also seem to have reduced revenue by multiple billions, though we cannot be sure of the causal relationship.
The other problem is that bureaucracies are hard to make interesting. Their work is technical and complicated, and most officials are taught to avoid saying anything engaging in public. By the time a journalist has explained what an agency does and why it is important, the reader may well have clicked on to the next thing.
So there are few better suited to the challenge of telling this story than Michael Lewis, one of the world’s bestselling nonfiction writers, who has a knack for finding an angle that cuts through the complexity. After a career spent getting readers excited about credit default swaps (The Big Short) and sabermetrics (Moneyball) he has decided to try to help people understand the importance of civil servants.
Blockers is a loose sequel to the The Fifth Risk, in which Lewis focused on the transition from the Obama to the Trump administration and the disruption caused by the new team’s almost complete lack of interest in their jobs. It focused heavily on what different departments and agencies do and why they matter. This time around the problem is not indifference but malicious intent to destroy. The “blockers” are the dedicated officials who try to stop the wanton and often illegal destruction of their life’s work by Elon Musk’s Doge or other agents of chaos. They range from a researcher working on preventing wildfires to a security guard trying to block Musk’s goons from entering his building, and a lawyer attempting to keep personal tax data from being used to deport undocumented migrants.
In truth, they don’t do much blocking — since they all either end up resigning when they’re asked to do something illegal, or are fired. The title refers more to the assumption by Musk and his fellow travelers that these are the people who are stopping progress and need removing. Much of the book is taken up with descriptions of the valuable work they did before being turfed out.
It would have been good to have a bit more on the villains, whose motivations for participating in Doge are varied. They range from the addled young coders with limited social skills deployed by Musk, to turncoat bureaucrats looking for any easy life, and some very strange characters such as health secretary Robert F Kennedy Jr, with his bizarre obsession with dead animal parts. Trump’s absurd commerce secretary Howard Lutnick also makes a brief cameo, deciding he needs to personally sign off any check for more than US$100,000. It feels as if there is more to say about the personal journeys that lead people to behave this way.
This is the particularly true of the boss baddie Russell Vought, the Republican operative central to developing the Project 2025 plans for Trump’s second term. Musk causes havoc, but quickly gets bored of Doge and heads back to Silicon Valley. Vought is the real deal, quietly and systematically deconstructing the state while keeping out of the spotlight and getting others to do his dirty work for him.
He appears in one of the book’s most engaging chapters, which zooms in on Francis Collins, a scientist who helped discover a successful treatment for cystic fibrosis, allowing those with the condition to live much longer. Collins ended up at the head of the National Institutes of Health under Obama, continued through Trump’s first term and part of Biden’s, before stepping down to run an NIH research lab. After Trump’s re-election he was effectively forced out, saying that his position had become “untenable.” Lewis runs through a series of possible culprits, of which Vought’s cost-cutting is one. What makes this particularly remarkable is that Vought’s own daughter has cystic fibrosis. Ideology is a powerful drug.
But perhaps the most interesting character of all is Sahil Lavingia. A successful software engineer, he bought into Musk’s vision and went to work for Doge in the Department of Veterans Affairs. He only lasted 55 days before giving an on-the-record interview in which he noted that “it’s kind of fine — because the government works. It’s not as inefficient as I was expecting, to be honest. I was hoping for more easy wins.” This was not on-message and he was shown the door.
A few months later, though, once Doge had fallen apart, he was invited back by one of the few survivors, who had stayed on at the Treasury department. Lavingia was tasked with improving the Internal Revenue Service’s computer systems, and despite not needing the money, seems genuinely committed to the task of making things work better. Through Lavingia, Lewis gives us a taste of what serious work to enhance the state might have looked like.
There are real problems with the way the government operates, both in the UK and the US, caused by poor resourcing, dysfunctional systems or low pay for technical staff compared with the private sector. Alongside Lewis’s star civil servants, there are people who have checked out or become institutionalized. Lavingia’s lengthy battle to get a water cooler replaced reminded me of how difficult it was to get the lifts working when I was at the Department for Education.

EDITORIAL: China cannot silence free speech
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
16:45:06 UTC
01:45:06 KST

Prosecutors on Sept. 29 indicted two men for allegedly throwing feces and paint at the Comedy Club in Taipei on May 29. A 33-year-old man surnamed Liu (劉), allegedly acting on instructions from an unidentified person in China, recruited a 35-year-old man surnamed Kuo (郭), who threw bags containing human feces and white paint inside and outside the club in Zhongshan District (中山), prosecutors said.
The incident happened on a night when comedian Huang Yi-hao (黃逸豪), who had mocked Chinese President Xi Jinping (習近平), was scheduled to perform.
Property was damaged, staff were frightened and some customers sought refunds, prosecutors said.
It was an act of Chinese “transnational repression” intended to restrict freedom of expression, they said, recommending that Liu be given a prison term of one year and 10 months, and Kuo one year and eight months.
China’s Taiwan Affairs Office denied knowledge of the incident and dismissed the accusation of transnational repression.
It was not the first time people apparently acting on behalf of Beijing have been accused of trying to intimidate or silence critics in Taiwan. In 2017, Hong Kong democracy advocate Joshua Wong (黃之鋒) was targeted by pro-China protesters, including in an alleged attempted assault, upon his arrival at Taiwan Taoyuan International Airport.
In 2019, Hong Kong singer and democracy advocate Denise Ho (何韻詩) was splashed with red paint while speaking to reporters before a rally in Taipei to support the territory’s democratic movement.
Prosecutors identified the main suspect as a member of the China Unification Promotion Party.
Other Hong Kong rights workers have also faced harassment. In 2020, former Causeway Bay Books manager Lam Wing-kee (林榮基), who had fled to Taiwan, was splashed with paint at a Taipei cafe.
Security officials have said that attacks and vandalism targeting Hong Kongers and their businesses in Taiwan are suspected of being carried out under Chinese direction.
Beijing has also sought to pressure Taiwanese to conform to its “one China” narrative through legal and economic measures. In June 2024, China published 22 guidelines allowing its courts to try in absentia and sentence to death “Taiwan independence separatists.” Beijing has since threatened Taiwanese politicians, including Democratic Progressive Party (DPP) Legislator Puma Shen (沈伯洋), and activists with prosecution, despite having no jurisdiction in Taiwan.
Taipei has condemned the measures as attempts to extend Chinese law into Taiwan and create fear.
Economic pressure is another avenue of intimidation. This week, TV host Kevin Tsai (蔡康永) attended a campaign event in Taipei for Shen, who is the DPP’s mayoral candidate for the capital. After Chinese social media users called for a boycott, Chinese electric-vehicle maker Leapmotor removed promotional material featuring Tsai, while Harper’s Bazaar China took down its interview with him.
These incidents show the potential consequences for Taiwanese entertainers and businesses that operate in China when Beijing interprets their political activity as support for “Taiwanese independence.”
Taiwan’s freedoms of speech and the press were hard won. After 38 years of martial law, restrictions on political parties and the press were dismantled, as Taiwanese fought for the right to criticize their government, challenge those in power and speak without fear.
Article 11 of the Constitution protects freedom of speech, while the Constitutional Court has repeatedly emphasized the importance of free speech concerning government and public affairs.
Political satire and making fun of politicians are generally lawful and strongly protected forms of expression.
Huang’s political satire of Xi and other politicians is protected by Taiwan’s constitutional guarantee of freedom of expression. Taiwanese must not be intimidated into self-censorship. If fear of Beijing causes people to silence themselves, Taiwan risks surrendering the freedoms that distinguish its democratic system from the Chinese regime while encouraging further attempts at transnational repression.
That is why prosecutors and courts must continue to hold accountable those who use threats, violence or other criminal acts to silence others. Defending free expression does not mean allowing intimidation to go unanswered; it means ensuring that intimidation never determines what Taiwanese are allowed to say.
Ultimately, Taiwanese — not Beijing — will decide what can be said in Taiwan. The nation’s democracy is strong when its people exercise the freedoms they fought hard for, rather than allowing fear of China to dictate the limits of their speech.
China prefers to win without firing a shot in its bid to strangle Taiwan’s strategic autonomy. Chinese military strategist Sun Tzu (孫子) would have approved. Its central tool at sea is the “cabbage strategy”: the Chinese People’s Liberation Army Navy (PLAN) layers fishing boats, maritime militia, coast guard cutters and warships around Taiwan’s contested waters in overlapping rings. Each layer normalizes daily coercion, narrows Taiwan’s freedom of movement and chips away at its maritime sovereignty — all while staying below the threshold of armed conflict. This is “gray zone” warfare at its most cost-effective — one of Beijing’s most promising

It would create what Chiang called Taipei’s version of Omotesando — an upscale, tree-lined boulevard and shopping district in Tokyo — to attract young people and international tourists.
