Do not cut ties after losing allies
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
16:45:06 UTC
01:45:06 KST

Honduran Legislator Jorge Calix traveled to Taiwan last month, the first since Tegucigalpa severed diplomatic relations with Taipei three years ago.
During his visit, Calix met Minister of Foreign Affairs Lin Chia-lung (林佳龍) and participated in the Yuan Peng Class (遠朋班), an annual training program for Latin American leaders.
The significance of his visit raises a point that Taiwan should consider as China continues its efforts to amputate its remaining diplomatic relationships: When Taiwan loses an ally, why should decades of political relationships disappear with the embassy?
Calix’ visit also raises a more immediate question: How was it arranged? He did not arrive in Taiwan and accidentally discovered the program. The Yuan Peng program has been running for decades. Participation requires some channel through which prospective participants learn about the program and coordinate their attendance with Taiwanese authorities. Publicly available information does not establish who initiated the contact, but Calix’s participation demonstrates that channels between Taiwan and Honduran political figures remain despite the absence of formal diplomatic relations.
Panama provides an even more developed example.
In November last year, nine Panamanian lawmakers traveled to Taiwan, its first legislative delegation to Taiwan since it switched recognition to Beijing in 2017.
The visit attracted attention after Panama’s president said his administration had not authorized it, while the Panamanian Ministry of Foreign Affairs accused China’s embassy of interference after Chinese officials sought to discourage lawmakers from making the trip.
That exchange did not end parliamentary contact with Taiwan.
Less than a year later, Panama’s National Assembly established an interparliamentary friendship group with the Legislative Yuan. Forty-five of Panama’s 71 lawmakers joined, including National Assembly President Shirley Castanedas and both vice presidents. More than 20 Panamanian legislators also visited Taiwan in the preceding six months.
The timeline is important. A parliamentary delegation was followed by legislative exchanges and eventually the institutionalization of those relationships through a friendship group representing more than 60 percent of Panama’s National Assembly.
This does not prove that Taiwan deliberately designed every step of that process, but shows that parliamentary diplomacy can accomplish much, even after diplomatic recognition has been lost.
It is important to remember that Panama’s friendship is not an international anomaly.
Some of Taiwan’s most important parliamentary relationships exist in countries that do not formally recognize it. The UK has a British-Taiwanese All-Party Parliamentary Group whose purpose includes promoting bilateral relations, trade and mutual understanding. The French Senate has a France-Taiwan Friendship Group, while the European Parliament maintains a Taiwan friendship group. Canada has a Canada-Taiwan Friendship Group and Lithuania has had a Lithuania-Taiwan Parliamentary Friendship Group. Germany has parliamentary Taiwan groups, including one established this year in Berlin’s legislature. India has a Taiwan-India Parliamentary Friendship Association.
Japan offers perhaps the most striking example. Tokyo has not maintained diplomatic relations with Taipei since 1972, but the Japan-Taiwan Diet Members’ Consultative Council was formed just a year later and includes members of the Japanese Diet from across party lines. The organization traces its history back more than half a century and changed its name this year specifically to include “Taiwan.”
These examples show that formal diplomatic recognition and parliamentary relations are different things. A government can recognize the People’s Republic of China (PRC) while its legislators maintain extensive political relationships with Taiwan.
What makes Honduras and Panama particularly interesting is that they are former diplomatic allies. Taiwan does not need to build those relationships up from nothing.
Before Honduras switched recognition in 2023, Taiwanese diplomats had operated there for decades. Taiwan had diplomatic relations with Panama for more than 100 years before the 2017 switch. During those years, Taiwanese ambassadors and embassy personnel interacted not only with presidents and foreign ministers, but with legislators, political parties, local officials, universities, businesses and civic society.
Closing an embassy ends a nation’s official presence, but it does not erase the personal relationships accumulated by the diplomats who worked there.
Taiwan could employ former ambassadors and diplomats who served in former allied countries in roles that aim to preserve those networks, using their understanding of local political institutions, legislators and personal connections, things that their successors stationed elsewhere might not possess.
Those relationships could help introduce foreign lawmakers to members of the Legislative Yuan, facilitate participation in programs such as the Yuan Peng Class, identify opportunities for parliamentary delegations and maintain communication with political parties regardless of whether they are the ruling party or the opposition.
This does not mean asking governments to immediately reconsider diplomatic recognition of Taiwan; instead it would preserve relationships underneath the diplomatic level.
Calix illustrates the advantage of such an approach. He is not a member of Honduran President Nasry Asfura’s governing party. He is the caucus whip of the opposition Liberal Party. Taiwan’s ability to receive and engage an important opposition legislator suggests that parliamentary diplomacy can reach political actors, no matter which party controls the executive branch.
Diplomatic relationships are vulnerable to elections. A new president can reverse recognition, but parliamentary networks have the potential to be broader, incorporating politicians from governing and opposition parties simultaneously.
Panama shows what the next stage could look like. Individual visits can develop into recurring exchanges, and recurring exchanges can eventually become institutional relationships between legislatures.
Taiwan already possesses much of the infrastructure required for such a strategy. The Legislative Yuan maintains extensive parliamentary relationships overseas, while the Ministry of Foreign Affiars already operates programs that bring foreign leaders to Taiwan. Friendship groups provide institutional counterparts in countries with which Taiwan has no diplomatic relations.
The missing element is treating former diplomatic allies as a distinct category rather than considering the termination of diplomatic relations to be the end of Taiwan’s political presence.
Beijing’s diplomatic victories have been measured by the number of governments that abandon Taipei, but Panama and Honduras illustrate the limitations of measuring influence solely through diplomatic recognition. Beijing can persuade an executive government to recognize the PRC. However, that does not determine how legislators, political parties, universities, businesses or other institutions interact with Taiwan.
For Taiwan, this creates an opportunity to redefine what losing diplomatic recognition means.
An embassy closing should not mean that decades of accumulated relationships must close with it. Former ambassadors can preserve contacts. Legislators can build relationships with their counterparts. Training programs can introduce political leaders to Taiwan. Parliamentary delegations can reopen channels, and friendship groups can eventually institutionalize them.
Panama demonstrates how far that process can go. Calix’s visit to Taiwan suggests that in Honduras, it might already have begun.
Juan Fernando Herrera Ramos is a Honduran journalist based in Taipei. His work on Taiwan-China-Latin America relations has been published in Nikkei Asia, The Diplomat and the Taipei Times.

Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
16:45:03 UTC
01:45:03 KST

The delivery last week of the first two of 66 F-16V Block 70 warplanes purchased from the US would significantly boost Taiwan’s air combat capabilities, a retired US Navy rear admiral said.
The jets arrived at Chihhang Air Base in Taitung County on Friday last week.
Once several more F-16V Block 70 jets are delivered, they “will represent a significant increase in Taiwan’s air combat capability,” Mark Montgomery, a retired US Navy rear admiral and senior fellow at the Washington-based Foundation for Defense of Democracies, told the Central News Agency by e-mail.
Photo: Yu Tai-lang, Taipei Times
The next major step should be for Taipei to acquire E-2D early warning aircraft and upgraded air-to-air missiles, which would enable the air force to make better use of its new F-16s, said Montgomery, who focuses on Taiwan defense issues.
Michael Hunzeker, an associate professor at George Mason University in Virginia, said that the arrival of the two F-16Vs, despite delays, showed that Washington intends to honor its arms sales commitments to Taiwan.
Taiwan is acquiring the 66 new F-16V Block 70 jets under the Feng Hsiang program. The first two single-seat aircraft departed from Texas, stopped in Hawaii and Guam, and underwent several midair refuelings before arriving at the air base on Friday last week.
Basing the new fighters in eastern Taiwan would increase the strategic depth of the nation’s defenses, help deter enemy forces and reduce the logistical burden on the air force, Taiwanese defense experts said.
Separately, the Ministry of National Defense is to expand a joint Taiwan-US defense assessment program.
The program, budgeted at more than NT$470 million (US$14.78 million) and scheduled to run from this year through 2028, would involve the US Department of Defense arranging for one representative from the Office of the Undersecretary of Defense for Policy and one from the Institute for Defense Analyses, a private nonprofit research organization, to be stationed at the ministry’s headquarters on a long-term basis, the Chinese-language Liberty Times (the Taipei Times’ sister paper) reported.
The arrangement would put US personnel closer to the center of Taiwan’s defense policymaking, and allow them to assist with policy coordination and military capability assessments, it reported.
The Pentagon declined to comment when contacted by the Central News Agency.
Placing US liaison personnel at the ministry could help with policy coordination and operational analysis, complementing technical and tactical training assistance already provided through US arms sales to Taiwan and programs such as the “English-language instructor” program, Hunzeker said, using a phrase that refers to US military trainers.
It remains to be seen how the relationship would develop, but the arrangement could indicate that Taipei and Washington are seeking to improve coordination at the tactical, operational, strategic and policy levels, he said.
Such developments would be more significant than the announcement of any new arms sales, he added.

The Japanese Chamber of Commerce and Industry Taipei yesterday urged Taiwan to make its administrative procedures more transparent and predictable to encourage greater investment, as it released its annual white paper.
Presenting the document to National Development Council (NDC) Minister Yeh Chun-hsien (葉俊顯), the chamber called for regulations aligned with international standards and measures to address shortages of skilled workers and electricity.
Chamber chairman Yuichi Masuda said that those challenges cut across industries and reflected concerns he regularly heard in conversations with businesses in Taiwan.
Photo: CNA
Resolving them could encourage larger investments, bring in advanced technology and strengthen supply chains, he said, adding that the issues require coordination across government agencies.
On administrative procedures, the white paper called for a more transparent and efficient process for permit applications, approvals and consultations, as well as more flexibility in responding to businesses’ needs.
The recommendations drew on the chamber’s survey of all member companies, which received 368 responses, representing more than 70 percent of its corporate membership.
Respondents rated Taiwan’s living environment and business infrastructure highly, but identified difficulties with administrative practices and with recruiting and assigning staff.
While Taiwan-Japan trade continued to expand, individual Japanese investments in Taiwan remained relatively limited in size, the white paper said.
Responding at the event, Yeh described the annual document as an important channel for assessing Taiwan’s investment environment and the needs of multinational companies.
The government has introduced a preliminary review process for electricity license applications to simplify procedures and improve predictability, while also addressing changes to offshore wind projects and financing issues, Yeh said.
Taiwan is also developing renewable energy, promoting energy conservation and storage, and strengthening grid resilience to ensure a stable electricity supply, he said.
Turning to skilled workers, Yeh highlighted changes to improve working, residency and social security arrangements for foreign professionals.
He also asked the chamber to help promote a bilateral trade agreement.
“We hope to continue deepening our relationship and work toward signing a bilateral trade agreement,” Yeh said, asking the chamber to help convey its support for an agreement to Japan’s government.
Masuda thanked the NDC for helping secure some progress on 15 of the 41 requests in last year’s white paper.
Four have been implemented or are scheduled for implementation, while 11 have seen progress, but need further follow-up, the chamber’s assessment said.
This year’s document contains 51 requests, including 26 continuing items and 25 new ones.
The chamber also proposed a regular forum, coordinated by the NDC, to sustain policy dialogue and regularly review progress.
Yeh pledged continued coordination with government agencies to review regulations and administrative procedures and help businesses grow in Taiwan.
The chamber began submitting policy recommendations to Taiwan’s government in 2008 and issued its first formal white paper in 2009. This year’s white paper is its 18th.

Nobel in chemistry awarded for mirror image mystery
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
16:45:02 UTC
01:45:02 KST

Scientists Henri B. Kagan and Kenso Soai yesterday won the Nobel Prize in Chemistry for untangling mysterious mirror images in molecules, a discovery that has been used to develop countless drugs and transformed modern medicine.
Many molecules come in versions that look alike but are not exactly identical, like right and left hands. For example, one mirror image of the chemical carvone smells like mint, while the other has a whiff of caraway, a spice often used in rye bread.
Even life itself prefers one mirror image over the other. DNA twists to the right, and the proteins in human bodies are made of mostly left-handed building blocks.
Photo: Reuters
Versions of the same molecule can behave differently when interacting with other chemicals. When designing drugs to treat diseases, scientists want to be choosy about which mirror image they get.
They want the version of a molecule to treat a cold, not one that will make the sniffles worse.
Kagan, who is from France, and Soai, from Japan, found ways to make chemistry pick a side, designing and manipulating reactions to produce the desired mirror image.
“This is probably the coolest experiment in organic chemistry,” Nobel Committee for Chemistry member Peter Somfai said. “Taken together, the groundbreaking discoveries by Henri Kagan and Kenso Soai have reshaped our understanding of molecular chirality,” a term that comes from the Greek word for “hand.”
Scientists paid tribute to Kagan and Soai’s work, which the Nobel committee described as a feat never previously achieved by anyone “other than life itself.”
“It might be difficult to say that this drug, or that drug, was developed using this,” Somfai said. “I would say all of them, because we use this as a tool, we use this as an understanding, how to develop catalysts, how they function.”
In the 1980s, Kagan’s work showed there might be a way to design reactions to produce one form of a molecule over the other.
Years later, Soai brought that dream to life. He created the first-ever chemical reaction to produce only one of a molecule’s mirror images, in what’s now known as the “Soai reaction.”
“The medicines we have today would not be possible without this chemistry,” American Chemical Society president Rigoberto Hernandez said.
Kagan, 95, is affiliated with the Universite Paris-Sud in Orsay, France.
Soai, 76, is affiliated with the Tokyo University of Science.

US, China, EU: three paths to regulating AI
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
16:45:01 UTC
01:45:01 KST

The US, China and the EU are taking different paths to govern artificial intelligence, as calls grow worldwide to rein in its most powerful systems.
Here is how they are going about it:
US
Photo: AFP
Nearly two years into his second term, President Donald Trump has built his AI policy almost entirely from voluntary industry pledges and executive orders intended to sustain an AI boom that is powering the US economy.
On his first day back in office, Trump scrapped his predecessor Joe Biden’s 2023 order requiring developers of the most powerful AI systems to share safety test results with the government.
The White House in July last year unveiled an “AI Action Plan” listing more than 90 measures to speed up development.
An accompanying order titled “Preventing Woke AI in the Federal Government” requires federal agencies to buy only models deemed ideologically neutral.
Congress, politically divided and heavily lobbied by Big Tech, has yet to pass a federal AI law, and is out of session until after the midterm elections.
Trump has pushed to block state AI laws, but Congress has repeatedly refused to override them, and state laws are taking effect nationwide.
This year, the release of AI models capable of powerful cyberattacks shifted the focus to security. A June order set up a voluntary system for developers to give the government up to 30 days of early access to their most powerful models.
With voter anxiety growing, the heads of major AI companies signed a White House accord on Sept. 29 pledging independent audits and board-level oversight of cutting-edge models.
The pact carries no penalties for companies that fall short, though Trump called it “morally binding.”
The same day, Trump ordered federal agencies to replace the term “artificial intelligence” with “super intelligence” in official communications.
CHINA
China already has a complex, evolving set of rules on how AI is used, including by children.
Regulations on AI companion bots took effect in July, aiming to curb emotional dependency and banning the creation of digital clones of real people without their consent.
President Xi Jinping (習近平) said this summer that AI should be “always under human control,” calling for more “laws and regulations, technological monitoring, early warning and emergency response systems.”
Premier Li Qiang (李強) has also warned that the world risks “losing control” of frontier technologies such as AI if governments are too slow to regulate them.
However, “a general pause or deliberate slowdown in AI development remains outside the mainstream Chinese policy posture,” Oxford China Policy Lab analysts wrote last month.
Some in China see calls to slow progress as hard to justify, “particularly given their perception that US measures such as export controls have already constrained China’s AI development for years,” they said.
China censors and controls AI-generated content much as it does other online information — and last month, its spy chief warned that AI could endanger national security.
“Hostile forces” are abusing generative AI to “fabricate political rumors and spread harmful information,” Minister of State Security Chen Yixin (陳一新) said.
EU
The European Union rushed to adopt its AI Act in 2024, which Brussels touts as the world’s most comprehensive rules on the technology.
But European companies, fearing the rules would stifle innovation as they race to catch up with US and Chinese rivals, later won a delay on rules covering high-risk systems.
Amid growing global calls for control, European Commission chief Ursula von der Leyen said last month that the AI rules put “Europe in the position to shape global efforts.”
She also said she would invite the main frontier labs “for a discussion on how we can support ongoing industry efforts to pace the frontier.”
European firms have been more wary of slowing down, fearing it could be an attempt by US giants to lock in their dominance.
The EU has other tools to regulate AI.
ChatGPT in August became the first AI chatbot added to the EU’s list of digital services subject to greater legal scrutiny under its online content rules.
Brussels last month also proposed forcing companies to make AI companions and chatbots safe before children use them.
AI chatbots must not “simulate interpersonal relationships in ways that create emotional dependency,” the EU said, following a spate of suicides worldwide linked to children’s interactions with such assistants.

Lionel Messi on Tuesday brought the curtain down on his 21-year international career, bidding farewell to adoring Argentina fans in an emotional final appearance for the former world champions in Buenos Aires.
In a perfectly scripted finale, the 39-year-old widely regarded as the greatest soccer player in history signed off with his 126th international goal in front of 85,000 supporters as Argentina cruised to a 3-0 victory over Benin.
Messi, playing in his record-extending 208th international, also provided the assist for the opening goal scored by veteran Nicolas Otamendi, with Nico Paz also scoring.
Photo: AP
However, the match was a footnote to the occasion itself, which saw Messi savoring the adulation of the Monumental Stadium crowd one last time for an event which had been billed as “the last tango.”
“It was a huge source of pride for me to defend this jersey for more than 20 years,” Messi told fans in a post-match address. “Not coming anymore is going to be deeply painful. I swear I’d like to play for the rest of my life, because playing for the Argentina national team is the most beautiful thing that can happen to you.”
Messi though said he had no regrets about his decision to retire, citing Argentina’s grueling FIFA World Cup campaign, which took place as his late father was seriously ill, as a factor.
Photo: AFP
“Even though I want to be here all my life, I feel that this is the moment. The last World Cup was too much, everything I had to live through,” Messi said.
Beforehand, he wiped away tears as the bus carrying him and his Argentina teammates made its way through crowds of well-wishers en route to the stadium.
Messi took the field alongside his three children and received affectionate waves from his wife, Antonela Roccuzzo, and his mother, Celia Cuccittini, who were watching from a VIP box. Shortly before kickoff, a giant Argentina jersey bearing the word “Gracias” (Thank You) above the soccer superstar’s No. 10 was laid out on the pitch as the crowd roared their approval.
Messi welled up again as Falklands War veteran Fabio Santana sang the national anthem beside a banner which read — “The Malvinas are Argentine” — the same banner held aloft by players after their 2-1 World Cup semi-final win over England.
The match was halted in the 10th minute — in tribute to Messi’s famous shirt number — for a minute-long ovation to the former Barcelona and Paris Saint-Germain star.
He crowned the occasion with a goal from the penalty spot in the 71st minute.
Photo: Reuters
At the final whistle, a drone show lit up the night sky above the stadium, showing Messi’s image and thanking the eight-time Ballon D’Or-winner for his career.
Messi’s farewell came two-and-a-half months after Argentina’s World Cup final defeat to Spain in New Jersey, where Messi exited in tears after making little impression in an ill-tempered 1-0 loss.
“I gave it my all; I have nothing left to give, and besides, there are great young players coming up who deserve their chance,” Messi wrote at the time.
Before Tuesday’s game, the University of Buenos Aires awarded Messi an honorary doctorate in a ceremony at the Argentine Football Association (AFA) headquarters. Messi, who has in the past spoken of his regret at not studying more, expressed pride at the distinction.
“To be able to say that I am an honorary doctor,” he said.
Outside the AFA headquarters, fans unfurled a huge Argentina flag with his image inscribed “The joy of my life.”
Former Barcelona teammate Neymar paid tribute to the departing champion on social media.
“It’s not just Argentina that thanks you, the world thanks you for everything you did for football. Thank you for making me love football even more,” he said.
Messi remains under contract with Inter Miami until 2028, although following the death of his father, Jorge, two months ago, he revealed he might hang up his boots for good sooner than anticipated.
Lionel Messi’s departure comes four years after his greatest triumph in international soccer, leading Argentina to victory at the 2022 World Cup to end the country’s 36-year wait for a third title, cementing his status as Diego Maradona’s heir.
“I believe Messi gave everything, absolutely everything, so it doesn’t bother me at all that he’s leaving. He has more than earned it, let him enjoy himself, let him rest,” Cecilia Adriano, 52, said.

The governor of the southern Japanese island of Okinawa yesterday demanded that the central government do more to ensure effective discipline among US service members following the arrest of a US Marine on accusations that he robbed and murdered a local woman.
Okinawa Governor Genta Koja, in Tokyo for the first time since taking office last month, met with Japanese Minister of Defense Shinjiro Koizumi to express outrage over the killing and ask for further efforts to reduce the burden of hosting US military bases on the island.
People in Okinawa have long opposed the heavy US military presence on the island and complained about noise, pollution and crime related to US bases, although some have come to see its strategic value due to what is widely viewed as a growing threat from China.
Photo: Reuters
Lance Corporal Jacob Ballard, a 20-year-old Ohio native belonging to the Marine Corps Air Station Futenma, was arrested over the weekend on suspicion of strangling Anna Yagi, 39, at a hotel and stealing her wallet and backpack. He has denied the allegations, according to Japanese media.
“Okinawa has requested preventive measures every time similar crimes were repeated in past, and now we have this case again,” Koja told Koizumi as they met in the minister’s office packed with reporters and cameras clicking.
“I must say past disciplinary measures and human rights education implemented by the US military have not worked at all,” Koja said.
Photo: AFP
Koizumi said that he was aware of Okinawa’s concerns and that his government would cooperate with the US to discuss effective preventive measures.
In a later meeting, Koja told Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi: “The robbery-murder this time hugely shocked local residents, and there is an urgent need to reduce base-related burdens.”
Hours earlier, the US military in Okinawa announced a 48-hour pause of all military operations for training through noon tomorrow, as well as restricting the ability of troops to leave their base and prohibiting consumption of alcohol.
Lieutenant General Benjamin Watson, commander of III Marine Expeditionary Force, wrote in a letter posted on Tuesday on X that episodes like these “demand we pause for reflection” and that serving on the Japanese island “comes with responsibility.”
US troops on Okinawa are to be under a curfew from midnight to 5am for 30 days following the two-day training period, Watson said.

Unknown Publisher

The New Taipei City Government’s Department of Environmental Protection is to host the New Taipei City 2026 International Youth Climate Action Forum(新北青年氣候論壇) on Oct. 22 on the 17th floor of the Banqiao Shinban Financial Building, with online registration open until Oct. 19.
The event has 100 places available to the public and is open to anyone interested in sustainability. It is to bring together climate experts, youth groups and young climate advocates from Taiwan and abroad for cross-border discussions and case studies.
Held under the theme “From Ideas to Impact,” the forum aims to encourage young people to turn climate ideas into concrete action and contribute to Taiwan’s transition toward net-zero emissions, the city government said.
Screengrab from the Web site of New Taipei 2026 International Youth Climate Action Forum
Now in its sixth year, the forum has evolved from a focus on raising climate awareness to promoting concrete youth-led initiatives, the city government said.
In 2024, New Taipei launched its “Open Call for Youth Climate Action,” guiding participants through four stages: a call for proposals, empowerment, implementation and a showcase.
The number of submissions has risen from 10 in 2024 to 38 this year, reflecting growing interest among young people in sustainability and climate action, the city government said.
This year’s proposals focus on four areas: energy design, the circular economy, ecological conservation and public engagement.
Eight of the 38 teams advanced to the implementation stage, where they are receiving guidance from mentors as they test and validate their ideas in real-world settings.
The forum is also to showcase the work of the eight Taiwanese youth teams and feature international youth advocates sharing their experiences and approaches to climate action.
The city government said international exchange should go beyond simply “seeing the world” and instead promote the principle of “Global Vision, Local Action.” By learning from international examples and adapting effective approaches to local circumstances, young people can develop solutions suited to Taiwan while sharing the nation’s sustainability efforts with the international community.
Climate action does not have to begin with large-scale projects, the city government said, adding that small observations and simple questions in daily life can lead to meaningful change.
New Taipei is committed to providing young people with a platform to experiment, refine their ideas and gain exposure for their work, it said.
Those interested in attending can register online by Oct. 19. Registration is available at https://forms.gle/BsxyRe9hHjsfxrZ19.

Before the strike, the Taoyuan union “encourages” members to join a protest in Taipei on Oct. 19, union chairman Jerry Lin (林哲瑞) told a news conference in Taipei.
The union did not rule out staging a snap strike, Lin said.
Photo: CNA
The union has 2,258 registered members, with 88.3 percent backing the strike, he said.
The vote comes as Micron’s board of directors is meeting today and tomorrow in the US. The union expects the board to respond favorably to its request to overhaul the company’s bonus policy, Lin said.
The union asked the Boise, Idaho-based company to set up a transparent, fair bonus distribution mechanism and allocate 15 percent of its operating profits to employee bonuses, Lin said.
Micron previously distributed 10 percent of its net profit as employee bonuses, demonstrating that such a profit-sharing scheme is a viable solution, the union said.
Most global semiconductor companies such as Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co (台積電) and Micron’s South Korean competitors, Samsung Electronics Co and SK Hynix Inc, have adopted similar approaches tying employee bonuses directly to corporate profits, the union added.
Taiwanese memory producers Nanya Technology Co (南亞科技) and Macronix International Co (旺宏) have allocated 6 percent of pre-tax profit and 15 percent of net profit to reward employees respectively, the union said.
Winbond Electronics Corp (華邦電) and Powerchip Semiconductor Manufacturing Corp (力積電) have also adopted a similar mechanism, it said.
Micron employees’ annual payouts are mainly subject to the terms of the incentives pay plan (IPP) with several limitations. At issue is the five-month boundary, which means a typical top-performing engineer’s actual IPP payout maxes at about five months of base salary.
Micron Taichung Union, which represents about 10,000 Micron employees in Taichung and Tainan, yesterday said it is to launch a second-round negotiation with management on Oct. 22.
The union would not rule out holding a strike vote if the company fails to address its request, Micron Taichung Union chairman Mark Hsu (徐志銘) said.
The unions said that manufacturing capacity from Micron’s Taoyuan and Taichung facilities represents more than 60 percent of the US memory chipmaker’s total global output.
Micron Memory Taiwan yesterday said in a statement that it “respects our team members’ lawful rights and the applicable legal process.”
“We hear the concerns our team members have raised and take them seriously,” the statement said.
To prevent widespread strikes in Taiwan, Micron on Sept. 11 temporarily stepped outside the standard IPP framework by offering extraordinary, one-off cash appreciation bonuses of NT$1 million (US$31,451) for Taiwan employees and 100 percent equity penetration to boost total employee rewards up to 35 to 68 months’ worth of pay for this fiscal year.

India’s Gen Z is facing down the artificial intelligence future
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
16:44:52 UTC
01:44:52 KST

It took India 250 years to catch a break after its textile artisans lost out to new technology in the 18th century. How long will it take for the country to find the next growth frontier in the age of artificial intelligence (AI)?
The upheaval of the past came in waves. First was James Hargreaves’ jenny. Drawing, twisting and winding 16 or more threads at a time, it outproduced the spinners making some of the world’s finest yarn. Then handlooms gave way to power looms. British protectionism did not help, either. A century later, Mahatma Gandhi turned the symbol of wounded pride — the ancient spinning wheel working a lonely spindle — into an emblem of India’s anti-colonial struggle.
Expect a similar story to play out as AI blunts India’s edge in modern craftsmanship: the maintenance of the world’s business software. Autonomous AI agents are already shrinking the value that coders in Bengaluru and Hyderabad bring to global enterprises. Technology services are a US$250 billion export engine supporting 6 million jobs. Now local politicians are wooing Western cloud computing companies with liberal land grants and subsidized solar energy, which could potentially make India a go-to source for cheap tokens (a measure of AI computing power). However, data center investments will create few new jobs.
Illustration: Mountain People
Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s vision to make India a developed economy by 2047 required 9 percent-plus growth in per capita dollar income even before coding tools such as Anthropic PBC’s Claude and OpenAI’s o3 arrived. With global businesses such as Starbucks seeking to become their own software companies by replacing companywide systems from International Business Machines, Microsoft and Oracle — applications Indian programmers specialize in maintaining — that ambition looks more daunting than ever.
The angry youth that clashed with police on the streets of New Delhi this summer were not putting up a Luddite resistance to AI; they were merely registering their frustration with the state’s failure to ensure the fairness of university entrance exams. Still, the fraying link between education and good jobs is a palpable subtext for the self-proclaimed “cockroach” movement, named after a perceived put-down by India’s chief justice of some unemployed youth. (The justice said he was misunderstood.) The stakes for a Gen Z population of almost 400 million are immense. If nominal per capita dollar income keeps growing at the past decade’s 5.5 percent rate, India would be old before it is rich.
To join the league of wealthier nations, a country must create jobs, especially better-paying ones, in export-oriented sectors.
However, despite committing billions of dollars in taxpayer-funded incentives over the past five years, India’s share of global merchandise exports is stuck at less than 2 percent. Vietnam is pulling ahead in manufacturing. What should New Delhi do differently?
Policymakers are fixated on industrial policy, or using the government to steer investment into favored sectors. Trouble is, nearly all countries — developed and developing — have exactly the same idea nowadays. What is more, the government and the entrepreneurial class in India are ill-suited for the mandate.
Local businesses like to corner fiscal incentives, such as those for producing electronics and smartphones. However, assembling iPhones with imported components creates jobs that pay 18,000 rupees (US$186) a month, which, as former Reserve Bank of India governor Raghuram Rajan said, is not all that different from what a chauffeur or household helper makes in a large city such as Chennai.
Low-tech assembly makes sense only if it leads to higher-value manufacturing. That is the true pathway to a solid middle class, but it requires formal research and development (R&D), and what development economists Ha-Joon Chang and Antonio Andreoni have described as “learning in production.”
This kind of learning takes place on one shop floor, before spreading to rival companies and adjacent industries. That is the logic behind the government’s latest US$13.4 billion package of incentives for semiconductor manufacturing. Learning in production powered the East Asian miracle, a period of rapid export-led growth from 1965 to 1990 that dramatically raised living standards. However, that is only because the governments of those countries helped firms through long patches of painful overproduction and poor profits with low interest rates and competitive exchange rates. Even when corporate restructuring became inevitable during the 1997 Asian Financial Crisis, Seoul protected the deep learning embedded in today’s SK Hynix Inc. India’s industrial policy is yet to be tested on its long-term strategic intent.
India’s public finances are too precarious for that model, and its business leaders are too risk-averse. A permanently undervalued currency cannot be a strategy either. The West would not enable the rise of another billion-person economy after being caught asleep at the wheel as China went from a supplier of inferior goods to a challenger in modern technologies.
Instead of trying to build an entire supply chain by coaxing a domestic private sector that has no technology of its own, India could rely on the existing R&D centers of global leaders. Large tech companies, including Advanced Micro Devices, Intel, Nvidia and Qualcomm, employ thousands of engineers in India for cutting-edge R&D. Give them tax breaks for investing in underfunded public universities. Let them set up advanced testing, simulation and verification labs — not just within elite institutions, but also the broader network of engineering schools. They can produce all the scientists and researchers they would need, and more. The surplus talent would drive a start-up boom where the founders’ ambitions go beyond 10-minute food delivery.
A similar logic applies to data centers. Token factories using local land and power could contribute, say, 5 percent of their high-bandwidth memory chips toward an existing national research cloud, accessible to universities and research centers. Any resulting scientific breakthroughs could finally spur the local industry to invest in real R&D.
However, multinational companies would do the heavy lifting. When I visited the John F. Welch Technology Center in Bengaluru two years ago, engineers were collaborating with colleagues at GE Aerospace’s Niskayuna, New York, operation on a novel hybrid-electric jet engine platform — an effort validated this July in the world’s first high-altitude hybrid-electric flight. Multinationals already employ 2.4 million professionals in India, generating nearly US$100 billion in annual revenue. The real policy question is how to supercharge this sum to US$1 trillion. Embedding local research directly in the gear and services global companies sell worldwide would be far more remunerative than getting paid for lines of code.
That is why young Indians care so deeply about fairness in university entrance exams. They can see the power of a good education even in the age of AI, and they do not want it denied to them. With a substantial lift to the quantity and quality of the 3 million undergraduate and graduate degrees India mints annually in science, technology, engineering and medicine, the nation can conceivably expand its frontier cutting-edge talent pool by 10-fold over a decade.
Each of these R&D professionals, earning globally competitive wages, can generate the badly needed tax resources for public employment and urban infrastructure. Better-paid teachers, doctors and frontline health workers would start filling out the middle of India’s employment pyramid, where income and wealth are far too concentrated at the top. Even as it boosts the quality of civic services and expands career opportunities for women and socially disadvantaged caste groups, the state must loosen the grip of paper-shuffling bureaucrats holding the economy back.
While this vanguard of future growth needs to be nurtured, those who are not at the same level of skills need to be pulled out of a low-productivity rut. More than 15 million Indians work as handloom weavers, knitters and tailors, very often in solo establishments. An additional 5 million are employed by mom-and-pop food-processing operations. When they get even a little bit of scale and capital, the value added per worker jumps from about US$4 a day to US$6 or even US$8. If India wants to emulate Taiwan’s success in manufacturing, then it must also follow its path and build up its small businesses first.
India’s window for this transition will not stay open forever. As AI agents proliferate and take over more tasks, there would still be demand for human engineers to supervise the code they write along the way. However, those specialist positions will not follow the logic of labor-cost arbitrage that made outsourcing such a lucrative trade. The jobs can come up just as easily in Nashville as Bengaluru. And if it is the former, Indian techies would be at a disadvantage, because Washington’s stance on immigration has also hardened.
In 1804, a few decades after the spinning jenny, Joseph Jacquard invented a mechanical loom to control the weaving of complex fabric patterns using a sequence of punched cards. Those cards contained the seeds of binary code — the zeros and ones that would eventually give birth to the modern computer. Between the factory automation that impoverished India’s artisans and the computer revolution that finally gave the country a way back in, one-quarter of a millennium was lost.
This historical arc features prominently in the author Amitav Ghosh’s 1986 novel, The Circle of Reason: “When the history of the world broke, cotton and cloth were behind it; mechanical man in pursuit of his own destruction... Who knows what new horrors lie in store?”
Well, the latest horror is AI, for which an overly timid India Inc has neglected to build foundational capabilities. Mimicking a smartphone and semiconductor-focused industrial policy will not create good jobs fast enough. And although capitulation to the West will backfire politically and economically, collaboration will keep the world’s most populous nation enmeshed in the warp and weft of the global economy.
“Think different,” urged Apple Inc’s iconic ad featuring Gandhi and his spinning wheel. It is time for a homespun solution.
Andy Mukherjee is a Bloomberg Opinion columnist covering industrial companies and financial services in Asia. Previously, he worked for Reuters, the Straits Times and Bloomberg News. China prefers to win without firing a shot in its bid to strangle Taiwan’s strategic autonomy. Chinese military strategist Sun Tzu (孫子) would have approved. Its central tool at sea is the “cabbage strategy”: the Chinese People’s Liberation Army Navy (PLAN) layers fishing boats, maritime militia, coast guard cutters and warships around Taiwan’s contested waters in overlapping rings. Each layer normalizes daily coercion, narrows Taiwan’s freedom of movement and chips away at its maritime sovereignty — all while staying below the threshold of armed conflict. This is “gray zone” warfare at its most cost-effective — one of Beijing’s most promising

Victims lose access to their accounts, but the public response to these scams often questions whether they clicked suspicious links or gave out verification codes. If anti-fraud efforts only focus on victim blaming, platforms and telecommunications operators easily escape

Caribbean hot spot loses men to war machine
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
16:44:51 UTC
01:44:51 KST

Halfway around the world from Russia, in a Caribbean tourism hot spot, men young and old are being lured by Moscow with tantalizing job offers, only to find themselves en route to the front lines in Ukraine.
Moscow and Kyiv have recruited thousands of foreign nationals into their armies since Russia launched its invasion of Ukraine in 2022.
Moscow is accused, in some cases, of using fake job ads to hoodwink men from deprived backgrounds in Africa, Asia and Latin America into traveling to Russia and then forcing them to fight on arrival.
Photo: AFP
From countries such as India, Kenya, Equatorial Guinea, Colombia and Brazil, the long arm of Russian recruitment has reached the Dominican Republic.
Jesus Campusano, a 52-year-old from the impoverished port city of Bajos de Haina, was offered thousands of dollars to work as a welder in the city of Kazan.
When he arrived in the country at the end of July he was transferred to a Russian military base, from where he fears being deployed to the war against Ukraine.
The government has identified 20 Dominicans who were tricked into enlisting in the Russian armed forces, Dominican President Luis Abinader said last month in New York, adding that the matter was under investigation.
Campusano applied for a job through an online link.
When he arrived at Kazan airport, about 1,000km from the Ukraine border, he was given a document in Russian to sign, his 54-year-old sister Cristina Campusano said.
The authorities then took his passport, gave him a uniform, and told him he was going to be trained up as a police officer.
However, last week, his sister said they told him “they were going to take him to the war to fight.”
“I need the authorities to help me, because we are desperate and I want our brother back,” she said.
Amnesty International last month said Russia was preying on civilians “from low-income countries in the global south” with false promises of jobs in security, logistics, construction, information technology and other sectors.
However, some of those enlisted volunteered to fight.
A Dominican man, Juan Carlos Savila, has posted videos on Instagram showing himself in action on the front line.
In one, he can be seen hiding in the undergrowth while gunfire and explosions ring out nearby.
In another, he related how he was injured after stepping on a landmine.
“We cannot forbid people from engaging in activities. What we want to do is warn them so they understand the reality of what they are signing up for”, Abinader said.
Carlos Sanchez Diaz, a Dominican human rights coordinator, said that most of the Dominicans wearing Russian uniforms were recruited under false pretenses.
He said up to 100 were the victims of entrapment.
“It’s clearly a scam. These are people from vulnerable sectors, living below the poverty line,” Sanchez Diaz said.
He related one device used by the recruiters: “an invitation to a cultural exchange in Kazan.”
“But when they arrive, there’s no cultural exchange. They’re put on a plane and from there taken to a military base,” he said.
Maico Enrique Campusano, also from Bajos de Haina, but no relation of Jesus Campusano, was offered work as an advertising professional.
He traveled to Panama, where a recruiter was waiting for him, and then flew on to Kazan via Istanbul.
He too ended up in a military base, being put through his paces “from four in the morning until six in the evening,” his mother, Jaqueline del Carmen Feliz, said.
Feliz said she could not sleep at night with worry.
“He’s not Russian, nor is he Ukrainian, so he shouldn’t be out there. I want him back,” she said.
When she asks him about the situation in Russia, he replies: “Don’t worry, I’m fine,” she said.
Feliz is skeptical.
“You only go to war to die,” she said.

Activists call for S Korea to recognize cancer cases
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
16:44:51 UTC
01:44:51 KST

South Korean activists campaigning for workplace safety in the nation’s booming semiconductor industry yesterday called on the government to recognize the cancer diagnoses of three former SK Hynix employees as work-related illnesses.
SK Hynix, along with fellow South Korean tech giant Samsung Electronics, has emerged as a key player in the booming artificial intelligence (AI) industry, with its cutting-edge memory chips crucial to powering the sector’s rapid growth.
Establishing direct links between semiconductor work and certain cancers can be contentious, with research inconclusive, but fabrication and assembly plant workers can face exposure to solvents, acids, toxic metals and chemical gases, the US Occupational Safety and Health Administration said.
Photo: AFP
Samsung issued a public apology in 2018 to workers — many of them young women — who had developed cancer after working at some of its factories, paying out 150 million won per case (US$112,055 at the current exchange rate) after a decade-long dispute.
Supporters for the Health and Rights of People in the Semiconductor Industry (SHARPS), one of the groups that had pressured Samsung, yesterday said that chemicals classified as carcinogens were being used by SK Hynix.
“We have confirmed that several substances on SK Hynix’s own list of prohibited chemicals are in fact being used, including nickel and its compounds,” SHARPS activist Lee Sang-soo told a news conference, citing data reported by SK Hynix to the South Korean Ministry of Climate, Energy and Environment.
SK Hynix said in a statement it was “taking various measures to more objectively identify the characteristics of disease occurrence” and was fully cooperating with government inquiries.
The company, which did not address the specific claims, said it had taken “proactive industrial health measures including the development of a comprehensive support and compensation plan.” The husband of a former SK Hynix worker who died from breast cancer called on the Korea Workers’ Compensation and Welfare Service to recognize his wife’s illness as work-related.
“I believe the nature of her job meant that she was inevitably exposed to various hazardous substances,” Kim Yong-il, the husband of Yoon Young-mi, told the briefing outside the offices of the service, which is a government agency.
Yoon began working at SK Hynix’s Icheon chip plant in 1996 and was diagnosed with cancer in 2018. She died in April.
“The company and the relevant authorities must protect workers’ right to health when it comes to occupational diseases in the semiconductor industry,” Kim said.
Korea Workers’ Compensation & Welfare Service representative Ko Seong-yong said that authorities would “process their cases as fast as possible.”
“An epidemiological investigation is necessary. While it is difficult to give an exact timeframe, it could take around a year before a decision is made,” he said.

AUSTRALIA
Ex-bishop sentenced
A former Catholic bishop was yesterday sentenced to six years and six months in prison for sexually abusing two young indigenous men. A District Court of Western Australia state jury convicted Christopher Saunders, 76, in August of 13 out of 19 charges of sexual abuse that occurred between 2008 and 2019 in his sprawling Broome Diocese on the country’s tropical northwest coast. Saunders would become eligible for parole in February 2031. Saunders was acquitted of six charges involving a third accuser. He was accused of indecent dealing with a child over the age of 16. The age of consent in Western Australia is 16, but the law raises it to 18 if the older person is in a position of trust, power or responsibility. Four charges involving a child younger than 13 were dropped on the first day of Saunders’ three-week trial.
Photo: AP
HAITI
Polls postponed indefinitely
The government has indefinitely postponed elections due to be held later this year, officials said on Tuesday. The country has not held elections since 2016, and its last president, assassinated in 2021, has not been replaced. The first round of presidential and legislative elections was set for Dec. 13, and the second round for Feb. 21 next year. “The period originally scheduled for the electoral campaign has been postponed,” the Provisional Electoral Council said in a statement, omitting any mention of a new election date and adding that the timetable “will be made public as soon as possible.” However, it added that voter registration is continuing. Holding elections has been seen as a crucial step to stabilizing the government and tackling rampant gang crime.
UNITED STATES
Eva Marie Saint dies
Eva Marie Saint, the pale, willowy actor who won an Academy Award for her first movie, On the Waterfront, and starred opposite Cary Grant in the Alfred Hitchcock thriller North by Northwest, has died. She was 102. Saint, whose acting work lasted well into her 90s, died at her home in Los Angeles on Tuesday, family representative Jeff Sanderson said. Saint had one of the most spectacular debuts in Hollywood history, as the love interest of Marlon Brando’s tormented Terry Malloy in On the Waterfront, and her first trip to the Academy Awards was memorable, too. Pregnant with her first child, Saint accepted her Oscar from Frank Sinatra and smilingly murmured a unique winner’s speech: “I think I may have the baby right here.” Her son, Darrell Hayden, was born two days later.
VIETNAM
Police bust cat meat ring
Police in Ho Chi Minh City arrested 12 men suspected of operating a citywide ring that stole and resold about 2,700 cats for meat, state media said. Police identified 39-year-old Luu Thanh Binh as the alleged leader of the network. He and 11 others were being investigated for theft, state media said. Investigators said Binh bought stolen cats, kept them at a facility in the city’s north and resold them for meat. He worked with suppliers who recruited others to ride motorcycles through residential neighborhoods between 11pm and 4am, hunting for cats and trapping four to 10 cats each night. Police raided the network on July 8 and found about 50 cats and dozens of traps, state media reported. The suspects told investigators they had stolen and sold about 2,700 cats, the reports said. Police did not say how long the operation had been running.

Death row inmate awake after failed execution in US
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
16:44:48 UTC
01:44:48 KST

Tennessee death row inmate Christa Pike is awake and speaking at a hospital, her lawyers said on Tuesday, six days after the state’s failed attempt to execute her by lethal injection left her unconscious and on a ventilator.
Pike, 50, survived two doses of pentobarbital as executioners attempted to put her to death on Wednesday last week for the 1995 beating and stabbing death of classmate Colleen Slemmer. Pike is believed to be the only person to survive after lethal injection drugs were administered.
Pike’s attorneys are seeking more information about what went wrong from the Tennessee Department of Correction.
Photo: Tennessee Department of Correction via Reuters
“Against all odds, Christa Pike is conscious, speaking, and continues to receive critical medical care,” attorneys for Pike said in a statement.
Pike’s prognosis remains unclear and, at a minimum, she faces a lengthy recovery, the attorneys said.
They said Pike’s arms were burned and blistered after the attempted lethal injection and that she is handcuffed to the hospital bed.
Pike’s attorneys are seeking a court order to require the prison system to preserve information from the attempted execution including drug lot numbers, needles, execution logs and other information.
Attorneys with the Tennessee Attorney General’s Office wrote in a Tuesday court filing that the court order is unnecessary because the prison system is “obliged to maintain this evidence in other cases and must assure it is preserved.”
They said state officials have taken “the necessary steps to obtain medical care for Pike and ascertain what occurred.”
Republican Governor Bill Lee called what happened “deeply disturbing” and ordered a “comprehensive, third-party review to determine exactly what occurred.”
The governor postponed the state’s only other execution scheduled for this year.

S Korea signals military exemption cuts for athletes
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
16:44:48 UTC
01:44:48 KST

The reward of a military service exemption for gold medal-winning South Korean athletes could be abolished or reduced in future after public backlash to some controversial comments from winners at the Asian Games.
Three players from the men’s soccer team came under fire for comments following South Korea’s 1-0 win over Japan in the Asian Games final last weekend in Japan.
All three apologized, but a broader debate had already reignited over whether athletes should receive special treatment for sporting achievements, particularly as ordinary citizens — and even members of BTS, the globally famous K-pop group — had to complete their mandatory service.
Photo: Reuters
Criticism intensified on Tuesday and, yesterday, South Korean Minister of Culture, Sports and Tourism Choi Hwi-young told the National Assembly’s Culture, Sports and Tourism Committee that the alternative military service exemption system for artists and athletes “will inevitably have to be scaled back.”
“It is true that the system has contributed to helping outstanding artists and athletes maintain and develop their abilities,” Cho said. “However, the values attached to fairness and public perceptions of military service have changed. I agree that the system should be comprehensively reviewed once again.”
Most South Korean men must start 18 to 21 months of military service by the age of 28. However, since 1973, Olympic medalists and Asian Games gold medalists have been able to replace the full term with a supplementary service which consists of three weeks of basic training.
Three of the soccer players, including Yang Min-hyuk, who assisted the winning goal against Japan, made comments that were viewed as insensitive.
“The medal and winning the championship weren’t important. I played the game with only one thing in mind — the reward of a military-service exemption,” said Yang, who joined Tottenham Hotspur last year and is currently on loan at Belgian club Westerlo.
Newcastle United midfielder Park Seung-soo posted a photo on social media showing him wearing a cap associated with soldiers who have completed their service. In a post-match interview, captain Lee Gi-hyuk held up his gold medal and said: “I’m not going to the military.”
A number of politicians, including Ahn Cheol-soo of the People Power Party, said it was time to change.
“Some players’ remarks after the match were outrageous,” Ahn posted on social media. “Even the captain bragged about not having to serve in the military. Are all the young people who enlist every year fools?”
Former lawmaker Yoo Seong-min said the flippant comments had provoked resentment and asked: “Is it really fair that BTS has to serve in the military while Asian Games gold medalists are exempt?”
In a Korea Herald editorial on Tuesday, the newspaper declared that the practice was outdated.
“South Korea now stands shoulder to shoulder with the world’s leading nations,” the newspaper said. “The days when finishing first in Asia could meaningfully enhance the country’s national prestige are long gone. It is time to reconsider.”
That was the message from South Korean Ministry of National Defense spokeswoman Chung Binna during a news briefing in Seoul.
“Ultimately, we have plans to cut back or scrap the supplementary service, including one designed for artists and athletes,” Chung said.
The soccer players were among many winners from the Asian Games who qualified for the military exemption.
Golfer Tom Kim on Saturday won the men’s singles after flying across the Pacific when the Presidents Cup competition ended so he could compete in Japan. Asked about the military exemption, he took the gold-medal approach.
“I’m more proud that I’m able to bring a medal for my country,” he said.
Sixteen South Korea baseball players are also exempt after defeating Japan 3-1 in the Asian Games final. So are three South Koreans who won gold in e-sports, an event at the Asian Games.

Ministry promulgates teacher complaint rule changes
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
16:44:48 UTC
01:44:48 KST

The Ministry of Education yesterday promulgated amendments to regulations governing the handling of complaints against teachers, with the changes designed to protect the rights of educators and reduce administrative workload.
The amendments, which are expected to take effect tomorrow, are centered on simplifying the complaints process, protecting teachers’ ability to teach and discipline students within reasonable limits, as well as students’ right to education, giving due respect for the profession of education, and having distinct types of incidents handled separately, the ministry said in a statement.
The new rules stipulate that schools must close the case without convening a campus incident resolution council if the teacher being reported had clearly acted within the bounds of what is reasonable.
Photo: Rachel Lin, Taipei Times
Schools would be required to inform the person who filed the report about the reason for the refusal in writing within 20 days of receiving the complaint, the statement said.
The party filing the report could appeal the school’s decision to a higher educational authority, which would also be authorized to decline taking up the case should it find the complaint to concern conduct clearly exempt from punishment, it said.
The amended regulations would curb the role of independent evaluators, who would be called upon to investigate a teacher’s performance in ordinary performance assessment and disciplinary cases only when the school lacks staff members or under special circumstances, it said.
Planned supplementary measures include guidelines for teachers to call on legal counsel, prevent educational workplace abuse and misconduct, and increase the responsibility of parents to discipline their children, the ministry said.
Parents who fail to cooperate with student guidance could be referred to family education centers or, where appropriate, reported to social welfare authorities for intervention, it said.
The regulatory changes mark the ministry’s second attempt to revise them after the legislature in July returned for correction and resubmission a previous iteration of amendments promulgated in January.
The earlier version did away with the system allowing reports to be filed against teachers anonymously, using different mechanisms to deal with distinct types of incidents and allowing support personnel to assist parties during the proceedings.
The proportion of reports being passed up to campus incident resolution councils had dropped to 22 percent from 82 percent before lawmakers made the ministry rewrite the regulations.
The National Federation of Education Unions in a separate statement said that the current regulations lack enforcement mechanisms and penalties for parents who refuse to cooperate with schools on student guidance and discipline.
The National Federation of Teachers Unions said that reducing the number of accusations being processed by incident resolution councils does not solve core institutional issues.
Teachers need protection against repeated, malicious and unsubstantiated accusations, and incident investigators who do their jobs poorly should be held accountable, it said.
Compensation should be provided to educators for missing out on promotion opportunities and lost income during suspension over unfounded accusations, it added.
The National Substitute Teacher Union said that the amendments promulgated yesterday do not provide enough safeguards to ensure procedural justice or the rights of substitute teachers.
Schools could refuse to renew one-year contracts of substitute teachers if they are reported, regardless of whether the accusations are truthful, it said.

Mourning, war and elections as Israel marks anniversary of Oct. 7 attacks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
16:44:47 UTC
01:44:47 KST

Israel yesterday marked the third anniversary of Hamas’ attack with silent tributes, new strikes on Gaza and intense political debate, weeks before elections in which the country’s deadliest day would be front and center.
At the site of the Nova music festival, where Hamas militants in trucks and paragliders opened fire around dawn on Oct. 7, 2023, family members bowed their heads quietly — although at least one instead put on techno music in tribute to the fallen.
At Nova and the Kfar Aza kibbutz, another site of mass killings three years earlier, loud bangs could be heard from across the border in Gaza during the commemorations as Israel carried out new strikes, despite a ceasefire officially in place for the past year.
Photo: AFP
Gaza officials said three people were killed in strikes in the territory, most of which has been reduced to rubble in relentless bombing in retaliation for the worst attack ever against Israel.
At the Nova site, Katia Zohar, whose daughter Bar Zohar was killed at age 23, called the start of the attack at 6:29am ”the minute that changed our lives forever.”
“Sadly I remember everything,” Zohar said. “The moment she called for me to come and pick her up because there were missiles in the air. Then the second time when she called from the road, screaming that they were shooting at her.”
Anna Davitashvili, 53, paid tribute to her eldest son, Shaun Davitashvili, who was killed at 25 at Nova alongside friends, by playing the last track of techno music that the partygoers were dancing to when the attack began.
“I feel him here. I’m terribly sorry that I couldn’t save him, I couldn’t help him get out of this massacre,” she said, tears filling her eyes.
In Tel Aviv, activists set on the beach the outlines of more than 1,100 bodies to symbolize the Oct. 7 dead and to urge accountability for the failure to prevent the attack.
On Oct. 27, Israel is to hold elections for the first time since the attack, with polls showing a tight race for Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who in three years has ordered the massive offensive in Gaza and fought wars against Hezbollah in Lebanon as well as Iran, whose cleric-run government backs Hamas.
At the Nova site, Naftali Bennett, a former prime minister seeking to oust Netanyahu, told reporters of the attack: “This was a colossal failure of the state of Israel, which was established to defend Jews in our land.”
The Democrats Party put online footage of the attack, without commentary.
“A government that for three years has not destroyed Hamas’ rule is a government dangerous to Israel,” Democrats leader Yair Golan said.

Smoking could worsen facial wrinkles: HPA
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
16:44:45 UTC
01:44:45 KST

Women aged 40 or older who smoke are 3.1 times more likely to develop moderate-to-severe facial wrinkles compared with women who have never smoked, the Health Promotion Administration said yesterday.
The agency cited a US study that examined the link between “pack-years of smoking” and facial wrinkling in men and women.
A study was conducted with 299 never-smokers, 551 former smokers and 286 current smokers, aged between 30 and 69, drawn from a health maintenance organization.
Photo: Tien Yu-hua, Taipei Times
The study assessed their smoking status, pack-years of smoking and other variables via questionnaires.
The facial wrinkles of the study’s participants were clinically examined and scored, using a standardized visual assessment method, by researchers who were blind to the subjects’ smoking status.
As prominent wrinkling was found to be very uncommon for people aged 30 to 39, analysis was restricted to subjects aged 40 or older, including 227 never-smokers, 456 former smokers and 228 current smokers.
The agency said the study concluded that with age, average sun exposure and body mass index controlled, the risk of moderate-to-severe wrinkling for current smokers compared with never-smokers was 2.3 times greater among men and 3.1 times greater among women.
The study found that “women may be somewhat more sensitive to the effects of smoking on facial wrinkles than men.”
The agency said cosmetic appearance is only part of the negative effects of smoking, and the chronic negative effects to health and quality of life are more impactful.
With Taiwan Girls Day’ on Sunday, the agency encourages girls to learn the health risks of tobacco and nicotine products and to make healthy choices for themselves.
Empowering girls requires building their knowledge, skills and confidence, it said, adding that by fostering health literacy early, girls would be more capable of protecting their own health when faced with peer pressure, external environment factors and aggressive marketing.
WHO research estimates 37 million children aged 13 to 15 use tobacco globally, the agency said, adding that the tobacco industry uses many tactics to target young customers, including using bright, stylish, high-tech product designs and aggressively marketing through social media and influencers.
When facing marketing messages such as “cute,” “trendy” or “everyone is using it,” girls should look beyond the packaging and not let it affect their health choices, it said.
Adolescence is a crucial stage for the development of the brain, lungs and the rest of body, the agency said, adding that the earlier one is exposed to nicotine, the higher the risk of addiction and continued use.
Girls should say “no” to their first try, and stay away from all cigarettes, e-cigarettes and other tobacco or nicotine products, it added.

Overseas Community Affairs Council (OCAC) Minister Hsu Chia-ching (徐佳青) yesterday tendered her resignation amid allegations that she and her family misused public resources during her overseas trips, saying she wanted to allow official investigations to proceed.
Premier Cho Jung-tai (卓榮泰) approved the resignation yesterday morning, Cabinet spokeswoman Michelle Lee (李慧芝) said.
Hsu’s resignation came after members of the Taiwan People’s Party (TPP) accused her of making unnecessary overseas trips as minister.
Photo: Tu Chien-rong, Taipei Times
The council, a Cabinet-level agency responsible for relations with overseas Taiwanese and ethnic Chinese communities, and Hsu have denied the TPP’s allegations.
Hsu said in a statement that during her six-and-a-half years at the OCAC, first as deputy minister from May 2020 to May 2023 and then as minister, she had repeatedly faced “unfounded accusations from certain lawmakers.”
Despite her best efforts to rebut those accusations, there was “no room for rational discussion,” and so she requested an official investigation into the allegations, she said.
She was also resigning to allow the administrative and judicial authorities to conduct their investigations independently and objectively, although she regretted leaving many projects unfinished, she said.
The Ministry of Foreign Affairs on Tuesday said it was investigating the allegations against Hsu and her family, asking Taiwan’s representative offices in Germany, France and the US to provide information about her visits to those countries.
The TPP lawmakers said Hsu has traveled abroad 47 times for a total of 526 days since 2022, spending NT$23.83 million (US$749,489), or about one-third of the council’s international travel budget.
At a news conference on Monday, TPP Legislator Hung Yu-hsiang (洪毓祥) played an audio recording of an unidentified person who said Hsu’s husband and son live in Washington, and that Hsu had traveled to the US capital or New York three or four times in 2024.
The trips exhausted staff at the OCAC’s overseas offices, the person said.
They also said that Hsu’s husband, American political analyst Bo Tedards, had used a Taiwan government vehicle to drive their son to see Hsu.
During an OCAC trip to Germany and France in 2022, Hsu, then deputy minister, had her son added to the delegation as a “staff photographer,” even though he was only teenager at the time, Hung said.
The TPP lawmakers said Hsu’s actions breached conflict-of-interest rules for public servants and violated the Criminal Code. They called for Hsu to be suspended pending an ethics investigation.

The burden of proof is on Chiang
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
16:44:44 UTC
01:44:44 KST

On Saturday last week, Taipei City Mayor Chiang Wan-an (蔣萬安) of the Chinese Nationalist Party (KMT) wrote on Facebook a post criticizing Democratic Progressive Party (DPP) Legislator and Taipei mayoral candidate Puma Shen (沈伯洋) for a 2014 op-ed on drug policy. The post amassed an astonishing 500,000 comments in less than 24 hours.
Chiang said the flood of activity was orchestrated by the ruling party. If he wishes to make such claims, Chiang cannot simply point to the volume of comments as evidence; he must look a little closer.
Amid the backlash, KMT Taipei City Councilor Chang Szu-kang (張斯綱) shared a DPP supporter’s post on X featuring a screen grab of himself programming a script to comment on the original post to “deal with” the number of comments being deleted. At most, this proves that people could have used bots to leave comments on the post, but there is no indication of what proportion of comments they might account for, how much traffic was due to coordinated behavior, or who implemented any of it. There is also no evidence to suggest that any accounts involved had ties to the DPP.
Chiang claimed that Threads had 90 million registered users in Taiwan, disproportionate to its population size of 23 million.
The Taiwan FackCheck Center has said that the 90 million figure is not from Meta’s official statistics. It was from a miscalculation in a report from the US market research company Resourcera, which mistook Taiwan’s share of traffic as a share of user accounts in its workings. Resourcera has since acknowledged the error and removed the statistic from its Web site.
In sum, Chiang’s first accusation offered no definitive evidence, while his second simply repeated debunked information. We can be certain that 500,000 comments is a startling number. However, we cannot be certain that someone posting about building a comment bot is grounds to dismiss the entire outcry as being the result of green-camp online armies and ruling party power privileges.
As the election heats up, Chiang must accept the burden of proof for his accusations seriously and point to verifiable accounts, coordinated behaviors or official platform data that support his case. Old pieces of misinformation do not suddenly become compelling simply because the mayor quotes them; nor should they be used to give unproven political allegations a second run.
Steve Ho is a retired engineer.
Translated by Gilda Knox Streader
China prefers to win without firing a shot in its bid to strangle Taiwan’s strategic autonomy. Chinese military strategist Sun Tzu (孫子) would have approved. Its central tool at sea is the “cabbage strategy”: the Chinese People’s Liberation Army Navy (PLAN) layers fishing boats, maritime militia, coast guard cutters and warships around Taiwan’s contested waters in overlapping rings. Each layer normalizes daily coercion, narrows Taiwan’s freedom of movement and chips away at its maritime sovereignty — all while staying below the threshold of armed conflict. This is “gray zone” warfare at its most cost-effective — one of Beijing’s most promising
