5 takeaways from Kemi Badenoch’s fighty Tory conference speech
The Conservative leader aimed brickbats at Labour, Nigel Farage — and any attempt to “unite the right.” Now she just has to persuade some of the public to vote for her.
BIRMINGHAM, England — Kemi Badenoch used her rare moment in the spotlight Wednesday to promise “a fight coming in British politics; a fight that we have not seen in this country for more than half a century.”
Britain’s opposition Conservative leader, speaking at the close of her party’s annual conference in Birmingham, started as she meant to go on. She attacked Prime Minister Andy Burnham’s Labour Party and her right-wing rivals, Nigel Farage’s Reform UK.
It was a speech more about positioning the Tories in a five-party system than about policy. What little she did announce was also about positioning.
Advertisement
Badenoch’s flagship pledge was to abolish inheritance tax on a person’s main home, which is currently set at a threshold of £500,000 (or £1 million for a married couple). It will overwhelmingly benefit the wealthiest families — but it’s part of Badenoch’s argument about being unashamedly Tory and pursuing growth.
On her own terms, and those of her members, Badenoch is seeing the conference as a success. This time last year her own party was muttering about her future; now it is united in pursuing a victory at the next general election.
Whether she can achieve that victory is another question. POLITICO’s Poll of Polls puts the Conservative Party on just 18% in a general election (due by 2029), beneath its historic low in 2024, and behind Reform on 22% and Labour on 26%.
POLITICO crunched the five biggest takeaways as Tory conference closed.
1) ‘Unite the right’ looks dead and buried
With most polls projecting a hung parliament, the shape of Britain’s next government could be decided by one thing: whether the Tories are willing — or able — to form a pact with the rival right-wing party Reform UK.
Badenoch’s speech suggests that they are neither — and made it personal. Badenoch, the first Black leader of a major U.K. political party, took aim at Reform politicians and outriders who have questioned if non-white Brits with foreign heritage can be classed as English.
Advertisement
“I don’t want to explain to my son when we’re watching our brilliant England team play football that some people don’t think our black players are English,” she said. “We must not let these people take us backwards. That is not the country we are … I am black. I am British. I am proud of my country.”
She added: “To those who say unite the right: We are not uniting with that.”
At the same time, her party is clearly turning its head to middle-class “shire Tories” in the south of England who switched to the Liberal Democrats in 2024. Some of the key policies announced this week — such as state-subsidized childcare for workers earning more than £100,000 a year, and scrapping inheritance tax on multi-million-pound family homes — will benefit wealthier voters in London and the south.
That is a very different voter coalition to the industrial heartlands in northern England, where low-income voters have turned to Reform. “None of our voters would benefit from this tax cut for the 2%,” boasted one Reform aide of the Tory inheritance tax policy. “They’ve abandoned going after our voters.” (Tory aides insist they have policies to win back both groups.)
So could Badenoch’s Conservatives form a pact with any other party? The jury’s out on that.
She spent little energy criticizing the hard-right Restore Britain – which could aid her party by splitting Reform’s vote – but Restore’s tally of seats at an election would be minimal.
Advertisement
And while the Tories governed with the centrist Liberal Democrats in 2010, both sides remain scarred from that. Meanwhile, Burnham has already laid out what sounded like a coalition pitch last week, when he argued for closer ties with the EU and electoral reform. Shadow Minister for Policy Renewal Neil O’Brien told a fringe event: “Not since Marilyn Monroe stood on that hot air vent and let her skirts billow have I seen such a ‘come hither’ gesture.”
2) Attack-dog Badenoch is in a fight of ideas
Badenoch’s speech focused overwhelmingly on attacking her rivals and creating clear space between her party and theirs.
Burnham was the “Paddington Bear prime minister who hopes our problems go away”; Tory defector Robert Jenrick was part of an “export boom of drama queens going to Reform”; the Green Party was guilty of “disgraceful antisemitism”; some Reform politicians are “measuring up the curtains for their prison cells.” Her autocue even instructed her to give “side eye” when mocking Farage’s ally George Cottrell, whose links to the Reform leader have come under scrutiny.
It was a deliberate contrast to Burnham’s speech last week, which avoided naming his rivals. In a five- or six-party market, the two leaders are taking opposite approaches to make themselves stand out: Burnham wants to rise above the melee while Badenoch thew the hardest punches.
They are united, though, in seeing politics as a battle of ideas — unlike former PM Keir Starmer, accused of focusing more on process than vision. Badenoch spent more than two months personally writing a 95-page treatise on her ideas about the future, “The Right Way.” She unveiled it on the conference’s first day; extraordinarily, it didn’t leak.
Badenoch also wants to cut through by presenting her party as the voice of fiscal responsibility and defense. The Tories announced what they said would amount to £13 billion a year in welfare cuts on top of £23 billion announced last year. “Our country is running out of money. Almost every other problem flows from this,” said Badenoch.
Advertisement
She added her party would end the “delays” and approve a third runway for Heathrow Airport (though the exact process for this was not clear), halve the 15 percent rate of employers’ national insurance for under-25s and overturn the Labour government’s reforms to employment rights.
The Conservatives are banking on Burnham’s star falling after the Oct. 28 budget and a difficult spending review next year, in which he will have to set out whether Britain spends 3% of its GDP on defense by 2030.
A shadow cabinet minister, granted anonymity to speak frankly, said: “It’s a make-do-and-mend budget; they’ll get through that — but they can’t get through the spending review. [Former Chancellor] Rachel [Reeves] left them a bomb primed to explode.”
3) There are still some no-go areas for the Tories
The ideological chasm being opened up between Badenoch and Burnham is forcing the Conservatives onto uncomfortable territory.
Burnham used his own conference speech to open the door to a possible return to the EU, but Badenoch was clear she didn’t want to take the bait.
“He [Burnham] wants to reopen the Brexit debate. Can you imagine having to go through that again?” the Tory leader said. “So much time lost arguing with ourselves, arguing with the EU, going round and round in circles, businesses not knowing whether they should invest. He wants to do it all again. I think that is a terrible idea.”
Advertisement
Public opinion has shifted in the decade since the EU referendum, which was triggered and implemented by the Conservatives. Renegotiating any new deal with Brussels will be a headache for Burnham and stacked with peril, but it’ll also serve as a reminder of what the Tories — and veteran Brexit campaigner Farage — delivered for the country.
Veteran Euroskeptic MP Bernard Jenkin was even blunter at a fringe event: “Do not defend Brexit. Brexit is toxic with the voters.”
The other big divide that Burnham opened up is on social care. He wants to fund a “national care service” for the elderly in part by changing the “triple lock” on state pensions.
That lock is cherished by many on the right — but there are also the small-state realists who want it axed to curtail the ballooning welfare bill. POLITICO reported that shadow cabinet ministers are debating not coming up with their own substantive offer on how to fix the care system.
“The Tories are ducking the big issues facing our country and instead of showing leadership, Kemi Badenoch is happy to fail a whole generation of older people who have contributed to society all their lives,” Labour Party chair Bridget Phillipson responded.
Whether or not the Tories want to talk about these issues, their rivals will try to ensure they have no choice.
Advertisement
4) The Tories are definitely ready for an election … honest
The Conservatives are living in constant fear of Burnham calling a snap election.
Despite the prime minister insisting he won’t trigger a vote until 2029, Tory figures know it’s within the PM’s gift to go to the polls whenever it suits him best. The right is deeply divided and Burnham may want to seek his own mandate instead of serving out predecessor Keir Starmer’s stifling manifesto. That could catch the Conservatives on the hop.
Badenoch’s top team privately feared that Burnham would announce an election in his conference speech last week, said three senior figures with knowledge of the conversations. That didn’t happen, but it underlines the anxiety the Tories are living under.
Badenoch’s team pulled together a draft manifesto after some “highly stressed” conversations over the summer, said a second shadow cabinet minister. It now sits waiting in a Word document ready to go in case of emergency.
Would-be candidates are already trooping into the party’s new headquarters in Westminster for regular assessment days, while Badenoch’s senior team is holding an election planning meeting once a week on a Wednesday afternoon, a person with knowledge of it said.
“We are ready for an election whenever it’s called,” Badenoch insisted on Wednesday. “We will need many more talented people in the next parliament. People who have had successful careers outside Westminster, not just people who know how to talk a good game, people who know how to get stuff done.”
Advertisement
But deep down the Tories know they’ve got some way to go to be fully prepared.
One party activist told POLITICO a mere 17 campaign managers are in post, despite around 80 being needed for a full-strength election battle. “If we have an election tomorrow we’re f*cked,” they added. (A Tory official said further recruitment would start shortly.)
5) It’s still the Kemi show
“We are under new management. There’s a new captain. There’s a new coach. There’s a new owner, effectively, which is all me,” is how Badenoch put it to GB News.
There’s a reason why she’s taking the “all me” approach. Badenoch easily out-polls her own party, which was unceremoniously dumped out of power by the electorate two years ago. “The party is a drag on Kemi,” as a third shadow cabinet minister put it.
Badenoch knows she must deflect some of that shine onto her colleagues. That’s why they were introduced, if somewhat awkwardly, in a parade into the hall before her speech — where she name-checked ministers who she said had helped trigger government U-turns.
At the same time, the party still feels a need to apologize for the failures that littered its 14 years in power. O’Brien made that point at one event on the conference fringe, arguing that the Tories failed to build enough prison places, failed to “stop the boats” and failed to deport illegal immigrants sufficiently.
The mission, said O’Brien, is to show “that you are serious, that you are different, and it’s not just another round of bullsh*t ‘hope again’ and fantasy … I feel seared by our experiences in government last time round. After we left, I felt a profound sense of disappointment and frankly shame.”
Badenoch put it best in her speech, where she insisted voters are at least peering through the shop window at the Tories. “They like what they see,” she said, “but let’s be honest: not enough of them are buying yet.”

Ukraine Working on Five Ceasefire Tracks With Partners, Foreign Ministry Says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
15:20:01 UTC
00:20:01 KST

Ukraine is working with international partners on five possible ceasefire formats as Kyiv continues efforts to find a path toward ending Russia’s war, Foreign Ministry spokesman Heorhii Tykhyi said on Oct. 7.
The proposals include a full and unconditional ceasefire, separate arrangements covering the Black Sea, food exports and energy infrastructure, as well as a US-backed energy ceasefire.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“These are initiatives developed with the involvement of Ukrainian diplomacy. They are realistic and mutually beneficial,” Tykhyi said at a briefing, sourced by RBC-Ukraine.
The five tracks are:
- Full and unconditional ceasefire: Ukraine agreed to a comprehensive ceasefire proposal in March 2025, and Kyiv’s position remains unchanged. Tykhyi said it now awaits a reciprocal decision from Russia.
- Black Sea security: Ukraine, Turkey and Egypt are working on proposals to ensure safe navigation in the Black Sea.
- Black Sea food security: Kyiv is working with India on protecting food exports through the Black Sea.
- India-led energy track: India is working to facilitate a halt to attacks on energy infrastructure.
- US-backed energy ceasefire: Ukraine and the US are discussing a separate arrangement to stop attacks on energy facilities, Tykhyi said.
“It takes two to tango,” Tykhyi said, stressing that Russia must agree to the proposed arrangements.
He said Kyiv considers the proposals both realistic and mutually beneficial.
Tykhyi also pushed back against claims that Ukraine is responsible for the lack of progress toward a ceasefire, calling such arguments an attempt to exploit public fatigue with the war.
“An attempt to shift the blame for the continuation of the war from Moscow to Kyiv is manipulation,” he said.
India has recently increased its involvement in diplomatic efforts between Ukraine and Russia, particularly on Black Sea security and energy infrastructure.
Indian Foreign Minister Subrahmanyam Jaishankar has been involved in efforts to explore an energy ceasefire and a halt to attacks on critical infrastructure, while Kyiv says it remains ready to work with New Delhi on practical proposals.
5 Children, Including Three 1-Year-Old Boys, Among 19 Killed in Russian Strike on Pryluky
Putin rejects proposal for mutual halt to strikes
Moscow has repeatedly rejected proposals for reciprocal ceasefires in different areas of the war.
In one of his latest statements, Russian President Vladimir Putin dismissed a proposal under which Russia would stop attacks on Ukrainian vessels if Kyiv halted strikes on Russian oil refineries.
Speaking at the Valdai Discussion Club on Oct. 1, Putin called the proposal “absurd,” arguing that Russia would gain little from stopping attacks on Ukrainian ships carrying civilian and agricultural cargo while its own oil and petroleum exports remain restricted by sanctions.
“We are supposed to stop striking targets that are sensitive to them. Well, it simply looks absurd,” Putin said.
Putin again claimed that Ukraine had initiated attacks on Russian vessels, saying Kyiv began striking tankers and other ships in early July. He claimed that 40 Russian vessels were “knocked out” in the first 10 days and more than 100 had been damaged since.
“We began responding,” Putin said, adding that Russia was now being asked to stop its attacks.
Asked directly whether he would agree to the proposed mutual halt to strikes, Putin replied: “No.”

France arrests brothers suspected of running site with nude images of 17,000 women and girls
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

00:19:32 KST

Platform that sold stolen sexual images of women and girls shut in France-US operation
PARIS - A joint French-US operation has shut down several websites associated with an online platform that sold private sexual content stolen from over 17,000 women worldwide, law enforcement authorities in both countries said on Oct 7.
Two brothers, aged 21 and 25, were arrested in northern France on Oct 6 on suspicion of having been the “main administrators” of the NudeLeaksTeens platform, a statement from the Paris prosecutor’s office said.
The platform sold “packs” of images and videos of thousands of women and girls stolen from sources including hacked accounts on Facebook, Instagram, TikTok and Snapchat.
More than 17,000 women of all nationalities were affected, the prosecutor’s office said, some of whom were children.
The US Attorney’s Office for the Eastern District of Virginia said in a separate statement that the site “offered for sale sexually explicit images and videos of children”.
It said the platform sold its content in specific albums, including one advertised as containing “6,200 private nude files” of mostly American teenagers or adults from hacked accounts, including child sexual abuse material.
French investigators also seized digital assets including bitcoin worth more than €700,000 (S$1 million).
Users on the platform were encouraged - in exchange for virtual currency - to provide identifying information about each victim, who were listed individually by their real names and categorised by age, location and occupation.
French prosecutors said the operation was part of a joint effort with US law enforcement to “combat child pornography, as well as the distribution and sale of stolen private sexual content involving women”. AFP

Pope Leo opens Vatican meeting likely to discuss remarriage, gay Catholics

Pope Leo opens Vatican meeting likely to discuss remarriage, gay Catholics
VATICAN CITY – Pope Leo urged an assembly of some 150 bishops from around the world to find “renewed ways” of helping modern families at the start of a week-long meeting at the Vatican, his biggest gathering of Church leaders so far.
The assembly, meeting through Oct 14 to discuss Catholic family life teachings, is expected to touch on contested topics such as the Church’s treatment of LGBT members and those who have been divorced and remarried, although those issues are not formally on the agenda.
Leo asked that God would “give us the freedom to listen to one another, the wisdom to recognise his work among his people, and the courage to follow where he leads us”.
The Pope has called the assembly, a meeting with the presidents of the world’s Catholic bishops conferences, to mark the 10th anniversary of a landmark 2016 document written by his predecessor, the late Pope Francis.
That text, titled Amoris Laetitia (The Joy of Love), urged the Church to be less strict and more compassionate towards “imperfect” Catholics, such as those who are divorced and remarried.
Under current Church teaching, remarried Catholics cannot receive communion unless they abstain from sex with their new partner, because their first marriage is still valid in the eyes of the Church.
Francis appeared to open the door for remarried Catholics to take communion, saying in a footnote of the 2016 document that they could receive “the help of the sacraments”, but never laid out a clear universal policy for the global Church.
Leo did not specifically mention the issue in his remarks on Oct 7 but said the Church must “recognise the work of grace even in situations marked by limits, wounds and apparent failure”.
Bishops from more than 115 countries are taking part in the assembly, including two from China, which negotiated a contested 2018 deal with Francis that normalised appointments of Catholic bishops in the country after decades of tensions.
Also taking part are 11 lay Catholic couples, who are expected to give testimonies about their lives. REUTERS

Ex-Barclays traders jailed for rigging interest rates have convictions quashed
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
15:19:25 UTC
00:19:25 KST

Five more former traders who were jailed for rigging interest rates have had their convictions quashed by the court of appeal in London, after a long battle to clear their names.
The court overturned the convictions of Jay Vijay Merchant, Jonathan Mathew, Philippe Moryoussef, Alex Pabon and Colin Bermingham – all of whom worked at Barclays.
Their acquittals on Wednesday came just over a year after the UK supreme court overturned a decade-old ruling against the former UBS and Citigroup trader Tom Hayes.
The five former Barclays traders were jailed between 2016 and 2019 on charges of manipulating the euro interbank offered rate (Euribor) or the now-defunct London interbank offered rate (Libor).
The Euribor and Libor rates affected the value of ordinary people’s pensions, mortgages and savings, as well as hundreds of trillions of pounds and euros worth of financial products around the world. Nine bankers accused of rigging the rates were given fraud convictions.
The five former Barclays traders applied to clear their names after Hayes, the first banker jailed for Libor-rigging in 2015, had his name cleared. Carlo Palombo, a former Barclays trader sentenced to four years in prison in 2019 for rigging Euribor, also had his conviction quashed on the same day in July 2025.
The supreme court overturned the convictions of Hayes and Palombo after finding faults in the original trials, ruling that had ultimately “deprived” them of a fair trial. They found trial judges had given “inaccurate and unfair” instructions to the juries that found the former traders guilty.
The cases of the American Pabon; Calcutta-born Merchant; Britons Bermingham and Mathew; and French national Moryoussef were referred back to the court of appeal by the Criminal Cases Review Commission in January.
The move came after the Serious Fraud Office (SFO), which brought the original charges against the men, found their convictions “may be considered unsafe” after the supreme court ruling in the cases of Hayes and Palombo. The SFO did not contest the appeals.
Mathew said: “For the last 10 years, the stain of a criminal conviction has been a burden I have carried every minute of every day.”
He added: “Having this conviction quashed is not simply about correcting the record, it’s about finally having validation that this is an injustice that never should have happened.”
In a statement, Pabon, thanked Hayes, who he said “refused to let it go and pushed this through for all of us”.
Tom Bushnell, a partner at the law firm Hickman & Rose, which represented Merchant, Mathew and Moryoussef, said: “In Jay Merchant and Jon Mathew’s case, it took over a decade for this wrong to be righted. In Philippe Moryoussef’s case, over eight years.
“Their lives have been turned upside down as a result. All involved in the criminal justice system should now ask themselves not only how this error came to be made and repeated, but also why it took so long to correct.”
Wednesday’s ruling marks a further blow for the SFO, with the unravelling of more of its high-profile prosecutions. It said: “After carefully considering this judgment and the full circumstances, we do not oppose the appeals of five individuals convicted by juries in relation to Libor and Euribor.”
The agency reiterated in a statement that the supreme court had “found that there was ample evidence on which a properly directed jury could have convicted Tom Hayes and Carlo Palombo”.
Jason Williams, the head of division at the SFO, added that it was not deemed in the public interest to seek retrials of Hayes and Palombo.
A further attempted appeal by Christian Bittar, a former Deutsche Bank trader who pleaded guilty in 2018, is expected to be heard on Friday. His case is the only one being contested by the SFO, which argues his conviction was safe.

IEA members back faster oil stock releases, prioritizing diesel
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
15:19:02 UTC
00:19:02 KST

Mucahithan Avcioglu
07 October 2026•Update: 07 October 2026
International Energy Agency (IEA) member governments backed accelerating previously announced oil stock releases and prioritizing diesel supplies amid tight markets, as prices rise and supplies tighten, Executive Director Fatih Birol said on Wednesday.
In a statement after a meeting of member governments, Birol said participants supported completing releases pledged under the March collective action as soon as possible.
Members also supported prioritizing diesel stock releases to the extent possible, given current tightness in diesel markets.
Approximately 325 million barrels have already been released under the March deal, with some countries supplying more than initially pledged, he said.
Releasing all remaining stocks pledged under that plan would bring approximately 100 million barrels to the market.
Participants reaffirmed their commitment to delivering the pledge and expressed appreciation for the IEA's response to the energy impacts of the Strait of Hormuz crisis, according to Birol.
They emphasized the agency's role in monitoring implementation and providing updated market analysis.
Participants also welcomed a recent statement by G7 leaders on global energy security and market stability, including its emphasis on maintaining the free flow of energy trade. The Group of Seven countries last week agreed to release 100 million barrels over the next four months to bring down oil prices amid pressure from US President Donald Trump.
IEA member governments still hold around 1.1 billion barrels of publicly held emergency oil stocks, including more than 200 million barrels of diesel, Birol said.
“The IEA stands ready to release more of these stocks to the market if and when required,” he added.
The agency will continue working with member governments to monitor the ongoing releases. Members agreed to reassess the situation at the next meeting of the IEA Governing Board next week.
The Iran war led to the largest emergency stock release ever of 400 million barrels in March, coordinated by the IEA.
Trump is seeking to bring down fuel prices ahead of the November midterm elections, seeking to ease the impact of the Iran war and high fuel costs on consumers and industries.

German chancellor alarmed after AfD elects first state parliament speaker
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
15:18:02 UTC
00:18:02 KST

Ayhan Simsek
07 October 2026•Update: 07 October 2026
Chancellor Friedrich Merz expressed deep concern on Wednesday after the right-wing Alternative for Germany (AfD) won its first state parliament speaker post, securing a key role in Saxony-Anhalt.
“I am deeply concerned and somewhat appalled by what happened yesterday,” Merz said in his address at a business forum of the Handelsblatt Media Group in Berlin. He called on democratic politicians to keep refusing any cooperation with the anti-immigrant party.
“It was a secret ballot. We do not know exactly who cast votes for the AfD candidate,” Merz said. “But anyone who casts their vote for the AfD is playing the extremists' game. And they are destroying credibility. It is certainly incompatible with the values of my party, the CDU.”
Lawmakers in Magdeburg on Tuesday elected Tobias Rausch of the AfD as speaker of the state parliament. In a secret first-round ballot, he won 48 of 82 votes, nine more than the 39 seats held by his own party.
German media and rival parties speculated that some lawmakers from Merz's conservative CDU cast those votes, and read the result as a crack in the long-standing firewall against the AfD, the policy of no coalitions, no joint votes and no other cooperation meant to isolate the party.
Germany's state domestic intelligence agency in Saxony-Anhalt has classified the AfD there as a confirmed right-wing extremist group, citing suspected anti-democratic goals and activities. The party is challenging the label.
Merz expressed concern over Tuesday’s result in Magdeburg, but also warned against hasty conclusions. He suggested lawmakers outside the CDU could have backed the AfD candidate in the secret ballot to raise pressure on his party and open divisions.
“False-flag operations don't just happen in the military; they happen in politics, too,” he said. “And that is why we need to be careful about drawing hasty conclusions. Here, we are dealing with at least two -- or in the Saxony-Anhalt state parliament, three -- factions that are doing everything they can to undermine democratic cohesion”
Merz said the results of September's regional election in Saxony-Anhalt had been a bitter outcome and a historic turning point, with the anti-immigrant AfD winning 43.8% of the vote and the left-wing populist BSW 5.3%. Calling them extremist parties with authoritarian tendencies, he said it was deeply concerning that the two had reached an absolute majority in the state parliament.
"Yet the election result is the election result," he said, adding that accepting results, even when they are unwelcome, is part of democracy.
"The question then turns back to us: what do we do so that something like this is not repeated?" Merz said. "Above all, so that it does not happen across the whole of Germany at the next federal election."
He said the parties in the governing coalition will draw lessons from the setback, continue the reform program and deliver concrete results to address people's concerns.

All hail the Kult of Kemi – captain, coach and owner of the Conservatives | John Crace
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
15:17:56 UTC
00:17:56 KST

Where’s AI slop when you need it? It could all have been so much simpler. Just ask ChatGPT to write me a leader’s speech in the style of Kemi Badenoch. Make it an hour and 10 minutes long, so plenty of room for padding. Go heavy on the slogans, cliches and the obligatory crap politician jokes. Ones we’ve all heard many times before. Not least at this conference.
Make the usual digs at Labour and put the boot in to Reform. The main aim of the speech is to try to reposition a party that is tanking in third place on 20% in the polls as the main opposition to the government.
And just to give everyone a reason to go home with a feeling of mild optimism, chuck in a retail offer at the end. An uncosted tax cut for people who are rich but don’t feel quite rich enough. The new multimillionaire common-or-garden lower middle classes.
Unfortunately, Kemi made the schoolgirl error of trying to write the speech for herself. And it was much the worse for it. What’s the point of having AI if you don’t use it? It was too long, too flabby. No real argument, just a collection of random thoughts. Andy Burnham in Liverpool it wasn’t.
Parts of it even seemed to bore Kemi herself. As if she was going through the motions. Lazy, even. That it was still by far and away the best speech of the entire conference is not really the point. More of a reflection of how dire the others have been. Four days of the Tories in Birmingham is a trial for anyone remotely sentient.
On the surface, the Tories have seemed a happy tribe this week. There has been a soporific tranquillity to the proceedings. Few members attending, nonexistent queues and above all no Robert Jenrick. Or even Liz Truss. How we miss her.
But the unity feels very fragile. The Tories are now Kemi and Kemi is the Tories. The party has bet the bank on her. Kemi even now calls herself the captain, coach and owner of the Tories. Everyone else is an also-ran.
This comes at a huge risk. Because Kemi has become almost too big for the Tories to allow her to fail. So they daren’t question her. Anything she does has to be acclaimed as a work of genius. Just walking on stage is enough to secure her a standing ovation. No one has ever quite walked like that before.
The party has been captured by the Kult of Kemi. It’s a self-fulfilling prophecy that could lead them to oblivion. They have no idea if Kemi is messiah or lemming, but they are happy to go over the cliff regardless. They are out of other options.
Just don’t stop to ask why nothing the Tories seem to do is cutting through. Why the polls are stubbornly flatlining. Why it’s odds-on that beyond the few hundred people in the hall, no one will pay a blind bit of attention to her speech. It will be forgotten within a day.
Wednesday morning’s proceedings began with the Tory chair, Kevin Hollinrake. Kev’s dog got a bigger cheer than Kev. Next up was the shadow justice secretary, Nick Timothy, a one-man cluster of antimatter. No man can suck the energy out of the room like Nick. The only thing that would cheer him up is a public execution.
Then the Philpster. The UK’s self-proclaimed superhero. The vigilante who took on the French. Endearingly, he still thinks the French navy knows who he is. Chris, most of the UK don’t know who you are. Nor do they care.
After this, things began to get surreal as each member of the shadow cabinet was announced and applauded as they took their seats. A bit like a third-rate talent show. The presenter still didn’t know who Nick Timothy was, despite having introduced him moments earlier. She also got Helen Whately’s name wrong. And there was one empty chair. Tom Tugendhat had invented an unmissable trip to India to get out of the embarrassment. Wise choice.
A spot of Elgar and then it was Kemi. There was a fight for the soul of the country. There’s always a fight for the soul of the country as far as the Tories are concerned. They don’t seem to realise that it was them that ripped the soul out of it.
“What a great conference we’ve had,” she said. It was hard to know if she was being ironic. Other than the fact that everyone has been wandering round in brain-dead surprise that the Tories still exist, it’s been a disaster.
After that things went weird. As if we were entering a weird dystopia. Being asked to believe the unbelievable. Like when she said that her shadow cabinet was a united team that listened to one another. This after Kemi had literally said she was the party and that anyone who disagreed with her could go fuck themselves. The whole point of Kemi is that she listens to no one.
She also had a pop at Labour for putting all their faith in one man. Pots, kettles. As for Reform, she had nothing but contempt. You’d like to think that would rule out a possible coalition.
The one moment when Kemi became truly passionate – believable even – was when she talked about race. This was Kemi at her best, talking about something she really cared about. Even if she did imagine there was no racism in football in the 1970s and 80s. But this bit was all too short and the speech began to feel like it was dragging into eternity. We’d still be trying to stay awake well into the afternoon.
Finally the reveal – the inheritance tax reduction that would be funded by as-yet-unspecified welfare cuts. There would be no inheritance tax on anyone leaving their home to their children. With an extra million-quid freebie thrown in, in case you needed to do it up after your parents had let it get tatty. You could hear the cheers from the country’s stately homes echo around the hall.
Here was a party that really got it. Which was prepared to do something about the cost of living for the mega-rich. Even as Kemi was speaking, millions of ordinary citizens were phoning their brokers to liquidate their stock market assets so they could upgrade their £1m homes to something far more palatial. The property market in mega-homes had just gone wild. The people’s earl, Charles Spencer, could breathe easy. Althorp was safe. Let them drink champagne.
There was just time for Kemi to pay tribute to Jeffrey Archer – the Tories have a soft spot for a convicted conman who ruined several lives – and then came the extended standing ovations. An echo chamber is going to echo.

Arriving in Paris, Steinmeier says Europe needs right mix of 'reason and heart'
German President Frank-Walter Steinmeier has begun a three-day state visit to neighboring France. He landed at Paris' Orly airport on a damp evening and made his way to the German Embassy.
He said Europe needed to face its various security and political challenges with a mixture of the head's reason and the heart's emotion.
"Reason and heart, that's what Europe needs again today, in a time of wars and crises, in which our democracies are under attack to an extent not seen since the second World War," Steinmeier said.
He said it was a mixture of reason, or head, and heart that had made the Franco-German reconciliation after the war possible.
Steinmeier was playing on a quote from French writer Victor Hugo, who in the 19th century said that in Europe, Germany was the heart and France was the head or the reason. Steinmeier said he would leave it open to debate whether the modern-day French or Germans might agree with this particular division of anatomical labor.
What mattered, he said, was that there could be only one response to the current circumstances: "Europe must, now above all, stand up confidently and in unison for the values that made us what we are: respect for human dignity, peace, freedom, democracy."
On Thursday, Steinmeier will visit the Pantheon monument in Paris with President Emmanuel Macron, to honor the Jewish historian and resistance fighter Marc Bloch, who was murdered by Nazi Germany.
Steinmeier also intimated that a new deal on Franco-German youth cooperation might be signed amid the visit, speaking of a "promise for a new generation of German and French youth, who want to learn to understand, value and love each other."
The visit coincides with considerable political unrest among French young people in the form of ongoing school funding protests.
Steinmeier also said prior to leaving Berlin that his state visit would be "something of a farewell tour with a truly committed European and a good friend."
Both he and French President Macron took office in 2017, and both will be leaving their posts early in 2027.
Steinmeier's post, however, is far more ceremonial and removed from daily politics than that of the French president.
Saxony-Anhalt AfD and BSW lawmakers call for end to Ukraine aid, sanctions on Russia
Immediately following its initial parliamentary session on Tuesday, Saxony-Anhalt state legislators from the far-right AfD and far-left BSW called for the federal government in Berlin to drop sanctions on Russia over its invasion of Ukraine, as well as demanding an end to all arms deliveries and financial aid for Ukraine as Kyiv defends itself from a nearly five-year Russian invasion.
Both parties are known for their Russia "friendly" stances and their ties to the Kremlin.
They have also latched onto Moscow's claim that Berlin and other EU and NATO governments are the true "war mongers" in Ukraine, baselessly claiming that Russia is a peace-loving nation forced to defend itself against hostile neighbors.
BSW founder Sahra Wagenknecht echoed AfD co-chair Alice Weidel in labeling the initiative "a signal for peace."
"Economic sanctions against Russia must end immediately," a statement said.
Germany's federal leadership, under two chancellors, has shown steadfast — if at times cautious — support for Ukraine and demanded Russia end its killing of civilians before entering into further dialogue.
Beyond dropping sanctions, the AfD and BSW insist Germany must normalize relations with Moscow, and stop "financing the war," arguing instead that money spent helping Ukraine defend its democracy would be better spent in Germany.
State governments in Germany have no say in federal foreign and energy policy, but the parties say they launched their effort in an attempt to force change in Berlin.
Merz rails against extremism, AfD sympathizers in own ranks
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz on Wednesday addressed the threat of political extremism to the existing social order, accusing the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) and far-left BSW parties of wanting to wipe out "the DNA of our democracy."
"Extremism," said Merz, "is forcing its way into our state legislatures with a vengeance."
Merz, speaking in Berlin, called this week’s election of an AfD politician as speaker of Saxony-Anhalt's state parliament — the first time a far-right politician has been tapped to lead a statehouse since 1945 — a "historic break."
Moreover, Merz slammed politicians — potentially from his own conservative CDU party — for casting ballots in favor of Tobias Rausch in the Saxony-Anhalt vote, saying he was "deeply concerned and somewhat appalled" when the AfD's candidate was elected to the speaker position.
Rausch received 48 votes but the AfD and BSW only have 44 between them. It is unclear from whom Rausch picked up four extra votes — he was elected in a secret ballot.
Observers assume these came from within the CDU, but Merz said "false flag" attacks also occur in politics, implying the Social Democrats, the Left party and the Greens, all of which are also represented in the state's parliament, could be attempting to weaken or sow division in the CDU.
"Anyone who casts their vote for the AfD is playing the extremists' game and undermining credibility," said Merz. "In any case, this is incompatible with the values of my party, the CDU."
IN DEPTH: German spy scandal threatens national security
The arrest of August Hanning, former president of Germany's foreign intelligence service, the Bundesnachrichtendienst (BND), and his former chief-of-staff, Manfred D., is threatening to cause a major rupture in Germany's intelligence relationships, according to analysts, as the full scale of the scandal begins to be understood abroad.

Police in Oberding, Bavaria, on Wednesday warned residents in Notzinger Moos near Munich airport to remain vigilant and urged them to keep children and small animals indoors amid a spate of puma sightings.
"According to initial expert assessments," a spokesperson for the local government said, "it could be a puma."

Frankfurt Book Fair kicks off with literature, politics and AI debates
The Frankfurt Book Fair opened with the Czech Republic as guest of honor. The program ranges from presentations of literary works to political debates. In addition, Latin America's 50th anniversary as the first guest of honor at the fair will be commemorated on a special stage, and Chile will present its plans as the guest country for 2027.

IN DEPTH: Did CDU lawmakers vote for AfD speaker Rausch?
The question of which lawmakers besides those of the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) and populist BSW voted to elect the AfD's Tobias Rausch as parliamentary speaker in Saxony-Anhalt on Tuesday continues to fuel speculation — and outrage.
The choice of a far-right figure to preside over a state parliament for the first time since World War II has been described as a "breaking of taboos" by the center-left Social Democrats (SPD).
Most observers suspect that politicians from the center-right Christian Democrats are the most likely to have backed Rausch, despite their party's official adherence to the "firewall" principle rejecting cooperation with the AfD.

New Hannover-Hamburg rail line set to be built by 2050
As mentioned at the start of this blog, railroad woes are one major theme in our Germany coverage.
But here is some very positive news for once: The parliamentary transport committee has finally endorsed a plan by railway operator Deutsche Bahn (DB) to build a new line linking Hannover and Hamburg by 2050.
The project for what is one of Germany's most important transport routes is planned to cost at least €9 billion ($10 billion) and had prompted years of wrangling.
It still requires backing by the full Bundestag, or lower house of parliament, on Thursday, but that is likely to be a formality.
High-speed train line
The new two-track line will be designed for speeds of up to 250 kilometers per hour (155 miles per hour), cutting journey times between the two cities by 18 minutes.
However, it will be some time before construction begins: The preliminary planning report that forsees submitting approval documents in 2034, with construction to start in 2036.
Renovation of the existing line between the two cities is also planned for 2029 under the agreement.
According to DB, that route is already heavily congested, carrying up to 147% of intended capacity.
The agreement was reached despite opposition from lawmakers representing constituencies affected by the new construction, including Vice Chancellor Lars Klingbeil of the Social Democrats (SPD).
Final day of Backstreet Boys mania in Düsseldorf
US group the Backstreet Boyswill play their final of 10 concerts in Düsseldorf tonight, capping off a week of street parties and sing-alongs to celebrate the band.
"We'll take you on a trip back in time," member Howie Dorough promised.
To the rhythm of "Larger Than Life", Nick, Howie, Brian, AJ and Kevin appeared floating above the venue, crossing the Merkur Spiel-Arena on hoverboards each night.
Against the backdrop of a giant screen displaying futuristic graphics, accompanied by pyrotechnics and a laser show, the American stars have almost finished their short German residency.
The five musicians had already presented the show, Into The Millennium, at the Sphere in Las Vegas.

The Boys' return to Germany
The concert series carried the subtitle Homecoming: Live in Germany, because the band have enjoyed a loyal fan base since their early days in Germany, as the singers emphasized in Düsseldorf.
"Germany, you were our first love. You loved us before everyone else, and we loved you," Kevin Richardson said. "So many years, so many memories," Nick Carter added.

Germany blocks sale of Hamburg logistics firm to China's COSCO
The German government has said the acquisition of a majority of shares in Hamburg logistics company Zippel by China's state-owned shipping giant Cosco could pose a security threat and has blocked the sale.
The purchase of 80% of shares in Zippel by a Chinese company "would have deepened dependencies and jeopardized the resilience of Germany’s and the EU’s supply chains," an Economy Ministry spokesman said.
Speaking after a Cabinet meeting in Berlin, the spokesman said that although Germany welcomed foreign investment in general, "there may be investments that threaten the country's security."
Reports at the end of April said that the BfV domestic intelligence agency already had reservations about the takeover, which had been approved by the Cartel Office in February.
The business daily Handelsblatt reported at the end of September that the government was intending to block the sale, though this was not confirmed by Berlin at the time.
Cosco already holds a 24.99% stake in the Hamburg container terminal Tollerort.
That deal prompted a debate at the time about China's participation in critical infrastructure in Germany.
Majority finds Merz a failure as chancellor — survey
Most people in Germany consider that Chancellor Friedrich Merz is not up to the job, a new survey has shown.
In all, 67% of respondents in the survey by the Ipsos institute were either wholly or fairly in agreement with the statement "The chancellorship of Friedrich Merz has failed."
A whole 48% completely agreed on Merz's insufficiency as leader, according to the survey published in the Spiegel news magazine.
There were regional differences in assessment's of Merz's performance, with 80% of people in eastern states completely or somewhat dissatisfied compared with 64% in the west.
However, there was much less agreement on which conservative politician could replace him if he were to step down or be ousted.
The survey gave a choice between the leader of the Bavarian Christian Social Union (CSU), Markus Söder, his party colleague Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt or the premier of the state of North Rhine-Westphalia, Hendrik Wüst.
Altogether 43% of those surveyed said none of those named came into question, while some 14% responded with "Don't know."
Söder was, however, the favorite with 20% support, followed by Wüst on 16%.
Dobrindt lagged far behind on just 5%.
SPD questions CDU, BSW role in election of far-right speaker
The co-leader of the Social Democrats (SPD), Lars Klingbeil, says coalition partner the Christian Democrats (CDU) has questions to answer after the election of Tobias Rausch, a politician from the Alternative for Germany (AfD), as parliamentary speaker in Saxony-Anhalt.
"The fact that the candidate of the AfD in Saxony-Anhalt, which is classified as 'confirmed right-wing extremist,' was elected as state parliament speaker with considerably more than just AfD votes raises very urgent questions," said Klingbeil, who is also deputy chancellor and finance minister.
"Electing right-wing extremists to such positions breaks with a taboo," he said.
"Not just the BSW, but also the CDU must urgently explain how this could happen."
The SPD federal parliamentary party staged a march through Berlin's Brandenburg Gate on Tuesday to protest at the election result.
The state chapter of the AfD, which won a landslide victory at September elections, is classified as "confirmed right-wing extremist" by domestic intelligence.
Mysterious extra votes for Rausch
Rausch was elected speaker with 48-29 votes, though just 44 votes for him would have resulted if only his party (39 seats) and the populist BSW (five seats), which had pledged to back him, had voted in his favor.
The CDU parliamentary leader, Sven Schulze, had recommended that the 15 parliamentarians in his party abstain from voting, but there were only five abstentions altogether in the secret ballot. One CDU member was absent.
The other three parties represented in the legislature — the SPD, the Left Party and the Greens — had all declared their opposition to Rausch.
Schulze said he could not believe that the four extra votes for Rausch came from the ranks of the CDU, although there has been widespread speculation that this was the case.
All mainstream parties in Germany have so far officially stated that they reject any form of cooperation with the AfD in keeping with the so-called "firewall."
Ex-spy chief August Hanning to face court for allegedly selling state secrets
August Hanning, the former president of Germany's foreign intelligence service (BND), who was arrested on suspicion of espionage, is due to appear on Wednesday before an investigating judge at the Federal Court of Justice in Karlsruhe, who will decide whether he should remain in custody pending trial.
Hanning, who stepped down as head of the BND in 2005, is under investigation on suspicion of espionage-related offenses, including high treason, obtaining state secrets, attempted high treason, and acting as an agent for a foreign intelligence service.
Merz reaffirms solidarity with Israel amid October 7 commemorations
Chancellor Friedrich Merz has reaffirmed Germany's support for Israel in remarks on the anniversary of the deadly October 7, 2023 attacks led by the Palestinian militant group Hamas.
"Germany stands firmly by Israel's side. Our Israeli friends can count on our commitment to ensuring that such a crime is never repeated," Merz said.
"We stand for the security and existence of Israel — this is a lesson drawn from the Shoah [Holocaust] and part of German identity," he said.
Merz said Germany believed that the two-state solution was the best way to establish peace in the region.
He also said the German government would do all in its power to combat rising antisemitism, adding that Jews had to be able to live in Germany without fear.
Merz said his thoughts on the anniversary were with the victims and their families, survivors and former hostages.
"And we hope that the deep pain and wounds inflicted by this day — by these monstrous, barbaric acts — can heal," he said.
Several events are being held in Berlin to mark the anniversary.
The Palestinian militant group Hamas led attacks in southern Israel on October 7, 2023 in which some 1,200 people were killed and more than 250 others abducted.
The attacks triggered the ongoing war on Hamas in Gaza, which left some 74,000 Palestinians dead, most of them civilians.

MOSCOW, October 7. /TASS/. Two reconnaissance aircraft spent nearly seven hours flying over the international waters of the Black Sea, a source in EU air traffic control services told TASS.

Artists including Noel Gallagher show support for Garvaghy Road residents in Drumcree dispute

Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
15:15:43 UTC

Dozens of artists, actors and musicians including Susan Sarandon and Noel Gallagher have expressed support for Garvaghy Road residents in the impasse over the Drumcree parade in Northern Ireland.
In an open letter to the secretary of state, Chris Bryant, they urged the government to protect residents and to appoint an international mediator to resolve the dispute between the Catholic residents and the Orange Order in County Armagh.
“Central to any just resolution must be the primacy and protection of the local community,” said the letter, which urged authorities to safeguard residents from “any form of forced processions that disregard their consent, safety and right to live in peace free from intimidation”.
It was signed by the writer Irvine Welsh, the film-makers Ken Loach and Jim Sheridan, the actors Adrian Dunbar, Maxine Peake and Siobhán McSweeney and the musicians Paul Weller, Johnny Marr and Imelda May, among others.
Twenty MPs and members of the House of Lords signed a separate letter exhorting Bryant to cancel the march.
The 11-day-old dispute fuelled fresh political tension on Wednesday when three unionist parties tabled a motion of no confidence in Michelle O’Neill, the Sinn Féin first minister, and other Sinn Féin ministers. The motion lacks cross-community support and is expected to fail when debated at the Stormont assembly on 12 October.
In the Dáil in Dublin, the Sinn Féin leader, Mary Lou McDonald, accused Bryant of allowing the stalemate to fester and leaving Garvaghy Road residents in “dangerous limbo”. She urged the Irish government to “apply all necessary pressure” on British authorities to prevent the parade.
The taoiseach, Micheál Martin, said he had discussed the impasse with Andy Burnham on Monday and urged renewed talks in Northern Ireland. “We need a mediated resolution,” he said. “The talks that have happened could result in an outcome if we maintain dialogue.”
The march around Drumcree is one of hundreds of parades that the Orange Order holds in Northern Ireland each year to commemorate Protestant forefathers who fell in battles. Critics say they are an attempt to intimidate Catholics.
Attempts by Garvaghy Road residents to block the march in the 1990s led to pitched battles between Orange Order supporters and police and sectarian violence. The dispute subsided after 1998 when the Parades Commission prohibited the route through Garvaghy Road, but last month the commission ruled that a scaled-down parade of 35 Orangemen could march down Garvaghy, reigniting protests by residents.
In a statement on Wednesday, the Orange Order’s Portadown district lodge said its members were ready to exercise a legal right to march the route – for the first time in 28 years – and urged the police to deal with the protesters who impeded them.
“We will not give up that legal right, as to do so would be to legitimise mob rule. We will continue our dignified, peaceful and lawful stand,” it said. “We have yet to see any action taken, as Michelle O’Neill and her comrades continue to flout the law.”

Oscar-winning actress Eva Marie Saint of ‘On the Waterfront,’ ‘North by Northwest’ dies at 102
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
15:14:34 UTC
00:14:34 KST

Halis Sunnetci
07 October 2026•Update: 07 October 2026
Oscar-winning actress Eva Marie Saint, known for her roles in the Hollywood classics On the Waterfront and North by Northwest, died Tuesday of natural causes at her Los Angeles home at the age of 102, her representative Jeff Sanderson said.
Saint made her film debut opposite Marlon Brando in director Elia Kazan’s 1954 crime drama On the Waterfront, playing Edie Doyle, the love interest of Brando’s dockworker Terry Malloy.
The performance earned Saint the Academy Award for Best Supporting Actress, while Brando won his first Oscar for Best Actor for the film.
Five years later, Saint starred opposite Cary Grant as Eve Kendall in Alfred Hitchcock’s 1959 spy thriller North by Northwest, another of her best-known performances.
Born in Newark, New Jersey, in 1924, Saint began her career in radio and television before appearing in Horton Foote’s The Trip to Bountiful on Broadway in 1953, a performance that helped lead to her casting in On the Waterfront.
Her other film credits included A Hatful of Rain, Exodus, Grand Prix, The Russians Are Coming, the Russians Are Coming and The Stalking Moon. She later appeared in Nothing in Common, Superman Returns and Winter’s Tale.
Saint also had an extensive television career, winning an Emmy for the 1990 miniseries People Like Us.
Her husband, television and stage director Jeffrey Hayden, died in 2016 after 65 years of marriage. They had two children.

Sa’ar must stand by his decision to close the British Consulate in Jerusalem - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
15:13:39 UTC
00:13:39 KST

Foreign Minister Gideon Sa’ar made a significant diplomatic decision last month – to close the British Consulate General in Jerusalem. Now comes the more important test – standing by that decision and seeing it through.
The UK makes no secret of its position regarding Jerusalem. The British government’s official website states that the British Consulate General in Jerusalem represents the UK government in Jerusalem, the West Bank, and Gaza, and works to advance political, security, and economic interests between the United Kingdom and the Palestinians.
Britain also makes clear that it does not recognize Israeli sovereignty over Jerusalem and regards east Jerusalem as occupied territory.
That is precisely the problem.
For years, a foreign diplomatic mission has operated in Jerusalem, the capital of the State of Israel, independently of the British embassy in Israel, with much of its diplomatic activity directed toward the Palestinian Authority. This exceptional arrangement is rooted in historical circumstances that predate the establishment of the State of Israel.
A sovereign state is not required to accept such an arrangement indefinitely simply because it existed in the past.
On September 8, Sa’ar announced the closure of the British Consulate General in Jerusalem as part of a series of measures taken in response to the UK government’s recent policy toward Israel. According to official statements and media reports, the decision was coordinated with Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.
Israel is now facing pressure to reverse course.
In Britain, arguments are already being made that Israel has no authority to close the consulate because the UK does not recognize east Jerusalem as part of Israel’s sovereign territory. A legal opinion published in Britain has even called on the British government to oppose the Israeli move.
That is precisely why Israel must not back down.
This debate is no longer merely about a building on Rajeib Nashashibi Street in Sheikh Jarrah. It concerns a much more fundamental question: Who determines the rules governing diplomatic activity in Jerusalem – the government of Israel, or a foreign government that does not recognize Israeli sovereignty in its capital?
Israel should not sever its relations with Britain. On the contrary, Britain is an important country, and Israel has a clear interest in maintaining strong diplomatic, security, and economic relations with it. That is the purpose of a British embassy in Israel.
Israel must retain its sovereignty
But good relations between countries cannot come at the expense of the principle of sovereignty.
If Britain wishes to provide consular services to its citizens in Jerusalem, it can do so through an appropriate framework acceptable to Israel. If it wishes to maintain relations with the Palestinian Authority, it can do so through accepted channels and in accordance with the relevant arrangements.
But there is no justification for an independent diplomatic mission operating in Jerusalem as though Israeli sovereignty in the city were something that could simply be bypassed.
Sa’ar’s decision could mark a turning point in Israel’s policy toward Jerusalem. For years, Israel has called on countries worldwide to recognize Jerusalem as its capital and relocate their embassies to the city. In recent years, additional countries have indeed opened embassies in Jerusalem or announced their intention to do so.
But alongside the effort to bring more embassies to Jerusalem, Israel also needs a clear policy toward diplomatic missions operating in the city while denying Israeli sovereignty over it.
The message needed to be conveyed to Sa’ar now: You made a clear decision consistent with the sovereignty policy you have presented. Now it must be carried through.
Do not be deterred by diplomatic pressure. Do not allow a principled decision to become the subject of endless negotiations. And do not create a precedent in which pressure from a foreign government is enough to make Israel reverse a decision concerning the status of its own capital.
Closing the British consulate need not be an act against Britain. It can and should be an affirmation of a simple principle: countries that wish to maintain diplomatic relations with Israel must do so while respecting its sovereignty.
Jerusalem is not a diplomatic no-man’s-land.
Mr. foreign minister, do not stop halfway. You made the decision – now see it through.
The writer is chairman of the Jerusalem Center for Applied Policy (JCAP).

Hezbollah receives $200 million cash infusion from Iran to support families tied to terror group

2026-10-07

00:13:29 KST

Hezbollah has received $200 million from Iran, which the Islamic regime claims aims to help Lebanese displaced by this year’s war with Israel, two people with direct knowledge of the transfer said, the first significant aid from the terrorist group to supporters.
The Jerusalem Post cannot verify that the Iranian funds transferred to the terror group will be used as aid for Lebanese civilians affected by the war.
Hezbollah received the cash last month despite a tightening US economic chokehold on Iran and increasing difficulties in getting funds to Tehran's Lebanese ally, said the people.
Intermediaries who moved the money charged a 20% fee, reflecting the risks of dealing with the group, they said. One said this was four times the normal fee.
Asked for comment, a Hezbollah official said an amount had been secured, and a plan for distributing it would be announced in the coming days, without elaborating on the source of the funds.
The Iranian foreign ministry, Iran's permanent mission in Geneva, the US Treasury Department and the Lebanese government did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
Israel’s operation against Hezbollah in Lebanon uprooted hundreds of thousands of Shi’ite Muslim constituents after the group entered the regional war in support of Iran on March 2.
But those displaced have so far received little to no assistance from Hezbollah, a terror organization founded by Iran’s Revolutionary Guards in 1982, which has suffered heavy Israeli blows in two wars since 2024 and is designated a terrorist group by Washington.
Payments to approx. 50,000 families
Hezbollah would use the funds to pay an initial $3,000 per family, and priority will go to those whose villages have been destroyed or are inaccessible due to Israeli occupation, the sources said. These number around 50,000 families, one of the sources said.
Iran has maintained financial support to Hezbollah through years of crippling US sanctions: it transferred $1 billion to the group in the first 10 months of 2025, according to the US Treasury Department.
Tehran has never acknowledged financing Hezbollah. Iran's policy of funding regional proxies has stirred domestic protester anger against the clerical rulers in the past and could prove particularly sensitive at a time of worsening hardship in Iran.
Iran had promised Hezbollah more funding after Tehran signed an interim deal with Washington in June that allowed Iran to sell its oil, Reuters reported at the time. That agreement collapsed in July.
Washington has since intensified economic pressure on Iran, tightening sanctions and imposing a naval blockade to block Iranian oil exports.
Hezbollah leader Naim Qassem said in a speech last month that the group would soon contribute to a project aimed at housing thousands of people displaced by the war, using “available resources and donations”, without elaborating.
Hezbollah's ability to fund local services and provide post-conflict aid has helped shore up its support in the past. Following a war with Israel in 2006, the group immediately handed out large cash payments to those impacted and moved swiftly to help rebuild Beirut's southern suburbs, a stronghold.
But this time there has been little sign of reconstruction. Lebanese Prime Minister Nawaf Salam said last month that the total reconstruction costs from the two wars since 2024 could exceed $27 billion.
Thousands of terrorists dead in a costly war
The two sources provided no details on how the money got to Lebanon.
One of them said it was increasingly difficult for Hezbollah to move funds via financial companies that once processed such transfers. Such firms based in Iraq and Dubai were no longer an option, and they were also now under pressure in Turkey, this source said.
Hezbollah’s foes believed money was currently the group’s “oxygen”, the source added. Despite the difficulties securing funding, the group had not stopped paying its fighters and the family members of those killed in combat, this source said.
In Lebanon, the war has inflicted a heavy price on the Shi’ite Muslim community from which Hezbollah draws support. Israel has razed villages across a swathe of territory it has seized in the south, saying it aims to shield northern Israel from Hezbollah attacks.
Israeli attacks in Lebanon have killed more than 4,300 people since March 2, according to Lebanon’s health ministry. Its toll does not say how many combatants may be among the dead. Hezbollah has not disclosed figures on its war dead. Reuters reported on May 4 that several thousand Hezbollah terrorists had been killed in the war.

Former hostage Iair Horn declared honored guest of Buenos Aires, shares story of Gaza captivity
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
15:13:29 UTC
00:13:29 KST

Former Hamas hostage Iair Horn said he considers it his responsibility to keep telling his story in interviews, public speaking events, and any other forum he can, according to a series of interviews with Argentinian media on Monday, after being declared an honored guest of Buenos Aires.
“It is my responsibility, that is how I see it, that is how we understand it in my family, and that is why I speak," he explained. "I have a story to tell, and I tell it. It is part of my responsibility as a human being, as a Jew, and also because of the way I was raised.”
Horn described his first awareness of the October 7 attack on his community of Kibbutz Nir Oz. A siren going off was routine, he said, but then the kibbutz's internal communication system announced that terrorists were inside the community, and he began to hear gunshots and screams.
Horn and his brother, Eitan, hid in the safe room, but Horn was forced to emerge with his hands raised after Hamas terrorists began shooting through the door. He said that he hoped that, by shielding the doorway with his body, he could hide Eitan from the terrorists' view.
“They took the first people, and Eitan stayed behind; he stayed at the house. But he did what he could, and some time later they took him too,” Horn recalled.
Horn was taken to the Gaza Strip on a motorcycle, where his abductors repeatedly shouted that he was a Jew, leading the crowd to beat him.
"Punches, punches, punches," Horn said, describing how his captors would stop every few hundred meters to allow more people to abuse him.
He was taken down into tunnels below Gaza, "the biggest maze I have ever had to visit in my life," where five days later he would be reunited with his brother. The two would spend the rest of Horn's time in captivity together.
The worst aspect of the situation, Horn explained, was the psychological torment.
“Nobody cares about you. Tomorrow I kill you, tomorrow I kill your brother, tomorrow we blow up the whole tunnel with everyone inside,” he explained. “The physical part, one way or another, you suffer from it more or less, but you can recover from it."
'The most normal thing was to accept that this was my reality'
His survival strategy, he said, was to accept all that he was going through.
“For me, the most normal thing was to accept that this was my reality. Okay, now I live down here, I live here in the tunnel. That's it, yes, I live here. I shower once a month. This is my reality. If I think all the time about my family, about something else that I had outside, that is when you go crazy. The moment I accept that it is here, that I am here, then I am calmer.”
Another trick he used to cope with his imprisonment was to consider himself to be dead.
“I was already underground," he said. "The moment I decided that, every second, every minute, every hour, every day was a gain.”
Eventually, after 498 days in captivity, Horn was released in a ceasefire deal, leaving his brother behind, which he called "the worst moment, the worst day of the entire captivity.”
Horn dismissed the idea of humanity in his captors.
“You could count those moments on the fingers of one hand," he said. "It is not enough. The numbers don't add up for it to be something worth highlighting.”
He also said that he cannot fully hate, describing a time when a young boy tried to stab his brother Eitan during their captivity.
“That kid is not to blame; he was educated, badly educated. I can't hate him, but I can send him very far away.”
Argentina is not antisemitic, Buenos Aires legislator says
During a ceremony for Horn in Buenos Aires on Monday, City Legislator Waldo Wolff addressed the October 7 massacre.
“Of the 197 countries in the world, only 39 condemned Hamas,” Wolff said. “It seems that for some people Jews do not count when they are murdered. Jews will never again get on the trains going to Auschwitz.”
He added that Argentina, in his view, was not an antisemitic country.
“I always say that there are antisemites, but Argentina is not an antisemitic country. This does not appear through spontaneous generation. It is built through communication. If barbarism becomes normalized, it advances.”

How Israel’s genocide in Gaza pulled Britons into the Palestine movement

Unknown Publisher

How Israel’s genocide in Gaza pulled Britons into the Palestine movement
From quiet lives to protest arrests, Britons are risking freedom and reputations to stand with Palestinians and challenge government policy.
London, United Kingdom – Claire, 52, lives in the Scottish countryside, not far from Edinburgh.
She describes her work as “low-level administration” and does not use social media. She lives a quiet life with her dog, reading and baking in her spare time. Until three years ago, she did not consider herself political.
Now, she faces 14 years in prison for her suspected show of support for Palestine Action.
Claire, who requested Al Jazeera withhold her surname, is one of the many people in the United Kingdom who are newcomers to the Palestinian cause.
Organisations like Artists for Free Palestine, Workers for Free Palestine, and virtually every other insert-profession-here for Palestine have cropped up across the UK over the past three years.
In the summer of 2023, Claire read I Shall Not Hate by Dr Izzeldin Abuelaish, a Palestinian physician in Gaza who lost his three daughters to Israeli tank fire in 2009. After finishing the book, Claire watched the aftermath of October 7 unfold online.
“For me, there wasn’t a delay between ‘Israel has a right to defend itself’ and then lies,” she told Al Jazeera.
She went to a pro-Palestine rally on Armistice Day, calling for a ceasefire, and was “horrified” when then-Home Secretary Suella Braverman called the protests “hate marches”.
“I was determined not to ignore [Palestine],” she says.
She continued to march, writing letters to lawmakers and fundraising for various Palestinian aid programmes.
In August 2025, she began publicly protesting against the proscription of Palestine Action with Defend Our Juries, the group behind a campaign of civil disobedience aimed at lifting the ban. To date, more than 3,000 people have been arrested for showing support for the pressure group that was banned in 2025.
Earlier this year, police arrived at her door to arrest Claire under Sections 11 and 12 of the Terrorism Act: “Being a member of a proscribed organisation and encouraging others to join a proscribed organisation.”
“I’ve never been in trouble before,” she says. “I’m not backing down.”
Marji, 70, lives in Colchester and had a similar feeling after hearing Braverman’s words.
“I had never been to a protest in my life,” she says, until she carried a “Ceasefire Now” sign at an Armistice Day march in 2023.
“I knew it wasn’t a ‘hate march’.”
Marji’s father served in the British Army, and her father-in-law was in the Royal Air Force and taken as a prisoner-of-war in Japan during World War II.
“Our parents’ generation fought fascism,” she says. “Now Britain is breaking British law.”
Marji, who also requested to be identified only by her first name, had a successful career in financial services, while her husband held an executive-level role.
They are now retired grandparents.
In July, they were arrested in Westminster under Section 12 of the Terrorism Act – also for alleged support of Palestine Action – and are now waiting to see if charges will be laid.
“We’ve had to decide … is it safe to have grandchildren here? When the police could come to the door?”
Her children remain supportive.
“I think they’re proud of us, even if there’s been fear on their part.”
Across sectors, from the arts to railways, financial services and administration, Britons have risked professional and legal repercussions for the sake of Palestinian solidarity.
Hundreds of thousands have taken to the streets to protest against Israel’s genocidal campaign in Gaza and what they see as the UK’s role in the conflict. They have urged the UK government to cease all arms sales to Israel and cut diplomatic and trade ties as the genocide goes on in Gaza and violence escalates in the occupied West Bank.
This week, tensions have flared again as the Metropolitan Police warned pro-Palestine protesters against rallying on the three-year anniversary of October 7. The force said on Wednesday that five people were arrested outside the Board of Deputies of British Jews in north London for “inciting racial hatred, involving allegedly shouting or chanting slogans calling for Intifada”.
Israel’s latest war on the Gaza Strip – it has waged several since 1948 – began after Hamas, the group that governs Gaza, attacked southern Israel. About 1,200 people were killed that day, while more than 240 were taken captive, including Israeli soldiers, citizens and some foreign nationals.
Since October 7, 2023, Israel’s relentless bombardment has killed more than 74,000 people and devastated Gaza, making life for survivors nearly impossible. The small territory is now home to the largest group of child amputees in modern history.
“The narrative that we had grown up with was wrong – that the people who were there and living peacefully have been cast as ‘terrorists’, when they have suffered terrorism,” Marji says.
Both Marji and Claire spoke about their belief that the UK government is “complicit” in the genocide.
“The government participation, complicity, and their lies. Their gaslighting makes people more determined,” says Claire.
As the legal dangers and rhetorical backlash mount against pro-Palestine protesters, Marji, whose maternal grandmother was Jewish, is only more resolved: “We knew that saying ‘stop the genocide’ doesn’t mean you’re an anti-Semite. We’re not stupid, we can differentiate between Jewish people and people who support illegal occupation.”
Workers for Free Palestine, which includes a range of trade unions, formed in late 2023 and soon began holding protests.
“Many people oppose how their labour is used to prop up an apartheid state, but have been told there is nothing they can do as individuals,” a spokesperson told Al Jazeera.
Still, for some, there is not just resolve but optimism.
“Doing nothing makes us feel sick, angry and powerless,” says Marji. “I hope people will wake up and see how our own civil liberties … are being eroded to protect the interests of Israel.”
