94-year-old Jewish woman arrested for opposing genocide in Palestine
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
14:55:23 UTC
23:55:23 KST

94-year-old Jewish woman arrested for opposing genocide in Palestine
At 94, former human rights lawyer Margaret Owen had been trying for months to get arrested.
Jewish and an old friend of the Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband's mother, she said she had persistently sat, along with hundreds of other pensioners, at silent vigils holding paper signs which read: “I oppose genocide. I support Palestine Action.”
But while others were hauled away by the police, she said she had “failed miserably”.
“I’ve been holding that sign a long time,” Owen told Middle East Eye. She even mounted it in her front room window, and sent photographs to the Metropolitan police, to no avail.
“Even if it’s behind glass, they should have arrested me,” she said.
But on 27 September, at a protest outside the Labour Party conference in Liverpool, she was finally granted her wish.
“I was quite proud to join the arrestees last Sunday,” she said.
Owen recalled that she was among around 200 other people, “many of us old, disabled. There were a lot of white hairs around, people with crutches, somebody was in a wheelchair.
“We were just sitting quietly with our placards round our necks, and then we see the police wandering through the crowd and photographing at random with their cameras, and then they begin to encircle people,” she told MEE.
Owen has a bad back and struggled to climb into the back of the police van, so she sat up front with a police officer.
“She looked really cruel and vicious when she was arresting me. But when I sat next to her in the van, I looked her in the face and said, “I’m so sorry for you. This is not what you joined the police force for.”
Owen said the officer's face “completely crumbled, she suddenly became human again”.
She said was driven “a long way away” to a police station where she was finger printed and issued her bail conditions which stipulate she must report to a police station on 27 December.
“I think they’re trying to ruin our Christmas,” she said, smiling.
“We are actually now descending and embracing all the features of a police state. It's very, very worrying indeed.”
Defend our Juries (DoJ), the campaign group that called the protest, reported that after over 16 hours, 150 arrests were made.
Merseyside Police told MEE that it does not comment on individual cases, but confirmed that " 83 people were arrested on suspicion of wearing or displaying an item, or publishing an image, in support of a proscribed organisation, and a further 105 people were reported for summons".
"As with all significant policing operations, a debrief process will take place to identify any learning and inform future operational planning," it added.
Starmer’s government proscribed Palestine Action in July 2025, making expressions of support for, or membership of the group a criminal offence punishable by up to 14 years in prison.
Since then, DoJ estimates that some 3,850 people have been arrested, with at least 2,250 charges for allegedly expressing support for the banned group.
The group’s co-founder, Huda Ammori, is appealing a Court of Appeal decision earlier this year upholding the proscription as lawful.
The case is due to be heard at the Supreme Court later this year.
A Home Office spokesperson told MEE that the proscription "followed a rigorous and evidence-based decision-making process, endorsed by Parliament".
They added that the Court of Appeal, which overturned a High Court ruling finding the ban to be unlawful, found that the group "carried out acts of terrorism, celebrated those who took part in them and promoted the use of violence".
“The proscription of Palestine Action does not affect lawful protest in support of the Palestinian cause, which remains a fundamental democratic right,” they said.
Match words with actions
As Owen was being hauled away, Miliband addressed the conference, declaring a “reset” in Labour’s approach to foreign policy.
He condemned “ethnic cleansing by the settler terrorists in the West Bank”, Israel’s “war crimes in Gaza”, and its “illegal occupation of Palestine”, vowing to “match words with actions”.
Addressing the "millions of people... who were moved and outraged by the plight of the Palestinian people," he said: "We hear you, you were right.”
“That gave us huge cause for hope,” Owen said, but warned that the raft of sanctions against Israeli settlements announced by the foreign secretary “wasn't enough for us".
"He didn't, and he couldn't go far enough, because he has to deal with a very fractured Labour party," she added.
Activists have pointed to the glaring discrepancy between Miliband’s words and the now-familiar sight of white-haired protesters being arrested for supporting Palestine Action.
Burnham’s government, and Miliband in particular, is facing mounting pressure to reverse the controversial ban.
Footage circulated online showed Miliband being accosted by activists in a Pizza Express minutes away from where protesters were being carted away for holding the signs.
In the recording, an activist is heard informing the foreign secretary that “200 people, 100 metres from here are being arrested” and inviting him to “have a conversation” with them.
“They’re being arrested for holding pieces of paper, Ed,” he said.
Miliband responds that he is “happy to have them chat to me”, but that he was currently speaking to his constituents.
Subsequently, Miliband said in an interview with LBC: “I believe in the right to protest”, but said he would let the ban's Supreme Court appeal hearing “play out”.
Responding to a question from Andrew Marr about the arrests of "grannies and vicars", Miliband said he didn’t think it was “anyone’s intent” to "criminalise" them as a result of the proscription.
On Tuesday, DoJ wrote to Miliband on behalf of Owen and another arrestee, 76-year-old Jonathan Porritt CBE, accepting his offer of a meeting to discuss the proscription.
Responding to Miliband's comments about the arrests, the letter says that the elderly arrestees "have not just been criminalised. They are being prosecuted by your government as terrorists, under the most draconian branch of the criminal law".
“That's an important concession that the government has made. This is not the intention. This is not working as it should be working,” former government lawyer and DoJ co-founder Tim Crosland told MEE.
He said that the acknowledgement is “really significant” to the appeal hearing at the Supreme Court which will assess the ban’s proportionality.
“When the government itself is saying this is a disproportionate interference, it's a bit difficult to see how they defend the case now.”
Crosland noted that Miliband's deferral to the courts “feels disingenuous”, noting that the Home Office is defending the appeal against a High Court ruling that the proscription should be quashed.
“The government's got a choice. At any moment it could concede the appeal,” Crosland said.
Burnham has been less explicit in critiquing the ban.
When asked by Nick Ferrari whether he considered the sign holding vigils to be “terrorist activity” he conceded that the elderly arrestees sit at one end of the Palestine Action “spectrum”, with activists who have “carried out attacks" on military sites on the “extreme end”.
‘She would have ticked Ed off’
Owen can claim a connection with Miliband. She was a close friend of his mother, Marion Kozak, a Polish Holocaust survivor and feminist-socialist campaigner who was a member of Jews for Justice for Palestinians.
Kozak, who died in May, witnessed the Nazi occupation of her hometown Czestochowa.
“She’s one of the women I really admire so much,” Owen said.
Owen said that she, Kozak and Marlene Hobsbawm - the wife of Marxist historian Eric Hobsbawm - were known as the “three M’s”.
“She was incredibly modest, but incredibly strong in her calls for justice and for supporting victims of injustice,” she said, adding that Kozak “had always been for the Palestinian people”.
Reflecting on what Kozak would have made of Miliband’s policy shift on Israel, Owen said: "I think she would have ticked Ed off."
“And yet I salute him, because I think he's made a dramatic shift in our foreign policy," Owen said.
"That is a chink of light in the dark tunnel. We must encourage that and support him and build on that, whatever the obstacles are and however difficult it is.”
Owen recalled that, when David and Ed Miliband were competing for the Labour Party leadership in 2010, she asked MP Jeremy Corbyn who should be the party leader.
“You know what he said? Their mother.”
When asked if Kozak would be among the people risking arrest outside the Labour party conference, Owen responded: “Absolutely, she’d be with us holding a sign.”

Denmark says Russia has conducted sabotage attacks against its defense firms
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
14:54:06 UTC
23:54:06 KST

Denmark says Russia has conducted sabotage attacks against its defense firms
COPENHAGEN, Oct 7 - Russia has begun sabotage operations against Danish companies supplying Ukraine after concluding that broader disruption efforts failed to curb Western military support for the country, a Danish intelligence official said on Wednesday.
The shift reflects a significant escalation in Moscow's hybrid warfare campaign, the official, from the Danish national security and intelligence service (PET), told a homeland security conference in Copenhagen.
"What we saw in the spring was a lot of planning, but very little carried out; what we saw in early summer is that they started to carry out a lot more," the official said.
Russia concluded that its previous broad-spectrum targeting "did not have the effect of deterring the Western (military alliance) NATO from supporting Ukraine," the official added, and while Moscow maintains political control over operations, its operational boldness is growing and Russia is now "trying to hit targets that have a direct impact on the front line. That means weapons production."
Moscow has repeatedly denied involvement in sabotage or hybrid warfare operations. The Russian embassy in Copenhagen rejected the allegations on Wednesday, accusing Danish authorities of making unfounded accusations against Russia.
The official cited a Russian defence ministry list of alleged European drone and drone component manufacturers that Moscow said in April amounted to potential military targets, without elaborating further.
Russia is increasingly using untrained proxies — including homeless people and people addicted to drugs — recruited via Telegram and other social media platforms. Recruitment typically starts with low-threshold tasks such as reconnaissance or photography, then escalates toward actual sabotage operations, PET has said.
"It could be anyone just looking for quick money," the official said. "If the first person isn't successful, they'll throw another one at the problem until they succeed."
Denmark's defence intelligence service last month said Russia is likely to intensify hybrid attacks against the West in coming months, after Germany blamed Russia for an attempted drone attack at Leipzig/Halle Airport in August.
In September 2025, before Denmark hosted an EU summit, drones disrupted air traffic at six Danish airports, including Copenhagen, the Nordic region's busiest, in what Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen called a hybrid attack on her nation. REUTERS

Ex-German spy chief arrested: A history of spooks working for enemy powers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
14:52:26 UTC
23:52:26 KST

Ex-German spy chief arrested: A history of spooks working for enemy powers
There have been many cases of top spies giving classified information to enemy nations. Here are some of the highlights.
Germany’s former spy chief, August Hanning, has been arrested on suspicion of passing state secrets to a foreign intelligence service.
Hanning, 80, headed up the Federal Intelligence Service, known by its German acronym BND, from 1998 to 2005.
A federal prosecutor’s statement said it strongly suspected him of “treasonous espionage, obtaining state secrets, attempted treason” through contact with foreign intelligence services since 2010, while working as a private consultant. He is accused of obtaining around 2,000 sensitive documents from a former bureau chief who has also been arrested.
But he isn’t the only high-ranking intelligence officer to have been discovered to have worked for foreign governments over the years.
Here are some of the highlights.
1940s to 1960s – Kim Philby and the ‘Cambridge Five’
Kim Philby was a British intelligence officer who secretly spent decades working for the Soviet Union during World War II and the early Cold War years.
He was recruited by Soviet Intelligence while studying at Cambridge University in the 1930s. He was the most prominent member of the “Cambridge Five” – a spy ring that gave away British secrets to the Soviet Union.
During the war, he joined MI6, where he rose to head its counter-Soviet division, and was later posted to Washington, DC. This gave him access to sensitive information through his close links to the CIA and FBI.
His tip-offs to his Soviet handlers are believed to have scuppered many Western operations and revealed the identities of agents. This included information operations to overthrow Albania’s communist leader Enver Hoxha as part of Western efforts to stop the spread of communism.
Philby came under suspicion in 1951 and was forced out of MI6 when Guy Burgess and Donald Maclean, two other members of the Cambridge Five, defected to the Soviet Union. Philby was suspected of having warned them that British intelligence officers were close to uncovering their identities as double agents for the Soviet Union, before being formally cleared of the allegations in 1955.
Then, in 1963, aware that the net was closing in on him because of his own involvement with Soviet intelligence, he fled to Russia, where he lived with his wife since 1971, Rufina Pukhova, until his death in 1988. Overall, he provided state secrets, the identities of agents, minutes from cabinet meetings, atomic research, diplomatic and military intelligence, and information about counter-intelligence operations to the Soviet Union for nearly 20 years.
Philby is regarded as the most damaging spy in British history.
According to the UK’s National Archives, one of the agents he unmasked to the Soviet Union was Constantin Volkov, a Soviet intelligence officer posted to Turkiye who wanted to defect to the UK in 1945. Volkov and his wife were seized and executed in Moscow as a result. The information he provided to the Soviet Union about a joint CIA-MI6 operation in communist Albania in the late 1940s and early 1950s resulted in the execution of hundreds of anti-communist agents.
1970s and 1980s – Oleg Gordievsky
Oleg Gordievsky was a KGB colonel who spied for British intelligence for more than a decade.
He was the son of an officer in the NKVD, which was the Soviet secret police and the direct predecessor to the KGB.
But he was recruited by MI6 in the early 1970s after becoming disillusioned by the Soviet crushing of mass protests during the Prague Spring in Czechoslovakia in 1968 and the building of the Berlin Wall.
While working for the KGB, he was stationed in Copenhagen and later in London, where he became KGB station chief in 1985.
The intelligence he provided to the British is thought to have revealed the KGB’s deep concerns that NATO’s 1983 Able Archer exercise might be cover for a real nuclear strike. This was invaluable for helping the West understand Soviet fears and to de-escalate.
Gordievsky came under suspicion and was recalled to Moscow in 1985. He was drugged and interrogated but had not yet been charged when MI6 ran a daring operation to rescue him and smuggle him out of Russia in the boot of a car across the Finnish border.
Russia sentenced Gordievsky to death in absentia.
He lived in the UK under protection until his death in 2025.
1980s and 1990s – Robert Hanssen
Robert Hanssen was a high-ranking agent at the US Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) who spied for the Soviet Union and later for Russian intelligence services between 1979 and 2001.
Hanssen initially studied dentistry at Northwestern University before switching courses and receiving a degree in accounting and information systems. He worked as a police officer in Chicago before joining the FBI in 1976.
He approached Soviet military intelligence in 1979, eventually working with the KGB and its successor, the SVR. He operated using the alias “Ramon Garcia”.
Hanssen never met his handlers in person, instead using “dead drops” when he would leave classified documents in prearranged outdoor locations, including parks, wooded areas, under bridges and on street corners in the Washington, DC area, in exchange for cash or diamonds.
He handed over thousands of pages of classified material, including details about US nuclear war plans and the identities of Russian officials working for the US. At least two of those sources, including Dmitri Polyakov and Valery Marynov were executed.
The arrest in 1994 of Aldrich Ames, another US spy caught working for Russian intelligence, eventually led to his arrest in February 2001.
He pleaded guilty to avoid the death penalty and died in prison in 2023.
2000s – Alexander Yuk Ching Ma
Alexander Yuk Ching Ma is a former CIA officer who was caught spying for China.
He worked for the CIA from 1982 to 1989 and became a US citizen, living in Honolulu.
In March 2001, officers of China’s Shanghai State Security Bureau asked him to arrange a meeting with a now-deceased former CIA officer who served from 1967 to 1983. The two met in a Hong Kong hotel room for three days. In exchange for $50,000, they provided classified information to China.
The FBI became aware of his ties to Chinese intelligence and hired him as a contract linguist in its Honolulu office so that his activities could be monitored.
He was arrested in a sting after admitting to an undercover FBI employee that he had facilitated the provision of classified information to Chinese intelligence.
Ma pleaded guilty in May 2024 and is currently serving a 10-year prison sentence.

Five times deadly pathogens escaped laboratories
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
14:51:40 UTC
23:51:40 KST

Laboratories exist to study the world's most dangerous microbes, and strict biosafety rules exist to keep those microbes contained. The record shows the rules do not always hold.
A review of reports from 2000 to 2024 identified 712 laboratory-acquired human infections and 17 deaths.
Here are five incidents that show how containment can fail.
California microbiologist dies after meningococcal infection
A 25-year-old microbiologist working with meningococcal bacteria in California became infected and died in 2012.
The US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) said investigators identified several biosafety breaches.
The case showed that even trained scientists handling Neisseria meningitidis in routine conditions can pay with their lives when safety procedures fail. It remains a stark reminder that laboratory-acquired infections are not only a risk of exotic, headline-grabbing pathogens.
Everyday bacteria can be just as dangerous when protocols slip.
Dozens exposed in CDC anthrax and H5N1 lapses
Dozens of workers at the CDC in Atlanta were potentially exposed in 2014 after anthrax was inadequately inactivated.
Separately, material contaminated with H5N1 avian influenza was mistakenly shipped to another laboratory. The CDC said no illnesses or deaths resulted.
The episodes are notable because the agency helps set biosafety standards for laboratories across the United States.
They show that near misses, not only fatalities, can reveal weaknesses in even the best-resourced institutions and raise questions about oversight.
French technician dies of prion disease after needlestick
A research technician in France died in 2019 from variant Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease (vCJD), a fatal brain disorder caused by prions.
French authorities said the infection could have resulted from a laboratory needlestick accident in 2010.
The Ministry of Agriculture made the assessment. Almost a decade passed between exposure and death.
Prions are neither bacteria nor viruses, and standard sterilisation methods struggle to destroy them, which makes accidental exposure particularly hard to guard against.
Lanzhou factory leak infects more than 10,000 people
Improperly disinfected waste gas from a vaccine factory in Lanzhou, China, released aerosolised Brucella bacteria in 2019 and 2020.
More than 10,000 infections were eventually reported, according to published research.
That makes it one of the largest documented accidental pathogen releases. Brucella causes brucellosis, a disease that normally passes from animals to humans and can bring prolonged fever and joint pain.
Unlike the other cases here, this one reached the wider community, not only staff.
Russian lab worker dies as plague link remains unproven
A 28-year-old employee of an anti-plague institute in Irkutsk, Russia, died in 2026 from severe pneumonia.
According to Reuters, reports alleged a laboratory accident involving plague.
Authorities said testing has not established a laboratory link or plague infection. The cause remains undetermined, so this is an open investigation, not a confirmed escape.
It shows how quickly speculation can fill the gaps when information about laboratory incidents is limited.
Laboratory accidents remain rare, but the cases above show the consequences can be severe when they happen. The CDC, French authorities and published research all point to the same lesson: biosafety depends on strict procedures and transparent investigation.
As the Irkutsk case shows, unanswered questions can fuel speculation, so clear and prompt reporting matters as much as containment.

‘All me’: Tory party riding high on Kemi Badenoch’s wave of popularity
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
14:50:41 UTC
23:50:41 KST

Kemi Badenoch has long said that the Conservatives were “under new management”, but in a TV interview to mark the end of a party conference at which she has been front and centre of more or less everything, she took the analogy further.
“Your viewers will know that sometimes you have a football team that’s disappointing,” the Tory leader told GB News. “There’s a new captain, there’s a new coach, there’s a new owner, effectively – which is all me.”
These are bold words even for a politician known to possess an iron-clad self-confidence. But they are no exaggeration. Badenoch is not only outperforming her party in polling terms, she is busy remaking it in her own image.
The broad ideological direction was already set, with Badenoch saying explicitly at the start of this year that centrist ideas were no longer wanted. Some more moderate figures remain in her shadow cabinet, but they are signed up to a right-leaning agenda, including opposition to net zero and a bonfire of human rights protections.
Those around Badenoch say, however, that her control goes further, with policy decisions such as the move to grant free childcare to people with incomes above £100,000, announced on the eve of the conference, made simply because she believes they are the right thing to do.
“With policies it’s not about chasing certain groups of voters,” one shadow cabinet minister said. “She focuses on what she thinks needs to be fixed, what she feels is wrong.”
Talking her out of a policy decision, they said, was a tall order: “It’s not going to happen – it’s tablets of stone. She’s not going to change her mind. She knows what the policies have to be.”
Many political parties are, to a greater or less extent, a cult based around the leader, but this is particularly the case for the 2026-period Conservatives, where MPs say Badenoch is talked about on the doorsteps with an admiration and respect not accorded to their party more widely.
MPs recount how her name is raised unprompted. One said: “She’s brought up in a positive way. Crucially, in a world where most people couldn’t name more than a handful of politicians, they know who she is.”
This starring role was obvious throughout the Conservatives’ conference in Birmingham, not least Badenoch’s arrival, which saw her greeted by a flag-waving crowd of activists chanting: “Kemi, Kemi.”
Inside the venue, Badenoch was the heroic centrepiece of the party’s “Birmingham tapestry”, shown in mocked-up 12th-century form doing everything from chastising Wes Streeting to sitting in the turret of a tank.
Such veneration is not just wishful thinking by a party eager to move on from a revolving door of previous leaders. While last year’s conference was viewed as make-or-break for Badenoch, even with her party still bumping along at 20% or so in the polls her position is now seen as secure, with the Conservatives more unified than they have been for years.
This is in part the result of some serial malcontents leaving for Reform UK, especially Robert Jenrick, as well as the party’s diminished size in the Commons, which as one shadow cabinet minister notes, is too small for factions: “We could just about fill a corner table in Pizza Express.”
There are still private doubts, including Badenoch’s instinct to lean into culture wars rather than focus on the economy, which those around her believe is the party’s strongest electoral card.
Some party figures also wonder if Badenoch is thinking about election strategy at all with her very personal suite of policy choices, which in Birmingham mainly consisted of giving tax breaks to wealthier people.
This was capped in her end-of-conference speech with the announcement that a Badenoch-led government would exempt people’s homes from inheritance tax, an idea which, given that the levy only begins on property worth more than £500,000, is a largely theoretical idea outside London and the south-east of England.
While such policies could be appealing to prosperous home counties voters who defected to the Liberal Democrats in 2024, this does not seem to be the plan. During another TV interview, Badenoch chided her questioner for suggesting her tax cuts were aimed at bringing back such support.
“I’m very sad that you’re looking at this in crude electoral terms,” she said. “That’s how we’ve all got into this problem where we keep thinking about winning elections rather than thinking about what works.”
One former Tory strategist said there was a risk of incoherence: “I can’t understand what is being achieved with these announcements. Forget lots of the small ones, just use the money and do a big tax cut for middle earners.”
There was, they added, little chance things would change: “People are scared of her, to be honest. I think a lot of her team don’t know how to say no to her.”
However, much like football, politics is not a one-person game, and a star player or manager will only get you so far. And while Badenoch was at pains to praise colleagues in her speech, it is fair to say that the rest of the shadow cabinet is lagging.
Andrew Griffith, Badenoch’s new shadow chancellor, was feted by his boss for his private sector business expertise. But on Monday he gave a speech widely seen as one of the worst delivered to any conference in years.
It is a matter of profile as well as ability. While Badenoch is recognised by 90% of voters, according to YouGov polling, only 22% say they know who Griffith is. A number of his colleagues are on similar ratings, with pollsters saying even these are likely to be inflated by people who don’t want to admit ignorance.
The experienced Tom Tugendhat, now in the foreign affairs brief, does slightly better, on 46%. Laura Trott, the shadow education secretary, hits 50%, but this is because some people mistake her for the Olympic cyclist, now Laura Kenny, formerly of the same name.
There was some unease in Birmingham about Badenoch blotting out everyone else. “Isn’t there a danger we are becoming a one-woman party?” one activist asked a fringe of shadow cabinet members.
Others disagree. “It’s a normal dynamic for an opposition party that is unpopular,” said Nick Timothy, the shadow justice secretary. “It needs a strong popular leader that can pull it up and we should thank our lucky stars that we have her.”
Either way, most Conservatives now accept that, for now, it is up to Badenoch to chart the Conservatives’ course, whatever it involves. One ally said: “We win elections on the economy but there’s no point telling Kemi not to do anything.”

George Galloway contests London byelection without setting foot in UK
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
14:50:37 UTC
23:50:37 KST

George Galloway has been elected seven times to parliament, but his attempt to succeed for an eighth this week, in the London seat formerly held by Keir Starmer, is undoubtedly his most curious effort yet.
Since the byelection campaign began, the leader of the Workers party of Britain has yet to set foot in the UK, let alone the Holborn and St Pancras constituency, because he is in what he describes as “self-exile” after being questioned by counter-terrorism police at Gatwick airport a year ago.
Prolific social media feeds show that the veteran leftwinger has spent the past few weeks on a speaking tour in South Africa, with his most recent public appearance on Saturday at a pro-Palestine rally in Cape Town, though posts in the last 24 hours suggest he is in Shanghai, China.
Prior to that he was in Moscow, repeatedly making his hostility to Ukraine and Nato as explicit as his support for Palestine and opposition to apartheid.
“The biggest issue in the H&StP byelection is the path leading us to WW3 in Ukraine,” Galloway wrote on X in the middle of September, an argument that has not gained much traction with voters, though he has chosen to repeat it online – the only way he can reach voters personally before Thursday’s byelection.
Meanwhile, social media feeds show handfuls of Workers party activists campaigning in the constituency without their candidate, fighting a peripheral campaign in a byelection considered to be a battle between Labour’s Sagal Abdi-Wali and Zack Polanski, standing for the Greens.
“Sincere gratitude to my campaigners who are performing miracles on the ground in my enforced absence. Salute to the supporters they are encountering every day. We can win this. And me and my family can come home. Thank you,” Galloway posted at the end of September.
The campaign highlights an anomaly with Britain’s electoral law. Any British, Irish or qualifying Commonwealth citizen over 18 may stand for parliament – as long as they are not bankrupt or members of the police, armed forces, civil servants or judges. There is no requirement to be a registered elector or other residency requirement, according to the Electoral Commission.
Last month, Galloway also revealed he had been “debanked” – his bank accounts suddenly closed – by the Lloyds-owned Bank of Scotland. “Thirty-nine years ago I opened a personal bank account with Bank of Scotland in Byres Rd Glasgow. Yesterday without explanation or notice they closed my accounts,” he posted on 4 September, threatening Lloyds with legal action.
The bank said it would not comment on individual cases, though account closures are rare. A Bank of Scotland spokesperson added: “Our policy is not to close a customer’s account based on political or personal beliefs and we make customers aware if we make the decision to close an account.”
Galloway chose to leave the UK after he and his wife, Putri Gayatri Pertiwi, were stopped for what he said was “a total of 11 hours” in September last year by “five armed police officers” after returning from the Russian city of Nizhny Novgorod and attending a World Youth Festival assembly.
Last month, the former MP said the first question police asked him was: “Why do you admire Mr Lavrov?” They were referring to Russia’s long-serving foreign minister, Sergey Lavrov. Posting on X, Galloway attached a photo of Lavrov smoking and added: “I could have just shown him this picture!”
Galloway told the broadcaster RT, the former Russia Today, in an interview in March this year that officers “took all our stuff and copied everything on our phones”, forcing them to miss a public meeting in London at which, his wife said in a post on Instagram, “the Chinese ambassador [was] waiting for us”.
Neither Galloway nor his wife were subject to any further legal action in a stop that took place under schedule 3 of the Counter-Terrorism and Border Security Act 2019. This allows police to detain people to determine if they have been engaged in hostile activity, considered by investigators to be a low bar.
The former MP had appeared on a discussion panel with Lavrov in Moscow in June 2025, at the Forum of the Future, an event described as “far-right” by the Moscow Times, where Elon Musk’s father, Errol, and Alex Jones, the rightwing founder of Infowars, were also speaking.
In Galloway’s March interview with RT, where he had hosted a talkshow for nine years until Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, he said he was “now in exile in the east, and I must say that Moscow in the spring is quite the place to be”.
He was in Moscow in late April, speaking at the inaugural conference of Sovintern, an international pro-Soviet socialist network led by the opposition A Just Russia party, where a welcome address from the Russian president, Vladimir Putin, was read out.
In early September, Galloway released a video promoting his online talkshow, filmed from Moscow’s Red Square where he also said he would appear at a roundtable event on security at the city’s “prestigious university”.
On 13 September he participated in a public Sovintern discussion with Zakhar Prilepin, a leading pro-war author and propagandist who has fought in Ukraine and called for “the return of Kyiv to Russia”.
A day later, Galloway was selected as the Workers party candidate, and he shortly afterwards went to South Africa for a speaking and fundraising tour with the leftwing activist and former journalist Yvonne Ridley. He continued to post on social media from South Africa, frequently on international affairs.
He places a particular emphasis on Russia and Ukraine. Earlier this month Galloway posted an anti-Andy Burnham image, with the prime minister dressed in blue and yellow, the colours of Ukraine. “I want you to die for Ukraine. Conscription coming soon!” the caption read.
Particular criticism has also been reserved for Polanski, his most obvious rival for political support. On 25 September, Galloway posted: “I am with Russia Zack is with NATO. I am with an end to the war in Ukraine Zack is with Zelensky and risking WW3.”
Galloway and the Workers party were approached for comment.

Israel rushing to make its West Bank land grab permanent
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
14:50:01 UTC
23:50:01 KST

Israel rushing to make its West Bank land grab permanent
'They want the land without its people'
TEHRAN — Itamar Ben-Gvir climbed onto a bulldozer in occupied East al-Quds (Jerusalem) on Tuesday. Beneath him lay the ruins of a five-story apartment building. Ten apartments, home to roughly 70 Palestinians, mostly women and children, were reduced to rubble in the al-Tur neighborhood.
Israel's national security minister arrived under heavy police escort, three weeks before the Oct. 27 election, to personally oversee the destruction.
The building belonged to Mustafa Abu Subaitan. Residents received their final eviction notice on Monday following years of fines and denied building permits.
The United Nations notes that obtaining these permits is nearly impossible for Palestinians in the city.
The al-Quds (Jerusalem) Governorate described Ben-Gvir's participation as electoral exploitation. Hamas condemned it as organized terrorism.
Between July and September, the governorate recorded 139 demolition and land-clearing operations. Officials logged another 150 eviction and property-seizure notices.
UN data indicates approximately 170 Palestinian structures have been destroyed in East al-Quds (Jerusalem) since January.
Across the wider West Bank, Palestinian officials recorded 341 demolition operations targeting 740 structures in the first half of 2026.
Near Hebron on Monday, bulldozers leveled a home in Khallet al-Deirat in 25 minutes, leaving two families homeless.
The International Court of Justice ruled in July 2024 that Israel's presence in the occupied territories is unlawful and demanded settler evacuation.
‘Settlement revolution’
Between 2013 and 2022, Israel approved three settlements. Since then, the government has approved more than 100. 34 were authorized in a single March cabinet session.
Outposts erected in violation of Israeli law have received retroactive state authorization.
Military chief of staff Eyal Zamir reportedly warned the cabinet that the military was severely overstretched. The cabinet approved the settlements anyway.
Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich inaugurated two new settlements on Sept. 27. Smotrich called it a continuation of the "settlement revolution" designed to prevent a Palestinian state.
The government is pushing forward a tender for E1 before election day. E1 is a highly contested plan that would drive a physical wedge of housing between East al-Quds (Jerusalem) and the interior West Bank.
Smotrich stated openly that the objective of E1 is to bury the idea of Palestinian statehood.
War Minister Israel Katz announced a target of one million Israeli settlers in northern West Bank during the August reopening of Ganim. In 2005, Israel evacuated Ganim, Kadim, Sa-Nur, and Homesh.
All four northern West Bank settlements are now reoccupied. Settler families moved into caravan homes in Sa-Nur under military guard.
The estimated settler population now exceeds 540,000, living among roughly three million Palestinians.
‘They want the land without its people’
The physical restructuring is most visible in the north. In July, the army issued 15 land confiscation orders covering roughly 200 dunams in the Jenin governorate.
The orders target land in Areas A and C to clear a bypass road connecting the new settlements of Emek Dotan and Noa.
This is the first time since the Oslo Accords that military seizure orders in Area A serve explicit civilian settlement infrastructure rather than a military cover.
Six new military camps have been established across Jenin. Dror Etkes of Kerem Navot called the operation a comprehensive land-grab machine. Settlers and state forces work together to break the contiguity of the rural Jenin region.
Palestinian communities face total isolation. In Abu al-Sharqiyah, east of Jenin, 26 businesses received demolition notices in August. Mayor Burhan al-Azamtah said the village is now surrounded like a prison.
In nearby Arrabah, the Israeli military has uprooted trees and restricted agricultural access. Mayor Ahmad al-Ardah said the objective is clear. "They want the land without its people," he said.
Near Sa-Nur, settlers forced the Asa'asah family to exhume the freshly buried body of their 85-year-old father. The settlers claimed the grave was too close to the settlement. The family reburied him in another town.
Olive harvest and 'Herod's Pool'
This autumn, the olive harvest opened under fire.
Settlers attacked a family harvesting trees at Jabal Qamas on Oct. 3. Hussam Adily was left in critical condition.
The attackers then entered the village of Osarin, ransacking a home and smashing vehicles.
Similar violence struck Rantis, Sebastia, Beit Imrin, Deir Sharaf, Aqraba, and Arrabuna. Farmers were beaten, pepper-sprayed, and run over.
Near Abu Dis, settlers burned about 55 olive trees. In Sinjil, Rafat, and Kafr Ra'i, settlers stole olives and ladders.
In Fasayil, settlers diverted irrigation pipelines from farmland owned by Saad Nemer to fill an ancient reservoir.
Smotrich announced funding to develop the site as "Herod's Pool," and Nemer's crops dried up.
In Taybeh, the West Bank's last entirely Christian village, the military declared the area a closed military zone. The order blocks Palestinians from their groves while settlers roam freely.
Lethal force accompanies the harvest violence. In Yasouf on Oct. 1, settlers shot dead 51-year-old Mashhour Yassin.
The Palestinian Foreign Ministry reported that soldiers threw away the keys to the responding ambulance. On Oct. 2, 19-year-old Bahaa al-Natsheh was shot dead near Kobar.
On Monday near Bani Naim, troops fired on a vehicle, killing 38-year-old Hossam Alaa al-Din Abdul Jabbar Walad Ali. The army claimed the car attempted a ramming.
'That is not my job'
Journalists documenting the violence are active targets. On Tuesday near Aqraba, armed settlers beat Agence France-Presse photographer Jaafar Ashtiyeh with gun butts.
They fired live rounds and stole his equipment. Around a dozen Israeli soldiers stood 500 meters away. They made no attempt to intervene. AFP global news director Phil Chetwynd called the attack unacceptable.
The daily intimidation is relentless. Near Taybeh, settlers from an illegal outpost ride donkeys to the Kaabnah family home every morning and evening. They throw rocks and rattle the property fence. Volunteers sleep on the floor in protective presence shifts.
The Palestinian Colonization and Wall Resistance Commission recorded 14,742 attacks by forces and settlers since October 2023.
These attacks have killed 66 Palestinians and damaged more than 147,000 trees. Over 100,000 of those were olive trees.
On Monday, soldiers bulldozed a memorial to slain students inside Birzeit University and detained 12 people across the West Bank. Roughly 9,350 Palestinians sit in Israeli prisons today.
The United States provides no restraint. Donald Trump lifted Biden-era sanctions against violent settler groups on his first day back in office.
Britain banned settlement goods last month, with Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband calling settler violence ethnic cleansing. Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu denounced "a handful of rioters" but immediately told settlers the land was theirs.
The regime apparatus functions as intended. Near Taybeh, an Israeli border police officer threatened to arrest a Washington Post photographer. Asked why he would not instead arrest a settler throwing rocks at a family, the officer answered: “That is not my job."

Reacting to an announcement today by France’s Interior Minister that the use of stun grenades in the policing of high school student protests will be temporarily suspended, Anne Savinel-Barras, President of Amnesty International France, said:

These dangerous devices, which have a long history of causing serious injuries, must be permanently banned from the policing of all protests
Anne Savinel-Barras, Amnesty International France
“Protests should not be battlefields. Stun grenades are designed to shock, disorient, and sow panic, often among dense crowds at demonstrations. Some can cause permanent hearing loss as well as life-changing mutilations due to the blast and shrapnel.
“A permanent ban on the use of all stun grenades in the policing of all public assemblies must be part of a complete overhaul of regulations around the use of force against all protesters, to ensure France fulfils all its obligations under international human rights law, including the right to peaceful assembly.
Background

Media and authorities have reported that this injury was caused by a stun grenade
In June 2026, Amnesty International called for a global ban on the use of stun grenades in the policing of protests.

UK PM Burnham's Labour Party faces challenge from Greens in Starmer's old seat
LONDON, Oct 7 - Andy Burnham needs to win over voters like tech worker Dani Arbid in a by-election on Thursday if he is to fend off a national threat to his Labour Party from the Greens — and the early signs are encouraging for Britain's new prime minister.
The vote for a parliamentary seat in the inner London electoral district of Holborn and St Pancras, made vacant by the resignation of former Prime Minister Keir Starmer, is a first test of whether Burnham can restore voters' faith in Labour, which saw its popularity among left-wing voters plunge over the war in Gaza.
Many, like Arbid, turned instead to the Greens, helping them to their strongest result ever in local elections in May. Now, he says he is undecided on how he will vote in Thursday's so-called by-election but welcomed Burnham's tougher messaging on Israel and his more ambitious approach to ties with the European Union.
"It's very important to read the room, which I think the current Labour government is doing a lot better job at," Arbid, 38, told Reuters. "There is still room for Labour to kind of claw back some of those losses for sure."
LABOUR TIPPED TO WIN BY-ELECTION
Unlike the national picture, where Nigel Farage's Reform UK poses a serious challenge to Burnham, the by-election is mainly a contest between Labour and the Greens, with thousands of activists from both parties out canvassing in recent weeks.
Burnham hopes to show he can consolidate the left-of-centre vote, strengthening his efforts to take on a British right now split between Reform UK and the Conservatives. But the by-election also offers him a chance to rob the Greens of the momentum they have built up under new leader Zack Polanski.
Polanski himself is the Greens' candidate in Holborn and St Pancras but Labour's Sagal Abdi-Wali, a local council leader, is tipped to hold the seat for the governing party.
Green gains in areas of London contributed to Labour's dismal local election results in May, which helped set in train a process that culminated on July 20 with Starmer's resignation and his replacement by Burnham.
Since then, however, Labour has rebounded in national opinion polls, while the Greens have suffered setbacks.
At a conference last weekend, Green Party members voted to class Zionism as a form of racism, drawing criticism from British Jewish groups, Israel and even some Green lawmakers. Polanski, who is Jewish, did not take part in the vote.
Burnham's government, which has taken a more critical approach towards Israel and banned the import of goods from West Bank settlements, said the Greens had overstepped a line.
On Camden High Street, an area of London brimming with market stalls and popular with musicians, artists and tourists, Kamran Ahmed, a local resident who works in AI, said Polanski could have managed the issues raised at conference better.
But on a local level he said the Greens had something new to offer, echoing frustration heard around the country that the previously dominant Conservative and Labour parties no longer have the answers.
"Nothing is set in stone, but some of the mainstream parties have over-promised and under-delivered... If you take an area like Camden, it could benefit from some of the fresher thinking that the Green Party offers," Ahmed said.
Damian Lyons Lowe, head of pollster Survation, said the seat was one of the Greens' top targets, and that governments rarely did well at by-elections. But the Greens' anti-Starmer message, which resonated so well in May, was being tested by Burnham.
"Burnham has made direct appeals to Green-minded voters in terms of some of the things they care about," he told Reuters.
"The Burnham vibe check is very different to the Starmer-led Labour government, and that's a problem for the Green Party." REUTERS

Hungary risks situation near energy catastrophe if cut off from Russian gas — expert
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
14:47:42 UTC
23:47:42 KST

MOSCOW, October 7. /TASS/. Hungary risks finding itself in a situation "bordering on an energy catastrophe" if it is cut off from Russian gas supplies in 2027, Artyom Ilyinsky, a junior research fellow at the Department of European Political Studies at IMEMO RAS, wrote in a column for TASS.
"Technically, Hungary is capable of weaning itself off Russian gas by October 2027. However, this is possible only under the most optimistic forecast. Romanian production must reach planned targets on schedule and without disruption, pipelines must operate at peak capacity, and Budapest will have to cover the shortfall through emergency spot-market purchases. Only in this way can the country bridge the gap to 2028 – the launch date for alternative contracts with Western gas companies," Ilyinsky noted. "For the European Union itself, there is a threat that a member state could find itself in a situation bordering on an energy catastrophe if these bold and optimistic scenarios fail to materialize."
The expert explained that the delivery of major volumes under non-Russian gas agreements is scheduled to begin only in 2028, creating a critical time gap that "will prevent Hungary from navigating the pivotal year of 2027 smoothly."
"At the same time, the stance of external actors – specifically the United States – remains unclear. Hungary has already appealed to the US Congress to avoid the imposition of penalties mandated by the new US sanctions law targeting buyers of Russian oil and gas. Marton Hajdu, head of the Hungarian delegation, stated that he had asked the US side to support the country's transition efforts leading up to 2027 and to allow the continued use of Russian oil and gas for the time being. However, Washington has not yet officially announced its decision. This places Budapest in an awkward position, where the verdict of its transatlantic partner will determine whether the country can weather 2027 or not," Ilyinsky pointed out.
"Hungary has a chance to gradually diversify away from Russian gas. However, an attempt to do so before autumn 2027 – even if new contracts are signed 'here and now' – risks exposing the country to an energy shock. Judging by the cautious tone of the Energy Minister's projections, Budapest might not actually take this painful step," Ilyinsky added.
On September 18, Hungarian Minister of Economy and Energy Istvan Kapitany stated that Hungary's new government, led by Peter Magyar, would be ready to phase out Russian gas by October 2027, the deadline set by the European Union. In an interview with the Telex online news outlet, he noted that negotiations were underway with neighboring countries and LNG suppliers. According to the minister, the necessary cross-border pipeline infrastructure is already in place.
The previous administration under Viktor Orban had launched efforts to diversify supply sources and routes several years ago, citing national security reasons. In 2024, Hungary began purchasing small volumes of gas from Turkey and Azerbaijan, and announced plans to import Qatari LNG starting in 2027. Furthermore, Budapest intends to expand cooperation with Romania to purchase gas from the major Neptun Deep offshore field in the Black Sea. Hungary is connected by gas pipelines to all its neighboring countries except Slovenia.

EU hopefuls fear new safeguard plans could create second-class members
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
14:46:54 UTC
23:46:54 KST

EU candidate countries fear safeguards designed to prevent democratic backsliding, like a planned 15-year probation period, could create second-class membership and be used to exert political pressure.
EU candidate countries have raised concerns that new safeguards designed to prevent democratic backsliding after accession could leave them with second-class membership – or give existing member states a powerful tool to exert political pressure.
The concerns follow proposed measures unveiled by the European Commission on Tuesday, including a 15-year probationary period during which new members could lose voting rights if they commit a serious breach of EU values and rules.
"We are counting on the European Union to ensure that the accession process remains ambitious, credible and predictable, and reflects the progress that Ukraine continues to make," Vsevolod Chentsov, Ukraine's deputy prime minister for European integration, told Euronews.
"Our starting point remains full integration into the single market, and any transitional arrangements must be justified, proportionate and time-limited," he added.
Two-tier membership
One of the biggest concerns among candidate countries is that the safeguards could create a second tier of EU membership.
Countries including the Netherlands and France called for tougher safeguards, citing the experience of Hungary under Viktor Orbán and the difficulty of tackling democratic backsliding once a country has joined.
"We do not want a two-tier membership to join our union. Countries need to meet very high standards on the rule of law. We need to be sure that after joining, they never fall below those standards again. And this is what we have learned from experiences in the past," Enlargement Commissioner Marta Kos said as she presented the measure.
Publicly, candidates have been cautious in their response. Apart from Ukraine, the other three frontrunners – Montenegro, Albania and Moldova – are small countries deeply invested in joining the bloc.
Behind closed doors, however, candidates make no secret of their unease, especially over the 15-year probation period. During that time, newcomers could be stripped of voting rights for serious breaches of EU values and rules. Several had hoped the period would be shorter.
The Commission says this "institutional safeguard clause" is not discriminatory because it is temporary. But while the proposal includes no renewal mechanism, candidates fear member states might push to add one.
"The Commission stresses that this measure is temporary, but there is a significant risk that it might turn into a permanent status. What happens if the probation period gets repeatedly extended or its expiration blocked?" Obrad Kesić, head of Bosnia and Herzegovina's mission to the EU, told Euronews.
Risk of misuse
There is also concern among candidate countries that the safeguards could be used for political purposes, particularly in bilateral disputes with existing member states.
"It is important that the new safeguards should not be abused," said Zlatko Vujović, president of the NGO Centre for Monitoring and Research. "New members should not be blackmailed by old members," he said, pointing to the potential instrumentalisation of bilateral issues.
The threshold for suspending a country's voting rights will therefore be crucial. Candidates want clear safeguards against arbitrary action or attempts to pressure a newcomer into abandoning a strategic national interest.
When the debate over stronger safeguards began, Montenegro's ambassador to the EU, Petar Marković, said any assessment of democratic and rule of law backsliding should rest on objective criteria and systematic breaches.
"We will have very active monitoring precisely in the fields that are covered by the new institutional safeguards," a Commission official told Euronews when asked how such decisions would be made.
The official added that this monitoring would complement an expanded version of the rule of law reports and the information collected under Article 7 of the EU treaty, which allows suspending certain membership rights if a member state seriously and persistently breaches the EU's core values.
The idea is to make triggering easier than under Article 7. That provision allows measures against a member state that undermines the Union's functioning, but only with the unanimity of all the other member states. In Hungary's case, a sympathetic Polish government stood in the way.
Under the Commission's proposal, however, a decision would go through unless opposed by a qualified majority of member states. That prompts fears it would be far too easy to act against a newcomer that does not toe the line.
The procedure could be triggered by the Commission or by a "reasoned request" from member states. But its details, which are crucial for newcomers, will be negotiated only in the accession treaty.
Political bargaining
The Commission's proposals are non-binding and are likely to become a major point of contention in the final stages of accession negotiations.
"The transitional periods have to be negotiated between the member states and the country that wants to become a member of the EU. When it is negotiated, it will become a part of the accession treaty," Kos said.
That means the safeguards will be tailored to each newcomer's circumstances, but also to its bargaining position and its eventual relations with current member states, friends and sceptics alike.
"Our objective remains full accession to the EU, with equal rights and responsibilities," Cristina Gherasimov, Moldova's deputy prime minister for European integration, said on Facebook after the announcement.
The calculation in Brussels is that stronger safeguards could make it easier for enlargement-sceptical countries such as France and the Netherlands to accept new members when the time comes to ratify their accession treaties.
There is also an expectation that Montenegro, first in line to join, may set the blueprint for future accession treaties. But its determination to complete the process may leave it with little leverage to resist tougher conditions.
"Montenegro would accept anything. They are very keen to conclude the process, almost at any cost," a diplomat from a candidate country told Euronews, speaking on condition of anonymity.
Sasha Vakulina contributed to the reporting.

07 October 2026•Update: 07 October 2026
Italy’s Chamber of Deputies approved the government’s third and final confidence vote Wednesday on an electoral reform bill, paving the way for a final secret ballot Thursday, according to public broadcaster Rai.
Lawmakers backed the confidence motion on Article 3 by a 228-144 vote, with three abstentions. The provision redraws several electoral constituencies in South Tyrol, including Merano, Bressanone and Bolzano.
The lower house approved confidence motions Tuesday on Articles 1 and 2, covering the electoral systems for the Chamber of Deputies and Senate.
Lawmakers also approved Article 8 on Wednesday in a 214-0 vote, while opposition parties abstained. The provision extends voting away from one’s place of residence to family caregivers. The government did not attach a confidence motion to that article.
The reform, which has passed the Senate and returned to the lower house following amendments, has drawn strong criticism from opposition parties.
Its provisions include voter preferences alongside fixed lead candidates on party lists, as well as changes to electoral rules.
Women’s associations in Modena have appealed to President Sergio Mattarella to return the legislation to parliament if he identifies constitutional concerns, arguing that its candidate selection rules undermine equal access to elected office.
A network opposing the reform also said it was preparing legal challenges to file once the law takes effect, seeking a referral to the Constitutional Court.
The parliamentary votes come amid debate about possible early elections in May. Deputy Prime Minister and Forza Italia leader Antonio Tajani said Tuesday that his party favored completing the parliamentary term.

And we are thankful to the Prime Minister for his ideas.”
Modi has repeatedly maintained that India is willing to support meaningful efforts towards peace. Responding to a question on India’s role, he said, “I have already indicated India’s willingness to support meaningful efforts aimed at achieving a peaceful resolution of the conflict.”External Affairs Minister S Jaishankar said on Sunday that India had moved beyond advocacy and intensified engagement with both Kyiv and Moscow. He said New Delhi was focusing on issues including the safety of shipping in the Black Sea, grain exports and energy supplies.India has consistently advocated dialogue and diplomacy to resolve the conflict, now in its fifth year. Ukraine, meanwhile, has called for an unconditional ceasefire, including an end to attacks on energy and port infrastructure and a halt to hostilities in the Black Sea.

Satellite images show attack jets at Chinese military facility in Laos
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
14:46:01 UTC
23:46:01 KST

Satellite images show attack jets stationed at a new Chinese military facility in Laos, which opened last week and gives Beijing’s air force its first foothold in mainland south-east Asia.
Images provided by the commercial satellite provider Vantor show eight light attack aircraft positioned at Ban Keun airport alongside what appear to be more than a dozen military vehicles lined up in rows.
The planes’ shape matches that of the Chinese-made Hongdu JL-8 jet, a two-seat trainer that can be deployed in combat to carry bombs. Laos is reported to have four such aircraft, according to the London-based International Institute for Strategic Studies.
In a rare example of Beijing’s overseas military expansion, China opened what it said was a joint “support and training centre” at Ban Keun on 29 September.
The airport, about 30 miles (50km) north of Vientiane, the capital of Laos, has been significantly expanded over the past year. Satellite images taken months ago show farmland and dirt paths where there are now new buildings and a paved runway.
Aside from its island bases in the South China Sea, Beijing does not have a significant network of military outposts in other countries, and the Laos airbase would be its first facility in another country capable of handling fighter jets.
The new satellite images, taken a day after the announcement and first reported by Reuters, show extensive construction work that appears to be focused on a future runway extension, which could make the airport capable of handling larger planes such as bombers.
In its announcement last week, China’s defence ministry said the new centre would “help Laos strengthen the training of its air force pilots” and was not “directed against any third party”.
Governments will be watching closely for signs of deployments or the installation of defence equipment that may serve wider military ambitions. After the announcement, the Singapore-based security analyst Collin Koh said it “may not be wrong to conclude this is the first full-fledged PLA [People’s Liberation Army] overseas base in south-east Asia”.
Over the past two decades, China has built up an extensive network of outposts on islands in the disputed South China Sea, including airbases with air defence installations. Otherwise, its navy’s sole overseas military base is a logistics base in Djibouti, on the coast of the Horn of Africa.
The Laos agreement follows a similar programme established in Cambodia, at the Ream naval base on the Gulf of Thailand, although that facility has no runway.
After years of speculation and denials, China announced in April last year that it had created the “joint logistics and training” facility in Cambodia. It said the centre would support the two militaries in “conducting regional counter-terrorism, disaster prevention and mitigation, humanitarian assistance, joint training and other operations”.
US forces are believed to have used Ban Keun airport in Laos during covert military operations at the height of the Vietnam war in the 1960s and 1970s. Its development will be monitored by Vietnam, which maintains disputes with China over the South China Sea, and Thailand, which shares a border with Laos.
After the announcement last week, Thailand’s defence ministry spokesperson said Bangkok considered itself a close partner of both Laos and China and saw it as Vientiane’s sovereign right to decide whether to grant permission for a Chinese base.
“Nevertheless, Thailand will continue to closely monitor developments and how the matter proceeds, particularly with regard to building mutual trust,” said R Adm Surasant Kongsiri.
China’s government did not mention sending aircraft to Laos in its initial announcement, while the government of Laos has not commented on the project.
The US-based Institute for the Study of War has described the Laos base as the “first PLA overseas military facility focused on air power”. In its assessment, the thinktank said the base was “not yet equipped to provide the PLA with the ability to execute major combat operations, unlike US military bases”.
It said the base would give the Chinese military alternate routes to access to the South China Sea and strategic air routes.
Reuters contributed to this report

Could the UK really rejoin the EU?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
14:45:52 UTC
23:45:52 KST

It was lobbed into the national conversation without fanfare or warning, almost a footnote in the UK prime minister’s first speech as leader to his governing Labour party’s annual conference. But Andy Burnham has kicked off a quiet U-turn on Brexit.
By stating bluntly that the decision to leave Europe’s core political community had done “more harm than good”, Burnham broke a taboo in his own party, in effect, discarding his predecessor’s paralysing ‘red lines’ on Europe, and signalling he will not be bound by these constraints after the next British election.
Over the coming six weeks Burnham will gauge public support before setting out future options for the UK’s long term relationship with the UK’s largest market. Rejoining the 27-nation bloc will be one of them, opening the door to Britain reversing Brexit.
The famous red lines, or non-negotiables, enshrined by Starmer in Labour’s 2024 election manifesto, were meant to reassure Brexit-supporting voters that under Labour there would be no return to a single market, customs union or the free movement of people. These pledges left Starmer with little room for manoeuvre with Europe beyond warm words.
The evidence that Brexit has stunted the British economy is not new. Estimates for the damage quitting the single market has already done range from 6% of 8% of GDP. What is new is a prime ministerial readiness to publicly acknowledge that harm and conclude that an ambitious new path is required.
“This is the first time that a UK politician in power has been willing to stand up and say that Brexit is a failure that we must address or redress in some fundamental way,” Joël Reland, an analyst with the UK In a Changing Europe thinktank, told me. “Keir Starmer’s public message was that we will be sticking with Boris Johnson’s [2019] Brexit deal, but we’re going to improve it to make Brexit work. Burnham is saying Brexit doesn’t work and that we need a different form of deal. That has never been said before.”
Burnham is not yet committing himself to fighting the next election on a particular course of action. Much will depend on the response he gets. But all options – Lisa O’Carroll details them here – are on the table, from a customs union to re-joining the single market and becoming, like Norway, a rule-taker, to “going all the way”.
But crucially, Burnham has already departed from the orthodoxy that makes questioning Brexit a heresy. Instead of shutting down the topic to limit his exposure to Eurosceptic attacks, the PM is meeting it head-on, Reland said. “And I don’t see why you would do that unless you wanted to take on the political argument”.
Why would Burnham choose this juncture and risk drawing down what Rafael Behr calls the Brexit curse?
The economic rationale is the obvious one. “Burnham’s ten year domestic agenda for the country promises radical reform of such things as the social care system, and somebody is going to have to pay for that,” argues Reland. “One of the ways you can get economic growth is by rejoining your largest and closest trading partner.”
The modest ‘re-set’ agenda launched by Starmer in May 2025 is stuck, bogged down in disputes, such as that over fees for EU students in the UK. A pencilled-in 20 November summit is still up in the air. Britain’s big impediment from outside the club is its lack of bargaining power. A cherrypicking attempt to coax the EU into a selective single market for goods only (without free movement of people) was firmly rebuffed by Brussels in May. And even if this reset were fully delivered, the government’s own figures estimate it would add at most 0.3% to GDP by 2040.
Labour meanwhile has lost votes to its left, particularly to the Greens, so a more progressive offer on Europe might be a gamble worth taking. New polling, as Pippa Crerar and Rowena Mason revealed at the weekend, shows that if Burnham’s preference is for rejoining the EU, almost half of the country already agrees.
Gaby Hinsliff noted that among Burnham’s opponents the only one to react to the surprise move with “unfettered glee” was Nigel Farage. Yet, she suggested, the Conservatives, also obsessed with economic growth, may not side with Farage given that most voters think Brexit has made them economically worse off. “It’s not in Tory long-term interests to strangle this at birth” wrote Hinsliff.
A warm welcome?
Events in Europe are also dictating the pace. “Welcome back!” was the French president Emmanuel Macron’s possibly tongue-in-cheek response to Burnham’s remarks. But it is a French-led project called “Made in Europe” that is both concentrating the PM’s mind and could ultimately undermine his ambition.
Made in Europe is a highly protectionist idea for remaking the EU as an industrial powerhouse, able to withstand competition from China. UK-made goods, if legally classified as non-European under the law, would be locked out, spelling trade devastation for the British car industry. France, facing its own domestic upheaval and crunch elections next April, is hardline about Britain’s exclusion: Macron’s ministers insist that if you’re not paying the costs of the internal market you don’t get to claim the benefits. Made in Europe is emerging as a symbol, Reland explained, of how geopolitics is driving the EU’s agenda, and widening its range of competencies to such areas as industrial policy, AI and tech sovereignty. “It is no longer just food and environment policy that is set at EU level but the big, strategic, hard security decisions too,” he said.
The more that EU countries strategically pool sovereignty to respond to shocks such as US antagonism or Russian hybrid warfare, and the more aggressively they protect that cooperation, the steeper the costs of being outside the club become. With Norway and Switzerland, both non-EU members with single market access, now also facing the Made in Europe battle, it’s no wonder Burnham is mulling the full rejoin option.
But, as Mujtaba Rahman’s prescient column advised, the coming debate will need to go beyond the question of whether Britain could contemplate rejoining, to an honest assessment of what Europe has become in the years since it left.

The Quiet, Careful Growth of Philippine-Taiwan Ties
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
14:44:00 UTC
23:44:00 KST

On October 2, the Philippine Coast Guard commissioned BRP Sarangani, a retired Taiwanese Coast Guard cutter formerly known as the Kinmen. The transfer is unusual because Taiwan only transfers decommissioned vessels to states that officially recognize Taiwan’s statehood, which the Philippines does not.
Furthermore, the vessel did not sail from Kaohsiung to Manila under the Taiwanese flag, government-to-government, the way Taipei’s other patrol-vessel donations have gone to Palau, the Marshall Islands and Tuvalu – states that recognize the Republic of China (Taiwan). Instead, the Philippine nongovernmental organization We Protect Our Seas (WPS) Foundation quietly acquired the Kinmen, renamed it, repainted it, and handed it to the Philippine Coast Guard in a ceremony that never mentioned where the ship had come from.
The reason for this indirect approach is obvious: the Philippines adheres to the One China policy and would not like to provoke China. Unofficial engagements with Taiwan, carried out by states like the United States, France, Singapore, the United Kingdom, and Germany that formally recognize China, are a global default. China explicitly tolerates their economic and cultural relations with Taiwan.
So what makes the Philippines’ engagement with Taiwan different, and why is Manila engaging with Taiwan so extensively now when its relationship with China is tenser than in the past two decades?
The Philippines as a Distinct Case
For most of the above-mentioned states, Taiwan policy is about standing up for democracy and alliance management, conducted at a safe distance – being geographically far away from the immediate threat of military conflict with China. However, the Philippines is in close proximity to Taiwan. The Philippine province of Batanes lies south of Taiwan, near the Bashi Channel, placing it closer to spillover from the Taiwan conflict.
Adding to this are 200,000 Filipino workers currently in Taiwan, whose evacuation during a Taiwan crisis would pose an emergency for the Philippine government. Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. has publicly stated that Taiwan’s security is inseparable from the Philippines’ own, making clear that Taiwan is a national security question rather than an elective foreign policy stance.
Yet Manila must tread carefully. Anything it does with Taiwan that upsets China is directly visible in Chinese assertiveness in the South China Sea, affecting Filipino sovereignty and fisheries.
The Philippines’ increased engagement with Taiwan predates the Marcos administration. Taiwan is the Philippines’ ninth-largest trading partner, with established cooperation in education, agriculture, and healthcare and growing interest in semiconductors and start-ups. Under Philippine President Rodrigo Duterte (in office from 2016-2022), the Philippines and Taiwan signed a bilateral investment agreement in 2017 – the first major investment agreement in the last 25 years – under Taiwan’s New Southbound Policy, with cooperation extending across trade, investment, education, and labor mobility. But this engagement made sense given that the Philippines was in a state of rapprochement with China.
What has changed now is the strategic significance of Philippines-Taiwan engagement. Economic and cultural ties are increasingly accompanied by institutional and maritime cooperation. In April 2025, the Philippines eased restrictions on official exchanges with Taiwan, facilitating travel for economic and trade-related purposes. This was highlighted by Taiwanese Foreign Minister Lin Chia-lung’s visit to Manila, the second such foreign minister visit to the Philippines since 1975. Taiwan’s subsequent proposal to open a second representative office in Cebu to deepen the “Taiwan-Philippine Corridor” further signaled an effort to deepen institutional engagement.
Maritime cooperation has become increasingly apparent. What began as crisis management following the 2013 killing of a Taiwanese fisherman by Philippine personnel has created a basis for maritime cooperation, despite the absence of diplomatic recognition.
The WPS Foundation confirmed that the recently transferred vessel, BRP Sarangani, will support maritime patrols, search and rescue, humanitarian assistance, disaster response, and training. The transfer of vessels between two coast guards without requiring an overt government-to-government transaction demonstrates how institutional informality can create political space for cooperation that formal diplomatic relations might otherwise constrain.
Last year, the Philippine and Taiwanese Coast Guard conducted patrols in the Bashi Channel. Taiwan’s Coast Guard is also planning to send vessels to visit the Philippines in 2027, the first visit since the Philippines switched its recognition from the ROC to the People’s Republic of China in 1975.
But why is the Philippines doing this now, when China has become more assertive? One plausible explanation is that the Philippines sees little benefit in restraining its engagement with Taiwan. Chinese pressure in the South China Sea continued despite Manila’s previously cautious approach to Taiwan, giving Philippine policymakers fewer reasons to believe that restraint will win China’s goodwill.
At the same time, the Philippines cannot match China militarily or economically. Deepening ties with Taiwan offer the Philippines a way to widen its strategic and economic options at a relatively low cost. Manila can strengthen cooperation with a partner that provides investment, technology, and security benefits, while also engaging with an issue that China considers highly sensitive. Whether this amounts to deliberate tit-for-tat is difficult to establish, but the effect is clear: the Philippines has less incentive than before to keep its Taiwan relationship within narrow limits simply to avoid displeasing China.
Keeping It Under the Threshold
While the Philippines has steadily expanded its engagement with Taiwan, it has stopped short of turning that engagement into overt alignment, as seen in the vessel transfer through a non-governmental organization and the Philippine government’s refusal to publicly recognize it as a formerly Taiwanese vessel. Manila has repeatedly affirmed that its One China policy remains “consistent, clear and unchanged” and that “economic, cultural, and functional cooperation with Taiwan” does not violate it. Military and security engagements such as tabletop exercises or patrols are consistently described as “unofficial and informal.” Even the April 2025 easing of visa restrictions excludes visits and exchanges over defense- and security-related issues. Furthermore, no agreements, Memoranda of Understanding (MoU), exchange of notes or similar documents can proceed without clearance from the Department of Foreign Affairs (DFA) and, where necessary, an authorization from the Office of the President.
This caution reflects Manila’s awareness that spillover from a Taiwan crisis would be unavoidable. Under the Enhanced Defense Cooperation Agreement, U.S. forces could rely on Philippine bases to support operations in a Taiwan crisis. Yet Filipino officials have been explicit that they do not want the Philippines drawn into such a conflict – a position echoed by the public, with roughly 86 percent of Filipinos saying that they want the country to remain neutral in a China-Taiwan conflict. Philippine Foreign Affairs Secretary Thersea Lazaro has said that Manila is open to discussions with China over evacuation plans for its citizens in the event of a Chinese invasion of Taiwan.
The throughline is consistent: Manila wants to preserve its One China policy so Beijing has less reason to treat Philippine security as fair game in any future crisis.

CIS countries concerned by forecast of arms race in outer space
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
