Romania buys 12 H225M helicopters to replace old Pumas
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
14:14:50 UTC
23:14:50 KST

- Romania signed a contract for 12 Airbus H225M helicopters, financed by the European Union's SAFE program, to begin replacing its IAR-330 Puma fleet.
- Romania's defense ministry valued the purchase order at about €757 million (about $848 million), including initial logistics support and training.
Romania has signed a contract for 12 Airbus H225M Caracal military helicopters, the first step in replacing the Romanian Air Force’s aging fleet of locally built IAR-330 Puma helicopters, Airbus Helicopters said on October 7.
The deal was concluded through France’s defense procurement agency, the DGA, and is financed under the European Union’s Security Action for Europe, or SAFE, loan program. Romania’s defense ministry said in July that its purchase order for the helicopters, including initial logistics support and crew training, is worth about €757 million (about $848 million), within a total approved SAFE project budget of €852 million (about $954 million).
Airbus said the H225Ms will start replacing the Pumas in both conventional and special operations roles. The first helicopter is due 38 months after the order was signed, Romanian news outlet HotNews reported.
“We are honoured that Romania has chosen the H225M to strengthen its defence capabilities. This selection will also bolster Romania’s industrial capabilities through our long term partnership with IAR, Romania’s sole helicopter manufacturer,” said Matthieu Louvot, chief executive of Airbus Helicopters.
The H225M is the military version of Airbus’ largest Super Puma family helicopter, a twin-engine medium-heavy transport used for troop transport, search and rescue and special operations. Airbus says more than 350 H225s and H225Ms are in service and have flown more than 1 million hours. Romania becomes the 13th H225M customer, joining Brazil, France, Hungary, Indonesia, Iraq, Kuwait, Malaysia, Mexico, Morocco, the Netherlands, Singapore and Thailand.
Romania’s state-owned IAR plant in Brasov license-built the Pumas the H225M will replace, starting in the 1970s. The defense ministry plans to buy about 30 more helicopters after 2030 from its national budget, a deal of roughly €2 billion (about $2.24 billion) meant to move H225M production to Brasov, HotNews reported from the ministry’s SAFE procurement list.
The order is Romania’s second with Airbus Helicopters under SAFE. In June, the Romanian Ministry of Internal Affairs ordered seven H160 and five H145 helicopters for emergency response, civil protection and public order missions. Romania also ordered two H215M helicopters in a naval configuration in 2023.
SAFE provides low-interest EU loans for member states to buy defense equipment quickly from European industry. Romania’s allocation is €16.6 billion, the second-largest among the countries that applied, and the H225M deal was approved by the Romanian parliament as part of a wider package that also includes Lynx infantry fighting vehicles and Piranha 5 armored personnel carriers.

Iranian president says US deal ‘not out of reach’ in call with Putin
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
14:14:41 UTC
23:14:41 KST

Sahin Demir
07 October 2026•Update: 07 October 2026
Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian said during a call with his Russian counterpart, Vladimir Putin, that reaching an agreement with the US is “not out of reach” if Washington adheres to international legal frameworks, according to the Iranian presidency.
The two leaders discussed regional developments, Iran-US negotiations and relations, according to a statement.
Pezeshkian briefed Putin on negotiations between Iran and the US mediated by Pakistan, describing Washington’s “double standards and maximalism” as the biggest obstacle to reaching a fair agreement.
He said Tehran was prepared to reach a “balanced and fair” agreement that would ensure lasting peace and security in the region.
“Our red line is Iran’s national interests and the rights of the Iranian people,” said Pezeshkian, adding that if Washington adhered to international legal frameworks, reaching an agreement would not be out of reach.
The Iranian president also described Gulf countries as Iran’s “brothers” and expressed regret about the use of US military bases in those countries for attacks against Iran.
He said Tehran was ready to cooperate with neighboring countries to achieve regional peace and security without the presence or involvement of powers from outside the region.
Putin reiterated Russia’s support for diplomatic efforts to reach a political settlement to the war and expressed Moscow’s readiness to continue helping to find a diplomatic solution, according to the statement.
He also stressed the need to respect Iran’s sovereignty and territorial integrity, and backed Tehran’s demands for compensation for damage caused during the war and long-term security guarantees against additional attacks.
The two leaders reaffirmed their commitment to expanding cooperation under the Comprehensive Strategic Partnership Treaty and maintaining close coordination in international forums.
Iran and Russia signed the Comprehensive Strategic Partnership Treaty in January 2025 to strengthen cooperation in several areas, including trade, energy, transport and security.
The US-Israel war with Iran erupted in late February with attacks against Iran, followed by Iranian retaliatory strikes in the region.
Washington and Tehran signed an initial agreement in June following mediation efforts by Pakistan and Qatar to halt hostilities and pave the way for negotiations.
Implementation of the agreement has since stalled amid disagreements, including on security and navigation in the Strait of Hormuz.

South West Water owner taps investors to fix infrastructure after sewage spills
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
14:14:35 UTC
23:14:35 KST

The owner of embattled South West Water has slashed its dividend and launched a cash call to investors as it attempts to fund infrastructure investment, days after it was hit by a record £7.9m fine for hundreds of sewage spills.
London-listed Pennon said on Wednesday it would tap investors for £550m, as part of a £1bn investment “to drive improved outcomes for customers and communities”.
Shares in the utility company, which supplies water to about 3.5 million customers across the south-west of England, as well as 380,000 business customers around the UK, tumbled in response to the announcement, making Pennon the biggest faller on the FTSE 250 index.
Pennon’s new chief executive, Keith Haslett, who was appointed in April, said he had conducted a comprehensive review of the business and had identified areas for improvement, including customer service and the company’s environmental performance.
Last month, a judge issued South West Water with the largest fine for environmental offences in the region, at nearly £8m, and said the company’s conduct amounted to reckless failures in management systems and response to known risks. The fine will be paid by shareholders rather than through bill increases.
The company was fined after hundreds of sewage spills during a six-year period at popular bathing spots including the coastal village of Harlyn in north Cornwall and in sensitive habitats, such as the River Camel, which is home to otters and Atlantic salmon and popular with birdwatchers and sailors.
In June, South West Water was fined £1.85m by a judge in a separate case. The company pleaded guilty to the criminal offence of supplying water unfit for human consumption, after a 2024 parasite outbreak in Brixham, Devon, made hundreds of people sick and forced thousands of households to boil their water.
Pennon said on Wednesday it would also slash its shareholder dividend by about 30%, including the impact of the equity raise, as part of its “operational reset”.
Shares in Pennon, which also owns Bristol Water and SES Water, slumped by as much as 22% on Wednesday after the company’s announcement, named “project Proteus”, after a sea god in Greek mythology.
Haslett told reporters the reaction to the company’s plans had been mixed, saying: “Investment is needed to achieve improvements – we’re funding the plans in the right way.”
He added this would not be funded by further increases to customers’ bills and said he was also bringing some critical roles back in-house, including leakage teams that were previously outsourced.
In its recent results for the year to 31 March, Pennon revealed it had incurred outcome delivery incentives from the water regulator for England and Wales, Ofwat, of about £42m for its water and wastewater performance. It said it had faced operational pressures from “exceptional storms and sustained rainfall coupled with a step up in targets and penalty rates”.
The company anticipates it will continue to incur the penalties until 2030 but is aiming to reduce them by at least 50% a year.
On Tuesday, South West Water applied for a ban on non-essential water use for some businesses across parts of Devon and west Dorset, after a lack of significant rainfall after the hot, dry summer. The proposed ban would restrict activities such as vehicle washing, the cleaning of buildings and the filling of non-domestic swimming pools and ponds.
Customers of South West Water are already seeing their bills rise to fuel £2.5bn of investment in infrastructure in the years to 2030.
The number of customer complaints received by South West Water more than doubled over the past year, according to the latest figures from a consumer watchdog. The Consumer Council for Water found complaints to the company soared by 153%, and rated South West Water and Thames Water “poor” for the number of complaints received and how they handled them.
In recent weeks, Andy Burnham has come under further pressure from a cross-party group of MPs to take control of indebted Thames Water.
The MPs are calling for ministers to break off talks with the US hedge funds that are effectively running the company and to consider emergency legislation to take charge of Thames’ financial affairs.
However, the environment secretary, Angela Eagle, has previously suggested a special administration regime – effectively temporary public control – could not be triggered for Thames Water and would require a change in the law.

“I reaffirm my invariable support for you and the Russian Federation, being firmly convinced that the Russian people’s sacred war of justice for defending the sovereignty, security interests and territorial integrity of the country will surely end with their victory,” Kim said in a congratulatory message to Russian President Vladimir Putin, carried by the state-run Korean Central News Agency (KCNA).
Russia has “firmly consolidated its dignity and position as a big power” over the last two decades, Kim said.
“I am pleased to have good friendship with you and open up a new chapter for the development of the relations between our two countries,” he added.
It is the “steadfast” policy of Pyongyang and “my unshakable option” to attach importance to the comprehensive strategic partnership and alliance with Russia and to “steadily expand and develop the joint work,” Kim said.
Relations between Pyongyang and Moscow have significantly deepened since the two countries signed a comprehensive strategic partnership treaty in June 2024.
The pact includes a mutual defense provision requiring either side to provide military assistance if the other is subjected to an armed attack.
In August 2025, North Korea sent around 1,000 military engineers to Russia’s Kursk region to assist Russian forces in clearing land mines planted during fighting with Ukrainian troops.
The deployment followed an earlier dispatch of an estimated 15,000 combat troops to support Russia’s war effort, according to South Korea’s spy agency, which claims North Korea has lost 2,000 troops in the war.

Manfred D, former head of cabinet to ex-intelligence chief August Hanning, was taken into custody on charges of aiding and abetting treason. He is accused of obtaining classified BND documents and passing them to Hanning in exchange for payment since 2010.
Following the arrest of former BND chief August Hanning on Tuesday in what has turned out to be Germany's biggest espionage scandal, his long-standing confidant and former head of cabinet Manfred D has now also been taken into custody.
Federal prosecutors accuse both men of having used state secrets over many years to support private consulting activities and foreign interests, a crime that constitutes treason.
Manfred D, 64, has been charged with aiding and abetting and remains in pre-trial detention, while Hanning is being brought before an investigating judge, according to reports.
Manfred D previously served as head of cabinet to former intelligence chief August Hanning. The two men have known each other since the late 1990s and worked closely together for many years at the BND and later at the Interior Ministry.
Prosecutors say Manfred D obtained classified documents from the intelligence service and passed them to his former boss Hanning for financial gain.
The arrangement is believed to have been in place since 2010.
"Presumably in spring 2010, the defendants agreed that Manfred D would continuously obtain valuable intelligence from the Federal Intelligence Service for the accused Hanning in return for payment," senior public prosecutor Dr Ines Peterson said.
Hanning is said to have used the confidential information to prepare, among other things, an analysis for foreign services to earn private income as a consultant.
Investigators bugged Manfred D's property and monitored him for months in a high-profile probe.
Azerbaijan on Wednesday denied a report by German magazine Der Spiegel, republished by German and other media, claiming that Hanning could have been in contact with an agent from Azerbaijan.
Azerbaijan’s state news agency APA reported that Baku denied the Der Spiegel reports and that “through its special services and diplomatic channels conveyed its protest on the matter both to the Office of the German Chancellor and to the German Foreign Ministry."
Meanwhile, Azerbaijan’s Media and Broadcasting Council issued a statement rejecting the reports as “unfounded disinformation and unacceptable information manipulation.”
In parallel, a senior Azerbaijani official told Baku-based international news channel Anewz the chancellor's office and representatives of Germany’s intelligence community confirmed through official channels that the ongoing probe was not connected to Azerbaijan in any way.
"The initial attempt to associate Azerbaijan with this case originated from Der Spiegel, rather than from any official German investigative or judicial authority," the official said.
"The Federal Prosecutor General’s Office itself has publicly identified neither Azerbaijan nor any Azerbaijani institution in connection with the investigation,” they added.
The allegations risk “causing unnecessary damage to the steadily developing relations between Azerbaijan and Germany," according to the unnamed official.

The panel "called for strict respect for ceasefire commitments, full cooperation with verification mechanisms and restraint from actions that could undermine the peace process," the statement said.

While in Congo, the delegation also met with representatives of the UN peacekeeping mission in the country before visiting Nyiragongo territory to assess the humanitarian situation of internally displaced people.
The panel called on the warring parties to ensure safe and unhindered humanitarian access and protect essential services and educational facilities.
Reaffirming its commitment to Congo's sovereignty, unity and territorial integrity, the panel said commitments must translate into tangible improvements for affected communities.
In August, Congo and AFC/M23 rebels agreed in Switzerland to develop a roadmap setting out sequenced steps and timelines for peace negotiations under the Doha Framework Agreement signed last year.
The facilitators' visit came as fighting continued in eastern Congo between the AFC/M23 rebel group and government forces, with both sides accusing each other of ceasefire violations.
The M23 rebels have been at the center of the conflict in eastern Congo.

From Congo, the delegation, led by former Kenyan President Uhuru Kenyatta, traveled Wednesday to Kigali, Rwanda, where it met Rwandan Foreign Minister Olivier Nduhungirehe.

UN Human Rights Council in Geneva calls for safeguards on AI
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
14:12:08 UTC
23:12:08 KST

UN Human Rights Council in Geneva calls for safeguards on AI
In its first resolution on the issue, the UN Human Rights Council warned on Tuesday in Geneva of the threats posed by artificial intelligence (AI) systems.
The resolution, which was adopted by consensus, states that AI systems must comply with international law at every stage, from their manufacture to their use. Any application that fails to respect human rights should be banned.
More
The ethics of artificial intelligence
States are urged to consider the impact of AI on human rights when introducing legislative and regulatory frameworks. They must combat discrimination and other adverse effects. The resolution also adds that any decision involving AI must be overseen by a human being. Responsibilities must be clearly defined.
Another requirement is that all countries, including developing nations, should be able to take part in discussions on how AI is regulated. The issue will be discussed at the next Global Summit on AI, which is due to take place in Geneva in June.
+ We asked an AI about the future – its answer might scare you
The resolution also calls for international collaboration to be strengthened and coherence between the various initiatives to be improved. Similarly, states, the UN and other stakeholders should champion digital public goods, particularly in terms of access to digital infrastructure.
The Council is due to discuss AI next June. The Office of the High Commissioner for Human Rights will submit a report within a year.
In a second resolution, also discussed for the first time and adopted by consensus, the Council urged states to protect the human rights of women and girls in the context of digital technologies. Gender-based violence facilitated by these technologies must be prevented, it added.

Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan on Wednesday said that Türkiye is taking decisive steps to address problems in part of its fund market, pledging that authorities will not tolerate negligence, legal violations or misconduct.
"We are addressing the issue that has emerged in a certain part of the fund market and are taking the necessary steps one by one with great determination," Erdogan said.
He made the remarks at a legislative year opening meeting with Justice and Development (AK) Party members in Ankara.
"Our economic management is following the issue, taking measures and implementing the steps needed to ensure that financial markets emerge from this crisis stronger," Erdogan said.
He said the State Supervisory Council is conducting a comprehensive investigation into the fund-related issue and pledged that authorities would not tolerate wrongdoing.
"Our State Supervisory Council is examining this matter in all its dimensions. We will not tolerate even the slightest negligence or any violation of the law and rules," he added.
The president also highlighted the newly established Fund Coordination Board, chaired by Vice President Cevdet Yilmaz, saying its primary task is to resolve the issue.
"The primary agenda of our Fund Coordination Board, established under the chairmanship of our vice president, is to ensure that this issue is resolved," Erdogan said.
"Our board will work intensively and will swiftly overcome this problem, which has cast an unfair shadow over our capital markets," he added.
Government vows to protect investors
Erdogan said the government was also monitoring the issue from the perspective of investors and working to ensure that citizens' savings are repaid without creating an additional burden on the public.
"We are following the investor dimension of the issue. Without imposing a burden on the public, we are carrying out the necessary processes to ensure that our citizens' savings are paid," he said.
He warned that those seeking to exploit the situation would ultimately lose, while Türkiye and its citizens would emerge stronger.
"Those who trade in disaster in an attempt to wear down the Turkish economy will lose, while our country and nation will gain many times more," Erdogan said.
"Turkish capital markets will rid themselves of their dead weight, be cleansed of parasites feeding on the savings of small investors, and our financial market will continue on its path," he added.
Erdogan also warned those accused of obtaining illicit gains that they would face accountability.
He added that the political dimension of the investigation could not be separated from broader questions of morality and faith.
"For us, the political dimension of the issue is never separate from conscience, morality and faith," Erdogan said.
Erdogan highlights economic performance

"We are determined to protect our people's jobs and livelihoods. No matter the cost, we are determined not to compromise on this," he said.

"We are proud to have increased our exports from $36 billion when we took over in 2002 to $284 billion," he said.

German radar already guarding Ukraine is picked to spot ballistic missiles. Its maker just signed a new deal with Kyiv
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
14:10:40 UTC
23:10:40 KST

German radar maker Hensoldt has signed a memorandum with Ukraine's Defense Ministry for more large-scale radar deliveries, the company said on 5 October. Ukrainian defense outlet Defense Express reads it as a step toward fitting Hensoldt's TRML-4D, already in Ukrainian service, into FREYJA, a planned shield against ballistic missiles.
Ballistic missiles remain the hardest threat in Russia's air war. After Russia's overnight barrage on 7 October, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Ukraine is still searching daily for Patriot missiles. The only other system Ukraine can use against them is the Franco-Italian SAMP/T, which fires Aster 30 interceptors made in small numbers. That gap is why Fire Point is reworking its FP-7 missile into a Patriot-like interceptor. Such an interceptor still needs radars to find its target first.
A memorandum signed during Merz's visit
Hensoldt CEO Oliver Dörre signed the document on the sidelines of German Chancellor Friedrich Merz's visit to Ukraine. Beyond deliveries, it covers further development of radar capabilities. The partners will also study options to deploy and jointly operate TRL-4D LR long-range radars. Hensoldt said this expands cooperation already agreed on in ballistic missile defense.
Russia’s air defenses can’t protect all its strategic sites once Ukraine’s ballistic missiles are ready, expert says
The TRL-4D LR is the land-based version of a long-range radar Hensoldt also builds for the German Navy, German outlet Sicherheit & Verteidigung reported. The outlet cited Germany's defense procurement office as giving the naval version a range of more than 400 km (250 miles) against air targets. That, it concluded, puts the range well beyond the TRML-4D's.
"The Ukrainian air defence forces urgently need our high-performance radars to help protect infrastructure such as bridges," Dörre said.
Defense Express, describing the same memorandum, tied both the mass deliveries and the joint-operation plan to the TRML-4D. Hensoldt's release names no model for the deliveries and links joint operation to the TRL-4D LR.
Eyes for FREYJA
Hensoldt and Fire Point signed a memorandum on FREYJA at the Eurosatory arms show in Paris in June, with the TRML-4D to play a key role, Hensoldt announced. Fire Point is set to act as prime contractor and hold design authority. Hensoldt is to produce, test, and deliver the radars.
Germany’s Hensoldt to supply Ukraine with six more TRML-4D radars to boost air defense capabilities
Defense Express expects any study of deployment options to focus on how well the radar detects ballistic missiles and relays that data. Hensoldt has its own unit in Ukraine to work closely with operators, the outlet noted. Earlier, the company began setting up a local hub so Ukraine can service and repair the TRML-4D itself.
Already on duty
Ukraine's military uses the TRML-4D both standalone and as the built-in radar of the IRIS-T SLM medium-range air defense system, Defense Express noted. Hensoldt lists an instrumented range of 250 km (155 miles) at altitudes up to 30 km (19 miles). Defense Express, citing the manufacturer, gives track ranges of more than 120 km (75 miles) for fighter jets and more than 60 km (37 miles) for supersonic missiles.
More radars give earlier warning of ballistic strikes, but they cannot stop them. Until the FP-7.X makes its first ballistic intercept, planned for mid-2027, that job stays with Patriot and SAMP/T missiles. Partners delivered three times fewer air defense missiles in the first half of 2026 than a year earlier, Zelenskyy said on 5 August.

Rubio woos NATO member Iceland after Greenland deal
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio has praised Iceland for allowing Washington to “project power” from the North Atlantic island nation into the Arctic.
Iceland is strategically positioned to help the Pentagon monitor Arctic airspace and conduct missions tracking Russian submarines in the Atlantic, not unlike Denmark’s autonomous territory of Greenland, which US President Donald Trump had notoriously threatened to annex. The US president and Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen have signed an agreement to substantially increase Washington’s military presence there.
On Tuesday in Iceland, which joined NATO when it was created in 1949, Rubio praised Rejkyavik for allowing “the US military to project power using your land, your air, your sea, giving us a critical outpost for monitoring clandestine behavior and deterring our adversaries.”
The secretary stressed that Washington would not take action in Iceland without Reykjavik’s consent. Questions about US intentions were renewed last month after Trump posted an image showing North America and nearby islands covered in the Stars and Stripes, including Greenland and Iceland. Foreign Minister Thorgerdur Katrin Gunnarsdottir responded by summoning US Ambassador Billy Long to lodge a protest.
Rubio and Gunnarsdottir both played down the diplomatic incident at their joint press conference.
”We’re not talking about social media posts,” Rubio said, while Gunnarsdottir said the two governments “are looking forward, not backward.”
.@SecRubio on Trump social media post depicting U.S. acquisition of Iceland: "We're not talking about social media posts, I'm here, we're here meeting with a country...everything's very positive in our relationship." https://t.co/ZVA5q5Bjq1
— CSPAN (@cspan) October 6, 2026
Long also apologized last year after joking that Iceland could become the 52nd US state, with himself as governor. A petition urging Gunnarsdottir to reject his posting as US ambassador reportedly gathered around 2,000 signatures.
The US first established a presence in Iceland during World War II, taking over from British forces in 1941. A 1951 defense agreement signed under the banner of the newly created NATO cemented Iceland’s role during the Cold War.
Naval Air Station Keflavik, once the main US military hub in Iceland, was formally handed over to the local authorities in 2006, although the US continues to play a critical role in the country’s national security.
Rubio’s visit was designed to highlight decades of cooperation and the legacy of the Cold War. He and Gunnarsdottir met at the same venue where US President Ronald Reagan and Soviet leader Mikhail Gorbachev held talks in 1986 on nuclear arms.
Washington’s ability to project military power worldwide is currently strained, with substantial assets tied down in the Middle East supporting the war with Iran. Rubio said the smaller US role in the joint Northern Viking exercise earlier this year reflected the need to “allocate resources” in response to current events and was not an “enduring decision” to reduce Washington’s attention to Iceland.

Woman from Rezekne sentenced to six years in prison for funding Russian military  - The Baltic Times
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
14:10:30 UTC
23:10:30 KST

RIGA - The Riga City Court on Wednesday sentenced pro-Kremlin activist Polina Kamlova from Rezekne to six years in prison for funding the Russian military, LETA learned.
The woman was tried for transferring approximately EUR 43 for the purchase of drone-jamming equipment to be handed over to the Russian military.
In addition to the six-year prison sentence, she was placed on probation for three years. The court counted the time she spent in custody and detention in her sentence. Taking this into account, the remaining length of the sentence to be served is five years, one month, and 25 days.
The court left the imposed security measure - detention - unchanged until the ruling takes effect.
Kamlova may still appeal the ruling to the Riga Regional Court.
Without naming the individual, the prosecutor’s office previously told LETA that criminal charges were brought against an individual for committing a criminal offense under the section of the Criminal Law regarding the financing of an armed conflict.
The State Security Service (VDD) investigated the case before it was referred to the prosecutor’s office. VDD’s investigation revealed that in December 2024, Kamlova responded to a request from a contact person in Russia to provide funds for the purchase of drone-jamming equipment for Russian soldiers on the front lines in Ukraine.
Since it is not possible to make a transfer from a Latvian financial institution to a Russian financial institution, Kamlova turned to an acquaintance in Belarus. Thus, acting on the defendant’s request and unaware of the true purpose of the payment, she made a payment of 157 Belarusian rubles (approximately EUR 42.86) from her private bank account at a Belarusian financial institution to the bank account of Kamlova’s acquaintance at a Russian financial institution.
VDD initiated criminal proceedings against her on November 25, 2025.
The Criminal Law provides for punishment for the financing of an armed conflict with imprisonment for up to ten years and probation supervision for up to three years. Kamlova is currently in custody.
VDD detained Kamlova on December 2, 2025, and conducted searches at two locations associated with her in Rezekne and Preili Municipality.

EU-China relations: Parliament calls for dialogue and fair trade  - The Baltic Times
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
14:10:20 UTC
23:10:20 KST

TALLINN - The European Parliament has adopted a recommendation addressed to other EU institutions, expressing support for a world order based on multilateralism and stressing the need for dialogue with China on global challenges, peace and security, climate, and human rights.
At the same time, the report notes that EU-China relations have reached a difficult stage, as China employs unfair economic practices and holds a position on the war in Ukraine that is very different from the EU's, considering that the Chinese military has trained Russian soldiers to fight in Ukraine. The EU should therefore coordinate its actions with the US, G7 countries, and other like-minded partners, and China should use its influence on Russia to end the war in Ukraine.
The EU must urgently reduce its excessive economic dependence on China, as this can be used against the bloc. The EU must also de-risk in areas such as critical raw materials, pharmaceuticals, batteries, electric vehicles, information and communication technology, and semiconductors, as well as in other strategic sectors. China's industrial overcapacity, state subsidies, and access restrictions imposed on European companies are increasingly problematic for the EU economy. Investments into Europe must be screened more thoroughly, and the EU's vital technology, infrastructure, and supply chains must be more robustly protected.
Parliament demands a level playing field for the EU in trade and investment with China and wants the EU to respond proportionately when China fails to open its domestic markets. It also calls for strengthening the "Global Gateway" strategy partnerships, particularly in Africa and Latin America, as they offer an alternative to China's Belt and Road Initiative. Parliament stresses its continued support for the EU's One China policy but opposes any unilateral change to Taiwan's status quo by force or coercion.
The report also calls for the EU to more strongly combat cyberattacks, foreign interference, espionage, and hybrid threats, as well as to take a more robust stance on human rights. Parliament believes that more pressure should be put on China over its repression, use of forced labor, and policies in Tibet and Xinjiang. Additionally, Parliament expresses deep concern about the adoption of the so-called law on promoting ethnic unity and progress in China, as it further entrenches the country's assimilation policies. Parliament also demands that China unconditionally release all political prisoners.
In the plenary session, 454 MEPs voted in favor of the own-initiative report, with 86 against and 110 abstentions.
Rapporteur Hilde Vautmans from Belgium said that European policy towards China is changing and that a broad consensus is emerging in the EU on rebalancing economic relations. "I hope that Commissioner Šefčovič will address this tomorrow in Beijing. However, the Parliament's report goes even further. It calls for the EU to cooperate with China where possible but to remain firm on its security and values. As long as fundamental disagreements persist between the EU and China, our relationship will also be characterized by systemic rivalry."
Direct relations between the European Parliament and Chinese authorities were frozen from 2021 to 2025 after the Chinese government imposed sanctions on several MEPs in response to EU sanctions on Chinese officials and organizations for human rights violations. Relations were restored in 2025, and between March and June 2026, three parliamentary delegations visited China. A fourth visit is expected in October 2026.

Kulbergs calls for issue of Istanbul Convention to be put to a consultative referendum  - The Baltic Times
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
14:10:19 UTC
23:10:19 KST

RIGA - Public opinion on the Istanbul Convention could be gauged through a consultative referendum, the results of which would not be legally binding, Prime Minister and future candidate for the office, Andris Kulbergs (United List), said in a conversation with members of the press on Wednesday following a meeting with President Edgars Rinkevics.
Kulbergs stated that the United List had discussed the idea of a consultative referendum with the President. In his view, the Saeima could use such a referendum to pose a question to the public, receive an answer, and act accordingly.
The politician noted that the issue of the Istanbul Convention has generated significant public interest, making it a suitable topic for gauging public opinion in this way. Other questions could also be posed in consultative referendums. Although the results would not be legally binding, they would provide a clear signal to political forces and eliminate speculation, Kulbergs believes.
When asked whether postponing withdrawal from the Istanbul Convention is a condition for forming a new government, Kulbergs denied this. He emphasized that the public has given the United List a mandate for change, not for addressing ideological and divisive issues, so such matters are not on the United List’s agenda.
"Whether we will at some point hold a consultative poll or a referendum, and what politicians should do afterward, that is an open question," added Rinkevics, while noting that introducing a consultative referendum would first require changes to the law, which would take time.
The President added that there are differing opinions among legal experts regarding the possibility of putting international treaties to a referendum. While working on this issue last year, a large number of legal experts pointed to the possibility of putting a bill to denounce a convention to a referendum - rather than the treaty itself - while others held the opposite view.
Rinkevics emphasized that he currently sees no argument why Latvia should rush to withdraw from the Istanbul Convention, thereby becoming the first European Union (EU) country to take such a step.
The President reminded that, when submitting the bill to the Saeima for a second review, he had called for the issue to be left to the next parliamentary session and discussed in pre-election debates. The positions of the political parties have varied - some supported remaining in the convention, some strongly advocated for withdrawal, while others were willing to consider various options.
In his view, this is not an issue that needs to be rushed. Rinkevics noted that the new Saeima and government will face many pressing issues that require immediate attention. In consultations with most of the parties, he heard a willingness not to lower human rights standards or to raise issues that divide society.
As reported, last fall the United List, then in the opposition, together with other political forces, pushed for Latvia’s withdrawal from the Istanbul Convention, and the Saeima supported it, but the proposal sparked widespread public protests. President Edgars Rinkevics did not promulgate the law and referred it back to parliament for further review. The Saeima essentially agreed to entrust the final decision on the matter to the next parliamentary session, in which the United List has now gained a dominant role.
The United List's candidate for Prime Minister, current Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs - whom the President would like to see form the next government as well - has promised to focus his efforts on putting the country’s finances in order, ensuring security, and promoting economic growth.
The President expressed his view that, in his opinion, this issue should not be raised at this time. He would support the position of allowing the new Saeima and the Cabinet of Ministers to settle into their roles, while acknowledging that the issue of the convention might resolve itself.
Rinkevics also noted that the Saeima had adopted a resolution to draft a special law that would incorporate the positive aspects of the Istanbul Convention, but the government has yet to implement this resolution.
As another option under consideration, the President mentioned keeping the convention in force while simultaneously initiating discussions with Council of Europe (CoE) member states to clarify the provisions open to interpretation. He acknowledged that this would take a long time and emphasized that the issue should be resolved in a way that does not divide society.

23:10:04 KST

TALLINN - The European Parliament debated the current state of negotiations on the EU's next Multiannual Financial Framework with representatives from the Commission and the Council in a plenary session. Parliament's rapporteur Siegfried Mureşan from Romania warned that Parliament will not agree to a smaller budget, as it would weaken Europe in the coming years and prevent the EU from achieving its goals, responding to crises, or dealing with unexpected events.
Mureșan reiterated that the Commission's initial budget proposal is at the same level as the outgoing budget period, despite growing challenges. The Commission's proposal for 2028-2034 amounts to 1.15 percent of the member states' Gross National Income (GNI), whereas the current Multiannual Financial Framework was 1.14 percent of GNI at the time of its presentation. "Reducing the budget would only weaken Europe," he stressed. Mureșan also emphasized that while member states' budgets have grown by 68 percent in absolute terms over the last seven years, the EU as a whole has not kept pace, meaning the perception of an ever-expanding EU budget is false.
Parliament's second rapporteur, Carla Tavares from Portugal, stated that Europe is no longer facing temporary crises but structural problems, and the EU's response must also be structural and far-sighted. Speaking on Parliament's position, she said: "We are not just demanding more money. We are demanding a budget that is consistent with the commitments assigned to the EU."
Tavares noted that while everyone generally agrees that Europe needs to spend more money to address priority issues in areas like competitiveness, energy independence, security, climate, education, and healthcare, some member states in the Council are still demanding a smaller budget and refusing new own resources. "It's as if we want a first-class Europe, but with a second-class budget! This isn't ambition; it's a contradiction. And it harms Europeans," she warned. "We don't have a choice between a cheap Europe or an expensive Europe. The choice is between an underfunded Europe mired in endless crises, or a Europe capable of anticipating problems, investing in its people and businesses, and shaping its own future," she concluded.
Most representatives of the political groups in the plenary also expressed support for Parliament's position, which was adopted in April 2026. In it, Parliament calls for a strong, realistic, and forward-looking budget that aligns with the EU's goals and is funded by new sources. The EU's long-term budget must serve the interests of its citizens, reduce inequality, and ensure sufficient funding for all key policy areas, including agriculture, regional development, cohesion, and social affairs. At the same time, the transparency and accountability of budget use must be improved.
Ireland's Minister for European Affairs, Thomas Byrne, confirmed that the Irish Presidency of the EU will present a new draft negotiating position for the Council on Saturday. "We want to move a step closer to an agreement, but a compromise will require difficult decisions," he said.
Piotr Serafin, the EU Commissioner for Budget, Anti-Fraud, and Public Administration, stressed that some countries continue to view the EU budget like an accountant's balance sheet: how much I put in versus how much I get out. "This approach was mistaken in the past, but with a modern budget, it doesn't work at all," Serafin said. He noted that the EU budget addresses common problems that member states cannot manage alone or that would cost everyone more if tackled separately.
Parliament adopted its position on the new Multiannual Financial Framework for 2028-2034 in April 2026. In it, Parliament called for an increase of approximately 10 percent to the budget originally proposed by the Commission to invest in key priorities such as defense and security, competitiveness, and cohesion and agricultural policies. Parliament also wanted to see new revenue streams to strengthen the EU budget, including a digital services tax, an online gambling tax, an extension of the Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM), and a crypto-asset income tax. More than 93 percent of the EU budget goes directly to EU programs that support people and projects in all member states, with less than seven percent spent on administration.
Member states, however, according to the Council's initial position, want to reduce the Commission's proposed budget by two percent. The Irish Presidency of the Council plans to release its new negotiating package on Saturday, October 10. The EU's next long-term budget requires the approval of both the Council and the Parliament.

TALLINN – The Estonian Traders' Association recognized four outstanding retail projects of the year at its annual Trade Congress.
Category awards were given to The Club at the T1 center, the crisis store network established by the Estonian Stockpiling Agency and six retail chains, the acquisition of Prisma Peremarket and its merger with Coop, and the new intranet of Viru Keskus.
From the four category winners, the jury selected the nationwide crisis store network as the overall winner of the Trade Act of the Year 2026.
The nationwide crisis store network, created in cooperation between the Estonian Stockpiling Agency and six retail chains, was chosen as the Collaboration Project of the Year and the overall winner of the Trade Act of the Year 2026. The network's goal is to establish 110 crisis stores across Estonia by the end of 2026. The stores will be prepared to continue operating during long-term power outages, and it will be possible to pay by card even if the data connection with the bank is down.
According to Nele Peil, CEO of the Estonian Traders' Association, the project highlights the broader role of retail in society. "Retail plays a fundamental role in society. The crisis store network demonstrates this very concretely: traders help keep people's daily lives functioning even in difficult situations and contribute to Estonia's crisis preparedness together with the state," Peil said.
Ando Leppiman, Chairman of the Board of the Estonian Stockpiling Agency, stated that crisis preparedness is primarily born from cooperation. "Crisis preparedness does not arise from stockpiled supplies in warehouses or written plans alone, but is born from the joint action of people, companies, and the state. Interest has also been shown in the crisis store experience outside of Estonia, which shows that a functioning cooperation model can serve as an example for others," Leppiman said.
In the New Concept of the Year category, the T1 center was recognized for creating The Club. The concept, which combines training, working, and relaxation, expands the traditional role of a shopping center from a place to shop to a leisure environment. According to T1 data, the center was visited by an average of over 12,500 people per day in August, and the total turnover of tenants was approximately 10% higher than in the same month of the previous year.
The Development Project of the Year award was given to Coop Estonia for the acquisition of Prisma Peremarket and its merger with Coop. On September 1, Coop became the owner of Prisma Peremarket and its 13 stores, with nearly 700 employees joining the company.
All 13 stores will be integrated into Coop's systems between September and November. For the Roo Prisma store, the first to be transitioned, the technical and visual changes were completed in just over 16 hours.
The Technological Innovation of the Year category was won by Viru Keskus for launching its new intranet. The unified work and self-service environment connects 107 shops and nearly 1,200 users.
Among other things, the intranet consolidates employee training, user accounts, and access permissions into a single workflow. Previously, manually issuing an access card could take up to a week.
With the Trade Act of the Year competition, the Estonian Traders' Association recognizes projects that create significant value for customers, companies, or the broader development of Estonian trade.

Baltic states responded appropriately to threat to their underwater infrastructure - Atlantic Council expert  - The Baltic Times
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
14:09:57 UTC
23:09:57 KST

RIGA - The Baltic states acted very appropriately by ensuring transparency regarding the threat to their undersea infrastructure and by cooperating closely with their allies to neutralize this threat, said Elisabeth Braw, a senior fellow at the Atlantic Council and a member of the UK National Preparedness Commission, in an interview with LETA.
The author of the forthcoming book The Undersea War, which focuses on threats to undersea cables and pipelines, acknowledged that cable and pipeline infrastructure - especially cables - is an area where we remain vulnerable, as the cables lie on the seabed and have no protection whatsoever.
The only protection is the proper action of nations and maritime traffic participants - ships and all others. "We have now reached a point where we can no longer be certain that ships sailing in our waters will take care not to damage the cables, she said, acknowledging that we may never know whether, if a cable is snagged by an anchor, and if this was done intentionally or not," she said.
The expert assessed the Baltic states' response to incidents on the seabed of the Baltic Sea very positively. "In my opinion, the Baltic states are doing the right thing by ensuring transparency regarding these threats. It is essential to gain public support, and that is something all three Baltic states have done well. It is also necessary to cooperate closely with allies, but one's own public must definitely be involved in this process," said Braw.
The expert noted that in recent years, during several serious incidents involving undersea cables in the Gulf of Finland, the Estonians and Finns cooperated very closely to coordinate their responses, while the Latvians cooperated very closely with the Swedish government when a cable belonging to the Latvian Radio and Television Center was damaged, as it was a cable connecting Latvia and Sweden.
"It is precisely in such cases that radical openness and transparency are crucial. If the crew of the vessel that snagged the cable truly acted so carelessly that they severed the cable accidentally, then we should name that crew and ensure that everyone knows that these specific people caused the accident or incident, which could have significantly impacted, for example, Latvia's ability to function. After all, we need digital connectivity every day, every second," Braw said.
She specifically praised Latvia for implementing a national security education program in high schools, as Latvia is a step ahead of everyone else in this area.
"Latvia has the most comprehensive curriculum in this area; it is something other countries can learn from. This is also linked to transparency - teaching and educating young people about national security and how they can contribute to ensuring it," said Braw. Everyone has a role to play in helping to protect their country, even if it is something very small, such as verifying information before sharing it on social media.

"Both countries have knowledge and experience that they can share with one another. For Estonia, the value of this transaction lies in combining this expertise to create something truly unique and in helping bring that competence to European markets," Vahtras added.
"Estonia is a global benchmark for a digital society, which is why ELEKS is headquartered in Tallinn. By partnering with ADM, we are fusing Estonia’s unparalleled public sector expertise with the scale and resilience of Ukrainian engineering excellence to deliver next-generation solutions for public sector and commercial clients across Europe," said Andriy Krupa, CEO of ELEKS.

ADM’s clients will continue to be served by the same team, now supported by the knowledge and experience of more than 2,000 ELEKS specialists worldwide.
"For nearly 30 years, we have been building digital services for a small country. It has been an exceptional testing ground where solutions are developed quickly and tested under public scrutiny. At times, however, we lacked the scale and, for certain projects, the specialised technical expertise needed to take the next step. With ELEKS, those limitations disappear. ADM and ELEKS have previously worked together on public sector projects in Ukraine and in emerging markets.
"We are grateful to the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, the Ministry of Justice and Digital Affairs, ESTDEV, and the Estonian Business and Innovation Agency for their contribution. Their visits, programmes and initiatives have helped build the partnerships that ultimately led to this transaction," Pihelpuu added.
"Ukraine has a strong technology sector, highly skilled people, and unique experience of maintaining and developing digital services under the extraordinary pressure of a full-scale war. Estonia brings its own remarkable experience in building a digital state, developing trusted public services and turning innovative ideas into practical solutions. When Ukrainian technological capacity meets Estonian experience, trust and access to the European market, we can create solutions that are valuable not only for Ukraine and Estonia, but for Europe and beyond," said Volodymyr Boiechko, Ambassador of Ukraine to Estonia.
About ELEKS
ELEKS is an international software engineering and IT consulting company founded in Ukraine in 1991, with its group headquarters located in Estonia. The company employs more than 2,000 specialists and operates approximately 20 offices across Europe, North and South America, and Asia. Its development centres are located in, among other countries, Ukraine, Poland, Croatia, Argentina and United States. More than 500 ELEKS employees are shareholders in the company. ELEKS holds security and compliance certifications including ISO 27001, SOC 2, HITRUST, CREST and Cyber Essentials Plus.
About ADM Interactive
ADM Interactive is a Tallinn-based digital agency founded in 1997. The company develops web portals, self-service platforms and business-critical software solutions for public and private sector organisations in Estonia as well as international clients.

ICONIC21 is expanding its presence in Lithuania with new offices in Vilnius and plans to create more than 350 local jobs. In this interview, Rokas Benetis, ICONIC21’s Country Manager for Lithuania, explains its choice of Vilnius, its recruitment ambitions and how it hopes to build lasting connections with the local community.
ICONIC21 has opened new offices in Vilnius. Why was the Lithuanian capital the right location for this next stage of the company’s growth?
Vilnius stood out because of its strong talent pool, modern business ecosystem and growing reputation as a destination for international investment and innovation.
As we continue to expand across Europe, we wanted a location where we could attract ambitious people, build a long-term operation and create meaningful career opportunities. Vilnius offered all of those.
What does the investment in the new Vilnius office tell us about ICONIC21’s longer-term ambitions in Lithuania and the wider Baltic region?
We wanted this investment to reflect a long-term commitment to Lithuania. Our new facility will serve as a key operational hub, supporting our wider European growth while creating more than 350 local jobs. We see Lithuania as a base that directly supports our European operations and as an important part of our future.
Vilnius has developed a growing reputation as a hub for technology and international business. What advantages does the city offer ICONIC21 when it comes to attracting talent, fostering innovation and supporting future growth?
Vilnius is home to a highly skilled and internationally minded workforce, which is essential for a fast-growing business like ours. The city attracts people looking to grow their careers, while its business-friendly environment and strong infrastructure offer the right conditions for innovation and sustainable growth.
How significant do you expect the Vilnius operation to become within ICONIC21’s wider international business, and are there plans to expand the local team further?

Alongside the new office, ICONIC21 has strengthened its presence in the city through its sponsorship of BC Rytas. What attracted you to the club, and why was this the right partnership for the business?
We were drawn to Rytas because of the depth of its roots here. This is a club Vilnius has supported for generations, and basketball is not something you can be indifferent to in Lithuania.
We’re a company that intends to stay in the city, so partnering with Rytas was the natural place to begin putting down roots of our own.
Sports sponsorships can be about much more than brand visibility. What do you want the BC Rytas partnership to achieve in terms of building relationships with the local community, employees and the wider Lithuanian market?
This partnership is about becoming part of the local community. It helps introduce ICONIC21 to potential employees, strengthens our connection with the city and demonstrates that we are investing in Lithuania for the long term.
We want people to see us not only as an employer but as a company that actively supports the communities in which it operates.
ICONIC21 operates within an industry that continues to attract debate around responsible gambling and the relationship between betting brands and sport. How do you approach that responsibility when entering into a high-profile partnership such as this?
Whenever any company enters the sporting world, there is a responsibility to ensure those partnerships are approached carefully and transparently.
ICONIC21 is not a sportsbook or gambling platform. We’re a provider and creator of game products. Responsible gaming considerations are crucial and at the forefront of our minds when we develop those products. Ultimately, our games are made to be entertaining.
That same principle guided us to sponsor Rytas. Basketball is a great, entertaining sport that brings people together, so we wanted to support it and help it grow.
Being involved in sport also raises the importance of acting responsibly, and we take this very seriously. We wanted to support that journey while continuing to invest in the Vilnius community.
Taken together, the new office and BC Rytas sponsorship suggest ICONIC21 wants to become part of Vilnius rather than simply operate from it. What would success in Lithuania look like for the company over the next three to five years?
Success would mean establishing Vilnius as a thriving, long-term operational hub, creating hundreds of career opportunities and building a reputation as an employer of choice.
We also want to be recognised as a company that contributes positively to the local community. If talented people in Lithuania see ICONIC21 as a place where they can start, develop and grow their careers, that will be a very strong measure of success.

More than a safe haven: Jewish schools after Oct. 7
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
14:08:46 UTC
23:08:46 KST

The aftereffects of Oct. 7 and the multi-front war that confronted the State of Israel have affected Jewish communities around the world in myriad ways. These conflicts, alongside the sharp rise in global antisemitism, are driving significant shifts in worldwide Jewish education.
In the wake of increasing antisemitism, enrollment in Jewish day schools is rising worldwide. Jewish schools, which have traditionally focused on connecting students to their heritage and fostering Jewish identity, must today also prepare students to confront challenges from peers, navigate hostile environments on university campuses, and engage daily with a Jewish identity that has become charged and intensely public.
Next week’s Global Jewish Educators Summit, a four-day conference in Jerusalem bringing together hundreds of international Jewish educators, will discuss these issues and help to shape the future of Jewish education.
The conference is organized by the Ministry for Diaspora Affairs and Combating Antisemitism and will be operated by UnitEd, a global initiative (NGO) established in partnership with the ministry, dedicated to strengthening Jewish day schools and supporting educational leadership worldwide.
With more than 850 Jewish schools in 54 countries, UnitEd fosters students’ Jewish identity, deepens community engagement, and strengthens connection to the State of Israel.
To gain greater insight into the state of Jewish education in the Diaspora, this writer spoke with two key Jewish educators – Rabbi David Meyer, CEO of PaJeS, a UK-based organization that supports Jewish schools, trains and assists teachers, and develops educational programming and resources; and Dvorah Serrao, CEO of the Alliance Israélite Universelle, which operates four Jewish schools in France, three in Morocco, and two French-speaking schools in Israel.
Both Meyer and Serrao say enrollment in Jewish schools has increased in their countries since Oct. 7, largely among families who previously had sent their children to secular schools. Antisemitism has played a major role in this increase.
Meyer says while UK Jewish schools have made a considerable effort to accommodate this increase, they do not have enough space to meet the demand.
Serrao notes there are over 90,000 Jewish children of school age in France. Two-thirds of that total, or 60,000 students, have not been educated in Jewish schools until now. Some attended public schools while others studied in private Catholic schools, which are often academically strong and somewhat less expensive than Jewish schools.
After Oct. 7, she explains, many of these Jewish students could no longer stay in public schools as their safety could no longer be guaranteed. To meet the growing number of Jewish children who want to attend their schools, the Alliance Israélite Universelle has begun expanding school facilities in two locations.
“Meanwhile, there are 90,000 Jewish children, and today there’s only space for 35,000 of them. We need to extend and expand our capacity,” says Serrao.
Another important focusin Jewish schools, both in France and the UK, is increased safety and security. Meyer states that every Jewish school in the UK has security guards, which the British government supports. Security is provided for school field trips, and schools frequently hold security drills.
In France as well, says Serrao, security is paramount. “Once you ensure a child comes into a Jewish school, you have to secure the building, and you have to secure the premises. It is very important to work with the local police and everyone who’s working on security and procuring funding for all of this.”
What is it like for young French Jews to grow up amid rising antisemitism, both on the streets and online?
Serrao says having pride in one’s Jewish identity is easy when students are among their peers in a Jewish school. The difficulties increase when students graduate from Jewish schools and begin university. “That’s when the test occurs. As long as they are in a Jewish day school, go to synagogue on Shabbat, go to Jewish summer camps, and participate in sports with other Jews, they don’t go out so much into the outside world.
“Once they finish Jewish day school, they do, and then it’s going to be a big challenge for them. That’s when they need to find other Jews.”
How have students in Jewish schools responded to the events of Oct. 7?
For Rachel Fink, director of education at UnitEd, these challenges underscore the importance of belonging. “The events of the past three years have brought into sharp focus something Jewish educators have always known: Jewish education matters most when it helps a young person understand where they belong and why that belonging matters,” she says.
“We are not seeing a retreat from Jewish education, but a renewed determination to make it deeper, more relevant and more meaningful.”
Meyer says many older students in the UK have developed a stronger connection to Judaism since the attack. “I think that we’ve seen an upsurge and uptick in their connection with Judaism.”
By contrast, some children who were nine or 10 years old at the time are questioning their link to Judaism. “They are the ones who are most likely to be turning around and saying, ‘Well, if it’s so difficult to be a Jew, am I not better off not being a Jew?’ So educating these children through these challenges is also really important.
“There have been highs and lows, and obviously seeing the hostages released was a huge high, and making the students feel the connection they had to that was enormous. Just seeing the news over the last week [when Israeli passengers on the Flydubai flight thwarted the co-pilot’s attempt to crash the plane] has also been a high. And that’s important as well, to be able to ensure that our students are enthused by what they are seeing.”
For her part, Serrao says that the goals of Jewish education in France have shifted somewhat since Oct. 7, from primarily text-based studies to shaping aspects of Jewish identity.
“Instead of starting with which texts we want children to study, we now ask: What kind of Jews do we want them to become in the world after Oct. 7? What adults do we want them to be? Instead of talking about Jewish identity, we’ll talk about Jewish behavior. How do we want them to behave as Jews, and therefore, what kind of teaching do we need to give them?”
She adds that one of the main principles of the Alliance is that students will both respect the values of France while understanding Jewish values and traditions, such as holidays, Shabbat, and dietary laws, while speaking Hebrew, knowing the story of Israel, and being committed to the State of Israel.
Both Meyer and Serrao will attend next week’s conference in Jerusalem and look forward to learning and sharing their ideas about Jewish education post-Oct. 7 with contemporaries around the world.
“We not only have collaboration between the schools in the UK,” says Meyer, “but now we are seeing greater collaboration – thanks in large part to the role of UnitEd and the Ministry for Diaspora Affairs and Combating Antisemitism – between communities around the world. Many of the people who will be at the conference have met repeatedly and interacted.
“The key opportunity for us moving forward is this network, which permeates from Israel supporting our Jewish schools. But the interaction between the Jewish schools around different communities across the Diaspora, and the opportunities we have as a global community for supporting, educating, and enthusing our children – this is the challenge and the opportunity for the next few years.
“Ultimately, what we’re turning around and saying is we’ve got challenges in the UK; they’ve got challenges in Australia; they’ve got challenges in Canada; everywhere we’ve got challenges, but actually, as a whole community, we have something really special. We are a Jewish world, and that allows us to collaborate, educate our children, and make them feel they are part of something special.
“I think there’s a huge opportunity there, and that is what I think this conference has got the potential to achieve – bringing these communities together not just so that we can come and take away an idea, but that we can forge those ideas together and see how we can interplay and intertwine between the communities to be able to ensure the success of that.”
Serrao says time is of the essence. “Before Oct. 7, we had time to think about things. Today, we need to address the issues ahead of us. I’m coming to the conference to express concerns, raise awareness about the situation we’re in, and be inspired by others on how they have addressed the consequences of Oct. 7 and come back with a strategy and an action plan.
“I am coming to hear from others how they analyze the situation, how they experience it, and how they come back with ideas and plans to address all the issues we’re facing today in a better and more experienced way.
“UnitEd and the presence of the Ministry for Diaspora Affairs and Combating Antisemitism have been a huge asset, an asset that today we cannot do without. We must continue to work together.”
This article was written in cooperation with the Ministry for Diaspora Affairs and Combating Antisemitism, UnitEd, Herzog College, and the World Zionist Organization’s Department of Education.

What we know about espionage, treason allegations against Germany's ex-spy chief
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
14:06:59 UTC
23:06:59 KST

What we know about espionage, treason allegations against Germany's ex-spy chief
A court on Wednesday ordered the former head of Germany's foreign intelligence service August Hanning to remain in pretrial detention after his arrest on suspicion of espionage and treason, along with a former deputy who allegedly supplied him with secret files. Here's what we know about one of the biggest security breaches in German history.
A former head of Germany ’s foreign intelligence service who is charged with passing state secrets to a foreign intelligence service was ordered held in pretrial detention after a judge issued an arrest warrant Wednesday.
August Hanning, 80, who is “strongly suspected of treasonous espionage, spying out state secrets, attempted treason, and espionage,” led the Federal Intelligence Service, known by its German acronym BND, from 1998 to 2005. He was arrested Tuesday.
A former aide of Hanning, identified only as Manfred D. in line with German privacy rules, was also arrested Tuesday and is already in pretrial detention. He is accused of aiding and abetting attempted treason and treasonous espionage.
Read moreGermany's former spy chief detained on suspicion of trading state secrets
Contact with foreign spy
The two men allegedly agreed in 2010 that Manfred D. would continuously provide Hanning – who had left office five years earlier – with valuable foreign intelligence information in exchange for payment. Manfred D. served as chief of staff for several subsequent BND presidents from 2012 until 2026.
The federal prosecutor's office says Hanning allegedly used this information to his financial advantage in his private consulting work.
To display this content from YouTube, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.
Based on the current status of the investigation, Manfred D. is said to have provided his former boss with approximately 2,000 documents over a 12-year-period through June 2022.
In one instance, Hanning is alleged to have used classified information to prepare an analysis for an employee of a foreign intelligence service. However, “it has not yet been possible to determine whether the report reached its intended recipient,” the federal prosecutor’s office stated.
“In another instance, Hanning is alleged to have passed on information following an extensive exchange – also with an employee of another intelligence service,” a spokesperson for the prosecutor’s office said Tuesday.
Classified information
According to prosecutors, Hanning may have had access to information intended exclusively for use within the BND. Many of the documents contained classified information for executive intelligence briefings.
Beyond that, prosecutors have not given any further details about the mostly classified material and are not expected to do so in the near future.
Read more‘Russian sleeper cell’: Can Germany’s far-right AfD be barred from sensitive intel?
The prosecutor's office did not reveal who exactly the two men were suspected of spying for or which foreign intelligence services they provided with classified information.
“No further information beyond what is contained in the press statement is currently being provided,” Ines Peterson, a spokesperson for the office, said Wednesday.
“The federal government takes this case extremely seriously and is providing full support to the investigating authorities,” a spokesperson for German Chancellor Merz told reporters Wednesday.
“The allegations being made are serious. We need to analyze the situation and get to the bottom of it,” Sebastian Hille said, adding that “we must await the results of the investigation in order to determine whether any changes are needed.”
International fallout
The chair of the parliamentary committee that oversees intelligence agencies said the security breach has shocked both the German and international intelligence community. He said Germany needs to reach out to allied intelligence agencies who may have lost their trust in the BND after the spying scandal became public.
“Although this has caused quite a stir, I am quite confident that the German services enjoy a very high reputation internationally,” said Marc Henrichmann, who is also a national lawmaker with Chancellor Friedrich Merz's center-right Christian Democratic Union.
Read moreGermany arrests Ukrainian national accused of spying on defence firm
Merz's spokesperson Hille said that he was not aware that foreign intelligence services had reached out to Germany about the incident so far.
Several German politicians have also called for stricter rules banning former officials with security clearances from engaging in private consulting work after leaving office.
The massive intelligence breach comes at a time when the German government is working on a reform designed to grant its intelligence agencies broader powers to take measures such as countering sabotage and hacking attempts – in response to a growing threat from powers such as Russia and extremists.
In August, the cabinet approved draft legislation aimed at strengthening the BND and its domestic counterpart, the BfV, and reducing the European Union’s most populous country’s reliance on intelligence from its allies.
(FRANCE 24 with AP)

‘Another coup d’état’: fears grow as Flávio Bolsonaro vows to ‘re-democratise’ Brazil
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
14:06:42 UTC
23:06:42 KST

Flávio Bolsonaro, the far-right frontrunner to become Brazil’s next president, has vowed to “re-democratise” the South American country, increasing fears about a move into authoritarian rule if he wins power.
Brazil was re-democratised in the 1980s after a brutal 21-year dictatorship that Flávio’s father, the disgraced ex-president Jair Bolsonaro, has long praised.
Last year, Jair Bolsonaro, a former soldier who served under that military regime, was jailed for 27 years for trying to engineer a coup after he lost the 2022 election to the current leftwing president, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva.
Flávio, 45, beat Lula, 80, in Sunday’s presidential election first round and goes into the runoff on 25 October as favourite. On Tuesday, the rightwinger vowed to capitalise on the hugely increased far-right presence in congress after the election to change the constitution and “re-democratise this country”.
“The only thing standing in the way of Brazil becoming a barbarity is called Flávio Bolsonaro as president,” he claimed at a campaign event in Goiânia, a city near the capital, Brasília.
The incendiary comments caused outrage among historians and opponents of Bolsonaro’s radical populist movement, who have accused him of co-opting the language of democracy to disguise an illiberal shift.
Talíria Petrone, the leftwing congresswoman, wrote on X: “This is the announcement of a coup.”
Marcelo Freixo, a newly elected congressman from Lula’s Workers’ party (PT), said: “Brazil was re-democratised in 1988. The person who tried to undo this was his father, who was convicted of an attempted coup. What they want, once again, is a coup.”
Bolsonaro did not spell out what he meant by “re-democratising” Brazil, a vibrant if polarised multiparty democracy that the Sweden-based V-Dem institute ranks 28th on its liberal democracy index, two places ahead of the UK and 23 ahead of the US.
But Jair Bolsonaro, who has praised authoritarian leaders including Chile’s former dictator Augusto Pinochet, has long hankered for a return to military rule.
Last September, the supreme court found Jair Bolsonaro guilty of trying to convince military chiefs to help him cling to power at the end of his 2018-22 presidency. The conspiracy culminated in the 8 January 2023 riots in Brasília, a far-right insurrection seemingly inspired by the 6 January 2021 storming of the US Capitol.
Writing in O Globo newspaper, Míriam Leitão, a prominent political and economic journalist, warned that if Bolsonaro won, Brazil faced “the extreme and concrete danger of … another coup d’état attempt”.
“Flávio follows the same ideas as his father and has already said that an intervention in the institutions is necessary,” Leitão wrote. “If Flávio Bolsonaro is elected, he will have more tools at his disposal to carry out his father’s authoritarian project: robust caucuses in the lower house and senate, a weakened supreme court, and the support of the Donald Trump administration.
“Political science shows that it’s in the second term that an autocrat doubles down on their plan. Look at the case of Donald Trump. The risk isn’t of the son repeating the father, it’s that he surpasses him.”
Miguel Lago, a political scientist, said Sunday’s far-right election triumph – in which Bolsonaro’s Liberal party (PL) secured the senate’s largest caucus, with 28 of its 81 seats – would permit radical changes, including the impeachment of supreme court ministers considered enemies of the Bolsonarismo movement.
Jair Bolsonaro and his jailed co-conspirators are likely to be freed if his son wins, with the former president expected to become an influential minister able to select the new heads of the armed forces.
“It’s better than a coup d’état … it’s almost like a coup d’état with the support of the majority of the population,” Lago said.
Nayib Bukele, El Salvador’s authoritarian president, has been accused of “killing” democracy by using control over the country’s congress and institutions to approve sweeping constitutional changes, including scrapping presidential term limits so he can seek indefinite re-election.
Flávio Bolsonaro recently met Bukele’s security minister, Gustavo Villatoro, in São Paulo, hailing the Central American country’s hardline security policies under which thousands have been jailed during a state of exception that has lasted nearly five years.
Bolsonaro told reporters that during their conversation, Villatoro “stressed the importance” of using control of congress to make the “necessary legal changes”.
Celso Rocha de Barros, a political scientist, said he believed that by using the word “re-democratise”, Flávio Bolsonaro sought “to smuggle his authoritarian purposes into acceptable language”.
Barros said Bolsonaro, unlike his father who always seemed to favour an “old school barracks uprising” to seize power, appeared to be part of “a new generation of authoritarians” who sought to dismantle democracy from within by undermining and occupying the institutions.
“Then you don’t need to break any laws to achieve authoritarianism … because you are the law,” Barros added, citing Hungary’s former far-right prime minister Viktor Orbán as an example. “Clearly, Flávio’s plan is a corrosion of democracy so [Brazil] becomes a Hungary or Bukele-style system.”
Danilo Araújo Marques, a historian, said the word “democracy” had been co-opted before in Brazil by undemocratic forces, when the military men and politicians behind the 1964 coup called their actions “an intervention to democratise the country”.
“They all talked about democracy … [but] democracy has a different meaning in the mouth of a coup-monger,” said Marques, who is from a research unit at the Federal University of Minas Gerais called Projeto República.
Marques noted that during the campaign, Bolsonaro had claimed his octogenarian opponent, Lula, represented the past while he was selling the future. “But this future means going back to what [Brazil] was before,” Marques said. “It’s a ‘future’ that is based on the order prior to the 1988 constitution, which is precisely the military dictatorship.”
Asked to clarify his plans on Wednesday, Bolsonaro rejected speculation he was seeking to finish “what his father didn’t do”. “Let’s stop lying. Let’s touch down in the real world,” he told reporters, adding: “Brazil needs to go back to normal, that’s all.”
