Russia will spend a record $200 billion on the war this year — Bloomberg
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
17:06:13 EEST
23:06:13 KST

Russia will spend a record $200 billion on the war this year — Bloomberg
Kyiv • UNN
Russia’s defense spending in 2026 could reach 17 trillion rubles. The budget deficit will rise to more than 7 trillion rubles.
Russia may set a record for military spending this year. Moscow has significantly increased funding for the war compared with its initial budget plans. Bloomberg reports this, writes UNN.
Details
Dictator Vladimir Putin decided to increase spending at the end of last year. This happened after he concluded that talks with the United States in Alaska would not lead to an acceptable deal to end the hostilities.
By the end of 2026, defense spending is expected to reach nearly 17 trillion rubles ($199 billion). This is approximately 40% more than provided for in the initial plan announced by the Russian government at the end of 2025. The current trend sharply contrasts with the situation a year ago, when Moscow planned to contain the growth of military spending in an attempt to reduce the budget deficit and replenish reserves depleted during the war.
In January, the Kremlin concluded that reaching an agreement with Ukraine was unattainable, and that U.S.-led efforts had failed to achieve a breakthrough. After that, the Russian government began accelerating advance payments to defense-industry companies and increasing other war-related expenditures.
As a result, the projected budget deficit for 2026 rose to more than 7 trillion rubles (over $81.9 billion), compared with the initially planned 3.8 trillion rubles (approximately $44.5 billion). The government financed the additional spending in 2026 through increased domestic borrowing and gold sales.
According to budget plans, Russia's military spending in 2027 will amount to 17.1 trillion rubles (approximately $200 billion). In 2028, it will decrease to 16.6 trillion rubles (approximately $194 billion), and in 2029 it will amount to 16.3 trillion rubles (approximately $190 billion).
"The government is finally building a scenario of a prolonged war in Ukraine into the budget, but at the same time it still underestimates its cost. Maintaining nominal defense spending at the same level will be difficult, as the war of attrition drags on and military production costs rise," says Kateryna Vlasova, an economist specializing in Central and Eastern Europe and Russia.
According to her, next year's war expenditures will again exceed the planned level, although the excess will be smaller than this year. This will make it possible to keep the budget deficit at around 3% of GDP.

Italians and Czechs push Brussels to ease green rules as energy crisis hits industry
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
14:05:16 UTC
23:05:16 KST

Rome and Prague have joined forces to protect industry ahead of the EU leaders' summit in Brussels next week.
Italy and the Czech Republic have warned Brussels that the European Union's industrial base risks lasting damage unless the bloc eases the burden of its green rules, according to a letter seen by Euronews.
The joint warning, issued amid an unprecedented energy shock, reflects mounting pressure from EU capitals to protect domestic manufacturing as high energy and carbon costs collide with the bloc's decarbonisation targets.
"While security of supply remains the immediate priority, the combination of some of the world's highest energy prices, high carbon costs and exceptional fuel prices risks further weakening European manufacturing and accelerating the relocation of production and investment," reads the letter.
Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni visited her Czech counterpart Andrej Babiš in Prague last week to coordinate the plan of action between Rome and Prague ahead of next week's summit of EU leaders in Brussels.
Rome and Prague are targeting the bloc's carbon market, currently under political scrutiny, as well as its recently weakened methane rules, as they seek a broader coalition within the European Council.
The joint proposal outlines several targeted interventions designed to provide immediate economic oxygen to struggling European factories. Chief among them are the extension of free carbon allowances for heavy industry under the bloc's carbon market, the Emissions Trading System (ETS), and freezing the phasing out of free carbon allocations for sectors affected by the bloc's carbon border tax.
The push comes amid growing concern over European competitiveness, which is set to feature prominently on the agenda when EU leaders meet on October 15.
Italy and Czechia framed these measures as "temporary" interventions that "preserve long-term climate objectives". But several of their demands would amount to significant changes to the way the EU applies its climate rules to industry.
"A temporary suspension of the EU ETS would provide immediate relief to European industry from carbon costs. However, in the absence of sufficient support for such an option, it is worth considering a number of targeted and immediately actionable alternatives that the European Council could promote to alleviate the impact of the current shock and complement measures already announced at European level," reads the letter.
Italian Defence Minister Guido Crosetto recently went further, arguing that the ETS should be suspended until economic conditions improve.
"There would be better times" to reintroduce the carbon market in order to protect the environment, he said.
"A tax like the ETS today is unjust, absurd, unsustainable in international competition, and creates inequalities because it falls indiscriminately and equally on all European end consumers," Crosetto wrote on X.
The Meloni-Babiš initiative is the latest sign of a broader push among EU capitals to give greater weight to industrial competitiveness when implementing the bloc's climate policies.
Austria's Energy Minister Wolfgang Hattmannsdorfer made a similar case on the sidelines of a competitiveness ministers' meeting in Brussels on 24 September.
Hattmannsdorfer called for "economic patriotism" to keep industries and jobs in Europe, arguing that maintaining European production is crucial for regional wealth, welfare and environmental standards.

Iran's army spokesman said Tehran's forces were prepared to strike first "should circumstances require it," while IRGC officials claimed tighter control of Hormuz, and Washington publicly pondered how much authority Pezeshkian and Araghchi actually wielded.
Iran's army spokesman said on Wednesday that the armed forces were prepared to carry out pre-emptive strikes in the war against the US, as senior IRGC figures claimed tighter control over the Strait of Hormuz and Washington questioned how much authority Iran's civilian leadership actually holds.
"Should circumstances require it, we will conduct pre-emptive operations down the line in order to prevent the enemy from committing any act of aggression or intrusion," spokesman for Iran's regular army Brigadier General Mohammad Akrami-Nia told the state-run IRNA news agency.
IRGC officials separately said Hormuz was firmly in Tehran's hands, despite a parallel US naval blockade of the vital waterway.
"The Strait of Hormuz is closed and the armed forces have full control over it, and this situation will continue until Iran's legitimate demands are met," Brigadier General Mohammad Reza Naqdi, a senior IRGC adviser, said in a media interview.
He claimed that some vessels were using small boats to smuggle oil through the strait to larger tankers.
"Soon, a small number of the routes that violators have created by blasting and destroying some of the existing rocky passages in the Strait of Hormuz will be blocked," Naqdi said.
A second IRGC adviser, Brigadier General Amirahmadi, said international bodies had recorded an average of around 10 ships per day transiting the strait, against nearly 125 before the war that began with US-Israeli strikes on Iran on 28 February.
"These ships are mainly those that pass through the waterway and designated route with the permission of the Islamic Republic of Iran," he said.

Iran's President Masoud Pezeshkian said in a speech on Wednesday that the government was engaged in negotiations while simultaneously facing what he called "an all-out war on every front."

"I think if they want to show a commitment to not building a nuclear weapon, they would do something meaningful on their enrichment capacity," Vance said.
Speaking in Maryland on Tuesday, US President Donald Trump said Iran was "no longer such a bully" and claimed full US control over the strait.
"They were the bully of the Middle East. They're not so much the bully anymore, but we have to finish up. And it's only a question of which way do we want to do it, the nice way or the not-so-nice way. And pretty soon you'll find out," he said.
Trump has repeatedly questioned its decision-makers, calling for "new leadership in Iran," and said the new Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei — who still has not made a single public appearance since he was appointed supreme leader in March — was "a sick man".
However, in a June podcast, Trump suggested the younger Khamenei is in charge. "They say he is giving approval, because that's the way it has been for a long, long time," the US president said.

South Korea on Wednesday vowed to review the military service exemption system for talented athletes and artists after a backlash over remarks and actions by some South Korean gold medalists at the Asian Games.
Culture, Sports and Tourism Minister Chae Hwi-young said his ministry would “listen to the views of the sports and arts communities and consult with the Ministry of National Defense and the Military Manpower Administration to devise comprehensive measures on the issue, as it has raised concerns among the public,” according to Yonhap News Agency.
Some members of the under-23 national men’s football team came under fire after they appeared to flaunt their military service exemptions following their gold medal victory at the Asian Games on Saturday, reigniting a long-running debate over the fairness of the exemption system.

The remarks and post drew public criticism.
South Korea requires able-bodied men to complete 18 to 21 months of mandatory military service, while artists and athletes receiving top awards at government-designated competitions, including Olympic medals or Asian Games gold, are eligible for exemption.
Chae said that while the exemption system had helped athletes and artists with outstanding abilities maintain and develop their skills, “the public perceptions of military service and the value placed on fairness seem to have changed considerably with the times.”
The Defense Ministry said Tuesday that it was considering scaling back or abolishing the exemption system, citing fairness among those subject to mandatory military service and the declining number of people available for military service, among other factors.

Raids on Overijssel livestock businesses over fraud and cruelty
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
14:03:35 UTC
23:03:35 KST

Raids on Overijssel livestock businesses over fraud and cruelty
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
Investigators from the food and product safety board NVWA have raided the homes and businesses of two livestock traders in Overijssel over suspected fraud and transporting sick animals.
The raids took place on September 30, the NVWA said on Wednesday. Investigators seized business records, phones, used ear tags and a pair of pliers for removing ear tags.
Every cow in the Netherlands must be registered and carry an ear tag with a unique number, so animals can be traced quickly if there is a disease outbreak or meat turns out to be contaminated.
Unregistered animals
At one trader’s premises, 88 animals were registered at a different address or not registered at all. At the other, 19 animals were incorrectly registered. Cattle without the mandatory ear tags were found at both sites.
With help from the police, investigators also stopped a lorry that had left one of the traders’ premises early in the morning. None of the 21 cattle on board were registered to his address. Another 32 cattle belonging to the same trader were found on a farm elsewhere in Overijssel. They had been imported but never registered in the Netherlands.
One trader’s business was registered on paper at the other’s address, keeping it out of sight. Cattle from the Netherlands and abroad were being kept there. Animals may only be gathered for sale or slaughter at approved collection centres, which have strict rules on cleaning and disinfecting livestock trucks to stop disease from spreading.
Sick cows
Inspectors also found a shed of cows in poor condition. Some could no longer stand and others had severe inflammation. One of the traders is suspected of transporting the animals even though they were too sick to be moved. The NVWA believes he then kept them because he could no longer sell them or have them slaughtered.
A vet put three cows down on the spot. The NVWA has taken administrative measures to make sure the rest get the care they need.
Neither trader has been arrested. The criminal investigation is being led by the public prosecution department’s specialist unit for environmental and fraud cases (Functioneel Parket). The NVWA told broadcaster NOS it could not say how it came across the pair.

Millions of Pakistanis get government fuel relief but some miss out
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
14:02:40 UTC
23:02:40 KST

Millions of Pakistanis get government fuel relief but some miss out
Pakistan has subsidised petrol for millions, but some economists caution that those most needing help are left out.
Islamabad, Pakistan – More than 9.5 million people have received subsidised petrol under a special fuel relief scheme launched by Pakistan’s prime minister, Federal Minister Shaza Fatima Khawaja told Al Jazeera on Wednesday.
The initiative, aimed at lower-income citizens, comes as the government attempts to help households deal with fuel price increases tied to the war on Iran.
The scheme, launched in September, offers 100 rupees ($0.36) off every litre of petrol to owners of motorcycles, rickshaws and small cars, through a text-message system.
Petrol prices have risen by nearly 50 percent since the war began on February 28, adding to Pakistan’s economic hardship and putting further pressure on consumers already grappling with rising inflation.
How the scheme works
Explaining the process, Khawaja, the minister for information technology and telecommunications, said applicants text their national ID number, vehicle registration, and province to 9771. A second message, sent before each visit to a pump, generates a token redeemable anywhere in the country.
Two- and three-wheelers get 500 rupees ($1.80) a week, capped at four tokens a month. Cars with engines of up to 800cc get 1,000 rupees ($3.60) every 10 days, for three tokens monthly.
After complaints, registration, once a paid service, was made free, and a five-litre minimum purchase was scrapped for the same reason.
Khawaja told Al Jazeera the system had been redesigned based on experiences of users on the ground.
Riders no longer need the vehicle to be registered in their own name, as long as they can supply the exact registration date shown on the documents.
“Even in my own house, there’s a bike registered in our name that our cook uses for daily errands,” Khawaja said, explaining why the ownership requirement for two- and three-wheelers was dropped on September 20.
An earlier cash-transfer scheme in April had reached just over a million bike owners, she said, largely because disbursement required a bank account most riders did not have.
‘The relief is decent’
Government officials say that the scheme has been expanded to include wider sections of society, especially those who depend on their vehicles to generate income.
“There’s a benefit; it’s not like there’s nothing,” Shakeel Ahmed, 45, an electrician in Islamabad, told Al Jazeera. “The relief is decent for people who use it normally, for local trips. But for people like us, who put in 1,000 to 1,500 rupees [$3.60-$5.40] of petrol a day, it’s not enough.”
Safiya Aftab, an economist, told Al Jazeera the scheme has reached the people it was meant to.
“The scheme has indeed reached low-income segments of society, people who typically use two-wheelers and 800cc cars. So yes, it’s a good thing that they are subsidising the poor,” she said.
Aftab, however, also pointed to a levy – 114 rupees ($0.41) for every litre – that the government charges. This, she said, was helping the government raise revenue. She said the government is now earning more than 100 billion rupees ($361m) a month from the levy, which is fuelling inflation.
“The levy was originally meant as a sort of environmental tax, to discourage the use of petrol. Now it has become a full revenue earner for the government, one that helps keep the fiscal deficit down,” the economist said.
What it costs and for how long
The Pakistani government has approved 75 billion rupees ($271m) for the scheme’s first three months, through November.
Petroleum Minister Ali Pervaiz Malik put the running cost at 25-30 billion rupees ($90m-$108m) a month at launch. By late September, he said, it had risen to 35-40 billion rupees ($126m-$144m).
Malik has said the government is prepared to run the scheme for up to 10 months, or “until the end of the war”, if needed.
Pakistan is currently under a $7bn International Monetary Fund programme, and an IMF team is in Islamabad this week for talks with the government as it seeks to keep its fiscal commitments on track while responding to the fuel shock.
Officials familiar with the government’s talks with the IMF say the Fund wants relief capped at three months and routed instead through the Benazir Income Support Programme, the country’s main cash-transfer scheme.
Khawaja said the IMF’s position from the outset was that relief had to be targeted, not universal, which was why the scheme was built around actual token use rather than a blanket price cut.
Who it leaves out
But there are claims that the relief is not reaching all. Cars with engines larger than 800cc, diesel vehicles and public transport are excluded entirely, leading some experts to suggest that the subsidy scheme risks missing the most vulnerable sections of Pakistani society.
“A poor household that uses public transport, walks to work, or relies on diesel-powered transport may receive nothing while still facing higher food and transport costs,” Khaqan Najeeb, a former adviser in Pakistan’s Ministry of Finance, told Al Jazeera.
More than 8.1 million tokens had gone to two- and three-wheelers by late September, compared with fewer than 380,000 for cars, Malik said. A November 2024 Gallup Pakistan survey found that 79 percent of respondents, in rural and urban areas alike, said they use public transport such as buses or wagons.
Does the relief go far enough?
At 100 rupees a litre, the maximum monthly saving is 2,000 rupees ($7.20) for a motorcycle user and 3,000 rupees ($10.80) for an eligible car owner, Najeeb said, calling it “useful household relief, but not enough to offset the broader cost-of-living shock”.
Petrol has climbed from 266 rupees ($0.96) a litre before the war to nearly 395 rupees ($1.42), despite a partial rollback in April. Inflation rose to 10.3 percent in September from 7 percent in February, Najeeb said.
Sajid Amin Javed, a senior economist at the Sustainable Development Policy Institute in Islamabad, said the relief was “minimal”, but added that this was understandable given the IMF constraints on Pakistan.
“The relief is minimal, and that is understandable as we are in an IMF programme,” Javed told Al Jazeera, arguing that cutting the petroleum development levy, which still adds 114 rupees to every litre, would deliver broader relief than a capped subsidy.
“The government is using the petroleum development levy to fill its revenue gap, but that comes at a significant cost in terms of inflation, growth and household welfare,” Javed said.
Najeeb, however, argued the scheme should not become a permanent fixture of Pakistan’s energy policy – and should be used only to make oil price shocks “less damaging”.

US midterms could bring new wave of Israel critics to Congress
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
14:02:21 UTC

Breadcrumb
US midterms could bring new wave of Israel critics to Congress
Data and ratings from the Cook Political Report, an independent US election forecaster, and Decision Desk HQ, an election monitoring and forecasting platform, indicate that several districts in the US House midterm elections are likely to be won by Democrats.
The races include several new candidates who have been vocal opponents of Israeli policies in Palestine and the wider region.
With just weeks to go before voting day, forecasts point to Democrats having the advantage in the battle for the 435-seat House of Representatives.
The picture is more complicated in the 100-seat Senate, where 35 seats are being contested in the midterms.
The vote comes amid public dissatisfaction with President Donald Trump and Republican candidates over the war on Iran, as well as rising prices and inflation.
According to the latest estimates, Democrats are widely expected to take control of the House, while holding a relative advantage in the battle for the Senate.
The following is a summary of the key races.
Districts 'safe' for Democrats
The main districts classified as "safe" for Democrats by the Cook Political Report and not considered battlegrounds by Decision Desk HQ include:
- New Jersey's 12th District: Adam Hamawy (+13 points)
- Colorado's 1st District: Yemi Mobolade (+29 points)
- New York's 13th District: Yalinda Gonzalez (+32 points)
- New York's 7th District: Claire Valdez (+25 points)
- New York's 10th District: Brad Lander (+32 points)
- Michigan's 13th District: Donavan McKinney (+22 points)
All of these candidates would become new members of the US House if elected.
The candidates are progressives or socialists who have vocally opposed Israel's genocide in Gaza, with many making opposition to US arms shipments to Israel and funding from lobbying groups, particularly the pro-Israel lobby, prominent parts of their campaigns.
Several other districts where two Democrats are competing are also considered safely Democratic. These are in states with open-primary systems where candidates who advance from the primaries compete in the November election regardless of party.
The American Israel Public Affairs Committee, or AIPAC, is spending millions of dollars in the general election to support pro-Israel candidates running against them.
- California's 34th District: progressive Angela Gonzalez Torres against incumbent Rep. Jimmy Gomez.
- California's 7th District: progressive Mai Phan against incumbent Democratic Rep. Doris Matsui.
- California's 14th District: progressive Aisha Wahab against Democrat Melissa Hernandez, who recently defeated her opponent in a special election to represent the seat for several months. The two are running against each other again in November.
The latest opinion polls indicate that candidates opposing US support for Israel could defeat candidates backed by AIPAC in several of these races, marking a potentially significant development in this year's elections.
'Swing districts'
Several districts where progressive Democrats are challenging Republicans remain competitive.
They include:
- California's 22nd District: progressive Randy Villegas against incumbent Republican Rep. David Valadao, with the Democratic candidate ahead by one point.
- Michigan's 7th District: progressive Democrat William Lawrence against incumbent Republican Rep. Tom Barrett.
The races are considered highly competitive, although Decision Desk HQ rates them as leaning Democratic.
Districts 'safe' for Republicans
The forecasts also classify several districts where progressive Democrats are challenging Republicans as safe for the Republican Party.
They include:
- Illinois' 11th District: Lebanese-American incumbent Rep. Darin LaHood against progressive Democrat Paul Nolley (+11 points).
- North Carolina's 10th District: incumbent Republican Rep. Pat Harrigan against progressive doctor Ashley Bell (+9 points).
- Arkansas' 3rd District: Republican Rep. Steve Womack against progressive Democrat Rob Wiers (+13 points).
- Indiana's 4th District: Republican Rep. Jim Baird against progressive Drew Cox (+15 points).
The US congressional midterm elections for the House and Senate, scheduled for 3 November, have now entered their decisive phase.
Trump, meanwhile, is relying heavily on his personal political appeal in an attempt to shift voter sentiment as Republicans grapple with domestic and foreign crises ahead of the vote.
Of the 435 seats in the House, a party needs 218 to secure a majority.
Republicans currently hold a narrow majority of 220 seats, compared with 215 for Democrats, meaning Democrats need a net gain of just three seats to take control of the chamber.
Republicans are also heading into the election facing the historical tendency for the president's party to lose congressional seats in midterm elections.
Trump's continued prosecution of the war on Iran has added to the challenges facing Republican candidates.
He has repeatedly insisted that the election will not force him to end the war, stressing that he was "not on the ballot".

Brittin said he wanted to ensure the BBC was prominent on other platforms such as YouTube, Netflix and Amazon Prime.
The government and the BBC are looking at plans that would lead to anyone who watches any streaming service being told to pay the BBC’s licence fee. It is designed to arrest an alarming fall in the number of households paying the fee.

Ukrainian drugmakers sold $114 million worth of medicines to Uzbekistan in six months. Now they may lose the right to sell there
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
14:01:10 UTC
23:01:10 KST

Ukrainian drugmakers could lose the certificates that let them sell in Uzbekistan, their most important export market, Ukrainian business outlet Ekonomichna Pravda reported on 7 October. Uzbekistan is ending remote factory inspections next year, and industry sources say its inspectors are wary of traveling to a country at war.
Russia's war keeps reshaping Central Asia's trade with both warring countries: Ukrainian refinery strikes pushed Russian fuel shortages into the region, and Kazakhstan gained leverage over a Russian retail giant.
A market worth a third of export earnings
Uzbekistan brings in about 30% of the Ukrainian drug industry's foreign-currency earnings, and one in 10 medicine packs sold there is Ukrainian, Ekonomichna Pravda wrote. By the outlet's count, at least three of Ukraine's five biggest drugmakers by revenue rank it as their top foreign market.
The currency from Uzbekistan lets manufacturers keep prices low in Ukraine and absorb losses from Russian strikes, three industry sources told Ekonomichna Pravda. Losing the market would force producers to raise domestic prices or pull low-margin medicines, which "will hit the Ukrainian patient," said Hennadii Vovk, former deputy head of Ukraine's State Service on Medicines and Drug Control.
Exports reached $114 million in January–June 2026, more than in all of 2021, said Yevheniia Piddubna, government relations head at Farmak, Ukraine's largest drugmaker. She said Uzbekistan takes 35% of Farmak's exports.
Data from the YouControl business registry, cited by the outlet, complicates that picture. In 2022, 30–35% of Farmak's products went to Uzbekistan. In 2025, Uzbekistan was not among its direct buyers. Farmak explained that wartime currency rules cap payment terms at 180 days, while foreign buyers often demand longer. So part of its trade runs through the group's Polish company.
Remote checks end, and inspectors hesitate to travel
Uzbekistan grants three-year certificates of good manufacturing practice (GMP) after inspecting the factory. Since the pandemic, it has allowed remote checks. That suited Ukraine, where Uzbek experts avoided traveling because of Russia's invasion, industry sources told the outlet. Remote inspections end on 1 January 2027.
Ukraine funds its war from wages, and a 1971 law keeps millions of women from earning them
Most Ukrainian certificates expire within a year. Farmak's runs out in November 2026, and the company may not manage to renew it in time. Three producers renewed under the old rules until 2029: Darnytsia, the Borshchahivskyi Chemical and Pharmaceutical Plant, and Farmex Group. According to Piddubna, Uzbekistan's regulator has drafted rules for remote inspections in force-majeure cases, but nothing has been put into practice. Industry sources said the Uzbek Presidential Administration must sign off.
Producers have asked the Office of the President, the Foreign Ministry, and the Health Ministry to raise the issue with Uzbekistan's government, but no Ukrainian experts have been sent there yet, the outlet reported. Russia, whose share of the Uzbek drug market is almost the same as Ukraine's, is ready to take Ukraine's place, its sources said.

‘Palestinians will bear the cost’: UK consulate in East Jerusalem prepares to shut its doors
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
14:00:53 UTC
23:00:53 KST

The UK consulate in East Jerusalem gave few signs it was at the centre of a geopolitical controversy this week, with little movement around the high-walled building save the fluttering of the union jack and the occasional car exiting the compound.
The mission is to shut its doors on Thursday after Israel ordered its closure in response to a UK ban on trade with illegal settlements in the occupied West Bank and sanctions on those who help build or finance them.
The forced closure marked the lowest point in UK-Israeli relations for decades, with reports of the UK considering a retaliatory expulsion of 27 Israeli diplomats from London.
It would be the Palestinians who pay the price for the consulate’s closing, warned Amjad Iraqi, the International Crisis Group’s senior analyst on Israel and Palestine. The UK consulate in East Jerusalem is separate from the UK embassy in Tel Aviv – which remains open – and provides services to Palestinians in East Jerusalem, the West Bank and Gaza, services they will now lose.
“It’s quite telling that the Israeli government response was primarily about blocking the UK’s ability to support Palestinians, rather than the core of UK-Israeli relations themselves,” Iraqi said. “For [the Israeli] foreign minister, Gideon Sa’ar, the response is low-cost, in their minds it’s just Palestinians bearing the cost.”
Israel has already curtailed the diplomatic activities of the Netherlands, Spain and Norway in the occupied West Bank.
Palestinian residents of Sheikh Jarrah, the East Jerusalem neighbourhood that is home to the consulate, appeared resigned when asked about the impact the closure might have on their lives.
“I mean, it was the British that were the basis of the issue, wasn’t it? They were the ones who signed the Balfour declaration?” said Abu Abdo, a 79-year-old former repairman and resident of Sheikh Jarrah, referring to a 1917 document by the British foreign secretary Arthur Balfour, which expressed support for a Jewish state in Palestine.
It was a dramatic end for the consulate’s tenure in East Jerusalem, which since its move to the Sheikh Jarrah neighbourhood in 1967 has experienced its fair share of political upheaval.
The UK government first bought the plot that would become its consulate in 1963, when East Jerusalem was still under Jordanian control. It was meant to be a direct liaison between the UK government and the Jordanian-administered West Bank and East Jerusalem. The compound took four years to build and was finally ready for the UK consul-general to move into by 1967.
By the time the new consul-general moved into the premises, however, East Jerusalem was no longer under the control of the Jordanians. Just weeks before John Henry Lewen was to move into the building, the six-day war broke out and Israel captured East Jerusalem from the Jordanian forces.
Lewen assumed his post at the consulate in a changed East Jerusalem under Israeli control. The consulate he oversaw occupied a unique position as the UK did not recognise Jerusalem as being under any single country’s control.
As the UK foreign secretary told parliament in June 1967: “Our consul-general in Jerusalem is subordinate neither to the ambassador in Tel Aviv nor to the ambassador in Amman, but directly to the Foreign Office.”
Lewen’s tenure was marked by the political problems that plagued Jerusalem in the aftermath of the six-day war and the birth of Israel. In 1969, a bomb was placed under the window of a consul secretary, harming no one but damaging the compound.
Years later, Palestinians would present their grievances to the British consulate in Sheikh Jarrah. In 2017, protesters demonstrated outside the consulate to mark the centenary of the Balfour declaration. Men placed flags in the consululate windows reading “Balfour is a crime”, while schoolgirls carried thousands of letters written by Palestinian students asking Britain to apologise for the declaration.
This week, however, there was little sign of the political turmoil which the British consulate had waded through during its 60 years on the site. The neighbourhood, mostly made up of diplomatic missions and UN and other international organisations’ offices, was quiet.
Residents in the area expressed disappointment over what they saw as a lack of international support for the Palestinian people in recent years.
“We have seen very little but studies and words, no action from the international community,” said Abu Abdo.

Physical attractiveness offers no protection for perpetrators of online misogyny
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
14:00:47 UTC
23:00:47 KST

People evaluating online misogyny judge the severity of the hateful content itself rather than giving attractive perpetrators a free pass. The findings suggest that when online harassment crosses an unambiguous moral line, users rely on message-based reasoning over heuristic shortcuts like physical appearance. The research was published in Computers in Human Behavior.
Social media users constantly encounter rapid streams of information and often rely on mental shortcuts to make quick judgments about what they see. This behavior is partly explained by the Elaboration Likelihood Model, a psychological framework describing how people process information through two distinct pathways. When individuals evaluate a message deeply, they use a central route of processing. When they lack the motivation or time, they tend to rely on a peripheral route, depending on accessible cues like a speaker’s visual appearance.
One well-documented mental shortcut is the attractiveness-leniency effect. This is a psychological bias where physically attractive people receive softer moral judgments after committing an offense. Because online environments are visually driven, a user’s profile picture can heavily influence how others interpret their intent and credibility. Yet research on online harassment has rarely examined whether this physical bias extends to perpetrators of digital misogyny.
Automated moderation systems often fail to capture the nuanced expressions of online hostility, shifting the responsibility of defining moral boundaries onto regular users. Rinat Meerson, Kevin Koban, and Jörg Matthes, researchers at the University of Vienna, sought to test whether an internet troll’s appearance alters how bystanders react to their posts. They also wanted to understand if the specific phrasing of the hostility changes those reactions.
Communication experts generally divide digital hostility into three categories: incivility, intolerance, and threats. Incivility involves rude or vulgar language that breaks social etiquette without necessarily targeting a demographic group. Intolerance communicates ideological exclusion or discrimination against a specific group, undermining democratic principles of equality. Threats involve explicit insinuations of physical or psychological harm, introducing an element of coercion and fear.
To test how these factors influence user reactions, the researchers designed an online experiment involving 884 adult participants in Austria. The participants first viewed three mock social media profiles featuring male faces. These faces had been scientifically validated in a prior database as having high, medium, or low physical attractiveness.
Next, the participants read three misogynistic comments that were ostensibly written by the men in the profiles. These comments were pre-selected by independent experts to represent either incivility, intolerance, or a direct threat. After viewing the material, the participants rated the comments on their acceptability and their level of sexism. They also reported their negative emotional reactions, their support for platform moderation, and their likelihood of intervening.
The researchers measured two types of behavioral responses: indirect and direct intervention. Indirect interventions involve low-risk actions like reporting a post or flagging it for community moderation. Direct interventions involve engaging in a social interaction, such as replying to the perpetrator or expressing public support for the victim.
The results showed that users categorized the hostility on a progressive scale. Participants rated both intolerance and threats as less acceptable and more sexist than mere incivility. The cognitive evaluations leveled off between the two more severe categories, indicating a ceiling effect. Once a comment crossed a certain boundary of unacceptability, users did not judge the direct threat to be much worse than the intolerant remark.
In contrast, emotional reactions continued to intensify across all three categories. Participants reported higher levels of anger and disgust as the comments escalated from incivility to intolerance. These emotional responses reached their absolute highest point when participants read direct threats.
When it came to taking action, the study revealed a split between private reporting and public confrontation. Participants expressed a higher intention to indirectly intervene as the severity of the hate increased. They also showed stronger support for platform moderation when viewing threats compared to uncivil or intolerant comments.
Yet their willingness to directly intervene remained consistently low across all types of comments. The researchers noted an asymmetry between moral condemnation and visible action. Users recognized the harm and felt negative emotions, but they remained hesitant to involve themselves in a public conflict. The authors suggest this reluctance stems from the reputational and emotional risks associated with public confrontation, such as the fear of retaliation.
Regarding physical appearance, the researchers found that perpetrator attractiveness had no effect on any of the outcomes. Participants evaluated the misogynistic comments with the same level of condemnation regardless of whether the profile picture showed a highly attractive or highly unattractive man. The researchers noted that these findings were not statistically significant for the attractiveness variable, meaning the pretty privilege bias failed to materialize.
The unambiguous nature of the misogynistic statements appeared to override any superficial mental shortcuts. The researchers propose that when a moral violation is highly explicit, users may engage in more systematic, central-route processing. In that case, the moral content of the message may dominate their evaluations, overriding any leniency typically associated with physical attractiveness.
The experiment relied on static text and images rather than a fully interactive social media environment. This limits how perfectly the study mirrors everyday scrolling, as real platforms feature moving elements and ongoing comment threads. The study also exclusively utilized male faces and focused solely on hostility directed at women.
Reactions to digital hate might shift if the comments were directed at a less uniformly protected social group. Different biases might also emerge if the perpetrator were female. Because attractiveness can sometimes work against women when it is seen as a sign of manipulativeness or deceptiveness, an attractive female troll might face harsher judgments for similar comments. Future research could explore how perpetrator gender interacts with physical appearance to shape bystander intervention.
The study, “Pretty privilege? Effects of perpetrators’ attractiveness and hate type on user responses against misogynist digital hate,” was authored by Rinat Meerson, Kevin Koban, and Jörg Matthes.

A love of intense sweetness shows a surprising link to financial choices
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
14:00:45 UTC
23:00:45 KST

People who have a strong preference for intensely sweet tastes tend to grab a small reward available right now rather than wait for a larger one. New research published in Frontiers in Psychology suggests that this impatience may be partly explained by a general aversion to risk, rather than a stronger pull toward bigger rewards. The findings may help clarify the psychological and biological mechanisms connecting reward sensitivity to decision-making.
Reward sensitivity describes how strongly a person is motivated by the prospect of a reward. Scientists usually measure it with questionnaires or behavioral tasks, but one more physiological method is testing a person’s preference for sweet tastes. The sweet-liking phenotype, an observable biological marker, sorts people into two groups based on whether they strongly prefer highly concentrated sugar solutions or milder sweetness. Being a sweet-liker, a characteristic that is about half heritable and stable across life, is considered a physiological indicator of heightened sensitivity to a basic sensory reward.
A 2014 study found that people who intensely enjoy sweet tastes are more prone to choosing smaller, immediate rewards over delayed ones, a behavior known as delay discounting. Delay discounting is an economic and psychological measure of impatience. It captures how much less a reward seems worth to a person as the wait to receive it grows longer.
Separate neuroscience work, such as a 2009 study, demonstrated that the human brain relies on partly overlapping neural circuits to calculate the value of both delayed rewards and uncertain gambles. This physical overlap suggests that time preferences and risk preferences share common roots. Building on that idea, a 2018 study showed that a person’s tolerance for risk systematically alters how impatient they appear on delay-discounting tests, highlighting risk sensitivity as a potential hidden driver of impulsive choices.
The new study connects these threads by investigating whether biological sweet preference is linked to impulsive choices specifically through a heightened sensitivity to risk. The research was conducted by Anna Davidovich, senior research fellow Ksenia Panidi, and their colleagues at the Centre for Cognition and Decision Making at HSE University in Moscow. The team aimed to determine whether the link between sweet-liking and impulsivity could be explained by an increased desire for larger rewards, a heightened urge for immediate gratification, or a general avoidance of the uncertainty that comes with waiting.
“The study was motivated by the observation that sweet-taste preferences were linked to various kinds of addictions, such as alcoholism and other substance use disorders,” Panidi told PsyPost. “This observation suggests that sweet-taste preferences might be more broadly linked to impulsive decision making, due to the possible involvement of the opioid system in the valuation of rewards.” The opioid system refers to the brain’s own opioid chemicals, such as endorphins, which help regulate pleasure and pain.
“If this is the case, these differences in sweet-taste preference should then show up in other contexts (not linked to food rewards) that also imply value-based choices,” she explained. “This was the hypothesis that we decided to test using economic choices.”
To explore this, the researchers conducted two experiments. In the first experiment, 49 healthy adults completed a series of behavioral tasks. Participants took a standardized sweet-taste liking test, where they sampled five water solutions with varying concentrations of sucrose and rated their pleasantness. Those who rated the highest sucrose concentration as their favorite were classified as sweet-likers, while the rest were classified as sweet-dislikers.
It is important to distinguish this biological metric from everyday dietary habits. “The results of this study are very commonly misinterpreted as indicating that people who ‘like sweet food’ are more impulsive than those who don’t,” Panidi said. “In fact, sweet-taste preferences are very different from ‘sweet food preferences.’ Some studies even show that the correlation between the two is rather small.”
“The major difference is that the sweet-taste liking test only shows whether a person favors a sugar solution with the highest concentration of sucrose (i.e., 3 times higher than that of Coca-Cola),” she explained. “It does not necessarily mean that the same person would prefer sugary food, as food contains many more nutrients than just sugar (fats, proteins), which also affects food preferences.”
Participants also completed a lottery choice task to measure their risk preferences. In this task, they made 60 choices between a guaranteed payout of 100 monetary units and a risky lottery that offered up to 500 units at varying probabilities of winning (25, 50, or 75 percent).
After the lottery, they played a computerized balloon game, where they could earn real rubles by inflating a virtual balloon but would lose that balloon’s earnings if it popped. The taste test came first for 24 participants and last for the other 25, and the researchers controlled for this order, along with age and gender.
Twelve participants were classified as sweet-likers and 37 as sweet-dislikers. Sweet-likers did not rate the solutions as sweeter than sweet-dislikers did; they simply enjoyed the stronger ones more. The researchers found that sweet-likers were more risk-averse in the lottery choice task. They were less likely than sweet-dislikers to choose the lottery, and this gap held regardless of the prize size or the odds of winning.
However, the balloon task showed no differences between the two groups. The authors suggest this discrepancy might reflect that the lottery task involves explicit probabilities, while the balloon task requires people to learn about risk gradually through trial and error.
This aversion to risk ran counter to the researchers’ expectations. “Our initial hypothesis was that sweet-likers would be more prone to making impulsive choices which would also imply making risky choices, i.e., preferring an option where one can win bigger reward with some probability rather than taking a smaller amount of money for sure,” Panidi said. “However, we were surprised to see the opposite – sweet-likers showed higher preference for sure options compared to sweet-dislikers.”
“This might suggest that our common understanding of ‘impulsivity’ in risky contexts might be wrong,” she added. “In fact, making impulsive choices does not necessarily mean making risky choices. It might mean preference for more ‘tangible’ reward. If getting a small amount of money for sure feels more ‘tangible’ than playing a lottery, an impulsive person might prefer that small amount.”
In the second experiment, the research team recruited a new sample of 100 healthy adults to see how sweet-taste preferences relate to both risk and time delays. Because the task order had affected lottery choices in the first experiment, this time the taste test was always given last.
Alongside the same lottery choice task, participants completed a delay discounting task, which required them to choose between a smaller monetary reward available sooner and a larger reward available later. The two tasks were mixed together in blocks. Some of the delay choices offered the smaller reward immediately, while others enforced a delay for both the smaller and larger options.
Out of 100 participants, 28 were classified as sweet-likers. “I think an interesting observation is how stable the proportion of sweet-likers and sweet-dislikers in the population seems to be,” Panidi noted. “In our experiments, 25-30% of participants were classified as sweet-likers, which is pretty close to the proportions found in other countries where a similar method was used, such as South Korea or the UK.”
Sweet-likers again leaned toward the safe option, though in this larger sample the difference appeared only when the odds of winning were 50 percent, the point of greatest uncertainty. In the delay discounting task, the sweet-likers exhibited a specific pattern of impulsivity. When one of the rewards was available immediately, sweet-likers were more likely than sweet-dislikers to choose the immediate option.
But when both options required a waiting period, sweet-likers were actually more likely to choose the delayed, larger reward. Sweet-likers and sweet-dislikers did not differ in how strongly the size of the rewards or the length of the wait swayed their choices. Together, these patterns suggest that sweet-likers’ impatience is tied specifically to the availability of an immediate, certain outcome.
When the researchers accounted for each participant’s general risk aversion, the link between sweet-liking and choosing the immediate reward weakened by about 40 percent and fell just short of statistical significance. The authors interpret this as a sign that sweet-likers’ impatience may stem at least partly from a wariness of uncertainty: for someone who dislikes risk, a reward that arrives later can feel less certain than one in hand.
The two groups also looked alike on questionnaires. In the first experiment, sweet-likers and sweet-dislikers scored similarly on measures of sensation seeking and novelty seeking, and in the second they also did not differ on a standard impulsivity questionnaire or in how risky they rated themselves. The authors suggest that physiological and questionnaire-based measures of reward sensitivity may capture different things.
Panidi sees implications that reach beyond taste. “I think the main takeaway from this study is that the neurobiology of economic choice might have a much deeper physiological grounding than we might commonly think,” she told PsyPost. “At first, the link between sweet-taste preference and monetary choices might seem very indirect (how these two things might even be related?), but as we look deeper, we find that economic choices might be guided by our physiology just as much as our taste preferences.”
The findings are in line with research covered by PsyPost earlier this year, which relied on long-running household surveys of about 14,000 people in the United Kingdom rather than laboratory choice tasks. That study found that people who felt more dread about possible financial losses tended to be both less willing to take risks and less willing to wait for rewards.
As with all research, there are a few things to keep in mind. The study relied on laboratory tasks with small real-money stakes, which might not fully capture how people make high-stakes decisions in daily life. The effects were relatively small; in the first experiment, sweet-liking accounted for about 0.2 percent more of the variation in risky choices, and there were only 12 sweet-likers. The sample was limited as well: participants were young adults recruited in Moscow, and people with math, physics, economics, finance, or computer science backgrounds were excluded.
The delay discounting task offered only three sizes of sooner reward. This restricted range might have made it difficult to detect whether sweet-likers are more sensitive to the sheer size of a reward.
“I would not say practical significance is very important here,” Panidi said. “Rather, the results might be important for researchers as they suggest that we should further look into the mechanisms of opioid system involvement in economic or any other value-based choices. This might open the way to further investigation of addiction mechanisms.”
For instance, she suggested that “people who have preference for very sweet taste might be more prone to impulsive choices in various contexts, and knowing this might help them create the environment which discourages them from making unhealthy choices. But further studies are needed to make more solid conclusions.”
In addition, the lottery tasks in the study only involved positive gains, avoiding any scenarios where participants could lose money. Because the biological opioid systems linked to sweet-taste preferences may also be involved in evaluating threats, future studies could explore whether sweet-likers show a similar aversion to financial losses.
The research team also plans to observe these mechanisms more directly. “The next steps for this line of research would be in digging deeper into the neural differences between sweet-likers and sweet-dislikers, i.e., exploring what happens differently on the brain level when they make economic choices,” Panidi said.
The study, “Sweet-taste liking is associated with preference for less risky and immediate rewards in economic decision-making,” was authored by Anna Davidovich, Anna N. Shestakova, Nina Arzumanyan, and Ksenia Panidi.

New tool aims to find terrorist material on devices
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
15:00:31 BST
23:00:31 KST

Police officers are to be given a way of checking a seized phone or computer against a library of more than a million files produced by recognised terrorist organisations, returning an answer in minutes rather than weeks, according to Cyacomb, the Edinburgh firm behind it.
The company has developed the capability with Human Cognition, using that firm’s Terrorist Authored Material Contraband Filter. The filter draws on a curated dataset of modern and historical terrorist material which has been checked by people rather than only by machines, and verified as having been produced by recognised terrorist groups.
Behind it sits an archive of more than 3.3 million files that have circulated in terrorist online ecosystems over the past three decades, of which more than a million have been identified as terrorist-authored. A suspect device is checked against that material using secure matching technology, with the stated aim of supporting faster action against people moving towards violence.
Chris Johnson, chief executive of Cyacomb, said: “Technology has completely changed the environment in which radicalisation can take place. Traditionally becoming involved with an extremist organisation would require physical contact, but today an individual can access huge volumes of extremist material without leaving their bedroom.”
Dr Ali Fisher, co-founder at Human Cognition, said: “The speed, agility and resilience of the terrorist networks that share content online, and the mobility of potential terrorists in the physical world, requires tools that enable law enforcement to rapidly identify content on digital devices.”
The companies say the process does not expose unrelated personal information held on the device, since it matches only against material already in the dataset rather than reading everything stored. That distinction is the one that usually decides whether a tool of this kind survives contact with the courts, and it is the same approach Cyacomb has taken in its existing work on child abuse imagery, where the firm built its reputation.
A full forensic examination of a modern phone can take weeks, and a backlog of devices waiting for examination has been a recurring theme in inspectorate reports on counter-terrorism and serious crime investigation. A triage tool that tells an officer within minutes whether a device holds known material lets investigators decide where to put the specialist effort. Language is the other claimed advantage, with the companies saying the matching works whatever the nature or language of the content, because it compares files rather than reading them.

Energy Independence of Business: Andriy Dorofeyev on UKRAVTONOMGAZ Solutions
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
17:00:30 EEST
23:00:30 KST

On September 9-10, as part of the specialized exhibition AUTONOMY: EXPO 2026, the company "Ukravtonomgaz" demonstrated comprehensive engineering solutions for backup power supply for Ukrainian enterprises. According to the company's owner, Andriy Dorofeyev, only the proactive implementation of autonomous electricity and heat supply systems will allow businesses and critical infrastructure facilities to avoid shutdowns during power and heat supply interruptions in the 2026-2027 season.
LPG Gas Generation as a Response to Gas Outages
The main focus at the company's booth was on modern gas generators. The central exhibit was a 100 kW unit operating autonomously on liquefied propane-butane (LPG). Experts detailed its operation, providing engineering calculations and technical consultations for various industrial sectors.
Today, representatives of territorial communities and entrepreneurs are concerned about a key question: how to continue operations if the power grid or the central gas pipeline is de-energized or damaged. Negotiations at the exhibition shifted to a practical level - from discussing problems to finding ways for the rapid deployment of backup mobile capacities on propane (such as gas reciprocating units, LPG gas tanks, and gas boiler houses).
Regulatory Risks: Who is in the Gas Disconnection Zone?
Unfortunately, power outages have already become a familiar stress test for the Ukrainian economy. However, a new challenge may lie ahead for Ukrainian enterprises - gas blackouts. Most entrepreneurs mistakenly believe that a central gas pipeline connected to their enterprise guarantees an uninterrupted supply of the resource.
The Ministry of Energy of Ukraine has developed and approved strict regulations in case of crisis situations. According to Order No. 330 (dated December 13, 2021) and Order No. 437 (dated November 26, 2024), all consumers using natural gas are divided into five disconnection categories. If an energy crisis is declared, industrial and municipal enterprises will be obliged to independently stop consuming blue fuel at the first demand of the "Gas Networks of Ukraine" operator.
"Today, energy security is not limited to simply having a generator. Enterprises need a holistic system: from a guaranteed resource source, which can be not only natural gas but also liquefied propane-butane, to safe storage and stable fuel supply," emphasizes expert Andriy Dorofeyev from the UKRAVTONOMGAZ company. "Only a comprehensive autonomous gas supply based on liquefied LPG allows continuing operations during blackouts. This is the very real instrument for protecting companies and the population."
Company Profile: LLC "Ukravtonomgaz" is a Ukrainian engineering company specializing in the design, installation, and full maintenance of autonomous gas supply systems for boiler houses and cogeneration units. During its activity, the company has implemented over 650 turnkey projects across the country, providing them with backup fuel — liquefied petroleum gas (LPG).

Yemen displacement surges past 200,000 following fresh Houthi offensive, UN migration body warns
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
14:00:17 UTC
23:00:17 KST

More than 200,000 people have been displaced from their homes since fighting in Yemen began in recent weeks, according to data released on Wednesday by the United Nations' International Organization for Migration.
IOM described the crisis sparked by renewed fighting between the Iran-backed Houthi group and Saudi-backed government forces in Yemen as alarming, with displacement figures surging from 76,000 in mid-September to more than 200,000 as of Wednesday - nearly all of whom fled since fighting began in early September.
"People are running for their lives and finding nowhere safe to go," said IOM Director General Amy Pope, who called for more funding amid rising needs for food and shelter.
Yemen is experiencing the most serious escalation in fighting between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis since a UN-brokered truce largely halted cross-border attacks in 2022. 
The renewed conflict could reshape control in Yemen, with implications for Red Sea shipping lanes.
Houthis seize Red Sea coast as thousands flee to Africa
The Houthis, who already control most of northern Yemen including the capital Sanaa, seized the country's entire Red Sea coast last month from Saudi-backed forces of the internationally recognized government, based in the southern port of Aden.
People have been displaced across 10 governorates, with Ta'iz the hardest hit.
More than 3,700 people have also fled by sea to Djibouti, IOM said.
On Friday, the UN World Food Program said that three in four families in parts of Yemen were going hungry from the "absolutely devastating" impact of a surge in fighting.

Georgia arrests man for selling radioactive uranium-238 to foreign national for $700,000

Georgia has detained a man who planned to sell uranium-238 to a foreign national for $700,000, the national security service said on Wednesday.
The Georgian citizen is accused of illegally handling nuclear material and faces up to 10 years in prison, it said in a statement, sharing a video of armed security personnel pulling a man out of a white sedan and handcuffing him on the ground.
It was not immediately possible to contact the man or a legal representative for comment.
The footage also showed agents testing two small containers in the trunk of the vehicle with a handheld radiation detector. One of them appeared to contain a light-colored powder.
Uranium-238 is the most common uranium isotope and, while radioactive, is not ordinarily usable on its own to make a nuclear bomb.
Securing nuclear materials a major concern after 1991 collapse of Soviet Union
The security of nuclear materials was one of the biggest concerns after the 1991 fall of the Soviet Union, of which Georgia was part. There have been several serious incidents involving the illicit trade in nuclear materials in Georgia over recent decades.
In February, Georgia detained two people who attempted to purchase $3 million worth of uranium and a cache of a radioactive isotope found in nuclear weapons testing programs.

Why China’s export engine may hit a ceiling as trading partners face limits

Why China’s export engine may hit a ceiling as trading partners face limits
Exports likely to keep growing in near term but could face pressure in the years ahead, analysts say
While China’s export engine still has room to grow, many of its trading partners may be approaching the limit of how much more they can absorb, which could place a ceiling on further growth over the coming years, according to a Goldman Sachs report.
“At least over the next few years, there is still room for Chinese exports to maintain their strong momentum,” analysts said in the report led by the American investment bank’s chief China economist Hui Shan on Wednesday.
“Over the longer term, however, stronger economic growth in importing economies will be required for continued Chinese export gains.”
Even under the bank’s most conservative projection, China’s real exports could grow by 8 per cent annually in the near term, despite the country posting a record US$1.2 trillion trade surplus last year.

Minister says risk of pneumonic plague spreading in Lithuania and Europe is very low
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
14:00:00 UTC
23:00:00 KST

The risk of pneumonic plague spreading in Europe is very low, Lithuanian Health Minister Linas Kukuraitis said Wednesday, adding that the country’s hospitals have enough antibiotics to meet demand for about a month.
“Antibiotic reserves exist both at the national level, and hospitals should also have enough for up to a month to meet such a demand,” Kukuraitis told reporters.
Kukuraitis said Lithuania’s health system is better prepared to respond to infectious disease threats following the Covid-19 pandemic. The country has functioning infectious disease management infrastructure and established response procedures, he said.
He stressed that it has not been confirmed whether there was actually a case of pneumonic plague in Russia. Lithuania can currently assess the situation only on the basis of publicly available information, with a lack of reliable data presenting the main challenge, he said.
Kukuraitis said the strong reaction from the United States indicates that serious developments could be taking place in Russia, but that Lithuania currently has no independently verified information about the reported case.
The National Public Health Centre also said there is no increased risk of plague infection for people in Lithuania. Lithuanian institutions are monitoring the situation, but available information is limited and does not allow authorities to independently confirm that the woman who died in Russia had pneumonic plague.
Russian and local media previously reported that 28-year-old Daria Shipilova, who worked at a plague research institute in the Irkutsk region, may have died from pneumonic plague. Reports also said a possible laboratory incident had occurred and that her contacts had been isolated.
Russian officials, however, said post-mortem tests did not detect plague.
Kukuraitis previously said that if reports of plague in Russia were confirmed and the situation posed a threat to Lithuania, authorities could consider restricting the transit of Russian citizens through Lithuania. Any such measures would be coordinated with European Union partners.
Pneumonic plague is a rare bacterial infection caused by Yersinia pestis. It can be treated with antibiotics when diagnosed promptly, and antibiotics to treat the disease are available in Lithuania and elsewhere in Europe.

Anna Mazepa Politkovskaya: A Witness Russia Could Not Silence
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
14:00:00 UTC
23:00:00 KST

Twenty years ago today, Anna Politkovskaya was shot dead in the lift of her Moscow apartment block. It was Oct. 7, 2006 – Vladimir Putin’s 54th birthday.
The gun and spent cartridges left at the scene pointed to a contract killing. The meaning was hard to miss: A journalist critical of the Kremlin could be murdered in central Moscow, while the people who ordered it remained safely out of sight.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Her murder marked a turning point for Russian journalism. Politkovskaya had reported about Russia’s war on Chechnya, the bombardment, torture, abduction and fear. She documented abuses by Russian forces and Chechen fighters alike, appealed to both sides to spare civilians, and refused propaganda’s tidy moral fictions
Her courage was practical rather than performative. During the 2002 Moscow theater siege, she entered to help negotiate because the hostage-takers had asked for her and, as she later said, she could not refuse. Two years later, on her way to Beslan, in the northern Caucasus, she was poisoned and forced to turn back.
Arrest, threats and even a mock execution did not stop her. In an AFP interview marking the 20th anniversary of her murder, Sergei Sokolov, her editor at Novaya Gazeta, recalled that “nothing could make her stray” from a subject or principle she had chosen.
She also recognized early what Putinism would demand. In a 2004 article, as Western governments embraced a leader who appeared to promise stability after the upheavals of the 1990s, Politkovskaya wrote that journalists would be expected to show “total servility to Putin” or face prison or death.
Petition Calling for Zelensky Press Conference With Independent Media Reaches 25,000 Signatures
Russia, she warned, was “hurtling back into a Soviet abyss.”
Sokolov told AFP that many readers dismissed such warnings as exaggeration. Today, with independent media banned or driven abroad, dissent criminalized and Russia in the fifth year of its full-scale war against Ukraine, her words read less like prophecy than clear-eyed reporting.
So the European Parliament’s commemoration in Strasbourg this week was more than a ceremonial gesture.
Politkovskaya’s granddaughter, Anna Victoria Politkovskaya, appeared alongside Mariana Katzarova, the UN special rapporteur on human rights in Russia, and Kirill Martynov, editor of Novaya Gazeta Europe. European Parliament Vice-President Nicolae Ștefănuță said Politkovskaya’s “fearless pursuit of the truth” had made her “a beacon of hope for those fighting for justice and human dignity in Russia.”
At the Strasbourg tribute, her granddaughter spoke in more personal terms. Politkovskaya, she recalled, wrote about people abandoned to war, violence, injustice and the system: Chechen families trying to survive, Russian conscripts sent to kill and die, and victims of torture, abduction and corruption. Above all, she “did not allow human stories to go unnoticed.”
That was Politkovskaya’s gift. She returned names, faces and consequences to those whom the state reduced to statistics or enemies.
One part of her story is still too often left out. She was born Anna Stepanovna Mazepa in New York. Her father, Stepan Mazepa, was a Ukrainian diplomat from the Chernihiv region who served with the Ukrainian Soviet delegation to the United Nations; her mother, Raisa Novikova, came from Kerch in Crimea.
Politkovskaya built her life and career in Moscow and became known by her married name. Acknowledging her Ukrainian family background does not enlist her in a cause after death. It completes the record.
The name Mazepa carries its own historical weight. In 1708, Cossack Hetman Ivan Mazepa broke with Peter I and allied with Sweden in an effort to preserve the Hetmanate’s autonomy from Moscow. Russian imperial mythology made him the great traitor; for Ukrainians, he became a symbol of resistance to imperial rule.
There is no evidence that Politkovskaya was related to him, and there is no need to invent one. The echo lies elsewhere. Anna Mazepa Politkovskaya spent her career challenging an old imperial bargain: submission offered as “order,” violence presented as necessity, and loyalty to the ruler placed above loyalty to the truth.
Chechnya was the testing ground; Ukraine is the war on a far greater scale. The methods Politkovskaya recorded – indiscriminate force, coerced allegiance, manufactured narratives and contempt for civilian life – did not remain in the North Caucasus. Neither did the assault on journalism.
After her death, the Kremlin steadily tightened its legal and coercive grip. Novaya Gazeta was branded a “foreign agent,” and many journalists she inspired now work in exile.
Six men were convicted for roles connected to the assassination. Yet those who ordered and financed it have never been publicly identified. That is not a minor loose end. It is the central fact of the case.
Sergei Khadzhikurbanov, the former police officer convicted of helping organize her murder, was recruited from prison to fight in Ukraine. After six months, he received a presidential pardon, then signed another defense ministry contract. Impunity had come full circle.
Europe should honor Politkovskaya by defending the work for which she died: supporting independent Russian, Ukrainian, Belarusian and Georgian media; protecting journalists in exile; documenting war crimes; and refusing to treat political murder as an unfortunate cost of doing business with Moscow.
Repression at home and aggression abroad are parts of the same project. Both depend on contempt for law, fact and human life.
Politkovskaya did not live to see the full disaster she had described in outline. But she left behind a way of working: go where power does not want witnesses, listen to those it would rather erase, check every fact and write without servility.
Twenty years after the shots in that Moscow lift, what matters is not that she predicted the future. It is that she described the present accurately – and too many people chose not to listen.
The views expressed in this opinion article are the author’s and not necessarily those of Kyiv Post.
