Trump says Islam 'wants to take over' France amid student protests
US President Donald Trump has blamed Islam and mass immigration for the wave of student protests sweeping France, claiming the unrest is driven by Muslims seeking to “take over” the country.
Trump made the remarks on Truth Social as hundreds of thousands of people took to the streets across France in support of a student-led movement demanding better conditions in schools.
“What’s happening in France is nothing less than out of control mass migration,” Trump wrote. “This isn’t about schools, this is about Islam wanting to take over a once great Country!”
Trump offered no evidence for his claims, while the protesters’ demands have focused on deteriorating school infrastructure, teacher shortages, overcrowded classrooms and education funding.
French Foreign Minister Jean-Noel Barrot responded to Trump’s intervention by warning against allowing other countries to define the unrest in France.
“If we do not write our own story, others will write it for us,” Barrot said, according to French broadcaster BFMTV, warning against France being forced to “endure the stories of others”.
Barrot said France’s “rivals, adversaries, and partners” were attempting to interpret the movement “in their own way”.
In separate remarks to a parliamentary committee, Barrot said: “You’ll get the Iranians’ version, perhaps the version from some Israelis, perhaps the version from some Americans.”
He said French diplomatic missions were working to present France’s account of the protests “so that we have our own narratives to disseminate, rather than being subjected to those of others”.
No link has been established between the student movement and religious or identity-based demands, with even Marine Le Pen’s far-right National Rally not publicly attributing the unrest to immigration.
Demonstrations swept across France on Tuesday as teachers and parents joined high school students in what Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu has described as the country’s most violent student demonstrations in decades.
More than 250,000 people took part in protests across France, according to the Interior Ministry, while organisers put the figure at 450,000.
Police fired tear gas and water cannons during clashes on the fringes of demonstrations in Paris, Strasbourg, Rennes and Toulouse.
The Interior Ministry said 488 people were arrested on Tuesday, while 43 law enforcement officers were injured.
Lecornu has said at least 215 teenagers and 85 school staff have been injured since the unrest began, describing it as “the heaviest toll in decades paid by the school system”. His office said more than 700 police officers had also been hurt.
The protests began in September in disadvantaged suburbs of Paris before spreading across the country.
Students have complained of chronic underfunding and poor conditions in schools, including overcrowded classrooms, teacher shortages and basic maintenance problems ranging from water leaks to rat infestations.
The High School Students Union said more than half of France’s high schools had been blockaded or closed, while some education authorities have attempted to move classes online.
Rights groups, students and parents have accused authorities of using disproportionate force against minors. The government says the movement has been infiltrated by outside groups and in some areas descended into urban violence.
More than 1,800 people are being prosecuted over alleged offences linked to the unrest, including 1,483 minors, according to the Justice Ministry.
The demonstrations come months before France’s presidential election and amid broader political and economic tensions over public spending and the cost of living.

NATO's Military Committee, the Alliance's highest military body, visited Kyiv on 6 October to reaffirm support for Ukraine, its chair, Admiral Giuseppe Cavo Dragone, said. It was the committee's first official visit to Ukraine's capital in eight years. The officers came to hear how Ukraine is fighting Russia and to draw lessons for NATO's own defense, and Dragone used the visit to warn Moscow.
Russia's war no longer stays inside Ukraine: its drones, saboteurs, and pressure campaigns increasingly reach NATO members. That turns Ukraine, the only European army facing Russia in combat, from a country the Alliance helps into one it learns from.
All 32 allies at the table
Dragone brought the military representatives of all 32 member states to hear the latest battlefield assessment directly from Ukraine's commander-in-chief, Mykhailo Drapatyi, and his staff. They also came to learn what more NATO can do to support Ukraine, he said in an address recorded in Kyiv.
"After eight years, the NATO Military Committee comes back to Kyiv for an official visit. But while we were not physically present here, Ukraine is in our thoughts, in our discussions, in our decisions and following action every single day," Dragone said.
The visit fulfilled a promise he made to Drapatyi during their last conversation in August, the admiral said. It also follows a June visit to Kyiv by the North Atlantic Council, NATO's main political decision-making body. "We are here in full strength with a clear message. The bond between NATO and Ukraine is stronger and stronger," he said.
Lessons from Ukraine's commanders
The talks with Drapatyi focused on Ukraine's military priorities and lessons learned to strengthen Allied preparedness for current and future threats, Dragone wrote on X. The delegation also paid respects at the Wall of Remembrance of the Fallen for Ukraine in Kyiv.
14 dead in Pryluky, two each in Kyiv, Kremenchuk, and Oleksandriia: Russia’s night of 70 missiles
In his address, Dragone said Ukraine's courageous and resilient spirit remains unbreakable and serves as an example to other nations.
"An example that combines with all the lessons we can learn from your commanders, from their experience, which will ultimately help our Alliance too to better face today's and tomorrow's threats," he said.
To Russia: "You are failing"
Dragone also addressed Russia directly. NATO stands unwavering with Ukraine in the face of Russia's continued aggression and its reckless hybrid activities in member countries, he said.
"To those who think that by perpetrating acts of sabotage, cyberattacks, and violation of the airspace in national NATO territory they will undermine this support and our resolve, I will respond: You are failing. NATO support for Ukraine continues to grow, and our unity is stronger than ever."
Russia bears full responsibility for such dangerous and unacceptable behavior, and allies will keep sharpening their tools and strengthening deterrence and defense, the admiral added.
Drapatyi became Ukraine's commander-in-chief in July, when President Volodymyr Zelenskyy replaced Oleksandr Syrskyi after a week of political turmoil.
Kyiv under fire, Russian troops pushed back near Lyman
The day after the visit, Russia struck Kyiv and 12 oblasts with about 70 missiles. In recent weeks, Russian attacks have cratered the capital's bridges and hit a school, a café, and warehouses, as well as a maternity hospital. Ukrainian troops also retook ground near Lyman in the Vivaldi counteroffensive.

Men drive surge in Swiss smart glasses sales, says Galaxus
Swiss online retailer Galaxus reports that sales of so-called smart glasses are rising sharply. It also says that men account for nine in ten purchases of the devices.
Manufacturers estimate that millions of smart glasses will be in use worldwide by 2026, Galaxus says in a press release. Switzerland is also contributing to the trend: sales at the online retailer have quadrupled this year compared with the same period last year, up 307%.
+ Smart glasses ban in swimming pools debated in Switzerland
“Several thousand pairs were ordered between January and September,” the company says, adding that the glasses are “flying off the shelves”.
According to the company, the camera and built-in speakers can help deaf people follow conversations in real time and take part more easily. They can also provide blind people with spoken descriptions of their surroundings.
But there is a downside. Some people use the glasses to film others without their consent and then share the footage online illegally.
More
The future is coming to your face soon
Ray-Ban, Xreal and RayNeo are the most popular smart-glasses brands sold by Galaxus, followed by Viture and Oakley. The devices also appear to have a particularly strong appeal among men, who account for 87% of purchases.
Galaxus acknowledges that the technology has also attracted criticism. Raphaël Mahaim, a Green Party member of the Vaud cantonal parliament, has tabled a parliamentary motion calling for a new legal framework.

The proposal would also require manufacturers to demonstrate that their devices meet privacy safeguards before they are allowed onto the market.
Several cantons have also seen political initiatives in recent months, including Zurich, Lucerne, Basel-City and St Gallen. Much of the debate has centred on whether smart glasses should be banned in swimming pools.
Supporters of a ban say it would help prevent people from using discreetly integrated cameras to film others without their consent, including children, girls and women in swimwear. In some cases, such footage is later shared online.

August Hanning, the former head of Germany’s Federal Intelligence Service (BND) whose arrest was announced on Oct. 6, may have passed classified documents to an agent from Azerbaijan, according to an investigation by Der Spiegel. Hanning, who was detained on suspicion of espionage and disclosure of state secrets, allegedly prepared an analytical report for Azerbaijani intelligence. Manfred D., the former head of Hanning’s office, was also detained.
According to investigators cited by Der Spiegel, the former BND head unlawfully obtained 2,000 classified documents and may have shared them while communicating with a foreign agent, though it remains unknown whether Hanning’s analysis reached the recipient, and German authorities have not officially confirmed that they suspect the former intelligence chief of working for Baku. His connection to Azerbaijan, however, is beyond doubt: he was officially a member of the board of the German-Azerbaijani Forum.
Hanning headed the BND from December 1998 to November 2005. According to prosecutors, in 2010 Hanning made an arrangement with Manfred D. to receive information from the BND in exchange for payment. Hanning intended to use the documents he received in his private consulting business. According to the German outlets Süddeutsche Zeitung, NDR, and WDR, the documents included materials from foreign partner agencies, documents on Iran’s nuclear program, and documents on the Russian military.
In at least one instance, Hanning is known to have prepared a security report for an unnamed foreign intelligence service (not a Russian one, according to media reports). Meanwhile, after leaving the BND, Hanning made at least seven trips to Russia, The Insider found — all of them within the period from 2015 to 2019.
Often, Hanning would fly into Moscow in the evening and fly out the next day. In the summer of 2016 he flew from Munich to Moscow on the evening of July 6 and flew out to Berlin on the afternoon of July 7. A similar trip between Berlin and Moscow took place in May 2019.
The investigation into Hanning has continued for several months. He came to the attention of law enforcement last year in connection with his possible involvement in the abduction of the children of Hamburg businesswoman Christina Block. As part of that case, Hanning’s home was searched in September 2025; some of the BND documents were found during those searches.

EU Highlights Bulgaria’s Reforms as RRF Payments Remain Tied to Milestones
Bulgaria is among the EU countries where Recovery and Resilience Facility (RRF) payments have been suspended over unfulfilled milestones, while the European Commission also recognizes progress in anti-corruption reforms and green investments.
The RRF implementation period ends on August 31, 2026, and the European Commission has entered the final stage of reviewing payments to Member States.
Since the facility was launched in 2021, €450 billion, or 79% of its total financial resources, has been distributed. The RRF is the largest instrument under NextGenerationEU and differs from traditional European funding because payments depend on the completion of previously agreed reforms and investments.
As of October 1, 2026, the European Commission had paid €450 billion to the 27 Member States after receiving 163 payment requests. These payments correspond to 4,082 of the 5,981 milestones and targets included in national plans, equal to 68% of the total.
A substantial part of the program remains unfinished across Europe. All Member States submitted their final payment requests by September 30, while the Commission is reviewing 32 requests worth a combined €123 billion. Payments on these requests must be made by December 31, 2026.
Bulgaria is highlighted in the report for the combination of progress it has made and financial constraints that remain. The Commission identifies three decisions concerning suspended funds for the country.
In November 2025, €214.5 million in funding was suspended before the decision was later reversed. In a separate case involving €152.9 million, the suspension concerning one measure was lifted, while the suspension affecting the second measure was definitively removed on August 3, 2026.
The latest decision, issued on July 24, 2026, involves €118.4 million and three milestones and targets. The suspension was lifted for one of them, while the six-month period available for corrective measures is still running for the other two.
Bulgaria is therefore part of the broader group of countries where RRF payments have not always been made automatically. Since the mechanism began, the Commission has suspended 34 milestones and targets across 18 payment requests, equivalent to 0.9% of all milestones and targets assessed through August 31, 2026.
In four cases, the outstanding requirements were not fulfilled during the six-month corrective period. Of €3.1 billion suspended through completed procedures, €266.3 million was permanently reduced.
At the same time, the report points to Bulgaria as one of the countries that has delivered concrete results under the reform-related part of the mechanism. The Commission cites the country's anti-corruption reform as an example.
The reform provides for a new anti-corruption body and a mechanism for independently investigating the Prosecutor General. The national plan has also introduced legislative changes covering whistleblower protection, lobbying, and the integrity of public officials and employees of state-owned enterprises. The Commission specifically notes that it has not yet formally completed its full assessment of these reforms.
Bulgaria has also made progress in the green transition. Along with Poland, the Czech Republic and Austria, it accounted for about half of the milestones and targets completed in renewable energy and electricity grids during the last reporting year. This forms part of a wider acceleration in implementing green measures toward the end of the programming period.
Across the EU, RRF spending on digital transformation has reached €140 billion. The Commission's initial estimates suggest that each euro invested in digital measures is expected to produce €1.50 in economic output within the EU.
The investments are also expected to reduce annual greenhouse gas emissions by approximately 54 million tonnes of CO₂ equivalent, equal to about 1.5% of the EU's 2021 emissions. Supported reforms are linked to an additional 2 million tonnes of annual reductions.
Bulgaria's participation in the final phase of the RRF therefore combines measurable progress in European green and institutional reforms with outstanding implementation requirements linked to some payments. Under the mechanism, the amount of funding ultimately received depends on the completion of the remaining stages.

Justice minister vows new gender equality bill will reach vote before elections
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
13:50:00 UTC
22:50:00 KST

Justice minister vows new gender equality bill will reach vote before elections
Justice Minister Liisa Pakosta says the long‑stalled gender equality and equal opportunities bill will be passed during the current Riigikogu term, though she has not yet explained the draft's contents or the timeline for its processing.
"We hope to complete the processing of the equal opportunities bill by the end of this Riigikogu term," Pakosta said.
She is not worried that time may be tight — under normal procedure, the bill should reach the Riigikogu by November at the latest.
"There is nothing unusual about this. It is completely normal that things are in progress and some take a bit longer. That is the case with many bills," she said.
Pakosta said it is not actually a problem that the gender equality and equal opportunities bill has remained unpassed for so long. She said the Constitution already provides protection that covers the bill's provisions.
"This bill changes almost nothing in people's lives because paragraph 12 of the Constitution is directly applicable," she said.
"Courts, the chancellor of justice and everyone else work on the basis of that constitutional paragraph, which guarantees protection for all people across all characteristics in all areas of life. Estonians are very well protected against discrimination because we have a very good Constitution. The changes achieved with this bill are extremely nuanced," Pakosta said.
She did not agree to discuss the content of the bill, including how the current draft differs from the version she withdrew from the process in 2024.
"Once again, the bill is still being drafted," she said.
When Pakosta halted the processing of the gender equality and equal opportunities bill prepared at the Ministry of Economic Affairs in May 2024, the Ministry of Justice commissioned a new perspective from the private sector — from the law firm Sorainen — without informing the NGOs and the office of the equal treatment commissioner who had worked on the earlier draft.
Although Pakosta insisted Sorainen was not commissioned to write a bill, as media reported at the time based on ministry information, but only preparatory materials, she still chose to keep those materials from the public. She also did not show the newly completed analysis to equal treatment commissioner Christian Veske, who requested it, or to the equality policy department at the Ministry of Economic Affairs.
As before, Pakosta justified the secrecy by citing the need to avoid confusion. "There was just a major public confusion over the statute of limitations for sexual crimes against children, which shows how easily confusion can arise. That is exactly why the law states that preparatory materials are not always public. In this case, the Data Protection Inspectorate has confirmed that," Pakosta said.
Commissioner skeptical about timeline
Although Pakosta said Estonians are currently well protected against discrimination, equal opportunities commissioner Christian Veske wrote to the minister in summer with a series of proposals, including a recommendation to complete the processing of the equal opportunities bill and ensure equal legal protection for everyone.
In her autumn response, Pakosta wrote that the ministry considers the issues addressed in the bill very important and added that the bill concerns socially significant and sensitive matters that require thorough consideration of different rights, interests and positions. "We consider it important that these positions be taken into account in shaping equal opportunities policy," she wrote.
Commenting on Pakosta's response to ERR, Veske said it seemed rather vague. Based on it, he finds it hard to believe the bill will be processed during the current Riigikogu term. "Especially considering that none of the relevant parties have received any substantive information about the bill," Veske said.
Because withdrawing the earlier bill angered the NGOs and the equal treatment commissioner's office that had worked on it, Pakosta repeatedly promised at the time that she would definitely submit the new bill for consultation, where all stakeholders could give feedback. "I confirm that we are ready for full cooperation with the relevant state agencies and advocacy organizations," Pakosta said.
Veske, who has had no information about the bill for the past two years, also has no knowledge of any planned stakeholder consultation. He hopes it will still happen. "It would be very poor legislative practice if the ministry wanted to skip the consultation round. There may be some legal obstacles to skipping it, but since this is a Ministry of Justice bill, they likely know that better," Veske said.
In response to ERR's question about whether consultation will take place, Pakosta said it is still planned. She did not say when.
Justice Minister Liisa Pakosta decided at the end of 2024 to halt and not send for official government coordination the gender equality and equal opportunities bill prepared at the Ministry of Economic Affairs.
The bill aimed to merge two existing laws — the Gender Equality Act and the Equal Treatment Act — into one comprehensive legal act. It sought to resolve a long‑standing legal gap in Estonia where protection against discrimination is not equal across all characteristics. Pakosta said she halted the bill because of extensive legal criticism and conflicting feedback.

Longevity: why do Poles live shorter than Western Europeans?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
13:49:58 UTC
22:49:58 KST

Poland still clearly trails Western Europe in life expectancy and years lived in good health. According to Robert Mordaka, a public health specialist, prevention and everyday habits are crucial.
"We are lagging behind not only in terms of average life expectancy, but also in the number of years we spend in good health. And that is a metric that really needs to be improved," Mordaka told Euronews during the Economic Forum in Karpacz.
He pointed out that around 60% of deaths are caused by two major groups of illnesses: cardiovascular diseases and cancers. In both cases, prevention and earlier intervention in response to risk factors can play a key role.
Prevention in Poland is still underfunded
According to the doctor, the problem does not come down solely to individual choices made by Poles. The way the healthcare system operates is also crucial. Poland is among the EU countries that devote the smallest share of health spending to preventive care.
"The EU average is around 6% of health budgets, while in Poland it is just under 2%. And without funding it is impossible to reverse this trend," Mordaka said.
At the same time, many of the factors that affect the length and quality of life remain in patients' own hands. Mordaka draws attention to the so-called Life's Essential 8 – eight areas that are critical to cardiovascular health.
These include keeping blood pressure, blood glucose and cholesterol under control, maintaining a healthy body weight, getting enough sleep, eating a balanced diet and not smoking. Regular physical activity is also vital.
"These are the small, everyday choices. Do we go to the shop and buy a sugary drink, or do we buy water instead?" the expert asked.
Obesity and smoking can cut life expectancy by many years
One of the biggest current threats to health is obesity. According to Mordaka, studies indicate that it can shorten life by as much as 15 years. Another major factor is smoking, which can take several years off life expectancy, depending on how many cigarettes are smoked per day and how long the habit continues.
A lack of physical activity also has a negative impact on how long we live. That is why one of the simplest ways to improve health is to increase the amount of movement in everyday life. The expert advises starting with two basic elements: reviewing your diet and increasing your physical activity.
"Let’s take a close look at how we eat. Let’s plan a healthy plate and adapt it to our age and state of health. And the second thing: let’s start moving," Mordaka urged. "Exercise is the best medicine," the expert concluded.
According to World Health Organization guidelines, adults should engage in at least 150 minutes of moderate physical activity per week. This does not have to mean intensive workouts; it can be brisk walking, cycling or other forms of moderate exercise.

Yemen displacement tops 200,000 amid funding shortages, says UN
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
13:48:51 UTC
22:48:51 KST

Ikram Kouachi
07 October 2026•Update: 07 October 2026
More than 200,000 people have been forced from their homes in Yemen since fighting began, with displacement accelerating sharply in recent weeks amid dangerously low funding, the UN migration agency said Wednesday.
The figure makes up more than 33,700 households, according to the latest data from the International Organization for Migration.
Nearly all of the people tracked have been displaced since Sept. 1.
“People are running for their lives and finding nowhere safe to go,” the agency's Director General Amy Pope said.
“They need a roof, food and safety today. Our teams are on the ground, but the funding is not. I am asking donors to act now, because every day of delay costs lives,” he said.
The scale of displacement has risen rapidly.
In mid-September, 76,000 displaced people were recorded. That figure exceeded 145,000 by the end of the month.
Displacement now spans 10 governorates, with the flashpoint province of Taiz the hardest hit, accounting for 57% of those displaced.
Taiz was followed by Lahej, Aden, Abyan, and Hudaydah.
Crisis spills across Yemen's borders
The crisis is also spilling across Yemen’s borders, with more than 3,700 people fleeing by sea to Djibouti.
Many arrive exhausted aboard overcrowded boats with little food or water, while families often leave with almost nothing.
Many make the journey at night, carrying whatever they can, with most of those arriving being women and children.
“Every day our teams meet families who have lost everything,” Pope said. “We know what they need. We know how to deliver it. What we lack is the means to reach them all.”
The most urgent need is shelter, cited by 35% of displaced people. Food follows at 33%, while 22% identify cash assistance as their most urgent need. One in 10 say protection is their primary need.
Relief stocks are running low as humanitarian needs grow faster than available resources.
The UN agency called on the international community to provide immediate funding to enable humanitarian partners to save lives in Yemen.
Yemen has been engulfed in conflict since the Houthis seized the capital Sanaa and several provinces in 2014, prompting a Saudi-led Arab coalition to intervene in 2015 in support of the internationally recognized government.

BERLIN, Oct. 7 (Xinhua) -- German industrial output rose 2 percent in August from the previous month, official data showed Wednesday, although a renewed decline in auto production and persistent weakness in key industrial sectors pointed to an uneven recovery.

Data from Destatis showed renewed weakness in Germany's key automotive sector, where production fell 5.4 percent month-on-month in August. Citing the country's automotive association VDA, Destatis said the decline partly reflected factory holidays, which were more heavily concentrated in August this year than in 2025.
"There can be no talk of a broad upswing in industry," said Jupp Zenzen, economic expert at the German Chamber of Commerce and Industry (DIHK).
Despite a slight recent increase, industrial production was still marginally lower than a year earlier, while output in energy-intensive industries had fallen to its lowest level since the end of 2023, Zenzen added.
Carsten Brzeski, global head of macro at ING Research, said the latest data showed Germany had carried some positive economic momentum into the third quarter, but cautioned that turning it into a sustainable recovery would require significantly more policy action.
"To fundamentally bring the German economy back on a sustainable growth path, the economy still needs more reforms that improve international competitiveness," Brzeski said, adding that the measures announced so far would not be enough. ■

Chinese scientists develop rice's full-lifecycle cell atlas
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
21:48:13 CST
22:48:13 KST

HAIKOU, Oct. 7 (Xinhua) -- Chinese researchers have developed the world's first three-dimensional spatiotemporal cell atlas that tracks the entire growth lifecycle of rice.
The landmark findings, published online Tuesday in the international journal Cell, resolve long-standing bottlenecks in observing and understanding how rice cells grow, divide and coordinate to shape the crop.
Led by Yazhouwan National Laboratory based in south China's Hainan Province, a consortium of 12 research institutions, including Chinese biotech firm BGI-Research and Huazhong Agricultural University, built a 3D spatiotemporal cell atlas covering rice's entire journey, from seed germination to flowering and grain filling. The resource supports future efforts to improve grain quality, according to the team.
Using the widely cultivated japonica rice variety Zhonghua 11 as the research subject, the scientists integrated self-developed spatial omics, single-cell omics and high-throughput sequencing technologies to build a comprehensive rice cell atlas.
Covering 10 types of rice organs and tissues and 61 continuous developmental stages, the atlas is built on more than 850,000 high-quality single-nucleus datasets and over 340,000 spatial data units. The team precisely identified and annotated 119 cell types and 133 cell subtypes, successfully matching each cell's molecular features with its spatial location and dynamic changes across growth stages.
The high-resolution atlas enables researchers to visually and systematically observe how different rice cells collaborate and self-organize to form a complete plant, offering an unprecedented tool for decoding rice developmental mechanisms.
To further support global rice research, the team also developed a single-cell foundation model for rice, which enables efficient identification, comparison and reuse of massive omics data, providing vital technical support for identifying key functional genes and advancing innovative, precision rice breeding research. ■

Feature: At 39, Djokovic turns back the clock in Beijing
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
21:48:05 CST
22:48:05 KST

by sportswriters Hu Jiali and Jiao Ziqi
BEIJING, Oct. 7 (Xinhua) -- "Let's go, Novak! Let's go!"
The chant rose from Diamond Court as Novak Djokovic returned to Beijing, 11 years after his previous appearance at the China Open.
The 39-year-old Serbian went on to lift the trophy for a record seventh time, battling physical discomfort and tough opponents along the way.
"I had a year filled with struggle and challenges, not many great results after the finals of Australian Open," Djokovic said after the final. "I didn't know how I was going to feel because the American swing was terrible in terms of feeling on the court, health-wise and physically."
Those concerns were evident from the opening rounds.
Djokovic received medical treatment during his first two matches, including for an abdominal issue during his second-round comeback against China's Bu Yunchaokete. He eventually overcame Bu 4-6, 7-6 (2), 6-2 after nearly three hours.
In the quarterfinals, top seed Alexander Zverev blasted 19 aces and took the opening set. Djokovic, however, stayed in the match and turned it around, breaking the German late in each of the final two sets to win 4-6, 6-4, 6-4.
"I managed to kind of push through and really dig deep, turned some matches around," Djokovic said.
The semifinal against Daniil Medvedev brought another test. Djokovic saved 16 of the 18 break points he faced before taking a 7-5, 5-3 lead. The match then ended abruptly when Medvedev was defaulted after hitting a ball into the stands and striking a spectator.
It was an unusual way to reach the final, but as Djokovic said, "winning against three top-10 players in a matter of three days back-to-back is a great achievement."
"I'm very proud of the achievement here," Djokovic said. "It came at the best possible time as a confidence booster, as a proof that I can still play on the highest level."
The final brought another physical twist. Against Australia's Alex de Minaur, Djokovic won a tight opening set 7-6 (3), before De Minaur retired after the first game of the second set because of injury.
The title was Djokovic's first of the season and the 102nd of his career. It also extended his perfect China Open record to 34-0 and his run of winning at least one ATP singles title to 21 consecutive seasons.
For Djokovic, however, the significance of Beijing went beyond the court.
"Beijing was always my happy place. It continues to be," he said.
From the opening round to the final, every Djokovic night session at Diamond Court was sold out. Fans traveled from different parts of China to see him play, while others waited outside his hotel, the tennis club and the stadium for a chance to meet him.
"I did not expect the stadium to be full for every single match from the first round and people to be so joyful and passionate about me being here, playing in front of them," he said. "It's just the best crowd support I have anywhere outside of Serbia, that's for sure, is here in China."
"I try to always remind myself how special that is, how privileged I am," he added. "Yeah, that also explains why I play well in China, why I feel good, because people make me feel like I'm Chinese, like I'm playing at home."
He even joked that there was only one thing missing.
"The only thing I need is to learn Chinese and get the passport and we are good."
Staying at a hotel near the Summer Palace, Djokovic made a daily habit of walking or running around the historic site. "No joke. I've been going there every single day."
At 39, Djokovic is no longer planning too far ahead. Recovery, physical condition and form have become part of every decision.
"I am not making plans for so much ahead right now," he said. "I'm kind of more really following of how I'm feeling, how good I'm playing, how quickly I'm able to recover."
Yet there is one commitment he was willing to make.
"I will be back in Beijing, for sure," Djokovic said. "I would also like this unbeaten run to stay unbeaten. It would be nice." ■

Countries should move beyond discussions about what "should be done" and translate scientific findings into concrete policies, policies into project investments, and investments into tangible and measurable results, he said.
The Pre-COP31 opened in Nadi on Tuesday, serving as an important ministerial-level political consultation mechanism ahead of the COP31.
It aims to help countries test ideas, understand each other's priorities, identify areas of disagreement and find possible landing zones for agreement before formal COP negotiations begin.
This year's meeting brought together ministers, government representatives, and climate negotiators from more than 50 countries and regions. Feature: A century on, new voices: Young Chinese singers join Turandot production in Malaysia
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
21:48:03 CST
22:48:03 KST

Three young students (L) from the vocal music department of the Wuhan Conservatory of Music attend a rehearsal in Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia, on Oct. 1, 2026. (Photo by Chong Voon Chung/Xinhua)
KUALA LUMPUR, Oct. 7 (Xinhua) -- In a rehearsal room, the melody of the Chinese folk song Jasmine Flower, or Mo Li Hua in Chinese, tinged with an exotic charm, fills the air. Several young Chinese faces move among performers from Malaysia, Britain, Australia and other countries, repeatedly adjusting their positions, vocal delivery and movements.
This is Kuala Lumpur City Opera in Selangor, Malaysia. In recent days, three young students from the vocal music department of the Wuhan Conservatory of Music, majoring in bel canto, have been rehearsing alongside opera singers from several countries for Italian composer Giacomo Puccini's classic opera Turandot.
This year marks the 100th anniversary of the premiere of Turandot in Milan. Set in an imagined ancient China and incorporating Chinese musical elements including Jasmine Flower, the Western operatic classic will be staged in Kuala Lumpur in mid-to-late October. It will also mark the first time in 20 years that the opera returns to the Malaysian stage in a large-scale, full production.
"An environment like this provides us with rich and diverse opportunities for cultural exchange," said baritone Zhang Enrui, who plays Ping.
Speaking about his experience rehearsing with performers from different countries, Zhang said that his first experience taking part in an overseas opera production had given him a more tangible understanding of what it means to live in a "global village," while deepening his appreciation of cultural exchange and mutual understanding.
Turandot is a three-act opera adapted by Puccini from a fairy-tale play and was the final opera of his career. Set in an imagined ancient China, the story follows the romance between Princess Turandot and the Tartar prince Calaf. The opera is renowned for its sweeping orchestration, large-scale choral scenes and the iconic tenor aria Nessun dorma.
Over the past century, the work has been reinterpreted by artists around the world. For the young Chinese singers taking part in this production, performing Turandot offers an opportunity to explore the European artistic imagination of "China" from a century ago, while experiencing its local interpretation in Malaysia and bringing to it the perspectives and expression of young Chinese artists today.
Jin Junxian, who plays Pang, said that Turandot presents an "Eastern world" imagined by European artists in the early 20th century, while also incorporating distinctive elements of Chinese culture.
"For example, the melody of Jasmine Flower is very well known and truly distinctive," he said. "But today, as young Chinese people of the 21st century taking part in this production, we also hope to showcase the spirit and vitality of our generation."
To prepare for the production, the students had already undergone several rounds of intensive rehearsals in China. After arriving in Malaysia, however, they faced a new dimension to their work: performers from different countries have different interpretations of the characters, the music and even the movements on stage.
"Everyone has a different perspective, but art can serve as a bridge for communication," Jin said. Performers from different cultural backgrounds can shape their characters according to their own understanding while learning from one another's approaches, he said. "This kind of cultural exchange can deepen our understanding of the opera."
Han Longxi, the young Chinese singer playing Pong, has had a similar experience.
"I find it quite amazing. Music knows no borders," he said. Compared with some of the versions he had encountered previously, Malaysian performers approached certain characters in a livelier way, which made him realize that "there are other ways of presenting them."
The arrival of the young Chinese singers has also brought a fresh "chemistry" to the Malaysian performers. Gui Foo Chen, the Malaysian opera singer playing the male lead Calaf, said the production brings together performers of different nationalities, ages and professional backgrounds, including experienced singers as well as young students.
"I just heard them sing, and they really sang very well," he said, adding that he looked forward to seeing new sparks emerge as the different performers came together on stage.
The cross-border collaboration came about somewhat by chance. Danny Cheng Heng Siong, co-founder and executive producer of Kuala Lumpur City Opera, said the production team had faced casting challenges while preparing Turandot. Last year, he worked with Liu Gang, an associate professor at the Vocal Music Department of the Wuhan Conservatory of Music and a baritone singer. This led him to an idea: Why not use the opportunity to bring young Chinese singers into the production and combine opera with cultural exchange?
"I asked Professor Liu Gang whether he could select and train outstanding students to take on these roles and then bring them to Malaysia," Cheng said. The idea quickly received a positive response, eventually bringing three students from the Wuhan Conservatory of Music to Malaysia to take part in the production.
In his view, having a Chinese conservatory undertake the initial preparation before the young performers travel to Malaysia and integrate into the wider production is itself a form of cultural exchange built on professionalism and trust.
"Perhaps in the future, we could also send our young singers to China for exchanges," he said, expressing hope that the collaboration would serve as a starting point for more exchanges among young artists.
Back in the rehearsal room, the music continues and rehearsals go on. A century ago, Puccini drew inspiration from a melody from the distant East and incorporated Jasmine Flower into Turandot. A century later, several young singers from China are standing in a rehearsal room in Malaysia, joining artists from different countries in bringing the work to life.
"We hope the audience response will be enthusiastic. When the curtain finally rises, we hope audiences will see more than just the revival of a classic opera," Zhang Enrui said. As young Chinese singers, he said, they hope to "bring new energy" to the production and encourage more Malaysian audiences to enter the theatre and experience how opera performers from different countries come together to tell this story. ■

South Sudan's road to elections remains uncertain
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
13:45:00 UTC
22:45:00 KST

South Sudan on an uncertain path to first election
October 7, 2026
South Sudan has scheduled a general election for December 22, the first since the country gained independence from Sudan in 2011.
But as preparations lag, political tensions are high and the debate has intensified since President Salva Kiir dissolved the transitional unity government on September 22 to form a caretaker administration.
Denis Logonyi, a journalist based in the capital of South Sudan Juba, said that many in the country, which has seen violent power struggles and political instability, were not only concerned about the logistics of the polls.
"People have different views on these elections," he told DW. "You hear discussions in political circles and on social media, but ordinary people are not talking much about them."
One voter complained that "there has been no voter education, no voter registration, and only a few months remain." Another told DW that while South Sudanese citizens were eager for a credible election process, the country was not adequately prepared.
Food prices are rising, civil servants are not being paid, and displaced people are struggling, they said.
Politicians admit to 'obstacles' but agree to adhere to election timeline
Political parties have until October 22 to present their manifestos and register.
On October 7, South Sudan concluded a two-week Inter-Party Dialogue, in which 39 parties participated, discussing key issues ahead of the election.
Logonyi said that some civil society groups had been left out of the dialogue, which was initiated by President Kiir.
Minister of Cabinet Affairs Martin Elia Lomuro outlined a few of the challenges: "Delayed funding could severely affect civic education and election infrastructure. There is a need for a clear legal framework to govern the participation of the country's administrative areas. The three administrative areas are not clearly reflected in the National Election Act, which is necessary for the election outcomes to be accepted."
He added that "a credible election requires security readiness throughout the entire cycle — including campaign rallies, polling stations, voting, counting, and results transmission. The unified security forces have not yet been fully deployed."
According to Albino Akol Atak, the deputy rapporteur of the Inter-Party Dialogue and minister of humanitarian affairs and disaster management, the parties unanimously agreed to adhere to the election timeline. "The election train has left the station, and it has no reverse gear," he said. "We are trying to smooth the pathway for this train to arrive on December 22, 2026, without obstacles."
Meanwhile, Changkuoth Bichok Reath, the secretary general of the South Sudan Opposition Alliance (SSOA), said he strongly believed "that successfully conducting the election on December 22 requires coordinated, inclusive action from all national institutions, political parties, security actors, civil society, and other stakeholders."
He added that "given the limited time remaining, priority should be placed on resolving outstanding legal issues and ensuring constructive dialogue among political actors. Furthermore, political parties must be funded to meet key requirements, because a lack of funding will only draw us backward."
South Sudan's checkered election history
South Sudan has endured decades of conflict, from long wars that preceded independence to a devastating civil war that erupted just two years after it became a sovereign state.
Power-sharing transitional governments have been in place under fragile peace deals, including the Revitalized Peace Agreement of September 2018. Elections have repeatedly been planned then put off.
Armed opposition groups remain active, and many citizens fear political tensions could trigger renewed violence.
"The absence of [former Vice President] Riek Machar from the political process is a major concern," Logonyi said. "If there is to be an election or a meaningful political dialogue, many believe he has to be part of it."
In 2018, a power-sharing deal that saw Kiir become president and Machar — his long-time rival and main opposition leader — vice president briefly stabilized the country.
However, tensions between the two men persisted and in March 2025, Machar was placed under house arrest. He was later put on trial for offences that include treason and murder.
Key conditions for elections not fulfilled yet
"The government has demonstrated that it is keen for the election to happen," said Wambui Njehu Nzigo, an analyst with Control Risks, a global consulting firm. "But there are important processes that have not yet taken place."
The lack of voter registration is among the biggest concerns. "If elections are to take place soon, you would expect there already to be a voter register," Nzigo said. "There is very little time for that to happen."
Security reforms required under the 2018 peace deal have not yet been finished. These include the unification of armed groups to create the conditions for a stable transition.
Analysts have long warned that if these key issues are not addressed the legitimacy of any election would be undermined.
"The elections would be taking place in an environment where there is still active fighting in some parts of the country," Nzigo said. "The fact that the main opposition leader is under house arrest raises questions about whether this will be a true competition."
According to Logonyi, civil society groups are calling for greater dialogue, political inclusion and protections for journalists and activists before the vote is held.
Ongoing flooding could interfere with the vote
Futhermore, South Sudan faces severe flooding, a displacement crisis and food insecurity. This could make it difficult for some citizens to reach polling stations, Nzigo said.
For those displaced by conflict, there's uncertainty over how they can register and cast their ballots.
Experts warn that a vote without broad participation could lead to a disputed outcome and instensify conflict.
Regional organizations such as the African Union and international partners are expected to continue encouraging an inclusive political process.
Analysts argue that the focus should be not only on ensuring elections take place, but also on creating conditions that make them credible.
For many South Sudanese, the choice is clear: elections alone won't guarantee stability.

Iraq looks to Syrian route for crude exports to bypass Hormuz: Report
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
13:44:48 UTC
22:44:48 KST

Mücahithan Avcıoğlu
07 October 2026•Update: 07 October 2026
Iraq is preparing to export crude oil by truck through Syria to the Mediterranean, seeking an alternative to the Strait of Hormuz as shipping risks threaten a key source of government revenue, according to Bloomberg News.
Yousef Qiblawy, CEO of the Syrian Petroleum Company, told Bloomberg that Baghdad requested help exporting crude alongside existing fuel oil shipments, with an agreement between the governments nearing completion.
He said the first crude convoys could arrive by mid-October and that his company planned to provide storage tanks at Baniyas before the oil is loaded onto vessels for onward export.
The proposed route would expand an existing overland corridor carrying Iraqi fuel oil to Syria’s Mediterranean coast.
Qiblawy said about 1,000 trucks currently transport fuel oil daily, each carrying 220 barrels. He anticipated a similar or larger fleet for crude.
At those figures, 1,000 trucks would carry 220,000 barrels a day, underscoring the route’s potential and the logistical demands of moving substantial oil volumes by road.
A Syrian official reporting separately confirms extensive Iraqi oil transit operations. Ahmed Qubbaji, the petroleum company’s deputy chief executive for transportation and storage, told state news agency SANA on Sept. 27 that between 1,000 and 1,200 trucks crossed Syrian territory daily.
The corridor also carries energy supplies in the opposite direction. Syria began transporting imported gasoline from Baniyas to Iraq in late September under a renewable three-month agreement, with plans to increase traffic to 200 trucks daily.
Beyond trucking, the countries are pursuing a larger export outlet through rehabilitation of the Haditha-Baniyas pipeline, historically linked to the Kirkuk-Baniyas route.
SANA reported in July that Syria signed agreements with Iraq and an international consortium to advance the project, targeting a capacity of 2 million barrels daily. That remains a planned capacity rather than an operating export route.

Missed approach: Russia falls back on 1940s “corn duster” aircraft after new projects stall
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
13:43:14 UTC
22:43:14 KST

Russian officials plan to resume production of the An-2 — a light “corn duster” aircraft designed in the 1940s — after years of failed attempts to develop a replacement for the Soviet biplane. Previously, officials tried to fill the gap by certifying the Il-114-300, but that aircraft turned out to be completely unfit for real-world operation — in addition to being too expensive for customers. As for the flagship projects MC-21 and SJ-100, even if they can be certified and put into production, they risk ending up as commercial failures.
A U-turn
News of Russia’s intention to resume production of the legendary Soviet An-2 aircraft, better known as the “corn duster” or “Annushka,” was delivered without fanfare in early September at the Eastern Economic Forum (EEF) in Vladivostok.
Yuri Trutnev, Deputy Prime Minister and presidential envoy to the Russian Far East Federal District, called for prioritizing the creation of new aircraft: “I might not call this solution ideal, because it’s a bit of a shame that we flew the An-2 for 60–80 years and are now bravely going back to it.”
With poorly concealed sarcasm, Trutnev added: “If our wonderful aircraft designers can’t offer us anything but the An-2 right now, then let’s keep flying the An-2.”
Citing data from the Ministry of Industry and Trade, Putin’s envoy specified that deliveries of “fully updated An-2s” would begin in 2027, and in 2028 the aircraft would be outfitted with the new domestic VK-800 engine (whose certification is still in the works).
Earlier, the presidential envoy repeatedly demanded that the price of new aircraft be cut significantly, talked about project failures, and criticized manufacturers for missing delivery deadlines. In this context, his new comment might be perceived as yet another round in a years-long dispute.
But the Ministry of Industry and Trade gave a new dimension to his words. Deputy minister Gennady Abramenkov claims that several companies are working in parallel to update the An-2, with Rusaviaprom, the Motor Aircraft Repair Enterprise, and Technoregion all being involved. What’s more, there are plans to use the new VK-1600S engine, which the Ministry of Industry and Trade has commissioned from ODK-Klimov (and which for now exists only as a mockup), with the VK-800 (currently in testing) seen as an additional option.
“We’re creating conditions to offer light aircraft developers and manufacturers the tools they need. In particular, we’re exploring the option of preferential loans through the Industrial Development Fund to help set up aircraft production,” Abramenkov explained, adding that domestically produced engines and avionics are not ready for production. Separately, Abramenkov noted that Russia has around 700 An-2 aircraft currently in storage, and that many of them have used up only a third of their service life.
Russia has around 700 An-2 aircraft currently in storage, and many of them have used up only a third of their service life
Remarkably, the launch of a serious civil aviation project was met with studied indifference from First Deputy Prime Minister Denis Manturov, Minister of Industry and Trade Anton Alikhanov, and Rostec CEO Sergei Chemezov (who is connected to the project through Rostec affiliate ODK, which is developing a new engine for the An-2). It is quite possible that, without Trutnev, the An-2 would not even have come up at the EEF — and for a good reason.
Interest in the “corn duster” arose some time ago. Russia’s air fleet is aging, and the cost of maintaining the An-2, which is essential for connecting remote regions to the mainland, is rising as repairs are needed more often and as replacement parts become more expensive. The planes do not only operate in the Far East, but serve remote communities and rotational work camps all across the country. The alternative to light transport aircraft is helicopters, but they are far more expensive and their use would thus need to be heavily subsidized.
Notably, the revival of the An-2 has nothing to do with Russia’s military needs, which are much better handled by helicopters. The Ural Civil Aviation Plant (UZGA) had specifically been preparing to localize the four-seat Diamond DA42 for the Defense Ministry, but the project, which relied heavily on imported parts, was quickly scrapped once the full-scale war began.
The pride of Soviet aircraft manufacturing
The light multipurpose transport aircraft An-2 is rightly considered one of the triumphs of Soviet civil aviation — the industry’s equivalent of the AK-47 for gunmakers, or the “bukhanka” all-road vehicle for automakers. The An-2 was produced for more than 60 years straight, a fact that put it into the Guinness Book of World Records (even if it was later surpassed by the American C-130).
The “Annushka” was designed by Oleg Antonov’s team at the Novosibirsk OKB-153 design bureau of the Chkalov Plant. After making its first flight on Aug. 31, 1947, it entered service in 1948 and was put into mass production in 1949 in Kyiv.
The aircraft’s first customer was the USSR Ministry of Geology, but other industries soon discovered it too. Depending on the modification, the aircraft was used for agricultural work, civilian and military transport, paratrooper drops, and as a training plane.
Production in the USSR ended in 1971 (a total of roughly 5,000 aircraft were delivered), but by then foreign plants had also begun manufacturing the model. Between 1960 and 2002, Poland built roughly 12,000 An-2s with various designations, and the aircraft was successfully exported to 26 countries around the world. In addition, just under 1,000 An-2s (Y-5) were produced under license in China under the names Fongshou-2 and Yunshuji-5.
The An-2’s advantages include the ability to take off and land on short, unprepared runways, including agricultural fields and unpaved areas, while the biplane’s low speed is offset by an exceptionally stable design. Together, these qualities made the aircraft versatile and simple to service and operate.
The An-2 biplane’s low speed is offset by its exceptional stability
But even Soviet engineers acknowledged that by the 1980s the design had become outdated — primarily due to very high fuel consumption and by the necessity to carry out overly frequent repairs. There were plans to update the aircraft in the 1980s, but they were thwarted by problems with engine production. After the Soviet Union collapsed, new aircraft were no longer a priority.
Independent Russia eventually resumed the attempts to replace the An-2. In 2010, Novosibirsk-based Chaplygin Siberian Aeronautical Research Institute (SibNIA) proposed an extensive modernization of the An-2 called the TVS-2MS — a model that would be fitted with an American Honeywell TPE-331-12 engine.
As of mid-2025, 28 such aircraft had been produced, but the process is slow due to difficulties with engine supplies via parallel imports, along with a lack of government attention and funding.
Keeping it simple
SibNIA was competing with the Ural Civil Aviation Plant (UZGA) for the right to create a replacement for the “corn duster.” The institute proposed the TVS-2DTS (LMS-9) model — a far more thorough modernization of the An-2 that is effectively an entirely new aircraft with an American engine, an all-composite carbon-fiber structure, and a brand-new fuselage and cockpit. Aircraft assembly was expected to begin at the Ulan-Ude Aviation Plant in 2021.
However, in 2019, the Ministry of Industry and Trade announced that UZGA had won the competition with its LMS-901 project. The ministry explained the rationale for creating such an aircraft as being to reduce the An-2 fleet and replace the Soviet model with an aircraft built on advanced scientific and technical solutions.
The Ministry of Industry and Trade chose the LMS-901 because many of the technologies its competitor relied on were no longer available domestically (a fact SibNIA openly acknowledged). Originally, it was the TVS-2DTS that was supposed to receive the name Baikal, but when the Ministry of Industry and Trade revised its plans, the name passed on to UZGA’s model instead.
A Baikal prototype for static testing was expected to be built by the end of 2020, and then in December of that year, Putin claimed the aircraft would appear in 2021. A year later, Denis Manturov, who was then Russia’s Minister of Industry and Trade, promised that the Baikal would make its first flight in early 2022.
In June 2022, the government approved the Comprehensive Program for the Development of the Air Transport Industry, which envisioned the production of 14 Baikal aircraft in 2024, with output set to reach 25 aircraft a year starting in 2026. In 2023, Prime Minister Mikhail Mishustin assured the public that the Baikal would be certified before the start of 2024, and that its trial operation would follow shortly thereafter.
The quiet failures of parallel projects
Although Russian officials presented the Baikal as the An-2’s main successor, this characterization is not entirely accurate: while the Soviet aircraft can carry 12 passengers, the replacement carries only nine.
For routes with heavier passenger traffic, there were plans to produce the L-410, which has a capacity of 15 to 19 passengers. However, the project was abandoned due to the fact that the aircraft was a licensed copy of the Czech L-410 fitted with American engines, and in 2023, operation of this foreign aircraft in Russia began to be halted due to a lack of components. Building such aircraft without deliveries from abroad is impossible.
As a result, this aircraft did not make it into the 2024 edition of the industry development program, replaced instead by the mysterious Russian-Belarusian Osvei project (LMS-192), also with a capacity of 19 seats. The two countries’ governments signed an agreement on its production in April 2024.
Airlines were scheduled to receive the first 20 aircraft in 2027, but in August of 2026, Manturov reported that an Osvei prototype would appear only the following year, and that the certification process would not begin until 2029.
In that same address, Manturov admitted that the aircraft is still at the stage of working design documentation development, meaning its estimated cost remains unclear for now. At a meeting with Russia’s first deputy prime minister, Belarusian leader Alexander Lukashenko publicly pointed to certain “misunderstandings” in the project’s implementation that need to be resolved “so that Osvei actually happens.” He did not specify the nature of the misunderstandings, but the project was fraught with tension right from the start.
Yuri Zakharchenko, executive director of the RKK-Nauka professional association, described Osvei as an aircraft unsuited to Russian conditions. The aircraft’s design includes retractable landing gear not built for soft, low-bearing-capacity ground — which makes it poorly suited for the unpaved runways typical of Russia’s remote airfields.
Osvei’s retractable landing gear is not designed for unpaved runways, making the aircraft unsuited to Russian conditions
If such a landing were attempted, mud would get into its gear wells and freeze, meaning that at some point the landing gear might fail to extend for landing, causing a crash. Under those circumstances, pilots end up flying with the gear down at all times, reducing the aircraft’s efficiency and driving up fuel consumption.
Zakharchenko’s comment was published on the NSN portal, but it survives only in news aggregators. Both the original source and the outlets that reprinted it soon deleted the material without explanation.
Certification sleight of hand
The failure of the “corn duster” replacement project — which had looked like the simplest task facing Russia’s aviation industry — needed to be offset somehow, at least in Putin’s eyes. The only aircraft suited to that role was the Il-114-300, a modernization of a Soviet turboprop designed to carry 68 passengers. On June 5, 2026, the aircraft ceremonially received its Rosaviatsia type certificate at the St. Petersburg International Economic Forum (SPIEF).
“The awarding of type certificates is another step by our country toward technological sovereignty in a complex and strategically important industry — aviation. Another aircraft in the lineup is ready to carry passengers. And another engine is ready to lift modern airliners into the sky,” Sergei Chemezov said at the ceremony.
The event was presented as a breakthrough: Russia’s first new airliner was finally complete. However, in order to create that impression, the manufacturer and the government had needed to resort to a whole array of tricks — after all, the aircraft will not be ready for real-world operation for at least several more years.
The state-controlled outlet Vedomosti found that the certificate issued for the Il-114-300 only permits the aircraft to operate within a very narrow temperature range — from minus 9 to plus 25 degrees Celsius, whereas its predecessor could operate from minus 30 to plus 45. The aircraft is also barred from flying in icing conditions or thunderstorms, and from operating on wet or muddy runways. In other words, the aircraft is not fit for regular flights at all, since in real-world conditions a dry runway can never be guaranteed.
The Il-114-300 is not fit for regular flights, since it can’t take off in icing conditions, thunderstorms, or from wet and dirty runways
Ilyushin managing director Daniil Brenerman announced that test flights are continuing and that the approved operating conditions will soon be expanded. To that end, the Il-114-300 was sent for testing in Uzbekistan and Yakutia. In August, Rostec and the Ministry of Industry and Trade assured the public that the tests had been a success and that the approvals would follow shortly. However, there was no official explanation for the expedited certification in June or the lack of approval to fly in low-temperature conditions after tests in Yakutia in February 2026.
In July, the government allocated 2.6 billion rubles ($30.4 million) to finish work on the first three aircraft. Notably, that same amount had previously been the estimated cost of a single aircraft. In terms of value, that works out to roughly a third of the work still unfinished for each of the three certified airliners.
In July, Anton Alikhanov was still promising that the first aircraft would be delivered to the customer in August, with the remaining two following in October-November. Nevertheless, by September the timeline had already shifted noticeably. The 2nd Arkhangelsk United Air Detachment will now only receive the first aircraft by the end of 2026.
A stillborn project
The 2nd Arkhangelsk United Air Detachment (Arctic Airlines) handles passenger transport in the north of European Russia, flying passengers to remote settlements using An-2 aircraft and Mi-8 helicopters exclusively. In other words, it does not even have routes on its schedule where an aircraft with capacity for up to 68 people could be used.
Meanwhile, according to Brenerman, no Il-114-300 production is planned for next year, and only six aircraft will be built in 2028. Ilyushin plans to eventually reach an output rate of 12 aircraft a year, and only then will the Far Eastern airline Aurora — the main prospective customer operating routes suited to an aircraft with these parameters — finally get the chance to receive them.
Another crucial question regarding the aircraft’s parameters is whether it can take off and land on unpaved surfaces. In September, Alikhanov said the necessary testing had not even begun, and that the plant has produced only a prototype of a shield to protect against loose ground debris. The plan is to obtain approval for operation under such conditions in 2028. However, the professional community has expressed some well-founded concerns about these ambitions.
The Il-114-300 is a low-wing aircraft — meaning its engines hang close to the ground. Officials call it a replacement for the aging Soviet An-24 and An-26 (and its popular foreign counterparts, the French ATR-72 and Canadian Bombardier Dash 8). While all of these aircraft are certified for unpaved runways, all of them are also high-wing, with the engines farther from the ground and better protected from mud and debris.
Among low-wing aircraft, the Il-114-300 is comparable in its parameters to the Swedish Saab 2000, which entered service in 1994 and has a capacity of up to 58 passengers. The aircraft did not gain commercial success, so its production stopped as early as 1999. Incidentally, one of the Swedish model’s shortcomings was its unsuitability for unpaved runways.
The remaining operators of the Saab 2000 explicitly attribute this limitation to its wing design, meaning the Russian manufacturer needs to solve — within a mere two years — a problem that Western market leaders never even set out to fix: how to protect the engines of a low-wing aircraft from damage during takeoff and landing on unpaved runways.
Russian designers must figure out how to protect the engines of a low-wing aircraft from damage on unpaved runways
Nevertheless, Alikhanov says that the Il-114-300 already surpasses all its Western counterparts in terms of flight performance, as Rostec and the Ministry of Industry and Trade are announcing agreements with three Indian companies to supply 105 new aircraft (even if the parties to these memoranda turned out to be highly dubious organizations that do not operate scheduled flights). Moreover, while one of the companies does offer charter flights on light aircraft and helicopters, the other two have not even started flying.
The only official offering a more sober view on Russia’s aviation agenda is Deputy Prime Minister Trutnev, who in early 2026 demanded that the price of the Il-114-300 be lowered. At the Eastern Economic Forum he stated the problem in simple terms: at a price of over a billion rubles ($11.7 million), an aircraft with these technical characteristics is of no use to the Far East because the investment would never pay off. “This is fantasy, this is absolute madness, no economy could withstand this,” Trutnev fumed.
The project was stillborn for other reasons too. Even before the full-scale invasion of Ukraine, Russia was developing the Il-112V military transport aircraft. Both projects were tied to the same engine — the TV7-117ST-01 by ODK-Klimov. After an Il-112V crashed in August 2021 and the investigation showed the crash had been caused by critical engine problems, work on both aircraft was suspended.
In January 2023, the TV7-117ST-01 engine received its type certificate, but only one of the projects in which it was involved was allowed to continue. Instead of the nearly finished Il-112V — which was only waiting on the engine — the decision was made to create an entirely new aircraft, the Il-212, using PD-8 engines that had originally been intended for the SJ-100. That decision required more time — as well as significant financial expenditure, design changes, and new testing.
The most probable rationale for this choice could be that the TV7-117ST-01 engine was unsuitable for the tasks at hand. In that case, the Il-114-300’s oddly poor performance — noticeably worse than its Soviet predecessor’s — can be explained by a problematic powerplant.
Airliners from generations past
The focus on the Il-114-300 is explained by the fact that the flagship MC-21 and SJ-100 projects are approaching a dead end. Officials have even stopped explaining the delays in their certification. Most recently, they’ve been pushed back to 2027, and it is already clear that these aircraft will be extremely weak competitors commercially — that is, if the projects are ever actually completed.
The official reduction in flight range of the MC-21 from a planned 5,100 kilometers to 3,800 kilometers at the same payload (same number of passengers, same fuel tanks) indicates that fuel consumption turned out to be one and a half times higher than planned. This makes the aircraft uncompetitive on the global market right from the outset. And that’s assuming it even makes it into serial production, which is far from guaranteed.
Similarly, the mass production of the modernized Tu-214 is not coming together as planned either. The Kazan Aviation Plant (KAZ) keeps missing deadlines, producing no more than one aircraft a year despite the benefits of financial infusions and experience. Sources at the plant cite a shortage of qualified engineers and difficulties producing components, as well as the need to retool production capacity.
In the case of the SJ-100, serious problems are evidenced by the suddenly emerging plans to replace the Franco-Russian SaM146 engine with the PD-8 for the SSJ-100 model. In 2022, Manturov explained that putting new Russian engines on old aircraft would be too costly and impractical.
In 2025, Rostec also complained about excessive work costs, and in 2026 it became known that the re-engining would be mass-scale and would cost at least 115 billion rubles ($1.3 billion) — a very conservative estimate, according to industry sources. That works out to 2.3 billion rubles ($27.1 million) each across 50 planes. In effect, they will try to replace the engines on every airframe that still has enough flight life left.
The effort does not suggest building new aircraft simultaneously with re-engining old ones, as there will not be enough PD-8 engines for both. ODK’s capacity is limited to 30 engines a year, and each airframe requires two of them. Therefore, the SSJ-100s will have to be re-engined instead of producing the SJ-100s. This decision can only be justified by serious problems with the import-substituted version.
Still, even the PD-8 engine itself is not without its problems. Although the powerplant received an operating certificate, the Ministry of Industry and Trade struggles to even name the engine’s price, encouraging interested parties to wait for serial production to begin.
This uncertainty suggests a host of unresolved issues. Meanwhile, Aeroflot is admitting in advance that it may not be able to re-engine the SSJ-100 without government subsidies. And if the money does not come, company CEO Sergei Alexandrovsky states, the aircraft will have to be written off.
Crucially, a civil aircraft engine is one of the most complex devices in the world. Neither China nor Japan produces its own engines, even though both countries have spent more than a decade trying to create them. Only Europe, the United States, and Canada possess the necessary technology, and the whole world buys engines from them. Soviet engines were far less efficient (higher fuel consumption, more frequent servicing needed), so they were abandoned across every aircraft class at the first opportunity.
All bluster
Officials traditionally compensate for failure with bombastic statements, and true to form, Vladimir Putin claims that Russian aircraft are on par with the world’s best — or even superior in a number of respects. Manturov, for his part, assures that the Il-114 “turned out, in terms of its characteristics, better than its direct counterpart — the European ATR-72.” SuperJet program director Alexander Dolotovsky goes even further, calling the SJ-100 the best offering in the world in the segment of aircraft carrying up to 100 passengers. United Aircraft Corporation chief Vadim Badekha asserts that Russia is the only country capable of producing civilian aircraft relying solely on its own resources. And Russian Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova went so far as to claim that Russian engineers have supposedly recreated critical technologies and production chains in the aviation industry and are now ready to become suppliers to the whole world.
Maria Zakharova claims that Russian engineers have recreated critical aviation technologies and are now ready to supply them to the whole world
In reality, the Russian government is preparing an update to the comprehensive aviation development program by the end of the year. They intend to cut production plans and stretch out timelines. Meanwhile, Russia’s Transport Ministry is searching the globe for ways to lease aircraft on a “wet” basis — that is, along with a crew. Among other things, Transport Minister Andrei Nikitin confirmed that one such offer has been made to Vietnam. Against this backdrop, Vladimir Putin is showing India not the actual MC-21 aircraft but only a mockup of it at the BRICS summit — just as was done 14 years ago.
As of the fall of 2026, the entry into service of Russian aircraft at airlines has been pushed back to 2028 — certification, as the Il-114-300 example showed, has become a PR move rather than an actual sign that real completion of work on the aircraft has been achieved. The future of the three projects (Baikal, Ladoga, Osvei) remains murky. The MC-21 and Il-114-300 — based on their announced specifications — will turn out to be commercial failures even if they do make it into production in a few years. And the SJ-100 is already losing to its predecessor before it’s even certified.
Still, as long as Russian airlines manage to keep their fleets running through parallel imports, manufacturers and officials can keep up the illusion of an imminent breakthrough.
