Circuit court orders DJ to serve actual prison time in rape sentence
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
13:43:00 UTC
22:43:00 KST

Circuit court orders DJ to serve actual prison time in rape sentence
A court has overturned a ruling ruling that suspended a three-year rape sentence, imposed on a DJ, ordering him to serve the term in prison.
The Tallinn Circuit Court overturned the earlier county court ruling on Meelis Eskola, known as DJ Cityflash,
He was convicted in April 2025 of raping a young mother at a party venue in Paide in May 2022. Eskola denies the charges.
The circuit court, the second tier of the Estonian court system and which acts as an appeal court, overturned that part of the Pärnu County Court's earlier ruling that left the three-year prison sentence for rape conditionally unenforced.
Under the circuit court's fresh ruling, Eskola must serve real prison time.
The county court had found Eskola guilty of rape and sentenced him to three years in prison with a four-year probation period. He was also ordered to pay €7,000 in non-pecuniary damages to the victim.
Eskola's appeal went through all three court tiers. The Supreme Court upheld his conviction and the civil claim in May of this year, but sent the question of enforcing the sentence back to the circuit court for reconsideration.
Since the conviction and civil claim had already entered into force, the circuit court considered the case solely on the basis of a prosecutor's appeal, which sought Eskola's incarceration.
Under Supreme Court precedent, actual imprisonment is the rule for more serious crimes, and deviation from that — e.g. a suspended sentence — is justified only in exceptional circumstances, which must be apparent both in the act committed and in the offender's personhood, the court found.
The circuit court found that the arguments presented by Eskola's defense — such as the one-off or unintentional nature of the act — did not constitute exceptional circumstances. The court noted that the rape provision itself provides for liability for a single act, and that the county court's assessment of the offense as "average" in fact confirms the absence of exceptional mitigating circumstances.
Given the gravity of the crime — raping the victim in several ways, exploiting another individual's helpless state and using violence — and the absence of mitigating circumstances, the court found no basis for more lenient treatment of Eskola than imprisonment.
The circuit court's ruling can be appealed to the Supreme Court within 30 days.
Eskola stood trial on charges under the Penal Code provision on rape. According to the charge, he had sexual intercourse against the victim's will, at a party venue in the central Estonian town of Paide, on May 7, 2022.
According to the indictment Eskola dragged the victim, a young mother, into a rest room and threw her onto a pool table. The victim attempted to push him away but was unable to, after which the defendant had intercourse with her, causing her pain during the act, pressing a pillow into her face and pulling her hair. An examination found bruises and abrasions on the victim's body, including on her legs, buttocks and genitals.
According to the charge, Eskola committed the rape with violence. He also exploited the fact that the woman was unable to resist due to alcohol intoxication and being physically weaker than him.
In the civil claim, the victim sought non-pecuniary damages from the defendant at the court's discretion.
At the first two court levels — Pärnu County Court and Tallinn Circuit Court — Eskola was acquitted. On November 1, 2024, however, the Supreme Court overturned that acquittal too, finding among other things that the courts had given the defendant's statements preferential treatment to the victim's and had not compellingly justify their positions.
The Pärnu County Court found Eskola guilty on April 8, 2025 and sentenced him to three years in prison, suspended with a four-year probation period, and ordered him to pay €7,000 in non-pecuniary damages.
On November 25, 2025, the Tallinn Circuit Court overturned that sentence and the damages award, imposing one year and six months, suspended with a two-year probation period, and €2,500 in damages.
On May 29 this year, the Supreme Court overturned the circuit court's ruling and reinstated the county court's, except for the part suspending the sentence, and sent the case back to the Tallinn Circuit Court for reconsideration in a different composition.

Sri Lanka arrests ex-first lady in graft probe
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
13:42:41 UTC
22:42:41 KST

Sri Lanka's anti-graft authority has arrested former First Lady Shiranthi Rajapaksa over allegations that her charity misused donations collected for a children's hospital.
President Anura Kumara Dissanayake's government has revived long-dormant graft investigations involving members of the once-powerful Rajapaksa family, which dominated Sri Lankan politics for nearly two decades.
The 73-year-old wife of former president Mahinda Rajapaksa was arrested in Colombo on Wednesday and driven to the Commission to Investigate Allegations of Bribery or Corruption (CIABOC) for further interrogation.
"The arrest is in connection with her Siriliya Saviya Foundation," a CIABOC official told reporters at the Rajapaksa home in the capital.
She is due to appear in court later, when a magistrate will decide whether she can be released on bail.
Her lawyer, Manoj Gamage, told reporters that she denied the allegations and will contest charges of misappropriating donations raised for charity.
The CIABOC also arrested the former head of a state-owned bank in connection with a 10 million rupee donation ($30,000) to the charity, the agency said.
Pradeep Kariyawasam, the then-chairman of the National Savings Bank, was accused of donating public funds to the Rajapaksa charity without following proper financial regulations.
Shiranthi Rajapaksa travelled to Singapore on September 16 for medical treatment and was served with a summons at Colombo airport to provide a statement to police about her charity.
She flew back on Monday after filing a court petition seeking to prevent her arrest, but the hearing for anticipatory bail was fixed for October 12.
Police said the authorities wanted to question Shiranthi Rajapaksa over the $30,300 of donations collected by her Siriliya Saviya charity for a PET scanner intended for a local cancer hospital for children.
Investigators told a court that the scanner had already been donated by the Chinese government, but the charity allegedly continued to solicit donations and misused the funds.
Shiranthi Rajapaksa has denied any wrongdoing, saying the money had not been misappropriated.
Other members of the family have also faced legal troubles.
Not just corruption
The former first lady's eldest son, opposition lawmaker Namal Rajapaksa, is in remand custody over allegations linked to a 2013 Airbus aircraft deal signed during his father's presidency.
The Rajapaksa family has consistently denied the corruption allegations and dismissed the cases against them as politically motivated.
Mahinda Rajapaksa served as president from 2005 to 2015 and remains one of Sri Lanka's most influential political figures, despite the decline in the family's fortunes since mass protests ousted his brother, Gotabaya Rajapaksa, from the presidency in 2022.
The family is not, however, only accused of corruption but also infamous for stoking anti-Muslim sentiments in Sri Lanka.
In 2019, Easter Sunday bomb attacks killed nearly 270 people months before the presidential election, and the Rajapaksas were quick to jump the gun on Muslims.
Gotabaya Rajapaksa declared his candidacy soon after and went on to win the November vote in a landslide after promising to stamp out “terrorism”.
Sri Lanka's criminal investigators later arrested the country's former intelligence chief in connection with the bombings for conspiracy and aiding and abetting the Easter Sunday attack.

Russia’s international reserves fall 4.85% in September to $731.76 bln
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
13:42:35 UTC
22:42:35 KST

MOSCOW, October 7. /TASS/. Russia’s international reserves stood at $731.76 bln as of October 1, 2026, down 4.85%, or $37.262 bln, from the beginning of September, the Bank of Russia said.
As of October 1, 2025, Russia’s international reserves stood at $713.301 bln.
Russia’s foreign currency reserves decreased by $5.386 bln in September 2026 to $430.153 bln, down 1.24%, while the value of monetary gold in the reserves fell by 9.56% to $301.607 bln.
International reserves are highly liquid foreign assets held by the Bank of Russia and the Russian government. They consist of foreign currency assets, special drawing rights, the reserve position in the International Monetary Fund, and monetary gold.
Western countries imposed sanctions on the Bank of Russia after Russia launched its special military operation in Ukraine. In addition to freezing Russia’s gold and foreign exchange reserves, they banned all transactions related to the management of the Central Bank’s reserves and assets, as well as transactions with any legal entity, organization, or body acting on behalf of or at the direction of the Central Bank.

Why are the “very expensive” lawyers of the doctors from Odrex accused of medical negligence missing court hearings?
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
16:42:21 EEST
22:42:21 KST

Why are the “very expensive” lawyers of the doctors from Odrex accused of medical negligence missing court hearings?
Kyiv • UNN
The hearing in the case concerning medical negligence by Odrex doctors Vitaliy Rusakov and Maryna Bielotserkovska was postponed again on October 7. The oncologist’s defense lawyer asked to adjourn the hearing because she was participating in another court proceeding.
The hearing in the case concerning medical negligence by doctors at the private Odrex clinic has been postponed once again. This time, at the request of the lawyer for the accused oncologist, Maryna Bielotserkovska, who was occupied with another court proceeding. At the same time, one of the defense lawyers for the accused surgeon Vitalii Rusakov also failed to appear in court. The next hearing is scheduled for October 8, UNN reports.
Details
The accused surgeon Vitalii Rusakov, speaking about his defense, emphasized that his lawyers are "very expensive." The cost of legal services, of course, has no procedural significance whatsoever. However, against the backdrop of defense lawyers’ failures to appear and court hearings being postponed due to their involvement in other proceedings, a question arises: why can even an expensive defense team not organize its work so that the criminal case does not stall for months because of clashes in the lawyers’ schedules?
It cannot be claimed that the regular failures of the doctors’ defense lawyers to appear are a pre-planned tactic. At the same time, Andrii Misiats, acting head of the High Qualification and Disciplinary Commission of the Bar, drew attention to the systematic nature of the postponements.
A combination of failures to appear may indicate not an accidental violation, but a certain pattern of conduct by the lawyer and their bad-faith attitude toward their professional duties
7 of the 13 September hearings did not take place or were postponed
However, this situation has become more of a rule than an exception. In September alone, seven of the 13 hearings were postponed or did not take place due to motions from the defense.
Presiding Judge Viktor Chaplytskyi deemed the reasons for the lawyers’ failures to appear at the hearings unjustified and sent the relevant information to the Qualification and Disciplinary Commission of the Bar. It must now assess whether the defense lawyers’ actions show signs of a disciplinary offense.
Will the delay in the Odrex case have consequences for the lawyers?16.09.26, 09:01 • 37087 views
The October 1 hearing was also telling: the court was considering extending the restrictive measures imposed on Rusakov and Bielotserkovska. Neither defendant’s lawyers were present, so, in order not to postpone the hearing, the court appointed defense lawyers.
Lawyers interviewed by UNN do not rule out that the combination of the defense’s procedural actions could eventually lead to the expiration of the statute of limitations. In that case, even if the doctors’ guilt is proven, they may be released from criminal liability and avoid the punishment prescribed by law.
Reminder
The Kyivskyi District Court of Odesa is hearing the criminal case involving doctors at the private Odrex clinic, Vitalii Rusakov and Maryna Bielotserkovska. They are charged under Part 1 of Article 140 of the Criminal Code of Ukraine — improper performance of professional duties by a medical worker.
According to the investigation, during the treatment of businessman Adnan Kivan, the medics’ actions or inaction may have led to the development of postoperative complications and sepsis, which, against the background of the patient’s oncological disease, may have caused his death. The court must provide the final assessment of the evidence, the medics’ actions, and the question of their guilt.

Higher fuel costs reshape US used-car market as EVs outperform
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
13:41:10 UTC
22:41:10 KST

Mucahithan Avcioglu
07 October 2026•Update: 07 October 2026
Higher fuel costs are reshaping the US used-car market, supporting electric and fuel-efficient vehicles while weighing on larger models as overall wholesale prices decline, according to Cox Automotive data released Wednesday.
The Manheim Used Vehicle Value Index fell to 205.9 in September, down 0.6% from a year earlier and 1.1% from August, after adjustments for vehicle mix, mileage and seasonality.
Electric vehicle values, however, rose 4.3% annually and 0.6% monthly. Non-electric vehicle values fell 1.6% from a year earlier and 1.7% from August. Compact cars also showed resilience, while pickups and SUVs weakened.
The divergence extends beyond electric vehicles. Cox's quarterly presentation showed that non-electric models achieving at least 40 miles per gallon gained 9.9% in wholesale value since January, while vehicles achieving less than 15 miles per gallon lost 15%.
That gap highlights how running costs are increasingly influencing vehicle valuations as buyers face pressure on household budgets.
Diesel vehicles accounted for a little more than 3% of wholesale inventory, but the supply rose to 39 days, 27% higher than a year earlier, as record diesel prices weighed on demand. EV supply declined as sustained high gasoline prices encouraged buyers toward more efficient vehicles.
Cox lowered its forecast for year-end wholesale price growth to 0.2%, from 2% projected in July, citing higher fuel costs, rising interest rates and broader economic pressures.
Growing supply adds to used-EV market
Used retail EV sales reached a record 124,000 vehicles in the third quarter, up 11.4% annually, although they still represented only 2.8% of used retail sales.
More electric vehicles are also returning to the market after leases expire. EVs are expected to account for about 16% of off-lease supply in the second half of 2026, compared to 10% in the first half.
Despite weaker valuations, Cox slightly raised its forecast for total used-vehicle sales this year to 38.5 million, suggesting demand remains resilient even as buyers become more sensitive to ownership costs.

How divorce works in Denmark, and what international couples need to know
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
13:40:00 UTC
22:40:00 KST

Getting divorced is almost never an easy experience, especially when it happens abroad. There may be unfamiliar rules to understand, documents to deal with and, for international couples, questions about which country has the authority to handle the case in the first place.
In Denmark, divorce can be relatively straightforward when both spouses agree. But for internationals, the process can become more complicated depending on where the couple lives, their connection to Denmark and whether children, residence rights or other cross-border issues are involved.
Over the years, stories of divorces involving foreign residents that turned into long and difficult legal disputes have also attracted attention. In some cases, the divorce itself is only one part of the problem, with disagreements over children, housing or the right to remain in Denmark creating further complications.
So how does divorce actually work in Denmark, and what should international couples know before starting the process?
Who handles it
All separation and divorce cases in Denmark begin with the Agency of Family Law, known in Danish as Familieretshuset, the public authority that handles family law matters.
Couples must submit an application to the agency, normally online. People who cannot complete the application themselves online can ask their municipality’s Citizen Service or the Agency of Family Law for help.
If both spouses agree to divorce and agree on the terms, they can normally apply for an immediate divorce without first going through a period of separation.
The situation changes when one spouse does not agree.
You do not need your spouse’s permission to separate
Under Danish rules, either spouse has the right to a legal separation.
A person does not have to give a reason or provide proof to obtain one, even if the other spouse wants to remain married.
Separation means the spouses remain legally married but live apart. It can give them time to decide whether they want to resume their marriage or proceed with a divorce.
A divorce does not happen automatically after separation. The spouses must apply again if they want the marriage formally dissolved. If both agree, they can begin divorce proceedings at any point after the separation.
If one spouse still opposes the divorce, the other has the right to divorce after six months of separation.
Some divorces can happen immediately
A spouse can also seek an immediate divorce without the other person’s agreement in some circumstances.
These include adultery, violence, including psychological violence and sexual assault, bigamy, the abduction of a child shared by the couple, or cases in which the spouses have lived apart for at least two years because of disagreements.
These grounds can allow the divorce to proceed without the usual six-month separation period. Couples with children under 18 can also divorce immediately if they agree, although additional steps apply as part of the process.
What couples have to agree on
When a couple applies for separation or divorce, two issues may need to be settled as part of the case: whether one spouse should pay maintenance to the other, and who should remain in a home rented jointly by the couple.
If the spouses agree on these points, they normally do not need to attend a meeting to negotiate the terms.
If they cannot agree, they must attend a meeting with the Agency of Family Law. A case officer can explain the consequences of the separation or divorce and the disputed terms can be addressed there.
If the couple still cannot agree, the Agency of Family Law can make a decision on those issues. This means more case processing and can make the divorce or separation take longer.
Other matters are handled separately. Child support and the division of property, for example, are not settled as part of the divorce or separation application itself.
Can foreigners divorce in Denmark?
For international couples, getting married in Denmark does not automatically mean they can also get divorced here.
As a general rule, Denmark must have a sufficient connection to the couple before Danish authorities can handle the case.
A divorce or separation can, for example, be processed in Denmark if the spouse responding to the application lives in Denmark.
It may also be possible if the spouse applying lives in Denmark and has lived here for the past two years or has previously lived in the country.
Other situations can qualify as well. A Danish citizen living abroad may in some cases apply in Denmark if their citizenship prevents them from bringing the case in the country where they live.
A case can also be handled when both spouses are Danish citizens and the other spouse does not object to Denmark dealing with it.
Another possibility is when a divorce application is based on a legal separation granted in Denmark within the previous five years.
There is also a specific rule for some same-sex couples. Denmark can process a separation or divorce when the couple married in Denmark and neither spouse lives in a country whose laws on same-sex marriage correspond to Danish law.
But simply having held the wedding in Denmark is not enough.
That distinction can be particularly important for international couples who travelled to Denmark specifically to marry but live elsewhere.
Applying from abroad
People who believe their divorce or separation can be handled in Denmark must submit an application to the Agency of Family Law and pay the required fee.
The agency does not begin processing a case until the fee has been paid.
According to the fee information provided for 2025, an application for either separation or divorce cost DKK 875. A meeting to negotiate disputed terms cost an additional DKK 2,150.
The fees are not refunded, regardless of the outcome of the application.
People paying from abroad who do not have a Danish CPR number, Denmark’s personal identification number, can identify themselves using their full name, date of birth and, if possible, their postal address.
For international couples, the first step is therefore not simply deciding whether they want a divorce, but establishing whether Denmark is legally able to handle the case.
The hidden traps of separation as an international
Many internationals going through a divorce report problems.
Henriette Johnsen, a UK-trained Danish psychotherapist and couples counselor who works with internationals in Denmark and abroad, says the problems she sees in her practice can be divided into different categories, and that having children can make a major difference.
“It varies very much depending on whether you have children or not,” Johnsen said. “Without children, it is easier to reset your whole life, unless you are on a spouse visa. In that case, you need to look at whether you are still allowed to stay.”
Having children can make separation considerably more complicated.
“It could be that one of the two parents wants to relocate to their home country with the children,” she said. “And this could go against The Hague Convention that says that you cannot remove children under 16 from their habitual residency without the consent of the other parent.”
That can leave an international parent in an extremely difficult position.
“You could be stuck in a country that is not your own, without being authorized to work, with non-recognised qualifications, or without knowing the language,” Johnsen said.
She pointed to GlobalARRK, a UK nonprofit that supports parents facing these situations around the world.
“They support stuck parents around the world in these difficult and challenging situations,” she said.
Money can become another major problem after separation.
“Then there are the financial problems, because you might not be able to have your own income, but at the same time you might not have the money or opportunity to relocate abroad, and you can end up in poverty,” Johnsen said.
“We see stress, anxiety and depression in the parents, and this could also affect the children.”

French wine harvest set to hit historic low
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

French wine harvest set to hit historic low
- France’s wine harvest is set to fall to a historic low of about 35 million hectolitres, down 2% on 2025 and 14% below the 2021-2025 average, the French agriculture ministry said.
- Heatwaves and a 1.9% fall in vineyard area drove the decline, though recent rain helped. Bordeaux and the south improved, but Champagne, Burgundy and Beaujolais were hit hard.
- Growers reported very uneven results across regions. Some saw good quality, and officials said the harvest was in “excellent health” with no major fungus or moisture disease.
AI generated
PARIS – With its wine industry hit by a swathe of summer heatwaves, France is set to see the 2026 harvest hit a historic low.
At around 35 million hectolitres, the total harvest would be down 2% on a mediocre 2025 yield and 14% below the 2021–2025 average, according to estimates published on Oct 7 by the French ministry of agriculture.
According to the International Organisation of Vine and Wine (OIV), which tracks global statistics on wine production and consumption, France had already recorded in 2025 its lowest production since 1957.
This latest decline is down not just to hot weather, which has been slightly mitigated by recent rainfall, but also a reduction in cultivated areas – pared back 1.9% in the past year.
Some southern areas, already battered by the heat in 2025, have nonetheless seen production rise in 2026, notably Bordeaux.
There, despite a 5% decrease in cultivated areas, production is set to come in up 10% on 2025, albeit still 11% below the 2021-2025 average.
For the south-west, the rise is around 12%, essentially a return to the previous four-year average.
The Champagne region fared less well as growers had to harvest exceptionally early after the extreme heat sped sugar build-up – and hence natural alcohol production.
The harvest there wrapped up in September 2026 for the first time with production down by half on 2025 and the five-year average.
In Champagne, producer Claude Mandois reported harvesting three-quarters of an average yield in terms of volume, although “in terms of quality visually and in terms of taste, we had an exceptional harvest”.
In Burgundy and the Beaujolais region, production is projected to be 30% lower than the five-year average.
“It’s a level of heterogeneity I’ve never experienced before,” said Jerome Despey, chairman of the wine advisory board at the public agency FranceAgriMer and a winegrower in the southern Herault department.
In the south, “we’ve seen that vines have been more resilient to the climate”, he said, with previous intense heat spells causing growers to adapt vineyard management practices such as largely leaving leaves to protect the grapes.
Southern regions also benefited from May rainfall.
The ministry and the industry emphasised overall the “excellent health” of the harvest, free of fungi and other moisture-related diseases. AFP

- The review of compliance with biosafety requirements in the Irkutsk Region has been completed, with no emergencies involving work with pathogenic microorganisms identified.

- The watchdog emphasized that a special set of measures had been implemented in response.

CIS foreign ministers adopt joint statement supporting steps to prevent arms race in outer space
Unknown

2026-10-07

22:39:09 KST

Burc Eruygur
07 October 2026•Update: 07 October 2026
Foreign ministers of the Commonwealth of Independent States (CIS) member states on Wednesday adopted a joint statement supporting steps to prevent an arms race in outer space.
The statement was adopted following a meeting of CIS foreign ministers in Turkmenistan’s Avaza National Tourist Zone on the Caspian Sea coast, ahead of a leaders’ summit of the organization scheduled for Friday.
According to a statement by the CIS, the document declares that its member states conduct activities related to the exploration and use of outer space “in the interests of developing international cooperation and mutual understanding, and maintaining international peace and security.”
“The CIS member states express serious concern regarding the real prospect of an arms race in outer space and its transformation into an arena of military confrontation, which undermines global stability,” it quoted the statement as saying.
It added that the parties believe a ban on the deployment of any weapons in space, among other measures, could help prevent the emergence of a serious threat to international peace and security.
The joint statement was among a number of documents adopted at the CIS Council of Foreign Ministers meeting, attended by the top diplomats of Azerbaijan, Belarus, Kazakhstan, Russia, Tajikistan, Turkmenistan and Uzbekistan.
Armenia’s deputy foreign minister and Kyrgyzstan’s first deputy foreign minister also attended the meeting.
The CIS was established in 1991 following the dissolution of the Soviet Union to promote cooperation in economic, political and security affairs.
Its full members are Armenia, Azerbaijan, Belarus, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Moldova, Russia, Tajikistan and Uzbekistan. Turkmenistan holds associate membership.
Moldova suspended its participation in CIS meetings in 2022.

MOSCOW, October 7. /TASS/. China may strengthen its position in the Arctic over the next 10 years and become an prominent economic and technological player in the region by taking part in resource development, logistics and research programs, Director of the Arctic Interdisciplinary Research Center at HSE University, senior researcher at the Institute of China and Contemporary Asia of the Russian Academy of Sciences and Arctic Council goodwill ambassador Irina Strelnikova told TASS.
"Over the next 10 years, China may consolidate its position and, as an major economic and technological player, take part in resource development, logistics and research programs -- essentially what it is doing now. However, it certainly will not become a full-fledged Arctic state," she said.
According to Strelnikova, China is already the most active and influential non-Arctic player in the region. Economic interests and investments in regional projects play a major role in expanding its presence. "China is investing more than any other non-Arctic country at present. It has many projects, including projects with Russia. These include energy and logistics projects, as well as Arctic Express No. 1, which we launched, and many logistics cooperation agreements between New New Shipping and Rosatom," the expert said.
Strelnikova also pointed to China’s involvement in major energy projects, the development of its own icebreaker fleet and its observer status in the Arctic Council, which Beijing has held since 2013. According to her, this allows China to monitor the regional agenda and participate in individual projects, including at the council’s working-group level.
At the same time, the expert stressed that the Arctic is not a priority foreign policy area for Beijing. China’s capabilities are also limited by its lack of Arctic territories and its dependence on cooperation with traditional Arctic states.

'Great moral courage: The French thought they knew de Gaulle and suddenly realised they didn't'
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
13:36:04 UTC
22:36:04 KST

'Great moral courage: The French thought they knew de Gaulle and suddenly realised they didn't'
To display this content from YouTube, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.
Issued on:
François Picard is pleased to welcome Julian Jackson, the British historian, author and Emeritus Professor of Modern French History at Queen Mary University of London. His biography of Charles de Gaulle laid the foundation for France's two-part biopic, "De Gaulle: Résistance". And on the heels of that surprise box-office hit, Jackson's book is now available in French as "La Chute : France, 1940". He takes us back to the occupation of Paris and the extraordinary collapse of France in the summer of 1940.
Rather than treating defeat as inevitable, Jackson focuses on the uncertainty that gripped France as the war continued to spread across Europe. His book does not shy away from the scale of the disaster: "It was a disaster. It was a catastrophe. It was a dramatic military catastrophe."
And it was from this catastrophe that Charles de Gaulle emerged as a veritable standard-bearer: the symbolic and political embodiment of Free France. He refused to accept that France had been definitively defeated. Yet just weeks later, in August 1940, the Vichy regime condemned this "renegade" French general in exile to death, in absentia.
We must also see this through the prism of the wartime alliance. Until Pearl Harbor, the United States was not prepared to come to the military aid of either Great Britain or France. Washington initially recognised the Vichy regime as France's official governing authority, while de Gaulle was regarded as a dissident general in exile. Even after the fall of France, American policy remained cautious about openly backing the Free French.
That makes de Gaulle's emergence all the more remarkable. He was not simply fighting the Germans. He was trying to persuade Britain, the United States and the wider world that France had not ceased to exist as a political and military power.
His evolution is inseparable from the extraordinary relationships he forged, and fought over, with the Allied leaders around him. With Winston Churchill, there was admiration, rivalry and mutual dependence: two formidable personalities who needed one another, but who rarely saw the future in quite the same way.
With Franklin D. Roosevelt, the relationship was even more complex. After the fall of France, the United States effectively wrote France off as a serious power. De Gaulle, however, insisted that France would not disappear from the map of history.
That refusal became central to his political identity. "We're not going to be written off" is, in many ways, the story of de Gaulle's emergence: a determination to preserve France's place in the war and, ultimately, to restore its place in the postwar world.
It also helps explain why de Gaulle continues to fascinate audiences today. The French may think they know him, but the films and the renewed interest in his story reveal how much more complicated the man was than the familiar national icon. Jackson takes us beyond the myth of de Gaulle.
Read moreSummer blockbuster: Why the French keep coming back to Charles de Gaulle
De Gaulle's subsequent role was equally uncertain. He had to persuade Britain, confront the United States, navigate his often difficult relationship with Churchill and Roosevelt, and convince a world that had largely written France off that Paris still had a crucial role to play on the world stage.
Seen from this perspective, Jackson tells a story about how political possibilities can survive even after apparent defeat, and how one extraordinary individual attempted to turn what seemed like a finished history back into an unfinished one.
Ultimately, Jackson would like us to take away a simple but powerful understanding: history reminds us that the future is not written in advance. He firmly believes we must resist the temptation to see the present through the certainty of hindsight, because what appears inevitable after the fact was often profoundly uncertain to those living through it.
As he puts it: "It's hard enough to explain what happened, let alone say what's going to happen next."

Lithuanian business representatives warned Wednesday that restrictions on hiring foreign workers could weigh on the country's economic growth, according to broadcaster LRT.
"Most of us probably encounter migrants in one way or another, so we look at this issue through the lens of personal experience and perception," said Zivile Simonaityte-Vasiliauskiene, an economist at the Lithuanian Confederation of Industrialists.
She made the remarks at a news conference attended by various business groups and representatives.
Around 227,000 foreign nationals reside in Lithuania, about 108,000 of whom hold temporary residence permits allowing them to live and work in the country.
"When we discuss migration, we very often focus on the quota, thinking that all migration is about the migrant quota, which is almost 25,000," Simonaityte-Vasiliauskiene said.
Lithuania currently has a quota system for workers arriving from non-EU countries.
"If we count only foreign nationals who have residence permits in Lithuania on various grounds, the quota accounts for about 10%," Simonaityte-Vasiliauskiene said.
"It is certainly a small part of overall migration, just one way of having legal migration to Lithuania, but certainly not the main one," she added.
Simonaityte-Vasiliauskiene said foreign nationals working in Lithuania generated 45% of GDP growth between 2019 and 2024, citing Bank of Lithuania calculations.
Maintaining the quota would mean lost GDP growth and tax revenue for the state, she warned.
"So, this year alone, we estimate that the quota running out before the end of the year could potentially mean about €100 million ($112 million) in GDP not being generated in Lithuania," Simonaityte-Vasiliauskiene said.
She warned that the figure could reach as much as €150 million ($168 million) under the worst-case scenario.
Simonaityte-Vasiliauskiene also estimated that quota restrictions could result in between €20 million ($22 million) and €25 million ($28 million) in lost tax revenue this year.
She said the impact could be greater in 2027 if the current restrictions remain in place, potentially costing Lithuania around €500 million ($559 million) in GDP and €90 million ($101 million) in tax revenue.

Ukraine’s international reserves fell to $47.1 billion over the month - what are the reasons
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
16:34:44 EEST
22:34:44 KST

Ukraine’s international reserves fell to $47.1 billion over the month - what are the reasons
Kyiv • UNN
Ukraine’s international reserves decreased by 3.2% to $47.1 billion in September. The NBU sold $5.45 billion in foreign currency, while the state made debt payments.
Ukraine’s international reserves stood at $47.1 billion at the beginning of October, decreasing by 3.2% over the month. This was influenced, among other factors, by the National Bank’s foreign currency sales and government debt payments. UNN reports this with reference to NBU data dated October 7.
Details
"As of October 1, 2026, Ukraine’s international reserves amounted to $47,101.8 million, according to preliminary data. They decreased by 3.2% in September. This dynamic was driven by the National Bank’s foreign exchange interventions and the country’s foreign-currency debt payments. These operations exceeded receipts from international partners and the conversion into hryvnia of the currency received under the Ukraine Support Loan program," the statement said.
The current volume of international reserves, as stated, "is sufficient to maintain the stability of the foreign exchange market."
How much was received from international partners
According to the NBU, $890.4 million was transferred to the government’s foreign currency accounts at the NBU through World Bank accounts.
In addition, Ukraine received $3.81 billion from the European Union as part of the defense tranche under the Ukraine Support Loan program.
"These funds are not included in Ukraine’s international reserves due to their limited (targeted) purpose of use. However, if the government sells them to the National Bank in exchange for hryvnias for subsequent use for their intended purpose, international reserves increase by the corresponding amount," the statement said.
As stated, "in September, the government converted $3.81 billion of these funds into hryvnias, which accordingly contributed to an increase in international reserves." "At the same time, it should be taken into account that hryvnia financing from these funds subsequently leads to increased demand in the foreign exchange market, which affects the volume of the National Bank’s foreign exchange interventions," the NBU noted. "Thus, the National Bank’s operations with these funds effectively perform a redistribution function."
How much foreign currency the NBU sold
"In September, the NBU sold $5,449.9 million on the foreign exchange market," the NBU statement said.
How much was paid toward government debt
$195.7 million was paid for servicing and repaying government debt in foreign currency, including:
-  $72.3 million – servicing and repayment of debt to the World Bank; 
-  $8.3 million – servicing foreign currency domestic government bonds; 
-  $115.1 million – payments to other creditors. 
In addition, Ukraine paid the International Monetary Fund $254.3 million.

EU Says Kosovo's Changes To War Crimes Court Law Violate International Obligations
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
13:34:29 UTC
22:34:29 KST

The European Union has expressed "deep concern" over Kosovo's adoption of legislation that seeks to narrow the jurisdiction of a Hague-based war crimes court, saying the changes violate the country's international obligations toward the bloc.
The amendments, approved by parliament on October 6, target the Kosovo Specialist Chambers, which last month convicted former President Hashim Thaci and three other former Kosovo Liberation Army leaders of war crimes.
In a response to RFE/RL on October 7, an EU spokesperson said the legislation "goes against Kosovo's international obligations toward the EU."
"Their current mandate and independence must be fully respected," the spokesperson said. "The Kosovo Specialist Chambers are rendering justice, based on the principle of individual criminal responsibility."
Perparim Gruda, a lawmaker from the opposition Democratic Party of Kosovo (PDK), which initiated the amendments, rejected the EU's assessment.
"I can assure the EU that we are not violating any international obligation with this law," he told a news conference.
Gruda said he had not personally seen the EU statement. He cited European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen's recent remarks in Pristina, which he characterized as affirming Kosovo's right to amend the law.
RFE/RL contacted Kosovo's government about the EU's criticism but had received no response by publication.
During the bill's first reading on October 5, Prime Minister Albin Kurti said his Vetevendosje party considered the changes rushed and had little time to analyze them but would support them nonetheless.
The Kosovo Specialist Chambers declined to comment directly on the legislation.
"The Specialist Chambers is fully focused on implementing its mandate to ensure fair, impartial, and secure judicial proceedings, and to ensure the protection of witnesses and victims," it told RFE/RL on October 7.
The amendments' adoption was part of a last-minute agreement between the PDK and Vetevendosje that also paved the way for Justina Shiroka Pula's election as president on October 7.
The legislation would restrict the court's jurisdiction to offenses directly linked to organ-trafficking allegations outlined in a 2011 Council of Europe Parliamentary Assembly report.
It would also limit jurisdiction to crimes allegedly committed in Kosovo between July 1, 1999, and December 31, 2000, excluding the earlier period beginning in January 1998.
Cases outside that remit would be transferred to Kosovo's regular courts. The amendments also envisage serving sentences in Kosovo and eligibility for presidential pardons.
The PDK introduced the initiative five days after the September 16 verdict. Thaci and Jakup Krasniqi each received 25-year sentences, Kadri Veseli 18 years, and Rexhep Selimi 13 years.
All four were convicted of war crimes and acquitted of crimes against humanity. Organ-trafficking allegations were not part of their indictment. The verdict is not final, and defense teams have announced appeals.
Parliament's approval does not itself overturn those judgments or mean those convicted will be released.
Gruda also said the final amendment sought to reserve constitutional review of the legislation for Kosovo's Constitutional Court in Pristina, excluding the Specialist Chambers' constitutional chamber in The Hague.
Legal experts have warned that changes to the court's mandate could raise constitutional issues and conflict with international obligations.
The EU stressed that the court operates within Kosovo's legal system and is enshrined in its constitution. It urged Kosovo to ensure accountability and justice for victims from all communities.
In an exchange of letters in April 2014 between Kosovo’s then-president, Atifete Jahjaga, and then-EU foreign policy chief Catherine Ashton, Kosovo made a series of commitments concerning the Specialist Chambers.
The exchange formed the basis of the agreement that paved the way for the institution widely known in Kosovo as the Special Court.
Among those commitments was an obligation to consult the EU on any proposed legislative changes affecting the court’s mandate or judicial proceedings arising from investigations by the Special Investigative Task Force (SITF).
Kosovo also committed to allowing the Specialist Chambers and the Specialist Prosecutor’s Office to continue their work until the relevant investigations and proceedings were completed.
Still, the bloc also welcomed Shiroka Pula's election, expressing hope for renewed institutional stability.
"While the EU is available to continue supporting Kosovo, our partnership implies not only shared interests but also shared responsibility," the spokesperson said.

81 US aircraft lost or damaged during Iran war, congressional document shows

Yasin Gungor
07 October 2026•Update: 07 October 2026
At least 81 US fixed-wing, rotary-wing, and uncrewed aircraft were lost or damaged during military operations against Iran, according to a recent report prepared by the nonpartisan Congressional Research Service.
The figures compile operational incidents recorded since Feb. 28 across Pentagon records, US Central Command (CENTCOM) statements, military inspector general findings, and press accounts.
The compilation shows extensive losses across uncrewed platforms, led by 45 MQ-9 Reaper drones and three MQ-1 multi-role craft downed during operations, along with one MQ-4C Triton that crashed in a flight mishap.
Manned combat airframes also sustained substantial hits.
Twelve F-15E Strike Eagle fighters were affected, including three destroyed by friendly fire over Kuwait, one downed over Iran, and eight that suffered light damage during an Iranian missile strike on Muwaffaq Salti Air Base in Jordan before returning to service.
Iranian ground fire damaged an advanced F-35A Lightning II, while two A-10 Thunderbolt II ground-attack jets were lost or heavily damaged.
Support fleets suffered major attrition as well.
Seven KC-135 Stratotanker refueling craft were affected, including one fatal crash in Iraq that killed six crew members and five reportedly damaged on the ground in Saudi Arabia.
One E-3 Sentry early warning plane took a direct hit, two MC-130J special operations transports were intentionally destroyed during a rescue mission, and seven military helicopters, including AH-64 Apache and AH-6 Little Bird models, were lost or damaged.
The disclosures arrive amid soaring financial tolls in the Iran war, which began Feb. 28 with coordinated US-Israeli strikes.
A Lead Inspector General report in September estimated total campaign expenses at $33.4 billion through late June, including $3.7 billion in equipment losses, while the Congressional Budget Office projected hardware replacement costs at up to $3.3 billion.
The Congressional Research Service noted that the number of aircraft may remain subject to revision due to classification, ongoing combat activity, and attribution.

European Commissioner for Defense and Space Andrius Kubilius urged European countries Tuesday to accelerate military mobility, warning that Russia's growing defense spending and production show Moscow is still "not being deterred."
Speaking at the Military Schengen 2026 Conference in Hamburg, Germany, Kubilius said Russia is expected to allocate €180 billion ($201 billion) for its 2027 military budget, about 3% more than this year's allocation.
"In purchasing power parity terms, Russia next year will spend the same amount, or even a little bit more, than all the EU member states," he said.
Kubilius said Russia is also outpacing Europe in defense industrial production and rapidly developing new military technologies, including drones.
"If the day X would come in terms of Russian possible aggression, we need to understand that we will face a battle-tested Russian army with the ability to use 10 million drones per year," he said.
He said this would amount to roughly 30,000 drones a day, adding that Russia is preparing for "a prolonged war and confrontation."
"Our defense readiness has to speed up," Kubilius said.
He stressed that Europe's ability to deter aggression depends not only on defense spending and military procurement but also on its ability to rapidly move troops and equipment across the continent.
Kubilius said military mobility should be treated as an urgent operational requirement rather than a theoretical issue.
He called for an ambitious EU military mobility package that he said should effectively function as a "Military Schengen."
Kubilius said the EU needs to replace the current patchwork of 27 national systems with a single European rulebook for military transport.
Under the proposed system, a single European permit would be valid across the EU and issued within a maximum of three days, he said.
For emergencies, Kubilius said the EU is proposing a new European Military Mobility Enhanced Response System that could be activated by the EU Council.

The governor of Okinawa has demanded that Japan’s central government do more to ensure effective discipline among United States service members on the southern island following the arrest of a US Marine on accusations that he robbed and murdered a local woman.

“I must say past disciplinary measures and human rights education implemented by the US military have not worked at all,” Koja said.
People in Okinawa have long opposed the heavy US military presence on the island and complained about noise, pollution and crime related to bases used by US forces.

The US military in Okinawa earlier announced a 48-hour pause of all military operations for training through Friday, as well as restrictions on the ability of troops to leave their base and a ban on the consumption of alcohol.
Benjamin T Watson, the Okinawa area coordinator and commanding general of III Marine Expeditionary Force, said that the 48-hour period would give commanders the time to lead training with all service members on “standards, discipline, and our responsibilities as members of the Okinawan community”.
The lieutenant general, the most senior US military figure on Okinawa, also announced a 30-day “period of reflection” beginning Friday.
“During this period, we will implement a curfew in which liberty will expire at 2400 for all hands, meaning you must be back on base in your assigned quarters or at your off-base domicile from midnight to 0500,” Watson said.
Takaichi said she regretted the “heinous crime” and shared the outrage.
Noting the new disciplinary measures announced by the US military, Takaichi said she expected the US government to take subsequent steps.
Japan and the US will discuss “how to implement preventive measures that are effective”, she said.
The presence of US troops in Okinawa has repeatedly stirred resentment among residents over issues such as noise, aircraft crashes and the conduct of personnel.
Last year, a Japanese court sentenced a US Marine convicted of choking and attempting to rape a woman in her 20s to seven years in prison.
In 2017, a former US Marine and civilian military base worker was sentenced to life in prison for the rape and murder of a local woman in Okinawa.
The same year, US Forces Japan banned all personnel from consuming alcohol after an intoxicated US Marine crashed his vehicle into a mini-truck, killing its 61-year-old local driver.

AI and the Risk to Democracy
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
13:31:00 UTC
22:31:00 KST

The Diplomat author Mercy Kuo regularly engages subject-matter experts, policy practitioners, and strategic thinkers across the globe for their diverse insights into U.S. Asia policy. This conversation with Dr. Matthew Botvinick – author of “AI and Political Reform: The Risk to Democracy and How to Respond” (Princeton University Press 2026), world-renowned AI researcher and neuroscientist, senior fellow at Yale Law School and member of the technical staff at Anthropic, leading research on AI and the rule of law – is the 529th in “The Trans-Pacific View Insight Series.”
Explain how AI will pose fundamental challenges to constitutional democracy.
We are in a remarkable political moment right now, where two trends are converging. First, AI is generating feelings of insecurity and vulnerability across society. Second, in many democracies, trust in government institutions is low – in the U.S., trust is at historic lows. This is a combustible combination, because it provides ideal conditions for what has been called “the demagogue’s playbook,” where populist sentiment is exploited by political leaders to undermine democracy.
Democracy has always been vulnerable to this risk. The problem now, though, is that AI dramatically raises the stakes. As others have noted, if an authoritarian government can get a foothold, AI makes it much easier for such a government to entrench itself, through surveillance and control of the information citizens can access or share. So the problem is two-fold: AI is creating conditions that can be exploited by aspiring authoritarian leaders, and it is also making available tools that such leaders might use to achieve their goals.
It is important to add that all of this is about risks, not certainties. In fact, if democracies rise to meet the moment, AI might prove to be a benefit to democracy, rather than a detriment. The first order of business is to get our institutional houses in order, instituting government reforms – in emergency law, surveillance law, separation of powers, and free speech doctrines – that increase democratic resilience. If we can do that and make it past the immediate challenge, then we can start thinking about how AI might be used to empower and inform citizens, support democratic deliberation, and enhance government transparency and accountability. If we are careful and strategic, AI may be a boon rather than a curse.
Examine the dynamics between rising powerful AI systems and eroding democratic institutions and implications for political and economic freedom.
Democracy depends on a balance between the power of government and the power of society. What keeps that balance in place is a combination of two things. On the government side, to keep power in check, it must be subdivided. Things must be structured to prevent perfectly coordinated action, which would make abuse of power too easy. This is why we have separation of powers and traditional checks and balances. On the societal side, in contrast, adequate power depends on factors that support coordinated action – the news media, the activities of civil society, a free marketplace of ideas, free and fair elections, and so forth.
All of this means that democracies face danger when (1) the checks and balances within government erode, and (2) when the ability of society to engage in collective action is diminished.
If we are not careful, AI will threaten to do both of those things. My book unpacks this in a number of ways but let me give just two examples. On the government side, AI might over-empower the executive branch relative to legislative and judicial branches, if AI is used to automate perfect obedience to central executive authority. On the society side, the ability of citizens to act in concert could be undermined by AI-enhanced surveillance or propaganda. Society’s power decreases, government power increases, and the balance required for democracy is lost.
Again, these are risks, not inevitabilities. If we act wisely, AI could enhance society’s capacity for collective action, and keep government’s power in balance, through exactly the means I mentioned earlier. But that won’t happen without strategic and proactive interventions.
Analyze how the propagation of AI fuels authoritarianism in China and the United States.
The situation in China stands as a warning of what is possible. China’s use of AI to monitor and control its people has been detailed in excellent books like Josh Chin’s and Liza Lin’s “Surveillance State.” The importance of AI is this: Cheap and ubiquitous sensors, cameras for example, and online activity like that on social networks generate huge amounts of data. Finding the most important bits within that flood of information, and making sense of larger patterns, is a difficult problem. AI solves that problem, matching analytic capacity to the scale of the data. The result is that there is no place to hide from an authoritarian government’s gaze – that, of course, is the situation in China.
The current challenge in the U.S. and other democracies is to leverage AI for legitimate law enforcement and national security needs, without creating tools that are too easy to abuse. The U.S. has a long history of such abuse, running from FDR and J. Edgar Hoover to the activities revealed by Edward Snowden. This time, we must act to ensure civil liberties and the rule of law ahead of such problems, rather than only in reaction to them.
Explain why there can be no genuine AI safety without democracy and the rule of law.
I’m really pleased to see that people across society, people who have no direct involvement in the AI industry, are now talking about AI safety. It’s the right moment for that conversation, as AI systems become more capable and also increasingly permeate our activities, from commerce to education to science and beyond.
But there is one part of the AI safety conversation that is not getting enough public attention, and it’s the one you’ve brought up: the fact that constitutional democracy is absolutely mandatory for AI safety. To see this point clearly, imagine an AI system that is safe in every way: It cannot launch cyberattacks, cannot escape human control, cannot create bioweapons, and so forth. Now picture this AI system in two settings. The first is a democracy with free and fair elections, an open marketplace of ideas, protection of civil liberties, and robust rule of law. The second is an authoritarian state, with none of those features.
In that latter setting, our hypothetical “safe” AI is anything but safe. It will, quite reliably, be used to oppress dissent and enforce political compliance. Again, we needn’t read science fiction to understand what that looks like; it is playing out in many countries today, not only China but also Venezuela, Russia, some Gulf states and elsewhere. The take-home message is very simple: As we pursue AI safety, through technical and regulatory means, we must also work to assure that our democracies are robust and resilient as well. Real AI safety absolutely requires that.
Assess how U.S., Chinese, and other AI companies should be held accountable for the political and economic impact of their technologies on their societies and the global community.
Here I should start by stating clearly that I am speaking in a purely personal capacity, rather than on behalf of Anthropic. That said, I think the answer to the question follows directly from the points I just made about the connection between AI safety and democracy. Any company that purports to care about AI safety – and this includes all of the major AI labs – has a responsibility to use whatever power it has to protect and enhance the health of democracy, both where the company is based and worldwide.
It is important to acknowledge that this responsibility faces the AI industry with an extremely tricky task. Our tendency is to worry about the economic and political power of AI companies, and of course corporate power has been a recurrent problem in the U.S. and other democracies. However, at the same time, people underestimate how vulnerable corporate power – including the power of the AI labs – is to government power, especially when authoritarian tendencies seep into a democracy’s leadership.
Over recent decades, democratic backsliding around the globe has more often involved the subjugation of corporate power by government than the opposite. And when authoritarian-leaning governments bring companies to heel, they gain access to their assets, which here include AI. So we need to watch the relationship between government and industry power very carefully and support the labs when – as we hope – they stick their necks out to defend democratic institutions and the rule of law.

Trading platform Webull's China ties create national security risk, congressional panel finds; stock down nearly 30%
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
13:30:36 UTC
22:30:36 KST

Digital investment platform Webull, which counts 28 million global users, is quietly "tied in structural ways" to China's government, representing a national security threat to U.S. finance, according to a bipartisan congressional panel's findings shared exclusively with CNBC.
The bipartisan House Select Committee on China in its new report being released Wednesday found "a profound gap" between Webull's public marketing as "an American company" and actual control of the St. Petersburg, Florida-based firm.
"Webull's ownership architecture, technical workforce, technology infrastructure, cross-border data routing, corporate financing, and compliance frameworks are tied in structural ways to the People's Republic of China," the committee found.
The panel asserted that national security concerns around the company have "escalated" since October 2025, when Webull began carrying customer cash directly, according to a regulatory filing the panel cited. The committee alleges that creates a "structural exposure of billions of dollars in American capital."
The committee said the company's corporate structure means the firm's "software development, data pipelines, and core engineering operations" are dependent on infrastructure subject directly to Beijing's laws. And those laws in China can compel firms to cooperate with the government in myriad ways, including data transfers.
Webull took issue with the report, saying via a spokesperson, "It is deeply disappointing that the Select Committee published a report containing significant inaccuracies and unsupported conclusions without ever seeking clarification from Webull."
"Webull's U.S. business is conducted from its global headquarters in St. Petersburg, Florida and its office in New York City, while U.S. customer data is stored in the U.S. and access to sensitive customer data is controlled by the U.S.," the spokesperson said via email. "We remain prepared to address any questions directly and with the same transparency we bring to the SEC, FINRA, and regulators worldwide."
Webull's stock plummeted 18% in morning trading.
Rep. John Moolenaar, R-Mich., told CNBC in a statement that Webull's "China-based operations put American investors and their data at risk."
"Using technology providers in mainland China and an opaque China-linked ownership structure, Webull exposes its data to our foremost adversary," said Moolenaar, who chairs the House committee that issued the report. "Investors should heed this information when choosing who they do business with."
Webull, which trades on the Nasdaq stock exchange, says it operates a "global network of licensed brokerages," offering investment services in 18 markets around the globe. The online brokerage says it provides retail and institutional investors with 24/7 access to global financial markets. Users of the platform can trade global stocks, exchange-traded funds, options, futures, fractional shares and digital assets on the service.
Former Alibaba and Xiaomi manager Wang Anquan founded Webull in 2016. Its competitors include Robinhood, Charles Schwab and E-Trade.
The congressional committee, which had requested information from the company in 2024, said Webull represents a national security risk because "critical backend systems, personnel and data flows may remain exposed to the Chinese Communist Party's mandatory intelligence laws and coercive demands."
The committee said in its report that Webull Financial's "intricate corporate and technology framework" is tethered directly to China.
Webull Corp. is a Cayman Islands-incorporated holding company, and the report found it holds $24.6 billion in customer assets. And although the company has a U.S. holding company known as Webull Holdings (US) Inc., the report says the company's technology structure also includes Webull Technologies Pte. Ltd, which is a Singapore-based entity. And the report says Webull uses a mainland China-based subsidiary that supports technology development and platform operations. The company traces its origins to Hunan Fumi Information Technology Co., Ltd., a Chinese company that originally launched the business.
The release of the report comes on the heels of a largely friendly summit between President Donald Trump and Chinese leader Xi Jinping in September, and it comes ahead of further meetings between the two leaders later this year. It reflects concerns on Capitol Hill that the Chinese government could be planting seeds inside the U.S. financial system that could later be used to disrupt the American economy in the event of further conflict.
The committee also alleges Webull misrepresented the number of its China-based employees. In the report, the committee said the company initially told the committee it "does not have any offices or employees based in the PRC," and that "all Firm employees are located in the United States." But the committee says the firm remains operationally concentrated in China, with its mainland subsidiary, Hunan Weibu, growing to 863 employees, or 62% of the company's global workforce.

Madrid versus Latin America: Where is housing more affordable?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
13:30:18 UTC
22:30:18 KST

Homes cost more per square metre in Madrid than in several major Latin American cities, but lower wages in those cities can make renting even less affordable.
For the price of one square metre of housing in Madrid, you can buy almost two in central Mexico City and nearly three in Buenos Aires, Bogotá or São Paulo. But higher property prices do not necessarily mean a heavier burden on local wages.
The key question is how much of their income locals need to spend to afford a home.
If you compare rents with wages, the gap shrinks and in some cases even flips.
In the Madrid region, renting an 80-square-metre flat at December 2025 asking prices would have absorbed 71% of the average gross salary advertised on InfoJobs that year, according to a study by Fotocasa and InfoJobs.
In Buenos Aires, a two-room apartment comes to almost 80% of an average worker's income.
And in parts of the Santiago metropolitan area, anyone on the minimum wage can end up spending between 78% and 96% of their take-home pay on the rent for a small flat.
These measures illustrate the pressure on incomes, although differences in flat sizes, geographical coverage and wage definitions mean they are not directly comparable.
A commonly used affordability benchmark is to spend no more than 30% of income on rent. Taking Spain's modal salary (the most frequently recorded salary, rather than the average), which was €16,520 in 2024, and dividing it by 12 gives approximately €1,377 a month before tax. Applying that benchmark leaves about €413 a month for rent.
At that price, searches on housing portals found nothing available in Madrid. The closest option was €500 for a flat of barely 30 square metres.
The exercise produces virtually the same result in Barcelona. For €500, you can find somewhere noticeably larger than in the national capital, but the search returned just three homes.
How much housing costs in Madrid
Existing homes in Madrid were advertised at an average of €6,471 per square metre in August, according to property website Idealista. This is 2.2% more than a year earlier and below the April peak of €6,619. The slowdown has not reached the cheapest districts: in Villaverde, the borough with the most affordable homes per square metre, prices have jumped 25% in a year.
Rents, meanwhile, show no sign of hitting a ceiling. In September, they set a record of €23.4 per square metre a month, 4.8% more than a year ago. A study by InfoJobs and Fotocasa, comparing advertised salaries with asking rents for an 80-square-metre home, put the cost at 71% of gross pay in the Madrid region in 2025, compared with a national average of 50%.
The Madrid regional government has not designated any “stressed” housing areas under Spain's Housing Act, which allows rent limits in those areas. Other regions, including Catalonia, the Basque Country and Navarre, have used the mechanism.
The national government has also sought to intervene. After parliament rejected two housing decrees on 2 October, the cabinet approved replacement measures on 6 October, including rental contract extensions, limits on annual rent increases and protection against evictions for vulnerable households. The new decrees still require parliamentary ratification.
Madrid versus other Spanish cities
Madrid is not the most expensive provincial capital for buying a home, although it is for renting. According to Idealista, in August San Sebastián was more expensive: €6,680 per square metre versus Madrid's €6,471. Behind them came Palma (€5,835) and Barcelona (€5,440).
For rentals, Madrid led the way with €23.4 per square metre in September, ahead of Barcelona (€20.1) and Palma (€19.6), while the national average was €15.1.
At the same time, Madrid’s asking house prices rose 2.2% in the year to August, the smallest increase among the cities compared here. Seville (11.5%) and Bilbao (10.6%) recorded the largest increases.
Barcelona, a cap Madrid does not have
Barcelona has been officially designated a stressed housing area since 2024.
According to the Catalan Land Institute (Incasòl), the average rent on new contracts was €1,137 a month in the first quarter of 2026, 4.7% less than two years earlier.
The latest asking-rent figures also show a contrast: rents in Barcelona fell 0.8% in the year to September, while in Madrid they rose 4.8%.
Supply remains contested. In the first quarter, 8,156 contracts were signed in Barcelona, 17% fewer than in the same period of 2024.
The regional government counters that the number of active contracts for regular residential rentals across municipalities with rent caps has increased by 20,994 since the measure was introduced. Idealista's spokesperson argues that advertised supply is falling most sharply in the most heavily regulated markets.
Housing costs still stretch wages across Spain
San Sebastián, the priciest provincial capital for buying, has seen advertised rents fall by 2.5% in a year. In Bilbao, advertised rents are down 0.3%, although sale prices are up 10.6%. The city has been declared a stressed area until October 2028.
In Valencia, which, like Madrid, has no declared stressed areas, rents are just 0.5% below their all-time high. Meanwhile, Seville's sale prices, despite a rise of 11.5%, remain 12% below the 2007 peak, when prices reached €3,322 per square metre.
Palma has seen the sharpest rent increase among the cities compared here, with prices up 7.3% to €19.6 per square metre. The Balearic Islands are the most expensive region in which to buy (€5,595 per square metre).
Despite these differences, renting remains expensive relative to wages. According to InfoJobs and Fotocasa, renting an 80-square-metre home at the end of 2025 would have absorbed 76% of the average gross salary advertised on InfoJobs in Barcelona province, 72% in Madrid province and 64% in the Balearics.
Latin America compared: Lower prices, but homes still out of reach
Mexico City is the most expensive Latin American city surveyed in Deutsche Bank’s Mapping the World's Prices 2026 report, which compares 69 cities worldwide. City-centre homes cost €3,441 per square metre, followed by Rio de Janeiro (€3,264), Santiago (€2,507), São Paulo (€2,397), Bogotá (€2,329) and Buenos Aires (€2,328).
These figures are below Madrid’s August asking price of €6,471 per square metre, although the comparison mixes Latin American city centres with Madrid’s city-wide market.
The picture changes when you set rents alongside minimum wages. In Madrid, an 80-square-metre flat at Idealista's average asking rent costs about €1,872 a month, roughly 1.3 times the minimum wage, equivalent to €1,424.50 gross a month when spread over 12 payments. In Mexico City, the average rent for a two-bedroom flat of 65 square metres is about 2.3 times the monthly minimum wage.
In Buenos Aires, the rent on a two-room, 50-square-metre flat also exceeds twice the minimum wage, and in Bogotá the average asking rent is about 2.1 times the monthly minimum wage.
The flat sizes differ, but the figures illustrate how lower prices can still leave housing beyond a low-paid worker’s reach.
Five cities, five housing crises
Behind these affordability pressures lie different policies and housing conditions. Mexico City and Colombia limit annual rent increases, while Argentina has relaxed rental rules. The following examples show how these approaches sit alongside the pressures on local incomes.
Mexico City: Rising rents despite limits on increases
Asking rents rose 9.6% in the year to June, more than double inflation, according to the Inmuebles24 index.
A two-bedroom flat costs an average of 21,921 pesos (€1,069) a month. Nearly two million people, one in four inhabitants, live in rented housing, according to the city government.
Buying is even further out of reach. A calculation by the financial publication 'Expansión' estimates that a monthly income of around 85,800 pesos (€4,187) is needed to buy a 60-square-metre home, almost nine times the 2026 minimum wage.
To improve affordability, the city already has a rent cap. The Supreme Court has upheld a rule limiting annual increases in agreed rents to the previous year's inflation. For 2026, that cap is 3.69%.
But it only applies to existing contracts. Meanwhile, the indices compiled by property portals track flats coming onto the market.
Buenos Aires: Rents after deregulation
Argentina took the opposite path. Javier Milei's decree scrapping the Rent Act came into force at the end of 2023, allowing rental terms to be negotiated freely.
Following deregulation, the supply of rental flats in the capital surged. Advertised supply in Buenos Aires is now 3.4 times greater than at the low point in February 2023.
Asking rents rose 19.2% in the first eight months of 2026, below estimated inflation of around 21.5%.
A two-room flat costs 886,527 pesos (€516) a month, close to 80% of what the average employed worker in Argentina earns, 1,104,227 pesos (€643), according to Indec, the national statistics office.
Buying is another story. A two-room flat on the market costs around €116,000 on average. According to a calculator by the Argentine daily La Nación, buying a 50-square-metre flat, depending on the neighbourhood, requires between six and 35 years of a person's entire income.
São Paulo: Rent weighs on low-income households
São Paulo has the highest asking rents of any Brazilian state capital, at 65.36 reais (€11.2) per square metre in August, according to the FipeZAP index. Asking rents rose 5.74% in 12 months, outpacing inflation at 4.22%.
Asking prices for houses in July were above 12,000 reais (€2,042) per square metre.
High rents are also the largest component of Brazil’s housing deficit. An estimated 5.77 million households in Brazil, representing 7.4% of the total, needed better or more affordable housing in 2024, with high rents the biggest reason.
In South America's biggest economy, 3.59 million low-income households spent more than 30% of their income on rent in 2024, accounting for nearly two-thirds of the country’s estimated housing deficit.
The state of São Paulo accounts for 26.9% of those households.
Bogotá: Rent limits in a tight market
In Colombia, a 2003 law limits annual rent increases to the previous year's inflation, setting the 2026 cap at 5.10%. Monthly rent cannot exceed 1% of the property's value either. Even so, the market is highly strained.
Bogotá’s rental vacancy rate is just 1.9%, and an average apartment was advertised in the first quarter at 3.76 million pesos (about €1,035) a month. That is more than double the 2026 minimum wage of 1,750,905 pesos (about €482), following a 23% increase.
The minimum-wage rise also pushed up the maximum permitted price of social housing. That ceiling is tied to the minimum wage and has risen 76% in four years. At the start of the year, the government published a draft decree to stop minimum-wage increases from automatically raising that price ceiling.
Santiago de Chile: 11 years' income to buy a home
A Chilean family on an average income would have to spend everything it earns for 11.4 years to buy a home at the average price, according to a late-2024 estimate from the Chilean Chamber of Construction. Beyond five years, the indicator classifies housing as unaffordable.
Renting also puts pressure on low-paid workers. In metropolitan municipalities such as Independencia or La Florida, a two-bedroom flat of under 50 square metres costs between 345,000 and 421,000 pesos a month, according to Fundación SOL. That absorbs roughly 78% to 96% of the take-home minimum wage used in its study.
Informal housing adds another layer to the crisis
In Latin America, between a fifth and a quarter of the urban population lives in informal settlements, according to CAF, citing UN-Habitat and ECLAC. More than 30% of the urban population lives in inadequate conditions, according to the housing yearbook produced by CAF and the Lincoln Institute.
The crisis also affects people who have built their own homes in neighbourhoods without basic services.
In Madrid, aside from exceptions such as the Cañada Real settlement, the problem is mainly one of affordability: there are homes available, but often at prices wages cannot support.
Across the cities examined, the common challenge is the gap between housing costs and what people earn. Lower prices alone do not make a home affordable if rent still consumes most of a worker’s income, leaving little for other essentials.
