Father of 3: The first child benefit should be very generous in Estonia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
13:08:00 UTC
22:08:00 KST

Father of 3: The first child benefit should be very generous in Estonia
Director Madis Ligema, who recently became a father for the third time, told ETV that while money does not necessarily motivate people to have children, more generous benefits could increase the number of births in Estonia.
"The benefit for the first child in particular should be massive to encourage people to have that first child because once you have the first, then the second and third — and perhaps even a fourth — will follow," Madis Ligema said.
Economist and Family Foundation supervisory board member Raul Eamets, however, stressed the importance of supporting families having a third child.
"When people are planning a third child, it actually means a kind of qualitative change in their living arrangements because it means needing an extra room or a larger car, as three child seats won't fit in every car. Why is the issue of a third child so important? Half of Estonia's children live in families with three or more children," Eamets explained.
Parental benefit and a fixed percentage of GDP
As one way of increasing the birth rate, Eamets suggested extending parental benefits to parents who stay at home: "There are certainly parents, whether fathers or mothers, who do this, but we have taken that option away from them. I, for example, really liked Heido Vitsur and Indrek Neivelt's proposal that if you have decided to raise children full time, you receive the Estonian median wage — their proposal was €500 per child, so if you have three children, that would be €1,500," Eamets said.
Member of the European Parliament Jana Toom (Center Party) said Estonia should make supporting families with children a national priority and allocate a fixed share of the budget to it.
"Our child benefits are shamefully low. We have an extraordinarily high percentage of children living in relative poverty and outright poverty," said Toom, a mother of five. "We need to develop a national policy specifically focused on children and allocate a certain percentage of GDP to it, just as we do with defense," Toom said.
Inconsistent support measures rob people of certainty
According to Elin Järvsaar, editor-in-chief of "Pere ja Kodu," stability in benefits is important to parents, while constant changes to legislation discourage young people from becoming parents.
"More important than the amounts is a sense of security. In recent years, we have made a great many changes to the system of family benefits and allowances. That provides no sense of security whatsoever — up and down, back and forth, the rules keep changing," said Järvsaar, a mother of four. "The system has been made so complicated and it gives me no confidence that I will have support for 18 years. Even if parental benefits or other benefits are extremely generous, I know that four years from now they could be completely different and I don't dare take that step," Järvsaar explained.
Raul Eamets agreed that the demographic problem requires a long-term agreement similar to that on national defense. "Family policy and demographic issues are every bit as important as security, meaning that we need a consensus across society and across party lines. By now, I think all parties have realized that this is a problem, but what we need now are decisions that extend beyond election cycles and strategic decisions. One coalition raises benefits, the next lowers them — I completely understand women wondering how they can dare take those risks under such circumstances. Otherwise, we will simply die out," Eamets said.
A total of 9,240 children were born in Estonia in 2025, a record low. During the discussion, Eamets predicted that the number of births could fall below 9,000 this year.

Judge signals support for Booking’s two-day office rule
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
13:07:26 UTC
22:07:26 KST

Judge signals support for Booking’s two-day office rule
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
An Amsterdam judge has signalled she is likely to back Booking.com in its attempt to make staff work at least two days a week in the office, the Financieele Dagblad has reported.
The travel platform faced off against its works council (an elected employee body whose consent is needed to change working conditions) over whether it is reasonable to require in-office presence at that rate for all its workers.
“Two days is really very little, I’m just telling it like it is,” the judge said during Tuesday’s hearing. For over three years, Booking has held the two-day-a-week rule as a recommendation, but now wants it enforced as a mandatory measure.
The headquarters, on Amsterdam’s Oosterdok, cover more than 65,000 square metres. Booking agreed in 2016 to pay €270 million for the building and its land-use rights, according to filings by its parent company with US regulators. The average attendance rate by staff is 27%, according to the FD.
Dozens of employees sat in on the hearing. The company told the court that making office attendance mandatory was a “small step”, and argued that working only from home can harm staff’s mental health.
The works council disagreed, and one employee told the court he commutes an hour to the office, only to sit on Zoom meetings all day with colleagues in other countries.
The council also spoke about mental wellbeing and said that making office days compulsory could harm staff by taking away their autonomy. A lawyer for the council also noted that Booking is economically thriving regardless of low office attendance.
But the judge seemed to lean towards the arguments of the business. “You might think Dutch judges are strange, but we find working 40% of the time in the office perfectly normal,” she told the courtroom, where the audience was partly international.
The two sides have been given a week to reach an agreement. If they fail, the court will rule at the end of October.

A bet on tech millionaires and the first criticism — how people are reacting to Jaguar's electric car and its price

Jaguar Land Rover presented its new electric vehicle, the Jaguar Type 01, in New York — a model with an exceptionally long hood, no rear window, and a wide range of technologies — as part of a strategy aimed at growth in the U.S. market, UNN reports.
Details
The British luxury carmaker, owned by Indian group Tata Motors, said that the Type 01 — a four-door GT electric vehicle in restrained, muted tones, with a starting price of $130,500 — marks “the beginning of a new generation of Jaguar cars and a new era of transformation.”
The high price is a risky move for the U.S. market, where interest in electric vehicles is lower than in Europe.

The Type 00 model and the brand’s relaunch process itself drew criticism from car enthusiasts and some politicians.
JLR is also trying to recover from the consequences of a cyberattack that led to a production shutdown and supply-chain problems last year. X-Bow to develop booster for future U.S. Navy interceptor
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
13:05:57 UTC
22:05:57 KST

- X-Bow Systems won a prototype agreement worth up to $69.7 million to develop a solid rocket motor booster for a next-generation U.S. Navy weapon.
- The deal funds tooling for a Luling, Texas, line able to build up to 500 motors a year, with initial Navy capability planned for early fiscal 2031.
X-Bow Systems has won a prototype agreement worth up to $69.7 million to develop and qualify a solid rocket motor booster for a next-generation U.S. Navy weapon, and to tool a production line in Luling, Texas, that can build up to 500 motors a year, the Albuquerque, New Mexico-based company said on October 7.
The agreement, administered by U.S. Army Contracting Command at Rock Island Arsenal, covers a $50.4 million Phase 1 development effort lasting 12 months and a $19.3 million Phase 2 qualification option. The government obligated $50 million at award to fund Phase 1 in increments. X-Bow did not name the weapon the booster is intended for.
The company said the Navy program replaces single-purpose interceptors with a common design, including variants that fit more interceptors into each launch system. The U.S. Navy plans to field an initial capability in early fiscal 2031.
“To be the Arsenal of Freedom, we must first break the decades-old bottleneck in solid rocket motor production,” said Jason Hundley, founder and chief executive of X-Bow Systems. “This award is a clear signal the Pentagon is investing in advanced manufacturing to solve that problem, and we are ready to deliver the affordable, mass-producible propulsion our nation needs.”
Solid rocket motors are the propellant-filled engines that launch most U.S. missiles and interceptors. X-Bow makes them partly through additive manufacturing of the propellant, and it will run the program across its facilities in California, New Mexico and Texas, using a design approach it calls Modular Motor Architecture. The rate tooling for the Luling line is funded under the new agreement.
The award is the sixth new propulsion program X-Bow says it has been selected for in 2026, across the U.S. Navy, the U.S. Army and the Missile Defense Agency. The company also says it recently completed its first major production contract, delivering more than 2,100 rocket motors.
In July, the Missile Defense Agency gave X-Bow an $11 million contract to develop a high-performance solid rocket motor, saying it wanted to widen an industrial base that relies on two primary manufacturers, Northrop Grumman and L3Harris’ Aerojet Rocketdyne. In 2024, X-Bow received prototype agreements to build the Mk 72 and Mk 104 motors used in the U.S. Navy’s Standard Missile family.
X-Bow’s Texas site has grown alongside those contracts. The company finished installing a full production version of its additive manufacturing system at Luling in November 2025, and in May 2026 it earned certification for full production operations there. The U.S. Air Force Test Center had awarded it a four-year, $191.3 million motor manufacturing contract in September 2025.
The 12-month Phase 1 effort covers booster development, with the government holding the option to fund qualification in Phase 2.

====================================================================================================

Hamas boasts of 'glorious day' amid the ruins | Snapshot of the situation in Gaza
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
13:05:24 UTC
22:05:24 KST

Three years after October 7, the Gaza Strip no longer looks as it did on the eve of Hamas’ invasion of southern Israel. From northern Gaza to Rafah, entire neighborhoods have been transformed and hundreds of thousands of structures have been damaged. Gaza in 2026 is fundamentally different from Gaza before the war.
A United Nations analysis based on satellite imagery estimated that about 82% of buildings in the Strip were damaged — more than 200,000 structures. According to the assessment, about two-thirds of the damaged buildings were destroyed. The number of housing units damaged is also estimated in the hundreds of thousands.
But the destruction is only part of the story. Three years after the October 7 attack, the larger question is what has happened to the attitudes of Gaza residents themselves, and especially to their views of Hamas.
Throughout the war, some Gaza residents tried to protest against Hamas and challenge its rule, though not always successfully. Last June, hundreds of Palestinians demonstrated against Hamas at several locations across the Strip, with signs bearing slogans such as “With God’s help, Hamas out.” But those movements were either suppressed or failed to gain momentum in the first place.
The anti-Hamas trend also was reflected in polling. In the latest survey by the Palestinian Center for Policy and Survey Research, conducted in August 2026, support for Hamas had declined. Support for the organization in Gaza stood at 33%, while support among Palestinians overall was 24%. The center described the trend as part of a broader “decline of Hamas” in Palestinian politics.
Satisfaction with Hamas’ performance also eroded. According to the survey, only 38% of Gaza residents said they were satisfied with the organization’s performance, compared with 51% 10 months earlier.
At the same time, declining support for Hamas does not mean Gazans are ready to accept its dismantling. Sixty-two percent of Gaza residents oppose Hamas disarming before a complete Israeli withdrawal, while 72% of Palestinians overall believe that if Hamas disarms the war will resume and Israel will not fully withdraw.
In other words, Hamas is losing support but still retains significant political strength and the ability to influence public opinion.
Alina, a Gaza resident, wrote that she feels “personal hostility” toward anyone who still celebrates October 7. For her, she said, this is not a political argument about resistance or Israel, but about a day after which “my family became numbers, and my city became rubble.”
“How do you expect me to respect your celebration of the day after which my family became numbers, my city became rubble and people’s homes became graves?” she wrote.
She later directly criticized those who turn the attack into a celebratory event: “Don’t tell me you love Gaza more than I do and then celebrate the day when the gates of hell were opened on it.”
Egyptian writer Abdullah Ibrahim called October 7 “the day the madmen opened the way for the Zionists to destroy all of Gaza, kill more than 70,000 martyrs and 200,000 wounded, and displace all of Gaza’s residents.”
He wrote: “May God curse whoever planned it, took part in it and supported it.”
IDF deepens control, Hamas boasts of a 'glorious day'
Against voices such as Alina’s and Ibrahim’s, many others continue to support Hamas’ surprise attack, which included rape, murder and looting.
Faiz Abu Shammala, a former mayor of Khan Younis who is identified with Hamas, wrote that October 7 was “a day of battle and heroism” for Muslims, Arabs and Palestinians.
Gaza influencer Aboud Battah wrote that October 7 “will remain the most beautiful memory,” despite “the pain and loss that came afterward.”
Palestinian writer and commentator Yassin Izz al-Din wrote that October 7 was a day when “God humiliated the tyrants and criminals” and marked “the beginning of the end of their arrogance.”
Hamas itself continues to present the attack as a historic turning point and a “glorious day,” while arguing that armed resistance is a legitimate right.
And what happened to the Gaza Strip itself? Satellite images of the territory, including those available to Google Maps users, show neighborhoods that were densely built before the war and have since become vast areas of destruction. Schools and universities were damaged, residential buildings were erased, and new roads, earthworks, trenches and deployment points appeared in various parts of the Strip.
The IDF says it currently controls about 64% of Gaza and has established roughly 40 new military outposts there.
On the humanitarian situation, an Israeli security official said conditions in the Strip today are “stable and much better” than they were a year ago. According to data presented by COGAT, more than 2.2 million tons of food have entered Gaza since the ceasefire in October 2025. About 70%-80% of aid trucks carry food, and Israeli officials say food prices in the Strip have fallen by around 83%.
According to Israeli figures, 41 bakeries operated by international organizations are currently functioning in Gaza, producing more than 3 million pita breads a day, alongside dozens of local bakeries.
Israel also cites significant figures in the medical field. More than 24,000 tons of medical equipment have entered the Strip since the ceasefire, according to COGAT. Israel says permanent hospitals and field hospitals are operating in Gaza, and that tens of thousands of Gazans have been evacuated from the Strip for treatment or onward travel to third countries.
On water, Israeli data indicate that more than 70,000 cubic meters are supplied to Gaza each day through four water lines, desalination facilities, wells and water trucks. According to COGAT, that amounts to more than 60 liters per person per day.
At the same time, Israeli security officials claim Hamas is exploiting aid mechanisms to preserve its rule by taxing merchants, seizing goods, stockpiling aid and influencing distribution systems.

Mercedes global sales fall 6% as electric car sales hit record high
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
13:04:38 UTC
22:04:38 KST

Mercedes-Benz shares fell after the German carmaker reported a 6% fall in global sales, driven by weakness in China. Sales outside China edged higher, supported by growth in Europe and North America.
Mercedes-Benz shares fell by 4% at around 1 pm CEST on Wednesday before paring their losses, after the firm announced sales of 491,700 cars and vans in the third quarter of 2026, 6% fewer than a year earlier.
Growth in Europe and North America, alongside record battery-electric vehicle (BEV) sales, was not enough to offset weakness in China
“Mercedes-Benz Cars achieved the highest quarterly BEV sales in the company’s history, led by the electric GLC, whose sales more than tripled compared with Q2,” said Mathias Geisen, the Mercedes-Benz board member responsible for sales and customer experience.
Global sales in the car segment alone dropped 8% year on year to 407,200 vehicles.
In Asia, Mercedes sold 25% fewer cars than a year earlier, a total of 132,300 vehicles. This was dragged down by a 31% decline in the Chinese market, where intense competition and challenging market conditions squeezed Mercedes’ sales, according to the carmaker. The best-performing models in China included the GLC and E-Class; together, these accounted for almost two-thirds of Mercedes-Benz Cars sales in the country.
China accounted for almost a quarter of Mercedes-Benz’s global car sales in the second quarter, underlining the importance of the market to the German manufacturer.
The latest decline follows a 30% fall in Chinese car sales in the second quarter. Mercedes cut its full-year car sales and group revenue forecasts in July, citing continued weakness in China, where tougher competition, subdued demand and changes to its model range had weighed on performance.
Excluding China, group sales increased 2%, while car sales alone rose 1%. “Outside China, car sales increased for the third consecutive quarter in 2026,” Geisen said.
Electric car sales reach record high
Growth in Europe and North America helped support sales. This came as interest in EVs grew significantly.
Electric car sales rose 61% year on year globally to 68,400 vehicles, up 29% from the second quarter.
In Europe, Mercedes-Benz Cars achieved record quarterly battery-electric vehicle (BEV) sales, up 78% year on year and 24% compared with the second quarter.
“Our new electric models GLC, CLA, GLB and GLA are sold out in Europe for the rest of the year, with order books extending into 2027,” Geisen said.
The company added that its plants in Bremen and Rastatt in Germany, and Kecskemét in Hungary, were operating on three-shift schedules to meet demand.
Fully electric vehicles accounted for a record 16.8% of global car sales, up 7.2 percentage points from the prior-year quarter, according to Mercedes.
Overall European car sales rose 5% to 168,700 vehicles. This was mainly driven by growth in Germany, where sales increased 13%, and the UK, where they rose 7%.
In North America, Mercedes-Benz Cars sales increased 4% to 83,200 vehicles in the third quarter, with US sales rising 6%.
In the first nine months of 2026, Mercedes-Benz sold 1,244,400 cars, down 7% from the same period a year earlier, while sales of fully electric cars rose 40% to 165,500 units.

22:02:18 KST

Mortgage rates last week rose to the highest level in nearly three years. That kept demand for both refinances and home purchases on their steep and steady decline.
Total mortgage application volume dropped 4.2% compared with the previous week, according to the Mortgage Bankers Association's seasonally adjusted index.
The average contract interest rate for 30-year fixed-rate mortgages with conforming loan balances, $832,750 or less, increased last week to 7.49% from 7.30%, with points rising to 0.84 from 0.75, including the origination fee, for loans with a 20% down payment.
Applications to refinance a home loan, which are highly rate-dependent, dropped 8% for the week and were 56% lower than the same week one year ago. As rates rise each week, the pool of eligible refinances drops.
"Very few homeowners have an incentive to refinance at these rates," said Joel Kan, an MBA economist, in a release. "With rates roughly a percentage point higher than a year ago, refinance applications last week were at the lowest level since 2025 and fell to less than half of last year's pace."
Applications for a mortgage to purchase a home declined 2% for the week and were 15% lower than the same week one year ago.
"Purchase activity decreased across all loan types with FHA purchase applications falling the most, declining 6%, as these higher rates add to ongoing affordability challenges for many homebuyers," Kan added. "As noted in recent weeks, a higher share of borrowers are opting for ARMs [adjustable-rate mortgages] to lower their initial payments, with the ARM share steady at 10.3% last week."
Adjustable mortgages offer lower interest rates but can adjust in either direction after their fixed terms. That is why they are considered riskier. As a comparison, in the first years of the pandemic, when fixed mortgage rates were hitting multiple record lows, the ARM share of applications was less than 3%.
Mortgage rates pulled back slightly this week, according to a separate survey from Mortgage News Daily. While the levels remain near the highest since 2003, they're near the lowest in just over a week at 7.56% for the average lender.
"What gives? Is this a sign that recent upward momentum is starting to wane?" wrote Matthew Graham, chief operating officer at Mortgage News Daily. "It's too soon to conclude such things, but it is somewhat encouraging that Monday's long-term high was basically right in line with the high seen on September 30th. This is the sort of 'double top' behavior that some analysts look for when trying to identify momentum shifts."

====================================================================================================

Inside Kazakhstan’s historic rock-hewn mosques now recognised by UNESCO
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
13:00:48 UTC
22:00:48 KST

Five rock-hewn mosques and associated sacred sites dating from the 12th to the 18th centuries make up Kazakhstan’s newest UNESCO World Heritage property. The complexes preserve centuries of Sufi tradition alongside much older beliefs.
The World Heritage Committee adopted the decision at its 48th session on 25 July in Busan, South Korea. This follows President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev’s 2024 instructions to pursue the inscription of these rock-hewn mosques on the World Heritage List.
Set amid the otherworldly landscapes of Mangystau, the newly recognised mosques and their associated sites are named after revered Sufi masters: Beket-Ata, Shopan-Ata, Karaman-Ata, Shakpak-Ata and Sultan-Epe.
In Central Asian Sufism, ‘Ata’, meaning ‘father’ or ‘ancestor’, is used as an honorific for a revered spiritual figure.
Their spiritual lineage traces back to the 12th-century Sufi master Khoja Ahmed Yasawi. His teachings helped spread Islam among the Turkic-speaking peoples of Central Asia, connecting Islamic practices with older Tengri beliefs and local shamanistic traditions.
The mosques welcome both pilgrims and visitors seeking to explore Kazakhstan’s spiritual, cultural and architectural heritage.
Mangystau – the cradle of nomadic spirituality
According to the UNESCO World Heritage Centre, the complexes reflect the evolution of a distinctive spiritual culture.
They represent “sacred practices in which Islamic Sufi spirituality organically continued and transformed more ancient practices related to ancestor worship, the sacredness of the landscape and the role of spiritual leaders”.
Developed over many centuries, the monuments show how spiritual traditions and practices were adapted to the region’s distinctive natural environment and geological features through local architecture.
Speaking at the 48th session in July, Erlan Karin, Chairman of Kazakhstan’s National Commission to UNESCO and ICESCO, highlighted the significance of the inscription for the country.
“The inscription of the sacred monuments of Mangystau on the World Heritage List was not only a recognition of their significance for humanity as a whole, but also a tribute to the rich history, spiritual heritage and cultural identity of the Kazakh people.”
For local resident Almagul Zhaiman, the sacred sites embody a faith passed down through generations.
“These sacred sites have been preserved because of the faith passed down through generations, the knowledge of that heritage, preserving it and passing it on to our future generations. I believe that is what makes all these mosques so meaningful to us,” she said.
The Sufi masters of the mosques
Karaman-Ata was a Sufi missionary who came to spread Islam in the region. His mosque is believed to date back to the 12th or 13th century, while its associated necropolis is one of the largest and oldest in Mangystau.
For the Kazakhs and Turkmens who lived on the Mangyshlak Peninsula, the necropolis was considered a sacred place. According to local tradition, it was also a site for resolving disputes and negotiating peace. Those who made vows there were expected to honour them, as breaking a vow was believed to bring death and the end of one's lineage.
Karaman-Ata is believed to have been the grandson of Shopan-Ata, a 12th-century mystic revered as the spiritual protector of shepherds and their livestock.
According to tradition, Shopan-Ata was a disciple of the renowned Sufi master Khoja Ahmed Yasawi. Once part of an ancient caravan route to Khorezm, Shopan-Ata’s site remains an important destination for Sufi pilgrims.
Beket-Ata is said to have regarded Shopan-Ata, who lived centuries earlier, as a spiritual mentor.
Local traditions attribute extraordinary abilities to the 18th-century scholar, healer and architect, including teleportation and levitation.
“He was also regarded as the last and highest-ranking spiritual master among other holy men, which is why he became known as Pir Beket,” said Bakhtiyar Esimbetov, caretaker of Beket-Ata’s mosque.
In Sufi tradition, the Persian word ‘Pir’ refers to a spiritual guide or master, often one who has attained a high level of spiritual wisdom.
The Shakpak-Ata complex served as one of the region’s principal Sufi centres for centuries. Shakpak-Ata is believed to have lived sometime between the 9th and 14th centuries.
Carved into a chalk and limestone cliff, the sanctuary is arranged around a central domed hall with a cross-shaped layout.
Local traditions say the scholar taught astrology and astronomy, as well as ideas linked to the cosmos.
Inside the mosques’ architectural layout
According to local belief, divine signs guided the Sufi masters to the places where they built their mosques.
The sanctuaries are scattered across Mangystau, in western Kazakhstan, a region shaped by its nomadic heritage and geological history. Much of the area was once covered by the ancient Tethys Ocean.
Locally known as “underground mosques”, the complexes were built in natural caves, carved into steep rock faces or dug into the ground, providing shelter in the semi-desert landscape.
Their architectural layouts vary. They include prayer halls, mihrabs, rooms for contemplation and self-reflection, multifunctional spaces and tombs of the Sufi masters, sometimes alongside those of their immediate families.
Some underground cells were carved out for silent meditation and ascetic isolation.
“These underground mosques were places of retreat from society, where people could withdraw from everyday life and devote themselves fully to spiritual purification,” said Yersultan Islam, a local sacred sites guide.
The complexes also feature courtyards, water sources, sacred trees, pathways and cemeteries, some of which date from the 10th to the 20th centuries.
Pilgrims
For centuries, Mangystau’s sacred mosques have been important destinations for pilgrims.
Visitors are expected to dress modestly, while women are required to cover their heads before entering the underground mosques as a sign of respect for the sacred sites.
The sanctuaries attract not only local worshippers but also pilgrims from abroad.
Among them is Dinara Farvazova, whose family travels from Bashkortostan, Russia, to visit Mangystau’s sacred sites year after year.
“We read the Quran here, pray and make wishes. People come here seeking healing, and many see their dreams come true. They then tell their relatives and friends about the place, who come here too.”
Some visitors come in search of a deeper understanding of Islam.
Kaahn Ozturk, a traveller from Turkey, stopped at Karaman-Ata’s mosque during a long-distance motorcycle journey across the country.
“I have lots of questions in my mind, and I just want to find answers. That’s why I’m trying to discover every mosque, every place, every idea about Islam, to understand it better.”
Rinat Aubekerov and his wife, ethnic Kazakhs from Russia, made a pilgrimage to Shopan-Ata, hoping their prayers to have children would be answered.
For Davide Passanante, a visitor from Italy, the appeal was different.
After experiencing the crowds of summer tourism at home, he found a sense of calm in the remote sanctuaries. Travelling with a group of friends across Mangystau’s Martian-like landscapes, he was struck by the region’s spiritual atmosphere.
“I'm very impressed because the religion here is very important. I see how people pray and how they feel, how they think of God every time.”
Easing travel for visitors to sacred sites
The remote sanctuaries are attracting growing numbers of pilgrims from around the world. Kazakhstan is now planning to improve access to the newly listed sites while preserving them for future generations.
A five-year comprehensive development plan, due to begin in 2027, is expected to support tourism at the sites, including restoration work and the development of new visitor infrastructure.
Each sanctuary already has basic facilities where visitors can sleep and eat free of charge, although donations are welcome to help cover maintenance costs.
Plans include building visitor centres at Shopan-Ata, Beket-Ata and Karaman-Ata, complementing the existing centre serving Sultan-Epe and Shakpak-Ata.
“An asphalt road will be built to the site as part of the development plan. We also hope that internet connectivity issues will be resolved,” said Baltabai Balapan, director of the Mangystau State Historical and Cultural Reserve.
The five rock-hewn mosques and associated sacred sites of Mangystau, now collectively inscribed on UNESCO’s World Heritage List, are bringing the region’s spiritual heritage to a global audience, inviting visitors to discover its sacred landscapes.

Researchers probe the oxytocin system for clues to functional neurological disorder
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
13:00:39 UTC
22:00:39 KST

A recent study investigated whether the body’s oxytocin system acts as a biological risk factor for Functional Neurological Disorder. The findings indicate that while genetic variations do not appear to directly cause the condition, interactions between genetics, epigenetics, and circulating hormones might explain how patients process physical sensations and childhood trauma. The research was published in Comprehensive Psychoneuroendocrinology.
Natascha Stoffel, a researcher at the University of Fribourg in Switzerland, led the investigation. She and her colleagues wanted to understand the biological mechanisms behind Functional Neurological Disorder. This condition sits at the boundary between psychiatry and neurology.
Patients with the disorder experience physical symptoms like tremors, weakness, or non-epileptic seizures. These symptoms are genuine and debilitating, but they are not caused by traditional structural brain diseases. People with the condition frequently report a history of adverse life events, such as childhood trauma or emotional neglect.
Patients also often struggle with interoception, which is the brain’s ability to sense and process internal bodily signals. Interoception allows a person to feel when they are hungry, when their heart is racing, or when their breathing changes. In many stress-related conditions, this internal sensory system becomes disrupted.
To explore potential biological mechanisms, Stoffel and her team focused on the oxytocin system. Oxytocin is a hormone and chemical messenger that regulates stress, emotional responses, and social behavior. The researchers suspected that changes in how the body processes oxytocin might alter a person’s stress response and their internal bodily awareness.
The team looked at three distinct components of the oxytocin system. First, they looked at genetics, specifically examining variations in the oxytocin receptor gene. Second, they examined epigenetics, which are chemical tags added to DNA that change how a gene functions without altering the genetic code itself. Epigenetic changes are influenced by a person’s environment and life experiences.
For the epigenetic component, the team specifically measured methylation, a type of chemical tag that typically reduces a gene’s activity. Finally, the researchers measured the actual levels of oxytocin circulating in the participants’ bodies.
To conduct the first part of their research, the scientists analyzed data from 89 adults, after three of the 92 originally enrolled participants were excluded because of missing genetic data. The group included 41 patients diagnosed with Functional Neurological Disorder and 48 healthy control participants. The research team collected blood samples to extract and analyze the participants’ DNA.
From the blood samples, the team identified each participant’s genetic variants for the oxytocin receptor gene. They also measured the degree of epigenetic methylation at two specific regions of this gene. To measure circulating hormones, the researchers collected saliva samples at four different times during the day.
The scientists compared the genetic and epigenetic data between the two groups. When looking at the genetic variants alone, the models showed no difference in how the gene variations were distributed between the patients and the healthy controls. They also found no statistically significant differences in the average epigenetic methylation rates between the two groups.
While the baseline genetic and epigenetic markers did not differ, the researchers found an interaction when they included the salivary oxytocin levels. Patients with the disorder who carried a specific variant of the oxytocin receptor gene (the GG genotype) had elevated levels of oxytocin in their saliva compared to healthy controls with the same genetic variant.
In healthy individuals, oxytocin levels typically rise in response to specific contexts, like social bonding, parenting, or physical exercise. For the patients in this study, the elevated oxytocin levels appeared independently of these specific triggers. The researchers suggest that a specific genetic variant might act as a vulnerability factor, causing an abnormal release of oxytocin in response to daily stress.
In the second part of the investigation, the researchers tested whether combining the genetic and epigenetic data could help explain the participants’ interoceptive abilities. Participants completed a breathing task that measured their physical sensitivity to respiratory resistance. They also filled out a questionnaire that assessed how accurately they felt they could detect their own bodily sensations.
The researchers used statistical models to see if combining the oxytocin receptor genetics, methylation data, and salivary oxytocin levels would predict the interoceptive test scores. The addition of these biological markers did not improve the models. The genetic and epigenetic variables did not explain the interoceptive dysfunction observed in the patient group.
The team then applied the same statistical approach to look at childhood trauma. Participants completed a standard questionnaire to self-report their history of childhood trauma and emotional neglect. The researchers built a model to see if the biological markers aligned with the variation in these trauma scores.
In this case, the addition of the biological markers improved the statistical model. Including the epigenetic methylation data and the salivary oxytocin levels helped explain the variance in the self-reported childhood trauma scores. Higher levels of methylation at a specific region of the oxytocin receptor gene were associated with lower reported trauma scores.
The researchers noted a few caveats regarding their findings. Because the investigation relied on a modest sample size of 89 adults, it lacked the statistical power needed to make definitive claims about genetic associations. A simulation conducted by the researchers indicated that a study would need about 400 participants to confidently detect the genetic effects they observed.
The study measured epigenetic markers using blood samples, which might not accurately reflect the methylation levels present in brain tissue. The levels of oxytocin measured in saliva also might not perfectly mirror the concentrations of the hormone functioning directly within the central nervous system.
The statistical models linking the oxytocin system to childhood trauma do not establish a directional mechanism. The researchers cannot say whether experiencing trauma causes changes to the oxytocin system, or if an altered oxytocin system changes how a person processes and reports traumatic memories. Future research will need to track larger groups of people over time to understand how stress, genetics, and hormones interact to trigger the condition.
The study, “The Oxytocinergic System in Functional Neurological Disorder: Preliminary Testing of Associations with Interoception and Childhood Trauma,” was authored by Natascha Stoffel, Juan Ansede-Bermejo, Cristina Concetti, Ángel Carracedo, and Selma Aybek.

Henri Kagan, Kenso Soai win chemistry Nobel for ‘mirror image’ breakthrough
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
13:00:32 UTC
22:00:32 KST

Henri Kagan, Kenso Soai win Nobel chemistry prize for ‘mirror image’ work
Scientists honoured for solving mystery of asymmetric ‘mirror image’ molecules that has helped in manufacture of pharmaceuticals.
Scientists Henri Kagan and Kenso Soai have won the 2026 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for solving a longstanding riddle of asymmetric “mirror image” molecules, a discovery hugely important for pharmaceutical manufacturing.
The Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences said on Wednesday the pair – Kagan, 95, from France; and Soai, 76, from Japan – were honoured “for the discovery of nonlinear effects and autocatalysis in asymmetric organic synthesis”.
Their findings showed how chemical reactions can be driven to favour a single molecular mirror image, work that has been key for chemists who design reactions for the manufacture of pharmaceuticals.
Many of the molecules essential to life exist in two forms that are mirror images of each other, like left and right hands. Yet living organisms almost exclusively use only one version, a phenomenon known as “homochirality” – from the Greek word for hand – that has puzzled chemists for more than a century.
“The left-handed version of the drug can have one effect, and the right-handed version can have another effect, and then we need methods for selectively preparing them,” said Peter Somfai, a member of the Nobel Committee for Chemistry.
“In developing such methods, the findings of this year’s laureates are important. They provided powerful tools for that,” he said.
Heiner Linke, chair of the committee, said the two scientists provided “a solution to a chemical mystery that is over a century old: how homochirality can emerge spontaneously”, calling the chemical reactions they developed “spectacular”.
‘Most exciting day’
Soai, speaking by phone to the Nobel Prize news conference, said he had been out shopping when he received the news.
“This is the most exciting day in my life, I am very glad to share this prize with Professor Henri Kagan,” he added.
Last year’s chemistry award went to scientists Susumu Kitagawa, Richard Robson and Omar Yaghi for the development of so-called metal-organic frameworks, molecular constructions that can help tackle challenges such as climate change and lack of freshwater.
The chemistry Nobel is always the third prize to be awarded during Nobel week, following those for medicine and physics.
The literature laureate will be revealed on Thursday, while the keenly anticipated peace prize is due on Friday.
Established in the will of Swedish inventor and businessman Alfred Nobel, the prizes for achievements in science, literature and peace have been awarded since 1901, with a few interruptions mostly due to the world wars.
Nobel, a chemist by trade, amassed huge wealth in the 19th century from inventions primarily tied to warfare, most notably dynamite. The economics prize is a later addition funded by the Swedish central bank.

US Navy tests autonomy that adapts a plan in flight
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
14:00:29 BST
22:00:29 KST

An uncrewed combat aircraft has been flown in an American trial in which the autonomy software was given the commander’s intent rather than a fixed route, and allowed to rework the plan as the scenario changed, according to General Atomics Aeronautical Systems.
The demonstration took place on 10 September with the company’s MQ-20 Avenger test aircraft, flown as an autonomous collaborative platform, and was run with the United States Navy’s Strike Planning and Execution Systems programme office during an exercise called Gray Flag 2026.
What was tested was less the aircraft than the plumbing between the planning system and the machine. The team extended the Navy’s existing planning tools with mission context compliant with the Autonomy Government Reference Architecture, a standard intended to let autonomy software from different suppliers understand the same description of a mission. That let the Navy’s baseline mission planner pass objectives, constraints and threat information to the autonomy layer, which could then reason over the plan and adapt it in real time.
Michael Roberts, advanced programs emerging technology director at the company, said: “By taking the Navy’s practices, adding A-GRA-compliant mission context, and connecting it to TacACE, we showed that autonomy can understand commander’s intent, coordinate a heterogeneous team of uncrewed aircraft, and adapt the plan using its judgment in real time alongside human pilots.”
TacACE is the company’s Tactical Autonomy Ecosystem, the software and platform environment used for mission planning, command and control, autonomy configuration, simulation and post-mission analysis. The demonstration mixed live aircraft with virtual and constructive participants, a standard way of running these events without putting a full package of real aeroplanes into the air, and covered the length of the kill chain using passive sensors.

====================================================================================================

Artificial Is a Hugely Entertaining Movie About Despair for the Future
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
13:00:14 UTC
22:00:14 KST

If you’re like most people, your preoccupations in late summer 2026 were fairly workaday: Maybe you were negotiating the eternal challenge of the life-work balance, or fretting about escalating prices for gas and groceries. Then, in early September, former Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon blew a whistle to drown out all other whistles: He warned that, given the current irresponsibility of the companies in charge, AI could easily spin out of control and “kill us all by the end of the decade.” If imminent human extinction—as opposed to the more slow-burning decline posed by global warming—hadn’t been on your list of worries, you now had a reason to add it.
Luca Guadagnino’s tragicomedy Artificial—which premiered at the New York Film Festival on Oct. 5 and opens in limited release on Dec. 25, provided the world hasn’t ended by then—lays out with alarming clarity how we got here, and offers only the most threadbare scrap of hope that we might avert disaster. Strangely, though, Artificial isn’t a total downer; it’s essentially about human ideals gone off the rails, a reflection on how wrong things can go when brilliant, optimistic scientists fail to grasp the real danger of the thing they’ve set in motion. Artificial opens in 2003, in the University of Toronto lab of Geoffrey Hinton, the man who’d come to be known as the godfather of AI, and ends with a postscript from Hinton about the necessity of curtailing the capabilities of AI, fast. Yet beneath its potentially oppressive, ominous layers, it's a movie filled with life, and in places, it’s laugh-out-loud funny. Ike Barinholtz, of The Studio, practically brings the house down as a circa-2015 Elon Musk, a guy who seems to shamble through life looking only vaguely, comically zonked, not dangerously so. If nothing else, Artificial shows us how naïve we all were not 50 years ago, or even 20; the world is spinning so fast now that a decade goes by in the blink of an eye.
Musk is a minor player in Artificial, almost a curlicue attached to the bigger story. But not even OpenAI CEO Sam Altman—played here, with unnerving malevolence by Andrew Garfield—is the movie’s star character. Artificial really belongs to OpenAI cofounder Ilya Sutskever (Yura Borisov), whom we first meet as a brash 17-year-old kid enrolled in the University of Toronto. He’s the one who first, shyly, knocks on the door of computer scientist, cognitive scientist, cognitive psychologist, and all-around genius Hinton (Mark Rylance, his eyebrows two sincere, somber, science-brain hyphens), hoping to be taken under his wing. Hinton isn’t immediately impressed. Ilya is quiet, lumbering, extremely awkward. But if his English is sluggish, his mind is quick as a lightning strike, and he has high hopes for the ways artificial intelligence might help mankind. His ideas align with Hinton’s, and by 2013 the two of them—along with a third partner, Fedor Fedotov’s Alex Krizhevsky—find themselves at Google, innocently pursuing their research.
When Ilia first meets Altman, there’s not even the faintest clang of an alarm bell. At that point, Altman, as portrayed by Garfield, is just a skinny, eccentric and possibly vaguely charming guy who’d just happened to make a pile of dough off a tech startup he’d founded, which he later parlayed into various lucrative investments. With Musk and others, he’d already started OpenAI, a nonprofit at the time, with the intent of keeping the development of AI technology in the hands of the people. It’s 2015, and he invites Ilya to a private event in Menlo Park called, somewhat ominously, A Dinner for the Future. The dinner is really just a noisy roundtable of badly dressed tech whizzes drinking shots and shoveling expensive food into their gobs. But somehow, in the midst of all this frat-boy revelry, Ilya is able to outline his vision for the future, one in which AI will have solved numerous human problems, including eradicating not only cancer but also loneliness and unhappiness. By now we can see that Altman, the man presiding over the table, is a wily, evil elf. Somehow, though, Ilya trusts him and leaves Hinton and Google for OpenAI, and the chain of sterling intentions that he’s taken such care in forging begins to tarnish.
Artificial is a story of unchained ambitions and betrayals, with its Altman an unqualified villain. Guadagnino, screenwriter Simon Rich, and Garfield have fashioned him as a pure sociopath, a conniving agent of chaos with Mr. Spock eyebrows and dark eyes that glint like a serpent’s. As Garfield plays him, Altman makes a practice of manipulating those around him for his own ends, though he’ll also run to his boyfriend, mewling with self-pity, when he feels he’s been wronged. (Guadagnino seems to have no compunction about fashioning Altman as an “evil gay”; sometimes you’ve just got to call it as you see it.) Garfield's performance is both hilarious and truly unsettling. His Altman—sucking down his green smoothies, pouting when things don’t go his way, visiting his neon-lit Napa Valley bunker filled with automatic weapons—is a big baby man who, along with a small handful of others, holds the fate of humanity in his hands. This is the way the world ends, not with a bang but a tech bro.
Artificial features a large, sprawling cast, including Cooper Hoffman as one of Altman’s original OpenAI cronies, and an underused Monica Barbaro as Mira Murati, the Tesla product manager who became one of OpenAI’s key players. But Borisov is the movie's key. The Ilya of Artificial is a fumbling genius who, unlike his tech compatriots, pads around in sandals instead of big, ungainly sneakers, who sits down at the keyboard when he’s feeling tense, who stumbles with shyness when he's first confronted with Murati's brains and beauty. Borisov, who broke through as a thug with a poet’s soul in the 2024 Anora, vests Ilya with the same spiritual contours. You could argue that Artificial is a movie of stark bad guys and good ones, with no middle ground. But maybe, here, there is no middle ground. Ilya’s principled belief in the ways AI might have been used to help mankind is the sort of thing to which you can’t attach a price tag. You can’t say the same about ChatGPT which, as the movie tells it, was rushed to market before anyone had bothered to check its tendency to “hallucinate,” let alone furnish users with dangerous or harmful information.
If Artificial is a movie you think you have no interest in seeing, think again—if only because the people developing, and profiting off, AI technology will surely hope you won’t see it. Guadagnino developed the movie at Amazon MGM, which ultimately declined to release it, not least because Amazon had already announced its own multi-billion-dollar investment in OpenAI. (The film will now be distributed by Neon.)
But it’s important to know that you needn’t approach Artificial with feelings of dread. What makes the movie distinctive is how enjoyably watchable it is. Shot by Malik Hassan Sayeed, it has a vital, vibrant look; its vibe is more teen comedy than Important Picture of Our Time. This isn’t an exceedingly noble, dutifully made picture like Aaron Sorkin’s The Social Reckoning, in which another Anora alum, Mikey Madison, plays a Facebook employee who blows the whistle on that company’s eagerness to court extremist groups as a way of driving up engagement. The Social Reckoning is hardly a terrible film, but it doesn’t have the verve and energy that Artificial does. Guadagnino has made an exhilarating movie that’s also ultimately despairing: Though he’s done a great job of laying out the story of how we got here, he can’t even pretend there’s an easy solution. Yet Artificial doesn’t come off as a helpless shrug. It’s too muscular a piece of filmmaking for that. If we really are being led to our doom by a small handful of greedy, power-mad players, let’s not go down without a fight. Let’s be like Ilya at the keyboard, picking out a tune even in a moment of duress. In the face of an almost incomprehensibly inhuman threat, being the ultimate human is the only answer, from our first breath to our last.

Hadi Rezaei: there are no guarantees in sport
TEHRAN - Iran’s men’s sitting volleyball head coach Hadi Rezaei says that Team Melli will be targeting a record-extending ninth Asian title at the upcoming Asian Para Games in Nagoya, however there are no guarantees in sport.
Rezaei also believes Iran’s women’s team have a strong chance of securing a place at the Paralympic Games following an impressive run of performances.
“Being a role model is not limited to able-bodied people. Athletes with disabilities can also inspire society and show that people with disabilities are capable of reaching the highest levels of sport,” Rezaei said. “They can become champions for their cities and country and win gold and silver medals at the world, Asian, Olympic and Paralympic levels.”
Speaking about the women’s national team, Rezaei said the squad’s seventh-place finish at this year’s World Championships demonstrated their progress.
“The women’s team finished seventh at the World Championships this year and had a very good performance. They have a strong chance of qualifying for the Paralympics, and we hope they can secure their place at the qualification tournament in Kazakhstan next July,” the technical director of Iran’s national sitting volleyball teams said.
Rezaei also discussed the men’s team, which claimed their ninth world title last month and will now compete at the Asian Championships with five changes to its lineup.
“We have entered the Asian Para Games with almost 40 percent of the squad changed compared with the team that competed at the World Championships,” he said. “This shows the growth and depth of Iranian sitting volleyball. We are able to bring other ready players into the national team within a short period of time.”
“Within one or two months, 18 players are ready to compete in two major events. That demonstrates the depth and strong pool of talent we have in Iranian sitting volleyball.”
Asked whether Iran can be expected to retain their Asian title, Rezaei acknowledged that sport offers no guarantees but remained confident in his team.
“There are no guarantees in sport, but these players deserve to be champions,” he said. “I hope we can win the medal that the people expect from this sport and that our athletes deserve.”

Feature: Myanmar's century-old market celebrates its enduring heritage
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
21:00:04 CST
22:00:04 KST

People visit Bogyoke Aung San Market in Yangon, Myanmar, Oct. 7, 2026.(Xinhua/Myo Kyaw Soe)
YANGON, Oct. 7 (Xinhua) -- Bogyoke Aung San Market, one of Yangon's best-known heritage landmarks, is marking its centenary with a five-day festival featuring traditional handicrafts, cultural performances and local products.
Running from Oct. 7 to 11, the festival features more than 100 stalls selling textiles, gems and jewelry, handicrafts and food.
The celebrations also include a Myanmar Thanakha exhibition, puppet shows, 1970s-style musical performances and commemorative photo sessions featuring traditional ethnic costumes.
"We organized this festival to showcase the history of Bogyoke Aung San Market, one of Yangon's heritage landmarks," said Daw Chaw Su Htwe, an organizer of the centenary celebrations.
"We also hope visitors will gain a better understanding of the market's architecture and that the younger generation will learn about its rich history," she said.
Today, more than 1,800 shops operate in the market, selling jewelry, antiques, paintings, silk and cotton fabrics, handicrafts, and food. Known for its architecture and inner cobblestone streets, the market remains a popular tourist destination.
For shopkeepers who have spent years working there, the market's history has become closely intertwined with their own.
Daw Nyein Nyein Oo, who is in her 60s and has run Nyein Jewelry, a shop selling jade, gems, and jewelry, for about 20 years, said she has developed a strong attachment to the market.
"Before COVID-19, there were more foreign visitors, so business was very good. Now, things have become a little quieter," she said.
She welcomed the centenary celebrations, saying the event had brought more activity to the market and created memorable moments for shopkeepers and visitors.
Ma Su Su, a sales in-charge at Zaw Store, an arts and handicrafts shop, said the market also provides an opportunity to introduce Myanmar's traditional culture to international visitors.
"Apart from doing business, we also want people from around the world to know about Myanmar's traditional handicrafts," she said.
"Through these handicrafts, foreigners can learn about Myanmar's traditional culture, traditional musical instruments, puppetry and the traditions of our people," she added.
Artist and businesswoman Winn Thant Thant, founder of Iris Pandaya Creative Art Studio, participated in the celebrations with a booth showcasing artworks. She said she felt proud to work in a place with such a long history.
"Being able to work with art in a place that is more than 100 years old makes me feel especially proud, both as an artist and as a businessperson," she said.
For Daw Kay Khaing Oo, 49, a Yangon resident who has visited the market since she was about 20, its well-preserved character is part of its appeal.
"For me, the market hasn't changed. It is just like it was in the past," she said.
As Bogyoke Aung San Market marks its 100th anniversary, the celebrations highlight not only its long history but also its continuing role in Yangon's cultural life, where traditional crafts and cultural heritage are preserved and shared with new generations. ■
