Omar Sy on Lupin Season 4 and His 'Stunned' Reaction to the Louvre Heist
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
13:00:03 UTC
22:00:03 KST

A door opens. The 6-foot-3 actor is sitting on a large leather sofa.
His eyes are bright, his smile infectious despite the French team's World Cup defeat, from which he's still recovering. "I feel like m’être fait ‘mêler,' as we say in the neighborhood when 10 guys jump you,” he says. “But if I'm complaining about the World Cup like it's a major misfortune, it means things aren't too bad." It's summer when we meet; he's just arrived at the studios in La Plaine Saint-Denis to promote the fourth season of Lupin, the series that saw him explode into global view, in the guise of a gentleman thief who, this time, faces off against a copycat.
The actor has reached a milestone by elevating the program—which he co-produces with his company Carrousel Studios—to the rank of the most-watched non-English language series in the world on Netflix.
It all started with a hunch. A few years ago, alongside director Louis Leterrier, the French duo sensed a great opportunity. “At the time, in France, Netflix was still a somewhat unclear thing,” he says. “But based on the United States, we knew perfectly well that the series would be watched all over the world. We simply said to ourselves: let's make a show that does France proud.” The bet paid off, close to hundreds of millions of views later, all without ever having taken a single drama class. “It also comes down to the people you meet; that's what I love most about this job.”
Having already appeared in the blockbusters X-Men and Jurassic World, he will soon be seen on posters for the next Ocean's Eleven, directed by Bradley Cooper, whom he met nearly 10 years ago on a film set and who has since become a close friend—the story of his life.
TIME France: What aspects of yourself do you see in Assane Diop, the elusive thief you play on Lupin?
OMAR SY: I don't know if there are similarities between us. But there are many things I envy, admire, and like about him. That elusiveness—the fact that he's always where you least expect him. He uses every means at his disposal. He has a bit of an aikido quality: he takes what others consider a weakness and turns it into a strength. I also like his way of dispensing justice. Even though he's a thief, he has this desire to right wrongs, a Robin Hood-like quality. And then there's his panache, his lightheartedness, his playfulness…
We see you a lot at times, then you disappear. Is that necessary for your well-being?
Yes, I work in a creative field, and creativity feeds on life. You can't create if you are constantly on. Otherwise, it becomes industrial. I need to go back to living, to feeling the strong emotions that shape you, define you, and then inspire you to express things. And that's, that’s happens off-set… You have to take a break, to recapture a bit of and ask yourself: “Where am I in my life? What moves me? What do I want to express?”
How did you react to the Louvre heist a few months ago, which echoed the series so strongly?
I was a bit overwhelmed by it. People were calling me and inevitably making the connection; there were all the jokes: “Give it back!” “Was it you?” It’s crazy to see the extent to which much we draw inspiration from real life… and the extent to which reality can also be inspired by us in turn, like communicating vessels. I was torn between a lot of feelings.
First, immense surprise. I was truly stunned to see that the robbers were capable of trying to reproduce something reminiscent of what we did on Lupin. You tell yourself there was some inspiration, then laugh at the absurdity of the thought. But then comes a moment when you feel guilty and ask yourself, “How much of all this is my responsibility?”
Perhaps one day they'll say they were inspired by Lupin, just as Rédoine Faïd was by Michael Mann's Heat …
That’s also one of the reasons why, in writing Lupin, we pay close attention to the moral of the story, to the values we convey. Because Assane Diop and Arsène Lupin are extraordinary characters, but they remain thieves.
Every second foreign tourist in Paris has watched the series. Do you consider yourself an ambassador for France abroad?
I felt like an ambassador for France long before Lupin. I've never been more of a representative of France than since I left. By living abroad, I've become even more French. Because the truth is you carry your country within you. And others see you that way. In my daily life in the United States, I'm "the Frenchman in the neighborhood." In my work, I'm "the Frenchman" in the story. I'm chosen for that reason too. Obviously, when we launched Lupin, we didn't expect to reach such a level of success. Today, I'm extremely proud of it. And what also touches me is that Lupin has rekindled the desire to read the writer Maurice Leblanc. Booksellers and publishers thank us for giving his character a new lease on life. Well… The inhabitants of Étretat [where the series was partly filmed] hate us a little bit. [laughs] It has become unbearable for them; I want to take this opportunity to apologize again.
You seem—through your choice of roles—to want to spotlight something deeper in society. Is that a fair impression?
My work is precisely that. When I say I take time to live before expressing my feelings, that's exactly why. I always have an image in my mind, which I've never articulated before: I think of the shelves at Fnac. I tell myself that in the end, when you look at all of an actor's films, there has to be a coherence. And that coherence is who I am. Yes, I always need to say something.
Sometimes it comes through a particular genre, sometimes through a character, a different story. But, deep down, there's always something I want to express. Regarding Assane Diop and Lupin, what interests me are injustices, the invisible people. All those who exist, but that we don't see, that we don't consider. Through this character, there's also a way to bring them to light. There's always a little Trojan horse in what I do. It's not some grand declaration. I'm not going on a crusade. But it's a driving force. No character interests me if he doesn’t carry a message, if he has nothing to say to the world. It has to be bigger than me for me to take it on. Otherwise, I'm too timid.
This series is also a consequence of The Intouchables, the film that transformed your life and brought you to the United States. What do you enjoy most about this life you've been living there for the past 14 years?
It's given me a much more global perspective on the world…and on my profession. It's allowed me to take a step back with the right amount of distance. One of the most important things I've learned there is that filmmaking is also an industry. In France, it's something we sometimes find hard to admit. Yet, here too, we strive to make films that are successful and profitable. We simply talk about it less openly. Over there, that aspect is much less taboo. We can discuss it, study it, understand it. Today, this knowledge helps me as a producer. When you better understand the economic mechanisms of our profession, you can ultimately better express yourself, with even greater impact. For example, if I was able to develop certain productions, if I was able to make Father & Soldier, if we were able to make Lupin, it's also thanks to this understanding of the business. It also allowed me to develop real estate projects in Senegal.
Do you perceive France differently from a distance?
When you live in France, you feel so many things. The French are passionate; they experience their country very emotionally. Being far away sometimes allows me to observe things with more perspective. I see my American neighbors’ view of France and, ultimately, I have both perspectives now: that of someone who experiences France from the inside, and that of someone who can also observe it from the corner of the room.
You have expressed concern in the past about the state of French society. Do you feel it even more today?
It’s not that I’m more worried—I’m just as worried as ever. I have the feeling that we are going toward what I fear most: a France that is deeply fractured at every level. A France where bridges are becoming more and more difficult to build. Not impossible, mind you, but much more complicated.
Has the idea of "vivre-ensemble" eroded?
It's an overused term. "Le vivre-ensemble" has been used so much, so politically co-opted by both sides… It no longer really means what it should. We've ended up making it lose its meaning.
Your filmmakers and friends Olivier Nakache and Éric Toledano recently made a film in which the banlieue of the 1980s were less fractured. Did you feel that was the case for you as well?
When I was a child in Trappes, I didn't have that feeling of division. That doesn't mean everything was great, but we were together. I didn't feel that there were divides between people, like today, where you sometimes feel like you have to cross a river to meet someone. I didn't feel that. There were shared spaces. Of course, there was already racism; I've never had any trouble saying it. And I continue to say it, it's real. But to truly understand it, you have to be Black or Arab in France. We've always experienced it. It's just that today, there's a different intensity. And above all, there is another way to express it… and to experience it.
We're a few months away from the presidential election, and the National Rally is leading in the polls. What does that tell you?
It goes along with everything I've been saying and it confirms the concerns I've been expressing for a long time. We're heading towards a France that's asking itself a lot of questions. And giving itself the wrong answers.
Do you know who you'll vote for in April 2027?
It's still quite unclear. Like many French people, I'm lost; it's been a while since we've had any innovative proposals… On the other hand, I know who I won't vote for.
Is it a delicate matter for you to express your views on the presidential election while living in the United States, or do you feel you have the right to do so?
I feel totally entitled to do so because I am French. France allows French citizens living abroad to vote. So, if my vote exists, it means my voice counts. The day they decide that French citizens abroad should no longer vote, then we'll talk about it again. But today, I have that right. I remain concerned about what is happening in my country. The fact of living elsewhere does not make me a foreigner.
What do you say to those who use that argument against you?
The simple fact that some people question my feelings about France, that I can express my opinion about the country, is clearly racism. It's not that I'm abroad that’s the problem; it's that I'm Black. When people tell me, “You should thank France”— why should I thank France more than anyone else? If everyone is supposed to thank France, then everyone should thank it in the same way. Why is this injunction directed more at me? That's also a form of racism.
I'm often told I'm ungrateful. That because I live abroad, I shouldn't criticize France or have a negative opinion. But what are they all doing all the time?
You arrived in the United States during Barack Obama's presidency. Now, Donald Trump is in his second term, and there too you live in a troubled society…
The world is troubled, the world is asking itself questions… We are part of that world. I've seen the difference, I still see it, but I don't have the right to vote because I'm not American, and therefore, I can’t legitimately speak on the subject.
You've said that you experience more racism in France than in the United States…
Of course, and in a very real way. There are acts that are punishable by law in the United States that aren't here. In France, we still see things occur without provoking the same reactions. Therefore, in my opinion, there is a different level of legal protection. And there is also a difference in behavior. Some attitudes that are still accepted here would be much harder to find there.
In recent months, there's been the Epstein affair, and, in France, scandals surrounding after-school programs are piling up. As a father of five, are you worried?
What worries me is how late we're discovering things about our children. What strikes me most is the density of the silence. How is the silence so pervasive and, at the same time, so opaque? How could so much have remained hidden for so long? How could we have taken so long to understand what was happening around our children? And I sometimes have the feeling we're fighting the wrong battles. We debate certain issues endlessly… while others, much more serious, are almost relegated to the background. I believe all parents everywhere are asking themselves questions today that our parents never asked. Sending a child to summer camp—if so, where? Enrolling them in an extracurricular activity? And so on.
When you were growing up, you didn’t need to worry about the climate, the impact of artificial intelligence on employment, or pensions.
But there's another difference: we knew less. This kind of ignorance also protected us, to a certain extent. In our society today, children are much more aware of the gravity of the world they live in. And especially of the consequences this can have on their own future. Us, we felt that anything was possible. The future was a blank page on which we could write whatever we wanted. Today, they already feel that there are limits in place in many areas.
Do you talk to them about it?
A lot. And what's really surprising is that they're perfectly conscious of all this. But they're not afraid. That's actually what gives me hope. I have the feeling that our children are just waiting for one thing: to take the reins. When I listen to them, I understand that they're looking at us and thinking: "You've messed everything up. You're incompetent. Now, let us do it.” I'm counting on them.
Will AI replace you on screen at some point?
That's impossible! [laughs] I don’t think it will replace actors of my generation—if it ever does manage to replace actors, which I don’t believe it will. On the other hand, it’s an extremely powerful tool that’s evolving so fast that by the time we finish this conversation and your article is published, something new will already be out there!
But are you worried about damage to the craft of filmmaking? Many people in Hollywood have spoken up on this subject.
Artificial intelligence must remain a tool in the service of creation. Not a tool that creates in place of creators. When I look at what it produces on its own, it doesn't interest me. Because what moves us in a work of art is precisely what belongs to humanity: the soul. And that soul, artificial intelligence doesn't have it.
How long will this last? Its deployment and its advances are happening every day…
There's no point fighting something that's already underway. It's already part of our jobs. From this point on, the real question is no longer: how do we stop it? But rather: how do we regulate it? How do we protect jobs? How do we support those whose jobs will disappear? How do we embrace this movement? It's exactly the same as when Netflix arrived. At the time, many thought it would kill cinema. Today, we clearly see that the two coexist. Because nobody wants to see cinema disappear. So we've found a balance. With AI, it's the same thing.
Our colleagues at TIME in the United States ranked you among the 100 most influential people in the world in 2021. Do you manage to stay grounded?
I do what I can to stay grounded. And anyway, when you're not grounded, you're not even aware of it. So I'm not the best person to answer that.
Sometimes people project their own struggles onto you. Is it exhausting to be seen as a symbol?
When someone projects something onto me, they're mainly projecting the image they have of me. It's their story. Not mine. I don't belong to anyone. I'm part of their imagination, but it doesn't belong to me. When you're an actor, you quickly come to understand one essential thing: people aren't always talking to you; they're talking to the image they've constructed of you. Once you understand that, you sleep much better. Otherwise, you go crazy. You can't live according to what everyone expects of you.
You have often spoken out on issues of migration and police violence. Is this a way of giving meaning to your fame?
When I speak out on certain social issues, it's not because I wake up in the morning thinking, "Today, I'm going to defend this or that cause." It doesn't work like that. I'm given a microphone. If the subject resonates with me, then I respond. If not, I don't respond. It's as simple as that. When you ask me about France, about certain realities I’m familiar with, then yes, I have something to say. But it's never a pose. It's never a strategy, much less an obligation.
It's often said, "Omar Sy is a socially engaged actor." But let's look at the questions asked of other actors and those asked of me. They're never the same.
Many don't want to step outside the promotional framework; it's a choice.
Yes, perhaps they don't want to express themselves, but above all, they're never asked certain questions. It doesn't matter which films they're promoting.
Conversely, you openly express your feelings and opinions on these subjects.
To understand my feelings, you first have to ask me questions. People want to hear my perspective on a topic, and by constantly asking me these questions, it makes me seem like someone who reacts to current events and takes a stand. It's the microphone they're holding out to me that ho creates this… You have to look at how I'm approached.
With some actors, you can promote the exact same type of film. And yet, we're not steered toward the same topics. Before I've even answered, there's already a projection: He's Black, Muslim, he comes from the banlieue. And in that, too, it's a form of discrimination.
Talking about the banlieue also means talking about your own journey and your story. It's not without reason…
But there are other actors from the banlieues; it's just that they don't represent the archetype. People assume they don't come from there. But they do, just as much as I do. At the same level of notoriety—I'm not going to name names, but I know others who grew up in the same neighborhoods, yet who are left alone on these subjects.
Your eldest daughter was born in Trappes, your youngest in Los Angeles—that pretty much sums up this life, almost elastic.
Yes, my eldest daughter was born in Trappes, on my 23rd birthday. In the same hospital, with the same doctor who delivered me. And my youngest child was born in Los Angeles. When I look at it, I think it tells a life story. I like to laugh about it. I often say there's the Trappes girl, the Versailles kid, and the Californian. It also shows that you can evolve without denying your roots. Evolving doesn't mean changing. You can go very far without losing your anchor and your roots. It's important to pass that on to my children, because that's how I was raised.
Despite the money and the change of scenery, has your current life retained some elements of your previous one? A lot has changed in my life; just look at this dressing room, it's an apartment. [laughs] In the beginning, there were 15 of us in a dressing room half the size. But the essentials haven't changed. I think that as you get older, you even return to certain things more. When you lose a parent, certain values become even more important. But I refuse to spend my time analyzing myself; the only time I do that is during interviews when I'm asked questions I never ask myself. Otherwise, I still enjoy very simple things like going to the market, cooking, and walking in nature.
Is it possible to make friends in Hollywood?
When I arrived in the United States, I was 34. At that age, your life is already built. You have your friends. You're a father, you have a wife. You don't go to the United States to make friends. You make some anyway, but it's not the primary goal. And then, there are a lot of clichés about California. You often hear that everything is fake. Honestly, I haven’t found that to be so. I'd even say that there's sometimes more transparency than in France. Over there, people might take a little longer before inviting you to their home. On the other hand, once they do, it's sincere. Here, sometimes you get invited to dinner very quickly, and then, two years later, the person pretends not to know you anymore on the street. [laughs]
Do you ever wonder what other path you could have taken?
Honestly, very rarely. But I believe that, one way or another, I would have built a life similar to this one, on a different scale... Not with the same encounters, not with the same resources. But I believe my curiosity would have led me to a fairly similar existence. Today, I live on three continents. I think that, even without this job, I probably would have lived on at least two. Because that's just how I am. I've always wanted to see other places, to discover. To build several things at once.
You were passionate about science, and you earned a technical baccalaureate specializing in heating and air conditioning.
My plan was very simple: I had a cousin who was an architect working in Senegal. I wanted to join his business, installing air-conditioning systems on his construction sites. That was my plan. In that life, I would probably have, for example, split my time between France and Senegal.
In your book Viens, on se parle, you say that your life is a merry-go-round and that someone will tell you it’s time to get off. Is that still the case?
This profession is a bit like that. Every film is a ride on the merry-go-round. And we all work so we can go on another ride. I know very well that one day, someone will tell me the merry-go-round is closed. I've been aware of that for a long time. And precisely because I know that, I'm already ready. That's also why I'm developing other projects. Paris Basketball [of which he is a co-owner]. Production. Things in Senegal, projects in agriculture. I always want to learn and discover other worlds.
And if that happened, where would you start?
Everything I just mentioned, but I would still find a way to stay involved in filmmaking. I might not be in front of the camera anymore, but I’d be somewhere else. Because this world is now part of my life. I need it. Sports work the same way. When I watch a basketball game, I find what I love about cinema: the emotion, the story, the suspense, the sense of connection. I think the common thread in everything I do has become very clear: I want to bring people together, create bonds, build bridges, unite people. When a project makes that possible, you’ll find me nearby!
Translated by TIME

JOHANNESBURG, Oct. 7 (Xinhua) -- South African President Cyril Ramaphosa on Wednesday officially launched the Council for Scientific and Industrial Research's (CSIR) FuturePharma facility in Pretoria to advance pharmaceutical innovation and domestic manufacturing.
The CSIR, South Africa's national scientific research organization, established the open-access biomanufacturing facility to bridge the gap between early-stage laboratory research and commercial production.
In his address, Ramaphosa described the launch as a milestone in South Africa's efforts to strengthen its pharmaceutical ecosystem and boost domestic capacity to manufacture medicines.
"The FuturePharma facility signals our resolve as South Africa to harness science, technology, and innovation in pursuit of sustainable development," Ramaphosa said.
He added that the new facility will provide specialized infrastructure and technical expertise for pharmaceutical process development, formulation testing, scale-up, and technology transfer, enabling local researchers and biotech enterprises to translate innovation into market-ready products, including indigenous active pharmaceutical ingredients and biotherapeutics.
Reflecting on the supply chain vulnerabilities exposed during the COVID-19 pandemic, where African nations rely heavily on imported medicines and vaccines, Ramaphosa stressed that developing local manufacturing capabilities is vital to safeguarding public health.
"The pandemic was a reminder that health security, economic resilience, and national development are interconnected," Ramaphosa said, noting that the initiative supports broader African Union goals for regional health self-reliance. ■

Remember the ‘caregiving kills’ study? Reality is more nuanced
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
13:00:00 UTC
22:00:00 KST

Remember the ‘caregiving kills’ study? Reality is more nuanced
Humans and other mammals are wired to care for others. But caregivers still need support
By Sujata Gupta
Social Sciences Writer
When social and affective neuroscientist Naomi Eisenberger’s dad developed dementia, she knew the popular wisdom. Caring for him could shave years off her life. But Eisenberger, of UCLA, was skeptical. Caring for her dad, who died in January, was stressful but also meaningful, she says. “It gave me a lot of joy to bring him some happiness.”
Caregiving kills as an idea first emerged in the scientific literature almost three decades ago. Distressed caregivers were 63 percent more likely to die within four years than non-caregivers, psychiatrists Richard Schulz and Scott Beach reported in 1999 in the Journal of the American Medical Association. The finding has since been cited almost 5,300 times, including almost 300 times in the past two years.
But researchers have largely failed to replicate that finding, with considerable research showing instead that caregiving links with living longer, Eisenberger and colleagues report in September in Biopsychosocial Science and Medicine. Caregiving stress may be softened by humans’ hardwired propensity to help others in need, the researchers suspect.
Silence surrounding caregiving’s positives is probably well-intentioned. In 2025, almost one-quarter of all adults in the United States, some 63 million people, provided care to adults or children with a medical condition or disability, according to a 2025 report by AARP and the National Alliance for Caregiving. Almost 65 percent of caregivers surveyed reported experiencing moderate or high emotional stress and almost half reported financial difficulties. Yet financial and emotional support for caregivers remains limited, the report notes.
Highlighting caregiving’s pros could jeopardize what little help is available, says sociologist and gerontologist Rebecca Utz of the University of Utah in Salt Lake City. “I don’t like to take our foot off the pedal and say that caregiving is so positive because it’s hard, and people need support.”
But painting caregiving as wholly negative, rather than nuanced, erases insight into how caregiving might also protect health, Eisenberger and colleagues argue. Most stressors, such as work-related burnout, link with chronic inflammation. Caregiving is less likely to show that link. Understanding that caregiving paradox could reveal how the body can withstand stress, Eisenberger says.
Moreover, helping a loved one may bring unexpected benefits, Eisenberger says. She cites a 2003 study in The Gerontologist showing that adult children who did not care for a parent with severe disabilities experienced more depression than those who did, though the researchers could not show causation. “I’m not suggesting everyone go out and engage in informal caregiving,” Eisenberger says. “I’m trying to make informal caregiving [feel] a little less scary.”
Caregiving was labeled as life-threatening
In highlighting the need for researchers to take caregiver well-being seriously, the 1999 study was groundbreaking, Eisenberger and colleagues write. But it had design flaws.
Schulz and Beach, both of the University of Pittsburgh, compared mortality rates across a four-year period from over 800 individuals. Roughly half the participants had disabled spouses, with some serving as caregivers and others not; the other half had nondisabled spouses and served as the control. Caregiving spouses filled out self-reports indicating their degree of mental strain.
Over the next four years, 103 participants died. Schulz and Beach zoomed in on mortality rates among one subgroup — spousal caregivers reporting considerable strain. Of those distressed caregivers, 17 percent died during the study period compared with 9 percent of control group members.
But buried in the data was another finding, Eisenberger and colleagues note: Individuals not providing care to their disabled spouses still died at the same rate as caregivers experiencing distress. Individuals with sick and healthy spouses occupy different realities, largely invalidating comparisons between those groups, Eisenberger says. In this case, the findings suggest that having a sick or disabled spouse, and not caregiving status, increases one’s likelihood of dying.
A nuanced picture
More than 6,000 caregivers were asked to evaluate both the sense of purpose and emotional stress associated with caregiving. Their answers illustrate the role’s emotional duality.
The team is not the first to dispute the idea that caregiving kills. That list includes Schulz himself, who coauthored a 2009 Psychological Science study titled, “Caregiving behavior is associated with decreased mortality risk.” (Neither Schulz nor Beach could be reached for comment.) That study, though, has been cited less than 400 times, with just a couple dozen citations in the past two years.
“I … assumed that the field would have taken notice,” says evolutionary and social psychologist Stephanie Brown, an author on the 2009 paper and a similar 2014 review of caregiving in Social Issues and Policy Review. But “slam pieces on caregiving” remain on prominent display in doctor’s offices and other medical settings, says Brown, of the Renaissance School of Medicine at Stony Brook University in New York.
Caregivers are stressed. Biology may help compensate
More recent research hints at why caregiving, a tremendously stressful undertaking, may not kill.
It’s increasingly accepted that stress can trigger systemic inflammation that then compromises the immune system. In theory, stressed caregivers should be inflamed. They’re not, researchers reported in 2020 in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences. That study relied on data from more than 30,000 U.S. adults. In surveys taken in the early 2000s and the 2010s, participants indicated their caregiver status, type and intensity of care being given, and experiences of strain. They also provided blood samples.
The scientists zoomed in on roughly 250 people who became regular caregivers and analyzed their blood samples for six inflammation-related biomarkers. Those biomarkers did not go up, on average, when people transitioned to caregiving, the team found. Nor did they go up relative to a matched control group of non-caregivers selected from the larger sample. Those findings held true for even the most stressed caregivers, including spouses caring for a partner with dementia.
How, though, are caregivers largely avoiding inflammation associated with chronic stress? “We don’t really know,” says gerontologist and clinical psychologist William Haley of the University of South Florida in Tampa. “There’s a lot of mysteries here.”
Eisenberger and colleagues theorize that the key to the caregiving paradox may lie in a biological system that evolved among mammals to protect offspring that remain helpless well after birth. That “mammalian caregiving system” seems to encourage caring and tamp down the normal stress response that tells people to flee danger, at least when their baby is involved, Eisenberger says.
Studies primarily in rodents hint at how that caregiving system works, Eisenberger notes. And emerging evidence in humans suggests that this system kicks on even in non-parenting contexts, such as holding onto a partner in pain or giving money to family. In preliminary work, Brown and colleagues even saw signs of it among strangers who bonded during an activity.
Researchers are missing fascinating questions
The contradictory feelings Eisenberger experienced while caring for her dad are common. Caregivers can’t disentangle the advantages of the mammalian caregiving system from the strain of helping. Yet over half of caregivers surveyed by AARP reported that caring for a loved one gave them a sense of purpose.
Ironically, minimizing potential positives to protect caregivers may do more harm than good, researchers say. Caregivers may hear only how awful their next several months or years may be. Others might run from the responsibility and later experience regret.
“What if we tell people that … helping others can be really fulfilling even if it can be stressful, too?” Eisenberger says.
Reticence around caregiving’s benefits has also hampered scientists’ ability to advise people undertaking such a difficult role, Eisenberger and colleagues note. Can feeling compassion for a sick loved one turn on the mammalian caregiving system, or does one have to provide care? What if someone has a fraught relationship with the sick family member? Ultimately, when does the stress of opting out of caregiving outweigh the stress of opting in? Framing caregiving as entirely negative means those questions rarely even get asked.

====================================================================================================

‘The Social Reckoning’ Already Feels Irrelevant
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
13:00:00 UTC
22:00:00 KST

When The Social Network hit theaters in 2010, it was fair to wonder if the film had come too soon. Facebook had been launched from Mark Zuckerberg’s Harvard dorm room just six years earlier, and nobody really knew how it would reshape digital community in the decade to come.
But, with a breakneck screenplay by Aaron Sorkin, a menacingly propulsive soundtrack by Trent Reznor and Atticus Ross, and a surgical performance from Jesse Eisenberg as Young Zuck, director David Fincher delivered a slick corporate thriller about the major drama to that point: intersecting lawsuits over who owned what percentage of the platform and who could lay claim as a founder. It was an electrifying film that seemed to only lightly fictionalize the newest and perhaps most cutthroat generation of Silicon Valley warlords.
Flash forward 16 years, and Facebook (now Meta) has accumulated more scandals than Hollywood could possibly hope to keep up with. Sorkin tells WIRED that he was approached many times over those years with pitches for a sequel, though he struggled to see an angle of approach. “Before a film can be anything else, before it can be relevant or thought-provoking, it has to be good,” he says. “It has to work as something that you watch while you're eating popcorn.”
Then, Sorkin says, he met Frances Haugen, the former Facebook data engineer who leaked damning internal memos to investigative reporter Jeff Horwitz. Horwitz wrote up what became known as the “Facebook Files” in a far-ranging 2021 series of articles for The Wall Street Journal, exposing much of what the company knew regarding harms to users—everything from hate speech and medical misinformation to body image issues and human trafficking—but had largely brushed aside in pursuit of growth.
Sorkin still wasn’t sure he had a film, but one day he asked Haugen why she finally decided to go to the media. “She just told me in kind of an offhand way, ‘Oh, I had this friend who was radicalized by Facebook after spending too many hours on the platform,’” he recalls. “And I began to get the idea for what is now the opening scene of the movie.”
The cold open of The Social Reckoning, written and directed by Sorkin, depicts an intoxicated woman pulled over on the side of the road in San Mateo, California, with an overheated car. Approached by police officers, she turns combative, pulling out her phone to record a video as she hurls racist abuse at the cops and is at last arrested for threatening to kill one of them. The video turns up on a Facebook page for far-right content, which is where Haugen (Mikey Madison) finds it in 2019, recognizing the woman as an acquaintance from her pilates class who used to hold progressive views. She also learns that this woman is a superuser, intensely active on Facebook for many hours each day.
Haugen first tries to get her colleagues at Facebook to recognize how their own algorithms are pushing many users, including her former friend, into extremist feeds. It’s only when she hits enough walls that she puts her tentative trust in Horwitz (Jeremy Allen White), a journalist whom Facebook staff have been explicitly warned not to speak to. As they develop the bickering rapport of two focused professionals with clashing ideals—Haugen wants to save the company from itself, while Horwitz suspects it’s too late for that—we see flash-forwards of Zuckerberg (Jeremy Strong) rehearsing for a congressional hearing on social media misinformation in 2021. In the room are a crisis PR adviser named Raya (Wunmi Mosaku) and Charlie (Bill Burr), a composite ex-employee (as in, not specifically based on any living individual). He’s been brought in as an agitator with the freedom to get under Zuck’s skin and dismantle his practiced talking points.
This plot structure is clunkier than the cross-cutting depositions of The Social Network, which neatly allowed for the characters to recount the early days of Facebook without narrative hand-holding. By comparison, The Social Reckoning is clogged with portentous intertitles (the first sequence is even labeled a “prologue”) and visual cues to remind us where we are in the timeline. From scene to scene, the sharp-edged performances and familiar crackle of Sorkinese dialog (which leaves room for the occasional and delightfully odd non sequitur) make for engaging fare. But the pieces fit together awkwardly—and you do wish Reznor and Ross were around to boost the momentum.
The movie arrives as part of a crowded slate of keenly anticipated tech films. There’s Artificial, Luca Guadagnino’s satire about the firing and rehiring of OpenAI CEO Sam Altman in 2023; it picked up significant buzz as Amazon MGM dropped it this summer following a $50 billion deal between Amazon and OpenAI. Alex Gibney’s epic documentary Musk covers the exploits of the world’s richest man up through his disastrous reign as a “government efficiency” czar in the White House. And don’t forget You Can See Everything, for which directors Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim gained close access to Theranos founder and convicted fraudster Elizabeth Holmes shortly before she began serving a decade-long prison sentence.
Amid these timely offerings, The Social Reckoning is just a touch out of step. Its climax (spoiler alert) is the January 6 Capitol riot, the horrors of which are blamed in part on Facebook’s failure to either get a handle on election fraud conspiracy theories or remove Donald Trump’s account as he stoked such inflammatory falsehoods. Now, halfway into Trump’s second term, is it all that much of a revelation that he and his movement are emboldened by the complicity of tech oligarchs, who openly backed him in 2024?
Nevertheless, there are big issues at play here. The debate over ethics in tech continually boils over into agonizing questions of how truth is negotiated and who gets the last word on it.
Whether you find Reckoning to be a worthy interrogation of this stuff will probably depend on your appetite for what amounts to a mashup of The Newsroom and The West Wing. There are mic-drop moments that plainly invite the audience to “lib out,” such as when Haugen accuses Horwitz of bias against tech because it’s stealing journalists’ jobs and he fires back that it’s actually because “you are so bad at it.” Or when Zuckerberg taunts his traitorous former friend Charlie for cashing out his Facebook stake for $200 million instead of holding on until it was worth $1.3 billion, and he counters by torching the presumption that he’s “supposed to be embarrassed by that.”
“I love that line, because that is the disease,” Burr tells WIRED. “What you're seeing with these robber baron nerds that are out there right now is the way somebody is addicted to methamphetamine, they are addicted to money. They literally cannot have enough. They are insatiable. They behave like addicts. And an addict will do whatever they have to do, hurt whoever they have to, to get that next fix.”
There is a definite satisfaction to seeing Burr, a caustic stand-up comedian, stick this observation directly into Zuckerberg’s craw. On the other hand, it’s a little naive to imagine that it stings a guy expanding his massive top-secret Hawaii compound to include ancestral burial grounds. In so many ways, Reckoning attempts to shame a ruling class that has proved itself, well, shameless.
At its best, then, the film may serve to underscore Haugen’s bravery in turning whistleblower while capably illustrating the difficulty and dangers of mounting an exposé on a Silicon Valley behemoth. It reminds us that there is always something else these tech firms are concealing. Both Madison and White tell WIRED that Sorkin’s screenplay jolted their understanding of the forces at work in the industry.
“I had an inkling about certain things, but then to be confronted with the real statistics and facts—that really confirmed how I was already feeling about social media as a whole and some of the negative effects it can have on people,” Madison says. White adds that people shouldn’t give companies like Meta the benefit of the doubt when something goes wrong. “What you find out in watching this film is, there's a business model, there's a plan, there's engagement,” he says. “They're hyper-aware of exactly what's happening, and they still choose to put their foot on the gas.”
Though as to an actual “reckoning” with this reality, the title may have been an overpromise. The movie’s postscript notes that millions of Americans still get news from Facebook and that in 2025, Meta ended its fact-checking program, opting instead to solicit crowdsourced context notes from users. It’s a downbeat conclusion after Haugen and Horwitz have beaten the odds to drag countless dirty secrets into the light. You wish you could walk away from The Social Reckoning with a sense that this forever changed Facebook, or Zuckerberg, or the internet itself, yet it’s hard to avoid noticing that everyone got away with it.

First Gripen E produced in Brazil makes maiden flight
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
13:00:00 UTC
22:00:00 KST

First Gripen E produced in Brazil makes maiden flight
The first Gripen fighter built outside Sweden through the collaboration between Saab and Embraer, marks another milestone in the Gripen programme.
The first Gripen fighter built outside Sweden has taken to the skies, completing its historic maiden flight from Embraer's Gavião Peixoto aerodrome in São Paulo State on 6 October at 10:21 local time.
Flown by Saab chief test pilot Jakob Högberg, the sortie aimed to verify the aircraft's basic system functions and assess its initial performance. The flight was classified as the fighter's first production acceptance test and initiated the final phase of the manufacturing process at Embraer.
Embraer flight engineers were responsible for flight planning and execution, with support from Saab, marking another milestone in the technology transfer plan delivered by the Gripen programme to Brazil.
“This maiden flight shows that Gripen production in Brazil has reached a new level of maturity. I am proud of our close cooperation with Embraer in the Gripen programme, which establish a solid foundation for Gripen´s future development in Brazil,” says Marcus Wandt, head of Saab´s business area Aeronautics.
“This first flight of a Gripen E produced in Brazil by Embraer is a historic milestone for the country’s aerospace and defense industry. It confirms the success of a long-term strategy that combined the vision of the Brazilian Air Force, Saab’s technological expertise and Embraer’s engineering and industrial capabilities,” said Bosco da Costa Junior, President & CEO of Embraer Defense & Security.
Following its production acceptance flight campaign, the aircraft will be certified and ready for delivery to the Brazilian Air Force (FAB). It will be transferred to Anápolis Air Force Base in Goiás State, to join the First Air Defence Group (1st GDA), currently operating 10 Gripen fighters.
This aircraft, officially presented on 25 March 2026 by Embraer, is the first of 15 to be produced in Brazil under the current programme. Embraer is home to South America's only supersonic fighter production line and an integral part of Saab’s global manufacturing and supply chain network.

Cambodia's bourse sees active trading in September amid rising investor interest
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
20:59:59 CST
21:59:59 KST

PHNOM PENH, Oct. 7 (Xinhua) -- Average daily trading volume on the Cambodia Securities Exchange (CSX) hit an all-time high in September 2026 as investor momentum continued to surge, the bourse said in a press release on Wednesday.
Trading activity on the CSX gained sharp momentum, setting a new record as the average daily trading value in September reached 5.8 billion riels (about 1.45 million U.S. dollars). This represents a roughly 63-percent surge from the previous record of 3.6 billion riels, set in April 2022.
The exchange added that the average daily number of orders placed reached 12,173 in September, with an average of 7.5 million shares ordered per day.
Concurrently, the CSX Index climbed to 650.62 points, marking a 20.26-percent rise that highlights solid market confidence and sustained liquidity inflows into the exchange.
"This historic breakthrough clearly reflects the potential and resilience of Cambodia's securities market," the CSX said. "Investors maintain strong confidence and continue investing in the Cambodian stock market amid global economic instability."
Appetite for the market was further underscored by 4,162 investors opening new trading accounts in September. This is the highest single-month figure on record, surpassing the previous milestone of 4,034 accounts registered in September 2018.
Since launching trade operations in 2012, the CSX has grown to feature a total of 28 listed companies, comprising 12 equity firms and 16 corporate bond issuers. ■

8 alleged gangmasters cited near Caserta
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
14:59:22 CEST
21:59:22 KST

Eight alleged gangmasters were cited
by police near Caserta north of Naples Wednesday for allegedly
exploiting clandestine immigrant agricultural workers mostly
from Pakistan and India.
                                    
The migrants worked up to 14 hours a day, seven days a week, in
both rain and heat, police said.
                                    
They were paid between 80 cents and 1.50 euros per crate. They
could not take time off for illness or use their phones. They
were subjected to constant supervision by "caporali"
(gangmasters) and faced losing their jobs if they failed to flee
during law enforcement raids, or if their productivity dropped
or they fell ill.
                                    
"This is the reality behind the exploitation of non-EU workers
lacking residence permits," said police.
                                    
Investigations coordinated by the Santa Maria Capua Vetere
Public Prosecutor's Office and conducted by the Carabinieri's
Labor Inspectorate Unit in Caserta lasted over two years; today,
enforcement actions were carried out in the Caserta area,
specifically in Villa Literno and Mondragone.
                                    
Three individuals, all residing in the province of Caserta, have
been ordered to report regularly to the judicial police, while
another individual has been placed under a mandatory residency
order.
                                    
Notices regarding the conclusion of the investigation have been
served to four additional people.
                                    
They are accused of illicit labor intermediation and
exploitation for having recruited and employed undocumented
workers.
                                    
The farmhands—numbering up to 80 a day—were recruited on the
street and transported to work sites in dilapidated vans, some
of which were intended for cargo transport.
                                    
They were paid on a piecework basis (between €0.80 and €1.50 per
crate), by the hour (€3-€4), or via a daily wage of €30 for new
hires and €50 for long-term workers.
                                    
They worked without medical check-ups, portable toilets, or rest
areas.
                                    
The investigation involved both physical surveillance and
technical investigative methods.
                                    
Farmhands who provided useful testimony have been relocated to
protected locations and offered prospects for protection and
social and professional integration.
                                    
"The facts that emerged from the investigation into the
"caporalato" (illegal labor brokering) system on farms in the
Caserta area are serious because worker recruitment took place
on public roads—in broad daylight—amidst the indifference of
many people who never reported the practice, likely because they
had become desensitized to such phenomena. On the positive side,
however, 17 farmhands cooperated with the investigation, finding
the courage to report their exploiters," said Pierpaolo Bruni,
the Public Prosecutor of Santa Maria Capua Vetere, during a
press conference at the Prosecutor's Office.
                                    
He was joined by Deputy Prosecutor Graziella Arlomede, who
highlighted the "persistent nature of the conduct,"
demonstrating "awareness on the part of both the exploited
workers—who knew where to find work—and the labor brokers and
business owners who were circumventing the rules."
The investigation led the Preliminary Investigations Judge (GIP)
to order three suspects to report regularly to the judicial
police, while a fourth was placed under an obligation to reside
within a specific municipality; all are accused of acting as
labor brokers, and all are foreign nationals, though their
specific nationalities have not been disclosed.
                                    
Four other suspects—including the owner of one of the farms that
employed the workers—have received a notice of the conclusion of
the investigation, a step that precedes a formal request for
indictment.
                                    
It is known that the victims are primarily of Indian and
Pakistani nationality.
                                    
The investigation (coordinated by Assistant Prosecutor Armando
Bosso) revealed that workers were recruited every morning at a
traffic roundabout in Villa Literno, and often in narrow side
streets as well.
                                    
From there, they were distributed to local farming areas—or to
places like Casal di Principe and Grazzanise—in vans certified
for nine passengers but crammed with 25 to 30 workers; often,
these were cargo vans lacking windows.
                                    
The courage of one worker, who was the first to report the labor
brokers, triggered the investigation; other workers subsequently
came forward, enabling investigators to piece together the
illicit system through stakeouts and video evidence.
                                    
The phenomenon of gangmastering of fruit and vegetable pickers
in Italy came into sharp focus with the case of  Satnam Singh,
an off-the-books 31-year-old Indian farm labourer who bled out
after being dumped outside his hut with an arm severed by
wrapping machinery placed beside him on a fruit picking box at
Latina south of Rome two years ago
In July Singh's boss got 16 years in jail for manslaughter in a
case that has shone a spotlight on often ruthless and callous
gangmastering.
                                    
The leftwing trade union CGIL, students and members of Singh's
large local Sikh community demonstrated outside the courthouse
in the city founded by Mussolini in 1932.
                                    
The gangmaster, Antonello Lovato, had told the trial that he had
lost his head after the accident in June 2024 and was "not
myself" when he dumped Singh.
                                    
"I found Satnam there and I lost my head: it wasn't me. I never
wanted his death. The news of his passing two days after the
accident destroyed me. There is not a day that I don't think of
him and his family. I will always be close to Satnam's wife,"
said Lovato, the thirty-nine-year-old whose crime has brought
attention back onto gangmastering and exploitation of mainly
migrant farm hands in Italy.
                                    
Prosecutors had requested 22 years for Lovato. 
                                    
ALL RIGHTS RESERVED © Copyright ANSA

40 thousand Bulgarians abroad register to vote in presidential election
Unknown

40 thousand Bulgarians abroad register to vote in presidential election
Wednesday 7 October 2026 15:45
Wednesday, 7 October 2026, 15:45
PHOTO BTA
Font size
Nearly 40,000 Bulgarians abroad have registered to vote in the October 25 presidential election, the Central Election Commission (CEC) said.
The commission has determined where polling stations will be opened abroad and how many will operate in each location. Political parties represented in parliament will hold consultations on October 8 on the composition of polling station commissions abroad, which the CEC must appoint by October 12.
Voting machines will be sent abroad as diplomatic cargo. They will be collected from storage and handed over to Foreign Ministry representatives for delivery to Bulgarian embassies and consulates. Each machine will travel in a sealed transport case, with its polling station, machine and seal numbers recorded in a handover document.

Poland’s President in the Philippines: Black Hawks, ASEAN, and US Defense Interests
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
12:59:00 UTC
21:59:00 KST

President of Poland Karol Nawrocki arrived in Manila on October 5 for a three-day official visit to the Philippines. It is the first visit by a Polish president to the Philippines since diplomatic relations were established in 1973.
According to Marcin Przydacz, secretary of state and head of the International Policy Bureau of the Chancellery of the President of the Republic of Poland, the visit is part of a broader Polish strategy to strengthen the country’s position among the countries of the Global South. Nawrocki described the visit as an opportunity to seek backing for Poland’s continued presence in the G20 by gaining informal support from the Philippines, which is chairing ASEAN this year. Nawrocki also described the trip in the context of a broader strategy of engaging with the Global South – a direction that has recently been highlighted in Polish foreign-policy discussions.
There is also a military cooperation angle, raising the question of possible broader American defense interests within the Polish administration and opposition.
In August, PZL Mielec, an aerospace manufacturer based in Poland, completed the delivery of 32 S-70i Black Hawk helicopters to the Philippine Air Force. The Philippines had previously ordered 16 helicopters from Mielec in 2019.
PZL Mielec presents itself as a Polish company: the helicopters are manufactured in Poland and the workforce is Polish. But since 2015, PZL Mielec has been owned by Lockheed Martin, one of the world’s largest U.S. defense contractors.
This makes Nawrocki’s visit to the Philippines particularly interesting.
Former Polish Defense Minister Mariusz Błaszczak, now a leading opposition figure and a strongly pro-American and Eurosceptic politician, has argued that Europe is effectively helpless against Russia and that Poland should rely on the United States rather than Europe for its security. He was also highly critical of the EU’s SAFE program, an EU initiative providing up to 150 billion euro in loans for defense investment. Błaszczak has argued that the program could push the United States out of Europe and questioned its compatibility with Poland’s reliance on U.S. defense technology.
In July 2026, Błaszczak, together with a group of MPs with the conservative party Prawo i Sprawiedliwość (PiS), submitted a parliamentary interpellation concerning the lack of new orders for S-70i Black Hawk helicopters from PZL Mielec. The MPs warned that the end of the Philippine contract could put the future of S-70i production in Poland at risk.
Supporting PZL Mielec can be presented as supporting Polish jobs and industrial capacity, but it also directly supports the commercial interests of Lockheed Martin.
Ironically, it may be easier for the Polish president to persuade the ASEAN countries to place an order than Poland’s own Ministry of Defense.
Given the tense relationship between Nawrocki and the Polish government led by Prime Minister Donald Tusk, as well as Nawrocki’s alleged close relationship with U.S. President Donald Trump, one possible aim of the Philippine visit could be to encourage the government in Manila to consider another contract, or to promote PZL Mielec and its capabilities through the Philippines at the ASEAN level.
Given the ownership structure of PZL Mielec, Błaszczak and Nawrocki’s political alignment, and support for stronger U.S. defense ties, the timing raises questions. Within the span of a few months, a parliamentary interpellation called for new orders for PZL Mielec, the factory completed its Philippine contract, and Poland’s president made his first-ever visit to the Philippines.
Could Nawrocki’s visit also serve to promote further Black Hawk sales across ASEAN, potentially benefiting U.S. industrial interests?

EU idea of defense policy seeking ‘confrontation’ with Russia a ‘dead end’: Kremlin
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
12:58:02 UTC
21:58:02 KST

Burç Eruygur
07 October 2026•Update: 07 October 2026
The Kremlin said on Wednesday that the EU’s idea of a defense policy that it argued seeks “confrontation” with Russia is a “dead end.”
In remarks to journalists at a press briefing, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov accused Europe of being “obsessed with plans to militarize the EU” and said the 27-member economic union is moving toward adopting a military-political element.
“This is problematic because they are building their defense and security identity on the basis of confrontation with the Russian Federation – a dead-end path that, as history shows, leads to no good outcome,” Peskov said.
Amid France’s test of a new ballistic missile launched from a nuclear-powered ballistic missile submarine a day earlier, Peskov said Russia remains vigilant and is closely monitoring the situation amid Europe’s “aggressive rhetoric” against his country.
Peskov further said that Russia has taken note of French President Emmanuel Macron’s remarks about the test’s “loud and clear” message, which he said in a video of him observing the launch that has been posted on US social media company X.
He added that while Russia is taking security measures in the context of the EU's “militarization,” Moscow remains open to dialogue with Europe.
Peskov also commented on a possible phone call between Russian President Vladimir Putin and US President Donald Trump, which the latter said Tuesday would take place “very soon,” saying such a call has not yet been specifically agreed on.
“If such an initiative is put forward, I have no doubt that it will be promptly approved,” Peskov added.
On Tuesday, Trump said that he has a call scheduled "very soon" with Putin concerning reports emerging of a pneumonic plague outbreak in Russia’s Siberian region of Irkutsk.
Local authorities in Irkutsk imposed quarantine measures for people and several departments of the district hospital amid reports, which said an employee of the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Research Institute of Siberia and the Far East has been diagnosed with “pneumonia of unknown etiology.”
Russia’s consumer and health watchdog Rospotrebnadzor announced Monday that the sanitary and epidemiological situation in the Irkutsk region is “calm,” while the development has raised concerns and public health fears on social media.
The US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention said Tuesday that it is closely monitoring reports in this context, while US Secretary of State Marco Rubio urged Russia that same day to provide full transparency and share detailed information with the international community regarding the incident.
“The media are reporting a great deal, and the overwhelming majority of what they are reporting regarding this situation is false information,” Peskov said, urging the public to rely on Rospotrebnadzor's statements regarding the situation.
He also said the World Health Organization has been informed of the situation “in accordance with established practice.”

Chentsov on new EU enlargement strategy: Ukraine needs clear perspective
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07

Chentsov on new EU enlargement strategy: Ukraine needs clear perspective
Ukraine's Deputy Prime Minister for European and Euro-Atlantic Integration Vsevolod Chentsov said this in a comment to Ukrinform.
"We welcome the European Commission's intention to continue updating and adapting the EU enlargement policy to the realities we are facing today. We fully support the goal of making the enlargement process more effective, credible and fit for a Union that will have more member states," the official said.
At the same time, Chentsov stressed that when considering indicative roadmaps and timelines for the leading countries in the process, it is important that they provide Ukraine with a clear, credible and sufficiently ambitious perspective.
He explained that the timeframe for completing the negotiation process is particularly important for Ukraine given society's efforts to implement reforms under difficult conditions and the fact that the European perspective is a source of confidence in the future.
Therefore, Chentsov said, it is important for the EU to send a clear political signal that Ukraine's efforts and progress are recognized, and that its accession trajectory remains ambitious and predictable.
"In this context, we would welcome an agreed approach to indicative timelines for the leading countries in the process, including a common political horizon for completing accession negotiations. Such an approach would provide greater predictability and strengthen confidence in the enlargement process," the official said.
He stressed that Ukraine is ready to do its part and expressed hope that the accession process would remain ambitious, credible and predictable and reflect the progress Ukraine continues to make.
As reported, on October 6, the European Commission proposed a comprehensive strategy to prepare the European Union for future enlargement, in which Ukraine was given a special place due to its significant potential in food security and defense.

Swiss researchers develop wire-shaped motor for robotic suits
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
12:53:48 UTC
21:53:48 KST

Swiss researchers develop wire-shaped motor for robotic suits
Researchers at the Swiss Federal Institute of Technology Lausanne (EPFL) have developed a wire-shaped motor that could one day be used in robotic suits to help people move.
The “FiberMotor” is between one and three millimetres in diameter, according to an EPFL press release published on Wednesday. The development is described in the journal Advanced Materials.
More
What does the future hold for the robotics industry in Switzerland?
The motor is made up of two hollow fibres, one inside the other. Thin copper wires are wrapped around both fibres. When voltage is applied, electrostatic forces pull the fibres closer together, causing the inner fibre to move back and forth inside the outer one.
+ Swiss robotics moves from research to delivering products
Unlike traditional motors, the wire motor does not require gears or a mechanical transmission system. This makes it more flexible and means it can be moved externally. For example, if an arm moves against the direction generated by the motor, it does not lock up.
Assistance for movement
Working together, four of the motors generated enough force to lift a 46-gram chocolate bar.
More
Swarm of Swiss robots could take part in future space missions
The researchers say the technology could have a range of applications, including wearable robotic suits that help people walk. As part of their testing, they built the motors into a pair of trousers. In future, large numbers of the slim motors could be woven into clothing as threads, providing support for movements such as bending or straightening the leg.
The researchers have already launched a start-up to commercialise the technology. For now, however, their focus is on making the motor more powerful and durable.

Ozel warns Saudi defence pact could drag Turkey into Yemen war
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
12:51:56 UTC
21:51:56 KST

Breadcrumb
'Saudis' problem will be ours': Turkish opposition leader warns Ankara over defence pact
Turkish opposition leader Ozgur Ozel has strongly opposed Ankara’s defence pact with Saudi Arabia and Pakistan, warning against Turkey being drawn into the Saudi-Houthi conflict and criticising Donald Trump.
Speaking at his New Party's parliamentary group meeting on Tuesday, Ozel said the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement amounted to Turkey becoming a party to a war involving Saudi Arabia, while accusing the government of committing to the deployment of Turkish troops before the agreement had been approved by parliament.
"An armed attack against one of the three countries will be considered an attack against all three. In other words, from now on, the Saudis' problem will be our problem," Ozel said.
Turkey, Saudi Arabia and Pakistan signed the agreement in Mecca on 7 August. It commits the three countries to mutual defence, with an armed attack against one member treated as an attack against all three.
Ozel also criticised what he described as the government's alignment with US President Donald Trump's regional strategy, saying Turkey should not become part of a new Middle Eastern order dictated from Washington.
"We do not accept being part of Trump's Middle East order," he said.
His strongest criticism came when he warned against Turkey becoming subordinate to Washington's regional policy.
"We do not accept being Trump's soldiers on command," Ozel said.
Turkey could provide drones, intel
The comments reflect broader opposition concerns that the pact could draw Turkey deeper into the Saudi-Houthi conflict, although analysts say a direct Turkish combat role in Yemen is unlikely, at least initially.
"The Mecca pact is quite new, and the Houthis forced an early birth of the defence clause," Omer Ozkizilcik, a political analyst at the Atlantic Council, told The New Arab.
"We should expect the Turkish and Pakistani role in defending Saudi Arabia to increase gradually," he said, adding that Turkey could provide significant support for Saudi Arabia's defence against drones.
However, Ozkizilcik said he did not expect Turkey or Pakistan to take an active and direct combat role in Yemen, at least in the initial stages.
"However, the more important and efficient Turkish role may be on the intelligence level and strategy planning," he said.
Turkey has significant experience operating in civil war environments and engaging with tribes and non-state armed groups, Ozkizilcik said. Ankara also maintains relationships with non-Houthi Yemeni actors that have remained at a distance from Saudi Arabia.
"Turkey could potentially alter Yemeni dynamics against the Houthis," he said, arguing that Turkish intelligence support to Saudi Arabia could ultimately prove more effective than direct airstrikes.
The pact comes as fighting between Saudi-backed Yemeni forces and the Houthis has intensified, with the Iran-aligned group carrying out attacks against Saudi targets including the kingdom’s vital oil infrastructure and its capital.
The fighting has shattered years of relative calm in the Saudi-Houthi conflict, which has now become another major front in the broader Middle East war.
'No troops a century later'
Ozel argued that signing a mutual defence pact with a country involved in an ongoing war risked making Turkey a direct party to the conflict.
"Mutual defence pacts are concluded in peacetime. They are established for deterrence," he said. "Signing this agreement with a country that is at war means directly becoming a party to the war."
He also criticised the reported decision to deploy Turkish military personnel to Saudi Arabia, arguing that such a move required parliamentary approval.
"They have decided to deploy troops there," Ozel said, accusing the government of making commitments on behalf of parliament before the agreement had been formally submitted for approval.
He cited Article 92 of Turkey's constitution, which governs the deployment of the country's armed forces abroad, arguing that any decision to send Turkish troops must be approved by parliament.
"Article 92 of the constitution is there. If soldiers are going to be sent, it must go through parliament again," he said.
Ozel also pointed to President Recep Tayyip Erdogan's earlier criticism of Saudi Arabia's role in Yemen, noting that Erdogan had previously questioned Riyadh's responsibility for the conflict.
Ozel argued that Ankara had now moved from criticising Saudi Arabia's intervention in Yemen to entering a defence arrangement that could require Turkey to stand alongside Riyadh in the event of an attack.
The Turkish government has said the agreement does not mean Turkey will directly intervene in the Yemen conflict. Ankara is instead expected to focus on defence cooperation, joint planning, military training and intelligence sharing with Saudi Arabia and Pakistan.
For Ozel, however, the agreement represents a fundamental shift in Turkish foreign policy.
"We do not accept the adventurism that would send our soldiers into the deserts of Yemen 100 years later," he said, in an apparent reference to Ottoman rule.
The comments come as Ankara seeks to deepen defence cooperation with Riyadh and Islamabad under the new pact, which comes more than seven months into regional conflict triggered by the US-Israel war on Iran. Before the Houthi escalation, Saudi Arabia, like the five other Gulf states, had come under repeated attack by Iran and Iran-backed militias in Iraq.
For now, analysts expect Turkey's role to focus more on helping Saudi Arabia defend its territory and on intelligence and strategic support than on sending combat forces into Yemen.

Three years after the Hamas attack: how October 7 changed Israel, Gaza and the entire Middle East
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
15:50:57 EEST
21:50:57 KST

Three years after the Hamas attack: how October 7 changed Israel, Gaza and the entire Middle East
Kyiv • UNN
Israel is commemorating the victims of the October 7, 2023 attack after bringing all the hostages back. The war in Gaza and the humanitarian crisis have not ended.
On October 7, 2026, Israel commemorates the victims of the attack by Hamas and other Palestinian groups, which became the deadliest day in the country's history. The 2023 attack claimed the lives of approximately 1,200 people, while militants took another 251 people hostage and transported them to the Gaza Strip.
Three years later, all the hostages—alive and deceased—have been returned to Israel, but the war caused by the attack has not, in fact, ended. UNN explains how its consequences continue to shape the situation in Israel, Gaza, and the entire region.
What happened on October 7, 2023
On the morning of October 7, 2023, at around 6:30 a.m., a massive rocket barrage against Israel began from the Gaza Strip. At the same time, Hamas militants and allied groups breached the border barriers and infiltrated Israeli territory by land, sea, and air. They attacked border kibbutzim, cities, military facilities, and the Nova music festival near Re'im. Approximately 1,200 people, mostly civilians, were killed in the attack. A total of 251 people, including civilians, military personnel, and foreigners, were taken to Gaza.
The attack was the largest single-day loss of life in Israel's history and triggered a major political and social crisis over the failure of the security system and the state's inability to stop the attack in time.
In response, Israel declared war on Hamas and launched a large-scale military operation in the Gaza Strip. Its stated objectives were to eliminate Hamas's military and political infrastructure, return the hostages, and remove the threat of a repeat of the October 7 attack.
Why the hostage issue became the most painful
The hostage issue remained one of the most important concerns for Israeli society for more than two years. Some people were released during ceasefire and exchange agreements, some were rescued during military operations, and the bodies of those who had died were returned to Israel throughout the war.
On January 26, 2026, the Israeli military announced the return of the body of the last hostage—a 24-year-old police officer, Ran Gvili, who was killed in combat on October 7, 2023. His remains were found after a special operation in the northern Gaza Strip. Thus, only 843 days after the attack, all the living and deceased hostages were returned to their homeland. Therefore, the third anniversary of the attack became the first that Israel commemorated without people remaining captive in Gaza.
The war in Gaza and the humanitarian crisis
Israel's campaign in the Gaza Strip became one of the most destructive wars in the region in recent decades. According to the Gaza Ministry of Health, more than 74,000 Palestinians have been killed since the hostilities began. A significant portion of the enclave's buildings was destroyed or seriously damaged. Most of its approximately two million residents were forced to leave their homes.
In October 2025, through U.S. mediation, the parties agreed to a ceasefire. It made it possible to return the hostages, increase the volume of humanitarian aid, and reduce the intensity of the fighting. However, the war in the region did not end there. As of October 2026, Israel continues to control more than 60% of the Gaza Strip, while Hamas retains influence over the rest of the enclave. Israeli strikes and Hamas operations continue.
According to Reuters, more than 1,400 Palestinians and five Israeli soldiers have been killed since the ceasefire took effect.
In addition, the reconstruction of Gaza has still not begun. The main political dispute remains the issue of Hamas's disarmament: Israel insists that it will not relinquish military control without the group's complete disarmament, while Hamas does not agree to the proposed terms and demands an end to Israeli strikes. The humanitarian situation also remains difficult. According to the United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs, from mid-April to the end of June 2026, more than 1.2 million Gaza residents experienced acute food insecurity at the "crisis" level or worse. The UN forecast indicated that between July and December, the number of such people could rise to 1.4 million.
How Israel commemorates the third anniversary of the Hamas attack
On the morning of October 7, Israeli President Isaac Herzog and his wife lit a memorial candle at 6:29 a.m.—the time when the attack began three years ago. Throughout the day, memorial events are being held in communities in the south of the country, near the sites of the mass killings, in cemeteries, and at the Nova festival site. Separate events were also held near the Knesset.
Families of those killed, former hostages, and civic activists continue to demand an independent investigation into the actions of state institutions before and during the attack. The issue of the authorities' responsibility remains one of the central issues in Israel's domestic politics ahead of the parliamentary elections.
Three years that changed the region
The October 7 attack and the war in Gaza became a turning point after which the conflict extended far beyond the Israeli-Palestinian confrontation. Fighting spread to Israel's border with Lebanon, where Hezbollah entered the conflict; the confrontation between Israel and Iran intensified; and the Houthis in Yemen began attacking shipping and targets linked to Israel and its allies.
Three years after the attack, the main questions that arose in the autumn of 2023 remain unresolved. Israel has returned all the hostages but has not achieved the complete disarmament of Hamas. More than 60% of the Gaza Strip remains under the control of Israeli forces, a significant part of the enclave has been destroyed, and there is still no political settlement that would determine the future of the Strip and a broader Palestinian-Israeli settlement.
