Ukraine Drops in FIFA Ranking, Spain Remains Top — Updated National Team Ranking
Kyiv • UNN
Ukraine dropped three places and 8.08 points after the Nations League matches. The Russian national team remained 35th despite being suspended from FIFA and UEFA.
Ukraine's national football team dropped three places in the updated FIFA ranking after disappointing performances in their latest 2026/27 Nations League matches. The national team fell to 36th place, below Russia's national team. This is stated in the updated FIFA ranking, UNN reports.
Details
Thus, Ukraine dropped from 33rd to 36th place in the FIFA ranking. Our national team lost -8.08 points and now has 1,535.27 points.
The ranking was calculated from the end of May. In Andrea Maldera's debut match against Poland (2:0), Ukraine gained 2.41 points; in the first match against Hungary (1:0), it gained 6.88 points; however, in the match against Georgia (0:0), it lost 2.85 points; in the match against Northern Ireland (0:3), it lost 9.98 points; and in the match against Hungary (1:2), it lost 8.08 points.
It should be noted that Russia's national team, which has not competed under the auspices of UEFA and FIFA since February 2024 and plays only "friendly teams," including Iran, Namibia, Trinidad, and Burkina Faso, remained in 35th place.
Overall, the top three remained unchanged: Spain is first, having won the World Cup; Argentina is second; and France is third.
Portugal's national team rose from 7th to 5th place, moving Brazil into sixth place and Morocco into seventh. Belgium, the Netherlands, and Mexico round out the top 10.
It should be noted that Rwanda's national team climbed by 8 places at once—from 128th to 119th. Guinea-Bissau's national team gained the most points.
Incidentally, the FIFA ranking determines the strength of national teams and is used to distribute teams (seeding) during the draws for major tournaments. A high position helps a team get into the first or second pot and avoid facing the strongest national teams in the group stage of qualification.
In addition, the ranking shows a national team's actual achievements on the international stage in recent years through calculation using the Elo system.
A national football team's position in the FIFA ranking depends not only on the number of wins and losses. The calculation takes into account the strength of the opponent, the expected match result, and the importance of the game itself. That is why a victory over a team near the top of the ranking can earn significantly more points than success in a match against a weaker opponent.

Simion Elected to ISC Board
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
12:49:40 UTC
21:49:40 KST

Mona Simion, professor of philosophy at the University of Oxford, has been elected to the Governing Board of the International Science Council (ISC).
The International Science Council (ISC) is a non-governmental organization whose members are major disciplinary academic organizations (such as the International Union of Pure and Applied Physics and the International Union of Geological Sciences) and major national academic organizations (such as National Academy of Sciences and the British Academy). The ISC was created in 2018 through the combination of two previously existing organizations: the International Council for Science and the International Social Science Council.
Its goals include promoting the value of science and “evidence-informed understanding and decision-making,” facilitating international interdisciplinary collaboration, publicizing scientific knowledge (especially as it relates to public policy), and defending “the free and responsible practice of science.”
While most of the disciplinary organizations that are members of the ISC are in the sciences, not all are. From what I can tell, just one philosophy organization is: the International Union of History and Philosophy of Science and Technology.
Professor Simion is not the first philosopher to have been appointed to the governing board of the ISC. Francoise Baylis, emerita at Dalhousie University, is currently a board member.
You can read more about why Professor Simion was elected to the position here. Her four-year term begins later this month.

Three years of Gaza genocide: Israeli assault leaves health system in ruins
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
12:49:01 UTC
21:49:01 KST

Serdar Dincel
07 October 2026•Update: 07 October 2026
Three years of Israeli war have devastated Gaza’s healthcare system, reducing its capacity to deliver even the most basic health services and undermining its ability to respond to needs of the population.
Israel's brutal military campaign has killed hundreds of health workers, destroyed health facilties, and deprived medical teams of equipment and supplies needed to care for patients. 
Health workers and medical facilities hit by war
According to WHO chief Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, more than 1,700 health workers have been killed in at least 920 attacks on health facilities and staff in the last three years. 
The attacks had also affected 386 ambulances.
The UN health agency’s latest situation update said only 2,253 inpatient beds and just 104 ICU beds, 343 maternity beds, 384 emergency room beds and 126 incubators remain available across Gaza health services to serve a population of over 2 million people. 
Healthcare system pushed to the brink 
Before the war in October 2023, the Gaza Strip had 36 hospitals operating within its healthcare system.  
According to the latest World Health Organization (WHO) assessment, only 19 remain partially fuctioning now.
Primary healthcare has also been severely affected.  
Of the 233 primary health care facilities, only 146 are functional, leaving large parts of the population with limited access to routine and specialized care. 
Shortages deepen pressure on patients 
Due to Israeli restrictions on "dual-use" items, essential medicines including insulin, diagnostic equipment and fuel are in critically short supply.
Cancer patients are unable to consistently access treatment, kidney patients face difficulties obtaining regular dialysis, and mothers and newborns face increased risks.
Thousands of people have also suffered amputations – often without anesthesia – and other life-changing injuries, while rehabilitation services remain severely limited.
Diagnostic capacity remains restricted by shortages of equipment, consumables, generator fuel and spare parts.
Overall, estimates showed at least 2,000 people in Gaza are being diagnosed with cancer each year, 45,000 patients are living with cardiovasculur diseases, and over 1 million have mental disorders.
Meanwhile, more than 500,000 women of reproductive age lack access to essential services including antenatal care, postnatal care, family planning, and management of sexual transmitted infections. 
Displacement and poor sanitation add to health risks 
The collapse of healthcare is compounded by deteriorating water, sanitation, shelter and living conditions.
According to WHO estimates, about 1.7 million people remain displaced, many living in overcrowded conditions with inadequate shelter, water and sanitation.
Health authorities and humanitarian organizations continue to report respiratory infections, skin diseases and acute watery diarrhoea, while water contamination and inadequate sanitation increase the risk of further outbreaks.
For patients whose conditions cannot be treated locally, medical evacuation remains a critical lifeline.
In a September report, the WHO said over 13,760 patients have been medically evacuated from Gaza since October 2023, but tens of thousands more still require specialized care unavailable inside the territory.
Reinhilde Van de Weerdt, WHO representative for the occupied Palestinian territory, told a media briefing in April that rebuilding Gaza's healthcare system will require an estimated $10 billion over the next five years.

Palestinian children leave Israeli prisons, but the prison does not leave them
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
12:47:19 UTC
21:47:19 KST

“I left one prison and entered another.”
For Ahmad, 19, leaving Israeli detention did not mean leaving prison behind. The fear and trauma of his 15 months in detention followed him home.
He was arrested on August 6, 2024, at 16, and released on November 3, 2025, at 18.
Now back in Balata Camp in the occupied West Bank, Ahmad says that fear continues to shape his daily life.
“If the army enters the city, I instantly disappear from the area. I’m afraid of going back to prison. I’m afraid of what is inside, of the hardships I experienced in there,” he tells TRT World.
Since October 7, Palestinian children in the occupied West Bank have faced a sharp rise in detention by Israeli forces, within a system that has long subjected Palestinian minors to arrest, interrogation and prosecution under Israel’s military courts.
Around 370 Palestinian children were being held in Israeli prisons as of early August, most of them in Megiddo and Ofer. Israeli forces detained 276 Palestinian children in the first six months of 2026 alone, according to the Palestinian Centre for Prisoners’ Advocacy.
But the numbers say little about what happens after the prison gates open.
For children who have spent months or years behind bars, release can mean returning to interrupted education, disrupted routines and strained relationships while carrying the physical and psychological effects of detention.
Even a few days in detention can leave a lasting mark.
When five days are enough
For brothers Omar, 13, and Faisal, 14, detention lasted just five days.
They were held at Megiddo Prison before returning home to their family. But those five days have continued to affect their sleep, friendships, education and work, while leaving them afraid to move freely outside their home.
Before his arrest, Omar had left school but was planning to return. He also worked at a local shop. Since his release, he has done neither.
“My mental health has deteriorated since I was released from prison. My friends stopped spending time with me. I had conflicts with many of them, and eventually they started avoiding me,” Omar tells TRT World.
He says the shop owner became afraid that Israeli forces might return to the area and damage the shop because of him, leaving Omar without work.
He also continues to experience pain after being struck in the head with the butt of a rifle before reaching the prison.
“The impact affected my head, and ever since then, I have experienced pain whenever I rest my head on a pillow.”
His fear of being detained again has also changed how he moves through his neighbourhood.
“Whenever I go outside into the neighborhood, I am afraid that the army might come and arrest me again, or that soldiers might come on foot and take me away,” Omar says.
“I am constantly afraid. I have stopped going outside and now I spend most of my time at home.”
Faisal describes a similar struggle, particularly at night.
“After I was released, my life became even worse,” Faisal tells TRT World.
“Every night, I struggle to sleep because I keep remembering what happened, the beatings, the humiliation, and the experiences I went through in prison.”
He says some friends have distanced themselves from him and that returning to ordinary life has become one of his biggest challenges.
“The hardest part has been trying to return to my normal life and reconnect with my friends and people around me. I feel like I have not been able to make my life normal again,” he adds.
A system that follows children home
What Omar, Faisal and Ahmad have been through occurs against a wider system in which Palestinian children can be detained without charge or trial.
Under administrative detention, Israel can hold Palestinians for renewable periods without charge or trial, based on undisclosed evidence.
Israel Prison Service data showed that 191 Palestinian minors were held under administrative detention in March 2026, a record high since the organisation began monitoring child administrative detainees in 2008.
Even those figures do not capture the full scale of child detention.
Israel Prison Service data cover prisons under its administration but exclude children held in military detention and interrogation centres. The number of children detained from Gaza remains unclear.
Palestinian children from the occupied West Bank are prosecuted under Israel’s military court system, while Israeli settler children living in the same territory fall under civilian juvenile law. Under Israeli military law, the age of criminal responsibility is 12.
Article 37 of the Convention on the Rights of the Child requires detention to be used only as a measure of last resort and for the shortest appropriate period.
A UNICEF review of Israel’s military detention system concluded that the ill-treatment of Palestinian children appeared to be “widespread, systematic and institutionalised” throughout the process, from arrest through prosecution and sentencing.
For Ahmad, the consequences of that system did not end when he was released.
He arrived home on a Monday but said it took him until Thursday to sleep properly.
“I couldn’t sleep. I didn’t know whether I was dreaming or awake, whether I had actually gone home or not.”
Even eating felt unfamiliar. After months in conditions where food was scarce, Ahmad says his body had become unaccustomed to eating normally.
“There was barely any food. It was a completely different life inside,” Ahmad says.
During his 15-month detention, he was held in Damon, Ofer and Megiddo prisons. He described beatings, stress positions and repeated exposure to gas, and said he suffered from scabies for four months without receiving medical treatment.
Some of his most disturbing memories, however, are of what he saw around him.
“When I entered the prison’s section for child prisoners, I saw the scene inside and thought, ‘Where have I come?’”
“For an entire week after I entered, I was in a state of shock. I couldn’t talk to anyone about what I had seen,” Ahmad says.
Outside prison, reminders of those experiences are difficult to avoid. Ahmad says he leaves conversations when people begin discussing the Israeli army or other prisoners.
“Anyone who starts talking about the army, I get up and leave the gathering,” he says. “And if someone brings up a story about a prisoner, I distance myself from those conversations. I tell them, ‘I don’t know.’”
Faisal, meanwhile, still thinks about friends who remain in prison. Even while working and spending time with his cousins, the possibility of being detained again remains on his mind.
“I am afraid that they will arrest me again while I am at work. I keep thinking that I just want to go home after work, but I am afraid that they might arrest me again,” Faisal says.
None of the children interviewed for this story has received support to help them process what happened.
They are trying to return to school, work, family and ordinary life. But for children who have learned that a street, a checkpoint or even a knock at the door can lead back to prison, freedom does not necessarily feel like freedom.
For Ahmad, that uncertainty has shaped how he thinks about his future.
“All I think about is how to leave. I want to live a normal life without fear and anxiety. I want to feel safe.”
For Palestinian children released from Israeli detention, the question is therefore not simply whether they have been allowed to go home.
It is whether they can ever feel at home again.

Scientists changed how zoo lions eat. Their wild side came out
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
12:46:44 UTC
21:46:44 KST

Scientists changed how zoo lions eat. Their wild side came out
- Date:
- October 7, 2026
- Source:
- Adelaide University
- Summary:
- Giving zoo lions whole carcasses on a feast-and-fast schedule appears to bring out more natural behavior. The lions spent nearly three times longer feeding, engaged in more tearing and manipulating of food, and rested more heavily after meals. Their activity then increased gradually during the fasting period, closely resembling the rhythm seen in wild lions.
- Share:
A new Australian study suggests that zoo lions behave more like their wild counterparts when they are given whole animal carcasses as part of a feast and fast feeding schedule.
Published in Applied Animal Behaviour Science, the research was conducted by Adelaide University and Monarto Safari Park in South Australia. Scientists studied a group of adult male African lions after animal care staff added whole carcasses every nine days to an existing feeding routine designed around periods of eating and fasting.
Continuous video monitoring over three months showed that the lions spent much more time eating when carcasses were provided, rested for longer afterward, and gradually became more active as the fasting period continued. Together, these patterns more closely resembled the natural feeding cycles seen in wild lions.
Lead author Lesia Hryhorenko from Adelaide University's School of Animal and Veterinary Sciences said the study provides new information about how feeding routines can shape the behavior of carnivores living in human care.
"Wild lions don't eat at the same time every day. They experience natural periods of feasting and fasting depending on hunting success," Hryhorenko said.
"We wanted to understand how African lions in human care respond when feeding routines more closely resemble those natural patterns."
Tracking Lions Around the Clock
The research team - which included visiting Belgium Masters student Florence Demoulin from the University of Liege - observed three adult male lions at Monarto Safari Park before and after whole carcasses were introduced.
During the experimental phase, the three lions received approximately 200 kilograms of carcasses. The food was left available for as long as three days, after which the lions entered a period of rest and digestion.
Researchers used eight infrared cameras to record the animals continuously. This produced one of the most detailed 24 hour datasets yet assembled for African lions in human care under a carcass feeding regime.
The difference on carcass feeding days was substantial. The lions spent almost three times as long eating as they typically did. They also fed more frequently and for longer stretches as they tore apart, pulled at, manipulated, and consumed the carcasses.
These activities gave the animals more opportunities to perform the kinds of feeding behaviors that are part of life in the wild.
A Natural Feast and Fast Rhythm
Once the lions had finished feeding, they spent considerably more time lying down and resting. As the fasting period went on, their movement gradually increased again.
This repeating pattern of intense feeding, extended rest, and rising activity closely matched the feast and fast rhythm documented among wild lion populations.
"Providing whole carcasses changes much more than the nutritional content of the diet," Hryhorenko said.
"It gives lions the opportunity to engage in behaviors such as tearing, pulling and manipulating food over extended periods, which are important components of their natural feeding ecology."
Pacing Appears Linked to Routine, Not Hunger
The researchers also tracked pacing, a repetitive behavior in carnivores that is often linked to anticipation.
Pacing increased slightly over the study period, but it did not consistently rise as the lions went longer without food. Instead, the largest increases occurred around predictable events such as keeper arrivals and times when the animals were moved between areas of their habitat.
That pattern suggests pacing may have been more strongly connected to familiar daily routines and the expectation of feeding than to hunger itself.
The researchers also found no increase in aggression or disruption to the lions' social stability during whole carcass feeding events.
Co-author Associate Professor Alexandra Whittaker said the findings demonstrate why animal behavior needs to be monitored over longer periods when researchers evaluate zoo management practices.
"Many zoo studies focus only on what happens immediately after food is provided," Associate Professor Whittaker said.
"Our results show that feeding schedules can influence behavior for days afterwards, making it essential to look at behavioral patterns across the entire feeding cycle rather than a single feeding event."
The researchers say future work could combine behavioral monitoring with physiological measurements to provide a more complete picture of how different feeding strategies affect animal welfare and well-being.
Story Source:
Materials provided by Adelaide University. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- Lesia Hryhorenko, Florence Demoulin, Alexandra L. Whittaker, Todd J. McWhorter, Jon Allon, Rachel Hemming, Justine K. Partoon, Eduardo J. Fernandez. Effects of implementing a whole-carcass feeding routine on the behaviour of zoo-housed African lions (Panthera leo). Applied Animal Behaviour Science, 2026; 301: 107041 DOI: 10.1016/j.applanim.2026.107041

How Quebec Separatists Win Poses New Challenge for Carney Amid Trump Trade War
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
12:45:34 UTC
21:45:34 KST

Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney’s “Canada Strong” strategy vows to “unite” and “secure” the nation in the face of an ongoing trade war with the U.S. Canadians are encouraged to support his efforts to “stand up to” President Donald Trump and help “build a stronger Canada.”
But Carney’s united front is being tested once more, following separatist Parti Québécois’ (PQ) win in Quebec’s provincial election on Monday. The win came just two weeks before Alberta is set to vote on Oct. 19 over whether to remain in Canada or move ahead with a second binding vote on separation. The PQ has already pledged its intention to hold a referendum on Quebec independence. “The courageous battle of Francophones to protect their language and culture will succeed when they have their own country,” said Paul St-Pierre Plamondon, Quebec’s incoming Premier, during his victory speech.
However, Plamondon has vowed that no such referendum will be held “as long as Trump is President of the United States,” citing the political upheaval of the trade standoff.
Even if he were to change his mind, holding a referendum without a majority in Quebec’s National Assembly would prove difficult, experts say. The party fell five seats short of the 64 needed to form a majority government. “In order to have a referendum, you need to have the question adopted by the National Assembly of Quebec, and Plamondon is not going to have the votes for that,” says Stéphane Paquin, a professor of public policy and international political economy at the École nationale d’administration publique (ENAP) in Montreal.
Still, the mere threat of a separatist agenda undoubtedly challenges Carney’s efforts to maintain a cohesive approach at a time when Canada needs to put its strongest foot forward. Carney congratulated Plamondon on his victory by stressing that “building a stronger Quebec is at the heart of our mission to build a stronger Canada.”
After trade negotiations between the U.S. and Canada collapsed in August, Carney met virtually with provincial and territorial Premiers to strategize. He used the opportunity to underscore his view that “Canada is strongest when governments stand together.” The trade standoff with the U.S. comes after months of escalating tensions, as Trump has repeatedly threatened to annex Canada and make it the “51st state” since returning to office.
Despite PQ’s victory, there are few outward signs that the majority French-speaking province is seeking independence. Polling by 338Canada found that around 70% of Quebecers opposed independence as recently as Oct. 4. In a Pallas Data-L’Actualité-Qc125 poll published on Sept. 15, 64% of Quebecers said they were against holding a third referendum on sovereignty—suggesting the unsuccessful attempts in 1980 and 1995 did little to whet Quebecers’ appetite
Nor should the separatist party's victory necessarily be interpreted as a rejection of Carney. The Prime Minister remains popular in Quebec—a poll by Abacus Data in late September found Carney had a net impression of +46, with 59% of Quebecers identifying Trump and his Administration as one of the three most important issues facing Canada.
Quebec has been particularly vulnerable to tariffs imposed by the Trump Administration.
An August analysis by the National Bank of Canada estimates that Quebec faces the highest average effective U.S. tariff rate in Canada at roughly 11%. According to provincial data, Quebec’s exports of metal ores and non-metallic minerals dropped by nearly 25% in 2025, alongside double-digit declines in autos, chemicals, and plastics products.
André Lecours, a professor of political studies at the University of Ottawa, says the presence of Trump was felt heavily throughout the Quebec election, as his trade threats had already dampened the separatist movement.
“It prompted PQ to commit to holding a referendum only after the departure of the President,” Lecours says. “Most Quebecers don't want an independence referendum at this point, anyway, so it helped to make the referendum something distant.”
Tensions between Carney and Plamondon
Lecours says it is “not in the DNA of PQ to collaborate with the government of Canada” and suggests there may be difficult conversations ahead.
That tension is already visible over the trade war, he notes. When Carney decided to match U.S. tariffs “dollar-for-dollar”, Plamondon publicly opposed the approach, saying “it directly harms” Quebec's economy.
“The intergovernmental relations with Quebec is going to be a challenge, especially in the context of the negotiations with the U.S.,” Lecours predicts. “If there's anything in these negotiations driving towards an agreement that seems to diminish Quebec, its economy, or its sectors, then PQ is going to denounce it.”
“PQ still wants to have a referendum on independence, so it has very few incentives to make this relationship [with Carney] work or seem productive,” Lecours adds.
The PQ has also voiced opposition to the federal government's proposed high-speed rail project that would connect Toronto to Montreal and on to Quebec City, which could cause further issues.
Alberta separatism movement adds plight to Carney’s unity efforts
Carney is facing a separatist challenge in the energy-rich province of Alberta. An Oct. 19 referendum, set to also include immigration and constitutional questions, will ask Albertans: “Should Alberta remain a province of Canada, or should the Government of Alberta commence the legal process required under the Canadian Constitution to hold a binding provincial referendum on whether or not Alberta should separate from Canada?”
The vote will not itself be a binding referendum on separation. Instead, it will determine whether the government should begin the legal process required to hold such a referendum.
Polling from 338Canada on Sept. 20 showed 74% of Albertans wish to remain in Canada.
Carney’s government has meanwhile sought to court support in Alberta through new business proposals, including a high-speed rail line that would connect Calgary to Edmonton via Red Deer, linking Alberta's two largest cities, and the Pacific Link oil pipeline project, which would carry crude oil from Bruderheim, Alberta, to a deep-water port near Delta, British Columbia.
“That’s the scale of what Alberta and Canada can achieve—and the speed with which we can achieve it–when we work together,” Carney said on Oct. 1, announcing that Canada will fast-track the approval process for the pipeline. “And we will build together—with Alberta, British Columbia, and every province and territory—in the true spirit of cooperative federalism, harnessing the full force of a united Canada.”
But experts say Carney must strike a careful balance, with efforts to address separatist discontent in Alberta potentially influencing perceptions elsewhere, particularly in Quebec.
“In order to prevent support for independence in Alberta, the Carney government’s strategy is to put more money and investment in the direction of Alberta,” says Paquin. “[Quebecans] might compare what he's doing to Alberta to what he does to Quebec. If he has a stronger stance against Quebec or a more aggressive approach, then it could lead to more support for Quebec independence.”

‘Now is the moment’: housing activists at Madrid encampment pin wary hopes on Spain’s early election
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
12:43:36 UTC
21:43:36 KST

At a makeshift lunch counter tucked within a maze of tents at a housing protest camp in Madrid, Sélpide San Luis pointed to the dizzying pace of change. “We built a city in a week,” said the 26-year-old, whose videos documenting day-to-day life at the encampment have attracted tens of thousands of views on social media, as she pointed to the more than 1,200 tents set up in the central Puerta del Sol square.
“We have urban planning, the streets have names and we’ve put surveillance systems in place. And thanks to what we’re doing here, media have not stopped talking about the issue of housing – something that we’ve been trying to get on the agenda for so long.”
This week marked another significant moment for the impromptu movement. After days of protests and encampments that have sprouted up across the country after the eviction from of 87-year-old Maricarmen Abascal from her home, the Socialist prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, announced a snap general election in response to rightwing parties torpedoing emergency legislation to tackle the housing crisis.
Housing campaigners vowed to keep up the pressure. “The power of the people has ushered in a new era,” said Alicia del Río, of the Madrid Tenants’ Union, as she floated plans for a general strike in November.
“An election campaign is now beginning that will be deeply shaped by the housing issue. So we ask the members of parliament, are you going to introduce the measures that people are demanding – ones demanded by the majority of voters across all parties – or are you going to continue to be the lackeys of the rentier economy?”
The election, which did not have to held until August 2027, is a high-stakes gamble for Sánchez. Polls suggest the most likely outcome will be a rightwing coalition between the People’s party and the far-right, anti-immigration Vox party.
But as anger seethes over rents that have surged 80% in a decade and housing costs that have risen by 63%, the protests also present Sánchez with an opportunity to keep his leftwing coalition in power.
“Bringing forward the elections is risky. But there’s also a feeling of ‘now is the moment’,” said Antonio Prieto, 36, as he and other volunteers transformed the steady stream of food donations into lunch for those at the Madrid camp.
“If we had waited until 2027, the right and far right would have crushed us. And now, at least with this momentum, putting the focus on housing, we can have a tiny bit of hope.”
Prieto is among the many closely watching the parties to the left of the Socialists, hoping they will unite to form a broad front before the election. “I’m hopeful that what we’re doing has really got through, so that parties on the left realise that this is a big issue and they start working on real solutions,” he said.
The eviction of Abascal, a wheelchair user who was carried from the home she had lived in for more than seven decades on a stretcher, catapulted the long-simmering frustration over the deepening housing crisis into public view. It cast a spotlight on the intense competition for housing across Spain, one that pits local people against tourists lets, investment funds and short-term rentals.
As a wave of outrage swept the country, the investment firm that bought Abascal’s home said she could return home without paying the 230% rent hike it had reportedly demanded. But the protests and encampments have continued to gain strength as people demand change.
Prieto described them as a “moral duty”, given that the Spanish constitution recognises the right to “decent and adequate housing” for all. “What we’re seeing is a systematic violation of the constitution … So we have to be here,” he said.
The growing tent city has had visitors too – some to snap photos, others to ask questions and some to provoke. But the vast majority express their support, said Juan Vázquez, of the Housing Union of Carabanchel, a district in the south of Madrid.
“People of all ages have stopped by to wish us strength, bring us water and food, and tell us to keep going,” he said.
The challenge now is to translate the groundswell of support into concrete change. “On the one hand we have a right wing that pursues policies of misery and directly attacks the working class,” Vázquez said. “But on the other hand, Sánchez and his government have not gone after the profits that speculative rentiers make from our misery.”
He described the coming weeks, as people across Spain prepare to vote, as crucial. “Basically, what we want is to channel all this energy so that it doesn’t just remain a footnote in a week-long encampment – to organise, apply pressure and secure our rights. We know that the organisation of the working class is the only means of looking after our interests.”
Jorge Rubio, 27, said the scale of the protests had hopefully made it clear to everyone just what was at stake. “If you don’t vote, the impact could be huge. You could end up without a place to live,” he said, citing rooms for rent that had surged from €180 to €700 (£150 to £600) a month in six years. “It’s crazy. It’s not viable. We’re all affected by this,” he said.
He was among the many hoping the movement would go further. “Housing is not just a problem here, it’s a European problem. The revolution needs to reach them too.”

Mourning, genocide and elections as Israel marks third anniversary of 7 October
Israel marked the third anniversary of Hamas-led 7 October attack on Wednesday with silent tributes, continued attacks on Gaza and intense political debate weeks before important elections.
Almost 1,200 Israelis died during the attack on Israeli military outposts and settlements within and around the Gaza envelope, with about 250 individuals captured and taken to Gaza.
The death toll also includes Israelis killed by Israeli forces during the chaotic response to the attack.
Israel has acknowledged at least one such case, while Israeli media have reported that the military invoked the controversial Hannibal Directive in several locations, authorising measures aimed at preventing captives from being taken into Gaza even at the risk of their lives.
At the site of the Nova music festival, one of the places which were hit that day, Israeli family members bowed their heads in silence—although at least one instead put on techno music in tribute to the fallen.
Both at Nova and the Kfar Aza kibbutz, AFP reporters heard loud explosions from across in Gaza during the commemorations as Israel carried out new strikes, despite an alleged ceasefire in place for the past year.
Gaza officials said at least two people were killed in overnight strikes in the territory, most of which has been reduced to rubble by a relentless Israeli genocide, which has killed at least 74,000 Palestinians, mainly women and children.
At the Nova site, Katia Zohar, whose daughter Bar Zohar was killed at age 23, called the start of the attack at 6:29 am (0329 GMT) "the minute that changed our lives forever".
"Sadly I remember everything," Zohar said. "The moment she called for me to come and pick her up because there were missiles in the air. Then the second time when she called from the road, screaming that they were shooting at her."
Anna Davitashvili, 53, paid tribute to her eldest son Shaun, who was killed at 25 at Nova alongside friends, by playing the last track of techno music that the partygoers were dancing to when the attack began.
"I feel him here. I'm terribly sorry that I couldn't save him; I couldn't help him get out of this massacre," she said.
Exploiting for elections
On 27 October, Israel will hold elections for the first time since 2023, with polls showing a tight race for Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who in three years has ordered the genocide in Gaza and launched wars on Lebanon, Syria, and Iran, and is wanted by the International Criminal Court for war crimes and crimes against humanity.
At the Nova site, Naftali Bennett, a former prime minister seeking to oust Netanyahu, told reporters of the attack: "This was a colossal failure of the state of Israel, which was established to defend Jews in our land."
The centre-left Democrats Party put online footage of the attack, without commentary.
"A government that for three years has not destroyed Hamas's rule is a government dangerous to Israel," Democrats leader Yair Golan said.
Netanyahu marked 7 October with official ceremonies in Jerusalem on Monday, which was closer to the anniversary on the Jewish calendar.
He said there would be "no forgiveness for the murderers" and vowed never to allow rule in Gaza by Hamas, which has faced major losses but remains in control of part of the territory.

3 years of Gaza genocide: The human toll of Israel’s assault
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
12:42:02 UTC
21:42:02 KST

Hind Rajab, the little girl who pleaded for rescue from a car under fire. Refaat Alareer, the poet and teacher. Khaled Nabhan, the grandfather who called his slain granddaughter the “soul of my soul.” Anas al-Sharif, the journalist who reported from northern Gaza.
Those are just four of the more than 74,000 Palestinians killed during three years of genocidal war in Gaza.
For those still alive, the losses extend beyond grief and injury.
Families have repeatedly fled their homes, parents have lost their livelihoods, and children have grown up amid displacement, hunger and the destruction of schools and health services.
A ceasefire in October 2025 reduced the intensity of fighting but did not end the killing or make a return home possible for much of the population.
Here is what available data shows about the human toll.
Gaza’s Health Ministry reported 74,237 deaths and 175,206 injuries as of Oct. 4.
The reported death toll alone is equivalent to about 3.4% of Gaza’s estimated prewar population of 2.2 million – roughly one in every 30 residents.
Of the 71,444 fatalities identified by age and gender through Dec. 31, 2025, 47.7% were men, 29.8% were children, 15.4% were women and 7.1% were older people, according to the UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA).
In October 2023 alone, 8,805 Palestinians were reported killed, according to World Health Organization Health Cluster data.
Thousands more Palestinians are believed to remain missing beneath destroyed buildings.
In an Oct. 3 statement, the Hemaya Center for Human Rights said it had documented the killing of 21,745 children and around 46,000 injuries among children since October 2023, including 11,000 cases of amputation of the lower limbs.
The center also reported 123 child deaths from malnutrition and dehydration, and 293 deaths among premature newborns amid deteriorating health services, electricity outages and shortages of medicines and supplies.
The extent of family loss was already evident within the war’s first year.
A Palestinian Center for Policy and Survey Research poll conducted between May 26 and June 1, 2024, found that 61% of respondents in Gaza said a family member had been killed. Some 78% said a relative had been killed or injured.
The survey covered accessible areas of central and southern Gaza, excluding the north and active combat zones.
Israel’s destruction of housing has created one of Gaza’s biggest long-term humanitarian challenges.
Nearly 1.9 million Palestinians – about 90% of Gaza’s population – have been displaced during the war, according to UN estimates. Many have been forced to move repeatedly.
For large numbers of families, displacement has become prolonged because their homes have been destroyed or are unsafe to inhabit.
An assessment by the World Bank, UN and EU, published in April, found that 371,888 housing units had been damaged or destroyed, representing about 77% of Gaza’s housing stock. Its findings covered damage through October 2025.
Separately, the Palestinian Central Bureau of Statistics said around 201,290 buildings had sustained damage through June 16, 2026 – about 82% of all buildings in Gaza. Of those, 134,422 were completely destroyed.
Around 94% of Gaza’s population needed shelter assistance and basic household items, according to a Shelter Cluster assessment cited by OCHA and based on surveys in June. At the time, up to 65% of households were living in tents or makeshift structures offering little protection from the elements.
The findings described inadequate protection from the weather, deteriorating temporary shelters and limited access to essential services, exposing families to serious health and safety risks.
More than half of households living in tents had used the same tent for more than a year, while more than half of assessed tents and makeshift shelters were in poor or very poor condition.
OCHA has also identified hundreds of displacement sites at risk of flooding, putting hundreds of thousands of people living in temporary shelters at additional risk.
The destruction has also stripped families of the means to support themselves.
A UN Trade and Development report released Sept. 24 estimated that 92% of Gaza’s economic establishments had been damaged or destroyed since October 2023, with the conflict destroying hundreds of thousands of jobs and erasing billions in unrealized labor income across the occupied Palestinian territory.
Gaza’s unemployment rate reached 78%, while more than 90% of the working-age population was not employed.
It's annual economic output per person fell to $212 in 2025, just 17% of its 2022 level.
Meanwhile, prices in 2025 remained 274% above their 2022 level, with essentials such as potatoes and cooking gas costing several times their earlier prices, according to the report.
The collapse has reached nearly every productive sector. Agricultural and industrial output were each 94% below their 2022 levels, while construction was down 99%.
The destruction of farmland and loss of household income have left families struggling to obtain enough food.
Less than 1.5% of Gaza’s cropland remained both accessible and undamaged, according to UN Trade and Development.
“Food security depends entirely on aid. Most Gazans, including children and pregnant and nursing women, face acute food insecurity and malnutrition,” the UN Trade and Development report said.
“Children under five risk irreversible damage, including stunted growth, cognitive impairment and developmental deficits that jeopardize their long-term health,” the report warned.
Gaza’s Health Ministry continues to report deaths and injuries despite the October 2025 ceasefire.
At least 1,460 Palestinians have been killed and 5,116 injured since Oct 2025 ceasefire alongside the recovery of 835 bodies.
More than half of Gaza’s hospitals and primary health clinics were non-functional, according to the assessment cited by UN Trade and Development.
Nearly 98% of school buildings in Gaza had been damaged since October 2023, with more than 93% requiring major rehabilitation or full reconstruction, according to UNICEF.
Around 541,000 students returned to school in September, according to Palestinian figures, many studying in makeshift classrooms without basic supplies.
The return followed years of disrupted education. UNICEF said 700,000 children aged four to 17 had missed formal face-to-face schooling for three consecutive years, including around 420,000 who had received no in-person learning at all.
The latest UN Trade and Development report put recovery and reconstruction needs at $71.5 billion, warning that the estimate could rise as further damage is recorded.

France suspends stun grenades as school protests sweep country
Finland
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
15:41:53 EEST
21:41:53 KST

France has suspended police use of stun grenades during school protests after a 15-year-old boy lost a hand, as demonstrations over teacher shortages, overcrowded classrooms and school buildings continue across the country.
Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez announced the measure on Wednesday following the incident near the Auguste Béhal high school in Lens on Monday. Nuñez told RTL radio that use of the grenades would stop during the high-school protest movement “until we know exactly what happened”.
The circumstances remain disputed. Authorities said the teenager picked up a grenade before it exploded. Students said a police officer fired the device directly at him.
The boy’s mother told BFMTV that doctors had amputated his hand and disputed claims that he had picked up the grenade.
Nuñez said 18 internal police investigations were under way over allegations concerning officers’ conduct during the protests. Other cases include a teenager who lost several teeth and another student who lost the use of an eye.
The protests began in September over conditions in France’s high schools and have since spread across the country, bringing pupils together with parents, teachers, university students and trade unions.
More than 250,000 people joined demonstrations on Tuesday, according to the Interior Ministry. Organisers put participation at 450,000. Marches and clashes have been reported in cities including Paris, Strasbourg, Rennes and Toulouse.
Police used tear gas and water cannon in some cities. The Interior Ministry said 488 people were arrested on Tuesday.
Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu told parliament that at least 215 teenagers and 85 school employees had suffered injuries since the protests began. Hundreds of police officers have also been injured.
The demonstrations focus on teacher shortages, crowded classrooms, long school days and the condition of school buildings. Students have reported water leaks, pest problems and difficulties securing replacement teachers when staff are absent.
More than 900 of France’s roughly 3,700 high schools faced blockades or closures on Tuesday, according to Education Ministry figures. Student organisations put the number higher. By Wednesday, the ministry said 528 schools had fully or partly suspended classes.
President Emmanuel Macron held an emergency meeting with Lecornu and senior ministers on Tuesday night as the government sought a response to the unrest.
Lecornu has instructed ministers to examine several demands from students, including replacement teachers, the length of the school day, lunch breaks and repairs to school buildings. Ministers are expected to submit initial proposals by the end of October.
The government has defended the overall police response while acknowledging that individual incidents require investigation. Nuñez said officers had acted proportionately in almost all cases.
Rights organisations and unions dispute that assessment. Amnesty France president Anne Savinel-Barras said images and testimony from the demonstrations raised concerns about the use of tear gas, batons and police tactics.
The unrest has also involved attacks on property and schools. 24 schools have been burned or ransacked since the demonstrations began. More than 6,500 people have been stopped or arrested during the unrest, while more than 1,800 people face prosecution.
The protests come as the government faces pressure over France’s public finances. The yield on French 10-year government bonds briefly exceeded 5% last week, reaching its highest level in 24 years.
The financial position limits the government’s room to meet demands for more education spending. French education spending has failed to keep pace with inflation, while results from the 2025 PISA assessment showed French students trailing the OECD average in overall performance.
Further demonstrations are planned in Paris and other cities on Thursday, according to student unions.

Which are Belgium’s busiest rail stations?

Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
12:41:08 UTC
21:41:08 KST

Brussels’ three largest railway stations remain the busiest in the country, according to the new counting method used by Belgium’s state-owned train operator NMBS. Brussels-North has the highest number of passengers, followed by Brussels-Central and Brussels-South (Zuid/Midi). In Flanders, the busiest station is Gent-Sint-Pieters.
In recent years, the NMBS has over-counted around 40 million passengers annually, but these figures have now been adjusted using a new counting method. Last year, the company carried 207.8 million paying passengers: an average of 740,431 per day on weekdays, 306,888 on Saturdays and 264,090 on Sundays.
The new counting method does not appear to alter the ranking of railway stations significantly. The Brussels stations Brussels-North, Brussels-South and Brussels-Central were once again the busiest stations in the country in 2025, with 61,362, 60,647 and 60,595 passengers boarding on weekdays respectively. This figure also includes passengers changing from one train to another.
In Flanders, the busiest stations are Gent-Sint-Pieters (56,779 passengers), Antwerp Central (38,681 passengers) and Leuven (37,379 passengers).
In Wallonia, Liège-Guillemins is the busiest station, with an average of 22,991 rail passengers per day. It is followed by Namur (21,597 passengers) and Ottignies (16,499 passengers).
Seven railway stations have barely 15 passengers per day or even fewer.

Estonia might struggle to fill conscript ranks with men alone in the near future
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
12:41:00 UTC
21:41:00 KST

Estonia might struggle to fill conscript ranks with men alone in the near future
Filling the required number of conscript positions with men alone could soon become difficult as the number of male births declines, Anu Rannaveski, director general of the Defense Resources Agency, said.
Rannaveski said the commander of the Estonian Defense Forces determines the number of conscripts each year. That figure, in turn, is based on the number of reservists needed. In recent years, the number of conscripts has ranged from around 3,600 to 3,800. Starting next year, up to 4,100 conscripts will be called up for military service.
According to Rannaveski, around 50 women enter military service each year. Women have been able to volunteer for military service since 2013 and the figure has generally remained at around 50 since then. "There have been a couple of years when there were 60 women and there have been years when there were 45, but it has remained at around 50," Rannaveski said. She added that women account for 1 to 2 percent of conscripts.
Conscript need must be met
Rannaveski noted that demographic trends show the number of boys being born is declining and the situation will get progressively worse. Rannaveski added that the Defense Forces will nevertheless have to find a way to reach the target of 4,100 conscripts.
In 2025, Estonia's total births came to 9,240, including 4,789 boys.
She explained that more than half of Estonian society currently has little opportunity to contribute to national defense. Rannaveski said women do have the option of entering military service, but they have to find the motivation to do so themselves. By contrast, the state actively reaches out to men, she noted.
Women can currently serve in a variety of units. "The concern that there are specific roles for women is certainly unfounded — women perform very well across the board," Rannaveski said.
Both men and women improve their physical abilities during military service. "When we talk about young men entering military service, only about a third meet the physical requirements that are actually needed," Rannaveski said.
She said that during military service, women want to have access to the same information as the rest of their unit. As a result, they stay in the same barracks and rooms as the men. "They use the lockers there to divide up the room and create some privacy for themselves," Rannaveski said. However, separate hygiene facilities are generally provided for women.
Changes in order
The director said that between 2035 and 2040, it will become difficult to fill the required number of conscript positions with young men alone. She added that in that case, a more compulsory system would have to be introduced.
Rannaveski said Estonia should develop a system that works for the country. She noted that in Norway, Sweden and Denmark, not all women are required to perform military service. "They have criteria: who is the most highly motivated and who has the knowledge, experience and skills that the Defense Forces need," she explained.
She noted she hopes Estonia will adopt a similar approach, adding that making military service mandatory for everyone would also not be a good fit as there would be more people than conscript positions.

Restaurant spaces in Tallinn do not stay empty for long
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07

Restaurant spaces in Tallinn do not stay empty for long
Many eateries in Tallinn have closed over the past year. Real estate agencies say, however, that there are still plenty of entrepreneurs who want to open new places. Interest from business owners coming from Asia has grown, for example.
This year, restaurants such as Tai Boh, Boheem, Vatikan, Manna La Rosa, Ülo and La Tabla have closed. Even Siili Sahver, a lunch spot that survived the COVID crisis, shut down.
Aira Veelmaa, a commercial real estate broker at Uus Maa, said the situation is not as difficult as media coverage might suggest.
"Looking at the commercial property market, I would say restaurant spaces are among the most sought‑after. There are quite a few people who want to start something new. There is also a more exotic group of clients who have come to Estonia and want to start a business here. Not knowing the Estonian market, they often have more enthusiasm than locals," Veelmaa said.
By "more exotic regions," Veelmaa means people from the Middle East and other parts of Asia.
Popular restaurant spaces often have several interested tenants. Still, some areas are more difficult, such as Narva maantee, where places constantly change. Despite the busy location, restaurants there often do not last long, Veelmaa noted.
The situation is most challenging for eateries located in office buildings because many people work from home. Owners also have to make sure there are not too many food places nearby, since there may not be enough customers for all of them.
But the trend is slightly positive, and more entrepreneurs are looking to open new places, Veelmaa said.
Tanel Tarum of the real estate agency 1Partner also said the situation is not as bad as it may seem from media reports.
"If we look at how many new places are opening, the balance in Tallinn is zero," Tarum said.
He acknowledged that people's movement patterns have changed over time, and areas like Telliskivi and the Volta quarter now see more foot traffic than a few years ago. He added that one reason for closures is insufficient groundwork before opening a restaurant.

Want to Stop Russia’s Jet-Powered Drone Attacks? Call the Belgian Embassy
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
12:40:00 UTC
21:40:00 KST

In Kyiv, we have learned to tell the difference between the softer sound of Russian jet-powered Geran drones and the throaty F-16s that are taking them out.
Unfortunately, the sound of the jet Gerans is much more prevalent than that of Ukraine’s defenders.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Almost half of Russia’s jet-powered Gerans are getting through Ukraine’s air defenses. Cumulatively, that is about 4,000 successful strikes this year, attacking bridges, schools and hospitals, with close calls on European embassies and passenger trains full of foreign dignitaries. Russia is building 3,000 per month and expanding production.
Many of these strikes could have been intercepted with a fully functioning F-16 fleet.
According to President Zelensky, about half of Ukraine’s approximately 43 F-16s are awaiting maintenance in Europe. The Wall Street Journal identified Belgian aerospace company Sabena as the place where some 23 Ukrainian planes sit in maintenance limbo.
The F-16 is one of the few weapons platforms available to Ukraine that can take out a Russian jet-powered drone. In fact, the faster drones are easier for an F-16 to intercept than the slow-moving propeller-driven Shaheds. Ukraine’s air defenses boast a 90-95% interception rate on those.
Ukraine’s F-16 flight wing is one of the most successful of all time. Ukraine flies one of the oldest F-16 fleets with the least experienced pilots, in one of the most brutal air defense environments of any war. Yet they have taken out nearly 700 Russian cruise missiles and more than 2,500 Shahed-type drones, both conventional and jet-powered. For perspective, Royal Air Force fighter planes downed 1,218 Luftwaffe planes in the Battle of Britain.
Sweden Sends Patriot to Poland to Guard Ukraine Aid Hub
But any airplane requires support. “Phase maintenance” is required for every 300 hours of flight time. Belgian aerospace company Sabena was awarded a $235 million contract by the United States Air Force (USAF) to conduct phase maintenance on Ukrainian F-16s in January of this year. Maintenance for a single plane is taking as long as 40 weeks, according to retired US Navy Rear Admiral Mark Montgomery, cited by the Wall Street Journal.
For comparison, Romanian TV reported in August that phase maintenance for F-16s of the same generation with similar modifications requires six weeks at Romanian aerospace company Aerostar. USAF technicians in 2012 in Kandahar, operating in 40-degree heat under enemy fire, compressed wartime F-16 phase maintenance to three and a half days.
Belgian Defense Minister Theo Francken, in an interview reminiscent of Monty Python’s “Dead Parrot” sketch, denied any problems, described the Sabena program as “running perfect” and implied that the Wall Street Journal editorial board and a retired two-star admiral might be Russian propagandists.
The Sabena contract was awarded in January, and Mr. Francken claims a turnaround of four F-16s per month. Were the program running perfectly, Sabena would have performed 32 phase maintenance procedures this year, and President Zelensky would not be telling the Financial Times about missing half his planes.
Certainly, the Dutch seem to think there is a problem, as the Netherlands just announced they will be pitching in on maintenance duties for Ukraine’s F-16s.
Other Ukrainian F-16 maintenance efforts through Sabena are taking even longer. Norwegian media reported in April of this year that all six F-16s donated to Ukraine in 2023 had been awaiting maintenance or assembly in Belgium for at least a year. Lockheed-Martin can build a new F-16 in less time.
But Mr. Francken seems more interested in saving face than saving lives.
Belgium is on both sides of this problem. Brussels should be commended for finally ceasing to import Russian energy in August and September, but Belgian importers have already sent €1.64 billion ($1.84 billion) to Russia for liquid natural gas (LNG) in 2026, according to RussiaFossilTracker.
This is enough money to fund the production of every jet-powered Geran Vladimir Putin has fired into Ukraine in 2026, with enough left over to fund about a third of Russia’s cruise missile attacks.
One of the last European importers of Russian energy, Belgium ranks among the top five European importers since Jan. 1, 2023, sending about €8.3 billion ($9.3 billion) to Russia in that time frame.
For years, we have listened to Belgian officials explaining that a billion-euro contractual obligation to Russia’s Yamal LNG required their gas utility to continue to fund the Russian war machine. Those of us hearing jet-powered Gerans overhead would like to see the same attention paid to contractual obligations by Sabena.
Even if Sabena turns over four planes a month going forward, this only addresses Ukraine’s current needs and doesn’t return the roughly 29 planes Ukraine has been awaiting.
But there is a solution. Belgian Prime Minister Bart De Wever was very clear at the Victor Pinchuk Foundation’s Ukrainian Breakfast in Davos 2026, when he explained why Russia’s frozen assets should not be used to aid Ukraine’s war effort. He said, “We are not at war with Russia. Europe is not at war with Russia.”
Since Mr. De Wever is not in urgent need of Belgium’s 50 or so F-16s, he could save a lot of lives by instructing the Belgian Air Force to immediately loan Ukraine 29 Belgian F-16s. One Belgian plane will be returned for each Ukrainian plane that returns from maintenance. Belgian loaners would dramatically increase the interception rate of Russian jet-powered Gerans and free Ukrainians from living under terror.
It is easy for people living in Ukraine to feel powerless as Russian drones and missiles destroy homes and infrastructure. Now Kyiv residents can act. Call the Belgian embassy and ask them to send replacement F-16s immediately until Sabena can solve its maintenance backlog. Or maybe it is time for the cardboard revolution to shift from Bankova to the Belgian embassy.

German spy scandal threatens national security
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
12:39:00 UTC
21:39:00 KST

German spy scandal threatens national security
October 7, 2026
The arrests of August Hanning, former president of Germany's foreign intelligence service, the Bundesnachrichtendienst (BND), and his former chief-of-staff, Manfred D.*, are threatening to cause a major rupture in Germany's intelligence relationships, according to analysts, as the full scale of the scandal begins to be understood abroad.
Manfred D. is accused of selling around 2,000 highly classified documents to Hanning over a period of 12 years, long after the latter stepped down from the BND in 2005 following seven years as its chief. Manfred D. continued to serve all of Hanning's successors, including the current BND chief Martin Jäger, before retiring in March this year.
On one occasion, the state prosecutor said, Hanning "used classified intelligence provided by Manfred D. to draft an analysis for an officer of a foreign intelligence service."
According to Florian Flade, a reporter for public broadcaster ARD, most of these documents were weekly intelligence briefings the BND delivered to the German government, including the latest findings from partner intelligence agencies in other countries.
"This is very, very sensitive because it involves partner agencies in other countries," Flade told DW's Berlin Briefing podcast. "And we heard this also involves information about the Iranian nuclear program, the Russian military, also the Ukraine war."
Broken trust, broken credibility
Some pundits now say that the biggest concern is what conclusions the intelligence agencies of allied countries will draw from this affair. In the past, the Central Intelligence Agency in the US is known to have shared information on radical Islamists in Germany, which possibly helped to prevent terrorist attacks in the country.
If it now emerges that information was leaving the BND via Hanning, that relationship could be undermined, particularly if it was also eventually ending up in the hands of the intelligence agencies of Russia and China — though there is no suggestion of that as yet.
"There's huge damage being done not only to the outer appearance and image of the BND," said Flade. "There's a damage assessment now happening within the BND. Also, they're talking to partners about this because they want to know if their information was given to other countries."
That could also potentially have consequences for Germany's national security in the growing confrontation with Russia. The BND, which is currently subject to more legal restrictions than other intelligence agencies around the world, considers its relationship with its US counterpart as vital.
"There might be a change in the amount of information that is coming from the US and others," Flade added. Ultimately, he pointed out, it might be difficult for the BND to know what they're not being told.
Only a day before the scandal broke, current BND President Martin Jäger reiterated his concern that Germany could slide into a military conflict with Russia, telling a parliamentary hearing that the Kremlin was already waging a "shadow war" and that further military rearmament was "unfortunately necessary" — though he did say that there was currently no indication of active preparations from Russia.
Flade said that, behind the scenes, Jäger is furious about the leak of information from Manfred D. and called a meeting on Tuesday of all BND officials to underline how serious the consequences of sharing information could be. New internal security measures are also being put in place.
The new case could not have come at a worse time for Jäger or the BND. For one thing, new laws are currently being prepared to expand the agency's powers, partly to improve the BND's standing among its foreign partners.
For another thing, another BND agent, Carsten L. and a businessman named Arthur E., are currently on trial in Berlin on treason charges for passing on classified documents to the Russian secret service in 2022.
New rules for old officials?
The case has also raised questions about what former intelligence officials should and shouldn't be allowed to do once they leave office. After leaving the BND, Hanning founded his own security consultancy business, where he apparently used his contacts and knowledge to advise his clients. This is legal and tolerated, but many think it shouldn't be.
Timo Lange of the NGO LobbyControl said that the Hanning case shows why former intelligence officials must be prevented from working as security consultants in any capacity for the rest of their lives.
"It is fundamentally problematic when high-ranking officials from the intelligence or military sectors, after leaving government service, act as consultants for various — and in some cases unknown — clients from abroad," Lange said in a statement. "This is an obvious gateway for illegitimate foreign influence and jeopardizes the security interests of Germany and the European Union."
But as Flade pointed out, Hanning's career path is not exactly unusual. "These people are trying to just make some money with what they can do best, which is networking and then selling the security assessments that they do," he said. "And yeah, working for companies or even for other countries as a consultant."

WHO urges Russia to release more info on plague institute death
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
12:39:00 UTC
21:39:00 KST

The World Health Organization said Wednesday it requested information from Russia regarding the death of a plague institute worker in Siberia, but the Kremlin accused the media of spreading lies and insisted it had shared all known details.
Russian authorities say the 28-year-old laboratory worker died Friday from pneumonia of an as-yet unestablished origin, in a case that has prompted international concern, including from U.S. President Donald Trump, and which saw around 200 people initially placed in quarantine.
Russia's health watchdog said Tuesday that no cases of plague had been detected among anyone who had come into contact with the deceased worker, Darya Shipilova, and a local official said that 60% of those placed in quarantine had been released.
But Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, the director general of the WHO in Geneva, said in a statement on X that his organization needed more information from Russia to fully understand what had happened.
"WHO has requested further information to clarify the cause of the severe pneumonia, the pathogen that prompted the public health measures, and media reports of a second employee with pneumonia of undetermined cause," he said.
"Timely, complete and transparent information sharing under the International Health Regulations is essential to clarify conflicting reports and enable an accurate assessment of potential public health risks."
The Kremlin said Russia had properly informed the WHO about the incident in line with established procedures.
When asked about the WHO's request to respond to reports about a second person in Siberia allegedly falling ill, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov urged caution when it came to using media reports as a reference for what was happening.
"There is a great deal of media coverage, and the vast majority of what the media are reporting about this situation is false information," said Peskov.
He advised the media and others to rely on information provided by Rospotrebnadzor, Russia's health regulator. It did not immediately respond to a Reuters comment request on Wednesday about the WHO's questions.
Some Western media outlets have reported – citing unnamed "Russian media" – that a second person in Siberia had died, saying they had died of plague.
Reuters was unable to find any such stories in Russian media or any evidence that a second person in Siberia had died although some bloggers on social media were making – without evidence – such assertions.
Contacted by Reuters, the WHO said it had nothing further to add on the matter beyond what Tedros – who was due to give a press conference later Wednesday – had already posted on X.
Tedros' call for more information echoed that of U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio who has said Moscow needs to share more information about the incident.
While Russia's health watchdog has said that Shipilova died after contracting pneumonia, it has not publicly explained what caused it or how she fell ill.
Pneumonia, a lung infection, can have a variety of causes including plague as well as other bacterial infections or viral respiratory diseases, such as flu or COVID-19.

Palestinian killed, 16 wounded in Israeli pogrom in occupied West Bank

Ali Hassan Yasser al-Bazzari, 44, from Burqa, northwest of Nablus, was killed in the attack on Palestinians harvesting olives on farmland near Burqa, west of Nablus, the Palestinian Ministry of Health said on Wednesday.

One such pogrom, backed by Israeli forces in the village of Marda, north of Salfit, injured a number of Palestinians picking olives on Wednesday. They were treated for tear gas inhalation by the PRCS, according to Wafa, which says Israeli forces detained at least three Palestinians.
Separately, a Palestinian was injured after being shot with live ammunition by Israeli forces during a raid near the al-Aqsa restaurant in Jenin. The injured man was taken to hospital by PRCS.
Israeli forces detained a Palestinian and imposed a curfew on residents in Burqa, as settlers raided the village east of Ramallah.

====================================================================================================

The UK Greens are wrong – Zionism is not racism
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
12:37:22 UTC
21:37:22 KST

UK Greens are wrong – Zionism is not racism
The party’s new policy reflects ignorance of Zionism and does nothing to advance Palestinian self-determination.
No notion has been so cynically exploited and distorted by both its supporters and its detractors as Zionism. Just when you think you have seen enough in politics to stop being genuinely surprised, let alone shocked, the Green Party of England and Wales has managed to do exactly that. The decision at its annual party conference on Sunday to vote, albeit by a small majority, in favour of a members’ motion declaring Zionism – which, at its broadest, asserts the Jewish people’s right to national self-determination in their historic homeland – to be racist, while supporting a “single democratic Palestinian state in all of historic Palestine”, was not only unexpected but deeply damaging: to the Palestinian cause, to the prospects for peace, and, to be completely honest, to the Green Party’s claim to be taken seriously as an emerging force in British politics.
Even before addressing the decision itself, one has to ask why, for a party whose raison d’être has always been saving the planet from the cataclysmic threat of climate change, the headlines at the end of its annual conference were about Israel-Palestine. They should have been about how best the UK could contain and reverse global warming, reach net zero, and address the many other issues that could unite the party rather than bitterly divide it. Such a focus might at least have given its MPs some spring in their step before returning to Westminster next week.
The decision itself to treat Zionism as “any other form of racism” is, in my view, a sad reflection of the sheer ignorance of those who supported it regarding the fundamental principles of Zionism, fuelled by hostility towards the state of Israel and, in some cases, intertwined with antisemitism.
The Zionist movement emerged in Europe as a reaction to rampant antisemitism, which in some places manifested itself through pogroms, displacement, persecution and systematic discrimination. It was also a reformist movement that rebelled against Jewish orthodoxy, seeking to change the course of Jewish history from within and enable Jews to become a nation like other nations, rather than remain a secluded and isolated minority living in the diaspora. Early Zionists regarded this condition as unnatural and ultimately disastrous, believing that it could be resolved not through emancipation alone but through self-emancipation – in other words, by establishing an independent Jewish state.
There is nothing inherently racist in the desire of a group of people who share a common identity, history, religion, traditions and language to achieve statehood. Judaism is not merely a religion; it is also a cultural identity and a sense of national and historical belonging. As the political scientist and historian Benedict Anderson famously argued, all nations are social constructs, or “imagined communities”. The Jewish people’s longing for self-determination was shaped by their biblical history of independence, followed by exile and persecution, as well as by the European ideology of a world composed of nation-states that took hold in the nineteenth century.
After much and bitter deliberation within the Zionist movement, it became apparent that the territory that appealed most to those who embraced the idea was the ancient Eretz Israel. This is not to exonerate the Zionist movement from internalising the deeply problematic notion, with strong colonial undertones, that the land of Israel was somehow a virgin territory. The slogan “a land without a people for a people without a land” encapsulated that profoundly mistaken perception.
The immense suffering of Palestinians as a result of the Zionist movement’s drive to establish a Jewish state in the land of their forefathers is indisputable: from the 1948 Nakba to the occupation of the West Bank and Gaza that began in 1967, to the expanding settlements in East Jerusalem and the West Bank, and to the horrors inflicted on Palestinians in Gaza in Israel’s response to the Hamas massacre of October 7, 2023.
Yet the most fundamental document produced by Zionism – Israel’s Declaration of Independence of 14 May 1948 – envisaged a state that was both Jewish and democratic, without one principle taking precedence over the other, at a time when the Zionist leadership accepted the partition of Mandatory Palestine into Jewish and Arab states. Is there racism in Israel? Yes. It exists within Israeli society and has become particularly pronounced under the current government. Do Palestinian citizens of Israel enjoy complete equality before the law and freedom from discrimination? No. Israeli society falls short in this respect, and the refusal by many parties representing predominantly Jewish voters to sit in government with Arab parties, regardless of their political positions, is discriminatory and unacceptable in a democracy.
None of this, however, makes the state of Israel, or the entire Zionist project, inherently racist. The Zionist movement has always been diverse and has unfortunately included racist elements, but they have never represented the totality, or even necessarily the dominant tradition, of Zionism.
Practically speaking, the Green Party’s call for a single state called Palestine to be established in place of Israel is a shocking call for the elimination of an existing UN member state. UN General Assembly Resolution 181 of 1947 called for the partition of Mandatory Palestine into Jewish and Arab states. Israel was established the following year and admitted to the United Nations in 1949. What remains unrealised from that partition plan is the establishment of a Palestinian state, which requires ending the occupation and creating the conditions for genuine Palestinian self-determination. That is where international efforts should be focused.
Moreover, this intervention by the Green Party could hardly have come at a worse time: in the midst of a bitterly fought Israeli general election campaign. It plays directly into the hands of Benjamin Netanyahu and his far-right partners, who thrive on the false narrative of “us against the world”. In this case, the Green Party has handed them precisely the ammunition they need.
The Green Party is entitled to its opinion on the Israeli-Palestinian conflict, as is any other political party. There is much to criticise about the current Israeli government, the occupation of nearly six decades and the expansion of settlements, all of which obstruct the possibility of a two-state solution. But attempting to smear the entire Zionist movement as racist, denying the Jewish people’s right to self-determination, and calling for a one-state solution that does not enjoy the support of most Palestinians ultimately reflects more on the Green Party’s political immaturity, ignorance and moral bankruptcy than it does on Zionism.
The views expressed in this article are the author’s own and do not necessarily reflect Al Jazeera’s editorial stance.
