Ukraine 3rd in world for recorded cyberattacks - Microsoft
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
15:28:03 EEST
21:28:03 KST

Ukraine ranked third in the world and first in Europe in the first half of 2026 among countries whose organizations and users were most often targeted by cyberattacks, compared with fifth in the world and third in Europe last year, Microsoft said in its Digital Defense Report 2026.
Ukraine accounted for 4.8% of all victims worldwide, with only the United States and Israel ranking higher, the report said.
Ukraine remains one of the main targets of Russian state actors, accounting for 14% of their recorded activity, it said.
Government institutions and services were the hardest-hit sector worldwide this year, with 27% of recorded activity against 17% in 2025, the report said.
"Government agencies attract malicious actors because they store confidential information, keep critical services running and sit at the center of a network of agencies, contractors, technology providers and critical infrastructure operators," the report said.
Phishing accounted for 23% of recorded intrusions in 2026 against 7% in 2025, confirming that compromised credentials remain one of the main ways in, it said. In 52.2% of intrusions using valid accounts, attackers stole additional credentials, which shows how quickly they expand access after the first breach, the report said.
The report also noted that artificial intelligence (AI) is shortening response time, and the time from when a vulnerability is first spotted in real attacks to its active exploitation can be well under 24 hours. It forecast that the number of publicly disclosed software vulnerabilities (CVEs) will reach 72,000 this year.
Experts also found that attackers increasingly stay undetected for longer, and the time between gaining access and detecting or stopping the attacker grew in several sectors this year.
"AI adds two new dimensions to this risk. First, attackers are already using AI, while many organizations still hesitate to bring it into security operations. Attacks now run continuously, at machine speed and without fatigue, so security teams need AI on their side to restore the balance," Microsoft Security Sales and Engineering Lead Nataliia Burlakova said in a press release.
Many AI agents act on behalf of users and with their access rights, she said. AI governance, credential protection, the principle of least privilege and visibility into agents' actions should therefore be part of a security strategy, she said.

No systemic risk to financial markets: VP Yılmaz
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
12:27:50 UTC
21:27:50 KST

Vice President Cevdet Yılmaz spoke at the parliament on Oct. 7, 2026. (AA Photo)
Payments to 43,643 investors in 17 funds under liquidation will begin on Oct. 8, Vice President Cevdet Yılmaz said, ruling out the use of Treasury resources to cover private losses.
Addressing parliament on Oct. 7, Yılmaz said the payments would cover funds managed by A1 Capital, Bulls and Pardus under ordinary liquidation procedures.
Separately, he said interim repayments of up to 1 million Turkish Liras in principal could be made in October for funds subject to extraordinary liquidation, provided parliament passes the necessary legislation.
Small investors and money market funds would receive priority. Interim payments would be deducted from investors’ final entitlements, he said.
Yılmaz said investors’ claims would primarily be met through each fund’s own assets, with proceeds distributed in proportion to their holdings. Additional resources would come from recovering excessive or unfair gains and selling seized or confiscated assets.
“Treasury resources will not be used for private losses incurred during this process,” he said.
Investment funds, including higher-risk hedge funds, do not carry the state guarantees that apply to bank deposits, he added.
Yılmaz reiterated that Türkiye’s financial markets faced no systemic risk. The 131 funds in liquidation represent 4.6 percent of the total number of funds and 7.7 percent of their combined portfolio value, he said.
“The problem emerged in a limited area,” he said, while stressing that its limited scope did not diminish its importance for affected investors.
He said liquidating troubled funds would strengthen capital markets by removing potential risks. Authorities would protect investors’ rights, maintain orderly market functioning and introduce measures to prevent similar problems.
Yılmaz also said 10 inspectors from the State Supervisory Council were examining the responsibilities of institutions and regulators. Anyone responsible for unlawful gains would be held accountable, he said.

Pranas Domšaitis Gallery of the LNMA invites where the summer never ends  - The Baltic Times
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
12:26:45 UTC
21:26:45 KST

On Thursday, 8 October, at 6:00 PM, the Pranas Domšaitis Gallery of the Lithuanian National Museum of Art (Liepų St. 33) Klaipėda opens Where the Summer Never Ends, an exhibition by American photographer Andy Sweet. Documenting the vivid life of Miami Beach, Sweet captured imagery of his immediate surroundings that powerfully reflects much broader complexities of the American social landscape from the late 1960s through the late 1970s. Exuding summer heat, his photographs capture profound shifts in American society – from the Jewish traditions permeating daily life and the emerging LGBTQ+ community to ongoing racial and ethnic segregation.
Following its 2024 debut at the Radvila Palace Museum of Art of the LNMA, the exhibition arrives in Klaipėda inviting viewers to soak up the warmth of Miami Beach’s sun-drenched views.
‘Audiences in Klaipėda are always enthusiastic about photography exhibitions, so we are delighted to present Andy Sweet’s work in our city for the first time. Living in a port city, no one can remain indifferent to coastal beachscape views,’ says Skaistė Marčienė, Director of the Pranas Domšaitis Gallery.
‘The people immortalized in Sweet’s photography also include Jewish Holocaust survivors from Lithuania – making this exhibition, in a sense, a homecoming. We owe a debt of gratitude to the artist’s family; these photography and video works have now entered the LNMA’s permanent collection and will remain accessible to the future generations. I am delighted that the exhibition arrives in Klaipėda. I believe the views of Miami Beach will take on a new life in our coastal city, reminding their viewers that summer continues regardless of a season,’ the exhibition curator Ugnė Marija Gausmanė presents the event.
The photographer who preserved the ancient colours of Miami Beach
In 1977, after earning his MFA from the University of Colorado, Andy Sweet (1953 – 1982) embarked on a photography career. Together with colleague Gary Monroe, he conceived The Miami Beach Photographic Project. Between 1977 and 1982, Sweet worked daily recording the swiftly changing world of Miami Beach. The town comes back to life in the bright-colour giclée prints made from his analogue photographs, accompanied by a video footage discovered in the artist’s family home in 2021.
In his MFA thesis, he wrote: ‘I want my pictures to reflect truth … that is why I work exclusively in colour. It is not the colours that matter most in each frame – they are only the means to enhance the potential of the media, which already absorbs a lot of reality by itself, to show even more.’
The drive to capture authenticity shines through the artist’s emphatic lens as he turns it at diverse communities of Miami Beach. The daily lives of elderly Jewish residents, together with drag performers, and other local figures come together to create a vivid portrait of a town in the midst of transformation.
An ode to the capital of sun and fun – and to its people
The photographer never distanced himself from his subjects: his images of everyday life speak to universal human desires: the need to belong to a community or simply to feel needed. Among his most striking subjects were elderly Jewish residents who had resettled to Florida’s South Beach from colder places across the United States. At the time South Beach was home to the largest in the country community of the Jewish retirees, including the Holocaust survivors of Eastern Europe and among them, of Lithuania. The scenes of their life, captured on the oceanfront, on city streets, and at local gatherings, evoke the sense of a vibrant ‘American Shtetl’, seamlessly weaving Jewish traditions into the rhythm of local life.
When in 1977, Miami became one of the first American cities to pass anti-discrimination protections to LGBTQ+ community, growing numbers of the community residents started moving to Miami Beach. This particular community contributed significantly to preserving the area’s historic architectural heritage, most notably, its iconic Art Deco buildings.
The exhibition Where the Summer Never Ends will run at the Pranas Domšaitis Gallery through 14 March 2027, inviting viewers to experience the artist’s deep love to his hometown and its people. Exhibition tours and educational activities will offer audiences a deeper look into the stories behind these vivid, colourful frames. For additional information please visit the LNMA website and social media channels.

Police have been investigating potential offences under electoral law since the broadcast in early September, saying they would widen an existing special inquiry relating to donations made to Reform.
Jukes, 30, and Orr, 47, will remain suspended by the party while the police inquiry continues.
Jukes and Orr were filmed talking about a scheme in which a US donor paid for three polls with favourable narratives for Reform, costing more than £30,000. Donations from overseas sources are not allowed under political funding laws.
Jukes also discussed the idea of the US donor giving £500,000 to Reform through his UK-based son. The men they thought were father and son were undercover reporters.
Farage later met the undercover reporters as would-be donors over lunch in Clacton, and did not object when the idea of the scheme was explained to him. He later said he had not been listening.
In its internal report, Reform said it did not excuse the “foolish” way in which Jukes and Orr discussed donations with an overseas donor. But it said the party had not commissioned the £30,000 polling from the US donor, as Jukes was a contractor rather than a staff member.
Orr was recorded suggesting the US businessman could pay for opinion polling to help with the party’s campaigns, which would “technically be a donation in kind” but “the reality is we could easily get away with it”.
However, the internal report found that because Reform did not make any payment for the polls or directly arrange for them to be carried out, “the payments made to JL Partners were therefore not donations to Reform UK within the meaning of the Political Parties, Elections and Referendums Act 2000”.
In relation to discussions about the £500,000, which was never handed over, the report said it found no evidence that Orr or Jukes knowingly entered into or acted in furtherance of an arrangement to facilitate an impermissible donation.
The report said: “Nothing was agreed, no donations were made and no formal position was presented to the party’s finance team, and nothing was accepted. The party’s procedures for checking the identity of a donor and the source of funds were never engaged, because nothing reached them.”
Orr had also told the undercover reporter: “If there’s a non-trivial chance of you guys directly giving a … five or six-figure sum, then we could do a lunch with Nigel.” The report said “the words used were unwise” but concluded that “they were not a price”.
It also dismissed an incident in which Jukes discussed other purported foreign donors who had given money through their children, which would be against the rules. Jukes insisted “he simply invented circumstances for the purposes of not derailing the conversation” and that it was “foolish, loose talk” without foundation.
The investigation “found no basis for the suggestion that any supporter of the party has given in the way described”.
As a result of the episode, which overshadowed Reform’s conference in early September, the party said it would bring in rules that the party treasurer’s office must be informed in writing of proposed donations and that no meetings with proposed donors should take place until background checks had been carried out.
But Labour’s chair, Bridget Phillipson, said “nothing in it exonerates Reform or Nigel Farage from the serious allegations that they still face”.
She added: “The scandals and multiple police investigations aren’t going away. It’s time to stop the desperate deflection and cover-ups.”
A Reform spokesperson said: “Following the allegations raised by Verbatim Investigations and Channel 4 on 3 September, Reform UK commissioned a comprehensive internal investigation.
“The investigation examined all relevant evidence, including witness interviews, documentary records and electronic communications.
“Having concluded the review, the investigation found no evidence that any laws were broken. Reform UK takes its obligations on governance and conduct extremely seriously.
“We consider that the production company – Verbatim – acted unlawfully and will be taking the appropriate legal action in due course.”
Jukes told the Telegraph, which first reported the findings of the internal investigation: “I welcome the finding of this investigation, which crucially has found I did not break the law, as I have maintained from the outset.
“I am also considering all appropriate legal remedies in relation to any false and damaging statements made about me.
“For now, I will continue to take a break from politics to pursue other opportunities.”
A spokesperson for Verbatim said: “We note that this report is an internal one authored by Reform’s own barrister and general secretary, and that a police investigation remains ongoing. We are confident in our journalism, which speaks for itself.”

Interlaken vs Innsbruck: How Europe’s adventure travel hotspots compare for a winter holiday
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
12:25:44 UTC
21:25:44 KST

These Alpine adventure destinations offers snow-covered slopes, unique hotels and local delicacies. But between Interlaken and Innsbruck, where should you choose to travel this winter?
Winter in Europe means time for outdoor adventures – often on the slopes. Few destinations offer quite the same combination of skiing, snowboarding, chilly winter hikes and other activities like in the continent’s Alpine resorts.
In central Switzerland, between Lake Thun and Lake Brienz, Interlaken sits in the heart of the Bernese Oberland region of the Swiss Alps. Despite the lower temperatures, the year-round resort surprisingly offers accessible hikes and kayak routes during the colder season.
While around 370 kilometres to the east, Innsbruck makes an equally strong claim for holidaymakers’ attention. The capital of Austria’s Tyrol state, it’s also regarded as the “capital of the Alps”, though Grenoble in France is another contender for that title.
So, with the winter upon us, where will you choose for your next adventure getaway?
Both Interlaken and Innsbruck share an Alpine setting and a serious appetite for outdoor pursuits, but each offers adventure travellers surprisingly different experiences – and not just skiing.
Interlaken, Switzerland
Interlaken is replete with lakes, mountain villages and the Bernese Alps with glaciers.
The winter landscape, especially the snowparks, broad pistes and vast downhill runs, can be explored with a pair of skis. And the Interlaken Holiday Region has five areas dedicated to skiing and snowboarding: Beatenberg-Niederhorn, Brienz-Axalp, Diemtigtal, Habkern, and Aeschi-Aeschiried.
The latter two are especially popular during very snowy winters. In Habkern, a single ski lift connects to its four pistes – each of varying difficulty. While in Aeschi-Aeschiried, skiing and snowboarding activities overlook Lake Thun and the Niesen peak.
Another way to enjoy the region’s panoramas is on two wheels through Interlaken’s trails – even during the winter.
The town’s bike-friendly infrastructure makes leisurely rides a breeze. Although snow and ice can make outdoor cycling a challenge in winter, cyclists need not fret. “Winterlaken” by Yellow Velo offers an easygoing two-hour e-bike tour guided by a professional to Interlaken’s old town, 13th-century castle ruins and the traditional town of Bönigen.
Another way to make tracks in the Interlaken snow is through the town’s extensive network of hiking routes – the region features 220 kilometres of winter trails. Come rain or snow, the trails are maintained to still be hikable during the winter. The circular Aeschi hike is always in view of the Niesen, Switzerland’s highest pyramid-shaped peak.
On neighbouring Lake Brienz, just east of Interlaken, it’s also possible to kayak and surf ski across its turquoise waters during winter. Surrounded by snowy peaks and equipped with a dry warm suit, lake-cruisers can go on a half-day tour through the calm waters in the heart of the Bernese Oberland.
Interlaken’s accommodation offerings range from properties perched thousands of metres above sea level, wellness hotels, as well as various camp sites where visitors can spend their nights in camper cans, caravans, mobile homes, tents or bungalows.
Within Switzerland, the region receives train connections every 30 minutes to and from major towns like Bern, Zürich, Geneva and Basel. It is also part of the country’s national road network, making car travel easy, too.
While Interlaken doesn’t have its own airport, the nearest is around 50 kilometres away in Bern or 135 kilometres away in Zürich.
Innsbruck, Austria
Winter in Innsbruck means speedy toboggan runs amid mountain landscapes, groomed slopes and ski tours through snow-covered Alpine valleys.
Taking its name from the River Inn, the Austrian city is home to Tyrol’s highest toboggan run. Situated in the Kühtai ski resort, and at an altitude of 2,127 metres above sea level, this 2,020m-long route takes roughly 45 minutes to ascend before the swift descent starts. When the sun goes down, the tobogganing doesn’t have to end as the run is floodlit well into the night.
Innsbruck is also home to the Bergisel Ski Jump, a 50m-high sports facility and landmark designed by Iraqi-British architect Zaha Hadid as part of a remodelling project.
While popular among ski-jump enthusiasts, visitors can also go to take in the sights from the viewing terrace, and also take in the scenery while dining at Bergisel Sky, a floor-to-ceiling glass-windowed restaurant.
For the skilled skier, almost 40 cross-country trails offer yet another way to explore the Innsbruck landscape. At the cross-country ski centre in Rinn, the Panoramaloipe trail winds through fields towards Judenstein, which is 900 metres above sea level. The free to ski trail also includes a diagonal and skating track.
After working up an appetite, skiers and tobogganers can head to the Graf Ferdinand Haus for a place to indulge in the “hot stone” dining concept and unwind over meat or cheese fondue (perhaps both?) or Graf Ferdinand's spare ribs. The mountain hut is open from December to April and also features a sun terrace – ideal for views of the surrounding mountains.
The region also offers an array of unique places to stay – from farmers renting out apartments for visitors to experience Tyrolean country life up close to mountain lodgings at various altitudes with spectacular views.
Unlike its Swiss counterpart, Innsbruck has its own airport, served by around 50 airlines. Lufthansa, Icelandair, British Airways, easyJet and Finnair are among the carriers operating flights to and from the city.
While on ground, Innsbruck has a dedicated coach terminal. Austrian, German, Italian and Swiss coaches, as well as trains, are also connected to the city's main train station. Train connections from Vienna run 20 times a day, twice daily from Venice and once daily from Frankfurt.

TOKYO, October 7. /TASS/. High energy prices will likely persist for some time, even if the war involving the US, Israel, and Iran ends in the near future, International Monetary Fund (IMF) Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva warned.
"In addition, natural gas supply from the Gulf remains severely impaired, reflecting more-limited LNG transport options for as long as shipping through the Strait of Hormuz remains threatened," Georgieva said.
"This has uneven impacts across the world, with Asia and Europe particularly hard-hit. And, to quote from Game of Thrones, winter is coming. Price pressures may build further as countries replenish reserves and demand rises with the approach of the Northern hemisphere cold season."
"Even if the war in the Gulf were to end soon, the problem of high energy prices would likely persist for some time," the IMF chief added. "Brent futures, for example, now predict high oil prices through 2027. Higher energy prices are pushing up inflation, policy rates, and benchmark yield curves."
Georgieva noted that the average price per barrel of oil has remained above $100 for an extended period. According to her, the high cost of diesel fuel and other petroleum products is "due to a global shortfall in refining capacity."

Tallinn Airport sets record for September, but winter traffic expected to fall
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
12:25:00 UTC
21:25:00 KST

Tallinn Airport sets record for September, but winter traffic expected to fall
Tallinn Airport reported it handled nearly 356,000 passengers in September, up 13 percent on the same month last year — the busiest September in the airport's history.
In the first nine months of the year, the airport reported serving a total of 2.89 million passengers, up 12 percent on the same period last year.
Despite the record, the airport expects a decline in numbers over the winter.
Tallinn Airport spokesperson Aet Härmaorg told ERR the past 12 months have all been records on the month, adding the "all-time record was exceeded in four months: May, June, July and August 2026."
Scheduled flights operated from Tallinn to 41 destinations in September. Passenger growth was driven primarily by no-frills carrier Wizz Air, which has expanded significantly in Tallinn over the past year.
In September, the airline carried 16 percent of all Tallinn Airport passengers and offered connections to nine destinations. airBaltic remained the airport's largest airline, with a market share of 27 percent. In total, 22 airlines operated scheduled and charter flights from Tallinn to more than 50 destinations during the month.
Scheduled flights accounted for 90 percent of passengers, while charter flights accounted for 10 percent. Antalya, Turkey, was the main charter destination, with holiday destinations in Greece and Montenegro also proving popular.
While winter is the off-season, there is a winter travel season, starting September, to destinations in Egypt.
Warsaw was the most popular direct destination for scheduled flights in September, followed by Helsinki, Riga, Stockholm and Frankfurt.
The number of aircraft movements also rose, by 5 percent compared with September last year. There were 4,031 landings and take-offs in total, averaging 134 aircraft movements per day.
Eero Pärgmäe, commercial director at Tallinn Airport, said the passenger records show the summer schedule was exceptionally dense. "The growth that Wizz Air started at the end of last year is still carrying us," Pärgmäe told ERR.
Nonetheless, some developments will lead to a fall in numbers over winter. "airBaltic has said it is cutting its schedule due to the restructuring it is currently carrying out. And the second thing is that, since the price of aviation fuel remains exceptionally high, most carriers have said that the high fuel price is hurting them and they will be scaling back their schedules in winter," Pärgmäe went on.
"If we look at next year, we are moving toward last year's level or even a little below," he added.
Passenger numbers also rose at Estonia's regional airports, which fall under the Tallinn Airport umbrella. Together, they served 9,078 passengers in September, compared with 8,191 in September last year. Tartu Airport took in 4,847 passengers, Kuressaare Airport 3,008 and Kärdla Airport 1,111. Pärnu Airport served 104 passengers and Ruhnu Airfield eight.
Tallinn Airport also says it expects higher passenger numbers during the busy school holiday travel period, October 21-November 4. For this reason the airport recommends arriving at the terminal at least two hours before departure time, as check-in, security screening and passport control can take longer than usual. Passengers arriving by car should allow extra time to find a parking space too.

Ukraine's General Staff reports damage to Samara oil station and Astrakhan gas processing plant supplying Russian forces
The General Staff has reported that the Samara oil pipeline control station and Astrakhan gas processing plant, which help meet the needs of the Russian Armed Forces, sustained extensive damage in strikes.
Source: General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine on Telegram
Quote: "As a result of the 2 October strike on the Samara oil pipeline control station in Prosvet, Russia's Samara Oblast, damage to 11 RVS-20,000 tanks, three RVSPK-50,000 tanks, a section of pipelines and an automated oil product loading station has been confirmed…
As a result of the 4 October strike on the Astrakhan gas processing plant in Astrakhan, Russia's Astrakhan Oblast, damage to elements of two gas treatment units, U-172 and U-272, as well as the secondary distillation unit U-1731, has been confirmed."
Details: The General Staff said both facilities targeted in the strikes contribute to meeting the needs of the Russian Armed Forces.
The Samara oil pipeline control station is a major hub for receiving, storing and blending oil. It is where Urals crude, which accounts for up to 50% of Russia's total oil exports, is produced.
The Astrakhan gas processing plant is one of the world's largest producers of gas sulphur, which is used to manufacture explosives and gunpowder. The facility has a designed capacity to process up to 12 billion cubic metres of formation gas per year and produces up to 3.5 million tonnes of technical sulphur annually, accounting for about 50% of Russia's total production.
Background: On 2 October, Ukraine's defence forces struck oil facilities in Russia's Samara and Volgograd oblasts, causing large fires.

F-1: Singapore Grand Prix — sprint history, race schedule
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
15:24:33 EEST
21:24:33 KST

F-1: Singapore Grand Prix — sprint history, race schedule
Kyiv • UNN
The Singapore Grand Prix will take place on October 9–11 in a new sprint format at the grueling Marina Bay circuit.
This weekend, from October 9 to 11, the 2026 Singapore Grand Prix will take place — the most grueling and hottest round of the Formula 1 season, which will be held in a sprint weekend format for the first time in history. Spectators can look forward to three days of uncompromising racing on the iconic Marina Bay circuit, where drivers lose up to three kilograms over the race distance, UNN reports.
Details
The first night race in F1 history will become a sprint weekend in 2026 — Marina Bay under the floodlights, with the opportunity to score points throughout all three days.
The Singapore race is the most physically demanding of the entire year: humidity exceeds 90%, temperatures rise above 50 °C, and there are almost two hours of uninterrupted concentration without a single break. The combination of the sprint format and a circuit where the appearance of the safety car is practically guaranteed makes this weekend one of the most strategically unpredictable of the entire season.
The Marina Bay circuit
"Marina Bay" is F1's first night race and the most physically demanding one. The circuit's defining features are narrow street corridors, numerous 90-degree corners, and constant braking and acceleration. Drivers complete 62 laps in hot and humid conditions under artificial lighting, making Singapore one of the most physically exhausting races of the season.
Drivers lose up to three kilograms over the race distance and describe the final 20 laps as a test of sheer willpower. As a result of the circuit's redesign in 2023, four corners along the waterfront were removed, but 19 remained, most of them merciless 90-degree street corners.
The circuit runs counterclockwise. Overtaking is formally possible at three corners — 1, 7 and 14 — but in practice, fighting for position in Singapore is extremely difficult, making a good qualifying result, a strong start and a successful strategy crucial.
The speed at the slowest corner is 75 km/h, while at the fastest it is 275 km/h. The probability of a safety car appearance is 100%, and teams will take this factor into account when developing their strategies.
The lap record at the Singapore circuit belongs to Lewis Hamilton — 1:33.808 (2025).
History of the Singapore sprint
The 2008 Singapore Grand Prix became the first night race in the history of the World Championship, and its inaugural running went down in history for all the wrong reasons. On September 28, 2008, Flavio Briatore ordered Nelson Piquet to crash into a wall so that Fernando Alonso would have the ideal strategy and be able to win the race.
At the 2008 Singapore Grand Prix, Fernando Alonso started only 15th after problems in qualifying and made an unusually early pit stop. Soon afterward, his teammate Nelson Piquet Jr. deliberately crashed the Renault, bringing out the safety car at precisely the moment that perfectly played into Alonso's strategy. As a result, the Spaniard surged through the field and won the first night race in F1 history.
For almost a year, everything looked like nothing more than a strange coincidence. But after being released by Renault, Piquet revealed that the crash had been planned. The investigation established that Flavio Briatore, technical director Pat Symonds and Piquet had conspired to arrange an intentional crash to help Alonso.
The consequences were serious: Briatore received an indefinite ban, Symonds a five-year ban, Renault a suspended two-year disqualification, while Piquet avoided punishment in exchange for cooperating with the investigation.
Singapore is famous for the fact that as soon as the winner takes the checkered flag, fireworks are launched. They fill the city's skyline and create an exceptionally spectacular celebration that not only looks fantastic on television but also adds a special flair to the spectacle.
The winners emerge from their cars against a backdrop of bright, saturated colors exploding across the night sky behind them. This has become such an important event for the race organizers that there are even fans who film the spectacle as a separate event.
Fireworks are launched both beside the circuit and over the water in Marina Bay, and similar post-race fireworks displays have since become a common feature at several other night races, including those in Bahrain, Abu Dhabi and Las Vegas.
Race format
The 2026 sprint format is an exciting stress test: the physical demands equivalent to two races packed into one weekend at the most demanding circuit of the season. Safety cars appeared in the vast majority of races in Singapore, so strategy teams view a stoppage as an inevitability to be planned for, rather than an opportunity. Under the floodlights, the cars run in cooler evening air than during a daytime race, but the humidity never lets up.
Ahead of the event, Andrea Kimi Antonelli (Mercedes) leads the drivers’ standings with 302 points. George Russell (Mercedes) is second with 236 points. At the same time, Mercedes confirmed that Russell will start from the grid due to a power-unit replacement.
If Andrea Kimi Antonelli has a clean weekend and finishes around the top three in both racing sessions, his lead over Russell could increase to nearly 100 points with six rounds remaining in the season.
The main question in the drivers’ standings is who will finish the season in second place. As noted, Russell currently holds that position, but a number of drivers are breathing down his neck, including Ferrari racers Charles Leclerc and Lewis Hamilton, reigning world champion Lando Norris of McLaren, and Max Verstappen, who secured Red Bull’s first win of the season in Malaysia.
Interestingly, Verstappen has never won in Singapore, and throughout the event’s history he has led on this circuit for only three laps.
Schedule:
-  Friday, October 9: 11:30–12:30 — first practice, 15:30–16:14 — sprint qualifying; 
-  Saturday, October 10: 12:00–13:00 — sprint, 16:00–17:00 — qualifying.  
It should be noted that the race itself will take place at 20:00 local time (15:00 Kyiv time) on Sunday, October 11. First and foremost, this late time is intended to allow it to be broadcast during prime time in Europe, while it also offers the additional benefit of somewhat cooler conditions on the track.
The Setanta Sports Ukraine+ television channel will broadcast live the qualifying session, sprint, and the Singapore Grand Prix race itself in Ukraine.

What to use to shoot down jet-powered drones: experts explain how Ukraine is adapting weapons to new threats
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
15:24:23 EEST
21:24:23 KST

What to use to shoot down jet-powered drones: experts explain how Ukraine is adapting weapons to new threats
Kyiv • UNN
Ukrainian defense companies are increasingly adapting weapons that have already been developed to new tasks instead of developing systems from scratch. Experts explained why the speed of such modifications is critical in the war against Russia.
Ukrainian defense companies operate in a low-profile mode and are in no hurry to say what weapons and modifications they are developing. New solutions often become known only at the testing or deployment stage. One such project could be a new configuration of the FP-1/FP-2, which Quantum WIY Industries presented as part of the cooperation between Quantum Systems and Fire Point. What this could offer Ukraine and why the ability to quickly modify existing weapons is critical in the technological race with russia was examined by UNN.
Details
Most Ukrainian defense companies operate under an extremely high level of secrecy. On the one hand, this is connected with the need not to provide information to the enemy so that it does not have time to develop countermeasures… Therefore, when information about a development that had never previously been publicly announced suddenly appears, this does not mean that it literally emerged yesterday. Companies often work in parallel on a large number of different projects, some of which never reach serial production
Concept of a possible FP-1/FP-2 modification with eight SPYS interceptor drones. Image taken from the Drone Wars X account.
In the case of the FP-1/FP-2 modification, the concept involves placing four SPYS interceptor drones under each wing of the unmanned aerial vehicle—eight in total. The main advantage of this configuration is the ability to launch the interceptors from the air.
Under the concept, the FP-1/FP-2 could deliver the SPYS drones to the required area and altitude without using up the interceptors’ own resources flying from a ground launch point. Aviation expert Valeriy Romanenko explains that this approach would expand the area in which the interceptors can be used.
As for the concept under which the FP-1 and FP-2 could serve as carriers for interceptor drones and launch up to eight interceptors against jet-powered drones, it is generally interesting. Why? First, because it sharply increases the operational range of such drones. They do not need to expend fuel climbing and flying over a fairly long distance. Essentially, the airborne platform lifts them to a considerable altitude
Interception of the "Geran-5"
It should be noted that during the presentation of the SPYS interceptor in July, WIY Drones stated that it was capable of hitting targets moving at speeds of up to 600 km/h. To this end, the company worked, among other things, on a head-on interception algorithm. In September, the first confirmed use of SPYS against the Russian jet-powered strike drone "Geran-5" emerged.
Interception of the Russian jet-powered UAV "Geran-5" by a SPYS drone. Video: WIY Drones.
This Russian jet-powered UAV has become a new threat to Ukrainian cities: it is significantly faster than earlier modifications of the "Geran," making it more difficult to intercept. The "Geran-5" has a tubular fuselage and, in terms of its characteristics, already more closely resembles a cheap cruise missile than a classic long-range drone, said Fabian Hoffmann, a senior research fellow at the Norwegian Defence Research Establishment.
As a senior engineer at one of the defense companies told The Kyiv Independent on condition of anonymity, the "Geran-5" flies approximately 150 km/h faster than the jet-powered "Geran-4." This also changes the very logic of interception: instead of chasing the target from behind, the interceptor must be brought toward it head-on, which significantly complicates the task.
According to Ukrainian intelligence, the "Geran-5" can carry a warhead weighing approximately 90 kg. The Chinese turbojet engine for such a drone is estimated to cost approximately $40,000, while the entire aircraft costs about $115,000. By comparison, older piston-powered modifications could cost around $30,000.
At the same time, Russia is rapidly scaling up its use of jet-powered drones. Yurii Ihnat, head of the Communications Department of the Air Force Command, notes that on some days, jet-powered drones may account for up to two-thirds of all drones launched by Russia. Production volumes are also growing—the enemy is already capable of producing around 3,000 Geran-4 and Geran-5 drones per month.
The problem for Ukraine lies in the difficulty of intercepting them. President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said that Ukraine is currently shooting down around 57% of jet-powered attack drones, calling this figure “significantly lower than necessary.” That is why finding new means of countering such targets is now becoming one of the key tasks for Ukraine’s defense industry.
“We are already seeing information that at least five manufacturers have proposed their solutions for countering jet-powered attack drones. At least 50 more Ukrainian companies are developing solutions to counter such targets. But if we are talking specifically about mass deployment, we will probably not see it any earlier than another three to four months from now. After the development stage, time is needed to scale up production, train personnel and, among other things, select appropriate tactics for their use,”
However, even after effective countermeasures against jet-powered drones emerge, the technological race will not stop: Ukraine will find a way to shoot them down, while Russia, in response, will try to improve its weapons once again.
“This means that, likewise, once interceptors have been developed and the percentage of jet-powered drones shot down reaches approximately 90–95%, we will see the enemy very quickly try to improve its solution. We are talking about several months. We will see the next stage in terms of speed. In other words, it will no longer be 400–650 km/h, but probably 750–800, perhaps even 900 km/h, which is, in principle, comparable to the speed of conventional cruise missiles,”
In fact, this concerns the ongoing evolution of systems that have already been created: a platform initially developed for one task can perform new functions as the adversary changes. In conditions where new means of attack and countermeasures against them emerge at intervals of several months, the ability to rapidly modernize existing weapons is a key condition for not losing the technological race to the enemy.
“I believe that Fire Point is demonstrating a very sound approach in this case—not simply creating a separate drone for each task, but using existing platforms and seeking new ways to employ them. This makes it possible to adapt more quickly to changes in the battlefield situation,”

EU agrees to sanction over 1,600 people and entities linked to Russia's war
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
12:23:12 UTC
21:23:12 KST

The EU will soon add over 1,600 names, including 77 lawmakers who stood for election in the occupied territories of Ukraine, to its Russia sanctions. The decision comes amid an unsettling rise in hybrid attacks.
The European Union has agreed the single largest expansion of its sanctions list against Russia, adding 1,646 names in one go.
The deal, sealed on Wednesday by ambassadors in Brussels, covers 743 individuals and 826 entities accused of supporting Moscow's full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
Separately, it targets 77 lawmakers who stood in the Russian-occupied territories of Ukraine for the widely discredited State Duma election in September.
Ambassadors wrapped up the agreement after several weeks of deliberations and legal scrubbing, which was particularly intensive given the sheer number of names.
It will be formally approved on Monday when foreign ministers gather in Luxembourg. The targeted people and entities will then be made public.
Sanctions entail a travel ban, an asset freeze and a prohibition on providing funding.
Member states were keen to close the agreement to portray a united front amid a rapid succession of hybrid attacks, some attributed to Russia. Work has already begun on new listings in response to the drone incident at the Leipzig airport in Germany.
Another reason to project unity is last month's contentious decision to remove two high-profile oligarchs, Alisher Usmanov and Mikhail Fridman, from the blacklist.
Usmanov's removal, at France's request, was tied to a prisoner release with Azerbaijan brokered by the Turkic states, which have long lobbied in the billionaire's favour. One French citizen has been released while a second remains in prison.
In exchange for the painful concession, the EU extended the sanctions list for an unprecedented three years. In total, the blacklist will soon cover almost 4,650 names.
Earlier this week, High Representative Kaja Kallas celebrated the three-year renewal but admitted it is unlikely that Usmanov and Fridman will be included again.
"Countries are free to put forward names that should be included in the sanctions list. But in the end, it is up to the member states to decide," Kallas said.
"And I do not see this on these two persons happening any time soon."
Brussels is still grappling with the aftermath of the Usmanov saga and the precedent it might have set for the common foreign policy, which relies on unanimity.
As the bloc prepares to admit new members, the European Commission has proposed using the so-called passerelle clause to move from unanimity to qualified majority voting on issues such as sanctions, thereby avoiding the multiplication of vetoes.
But the clause creates a textbook Catch-22: it requires unanimity to end unanimity.

Kremlin responds to French ballistic missile launch
Russia views France’s nuclear-capable missile launch as a “loud and clear message” and will take “all necessary measures” to protect itself, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov has said.
The French military test-fired a submarine-launched M51.3 ballistic missile on Tuesday, in an exercise in the Atlantic Ocean watched by French President Emmanuel Macron. The weapon, a new variant of France’s 16-year-old M51 missile family, was launched without a warhead and splashed down in the North Atlantic, “hundreds of kilometres from any coastline,” according to the French military.
In a video message, Macron described the test as “a new demonstration of the credibility of our deterrence,” and “a clear message… for wherever it must be received.”
Speaking to reporters on Wednesday, Peskov said: “Problems should be resolved through dialogue, not demonstrative missile launches.”
“Europe has become obsessed with plans to militarize the European Union,” he continued. “This is bad because they are building their defense and security identity on confrontation with the Russian Federation. This is a dead end. As history has shown, this leads to nothing good.”
“Against the backdrop of such aggressive actions and such plans, Russia is on alert,” Peskov added. “We are taking all necessary measures to ensure our national security at the strategic level.”
Outside the US, France possesses NATO’s only independent nuclear arsenal, which Macron is currently modernizing and expanding. France plans to spend €7.4 billion ($8.3 billion) on nuclear deterrence in 2026, while its updated military program adds €36 billion to overall defense spending through 2030. Much of this money will be spent on multi-year submarine, missile, and warhead contracts, but a substantial sum will go toward Paris’ controversial “forward deterrence scheme.”
Under this scheme, Belgium, Denmark, Finland, Germany, Greece, the Netherlands, Norway, Poland, Sweden, and the UK will potentially host French nuclear weapons on a temporary basis and take part in French nuclear exercises.
Russia, which possesses the world’s largest nuclear arsenal, cannot view the deployment of atomic weapons on its borders “as anything other than a step toward escalating tensions,” Peskov said on Tuesday. Peskov was responding to the Lithuanian parliament’s vote to remove a constitutional ban on hosting nuclear weapons on its soil. Although Lithuania has not signed on to France’s “forward deterrence” plan, Defense Minister Robertas Kaunas has expressed interest in hosting American nukes in Lithuania.

Ukrenergo Management Board Chairman Vitaliy Zaichenko told Energoreforma in April 2026 that stabilizing the balancing market requires stopping the accumulation of debts first. He said this means removing from the market those who constantly consume electricity but do not pay for it and cannot be disconnected, including some water utilities, consumers in frontline areas and military units. At that time consumers owed Ukrenergo UAH 46.5 billion on the balancing market, and the company owed generators UAH 25.8 billion.
Experts familiar with Ukrenergo's work said balancing market debts grow by UAH 1 billion a month. They said non-paying consumers use about 120 MW but draw it from the balancing market, where the price is much higher than in other segments. The experts assume Ukrenergo's debts now stand at UAH 38 billion, while debts owed to the company are much higher.

Three years of genocide: How Israel destroyed education in Gaza
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
12:19:40 UTC
21:19:40 KST

- More than 20,000 students have been killed since October 2023
- Nearly 98% of Gaza’s school buildings have been damaged, according to UNICEF
- 700,000 children have missed nearly three years of formal, in-person schooling
Even in war, education remains a fundamental right for every child.
Yet three years into Israel’s genocide in Gaza, thousands of school-age children have been killed along with hundreds of education workers, while tens of thousands more have been deprived of regular schooling.
Despite a partial resumption of learning for the academic year that began Sept. 19, approximately 200,000 children in Gaza remained without access to structured education, according to the UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA).
The scale of the devastation is also evident in the destruction of Gaza’s schools: 98% of school buildings have sustained damage, according to UNICEF.
More than 93% require major rehabilitation or full reconstruction, while approximately 81% were directly hit, it said.
According to figures from Gaza’s media office, 165 educational institutions were completely destroyed, while 392 were damaged as of April.
An August assessment by Save the Children found that 86% of kindergartens it surveyed had been destroyed, damaged or were inaccessible because they were located behind the Israeli military-controlled “yellow line.”
The destruction and disruption have kept hundreds of thousands of children out of classrooms.  
Some 700,000 children aged 4-17 missed formal, in-person schooling for almost three consecutive academic years, UNICEF reported.
By September, approximately 495,000 preschool and school-aged children were enrolled in UN- and partner-supported learning spaces. Another 70,000 reportedly attended community-led and private spaces.
Even with those efforts, 200,000 children still lacked access to any structured learning, according to the UN. 
Deaths and injuries
More than 20,000 students have been killed since October 2023, according to a Gaza Government Media Office report. To put that toll in perspective, attending one funeral every day for 20,000 deaths would take nearly 55 years.
Palestinian Education Ministry figures recorded 1,379 university students killed and 3,017 wounded. 
In the same period, 830 teachers and 194 university professors and academics were killed, the report further said. 
The ministry’s broader June tally recorded 802 school staff killed and 3,291 injured, alongside 246 university staff killed and more than 1,493 injured. 
Destruction of schools and universities
A UNESCO-backed assessment published in November 2025 examined 21 higher education institutions across 38 campuses.
22 campuses were completely destroyed and 14 damaged, affecting 95% of campuses assessed. 195 of 206 buildings assessed were destroyed or severely damaged and non-operational.  
620 specialised laboratories and facilities were destroyed or severely damaged and unable to operate.  
Infrastructure damage was estimated at $373.25 million. School buildings continue to house displaced families, limiting the space available for teaching. OCHA documented two UN schools serving as shelters in Al Bureij in September.  
Financial losses and recovery challenges
Preliminary estimates attributed to Gaza’s Government Media Office put direct education sector losses at approximately $4 billion.
The Education Cluster had received only 13% of the $170.8 million requested under the 2026 occupied Palestinian territory Flash Appeal, OCHA reported in September. The appeal covers Gaza and the West Bank.
Teacher shortages, disrupted pay, insufficient classrooms and supplies, rubble and explosive hazards continue to hinder learning.  
UNICEF warns that prolonged disruption is eroding literacy and numeracy skills, while trauma and economic pressure increase the risks of permanent dropout, child labour and early marriage.  
Almost all of Gaza’s 1.2 million children need mental health and psychosocial support, according to the agency.
Since Oct. 8, 2023, Israel’s genocidal war on the Gaza Strip has killed more than 74,000 Palestinians and injured over 175,000 others, while around 90% of the enclave’s infrastructure has been destroyed.

Scientists identify ancient Egyptian crocodile whose skull is missing its nose like the Sphinx
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
12:18:48 UTC
21:18:48 KST

A skull found nearly a century ago has helped Egyptian and European researchers revise part of the crocodile family tree, shedding light on the Mediterranean's prehistoric wildlife and revealing an unexpected connection to the Great Sphinx.
Scientists have identified a new crocodile genus from a 45-million-year-old Egyptian fossil after using CT scans to re-examine a skull recovered nearly a century ago.
The fossil comes from the Mokattam Formation, the same limestone formation from which the Great Sphinx was carved. Like the monument, the skull is missing the tip of its snout.
Researchers from Egypt, the UK, Sweden and Germany have named the animal Herugavialis cairensis. The findings were published in Royal Society Open Science.
The animal was first described in 1927 as Tomistoma cairense, placing it in the same genus as the living false gharial, which has a long, narrow snout.
But the new examination revealed differences in the skull's structure and the animal's evolutionary relationships. Among its distinctive features were raised, projecting eye sockets.
Those differences prompted the researchers to place the species in a separate genus, changing a classification that had stood for almost a century.
Paul Burke of the Swedish Museum of Natural History led the study, co-led by Philip Mannion of University College London.
Mannion said in a statement that the resemblance between the fossil's missing snout tip and the Sphinx's absent nose helped inspire the name, which honours the Egyptian god Heru.
About 45 million years ago, much of the region lay beneath shallow seas. Herugavialis lived alongside at least two other species of long-snouted crocodiles.
The animal belonged to a group whose only surviving members are the Indian gharial and false gharial. Fossils show that their relatives once had a far wider distribution, with more than 40 species recognised.
The researchers suggest that cooling and falling sea levels reduced suitable habitats around the Mediterranean, while later warming may have allowed their diversity to recover.
Studying more fossils could help explain how these ancient crocodiles spread around the Mediterranean and why they later disappeared from the region.

Three years of Gaza genocide: How Israel devastated key infrastructure
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
12:18:14 UTC
21:18:14 KST

In Gaza, getting enough water has become a daily struggle. Families carry buckets, queue for water trucks and ration supplies for drinking, cooking and bathing.
Children spend hours collecting water instead of attending school.
“Before the war, we did not have this struggle,” Hanadi Al Aff, a displaced Palestinian living with her five children in Gaza City, told the International Committee of the Red Cross in June.
“We save water and keep it for the most important thing, which is drinking, cooking and bathing the children,” she said.
Three years after Israel began its genocidal war on Gaza in October 2023, the territory’s water, sanitation and electricity systems remain severely damaged, leaving millions dependent on emergency supplies and infrastructure operating far below capacity.
According to figures cited by the UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs in September, 91 percent of households experienced moderate-to-high water insecurity.
Nearly one-third had water access below minimum humanitarian standards, while 88 percent reported difficulties accessing safe sanitation facilities.
The damage caused by Israel’s attacks on the enclace is extensive: 88 percent of above-ground water, sanitation and hygiene assets and 76 percent of underground networks had been damaged, according to a separate report cited by the UN.
The Red Cross said water production had fallen to around 40 percent of pre-war levels.
Electricity shortages deepen the crisis
Water production remains vulnerable to disruptions. Supplies through three Israeli water lines fell about 40 percent below contracted quantities during a reporting period in late September, according to a UN humanitarian report.
A desalination plant in Deir al Balah was also operating below capacity because of a brine-pumping failure and heavy reliance on generators.
Electricity shortages further undermine water and sanitation services. UN figures cited in September indicated that 90 percent of energy infrastructure, including the electricity distribution network and related assets, had been destroyed.
Generators are essential to keeping remaining facilities running, but they depend on scarce fuel.
Unsafe water raises health risks
The shortage is compounded by concerns over water quality. In August, more than 73 percent of 938 water samples collected across Gaza failed to meet WHO-recommended levels for residual chlorine, while 18 percent showed microbiological contamination.
Reinhilde Van De Weerdt, the WHO representative in Palestine, said in September that microbiological contamination had risen from below 6 percent in January to more than 18 percent in August. Cases of acute watery diarrhoea nearly doubled over the same period.
Sanitation conditions are also deteriorating. Thirty-nine percent of assessed households reported solid waste accumulating around their shelters, while 36 percent observed sewage or sludge nearby.
Overcrowded displacement sites, unsafe latrines and poor drainage raise further concerns as the rainy season approaches.
Doctors Without Borders (MSF) has reported widespread illness linked to poor water and sanitation conditions, as well as psychological distress among people struggling to maintain hygiene and dignity.
Skin diseases accounted for nearly 18 percent of MSF primary healthcare consultations in 2025, while poor water and sanitation conditions have also contributed to the spread of scabies and lice.
Aid groups warn of deliberate deprivation
MSF also said in April that Israeli authorities had used water access as a weapon against Palestinians in Gaza, describing the deprivation as part of a pattern of collective punishment.
The organisation cited damage to infrastructure, restrictions on humanitarian access and the blocking or delay of essential supplies.
It also said its clearly identified water trucks and boreholes had been shot at or destroyed.
“Since 1 January 2026, all MSF requests for the entry of any supplies through the dedicated system, where approval is determined by the Israeli authorities, were denied,” the organisation said.
Humanitarian partners continue to repair infrastructure and use alternative water sources, but shortages of fuel, generators, spare parts, chlorine and other essential supplies threaten remaining services.
For families in Gaza, recovery means restoring basic necessities: safe drinking water, functioning sanitation and reliable electricity.
For children like those in Al Aff’s family, it could also mean putting down the water bucket and returning to school.

Breadcrumb
Who will govern Gaza? The battle over its post-war future
Khan Younis, Gaza Strip - A year after a US-brokered ceasefire halted Israel’s full-scale war on Gaza, the Palestinian technocrats appointed to govern the territory remain in Cairo, waiting for Israel to allow them to enter.
Palestinian analysts say the delay is a symptom of a deeper problem over Gaza’s future, with those chosen to govern the territory still unable to enter, while Israel continues to control the conditions for its governance and reconstruction.
The National Committee for the Administration of Gaza, chaired by Ali Shaath, a civil engineer and former deputy minister in the Palestinian Authority (PA), was formed in January under UN Security Council Resolution 2803.
It was endorsed by US President Donald Trump's 20-point plan and authorised a Trump-led Board of Peace to oversee Gaza's transition until the end of 2027.
Hamas dissolved its governing body in July to make way for the committee, but Israel has still kept it out. Israeli forces, which were to hold 53 per cent of Gaza behind the so-called yellow line under the ceasefire's first phase, now control around two-thirds of the territory.
Mohammed Daraghmeh Abu Allan, a researcher on Israeli affairs, argues that Israel has framed its demands, from disarmament to the destruction of the last Hamas tunnel, “in terms that can never be shown to be met,” allowing it to hold a long-term buffer zone and defend Israeli communities from inside Gaza.
"Israel's acceptance of the Gaza administration committee is conditional on guaranteeing the Israeli military's freedom of action across the entire Gaza Strip, including assassinations and thwarting any immediate threat," he told The New Arab.
"These are the very reasons Israel uses to reject any real solution in Gaza."
A Palestinian committee kept out
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu rejected Trump’s plan in August, saying Israel would not withdraw until Hamas was fully disarmed.
Abu Allan sees Hamas's decision as an attempt to strip Israel of its main argument for keeping the committee out. On the other side, Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Sa'ar dismissed it as a ploy to copy Hezbollah's arrangement in Lebanon.
Meanwhile, the Board of Peace said it would judge Hamas by its actions, insisting on "one authority, one law, and one weapon".
Writer and political analyst Iyad al-Qarra expects the status quo, with Israel holding 70 per cent of the Strip and the committee stuck outside it, to last at least until the end of the year and until the shape of Israel's next government is clear.
“Hamas deserves credit for stepping back from government, but Shaath’s committee has done very little. They’ve spent months talking without actually getting anything done,” he told The New Arab.
Abu Allan is harsher still, describing the Board of Peace as “aligned with Israel's goals,” given its failure to take practical steps in Gaza since the ceasefire and its silence over what he calls Israeli crimes, assassinations, and the siege.
The committee, he says, is "nothing more than an amorphous body with no real existence, which is why Israel may accept dealing with them as governing bodies in Gaza".
The Palestinian Authority's road back?
Saeed Abu Rahma, a researcher on conflict affairs, argues that the end goal should be a unified Palestinian political system with Gaza inside it, on the road to statehood, rather than a separate entity called the Gaza administration.
"It is hard to imagine rebuilding the Palestinian political system without [the PA], and equally hard to imagine Gaza without any link to the Authority, whether direct or indirect," he explained.
Ramallah's position rests on the same premise, according to Munther al-Hayek, a Fatah spokesman and member of the movement's Revolutionary Council, who tells The New Arab that the PA accepted the Board of Peace and its committee “reluctantly,” given the scale of the catastrophe, for the sake of ending the genocide.
"The best solution from the start was for Hamas and the occupation to allow the [Palestinian] Authority to take up its responsibilities in Gaza, but that did not happen," he adds
"Now, we have few alternatives other than accepting that the national committee that emerged from the Board of Peace handles the recovery phase, provided that the Palestinian Authority takes over the entire reconstruction file according to the plans already prepared."
Al-Hayek sees elections as the way to reunite Gaza and the West Bank under the Authority's legal jurisdiction. PA President Mahmoud Abbas has set legislative elections for 28 November, the first since 2006, when a Hamas victory triggered the split that ended with the movement taking over Gaza in 2007.
Israel holds its own general election on 27 October, and the Palestinian Center for Policy and Survey Research has warned that the month between the two votes leaves almost no time for a new Israeli government to set its policy, making a postponement close to inevitable.
Al-Hayek still hopes any new government will be less damaging than Netanyahu's, whose far-right ministers, Itamar Ben-Gvir and Bezalel Smotrich, he says, have left Palestinians with nothing.
Abu Allan, however, expects no such change, arguing that Israel will not accept the PA's return to Gaza because it would join the West Bank and Gaza in a single entity that could become the nucleus of a Palestinian state, and that only Washington could shift that position.
"Neither Hamas, nor the Authority, nor the Palestinians as a whole, nor even the Arab and Islamic states, nor even the European Union has the tools to confront Israel in its drive to keep Gaza outside any Palestinian governance or administration," he says.
Al-Qarra also rejects the idea that Hamas has lost its base, arguing that Fatah has suffered as much in the West Bank, where Israel has expanded settlements and checkpoints and stepped up killings.
“Gaza’s future,” Abu Allan says, “will depend less on who is in charge and more on the deal between the different parties over who governs, who pays for reconstruction, who provides security, and who ultimately gets to make the political decisions.”
A political and security vacuum
For human rights activist Hussein Hammad, the absence of the PA, or of any unified and internationally accepted government, leaves Palestinians to face the war machine and collapse alone, a view widely shared among Gaza's elite and public alike.
"This administrative vacuum obstructs the organisation of relief operations, prevents strategic recovery plans from being drawn up, and turns the Strip into a chaotic environment where needs collide with scarce resources," he says.
The situation in Gaza is dire; an estimated 1.98 million people, 94 per cent of Gaza's population, need shelter and basic household assistance, according to a Shelter Cluster survey led by the Norwegian Refugee Council, while the global hunger monitor IPC says more than 1.2 million people face acute hunger.
He also warns against sidelining UNRWA, the UN agency for Palestinian refugees, which he says is “the only logistical backbone” capable of distributing aid on the scale of the disaster. Already hit by Israeli bans on its operations, the agency laid off 600 staff and cut Gaza salaries by 20 percent in January to cover a $220 million shortfall.
The organisations filling the gap, from the World Food Programme and UNICEF to Arab institutions and local charities, lack UNRWA's staff, databases, and premises, Hammad says, and in his experience in the field they cover less than 10 per cent of actual needs.
Reconstruction has barely begun, with the Board of Peace unveiling a $2.45 billion plan in September to start rebuilding, a fraction of the $71.4 billion in needs over the next decade estimated by the EU and UN in April.
Abu Allan says there will be no reconstruction without disarmament, a position he says Israel and the Board of Peace share, and that Israel wants Gaza to remain "a place that drives life out" to advance a displacement project now back on Israeli campaign platforms.
Defence Minister Israel Katz said in September there was "no real solution for Gaza in the end without this migration," and analysts have warned that Israel's exit rules at the Rafah crossing are designed to ensure that more Palestinians leave than return.
Even Fatah, which has staked its return on the transition, expects it to drag on, with al-Hayek predicting that the Board of Peace's mandate, due to end in 2027, will be extended because nearly a year has passed without anything being done.
He also rules out any real improvement without an immediate and comprehensive end to the war, warning that after three years every coping mechanism, among residents and relief institutions alike, has been exhausted. A lasting administration, he argues, “can only spring from Palestinians' own free will”.
"Whoever ends up running Gaza cannot be a body imposed by tanks or by international resolutions detached from reality," he says.
Mohamed Solaimane is a Gaza-based journalist with bylines in regional and international outlets, focusing on humanitarian and environmental issues

Laws, pledges or an iron grip? How the EU, US and China are reining in AI
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
12:14:04 UTC
21:14:04 KST

The US, China and the EU are taking sharply different approaches to regulating artificial intelligence. Here is how the world's biggest economies are tackling the technology, and what is at stake.
Pressure is growing worldwide to rein in the most powerful artificial intelligence systems, and the world's three top AI heavyweights are answering in three very different ways.
The worries are much the same everywhere, starting from AI-powered cyberattacks, threats to national security and chatbots linked to children's suicides. The responses, it seems, are significantly different.
The EU has bet on binding rules, though it has already loosened some of them under pressure from industry. The US relies on voluntary promises and executive orders meant to keep its AI boom going. China is building its own rulebook under tight state control while rejecting calls to slow down.
Here is how each is going about it.
EU: "The world's first comprehensive rules on AI"
The European Union adopted its AI Act in 2024, which Brussels calls the "world's first comprehensive rules on artificial intelligence".
The Act regulates AI based on a four-tier risk framework, with rules escalating according to the threat level the AI system poses, going from those posing limited to no threat — such as video game elements and spam filters being able to operate freely — all the way to unacceptable systems with wide-reaching powers being outright banned such as social scoring, emotion recognition and manipulation.
But European companies, fearing the rules would stifle innovation as they race to catch up with US and Chinese rivals, lobbied hard and later won a delay as part of the AI Omnibus bill on rules covering high-risk systems, thanks in part to the Commission’s shift to the right following the EU elections.
Amid growing global calls for control, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said last month that the AI rules put "Europe in the position to shape global efforts".
She also said she would invite the main frontier labs "for a discussion on how we can support ongoing industry efforts to pace the frontier”.
European firms have been more wary of slowing down, fearing it could be an attempt by US giants to lock in their dominance.
The EU has other tools to regulate AI.
In August, ChatGPT became the first AI chatbot added to the EU's list of very large digital services subject to greater legal scrutiny under its online content rules known as the Digital Services Act.
Brussels last month also proposed forcing companies to make AI companions and chatbots safe before children use them.
The EU Kids Act calls for banning AI chatbots from "simulating interpersonal relationships in ways that create emotional dependency," the EU said, following a spate of suicides worldwide linked to children's interactions with such assistants.
US: 'Super intelligence'
Nearly two years into his second term, President Donald Trump has built his AI policy almost entirely from voluntary industry pledges and executive orders intended to sustain an AI boom that is powering the US economy.
On his first day back in office, Trump scrapped his predecessor Joe Biden's 2023 executive order requiring developers of the most powerful AI systems to share safety test results with the government and directing federal agencies to set guidelines for privacy to prevent algorithmic discrimination.
In July 2025, the White House unveiled an "AI Action Plan" listing more than 90 measures to speed up development, ramp up investment in infrastructure and deregulate the US sector as a whole.
An accompanying executive order titled "Preventing Woke AI in the Federal Government" requires federal agencies to buy only models deemed ideologically neutral.
The order was issued without any formal methodology to assess their neutrality other than sharing their platform’s technical documentation with the US government, something Dario Amodei’s Anthropic and Elon Musk’s xAI were all too happy to do especially given the latter’s history of controversial incidents.
Congress, politically divided and heavily lobbied by Big Tech, has yet to pass a federal AI law and is out of session until after the midterm elections in November.
Trump has tried to block state AI laws, but Congress has repeatedly refused to override them, and state laws are taking effect nationwide including California’s AI Transparency Act.
This year, the release of AI models capable of powerful cyberattacks shifted the focus to security. A June executive order set up a voluntary system for developers to give the government up to 30 days of early access to their most powerful models.
With voter anxiety growing, the heads of America’s six largest AI companies signed a White House accord on September 29 pledging independent audits and board-level oversight of cutting-edge models.
The pact allows the companies to self-regulate and carries no penalties should they fail to comply, though Trump called it "morally binding”.
The same day, Trump ordered federal agencies to replace the term "artificial intelligence" with "super intelligence" in official communications.
The latest figures show that AI infrastructure and investment make up roughly a fifth to a third of overall US economic growth at the moment, equal to .45 to .97 percentage points to overall US growth at of 2.1% to 2.3% in 2026, according to the Peterson Institute for International Economics.
China: 'Always under human control'
China already has a complex, evolving set of rules on how AI is used, including by children.
Regulations on AI companion chatbots took effect in July, aiming to curb emotional dependency and banning the creation of digital clones of real people without their consent.
President Xi Jinping said this summer that AI should be "always under human control", calling for more "laws and regulations, technological monitoring, early warning, and emergency response systems”.
Premier Li Qiang has also warned that the world risks "losing control" of frontier technologies such as AI if governments are too slow to regulate them.
However, "a general pause or deliberate slowdown in AI development remains outside the mainstream Chinese policy posture," Oxford China Policy Lab analysts wrote in September.
Some in China see calls to slow progress as hard to justify, "particularly given their perception that US measures such as export controls have already constrained China's AI development for years," they said.
China censors and controls AI-generated content much as it does other online information. And last month, its spy chief warned that AI could endanger national security.
"Hostile forces" are abusing generative AI to "fabricate political rumours and spread harmful information," Minister of State Security Chen Yixin said.
