Why Audiobook Walking Clubs Are Taking Off
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
12:00:04 UTC
21:00:04 KST

Kelsey Bettis discovered the Fleuria Audiobook Walking Club the way people discover many things they didn’t know they needed: Instagram’s algorithm served it to her. Perhaps, she suspects, the app had picked up on how many romance novels she was reading. Bettis had been looking for ways to be more social, but she was also struggling with anxiety and finding it difficult to connect with people. A walking club seemed manageable. She could talk if she wanted to—or retreat into her book if she didn’t.
“The audiobook walks allowed me to be social in a way that didn’t require talking to other people if I didn’t want to,” she says. “I had the option.”
Bettis soon became part of the small army of women wearing headphones that gathers at least once a month—sometimes more often—on beaches and trails across Southern California. She ended up going for coffee with some of the women she met on her first walk. “The best part is the connection with other people,” she says. She kept coming back, and eventually began inviting friends, too. There was something irresistible, she says, about watching “a bunch of women mobbing down the beach” while enjoying something they collectively loved.
The person responsible for that delightfully strange scene was Stephanie Pao, who owns The Fleuria, a mobile bookstore housed in a book truck. Pao has loved audiobooks since the cassette-tape era, and in July 2025, she invited her social-media followers to join her for a walk. She had no idea whether anyone planned to come. If five people appeared, she decided, it would be fun. As it turned out, 50 showed up. At a later event in Long Beach, nearly 200 people joined. “Reading is often such a solitary hobby,” Pao says. “But readers want to meet other readers.”
Audiobook walking clubs are now emerging around the country, turning an activity typically enjoyed solo into a low-pressure social event. For about an hour, everyone listens to a book of their choosing as they walk, then gathers afterward to compare notes, trade recommendations, and—in many cases—make plans to see each other again. It’s a book club without assigned reading, a walking group without racing, and a social activity that allows you to stop socializing whenever you’d like.
How audiobook walking clubs work
In a conventional book club, people read the same book by a specific date, then arrive prepared to say something reasonably intelligent about it.
Audiobook walking clubs require no such advance planning—or the social pressure of sitting around in a circle. All you need is a book on your phone, a pair of headphones, and comfortable shoes.
At Pao’s events, people often spend about 30 minutes mingling before the walk. Then they put on their headphones and separate into faster and slower groups, each person absorbed in a different story. “Everyone can participate, no matter your book taste,” Pao says. When the group is small enough, she asks people to share what they’ve selected—and inevitably, someone lights up because another walker is listening to the same book or adds a new title to their list.
When the walk ends, many linger around the book truck to discuss what they listened to or make plans for coffee. Pao sometimes organizes walks in conjunction with craft markets, bookstores, or library events. After one of her favorite events, everyone enjoyed the sunset together. “We all got to watch something beautiful together,” Pao says.
In the Washington, D.C., area, Morgan Menzies runs a similar group called Pages on the Path. Menzies moved to D.C. from New Jersey and wanted to make friends, so she started the group with one other person. Now, around 30 readers typically attend its monthly outings.
Participants have ranged in age from 13 to around 80; new parents push babies in strollers or carry them strapped to their chests.
“There are like a thousand run clubs in D.C.,” Menzies says. But not everyone wants—or is able—to run. An audiobook walking club offers another route to the same basic destination: movement, fresh air, and potential new friends.
The rise of these groups also coincides with a long-running audiobook boom. U.S. audiobook sales reached $2.43 billion in 2025, up 9% from the previous year, according to the Audio Publishers Association. “It’s not quite a rocket ship, but it’s pretty nice growth,” says Jim Dinegar, the association’s executive director.
Part of the appeal of audiobooks is their efficiency: People can listen while driving, exercising, cooking, cleaning, or unloading the dishwasher. But Dinegar has also noticed that people are becoming more open about their enthusiasm. Listeners once admitted they loved audiobooks almost sheepishly. “It’s OK. It’s not a confession,” he would tell them. “You’re not alone.” Now, he says, those people are finding one another.
Why audiobook walking clubs make socializing easier
Silently walking next to strangers while wearing headphones might sound antisocial. Yet for some, it can make socializing feel more natural.
At Pages on the Path events, participants can talk with one another, or they can simply “press play and just be in [their] own world,” Menzies says. There are no forced introductions or icebreakers. Sometimes she’ll ask what everyone is listening to, who their favorite author is, or whether they’ve recently encountered a five-star book. “It’s fun to hear when someone loved a book and a different person hated that book,” she says.
A group of women who met on one walk formed a text chain and began getting together outside the club. Menzies has watched similar connections unfold countless times. “I think the meaning of life is to form human connections,” she says. “Whatever that looks like.”
At Hedberg Public Library in Janesville, Wis., young-adult librarian Gabrielle Draxler and programming librarian Amy Christian organize an audiobook walking club called These Books Are Made for Walkin’.
“At first, it was a little awkward,” Draxler says. “We’re walking all together, but nobody’s talking to each other.” As soon as the walk ended, however, everyone started talking so fast that it was difficult to keep up. They ate snacks, compared books, and swapped recommendations. “It’s very low-stakes social engagement,” she says.
Once the earbuds come out, everyone has an obvious conversation starter: “What are you listening to?” That question can feel especially refreshing in Washington, D.C., Dinegar says, where strangers often lead with what you do and where you live. Talking about a book comes with “no baggage” and “no pressure.”
The health benefits of audiobook walking clubs
An audiobook walk can be exercise, entertainment, alone time, family time, social time, or all of the above, depending on what someone needs that day.
Dr. Mariah Stump, a primary-care physician at Brown University Health who specializes in lifestyle medicine, sees such walks as a form of “social prescribing”—connecting people with community activities that support their health and well-being. They combine several things known to help people feel better: physical movement, time outdoors, and contact with other people.
The pace doesn’t need to leave anyone huffing and puffing. Walking at a speed that allows people to chit-chat still counts as physical activity, Stump says. “Five minutes a day can go a long way,” she says. “Any movement for your body is helpful.”
Of course, the headphones that make these clubs possible come with a risk: It’s easy to tune out more than intended. Listeners need to remain alert to traffic, other people, and changes in the terrain, Stump cautions. In other words: Enjoy the plot twist, but don’t let it make you miss the curb.
Being part of a crowd can help people feel more comfortable. Pao has heard from women who are more at ease walking with headphones when they’re surrounded by a large group. A solo walk on an empty path might feel unnerving, but a walk with 199 other audiobook fans is a different story.
How to start your own audiobook walking club
If an audiobook walking club doesn’t exist nearby, “just start it,” Menzies says. If only one person shows up, congratulations—you’ve got a walking buddy. “There’s been a lot online about wanting a village, but not being a villager,” she says. “It takes effort to build a village.”
Organizers recommend choosing a flat or paved route, clearly identifying the meeting place, and giving participants a chance to chat before or after the walk. Conversation during the actual walking portion should remain optional. It’s also smart to have a bad-weather backup: When Wisconsin’s limited outdoor-walking season ends, the Hedberg club moves to the local mall.
Partnering with a library can also help people access audiobooks for free. Hedberg brings Playaways, small devices preloaded with a single audiobook, along with earbuds and spare batteries. Patrons can also download digital audiobooks through library apps like Libby.
Christian believes the format works particularly well for people who want to be around others but find large social gatherings overwhelming. During the walk, “no one’s really talking to each other,” she says. Afterward, everyone chats for a little while—a manageable dose of socializing for people who’d rather not work a crowded room.
“You’re going to go out, you’re going to enjoy nature, and you’re going to listen to a book,” Draxler says. “Just do it. I think you’re going to find your people.”

Compounding Pharmacies for Weight-Loss Drugs Are Booming. Should You Trust Them?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
12:00:03 UTC
21:00:03 KST

Before the pandemic, Diane Kinkade lost weight with diet and exercise. But by 2026, she decided she needed to try something else. She had prediabetes and high blood pressure, in addition to being overweight, but her doctor declined to prescribe her a GLP-1 weight-loss medication, saying he thought the side effects outweighed the benefits. So she asked around and found a telehealth site that seemed more than happy to send her a prescription for a GLP-1 after a brief questionnaire.
But the telehealth site didn’t send her a brand-name drug. It instead partnered with a compounding pharmacy to send her tirzepatide, the active ingredient in Eli Lilly’s popular drug Zepbound. The compounded drug represented significant cost savings—$250 a month versus the $399 a month she would have paid through LillyDirect, the direct-to-consumer site that people often use when their insurance doesn’t cover the drug.
Kinkade, who is 72, says she wasn’t too worried about injecting herself with what the compounding pharmacy had sent, a combination of tirzepatide and vitamin B12. At first, she started to lose weight. But a few months into her injections, the telehealth site switched compounding pharmacies, and she had such bad side effects from the new medication (ordered with the same prescription) that she says she could barely function. Brain fog, nausea, diarrhea, and exhaustion all plagued her.
“I could barely get up from the couch for a week,” she says. She tried reaching out to the telehealth site for help, but they just sent her canned, AI-type responses, she says. So she stopped taking the medication.
If Eli Lilly had its way, patients seeking tirzepatide would not be able to receive anything but Zepbound, which is approved by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA). The company’s patent on the drug does not expire until 2036.
In a 2024 news release from Eli Lilly about litigation it had pursued against compounding pharmacies, the company says that it is “the only lawful supplier of FDA-approved tirzepatide medicines in the United States” and that “patients taking a product referred to only as ‘tirzepatide’ are not taking an FDA-approved product.”
But because of a loophole—or a lack of enforcement, depending on who you ask—compounding pharmacies have still been sending patients compounded versions of tirzepatide.
An estimated 5 million people are using compounded GLP-1s in the U.S., according to a Gallup poll released in July; of the 11% of U.S. adults taking GLP-1 medications for weight loss, nearly one in five uses compounding pharmacies.
Compounding pharmacies are set to boom even further because people may soon use them to get more peptides—short chains of amino acids that have become popular among influencers who tout their benefits (absent robust scientific evidence, in most cases) for a wide variety of ailments—than they previously could. In July, an FDA committee decided that compounding pharmacies should be allowed to prepare six peptides for consumers; the FDA has not yet decided whether it will adopt the recommendations.
But compounding pharmacies are much less regulated than the drug manufacturers that make brand-name drugs. As more telehealth sites prescribe these medications and pitch them as a way to lose weight while saving money, some patient advocates argue that more people like Kinkade will fall through the cracks of a broken regulatory system.
What are compounding pharmacies?
Many pharmacies can compound medications. Compounding involves preparing a customized medication for a specific patient’s needs.
“Compounding is absolutely essential,” says Dr. Anjali Deshmukh, a pediatrician and law professor at Seton Hall University. Deshmukh uses compounding pharmacies when, for example, she treats a 3-year-old with a serious disease who can’t swallow tablets and needs medication in a different form.
For much of U.S. history, pharmacists had to mix individual medicines themselves: in the 1930s, three-quarters of prescriptions required in-pharmacy compounding. In this sense, compounding pharmacies have existed for as long as pharmacies have. For decades, pharmacies that compound small amounts of medication have operated under what’s called Section 503A of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act. Called 503As for short, they’re regulated by state boards of pharmacy.
Because they dispense small amounts of medications for individual patients, only with a doctor’s prescription, most 503As aren’t subject to certain FDA rules that apply to traditional larger drug manufacturers. That includes what’s called “current good manufacturing practices,” which are regulatory standards that ensure drugmakers record and trace every batch of product they make and have their equipment tested regularly.
They must adhere to other regulations, however. For instance, they must follow U.S. Pharmacopeia (USP) guidelines, which are set by a private non-profit that develops science-based standards for medicines, dietary supplements, and food ingredients. And they must source their active ingredients from FDA-registered suppliers, says Scott Brunner, the chief executive officer of the Alliance for Pharmacy Compounding, a trade group.
Struggles with regulation
This regulatory system has broken down before. In 2012 a compounding pharmacy called the New England Compounding Center started mass-producing medications in a setting that had been flagged as unsanitary numerous times. It shipped thousands of vials of contaminated steroid injections to patients. Dozens of people died, and investigators later found severe safety lapses in the pharmacy’s production of sterile drugs. The owner of the pharmacy was later convicted of racketeering and other offenses by a federal jury.
In response, in 2013 Congress passed a law creating a new category for compounding pharmacies that serve a large number of people, which it calls outsourcing facilities. These compounding pharmacies, known as 503Bs, are more tightly controlled and closely watched; they are required to follow current good manufacturing practices and are subject to routine FDA inspection. Those pharmacies can compound and distribute drugs on a large scale to help overcome national drug shortages, or when drugmakers stop making a certain drug. Unlike 503As, they can prepare batches of drugs without an individual prescription from a provider. But there are less than 100 of them in the U.S.
Both of these types of compounding pharmacies were essential when GLP-1 drugs were first released, says Brunner. Almost immediately after Zepbound, Wegovy, and Mounjaro hit the market, there were shortages. Physicians who knew that 503As could make compounded versions of the drugs with a prescription reached out to 503As to see if they could help their patients, Brunner says.
“Prescribers knew that this was a wonder drug and started sending prescriptions, saying, ‘Hey, can you make this?’” he said. “And if you were a sterile compounding pharmacy, you determined whether you could acquire the [active ingredients], and that’s how it started.”
Once the drugs were officially added to FDA shortages lists, 503Bs revamped their facilities to start mass-producing them. (It takes much longer for a 503B to ramp up because they produce large amounts of medication and must adhere to current good manufacturing practices, Brunner says.)
Seeing that compounding pharmacies were making these drugs, telehealth sites started advertising that they could provide consumers with cheap versions of GLP-1s, and patients and doctors alike became more comfortable with the idea of buying them from pharmacies they’d never visited. The initial high cost of the drugs motivated many patients to seek out cheaper versions, Brunner says.
This is not supposed to be how compounding pharmacies work, says Shabbir Safdar, executive director of the Partnership for Safe Medicines, a public-health group that aims to protect consumers from counterfeit or unsafe medicines. In 2012, when Congress created 503Bs in response to the New England Compounding Center tragedy, it assumed that 503As would stop mass-producing drugs, he says. But “they didn’t count on the 503As saying, ‘Yeah, I know you did that, but I don’t care. I’m going to mass produce drugs.’” (The FDA said, in a response to a query from TIME, that federal law limits when compounders can make copies of FDA-approved drugs.)
Eli Lilly has taken a position similar to Safdar’s on compounding. “Everyone who needs medicine deserves real medicine that has been trialed, tested, and manufactured in compliance with the law,” an Eli Lilly spokesperson wrote in a statement to TIME. Many compounding pharmacies, the spokesperson said, have been “unlawfully mass-producing knockoff drugs.” The spokesperson added that “anyone selling mass compounded products—including by referring to them as ‘personalized’ or ‘tailored’—is breaking the law and putting patient safety at risk.” (Novo Nordisk did not return TIME’s request for comment.)
Why compounding pharmacies are growing
The GLP-1 boom that began in 2021 was great news for compounding pharmacies. That’s because at the time, many pharmacies were struggling. Consumer behavior was changing, and people were buying more of their goods and medications online. Pharmacists have long argued that middlemen called pharmacy benefit managers (PBM)—which manage prescription drug benefits for insurers—reimburse pharmacies too little for many medications, cutting into pharmacy margins.
Compounding provided a rare opportunity for many small pharmacies to turn a profit. With GLP-1s, “I don’t want to compare it to a gold mine, but it’s a very good revenue source for pharmacies,” says Dae Lee, an attorney who focuses on pharmacy at Buchanan Ingersoll & Rooney, a law firm. “PBM reimbursement rates are very bad, and pharmacies are losing money left and right.”
Pharmacies that submit claims for GLP-1s very often lose money by filling those prescriptions, he says, because the cost of acquiring the drugs is higher than the reimbursement they get from insurers.
With compounded GLP-1s, on the other hand, pharmacists don’t have to deal with insurance because consumers pay cash. (Because compounded drugs are not FDA-approved, insurance will largely not pay for them.)
Compounding allows pharmacies that may otherwise have to shut down to stay open, says Ilisa Bernstein, who worked at the FDA for 31 years in roles including heading human drug compounding. She is now a consultant for compounding pharmacies.
“Independent pharmacies are struggling, and they’re looking for ways to keep their doors open,” she says. “If they can meet their community's needs through compounding, they’re trying to figure it out.”
The rush in demand for peptides could provide a new revenue stream for many small pharmacies. Demand for peptides “is large and growing, and the potential volume is likely to dwarf the volumes seen with GLP-1s,” the National Association of Boards of Pharmacy wrote in its testimony for the FDA committee’s July hearing on peptides.
Can compounding pharmacies even legally sell GLP-1s?
It was easy for Kinkade to get her compounded drug. All she had to do was fill out a form with her current weight and the medications she was taking. She asked for tirzepatide and received it within a couple of days. Some telehealth sites do sell brand-name GLP-1s, but many instead sell compounded drugs; one 2026 study in which a secret shopper easily obtained GLP-1 prescriptions from telehealth sites found that out of 45 telehealth websites, only 6 offered brand-name drugs.
Compounding pharmacies claim that the drugs they are selling are different from what the big drug companies are selling. They do this by working with medical providers to get a prescription for a different formulation of the drugs, changing the dose that they sell so that it is slightly different from what the drug manufacturer makes. The active ingredient often comes from an overseas lab. In 2025, the FDA launched a “green list” to ensure that compounding pharmacies were getting their active pharmaceutical ingredients from facilities that the agency has inspected or evaluated.
Kinkade’s vial of tirzepatide, for instance, included the vitamin B12. Adding extra ingredients is one way compounding pharmacies have been trying to distinguish their product so that they’re not just appearing to sell a copy of a brand-name GLP-1.
“So long as the product is not essentially a copy of a commercially available product, then compounding pharmacies can compound ingredients using semaglutide and tirzepatide,” says Lee.
But what counts as “essentially a copy” is up for debate. In April 2026, the FDA clarified policies for compounders, saying that a drug is essentially a copy if it has the same active pharmaceutical ingredient as the commercially available drug product “in the same, similar, or an easily substitutable strength,” or if the commercially available product can be used by the “same route of administration” (injection, for instance) prescribed for the commercially available products.
Then in September, it issued the first warning letter to a compounding pharmacy that included violations based on making copies of FDA-approved GLP-1 drugs. “The FDA will continue taking action, where appropriate, to protect patients and consumers from illegally marketed drugs and to protect public health,” an FDA spokesperson said in a statement to TIME.
That warning letter was one of the first actions the FDA has taken on this topic, says Bernstein, the former FDA staffer. “FDA recently issued a novel warning letter that focuses on copies of GLP-1s,” she says. “The agency picks and chooses its actions—they can’t go after everything.” But, she adds, “the law was not intended for 503As to mass-produce these products in the volume that we’re seeing.”
Eli Lilly and Novo Nordisk have sued some telehealth sites for saying that they were selling name-brand drugs, but have been hesitant to sue compounding pharmacies for making copies of their drugs, says Zachary Silbersher, a patent attorney. That’s because such patent lawsuits can be extremely expensive, and it can be difficult to prove that compounders did anything wrong, especially if they have a valid prescription from a doctor. Proving patent infringement is much more difficult than most people think, he says.
“Suing individual pharmacies can take a lot more time and energy than you might realize,” he says. “The lawsuits might start costing more than they’re worth.”
Is it dangerous to buy drugs from compounding pharmacies?
Besides the deaths of a dozen people from the compounding pharmacy in New England, some groups have raised broader safety concerns about drugs from compounding pharmacies.
One research paper published in Expert Opinion on Drug Safety in 2025 found that people who had taken compounded GLP-1s tended to have worse side effects—including abdominal pain, diarrhea, and nausea—than people who had used the brand-name products between 2018 and 2024. Reports of prescribing and preparation errors were also higher for compounded medications, the researchers found.
Anecdotal examples of people having bad reactions to compounded GLP-1 drugs include a woman in North Carolina who says she was hospitalized for three days after being prescribed too high a dose of a compounded GLP-1, according to an investigation by KFF Health News, and a Kentucky woman who wrote in the Washington Post about needing a liver transplant after taking a compounded GLP-1 drug mixed with vitamin B12.
“I’m actually a little appalled that we’re very comfortable injecting ourselves with these substances,” says Safdar, whose group Partnership for Safe Medicines helped fund the 2025 study. “I don’t know when we crossed the Rubicon.”
Safdar argues that there’s no way to know if the GLP-1s from compounding pharmacies are safe because they are not getting the drug from an FDA-inspected manufacturer. (They are, however, supposed to be getting the active ingredient from an FDA-approved supplier.) And while manufacturers like Eli Lilly or Novo Nordisk have to follow current good manufacturing practices, he reiterates, compounding pharmacies don’t.
“When Lilly or Novo went to the FDA and got an approval for its drug, it was for an approval of the drug that included a quality control manufacturing process,” he says. “So if you’re a compounder and you’re saying it’s the same active ingredient—well, that’s just not true.”
Brunner says that the blanket statement that compounded drugs are less safe is “subjective and unprovable.”
And many compounding pharmacies take extra steps to ensure that the active ingredients they are using are safe. Lawrence Rossetti, the CEO of Drug Crafters, a 503A in Texas, says that in addition to sourcing active pharmaceutical ingredients from FDA-registered suppliers, Drug Crafters tests the raw material before making any order. If the testing confirms that the drug is what the pharmacy claims, that specific lot is approved for compounding. The pharmacy’s finished-product formulations “are tested for potency, antimicrobial effectiveness, container closure integrity, method suitability, and undergo endotoxin and sterility testing before they can be sent to any patient," he says.
Some providers and patients say that despite the lessened FDA oversight, compounding pharmacies may be the best option many people have to get the medication they want at the price they want. “I would argue that the drug makers have overpriced their drug, and compounding pharmacies have been the only reason that those prices have come down over the past three years or so,” Brunner says.
Of course, you could argue that you get what you pay for. After receiving unhelpful, automated emails from her telehealth site, Kinkade finally got a response from a nurse practitioner who had a suggestion for why the tirzepatide had made her so sick: it may have had to do with the fact that the telehealth site had switched the compounding pharmacy it used. She says that the nurse practitioner emailed her that different pharmacies can prepare the same drug at different concentrations, even with the same prescribed dose, and that she accidentally might have gotten a much stronger dose of tirzepatide than she’d been used to taking. If she developed severe or worsening symptoms, the nurse practitioner wrote, Kinkade should seek urgent medical care right away. The email did not tell her whether she should take any more doses of the medication.
Kinkade decided to lower the dose she was taking on her own, and she hasn’t had bad side effects since.
She hesitates to return to telehealth or compounding pharmacies since her experience. Kinkade recently went to her annual checkup, and her doctor was impressed by how much weight she’d lost, and how good her glucose and other numbers looked. This time, he agreed to prescribe her a brand-name GLP-1.

I Put on Meta and Xreal’s XR Glasses. Face Computers Are Finally Getting Good
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
12:00:00 UTC
21:00:00 KST

I’m sorry to say, but the $1,299 Meta VR Glasses might just be very good.
That's despite the company's well-earned flak over privacy issues with its smart glasses and the general uneasiness people feel about being recorded. But in the 30 to 45 minutes or so I spent wearing the mixed-reality glasses at Meta’s Connect event in September, I was astounded by the video quality and wearability of a device that has for so long come in the form of a heavy, hot headset.
But it’s not the only big dog in the face computer world. Not by a long shot. Xreal, known for its virtual-display glasses, has partnered with Google to build mixed-reality smart glasses on the Android XR platform—the Xreal Aura. On Wednesday, the company announced the official price, starting at $1,279. That’s 20 bucks cheaper than Meta’s VR glasses. Unlike Meta’s option, the Aura glasses come out this year.
The Auras are available for preorder, but only for people who have already placed paid reservations. Preorder options will open up for the general public “in the coming weeks.” The starting price is for a model with 12 GB of RAM and 256 GB storage. Xreal says units will ship in the US, Canada, Japan, and South Korea. It will launch in more regions in 2027.
I tried both. I attended a demo of the Aura glasses, which was deliberately held a day after Meta announced its VR Glasses at Meta Connect. My immediate takeaway was that these glasses are direct competitors, with very similar experiences. Put on a pair, and you can watch videos, play games, or project a multi-monitor workplace setup. Some of those experiences work better on one device or the other.
Same but Different
Smart glasses come in several varieties. The simple ones plug into your phone or laptop and project the screen onto the glasses, acting like a portable monitor that doesn’t require you to crane your neck. Then there are glasses like the Ray-Ban Meta, which feature a camera to capture photos and videos and an AI assistant you can talk to. Display versions of these glasses—and ones coming from Google and Samsung—add a visual component so you can see real-time captions when people speak, translations, navigation instructions, and more.
But mixed reality glasses go a step further, bridging the world of virtual and augmented reality. They’re more akin to headsets like the Apple Vision Pro or the Meta Quest, but in slimmer, lighter designs that aren’t as cumbersome to wear. Snap also recently announced a competing pair called Specs, which cost $2,195 and are shipping later this year.
Neither Meta nor Xreal’s glasses can be mistaken for regular everyday glasses. Meta’s futuristic frames fit like the front half of a VR headset. The Xreal frames are more glasses-forward; chunky but nowhere near as thicc as Snap's Specs. Both have an attached wired compute puck (the thing that houses all the memory and processing power) that you'll need to put in your pocket.
On the Meta VR Glasses, the interactive experiences feel smooth and fluid. The glasses can run all the services that already exist on Meta’s Quest devices on a gorgeous 5K micro-OLED screen. They also have more cameras. (Two point straight down at your lap, so you should probably keep pants on when using these things.) That enables hand tracking features that feel very precise. Typing sentences out on a virtual keyboard feels almost seamless. On Xreal’s glasses, it feels more like hunting and pecking.
The Xreal Aura glasses generally feel less polished. The glasses can run anything built in Android. That works most of the time, but in my demo it also led to some apps not syncing right. Android is a huge platform, and not everything will adapt to mixed reality.
What you can do in the Aura much better than Meta’s VR Glasses is walk around. The Aura has lenses with real-world passthrough, meaning when you turn the screen off, it’s like looking through a regular pair of glasses. Meta’s VR Glasses have video passthrough, which can look fuzzy.
Ultimately, the Meta VR Glasses feel better for sitting and experiencing content, or typing something out. But the Xreal Aura adapts to the real world better—or at least makes it easier to see what’s in front of you while you’re walking around.
Meta’s glasses launch early next year, so we’ll have a clearer verdict once we get extensive time with the final hardware.

US President Donald Trump came to the European Parliament in Strasbourg on Oct 6 naked and in gold, with a golf club in his hand and a smaller man carrying his weight.

Can Switzerland adapt to a 'monsoon-like' future?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
12:00:00 UTC
21:00:00 KST

Can Switzerland adapt to a ‘monsoon-like’ future?
The total amount of water on Earth remains stable, but climate change is altering its distribution. As a result, some regions face growing water shortages, while others are increasingly affected by flooding, fuelling geopolitical tensions. Switzerland is not immune.
In Switzerland, turning on a tap for a glass of water is something most people take for granted. Yet for many people around the world, access to water is not guaranteed.
Freshwater resources are becoming increasingly scarce in many regions. According to a reportExternal link published in September by the World Meteorological Organization (WMO), river levels fell to their lowest point in more than three decades in 2025. These figures do not yet include the exceptionally hot and dry European summer of 2026.
More
Switzerland sees hottest and driest summer on record
The total amount of water on Earth is not decreasing. Instead it continues to circulate between oceans, soils, groundwater, lakes, rivers and glaciers.
As the French chemist Antoine Lavoisier famously observed, “nothing is lost, nothing is created, everything is transformed”. The principle applies particularly well to water, Thibault Datry told Swiss public broadcaster RTS.
A change in distribution
But the director of research in ecohydrology at the French National Research Institute for Agriculture, Food and the Environment points to a shift where freshwater is found.
“Since the creation of the Earth, the amount of water has remained unchanged. What has changed is its distribution between different reservoirs: surface and groundwater, freshwater and saltwater,” he explains. As glaciers and polar ice caps melt, more freshwater flows into the oceans. “We gain salt water and lose freshwater.”
Depending on its cycle, ocean water continues to evaporate, forming clouds that eventually return moisture to the land as precipitation. But winds and atmospheric currents do not redistribute this moisture evenly across the globe.
Africa, for example, experienced an exceptionally dry year in 2025 while also suffering severe floods, according to the WMO report.
Long associated with drought and famine, the Sahel is experiencing a return of water. Since the 1990s, rainfall has increased and groundwater levels have risen. But the trend has also brought more flooding and new challenges for agriculture.
One explanation is the return of the West African monsoon. Reduced pollution from coal burning has contributed to warming in the North Atlantic, allowing more moisture to penetrate further into the region.
Changes in land use also play a role. Replacing grasslands with shallow-rooted crops reduces evapotranspiration, meaning more water remains in the soil. But explosed soils sometimes form a crust that are not very permeable, causing rainwater to run off rapidly and increasing the risk of flooding.
The Sahel must therefore adapt to this new situation. Rainfall is becoming more intense but also more irregular, while dry periods are common. This can disrupt sowing and harvests. The return of water offers opportunities, but it does not remove the challenges posed by climate change.
“The moisture is not redistributed homogeneously, but the fresh water did come back at some point,” says Datry.
More erratic rainfall
Climate change is amplifying these contrasts. “All the most extreme years have occurred within the last twenty years,” says Bettina Schaefli, professor of hydrology at the University of Bern and president of the Hydrology Commission of the Swiss Academy of Sciences.
According to Scheffler, the trend is likely to intensify. “We know that regions that are already dry today are likely to become even drier. Other regions, such as Switzerland, may see little change in total annual rainfall.”
The challenge lies in how that rainfall is distributed throughout the year. “In France and Switzerland, we are moving towards a system that, if I exaggerate, resembles a monsoon climate, with six months of rain and six months without,” says Datry.
More
Switzerland braces for more heatwaves, droughts and violent storms
Heavy rainfall and flooding do not necessarily replenish water reserves. In Switzerland and France, aquifers and rivers still held abundant water in mid-May. Just a few weeks later, however, the situation had become exceptional, Datry notes.
Switzerland must also negotiate
The changing distribution of water is affecting agriculture and industry, and is increasingly becoming a source of geopolitical tensions. India and Pakistan have long disagreed over the management of dams and canals. Ethiopia and Egypt, meanwhile, remain at odds over the use of Nile waters following Ethiopia’s construction of the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam. Egypt considers the project a potential threat to its water security.
Switzerland is not exempt from such challenges. One recurring question concerns Italy: should Switzerland release more water so Italy can irrigate the Po Valley more?
More
Switzerland gives Italy more water from Lake Lugano
“We were not used to having to worry about coordinated water management. Now we are seeing new conflicts that did not exist before. Until five or six years ago, people assumed that we had enough water for everyone. Suddenly, we are having to discuss it,” says Scheffler.
France faces similar concerns. According to Datry, the flow of the Rhône could decline by 25% by 2050. Several French nuclear power plants depend on the river for cooling water.
“It’s already a political issue today,” he says.
More
Switzerland’s worst-case climate scenario now more likely, say scientists

Critical funding gap threatens health response in Yemen

Critical funding gap threatens health response in Yemen
The World Health Organization (WHO) warned that significantly more resources are required to scale up its response in Yemen amid escalating conflict and rising needs.
Renewed clashes between Saudi-backed Yemeni Government forces and Houthi rebels supported by Iran, have intensified in recent weeks.
More than 200,000 people have been displaced, according to latest figures from UN migration agency, IOM, while close to 3,800 have fled to Djibouti across the Red Sea.
WHO said its immediate funding requirements have increased from $9 million to $31 million. An additional $700,000 is also needed to support refugees in Djibouti.
“The situation is evolving into a complex emergency, with health needs rising as resources are already severely stretched,” said Dr. Syed Jaffar Hussain, WHO Representative in Yemen.
Health services struggle to cope
Fighting has mainly occurred on the coast in Lahj governorate in southwestern Yemen near the strategic Bab al-Mandeb Strait, in neighbouring Taiz governorate and in Marib governorate in northern Yemen.
As of 2 October, there were 959 reported deaths and 4,207 injuries across 10 governorates, according to the Yemeni health authorities.
Health services in conflict-affected governorates are struggling to cope with mounting needs. Nearly half of health facilities in these areas lack partner support, with critical gaps in frontline trauma care and outpatient services.
Critical hour for care
“For people with severe injuries, access to trauma care within the first hour can determine whether they survive,” said Dr. Hussain.
“Yet trauma stabilization points on the Lahj coast and in Al-Dhale have no partners to operate them. Few agencies are able to provide trauma care, leaving critical gaps along the front lines.”
WHO noted that displaced families are among those most affected. Of the nearly 198,000 people who have been uprooted, less than one per cent had received health services as of last week.
Supply shortages, disease outbreaks
Hospitals are facing shortages of surgical supplies, anaesthetics, blood-bank materials and fuel, while delivery of essential supplies is becoming slower and more expensive. Emergency maternity services have also been suspended in Marib and Ras Al-Arah in Lahj governorate.
Meanwhile, disease outbreaks are further complicating the emergency response. Cholera cases have tripled in three weeks, including infections detected in displacement camps, while dengue and malaria cases are also rising.
More than 22,000 suspected measles cases and 128 deaths have been reported this year, as the disease spreads among unvaccinated displaced children. Malnutrition among these groups is also a growing concern. The coming El Niño is likely to worsen disease outbreaks and malnutrition.
WHO is preparing to scale up trauma and emergency care, outbreak response and essential health services and supplies, including maternal and newborn care services.
As the main health coordinator in Yemen, the agency also acts as the provider of last resort where no partner can deliver services.
Yet without urgent additional financing, WHO warned that the gaps between available services and needs will continue to widen.

Reform, or lose trust: Governments press the UN to reflect the world as it is
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
12:00:00 UTC
21:00:00 KST

Reform, or lose trust: Governments press the UN to reflect the world as it is
Can the UN still remain relevant if it still looks and acts like the organization it was when it was formed in 1945? The debate over UN reform at the General Assembly in New York last month produced a striking common refrain from a diverse range of Member States.
Many governments believe the United Nations can only remain credible and effective if its institutions better reflect the realities of the 21st century.
From questions of Security Council representation to institutional effectiveness, delegates repeatedly returned to the relationship between power, fairness and legitimacy.
For this third and final analysis piece highlighting key themes, UN News looked at some of the speeches during the annual General Debate of the 193 Member States attending the UN General Assembly.
As Secretary-General António Guterres put it: “The United Nations exists because power requires rules – and humanity needs a place where power answers to principle.”
Who gets a seat at the table?
Security Council reform sat at the centre of discussions about UN reform.
Speaker after speaker argued that representation and legitimacy can't be separated, and Africa's continued absence from permanent membership was a recurrent theme.
Kenya put it bluntly: “The equality proclaimed in this Assembly ends at the doors of the Security Council."
Guyana made a similar case for the wider world: “We need a Security Council that reflects the geopolitical realities of the 21st century, not the power structures of 1945; a Council that embraces the emerging multipolarity of our world, including permanent representation from Africa, and Latin America and the Caribbean.”
The UN chief Mr. Guterres agreed, calling the status quo indefensible: “A 21st century Security Council without permanent African seats is unjust and indefensible.”
General Assembly President Khalilur Rahman echoed this sentiment: “Africa cannot be asked to wait indefinitely for its rightful place on the Council.”
Consensus on reform, disagreement over how
While support for reform was widespread, governments proposed different solutions.
Spain went furthest, calling for both fairer regional representation and scrapping the veto outright: “We need to reform the Security Council so that all of the regions in the world have fair representation, and so that we can do away with the right of veto of the permanent members.”
Russia, one of the five Permanent Members of the Council, took a more cautious approach backing “the expansion of representation by Asia, Africa and Latin America” but adding that reforms shouldn't “undermine the intergovernmental nature of the UN system or erode the prerogatives of the UN Security Council and its Permanent Members."
Trust has to be earned
A second thread ran through the week: Trust, and how easily it erodes when rules get applied selectively.
Hungary argued cooperation and self-interest aren't actually in opposition: “We believe that national interest and international cooperation do not have to stand against each other,” adding that “the United Nations cannot demand trust. It must earn it.”
Several delegations linked public confidence in international institutions to the consistent application of rules and principles. Concerns were raised about unequal treatment, selective implementation of international law and failures to respond effectively to crises.
A leaner UN?
While the UN has championed its UN80 Initiative, that aims to make the United Nations more coherent, effective and responsive to today's challenges, countries also offered competing visions of operational reform.
Switzerland and Costa Rica emphasized clear priorities, efficiency and measurable results.
The President of the General Assembly highlighted overlapping mandates, bureaucratic silos and the need for better coordination at the country level.
However, several speakers warned against treating reform as a cost-cutting exercise.
China said reform should improve institutional performance rather than merely reduce budgets and mandates.
Guyana argued that resources should match the responsibilities assigned to the Organization.
Spain called for United Nations agencies, funds and programmes to receive more resources and greater executive capacity.
The differences were not simply about spending. They concerned what the United Nations should do, how much authority it should have and whether better delivery requires stronger operational capacity – or a narrower institutional role.
Is the UN fit for purpose?
A recurring question throughout the debate was not whether the United Nations should exist, but whether it can produce results.
General Assembly President Rahman put it most sharply: “Outside these walls, people are not asking whether the United Nations still exists. They are asking whether it works.” He maintained that it is people which matter, not process: “Every penny must be invested to achieve impact on the ground for the people we serve.”
The United States offered a contrasting model based on institutional retrenchment: “We cut the UN budget for the first time ever, slashing it by 15 percent in 2026 and eliminating more than 4,000 positions from the UN bureaucracy,” while rejecting international involvement in areas considered national prerogatives.
One line united almost everyone
For all the disagreement over vetoes, institutional power and competing reform models, delegates kept circling back to the same core concern.
Namely that the scale of today's problems has outgrown the structures meant to solve them and that Member States need to work towards building a more resilient and effective organization.
As Guyana noted: “This is why we must not abandon multilateralism because it is imperfect; we must renew it because humanity still needs it.”

Kenya races to trace all contacts after first Ebola death, WHO official says

Kenya races to trace all contacts after first Ebola death, WHO official says
Kenya’s first Ebola death has triggered a race to trace everyone the victim came into contact with, as the United Nations and partners provide full support, the World Health Organization’s (WHO) top official in the country has told UN News in her first interview on the case.
Speaking in Nairobi on Wednesday, WHO Representative Dr. Neema Rusibamayila Kimambo said the coming days would be decisive in preventing community spread of the Bundibugyo strain of the virus, which has now claimed its first life in Kenya.
The victim, a local man who had lived in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) for several years, fell ill there, where a deadly outbreak continues to spread in the east.
He flew to Nairobi via Kampala and Entebbe in Uganda on 3 October, went straight to hospital and died in the Kenyan capital on Monday.
Authorities have since identified the people who had come in direct contact with him from social contact and his admission to hospital. So far, there have been no other infections.
“This is an outbreak of an imported case, one who came in and went straight to hospital, but the Government is working to identify all the relevant contacts as part of their response to this outbreak,” Dr Kimambo told UN News.
Contact tracing underway
She said a list of contacts has been identified, including around 10 of the man’s relatives who “have been very cooperative, and some actually volunteered themselves and they are now already placed under quarantine.”
Meanwhile, 21 health workers who served him in hospital, as well as lab nurses and others, have also been contacted.
Even though these professionals used infection prevention and control (IPC) measures, “the plan is to make sure that they are all under quarantine and decisions have already been made where the staff of the Nairobi Hospital are to be quarantined,” she said.
The Kenyan Government is also working with the airline to contact the roughly 23 passengers and four crew members who were on the flight from Entebbe to Kampala.
She said the Government was making “every effort” to find all possible contacts: “Because to make sure that we contain this and we do not get community spread, it is critical that all contacts are identified and are quarantined.”
Agencies on the case
WHO is supporting Kenya, the DRC and Uganda in contact tracing, surveillance, screening and other response measures to rapidly identify potential cases and prevent any further spread of the virus.
It is also working with the Africa CDC (Centres for Disease Control and Prevention) to both support Kenya and mobilise Member States.
Understanding Ebola
Dr. Kimambo stressed that it is important for people to know how Ebola is spread, namely through contact with the bodily fluids of an infected person such as sweat, blood and saliva.
She highlighted the need to “maintain utmost hygiene” through regular handwashing, use of hand sanitizers, and avoiding “a lot of hand holding”, in addition to identifying symptoms and seeking medical care early.
“I think one key message is not to panic,” she said. “And the second one is let us take necessary precautions and quickly. If someone is feeling unwell, they should go to a health facility to seek care.”
Preparedness and support
Even before the confirmed case in Kenya, WHO and other UN agencies were supporting Ebola preparedness in the country following its emergence in the DRC in May.
The International Organization for Migration (IOM) monitored movements at borders, for example, while children’s agency UNICEF worked on community risk management and issues around water, sanitation and hygiene.
WHO focused on measures such as strengthening surveillance, training case managers and conducting simulation exercises.
Asked about the risk of Ebola spreading in Kenya, Dr. Kimambo underlined the importance of quarantining so that contacts can be monitored and quickly tested should they develop symptoms.
“I think these next few days are critical because we know the incubation period will start from between two to eight days,” she said.
“If we are able to ensure that we do proper contact listing, get all contacts, put them in quarantine, then that will be the key to really contain and stop any community spread.”

France suspends use of stun grenades to police student protests
PARIS, Oct 7 - The French government said on Wednesday it was pausing the use of stun grenades in its policing of student protests, after a 15-year-old boy's hand was blown off during a clash with riot police, fuelling protesters' accusations of police brutality.
Protests showed no sign of easing, with more than 500 schools closed a day after demonstrations swept across the country, and unions representing high-school students, teachers and other workers planning more marches for Thursday.
The wave of protests has been going on for more than two weeks and has exposed widespread public anger six months ahead of an election to replace President Emmanuel Macron.
Speaking to the nation on Wednesday evening, Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu said the government would review the demands made by students and present proposals at the end of October on issues ranging from renovating buildings to make more teachers available, but gave no details.
"In the past, too many promises were not kept, quite simply because they were untenable," Lecornu said. "What I want are concrete, quick and fully funded answers."
The lack of an immediate government response, which was decried by student leaders after talks at the education ministry earlier on Wednesday, appeared unlikely to quell the protests. At Lycee Lamartine, a high school in central Paris, protesters sang the Marseillaise, chanted slogans and performed Mexican waves as they blockaded the entrance to the school.
"We saw there were lots of crumbling walls, a shortage of teachers in public schools, absent teachers," said Gabriel Fillieule, who used to attend a public school but now goes to a private one. He and others said they were protesting to demand better learning conditions for all.
POLICE'S USE OF FORCE BEING INVESTIGATED
While most of Wednesday's blockades were peaceful, police used tear gas and pushed back protesters in a street barricaded by rubbish bins outside Sciences Po university in central Paris.
Rights groups, labour unions, students and some opposition politicians have accused the police of using disproportionate force to quell the wave of protests.
Interior Minister Laurent Nunez said he had ordered the suspension of the use of stun grenades following an incident in the northern city of Lens on Monday in which there was a "strong possibility" the firing of a stun grenade had caused a teenager to lose his hand.
"I am suspending their use for the high-school students' movement until light has been shed on what happened in this case," said the minister, who added that 18 incidents in total had been referred to the police inspectorate for investigation.
Protesters have said they blame poor learning conditions for a sharp drop in French teenagers' scores in reading and maths over the past decade.
French 15-year-olds scored 43 points lower in reading in 2025 than in 2015, according to the OECD's Programme for International Student Assessment, the biggest drop among the OECD countries. Their maths scores also dropped the most.
But the government, under pressure to tame public debt amid weak growth, has little spare cash to address students' complaints of teacher shortages, ageing school buildings and inequalities between schools in affluent and poor areas.
TWENTY-FOUR HIGH SCHOOLS DAMAGED BY FIRE OR VANDALISM
Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu has acknowledged the "legitimate" demands of France's students but also described the unrest as the most violent student demonstrations in decades.
Education Minister Edouard Geffray told parliament that 24 high schools had been damaged by fire or vandalism to the extent that they would remain closed for weeks, meaning some 30,000 students would receive no in-person teaching until they reopened.
He estimated it would cost €20 million to €30 million ($22 million to $34 million) to fix the damage.
Far-right presidential candidate Marine Le Pen, the frontrunner according to opinion polls, said those who damaged schools should pay for the repairs rather than taxpayers.
The government has adopted a similar stance and has a bill going through parliament that aims to set up such a system.
According to an Elabe poll for BFM TV, 72% of French people think the students' demands are legitimate, but 55% of them think the protests should stop.
UNREST ELSEWHERE
Elsewhere in Europe, where budgets have been under pressure as governments respond to successive cost-of-living and energy crises, students in parts of Belgium staged similar protests.
In the Belgian city of Liege in the southern French-speaking Wallonia region, at least 107 people have been arrested in connection with student protests this month, the Belga news agency reported.
Teachers are also on strike.
In Portugal, the main teachers' union FENPROF launched an indefinite strike in mid-September over working conditions, with teachers refusing to do any unpaid work beyond the 35 hours a week mandated by law.
And in Spain, teachers' unions have been protesting conditions in state schools. Teachers in Madrid plan a strike on October 14 to press demands including a reduction in hours, smaller class sizes and higher salaries. REUTERS

Webb finds a surprising atmosphere on a scorching lava world
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
11:58:25 UTC
20:58:25 KST

Webb finds a surprising atmosphere on a scorching lava world
- Date:
- October 7, 2026
- Source:
- University of Chicago
- Summary:
- The James Webb Space Telescope has found strong evidence that the rocky lava world HD 3167 b has an atmosphere, despite circling its star every 24 hours under extreme heat. The surprising discovery could help scientists understand how rocky planets retain atmospheres and what the young, molten Earth may once have looked like.
- Share:
For scientists searching for life beyond Earth, rocky planets with atmospheres are among the most promising places to investigate. An atmosphere is essential for maintaining liquid water on a planet's surface. Yet among the more than 6,300 exoplanets cataloged thus far, most are not rocky, and only a small number of known rocky planets appear to possess atmospheres.
Now, researchers have added another world to that short list. In a study published in The Astrophysical Journal Letters, a team led by University of Chicago scientist Brandon Park Coy reports evidence of an atmosphere surrounding HD 3167 b, a rocky super-Earth located 154 light-years away in the constellation Pisces. The intensely hot planet, classified as a "lava world," completes an orbit around its star in only one Earth day.
"What's so surprising is that the closer a rocky planet orbits its star, the harder it should be to have an atmosphere, because it's bombarded by stellar wind and gets more high-energy photons from the star. But it seems that many of these lava worlds do," explained Edwin Kite, UChicago associate professor of geophysical sciences and co-author of the study. "These planets are too hot for life, but by studying them, we can say something about the processes that matter for other rocky worlds."
In the Q&A below,Coy, a graduate student in Kite's group and first author on the study, explains why atmospheres on lava worlds are scientifically valuable, how researchers detected evidence for this one, and what they hope to learn next.
What was the goal of the survey that found this atmosphere-bearing exoplanet?
One of the driving questions that the James Webb Space Telescope is being used to answer is whether planets orbiting stars much smaller than the sun have atmospheres. It appears that most of those terrestrial planets don't -- they're just bare rock.
But surprisingly, we've found evidence that the majority of lava worlds -- similar in composition to Earth and Venus but much, much hotter -- might have atmospheres. Five terrestrial planets found with atmospheres, including the one described in this study, have been ultra-hot.
This planet, however, is the coldest lava world found so far with evidence of an atmosphere. This is interesting because we're trying to understand the temperature transition between planets with and without atmospheres.
The result is the first from a program led by Megan Weiner Mansfield, PhD'21, who's now at the University of Maryland. The goal of the program, which is looking at 10 ultra-hot lava worlds, is to see if there's a critical temperature over which you start seeing planets with atmospheres.
"We're interested in studying these kinds of planets because we think early Earth might have looked a lot like a lava world." -- Study author Brandon Park Coy
How can you tell if an exoplanet has an atmosphere?
Right now, directly looking at Earth-like planets for signs of life is out of reach. Instead, we can use the Webb telescope to detect light in the mid-infrared wavelength range to estimate the temperature of exoplanets, which can tell us if they might have atmospheres.
There are two primary ways that we study exoplanets. One is called transit, when the planet goes in front of the host star. Another called secondary eclipse, which is the method we used for this study, is when the planet passes behind its star, and we can measure how much light is lost. That difference tells us how much mid-infrared light comes from the planet itself, which essentially tells us how hot the planet is.
If a planet doesn't have an atmosphere, its star-facing, day side should be as hot as theoretically possible based on how reflective its surface is and its distance from the star. But an atmosphere would help redistribute heat from the day side to the night side. We see this happen on Venus -- there's almost no difference in surface temperature between the day and night sides, or between the poles and the equator. If a planet has an atmosphere, it might also have clouds that reflect incoming starlight and cool the dayside. So if a planet's day side is cooler than the maximum possible, it likely has an atmosphere.
The subject of this study, HD 3167 b, is noticeably cooler than its expected maximum, providing strong evidence that it has an atmosphere.
What do you think HD 3167 b's atmosphere is made of?
These lava worlds are so-named because the surface facing their star is likely melted rock. We think that HD 3167 b might have a silicate-rich composition, with a similar mixture of minerals that make up Earth's mantle. Before this study, we expected that any atmosphere on these ultra-hot planets would be composed of vaporized rock, but we're starting to see evidence that some might have heavier gases like carbon dioxide, carbon monoxide, or water in their atmospheres.
The makeup of HD 3167 b's atmosphere is still up in the air. That's one reason we're so interested in getting new observations.
Why is this result important?
Because the four other lava worlds found to have atmospheres are in the ultra-hot regime, it raises questions about whether there's a critical transition temperature when silicate atmospheres start becoming very thick. Is there a temperature where these planets form silicate cloud decks that might reflect incoming radiation to space and cool its day side? This relatively cooler planet helps us better characterize and nail down this transition.
Despite how inhospitable they are for life, we're also interested in studying these kinds of planets because we think early Earth might have looked a lot like a lava world. We think that very early in the solar system's history, when the terrestrial planets formed, they were extremely hot due to the energy from all of the planetesimal collisions. Earth had what's known as a magma ocean stage with an entirely liquid surface. This result gives us a window into studying what conditions may have been like in Earth's first couple of million years.

Kulbergs reveals how he will choose Latvia’s next coalition partners
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
11:58:24 UTC
20:58:24 KST

The United List (AS) will choose as its next coalition partners those political forces that agree to implement changes, Prime Minister and candidate to continue in the post Andris Kulbergs (AS) told journalists on Wednesday at Riga Castle following a meeting with President Edgars Rinkēvičs.
Kulbergs said the coalition must be capable of implementing changes with full commitment, without fearing them, while also explaining them to the public. He acknowledged that the changes would not be comfortable for everyone but stressed that they are necessary for the country.
In the prime minister’s view, voters have clearly voted for change, and willingness to implement it will determine the choice of coalition partners.
Speaking about the structure of the government, Kulbergs said the number of ministries should not be an end in itself. In his view, the focus should be on achieving the greatest impact and economic benefit while using as few resources as possible. As examples, he mentioned governments consisting of 14, 12 or 11 ministers.
President Rinkēvičs, meanwhile, stressed that he had not drawn any red lines during consultations with the political forces but had instead set out three key principles.
The first is an unchanged course on national defence, security and foreign policy, including spending 5% of gross domestic product on security and defence and continuing support for Ukraine. Rinkēvičs said he had heard fairly broad support for this course during consultations, with the possible exception of one political force, which he did not name.
As his second principle, the president highlighted effectiveness rather than the size of the coalition. He stressed that the candidate for prime minister and his political force, the United List, had been given a strong mandate.
Rinkēvičs said the public would primarily hold the prime minister accountable because a large part of society had placed its trust in him. How that mandate is implemented is now a task for the prime ministerial candidate, the president noted.
As his third principle, Rinkēvičs said he wanted the coalition to be formed with the aim of governing for the full four-year electoral cycle.
 The next elections will take place in 2029, when European Parliament and municipal elections are scheduled, followed by the Saeima election in 2030.
Rinkēvičs stressed that there are effectively two years until the next election cycle in which much can be accomplished without worrying about how social media, experts, journalists or particular groups in society might react.
The president also acknowledged that changes may initially be unacceptable to certain sections of society or professional groups. He said he had heard from the parties that they were prepared to work on such changes.
Speaking about the formation of the coalition, 
Rinkēvičs also referred to Kulbergs’ list of priorities and whether political forces would agree to them.
The president said that when he met Kulbergs and the United List on the first working day after the election, they discussed their vision for the work ahead. He said he had heard proposals from AS aimed at putting public finances in order and creating a more efficient state administration.
Rinkēvičs stressed that this would require a broad package of measures.
He acknowledged that reducing the number of ministries is currently seen as a symbol of efficiency, but increasing the efficiency of public administration is a much broader process. Rinkēvičs explained that ministries themselves are not the largest institutions, while the systems under their supervision are often extensive. Therefore, subordinate institutions and their functions must also be reviewed.
In his view, merging ministries will only be effective if accompanied by a review of functions and the entire administrative system.
At the same time, Rinkēvičs noted that, from the perspective of the political distribution of posts, merging ministries or reducing their number would also reduce the size of the Cabinet and therefore have political consequences.
The president stressed that other parties had also expressed readiness during consultations to begin by merging ministries. However, there are differing views on what the future structure should look like, and more specific solutions will have to be found through political negotiations.

Egyptian media channels widely aired threats against Israel, Tel Aviv, and Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu this week as they reacted angrily to Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich’s warning Monday that Israel would destroy Sinai if Egypt attacked Israel, delivered during an interview with the haredi (ultra-Orthodox) news site Hashtiblach.
“What will cause Egypt not to attack us? They know that if they attack, there will be no Sinai,” Smotrich told the channel. “It won’t happen again. There is no [Menachem] Begin.”
Then-prime minister Menachem Begin made peace with Egypt by signing the historic Egypt-Israel Peace Treaty on March 26, 1979. Under the treaty, Israel agreed to withdraw its forces and civilians from the Sinai Peninsula in phases, while Egypt regained full sovereignty over the territory, and the two countries established security arrangements governing their forces in the peninsula.
“At least half of Gaza under tomorrow morning, and the same thing with Lebanon, up to 8, 9, [or] 12 kilometers that are ours. Guys, it won’t be [yours], you’re not coming back. Why? Because you started with us, and that’s the price of war,” Smotrich said.
Though his threat made clear that such an action would only be taken if Egypt attacked Israel, in the wider context of Israel’s post-October 7 security, his words were poorly received in Egypt. Egyptian parliamentarian and journalist Mustafa Bakri described the minister as an “extremist Zionist… thug” and insisted that Cairo could “crush” Israel’s military.
“[Smotrich] thinks Egypt is an open playground. I wish you would read how we crushed your army, you ignorant fool – the ones who did it once are capable of repeating it again.
“The Egyptian army is ready to confront and crush anyone whose soul dares to tamper with national security,” Bakri wrote. “You will surely be taken prisoner, and we’ll throw you in the mental hospital in Khanka. Don’t you dare overstep again, you madman [he said, addressing Smotrich].”
Egyptian TV host: Israel would pay 'heavy price' if it attacked
Egyptian TV host Ahmed Moussa, on Ala Mas’ouleety [Egyptian nightly talk show broadcast on the satellite channel Sada El Balad], also commented on Smotrich’s remarks, responding by insisting that “all 120 million Egyptians would die defending Egypt, and Israel would pay a heavy price if it took any step threatening Egyptian national security.”
Moussa noted Egypt’s success in the Yom Kippur War, during which more than 200 Israeli soldiers were taken prisoner by Egyptian forces, saying that this time there would be no hostages to exchange.
“If you act recklessly, there will be no Israel. You cannot get near an inch of Sinai, and what happened in 1967 will not be repeated with Egypt.”
“We are advocates of peace, but some extremists in the Zionist entity do not want peace. Egypt is a strong country. The war criminal says he will take Sinai. This is harassment and a threat to Egypt. We know what the lesson of 1973 was like for you,” Moussa said.
“You are an illegitimate state. We brought you back with the prisoner exchange, and after that there will be no prisoner exchange because there will be no prisoners.”
'There will be no Tel Aviv, there will be no Ben-Gurion Airport'
Amr Adib, on MBC Egypt, insisted that Cairo had actively worked to defend the border with Israel from any instability, and if the IDF attacked, “There will be no Tel Aviv, there will be no Ben-Gurion Airport, and there will be no Netanyahu.”
“Before you decide to finish us, you will be finished,” he said. “Before you throw us into the sea, you will be in the sewer.”
Egyptian political science professor Hamed Fares told Sky News Arabia that Smotrich’s comments reflected a form of “political adolescence” and demonstrated, in his view, the minister’s ignorance of the region’s power dynamics.
Fares added that he believed Smotrich’s comments, which he described as a “redline” for Egypt, reflected the finance minister’s efforts to maintain a hardline image ahead of the upcoming elections.
Fares said that by portraying neighboring countries as unstable, Smotrich was seeking to create a perceived need for territorial expansion on national security grounds.

Over 400 bereaved partners of IDF soldiers left mourning since Oct. 7, GFIDF reveals on anniversary
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
11:58:01 UTC
20:58:01 KST

Since the start of Israel's war against Hamas, 412 fallen IDF soldiers left behind a bereaved partner or significant other, the organization "A Partner Left Behind" (GFIDF) revealed on Wednesday, the third anniversary of the October 7 massacre.
From the establishment of the organization in 1998 until October 7, only around 500 bereaved partners of killed soldiers had been recorded.
Over a quarter of the soldiers in question, 118, were killed on October 7, 2023. Another 23 bereaved partners faced the death of their significant others only in the last year.
While the oldest recorded bereaved partner was 60 years old, only 4% were over the age of 32. The youngest bereaved partner was 16, with over half (57%) being 21 or younger.
Bereaved partners lose their envisioned future
"Bereaved partners have lost not only the person they loved but also the future they had envisioned together," GFIDF CEO Attorney Adi Alon Sheinberg stated.
"Because they had not yet married, their place within the circle of bereavement is often not fully acknowledged - a fact that only intensifies the difficulty of coping with the loss," she added.
Only 8% of fallen IDF soldiers left behind a bereaved significant other, the organization reported.
"The pain remains; at the organization, we support bereaved partners by providing a therapeutic safety net and a warm community, enabling them to return to a full life - living alongside their grief rather than in its shadow," Sheinberg said.

Ammunition Hill hero and defense innovator Yaki Hetz passes away at age 80
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
11:57:55 UTC
20:57:55 KST

Yaakov (Yaki) Hetz, a decorated veteran of the battle for Jerusalem’s Ammunition Hill and an Israel Defense Prize laureate, has died, the Ammunition Hill memorial center announced on Facebook on Tuesday.
Hetz, who fought with the 66th Battalion during the Six-Day War, received the Medal of Courage for his actions in the battle and lit a torch at the state ceremony marking Israel’s 69th Independence Day.
Hetz (Haimovitch) was 21 when he fought at Ammunition Hill, becoming one of the figures most closely associated with the historic battle to liberate Jerusalem. After his platoon commander, Yoram Eliashiv, was hit, Hetz took command and continued leading his comrades under heavy fire. He was awarded the Medal of Courage for his bravery and conduct during the battle.
During the fighting, Hetz and fellow soldiers Yehuda Kendal and David Shalom helped overcome a fortified Jordanian bunker that blocked the Israeli advance. After a grenade failed to put the position out of action, the three gathered approximately 20 kilograms of explosives and detonated them against the bunker. The blast brought down a wall and part of the roof, clearing the way forward.
Hetz received a special commendation for his actions at the Battle of the Chinese Farm
Hetz also fought in the Yom Kippur War. Forty years later, he received a special commendation for his actions at the Battle of the Chinese Farm, where he risked his life to rescue wounded soldiers.
His story, however, did not end in the trenches of Ammunition Hill. He later worked in defense development and innovation, contributing to advanced weapons systems at Rafael Advanced Defense Systems.
Among his contributions was the idea that led to the development of the Maoz system, an advanced attack drone used by IDF soldiers. The concept grew out of his experience at Ammunition Hill and his determination to give future soldiers capabilities that he and his comrades had lacked in 1967.
In 1982, Hetz received the Israel Defense Prize for his defense work. In 2017, he was selected to light a torch at the official Independence Day ceremony.
Alongside his military and technological achievements, Hetz dedicated himself to remembrance, education, and preserving Israel’s heritage. For decades, he shared the stories of the soldiers who fought for Jerusalem, meeting generations of young people and recounting the battle and the experiences of his comrades.
Hetz published his autobiography in 2023, three years before his passing
In 2023, he published his autobiography, Baptism of Fire, describing the battle from his own perspective.
His bravery is commemorated at Ammunition Hill’s Six Day War Museum, which preserves the history of the war, the battles for Jerusalem’s liberation and reunification, and the personal stories of those who fought. His testimony and life story form part of the heritage passed on to visitors and future generations.
For Ammunition Hill, Hetz was much more than one of the battle’s heroes. He was an inseparable part of its community, belonging to the generation of soldiers who transformed a battlefield into a living center of remembrance, heritage, and education.
“Yaki Hetz was an inseparable part of Ammunition Hill, not only as one of the heroes of the battle for Jerusalem’s liberation and reunification, but also as a man who devoted his life to action, creation, and passing on our heritage to future generations,” said Menachem Landau, chairman of the board.
“Yaki was a man of many talents, with vast knowledge, a youthful spirit, and boundless curiosity. To us, he was much more than a soldier and a hero of Israel; he was one of the family, a partner on our journey, and a dear friend. His bravery is commemorated in the hill’s Six-Day War Museum, but his legacy lives far beyond the museum’s walls. Today we bid farewell to a man whose life story is intertwined with that of a united Jerusalem, and whose memory will continue to accompany us and future generations.”
