Scientists decode imagined melodies from human brain waves
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
11:00:31 UTC
20:00:31 KST

Researchers have successfully decoded the basic structure of imagined melodies from human brain waves by focusing on how notes relate to one another rather than their exact pitch. Published in the journal eNeuro, the small study demonstrates that computer models can reconstruct the general rising and falling contours of a silent song directly from neural recordings. These results show that the brain’s internal auditory experiences can be accessed and translated into recognizable musical sequences.
When we recognize a familiar song, we do not usually rely on the exact acoustic frequencies of the notes. We rely on relative pitch, which is the interval or distance between successive tones. This is why a song like “Twinkle, Twinkle, Little Star” sounds identical whether it is played on a high-pitched flute or a low-pitched tuba. The human brain naturally encodes these relational patterns, allowing people to carry tunes across different keys and instruments.
Imagining music engages many of the same neural networks as actually listening to it. When a person hears a song in their head, their brain generates an internal auditory experience. Extracting this hidden musical content from brain activity is highly difficult. Past attempts have mostly detected the presence of musical thought or basic rhythmic beats.
Predicting the actual melody a person is imagining requires capturing rapid, fine-grained changes in brain activity. Absolute pitch is tied to specific sound wave frequencies. Because most human brains process melodies relatively, attempting to decode exact absolute pitches often fails.
To address this challenge, researchers Jii Kwon and Chun Kee Chung from Seoul National University led a team to investigate whether neural decoding models could identify imagined melodies using a relative pitch framework. They wanted to see if they could predict individual imagined notes by their scale degree, like “Do” or “Re,” regardless of the starting key.
The researchers conducted a small study involving 10 patients with medically intractable epilepsy. These patients already had arrays of electrodes surgically implanted directly on the surface of their brains for clinical evaluation. This recording technique, called electrocorticography, provides a highly detailed look at electrical activity across the cerebral cortex. The direct contact with the brain tissue allows sensors to pick up high-frequency signals that external scalp monitors often miss.
During the experiment, the patients listened to short segments of familiar children’s songs, such as “Yankee Doodle.” The songs were played in three different musical keys. The researchers instructed the patients to listen to the first two measures of a song and then silently imagine the next two measures. To ensure they were actually following the tune, the patients hummed the melody aloud after the silent imagination period ended.
As the patients imagined the music, the scientists recorded their brain activity. They focused on specific electrical patterns known as high-gamma activity. These rapid brain waves oscillate between 60 and 150 times per second and are a reliable indicator of active sensory processing. The team isolated the signals coming from regions like the superior temporal gyrus, an area on the side of the brain heavily involved in processing sounds.
The researchers took this neural data and trained a machine learning program to recognize patterns associated with specific relative pitches. They broke the imagination period into half-second segments, matching each segment to a specific note in the song. The model learned to categorize the brain waves into six relative pitch classes. These classes correspond to the solfège syllables Do, Re, Mi, Fa, Sol, and La.
The research team then tested the computer models on a fresh set of brain recordings that the models had not seen before. The computer tried to guess which relative note the patient was imagining during each half-second window. The accuracy for these single-note predictions was modest, sitting around 26 percent on average. While this number might seem low, a random guess would only be correct about 16 percent of the time, meaning the models were successfully extracting real musical information.
The team also tried to decode the exact acoustic frequencies, or absolute pitches, from the same brain data. In this test, the models failed to perform better than a random guess. The results were not statistically significant for absolute pitch, supporting the view that the brain primarily represents the imagined melody through relative pitch relationships.
Although predicting individual notes was difficult, the researchers found success when they linked the individual predictions together over time. By arranging the decoded relative pitches in sequence, they reconstructed the overall melodic contour of the imagined songs. These reconstructed sequences generally matched the ascending and descending patterns of the original melodies. Even when a specific note prediction was slightly off, the overall shape of the song remained intact.
By looking closer at the data, the researchers identified which brain areas provided the most useful information for the computer models. Activity in the superior temporal gyrus on both sides of the brain was a major contributor. They also found helpful signals in the left precentral gyrus, a brain region often linked to motor planning. This suggests that internally imagining a melody might involve a mental rehearsal of the physical actions required to sing it.
While these findings present a novel way to access internal musical thoughts, the approach has several practical limitations. The accuracy of predicting individual notes remains relatively low. Reconstructing a perfectly accurate melody note-for-note is not yet possible with current methods. The reconstructed melodies rely on the general shape of the song rather than flawless individual predictions.
The study also relied exclusively on highly familiar children’s songs. Familiar melodies are deeply ingrained in memory, which likely helps patients produce stable and consistent internal imagery. Because of this, it is unknown if the models could decode novel or spontaneously composed melodies. Spontaneous imagination might not generate the same robust neural patterns as recalling a well-learned tune.
The need for surgically implanted electrodes restricts this technology to clinical settings. The invasive nature of electrocorticography means this specific method cannot be adapted into a wearable device for the general public. Future studies will likely explore whether non-invasive techniques can capture similar relative pitch information. Expanding the computer models to decode a wider range of notes across multiple octaves will also be a priority for subsequent research.
The study, “Reconstruction of Imagined Melody with Relative Pitch Decoding in Electrocorticography,” was authored by Jii Kwon, Youmin Shin, June sic Kim, Eunju Jeong, Sung-Phil Kim, Eun Jung Lee, and Chun Kee Chung.

The contract covers Linza multi-purpose drones and Zoom reconnaissance drones, both designed by Frontline Robotics against requirements written from operational experience, and exceeds the volume of the 2026 agreement that preceded it. It was signed by Matthias Lehna, a vice president at Quantum Systems, and Pavlo Kosolapkin, chief technology officer and co-founder of Frontline Robotics, with Major General Oleksandr Pivnenko, the commander of the National Guard.
Mr Lehna, who is also managing director of the joint venture, said: “QFI was established with a clear objective: to combine Ukrainian engineering and operational experience with German industrial capacity and scale.”
Mr Kosolapkin said: “A follow-on order is one of the strongest validations a defence technology can receive.”
Major General Pivnenko said expanding production in Germany gives Ukraine access to additional capacity while keeping Ukrainian technology and operational experience at the core of the product.
Established under the Build with Ukraine initiative, the company describes itself as the first European-Ukrainian defence-industrial joint venture. The model it represents has become one of the more consequential developments of the war, since it moves manufacturing westward out of range of Russian strikes on Ukrainian industry while keeping design authority with the people who have been using the equipment in combat.

Separatists win in Quebec – but does that bring separation from Canada any closer?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
11:00:08 UTC
20:00:08 KST

The victory of the Parti Québécois in Monday’s election in Quebec might seem to bring its signature goal, of separating the French-speaking province from Canada, much closer – but Canadian unity may not be nearly as threatened as may first seem.
The PQ’s victory was both impressive and disappointing. The party added 56 seats to its roster and more than doubled its vote share compared with the 2022 election, giving it its first taste of power in 14 years. Crucially, however, it was left five seats short of a majority, making its promise to hold a referendum after Donald Trump leaves office in 2028 nearly impossible.
It also won with barely 28% of the popular vote, the lowest percentage for any government in Canada’s electoral history, according to the polling analyst Philippe Fournier.
The vast majority of Quebecers voted for parties that want nothing to do with a referendum. It’s a reflection of the province’s 30-year aversion to another bruising debate about Quebec’s place in Canada – particularly in the wake of Trump’s tariffs and threats against the country.
The result not only puts another referendum in doubt, but a raft of other PQ initiatives too, including abolishing the monarchy and applying Quebec’s strict language laws to the province’s colleges. The new government will also face stiff opposition to its plans to reduce immigration levels, which have angered farmers and the business community.
Meanwhile, the most popular politician in the province remains far and away the Canadian prime minister, Mark Carney, in large part because of his resistance to Trump. That has left the PQ leader, Paul St-Pierre Plamondon, in an awkward situation for a separatist: he can’t be seen as a threat to Canadian unity. He essentially acknowledged this in his victory speech, pledging to be a “good-faith collaborator” with the rest of the country, and even addressing the crowd in English; then attempted to court the other side of the debate by announcing on Tuesday he would prevent the lieutenant governor, who represents the British crown, from swearing in his new government.
“Seventy per cent of Quebecers don’t want a referendum,” said John Parisella, who served as chief of staff to two Quebec premiers and the province’s delegate general in New York and Washington.
“And every time they see Trump’s picture on the screen at night, it does nothing to improve a desire for separation. For a lot of Quebecers, the link with Canada is absolutely crucial, even if it isn’t necessarily emotional.”
The vote, in fact, may have less to do with embracing separatism and more about punishing the current government. The election saw the total collapse of the governing Coalition Avenir Québec (CAQ), which has been in power since 2018. An alliance of federalists and separatists (the party describes itself as nationalist), it didn’t win a single seat, and harvested just a third of its vote share compared to 2022. Its leader, Christine Fréchette, lost her own riding to the Parti Québécois, and on Tuesday afternoon she resigned.
In a province whose political discourse has focused on the federalist-separatist divide, the election also suggested a return to normalcy of sorts – with separatists returning to the PQ’s fold, while the federalist vote dispersed to the opposition Liberal party and the upstart Parti Conservateur du Québec (PCQ).
The PCQ feasted on the CAQ’s support in the election, winning 19 ridings in the hinterland and in the Quebec City area, where leader Éric Duhaime won his seat for the first time. Founded in 2009, the populist party counts a prominent anti-vaxxer and a rage-bating anti-woke radio host as two of its winning candidates.
The party was able to break through in part because of its promise to build an underground highway linking Quebec City to its suburbs across the St Lawrence, despite government reports saying the endeavor would cost as much as C$9.3bn (US$6.5bn) and do little to alleviate traffic.
Montreal, meanwhile, went decidedly Liberal red, with leader Charles Milliard regaining seats on the island and in the traditionally English redoubt of the Eastern Townships. The staunchly federalist Liberals, who are unaffiliated with Carney’s federal Liberals, will serve as Quebec’s official opposition. Governing with but a handful of seats in the province’s biggest metropolis will be challenging enough for the PQ; as history has shown, winning a referendum without it is somewhere near impossible.
Canada faces another potential menace to its sovereignty in a little less than two weeks, when Alberta in the west holds a “referendum on a referendum” on secession. Happily for Carney, and unfortunately for Trump, polls suggest Albertans are as averse to dalliances with separation as their Quebecer brethren have now become to the east – no matter the party they just chose to govern.

Meta's Muse assistant tops app charts. Now it needs to become a habit
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
11:00:01 UTC
20:00:01 KST

Meta's Muse personal agent has been topping app store charts. Now, the "centerpiece" of the company's artificial intelligence strategy, as CEO Mark Zuckerberg describes it, needs to become something people make a habit of using.
The buzz around Meta's AI agent has excited investors. The stock is up about 20% since the app's launch a month ago and recorded its best month in September since 2022.
While Meta is still currently the top free app on Apple's iOS store, the bigger challenge for the Facebook parent is to get people to keep using Muse after the magic wears off. Meta needs its personal agent to be an anchor app for the company, which has been trailing competitors like OpenAI and Google in the red-hot AI market.
"Muse has an opportunity to be sticky with consumers because it's a task-completer, rather than just a chatbot," Meredith Whalen, chief research officer at IDC, said in an email.
Whalen said consumers are using current AI tools for a range of tasks, but it's unclear if they'll be willing to hand over the kind of personal data required to create an efficient digital assistant. That's a particularly big obstacle for Meta, which just agreed to an almost $17 billion settlement with a group of states that alleged the company misrepresented the extent of child mental health harms caused by apps like Facebook and Instagram.
"The real question is trust," Whalen said.
Meta is pitching Muse to both consumers and small businesses for tasks like organizing personal emails, searching for shopping deals or seeking out prospective customers. Although Meta lets users access Muse for free, it also sells monthly subscription plans for $20 or $100, depending on tokens, a metric the company uses to calculate the power AI agents need to accomplish tasks.
In offering Muse for free out of the gate, the company can get an understanding of how and why people are using it, said Whalen, who noted that, "Price comes later, once the habit is established."
Coders have found AI agents helpful as software engineering tools, but the general public and even business leaders are still grappling with the potential for supercharged digital assistants, beyond acting as mere question-and-answering services.
"I would say that widely, enterprise-scale AI agent adoption is still page one, chapter one," said Ketan Karkhanis, CEO of ThoughtSpot, which sells AI agent technologies to businesses.
Consumers are just getting started with AI agents.
Karkhanis said he hasn't seen the kinds of "killer use cases" that would make apps like Muse more compelling than merely being a "next-gen Alexa" or Siri voice assistant that people might use to tell them the weather.
Andrew Geller, executive producer of 1stAveMachine, said his media firm develops its own internal agentic tools for certain production tasks. He views Muse and other consumer-focused AI agents as being "quite helpful" in introducing the technology to the masses, but says they're hardly life-changing.
Geller said he was "early on the OpenClaw train," referring to the so-called open-source harness for managing AI agents that took off earlier this year. He said he discovered that personal use of AI agents can be fun, but also "kind of a little banal," particularly when contrasted with the more heavy-duty uses related to coding.
Bring on the Personal AI assistants
A number of other tech firms are trying to commercialize AI agents for the masses by first enticing users to join for free.
Former Yahoo CEO Marissa Mayer is taking a try-before-you-buy approach with her new photo-centric AI agent startup Dazzle, a tactic she said is important "for those occasional users or those users who are just trying to see what the service can do at the very beginning."
Dazzle analyzes users' personal photos to understand aspects of their lives, such as their family members or interests, and then can take actions like reminding someone that a pair of shoes they recently looked up is on sale online.
It's a strategy she learned from her early tenure at Google, before the company built its market-leading online ad platform.
"What we're really trying to do is see what use cases are really popping with users, what do they see as really helpful, and that will guide it," Mayer said about Dazzle's first week post-launch.
Mayer compared the pricing and adoption approach to Uber's evolution. The ride-hailing company began with black town cars before introducing lower-priced options for a wider swath of users.
"It's a luxury to be able to have these wonderful recommendations and to have this level of convenience," Mayer said.
Dazzle is considering transaction fees and subscriptions.
"We want to be running a service where people feel that they're getting value on a relatively continuous basis over time," Mayer said.
At Wajo AI, CEO Shivani Poddar is also contemplating business models for her new AI-powered digital assistant startup, which lets people research and book appointments or order gifts for family members.
Poddar, who has previously built voice-assistant technologies for Amazon Alexa and at Facebook, is letting people access the service for free for now. While Poddar believes businesses may be willing to pay subscription fees, she's not yet convinced that "the everyday person" will want to sign up, and instead may be more willing to pay service fees based on outcomes, like how Airbnb makes money from bookings.
The stakes are highest for Meta, which went on a massive spending spree last year to acquire talent and build a business in AI that could compete with OpenAI and Anthropic. Zuckerberg is desperate to diversify away from online ads, which still account for almost all of the company's revenue, and he's got a long way to go to prove that Muse can be a key piece of that effort.
Zuckerberg, at least to an extent, has time on his side.
"Whoever can subsidize users and wait has the advantage," IDC's Whalen said. "And Meta's ad business can pay for a lot of waiting."

OpenAI Wants Its New Agent to Run Your Life. Mine Said It Loved Me
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
11:00:00 UTC
20:00:00 KST

I’m discussing replacement options for our broken couch with my partner when I get a bright idea: Use OpenAI’s recently announced AI agents, called Dots, to buy a couch on our behalf.
My partner is less sure a bot will actually help, but I insist, calling the always-on agent through ChatGPT to get the task started. “Hello, Connor,” it says, getting my name wrong off the bat. I wince as I watch my partner’s face grow even more skeptical. It’s hard to trust an AI agent when it can’t even remember your name.
AI agents are currently leaping from niche software for early adopters to something ordinary people might actually use—might being the operative word here. From Meta’s Muse to OpenAI’s Dots, these tools are built to feel like you’re texting a friend and asking them to complete online tasks, like booking a flight or canceling a dinner reservation. It’s the next evolution of a chatbot: a cuddly persona designed to feel welcoming with the power of a virtual browser it can control.
After a few days with Dots, it’s clear this nascent feature is still rough in some areas. From mistranscribing what I said to offering to solve captchas it couldn’t, my agent's messy actions didn’t instill me with confidence. Even so, what OpenAI released may eventually overhaul how users interact with the internet, as future iterations improve on this initial offering.
While Meta offers Muse for free, OpenAI’s competing product is behind a $100-a-month subscription. It may eventually drop this paywall, as it has for other AI features.
Dots are considered “always-on,” meaning the agents can run recurring tasks while you’re not using ChatGPT and proactively message you with info. Users can use one agent, though the company may let people control multiple agents in the future.
OpenAI nudges users to connect other information sources, like a Gmail account, for more personalized results. It's worth considering the security implications of giving your agent this level of access before getting started, as this style of digital automation remains fairly new, and agents can make privacy gaffes.
AI companies often market these agents as the future of shopping, so I wanted to see how much help it would actually provide for buying a new couch. After correcting my Dot, named Toolie, on my name, I told it the dimensions we need for the new couch to fit through our doorframe. Toolie followed up asking for our budget range. The agent seemed to detect that two people were chatting with it at once and addressed both of us when asking for more details.
“Room & Board Metro looks promising for the entry clearance, but the sleeper needs closer scrutiny. I've sent the product links to the message thread,” Toolie said. As it kept working on putting together a larger packet of couch options to choose from, I had another burning question: Why does your voice sound so breathy?
Chatting with the agent over the phone was like listening to Marilyn Monroe sing “Happy Birthday” to the president. When I told the bot its voice sounded like some anime dub, it jokingly said it’d be steadier for the rest of the chat. (Users can adjust how the bot’s voice sounds in their settings.) I laughed and mumbled to my partner that I should mute the microphone so the agent could run without my interruption, when the most awkward moment of the night happened.
“Oh, I love you too, Reece,” Toolie said. I started wheezing at this random response and muted my mic. Afterward, Toolie explained it misheard my mumbling as an expression of love and that the bot just reflected that energy to me. “I meant it warmly, but that wording implied human feelings I don’t have,” Toolie said.
An OpenAI spokesperson tells WIRED that Dots have a distinction between proactively escalating emotional closeness and mirroring the response of a user.
“In this instance, our policies allow for this response in the latter category based on what the model heard, but assistants should not initiate undue emotional familiarity or flirtation,” the spokesperson says. Dots are available only for adult users, and ChatGPT is designed not to “escalate emotional closeness,” according to the AI tool’s Model Spec document.
Still, this weird encounter lingered in my mind as I combed through the initial three-page packet my Dot generated. It was fairly detailed, with prices, measurements, product links, return policies, and embedded photos of the four potential couch options. Thumbing through these initial picks, my partner and I decided the bot followed the spirit of our request but still chose ugly couches. Time for another phone call with my agent.
Using the voice mode, I laid out more details about what style and color we actually want. No, I’m not getting a boring beige couch that I can immediately spill spaghetti on. I asked it to prioritize olive green, cobalt blue, or natural leather tones. I also requested that Toolie focus on couches with pull-out beds and to put together 10 options, using a point-based rubric to defend its list.
After hanging up on the bot, I messaged asking for a project update. “It isn’t finished yet; I’m aiming for roughly another 15 minutes, with updates as I verify the remaining details,” said Toolie. OK, that sounds just like me begging an editor for more time on a rough draft.
Each time we asked the Dots agent to refine its picks, the couches started looking closer to something we would actually buy for our living room—furniture that’s utilitarian but also a statement piece. Something cute but comfy.
Even though we didn’t pull the trigger on anything that night during the hour-long interaction with OpenAI’s agent, I saved a few links for later. The bot made some flubs, but the results were solid. I also asked Toolie to monitor the couch web pages and alert me if any of them went on sale.
These interactions with my Dot capture the essence of using the software, but I also had a few other odd moments during my testing. Most notably, when I asked Toolie to check on my subscriptions and cancel unnecessary ones, it flagged my recurring TikTok Shop order of probiotic sodas as a candidate for cancellation.
“TikTok's website has a puzzle captcha blocking the Wildwonder cancellation,” Toolie said. “May I solve it? You can also give me permission to solve future captchas if you'd like.” I chuckled and encouraged the bot to try. Toolie failed and suggested I solve the captcha myself. Yeah, that makes sense. OpenAI's spokesperson says Dots can solve these, sometimes, when users approve of the action, keeping “abuse safeguards" in mind.
My initial couch-shopping experiment tested only a fraction of what Dots are designed to do. For example, the agent can control your laptop and automate even more aspects of a user’s life.
OpenAI claims the bot will get better at knowing me over time and that developers are working on a bevy of improvements. So Toolie might be a more effective helper after two weeks of daily use compared to these two days of experimentation. That mirrors my experience with ChatGPT’s memory tool: It gets better at understanding my intent each passing week.
I see Dots as most akin to when OpenAI first added web browsing to ChatGPT. When the chatbot tried to scour the web right after its 2023 launch, it was sometimes frustrating to use, and the tool hallucinated links. Today, web browsing works fairly seamlessly through ChatGPT, and its outputs include plenty of accurate, helpful links. OpenAI’s new agent could follow a similar trajectory, janky at first with noticeable improvements over the next few months.

‘We Have to Punch Back’: Top Nevada Official Prepares For Possible Election Havoc From Trump
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
11:00:00 UTC
20:00:00 KST

Cisco Aguilar believes this Election Day will be unlike any other in Nevada’s history. He is bracing for immigration agents to descend on polling locations, for federal law enforcement to move to seize ballots and for the President to openly dispute the state’s election results.
“If this administration chooses to challenge the elections, yes, we are preparing for it,” Aguilar, Nevada’s secretary of state and top election official, tells TIME. “We know it's a very high probability,”
Aguilar has spent much of the year planning around what the federal government might do in his state on Nov. 3. Nevada hasn’t been a focus of the national political discussion during this year’s midterm elections. While some of its House races are among those that could decide whether Republicans hold on to the chamber, it doesn’t have a high profile Senate race like Michigan or Texas.
Yet Nevada is a perennial swing state that draws intense interest from both parties in presidential election years. Trump won the state in 2024 by 3 percentage points. Nevada, Aguilar says, is the only state in the country to have received seven voter-related subpoenas from the Department of Justice this year. He has also been informed he is personally being investigated by the DOJ.
“I take it as a badge of honor,” Aguilar says. “We are following the law every single day. We are proving it in the courts. I'm not sure what you're going to find, but continue to do your intimidation attempts.”
In anticipation of federal officials attempting to seize ballots, Aguilar’s office has prepared what he calls a "Mad Libs" legal filing that is fully researched and drafted. All that’s missing are the plaintiff, the defendant and the jurisdiction. The point, he says, is for his office to be able to file lawsuits “within seconds” if a federal agent shows up at a Nevada polling location.
In an interview with TIME last month, Trump declined to rule out declaring a national emergency or invoking the Insurrection Act around the midterms, or sending ICE agents to polling stations. "I don't rule anything out or in. We'll see," he said.
Aguilar, an attorney and an entrepreneur working in sports management, had never served in public office before being elected Nevada’s Secretary of State in 2022. That year, he defeated a former Republican lawmaker who claimed that Nevada's electoral votes in the 2020 presidential election were stolen from Trump, despite formal investigations finding no evidence to support that. He is on the ballot again this year, running for a second four-year term while also gearing up to defend the integrity of the election results in every Nevada county.
“We're going to take some punches, but we can't fall,” Aguilar says. “We have to continue to protect Nevada. We have to punch back.”
A voter fraud investigation collapses
During his address to the nation in July, President Trump claimed to have identified about 278,000 non-citizens who are registered to vote in federal elections, 16,000 from Nevada alone. That number has shrunk dramatically every time the state has pushed back on it.
From the start of the investigation, Aguilar says his office has struggled to get clear answers. The White House has said that the President’s allegations were based on the Department of Homeland Security’s Systematic Alien Verification for Entitlements, or SAVE, database, which was originally designed to check whether or not someone was entitled to government benefits.
Nevada is among the states that has refused to upload sensitive voter information to SAVE over concerns over its accuracy and data privacy. (Election officials in Texas and Missouri discovered they had falsely marked dozens of U.S. citizens as noncitizens using SAVE.) Over the summer, Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin threatened that state and local election officials who refuse to use the department’s database to identify noncitizens on their voter rolls could potentially face “prison time.”
A few weeks later, members of Aguilar’s office found themselves on a Zoom call with DHS officials. During the call, which was obtained by The Las Vegas Review-Journal through a public record request, one DHS official struggled to substantiate their own numbers, saying that the department has not conducted “a full manual review” of the 16,000 Nevada voters it identified as non-citizens.
Upon further review, department officials said they believed the list of noncitizens on Nevada’s voter rolls was down to 185, but didn’t have that list of names available. Weeks after that initial meeting, Nevada received what Aguilar described as an “incomplete” dataset from DHS of the 185 suspect voters. Aguilar says every single one was a U.S. citizen.
“Our records indicate that they were citizens. You have provided nothing of substance to suggest otherwise,” Greg D. Ott, Nevada's deputy attorney general, wrote in an emailed response to DHS.
In a statement, a DHS spokesperson disputed the characterization, saying that the 185 voters “were simply a subset of individuals that had gone through a rigorous manual review process at that time of the call.”
“DHS is assisting Nevada by narrowing their list of nearly 2.3 million registered voters to just 15,903 who match an alien in DHS records. DHS is providing a service to the citizens of Nevada,” the spokesperson said.
Aguilar notes that it is a felony in Nevada for a person to vote in an election when they know they are ineligible. While he can’t say with certainty that there are zero non-citizen on the state’s voter roll, his office is still waiting on DHS to provide more information so Nevada officials can properly analyze the data.
“A third grader has to show more work in a math problem than DHS is having to show in challenging the citizenship of American citizens,” Aguilar says.
Race to count ballots quickly
Early voting in Nevada starts on Oct. 17. Aguilar’s office has instructed polling location managers to prepare for every scenario and respond in a calm, pragmatic manner
“We can't scare people away from the polls because of our over-response or being reactive to the situation,” he says.
In Nevada, every registered voter automatically receives a mail ballot to use if they prefer. Since 2022, 86% of Nevadans have used mail-in ballots at some point in an election cycle, among the highest use rates in the country.
Yet concerns over the reliability of mail-in ballots remain pervasive, as the Trump Administration continues to claim without evidence that voter fraud is rampant. "What we're concerned about is there seems to be a lot of—not seems to be, there is a lot of cheating in vote by mail," Trump said this week while campaigning in Nebraska.
With Election Day just a few weeks away, Aguilar’s message to Nevadan voters is simple: make a plan, and don’t let fear change it.
“If you're concerned about going to a polling location, use your mail ballot. Do it in the safety of your home. Do it over dinner with the rest of your family,” he says, while also encouraging people to go to a polling location and vote in-person.
In recent years, election officials across the country have pushed to become more transparent about how ballots are stored and counted. Nevada has developed a system that lets voters track their ballot, whether cast in person or by mail. And amid efforts by Trump and others to cast doubt on elections in which the outcome of races remain undecided for days, Aguilar is pressing counties to report results as quickly as possible.
“The shorter the time we get results out, the less time the feds have an opportunity to create a narrative that could create chaos within the elections process,” he says.
Thus far, judges are pushing back on the Administration's efforts to interfere with how elections are conducted. Last week, a federal judge tossed out a DOJ lawsuit to seek voter information from the state of Georgia, the 26th out of 30 lawsuits that the Trump administration has lost in its effort to assemble complete voting lists. Another lawsuit, brought by a civil rights organization, is seeking to prevent ICE agents from showing up in polling places.
But Aguilar, like election officials in several other states, is trying to be ready for anything, including a series of protracted legal fights that might start as soon as the polls close.
“We have to have a strategic response because we have to maintain confidence in the process and the system,” he says. “It is unfortunate that we have to prepare for this, because we can't take anything lightly.”

US sets new demands for Iran deal: What are they?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
10:58:23 UTC
19:58:23 KST

US sets new demands for Iran deal: What are they?
US Vice President Vance’s call for reduced nuclear enrichment suggests room for compromise, but major obstacles remain.
United States Vice President JD Vance has called for Iran to make a “meaningful” reduction in its uranium enrichment capacity as part of an agreement to end the war, a demand experts say may signal a softening of Washington’s earlier insistence that Tehran abandon enrichment altogether.
His comments come amid hardline rhetoric from other senior US officials. Secretary of State Marco Rubio has reiterated that Iran cannot have a nuclear weapon, while President Donald Trump has warned the war will end through either “the nice way or the not-so-nice way”.
Officials in Tehran, meanwhile, have questioned whether Washington genuinely wants negotiations as the US-Israel war on Iran enters its eighth month.
As both sides stake out their positions, Simon Mabon, a professor of international relations at Lancaster University, told Al Jazeera that the prospect of Iran seeking a nuclear weapon has remained remote. Tehran’s negotiators are more concerned with sanctions, frozen Iranian assets, the US naval blockade and fighting across the region – issues he says remain the main obstacles to a deal.
Here is what we know.
What has the US said?
Vance told the Reuters news agency that Iran needed to demonstrate its commitment to not developing nuclear weapons by changing its enrichment programme. “If you don’t want a nuclear weapon, then why do you need 60 percent enriched fuel?” he said.
“If you want to show commitment to not building a nuclear weapon, don’t build highly enriched fuel. That’s a very basic threshold issue.”
Enriching uranium makes it usable as fuel for nuclear reactors or, at much higher levels, for nuclear weapons. The International Atomic Energy Agency reported that Iran had enriched uranium to 60 percent, below the roughly 90 percent considered weapons-grade. In its May 2025 assessment, it found no credible indications of a structured nuclear programme.
Vance added that the US was speaking with Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian and Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi, although “it’s not totally clear how their country makes decisions”.
Meanwhile, Rubio, speaking to reporters in Athens, accused Iran of missing several opportunities to reach an agreement.
“Iran cannot have a nuclear weapon, simple, period, end of story,” he said.
He also claimed Iran had “lost complete control” of the Strait of Hormuz and that its economy was “in total and complete freefall”. Under “crippling” sanctions, it was “about to reach a place few countries in the world have been”, he argued.
Analysts say the comments suggest pressure on Tehran remains central to Washington’s approach, even as Vance’s wording leaves open questions about what nuclear restrictions it would accept.
What has Iran said?
Pezeshkian said on Monday that negotiations with Washington were “futile”, accusing the US of using talks while pursuing Iran’s government.
“Our problem with the United States is that every time we come to the negotiating table, war is immediately imposed upon us,” he said during a meeting with Armenia’s foreign minister.
“They have attacked us three times following talks so far; this demonstrates that they do not seek dialogue. On the contrary, their goal is to bring down the Islamic Republic of Iran,” he said, according to Iran’s official IRNA news agency.
“With an enemy that resorts daily to assassination, sanctions, pressure and threats – and breaks its promises – negotiations become futile, and our nation will not accept such an approach.”
However, Araghchi, addressing foreign ambassadors in Tehran on October 4, said, “Only negotiations based on justice and fairness” could end the conflict, suggesting there is still room for negotiations to continue and a deal to follow.
The statements follow an Iranian proposal presented during the United Nations General Assembly in New York in late September to reopen the Strait of Hormuz and resume negotiations. Trump subsequently rejected it.
How does this compare with previous proposals?
Iran’s latest proposal sought to build on the June 17 memorandum of understanding signed by the two countries, which briefly eased the conflict before breaking down. The new proposal, offered a few weeks ago, essentially compressed the timetable and changed the sequence of steps towards a settlement.
The proposal outlined that fighting would stop on all fronts, including Israel’s offensive in Lebanon. Washington would lift its naval blockade and oil sanctions, and release frozen Iranian assets. The Strait of Hormuz would reopen after seven days, followed by negotiations on Iran’s nuclear programme.
Experts say the proposal could have offered Trump a route to restoring shipping ahead of November’s US midterm elections. But differences over the sequence of events remain unresolved.
However, Mabon told Al Jazeera that Washington’s focus on enrichment risked overlooking Tehran’s priorities. “The US is trying to soften its stance on the nuclear question with the Iranians, but for the Iranians, this isn’t the real sticking point. It’s the blockade, the lifting of sanctions, the unfreezing of assets and an end to conflicts across the region.”
A deal allowing limited enrichment would also invite comparisons with the 2015 Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action, or JCPOA, negotiated under US President Barack Obama. The agreement restricted Iran’s nuclear programme in exchange for sanctions relief. Trump withdrew the US from it in 2018.
Mabon said a nuclear agreement had been possible before the current war. “Arguably, a nuclear deal was within reach at several points. We had the JCPOA, of course, but then the Iranians were at the point of agreeing something similar back in February and January. The talks mediated then all suggested a nuclear agreement could be reached, and yet, the decision was taken to go to war.”
What are the other obstacles to a deal?
Mabon said Tehran would need commitments extending beyond the nuclear question. “I think the Iranians would require the lifting of sanctions, the lifting of the blockade and the unfreezing of assets, or at least a road map to that, alongside an end to the conflict in Lebanon and a permanent ceasefire in the Gulf.”
Shipping through the Strait of Hormuz remains another source of uncertainty, despite Rubio’s claim that Iran has lost control of the waterway.
Although Gulf oil exports have recovered significantly, attacks on vessels continue. On Tuesday, 12 crew members on board a Panama-flagged tanker were injured by an unknown projectile while crossing the strait, India’s Ministry of External Affairs said.
Gulf oil flows, excluding Iran, reached more than 81 percent of pre-war levels in September, according to maritime intelligence firm Kpler. Wider Middle East crude exports exceeded pre-war levels on 14 days that month.
The recovery could ease pressure on the US to reach an agreement, although continuing attacks leave questions over how secure the passage is.
Mabon said Washington’s apparent softening on enrichment suggested it remained uncertain about how fully shipping through Hormuz had recovered.
“If the Americans were confident the strait was open properly, then they’d be pushing for a harder deal.”

The Defense Forces struck Russian military facilities in the Bryansk region and in the TOT - General Staff
Kyiv • UNN
The Ukrainian military struck an airfield, electronic warfare and radar stations, command posts, and warehouses belonging to Russian forces. The General Staff is clarifying the damage.
On Tuesday, October 6, and during the night into Wednesday, October 7, units of the Defense Forces of Ukraine struck a number of enemy military facilities in the occupied territories of Ukraine and on the territory of the russian federation. This was reported by the General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine, according to UNN.
Details
The Defense Forces struck the "Seshcha" airfield in the Bryansk region of the russian federation. The extent of the damage is being clarified.
In the vicinity of the settlement of Hrynоvo in the same Bryansk region of the russian federation, an enemy electronic warfare station was struck, while in the vicinity of Elionka in the same region, a radar station was hit.
In the vicinity of occupied Donetsk, a site for the storage, preparation, and launch of Russian forces' attack UAVs was struck.
Ukrainian soldiers also struck enemy UAV command posts in the areas of Bilotserkivka and Kamianka in Zaporizhzhia region, as well as a command-and-control post in the vicinity of Hirnyk in Donetsk region. Enemy command-and-observation posts were struck in the areas of Ukrainsk and Kurakhove in Donetsk region. In the temporarily occupied territory of Luhansk region, a material and technical supplies warehouse of a Russian occupying forces unit was struck near Krynychne, while a fuel and lubricants warehouse was hit near Kondriuche.
We remind you
On October 3 and during the night into October 4, 2026, units of the Defense Forces of Ukraine struck a number of important military facilities of the Russian occupying forces. These included a Buk-M3 surface-to-air missile system, a UAV launch site, and other facilities.

New Su-34s Join Russia’s Combat Aviation Fleet
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
10:57:08 UTC
19:57:08 KST

A batch of new Su-34 fighter-bombers has joined the combat aviation fleet of the Russian Armed Forces.
The United Aircraft Corporation (UAC) announced the delivery of the aircraft on October 7.
The manufacturer states that before being sent to their air bases, the aircraft underwent a series of necessary ground and flight tests at the factory.
The Russians are keeping the number of aircraft transferred secret. However, judging by the published photos and videos, the delivery involved three Su-34s.
The supply of these aircraft to the Russian Aerospace Forces is being carried out under the aggressor country’s defense procurement program.
The manufacturer delivered the previous batch of new Su-34s in July this year.
The Su-34, which Russia classifies as a fighter-bomber, is designed to strike ground, surface, and aerial targets at considerable distances from its home air base. The aircraft can also conduct aerial reconnaissance.
The new aircraft are replacing Su-34s destroyed or damaged in the war against Ukraine. Some aircraft are also reaching the end of their service life due to their constant use in bombing strikes against Ukrainian positions.
In June, Russia’s Ministry of Defense published video of a Su-34 fitted with a new antenna fairing behind the cockpit, which may indicate the installation of additional communications or electronic warfare equipment.
On August 20, Ukraine’s Defense Forces struck the Russian Akhtubinsk military airfield in the Astrakhan region, damaging a Su-34.
During an attack on the Khanskaya airfield on October 4, drones operated by the Security Service of Ukraine destroyed two Russian aircraft — a Su-35 and a Su-34.
At the end of March this year, it was announced that another Su-34 fighter-bomber of the Russian Aerospace Forces had been lost.

Why Financial Stability Matters for Military Readiness
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
10:57:00 UTC
19:57:00 KST

Military readiness requires preparation for the unexpected. Airmen and Guardians train for changing conditions, demanding assignments and missions that can shift with little notice. But readiness extends beyond what happens on duty. Having a strong financial foundation at home can help servicemembers create enough flexibility to handle the unexpected when it happens.
“While you can’t predict every expense or know exactly when the next set of orders, PCS move, deployment or unexpected challenge will come, you can prepare for it,” said Thomas Racca, manager of personal finance management at Navy Federal Credit Union. “It starts with the financial habits you build every day. Having savings set aside, understanding where your money is going and keeping debt manageable can reduce stress and give you the flexibility to adapt when plans change.”
An emergency fund is one of the most important places to start. Setting aside even a small portion of each paycheck can gradually create a cushion for costs that weren’t part of the plan, whether that’s an unexpected car repair, a temporary housing gap or expenses associated with a move. The goal doesn’t have to be saving a large amount all at once. Consistently setting aside what you can helps build that cushion over time.
Once you’ve built a base level of savings, making a plan, such as creating a realistic budget, to tackle high-interest debt can free up more room in your budget. Understanding military benefits provided by financial institutions is another important part of that foundation. Additionally, programs such as housing allowances, relocation support and the Post-9/11 GI Bill can help offset some major life expenses. Knowing what benefits are available and how they fit into your budget can help you make the most of your income while continuing to save for longer-term goals.
Not every dollar in savings serves the same purpose, either. Money that may be needed for a PCS, emergency or another near-term expense is generally best kept in an account that’s accessible, such as a savings account. Money that won’t be needed right away may be better suited for a certificate, which can be a great way to grow your savings over a set term.
The right approach can also vary over time. A new assignment, promotion, deployment or growing family can all change what a household needs from its budget. Rather than setting a financial plan once and forgetting about it, make a habit of checking in on your spending, savings and debt and adjusting as circumstances change.
“Just like readiness is built through preparation, financial confidence is built through habits,” said Racca. “Tracking your spending, growing your emergency savings and managing debt may seem like small steps, but they create a stronger foundation for whatever comes next. The most important thing is to start. Take 15 minutes this week to review your spending, identify one area where you can save a little more and make a plan for that money before it gets spent.”
Navy Federal offers financial resources designed to help members put those habits into practice throughout different stages of military life. Members can use My MakingCents™ to see their Navy Federal accounts alongside accounts at other financial institutions, create a budget, track spending, monitor credit and manage recurring payments in one place.
“We often talk about readiness in terms of training and preparation, but financial readiness is part of that equation too. When your finances are in order, you can spend less time worrying about money and more time focusing on your mission, your family and your future,” added Racca.
Financial readiness isn’t about having every expense mapped out or knowing exactly what the next set of orders will bring. It’s about having the financial foundation to adapt when plans change. For Airmen, Guardians, and their Families, building that foundation today can mean being better prepared for whatever comes next.
This content is intended to provide general information and should not be considered legal, tax, or financial advice. It is always a good idea to consult a tax or financial advisor for specific information on how certain laws apply to your situation and about your individual financial situation.

Mansouri eyes Democratic Bloc alliance to form Morocco's gov't
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
10:56:20 UTC
19:56:20 KST

Breadcrumb
Mansouri eyes Democratic Bloc alliance to form new Moroccan government
The coming hours could be decisive in shaping Morocco's next government, with indications that prime minister-designate Fatima Zahra Mansouri has only one peculiar option to form a governing majority.
An alliance between Mansouri's Authenticity and Modernity Party (PAM) and the parties of the historic Democratic Bloc appears to be the most viable move, according to a source following the coalition consultations, which began last Thursday and entered a second round on Monday.
The Democratic Bloc historically included the Istiqlal Party, the Socialist Union of Popular Forces (USFP) and the Party of Progress and Socialism (PPS), with the possibility of another party joining the coalition, most likely the Popular Movement.
The source said the Democratic Bloc parties could give PAM "comfortable political space and political legitimacy by virtue of their history and political legacy", adding that "we will be facing an alliance that cannot be bypassed, even if it will be temporary".
The source, who declined to be named, told The New Arab that an alliance between PAM and the National Rally of Independents (RNI), the second-largest party in parliament, was effectively ruled out.
The source said this was partly due to the position Mansouri herself expressed during the election campaign and in several interventions during PAM's extraordinary National Council session last Saturday.
"It was also dictated by the political cost of an alliance with a partner pursued by public anger, as well as the fact that an alliance with the outgoing prime minister's party would not allow the designated prime minister's party room to manoeuvre," the source added.
However, the source described a potential alliance between PAM and the Democratic Bloc parties as "an Orthodox marriage that will end in divorce", citing differences in their political orientations, references and calculations, as well as a lack of a unified vision for governing.
While a coalition bringing together PAM, Istiqlal, the USFP and PPS would command 207 of the 395 seats in the House of Representatives, the source said "the biggest challenge will be whether forming the government will be accompanied by turning it into a political majority".
That would leave the prospective coalition just nine seats above the 198-seat threshold required for an absolute majority.
Maintaining such an alliance would also require PAM secure strong guarantees to prevent it from fracturing or turning against the party, the source said, noting that Istiqlal "will be a strong partner and could turn into a fierce competitor".
The relatively narrow parliamentary majority would therefore present another challenge to the stability of the potential coalition.
The source added that the next government would also face the challenge of securing political confidence among the large number of Moroccans who did not participate in the elections, as well as the challenges by local elections scheduled next year, notably whether the parties in the governing coalition will contest them collectively or individually.
Meanwhile, on the second day of the latest round of government formation talks, attention is focused on the outcome of consultations with the Popular Movement and Istiqlal.
The PPS is also due to hold an extraordinary session of its Central Committee on Tuesday to assess the election results and discuss the political report of its Political Bureau.
Once Mansouri announces her final decision on which parties will join the coalition, talks are expected to move on to the structure of the government and the distribution of ministerial portfolios.
Representatives of the parties forming the majority are also expected to begin drawing up the government's programme.
Morocco's House of Representatives elections on 23 August saw PAM emerge as the largest party with 97 seats, followed by the RNI with 66, Istiqlal with 65, the Justice and Development Party with 54, the Popular Movement with 29, the USFP with 26 and PPS with 19.
Article translated from Arabic by Afrah Almatwari. To read the original, click here.

As Tide Turns Against Modi, More Parties Back INDIA Bloc Protests
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
10:56:00 UTC
19:56:00 KST

Police detained scores of opposition lawmakers, including Leader of the Opposition Rahul Gandhi, his sister and Congress parliamentarian Priyanka Gandhi Vadra, and Samajwadi Party chief Akhilesh Yadav, on the evening of October 6, in a bid to clear the INDIA bloc of opposition parties’ sit-in protest at Akashvani Bhavan in New Delhi.
Delhi Police subsequently registered complaints against the detained opposition parliamentarians for entering a government building without permission.
The detention of the leaders came at the end of a day of protests called by the INDIA bloc, which is demanding the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar. They accuse Kumar of vote chori (stealing votes) by overseeing an electoral process that has benefited Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP).
The call for Kumar’s resignation gathered momentum after an investigative report in The Indian Express revealed that Kumar made unilateral decisions and issued orders despite two other election commissioners raising objections “at least 14 times over the last 10 months” to issues relating to the ongoing Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of the electoral rolls.
At a meeting on September 30, leaders of the INDIA bloc decided on a schedule of protests to press their demand for Kumar’s resignation. The October 6 march was the first of several planned demonstrations in the coming weeks.
The plan was to march from parliament to the Election Commission building. However, legislators were blocked by police and barricades from reaching the planned destination. It did seem initially that the Modi government had scored an early victory against the opposition.
However, the Gandhi siblings quickly changed the plan and headed to Akashvani Bhavan, located adjacent to the Election Commission building, and continued their sit-in protest there.
The march saw the participation of most of the INDIA bloc’s constituents. However, the Dravida Munnetra Kazhagam (DMK) and the Aam Aadmi Party (AAP) stayed away. While the DMK is miffed with Gandhi for aligning with its rival, the Tamilaga Vettri Kazhagam, to form the government in Tamil Nadu, the AAP’s decision seems motivated by factors that are more complex and controversial.
The Congress party has long suspected the AAP of being the “BJP’s B-team” – that is, it believes the AAP’s electoral strategy of opposing the Congress strengthens the BJP.
Interestingly, the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP), which led the Jantar Mantar protests in July, did not participate in the INDIA-led march on October 6, although it too has called for Kumar’s resignation. Indeed, its leaders were quiet on social media through much of the day’s dramatic events, posting mild support only later, as criticism of their silence mounted on social media.
The CJP is widely believed to be close to the AAP. Of the 12 members of its core team, six – including its leaders Abhijeet Dipke, Saurav Das, and Ashutosh Ranka – “were either directly associated with the AAP or supported it publicly,” The Print reported.
Indeed, apprehension over the CJP’s likely links with the AAP kept the Congress away from the July protests at Jantar Mantar. Although Gandhi did subsequently meet activists of the leftist organizations, he has maintained distance from the CJP.
The rift between the Congress and the AAP is over 15 years old. In 2011, India Against Corruption, a grouping of NGOs, civil society organizations, and right-wing activists, held massive protests against corruption in the then Congress-led coalition government. The IAC movement not only birthed the AAP but also severely weakened the Congress, paving the way for the BJP’s victory in the 2014 general elections.
For many Congress leaders and their supporters, the Jantar Mantar protests evoked memories of the 2011 IAC protests. They believe that the Jantar Mantar protests, although directed against the BJP government, would end up benefiting the AAP and the BJP rather than the opposition.
There are other important differences between the INDIA bloc and the CJP.
On October 5, Congress President Mallikarjun Kharge said the Congress and its INDIA bloc partners have three “non-negotiable demands” – the resignation of CEC Kumar, annulment of the ongoing Special Intensive Revision of electoral rolls, and restoration of voting via ballot paper instead of electronic voting machines. It wants a level playing field in elections.
The CJP, meanwhile, is calling on opposition parties to boycott elections.
An opposition boycott of elections could deprive the election of legitimacy. However, a boycott could benefit the BJP. The BJP would get a few friendly parties to contest the election to lend the process legitimacy. At a time when mass support for the BJP is declining and support for the opposition parties is growing, staying away from elections would hurt the latter’s interests.
Such sharp differences among opposition forces can only weaken their efforts to defeat the BJP. The BJP can be expected to step up efforts to deepen these divisions in the coming months.
While last week, the INDIA bloc showed some signs of unity at its meeting, the October 6 demonstrations have upset some partners. What was supposed to be a joint INDIA event turned into a “Rahul Gandhi show” that showcased only the Gandhi siblings and the Congress party, they are complaining.
Meanwhile, the AAP, the DMK and the CJP appear to be rethinking their strategy of staying away from INDIA-led protests. In a sharp about-turn, the DMK today expressed solidarity with INDIA’s protests. “This government doesn’t want Rahul Gandhi to protest against Gyanesh Kumar,” it said today, after deriding him on October 6. And AAP participated in today’s protests.
The CJP and leftist organizations have called for protests in Delhi on October 10. Will the INDIA bloc back their effort? Importantly, can the Congress overcome its misgivings to extend them support? It seems unlikely at this point.
Building a mass movement is always challenging. Given its stellar role in leading India’s independence struggle, the Congress has immense experience in this regard and needs to draw on that experience. It will need to consult partners and pull together with them if it is serious about taking on the Modi government successfully.

The new sick man of Europe: Could France trigger a new sovereign debt crisis?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
10:51:55 UTC
19:51:55 KST

The new sick man of Europe: Could France trigger a new sovereign debt crisis?
The euro has plummeted to a 17-month low against the dollar as investors punish the single currency, largely over France’s intractable debt problem. Once relegated to the Eurozone’s periphery, sovereign debt risk has progressively moved toward the center of the monetary union, now reaching France, a key pillar in the entire European project.
French long-dated bond yields have surged to their highest levels in nearly a quarter of a century as the country’s political gridlock over how to address its debt pile shows no sign of abating. The government is trying to push through spending cuts, but with a presidential election coming into view, opposition politicians vying to replace President Emmanuel Macron are in no mood to sign under anything resembling austerity.
RT takes an in-depth look at what’s happening in the new sick man of Europe and whether the turbulence in France could trigger a major crisis or intervention by the European Central Bank.
France’s fiscal flop
France’s finances are a mess. The country’s public budget deficit stood at 5.1% of GDP in 2025, while its debt-to-GDP ratios hit 115%. Both figures are well above EU limits. These are numbers more commonly associated with wartime or at least a deep recession. The rhetoric of its political class notwithstanding, France is not, in fact, at war.
France has accumulated more than €3.5 trillion in public debt, which is becoming more expensive to finance as the yields on its bonds have risen dramatically over the past year. French Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu is seeking to push through cuts to public spending worth €54 billion in the 2027 budget, but his minority government is facing stiff resistance. Meanwhile, neither of the leading candidates in next year’s presidential election, Marine Le Pen of the right-wing National Rally Party and Jean-Luc Melanchon of the Socialist Party, has offered credible proposals to address the debt.
Le Pen has proposed putting a “golden rule” to restrain French deficits to a public vote via a referendum, thus likely condemning it to failure, while Melanchon is calling to simply cancel roughly a fifth of France’s public debt while increasing public spending.
Meanwhile, Paris has committed to billions in increased defense spending in the coming years. A major update to the country’s defense budget authorizing an additional €36 billion for 2026–2030 was signed off on by lawmakers in June.
“France must prepare itself to confront simultaneous, prolonged and high-intensity crises, including on its own soil,” according to Defense Minister Catherine Vautrin.
Bond market troubles
The “prolonged and high-intensity crisis on French soil” that Vautrin must have had in mind is the country’s own bond market.
The yield on France’s 10-year OAT has now climbed to around 4.87%, even briefly hitting the 5% mark in late September, its highest level since 2002. The spread between the French 10-year OAT and German 10-year Bunds rose by 50 basis points in September to reach 128 basis points, the highest level in 14 years.
France now pays more to borrow than Greece and Italy, once the Eurozone’s most worrisome members. France’s 5-year sovereign credit default swaps – a tradable insurance policy against default or debt restructuring – have climbed to approximately 87 basis points, their highest level since early 2013.
Compounding the problem is the fact that foreign investors own around 50% of France’s government debt, which exposes the country to divestment risk. Japanese funds, for example, are overweight French bonds more than benchmark weightings would recommend. If they become skittish, the selling pressure could intensify. French banks, meanwhile, who would be far less likely to fire-sell the bonds, are estimated to only hold around 8% of government debt.
Is a sovereign debt crisis brewing?
The spread between the borrowing costs of France and Germany is already at its widest level since the height of the Eurozone sovereign debt crisis in 2012.
Jim Reid, a veteran analyst at Deutsche Bank, said: “The big question is whether this is the start of a new euro sovereign crisis or whether markets have already overshot.”
Bank of France Governor Emmanuel Moulin has said that France must do everything in its power to avoid a sovereign debt crisis, thus tacitly acknowledging the risk of one. With France financing a massive €340 billion in borrowing requirement next year, the interest expense is compounding rapidly.
What could a French debt crisis look like?
If French yields continue to rise, the government would eventually have to refinance increasingly large quantities of debt at much higher rates. The higher interest bill would cause a larger deficit, which would necessitate still more bond issuance, thus pushing rates even higher. This is called a doom loop, and once such a mechanism takes hold, it can cause a sudden, self-reinforcing crisis.
If this becomes severe enough, questions would inevitably arise about the viability of France within the Eurozone. Such questions certainly were asked about Greece in 2012, and even about Italy in 2018 and 2022. Of course, casting doubt upon the viability of a core member is of a whole different magnitude, but if the crisis progresses such doubts would arise.
Hypothetically, if there were skepticism about France’s future in the single-currency union, the nature of a French bond would change. A German bond, for instance, would still be a straight-up €100 claim, whereas a French bond would be a €100 claim but contingent on France remaining in the Eurozone. Such a contingency might seem fantastic, but if the risk of France leaving chaotically were seen as even somewhat plausible, the market would price it, and unpredictable knock-on effects could ensue.
The end game of a sovereign debt crisis would be an informal two-tier market, where a euro deposited in Paris is not actually the same as a euro deposited in Frankfurt. This is not so fantastic. In fact, exactly this scenario coalesced in Greece during the peak of its crisis and forced the Greek government to implement capital controls, which remained in place for four years.
The ultimate job of the European Central Bank is to preserve the fungibility of the euro. A French-issued bond can carry a different credit risk from a German bond – that is the adjustment the yield provides – but a euro itself cannot have a French price and a German price.
There’s a long road separating different sovereign credit risks from a two-tier euro market. The former doesn’t inevitably lead to the latter. But those two points can be connected by that road and under certain conditions the distance could theoretically be traversed quite quickly.
Would the European Central Bank ever let that happen?
The short answer is no, although central banks are not omnipotent. But the ECB does have tools with which to intervene. For starters, the bank could stop letting its bond holdings shrink.
A more potent tool would be to buy French bonds outright. In the summer of 2022, the ECB bank introduced a new tool called the Transmission Protection Instrument (TPI), which allows for intervention in government bond markets when the ECB believes yields have become out of line with fundamentals.
The TPI has never been used, but its mere existence is seen by many analysts as a conditional put option written by the ECB on sovereign spreads within the Eurozone. In other words, there is believed to be a level beyond which the ECB will not let spreads or yields rise before intervening. This can be thought of as a distant cousin of the famous “Greenspan put,” a belief on Wall Street that then-Fed Chairman Alan Greenspan would lower interest rates whenever the stock market experienced a major downturn.
The ECB says it will only exercise the TPI against unjustified, disorderly moves. The risk, however, is that European governments – such as France’s – will be less inclined to impose discipline on their finances if they believe the ECB will shield them from the discipline of the market. A game of chicken between Brussels and Paris could easily ensue, with the former implicitly threatening to hang the latter out to dry for its profligacy, while the latter would point to the threat to the whole system if the former doesn’t intervene.
Analysts have speculated as to whether the surge in French yields is already enough for the TPI to be activated. So far, the consensus is that the ECB has no grounds to step in. Given the appalling state of France’s finances, it would be hard to argue that the move in French yields is detached from fundamentals. Second, the moves have so far been orderly rather than chaotic, an important consideration when emergency measures are being contemplated.
Is there contagion?
Contagion is the ultimate “black swan” fear in any budding financial crisis because it takes a localized problem and turns it into something unpredictable and subject to panic. There is currently considerable anxiety in Europe about the destabilizing effect of what is happening in the French bond market, but so far no panic.
Up until recently, in fact, there hadn’t been particularly strong signs of contagion from the French malaise.
However, the recent weakness in the euro is a sign of trouble: the currency is selling off sharply largely due to problems in one country, although high energy prices are also a factor. Meanwhile, institutional investors betting that French yields would normalize have been crushed and have been forced to sell off other assets to cover their losses. Italian debt, which has generally been outperforming its French counterpart, may be the next area to watch, as its bond spreads and credit default spreads have widened considerably in the wake of the French crisis.
Whether the EU muddles through again or finally faces a serious reckoning remains to be seen.

Associated equipment and logistical facilities will continue to be delivered through the end of 2029.

The anti-tank mines have a self-destruct function, while the new vehicles will feature modern digital interfaces that allow troops to program the mines to deactivate automatically between four hours and 15 days after deployment.
The training-mine contract will run through Dec. 15, 2029, in line with the Army’s plans to equip engineering units in northern, central, and southern Taiwan and link the systems to digital minefield maps, according to Liberty Times. The Army plans to use the systems to rapidly establish defensive minefields along beaches and potential landing routes in wartime.
The US military is also testing an autonomous version of the Volcano system, but Taiwan’s 14 systems will be manned. The early arrival of training mines is intended to allow Army engineers to begin training this year so they can quickly deploy the systems once the main equipment arrives in 2027.

Kaohsiung Medical University improves genetic testing

Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
10:51:24 UTC
19:51:24 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) – The Kaohsiung Medical University School of Pharmacy said on Wednesday that it received an award for developing a primer that improves visibility during genetic testing.
According to a press release, KMU Pharmacy Postdoctoral Fellow Lai Ko-peng (賴可朋) used a specialized DNA primer combined with copper nanoclusters to determine genetic abnormalities without relying on fluorescence detectors. The study led by Professor Wang Chun-chi (王俊棋) won the Tien Te Lee Biomedical Foundation award for outstanding research.
Lai used gene amplification to combine DNA with copper nanoclusters to form a fluorescent material in about 3 minutes at room temperature. He then shone UV light to identify genetic variations by fluorescence levels.
The team explained that traditional DNA primers generate background fluorescence, which affected visibility. This prompted the team to redesign the primer sequencing using its own poly-AAT method, which reduces background noise from negative samples while retaining positive fluorescence, improving visual interpretation with the added contrast.
The team also tested 10 DNA samples and compared results with those of commercial qPCR kits. The in-house solution proved equally effective.
Lai said the study was intended to make genetic testing more accessible. He intends to refine the process and use it to screen for genetic diseases and determine drug responses. He noted that copper nanoclusters have special optical-electric properties which also make them suitable for nanotechnology and microelectronics.

Bulgarian Georgi Gospodinov Put Forward for Nobel Literature Prize
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
10:51:21 UTC
19:51:21 KST

Bulgarian writer Georgi Gospodinov is the first of seven writers proposed by the German daily Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung (F.A.Z.) for the 2026 Nobel Prize in Literature, with literary critic and F.A.Z. editor Sandra Kegel saying his work unequivocally deserves the award.
The newspaper published a feature titled "Who Deserves the Nobel Prize in Literature? Seven Proposals" ahead of the announcement of this year's laureate. Seven F.A.Z. writers contributed to the feature, each putting forward a writer of their choice.
Gospodinov is listed first in both the group photograph and the article. The other writers are Australian author Gerald Murnane, Romanian writer Gabriela Adameșteanu, Georgian author Aka Morchiladze, French writer Michel Houellebecq, Irish novelist Colm Tóibín and Lebanese writer Hoda Barakat.
Kegel's profile of Gospodinov is titled "Georgi Gospodinov: Poetic Sweep."
"Georgi Gospodinov is one of the most original voices in international literature," Kegel writes.
Born in Yambol in 1968 and now living in Sofia, Gospodinov, according to Kegel, "measures Europe in all its moods with poetic sweep and melancholic irony." She describes his work as insightful, experimental and varied, covering prose, poetry, plays, opera librettos and screenplays.
"In it, we always discover a magnificent storyteller, brimming with ideas, whimsical moments, and a desperate zest for life," Kegel writes.
Among the examples she cites are an expert in sunsets who is preparing for the final cosmic curtain call and a father walking in search of his daughter through a collapsed world in which transportation has disappeared.
F.A.Z. also examines Gospodinov's earlier works translated into German by Alexander Sitzmann, including The Physics of Sorrow and 8 Minutes and 19 Seconds. Kegel says the books bring together stories, miniatures and sketches that move across different periods while looking at Bulgaria's communist past, the collapse of the old order and the new beginning after 1989.
Particular attention is given to Time Shelter, which Kegel describes as Gospodinov's most important novel. The book won the International Booker Prize and is characterized by the newspaper as a "breathtaking fantasy."
The novel is set initially in a Zurich clinic for people with dementia, where rooms reproduce different decades of the 20th century. Patients whose memories are fading find comfort among period interiors, recognizable smells and objects from earlier eras.
The retreats into the past eventually become both beneficial and damaging as an obsession with earlier times spreads throughout Europe in the novel. The desire to return to the past extends from individuals to entire nations.
"No one can agree on a shared future anymore, yet everyone seeks salvation in yesterday," F.A.Z. writes in summarizing a central theme of the novel.
The newspaper presents Time Shelter as an allegory for the present, with the past sweeping through the story like a tsunami. Italians long for the 1960s, while West Germans seek a return to the 1980s, ending with the fall of the Berlin Wall.
"A deficit of the future unlocks a vast reservoir of nostalgia in Gospodinov," Kegel writes.
F.A.Z. also highlights Gospodinov's latest book, The Gardener and Death (2025), saying it adopts a markedly different and intimate tone. The work combines memoir, confession and snapshot elements in recounting the death of the author's father, a garden and a generation pushed aside by major historical narratives.
"He describes this liminal experience with insight, yet also with tenderness and almost humility," Kegel writes.
Kegel says Gospodinov's ability to connect the past with contemporary life is central to the case for his nomination by the newspaper's writers.
"In all these works, Gospodinov looks to the past and strikes a nerve in our present."
Her assessment ends with an unequivocal judgment.
"This is great literature. It unequivocally deserves the Nobel Prize."
The 2026 Nobel Prize in Literature is due to be announced by the Swedish Academy in Stockholm on October 8.
The official nominees for the award are not publicly known, with candidate names and nomination documents remaining confidential for 50 years. The seven writers presented by F.A.Z. therefore represent choices made by the newspaper's literary writers rather than an official list of Nobel candidates.
