children’s illustrated worlds meet realities of seoul in yeondoo jung’s photographs
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
10:50:31 UTC
19:50:31 KST

children’s illustrated worlds meet realities of seoul in yeondoo jung’s photographs
the series takes on new meaning at a time when images can be generated without the physical process once required to make them.
Yeondoo Jung’s Wonderland brings children’s drawings to life
Korean artist Yeondoo Jung collected 1,200 drawings from children between the ages of five and seven, selecting 17 to reconstruct as large-format photographs. Working with teenage models, costume and prop designers, and locations across Seoul, the artist carefully translated the imagined worlds from sketches into physical scenes, including details that could not exist according to the usual rules of photography. Twenty years later, this painstaking process feels especially relevant as images that once required sets, costumes, models, and physical tricks can now be created instantly. ‘When producing the work back in 2004, digital cameras certainly existed, but I intentionally insisted on using a 4×5 inch large-format film camera,’ Jung tells designboom. ‘This was to create the most theatrical and hard-to-realize scenes—for instance, using a trampoline to capture the exact moment models floated in mid-air to recreate a drawing where gravity is ignored.’
Jung wanted to stay as close as possible to the children’s drawings, even when their ideas were difficult to reproduce in real life. Turning these into photographs meant working out how to make those details happen in front of the camera. Some required finding the right location, while others involved costumes, props or a trampoline. The photographs keep the strange logic of the original drawings, but bring it into the real world.
from 1,200 drawings to 17 photographs
Over four months, Jung collected 1,200 drawings from children between five and seven, from which he selected 17 to recreate as photographs. He chose teenagers to play the characters because, as he explains, ‘they visually convey the bodies of adults and at the same time, their minds are more similar to that of the child that created the original drawings.’
Turning the drawings into photographs involved a team of fashion designers, prop designers, makeup artists and teenage models, all working out how to translate the children’s simple images into real spaces. ‘Fashion designers, prop designers, makeup artists, and teenagers gathered around a 6-year-old’s drawing, holding serious planning meetings for hours,’ Jung shares with us. They had to decide everything from the fabric of a costume to how a piece of furniture drawn on a flat page could be made in three dimensions.
 Color was another part of the process. Jung followed the colors chosen from a 12-color crayon set and went to Seoul’s Dongdaemun fabric market with a costume designer to find matching fabrics to stay as close as possible to what the children had drawn, without trying to make the images look more polished or realistic.
The same attention went into details that could easily be missed. In one seven-year-old girl’s drawing of Cinderella, the palace carries a sign reading Kingdom, which Jung connects to the amount of signage the children see around Seoul. ‘Unlike written words, children’s observations of society are directly revealed through their drawings,’ the South Korean artist says. ‘This reflects a dimension of reality that is completely different from the knowledge and understanding conveyed through text.’
when fantasy exposes the city
In some cases, the drawings may reveal things about the world the children see around them. In Rich and Poor, for instance, the two houses are only slightly different in size, while a wealthy person hands a lump of gold to a poor person. Recreating the drawing as a photograph forced Jung to look at how differently wealth and poverty are actually represented in Seoul, where wealthy residents live in high-rise apartments while poorer communities often occupy homes in areas marked for redevelopment. ‘If we were to photograph this, what kind of image would it become?’ Jung asks. ‘We would definitely have to find a location where both a wealthy house and a poor house fit into a single frame.’
The photographic medium forces Jung to find an actual relationship between the spaces represented abstractly in the drawing. The difference between rich and poor can no longer remain a symbolic difference in scale. ‘In the reality of Seoul, the wealthy live in high-rise apartments, while the poor live in redevelopment zones,’ he continues. ‘They live in houses they cannot even afford to repair, in areas that will soon be demolished to make way for new apartments.’
The photograph brings another layer to the original drawing, revealing how much of the children’s everyday surroundings has made its way into their imagined worlds. What looks like a simple story about two houses and a gift of gold also reflects the realities of housing and inequality in Seoul. ‘The realization that a child’s innocent drawing actually deals with the heavy reality of metropolitan expansion and housing culture is only possible through the medium of photography,’ the visual artist highlights.
photography after the digital turn
 When Jung made Wonderland in 2004, he chose to work with a 4×5-inch large-format film camera, even though digital photography was already available. He wanted to make the scenes as physically real as possible, which meant finding practical ways to recreate things that could only exist in a child’s drawing.
That approach feels different today. ‘Times have changed, and now, by simply inputting a few lines of text into an AI program, one could easily generate an image of teenagers floating in the air,’ Jung comments. For him, this is part of why Wonderland has drawn attention today, as the effort that went into making each photograph is now much harder to separate from the image itself. ‘I believe the reason the Wonderland series is receiving renewed attention recently is, ironically, because of the immense physical effort and the highly inconvenient methods chosen to take a single photograph,’ he reflects.
The difference is also in the way the images were made, with people, materials, locations and physical tricks all coming together to reproduce something that began as a child’s drawing. As Jung puts it, ‘Children’s ideas do not come from text (as they haven’t yet learned to write), but rather from their sharp ‘’observation,’’ much like looking at the world through a camera lens.’
two ways of seeing
 The difference between the drawings and the photographs is part of what makes Wonderland work. The children could ignore gravity, perspective and proportion, while Jung had to find a way to make those ideas work in front of a camera. The teenagers, costumes, props and locations became part of that process.
‘The medium of photography traditionally captures a resemblance of reality on a flat surface through a lens,’ Jung notes. He describes the making of the photographs as a group of people gathering around a child’s drawing and trying to work out how each part could be made real.
For the artist, the drawing and the photograph are meant to be seen together. ‘The children’s drawings and the photographs interpreting them form a pair, creating a single artwork,’ he suggests. The first thing viewers might notice is how closely the photograph follows the drawing, but looking longer reveals the differences between the two. That gap between the original drawing and the finished photograph is where much of the work’s meaning sits. What begins as a child’s simple idea becomes something more complicated once it is placed in the real world.
the weight behind the wonder
Yeondoo Jung describes Wonderland as one of the lightest subjects in his body of work. ‘The Wonderland series deals with what appears to be the lightest subject matter among my works,’ he tells us. ‘Therefore, I tried to give it as much weight and fidelity as possible through the highly realistic medium of photography.’
That balance is still visible in the photographs. A person floats above the ground, a palace carries a Kingdom sign, and houses sit together in ways that would be difficult to find in the real city. At the same time, the photographs bring these scenes back to Seoul, with its streets, buildings, signs and social realities. For Jung, the drawings and photographs remain closely connected. ‘The children’s drawings and the photographs interpreting them form a pair, creating a single artwork,’ he says. Looking at them together, the differences become as important as the similarities, showing what happens when a child’s way of seeing is brought into the adult world.

Tomorrow will be the warmest day in Ukraine! And tomorrow Ukraine will be one of the warmest countries in Europe! During the day, air temperatures in most regions of Ukraine will range from +20 to +24°, while in the western regions, +21 to +26° is expected

In Kyiv, October 8 will also be the warmest day of the coming period. No precipitation is expected, while the daytime temperature will rise to +22…+23 degrees.

Earlier it was also reported about traffic closures on the largest bridges across the Dnepr River - Yuzhny, Metro and Patona.
In recent days, Kiev has been experiencing serious transport problems and major traffic jams. Mayor Vitaly Klichko called the situation very dramatic. The Ukrainian edition of Insider said that a transport collapse has started in the Ukrainian capital.

My goal is to have 100. I want 100 FIRs to be registered against me. Every FIR is a medal for me," he told reporters.
Delhi Police beefed up security in anticipation of a possible opposition protest. The force also cited a Supreme Court directive to justify its decision not to grant permission for a sit-in at Jantar Mantar, Delhi’s designated protest venue.
“As per the order of the Supreme Court in Writ Petition (Civil), Mazdoor Kisan Shakti Sangathan vs. Union of India & Others, and the Delhi Police Standing Order issued in compliance with the said order, prior permission of the competent authority is mandatory for organising any meeting, demonstration, sit-in, or protest at Jantar Mantar,” a Delhi Police statement read.“Applications seeking such permission are required to be submitted to the Deputy Commissioner of Police, New Delhi District, at least 10 days prior to the proposed event,” the statement added.

Germany blocks Chinese takeover of Hamburg logistics firm
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
10:47:49 UTC
19:47:49 KST

Ayhan Şimşek
07 October 2026•Update: 07 October 2026
Germany has blocked Chinese state-owned shipping company Cosco from acquiring an 80% stake in Hamburg logistics firm Zippel, citing security concerns.  
An Economy Ministry spokesman said after a Cabinet meeting Wednesday that the ministry would issue a formal prohibition order, German news agency dpa reported.  
"The reason for the prohibition is security concerns. The acquisition would have deepened dependencies and jeopardized the resilience of supply chains in Germany and the EU,” the spokesman said. 
Germany welcomes foreign investment, he said, but its laws allow the government to review foreign acquisitions of German companies on a case-by-case basis.
The standard considers whether a deal is likely to threaten public order or security, he added.  
Cosco is among the world’s largest shipping companies by cargo volume. It already holds a 24.99% stake in Hamburg’s Tollerort container terminal.

October 7 and the forever war it unleashed, from Gaza to Yemen
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
10:47:45 UTC
19:47:45 KST

Breadcrumb
October 7 and the forever war it unleashed, from Gaza to Yemen
The war triggered by the events of 7 October 2023 will drag on for years to come. What began that day quickly revealed much broader objectives, many of which had been taking shape well before the fighting erupted.
Just a month earlier, in September 2023, the India-Middle East-Europe Economic Corridor, or IMEC, was announced in New Delhi. The project, backed by the United States, India, the European Union, France, Germany, Italy, Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates, was designed to connect Asia with Europe through the Middle East.
IMEC was conceived as an integrated network spanning energy, oil, telecommunications, technological infrastructure, subsea cables, ports and railways. The aim was to bind these countries together economically and strategically, partly as a counterweight to China’s Belt and Road Initiative.
In political terms, the corridor would connect South Asia to the Middle East and Europe, while helping contain China and its allies. It would also create a framework for deeper integration between Israel and regional states, reinforcing the path towards normalisation and the Abraham Accords.
Then came 7 October.
Israel soon made clear that it saw the war as part of a much broader regional project. It openly spoke of reshaping the Middle East and began pursuing geographic and demographic changes in the arenas where it was fighting, particularly Gaza and Lebanon. It has continued along the same path in both, while extending its military operations into Syria.
With firm US backing, Israel remains committed to that wider project. The war eventually led to direct confrontation with Iran, a conflict Israel still appears keen to revive, with preparations seemingly continuing in coordination with Washington.
Iran is no minor regional actor. It has built a project of its own and, for years, wielded considerable influence across the Middle East. Israel wants to dismantle that influence and replace it, particularly in Lebanon, while consolidating its position in Syria, pushing the Palestinian issue out of the regional equation, and forcing other states towards peace agreements and normalisation.
Washington has its own objectives. It wants to bring Iran to heel while opening the country to Western investment and economic influence, including in its oil sector. The broader aim is to loosen Tehran’s ties with China and pull it closer to the West. If that effort fails, Washington may once again turn to war.
But the conflict is about more than the Middle East. At stake is the wider balance of power that will emerge globally.
The United States wants to preserve a world in which it remains the dominant power, without a serious rival. To achieve that, Washington is willing to pressure allies and adversaries alike, and at times even exploit the pressure exerted by its rivals to keep its own partners in line.
Donald Trump’s approach to the Russia-Ukraine war offers one example. His strategy towards Europe is based on extracting concessions, reminding European states of their military and political dependence on Washington, and reinforcing the idea that they remain vulnerable without US support.
A similar logic is at work in the Gulf, where regional states are now confronting a major war in Yemen.
At the start of the latest fighting, Trump signalled that he was unwilling to enter the war directly on Saudi Arabia’s side. At the same time, contacts between Washington and the Houthis came to light. Rather than shutting down that channel, Trump appears content to keep it in play, allowing pressure on Riyadh to build while steering events towards the political outcome he wants.
None of this means the United States has abandoned Saudi Arabia. Security, military and intelligence coordination continues, and Secretary of State Marco Rubio has publicly insisted that Washington will stand by the kingdom.
But for Trump, support is never free. Every war, intervention or security guarantee comes with a political price. In this case, that price is to draw the Gulf states, much like Europe, more firmly into Washington’s confrontation with Iran.
Some now see the war in Yemen as preparation for another strike on Iran and for the formation of a new coalition built around that objective, just as the wars in Gaza and Lebanon preceded the direct confrontation with Tehran.
There is no consensus, however, on how the Yemen war will unfold.
Some expect a prolonged war of attrition that drains all sides. Others believe it could be decided far more quickly, pointing to changes in military tactics since Operation Decisive Storm, shifts in the regional balance of power, the emergence of the Mecca Alliance, and US support for Saudi Arabia against the Houthis at a time of continuing US-Iranian hostility and renewed fears of war.
What is clear is that this is no longer simply a war over Palestine. It has become a struggle over the regional order itself, with consequences for the balance of power both in the Middle East and beyond.
Israel sees the Yemen war as another opportunity to expand its influence. It has little interest in seeing large, powerful states emerge around it and will continue trying to weaken those it regards as potential rivals.
Netanyahu has hinted at this logic before. After Israel struck Iran and its regional allies, he spoke of turning next to what he described as an emerging “radical Sunni axis”. The author understood this as a reference to the growing alignment between Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Turkey.
The Yemen war gives Netanyahu an opening to offer Israel’s services to Riyadh, while trying to pull Saudi Arabia away from Turkey and Pakistan and towards an agreement under the Abraham Accords framework.
Trump is likely to push in the same direction, while also seeking to recalibrate relations between Turkey and Israel.
The war therefore presents a major test for the states of the region, particularly the members of the Mecca Alliance and, above all, Turkey and Saudi Arabia.
The interests of Ankara and Riyadh have already converged in Syria. There, both have faced serious challenges but have so far managed to avoid the worst outcomes, while helping preserve Syria’s territorial unity against Israeli efforts to fragment the country. That has also been aided by a degree of strategic overlap with the United States.
Yet the Israeli threat has not disappeared.
Israel has little interest in seeing Syria re-emerge as a unified, strong state with the ability to rebuild economically. Its incursions and attacks continue, as does the seizure of additional Syrian territory.
The latest war in Yemen has added another layer to this competition.
As the fighting began, the members of the Mecca Alliance quickly convened and announced the activation of its collective defence mechanisms. In practical terms, that means greater Turkish and Pakistani support for Saudi Arabia through military technology, weapons and intelligence, while also limiting the space for Israel to exploit the war or insert itself into the conflict.
Only hours after the meeting, Syrian President Ahmad al-Sharaa arrived in Riyadh for talks with Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, raising the prospect that Syria could also move closer to the Mecca Alliance.
Such a development would deepen security and military cooperation and help fortify other regional fronts, particularly if the Yemen war intensifies, if Iran and its allies retaliate elsewhere, or if Israel decides to expand its military operations in southern Syria.
Damascus is already preparing for such possibilities. It has reinforced its military presence along the borders with Iraq and Lebanon in anticipation of further escalation.
Israel, meanwhile, could look for other ways to increase pressure on the Mecca Alliance. That could mean further action against Syria, or moves elsewhere, including in Somaliland and the wider Horn of Africa.
Lebanon is also firmly in the eye of the storm.
The war there has not ended. Israel continues its military operations and territorial encroachments while maintaining intense political pressure.
Lebanon says it wants to be the last Arab state to sign a peace agreement with Israel. Israel, by contrast, wants to pull Beirut into such an agreement far sooner.
Its strategy is to isolate Lebanon through political, military and economic pressure, force it to the negotiating table, and prevent it from remaining part of a broader Arab bargaining position.
If Israel succeeds in drawing Lebanon into this framework, the consequences would extend beyond Beirut. It would increase pressure on Arab states more broadly, place Syria under even greater strain, and help constrain Turkey’s position in the Mediterranean.
The war, then, did not truly begin on 7 October, and it will not end any time soon.
When it does, the regional order that emerges will bear little resemblance to the one that existed before it.
Mounir al-Rabih is editor in chief of Beirut-based Al-Modon

Dalia Kayed survived the genocide. She now tells her story through photos and embroidery.
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
10:46:40 UTC
19:46:40 KST

For Dalia Hammad Kayed, the morning of October 7, 2023 began like any other. She woke before dawn to pray at her family home in Gaza.
“When I finished (praying), we started hearing the sound of rockets everywhere. It was a shock for everyone,” the Palestinian photographer and embroiderer tells TRT Espanol.
Three years later, that morning still shapes her life. Dalia was 21 at the time, studying digital media and living in Gaza with her father, Palestinian journalist Kayed Hammad, her mother and three brothers.
She could not have imagined that the next 500 days would be marked by genocide, displacement and loss, including the death of her 24-year-old brother Omar Hammad, who was killed by Israel.
Nor could she have imagined that she would eventually have to begin an entirely different life, far from Gaza, in Spain.
On October 7, after hearing the explosions, the Palestinian family turned on the news to follow the events.
“Shortly after, we began to hear that the Palestinian resistance had entered the occupied territories,” she recalls.
“For a few moments, I felt we were going to liberate Palestine and would soon return to the land taken from us,” she says.
But that was not what followed.
The day marked the beginning of one of the darkest periods in humanity, with Israeli attacks, siege and the deprivation of basic necessities.
From the 12th floor of the building where the family lived, they could see what Dalia describes as “the whole” enclave, with “bombings here and there, and people being killed every minute” by Israeli attacks.
Displacement, forced starvation
At first, Dalia thought it would be like “previous wars”, lasting only a few weeks.
Then they received an order to evacuate their area. The family spent three days at her aunt’s house before receiving another order and having to move again.
The pattern repeated itself, taking them from one evacuation to another and from one relative’s home to another, in what Dalia describes as “one of the most difficult experiences of my life”.
To prepare for emergencies, they kept small backpacks by the door containing water, flashlights and food.
“If there was an emergency, everyone would grab their backpack and leave,” she recalls.
“Many times we left our personal belongings behind because we knew we would have to walk long distances and couldn’t carry everything on our backs.”
For Dalia, who was raised in a family with strong cultural roots, displacement also meant losing the routines of everyday life—school, university, work—and her favourite foods, including qidra, a spiced rice dish with meat and whole garlic cloves, slowly cooked in a clay pot.
As the siege tightened, access to food became increasingly difficult, while Israeli forces separated northern Gaza, where the family lived, from the south.
The Kayed family refused to flee, even as what Dalia describes as “a severe famine” took hold.
“I’ll never forget that we ate rice for almost three months. Rice, water, and a little bit of spice, just to give it some flavour,” she recalls of the food they had stored.
“We ate it simply to stay alive, and we thanked God for having it,” she adds, acknowledging that her family was among the more fortunate because they had something to eat at night, which also helped them fall asleep.
Alongside the hunger came the loss of loved ones, including her brother Omar.
In May 2024, Omar went to collect medicine for a friend receiving treatment at Al-Awda Hospital in northern Gaza. When he reached the entrance of the hospital, the area was bombed. He and several others were killed.
Dalia says the friend he had gone to help later died as well because of the shortage of medicines.
Safeguarding memory
Amid the grief, Dalia returned to something that allowed her to preserve memories: photography.
She began with “family photos” and then started photographing “everyone and all the circumstances we were experiencing”.
During this period, Spanish journalist Mikel Ayestaran, a friend of her father, remained in contact with the family and regularly checked whether they had been able to find food.
“We kept telling him that everything was fine and not to worry, but he wanted us to prove it to him with a photo of our meal of the day. My father asked me to photograph the plate every day and send it to Mikel,” Dalia recounts.
Ayestaran asked for permission to post the photographs on Instagram, and the family agreed. Each image was accompanied by a short account of what they were experiencing.
The response came quickly. People in Spain began asking about the family and offering help. Little by little, Dalia began to understand the value of those photographs.
“That photo, accompanied by a few words, showed the world what our people were experiencing and carried our voice and our news through the image of a plate,” she says.
From those photographs came another idea. Ayestaran proposed preserving the story of the meals in a physical book.
The idea developed into a collaboration involving Ayestaran, Dalia’s family and Spanish magazine 5W, eventually becoming the “Gaza Menu” project.
“The book brings together photographs, recipes, and our family’s memories during the war. It also shows another side of our life in Gaza: not just the hunger, but also our family life and our attachment to life,” she says.
In 2025, a crowdfunding campaign raised 119,830 euros from 2,553 contributions, far exceeding its 35,000-euro target and allowing more copies of the book to be printed and distributed than originally planned.
Embroidering among the bombs
Photography was not the only way Dalia found to cope with what was happening around her. She also returned to another practice she had learned as a child: embroidery.
When she was young, an aunt living in Libya visited Gaza, and Dalia learned to work with a needle and thread alongside one of her cousins. She still remembers making a small coin purse embroidered with a rose.
Years later, amid the hardships of life under siege in Gaza, she found a needle and thread and returned to that childhood passion.
“Every time I started embroidering, I forgot about what was happening around me and could concentrate solely on the embroidery. I began to dedicate most of my time to it. It helped distract me from the bombings and the death that surrounded us, and reduced the psychological pressure,” she recalls.
“I felt happy every time I finished an embroidered piece and could wear it or give it to someone in my family.”
Despite everything they had endured, the family had never seriously considered leaving Gaza.
That changed when Ayestaran suggested that Dalia’s father and several well-known journalists sign a petition to the Spanish Ministry of Foreign Affairs requesting their evacuation from Gaza.
Dalia says the family did not expect a “concrete result”. Then they received “a call informing us that our names had been accepted and that we would soon be leaving Gaza for Spain”.
The news meant leaving behind the place where she had spent her entire life, from childhood into adulthood. For Dalia, “it was much harder than I could have imagined”.
Seeing the destruction of her homeland as she left made the departure even more painful.
“The roads had practically disappeared and there was rubble everywhere. It took us a very long time because the bus was completely controlled by the Israeli forces: they decided when it could move forward, when it had to stop, and when it was not allowed to continue,” she recounts.
But the most painful part was saying goodbye to those who remained in Gaza.
For Dalia, the uprooting and the farewells were “the most difficult moment” and a weight she does not believe will ever go.
“We left our families and loved ones behind. We carried with us a deep sense of guilt and regret, as if we were doing something wrong to survive. We left them in the midst of death and hell while we managed to get out. We left parts of ourselves behind and kept going because we had no other choice,” she says.
A new life in Spain
Dalia arrived in Spain with her family on June 28, 2025. Their first stop was an uncle's home in a small town in Málaga, southern Spain.
But her thoughts remained with the relatives they had left behind in Gaza.
“I felt guilty because I had survived while they were still there, and I was constantly afraid of receiving devastating news about them,” she says.
“It was also a shock to go from months of fleeing death to suddenly being in a normal, safe place. I had to face a new language and culture, and at the same time, I felt like I was starting all over again.”
As Dalia adjusted to her new life, “Gaza Menu” began opening new doors for her.
In 2025, the project won the Ortega y Gasset Journalism Award for Best Multimedia Coverage, featuring photographs of Dalia’s family and their daily life in Gaza. It also received the Zampa Photojournalism Award.
Dalia began taking part in events where she could tell Gaza's story herself. On February 19, 2026, she presented the book at the Finestres bookstore in Barcelona alongside her father, Ayestaran and photographer Anna Surinyach.
“I never imagined that one day I would be standing in front of such a large audience, presenting our book and speaking to people face to face, after our stories had been confined to phone screens during the war,” she says.
“I felt nervous, but I also felt a great responsibility: to be the voice of my family and the people of Gaza.”
The experience also allowed her to witness what she describes as “the enormous solidarity” in Spain towards the Palestinian people.
“That made me feel that we were not alone,” she says.
Dalia has also intensified her Spanish studies, helping her communicate her work to new audiences.
In her workshops, including one with the Ferrer Foundation in Barcelona, she explains the origins and history of Palestinian embroidery.
Art as resistance
“This traditional art is not simply a hobby or just any craft. It is an essential part of Palestinian identity and an inherited history that has faced attempts to erase, silence, and appropriate it. Through these threads, I seek to preserve our heritage.”
Dalia´s embroidery incorporates symbols including Palestinian birds, olive trees and wildflowers, each carrying its own meaning.
“Some represent the richness and beauty of our land and its nature, while others express meanings of resilience, firmness, and resistance. Still others document details of the lives of our ancestors and the tools they used in their daily lives.”
Today, from Segovia, Spain, Dalia continues that mission: sharing the richness of Palestinian culture and preserving part of its history through embroidery.
“I don’t just teach a craft,” she says. “With this art, I’m placing in their hands a living document that speaks of our history and tells the world that we are a people with deep roots. A civilization that continues to live on and cannot be erased.”
This article was first published on TRT Espanol.

The Week of Italian Cuisine in the World, the annual event organized in Portugal by the Italian Embassy, is now in its 11th edition. The 2026 edition aims to highlight the historic recognition of Italian cuisine as a UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity and has as its theme: “Italian Cuisine, a UNESCO Heritage: Regions and Chains of Excellence.” The event runs from October 17 to 25, but will kick off on the 15th with the opening of Expo Italia at the Oeiras Municipal Market, which will host the finest “Made in Italy” products through October 18, featuring culinary experiences and networking opportunities for Italian and Portuguese professionals. This initiative is organized by the Italian Chamber of Commerce for Portugal, in collaboration with the Embassy and the Municipality of Oeiras.
                                    
On the 19th, the Embassy will host renowned food historian Massimo Montanari for a discussion with journalist Rita Caetano focused on the themes of “Tutti a tavola. Perché la cucina italiana è un patrimonio dell’umanità” (Everyone to the Table: Why Italian Cuisine Is a World Heritage), Montanari’s recent book.
                                    
Pasta will take center stage at the October 21 seminar “From Grains to Table,” conceived and organized in collaboration with Alessandra Lauria’s Pasta Week, an event that partners with various organizations, including Slow Food Portugal. The seminar will bring together Italian and Portuguese speakers at the Embassy to discuss the themes of biodiversity and sustainability.
                                    
As is the case every year, the presence of a Michelin-starred chef brings Italian haute cuisine to Lisbon: this year’s guest is Michelin-starred chef Andrea Berton, who on the 22nd will host a gala dinner titled “An Italian Story” in the halls of Palazzo Pombeiro, organized in partnership with the luxury brand Eleventy.
                                    
There will also be opportunities to support social causes, such as the charity dinner taking place on October 23 in Cascais, organized by the City of Cascais and the Cascais Food Lab. The cost to attend is 20 euros, and all proceeds will be donated to the Portuguese League Against Cancer.
                                    
Finally, the event “Il Gusto nell’Arte,” promoted by COMITES Portugal, will enliven the day on October 24 with a workshop for children at The Therapist LAB, and the GIARDINIERA workshop, dedicated to making Italian-style pickles, accompanied by an aperitif featuring a tasting of artisanal fermented beverages.

‘Digger’ is a Box Office Flop. It Might Be the Most Relevant Film of the Year
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
10:45:00 UTC
19:45:00 KST

The trailer for Alejandro González Iñárritu’s Digger promised an over-the top, prosthetic-laden Tom Cruise comedy—a caricature of an oil baron who has to save the world from his own actions. But despite an underwhelming opening at the box office, this sprawling, grotesque satire may be the most relevant film of the year.
Given the way the plot layers, key moments being recontextualized as the story progresses, this movie is difficult to market—or to review—spoiler-free. The broad strokes are that Digger is an oil tycoon whose drilling broke off an iceberg and sent it toward Europe, threatening to kill 100,000 people and displace more than a million. He’s a man who takes painstaking care of his sick cat while watching footage of the wildlife dying as a direct result of his actions. A man purely interested in profit, working alongside the US president, played by John Goodman, to save the world.
There are moments that are directly lifted from real life. It is an obvious, purposely heavy-handed satirization of Bush-era politics as well as the modern US political climate. Before getting into spoiler territory, the movie is also visually striking and ambitious with surreal set designs delivering pointed messages about the world the characters live in, with incredible performances from a star-studded cast.
If you want to go into the movie without any spoilers—and I really think you should—stop here and come back once you’ve watched it.
You expect to see a movie about a wealthy man grappling with a problem he created in the world, but Tom Cruise isn’t actually playing Digger Rockwell. He is playing Curtis Markson, an actor portraying Digger in a satirical play about the events that caused the climate crisis of this world. The play is directed by Hannah (played by Sophie Wilde) and funded by Kenny Rockwell, Digger’s nephew (played by Jesse Plemons).
This context comes in bits and pieces over the course of the movie, and each reveal shines a new light on the film—Goodman’s vulgar, larger-than-life president makes lowbrow jokes for laughs, his team members have minimal reactions to the potential death toll of the climate disaster and overreact when the financial cost is declared. When Europe is struck, the president and his team are eating popcorn and shouting at the screen, telling the victims—of a catastrophe that they created—to run, as though watching a slasher film. It is horrifyingly cartoonish.
The whole movie is a striking caricature, not just of politics but of making art today. The play only happens because Kenny decides to fund it, and while the play has elaborate sets, ample staff, and high-tech production, the theater has intermittent air-conditioning. The audience and director sweat inside while mold grows in the green room, and the world falls apart around this decadent spectacle.
In the context of a play written for the catharsis of the masses, it reveals a wider tension that runs throughout the movie—and which it argues about out loud. Cruise, playing Markson, hates the caricature of Digger, complaining to the director that he was a terrifying, intimidating, “seductive psychopath,” not a buffoonish cowboy. Hannah says it’s what the people need—a didactic, sensationalized, cathartic play with villains to laugh at.
Kenny also isn’t putting on the play as an act of remorse. Instead, it’s a deflection, placating the audience by giving them a villain in the past so they can accept the present, while he profits off of the catastrophe the play satirizes. When Curtis’ daughter, Hope, disappears after boarding a plane to come to the opening night, Kenny is able to locate her using only her phone number. He runs a security company—read as likely in the business of surveillance.
His decision to fund a play exaggerates the current tech and cultural climate. The tech moguls of today are increasingly seeking cultural clout, and culture is now largely dispersed through technology: Jeff Bezos owns Prime Video; Apple has Apple TV. This can be extended to how social media platforms—and the algorithms that govern them—are cultural gatekeepers of sorts.
As the movie nears its end, we see the conclusion of the play, where Digger dies, met with applause, tears of joy, and cheers from the crowd. Catharsis. The audience then puts on their breathing masks, filing out into a flooded, dystopian city. The catharsis, the spectacle, even Cruise’s agonizing over the portrayal of his character, are all meaningless out here.
Just like the audience of the play, I laughed throughout the movie. I laughed at lines that were clearly pulled from real events, at the gaudy recreation of people more than happy to convert breathable air into dollars and cents and their familiar deflections and excuses. When the lights came up and the credits rolled, I too left the theater and returned to a world where surveillance companies track us, where militaries remotely wage war with AI, and where the climate slips closer to further disaster.
This story originally appeared in WIRED Middle East.

With the aim of building bridges for Italian business in Astana, Italian Ambassador Antonello De Riu met with Ainur Amirbekova, Deputy Director General of QazTrade. Man appears in UK court accused of trying to break into Reform leader Farage's home
LONDON, Oct 7 - A man accused of murdering former British minister Ann Widdecombe appeared in court on Wednesday charged with a terrorism offence which includes trying to break into the home of Nigel Farage, the leader of the Reform UK party.
Joshua Kerry, 28, is charged with engaging in conduct in preparation of terrorist acts between May 2024 and July this year, and is accused of carrying out research on prominent people and institutions, and of travelling to, and attempting to gain entry to Farage's house.
Kerry, from Rotherham in northern England, appeared at London's Westminster Magistrates' Court where he spoke only to confirm his name and age. He was remanded in custody and will appear at London's Old Bailey court on Friday.
Prosecutor Kashif Malik told the court that in April 2025, Farage's partner had returned to their home to find the front door had been damaged and part of the wooden frame was hanging off. There was also a bottle of lighter fluid in the porch.
"The inference being that an attempt was made to gain entry to the house," Malik said.
Kerry has already been charged with murdering Widdecombe, 78, a prominent figure in Reform UK, who was found dead at her home in rural southwest England on July 9 after being attacked the day before.
He is yet to enter a plea to any of the charges he faces.
Prosecutors say Widdecombe was struck 21 times with a hammer, shocking British politics and raising further concerns about politicians' security, coming after the killing of two serving British members of parliament since 2016.
Farage, 62, often credited with forcing the 2016 referendum on whether Britain should stay in the European Union, has been one of the most influential, but also one of the most divisive, figures in British politics for more than a decade.
When campaigning for parliament in 2024, Farage had a milkshake thrown at him by a woman and on another occasion objects were hurled towards his open-top bus by a man.
Reform UK, which has a policy of deporting all immigrants who have come to Britain illegally, was leading in the polls until recently, though a combination of allegations over party funding and Andy Burnham taking over as Labour prime minister has seen a weakening in its support. French and Japanese scientists win 2026 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for what could change how medicines are made
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
10:44:08 UTC
19:44:08 KST

Two researchers have won this year's Nobel Prize in Chemistry for work that could change how medicines are made.
Henri B. Kagan and Kenso Soai have won the Nobel Prize in Chemistry for research into molecules' mirror images, “decisive for chemists who design reactions for the manufacture of pharmaceuticals", the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences in Stockholm said on Wednesday.
The French and Japanese researchers were awarded for the discovery ofnon-linear effects and autocatalysis in asymmetric organic synthesis. Many molecules, such as amino acids, have two mirror versions of themselves, but only one version of them is found in living organisms; this is known as chemical asymmetry.
This asymmetry creates challenges when developing new pharmaceuticals. Many of the drug molecules occur in two variants that are each other’s non-identical mirror image; one has the therapeutic effect, while the other can cause unnecessary and sometimes harmful side effects, the Committee explained.
"Henri Kagan and Kenso Soai have provided a solution to a chemical mystery that is over a century old: how homochirality can emerge spontaneously," said Heiner Linke, chair of the Nobel Committee for Chemistry, in a press release. "The chemical reactions they have developed are spectacular."
Kagan is affiliated with Université Paris-Sud in Orsay, France, and Soai with the Tokyo University of Science.
“I'm very excited to receive the very nice news about the Nobel Prize,” said Soai after the announcement.
“This is one of the most exciting days in my life. I'm really glad to share the prize with Professor Henri Kagan, such a famous organic chemist,” he added.
The prize this year is 12 million Swedish kronor (about €1.09 million), whether for an individual, a small group of laureates, or an organisation.
The remaining 2026 Nobel Prizes, in literature, peace and economics, will be announced in the coming days. The awards for medicine and physics were announced earlier this week.
Following the announcement of Friday’s peace prize, the Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences will be announced on 12 October.
The award ceremony will be held on 10 December, the anniversary of the death in 1896 of Alfred Nobel, the Swedish industrialist and inventor of dynamite who founded the prizes. He died in 1896.
Previous Nobel Prizes in Chemistry
From 1901 to 2025, 117 Nobel Prizes were awarded in chemistry. Eight of the 198 chemistry winners have been women, including Marie Curie in 1911.
Last year’s chemistry award was shared among Susumu Kitagawa from Kyoto University in Japan, Richard Robson from the University of Melbourne in Australia, and Omar M. Yaghi from the University of California, Berkeley, in the United States.
They were awarded for creating a new molecular structure used to extract carbon dioxide from the air and separate pollutants from water.

EU ambassadors clear path for Ukraine to open two new accession clusters
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
10:44:05 UTC
19:44:05 KST

BRUSSELS, Belgium — EU ambassadors on Oct. 7 took the next step in advancing Ukraine and Moldova's push for membership, paving the way for the opening of two so-called enlargement clusters next week.
Candidate countries for EU membership have to align with the bloc by completing reforms, split into six so-called clusters.
Ambassadors agreed on Oct. 7 to take the next step on the two largest clusters, internal market and competitiveness, which address broad parts of the economy.
The decision also applied to Moldova because the EU politically linked the two countries' accession efforts.
In practice, that means Chisinau has had to wait as Hungary stalled Ukraine's EU bid until the country strengthens the rights of its Hungarian-speaking minority.
Budapest and Kyiv reached a political deal on minority rights in early summer, which led to the opening of the first two clusters in June and July, on the rule of law and external relations, respectively.
But progress stalled again as Hungary demanded that Ukraine adopt a law implementing changes to education for national minorities as outlined in the summer agreement.
The bill was submitted to the parliament on Oct. 2, which was enough to allow EU ambassadors to proceed, but between then and now, much remains to be done.
Ukraine first needs to submit a written negotiating position to the EU, which is understood to be already ready.
Then an EU working group of technical experts from the 27 countries needs to agree on the bloc's common position, which must, in turn, be adopted by ambassadors and ministers from the 27 EU countries.
And if Ukraine's parliament fails to pass the minorities law on Oct. 12, then the formal meeting to open the clusters the day after will not be allowed to take place.
But assuming all goes as planned, the EU should open the next two negotiation clusters with Ukraine and Moldova at the Intergovernmental Conference in Luxembourg on Oct. 13.
The amount of bureaucracy involved has prompted the European Commission to propose paring back some of that paperwork.
"Based on the treaties, we need two unanimity decisions, giving candidate status, and finishing," said the EU's Enlargement Commissioner Marta Kos in a discussion with European Parliament members on Oct. 7.
"But now, in between, we have 150 steps also for sending a letter to a candidate country," the commissioner fumed.
Assuming all goes as planned, opening the two clusters could help Ukraine benefit from the European Commission's new "gradual integration" idea pitched on Oct. 6.
This would mean that as Ukraine completes reforms, it should already begin to enjoy some EU benefits, and a senior EU official told the Kyiv Independent that progress on the internal market cluster is critical because it addresses "economic security and critical infrastructure."

EU enlargement commissioner calls for stronger rule-of-law safeguards for member states
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
10:43:57 UTC
19:43:57 KST

Melike Pala
07 October 2026•Update: 07 October 2026
The EU should strengthen its safeguards for upholding the rule of law not only in future member states but also within the bloc's existing membership, European Commissioner for Enlargement Marta Kos said Wednesday.
Speaking at the European Parliament in Strasbourg, France, during an exchange of views on the pre-enlargement policy reviews, Kos said the EU should examine how to make its existing mechanisms, including Article 7 of the EU treaties, more effective.
"When it is about the rule of law. ... We should also do something among the member states, so we suggest that we sit down with the member states and also go through Article 7, how to make its use, how to make it more efficient," Kos added.
Article 7 allows the EU to respond to a serious risk of, or a serious and persistent breach of, the bloc's fundamental values, including the rule of law.
Kos said the commission is proposing a common framework of safeguards for future accession treaties.
The framework would build on existing sectoral safeguards while introducing additional measures that could be used if new members seriously breach EU values, including democracy and the rule of law.
In the most serious cases, measures could include suspension of voting rights, with the proposed measures operating during a transitional period of up to 15 years.
She added that rule-of-law monitoring will begin before accession and continue after a country joins the EU, with new member states covered by the bloc's full rule-of-law toolbox.
Kos also rejected the idea that the EU's enlargement drive is based solely on geopolitical considerations.
"Geopolitics means why enlargement is important and why this is priority. Merit-based means conditions under one country can join and when," she said.
The broader package proposes enhanced gradual integration for candidate countries, allowing them to participate more closely in selected EU policies before full membership, while requiring continued progress toward accession.
Kos stressed that gradual integration is not a substitute for EU membership.
"Only those candidates who are serious about becoming a member of the EU will be able to get part of this enhanced gradual integration," she said.

"There are a whole number of networks, including <...> Telegram, whose founder, unfortunately, has taken an anti-Russian position. VEPR UGV to Receive Saber Combat Modules from ROBONEERS
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
10:43:34 UTC
19:43:34 KST

Ukrainian companies Partner-VS and ROBONEERS have signed a memorandum of cooperation to integrate five variants of the Saber remote weapon stations onto the VEPR unmanned ground vehicle.
ROBONEERS told Militarnyi about the joint development.
The partnership aims to create a mobile combat platform for military units that can be adapted to specific front-line missions.
The modules under consideration for integration are the Saber 7.62 for the PKT machine gun, Saber M240 for the M240 machine gun, Saber K-2 with two AK-74 assault rifles, Saber M2 for the M2 Browning machine gun, and Saber Mk.19(M) for the Mk.19 automatic grenade launcher.
ROBONEERS’ flagship Saber turret module has been actively used in combat since 2023.
Depending on the version, the weapon stations offer an effective firing range of 300 meters to 2.4 km and can operate autonomously in surveillance mode for up to 120 hours.
Operators can control the turrets remotely from up to 100 meters or via Wi-Fi using a control unit, and the system includes surveillance, targeting, and thermal imaging cameras.
ROBONEERS’ proprietary software provides the operator with a ballistic calculator, coordinate-based firing, target memorization, and digital zoom.
The VEPR unmanned ground vehicle, developed by Partner-VS, has been used on the front line since 2024 for logistics, remote mine clearance, and casualty evacuation.
The platform weighs around 400 kg, can carry up to 250 kg of cargo, reach speeds of over 12 km/h, and has a range of more than 50 km.
The UGV is equipped with two 1,500 W electric motors and six communication types, including LTE and Starlink.
Earlier, German company ARX Robotics and Ukrainian company ROBONEERS entered into a strategic partnership to jointly develop and integrate unmanned ground systems.

WHO chief urges transparency amid Russia plague reports
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
10:42:59 UTC
19:42:59 KST

A razor wire sits on a fence of the anti-plague institute in the city of Irkutsk on October 7, 2026. (AFP Photo)
The World Health Organization (WHO) said on Oct. 7 that it wanted more information from Russia on the death of a plague laboratory technician, and on reports of “a second employee with pneumonia of undetermined cause.”
The WHO’s chief Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus said full transparency was needed in order to make a proper assessment of the public health risk.
He reiterated that the WHO stood ready to help Moscow with technical support, if asked.
“WHO has been actively following up on the reported death of a laboratory worker at the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Research Institute,” he said on X.
“The individual died on Oct. 2 after being hospitalized with severe pneumonia. Initial media reports suggested pneumonic plague following an alleged accidental laboratory exposure.”
On Oct. 3 the WHO contacted the Russian authorities to get more information, under the International Health Regulations (IHR).
The IHR provide a legally binding framework defining countries’ rights and obligations in handling public health events and emergencies that could cross borders, and countries are asked to respond within 24 hours.
Russia got back to the WHO on Oct. 6.
“WHO has requested further information to clarify the cause of the severe pneumonia, the pathogen that prompted the public health measures, and media reports of a second employee with pneumonia of undetermined cause,” said Tedros.
“Timely, complete and transparent information sharing under the International Health Regulations is essential to clarify conflicting reports and enable an accurate assessment of potential public health risks.”
The WHO’s initial risk assessment from the information available estimates the risk to be moderate to low for the Irkutsk region; low for Russia as a whole; and very low for Europe.

We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.

After FrankenSAM, Ukraine Mashes Kub and Buk Together—and Scores About 20 Air Kills
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
10:42:31 UTC
19:42:31 KST

- Category
- Defense Tech
After FrankenSAM, Ukraine Mashes Kub and Buk Together—and Scores About 20 Air Kills
Ukraine has combined components of the Soviet-era Kub and Buk air defense systems into an unconventional battlefield pairing that has already destroyed roughly 20 aerial targets, most of them Russian jet-powered Shahed-type drones.
Ukraine’s 156th Anti-Aircraft Missile Regiment released footage of the hybrid configuration in combat on October 5, showing a Kub launcher operating together with a Buk self-propelled fire unit.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Ukrainian defense outlet Militarnyi noted that the unusual combination is possible because the two systems share related technical architecture dating back to the Soviet transition from Kub to Buk air defenses.
The setup helps compensate for one of the Kub system’s biggest limitations. A standard Kub launcher does not have its own autonomous target-illumination and guidance radar, while the Buk self-propelled fire unit carries an integrated radar capable of detecting, tracking, and continuously illuminating airborne targets.
At the same time, Ukraine can use remaining Kub-compatible missiles without consuming scarce Buk interceptors.
In practice, the Buk unit either detects the target itself or receives targeting information from another source, locks onto it, and maintains continuous radar illumination.
It then sends the launch command to the Kub 2P25 launcher carrying 3M9 missiles. After launch, the missile flies toward the target and its seeker homes on the radar energy reflected from the aircraft or drone being illuminated by the Buk.
“This combination has performed very well in destroying aerial targets. The Kub-Buk pairing alone has accounted for around 20 aerial targets,” Ukrainian troops said.
Most of those kills, according to the regiment, were Russian jet-powered Shahed-type drones, which are significantly faster than the original propeller-driven variants and present a growing challenge for Ukraine’s air defenses.
Although the configuration looks improvised, the underlying compatibility is not entirely accidental. Soviet engineers anticipated some degree of interoperability during the transition from the Kub to Buk systems in the 1970s and 1980s.
The 9A38 self-propelled fire unit developed for the Kub-M4 could be adapted to carry either three 9M38 Buk missiles or three 3M9M3 Kub missiles. The system shown by the Ukrainian regiment, however, uses a separate Kub launcher working together with a Buk fire-control vehicle rather than mounting both missile types on the same platform.
Ukraine has pursued a similar philosophy with its better-known FrankenSAM program, adapting Buk launchers and fire-control systems to use US-made RIM-7 missiles as Soviet missile stocks become increasingly difficult to replenish. The 156th Regiment also operates that configuration.
One Ukrainian crew commander said individual FrankenSAM vehicles have already accumulated dozens of confirmed aerial kills, while one launcher has fired RIM-7 missiles 131 times.
“We operate a modification of the Buk air defense system that is popularly called ‘Frankenstein’ and is equipped to fire RIM-7 anti-aircraft missiles. It has already proven effective in one sector. There are many destroyed targets—34. Some other vehicles have more, some have fewer,” the commander said.
Previously, reports emerged that Ukraine’s hybrid FrankenSAM air defense systems—combining Soviet-era BUK launchers with US-supplied RIM-7 or AIM-7 missiles—have already destroyed 105 Russian aerial targets.

Heavy casualties in Ukraine after Russian strikes
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
10:42:18 UTC
19:42:18 KST

A handout picture taken and released by Ukraine's National Police on Oct. 7, 2026 shows a bomb disposal expert neutralising an unexploded Russian missile near residential buildings in Kiev following a mass missile attack on the Ukrainian capital, amid the Russian invasion of Ukraine. (Photo by Handout / Ukraine's National Police / AFP)
At least 15 people were killed in Russian strikes across Ukraine on Oct. 7, the authorities said, including nine when a missile destroyed an apartment block in the north of the country.
Emergency services picked through the rubble of the destroyed five-story building in Pryluky, in the Chernigiv region, in a frantic search for survivors.
Police said that by late morning, the death toll had risen to nine. “Unfortunately, the bodies of three children were recovered,” they wrote on Telegram.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky had warned the public on Oct. 6 night that Russia was planning “massive” strikes, particularly against the country’s energy infrastructure.
“The Russians wanted to strike painfully and demonstratively,” he said on Wednesday, calling it “one of the most vile strikes” in the nearly five-year conflict.
Two people were killed when missiles slammed into high-rise buildings in Dnipro and Kremenchuk in central Ukraine, while two others lost their lives in Oleksandriya, he added.
In the capital, Kiev, strikes killed two people.
Kiev has come under increased attack in recent weeks as winter approaches, with air raid sirens wailing nearly constantly to warn of incoming Russian strikes.
Residents hunkered down in subway stations overnight, hauling duffel bags, sleeping mats and blankets, after air alerts sounded warning of attacks.
“We grabbed our things and came here, we live right next door,” Iryna Rybalchenko, who works in a bank, told AFP, sitting on the platform wrapped in a dark hoodie and surrounded by bags.
“The whole of Kiev is in a state of fear. We were stuck at work today and everyone, our group chats, our bosses, were messaging us to be careful.”
Russia launched at least 50 missiles and 130 drones overnight against several regions including Dnipropetrovsk, Kiev, Kharkiv, and Poltava, Ukraine’s air force said.
Zelensky said that although some were shot down, ballistic missiles were “the greatest challenge”, and new air defenses were “a vital necessity” to help Ukraine defend itself.
The two victims in Kiev died in a fire in the densely populated Darnytskyi neighborhood as a result of on Oct. 7’s attack, the city’s mayor Vitaly Klitschko said.
He had warned last week the capital should now be on a war footing as the enemy was “tearing Kiev apart” with strikes on bridges and energy infrastructure.
The renewed attacks had triggered scheduled power cuts on Oct. 6, which plunged parts of Kiev into darkness to ease the pressure on the battered grid.
A familiar rumbling sound of the generators, used to get through power cuts, filled the streets again, bringing back memories of the previous winter, when systematic Russian attacks regularly cut power and heating.
The air force said on Oct. 7 that it intercepted five ballistic missiles, as well as 39 cruise missiles and over 100 drones.
Ukraine has been struggling to down the new and fast-moving jet-powered drones, as well as the ballistic missiles that are harder to intercept.

Details
Do not touch any military debris it may be dangerous. Please note the location and inform a Training Safety Officer (TSO) or police.
Warning signals: red flags by day and red lamps by night, indicate that live firing is taking place within the range boundaries, which are marked by red and white poles. When warning signals are displayed do not cross the range boundary.
Learn more about accessing MOD training areas safely.

Unemployment Insurance Fund: Prejudice standing in the way of hiring the elderly
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
10:41:00 UTC
19:41:00 KST

Unemployment Insurance Fund: Prejudice standing in the way of hiring the elderly
Although older people want equal treatment in the labor market and employers see them as having an important role in the workforce, prejudices on both sides can pose an obstacle to hiring.
According to Statistics Estonia, there were more than 8,300 job vacancies in Estonia in the second quarter of this year. The largest number of vacancies were in education, public administration and retail.
Ain Käpp, head of the labor market working group at the Estonian Employers' Confederation, said that as a small country, Estonia cannot afford to have people who are able to work remain outside the labor market. Golden League (Kuldne Liiga), an advocacy organization for older people, aims to create an age-friendly society in which the equal treatment of older people in the labor market also plays an important role.
"It also depends on whether employers are interested in hiring older people because not everyone is able to work eight hours a day and some need workplace accommodations," said Agu Laius, head of advocacy at Golden League. "The state should consider how to make greater use of our older population because our working-age population will decline significantly over the coming decades," he added.
Both Laius and Käpp said amendments to the Employment Contracts Act that took effect this year and allow flexible working hours represent a major step forward.
"We need to offer greater flexibility — whether people do not want to work full time because of their health, need to look after their grandchildren from time to time or want to work small amounts at several different jobs," Käpp said.
"Today, the law allows all of this and we as companies need to give it more thought ourselves because these people's experience is extremely valuable. A team made up of people of different ages is very strong and capable," Käpp added.
In July, the Unemployment Insurance Fund began paying wage subsidies to employers for hiring people aged 55 and older who have been out of working life for an extended period. Ulla Saar, a member of the Unemployment Insurance Fund's management board, said more people in this age group have found jobs compared with last year. Saar added that prejudice often affects both job searches and recruitment.
"In my view, short-term work gigs, trial work or job shadowing, for example, are very good measures," Saar said.
"I've visited various employers while touring the counties and quite a few have been willing to admit that they had prejudices about hiring people aged 55, 60 or even 65 and older. They tried trial work, hiring someone for a couple of days and every employer I spoke with was pleasantly surprised. They learned that age is just a number and that the person was perfectly capable of doing the job," Saar said.
Pirjo Turk, head of the equality policies department at the Ministry of Economic Affairs and Communications, said the state has introduced distinctions in legislation, but discussions are continuing and the issue remains on the agenda.
"There are many different parties involved and we need to make sure the burden does not fall too heavily on one side or the other. As a result, changes are not always easy and take time," Turk said.
--
Editor: Marcus Turovski, Mari Peegel

Kosovo rushes war crimes court change to avoid snap poll
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
10:40:51 UTC
19:40:51 KST

Kosovo's newly elected President Justina Shiroka Pula receives a bouquet of flowers during an extraordinary parliament session in Pristina on October 7, 2026. (Photo by Armend NIMANI / AFP)
Kosovo parliament voted to curb the powers of its special war crimes court in a last-minute session that narrowly avoided another governmental collapse in the early hours of Oct. 7.
The amendment, which was tightly negotiated ahead of a looming deadline to elect the country’s president at midnight, came after the Kosovo Specialist Chambers (KSC) found four senior guerrilla figures guilty of war crimes last month.
The conviction of the men, which included former President Hashim Thaci, sparked outrage in a country where the former Kosovo Liberation Army (KLA) figures are largely viewed as heroes.
Protests broke out after Thaci was sentenced to 25 years for crimes committed during the struggle for independence from Serbia in the 1990s.
The amendment was passed minutes before parliament’s deadline to elect its president, a trigger that had threatened to send voters back to the polls for a fourth time in less than two years.
In a deal with the opposition, Prime Minister Albin Kurti’s government secured the two-thirds majority needed to elect Justina Shiroka Pula as president, ending a long-running political crisis.
Opposition parties and war veteran organizations have long criticized the KSC, which is established under Kosovo law but based in The Hague.
According to the original text of the amendment, the court, which was specifically set up to prosecute crimes committed by ethnic Albanian guerrilla fighters during the war, will have its powers dramatically shrunk, with its jurisdiction would be limited to crimes committed inside Kosovo in the immediate aftermath of the war.

Gaza has no MRI machine, only one or two CT scanners, MAP warns
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
10:40:07 UTC
19:40:07 KST

Breadcrumb
Gaza has no MRI machine, only one or two CT scanners, MAP warns
War-torn Gaza has no functioning MRI machine and only one or two operational CT scanners for a population of more than two million, a year after the fragile October 2025 ceasefire was implemented, Medical Aid for Palestinians (MAP) told The New Arab on Tuesday.
The severe shortage of diagnostic equipment comes after three years of Israel's war on Gaza devastated the enclave's health system, destroying and damaging hospitals and other medical facilities and leaving those still functioning struggling with shortages of medicines, equipment, fuel and staff.
The crisis has continued despite the October 2025 ceasefire, with Israel maintaining tight restrictions on the entry of medical equipment and other supplies it classifies as so-called "dual-use" items, meaning goods it alleges could have both civilian and military use.
Citing figures from Gaza's Ministry of Health, MAP told The New Arab that as of August, 22 of Gaza's 34 oxygen stations were out of service, leaving only 12 operating.
"Just four of 30 machines used to fill oxygen cylinders were still working," a MAP spokesperson said. "The Ministry warned that the remaining stations could also fail without access to the spare parts needed for repairs."
More than 500 patients across Gaza depend on oxygen, some around the clock, according to MAP. They include people with cancer, pulmonary fibrosis, liver disease and heart conditions, as well as babies and children requiring intensive care.
More than 72 intensive care units, 19 paediatric units and around 54 neonatal intensive care beds rely on the remaining oxygen stations, the organisation said.
The figures highlight the continued crisis facing Gaza's health system a year after the so-called ceasefire, with hospitals still struggling to obtain medicines, fuel, spare parts and essential equipment needed to diagnose and treat patients.
MAP raised further concerns in a separate report on Tuesday, in which Sally Saleh, the group's Head of Emergency, described how initial hopes that the ceasefire would allow Gaza's health system to begin recovering had failed to materialise.
Following warnings that hospitals across the devastated territory continue to face shortages of medicines, fuel and essential supplies, MAP said Israeli restrictions continue to affect equipment ranging from laboratory and imaging machinery to ventilators and neonatal intensive care equipment.
"When the ceasefire was announced on 10 October 2025, I think many of us had hoped that it would mean more than a reduction in Israel’s military attacks," Saleh said.
She said humanitarian workers had hoped the agreement would allow Gaza's health system to move from "emergency survival towards early recovery", with medical supplies entering more consistently, hospitals being rebuilt and renovated, patients receiving specialist treatment outside Gaza and Emergency Medical Teams entering the territory more easily.
Instead, she said, heavy restrictions remain on items classified as "dual use".
"These can include laboratory equipment, reagent components for laboratory machines, imaging equipment, neonatal intensive care units and ventilators, which are very essential for neonatal ICUs. Even relatively basic items needed for disease surveillance, such as tablets and laboratory supplies, have faced restrictions as well," Saleh said.
"From a health perspective, these restrictions can have very dire consequences, such as delays in diagnosis, disease surveillance, and treatment."
Saleh warned that the restrictions risk turning "an acute emergency [into] a prolonged health crisis that becomes normalised" in the Gaza Strip.
The continuing shortages come after Israel's war and siege devastated Gaza's medical infrastructure and repeatedly forced hospitals and health facilities out of service. Restrictions on the movement of people and goods have also complicated efforts to repair damaged facilities, replace medical equipment and evacuate patients requiring treatment unavailable inside the enclave.
The effects are particularly acute for newborn babies and their mothers.
Dr Amjad Salman, Head of the NICU at Sahaba Medical Complex, said the facility had seen a significant increase in newborn admissions over the past month, both among babies delivered there and those transferred from elsewhere.
"The conditions people are living in Gaza are directly affecting the health of mothers and newborns. Repeated displacement, overcrowding in makeshift shelter, high temperatures, lack of food and the difficulty of maintaining hygiene all increase the health risks faced by newborn babies," Salman said.
International aid organisations and UN officials have repeatedly warned that medical supplies, fuel and hospital equipment remain critically scarce in Gaza, while calling for the unhindered entry of humanitarian aid and equipment needed to restore basic health services.
Doctors, nurses, paramedics and support staff are meanwhile continuing to work under extraordinarily difficult conditions, with hospitals operating beyond capacity and severe staff shortages compounding the lack of equipment and supplies.
A year after the ceasefire, MAP warned that without the equipment, spare parts and supplies required to rebuild Gaza's health system, facilities risk remaining trapped in emergency conditions rather than moving towards meaningful recovery.

Mayor of Turkey's secular stronghold Izmir joins Erdogan's party
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07

19:39:23 KST

Mayor of Turkey's secular stronghold Izmir joins Erdogan's party
ANKARA, Oct 7 - The mayor of Izmir, Turkey's third-largest city and a bastion of its secular opposition, joined President Tayyip Erdogan's ruling AK Party (AKP) on Wednesday, amid a crackdown on the opposition in which dozens of mayors have been jailed.
Cemil Tugay, elected mayor in 2024 as a candidate of the opposition Republican People's Party (CHP) before quitting in June, formally joined the AKP at a ceremony in Ankara, handing Erdogan's party the mayoralty of a city it has never managed to win at the ballot box.
"I have no doubt that, with harmony between the local administration and central government, we will achieve great things," Tugay said.
The move is a significant symbolic gain for Erdogan's party in the western coastal city, long regarded as the heartland of Turkey's secular, social democratic opposition.
The religiously and socially conservative AKP, founded by Erdogan in 2001, has never won the Izmir metropolitan municipality despite dominating national politics for more than two decades.
Tugay won the March 2024 election with 49% of the vote, against 37% for the AKP candidate. The CHP also won 28 of Izmir's 30 district municipalities.
MANY MAYORS ARE IN JAIL AWAITING TRIAL
Erdogan's AKP suffered a major electoral blow in the March 2024 mayoral elections but since then Turkish authorities have launched an unprecedented crackdown on opposition municipalities that saw many mayors targeted with corruption charges that critics say are unfounded.
Dozens of mayors, including Istanbul's Mayor Ekrem Imamoglu, who is seen as Erdogan's main rival, are in jail pending trial. Tunc Soyer, who was the Izmir mayor before Tugay, is also among those jailed as part of a corruption probe.
The opposition has rejected the corruption accusations and says the investigations are politically motivated. The government says the judiciary is independent.
Tugay resigned from the CHP in June after a court ruling that annulled the CHP 2023 congress and stripped Ozgur Ozel of his title as CHP chairman. However, he did not join the New Party founded by Ozel and 90 opposition MPs in protest over the court ruling and continued as an independent mayor.
Ozel accused the AKP on Tuesday of using blackmail and the threat of imprisonment to pressure Tugay into defecting.
"Those who refuse to bow to this pressure ... and do not betray their friends or their party will remain our brothers until the day we die. Those who sell out and leave are genuine traitors," Ozel told his party's parliamentary group.
Erdogan rejected such accusations at Wednesday's ceremony.
"Those who want to serve their cities in peace see the AK Party as the safest address," Erdogan said.
"This is the reason for the growing support for the AK Party. Any suggestion otherwise is slander and speculation."
Tugay is the second mayor of a large city to defect to the AKP from the CHP, after Ozlem Cercioglu, mayor of Aydin, another western coastal city. Dozens of district mayors elected from opposition parties in 2024 have also joined the AKP since then. REUTERS

Russia-Africa Summit sets out priorities for Moscow gathering

Russia-Africa Summit sets out priorities for Moscow gathering
The agenda for the third Russia-Africa Summit has been released ahead of the gathering in Moscow later this month.
The summit will take place on October 28-29. Its program, released by the Roscongress Foundation, one of the organizers, is divided into four main tracks covering sovereignty and sustainable development, the economy, humanitarian cooperation and human capital, and technology and innovation.
Previous summits “marked a key stage in the strengthening of Russia’s relations with the countries of Africa,” Anton Kobyakov, an adviser to the Russian president and executive secretary of the summit’s organizing committee, said. He added that this year’s gathering would focus not only on reaching agreements, but also on “adopting practical solutions.”
Panel discussions will focus on trade and investment, industry, technology transfer, food and energy security, digitalization, healthcare, education, and science.
A separate Russia-Africa Media Forum is expected to bring together executives from African news agencies and media companies to discuss the role of media in Global Majority countries, the development of independent African media, disinformation, and the decolonization of media content.
The agenda has been unveiled days after Moscow accused Western countries of pressuring African states to stay away from the summit. Russian Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova said last week that Western nations are attempting to dissuade African partners from attending.
The inaugural Russia-Africa Summit in Sochi in 2019 drew official delegations from all 54 African countries, with 45 represented by heads of state or government. The second summit in St. Petersburg in 2023 drew official delegations from 48 countries, with 27 represented by a head of state or the second-highest-ranking official.
More than 30 African countries have confirmed their participation in this year’s summit, according to the Russian Foreign Ministry. The leaders of Burkina Faso, Mali, and Niger are among those expected to attend, Russian Deputy Foreign Minister Aleksandr Alimov said last month. The presidents of Ghana, Kenya, Uganda, and Zimbabwe are also expected to take part.

 A robbery and murder case allegedly involving a US Marine in Japan has left local residents “worried,” as the Japanese prime minister on Wednesday again expressed “outrage” over the incident.
Japan saw protests and widespread outrage after Lance Cpl. Devin Jacob Ballard, 20, assigned to Marine Corps Air Station Futenma in the southernmost Okinawa prefecture, was suspected of killing Anna Yagi, 39, at a hotel in Naha’s Wakasa district last Saturday.
