The Okinawa governor also met Japanese Defense Minister Shinjiro Koizumi and urged him to take “effective and fundamental” measures following the incident in the prefecture, which hosts the majority of US military facilities in Japan.
Approximately 50,000 to 55,000 US military personnel are currently stationed in Japan under the US-Japan Security Treaty, which was originally signed in 1951 and revised in 1960.
Amid the outrage, US forces in Okinawa imposed a 48-hour operational pause, a complete alcohol ban, restrictions on off-base liberty and a midnight-to-5 am curfew for one month following the arrest of the US Marine on suspicion of murder.
US Forces Okinawa Area Coordinator Lt. Gen. Benjamin Watson, joined by US Marine Air Ground Task Force Sgt. Maj. Christopher Adams, met US military leaders Wednesday to “reinforce expectations for the operational pause, period of reflection, standards, discipline, and responsible liberty,” according to a statement.

Fuel: government ends duty discount and waits for EU
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
10:38:27 UTC
19:38:27 KST

The Meloni government has neither renewed the diesel tax cut nor launched the replacement scheme it had promised. EU leaders meet on 15–16 October, while European governments pursue different measures to ease fuel costs.
Italy’s diesel tax cut expired on Monday 5 October without a replacement, adding to pressure on prices at the pump.
The cut in diesel excise duty had helped cushion motorists against rising fuel costs in previous months.
Eni raises its diesel price cap
By the time it expired at midnight, the measure was worth only 6.1 cents per litre, having fallen over time from the initial discount.
In its place, the Meloni government had promised a mechanism using additional VAT revenue from higher oil prices to fund excise duty cuts. This required a joint decree from the economy and energy ministries, which had not been issued when the existing cut expired.
The government is still considering whether and how to renew the support.
Eni has kept its temporary price cap but raised the diesel ceiling from €2.19 to €2.25 per litre to reflect the end of the tax cut.
Von der Leyen floats joint purchases and flexibility on climate rules
Last week, G7 countries agreed to release 100 million barrels of diesel and crude oil from strategic reserves to increase supply and help ease energy prices.
European Commission president Ursula von der Leyen has also proposed pooling Europe’s energy demand and arranging joint purchases to strengthen its buying power.
She said exporters would be given another year to prepare for EU methane rules. These require suppliers to declare the greenhouse gas emissions linked to their production. This obligation could therefore be pushed back to 2028.
The Commission also plans talks with European refineries to help lower costs and secure supplies.
Meloni calls for changes to EU carbon pricing
Attention now turns to the European Council meeting scheduled for 15 and 16 October.
Giorgia Meloni has called on Europe to provide "clear and concrete political guidance", particularly on lowering energy costs and protecting industrial competitiveness.
In a statement, she added that she had "referred back to the joint contribution drawn up with Czech prime minister Andrej Babiš with proposals to ease the costs linked to the ETS system, support the most exposed industrial sectors, limit the impact of the cost of CO2 on the price of electricity and postpone further the entry into force of ETS2".
This is the Emissions Trading System, the mechanism under which, on the one hand, a price is set for each tonne of CO2 equivalent, which companies can buy or sell according to their needs; and on the other, a cap on total emissions is imposed on a range of sectors, to ensure an overall reduction.
Another measure on the table is a possible ad hoc tax on the extra profits of oil and gas companies. The idea is also backed by Economy Minister Giancarlo Giorgetti and is viewed favourably by other European governments. While awaiting details of the measures that will actually be adopted at EU level, European governments are nonetheless moving ahead in an uncoordinated fashion.
France expands commuter support, Germany cuts fuel taxes
In France, a support scheme for those who have to travel long distances for work has recently been extended and broadened. In particular, 100 euros will be paid to each of the 5.5 million French beneficiaries of the measure, plus a discount on the price at the pump. In addition, up to 1,000 euros in company aid granted to employees who need to use a private vehicle to get to work will be tax-free.
A rule has also been introduced that prevents the state from "profiting" from fuel price increases: any surplus tax revenue (VAT and excise duty) will be used to fund support schemes in the face of the crisis. Overall, these measures are expected to cost 450 million euros to the French public purse.
In Germany, from 1 October the Merz government introduced a temporary cut in excise duty on fuel of 17 cents per litre, both on diesel and petrol. The reduction will remain in force until the end of the year.
Spain extends fuel tax cuts until December
The Spanish government has also announced support measures for households and businesses, extending measures first adopted in March until 31 December.
The tax cut on diesel and petrol remains at 20 cents per litre in October and is scheduled to fall to 13 cents in November and 6 cents in December.
This is an urgent necessity for the government of Pedro Sánchez, which is contending with inflation that has reached 4.9% year-on-year, according to figures published at the end of September by the National Statistics Institute. For Madrid, the overall cost of the package in force since March has been around 5 billion euros, from which 20 million households and three million businesses have benefited.
Belgium’s diesel price ceiling hits a record of €2.501 per litre
In Belgium, regulated maximum prices limit how much filling stations can charge for fuel. The ceilings change with market conditions, so they do not prevent prices from rising.
The maximum price for diesel reached a record €2.501 per litre on 22 September. Stations can charge less than that ceiling.
In the United Kingdom, the average diesel price reached 199.52 pence per litre in the weekly figures for 5 October.
The government has extended the 5-pence-per-litre fuel duty cut, first introduced in March 2022, until 31 December 2026.

How Israeli and Palestinian kids are coping 3 years after the Oct. 7 Hamas attacks ignited the Middle East
Three years after Hamas militants launched their assault on southern Israel, killing 1,200 people, taking 251 others hostage and triggering Israel's war in Gaza that has killed tens of thousands of Palestinians, CBS News met two teenagers on both sides of the Gaza border to find out how they are coping.
"Some kind of nightmare"
Ron Shargian, 15, said growing up in southern Israel has meant learning to live with fear. He was 12 when he watched Hamas militants on paragliders soar over a wall meant to protect his community.
"It feels like some kind of nightmare," he told CBS News three years later, calling the experience on that fateful day surreal, "and something I wouldn't believe if anyone told me it's going to happen."
The attackers killed 17 of his neighbors in Netiv HaAsara, the Israeli community that was closest to the Gaza border.
As the assault unfolded, he and his family locked themselves inside their home's bomb shelter.
"Every time the gunshots get close to you, you think that that's the end, that they're coming to your house now," he recalled.
His family escaped after 11 hours, when security forces came to the rescue, but like thousands of other Israelis displaced by the war, they couldn't go back home, at least not right away.
After Oct. 7, Shargian's family lived in a hotel for evacuees, and then in Tel Aviv, and then in another hotel, and then a year and a half in the coastal town of Gan Yavne. Finally, a little over a year ago, his family returned to their home.
"It was really hard to come back," he said. "But I also anticipated it very much. I really missed my home, my friends, the community — it's something that you don't have anywhere else."
"War has been not finished"
Across the border in Gaza, safe places have been hard for Palestinian children to find since Israel launched its full-scale military assault in retaliation for the Hamas attack.
"Lots of things has been destroyed for me," Kazem Doghmash told CBS News. He was 11 when the war started.
Israel pummeled Gaza for years with daily airstrikes in a grueling war that, despite a cease-fire in place since last October ending major combat, continues to claim lives three years later. Palestinian officials in Gaza say more than 1,400 people have been killed in Gaza since the cease-fire officially came into effect.
"They say a lot of times that the war will finish, but the war has been not finished, the war has been more difficult," said Doghmash, who is now 14.
"Before the war, I am just being a kid," he said, remembering it as "a good life."
"Used to this reality"
In Israel, Shargian said he struggles with how to think about people on the other side of the Gaza border after everything that happened.
"I don't know if there are good people there," he said. "Up until October 7th, I thought that we could make peace. But from that day, something inside me broke."
He is trying to move forward and lead a normal teenage life — learning the guitar, hanging out with friends at the beach, and he told CBS News the wider conflict now engulfing the Middle East can, at times, even feel distant.
"I don't think we feel the war so much, like, it's in other countries," he said.
When the sound of a rocket or an air raid siren jolts him back to reality, he said like most Israelis, he takes it in his stride.
"Because we're so used to this reality," he said. "So, we just don't make a big deal out of it."
But even though it has happened throughout his life, he said he still feels it inside, every time he and his family or friends hear an alarm and have to rush for shelter.
"Your muscles get tight and you have an adrenaline rush," he said. "It's something we just got used to."
"My life has been destroyed"
Moving forward has been hard for Doghmash, too. He still can't think about returning to normal teenage pursuits.
"My life has been destroyed," he said. "My school has been destroyed, a lot of things have been destroyed for me."
"We are focusing [on] how we're going to live," he said.
But he hasn't given up on his dreams. He told CBS News he hopes to become a doctor, and he has resumed studying at the British International School in Gaza — in its new location, as the original building was destroyed by Israeli airstrikes — where his favorite subject is English.
As he led CBS News through the rubble of what used to be his family's home, he longed for anything resembling a return to his life before the war.
"We need to live in a good life, not to just, thinking how we're gonna get food and the water," he said. "We're gonna need to go to school, to go, to be happy and smile."
The United Nations Children's Fund says more than 21,000 Palestinian children have been reported killed in Gaza since Oct. 7, 2023, as a result of Israel's counteroffensive.
Dozens of Israeli children have died, too, including 37 killed in the initial Hamas attacks.
Despite everything they've been through, both boys are still finding moments in life to just be kids.
CBS News' Becky Perlow and Anas Zeyad Fteiha contributed to this report.

Trump said he plans to speak with Putin - Kremlin says this has not yet been "agreed"
Kyiv • UNN
Trump announced an upcoming conversation with Putin following the death of a laboratory technician at an anti-plague center in Siberia. The WHO called on Russia to be transparent.
U.S. President Donald Trump said he would soon speak with Kremlin head Vladimir Putin about the death of a laboratory assistant at a research center studying plague in Siberia. UNN reports this, citing the BBC.
Details
"For now, we are engaged in very deep discussions," Trump said, adding that he would be able to report on his talks with Putin, "probably," on Thursday, October 8.
Russian officials say they are investigating the cause of the 28-year-old woman's death. They say that everyone who came into contact with the victim tested negative and have not confirmed that the suspected illness was pneumonic plague—a serious lung infection often described as the most virulent form of plague.
What the Kremlin said
Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov, as quoted by Russian media, said that "if the United States takes the initiative for a conversation between Vladimir Putin and Donald Trump, the conversation will be promptly arranged."
He added that "for now, a telephone conversation between the presidents has not been substantively agreed upon."
What the WHO said
The head of the World Health Organization (WHO) called on Russia to be transparent.
"Timely, complete, and transparent information-sharing in accordance with international health regulations is important for clarifying contradictory reports and ensuring an accurate assessment of potential risks to public health," said WHO Director-General Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus.
According to the WHO, pneumonic plague has a very short incubation period—sometimes as little as 24 hours—and can be fatal if it is not diagnosed and treated in time. Symptoms include shortness of breath and coughing, often with bloody sputum.
Reports first emerged on Friday that nearly 200 people had been placed under observation in the Irkutsk region of Siberia following the death. The laboratory assistant, identified in Russian media as Darya Shipilova, reportedly fell ill several days earlier.
Unconfirmed reports suggest that she fell ill after breaking a test tube containing a pathogen at the anti-plague institute in Siberia where she worked, or after traveling to a region where plague occurs naturally among wild rodents.
But Russian officials played down these reports. Russia's health authorities said that the woman died from "pneumonia of undetermined etiology."
Persistent speculation about the laboratory assistant's death has sparked controversy between Russia and the United States, including questions about possible spread beyond Russia.
U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said that the United States has "measures" to help Russia if the situation turns out to be more serious than claimed.
The bacterium that causes plague, Yersinia pestis, has been found among rodents such as marmots in the area.
In the 14th century, when plague was known as the "Black Death," it wiped out up to half of Europe's population.
It was precisely in response to a plague outbreak in the 1920s, a little more than 100 years ago, that the anti-plague institute in Siberia was founded.

EU to put energy security at heart of COP31 push for faster green transition
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
10:33:54 UTC
19:33:54 KST

EU ministers are set to confirm their commitment to the green transition despite soaring energy prices and supply concerns, according to a draft COP31 position seen by Euronews.
The EU plans to make energy security a central argument for accelerating the shift away from fossil fuels at next month’s UN climate summit, as the latest supply crisis exposes its dependence on foreign suppliers.
A Council document seen by Euronews sets out the bloc’s position for COP31 in Turkey, linking the clean energy transition to more secure, affordable supplies and reduced strategic dependencies.
The EU has become increasingly reliant on US liquefied natural gas (LNG) as Washington takes a more confrontational approach to energy relations.
It is also still grappling with the loss of Russian supplies, which drove up energy bills for households and industry. The war in the Middle East and disruption to oil and gas supplies from Gulf states have further exposed its vulnerability.
Brussels argues that these pressures strengthen the case for the clean energy transition as it pursues climate neutrality by 2050.
"(The EU) recognises the transition away from fossil fuels in a just, orderly and equitable manner, and towards renewable and low-carbon energy sources and energy efficiency as being central to ensuring energy security, affordability, and availability for all," reads the document dated 5 October.
The EU acknowledges that global warming is likely to exceed the Paris Agreement’s 1.5°C target in the coming decades, as the UN recently warned, but insists governments must minimise the scale and duration of that overshoot.
Its argument is that a temporary breach makes immediate action more urgent, rather than justifying abandoning the target.
“We don’t do climate policy only for the climate, but also for economic reasons and for geopolitical reasons. It’s basically an economic modernisation and liberation agenda,” a senior Commission official said, on condition of anonymity.
But the EU can push its own climate policies only so far if other major economies do not follow.
Who pays for climate action?
The US retreat from climate cooperation, alongside the absence of Chinese and Indian leaders from last year’s COP30 summit in Belém, Brazil, left the EU pushing for progress on climate finance.
"We learned a lesson in Belém: it’s increasingly difficult to reach consensus. We don’t want to go in with expectations and come back with frustrations," the senior Commission official said.
At COP29 in Baku in 2024, countries agreed a goal of at least $300 billion (€261 billion) in climate finance for developing countries by 2035, with developed countries taking the lead. They also called for funding from all public and private sources to reach at least €1.1 trillion ($1.31 trillion) annually by then.
EU officials are resisting additional financial commitments, pointing to the bloc’s substantial contributions and its relatively small share of current global emissions.
Together, China (29.2%), the United States (11.1%) and India (8.2%) account for nearly half of the world's emissions, compared to the mere 5.9% by the EU, according to 2024 data from the EU's Joint Research Centre.
In 2024 alone, the EU and its member states contributed €42.7 billion in international public and private finance, according to the Council.
"We’re happy to deliver on the past commitments but nothing additional," the senior Commission added.
The EU is calling on other major emitters to raise their ambitions and submit stronger national climate plans.
It wants countries to align their policies with the 1.5°C pathway and incorporate climate plans into national investment strategies — a tough sell for the US, which ranks second as the biggest carbon polluter, after China.
At a pre-COP visit to Fiji and Tuvalu this week, Climate Action Commissioner Wopke Hoekstra said climate change is essential for the islands.
"We need to accelerate implementation of the Paris Agreement, guided by science, deliver on commitments already made and ensure better access to climate finance, particularly for the most vulnerable,” said Hoekstra.
EU finance ministers are set to confirm the Council position on climate finance on 9 October. A second Council document seen by Euronews calls for greater private investment, arguing that public funding alone cannot meet the costs of the transition.
"Public finance, including concessional finance and export credit support, plays a catalytic role in unlocking private finance flows for the transition," reads the Council document dated 30 September on climate finance.
The COP31 will kick off on 9 November and run until 20 November.

A bill presented by the parties of
Premier Giorgia Meloni's ruling coalition to bring in a new
election law passed the last of three important confidence votes
in the Lower House on Wednesday, clearing the way for the final
vote, which will be a secret ballot, on Thursday.
                                    
After articles 1 and 2 of the bill got the green light with ease
in confidence votes on Tuesday, article 3 was approved in
similar fashion with 228 votes in favour and 144 against.
                                    
This show of unity from the ruling alliance suggests the bill
should have no problem passing the final vote, even though the
secret nature of the ballot makes it easier for lawmakers to
buck the line of their parties without facing consequences.
                                    
The opposition has cried foul about the drive to overhaul the
electoral system, saying the ruling alliance is changing it
because it fears losing the general election set to take place
next year and wants to minimize the chances of this happening.
                                    
The bill will see the current system, a mix of
first-past-the-post and proportional representation, replaced
with a proportional-representation system with bonus seats for
the coalition that obtains the most votes, as long as it reaches
a threshold of 42%, to ensure it has a working majority in
parliament.
                                    
If no coalition reaches the threshold, or the votes for the
Lower House and the Senate produce different results, a purely
proportional system is used.
                                    
The opposition have said that, among other things, the
envisioned system of bonus seats is unconstitutional.
                                    
Coalitions will have to say who their candidate to be premier is
before the election.
                                    
The bill will also give voters the option to express preferences
for up to three candidates out of six on a party list in which
candidates names must alternate according to gender.
                                    
The opposition says that in reality this gives "fake
preferences" as the head of the ticket would always be
"blocked", arguing this was also be a step back for equality,
as, in theory, it would be possible for all the ticket heads to
be men.
                                    
The current system does not give voters any option to express
preferences about which of the candidates on a party list they
want to represent them.

Ukrainian Steel Construction Center urges national plan for bridge resilience
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
13:32:28 EEST
19:32:28 KST

Ukraine needs to develop a comprehensive program to protect and strengthen the resilience of bridge infrastructure, with the foundation for such an approach having been laid back in 2022, according to the website of the Ukrainian Steel Construction Center (USCC).
The USCC explained that Ukraine developed the "Fortress Country" concept for the comprehensive protection of critical infrastructure facilities at that time, which was subsequently approved at the state level. Among other things, it provides standard solutions for protecting road and railway bridges.
"Today, it is important to implement these solutions as part of a systematic bridge infrastructure protection program. It is necessary to assess critical bridges, establish priorities, develop appropriate engineering solutions, create reserves of materials and structures for repairs, and determine the responsible organizations and action protocols following damage. Otherwise, every time we will act reactively: first damage occurs, then an assessment, the search for engineering solutions, materials and contractors. And only after that does restoration begin," serviceman Artem Bilyk, a member of the Coordination Headquarters for the Engineering Protection of Critical Infrastructure Facilities and a lead co-author of the "Fortress Country" concept, said.
According to him, such a model is too slow for critical infrastructure. Action must be taken proactively, anticipating what the enemy may strike and protecting vulnerable points in the infrastructure.
The comprehensive program should include at least five areas, namely: assessment and ranking of bridges by their level of criticality and the potential consequences of their damage; engineering protection of the most critical structural elements and facilities; organizational and technical measures, including monitoring, security and countermeasures against drone and missile threats; preparation of reserves for rapid restoration, including engineering solutions, materials, metal structures and equipment; and the creation of a network of Ukrainian manufacturers capable of producing the necessary structures and ensuring their installation as quickly as possible.
According to Bilyk, the top priority for bridges should be to identify the most critical elements of a particular structure and reinforce them, taking into account possible damage scenarios.
Depending on the structural design and operating conditions, various solutions may be used, including protective structures, gabion structures, concrete and other barrier elements, steel protective structures and so forth.
A separate area is the creation of blast barriers, which make it possible to increase the distance between the source of an explosion and the main structural elements. Such projects should be designed individually for each facility and must not create additional risks for bridge operation, the expert believes.
No less important is protection against secondary effects of damage, including fires, fragmentation damage and damage to auxiliary systems. Vulnerable bridge infrastructure elements should appropriately be protected with fire-resistant structures.
As for alternative crossings, the expert estimates that it would be extremely difficult to fully replace existing urban bridges across the Dnipro with temporary structures. A temporary crossing must be integrated with road and railway infrastructure, have the necessary capacity and meet safety requirements, Bilyk explained.
In addition, it is noted that a modern bridge is far more than just a road traffic facility. Railway tracks, metro lines, utility networks, pipelines, cables and other systems may run across bridge crossings. Therefore, a pontoon or other temporary crossing can serve as a backup option, but not as a full replacement for the developed bridge infrastructure of major cities, the website says.
As noted in the press release, the strategy should not be about choosing between a bridge and a pontoon, but about creating a multilayered resilience system in which a protected primary bridge is supplemented by rapid restoration capabilities and backup transportation solutions.

Sweden will deploy a Patriot air defense system and approximately 100 troops to southeastern Poland to protect a key NATO logistics hub supplying Ukraine, the Swedish government announced on Tuesday, Oct. 6.
The mission will begin in December and Sweden will deploy its Patriot system as part of a NATO operation, according to the Swedish Armed Forces.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
The Swedish unit will be stationed in Rzeszów, a major transit point for military equipment and civilian assistance headed to Ukraine. It will operate under NATO Air Command and contribute to the alliance’s Integrated Air and Missile Defense system.
“For the second time, Sweden is participating with Gripen fighter jets in support of NATO’s operation to protect NATO’s logistics hub in Poland. Sweden will also, starting December, provide the Patriot air defence system,” Swedish Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson said.
“The purpose is to protect the logistics hub and thereby ensure that important materiel reaches Ukraine,” he added.
Sweden’s first NATO Patriot mission
The Patriot system will be operated by personnel from Sweden’s Air Defence Regiment, with support from the Blekinge Air Wing.
The Swedish Armed Forces said the unit would carry out the mission from the beginning of December through the end of 2026. Preparations are also underway to allow the deployment to continue during the first half of 2027.
“As Allies, we share responsibility for protecting and defending NATO territory. At the same time, supporting Ukraine remains a priority for Sweden,” Swedish Army Chief Johan Pekkari said.
How NATO Plans to Win: ‘Theory of Victory’ Against Russia to be Unveiled in Poland
Air Defence Regiment Commander Sofia Westermark said the unit was “well trained, well prepared” and had the personnel needed to complete the mission.
Sweden refers to its Patriot system as Air Defence System 103. It is designed to detect and intercept aircraft, cruise missiles, and certain ballistic missile threats.
Gripens already protecting Polish airspace
The Patriot deployment will reinforce a separate Swedish contribution involving Gripen fighter jets.
Beginning in October, Swedish Gripens joined NATO’s air and missile defense operations over Poland. Most of the aircraft are based in Sweden, while a smaller forward operating base has been established in Poland.
Stockholm said the aircraft would help protect NATO airspace and secure the continued flow of assistance to Ukraine amid repeated violations of allied airspace and other threats connected to Russia’s war.
Swedish Foreign Minister Maria Malmer Stenergard said Russia’s recent attempts to disrupt support for Ukraine had increased the importance of protecting the Polish logistics hub.
“The purpose behind the Swedish contribution is to ensure that military and civilian support reaches Ukraine. This is simultaneously also part of our collective contribution to NATO’s deterrence and defence,” she said.
Poland moves its own Patriots east
Sweden’s announcement comes as Warsaw strengthens air defenses along Poland’s eastern frontier with deployment of its own Patriot batteries to the Lublin region near Ukraine.
The move is part of a broader military buildup that includes new ground units, drone forces, and aviation infrastructure. Polish authorities say the eastern regions face heightened risks because of Russia’s repeated strikes near the border and previous incidents involving missiles and drones entering or approaching Polish airspace.
The Swedish system in Rzeszów will have a more specific mission: shielding the NATO-operated supply route through which weapons, equipment, and humanitarian assistance continue to reach Ukraine.

Analysis: Oct. 7, 2023, Pearl Harbor and 9/11 echo the same failures
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
10:30:38 UTC
19:30:38 KST

What links Israel's Oct. 7 and America's Pearl Harbor and 9/11 disasters?
Tel Aviv — With the first Israeli election since the Oct. 7, 2023, Hamas attack just three weeks away, the country is grappling with conflicting accounts about whether Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu had warnings from regional allies that a massive attack was coming, even if there were no specifics on the timing or location.
Netanyahu has denied getting any warnings, and the fierce internal debate about it may be overshadowing a wider problem — with clear precedent — of overwhelming intelligence signals being misinterpreted or underestimated at the cost of thousands of lives.
Israel is not the only country to have failed to take action despite ample intelligence suggesting a catastrophic attack was imminent. The phenomenon has a name in intelligence circles: strategic intelligence failure. It happened 84 years ago at Pearl Harbor, and on Sept. 11, 2001.
Israel had in its possession Hamas' own secret plan for the attack a year before it occurred, according to Israeli officials. In the months and weeks before the invasion, Hamas both talked about it in public statements and shared videos showing them practicing for it.
In the hours leading up to the attack, Israeli intelligence agencies saw some Hamas leaders go underground and Hamas commandos gathering at different spots. Israel's domestic intelligence agency, Shin Bet, was alerted to the fact that Israeli SIM cards that had been distributed to Hamas fighters were activated — a sign of their imminent intention to cross into Israel.
A female Israeli soldier stationed at the Gaza border had warned her commander for months that she had seen Hamas operatives making apparent preparations for an attack.
Yet, on the evening of Oct. 6, 2023, Israeli military and intelligence officials likely never imagined what was about to happen early the next morning, when thousands of Hamas militants stormed across the border in pickup trucks, on motorcycles and even by motor-powered hang glider to rampage through communities and military bases.
"There was a lot of information. They just didn't understand it correctly," Shlomo Mofaz, a former senior Israeli military intelligence official who now heads the independent Meir Amit Intelligence and Terrorism Information Center, told CBS News.
America's intelligence failures
Before Japan launched its surprise attack on the U.S. Pacific Fleet in Pearl Harbor, as well as several other U.S. naval bases in the region, on Dec. 7, 1941, dragging the U.S. into World War II, there were signs of an impending strike.
U.S.-Japanese talks to avoid a clash had just broken down, and weeks earlier, the Japanese fleet had disappeared into the Pacific Ocean. Even as U.S. radar picked up over 180 Japanese aircraft on their way to Hawaii, American officers failed to understand what was happening.
That's due in part to an overriding belief at the time among the top American brass that Japan was focused on battles closer to its borders, and wouldn't dare spark a war with the U.S.
Before the 9/11 attacks, U.S. intelligence agencies knew al Qaeda leader Osama bin Laden was planning something. They had noted suspicious individuals from the Middle East were learning how to fly planes, but not land them. But they never connected the dots.
It was, in the words of the 9/11 Commission, a catastrophic failure "of imagination."
For decades, the U.S. had been concentrated on conventional threats posed by foes in a similar weight class, like the Soviet Union. Few had considered that small but determined terrorist groups like al Qaeda could cause such catastrophic damage, the commission said.
In all three cases, Pearl Harbor, 9/11 and Oct. 7, the stronger party failed to see that the weaker party wasn't deterred, but rather determined to keep fighting by any means necessary.
Israel thought it could contain Hamas while devoting most of its resources to much clearer and more potent threats, such as Iran and the Lebanese militant group Hezbollah, former senior Israeli security officials have said.
"Even when they understood that Hamas was going to do something, it was never in the dimension and in the force that they eventually did," Mofaz told CBS News.

A Mysterious Nonprofit Run by SpaceXAI’s Top Lawyer Is Paying the Salaries of Government Workers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
10:30:00 UTC
19:30:00 KST

Following billionaire Elon Musk’s departure from the so-called Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE) in late spring 2025, several of the group’s members found a new home within the federal government: the National Design Studio. Led by Joe Gebbia, a cofounder of Airbnb, a former member of DOGE, and currently the chief design officer of the US, the NDS is nested in the Executive Office of the President and has been tasked with redesigning government websites and services.
As with DOGE before it, who exactly is a part of NDS—and what they’re working on—often remains opaque. But a WIRED investigation has found that at least two members of NDS are on loan to the government and are actually employed by a recently formed nonprofit, the America by Design Foundation. This entity appears to be run by James Burnham, a former member of DOGE and the current general counsel of SpaceXAI, the artificial intelligence space company founded by Musk. It is not clear who is funding the foundation or how much money it has.
These findings raise questions about whether NDS, like DOGE, is skirting rules and regulations to bring its chosen staff into government and is functioning as an arm of the tech industry as much as a government initiative.
“The fact that we wouldn’t know who is employing and paying these people is troubling in any context,” says Don Moynihan, a professor of public policy at the University of Michigan. “Especially in the context where there is a back-and-forth movement from the private sector to the public sector.”
The White House announced the creation of the National Design Studio in August 2025 as part of a broader initiative called America by Design, which an executive order described as “a national initiative to improve experiences for Americans.” In the past year, NDS was responsible for launching websites such as TrumpRx and RealFood.gov. In addition to Gebbia, several other DOGE members have worked for or contributed to NDS. Edward “Big Balls” Coristine, one of the young engineers who formed the early core of DOGE and who entered the government at just 19 years old, now serves as the group’s head of engineering. Akash Bobba, another young engineer whose work spanned several government agencies, and Zachary Terrell, the chief technology officer at the Department of Health and Human Services, have also been part of both NDS and DOGE.
Many DOGE operatives also entered government as special government employees, a designation that allows people to work in government for 120 days out of a year without going through the full federal hiring process or requiring the usual level of transparency disclosures. NDS appears to be using a similar strategy by bringing in staff under the Intergovernment Personnel Act, a law meant to allow people with specialized skills from institutions like universities and nonprofit organizations to work in government for up to two years.
Documents reviewed by WIRED indicate that two members of NDS, Amittai Groot and John Cafazza, are actually employed by America by Design and have been detailed to the Office of Personnel Management. Both men reported to Christina Bonarrigo, who until last month was OPM’s chief of staff. According to her LinkedIn, she is now chief of staff at NDS. Bonarrigo did not respond to a request for comment.
Groot lists himself on LinkedIn as having begun work with NDS in April 2026, the same month, according to documents reviewed by WIRED, that he began employment with the American by Design Foundation. Groot’s term with OPM is also part-time and is listed on those documents as spanning from May 5, 2026, to September 30, 2026. On his LinkedIn, Groot says he was previously an “IT cybersecurity expert” at the Social Security Administration from July 2025 to April 2026. He did not respond to a request for comment.
Cafazza, according to his LinkedIn, works as a senior product designer with NDS and previously worked as a product designer at Trump Media & Technology Group, the parent company of President Donald Trump’s Truth Social platform. In documents reviewed by WIRED, Cafazza’s term in government is listed as part-time and as running from May 7, 2026, to May 7, 2028. Cafazza did not respond to a request for comment.
The agreements to loan Cafazza and Groot to OPM were signed by a representative of the America by Design Foundation.
It is not clear what projects Groot and Cafazza have been brought into OPM to work on. Last week, however, the group launched its latest project, an AI-driven website called America.gov, the goal of which is to consolidate several government services, including tax filing and passport renewal, into a single site. Coristine attributed work on the new site to Groot in a post on X. (Earlier this year, the The Guardian reported that NDS-designed websites had installed commercial software to track visitors in a way that appears to violate the 1974 Privacy Act. The code was removed during the course of The Guardian's reporting.)
Erie Meyer, chief technologist of the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau under the Biden administration, hired several IPAs, as workers brought in under the Intergovernment Personnel Act are known, during her time in government and says that generally IPAs are not meant to be at the core of any agency.
“I used to bring in AI experts in 2021, when the government did not have any. And it was important that they did not have the same job duties as a federal employee, that they weren’t taking a federal employee’s spot,” she says. “If the National Design Studio is bringing in designers and engineers now, the government is actually now full of those. You can't just use the IPA system to evade hiring protections.”
Meyer also noted that IPAs need to be employed for at least 90 days at their home organization before they can be loaned to the government. This does not seem to have been the case for Groot, who started in government less than a month after being hired by the America by Design Foundation.
In some cases, the government will reimburse the IPA’s home organization for the cost of their salary or, in cases where their salary is substantially higher than a government salary, for part of their salary. In the documents, OPM says it will reimburse the foundation $13,691 a month for Groot’s work. This amounts to only a portion of his actual salary, which the documents indicate is too large for the government pay scale, meaning the foundation will pay the "remaining employee's salary requirements and all benefits." In Cafazza’s case, it appears that the Foundation will be covering the full cost of Cafazza’s employment.
Meyer says that having multiple people from the same organization who have different payment agreements with the government is “very, very weird.”
A White House spokesperson did not respond to questions about the relationships between the America by Design Foundation, OPM, and NDS. Instead, they referred WIRED to OPM, which did not respond to a request for comment.
“It makes you ask, What does this outside organization get out of this?” says Moynihan. “We should know who is paying the salaries of government employees.”
How the foundation plans to pay Cafazza—and with what money—is unclear. The America by Design Foundation was registered on August 25, 2025, just four days after the NDS was officially established, and received its exemption on September 22, 2025. Tax filings for the organization are not yet available, and it is not clear who is funding the foundation. According to documents viewed by WIRED, the foundation’s “core mission is to enhance the visual design, usability, and overall experience of web-based federal government services.”
What is clear is that James Burnham, SpaceXAI’s top lawyer, has been listed on documents as its managing director. In his biography on the website of the conservative legal group the Federalist Society, Burnham is described as the former general counsel of DOGE and having “designed the legal structure” of the organization. In the System for Award Management, the procurement website where US government contractors and grantees are required to register, the America by Design Foundation's address is listed as a residential property in Alexandria, Virginia; when cross-referenced with Nexis, that location appears to be Burnham's house. (Organizations seeking reimbursement from the government for their employees’ salaries while they are IPAs must be registered in the System for Award Management.) The Internal Revenue Services letter confirming the foundation’s registration is also addressed to Burnham.
While it is unclear who is funding the America by Design Foundation, Burnham serves as a direct link between it and SpaceXAI, which has received billions of dollars in federal contracts, works closely with the government to integrate its Grok AI systems with government ones, has substantial regulatory business before the government, and is run by the GOP’s top funder. Burnham is also president of Vallecito Capital, a fund that supports litigation against companies who litigants believe have broken the law with progressive policies.
Further documents from the Department of Labor also reveal that the foundation applied for an H-1B visa for someone designated as a “member of technical staff.” In these documents, Burnham is listed as the foundation’s managing director, and its address as 800 Connecticut Ave NW, Suite 300, in Washington, DC, the same address as King Street Legal, where, according to LinkedIn, Burnham was a managing partner until November 2025.
The immigration documents that list Burnham as the foundation’s managing director do not show who the H-1B visa application was for. Burnham did not respond to a request for comment. (The documents do show the visa’s start date is listed as April 6, 2026, and expires April 5, 2029, effectively spanning the remainder of the second Trump administration.) But both DOGE and NDS have a history of including noncitizens in their operations. Baris Akis, a Turkish national and a close associate of Musk’s, acted as a recruiter for the group, even attending a DOGE meeting hosted by Musk. Akis did not respond to a request for comment.
Previous reporting from WIRED also identified one apparent foreign national in the DOGE orbit. Yat Choi, an NDS member who previously worked for Airbnb, has described Canada as “home” in social media posts. Choi’s LinkedIn says that he has been a senior technologist at OPM since April 2025 and lists the role as a “contract.” On his profile on X, Choi indicates that he was a member of DOGE and NDS. Choi did not respond to a request for comment.
The salary for the role, also listed in the documents, ranges from $175,427 to $340,000. $175,427 is toward the highest end of the federal pay scale, which tops out at $197,200. Foreign citizens are not generally permitted to work in the US government, and Meyer says that while it is not unprecedented to have foreign nationals working as IPAs, it’s “not common.”
A search for the America by Design Foundation on the Department of Homeland Security’s website that tracks H1-B employment visas returns “Jennifer Michelsen America by Design Foundation.” Jennifer Michelsen is the cofounder of an eyewear company called Gunnar. Her husband is Matt Michelsen, the founder of Gothams LLC, which won a $33 million contract for the “Alligator Alcatraz” immigration detention facility in Florida and, according to reporting from the Guardian, sought further contracts from the Trump administration to develop a “fully integrated humanitarian logistics system” for the administration’s efforts to rebuild the Gaza Strip.
For her part, Meyer says that the whole setup of the foundation and the way it is bringing people into the government appears to be suspect. “The thing that you wouldn't want is an outside organization to be able to use an external rich person's preference to exert power over how the government works,” she says.

The loss of Jefferey Archer feels personal to us because we miss the India of the 1980s – the India of simple pleasures
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
10:29:56 UTC
19:29:56 KST

That simple pleasure and anticipation of finishing one more chapter
Jeffrey Archer page-turners helped Indians fall in love with reading
That simple pleasure and anticipation of finishing one more chapter
Jeffrey Archer page-turners helped Indians fall in love with reading
That simple pleasure and anticipation of finishing one more chapter
The 1980s was a good decade to grow up in India. Not too far off from Independence, and two decades shy of the 21st century; it was an India that gave children enough room to discover and know themselves before they went out to the big, bad world out there. Mornings were rushed. Afternoons were lazy. Evenings were long and a time to catch up with neighbours from verandahs and terraces. This was also an India where young people had the freedom to play outdoors — though strict rules applied. And when night came, it was full of promise to read our favourite books. And on top of the reading list was Jeffrey Archer.Which is why when the news of his death broke Monday, there was this whole generation — Gen X mostly but Boomers and Millennials too — who were promptly transported to a time when living life used to be a peaceful affair. When parents, grandparents and teachers were all guides who would tell children how to brush up their English-speaking skills. And British author Archer was on top of the list because he knew how to write page-turners in the simplest language.In this India, privilege was education. And going to an English medium school or Bengali medium, where English was the second language was why our parents worked hard. Dads at their workplace, and moms at home helping finish our homework.
Even in homes where both parents worked, the setting wasn’t too different. Grandparents bright a lot of us up. The 1980s was a decade and half shy of the nuclear family. There were mini-libraries in every house (read two to three cupboards full of books). There would be a mix of literature — mostly fiction — in our first language and English.In Bengali households, after Bengali literature, it was the Russians who sat pretty and fat in those library cupboards. But then there were easy English fictions. Enid Blyton, Agatha Christie, Sherlock Holmes and Jeffrey Archer. Well, there was also Sydney Sheldon. But we were told those were “adult” books not to be touched till we were 16. But as things go, almost everyone we knew had read all Archers and all Sheldons by 16 years of age.There was something about those books that made them travel easily from one generation to another, and from one house to another. You didn’t have to be a serious reader to pick up a Jeffrey Archer. You didn’t need to know anything about literary criticism or understand what made a novel important. You simply needed to be curious about what happened next. That was Archer's great gift. That’s also essentially how generations of people fell in love with reading.Then came the imagination of what adult worlds look and feel like. As school students in the 1980s India, we knew of worlds far off and very different from ours through fiction. Also, as teenagers, when hormones are running wild, there was this insane urge to know about all kinds of unfelt emotions we watched in movies and read in books — but didn’t fully comprehend ourselves because those worlds seemed far off. But very attractive. And full of tales of people who wanted something badly.
The lure of the glitzy and gritty world between the pages
Money, power, revenge, love, recognition, another chance at life. There were families, rivalries, fortunes, secrets, political ambitions and people who seemed to have everything until one twist of fate changed it all. The stories were set in worlds that were far removed from the India most of us knew, but the emotions were not. Ambition was ambition. Jealousy was jealousy. A family feud was a family feud. And a person who had lost everything and wanted to start again was a character anyone could understand.That was also why Archer became such an easy entry point into English fiction. The language didn’t stand between you and the story. At a time when many Indian children were learning English as a second language, Archer books became handy. Almost an already-available tool that helped out both parents and teachers.Parents wanted us to read because they believed good English could change our lives. Teachers recommended books because they knew that children who read would eventually write and speak better. And Archer didn't feel like homework. His books were what you read after the homework was done. At times even when mom had asked us to turn off my light. We would turn off the light, say goodbye, listen intently—like a cheetah hunting its prey—to our parents’ steps withdrawing from our rooms. Hold our breaths for 10 minutes, and then promptly turn on the torch inside our sheet covers to read a couple of more chapters.That was the beginning of the relationship between India and Jeffrey Archer. He arrived at the precise moment when books still had enormous power in middle-class homes. There was no internet to tell you what was trending. No Instagram account to follow. No streaming platform recommending the next series. There were just newspapers, magazines, television and books. And books could take you somewhere else for as long as you wanted.An Archer novel was particularly good company on a long afternoon or a long train journey. It could make a railway compartment disappear. It could turn a summer holiday into something you remembered years later. It could keep you awake under the blanket with a torch because you were determined to finish one more chapter and then another. And the next day as one would inevitably fall asleep in the classroom, the teacher would gently pat us awake and ask which book we were reading last night. The whole class would laugh. Then it would be another student’s turn. This was a ritual in 1980s school life.Archer himself knew that no country held him close quite like India. By his own estimation, more than 50 million Indians had read his 1979 masterpiece, Kane and Abel. When he toured the Western world, a typical book signing in New York or London might bring in 200 or 300 readers. But when he stepped off the plane in Delhi, Mumbai or Bangalore, he was greeted like a pop star by crowds of 2,000 to 3,000 eager fans. What moved him most was how young these readers were. At a 2013 gathering of 1,000 fans in Bangalore, eight out of ten people in the room were under 20 years old.That tells us about the peculiar place Archer occupied among Indians. He wasn't just a bestselling foreign novelist. He was the author who introduced us to the pleasure of reading for pleasure. He was the book we borrowed from an older cousin, the paperback that travelled through a classroom, the novel somebody recommended with a slightly conspiratorial “You must read this.” He became part of the informal education of a generation.
That simple pleasure and anticipation of finishing one more chapter
Of books borrowed and dog-eared
Many of us discovered him in school libraries or through friends, and then went looking for the rest of his books. Kane and Abel, A Twist in the Tale, Not a Penny More, Not a Penny Less. Once you had read one, you knew there were more waiting. That excitement is still palpable and was felt by most of us as we heard of the author’s demise.Books were not as easily available back in the day as they are today. Finding another Archer could itself feel like an achievement. At times two people would read it and two different pages would be dog eared. That’s how people read books in those times. It seemed the world would fall apart if the next chapter was not finished by the end of school.Teachers and librarians played their part too. In an India where parents saw English as one of the most important gifts they could give their children, books that were accessible but exciting were invaluable. Archer’s stories offered unfamiliar worlds. But we could dream we would be a part of this world some day. We could read about international banking, political campaigns, art auctions or courtroom battles and still follow the story not just because we saw ourselves as the protagonist but also because the language was simple and clear.A paperback could be finished by one person on Monday and be in somebody else's schoolbag by Tuesday. Pages became dog-eared, covers disappeared, names were written inside them. Books were rarely pristine possessions. They were used, borrowed, exchanged and sometimes never returned.Archer's stories also had something that felt instinctively familiar to Indian readers: a love of drama and fate. Kane and Abel is essentially the story of two men born on the same day but into completely different worlds, whose lives become intertwined through ambition and rivalry. William Lowell Kane is born into privilege in Boston, while Abel Rosnovski grows up in poverty and survives extraordinary hardship before building an empire of his own. It is an enormous story, but its emotional core is simple. Two men want to make something of their lives and neither is willing to give way.For an ambitious Indian middle class, particularly the generation that came of age around and after the economic reforms of 1991, there was something irresistible about that. The idea that circumstances did not have to determine your destiny was deeply appealing. Archer’s characters were forever trying to escape the lives they had been given and build better ones.
Hollywood dreams mashed with Bollywood masala
His stories also understood that people were rarely entirely good or entirely bad. They were complicated by family, pride, love, money and circumstance. That too was familiar. Indian storytelling had long been comfortable with characters who could be generous and selfish, noble and flawed, loving and resentful at the same time. In that sense, Archer's worlds, however Western they appeared on the surface, did not feel entirely alien.And then there were the twists. Archer understood the sheer pleasure of making a reader gasp. Separated twins, secret identities, unexpected inheritances, betrayals, reversals of fortune, family ambitions, betrayals — his stories were constantly nudging you towards one conclusion and then taking you somewhere else. Shall We Tell the President? took the reader into the world of American politics and a plot to assassinate the President.A Quiver Full of Arrows showed just how much drama could be packed into a short story, with its tales of deception, revenge and unexpected reversals. And The Prodigal Daughter, the sequel to Kane and Abel, took the saga into another generation, following Florentyna Rosnovski as she rises through American politics and pursues the ambition of becoming the first woman President of the United States.These were stories that could have been written for an Indian movie audience. And Indian filmmakers noticed. It was no surprise that his books found their way into Indian cinema, sometimes with permission and sometimes without it. Rakesh Roshan's 1987 film Khudgarz, starring Jeetendra and Shatrughan Sinha, drew heavily from Kane and Abel. The story travelled further through regional cinema, and years later Not a Penny More, Not a Penny Less provided the inspiration for the trickster plot of Yash Raj Films' Ladies vs Ricky Bahl.Archer was not particularly amused by this. He famously referred to Bollywood as “a bunch of thieves”. But the irony was that the very industry borrowing his stories was also proof of how naturally his storytelling fitted the Indian imagination.But long before streaming platforms discovered him, Archer belonged to another India — one where his books travelled through railway stations and pavement stalls. The extraordinary parallel world of India's street book trade. Pirated copies of popular books could appear almost as quickly as the originals. Archer himself recalled how, within days of a new book being released abroad, copies could find their way to Indian streets. Someone would buy the new edition, fly back to India and the presses would get to work.
Archer was a good friend of the late Nawab Pataudi
From 2008 onwards, India became a regular part of Archer’s international tours, and he often seemed to enjoy the enthusiasm here in a way that was quite different from the more restrained response he received elsewhere. He called Indians among the biggest readers in the world and spoke warmly about the country's love of physical books.He had his own affection for India too. RK Narayan was a writer he admired deeply, and he considered him worthy of the Nobel Prize in Literature. Cricket gave him another connection with the country. He became friendly with Indian cricketing greats including Sunil Gavaskar, Kapil Dev, Rahul Dravid, Anil Kumble and Mansur Ali Khan Pataudi. With his usual flair, Archer once called himself the “Sachin Tendulkar of England”.Indian readers wanted even more from him. But Archer didn't have to write an India novel to become part of Indian literary memory. India had already made him its own.That is why his death brings back more than memories of a bestselling author. It brings back an entire reading culture. The book cupboards in our parents' homes. The school libraries. The railway stalls. The borrowed paperbacks. The books we were told were too adult for us and read anyway. The evenings when there was nothing urgent to do and a novel could fill the entire night.For this generation of Indian readers, Archer was never quite a foreign author. He was the writer whose novels moved from one bedroom to another, from one cousin to another, from one schoolbag to another. He was there when many of us were discovering that reading could be more than something you did for school.
Archer didn't change the way we read because he was a great literary stylist. He changed it because he made reading irresistible. He understood that a book does not have to teach you anything, improve you or make you more sophisticated. It simply has to make you want to turn the page.For millions of Indians, opening an Archer novel still brings back a particular kind of memory: the smell of platform tea on a train journey, a dog-eared paperback borrowed from a classmate, a book pulled out of a crowded cupboard on a lazy afternoon, or the quiet excitement of staying awake under the covers because there was only one more chapter left.For those who grew up with his books and in those times, saying goodbye to Jeffrey Archer feels a lot like saying goodbye to a part of the India we grew up in and loved dearly. An India we miss sorely in these crazy times.
While not jumping with joy seeing every dog that comes her way (to the bewilderment of the dog owner and the dog), Haimanti fantasizes about fantasy books or classics to read and re-read. That could be the gist of it all, except for the aroma of biryani that beckons; or that idea that's stuck in the head and refuses to go till it's penned down.

Ten injured in knife attack at Polish school
WARSAW – Ten people were injured in a knife attack at a school in Ostroleka in north-eastern Poland on Oct 7, the town’s mayor said, with police detaining the 19-year-old suspect, who was among those hurt, shortly after the incident.
Mayor Pawel Niewiadomski told reporters that nine people had been taken to hospital but that none of them was in a life-threatening condition.
“The injured included five students, two teachers, and two bystanders, as well as the perpetrator, who inflicted self-harm,” he said.
Police said the suspect was a student at the school and that he had attacked people with a machete.
They confirmed that bomb disposal experts were checking the attacker’s backpack but were unable to say if anything had been found.
Students barricaded themselves in classrooms
The attack took place at a vocational school for teenagers.
Fire brigade spokesman Adrian Stupski told state news channel TVP Info that students had barricaded themselves into classrooms in self-defence before they were evacuated.
The authorities said the attack happened around 9am GMT.
Police said they detained the suspect about 20 minutes after the attack and posted a photo on social media platform X showing a man they appeared to have apprehended lying face down in a wooded area.
Town hall spokeswoman Katarzyna Ogniewska told reporters that all schools in Ostroleka were closed and that children were safe.
The motives behind the attack were unclear. Such incidents are rare in Poland, but in September police detained a 13-year-old suspected of planning an attack and found a knife in his bag. REUTERS

Hungary agrees to opening of negotiating clusters 2 and 3 for Ukraine
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
13:29:00 EEST
19:29:00 KST

Hungary agrees to opening of negotiating clusters 2 and 3 for Ukraine
Hungary has agreed to allow Ukraine to move forward in its EU accession negotiations, clearing the way for the opening of Clusters 2 (Internal Market) and 3 (Competitiveness and Inclusive Growth).
Source: European Pravda, citing an EU source familiar with the negotiations
Details: Budapest has lifted the block that until now had prevented Ukraine from moving to the next stage in the procedure for opening negotiating clusters 2 and 3.
"COELA [the Working Party on Enlargement and Countries Negotiating Accession to the EU] has approved the screening results for Clusters 2 and 3 for Ukraine, and today at Coreper, the EU member states' ambassadors agreed to send letters to the governments of Ukraine and Moldova inviting them to present their negotiating positions," the European Pravda source said.
The source said the next procedural steps could be completed very quickly.
The EU's draft negotiating position on both clusters is due to be drawn up at a COELA meeting in the coming days.
EU member states are expected to be able to agree on the negotiating position for opening the clusters as early as Monday 12 October, after the Verkhovna Rada (Ukrainian parliament) adopts legislative amendments on education in national minority languages.
Once the EU negotiating position has been approved, a Ukraine-EU intergovernmental conference could be held the following day, 13 October, and Clusters 2 and 3 could be formally opened.
Hungary had blocked approval of the screening results for these clusters for several months, preventing Ukraine from moving on to the next procedural stages required for them to be opened.
Background:
- A bill on education in national minority languages was registered in the Verkhovna Rada on 1 October. Its adoption was expected to help lift Hungary's veto, which had blocked progress on the two negotiating clusters.
- On 6 October, the European Commission adopted a package of proposals on pre-enlargement policy reviews, which are intended to enable the EU to admit new members, including Ukraine.
- European Enlargement Commissioner Marta Kos outlined five groups of measures proposed by the European Commission for future EU enlargement: greater use of qualified-majority voting and limits on vetoes in certain areas; closer integration of candidate countries into parts of the EU before membership; safeguards to prevent new members from backsliding on the rule of law, democracy and fundamental rights; adjustments to EU policies to accommodate enlargement, including targeted measures for sensitive Ukrainian agricultural products; and roadmaps for the four most advanced candidate countries.

US troops slapped with curfew, alcohol ban over Okinawa murder
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
10:29:00 UTC
19:29:00 KST

U.S. forces on Okinawa were hit with a 48-hour alcohol ban and a 30-day curfew Wednesday following the murder of a woman allegedly committed by a U.S. Marine.
The case has triggered outrage in Japan, where any crimes involving U.S. forces have long inflamed criticism of the troops' presence.
Genta Koja, the governor of Okinawa – where the bulk of the 54,000 U.S. military personnel in Japan are based – told Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi during a meeting in Tokyo Wednesday that there was an "urgent need to reduce base-related burdens" on the island, without providing specifics.
"The robbery-murder this time hugely shocked local residents," he said, requesting a committee be convened swiftly to discuss the issue.
Earlier Benjamin T. Watson, Okinawa area coordinator and commanding general of III Marine Expeditionary Force, announced a "complete prohibition of alcohol consumption on or off base" starting Wednesday.
Watson said that the 48-hour period – described as "an operational pause" – would give commanders the time to lead training with all service members on "standards, discipline, and our responsibilities as members of the Okinawan community."
Operations will cease during this period and "we will not allow off-base liberty," said Watson in a statement posted on X late Tuesday.
The lieutenant general, the most senior U.S. military figure on Okinawa, also announced a 30-day "period of reflection" beginning Friday.
"During this period, we will implement a curfew in which liberty will expire at 2400 for all hands, meaning you must be back on base in your assigned quarters or at your off-base domicile from midnight to 0500."
Police said Sunday that a US Marine stationed on Okinawa was arrested on suspicion of killing a 39-year-old woman at a hotel in the city of Naha and stealing her wallet.
Local media reported she was choked to death and that the Marine is denying the allegations.
The United States has around 54,000 military personnel stationed in Japan, mostly on Okinawa.
Crimes committed by U.S. personnel have been a thorn in relations between the close security allies.
Koja, who won the gubernatorial election last month, is the first Okinawa leader in 12 years who approved of a contentious U.S. military base relocation plan.
The central government plan is to keep the U.S. Marine Corps' Futenma air base on Okinawa's main island, but move it to a less populated location.
On Wednesday, Koja also met Defense Minister Shinjiro Koizumi in Tokyo where he said the murder case had "caused deep anxiety" among Okinawa residents.
"The prefectural government has repeatedly demanded that the U.S. military take measures to prevent a recurrence every time an incident occurs, but the fact that such an incident has happened again forces us to conclude that discipline within the U.S. forces and their human rights education are not functioning at all," he told Koizumi.
Koizumi said that he would "advance discussions with the United States on how to implement effective measures" to prevent such incidents occurring.
Last year, a Japanese court sentenced a U.S. Marine accused of choking and attempting to rape a woman in her 20s to seven years in prison.
In 2017, a former U.S. Marine and civilian military base worker was sentenced to life in prison for the rape and murder of a local woman in Okinawa.
The same year, U.S. Forces Japan banned all personnel from consuming alcohol after an intoxicated U.S. Marine crashed his vehicle into a mini-truck, killing its 61-year-old local driver.

Bill for new election law passes confidence tests before final vote
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
12:28:25 CEST
19:28:25 KST

A bill presented by the parties of
Premier Giorgia Meloni's ruling coalition to bring in a new
election law passed the last of three important confidence votes
in the Lower House on Wednesday, clearing the way for the final
vote, which will be a secret ballot, on Thursday.
                                    
After articles 1 and 2 of the bill got the green light with ease
in confidence votes on Tuesday, article 3 was approved in
similar fashion with 228 votes in favour and 144 against.
                                    
This show of unity from the ruling alliance suggests the bill
should have no problem passing the final vote, even though the
secret nature of the ballot makes it easier for lawmakers to
buck the line of their parties without facing consequences.
                                    
The opposition has cried foul about the drive to overhaul the
electoral system, saying the ruling alliance is changing it
because it fears losing the general election set to take place
next year and wants to minimize the chances of this happening.
                                    
The bill will see the current system, a mix of
first-past-the-post and proportional representation, replaced
with a proportional-representation system with bonus seats for
the coalition that obtains the most votes, as long as it reaches
a threshold of 42%, to ensure it has a working majority in
parliament.
                                    
If no coalition reaches the threshold, or the votes for the
Lower House and the Senate produce different results, a purely
proportional system is used.
                                    
The opposition have said that, among other things, the
envisioned system of bonus seats is unconstitutional.
                                    
Coalitions will have to say who their candidate to be premier is
before the election.
                                    
The bill will also give voters the option to express preferences
for up to three candidates out of six on a party list in which
candidates names must alternate according to gender.
                                    
The opposition says that in reality this gives "fake
preferences" as the head of the ticket would always be
"blocked", arguing this was also be a step back for equality,
as, in theory, it would be possible for all the ticket heads to
be men.
                                    
The current system does not give voters any option to express
preferences about which of the candidates on a party list they
want to represent them.

NATO Military Committee delegation in Kyiv: Russia will not succeed in undermining support for Ukraine
Cavo Dragone made this statement in a video address from Kyiv, according to a Ukrinform correspondent.
“After an eight-year hiatus, the NATO Military Committee comes back to Kyiv on an official visit. But while we were not physically here, Ukraine is in our thoughts, discussions, decisions, and following action every single day. This visit fulfills the promise I made to the Commander-in-Chief of the Armed Forces of Ukraine, Mykhailo Drapaty, my good friend, during our last conversation in August of this year,” he emphasized.

“We are here in full strength with a a clear message: the bond between NATO and Ukraine is stronger and stronger. In facing Russia continued aggression against Ukraine and its reckless hybrid activities in NATO countries. We stand unwavering with Ukraine in the heroic defense of its sovereignty, territorial integrity, and the future of its people,” Kavo Dragone emphasized.
The delegation included military representatives from 32 Alliance member states. They arrived to hear the latest assessment of the situation on the front lines from the Commander-in-Chief and the General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine and to learn how they could further support Ukraine.
The Chairman of the Military Committee added that the delegation members paid tribute to all Ukrainian soldiers, especially those who gave their lives or were wounded.
“To those who think that by perpetrating act of sabotage, cyberattacks, and violations of the airspace in national NATO territory, they will undermine this support and our resolve, I will respond. You are failing. NATO support for Ukraine continues to grow and our unity is stronger than ever. Russia bears full responsibility for this dangers and unacceptable behavior,” Kavo Dragone emphasized.
As reported by Ukrinform, NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte stated that the allies must be prepared for further hostile actions by Russia against the Alliance, and the response to them must be increased support for Ukraine.

UK Detains Seventh Suspect Over Possible Attack on Fairford Air Base
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
10:27:33 UTC
19:27:33 KST

UK police have detained a seventh suspect in connection with an alleged plot to carry out a terrorist attack near Fairford Air Base in Gloucestershire.
Reuters reported that the 22-year-old British man was detained in Westminster, London, on Tuesday. He is suspected of preparing terrorist attacks.
Law enforcement officers also searched a property in the area but provided no details about what they may have found. The man remains in custody.
“This investigation remains ongoing, and our specialist teams continue to carry out extensive inquiries into the circumstances surrounding the events near RAF Fairford,” said Vicki Evans, the senior national counter-terrorism coordinator.
Earlier in the investigation, six men aged between 23 and 25 were detained, including a man who holds both British and Iranian citizenship.
All six were later released on bail. However, they remain under investigation and must comply with restrictions on their movements and contacts.
UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham said there are signs that Iran may have been involved in an alleged plot to carry out a terrorist attack near Fairford Air Base.
On September 27, British police were alerted to three suspicious vehicles traveling toward the airfield. Bomb disposal officers were sent to the scene, and around 85 households in the area were evacuated as a precaution.
After examining the three vans, police said they had found no improvised explosive devices. However, they did find a quantity of petrol.
UK counter-terrorism police reported that they were investigating several possibilities, including whether the suspects may have been acting on behalf of a foreign state. At the time, officials did not publicly name any specific country.
The Iranian Embassy in the UK rejected claims of possible Iranian involvement, calling them baseless. Following Burnham’s remarks, Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi also denied the allegations.
Fairford is one of the UK’s key air bases and is also used by US military aircraft, including aircraft involved in strikes on Iranian territory. Amid the investigation into the alleged terror plot, the US withdrew all of its B-1B bombers from the air base on October 4.
