25-year-old Natalia, born in Russia, served in the Israeli army, returned to Ukraine during the full-scale invasion, and join the Armed Forces of Ukraine
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
10:10:13 UTC
19:10:13 KST

Natalia is 25 years old and from Odesa. She has served in two armies—the Israeli and Ukrainian militaries. In the Armed Forces of Ukraine, she has, among other things, carried out missions as part of a UAV, FPV drone, and strike-wing crew on the Zaporizhzhia and Kupiansk fronts, NV reported on 5 October.
During the Russo-Ukrainian war, women in Ukraine have the right to voluntarily enlist in the military. As of March, more than 75,000 women were serving in the armed forces, more than 55,000 of them as service members, the commander-in-chief said, and their number has been growing every year. Recently, discussion around the mandatory mobilization of women has intensified. Keith Kellogg, former US Special Presidential Envoy for Ukraine under President Donald Trump, said that he considered mobilizing women in Ukraine appropriate. In response, Iryna Vereshchuk, Deputy Head of the Office of the President of Ukraine, said she would rather see more missiles and more will from the United States than advice to mobilize women.
In Israel, Natalia served in a search-and-rescue brigade as a rescue soldier and in the engineering corps during a deployment along the northern border.
Natalia was born in Russia’s Saint Petersburg but does not remember her life there
The young woman was born in St. Petersburg, where her family lived at the time. When she was a year and a half old, her mother returned to Odesa with her and her older son. Natalia says she remembers her life exclusively in Ukraine.
She spent the first nearly two years studying at Lviv University, but later decided to leave the university and look for other educational opportunities. Natalia studied, among other places, in Denmark through a scholarship program. After completing it, she planned to enroll at a European university to study sound engineering, but the coronavirus pandemic began at that time.
She moved to Israel under a program for Jewish youth at the end of 2020. After the program ended, due to quarantine restrictions and closed airports, Natalia faced a choice: obtain a work visa or acquire citizenship under the Law of Return. She chose the latter—and with it, she also became obligated to perform military service.
In May 2022, Natalia joined the Israeli military and chose a combat unit.
“When the war started in Israel itself, I still had six months of mandatory service left. I was discharged and immediately transferred to reserve service. Once I managed to resolve all the bureaucratic issues so that this would not be considered desertion, I returned to Ukraine,” the young woman says.
Natalia returned to Ukraine in March 2025, and in August signed a contract with the Armed Forces of Ukraine.
“The army—both Israeli and Ukrainian—gives you a deeper understanding of what society is made of”
Among the advantages of the Ukrainian army, she highlights its ability to quickly adapt to circumstances. In particular, she mentions the use of drones, OSINT, and solving complex technological tasks with minimal resources.
“The West could learn from this situational agility. They often spend huge budgets on developments that should be cheap and mass-produced,” the veteran says.
However, such Ukrainian ingenuity is largely a consequence of a lack of funding, Natalia notes.
In the Israeli military, Natalia highlights society’s readiness for the constant threat of war and more systematic planning of military service.
“There, preparation for and perception of the army begin at school: by the age of 14–15, teenagers already understand where they want to go, what skills they need, and undergo selection for special or intelligence units,” the young woman says.
She then gives the opposite example of the situation in Ukraine.
This Ukrainian female soldier flies one of war’s heaviest drones. She turns down promotion twice to keep doing it
“In Ukraine, with very rare exceptions, people hide until they are mobilized, and suddenly face the reality of conscription without having any understanding of the system,” the veteran says.
Asked how adapted the Ukrainian army is to women, she answered: “In no way,” adding that the Israeli army is “also largely not fully adapted.”
In Ukraine, this is reflected, in particular, in the provision of clothing and equipment that often does not correspond to women’s sizes and physiology. She says she had to purchase her own anatomically fitted body armor. She cited the example of veteran Natalia Lishchyshyna, who had her breasts amputated due to prolonged wearing of body armor that was not adapted to the female anatomy.
In Israel, by contrast, there is a practice of reimbursing expenses for equipment that service members purchase at their own expense.
Serving in the military in both countries provides an opportunity to better understand what society is actually made of, the young woman says.
“The army—both Israeli and Ukrainian—gives you a deeper understanding of what society is made of. You encounter people you would never have crossed paths with in your civilian bubble because of differences in views or socioeconomic circumstances,” Natalia says.
She believes this makes it easier to accept mistakes, difficulties, and new challenges.
The Ukrainian army is not adapted to women in any way, Natalia says
In Natalia’s view, the problem is not only the living and working conditions but, above all, the lack of mechanisms necessary for the systematic mandatory mobilization of women. At the same time, she believes voluntary recruitment should be encouraged and expanded.
One of the problems is the lack of a legal procedure for temporary childcare in cases when both parents are simultaneously carrying out combat missions, Natalia says, stressing that she means the period of their service, rather than situations involving the death of one of the parents.
Another shortcoming is insufficient protection against sexual violence and harassment in the Ukrainian military.
“Here, any complaint goes through the direct chain of command. If the commander is not interested in resolving the problem or is involved in it themselves, the woman is left defenseless,” the veteran says.
In Israel, by contrast, there is a separate hotline and mechanisms for documenting such cases without directly approaching a commander.
Women in combat positions can also still be taken insufficiently seriously, denied participation in combat missions, or transferred to staff positions without their consent.
Natalia also emphasizes the lack of systematic military training for civilian women “at any level” and gives school education as an example.
“Even with the weak level of the school curriculum for the subject ‘Defense of Ukraine,’ boys had at least some basic knowledge. Girls were not involved in it at all,” the veteran says.
For now, Natalia believes that women’s military service should remain voluntary, as society as a whole is still not ready to fully accept women in the military.

PRYLUKY, Ukraine -- Rescuers frantically picked through rubble and debris of a destroyed apartment building in northern Ukraine as they search for survivors of a Russian missile attack that killed at least 18 people.
At least 20 people nationwide, including two in the capital Kyiv, were killed in the October 7 barrage.
The bombardment was part of near-daily attacks that have steadily increased in frequency and ferocity, as the Kremlin struggles on the battlefield front line.
President Volodymyr Zelenskyy called it one of the "most vile" attacks in recent memory, and he noted they occurred on the birthday of Russian President Vladimir Putin.
Russian forces "destroyed" a residential building "as a birthday 'gift' to Putin," Zelenskyy said in a post to X.
At least 10 other such buildings were damaged elsewhere, along with Ukraine's energy infrastructure, one of Moscow's other "key targets," he said.
In Pryluky, which is about 150 kilometers east of Kyiv, firefighters, emergency workers, and local volunteers dug through bricks and building debris searching for survivors of the attack. The five-story building was mostly torn apart by the Russian strike with its roof destroyed, windows blown out.
"The fire was right in front of my eyes. There were explosions. I was screaming in my apartment. Extremely scary. I can't describe it," one woman, who gave her name as Lidiya, told Current Time.
"So many people have died. I knew everyone here," she added, holding back tears.
With a fifth wartime winter approaching, Russian strikes on Ukraine have become a daily occurrence.
Moscow has previously sought to pressure Kyiv into accepting its hard-line demands by attacking the country's energy infrastructure and leaving thousands without heat or electricity amid freezing temperatures.
Since this year, however, Kyiv has increasingly responded to Russian attacks with a campaign of long-range strikes targeting military and energy sites inside Russia and middle-range strikes targeting its key logistics in Ukraine's occupied eastern and southern regions.
Tanker Hit In Black Sea
Following the latest Russian attacks, Zelenskyy later reported on what he called Kyiv's "just responses." He said Ukrainian forces had targeted two of Russia's oil facilities and a military training ground overnight on October 7, adding, "There was also a response in the Black Sea."
Hours earlier, Russia's Transport Ministry said a Liberian-flagged tanker had been attacked by "naval drones" near the Black Sea resort city of Sochi.
The ministry reported an intense fire following the attack, saying that "crude oil is burning openly" on the surface of the Black Sea. It later added that the crew of 23, all Indian citizens, had been rescued and the fire had been extinguished.
According to the Ukrainian monitoring site BlackSeaNews, the vessel was used by Russia as part of its so-called shadow fleet, a network of vessels used to transport Russian fuel and evade sanctions.
Sochi's local authorities said access to the city's coast and beaches was being restricted. Previous Ukrainian strikes on energy targets in southern Russia have caused oil slicks, prompted beach closures, and led to toxic black rainfall.
The developments came amid renewed US interest in negotiating a diplomatic settlement to the long-running war.
While US President Donald Trump has long said it is one of the key goals of his presidency, Kyiv and Moscow remain far apart in their negotiating positions.
Since the beginning of Russia's full-scale invasion in February 2022, the Kremlin has shown no willingness to compromise on its key demands, including full control over Ukraine's key eastern Donetsk region, a stronghold Russian forces have not yet been able to capture.

Geert Wilders, the right-wing Dutch leader known for his strong support for Israel, responded by accusing Jetten of betraying Israel and the Jewish people through measures including boycotts, condemnations, support for the International Criminal Court and sanctions. He also accused the government of leaving the Netherlands vulnerable to the type of violence Israel experienced on Oct. 7. AI generated
MOSCOW/LONDON - Russia's health regulator said on Oct 7 there were no risks of an epidemic breaking out in Siberia after a plague institute worker there died, as the World Health Organization pressed Moscow for more information about her cause of death.
Russian authorities say the 28-year-old laboratory worker died on Oct 2 from pneumonia of an as-yet unestablished origin, in a case that has prompted international concern, including from US President Donald Trump, and which saw around 200 people initially placed in quarantine.
Rospotrebnadzor, Russia’s health watchdog, said in a statement it was winding down precautionary measures it had put in place after concluding there was no risk of an epidemic and that it had shared its latest information with the WHO.
No cases of plague had been detected among anyone who had come into contact with the deceased worker, Darya Shipilova, it said, and 90% of those placed in quarantine had been released after nearly 5,000 lab tests had failed to detect any dangerous pathogens.
It said Shipilova had been vaccinated and had therefore been “immune to the dangerous infections with which she worked”.
It did not say though what had caused the pneumonia which killed her or how she fell ill.
More information
Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, the director general of the WHO in Geneva, said in a statement on X earlier on Oct 7 that his organisation needed more information from Russia to understand what had happened.
“WHO has requested further information to clarify the cause of the severe pneumonia, the pathogen that prompted the public health measures, and media reports of a second employee with pneumonia of undetermined cause,” he said.
“Timely, complete and transparent information sharing under the International Health Regulations is essential to clarify conflicting reports and enable an accurate assessment of potential public health risks.”
‘False information’
The Kremlin said Russia had properly informed the WHO about the incident in line with established procedures.
When asked about the WHO’s request to respond to reports about a second person in Siberia allegedly falling ill, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov urged caution when it came to using media reports as a reference for what was happening.
“There is a great deal of media coverage, and the vast majority of what the media are reporting about this situation is false information,” said Peskov.
He advised the media and others to rely on information provided by the health regulator. It did not immediately respond to a Reuters comment request on Oct 7 about the WHO’s questions.
Cause of death unknown
Some Western media outlets have reported — citing unnamed “Russian media” — that a second person in Siberia had died, saying they had died of plague.
Reuters was unable to find any such stories in Russian media or any evidence that a second person in Siberia had died although some bloggers on social media were making — without evidence — such assertions.
Contacted by Reuters, the WHO said it had nothing further to add on the matter beyond what Tedros — who was due to give a press conference later on Oct 7 — had already posted on X.
Tedros’ call for more information echoed that of US Secretary of State Marco Rubio who has also said Moscow needs to share more information about the incident.
Pneumonia, a lung infection, can have a variety of causes including plague as well as other bacterial infections or viral respiratory diseases, such as flu or COVID-19. REUTERS

EU wants to impose a tax on U.S. big tech - media
Kyiv • UNN
Brussels is considering expanding the CORE levy to large companies, including Apple, Meta and Google. In this way, the EU seeks to increase revenue and avoid conflict with the United States.
Brussels is considering taxing large American technology groups (Big Tech) by expanding the levy on large corporations in an effort to increase EU revenues while avoiding a backlash from the Trump administration. Financial Times reports, writes UNN.
Details
The European Commission is reportedly working on new ways to generate more revenue from technology groups such as Apple, Meta and Google without singling them out, Reuters writes.
The report says that Brussels has been considering changes to its "Corporate Resource for Europe" (CORE) proposal, which would require all companies operating in the EU with annual revenue exceeding €100 million ($112.32 million) to pay a one-off annual tax contribution.
In its current form, CORE requires these companies to pay a fixed annual levy of between €100,000 and €750,000, covering only a small portion of a multinational company's profits.
"Some (EU) capitals are opposed to a purely digital tax because they do not want to upset the Americans, while many others are opposed to CORE," an EU official told the FT. "The solution is to expand (the tax) so that it covers virtually all large companies."
"The European Commission remains ready to support the Council (of the EU) and the European Parliament in reaching an agreement on a new own-resources package... as these are essential to ensuring adequate funding for our shared priorities over the next decade," a spokesperson for the EU executive told Reuters.
Apple, Google, Meta and the Computer & Communications Industry Association (CCIA), which represents several U.S. technology companies, did not immediately respond to Reuters' requests for comment outside normal working hours.
U.S. President Donald Trump threatened in June to impose a 100% tariff on all goods from any country that levies a digital services tax on American companies.
The Office of the U.S. Trade Representative, which has long threatened European countries with retaliatory tariffs if they impose such taxes, claims that these levies discriminate against American companies, which dominate the sector worldwide.

Lithuania gets its first Switchblade 600 attack drones
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
10:07:57 UTC
19:07:57 KST

- Lithuania has received its first batch of AeroVironment Switchblade 600 anti-armor loitering munitions, the country's defense ministry said.
- The drones come from a December 2022 deal worth about €45 million (about $50.4 million) signed with the U.S. government.
Lithuania has received its first batch of Switchblade 600 loitering munitions, U.S.-made attack drones built to hunt tanks and other armored vehicles, the Lithuanian Ministry of National Defence said on X.
The ministry did not disclose how many drones arrived, which units will operate them, or when the remaining deliveries are due. Lithuania signed the purchase with the U.S. government in December 2022 in a deal worth about €45 million (about $50.4 million) that also covers launch and control equipment, a maintenance package and a training simulator.
“The system gives the Lithuanian Armed Forces a new long-range precision strike capability against armored targets,” the Lithuanian Ministry of National Defence wrote.
AeroVironment, based in Arlington, Virginia, builds the Switchblade 600. Soldiers launch it from a tube and guide it with a tablet-based control unit, letting the drone circle over an area until they pick a target and send it diving in. The company lists more than 40 minutes of flight time and a demonstrated standoff range of more than 40 km (25 miles) for the original version, which carries the same type of anti-armor warhead used on the Javelin missile.
When the contract was signed, then-Defence Minister Arvydas Anušauskas said the drones would let Lithuanian forces destroy enemy tanks and other armored equipment up to 40 km away, a capability the military had not had before. The ministry said Lithuania was the first country after the United States to buy the system, and a ministry spokesperson declined at the time to say how many Switchblade 600s had been ordered. Deliveries were scheduled for 2025 and 2026.
The 2022 announcement also said the United States would supply the smaller Switchblade 300, paid for with U.S. military assistance funds. The ministry’s latest post did not mention the Switchblade 300.
AeroVironment unveiled an upgraded Switchblade 600 Block 2 in October 2025, with about 20 percent more endurance, more than 50 minutes of flight time and a reach of more than 100 km (62 miles) when control is handed off between operators. The company said it had raised Switchblade 600 production from 40 to 240 systems a month over the previous year. The ministry did not say which version Lithuania received.
Ukraine has used the Switchblade 600 in combat against Russian armor after the United States began sending the drones following Russia’s full-scale invasion in 2022.
The Switchblade order is one of several major U.S. purchases Lithuania has made in recent years, alongside HIMARS rocket launchers, Joint Light Tactical Vehicles and UH-60 Black Hawk helicopters.

Three Years After October 7, Netanyahu Faces Accountability Questions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
10:07:00 UTC
19:07:00 KST

Israelis began marking the third anniversary of the October 7, 2023 Hamas attacks on Wednesday, with 1,200 people killed and 251 hostages taken in the assault, while this year's commemorations are the first in which all hostages or their remains are back in Israel.
At the site of the Nova music festival, where more than 300 people were killed three years ago, families gathered at dawn and observed a moment of silence. Hamas militants had entered the festival site on October 7, 2023, using cars and paragliders, and mourners bowed their heads at 6:29 a.m. (03:29 GMT) among portraits of those killed, with flowers placed beneath them.
Israel also launched new strikes on Gaza on Wednesday as the anniversary was marked, with Palestinian officials reporting two deaths. Loud explosions from Gaza could be heard across the border from the Nova festival site as relatives gathered to remember the victims.
Al-Shifa hospital in Gaza City said two people had been killed in an Israeli strike overnight. Gaza's civil defense identified one of them as Mohamed Tamous, saying he was a volunteer with the agency, which operates as an emergency rescue service under Hamas.
The military campaign has left extensive destruction across Gaza over the past three years. Satellite images show that the Israeli military has systematically demolished Rafah and other cities, towns and districts in some areas, with rubble also cleared away.
Demolition operations involving bulldozers and explosives have continued since the Israel-Hamas ceasefire agreement reached a year ago, while the military has consolidated control over about 60% of the territory it still holds.
Three years ago, thousands of Hamas-led militants crossed from Gaza into Israel in a surprise assault, killing 1,205 people and taking 251 hostages back to Gaza, according to figures cited by France 24. Israel responded with a major military campaign in Gaza, in which at least 74,347 people have been killed, according to the enclave's Hamas-run health ministry.
The attacks have left a deep impact on Israel, where voters are due to elect a new parliament on October 27, making the events a central issue in the election campaign.
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu is seeking another term, while questions about what he knew before the attacks continue to surround Israel's longest-serving leader. Reports that Arab leaders warned him about a possible Hamas offensive have continued to emerge.
Israeli journalists Shlomi Eldar and Ruth Yuval reported that UAE President Mohammed bin Zayed al-Nahyan warned Netanyahu by phone about 10 days before the October 7 attacks that a major confrontation with Hamas was approaching.
In excerpts from their book first published by Haaretz on September 8, the journalists cited three foreign senior sources and a Palestinian adviser to bin Zayed as confirming the call. They reported that the 45-minute conversation included a warning that former Hamas leader Yahya Sinwar was preparing a major operation that could cause “bloodshed” and even “destabilize the region.”
According to the report, bin Zayed was surprised by Netanyahu's reaction, as the Israeli prime minister “reacted calmly” and said “Israel was prepared for any scenario.”
The report said bin Zayed later told former CIA Director William J. Burns about the conversation. It also alleged that Netanyahu did not inform the Shin Bet security agency, the Mossad intelligence agency or his army chief of staff about the call.
Netanyahu's office rejected the allegations, calling the report a “wicked fabrication with clear political timing” by left-wing Israeli officials and saying that no warning had been given.
Netanyahu subsequently sued Haaretz for defamation, while the newspaper has stood by its reporting. The New York Times has also supported the account and published additional details.
The question of whether Netanyahu had advance knowledge of the October 7 attacks has also been fueled by reports that Egyptian intelligence chief Abbas Kamel warned him days before Hamas crossed the border. Those reports were published by The Atlantic and the Wall Street Journal.
The UAE has not directly responded to the allegations but has said that “when necessary, all relevant intelligence has been and continues to be communicated” since Abu Dhabi restored relations with Israel in 2020.
Netanyahu made a secret visit to Abu Dhabi on September 27 and met bin Zayed for about an hour, according to Israel's Channel 12. One source said the two discussed the Haaretz report and that Netanyahu asked the Emirati leader to deny warning him about an impending attack.
Netanyahu's office dismissed that account as “fake news,” while the official Emirates News Agency said the meeting focused on “bilateral relations.”
Netanyahu's response to the allegations has largely involved shifting responsibility elsewhere, in contrast with several senior Israeli security officials who have accepted responsibility for failures surrounding October 7.
Former military Chief of Staff Herzi Halevi took responsibility for failing to prevent the attacks and resigned in January 2025. An internal Israel Defense Forces investigation conducted after his resignation described the events as one of its “greatest failures.”
Several months later, the Israeli government dismissed Shin Bet chief Ronen Bar. The decision was partly linked to an internal report on the October 7 attack, while Netanyahu also cited an ongoing “lack of trust” in Bar as a reason for the dismissal.
Bar responded in a letter that Netanyahu's arguments amounted to “unsubstantiated accusations” and accused him of seeking to “prevent investigations into the events leading up to October 7.”
On September 28, only hours after Netanyahu renewed his accusations against Bar, the former intelligence chief threatened to sue him for defamation. According to The Times of Israel, Bar accused Netanyahu of “attempting to deflect blame away from himself by levelling accusations at those who warned him in real time.”
Israeli journalist Nicolas Rouger, author of "Netanyahu – Agent of Chaos," said Netanyahu had responded to the allegations by directing blame toward what he described as a “deep state” made up of security services and left-wing bureaucratic elites.
Netanyahu has also alleged that his security chiefs deliberately allowed him to sleep for hours after Hamas began its assault because they feared he would respond aggressively and immediately place the entire military on alert.
"If they would have woken me up, everything would have looked different," Netanyahu said in a campaign video posted on X in August.
A schedule released by Netanyahu's office disputes that account, stating that he was informed at 6:29 a.m. of an attack originating from the Gaza Strip.
Sylvaine Bulle, an expert on Israeli society and sociology professor at Paris's EHESS university, said the allegations had not seriously damaged Netanyahu politically.
"Whether it’s his ongoing corruption trial or the allegations of ignored warnings, scandals seem to roll off him like water off a duck’s back," Bulle said. She described him as politically agile and argued that his efforts to avoid responsibility had strengthened his support.
Netanyahu has repeatedly opposed calls for a state inquiry into the October 7 attacks, even though the military and intelligence agencies have conducted their own investigations. He has argued that such an inquiry should only begin after the war ends.
Despite broad public support in Israel for an independent investigation, Netanyahu said in November last year that most Israelis did not support such a commission and proposed a separate committee to be established by the prime minister.
Gadi Eisenkot, a former military chief and Netanyahu's main challenger ahead of the October 27 election, has accused the prime minister of avoiding responsibility for security failures. Eisenkot rejected Netanyahu's explanations, including his claim that he was not awakened early enough on the morning of the attack.
In a post on X, Eisenkot said Netanyahu had “ignored” dozens of warnings before October 7 and declared him “unfit” to lead.
Eisenkot and other opponents of Netanyahu have pledged to establish an independent commission of inquiry if they win the election.
Some analysts believe Israeli voters may not be persuaded by a centrist bloc led by Eisenkot as the electorate continues shifting to the right, particularly among younger voters.
Bulle said the opposition had limited political weight and that its campaign lacked sufficient focus on domestic policy, social justice, housing and regional inequality, allowing religious parties to take greater control of social issues among religious working-class voters.
Netanyahu may have been weakened somewhat by the reports, but he retains a loyal base.
Rouger said Netanyahu presents himself as a leader capable of guiding Israel through existential threats, while Bulle argued that the trauma of October 7 had strengthened rather than weakened his traditional supporters.
"He is the only person who can turn an entire nation’s fear of existential threat into votes. He has been doing it for three years and it’s working," Bulle said.
The latest polls cited by Haaretz show Eisenkot slightly ahead of Netanyahu before the election, with 54 Knesset seats projected for his bloc against 49 for Netanyahu's current coalition.
Rouger said international criticism had limited influence even among Israelis who oppose Netanyahu, acknowledge corruption allegations against him and consider his leadership chaotic.
He said the International Criminal Court's arrest warrant against Netanyahu over alleged crimes committed in Gaza had been met primarily with accusations of anti-Semitism.
"Israelis only trust the Israeli media," Rouger said. “The rest – who are reporting on the destruction of Gaza, for example – are virtually invisible.”
Separately, Iran-backed Houthis targeted Aden International Airport in Yemen with two ballistic missiles and explosive-laden drones, the government news agency Saba reported Wednesday.
"The terrorist Houthi militias targeted Aden International Airport with two ballistic missiles and explosive-laden drones," Saba said in a post on X.
The Saudi-led coalition fighting Yemen's Houthis said it had intercepted and destroyed a ballistic missile north of Riyadh.
"A ballistic missile launched by the terrorist Houthi militia north of Riyadh was intercepted and destroyed," coalition spokesman Major General Turki al-Maliki said on X.
The two missiles fired toward Aden caused no reported casualties, according to the media office of Aden's security department. The attack came during renewed fighting after weeks of Houthi advances along Yemen's Red Sea coast and a counteroffensive by the Saudi-backed government, which has retaken areas around the strategic Bab al-Mandab Strait with coalition air support.
The airport serves as the main international gateway for parts of Yemen outside Houthi control.
Oil prices climbed on Wednesday while stocks declined as renewed concerns over Middle East energy supplies followed warnings that Iran appeared to be increasing attacks in the Strait of Hormuz.
Investors had earlier looked past another record session on Wall Street, where the Nasdaq and S&P 500 benefited from renewed demand for artificial intelligence stocks and Nvidia moved toward a USD6 trillion market capitalization.
Reports that Middle Eastern exports excluding Iran were returning toward pre-war levels had supported confidence during the week.
The development helped push Brent crude below USD100 a barrel and West Texas Intermediate below USD90, easing inflation concerns and giving central banks more room to avoid raising interest rates.
Both contracts recovered on Tuesday and gained in early Asian trading after figures indicated that Tehran had stepped up attacks on tankers in the Strait of Hormuz.

The Concert for Peace in Maputo commemorates the 1992 Agreements
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
12:05:41 CEST
19:05:41 KST

The Cine Teatro Scala in Maputo, which was sold out for the occasion, hosted the second edition of the Concert for Peace on October 3, an initiative promoted by the Italian Embassy in Mozambique to commemorate the 34th anniversary of the signing of the General Peace Accords in Rome on October 4, 1992. 
   The evening brought together Italian and Mozambican musicians and singers, along with the young members of the Xiqitsi orchestra and choir, conducted by the renowned Mozambican oboist Kika Materula.
                                    
In his opening remarks, the Italian Ambassador to Maputo, Gabriele Annis, highlighted the role of dialogue in building peace and the process that—through the mediation of the Italian government and the Community of Sant’Egidio—led to the end of the Mozambican civil war. “People who had fought each other for years chose to sit at the same table and recognize themselves as part of the same humanity and the same nation,” he stated.
                                    
The ambassador attributed a special role to music, “one of the oldest and most universal languages,” capable of building bridges even in times of division, and which did not fade away during the years of conflict. “It is important to remember: to keep in mind the result achieved and everything that was learned to achieve it. So that we don’t have to start over from scratch every time,” he emphasized.
                                    
Under the artistic direction of Girolamo Deraco and Kika Materula, the concert featured the world premiere of four works, including Deraco’s “United We Sing.” The event is part of the Mozita 2026 festival, organized by the Italian Embassy as a tool for integrated promotion and to launch collaborations between Italy and Mozambique in the field of the creative economy.

Swiss property prices continue to rise in third quarter
Switzerland’s property market continued to rise in the third quarter. Buyers paid an average of 0.8% more for properties than they did in the previous quarter, and 3.3% more than a year earlier, according to the CIFI private property price index published on Wednesday.
In the market for owner-occupied flats, prices rose by 0.8% between July and September, while detached house prices increased by 0.7%, according to a press release. Compared with the same period a year earlier, prices were up 2.8% for flats and 3.9% for detached houses.

Switzerland’s housing shortage: how bad is it?
As a result, property transactions have fallen, leading to a decline in mortgage lending volumes. Despite favourable borrowing conditions, many households still find it difficult to get on the property ladder, the property consultancy said. The firm is a subsidiary of Swiss Marketplace Group.
Investment property, by contrast, continues to attract strong demand, particularly apartment blocks and mixed-use properties with commercial space. This is despite prices rising by 1.4% compared with the second quarter.

Most Republicans in tight midterm distance themselves from Trump, Reuters review finds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
10:04:43 UTC
19:04:43 KST

Most Republicans in tight midterm races distance themselves from Trump, Reuters review finds
Oct 7 - Two-thirds of Republican candidates in competitive US House and Senate races have broken with President Donald Trump on policy or played down ties to him, a Reuters review found, revealing a widespread effort to distance themselves from the president as his unpopularity threatens the party's hold on Congress.
The review of voting records, public statements and campaign materials found candidates in 41 of 62 competitive congressional races seeking some distance from Trump ahead of the November 3 midterm elections.
The candidates have largely criticized or diverged from Trump on individual issues rather than repudiated his broader agenda. The findings suggest an effort to attract independent voters while avoiding a direct break with their party leader.
Policy differences were the most common point of divergence, appearing in 23 of the 62 races.
In 12 contests, the split centered on the Iran conflict, with vulnerable Republicans either voting to curb Trump's war powers or calling publicly for an end to the fighting that has raised gas prices and squeezed household budgets.
Data centers are among the issues dividing Trump and some Republican candidates. Reuters identified three candidates in competitive races who have criticized or sought to slow such projects despite the president's support for faster development.
The shift is notable because Trump has spent the past decade remaking the Republican Party in his own image and has been swift to punish lawmakers and candidates who defied him through primary challenges, personal attacks or public pressure to fall into line.
In response to questions about the Reuters findings, White House spokesman Davis Ingle pointed to the administration's accomplishments and said Trump was "the unequivocal leader, best messenger and unmatched motivator" for the party.
While news organizations have highlighted individual cases of distancing, the Reuters review is the first to systematically measure the trend across competitive races that will decide whether Republicans retain control of either or both chambers of Congress.
A new Reuters/Ipsos poll underscored the challenge facing Republicans: Trump's approval rating remained stuck at a career-low 32%, while registered voters favored Democrats over Republicans 44% to 37% ahead of the midterms. Among independents, Democrats led 37% to 21%.
CREATING DISTANCE FROM TRUMP
Reuters also found a broad effort to play down ties: A dozen candidates removed his name, image or endorsements from campaign websites, most after securing their party's nomination.
Others acted in subtler ways, skipping his events or declining to say whether he should campaign on their behalf.
Direct criticism was relatively rare, underscoring Trump's dominance of the Republican Party and the risks candidates face in openly challenging a president who still commands the loyalty of many ardent supporters.
Candidates distancing themselves from an unpopular president before an election is not unusual. Democrats employed similar tactics in the 2014 and 2022 elections.
While Reuters did not conduct a comparable review of competitive races in the 2018 midterms during Trump's first term, analysts said Trump has rarely faced such widespread pushback by vulnerable Republican candidates.
"(Candidates) are reflecting voter attitudes in these races," said Republican strategist Ron Bonjean. "If (voters) are not with Trump, then they need to show a break."
Privately, campaign advisers told Reuters that candidates needed to dial back ties to Trump to attract independent voters. Publicly, they dismissed criticism of the repositioning.
BALANCING ACT
Republican Senator Pete Ricketts, who faces a tough challenge from independent Dan Osborn in Nebraska, exemplifies the 11 candidates identified by Reuters who broke with Trump on one policy issue while backing him on everything else.
The balancing act was on display this week when Ricketts, who criticized Trump's plan to expand beef imports, joined the president at a Nebraska rally.
"President Trump, I have been fighting for you in Washington," Ricketts told the crowd.
Mariannette Miller-Meeks, a Republican in one of the country's most competitive House races in Iowa, has also shown a growing willingness to break with the administration. She was among 12 candidates identified by Reuters who split with Trump on multiple issues, criticizing his beef-import policy and later voting to limit his war powers in Iran after previously opposing similar measures.
Yet, less than two weeks after her war-powers vote, Miller-Meeks joined Trump at the White House to announce a major steel plant investment in Iowa.
"It is a balancing act," said Republican consultant Jeanette Hoffman, adding that candidates are trying to capitalize on the administration’s successes while creating some distance from Trump because of “how toxic the Trump brand is at the moment.”
SCRUBBING TRUMP REFERENCES
As Republicans in competitive races seek to expand their appeal beyond Trump's core supporters, some candidates have begun dialing back public displays of loyalty to the president.
Mike Beltran, a former Florida state representative running against Democratic US Representative Kathy Castor, is among candidates who have scrubbed prominent references to Trump from their campaign websites.
In August, his homepage featured a photo of Trump and said he stood with the president, according to the Wayback Machine, an internet archive website. Now Beltran's homepage shows only him and his family and makes no mention of Trump.
Beltran's campaign had no immediate response to a Reuters request for comment.
Representative Mike Lawler of New York, facing one of the most competitive US House races, embodies the balancing act confronting many Republicans in battleground districts: staying close to Trump while demonstrating independence from him.
Lawler has highlighted breaks with Trump on issues including temporary legal protections for Haitian immigrants and a Trump-backed proposal to restore Turkey's access to F-35 fighter jets.
His campaign manager Ciro Riccardi said Lawler acts on behalf of his constituency regardless of a president's stance.
Lawler acknowledged the disagreements in a speech to Trump supporters at the Republican midterm convention in September, saying, "The truth is that the president and I don't always agree. And that's OK." REUTERS

Trump makes third Texas trip in a month as Republicans defend longtime stronghold
Oct 7 - US President Donald Trump heads to Texas on Wednesday for the third time in a month, placing unusual focus on a state he won easily in 2024 but where Republicans now face unexpectedly tight midterm election battles as they seek to retain control of Congress.
Trump is due to speak in San Antonio alongside Republican Senate candidate Ken Paxton, who is locked in a close race with Democrat James Talarico. A loss on November 3 would complicate the party's path to retaining its slim Senate majority and mark a major setback in a Republican stronghold.
The rally is Trump's latest effort to mobilize his supporters for Paxton after staging an unusual midterm conventionin Dallas, in part to boost him. But Trump has also publicly criticized his longtime ally, calling Paxton "a pain in the ass sometimes" last week before adding that Republicans "need Ken so badly."
Trump's repeated trips to Texas are part of a broader push in Republican-leaning states, which were expected to be safely in hand but have instead become midterm battlegrounds. His 32-day campaign blitz has taken him through Texas, Oklahoma, Alabama, Ohio and Nebraska, while Vice President JD Vance has campaigned in Alaska. Trump and Vance carried all six states in the 2024 presidential election.
Republicans are struggling as voters focus on high costs and the war with Iran, giving Trump record-low approval ratings. A Reuters/Ipsos poll completed Monday put his approval at 32%, with Democrats leading Republicans 44% to 37% among registered voters.
Trump surprised some Republicans in May by backing Paxton in a party runoff over longtime Senator John Cornyn, whom party leaders saw as a safer bet. Republicans are now spending heavily to defend territory they once expected to win comfortably.
Trump won the state by 14 points in 2024, but recent polls have shown Talarico ahead of Paxton. Republicans are also defending competitive House of Representatives seats in South Texas.
For Trump, the stakes are also personal. James Henson, director of the Texas Politics Project at the University of Texas at Austin, said losing the Senate race would be "devastating for Republicans and devastating for Donald Trump" given his support for Paxton. "I think the president clearly will do a lot to try to avoid that outcome," Henson said.
Trump's political operation has also poured millions into competitive House races. In San Antonio, Republican Carlos De La Cruz, an Air Force veteran, is running in a newly redrawn district, part of a Republican-led remapping that Democrats have called a partisan gerrymander. De La Cruz is expected to speak at Wednesday's rally.
AN UNEASY ALLIANCE
Trump and Paxton's relationship has appeared awkward at times. Paxton was recorded telling donors that Republican candidates' numbers fell after the Trump-centered convention in Dallas, according to The New York Times, while Trump has publicly mocked Paxton's clothes, speaking style and appearance.
"So to be honest with you, the numbers, when we did that convention, it dropped our numbers. Everybody's numbers dropped," Paxton said in the recording. His campaign has disputed suggestions that the remarks amounted to criticism of Trump. A spokesperson did not respond to a request for comment.
A Siena College poll released October 3 showed Talarico leading Paxton 51% to 45% among likely voters. Brandon Rottinghaus, a political science professor at the University of Houston, said rallying Trump's base was "necessary but not sufficient" for Paxton.
"Trump's visits are a Catch-22," Rottinghaus said. "The president can inspire as much as he can repel."
Texas Republican Governor Greg Abbott, a close Trump ally who is also in a closer-than-expected re-election race, plans to skip Wednesday's rally, citing other campaign events.
"My rallies are saving the Republican Party, again," Trump said in an all-caps post on Truth Social on Tuesday.
Republicans are betting Trump can still turn out the voters who powered his 2024 victory even as his broader standing has weakened.
The latest Reuters/Ipsos poll showed that just 24% of Hispanic voters approved of his performance. They were an important part of Trump's success in 2024, when he won nearly half the Hispanic vote, and are a bigger demographic in Texas than most states.
Wednesday's rally is scheduled for the Freeman Coliseum in San Antonio, with Trump expected to speak at 6 p.m. Central Time (2300 GMT). REUTERS

Three years of Gaza genocide: How Israel devastated water and power lifelines
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
10:03:56 UTC
19:03:56 KST

In Gaza, getting enough water is no longer a routine part of daily life.
Instead, families must carry buckets, wait for water trucks and decide how much they can spare for drinking, cooking, bathing or washing clothes.
For children, it means spending hours helping their families collect water instead of going to school.
“Before the war, we did not have this struggle,” Hanadi Al Aff told the International Committee of the Red Cross in June.
Al Aff, one of the many displaced Palestinians, lives with her five children opposite a rehabilitated desalination plant in Gaza City.
“We now carry water in buckets. It has become a burden on our children. Instead of going to school and studying, they carry water,” she said. 
Al Aff said her family did not have enough water for all their needs.  
“We save water and keep it for the most important thing, which is drinking, cooking and bathing the children. If there is extra, we use it for washing the dishes and doing the laundry.”
Three years after Israel began its genocidal war on Gaza in Oct 2023, the territory's water, sanitation and electricity systems remain severely damaged, leaving millions of Palestinians dependent on emergency measures and infrastructure operating far below its former capacity.
According to a survey cited by the UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) in September, 91% of households experienced moderate-to-high water insecurity.
Nearly one-third, 31% of households, had total water access below minimum humanitarian standards, while 57% fell below minimum standards specifically for drinking water.
Meanwhile, 88% households reported difficulties accessing safe and clean sanitation facilities.
The shortages are compounded by damage to the infrastructure on which Gaza's water supply depends.
Another report cited by the UN in September, showed that 88% of above-ground Water, Sanitation and Hygiene (WASH) assets and 76% of underground networks had been damaged.
Red Cross also said in June that water production in Gaza had fallen to around 40% of pre-October 2023 levels, while independent production from wells was less than a third of what it had been before the war.
Gaza's remaining water supply also remains vulnerable to disruptions.
According to a UN humanitarian situation report issued in late September, the three Mekorot water lines from Israel supplied about 40% below contracted quantities during the reporting period because marine algae affected desalination plants in Israel.
In Deir al-Balah, the Al Basa Desalination Plant was operating below capacity because of a brine-pumping failure and overuse of generators.
Humanitarian partners were working to increase groundwater production through wells to partially offset the shortfall.
In August, a UNICEF-supported water well and desalination facility in Deir al-Balah was also severely damaged by a strike, disrupting access to safe drinking water for more than 4,000 people, including about 2,000 children.
The water crisis cannot be separated from Gaza's electricity shortage.
Wells, desalination plants and sewage pumping stations all require electricity to operate.
Yet September UN figures indicate that 90% of energy infrastructure, including the electricity distribution network and associated assets, has been destroyed.
With the electricity system largely unavailable, generators have become essential for keeping remaining water and sanitation infrastructure operating.
But generators themselves depend on fuel.
The Red Cross reported that Gaza has gone for more than two-and-a-half years without a regular electricity supply, leaving people dependent on generators.
Officials cited by the Alliance for Water Justice in Palestine in June estimated that rebuilding the electricity system could take three to five years, even if reconstruction materials were allowed to enter immediately.
The work would require thousands of utility poles, hundreds of kilometers of power cables, transformers, heavy equipment and specialized machinery simply to restore basic services.
The question is not only how much water Palestinians can obtain, but whether it is safe to drink.
In August, health partners collected 938 water samples across Gaza and tested them at the seven water-quality monitoring laboratories that remain functional despite severe operational constraints.
More than 73% of the samples did not meet WHO-recommended free residual chlorine levels, while 18% showed microbiological contamination.
Reinhilde Van De Weerdt, the WHO representative in Palestine, said at a September press briefing that over 6,700 water samples had been tested between January and August.
Microbiological contamination nearly tripled during that period, rising from below 6% in January to more than 18% in August.
She said cases of acute watery diarrhea nearly doubled over the same period.
The deterioration of sanitation is closely linked to the water crisis.
Thirty-nine percent of assessed households reported solid waste accumulating around their shelters, while 36% observed sewage or sludge near where they were living.
The situation is particularly difficult in displacement sites, where families live in overcrowded and makeshift shelters.
Site safety audits covering about 230 displacement sites hosting at least 187,400 people reportedly found unsafe latrines, open pits, wastewater hazards and poor drainage in low-lying areas, alongside inadequate lighting and overcrowding.
The approaching rainy season adds another layer of danger.
Humanitarian agencies warn that damaged sewage and stormwater drainage systems will increase the risk of flooding and disease.
According to a Doctors Without Borders (MSF) survey, almost one in four people interviewed between May and August 2025 had experienced diarrhoea in the previous month.
Skin diseases accounted for nearly 18% of MSF primary healthcare consultations in 2025, while poor water and sanitation conditions have also contributed to the spread of scabies and lice.
The effects extend beyond physical health.
MSF said its mental health professionals observed high levels of distress linked to the struggle to obtain sufficient water and hygiene supplies, with children carrying heavy responsibilities.
“The inability to maintain hygiene has become a source of distress and undermined people’s sense of dignity,” it wrote.
“Israeli authorities have used access to water as a weapon against Palestinians, systematically depriving people in Gaza, Palestine, of water in a campaign of collective punishment,” MSF said in April.
It noted that the “deliberate denial” of water from Palestinians was an integral part of Israel’s genocide and was part of a “recurrent, systematic and cumulative pattern” rather than being isolated acts.
The organization stressed that the destruction and attacks on infrastructure, obstruction of humanitarian access through forced displacement and denial of movement, and the blocking or delay of essential supplies were the main mechanisms Israel’s weaponization of WASH access.
MSF said it had documented several incidents involving the shooting at or destruction of its clearly identified water trucks and boreholes.
“Since 1 January 2026, all MSF requests for the entry of any supplies through the dedicated system, where approval is determined by the Israeli authorities, were denied,” MSF said.
Some water infrastructure has been repaired and humanitarian partners continue to use alternative sources.
Yet restrictions on equipment, generators, spare parts, chlorine and other essential supplies, alongside fuel shortages, continue to threaten the operation of remaining systems.
UNICEF says 19.4% of its $746.8 million humanitarian funding requirement for the occupied Palestinian territory is allocated to water, sanitation and hygiene.
For Palestinians living through the crisis, recovery starts with what should never have become a struggle.
A tap that works. Water that is safe to drink. Functioning sanitation and reliable electricity.
And for children like those in Aff's family, it is the possibility of putting down the water bucket and picking up a schoolbook instead.

STRASSBURG – Im Europäischen Parlament versammeln sich Politiker aller Lager zunehmend hinter einem härteren Kurs in der China-Politik der EU - auch über Handelsfragen hinaus.

„Ich möchte, dass er mit einem möglichst starken Mandat dieses Hauses dorthin reist“, sagte Hilde Vautmans, die Verfasserin des Berichts, am Dienstagabend in einer Debatte. „Europa verfügt über wirtschaftliche Macht. Es ist an der Zeit, diese einzusetzen.“
Die Äußerung deckt sich mit Positionen, die Bundeskanzler Friedrich Merz und Frankreichs Präsident Emmanuel Macron Anfang der Woche in einem gemeinsamen Papier vereinbart haben. Sie sprechen sich dafür aus, der EU-Kommission mehr Befugnisse zu geben, um Importe aus Ländern, die „schwerwiegende und systematische Verzerrungen“ in der EU verursachen, zu beschränken oder sogar zu unterbinden.
Mehrere Europaabgeordnete lobten die gemeinsame Haltung der beiden größten Volkswirtschaften der EU. Der polnische Europaabgeordnete Mariusz Kamiński von den Europäischen Konservativen und Reformisten ging weiter. Er nannte „pragmatische wirtschaftliche Beziehungen“ zu China unverantwortlich oder schlichtweg dumm. China sei eine „kommunistische Diktatur, die eine Bedrohung für die freie Welt darstellt“, sagte er.
Damit steht er nicht allein. Vielen Abgeordneten genügt es nicht, lediglich gegen Chinas aggressive Exporte aus subventionierten Überkapazitäten vorzugehen. Die EU-Kommission müsse sich auch mit Menschenrechtsverletzungen in China, der Aggression gegen Taiwan und Chinas Rolle bei Russlands Krieg gegen die Ukraine befassen.
„Wir müssen anerkennen, dass China sich in einer Weise verhält, die unsere Interessen gefährdet. Nicht nur im Handel, sondern auch in den Bereichen Sicherheit und Verteidigung“, sagte der spanische Europaabgeordnete Nicolás Pascual de la Parte von der Europäischen Volkspartei. „Die Menschenrechtslage hat sich nicht verbessert, ist aber in den letzten Jahren von unserer Agenda verschwunden.“
Vautmans wertete die Debatte als Beleg dafür, dass die EU dabei sei, eine einheitliche Haltung gegenüber China einzunehmen. „Das ist nicht mehr nur die Position des Europäischen Parlaments oder einer einzelnen Fraktion“, sagte Vautmans nach der Debatte. „Es setzt sich zunehmend die Erkenntnis durch, dass Europa eine kohärentere China-Politik braucht: offen für Dialog und Zusammenarbeit, aber viel entschlossener, seine Interessen zu verteidigen, wenn es nötig ist.“
Der Artikel ist zuerst auf Englisch bei POLITICO erschienen.

Disinflation expected to accelerate: Karahan
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
10:03:47 UTC
19:03:47 KST

Disinflation is expected to accelerate in the coming period if supply-side pressures continue to fade, said Fatih Karahan, the Central Bank Governor.
Speaking at an event in Istanbul on Oct. 7, Karahan said the underlying inflation trend rose during the March-June period when the effects of the war became more pronounced but resumed its decline from July onward.
“On an annualized basis, the underlying trend, which climbed to around 30 percent during the war period, stood at 23.7 percent as of September. This level is approximately 6 percentage points below the current annual inflation rate,” he said.
Karahan said the fact that the underlying trend remains below annual inflation provides an important signal for the period ahead, adding that disinflation would continue at an accelerating pace if supply-side pressures ease.
He said the development reflects the impact of tight monetary policy on demand conditions and pricing behavior, adding that the disinflation process is expected to regain momentum as the effects of shocks diminish, supported by the central bank’s tight policy stance.
Karahan said the slowdown in domestic demand has become more evident thanks to tight monetary policy and noted that disinflation has been more pronounced in components directly affected by monetary policy.
“Inflation expectations and pricing behavior will remain important for the course of disinflation. In this framework, we will continue to use all our tools decisively in line with our objective of achieving price stability,” Karahan said.

U.S. Air Force breaks ground on new B-21 assembly line
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
10:03:27 UTC
19:03:27 KST

- The U.S. Air Force and Northrop Grumman broke ground on more than 1 million square feet of new B-21 final assembly facilities at Plant 42.
- The construction supports a February agreement to raise annual B-21 production capacity by 25 percent, funded partly by $4.5 billion in reconciliation money.
The U.S. Air Force and Northrop Grumman have broken ground on a new final assembly line for the B-21 Raider stealth bomber, adding more than 93,000 square meters (1 million square feet) of facilities at Air Force Plant 42 in Palmdale, California.
The construction is tied to the agreement the Department of the Air Force and Northrop reached in February to raise annual B-21 production capacity by 25 percent. Neither the service nor the company disclosed the cost of the new facilities, a completion date, or how many bombers the expanded line will produce each year.
“It’s more than construction… we’re moving fast to build B-21s!” the Office of the Secretary of the Air Force posted on X.
“The B-21 isn’t the only thing taking off,” Northrop Grumman wrote, adding that more than 1 million square feet at Plant 42 is now dedicated to building the bomber.
Northrop builds the Raider at Plant 42 in the same Palmdale complex where it assembled the B-2 Spirit in the 1980s and 1990s, and the first B-21 was unveiled there in December 2022.
The U.S. Air Force is financing the faster schedule with $4.5 billion from fiscal 2025 reconciliation legislation. Northrop CEO Kathy Warden said in April that the company will add $2.5 billion of its own money, including about $200 million in 2026. Northrop says it has already invested more than $5 billion in digital engineering and manufacturing infrastructure for the program.
The production rate is classified, and low-rate initial production has been understood to cover 21 aircraft across five lots. The U.S. Air Force has set a requirement of at least 100 Raiders, with a unit cost reported at around $700 million. In 2025, Northrop took a $477 million charge on the program connected to a production process change for a higher rate.
Northrop has also expanded B-21 work outside California, opening a new manufacturing building called East Gate 3 in Layton, Utah, on September 9. The program draws on more than 400 suppliers in at least 40 states, with final assembly remaining at Plant 42.
In 2025, an Air Force spokesperson told Air & Space Forces Magazine that the planned production increase would be carried out within Northrop’s Palmdale campus and at some major supplier sites. The new assembly line now adds more than 1 million square feet of construction on that campus.
The B-21 is designed to penetrate modern air defenses and strike heavily defended targets with conventional or nuclear weapons. It is set to replace the B-1B Lancer and the B-2, and its design allows for both crewed and uncrewed missions.
The first B-21 flew on November 10, 2023, from Palmdale to Edwards Air Force Base, California, and a second test aircraft joined flight testing at Edwards on September 11, 2025. Low-rate initial production was approved in late 2023 and made public in January 2024.
Ellsworth Air Force Base in South Dakota will be the bomber’s first operational base and training site, and Northrop and the U.S. Air Force say the first aircraft is on track to arrive there in 2027. Air Force Global Strike Command will decide when the B-21 reaches initial operational capability.

Trade Minister Bolat meets EU Ambassadors
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
10:02:29 UTC
19:02:29 KST

Turkish Trade Minister Ömer Bolat
Turkish Trade Minister Ömer Bolat met with ambassadors of European Union member states in Ankara to discuss bilateral trade and economic relations, according to a statement from the Trade Ministry.
The meeting, hosted by Aivo Orav, head of the European Union Delegation to Türkiye, followed up on talks held at the ministry in April.
Discussions focused on the current state of Türkiye-EU trade and economic relations, the European Commission’s proposed Industrial Acceleration Act under its “Made in EU” policies, the functioning of the Customs Union and trade barriers faced by the Turkish business community.
Bolat said economic integration between Türkiye and the EU is deep and strategic in nature.
He noted that bilateral trade between Türkiye and the EU reached a record $233 billion last year, with EU countries accounting for 43 percent of Türkiye’s exports and 32 percent of its imports. He also said around 62 percent of Türkiye’s foreign direct investment stock originates from European companies.
Commenting on the European Commission’s proposed Industrial Acceleration Act, Bolat said vehicles and components produced in Türkiye should be fully recognized as having “Union origin” status.
Emphasizing the importance of preserving Türkiye’s position within the EU value chain, Bolat said Türkiye was not seeking special treatment but rather recognition of its unique position and the rights stemming from its 30-year Customs Union relationship with the bloc.
He also highlighted the need for practical solutions in Türkiye-EU relations, saying lengthy visa procedures faced by businesspeople and road transit quotas that directly restrict trade prevent the Customs Union from reaching its full potential.
Bolat recalled Türkiye’s reciprocal steps toward opening public procurement markets and said one of the main agenda items discussed was the upcoming Türkiye-EU High-Level Trade Dialogue Meeting, which he will co-chair with Maros Sefcovic, the European Commission’s trade chief, in Brussels on Oct. 13.
He said the meeting would provide an important opportunity to develop constructive and concrete solutions for Türkiye-EU trade and economic relations.

Air quality has deteriorated in six cities in the Kyiv region — what is known
Kyiv • UNN
Air quality has deteriorated in Ivankiv, Vyshneve, Boiarka, Vasylkiv, Obukhiv, and Brovary. Residents are advised to close their windows and spend less time outdoors.
Air quality temporarily deteriorated in six settlements in the Kyiv region due to elevated levels of fine particulate matter. Experts advise keeping windows closed, spending less time outdoors, and using an air purifier if possible. The Kyiv Regional Military Administration reported this, UNN writes.
Air quality temporarily deteriorated in Ivankiv, Vyshneve, Boyarka, Vasylkiv, Obukhiv, and Brovary. The main pollutant is fine particulate matter
It is noted that prolonged exposure to such dust can cause breathing discomfort, particularly among children, older people, and those sensitive to irritation. Therefore, experts advise keeping windows closed until the situation improves, avoiding spending a lot of time outdoors, and drinking enough water. If you have an air purifier at home, turn it on at the maximum setting.
At the same time, no exceedances of the permissible levels of chemical and biological substances in the ambient air were observed in other settlements of the Kyiv region.
The level of gamma radiation in the region is consistent with the natural background level.
Ambient air monitoring is carried out at 15 observation points in the cities of Brovary, Boryspil, Pereiaslav, Vyshhorod, Boyarka, Obukhiv, Kaharlyk, Bohuslav, Uzyn, Vasylkiv, Irpin, and Vyshneve; the towns of Ivankiv and Velyka Dymerka; and the village of Pidhirtsi in Obukhiv district. The observation post in the city of Bila Tserkva is temporarily not operating.

According to Hung Cao, the acting US navy secretary, eight US navy personnel assigned to the Lincoln carrier strike group attempted suicide since the start of their lengthy assignment – the longest continuous period at sea without a port call.
On Wednesday, Hegseth repeated his frequent critique of the media, and accused some members of the press of turning the record-breaking deployment into “some sort of symbol of dysfunction, or a symbol of low morale or a symbol of a failed mission”.
Last week, Hegseth appeared to reference the mental health crisis on board while speaking to lower-ranking troops at the Marine Corps Base, insisting there are “disingenuous headlines about deployment lengths, patently false claims of low troop morale, or flat-out propaganda, as if it’s written by our adversaries”.
MS Now also reported in August on alarming allegations of mold in the ship’s showers and dwindling supplies of food and soap, among other basic necessities. At the time, Hegseth dismissed reports about deteriorating conditions on board as “completely misrepresented”.

Why do billionaires have so many children if they’re not prepared to parent them? | Arwa Mahdawi
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
10:00:41 UTC
19:00:41 KST

“I have the best advice for women in business,” Kim Kardashian told Variety in 2022. “Get your fucking ass up and work. It seems like nobody wants to work these days.”
The billionaire got a lot of flak for this comment but no one can accuse her of being a hypocrite. It takes serious graft to spin a sex tape into lasting fame and a business empire. That said, like many high-flyers who preach the importance of hard work, the Skims co-founder isn’t above outsourcing the less glamorous domestic labour. She has primary custody of the four kids she shares with her ex-husband, Kanye West, and, according to an interview with the Sunday Times, employs five nannies to take care of them: “One nanny on duty, four on rotation,” she said. Despite having more nannies than kids, she apparently still does the school run. And I bet she doesn’t turn up at the school gate with yoghurt on her shirt like I do.
The revelation about Kardashian’s numerous nannies has caused a bit of a ruckus. Largely because there’s nothing people love more than judging how a woman mothers while ignoring the dad. And I’ll admit I was a bit judgy at first. But, look, if I could afford to contract out all the boring bits of parenthood I would too. You’re not a better mother because you’re running yourself ragged doing absolutely everything.
Back to being judgy though: while there’s nothing wrong with getting help, I don’t really understand the point of having four kids if you don’t have time to parent them all. Particularly as Kardashian’s kids weren’t oopsies: numbers three and four were born via a surrogate because of complications in her earlier pregnancies.
But of course, four kids is rookie numbers compared with some other breeding-obsessed billionaires, many of whom seem keen on procreating but not parenting. The Russian-born tech mogul Pavel Durov has more than 100 biological children in 12 countries via sperm donation. The Chinese billionaire Xu Bo is reported to have more than 100 children via surrogates. And obviously there’s Elon Musk, who has 14 known children.
Meanwhile, for the rest of us it’s getting tougher to afford kids at all. A 2024 Pew Research Center study found that, among adults under 50 who say they’re unlikely to have kids, 36% cited costs as a key factor. Having big families used to be associated with lower economic status. But research shows that’s gradually being flipped on its head. Having multiple kids, and a team of nannies to take care of them, has become the ultimate status symbol. Albeit the only status symbol that’s going to grow up demanding therapy.
Arwa Mahdawi is a Guardian columnist

“One thing we agree on, for example, is that the nations of Europe need to take on a greater share of the burden in defending their continent, and Greece is doing just that,” Rubio told reporters alongside Greek Foreign Minister Giorgos Gerapetritis, noting that Athens remains on track to allocate 5% of its gross domestic product to defense.
