====================================================================================================

'I never imagined that in less than two hours, I'd be picking up body parts'
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
09:45:45 UTC
18:45:45 KST

Two months before Oct. 7, Tomer Peretz stood facing Mount Everest. He had reached base camp and felt, quite literally, that he was at a high point in his life: a successful international artist living in Los Angeles, traveling the world, seeking out extraordinary people, living among them and creating art inspired by their stories.
In a moment of exhilaration, he began talking to the mountain. “I told it, ‘Listen, what’s the next story? What’s next? I’ve already done everything. What are you planning for me?’” he recalled. The mountain did not answer. But a gray cloud appeared and covered the summit. Peretz now jokes that the message was clear: “Your call is important to us. Please hold.”
Two months later, in October 2023, Peretz landed in Israel with two of his children, Roi and Ziv, for a two-week vacation and a relative’s wedding. The previous evening, he had attended a reunion with old army friends on a Tel Aviv beach.
On the morning of Oct. 7, like so many Israelis, he woke to the sound of an air-raid siren. He and his children ran to the safe room, where he tried to explain to two children he describes as having grown up extremely sheltered what a terrorist was.
Twenty years had passed since his discharge from the military, where he had served as a combat officer and later been diagnosed with PTSD. But now all he could think about was getting into the battle zone. 
His calls to friends from the army went unanswered. They had all already been called up. Only that evening did he manage to reach Natan Sabag, a childhood friend from Jerusalem who volunteered with ZAKA, Israel’s emergency response and recovery organization.
Peretz rushed to Jerusalem, left his children with his wife Lital’s family and told her he was going to help distribute food. The next morning, he climbed into a ZAKA vehicle. Less than two hours later, he found himself inside the scenes of the massacres at the Nova music festival and Kibbutz Be’eri.
The instinct of someone with trauma is usually to stay away from a battlefield, not rush toward one.
“I come from a family with deep ties to the security world,” Peretz said. “I come from a culture where, when something happens, you run toward the fire. It doesn’t matter what you’re carrying, physically or mentally, you go. Nobody stops to say, ‘Sorry, I can’t, I have PTSD.’ That wasn’t even a thought.”
What did you think you were going there to do?
“I thought I’d hand out sandwiches to soldiers, drive a vehicle, do anything that might help. When they picked me up, I still assumed they wouldn’t actually let me do what they were doing. They were trained volunteers with experience. Who was I? I hadn’t been here in years. I never imagined that less than two hours after getting into the car, I’d be picking up body parts.”
Weren't you afraid of dying?
“I didn’t really have time to think about dying. My trauma from the army was never about fear of death. I didn’t have nightmares about gunfire or shelling. For me, the trauma was always rooted in guilt.”
Once inside Be’eri, Peretz began filming. “I filmed 40 bodies and immediately uploaded the video to Instagram and YouTube,” he recalled. “By then I was completely focused. I couldn’t understand how we could be doing this work while no one was documenting it. We were about to clear everything away, and I kept thinking: Is no one going to see what happened here?”
“So I said, screw it, I’m filming,” Peretz recalled. “People shouted at me, and ZAKA’s leaders nearly threw me out. I already stood out; they had sidelocks and their religious sense of mission, and I was covered in tattoos. I was an outsider, and that only made me work harder to prove myself. I went from body to body without stopping, filming on my phone as I worked. I wasn’t getting sick, I wasn’t fainting, and I wasn’t taking breaks.”
Within 10 minutes, Peretz said, the videos had accumulated millions of views. Then the messages began pouring in. “My phone completely crashed from messages sent by families of missing people,” he said. “I suddenly went into some kind of trance that lasted several days.”
While working, he said, he would climb into trucks carrying bodies. “Each truck had between 30 and 50 bodies. I would open the zipper around the face, photograph it and check. People sent me passports and ID cards of their missing relatives. Of course, I did it privately. Most of the ZAKA guys didn’t really know, except for one person who helped me.”
How was it seeing your sons afterward?
“Every night I came home, and most of the time the kids were already asleep. Roi found out what I was doing from friends in the community. At some point, packages and chocolates started arriving at our home in Los Angeles from different people, and suddenly Lital discovered that I had been collecting bodies. She was really angry with me.”
“She had already lived through some of my worst triggers and flashbacks from the army, and in the years before Oct. 7 she dealt with things most people could barely imagine. For her, this felt like going backward. She was basically saying, ‘You dumped the kids at my parents’ house, decided you were Rambo and, thanks a lot, wrecked our lives.’
“That was how she saw it, and at the time I fought with her over it. But she wasn’t the only one. A lot of people close to me, people who knew what I had been through with PTSD, were furious with me.”
To them, it looked like a relapse.
“Yes. Because by then I had really come a long way. Between COVID and 2023, I had several years without nightmares, anxiety or triggers. I had done a huge amount of work on myself.
“I was in a very good place financially, professionally, socially and with my family. I had seen every kind of therapist imaginable. I even traveled to China to meet an old Chinese healer. I tried every ritual, every medication, every approach, from holistic treatments to conventional medicine, ayahuasca and rehabilitation. For nearly 20 years, I dug as deep as I could, and it had worked.”
Then guilt appeared and sent you back into a battle zone within minutes.
“Exactly.”
‘Just go as far away as possible’
The day after leaving the IDF, Peretz boarded a plane to South America. A Jerusalem native raised in a religious-Zionist family, he grew up supporting Beitar Jerusalem and at times mixed with the club’s more hard-line fans, while moving back and forth between religious and secular life. “My father still studies in a yeshiva,” he said.
After four years in the military during the height of the Second Intifada, including one year as a career officer, Peretz left Israel on a one-way ticket. An incident during fighting in Jenin in which one of his soldiers, David Solomonov, was killed, along with intensive operations in Gaza and the West Bank, left him with severe PTSD.
“I didn’t know where I was going,” he said. “Just go as far away as possible. Run and don’t come back.” In hostels across South America, he developed a system: accommodation in exchange for painting murals. For 10 months, he returned to an interest from his school days, when he had channeled his restless attention into doodles in notebooks and later graffiti on the streets of Jerusalem.
When he arrived in Los Angeles, one of the first things Peretz did was buy canvases and start figuring out how to build a life that would let him keep painting without interruption.
Years later, after meeting Lital, also from Jerusalem, starting a family with her and establishing himself as an artist, including a series of solo exhibitions in Los Angeles such as “Unbreakable,” dedicated to IDF soldiers, Oct. 7 forced another dramatic turn.
In retrospect, Peretz says, as strange as it may sound, the catastrophe became a positive turning point in his life, transforming him from someone who ran from his trauma into someone willing to live alongside it. But that did not happen immediately. To climb again, he first had to hit bottom.
“What I did on Oct. 7 and in the days afterward included some of the best things I’ve ever done and some of the best decisions I’ve ever made in my life,” he said. “I would do it another 30 times, including Be’eri. “I can say that now, in hindsight. If you had asked me during the first six months, I would have told you, ‘Shoot me.’ I was a walking dead man.
“In those six months, I lost everything. I lost my business partner, my manager, my gallery representation, my entire career, all my money and all my savings. I grew distant from my wife and my children. I lost friends. Everything I had was falling apart.
“When PTSD is at its worst, you can end up losing the people who love you most, and the people you love most. That’s the blast wave of trauma. It hits the people closest to you.”
Was that a direct response to what you experienced on Oct. 7, or did it also bring back things from your military service that had never fully been resolved?
“Mostly things from the army that came rushing back. I started having flashbacks I hadn’t experienced since the first year or two after I was discharged. Oct. 7 also dealt a serious financial blow to my career. A lot of people distanced themselves from me, and I could no longer maintain the business relationships I had built because I had entered this completely different world. At that point, I didn’t have the motivation to keep them going anyway.”
Did your manager simply leave because you were Israeli?
“To this day, I honestly don’t know. I never spoke to him, and I’m not interested in doing so. I’m not particularly curious. He simply stopped answering me. Projects were canceled. Galleries where I used to show took my works off the walls. Nobody informed me. I found out afterward that the works weren’t even hanging anymore and there were no sales.
“Nothing was happening. No money was coming in. “But the point is that at the time, I didn’t care either. Everything had lost its meaning. I’m still suffering from that loss today, but I’m at peace with where I am. I don’t want it back. I’m building a new life now, one that includes both Oct. 7 and everything I carry from my military service.”
‘On the eighth day, we began to live’
The turning point came through a Nova survivor living in Los Angeles who had lost her father. She contacted Peretz while her father was still considered missing and Peretz was moving through the kibbutzim. Their connection continued after he returned to the United States. Her father’s body was found some time later, and she and other survivors began coming to Peretz’s studio.
“We talked, and the next time she came back with more people, and then more. By then I was completely broken. I was spending all my time in the studio and barely leaving. Soon, people displaced by Oct. 7 started coming through the door: evacuees, Nova survivors and survivors from the kibbutzim.”
“We would create together. We all felt the same thing: We didn’t want to sit around a table and talk about something other than what we had been through. There was a lot of crying, a lot of pain.”
When people Peretz did not know began reaching out, he started organizing the studio sessions more formally. He brought in groups of survivors at scheduled times, prepared specific activities and developed concepts for them. He would spread a canvas across a wall or floor and groups of 10 to 20 people would paint together. As they worked, conversations began.
“These were people who weren’t involved in art, so their work was very naive,” he said. “Technically, I loved the fact that they would paint something that looked like a four-year-old’s scribble, then I would add some realistic element. Then you would see this collection of elements in a painting that told a story. The problem was, I ran out of money. I couldn’t keep financing it.”
Peretz decided to establish a nonprofit that would raise funds to fully subsidize flights and accommodation for survivors. He called it Project 8. “Creation lasted seven days, and on the eighth day, we began to live.”
Hostages, reservists, active-duty soldiers, children and bereaved families all came through his studio. “But eventually I started asking myself, what happens to them afterward?” Peretz said. “They come here, let everything out, and that helps. But then they go home and have to face the nights, when everything comes back.”
That question led Peretz to rethink his approach. Instead of working with groups, he began spending three months at a time with a single participant, creating what became the residency program.
He drew on an earlier chapter of his life in Los Angeles. “Two or three years after I arrived, I started a marketing company with 60 people doing telephone sales,” he said. “I recruited many of them through a government program called Plan C, which helped people leaving prison gradually reintegrate into society. They would work from nine to five and then return to supervised housing.
“That meant I worked with people convicted of murder, rape and drug dealing, and I learned a lot from recovery programs like Alcoholics Anonymous. If I was short on salespeople, I’d sometimes bring in people who were using crack on the street. We’d get them cleaned up, wait for the high to wear off and put them on the phones. I swear. I would drive around looking for people who were completely down and out, because sometimes they turned out to be the best salespeople.”
How come?
“Because they would do anything for $10. I spent years working that way, and I learned a lot about how to see the person underneath everything, but also not to embrace them too much. You also have to know when to be firm. 
“If someone genuinely wants to rehabilitate themselves and all you do is comfort them, you can lose them. You need to create a certain kind of structure, and they need to feel that they don’t want to let you down. It’s a very particular relationship, and that’s what I brought into the residency program.
“I brought therapists in to make sure I wasn’t doing something reckless, and they were always stunned by the results.”
Do you focus on a particular group?
“Reservists with families, with wives and children.”
Is that who you identify with most?
“That’s where I’m able to see the woman I failed to see in my own life,” Peretz said. “A lot of this is about lessons I’ve learned. I think the wife is the most important caregiver, and in many cases the first person who should receive support, even before the person suffering from the trauma. She’s with him all day. If she gets the tools to understand how to deal with what he’s going through, we can save a lot of marriages and families, and that ultimately reaches the children too.
“I think most of the resources should go to the women, because they’re the ones who will hold all of us together.”
But that can be complicated. You risk turning the wife into his caregiver.
“But she already is his caregiver. Who holds him when he’s vomiting or having flashbacks? The psychologist who sees him once or twice a week on Zoom? Who makes him food? Who answers the phone? Who sees him crying when he comes home after being ‘Rambo’? Who sees him shattered on the floor and tries to help him get back up? She’s the person living through all of it with him. If she isn’t given the tools to cope, she’ll collapse too.”
What is this period like for you personally?
“On one hand, I’m doing the most incredible thing in the world. I’m painting, I’m making art. We put together an exhibition from everything we created in the studio over the course of a year, and their works were shown in a museum. My professional world has developed enormously, just in a completely different direction. On the other hand, everyone who used to buy my work before Oct. 7 disappeared. Everyone buying my art today is someone who came to it after Oct. 7.”
How do you manage the trauma?
“I think I arrived at Oct. 7 as patient No. 1,” he joked. “It’s financially very difficult to replace a clientele, a collector base and a network of galleries that you built over 20 years. Personally, I’m still picking up the pieces. Socially, I’m disconnected too, because I’m so focused on one thing. I gave up a lot.
“But for the past year and a half, I’ve been in the best mental place of my life. I fall asleep instantly. I sleep well. I don’t dream about anything. I don’t use any substances to function. I feel very good about myself.
“I think I’m doing the most incredible thing in the world, but it comes with enormous sacrifice. I’m currently separating from my wife, who couldn’t join me on this journey. I don’t blame her at all. I don’t know anyone who could have.
“I applaud her for making it this far. I honestly don’t know how she did it. I was always traveling as far away as possible, while she stayed home waiting for this crazy person to return with some ridiculous story after she’d been alone for two or three weeks. Then I’d disappear into the studio for another three months to create work about whoever I’d met.”
Do you think things might have been different between you and Lital if she had been given the right tools?
“I don’t know how to answer that. I don’t blame her. What I do know is that I see it in other couples. I can see the relationship now. I can see the women. That’s the most important thing in this whole story. When something good happens between the couple, something good happens with the children too. They need to see their parents standing strong together.”
‘I’m not focused on advocacy, but on healing ourselves’
Last week, Peretz completed his first work in Israel, a mural commemorating hostages Ori Danino and Hersh Goldberg-Polin, who were held together and later murdered in Hamas tunnels.
The two are depicted wearing the jerseys of their favorite soccer teams, Danino in Beitar Jerusalem colors and Goldberg-Polin in Hapoel Jerusalem colors. They are shown embracing in front of the stands at Jerusalem’s Teddy Stadium, conveying a simple message: If supporters of bitter rival clubs can come together, perhaps the rest of the country can too.
“There will probably be people who don’t like seeing it, but that’s fine. The focus today needs to be on strengthening the connection among ourselves and worrying less about how people outside see us. I’ll stand with my brothers and sisters no matter what, with my eyes closed. But I’m focused on healing ourselves.
“All this antisemitism doesn’t interest me. I’m not focused on advocacy. If someone calls me a ‘baby killer’ in the street, I’m basically like, ‘Fine.’”
People threw stones and smashed windows at your studio in Los Angeles.
“My studio was broken into six times. They wrote ‘Free Palestine’ on the windows and came to threaten me. One day, two people came up and asked if I was Tomer Peretz. I was carrying a gun, so I felt protected and said yes. One of them said something about babies in Gaza and told me we’d meet again. I said, ‘Why meet again? Let’s meet now.’
“During the first year and a half, I got into a lot of trouble because I was very outspoken. Twice I ended up in physical fights with protesters outside the studio, but that rarely happens anymore. I carry a gun openly. When I filed my sixth complaint after another break-in, I told the sheriff very simply, ‘Be prepared. The next time this happens, I’m shooting anyone who comes near me.’ “That was the end of it. The sheriff is Jewish and a decent guy. He understood.”
So have you become a different person?
“I don’t think so. Even before Oct. 7, I would travel to Mexico and India looking for unusual people with extraordinary stories, sometimes people involved in illegal things. I would live with them for a week, two weeks, three weeks, and tell my story through them. I would create work about them. So before, it was Mexico, India, Nepal or Bhutan. Now it’s Israel.
“My attraction to unusual stories is still there, and some of them are also about trauma. The only real difference between who I was before Oct. 7 and who I am now is that today I use all my resources to help people.
“The only problem is that it’s harder now to find a story that truly moves me, because it’s become harder for me to be moved. There just aren’t that many things left that can surprise me.”

Individual heating powers 37% of urban, 71% of rural households in Ukraine
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
12:45:13 EEST
18:45:13 KST

Individual heating is available in 37.2% of Ukrainian households in urban areas and 71.4% in rural areas, while centralized heating is available in 61.3% and 2.5%, respectively, the State Statistics Service reported following its 2026 household budget survey.
According to the sample survey, Ukraine has 12 million 452,500 households, of which 7 million 462,700 live in urban areas (including 5 million 255,900 in large cities) and 4 million 989,800 in rural areas. The average household size is 2.28 people, including 2.19 people in urban areas and 2.40 people in rural areas.
In rural areas, 94.5% of households live in private houses or parts thereof, while in urban areas, 73.8% live in apartment buildings (81.8% in large cities).
A total of 90.8% of households live in housing privately owned by their members, while another 0.6% live in homes they own but are still paying off through a mortgage. A total of 6.6% of households live in housing rented at market rates, with the figure reaching 12.8% in large cities.
According to the survey, among households that obtain water for drinking and cooking from a public standpipe, public well, spring, river, lake, stream, and among those living in rural areas, 47.6% live less than 100 meters from their main water source. Another 24.5% live 100-200 meters away, 14.4% 200-500 meters away, 3% 500 meters to 1 kilometer away, and 10.5% more than 1 kilometer away.
In cities, 20.7% of households live up to 100 meters from their main water source, 35.5% 100-200 meters away, 33% 200-500 meters away, 7.3% between 500 meters and 1 kilometer away, and 3.5% more than 1 kilometer away.
A total of 54.1% of households use a centralized water supply to obtain water for drinking and cooking (65.2% in urban areas and 37.9% in rural areas). For 56.0% of rural households, wells in their yards remain the main source of water for drinking and cooking.
According to the survey, 99.1% of households in urban areas live in housing equipped with running water, compared with 77.2% in rural areas. A total of 98.4% of households in cities live in housing connected to a sewerage system, compared with 75.3% in rural areas. Housing is equipped with a bathtub or shower for 98.4% of households in cities and 74.7% in rural areas. At the same time, hot water supply is available in the homes of 60.3% of urban households and 31.6% of rural households.
The State Statistics Service noted that housing is connected to a centralized gas supply for 89.8% of urban households and 68.6% of rural households. Centralized heating is available in the homes of 61.3% of households in cities and only 2.5% in rural areas. At the same time, housing is equipped with individual heating for 37.2% of urban households and 71.4% of rural households.
The State Statistics Service conducted the main survey in 22 regions of Ukraine (excluding Donetsk, Luhansk and Kherson regions, the temporarily occupied territories of the Autonomous Republic of Crimea and the city of Sevastopol, as well as territories of the regions where active hostilities are taking place and which are temporarily not controlled by the Ukrainian government) from December 2025 through February 2026.

Hardline Iranian MPs move to impeach foreign minister over UN General Assembly talks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
09:44:34 UTC
18:44:34 KST

The motion, filed by MPs aligned with the Paydari Front, accuses Araghchi of meeting US envoy Steve Witkoff at the UN General Assembly without authorisation, a claim directly opposed by Supreme National Security Council chief Mohsen Rezaei, who said the talks had prior approval.
A group of hardline Iranian MPs has filed a motion to impeach Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi over his talks with US special envoy Steve Witkoff on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly last month, exposing divisions within the Islamic Republic over how and whether to pursue negotiations with Washington to end the war.
Member of parliament's presiding board Mohammad Rashidi confirmed on Tuesday that the request had been registered in the parliamentary system but had not yet been referred to the board or placed on the agenda.
The MPs behind the motion, led by Amirhossein Sabeti of the hardline Paydari Front, argue that Araghchi's meeting with Witkoff on 22 September was conducted without authorisation from Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei or coordination with the Supreme National Security Council.
The talks were held with Qatar acting as an intermediary and focused on conditions for reopening the Strait of Hormuz, a key stumbling block in negotiations between Tehran and Washington since the war began in late February.
Supreme National Security Council's secretary Mohsen Rezaei directly contradicted that claim.
"It was agreed that Mr Araghchi, during his trip to New York, would convey Iran's conditions to the intermediaries," Rezaei said, indicating the talks had the prior approval of Iran's higher authorities.
Araghchi set out Tehran's conditions in the New York talks, including the immediate lifting of the US naval blockade, the immediate transfer of frozen Iranian assets and an end to the war on all fronts. US President Donald Trump rejected the proposal.
A second signatory, MP Hosseinali Hajideligani, accused Araghchi of "repeatedly, through targeted interviews, helping to lower oil prices for the United States."
Sabeti listed "crossing red lines" during negotiations, "serious miscalculations" in political analysis and mishandling of the US file as the main grounds for impeachment.
Araghchi's name has appeared on impeachment lists drawn up by hardline MPs multiple times over the past two years, and Hajideligani said in August that they were gathering documentation for a formal motion.
Alireza Salimi, himself a signatory of the letter and a member of the presiding board, told Mehr news agency that filing an impeachment motion does not mean the speaker supports it or that it will reach the floor.
The motion was filed while parliament speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, one of Iran's main negotiators with the US side, holds the chair.
'A sign of weakness'
Some MPs oppose the move. Ruhollah Lak Aliabadi said "impeachment proceedings, especially impeaching the foreign minister in this wartime situation, are definitely not in the country's interest" and could send "a negative signal and a sign of weakness to the enemy."
Aliabadi said a recent parliamentary meeting with Araghchi lasted four and a half hours, during which the IRGC commander called Araghchi by phone at least three times, which he cited as evidence of coordination between diplomacy and the military.
Conservative political figure Mansour Haghighatpour also pushed back. "You do not change saddles in wartime," Haghighatpour said.
Araghchi's position appears secure for now. After he returned to Tehran following the New York trip — during which social media speculation circulated that he had sought asylum abroad — the foreign ministry formally described him as a member of Iran's six-person decision-making team, a signal that he retained the regime's confidence.
The memorial service for his sister, who died while Araghchi was at the UN General Assembly, drew one of the largest gatherings of Iranian officials since the start of the war. Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei did not attend, continuing his absence from public events more than seven months after assuming power.

Eesti Energia given conditional permit to heat Narva with shale oil
The Environmental Board has granted Eesti Energia permission to use shale oil instead of natural gas to heat Narva. However, it may only do so if there is a risk of disruption to gas supplies.
Narva was last heated using shale oil four years ago when natural gas prices were extremely high. At the time, Enefit Power was permitted to use shale oil throughout the heating season.
Enefit Power is indeed forecasting supply problems this year, but it remains uncertain whether it will be able to use cheaper shale oil.
"I can't confirm with 100 percent certainty right now, although I'm optimistic that we will be able to use it. The analysis is still underway, so I'll be able to give a definitive answer once it is complete. They granted us an environmental permit, but it is conditional, so we now have to analyze it — what we can offer the city on the one hand and, on the other, the risk of disruptions to the gas supply," said Enefit Power CEO Raine Pajo.

France halts police use of stun grenades at student protests

France halts police use of stun grenades at student protests
Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu to make public address after hundreds of thousands rally to demand more funding for education.
France has temporarily banned police from using stun grenades at student-led protests, the interior minister said, amid growing accusations of police brutality following several days of student demonstrations nationwide.
The announcement on Wednesday came a day after hundreds of thousands of students and supporters marched across France to demand more funding for education and better conditions in high schools, prompting President Emmanuel Macron to convene an emergency meeting with Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu and other key ministers to try to defuse the crisis.
Lecornu will make a public address later on Wednesday on the school protests as well as the country’s finances, his office said.
Interior Minister Laurent Nunez told radio broadcaster RTL early on Wednesday that he had suspended police use of stun grenades at the protests.
A 15-year-old lost a hand in the northern city of Lens on Monday after police fired a stun grenade.
Earlier, a 14-year-old student was hit in the face by a tear gas grenade at such close range that he lost several teeth. A policeman was charged on Tuesday over the incident in the capital, Paris.
Police have opened 18 internal investigations into allegations of misconduct since the protests began, Nunez said.
Rights groups, students and parents’ groups have accused authorities of using disproportionate force against minors. The government says the protest movement has been hijacked by outsiders and morphed into urban violence.
The Ministry of the Interior said 6,100 people have been arrested since the protests began last month, the overwhelming majority of them minors.
More than 1,800 people are being prosecuted, including 1,483 minors, the Ministry of Justice said, without specifying the crimes.
At least 715 police officers and 215 teenagers have been injured in clashes, according to Lecornu’s office.
Students demand school funding
Protests started in late September with students blocking entrances to hundreds of high schools for 15- to 17-year-olds over complaints of dilapidated facilities and teacher shortages and demands for more funding for education.
Parents, teachers and union workers joined the demonstrations in Paris and other cities on Tuesday amid accusations that police were using disproportionate force.
Sporadic violent clashes have broken out between police and protesters at what otherwise have been largely peaceful demonstrations.
Lecornu on Tuesday condemned the violence and told lawmakers that it would not be tolerated, while also rejecting accusations that the government had ordered “police repression” against protesters.

Although funding for the Italian
national health service has grown in nominal terms since 2023,
it has lost around 18.8 billion euros in that period in terms of
the amount of money needed to keep its share of funding stable
in relation to GDP, the GIMBE health institute said in a report
on Wednesday.
                                    
It added that an additional 32 billion euros in funding will be
needed over the next three years to avert the danger of the
burden of health-care spending being increasingly shifted to
citizens.
                                    
"Nominal funding has certainly increased, yet the share of
national wealth allocated to the National Health Service has
shrunk," said Gimbe President Nino Cartabellotta.
                                    
"It is a phenomenon of 'invisible cuts: not nominal cuts, but
fewer resources than the national health service would have
received had the health-service-fund-to-GDP ratio from 2022
remained unchanged".
                                    
The report said the national health service fund increased by
17,5 billion euros between 2023 and 2026, going from 125.4
billion in 2022 to 142..9 billion 2026 this year.

Sümeyye Dilara Dinçer

The UK and Türkiye have numerous opportunities to strengthen their space capabilities through cooperation, a senior UK Space Agency official told Anadolu.
“There are many different areas in which we will be much stronger when we work together,” Alice Bunn, co-director of the UK Space Agency, said during the 77th International Astronautical Congress (IAC) in Türkiye’s Mediterranean resort city of Antalya.
Bunn welcomed a new cooperation agreement signed Tuesday between the UK Space Agency and the Turkish Space Agency.
She said the two sides could expand joint work in science, research and development, and technology, as well as in developing regulations governing space missions and activities in orbit.
The agreement establishes a road map for developing that cooperation, according to Bunn.
The signing ceremony was also attended by British Ambassador to Türkiye Jennifer Elizabeth Anderson, whose presence Bunn said demonstrated the importance attached to the partnership.
“Science and technology are often used as instruments of cooperation between countries,” she said. “We are excited to see the next steps in our cooperation in science and technology.” 
Space technology largely invisible in daily life
Bunn also emphasized the central role space-based systems play in modern society, despite often operating unnoticed in the background.
“All of our modern lives are absolutely dependent on space technologies,” she said.
“Most of the time, we are not even aware of it because space technologies are invisibly integrated into our daily lives. But we are talking about an extremely important field of technology that makes our modern way of life possible.”
Commenting on the congress, Bunn described its atmosphere as energetic and said she had participated in a session bringing together global space leaders.
She said the packed session produced an intense but exciting discussion about how countries and organizations could work together.
Organized by the International Astronautical Federation, the congress brings together representatives of space agencies, companies, universities and research institutions from around the world.

U.S. Embassy Urges Citizens to Leave Russia Over Siberian Plague Suspicions

Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07

18:40:10 KST

The U.S. Embassy in Moscow issued a health alert on Tuesday over the death of a plague lab worker in the Irkutsk region, urging Americans to leave Russia and those in the affected area to follow local health guidance.
The death of an Irkutsk anti-plague institute employee last week has fueled fears of a possible outbreak, though authorities have not publicly confirmed that she had the disease.
U.S. State Secretary Marco Rubio urged Russia to share more information, while President Donald Trump said he planned to address the matter in a call with President Vladimir Putin.
“U.S. citizens in the area should follow the guidance of local health authorities, avoid affected facilities, and seek medical care promptly if they develop fever or respiratory symptoms,” the U.S. Embassy in Moscow said in a statement.
It emphasized that the U.S. government has “limited ability to help U.S. citizens in Russia, especially outside of Moscow,” citing reports of hospital quarantines following the death.
The embassy reiterated that U.S. citizens are advised to depart Russia and not travel due to security concerns. The U.S. State Department’s Level 4 “Do Not Travel” advisory for Russia has been in place since January 2022, on the eve of the full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
The State Department has sent a formal diplomatic demarche to the Russian government requesting clarification, a source close to the matter told AFP.
The World Health Organization said no cases have been recorded within Irkutsk, but Director-General Adhanom Ghebreyesus called for “timely, complete and transparent information sharing.”
Russian authorities have denied any active public health crisis, insisting the situation is under control. The Kremlin urged the public to ignore online rumors and rely only on updates from Russia’s consumer health watchdog Rospotrebnadzor.
Speaking to the press on Wednesday, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov accused the media of disseminating false information about the case, saying Russia informed the WHO about the death of a laboratory worker at a Siberian plague research institute last week in line with established procedures.
Peskov was commenting on an ABC News report that the United States had lodged a formal diplomatic complaint over Russia's handling of the reported death, urging Moscow to provide greater transparency about the incident.
Peskov said much of the reporting surrounding the incident was false and that people should rely on information released by state health watchdog Rospotrebnadzor.
In response to Trump’s offers of assistance, Rospotrebnadzor offered to aid the U.S. with its own domestic health challenges, citing rising measles cases and a “fatal case of plague” recorded in New Mexico in June.
AFP and Reuters contributed reporting.

Hamam al-Hammami hired by flydubai as part of airline's mass hiring push - report
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
09:38:28 UTC
18:38:28 KST

Omani national Hamam al-Hammami, the pilot who attempted to hijack an Israel-bound flydubai flight, was hired by the airline during a push by the United Arab Emirates-based carrier to expand its pilot staff, according to a Wall Street Journal report published on Tuesday.
The report came after it was alleged that Hammami had previously been banned from flying by Omani authorities over concerns regarding his radical ideological views and that flydubai may have hired him in February without conducting thorough background checks.
According to the WSJ, the airline’s recruitment spree began after the COVID-19 pandemic, as the carrier worked to expand its model of providing low-cost, high-volume flights amid an industry-wide shortage of pilots.
Flydubai launched recruitment initiatives, lowered requirements for some pilot programs
Flydubai’s total number of employees reportedly swelled from 3,682 at the end of 2012 to 6,763 by the end of 2025. Around 1,500 pilots were employed at flydubai at the time of the attempted hijacking.
Over the past three years, flydubai launched several initiatives to increase hiring, including recruitment events in Italy, Ireland, and Poland. Last year, the airline launched a new training program for pilots aged 18 to 30, opened a 38,000-square-foot flight training center in Dubai, and began a cadet program to train foreign pilots, according to the WSJ.
It also lowered the required flight hours for individuals applying for a junior, second-officer pilot program, while increasing salaries offered to new captains and first officers.
According to the report, flydubai categorizes airports by difficulty, allowing pilots without major experience to fly routes to easier destinations. Pilots told the WSJ that Ben-Gurion Airport was considered to be among the network’s most desirable trips, despite security sensitivities.
While the WSJ could not establish how Hammami was assigned the flight to Tel Aviv, it noted that authorities and aviation industry insiders are questioning whether flydubai’s hiring process may have contributed to the circumstances that allowed the first officer access to the sensitive route.

URCS shares wartime operational experience with Norwegian counterparts
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
12:38:28 EEST
18:38:28 KST

The Ukrainian Red Cross Society (URCS) has shared its operational experience during wartime with colleagues from Norway.
"A delegation of the Ukrainian Red Cross Society, led by organization President Maksym Dotsenko and Director General Illia Kletskovsky, visited Norway on a working visit. The main goal was to exchange experience in responding to humanitarian crises and discuss further cooperation with the Norwegian Red Cross," the URCS reported on Facebook on Wednesday.
The parties outlined key partnership priorities under a new three-year agreement during meetings in Bergen and Oslo. Specifically, discussions focused on cooperation in healthcare, humanitarian diplomacy, the dissemination of knowledge regarding international humanitarian law, financial resilience, and the development of organizational capacity.
In addition, Dotsenko spoke at the humanitarian forum titled "War in Europe, Crisis in Norway: Is the Volunteer Sector Ready?". He shared the Ukrainian Red Cross's experience amidst the full-scale war, emphasizing the importance of advance team preparation, public trust, and streamlined interaction with public authorities.
URCS representatives also participated in the General Assembly of the Norwegian Red Cross and held meetings with the leadership of the national society. The delegation met with State Secretary and National Security Advisor Thomas Hornburg, representatives of the Norwegian Ministry of Foreign Affairs and the Norad agency, as well as members of the parliamentary Committee on Foreign Affairs and Defense. Key topics included the humanitarian situation in Ukraine, emergency preparedness, security challenges, the role of volunteers and civil society during wartime, and future opportunities for long-term cooperation.

Mali and Liel Yahalomi arrested in Namibia nearly two months after detention in Argentina - report
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
09:38:14 UTC
18:38:14 KST

Two Iranian women arrested in Namibia after claiming to be Israeli were initially misidentified in Wednesday media reports as Israeli mother and daughter Mali and Liel Yahalomi, who were found in Argentina nearly two months ago.
The two women were arrested after being found with fake Hungarian passports and claiming to be Israeli. After the passports were determined to be fraudulent, Namibian authorities contacted Israel’s Consulate in South Africa to verify the women’s identities.
The women were subsequently found to be Iranian nationals with no connection to the Yahalomis, an Israeli mother and daughter whose disappearance sparked an international search before they were located in Argentina.
Namibia rabbi: I realized immediately - these aren't Israelis, they're Iranian
Rabbi Yosef Rahimi, the Chabad Lubavitch emissary in Namibia, told Walla that he immediately realized the two women were Iranian when he met them at the police station.
Rahimi explained that he had heard reports of Israelis detained at the station and went to bring them breakfast there.
"I looked at them, said, 'Hello, good morning,' and realized immediately - these aren't Israelis, they're Iranian," Rahimi recounted. "They looked at me in shock, like they were trying to figure out who I was and what I was doing there."
Rahimi added that his father was born in Iran and still has family there, so he was familiar with the Persian language enough to converse with the two women and "see how they were doing."
He also told Walla that although he discovered the two were not Israeli, he still gave them the food he had brought. "At least they got an Israeli breakfast out of it," he said. "Everything was strictly kosher."
He expressed frustration that the matter had been leaked to the media before the information was verified, leading people to believe that the Yahalomis were actually in Namibia.
Mali Yahalomi, 50, and her 23-year-old daughter, Liel, both residents of Modi'in, left Israel on August 4, 2026, for a trip to Europe.
The two later traveled to Vienna, where contact with them was lost. When they failed to return to Israel on their scheduled flight, their family reported them missing, prompting an international search.
The investigation was later transferred to Lahav 433, with authorities examining several scenarios, including kidnapping or a security-related incident. Investigators subsequently gathered indications suggesting that the women had left of their own free will and had taken steps in advance to make themselves difficult to locate. Reports said they had purchased replacement phones, turned off or disrupted location services, and deleted applications.
According to published findings from the investigation, the women traveled through the Czech Republic, Austria, and Germany before continuing to South America.
Authorities found no indication of criminal offense or kidnapping
On August 14, they were located on a bus in Argentina after nearly a week of searches spanning several continents. Supt. Walter Kogan, the Israel Police representative in Latin America, boarded the bus, identified himself to the women, and confirmed that they were in good health and not in danger.
Following brief questioning in Argentina, authorities found no indication at the time of a criminal offense or that the two were being held against their will. They were released and allowed to continue their journey after police determined that they were two adult women who had left voluntarily.
Their reported arrest in Namibia is therefore a separate, later development, following their disappearance in Europe and subsequent discovery in Argentina in August.
Anna Barsky and Alon Hachmon contributed to this report.

Shahar Nevo named as Bar-Ilan prof. accused of planning mass terror attack against Palestinians
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
09:38:09 UTC
18:38:09 KST

Shahar Nevo, 59, was named on Wednesday as the mathematics professor at Bar-Ilan University accused of plotting terror attacks against Palestinians and Arab-Israelis.
On Monday, the State Attorney’s Office indicted Nevo for allegedly planning a series of mass terrorist attacks motivated by nationalist ideology against hundreds of Palestinians and Arab-Israelis.
Authorities did not immediately release his name because of a court-issued publication ban, which expired on Wednesday.
The goal of Nevo’s plan, according to the indictment, was forced mass transfer. He named his plan AYT, a Hebrew acronym for Am ya’aseh transfer, which translates as, “The people will carry out transfer.”
Nevo’s vision was to simultaneously activate terrorist cells in different locations across Israel, led by 72 individuals – including Nevo himself. They were to be divided into 12 cells of six people each and use a variety of weapons, including handguns, rifles, axes, and hammers.
Mixed cities, Arab Israeli communities intended targets
The intended targets were mixed cities and Arab communities across the country.
Bar-Ilan University immediately suspended Nevo, and already on Monday said that it “condemns in the strongest possible terms” and is “deeply appalled by the acts” attributed to Nevo. The university called on authorities to “pursue the matter to the fullest extent of the law, should the allegations be substantiated.”
It added, “The University has, and will continue to have, zero tolerance for conduct of this nature – conduct that is fundamentally incompatible with the values we share as Jews, as Israelis, and as human beings, and that stands in clear opposition to the values” of the university.
According to the indictment, the plan was to instruct members of the public to join in “carrying out mass killings and rapidly seizing areas of friction, roads, entrances to and exits from Arab communities, mixed cities, and hospitals… Do not show mercy even to the women or their cruel and repulsive children; do not stop in the face of pleas; harden your hearts. Any pause will lead to an intolerable state of chaos, followed by the massacre of Jews.”
Attacks intended to cause Arabs to flee Israel
According to the plan, the simultaneous mass terrorist attacks, which were to be amplified and publicized on social media in real time, were intended to cause all Arab citizens of Israel, including Bedouin, as well as Palestinians living in east Jerusalem and the West Bank, to flee or be permanently expelled to Jordan, Lebanon, and the Gaza Strip, according to the indictment.
For about a year-and-a-half, he tried to recruit supporters to join him, with no success. He sought out Zehut chairman Moshe Feiglin – No. 2 on the joint Religious Zionist Party-Zehut electoral list – intending to enlist him and, with his help, recruit more activists.
Nevo attended public events that Feiglin appeared at, tried to arrange a meeting with him, and even left the politician a threatening letter, which he later threatened to circulate. He claimed that its publication would harm Feiglin’s image ahead of elections.
Nevo was charged in the Central District Court in Lod with preparing to commit an act of terrorism, extortion by threats, and obstruction of justice. Prosecutors asked the court to keep him in custody until the conclusion of legal proceedings against him. A hearing in the case is scheduled for later this month.

FACTBOX: Russian forces hit enterprises producing Flamingo missiles in Ukraine

MOSCOW, October 7. /TASS/. Russian forces delivered a massive strike overnight, hitting industrial sites producing Flamingo missiles and drones in Kiev and six regions in Ukraine, Russia’s Defense Ministry said on Wednesday.
TASS has compiled the main details on the strikes.
Defense Ministry’s statement
- Russian forces delivered a massive strike by ground-, sea-and air-launched precision-guided weapons and unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs), hitting Ukrainian targets, the Defense Ministry reported.
- According to the ministry, as a result of the strike, Ukrainian military industrial sites involved in the production and storage of Flamingo cruise missiles and long-and medium-range UAVs for the Fire Point company in the city of Kiev and the Kiev, Chernigov, Kirovograd, Dnepropetrovsk, Poltava and Kharkov Regions were hit.
- In addition, Russian forces struck port and ship-repair infrastructure in the Odessa Region and vessels used by the Ukrainian army.
- Russian troops hit a dry cargo ship with supplies for Ukrainian forces at the port of Yuzhny in the Odessa Region, using Geran-4 Seeker drones, the Defense Ministry said, releasing footage of the strike.
- Russian forces also struck a storage facility for fuel and lubricants at the Chernomorsk port in the Odessa Region, using Geran drones.
Targets hit
- The Defense Ministry later stated that Russian forces struck the Smart Ammunition industrial facility for the assembly and storage of FP-5 Flamingo cruise missiles, FP-9 tactical missiles and their components in the city of Kiev.
- Russian troops also struck the Kiev Cardboard and Paper Mill plant that served as a production and storage facility for FP-5 Flamingo cruise missiles and their components in the settlement of Obukhov in the Kiev Region.
- In addition, the Trading House Plastmas-Priluki industrial enterprise, which produced and stored components for FP-5 Flamingo cruise missiles, was hit in the town of Priluki in the Chernigov Region.
- A workshop belonging to the Alexandria Group of industrial enterprises that manufactured components for long-and medium-range unmanned aerial vehicles, including fixed-wing drones, was hit in the settlement of Alexandria in the Kirovograd Region.
- Russian forces also struck a rocket and space industry facility of the State Enterprise Production Association Yuzhny Machine-Building Plant named after O.M. Makarov, which produced, stored and supplied FP-5 Flamingo cruise missiles to the Ukrainian army, along with FP-1 and FP-2 long-and medium-range drones, in the city of Dnepr in the Dnepropetrovsk Region.
- In addition, the AvtoKrAZ factory, where transporter erector launchers for FP-5 Flamingo cruise missiles were produced and stored, was hit in the city of Kremenchug in the Poltava Region.
- Russian forces also struck the JTI Ukraine tobacco factory in the city of Kremenchug, where the production lines were being used to manufacture small arms ammunition for the Ukrainian army.
- Moreover, the Russian army hit a mechanical plant in the settlement of Lozovaya in the Kharkov Region, where FP-5 Flamingo cruise missiles and their components were assembled and stored.
- The Danube Ship Repair plant at the Izmail port in the Odessa Region that manufactured and stored uncrewed boats and their components was also hit.
- In addition, Russian forces struck a dry cargo ship carrying military supplies and dual-use goods for the Ukrainian army at the port of Odessa.
Situation in Ukraine
- Non-residential buildings in Kiev’s Obolonsky District and warehouse facilities in the Podolsky District were damaged, Mayor Vitaly Klitschko said on his Telegram channel.
- Later he said that debris caught fire in an open area in the Darnitsky District and fragments hit non-residential buildings in the Shevchenkovsky District.
- An industrial enterprise was damaged in Dnepropetrovsk, the RBC-Ukraine news agency reported.
- No details have been provided.
- Explosions damaged a warehouse and energy facilities in the city of Kiev and in the Kiev Region, the Strana news outlet reported.
- The outlet did not specify where the damaged sites are located.
- However, the publication posted on its Telegram channel footage of large-scale fires at the sites of explosions.
- Explosions damaged the Tripolskaya thermal power plant in the Kiev Region, Strana later reported.
- The publication provided no further details, only noting that the authorities said nothing about it.
- Trams on several routes stopped after explosions disrupted power in the overhead contact system in Kiev, the city administration said.
- A transport infrastructure facility was damaged in the Kiev-controlled city of Zaporozhye, acting head of the regional military administration, appointed by Ukraine, Mikhail Semikin said.
- No details have been provided.
- According to Semikin, temporary traffic restrictions are possible on some road sectors.
- Over a thousand residents have been left without power in the town of Izyum in the Kharkov Region after infrastructure was damaged, the district military administration reported.
- Head of the Kharkov Region administration Oleg Sinegubov said that railway infrastructure and warehouse facilities were damaged in the Izyumsky District.

Kabul rejects ICC’s Afghan arrest warrants, says no association with top court
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
09:37:28 UTC
18:37:28 KST

Riyaz ul Khaliq
07 October 2026•Update: 07 October 2026
Kabul Wednesday rejected unsealing of four arrest warrants by the International Criminal Court (ICC) against ruling Taliban figures over alleged crimes against humanity involving persecution on gender and political grounds in Afghanistan.
Calling the ICC move a “clear violation of Afghanistan’s national sovereignty, independence,” the Afghan Foreign Ministry accused the top international court of having a “selective and politicized” approach.
The ICC's Pre-Trial Chamber II Monday made public warrants against Haibatullah Akhundzada, Abdul Hakim Haqqani, Habibullah Agha, and Neda Mohammad Nadim.
The warrants were issued on July 8 and Sept. 9, 2025.
The ICC’s “efforts to use international judicial mechanisms for political purposes, have raised serious concerns regarding its impartiality and credibility,” said the ministry, adding Kabul has “no form of cooperation or engagement with the said entity (ICC) and categorically rejects any jurisdiction it purports to exercise over” Afghanistan.
“The entity’s previous association with the former administration (pre-Taliban era), which was established under foreign occupation, has no legal validity for present-day independent Afghanistan,” it added.
The alleged crimes, according to the ICC, occurred from the Taliban’s return to power on Aug. 15, 2021, until at least Jan. 20, 2025.
Emphasizing that Afghanistan’s “sovereignty, independence, and the Afghan people’s sovereign domestic choices” be “respected,” the ministry said Kabul remains “ready to engage with the international community in a constructive and meaningful manner based on mutual respect.”
“Interference in the country’s internal affairs, the imposition of judicial jurisdiction, and any attempt to exert political pressure are unacceptable,” it added.

Syria is depleting its groundwater, but recovery is possible
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
09:37:20 UTC
18:37:20 KST

Breadcrumb
Syria's groundwater reserves are being drained. Can they recover?
A sharp rise in groundwater extraction could deepen Syria’s water crisis, driving down water levels, raising pumping costs and putting further pressure on agriculture and vulnerable rural communities, a researcher who has studied the country’s groundwater has told The New Arab.
Already facing the consequences of conflict, environmental degradation and climate change, Syria is increasingly turning to groundwater as declining surface-water supplies put further pressure on its strained water resources.
Around 6 billion cubic metres of groundwater were extracted during the 2024–25 hydrological year, according to figures reported by Beirut-based pan-Arab news site Almodon, highlighting the growing pressure on Syria’s underground reserves.
"Groundwater depletion is certainly a serious issue in Syria and one that should be given considerable attention by local stakeholders and water managers," said Saeed Mhanna, a researcher at the Centre for Hydrogeology and Geothermics at the University of Neuchâtel in Switzerland.
The reported extraction comes amid years of declining rainfall, drought and reduced surface-water supplies, which have increased reliance on wells for irrigation and drinking water.
However, Mhanna said the reported national extraction figure should be treated with caution because the underlying data and methodology were not available to him for independent assessment.
The figure, drawn from Syria’s water balance for the year, comes as several of the country’s main water basins face increasing pressure from groundwater pumping, particularly for agriculture.
The Barada-Awaj, Yarmouk and Orontes (Assi) basins are among those experiencing significant pressure, with officials warning that extraction in some areas has exceeded permitted levels.
The number of irrigation wells has also increased substantially in several parts of northwest Syria since before the war, as farmers have increasingly turned to groundwater as surface-water supplies decline. In southern Syria, some wells are now being drilled to depths of more than 500 metres, according to the report, increasing the energy and cost required to bring water to the surface.
Syria is emerging from more than 13 years of civil war that began with the Assad regime’s brutal crackdown on anti-regime protesters. The war left much of the country’s infrastructure in ruins, with reconstruction needs estimated at around $216 billion, according to a 2025 World Bank report.
The new government is seeking to reunify the country amid severe security and economic challenges, while relying on international support to help rebuild basic infrastructure and services. Managing the country’s increasingly strained water resources will be another major challenge as it attempts to rebuild.
Solar pumping adds to the strain
Mhanna said one factor that could be contributing to increased groundwater pumping is the growing availability of solar-powered pumping systems.
Solar panels have become substantially cheaper and more widely available, he said, potentially making it easier to extract groundwater in areas where access to electricity and fuel has been limited.
The increasing use of groundwater comes as Syria’s surface-water resources face mounting pressure.
Almodon reported a long-term decline in flows in the Orontes River and other water sources, while climate change is altering rainfall patterns and increasing pressure on water resources.
The country’s dependence on groundwater is particularly important for agriculture, which is one of its major users.
Depleted aquifers can recover
But Mhanna said groundwater depletion is not necessarily irreversible.
"Aquifers can indeed recover when groundwater abstraction is reduced sufficiently," he said, adding that recovery also depends on there being sufficient precipitation to replenish groundwater reserves.
Research conducted by Mhanna and colleagues in the Orontes River Basin found evidence of groundwater recovery after the Syrian war led to widespread abandonment of irrigated farmland and a sharp reduction in pumping.
The researchers used satellite observations to examine changes in groundwater storage and land levels across the region. They found that areas where groundwater abstraction declined experienced groundwater recovery, with springs re-emerging, river discharge increasing and land surfaces rising by up to 4 centimetres a year during wet years.
By contrast, areas where groundwater pumping remained intensive continued to experience land subsidence.
The research provides evidence that reducing groundwater abstraction can allow depleted aquifers to recover, although the extent and speed of recovery depend on factors including rainfall and the characteristics of individual groundwater systems.
A test for the new government
For Syria, that puts irrigated agriculture at the centre of the country’s groundwater challenge.
"If extraction continues to increase without effective management," Mhanna said, the consequences could include declining groundwater levels, higher pumping costs, reduced agricultural productivity and increasing pressure on already vulnerable rural communities.
The next five to 10 years will depend heavily on how Syria’s authorities approach groundwater regulation, irrigation policy, agricultural development and access to energy for pumping, he said.
The challenge is complicated further by the fact that Syria’s groundwater resources cannot be considered in isolation.
The country also depends heavily on transboundary rivers, while climate change and increasing drought frequency may put additional pressure on both surface-water and groundwater resources, Mhanna said.
For water managers, the issue is therefore not simply how much groundwater Syria can extract, but how much it can pump while allowing its aquifers to replenish.
The reported 6 billion cubic metres of extraction in 2024–25 highlights the scale of that challenge, but the evidence from northwest Syria also suggests that Syria’s underground water reserves may not be beyond recovery if pumping can be brought back to sustainable levels.

National health system endured 18.8 bn in 'invisible' cuts 2023-2026 - Gimbe
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
11:37:02 CEST
18:37:02 KST

Although funding for the Italian
national health service has grown in nominal terms since 2023,
it has lost around 18.8 billion euros in that period in terms of
the amount of money needed to keep its share of funding stable
in relation to GDP, the GIMBE health institute said in a report
on Wednesday.
                                    
It added that an additional 32 billion euros in funding will be
needed over the next three years to avert the danger of the
burden of health-care spending being increasingly shifted to
citizens.
                                    
"Nominal funding has certainly increased, yet the share of
national wealth allocated to the National Health Service has
shrunk," said Gimbe President Nino Cartabellotta.
                                    
"It is a phenomenon of 'invisible cuts: not nominal cuts, but
fewer resources than the national health service would have
received had the health-service-fund-to-GDP ratio from 2022
remained unchanged".
                                    
The report said the national health service fund increased by
17,5 billion euros between 2023 and 2026, going from 125.4
billion in 2022 to 142..9 billion 2026 this year.

Bulgaria calls off search for crew of sunken cargo ship Alpha Watan
Unknown

Bulgaria calls off search for crew of sunken cargo ship Alpha Watan
Wednesday 7 October 2026 11:15
Wednesday, 7 October 2026, 11:15
Rumen Nikolov
PHOTO BTA
Font size
The search operation for the crew of the cargo ship Alpha Watan, which sank off the coast of Bulgaria's Byala, has been called off and will not be resumed. No trace of the sailors has been found, said Rumen Nikolov, director of the General Directorate for Emergency and Rescue Activities at Bulgaria's Executive Agency Maritime Administration.
Drones hit two ships in the Black Sea 80 nautical miles off the Bulgarian coast
According to Nikolov, the operation was terminated at 5 p.m. on October 6, as the search and rescue phase had been completed. The only items found at the scene were an overturned lifeboat, three life rafts and parts of the vessel’s equipment, which remained afloat on the surface of the sea.
According to information received from a Bulgarian vessel that came to the ship’s assistance following the drone attack, the vessel sank within seconds after an extremely powerful explosion. Given the speed with which it went down, hopes of finding survivors are extremely slim.
Rumen Nikolov also said that the wreckage would not be inspected underwater by Bulgarian authorities, as this does not fall within Bulgaria’s responsibilities.
The condition of the second vessel that was hit also remains critical, although its crew was rescued. The ship sustained severe damage to its stern, while the engine room is almost completely flooded. According to Nikolov, there is a very high likelihood that the vessel will also sink, BNR correspondent in Varna Daniela Stoynova reported.

Taliban and North Korea Hold Talks During Military Exercises in Russia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
09:35:11 UTC
18:35:11 KST

The Taliban and North Korea held talks during Russia’s Center-2026 strategic military exercises.
Afghanistan’s Ministry of Defense reported the talks on October 3.
The exercises were held from September 28 to October 3. Representatives from Afghanistan and North Korea attended the drills as observers.
Nasibullah Madani, commander of the Joint Combat Training Command, led the Afghan delegation. He met with North Korean military attaché Ro Ki Chol. A photo released by the Afghan ministry shows the two together at an arms exhibition.
According to Safir TV, during the visit, Taliban representatives also held talks with military officials from China, India, Vietnam, Colombia, Uzbekistan, Tajikistan, and other countries.
The ministry said the discussions covered bilateral relations, the exchange of military experience, professional training, and opportunities for cooperation.
These topics referred to the Afghan delegation’s meetings in general. The statement did not provide any specific details about the talks with North Korean representatives or mention any concrete agreements with Pyongyang.
In addition to observing the exercises, the delegation visited a military equipment exhibition. The exhibition featured heavy weapons, drones, long-range missiles, and robotic systems.
The Taliban is also strengthening its military ties with Russia. As Militarnyi previously reported, on May 27, 2026, the two sides signed an agreement on military-technical cooperation.
The agreement’s text was not made public. According to Zamir Kabulov, Russia’s special envoy for Afghanistan, the agreement primarily provides for the restoration of military equipment already in the Taliban’s possession.
The Russian side has also said it could establish training centers to maintain the equipment.
Meanwhile, Russia is expanding its military partnership with North Korea. In June 2024, Moscow and Pyongyang signed a Comprehensive Strategic Partnership Treaty.

Israel marks third anniversary of October 7 attacks with tributes, Gaza strikes and political debate
France
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
11:35:01 CEST
18:35:01 KST

Israel marked the third anniversary of Hamas's October 7, 2023, attack on Wednesday with silent tributes, new strikes on Gaza and intense political debate, weeks before elections in which the country's deadliest day will be front and center.
At the site of the Nova music festival, where Hamas militants in trucks and paragliders opened fire around dawn on October 7, 2023, family members bowed their heads in silence, although at least one instead put on techno music in tribute to the fallen.
Both at Nova and the Kfar Aza kibbutz, another site of mass killings three years earlier, Agence France-Presse (AFP) reporters heard loud bangs from across the border in Gaza during the commemorations as Israel carried out new strikes, despite a ceasefire officially in place for the past year. Gaza officials said at least two people were killed in overnight strikes in the territory, most of which has been reduced to rubble in relentless bombing in retaliation for the worst attack ever against Israel.
Election battle
On October 27, Israel will hold elections for the first time since the attack, with polls showing a tight race for Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who in three years has ordered the massive offensive in Gaza and fought wars against Hezbollah in Lebanon as well as Iran, whose cleric-run government backs Hamas.
At the Nova site, Naftali Bennett, a former prime minister seeking to oust Netanyahu, told reporters of the attack: "This was a colossal failure of the state of Israel, which was established to defend Jews in our land." The center-left Democrats Party put online footage of the attack, without commentary. "A government that for three years has not destroyed Hamas's rule is a government dangerous to Israel," Democrats leader Yair Golan said.
Netanyahu marked October 7 with official ceremonies in Jerusalem on Monday, which was closer to the anniversary on the Jewish calendar. He said there would be "no forgiveness for the murderers" and vowed never to allow rule in Gaza by Hamas, which has faced major losses but remains in control of part of the territory.
Hamas, while battered, remained defiant on the anniversary, issuing a statement calling October 7 "a glorious day of our people's history." The group said it had "smashed the myth of the invincible army" and called the attack "a natural response to, and culmination of, decades of bitter suffering," including the blockade of Gaza that Israel has imposed since the Islamist movement seized the territory in 2007.
Shock to Israeli psyche
October 7 delivered a deep shock to the psyche of Israel, which has prided itself on protecting its borders despite long odds.
Israelis had a more triumphant narrative last week when passengers helped foil an attack by the co-pilot of a flydubai flight to Tel Aviv, although questions were soon raised on why he was allowed to fly.
On October 7, 2023, Palestinian fighters breached the border, storming southern Israel with gunfire, rockets and grenades. A total of 1,221 people died in the attack, according to an AFP tally based on official Israeli figures. Militants also dragged 251 hostages into Gaza, 44 of them already dead.
Israel's military offensive has displaced nearly the entire population of Gaza and killed more than 74,200 people, according to Gaza's health ministry, which is under Hamas authority and whose figures are considered reliable by the United Nations.

KYIV – Russian strikes killed at least 12 people and injured over 40 across Ukraine on Wednesday — the same day that Russian President Vladimir Putin celebrates his 74th birthday.
“As a birthday ‘gift’ to Putin, the Russian army destroyed a residential building in Pryluky, in the Chernihiv region. It was an ordinary five-story apartment building,” Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Wednesday morning, adding that there may be more victims trapped under the rubble.
The Ukrainian air force reported it had shot down most of the 130 killer drones and cruise missiles but only five of about 20 ballistic missiles. Pryluky was the worst-hit area, with five people killed and 26 injured, including five children, according to Zelenskyy. Advertisement

“The Russians wanted to strike painfully and demonstratively. This was one of the most vile strikes. Russian ballistic missiles remain the greatest challenge. And air defense packages for us right now are a vital necessity,” Zelenskyy added.
“Mr. Putin, is this what you wanted for your birthday? People killed in their sleep, injured children, shattered homes?” EU Ambassador to Ukraine Katarína Mathernová wrote on Facebook.
In the past 24 hours, Ukraine has also burned a Russian oil tanker in the Black Sea, struck two oil facilities and a military training ground in the Perm, Samara and Astrakhan regions. The Russian defense ministry reported shooting down 311 drones over 16 Russian regions and the Black Sea.

Rubio says US, Greece to jointly combat security threats
ATHENS, Oct 7 - US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said on Wednesday that "strong and model NATO ally" Greece and the United States are launching new counterterrorism information sharing between their law enforcement agencies.
During an official visit to Athens, Rubio said Greece was particularly exposed to the threats posed by mass migration and human trafficking.
"As part of our efforts to combat these common threats to our nations, we're proud to announce a new memorandum of understanding establishing a joint security program to strengthen the counterterrorism information sharing between our respective law enforcement agencies," he told reporters alongside Greek Foreign Minister George Gerapetritis.
Greece has been an important NATO ally to the United States, offering key military facilities to safeguard security in the Eastern Mediterranean, and it leads an EU maritime mission to protect commercial shipping in the Red Sea.
Rubio and Gerapetritis presided over the sixth round of a US-Greece strategic dialogue that began in 2018 in which the sides agreed "to deepen defense ties, bolster trade and investment, and promote cultural ties," according to a joint statement.
Greece, it said, would receive $4 billion to support a long-term defense plan to increase interoperability between the two militaries and to "explore future opportunities for defense industrial base cooperation."
Gerapetritis said that Greece was willing to cooperate with the United States and offer maritime aid in the Strait of Hormuz if there is a viable peace process there.
Rubio stood by US Ambassador to Greece Kimberly Guilfoyle after US senators expressed concerns over allegations that she had threatened that the US could use its influence to undermine the Greek government.
Asked if her conduct was in compliance with State Department ethics, Rubio said: "Suffice it to say, our embassy here is doing a great job. Our ambassador has been a strong ambassador here." REUTERS
