Victoria Roshchyna, Tortured to Death by Russia, and Imprisoned Ukrainian Journalists Receive Human Rights Award
The international human rights organization Reach All Women in War (RAW in War) has named several journalists held in Russian captivity and occupied territories as recipients of the 2026 Anna Politkovskaya Award , as reported by Detector media on October 6.
The announcement honors media workers reporting on Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine and human rights abuses while detained by Russian authorities.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Prominently recognized among the recipients is Victoria Roshchyna, a Ukrainian journalist who documented war crimes during Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine and died in Russian custody in September 2024 following torture and mistreatment.
Other Ukrainian media professionals awarded include Melitopol journalist Iryna Levchenko, who was sentenced by Russia to 15 years in a penal colony on espionage charges.
The honors also recognized RIA Melitopol reporter Anastasiya Hlukhovska, held in Russian captivity since August 2023, and Yana Suvorova, a local Telegram channel administrator sentenced to 14 years on terrorism and espionage charges.
Crimean journalist Iryna Danylovych, who was detained in April 2022, was also recognized. She received a 7-year sentence from an occupation court and has suffered severe health deterioration due to poor conditions and torture during her imprisonment, Detector media reported.
The nomination committee cited the courage of these Ukrainian media workers who risked their lives and freedom to report on Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine and protest human rights violations. RAW in War called for the immediate release of all detained journalists and stated that those responsible for abuses and torture in custody must face justice.
The award marks 20 years since the assassination of Russian investigative journalist Anna Politkovskaya on October 7. Founded in 2006 by Bulgarian journalist and human rights defender Mariana Katzarova, RAW in War presents the annual prize to honor women working in active regions who protect human rights at great personal risk.
Anna Politkovskaya was a prominent Russian investigative journalist, author, and human rights activist known for her reporting on Russia’s full-scale invasion of Chechnya and exposure of state corruption and human rights abuses by Russian forces.
She was assassinated on October 7, 2006, after being shot dead in the elevator of her Moscow apartment building in a targeted contract killing linked to her reporting.
The persecution and illegal sentencing of Ukrainian media workers coincides with broader violations of international law by Russian forces against Ukrainian captives. Previously, it was reported that Russian forces have established a specialized combat brigade made up of Ukrainian prisoners of war and Ukrainians coerced into defecting.
Forcing prisoners of war into military service would violate international law governing the treatment of captives. The reported use of POWs for military purposes also follows broader patterns of coercion and abuse documented in Russian detention facilities, where Ukrainian captives have reported systematic torture, deliberate deprivation of food, and other forms of physical and psychological abuse.

Germany’s Merz renews backing for Israel, also calls for Palestinian state
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07

Ayhan Şimşek
07 October 2026•Update: 07 October 2026
Chancellor Friedrich Merz reaffirmed Germany’s support for Israel while also calling for a Palestinian state alongside Israel as the best path to peace and security in the region.
Merz, a conservative politician who has long backed Israel, renewed that stance in a written statement Wednesday. He said Germany stands firmly by Israel and that Israeli friends can count on Berlin’s commitment.
Blaming Hamas for the conflict, Merz said Germany’s thoughts were with the victims of the October 2023 attacks, the survivors and former hostages. The country, he said, stands in solidarity with the victims’ families and mourns the dead. 
Security and Palestinian state
“We stand for the security and existence of Israel. That is a lesson from the Shoah and part of German identity,” Merz said.
The Shoah, the Hebrew term for the Holocaust, was the systematic murder of about 6 million Jews by Nazi Germany during World War II.
Merz renewed his call for a political solution to the Israeli-Palestinian conflict, saying the task now is to lay the foundation for a new order in which Israelis, Palestinians and their neighbors can live in peace and security.
“The German government is committed to this,” he said. “In our conviction, this goal is best achieved through the establishment of a Palestinian state alongside Israel.” 
Antisemitism in Germany
Merz also warned of growing antisemitism in Germany that, he said, too often goes unchallenged. He pledged that the government would do everything in its power to fight antisemitism in all its new and old forms.
“Jews must be able to live without fear throughout Germany. Jewish life must be able to continue to flourish in our society,” he said. “That is why we are acting with all determination against antisemitic incidents and attacks.”
He said the government would oppose those who relativize or question Israel’s right to exist, not only on this anniversary, but every day.

EU Considers Limits on Market Access and Funding for Sensitive Ukrainian Agricultural Products
The European Commission is proposing targeted arrangements that would significantly limit financial support and market access for certain sensitive Ukrainian agricultural products after Ukraine joins the EU, according to Hromadske.
The measures are part of a broader document package adopted on October 6, aimed at updating policies in preparation for future expansion of the European Union.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
European officials highlighted the substantial scale, structure, and high efficiency of Ukraine's farming sector as key reasons behind the proposal.
To manage the impact on the bloc, targeted mechanisms would substantially cap both funding and market access for specific sensitive items.
While Brussels did not specify which goods would face constraints, the policy document stressed the importance of helping Ukraine re-establish trade access to its historical export markets outside the European Union.
Ukrainian authorities expressed strong opposition to long-term trade caps during membership talks. Ukrainian Minister of Agrarian Policy and Food Taras Vysotskyi stated in an interview with Politico that Ukraine cannot agree to an accession framework that permanently restricts sales within the bloc.
Vysotskyi noted that temporary transitional periods are acceptable, but permanent restrictions contradict the core logic of full European Union membership.
He urged European partners not to view Ukraine solely as a competitive threat to local producers, pointing out that Ukrainian agriculture can help lower Europe's reliance on third-country imports of fertilizers, soy, and lysine, while expanding access to Black Sea shipping routes, according to Politico.
He added that the goal is to enter the single market not just as a supplier of raw grain, but as a producer of animal feed, food ingredients, processed products, and biofuels.
Previously, Ukraine’s Ministry of Agrarian Policy and Food requested €220 million ($254 million) in non-repayable aid from the European Commission to support small and medium agricultural producers following Russian attacks on Black Sea ports.
The requested funding was intended to subsidize loan interest rates under the state "Accessible Loans 5-7-9%" program, helping farmers secure financing for the autumn sowing campaign amid sharp drops in crop prices and severely restricted export routes.

Germany’s Foreign Minister Names Five European Countries Russia Could Target Next
German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul has stated that Russia may hold broader ambitions beyond Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, naming five countries that could potentially face future threats.
Speaking on the German television channel n-tv on October 6, Wadephul outlined potential targets based on historical assertions, according to ZDFheute.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
"And so we must assume that Russia has further plans," Wadephul said. He rooted his assessment in previous statements made by Russian leader Vladimir Putin regarding the dissolution of the Soviet Union, an event Putin previously referred to as the "greatest geopolitical catastrophe" of the 20th century.
When questioned about which specific nations could be included in such ambitions, Wadephul identified Ukraine, Georgia, Moldova, Estonia, Latvia, and Lithuania.
"Ukraine belongs to this. Georgia also belongs to this. We also see Russian activity in Moldova. And, of course, the Baltics would belong here as well," the German Foreign Minister declared, ZDFheute reported.
Addressing the situation in the Baltic region, Wadephul noted that Estonia, Latvia, and Lithuania are members of both the European Union and NATO.
He emphasized that in the event of an attack against any of these nations, Germany, as an allied partner, would be directly involved. In addition to future military concerns, Wadephul stated that Berlin is already experiencing Russian hybrid tactics firsthand, citing recurring cyberattacks and unmanned aerial vehicle incidents.
"We are already under attack right now. Remember the drones in Leipzig," the German Foreign Minister said.
Wadephul clarified that while he does not classify current hostile actions as full-scale warfare, Berlin views them as ongoing hybrid attacks.
In August 2026, Russia launched a targeted hybrid attack on Germany using explosive-laden drones that infiltrated the Leipzig/Halle airfield.
One drone, intended to detonate near a Ukrainian Antonov-124 cargo aircraft carrying ammunition, failed to explode and was discovered on the ground, while another struck a plane mid-flight, forcing an emergency landing in Hannover.
Following the initial incident, additional suspicious drones were spotted near German military installations, and a third device bearing traces of explosives was recovered.
By early September 2026, German authorities and US intelligence confirmed that the operation bore the clear hallmarks of Russian intelligence services, with Chancellor Friedrich Merz condemning the months-long planned attack as a deliberate strike against German infrastructure.

Bulgaria to Add Five Air Defense Missile Systems Following Black Sea Drone Attack
Prime Minister Rumen Radev said the government will approve an investment expenditure plan for five additional air defense missile systems, while warning that developing capabilities against unmanned systems in the air and maritime domains requires time, funding and a systematic approach.
Radev made the remarks before the regular Council of Ministers meeting, hours before the Consultative Council for National Security (CCNS) convenes following drone attacks on commercial vessels in the Black Sea.
He thanked the crew of the Bulgarian ship DIOSCURIA, as well as rescue teams from the Navy and Air Force, Border Police and medical teams, for their professional response in helping people in distress after two vessels were attacked.
"Once again, we have demonstrated that human life is a supreme value for us and that Bulgaria possesses emergency rescue capabilities within its Exclusive Economic Zone, in accordance with international conventions," Radev said.
The Prime Minister said the CCNS should not become a venue for political campaigning and called for restraint in the wake of the attacks.
"The CCNS must not turn into a stage for pre-election demagoguery. There is no room for hysteria. Composure and sober judgment are required," Radev stated.
He said establishing the necessary capabilities to counter unmanned systems at sea and in the air is a complicated process that cannot be completed quickly.
"It requires time and funding," Radev said.
The Prime Minister recalled that plans had been initiated in 2023, during a caretaker government he had appointed, to purchase high-end unmanned aerial systems capable of monitoring Bulgaria's entire Exclusive Economic Zone. He said the initiative had not progressed since then.
"Many governments have come and gone since then. Absolutely nothing. Zero," Radev said.
He added that the Defense Minister had now prepared the required documentation and that a procurement procedure had been launched, including a Request for Information sent to leading global companies.
Radev also recalled that Bulgaria joined the European Sky Shield Initiative in 2022, again at the initiative of the Defense Minister of his caretaker government.
He said a contract had already been signed for one IRIS-T air defense system and that the government would approve an investment expenditure project for five more systems.

Instead, Radev focused on the operation in Plovdiv targeting abuses involving clinical pathways, hospital activities and high-cost medications, as well as the siphoning of funds from the National Health Insurance Fund (NHIF).
He praised officials from the Ministry of Health, Ministry of Interior, Prosecutor's Office and SANS who took part in the operation and said cross-checks would continue throughout the country.
"Cross-checks are continuing across the country. We are preparing amendments to the Public Procurement Act to curb the siphoning of funds from the NHIF," Radev stated.

Morocco’s First F-16 Block 72 Fighter Takes Flight
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
09:04:26 UTC
18:04:26 KST

Lockheed Martin conducted the first flight of an F-16 Block 72 fighter intended for the Royal Moroccan Air Force.
The company said the aircraft is moving into the flight-testing phase before being transferred to the customer.
The Block 72 is the latest and most advanced F-16 version, featuring upgraded avionics, cutting-edge sensors, enhanced combat mission systems, and improved safety and reliability features.
“The F‑16 remains a vital component of today’s and future air defense, and we’re proud of the role it will continue to play in supporting Morocco’s sovereignty and contributing to regional stability for decades to come,” the company stated.
In 2019, the U.S. Department of State approved the sale of 25 F-16V Block 72 fighters to Morocco, valued at an estimated $3.8 billion.
The package also includes 29 Pratt & Whitney F100-PW-229 engines and 26 AN/APG-83 radars.
The AN/APG-83 radar is a key component of the Block 72’s combat capabilities.
The AESA radar provides improved target detection and tracking, greater reliability, and better resistance to electronic warfare compared with older F-16 systems.
Combined with modern onboard computing systems, a helmet-mounted cueing system, and precision-guided munitions, this creates a fighter designed to detect and engage threats more quickly.
The contract also deepens Morocco’s integration into the U.S. defense ecosystem.
In 2004, Washington designated Morocco a major non-NATO ally of the United States. Since then, U.S.-Moroccan security cooperation has expanded to include combat aviation, ground forces, and long-range systems. Procurement has included F-16 fighter jets, M1 Abrams main battle tanks, AH-64E Apache attack helicopters, and HIMARS multiple rocket launchers. Last year, the Royal Moroccan Air Force received the first six of the 24 AH-64E Apache attack helicopters ordered.

Taiwan aims to halt birth rate decline next year
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
09:03:55 UTC
18:03:55 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Taiwan aims to stop its birth rate from falling further next year, Premier Cho Jung-tai (卓榮泰) said Tuesday.
The country has continued to expand childcare subsidies in response to its low birth rate. More than NT$210 billion (US$6.6 billion) is earmarked for related measures in next year’s central government budget, according to CTEE.
Cho said the package draws on the experiences of neighboring countries and covers several areas, including expanding education support, strengthening childcare services, promoting family-friendly workplaces, and reducing housing costs. He acknowledged that the policies would not produce immediate results, saying it could take one to two years for their effects to become apparent.
The initial goal is therefore to stop the birth rate from falling further before gradually raising it in subsequent years, Cho said. Taiwan recorded 107,812 births last year, marking the 10th consecutive year of decline and a new low, according to CNA.
The National Development Council projects that Taiwan’s population will continue to shrink as low fertility and an aging population reshape the country’s demographics. The number of newborns is projected to fall below 100,000 this year, according to CNA.
The package includes about NT$185 billion (US$5.82 billion) for a monthly NT$5,000 (US$157) child development allowance. Under the plan, children aged 0 to 18 would receive NT$5,000 per month, according to InsFeel.
For children aged 0 to 6, the allowance would be paid directly to their families. For those aged 6 and above, half of the monthly amount would instead be placed in a child savings account and could be withdrawn after the child reaches adulthood.

The bureau said that it has completed 282 beams and two piers. It added that southbound construction is currently at 66.51%, about 5.71% ahead of schedule.
Highway Bureau Director Lin Fu-shan (林福山) said joining the northbound section marks the final construction phase. Chen noted that builders Kseco and Cheng Shine Machinery also built New Taipei's Danjiang Bridge.

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Taipei Mayor Chiang Wan-an (蔣萬安) on Wednesday visited a methadone clinic to observe the city's opioid addiction treatment program as drug policy becomes an issue in the upcoming Taipei mayoral election.
Chiang visited the Taipei City Hospital Kunming Branch to learn about treatment practices. Staff explained that patients first consult a doctor and receive a prescription, and at the dispensing counter, their identity and prescribed dosage are verified before a nurse measures the medication.
Patients must drink the full dose and open their mouths so staff can confirm it has been swallowed. Throughout the process, patients must receive methadone under medical supervision and consume the medication at the clinic, per Upmedia.
Methadone is an opioid medication used to treat dependence on illicit drugs such as heroin. In Taiwan, it is classified as a Schedule II controlled drug and requires medical supervision for treatment and to reduce intravenous drug use health risks.
Taipei has provided such treatment since 2005, and is offered at four medical institutions: Taipei City Hospital's Kunming, Yangming, and Songde branches and the Beitou branch of Tri-Service General Hospital. Wang Chien-chun (王建淳), director of the Kunming Branch, said approximately 600 people receive methadone treatment in Taipei each year, per TVBS.
The mayor's visit comes amid a dispute with DPP Taipei mayoral candidate Puma Shen (沈伯洋) over drug prevention and harm-reduction policies. On Wednesday, Shen said methadone treatment and other harm-reduction efforts by health care workers had been unfairly politicized during the election campaign.
He welcomed Chiang's visit to the clinic and said he hoped it would help ease concerns among frontline medical workers. The Kunming center also operates a clean-needle program. Taipei has 19 automated clean-needle vending and collection machines, according to a Taipei City Hospital press release.

‘I thought the baby would change him’: the women whose pregnancies are blighted by domestic abuse
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
09:00:45 UTC
18:00:45 KST

Evie bought the baby monitor with a rare flicker of enthusiasm, having become increasingly numb as her pregnancy progressed. She liked that it would send video footage to her phone. “I thought, ‘This is really good. Not only can you hear the baby – you can see the baby.’” Unfortunately, her partner appreciated the monitor too. Soon she was carrying it around the house on his orders, so he could watch her. “He used it as surveillance,” she says.
By then she was worn down, and terrified. He had become more controlling since they learned she was pregnant. By the seventh month he had become physically abusive, too. “We were just lying in bed watching something,” she recalls of the first attack. “An argument broke out but it started getting overly aggressive … It just felt more threatening and he looked really agitated. So I ended up shimmying over and sitting on the edge of the bed. All of a sudden he just swung the biggest punch at my arm. Then he did it again. The impact was like whiplash.”
Trauma makes her memory hazy, Evie says, but somehow she ended up lying on the bed again. “Then he climbed over me, putting his knees either side. As he put his arm down, it squashed my belly.”
She shrieked. “Then he just snapped out of it.” As she cried he apologised and put his arms around the bump. “He talked to the baby, sang to the baby …” she recalls. He claimed he had lashed out due to his anxiety. “I accepted it wouldn’t happen again because he was so apologetic.”
The Domestic Abuse Commissioner estimates that in England and Wales, 30% of domestic abuse begins during pregnancy, but the real figure is almost certainly higher because of underreporting. New research published by the For Baby’s Sake Trust, which supports young families experiencing domestic abuse, estimates that 20,000 cases of domestic abuse are disclosed to maternity services in England every year.
Lauren Seager-Smith, the chief executive of For Baby’s Sake, stresses “pregnancy does not cause abuse”, but explains: “It can be a context in which we see an increased use of abusive behaviours … This could include increased monitoring, isolation from family, friends and colleagues, financial control, coercion around healthcare or reproductive rights, physical, emotional and sexual abuse, and even jealousy and resentment towards the developing baby.”
Elaha Walizadeh, a senior programme manager at Refuge, the biggest specialist domestic abuse organisation in the UK, says that between 2024 and 2025 “14% of our service users reported being pregnant”, but believes this is the “tip of the iceberg”. Women may come into more contact with healthcare professionals during pregnancy, but “because not all healthcare professionals and advisers are trained in recognising the signs and having the right conversations with these survivors, survivors are being missed”.
Evie became pregnant early in her relationship. She describes “lovebombing”: gifts, flowers, chocolates. She now sees signs of control were there, dressed up as love. “‘Oh, you’re going to see your mum?’ he would say. ‘I was going to get a movie night ready …’”
He was “over the moon” when she became pregnant but his control intensified. “It started with tracking apps – he ‘wanted to know I was safe’,” she says. “Or he’d say: ‘I’d rather you not go there. I’ve got a bad feeling.’” He even started accompanying her to work sometimes. “He had to be with me constantly. Every midwife appointment. I couldn’t go to doctors on my own, couldn’t have my flu jab on my own.” Evie was asked routine questions concerning domestic abuse. She said everything was fine because she thought it was.
Later her partner became aggressive. Arguments escalated, usually triggered by an accusation she was not paying him enough attention. Doors would slam, and the name-calling began: “slag”, “stupid bitch”. But the apologies afterwards and excuses of anxiety convinced her, until the physical attack. Even then, she felt too vulnerable to leave or seek help. “No one wants to bring a child up in a broken home,” she says. “I thought the baby would change him and make him happy.”
A month before the birth, another violent outburst led to the authorities finally becoming involved. He eventually moved out, but would “sneak back” and continued to demand Evie carry the baby monitor. Fear kept her silent. She allowed him to attend the birth and he had supervised contact with the new baby, who he bonded with, but the physical abuse against her escalated until she secured a non-molestation order, granted by courts to prevent domestic abuse. She has not had any contact for years.
“I feel like I died and my body just carried on,” is how Evie describes her emotions towards the end of her pregnancy and early motherhood. There is a blankness to her voice even now. “I hold a lot of guilt,” she says, believing she “failed” her child. “I am hypervigilant, extremely jumpy …” She still ruminates on why the abuse began. “I believe at first he thought it was a good idea to have a child because then: ‘She can’t leave me.’ But then the baby was getting all the attention.”
Dr Panos Vythoulkas, a lead perinatal clinical psychologist at the North London NHS foundation trust, says this is common. “The baby introduces another person whose needs must be recognised. Someone who feels entitled to control their partner may experience these changes as a threat to their position, attention or authority.” He cites survivor accounts that repeatedly describe “increased possessiveness”. Abusers resent “the attention given to the pregnancy or experience the baby as a rival. A woman’s need for rest, support or choice not to have sex may be interpreted as rejection or a challenge to their authority.”
The clinical psychologist Dr Jill Domoney has worked with abusers who have faced up to their actions. “In some of those cases there was a real tension between what they’d internalised about masculinity – needing to be strong and in control and to look after the family financially – and what was being expected of them as fathers, needing to provide in circumstances where that might not be possible,” she says. “Maybe they’re feeling quite vulnerable and scared – but not feeling they were allowed to express that.” Some had difficult relationships with their own fathers.
Like Evie, Vythoulkas believes that abusers may initially desire pregnancy because it offers opportunities for control. “Financial pressures, insecure housing, isolation and increased dependence can restrict a woman’s options. An abusive partner may exploit these circumstances by withholding money, limiting contact with others or obstructing healthcare,” he says.
Riley says her partner was desperate for children. Although they were in a long-distance relationship, “within a matter of weeks” he was talking about babies. She eventually agreed. However, when she rang to tell him the news, his reaction was staggering. As well as asking her to do a pregnancy test on video to prove she wasn’t lying, “He immediately said: ‘Is it mine?’” Shaken, she refused to do the test but still found herself desperately reassuring him. Vythoulkas confirms that “accusations of infidelity and doubts about the baby’s paternity” are regularly observed as part of abusers’ insecurity.
The abuse Riley then began to experience was initially a disorientating combination of lack of interest and manipulation. Her partner would look at his phone if she put his hand on her stomach to feel the baby kicking, and insisted he felt nothing. He did not want to discuss baby names. No plans were made to move in. Yet he would regularly visit unannounced. “He would turn up on my doorstep at 2am; it was like he was trying to catch me out or put fear into me,” she says.
Then the verbal insults and aggression escalated, especially when Riley declined sex. “He used to call me a rhino and said I looked disgusting. If I cried he would tell me to stop turning on the waterworks and ask if I agreed it was pathetic. My self-esteem was at an all-time low.”
She tried to end the relationship but he kept showing up. Her low confidence made this harder to resist. “I felt very alone. I didn’t share the things he was saying to me, partly because I felt ashamed and partly I had become so used to what was happening.”
Then the physical intimidation began, stopping short of contact. “He was once boiling a pan of water and we got into an argument and he held this big pan of water in front of me and kind of lunged.” He didn’t throw it. “It creates a really confusing emotional situation because you can be genuinely frightened of someone while still desperately wanting the relationship to be OK.”
Fear stopped her taking action: fear of his response and fear of having her baby removed. “He would say: ‘Don’t go and pull something where I’m not at the birth because you’ll regret it,’” she recalls. He was present, but they did not move in together afterwards. When he visited, the violent outbursts intensified, usually when Riley was holding the baby. It culminated with Riley being held hostage in her home with her baby, punched as she fed the infant, strangled and raped. She believes she could have died. Her partner was convicted and is now serving a prison sentence. “At no point did he ever beg for forgiveness,” she says. “He would talk about work stresses, money pressures, his childhood or the way he had been treated himself.”
Abuse during pregnancy can be fatal. A Byline Times investigation based on police information found at least 223 women experienced pregnancy loss linked to domestic abuse in England and Wales between 2017 and 2021. Victims of intimate partner violence are also twice as likely to forgo prenatal care, exacerbating the risk of pregnancy loss. The MBRRACE Confidential Enquiry into Maternal Deaths found that suicide was the leading cause of maternal death in the first postnatal year, and that domestic abuse was documented in 43% of women who died. Evie says she felt suicidal after her child’s birth. “I drank to numb myself and I wanted to end my life because I couldn’t cope,” she says.
Evie also points to another potential result of abuse: the behavioural challenges she now observes in her son. Walizadeh says Refuge sees children with brain injuries potentially caused by physical abuse during pregnancy, as well as “children who later in life go on to develop symptoms of ADHD [attention deficit hyperactivity disorder] and other forms of developmental conditions”.
For Baby’s Sake and Refuge stress the need for continued training in perinatal services about domestic abuse. It needs to be spotted early. “By the time you’ve actually realised how dangerous it is, it’s too risky to leave,” says Riley.

As many as 450,000 people have taken part in nationwide protests across France, according to student and youth organizations, in the biggest day yet of a growing movement over deteriorating school conditions, as police fired tear gas and used batons and water cannon to disperse protesters in several cities.
The Interior Ministry put the turnout on Tuesday at more than 250,000, including 56,000 in Paris, compared with the organizers’ estimate of 450,000 nationwide and 100,000 in the capital.
The protests, which began in September in the deprived suburbs of Paris and have since spread across the country, have brought together high school students, teachers, parents and trade unionists demanding more funding for education, additional teachers, better-maintained school buildings and improved classroom conditions.
The scale of Tuesday’s demonstrations, coupled with increasingly violent clashes between protesters and police, has intensified pressure on Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu’s government, which has promised to address the students’ demands while defending the police response.
Lecornu told lawmakers that at least 215 teenagers and 85 school staff had been injured since the protests began, describing the toll as “the heaviest toll in decades” paid by France’s school system. His office said more than 700 police officers had also been injured.
Most of Tuesday’s demonstrations passed without serious incident, but some, including in Paris, ended in clashes with riot police. Nearly 500 people were arrested, according to Interior Ministry figures reported by French media, while the ministry said dozens of police officers were injured, according to Press TV.
Trade unions and human rights groups have accused police of using excessive force against young protesters. Amnesty International called on French authorities to end what it described as “disproportionate police repression.”

Bar-Ilan professor named in alleged plot to kill hundreds of Arabs and Palestinians
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
09:00:00 UTC
18:00:00 KST

Prof. Shahar Nevo, 59, of Petah Tikva was identified Wednesday as the Bar-Ilan University mathematics lecturer charged with planning large-scale terror attacks that prosecutors say were intended to kill hundreds of Arab Israelis and Palestinians.
Nevo was indicted two days earlier at the Lod District Court on charges including preparation to commit an act of terrorism, extortion by threats and obstruction of justice. Prosecutors allege that he developed the plan out of a nationalist and ideological motive, initially against the backdrop of the May 2021 riots and with increasing intensity after the October 7 massacre.
According to the indictment, Nevo sought to carry out numerous coordinated attacks across Israel that would kill large numbers of Arab citizens, including Bedouins, as well as Palestinians in east Jerusalem and the West Bank. Prosecutors say his ultimate objective was to force them to flee permanently to Jordan, Lebanon and the Gaza Strip.
The indictment alleges that for more than three years, beginning in February 2023 and continuing until his arrest about two weeks ago, Nevo developed a detailed plan he called “AIT,” a Hebrew acronym for a phrase meaning “the people will carry out transfer.”
Prosecutors say he took concrete steps to advance the plan, including conducting reconnaissance trips, drafting documents laying out its operational methods and ideological justification, and attempting to recruit participants.
72 attackers in 12 cells
Under the alleged plan, 72 Jewish participants, at least half of them licensed to carry firearms, would be divided into 12 cells of six people each. They would arm themselves with weapons including pistols, rifles, axes and hammers and launch simultaneous surprise attacks in mixed Jewish-Arab cities and Arab communities across Israel.
The indictment says Nevo also envisioned support from subversive elements recruited from within the IDF. According to prosecutors, the plan included possible strikes on Arab population centers by the Air Force, Artillery Corps and Armored Corps.
In a section of the plan titled “How to carry out AIT here and now,” prosecutors say Nevo outlined instructions for what he described as mass killing, rapid seizure of friction points, roads and entrances to Arab communities, mixed cities and hospitals.
The indictment quotes him as calling on participants not to show mercy, including toward women and children, and arguing that hesitation would lead to chaos and the killing of Jews.
Prosecutors allege that the coordinated attacks, combined with their immediate amplification on social media, were intended to cause Arab citizens of Israel, Bedouins and Palestinians in east Jerusalem and Palestinian Authority-controlled areas to flee beyond Israel’s borders.
The indictment further alleges that Nevo devised a covert recruitment plan under which he intended to approach Zehut chairman Moshe Feiglin and seek his participation before recruiting additional activists with his help. Feiglin is running in the upcoming election on the joint Religious Zionist-Zehut slate.
According to prosecutors, Nevo planned to identify potential recruits in advance and invite them to a Zehut election event, where they would be told they had been selected to participate in a terror attack the following day and would receive detailed operational instructions.
In its request to keep Nevo in custody until the end of proceedings, the prosecution said the plans reflected what it described as an “extreme and murderous ideology” that led him to formulate a detailed, multi-stage program intended ultimately to cause the mass killing of Arab Israelis and Palestinians.
Prosecutors said the alleged ideology and efforts to advance the plan demonstrated an immediate danger to individuals, the public and the state, adding that the nationalist motive and the security tensions during which the acts allegedly took place heightened that danger.
‘I have exams to grade’
At a court hearing Sunday, Nevo argued that he should be released to house arrest.
“In my opinion, I am not currently a danger to anyone,” he told the court. “My life has been completely turned upside down. I have so many things to do and financial matters to take care of. I don’t see who I am dangerous to.”
Nevo also expressed concern about remaining in custody and said that people around him knew the allegations against him. “I’m a professor at Bar-Ilan and worked until my arrest,” he said. “I have exams to grade at home.”
Nevo began studying mathematics at Tel Aviv University in 1984 and received his bachelor’s degree three years later. He later studied mathematics at Bar-Ilan University, earning a master’s degree in 1992. He joined the university’s permanent academic staff in 1999 and later became an associate professor in the mathematics department.
His attorneys, Hadar Sharir and Alon Porat of the Public Defender’s Office, said the case was still at an early stage. “After we study the investigation materials, we will consider our next legal steps,” they said.
Bar-Ilan University said after the indictment that it was “shocked” by the allegations and condemned the acts attributed to Nevo. The university said he would be suspended immediately pending completion of the legal proceedings.
Zehut and Feiglin said that after receiving alleged extortion and threatening letters from Nevo, they immediately contacted police and filed a formal complaint. The party said it trusted law enforcement and judicial authorities to handle the case fully.

ChatGPT's teen safeguards failed to alert parents during suicide conversations, report finds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
09:00:00 UTC
18:00:00 KST

ChatGPT’s teen safeguards failed to alert parents during suicide conversations, report finds
- Click here to listen to this article
-   Share via
See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search. Set us as preferred
- Common Sense Media’s Youth AI Safety Institute rated ChatGPT for Teens as an “Unacceptable Risk,” urging OpenAI to stop marketing it to minors until it can provide a safer experience.
- In tests of more than 4,000 prompts, researchers found that prolonged conversations about suicide and self-harm rarely triggered parental alerts, and some chats lacked referrals to professional help.
- OpenAI disputed the findings, saying the testing may have preceded full activation of parental controls; the report also said the safeguards failed requirements of California’s Adam’s Law.
The guardrails OpenAI put in place to protect teens don’t seem to be working, according to a new report.
Common Sense Media’s Youth AI Safety Institute rated ChatGPT for Teens an “Unacceptable Risk” for children under 18 in a study published Wednesday. The media and technology watchdog organization urged OpenAI to pause marketing the product and keep minors off the platform until it can offer a safer experience.
OpenAI announced ChatGPT for Teens in August, promising “stronger built-in safety protections” for users under 18, including limits on discussions around suicide, eating disorders, violence and sexual content. Parents who link their accounts can set times when ChatGPT can’t be used and schedule study hours when the teens’ chats start in study mode. Parents also can choose to receive alerts if their teens use the bot for high-risk behavior or research.
Researchers posing as teenagers with San Francisco Bay Area-based accounts tested more than 4,000 prompts before and after the launch of ChatGPT for Teens. A group of experts reviewed the chatbot’s responses.
“Some protections, including refusing sexual role play, worked — but others failed to deliver on their commitments, or even got worse with the launch of ChatGPT for Teens,” the report said.
Testers spent up to an hour discussing suicide, self-harm or eating disorders on more than a dozen new accounts registered to 13- to 17-year-olds. 
After dangerous discussions that went as long as an hour, only a handful of alerts were sent to the accounts registered as the users’ parents. 
Clinical reviewers found that much of ChatGPT for Teens’ crisis response content was “clinically sound” but many conversations that should have forced the bot to refer teen users to professional help didn’t lead to referrals. Meanwhile, some safeguards were easy to turn off or circumvent.
The report says ChatGPT failed tests tied to three requirements of California’s Adam’s Law: crisis referrals, parental alerts and age assurance. Signed by Gov. Gavin Newsom last month, the law will go into effect in July 2027. Sponsored by Common Sense Media and endorsed by OpenAI, the bill is named after 16-year-old Adam Raine, whose parents sued OpenAI alleging ChatGPT encouraged his suicide.
OpenAI said the report’s conclusions are based on flawed testing.
“We welcome rigorous independent evaluation, but we do not believe Common Sense Media’s testing accurately reflects how ChatGPT’s teen safeguards work in practice or expert perspectives on how AI can support teens,” an OpenAI spokesperson said in an email. “Our review of Common Sense Media’s methodology shows that the bulk of their testing may have begun and concluded before activation of parental controls was complete, making their findings inaccurate.”
Tom Siegel, executive director of the Youth AI Safety Institute, said
it hopes OpenAI will share company data and partner with outside researchers and organizations to look into ways to reduce risks associated with AI for kids.
“Teens are vulnerable and unprotected and we’re letting them loose on a product that is not just unproven, but proven to be high risk and dangerous,” Siegel said.
The institute is partly industry-funded, including by the OpenAI Foundation. It said OpenAI reviewed a draft of the report for factual accuracy but had no say over its findings.

Prof. Shahar Nevo, 59, of Petah Tikva was identified Wednesday as the Bar-Ilan University mathematics lecturer charged with planning large-scale terror attacks that prosecutors say were intended to kill hundreds of Arab Israelis and Palestinians.
Nevo was indicted two days earlier at the Lod District Court on charges including preparation to commit an act of terrorism, extortion by threats and obstruction of justice. Prosecutors allege that he developed the plan out of a nationalist and ideological motive, initially against the backdrop of the May 2021 riots and with increasing intensity after the October 7 massacre.
According to the indictment, Nevo sought to carry out numerous coordinated attacks across Israel that would kill large numbers of Arab citizens, including Bedouins, as well as Palestinians in east Jerusalem and the West Bank. Prosecutors say his ultimate objective was to force them to flee permanently to Jordan, Lebanon and the Gaza Strip.
The indictment alleges that for more than three years, beginning in February 2023 and continuing until his arrest about two weeks ago, Nevo developed a detailed plan he called “AIT,” a Hebrew acronym for a phrase meaning “the people will carry out transfer.”
Prosecutors say he took concrete steps to advance the plan, including conducting reconnaissance trips, drafting documents laying out its operational methods and ideological justification, and attempting to recruit participants.
72 attackers in 12 cells
Under the alleged plan, 72 Jewish participants, at least half of them licensed to carry firearms, would be divided into 12 cells of six people each. They would arm themselves with weapons including pistols, rifles, axes and hammers and launch simultaneous surprise attacks in mixed Jewish-Arab cities and Arab communities across Israel.
The indictment says Nevo also envisioned support from subversive elements recruited from within the IDF. According to prosecutors, the plan included possible strikes on Arab population centers by the Air Force, Artillery Corps and Armored Corps.
In a section of the plan titled “How to carry out AIT here and now,” prosecutors say Nevo outlined instructions for what he described as mass killing, rapid seizure of friction points, roads and entrances to Arab communities, mixed cities and hospitals.
The indictment quotes him as calling on participants not to show mercy, including toward women and children, and arguing that hesitation would lead to chaos and the killing of Jews.

Prosecutors said the alleged ideology and efforts to advance the plan demonstrated an immediate danger to individuals, the public and the state, adding that the nationalist motive and the security tensions during which the acts allegedly took place heightened that danger.

French investigation spotlights Hamas links to crypto funding, local NGOs
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
08:59:58 UTC
17:59:58 KST

An investigation in France and the US has spotlighted how Hamas appeared to channel money to terrorist operations using groups posing as humanitarian associations and cryptocurrency.
A report at Al-Ain media in the UAE noted on October 6 that there was a “French investigation into Hamas funding through cryptocurrencies; head of association imprisoned.” The report added that “the head of an association in the Gironde region of southwestern France was placed in pretrial detention on Tuesday as part of a judicial investigation opened in Paris into suspicions that funds reached Hamas through humanitarian associations, according to a judicial source.”
The report appears linked to a statement by the US Department of the Treasury’s Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) which said on October 2 it had “designated a member of Hamas’s military wing, along with two France-based individuals and two affiliated entities that provide critical financing to Hamas.
These designations expose a sophisticated, multi‑year financing architecture that moved more than $2 million to Hamas through deceptive charitable fronts and cryptocurrency channels, demonstrating the organization’s persistent ability to adapt its fundraising mechanisms to evade detection.”
According to the Treasury Department, the network had several levels. It identifies Saleem Abdallah Saleem al-Zaq (al-Zaq) as “a Gaza-based battalion deputy in the Hamas military wing who oversees a financial network that has used various money services businesses and cryptocurrency wallets to transfer significant funds to the Hamas Al-Qassam Brigades.”
French 'sham fundraisers' used to finance Hamas
Meanwhile, in France, a group of “sham fundraisers” was used. “Faouzi Barika (Barika) and Amel Oualid (Oualid) operate from France, where they run purported charities ostensibly to raise money for humanitarian purposes to aid Gazan civilians. In reality, they partner with al-Zaq to raise and transfer money directly to him, which al-Zaq in turn funnels to Hamas. The Treasury says that “during the six years from 2020–2026, Barika, Oualid, and al-Zaq collected more than $2 million for Hamas, of which $1.5 million was collected after the October 7, 2023 Hamas attack on Israel. Barika and Oualid sent hundreds of thousands of dollars in cryptocurrency to al-Zaq, and al-Zaq has advertised both Barika’s and Oualid’s fundraising accounts on his own social media accounts.”
In France, Barika is accused of jointly establishing “France-based Association Baraka with al-Zaq, which he uses as a mechanism to solicit public donations that are sent to al-Zaq for transfer to Hamas. Oualid established France-based Ensemble C Mieux, which, like Association Baraka, she uses to raise money to send to al-Zaq and Hamas.”
The report at Al-Ain appears to reference this connection, noting that Faouzi I the head of Barika and “along with four other people, faces charges brought by the judicial authorities in Paris on Friday, including ‘financing a terrorist entity, specifically Hamas,’ ‘breach of trust within an organized gang,’ and ‘money laundering resulting from breach of trust within an organized gang linked to a terrorist entity.’”
The report goes on to say that “the National Anti-Terrorism Prosecutor’s Office [in France] had requested that Fawzi B. be placed in pretrial detention, while the suspect requested a postponement of the hearing to prepare his defense. He appeared before a judge on Tuesday who ordered his detention, according to the judicial source.”
The October 2 statement from the Treasury in the US appears to have enabled or been timed with the French arrests. Arab News said on October 3 that “five people have been charged in France on suspicion of sending funding via humanitarian groups to a third party seeking to collect money for Hamas, the French National Anti-Terrorism Prosecutor’s Office (PNAT) said Saturday.”
The report noted that PNAT had told the AFP that “five were taken into custody on Tuesday by investigators from the General Directorate for Internal Security (DGSI), which is leading the investigation.” The inquiry had been opened Friday, the same day that the Treasury released its details. “Three of the five suspects were placed under judicial supervision on PNAT’s recommendation.”
France “requested the pretrial detention of the two association presidents”, but the first “was placed in pretrial detention pending a postponed adversarial hearing he had requested”, the public prosecutor’s office said. A lawyer told AFP that “my client participated in fundraising efforts for exclusively humanitarian purposes; his detention would be scandalous.”
The investigation focuses on the Gironde region of France, an area along the coast in southwest France not far from the Spanish border. The area is usually known for wine vineyards. The French news site Ouest France reported similar details to AFP and Al-Ain.
CoinDesk, which reports on crypto generally, noted on October 5 that “Treasury crackdown exposes crypto’s role in $2 million Hamas fundraising network.” They add that “the action is the latest indication that US authorities are focusing on crypto’s role inside wider fundraising and payment networks, rather than portraying it as Hamas’s primary funding source. Treasury officials have previously said Hamas and other groups still rely mainly on conventional finance, despite previously already being levied crypto-related sanctions and seizures.”
Wohl: US Treasury designations leave gaps
CoinDesk also noted that “it also follows reports last month that the Al-Qassam Brigades advised donors to avoid sending funds directly from Binance and instead use other crypto services before moving money to a TRON wallet.”
Ryan Wohl at the Foundation for Defense of Democracies noted, in a report on October 6 about the Treasury sanctions, that “The designations block the targets’ property in the United States, or in the possession or control of US persons, such as US banks, and generally prohibit US persons from dealing with the targets. But they leave two gaps: they cannot compel French banks to freeze euro-denominated accounts, and they do not identify the network’s cryptocurrency wallets.”
Wohl, an Education and National Security Research Associate at FDD, added that “French prosecutors have charged Barika and Oualid with financing Hamas, which they dispute. Neither of the designated associations appears in France’s national asset-freeze register, though their funds may already be restricted through the criminal proceedings. Three days after the designations, Association Baraka’s website was still asking donors to give through PayPal and to contact “our brother” in Gaza on Snapchat and WhatsApp.”
A document on the website of the US Congress notes some background on the role of cryptocurrencies in terror finance. “Although Hamas has reportedly solicited cryptocurrency donations, the scale and effectiveness of these efforts remain unclear.
Citing two cryptocurrency analytics firms and Israeli government seizure orders, the Wall Street Journal reported on October 10, 2023, that cryptocurrency wallets connected to Hamas received about $41 million between 2020 and 2023 and that wallets connected to another US-designated terrorist organization, the Palestine Islamic Jihad (PIJ), received as much as $93 million over a similar period.
Some observers have questioned whether the figures overestimate the amount Hamas received and the potential role of other, larger funding sources. The Wall Street Journal subsequently reported that Treasury is “investigating $165 million in cryptocurrency-linked transactions that may have helped finance Hamas” before the October 2023 attacks.”
This report added that “in 2019, Hamas engaged in a cryptocurrency donation campaign that led to the US seizure of several websites and 150 cryptocurrency accounts linked to the armed wing of Hamas, the Izz al Din al Qassam Brigades, in 2020.”
It goes on to note that “in connection with these enforcement actions, the US Department of Justice (DOJ) charged two foreign nationals for money laundering crimes related to their involvement in converting cryptocurrency into other forms of value. DOJ also prosecuted an individual for concealing material support to Hamas, including through Bitcoin. US enforcement actions in 2023 revealed that Qassam Brigades used Binance, a cryptocurrency exchange, to facilitate cryptocurrency transactions as early as 2019.”

Support for the students’ demands is even higher, with 72% considering them legitimate – a view shared by majorities across the political spectrum, from left to right.
However, the public is far more divided over what should happen next: 55% believe students have made their point and should end the protests, while 27% think they should carry on.
'Impunity must end,' Le Pen says, as she offers her support to police over student protests
French far-right National Rally leader Marine Le Pen offered her strong support for the police, saying “impunity must end,” and “those who vandalise our schools, and their parents when they are minors, must pay for the damage they cause.”
“The French people should no longer have to finance the vandals,” she told reporters on a visit to Cournon-d’Auvergne.
She also said the police should have the support of the nation, and “not face constant accusations from those in power,” as she chose to use the protests to criticise the French president, Emmanuel Macron.
“While the far left spreads false accusations to stoke violence, Emmanuel Macron once again chooses to undermine those who protect the French people,” she said.
Le Pen leads the presidential polls ahead of next year’s election, with 33-34% of vote share in the first round, well ahead of Édouard Philippe and Jean-Luc Mélenchon at around 16-18%.

Brussels has yet to find a way to curb Chinese imports, while EU leaders demand results from Beijing talks as a trade war looms.
EU Trade Commissioner Maroš Šefčovič heads to Beijing on Wednesday for two days of talks aimed at rebalancing trade relations that Brussels sees as heavily skewed in China’s favour.
His meetings with Chinese Commerce Minister Wang Wentao come as the EU’s trade deficit with China has reached a record €1 billion a day – and an October deadline for progress approaches.
The Commission opened negotiations in June to address what officials describe as trade-distorting Chinese exports, giving Beijing until October to deliver “tangible” results.
At the heart of the talks is access to the EU market. Brussels wants product-specific quotas on Chinese imports, but has yet to persuade Beijing to curb exports. China recently rejected its proposal for “voluntary export restrictions” on electric vehicles.
The pressure is mounting as a wave of low-cost Chinese imports threatens entire sectors of European industry.
EU leaders, whose countries all now run trade deficits with China, expect Šefčovič to return with concrete results ahead of their summit in Brussels next week.
"Harsher measures"
“They [EU27] want to see the direction of travel. They want to even have a concept for the solution of this issue, a pilot scheme,” Šefčovič told Euronews in an exclusive interview in early September.
“I’m trying to do it through these negotiations, but they have to bring us very concrete results.”
He warned that a failure to deliver tangible results this month would trigger “a strong political movement” among EU leaders for “harsher measures”.
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz and French President Emmanuel Macron pushed on Monday for a new tool that would allow the Commission to react quickly to economic threats, including measures that could lead to “an immediate cut-off from the internal market if needed.”
Trade tensions have escalated in recent months, with Beijing threatening retaliation over EU proposals to restrict access to its market.
Since the launch of the talks, the Commission has also launched several probes into Chinese products over unfair trade practices and imposed anti-dumping duties on Chinese firms.
Euronews has also learned that EU member states were holding back investigations into the chemicals sector that could lead to safeguards — quotas and tariffs — to protect an industry particularly hit by Chinese competition.
Meanwhile, China opened an investigation into EU chemicals on Saturday, a move seen as retaliation for EU investigations into Chinese chemical producers.

Nobelitis — How winning a Nobel Prize can give you delusions of grandeur
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
08:58:00 UTC
17:58:00 KST

How winning a Nobel Prize can give you delusions of grandeur
October 7, 2026
Linus Pauling won not one, but two Nobel Prizes — the first, for chemistry, in 1954 for his research into the nature of the chemical bond, and the Peace Prize in 1962 for his work in the anti-nuclear weapons movement.
The American chemist not only won two Nobel Prizes, but won them on his own, a rare feat for any scientist. Such an honor often turns laureates into global superstars overnight, with millions hanging on their every word.
Nobel laureates can fall victim to Nobelitis
That instant fame can be dangerous, said Nils Hansson, a professor in the Department of History, Theory and Ethics of Medicine at Heinrich Heine University in Düsseldorf. Especially, he said, when these world-renowned experts "start spreading crazy, unproven scientific theories" — ideas that, when disseminated by Nobel laureates, risk being taken seriously.
That's what happened with Pauling. Beginning in the mid 1960s he began claiming that vitamin C was a universal remedy, a cure for everything from cancer to cardiovascular conditions and degenerative diseases like Alzheimer's disease, multiple sclerosis or osteoarthritis.
Pauling developed an alternative treatment he called orthomolecular medicine, based on specific doses of vitamins and minerals for each patient. To this day, some 60 years later, evidence for his methods remains inconclusive.
Pauling's case is a classic example of "Nobelitis," or "Nobel disease" — not an official diagnosis, but an informal term used to describe how some laureates begin to suffer delusions of grandeur later in life. It was first coined by Paul Nurse, president of The Royal Society, the UK's national academy of sciences, and himself a winner of the Nobel Prize.
'Be skeptical of everything'
"Be skeptical of everything, including yourself and your own ideas," Nurse said in a 2019 interview with KU Leuven University in Belgium, when asked what made someone a good scientist. In cases of Nobelitis, that self-skepticism is the first to go.
That was also the case with virologist Luc Montagnier, who was jointly honored in 2008 for his discovery of the human immunodeficiency virus, HIV, with colleague Francoise Barre-Sinoussi in the early 1980s.
Montagnier would later go on to support homeopathic medicine, another alternative treatment of disease and claim that HIV transmission in Africa could be diminished through better hygiene and nutrition.
During the COVID-19 pandemic, Montagnier said the SARS-CoV-2 virus had been created in a lab with parts of the HIV genetic code. "It's difficult for a practicing virologist to say that a Nobel laureate in virology is spreading nonsense," said German virologist Christian Drosten on NDR's Coronavirus Update podcast in May 2020. "But that is utter nonsense."
James Watson, who was never known for his modesty, also let fame go to his head. In 1962, he was awarded the Nobel Prize along with Maurice Wilkins and Francis Crick for their discovery of the structure of the DNA molecule. But in the early 2000s, Watson repeatedly spread racist theories that Black people were less intelligent than white people.
For medical historian Hansson, Watson is a prime example that the Nobel Prize is not automatically awarded to a person who should be considered as a role model.
"You may have made a fantastic discovery, but that doesn't make you a universal genius," he said.
Even Noble Prize winners need to be challenged
But the great expectations of an admiring public may also contribute to the development of Nobelitis. Paul Nurse, who won the Nobel Prize in physiology or medicine in 2001, soon found himself getting daily requests for interviews on all sorts of topics.
"As if suddenly I was acknowledgeable about all workings of the world and of human beings," he told DW.
Nurse had this advice for researchers: "Be careful quite what you say. Talk about things that you do know something about that would be fine. And if you don't know so much or you're not sure about something, be really clear that you're not sure."
Hansson has also noticed that the media eagerly report whatever Nobel laureates say — even when prize winners stray far from their area of expertise.
Nobelitis sufferers are leaders in their fields, and rightly honored for their work with the Nobel. But they're also regular individuals, not immune to megalomania and other behavioral problems — meaning that homeopathy, orthomolecular medicine and other pseudosciences don't automatically become credible just because they're backed by a Nobel Prize winner.
This article was originally written in German.

Trump blames French unrest on ‘mass migration’ (VIDEOS)
US President Donald Trump has blamed the violent student protests in France on the country’s migration policies, rejecting rioters’ claims that the unrest is driven by poor school conditions and teacher shortages.
On Tuesday, France saw the largest day of demonstrations demanding that the government of President Emmanuel Macron provide more resources and better funding for schools since the student protest movement began in mid-September.
Some 266,000 people took to the streets across the country, with 56,000 joining the march in Paris and major rallies also taking place in Marseille, Strasbourg, Nantes, Lyon, and other cities, the Interior Ministry said. The organizers put the attendance at 450,000.
In some locations, including Paris, protests escalated into vandalism and clashes between demonstrators and police, who employed tear gas and batons to disperse the crowds. A total of 488 people were arrested on the day nationwide, according to the French authorities.
Teachers, parents, and rights groups have accused police of excessive force, with around 215 students injured over the past three weeks. They include a 15-year-old who lost his hand after reportedly picking up a police stun grenade and a 16-year-old who lost sight in one eye, allegedly after being hit by a rubber bullet. On Wednesday, the French government banned the use of stun grenades during the student protests. More than 6,500 people, mostly minors, have been arrested, according to AP.
In a post on Truth Social on Tuesday, Trump insisted that “what’s happening in France is nothing less than out of control mass migration,” rather than a dispute over schools, claiming that “Islam [wants] to take over a once great Country!”
France, which has been one of the main destinations for migrants in the EU in recent years, has a foreign-born population of 9.6 million, the second largest in the bloc after Germany.
Migration has also caused tensions elsewhere for Western European countries. More than 72,000 migrants crossed from Morocco into the Spanish North African enclave of Ceuta in late July, according to Reuters. At least 10,000 were reported to still be in the territory this week, straining local resources and prompting protests by residents.
Trump’s words were echoed by the US envoy to the UN, Mike Waltz, who told Fox News that Washington would “always condemn lawlessness” and the violence in Paris, but argued that Europe’s “open borders” and “unchecked immigration” policies had caused “a level of frustration” to boil to the surface.
French Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu rejected claims that the government had ordered “police repression” or that officers were being racist. He said “ultra violence” would not be tolerated, while promising investigations into what he described as “accidents” during the protests.
Interior Minister Laurent Nunez insisted that the response by police had been proportionate in “almost all cases.” A total of 715 officers have been injured in the clashes over the past three weeks, he said. According to the Education Ministry, 24 schools have been burned or ransacked by demonstrators since mid-September.
Some student groups have called for new nationwide rallies to be held on Thursday.

Pig disease outbreak leads to mass cull across Switzerland
More than 10,500 animals are being culled across Switzerland following an outbreak of highly contagious enzootic pneumonia. The disease has affected 60 breeding and fattening farms in 14 cantons.
An outbreak of enzootic pneumonia was detected on September 9 at a large network of pig farms across several cantons, the Lucerne cantonal veterinary service said on Tuesday.
+ High risk of contagious swine fever spreading in Switzerland
Authorities have ordered the complete clearance of 20 farms across six cantons in an effort to stop the spread of the disease. So far, around 10,500 animals have been slaughtered or put down nationwide. Movement restrictions remain in place at 40 affected pig-fattening farms across 14 cantons.
Canton Lucerne hardest hit
Canton Lucerne has been the hardest hit. Authorities there have culled pigs on 10 breeding farms and one fattening farm, with a total of 5,200 animals either slaughtered or put down. In canton Bern, three breeding farms housing around 1,700 animals were affected.
More
Swiss pig farmers face new biosecurity rules
In canton Vaud, 950 pigs were culled on an affected farm. A second farm will be allowed to complete its fattening cycle before being sanitised.
The 14 affected cantons include Neuchâtel and Valais in French-speaking Switzerland.
+ Dutch cities are banning meat advertising – will Switzerland follow?
Animal transfers prohibited
Each farm is assessed individually to determine the risk of the disease spreading. Cantonal vets are also visiting neighbouring farms to check the health of pigs kept there.
More
How Switzerland’s pig’s feet export gamble in China faltered
So far, there is no indication that any farms outside the affected area have been infected. Restrictions on the movement of animals will remain in place until infection can be ruled out or the herd has been cleared of infection.
Farmers whose animals are culled by order of the authorities will be compensated for their losses. Authorities are urging pig farmers to remain vigilant and follow biosecurity measures strictly.
The disease affects pigs but poses no risk to humans. There is also no risk from eating pork.

Rubio In Iceland Signals Deeper NATO Push As Russia, China Challenge Arctic Security
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
08:55:02 UTC
17:55:02 KST

REYKJAVIK -- US Secretary of State Marco Rubio has signaled a renewed American push to strengthen security in the Arctic, warning that US adversaries and competitors are already acting in a region of growing strategic importance.
Rubio, standing alongside Iceland's foreign minister, Thorgerour Katrin Gunnarsdottir, on the first stop of a three-nation tour of NATO allies, cast the strategically located NATO member as a critical link in the defense of North America and Europe.
The trip comes as Russia's military and covert capabilities and China's expanding Arctic ambitions drive greater attention to the north.
"Iceland sits at the center of many of the questions surrounding the security and defense of our shared region," Rubio said.
"Those threats are growing, which is why this focus on the Arctic in general and Iceland, in particular, is so critical."
His visit included a stop at Hofdi House, the site of the 1986 summit between US President Ronald Reagan and Soviet leader Mikhail Gorbachev.
Forty years later, Rubio and Gunnarsdottir recreated the leaders' famous handshake, highlighting Iceland's enduring role in the strategic relationship between North America, Europe, and the Arctic.
Rubio did not announce plans for a new permanent US military base in Iceland, but he signaled Washington is open to expanding its security presence.
Asked whether the United States could increase its military footprint or surveillance capabilities following a new US-Danish-Greenland defense agreement, Rubio said Washington would work with Icelandic authorities to determine what more could be done.
"I think there's a willingness to do more together," he said, pointing to Iceland's infrastructure, technology, and ability to provide surveillance and domain awareness.
The United States ended its permanent military presence at Keflavik in 2006, but allied activity has continued through exercises, maritime patrols, and rotational deployments.
Rubio said the strategic environment has since changed. "The world has changed over the last 20 years. There's a lot of focus on the Arctic," he said, arguing Iceland's location is important not only to NATO's defense of Europe but also to the defense of the US homeland.
More than 1,200 Americans participated with allied forces in the Northern Viking 2026 exercise last month, part of annual military cooperation in and around Iceland.
Rubio stressed that Iceland's lack of a conventional military does not prevent it from making an important contribution to NATO.
Instead, the country provides territory, infrastructure, surveillance capabilities, and access for allied forces.
"We want to continue to build upon that as a way to prevent conflict," Rubio said. "History teaches us that deterrence is the best prevention of violence and the best preventer of war."
Rubio said the security risks facing Iceland and its allies extend beyond conventional military threats.
Asked whether Iceland faces a direct threat from Russia, he cited covert activity, threats to undersea cables, and vulnerabilities around shipping lanes.
"There are direct threats," Rubio said. "And those threats in the 21st century aren't just military threats; they're also economic, commercial threats that have implications on the national security of our respective countries."
The comments reflect a broader NATO concern that the Arctic and North Atlantic are becoming increasingly important strategic spaces for submarine activity, maritime routes, communications infrastructure and access to North America.
Erlingur Erlingsson, a senior visiting fellow at the Institute of International Affairs at the University of Iceland, told RFE/RL that Iceland has welcomed improved allied security awareness in the High North, including NATO's Arctic Sentry initiative and growing European capabilities.
But he cautioned against losing sight of the larger European security picture.
"Russian capabilities, particularly gray-zone warfare, long-range strike, and submarine, remain a significant threat," Erlingsson said.
He said NATO's eastern flank remains the alliance's primary security concern and continued support for Ukraine is critical to European security.
Kristinn Arni Lar Hrobjartsson, co-founder of the Icelandic security think tank Varda, said Reykjavik is also seeing heightened Russian interest in the region.
Arctic Focus
"Iceland certainly feels the increased focus on the Arctic, driven by Russian activities and continued war of aggression," he told RFE/RL, pointing to the presence of a Russian spy ship around Iceland during the summer.
Hrobjartsson also cautioned against overstating China's role in Iceland, saying Chinese activities are "largely exaggerated" compared with the more immediate military dangers facing NATO on its eastern flank.
Iceland's importance is likely to grow as the United States strengthens its position in Greenland and the wider Arctic.
Rubio welcomed a recent agreement involving the United States, Greenland, and Denmark on Greenland's defense, saying it was important for regional security.
Hrobjartsson said Iceland's strategic location and support for allied forces make it an important part of the emerging Arctic defense network.
"The new Greenland agreement and potential build out of more bases there will undoubtedly call for even more contribution from Iceland," he said.
Rubio also sought to broaden the relationship beyond defense, highlighting opportunities in geothermal energy, biotechnology, marine industries, and other areas.
But he stressed that security remains the foundation for economic cooperation. "Security underpins everything else," Rubio said. "If you're not secure, you can't be prosperous."
He suggested that while a traditional US-Iceland free-trade agreement may be difficult in the current environment, the two countries could pursue closer bilateral trade and investment ties.
For Iceland, the challenge will be balancing its growing strategic importance with the need to maintain a strong and predictable transatlantic alliance.
Erlingsson said Rubio's visit could help repair some of the damage caused by recent tensions over Greenland, but warned that wider questions about US commitments to NATO remain.
For Washington, Iceland's strategic value is tied to its location between North America, Europe and the Arctic, as NATO increases its focus on the High North and the North Atlantic.
Rubio said the goal was not to provoke conflict but to strengthen deterrence.
"We want to continue to build upon that as a way to prevent conflict, not as a way to encourage conflict or provoke conflict, but prevent it," he said.
"History teaches us that deterrence is the best prevention of violence and the best preventer of war."

Thick haze from forest and land fires disrupted flights in Indonesia on Wednesday, while dozens of areas across neighboring Malaysia recorded unhealthy air quality.
Two flights from Jakarta failed to land at Sultan Syarif Kasim II Airport in Pekanbaru, Riau province, after visibility dropped to about 600 meters (1,969 feet), Indonesia’s state-run Antara news agency reported.
Lion Air flight JT292 returned to Jakarta, while Citilink flight QG936 was diverted to Batam in the Riau Islands, according to airport authorities.
The Lion Air flight turned back at 6.44 am local time (2344GMT Tuesday), local outlet Detik reported.
Haze also blanketed Batam, reducing visibility to 2-3 kilometers (1.2-1.9 miles), Detik reported, citing Indonesia’s Meteorology, Climatology and Geophysics Agency (BMKG).
The agency said smoke from forest and land fires in other parts of Sumatra and Kalimantan had been carried into Batam and surrounding areas.
In Malaysia, 36 areas recorded unhealthy Air Pollutant Index readings as of 10 am local time (0200GMT), local newspaper The Star reported, citing the country’s Air Pollutant Index Management System.
Johan Setia in Selangor recorded the highest reading at 191, followed by Cheras in Kuala Lumpur and Nilai in Negeri Sembilan at 189.
Malaysian authorities said Indonesia had accepted Kuala Lumpur’s offer to assist firefighting operations, including aerial water bombing and amphibious aircraft.
Malaysia and Indonesia are coordinating the deployment of firefighting assets through diplomatic channels.
