Fear and a far-right lurch: How October 7 reshaped Israel
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
08:53:23 UTC
17:53:23 KST

Fear and a far-right lurch: How October 7 reshaped Israel
Three years on, the trauma of October 7, 2023, continues to reshape Israel’s politics, wars and place in the world.
For the vast majority of Israelis, modern history is divided between the period before the Hamas-led attacks of October 7, 2023, and after. In the three years since Israel launched its genocidal war on Gaza following the attacks, Israeli society has undergone fundamental changes.
A sense of collective trauma has been amplified through political rhetoric and media hysteria to hitherto unseen levels in modern Israel, observers say.
Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza has killed more than 74,000 Palestinians, and Israel has expanded its attacks to several regional states.
The war on Gaza and a series of settler pogroms in the occupied West Bank, fuelled by the Israeli far-right, have contributed to Israel’s growing isolation from much of the world.
Daniel Bar-Tal, an Israeli political psychologist at Tel Aviv University, said October 7 shattered the myth of Israeli military invincibility.
Before October 7, 2023, a powerful sense of confidence regarding Israel’s supposed technological and military superiority was common.
That ended when Hamas and other groups stormed into Israel: Nearly 1,200 people were killed, and Palestinian groups took about 250 others captive.
The Israeli public had been generally isolated from the consequences of the military’s violent actions in Gaza and the occupied West Bank, and Bar-Tal said many were shocked that Israel’s Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu might have had prior intelligence about Hamas’s plans.
Inside Israel, the psychological impact of the attacks was palpable. “It disrupted [everything] immensely. It is a crisis that doesn’t leave the population,” he told Al Jazeera.
Palestinians, in particular, have lived with Israel’s genocidal response ever since.
The lurch rightward
Politicians have exploited the fear and trauma of the October 7 attacks to further their own ends, and are using them to target Palestinians as a whole.
“There is no doubt that many Israelis were gripped by genuine fear after October 7, but there is also no doubt, in my view, that political forces have exploited that fear to erase virtually every achievement made over the years in Jewish-Palestinian relations,” Israeli sociologist Yehouda Shenhav-Shahrabani said.
Countless polls suggest that Israeli society has lurched even further to the right over the past three years. Mainstream newspaper headlines have asked the question whether the left, which was the main bulwark for a two-state solution in Israel, still exists.
A huge number of Israelis continue to support the execution of Palestinian prisoners charged with “terrorism” and the continued expansion of illegal settlements in the occupied West Bank.
In a May 2025 survey of Israelis by Penn State sociologist Tamir Sorek, an overwhelming majority of respondents said they supported expelling Gaza’s residents. A significant minority also backed the “mass killing” of all residents of cities invaded by Israeli troops, as the biblical Israelites did at Jericho.
“October 7 was undoubtedly a watershed moment in contemporary Israeli politics,” noted Shenhav-Shahrabani. “I would say that it has taken us back a hundred years – in our collective consciousness, in our willingness to engage with one another, and, above all, in the level of mutual trust. This is an enormous setback, one that will be extremely difficult to overcome.”
Israel’s former Defence Minister Yoav Gallant has described Palestinians in Gaza as “human animals” and National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir boasted of handing out thousands of government arms to settler groups already known for their often-deadly pogroms against Palestinian towns and villages in the occupied West Bank.
“The messianic and racist right has seized upon the catastrophe, not merely to justify its existing positions, but to push the boundaries of what can be said and done in Israeli politics,” said Shenhav-Shahrabani.
He acknowledges that October 7 did not create the Israeli right, but it had normalised positions previously considered extreme.
“Fear is undoubtedly a major factor in this transformation. But fear alone does not explain it. Fear is also being politically mobilised,” he said.
‘Repression… became more violent’
Anti-Palestinian views did not begin with October 7, 2023, either. Such abuses go back to the foundation of the state of Israel in 1948, the subsequent forcible displacement of some 750,000 Palestinians, and the erasure of Palestinian villages from the land.
In the years since, a growing number of international bodies and rights groups have described Israeli rule over Palestinians as apartheid. Systematic violence, including military assaults on blockaded Gaza, deadly West Bank pogroms and ongoing settler attacks and land seizures, which largely go unpunished, has also been widely documented by rights groups, particularly after October 7.
B’Tselem has noted an explosion in violence across the occupied West Bank, recording 1,107 Palestinians killed in “a single political project” between the Israeli military and settlers that appears aimed at forcing out the local population.
“October 7 allowed processes that were already under way to gain momentum and escalate,” Yair Dvir, from B’tselem, told Al Jazeera.
“The infrastructure of apartheid, repression and control over Palestinians became more violent, while the broader trajectory of eliminating Palestinian collective existence became clearer and more normalised – through the genocide in Gaza, the ethnic cleansing and dismantling of Palestinian society in the West Bank, and the intensification of discrimination and dehumanisation against Palestinian citizens of Israel.”

Russia Drops Criminal Case Against Children’s Hospice Founder Lida Moniava
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
08:49:00 UTC
17:49:00 KST

Russian investigators have dropped a criminal case against Lida Moniava, a prominent advocate for critically ill children’s care, after finding no grounds for prosecution, her supporters said Tuesday, citing her lawyer.
Moniava was arrested on Sept. 2 and charged with spreading “false information” about Russia’s military over a social media post about Ukrainian civilians killed in Russian attacks. The charge carries a maximum sentence of 10 years in prison.
Her support group said lawyer Mikhail Biryukov had confirmed the decision and that an official notice closing the case had been sent by mail.
“This is a miracle. But it didn’t happen on its own. You made it happen,” the group wrote, thanking those who attended her court hearing, wrote letters in her defense and publicly supported her.
The group gave special thanks to hospice patients who came to court, some of whom were in wheelchairs or using ventilators.
Moniava is the founder of the Moscow-based charity Lighthouse, which operates hospices for seriously ill children and young adults in the Russian capital and surrounding region.
Her case had prompted an outpouring of support from families whose children had received care from the charity.
After Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, Moniava created a foundation that provided shelter, medical supplies and food to people fleeing from the war. That foundation suspended operations in 2025 due to the dwindling number of refugees arriving in Moscow and the Moscow region.
Following her Sept. 2 arrest, Moniava announced that she was stepping down as Lighthouse’s director and leaving its board but said she intended to stay in Russia.
However, on Wednesday, Biryukov said Moniava would remain Lighthouse’s director.
“If there’s no verdict and no judicial investigation, and the case is closed, that means there’s no reason for her to step down as director,” Biryukov told RBC.
The dismissal of her case marks a rare outcome in Russia’s crackdown on anti-war speech. In a February 2025 report, rights group OVD-Info said it knew of just over 20 instances in which anti-war criminal cases had been dropped at various stages since the full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

Lithuania’s Foreign Ministry on Wednesday condemned a Moscow court decision labelling 13 people from the Baltic states and several organisations as “accomplices of Nazi Germany”, calling the ruling a falsification of history aimed at smearing Baltic resistance fighters.
“This is not the first time Russia has falsified history to smear the Baltic states and our freedom fighters, thus trying to divert attention from its war crimes and other atrocities in Ukraine,” the ministry said.
The Moscow court this week said it had recognised the individuals and organisations as “accomplices of Nazi Germany in committing war crimes and crimes against humanity against the Soviets during the Second World War”.
Among those named were Juozas Ambrazevičius-Brazaitis, head of Lithuania’s 1941 provisional government; partisan commander Juozas Lukša; writer Bronius Krivickas, who was killed while fighting in the postwar resistance; the Lithuanian Activist Front; and the Lithuanian Nationalist Union.
The court said it based its decision on archival documents from various Russian state agencies and explanations concerning the alleged “criminal actions” of the individuals and organisations from Lithuania, Latvia and Estonia.
Lithuania’s Foreign Ministry said Russia was distorting historical facts by relying on biased archival material while ignoring crimes committed by Soviet repressive institutions.
The ministry said the campaign was primarily aimed at a domestic Russian audience and was intended to indirectly justify Russia’s aggression against Ukraine.
In a separate development, a memorial to Lithuanian and Polish deportees in the Siberian city of Yakutsk was reportedly replaced in September with a monument honouring Russian soldiers killed in the war in Ukraine.
Lithuania’s military has repeatedly said Russia uses historical issues as part of its propaganda efforts, particularly to portray the Baltic states and their resistance to Soviet rule in a negative light.
Historians generally agree that the 1941 provisional government of Lithuania, headed by Juozas Ambrazevičius-Brazaitis, collaborated with Nazi Germany that attacked the Soviet Union and pushed its forces out of Lithuania in June 1941. The provisional government, however, was soon disbanded by the Nazis. The provisional government was established by the Lithuanian Activist Front which was notoriously anti-Semitic, pledging in its manifesto “to carry out an immediate and fundamental purging of the Lithuanian nation and its land of Jews”.

Russia asks Vietnam for planes as illegally re-registered Western fleet falls apart
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
08:47:18 UTC
17:47:18 KST

Moscow proposed wet-leasing Vietnamese aircraft, crews and maintenance, but any transfer would involve Airbus or Boeing jets, exposing Vietnamese carriers to secondary sanctions. Nearly a fifth of Russia's largest airlines' planes are already grounded, double the normal downtime rate.
Russia has asked Vietnam to lease its passenger jets complete with crews and maintenance, as the fleet it seized from Western lessors in 2022 deteriorates and nearly a fifth of the country's largest airlines' planes sit grounded.
Transport Minister Andrei Nikitin said Moscow had proposed that Vietnamese carriers transfer aircraft to Russian airlines under wet lease — an arrangement that covers jets, crew, maintenance and insurance — and that Hanoi was studying the proposal.
Vietnam's main carrier exclusively operates Airbus and Boeing aircraft, meaning any transfer to Russia would involve Western-built planes. That creates the same secondary sanctions risk that led Ethiopia to decline a similar proposal, as companies could face US penalties for facilitating the operation of sanctioned aircraft types on behalf of a Russian carrier.
Approaches to other countries in Asia, Africa and the Middle East have so far produced nothing.
Russia's request to Vietnam shows how far Russia's seized and cannibalised fleet of passenger jets — built on legally contested re-registrations and parts that do not meet international airworthiness standards — has deteriorated.
Cobbling things together
When sanctions were imposed after Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, Moscow passed a law allowing airlines to re-register more than 400 foreign-leased Western aircraft domestically rather than return them to their owners.
Under international aviation law, dual registration of a single aircraft is prohibited, meaning Russia's re-registrations are illegal, but the International Civil Aviation Organisation (ICAO) has no enforcement mechanism to compel their return.
Lessors have filed insurance claims totalling around $8 billion (€7.1bn) to recover their losses, with many cases still ongoing.
Before the full-scale invasion of Ukraine, roughly 850 of Russia's 900 commercial aircraft were US and European-made Boeing or Airbus planes, of which around 85% were leased from foreign companies.
With Western spare parts and technical services now sanctioned, airlines have been cannibalising the seized fleet for components, making legal matters worse.
Under international airworthiness standards, every component must have a certified and traceable maintenance history.
Parts stripped from aircraft cut off from Western-certified maintenance chains cannot legally be used on internationally operated aircraft.
Russia's aviation regulator Rosaviatsia has been issuing its own certificates for such parts, which are not recognised by the EU or US aviation authorities.
Of 673 aircraft operated by Russia's 11 largest airlines, 130 or nearly one-fifth are not in service, according to Russian industry data. The normal downtime rate is around 10%.
Airlines outside the Aeroflot group are in worse shape: 93 of their 322 planes, close to a third, are idle.
No kerosene for passenger jets?
Fuel supply is a separate problem. Restrictions on refuelling have been introduced at at least 26 major airports, according to the outlet Verstka.
At airports in St Petersburg, Kaliningrad, Yekaterinburg, Kazan, Ufa, Irkutsk and Vladivostok, fuel is rationed to the volume needed for a single flight.
Restrictions are most severe in southern Russia: Sochi, Volgograd and Astrakhan have applied limits to all carriers. Ukrainian drone strikes on Russian oil refineries have reduced fuel production, and the government has restricted aviation fuel exports in response.
The transport ministry, industry ministry and state defence conglomerate Rostec are also discussing a new passenger levy to fund the purchase and operation of domestically produced aircraft, according to Russian media.
The charge is estimated at up to 500 roubles (€5.22) per domestic ticket and up to 1,000 roubles (€10.44) for international flights.
Russia's domestically produced MC-21 and Tu-214 jets are significantly more expensive to operate than the Boeing and Airbus aircraft they are meant to replace, requiring state or passenger subsidies to remain viable for airlines.
Analysts warn that higher fares could reduce passenger numbers and cut airline revenues.

Morocco gets another Indian defense factory, this time MKU
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
08:45:08 UTC
17:45:08 KST

- Indian defense company MKU plans a factory in Nouasser, Morocco, to produce body armor, helmets and electro-optical systems for local use and export.
- MKU has supplied Morocco's armed forces for five years and has not disclosed the plant's investment, size or production timeline.
Indian defense company MKU plans to build a factory in Morocco to produce body armor, ballistic helmets and electro-optical sensors, and to use the site as its base for exports to the rest of Africa.
MKU said the facility will be located in the SGZID zone in Nouasser, south of Casablanca. The company has not disclosed the plant’s size, the amount of the investment, the number of jobs or when production will start, saying those details will be announced later.
The factory will build products from MKU’s two main lines. Netro Optronics makes multi-sensor electro-optical systems used for surveillance, reconnaissance and target acquisition. Kavro Protection covers body armor, ballistic helmets, shields and armor kits for vehicles and other platforms. MKU did not say which specific products will be made in Morocco or how much of their content will be sourced locally.
The company already has a track record with the Moroccan military. Over the past five years, MKU has supplied optronics and personal protection equipment to Morocco’s Royal Armed Forces, and it says local production will cut delivery times, make it easier to adapt products to new requirements and put after-sales support inside the country. MKU said the plant will also train Moroccan engineers and technicians and transfer production know-how to local staff.
“Five years of working with Morocco have shown us the calibre of its institutions and its people. This factory turns that relationship into a long-term commitment, and it will be a cornerstone of our international growth strategy,” said Karan Gupta, vice president of international sales at MKU.
MKU says its equipment is used by more than 230 forces in over 100 countries. The company runs manufacturing and operational sites in India, Brazil, Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates and has a European research center in Germany. Products from the Moroccan plant will be offered to forces across Africa and Europe, according to the company.
MKU would be the second Indian defense manufacturer to set up production in Morocco. Tata Advanced Systems opened a plant in Berrechid, near Casablanca, in September 2025 to build its WhAP 8×8 wheeled armored vehicle, the first overseas defense factory by a private Indian company. The Royal Moroccan Army received its first locally produced WhAP vehicles from that plant early this year.
Morocco has been working to build a domestic defense industry and cut its reliance on imports, including through legislation that allows foreign companies to manufacture weapons and military equipment in the country under government license. Nouasser, home to Casablanca’s Mohammed V International Airport, already hosts a cluster of aerospace manufacturers.

Faisal Mahmud
07 October 2026•Update: 07 October 2026
Pro-Palestinian demonstrators gathered in Australian cities Wednesday, a day before the third anniversary of the start of Israel’s war on Gaza on Oct. 8, 2023, as Muslim groups called on Canberra to impose sanctions and a two-way arms embargo on Israel.
About 70 activists gathered outside the State Library of Victoria in Melbourne for a day-long vigil, the Melbourne-based Herald Sun reported.
Palestinian flags were displayed across the library grounds. A cutout depicting Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu holding a sign reading “Genocide Criminal” was also displayed.
The International Criminal Court issued an arrest warrant for Netanyahu in November 2024 over alleged war crimes and crimes against humanity in Gaza. The court lists him as at large.
On the library steps, demonstrators spread a large Palestinian flag alongside photographs and other displays, while a banner read: “We shall remain, we shall rebuild.”
The vigil began as scheduled and was due to continue until 6 pm local time (0700GMT), with organizers calling on participants to peacefully mourn Palestinians killed in Gaza.
The Herald Sun reported brief verbal confrontations during the gathering, with organizers urging demonstrators not to engage. Additional police officers were deployed after counter-protesters arrived.
In Sydney, a separate pro-Palestinian vigil was scheduled at Town Hall on Wednesday evening, while another gathering was planned in Wollongong, Australian public broadcaster ABC reported. Further pro-Palestinian rallies are scheduled across Australia on Sunday.
The Alliance of Australian Muslims (AAM) and Australian National Imams Council (ANIC), in a statement shared on US social media company X, said three years of Israeli attacks had brought “killing, destruction, displacement, starvation and immense suffering” to Palestinians.
The groups called on the Australian government to impose “meaningful sanctions” on Israel and “a comprehensive two-way arms embargo” and ensure that Australia does not contribute, “directly or indirectly, to violations of international law.”
They also called for unhindered humanitarian access to Gaza and support for rebuilding civilian infrastructure.
The demand comes amid scrutiny of defense ties between Australia and Israel. The two countries signed a memorandum of understanding on defense industry cooperation in 2017, while annual strategic defense talks began in 2018, according to Australia’s Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade.
Australia also participates in the global supply chain for F-35 fighter jets operated by Israel, with more than 70 Australian companies having contributed components to the program. The Australian government, however, maintains that it does not directly supply weapons or ammunition to Israel.
The Muslim groups said Australia’s recognition of the State of Palestine in September 2025 was an important step but should be followed by concrete political and diplomatic action.
Since October 2023, Israel's genocide in Gaza has killed more than 74,200 Palestinians and injured over 175,200 others, according to Palestinian figures.

====================================================================================================

Christa Pike wakes and speaks after surviving Tennessee lethal injection attempt, lawyers say
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
08:45:00 UTC
17:45:00 KST

Christa Pike, the 50-year-old convicted murderer who survived a lethal injection attempt in Tennessee last week, has regained consciousness and is speaking, her attorneys announced overnight Tuesday into Wednesday, nearly a week after her execution ended with her being taken from prison in an ambulance rather than a coffin.
“Against all odds, Christa Pike is conscious, speaking and continues to receive critical medical care,” her attorneys said. Despite severe damage to her arms during efforts to establish intravenous access, they said, Pike remains shackled by her hands and feet to her hospital bed.
“Her recovery is medically unprecedented. Her prognosis remains unclear, but at a minimum we expect a lengthy rehabilitation,” the attorneys added.
As recently as Sunday, Pike’s legal team said she remained unconscious and on a ventilator. Dr. Joel Zivot, an anesthesiologist and surgeon who has advised her legal team, told the Associated Press that her ability to speak was encouraging, but warned that it could take weeks or months before doctors understand the full extent of the damage.
Pike is no longer on a ventilator but remains in intensive care and is still considered medically at risk, he said.
Pike was sentenced to death for the 1995 murder of 19-year-old Colleen Slemmer. Pike was 18 at the time and, according to the court record, went with her boyfriend, Tadaryl Shipp, and another young woman, Shadolla Peterson, to a wooded area near the University of Tennessee campus in Knoxville.
Prosecutors said Pike feared that Slemmer was interested in Shipp. Pike and Shipp attacked and killed her while Peterson reportedly acted as a lookout. At trial, evidence showed that Pike slashed Slemmer more than 100 times with a box cutter and struck her with a large piece of asphalt, while Shipp carved a pentagram into her body. Pike also took a piece of Slemmer’s skull as a souvenir.
Pike and Shipp were convicted of first-degree murder. Pike was sentenced to death, while Shipp received a life sentence.
Two supposedly lethal doses, but she kept breathing
Pike was scheduled to become the first woman executed in Tennessee in more than 200 years on Sept. 30.
She was strapped to a gurney at Riverbend Maximum Security Institution in Nashville, and the execution team began administering pentobarbital, the drug Tennessee uses for lethal injections. But something went wrong.
Despite receiving two doses intended to be fatal, Pike continued breathing for more than an hour. Witnesses heard her groaning and snoring, and at one point she complained, “My arm feels like it’s going to explode.”
According to court filings by her attorneys, the execution team used at least seven needles while trying to find a suitable vein. One needle reportedly emerged from her arm bent at roughly a 90-degree angle.
Both of Pike’s arms were left swollen, burned and blistered. Her attorneys argue that the pentobarbital, a highly alkaline and caustic substance, leaked from the IV into tissue beneath the skin instead of entering her bloodstream properly.
Slemmer’s mother, May Martinez, traveled to the prison last week to witness the execution. After it failed, she said she had not received justice for her daughter.
“I watched the whole thing. She was awake. That wasn’t justice for Colleen,” Martinez said.
Pike’s lawyers also argue that authorities ignored advance warnings from doctors that she had small veins and a blood disorder that could complicate intravenous access.
The Tennessee Department of Correction has maintained that its personnel “followed all steps of the state’s lawful and approved execution protocol,” but has not yet publicly explained why the execution failed.
In the aftermath, Tennessee Gov. Bill Lee halted the state’s remaining executions scheduled for this year and ordered a comprehensive external review.
Tennessee correction commissioner Frank Strada also announced over the weekend that he would resign and leave his post this month. Strada continued to insist that prison officials had followed procedures, but said his departure was “in the best interest of the people of Tennessee” while the independent investigation continues.
Can Tennessee try to execute her again?
Pike’s survival now raises an almost unprecedented legal question: Can Tennessee attempt to execute her a second time?
She is believed to be the first known person in the United States to survive after the drugs intended to carry out an execution were actually administered. Previous executions have been called off when teams were unable to establish intravenous access, but in Pike’s case the state went through the lethal injection protocol and she remained alive.
Legal experts are divided over whether another attempt would be constitutional.
Fordham University law professor Deborah Denno told AP that Pike could have substantial arguments that a second attempt would constitute “cruel and unusual punishment,” prohibited by the U.S. Constitution, and could also raise concerns under protections against double jeopardy.
Other legal experts, however, have suggested that the U.S. Supreme Court could find that Pike’s sentence is death and, because that sentence has not yet been carried out, the failed attempt does not necessarily bar the state from trying again.
Pike’s attorneys have meanwhile asked a Davidson County court to order Tennessee to preserve all evidence connected to the failed execution, including needles and syringes, the production details of the pentobarbital, correspondence, documents and records involving the execution team.
They say the material could be used in future litigation alleging that Pike’s constitutional rights were violated and that she was subjected to cruel and unusual punishment. Her attorneys are also continuing to urge Gov. Lee to commute her death sentence to life imprisonment without the possibility of parole.
Pike’s 1996 sentence made her one of the youngest women ever sent to death row in the United States. Her attorneys and supporters have since argued that the punishment was excessive because she committed the crime at a very young age and suffered from untreated mental illness following a childhood marked by severe neglect and sexual abuse, including rapes at ages 11 and 17.
She was later diagnosed with bipolar disorder and post-traumatic stress disorder.
Her current attorney, Stephen Ferrell, has argued that Pike’s trial lawyers failed during the sentencing phase to present jurors with critical information about her background or ask them to give sufficient weight to her youth.
Ferrell has also pointed to advances in understanding adolescent brain development and to the different sentence imposed on Shipp, who was 17 at the time of the murder and received life imprisonment with the possibility of parole because of his age.

"In light of the ongoing budget adjustments, Czech Television has decided not to participate in the 2027 edition," the broadcaster announced on Tuesday.

Türkiye advances regulation of Booking.com, Airbnb
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
08:44:18 UTC
17:44:18 KST

Türkiye is moving to tighten oversight of foreign digital accommodation platforms such as Booking.com and Airbnb after a parliamentary commission approved a bill setting out new operating requirements, fees and penalties.
The bill will regulate foreign digital accommodation platforms’ activities conducted online in Türkiye. It is expected to enter into force on Jan. 1, 2027.
Under the proposed framework, platforms will be required to obtain a two-year operating permit from the Culture and Tourism Ministry. The permit will cost 5 million Turkish liras ($101,000), with the fee to be adjusted annually according to the official revaluation rate.
Platforms will also have to be registered for digital services tax, have no outstanding tax debt and designate a representative in Türkiye who is a Turkish citizen or a Turkish-registered legal entity. They will be required to provide a local address for official notifications and respond to information requests from authorities within 15 days.
The bill would allow licensed platforms to directly facilitate online sales of ministry-certified accommodation facilities, tourism-purpose rental properties and airline tickets.
The platforms would also face restrictions on their relationships with accommodation providers. They could not unfairly lower a provider’s ranking, suspend its services or restrict its ability to offer the same service through alternative channels.
Their commissions on domestic sales would be capped at 17 percent of the service price, excluding taxes. Violations could result in fines of up to 500,000 liras, while charging fees in breach of the rules could trigger a penalty equal to 10 times the unlawfully collected amount. Repeated violations could lead to cancellation of the operating permit.
Existing foreign digital accommodation platforms operating in Türkiye when the law takes effect will have three months to apply for a permit. The bill also introduces a tourism contribution of 0.075 percent on the tax base applicable to digital services.

Burger King one of a wave of restaurant closures in Tartu
Restaurants as old and new and as diverse as Burger King and a long-open chocolaterie have been closing in Tartu amid soaring overheads and stifled demand, Postimees reported.
Pierre, a café-chocolaterie which had operated on Tartu's Town Hall Square for around two decades, announced its closure last week, joining Gastronomist, Puente, Ralf Cafe and Burger King among this year's departures in the city.
Burger King closed at the Kvartal mall last month, with Laura Maarand, board member at franchisee Tallink Fast Food OÜ, citing fierce competition in central Tartu and unfavorable rents; Burger King's Lõunakeskus outlet, open since 2020, is staying — even as the franchise last year posted losses of over €3 million on revenues of €7,083,014.
A newer restaurant, Sinimandria, which only opened last summer, announced today it will close in November after failing to attract enough customers; owner Ivo Mägi said the financials were decisive and that the restaurant never managed to find its place — last year it posted losses of €187,534 on sales revenues of €170,496.
Mägi noted the sector as a whole is struggling, adding demand remains weak at a time of rising costs and that Sinimandria will fulfill all obligations to partners and employees before closing; Jaanus Sults, who sits on the boards of the more profitable Pahad Poisid, RP9 and Chaplin venues, attributed recent difficulties more to cooler summers and seasonal trade than to the tax rises, though he noted VAT increases and the upcoming excise duty hike have hardly helped.
Tartu Deputy Mayor Priit Humal (Isamaa) said the catering sector's difficulties are well known but not something the city government can do much to alleviate, as the VAT and excise hikes are set by the national government.

Draconid meteors to look red on night of October 9 — expert
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
08:43:51 UTC
17:43:51 KST

MOSCOW, October 7. /TASS/. Meteors from the Draconid meteor shower this October will have a reddish tint during the peak of its activity, making them easy to spot in the night sky, Evgeny Burmistrov, an astronomy expert from the Perm National Research Polytechnic University, told TASS.
The meteor shower will reach its maximum intensity on the night of October 9. Astronomers expect up to 15 "falling stars" per hour. This is one of the few meteor showers where the meteors catch up to Earth rather than flying toward it. Their atmospheric entry speed is relatively low because of that and is about 20 kilometers per second.
"The Draconids are characterized by a distinctive reddish tint, and such slow speed by cosmic standards explains their smooth and leisurely movement across the sky – these two features allow observers to easily distinguish genuine Draconids from random 'falling stars,' " he said.
The shower gets its name from the constellation Draco, which hosts its radiant – the point in the sky from which the meteors appear to originate.

Romanian President Nicușor Dan urges Romanians in the diaspora to 'test’ Romania
Unknown

News
Romanian President Nicușor Dan urges Romanians in the diaspora to 'test’ Romania
Wednesday 7 October 2026 15:20
Wednesday, 7 October 2026, 15:20
Romanian President Nicușor Dan
PHOTO presidency.ro
Font size
By 2080, Romania could have 3.4 million fewer inhabitants than it does today, with a quarter of the population aged over 65. Low birth rates, a deteriorating ratio of children to the elderly and high levels of migration are among the primary causes of this demographic decline.
Actually, demographic trends over recent decades have been strongly linked to Romanians leaving the country. According to migration experts, approximately 4.5 to 5 million Romanian citizens currently live abroad, a group that practically represents one of the country’s key assets. Consequently, in recent years, authorities have been taking steps to persuade as many of them as possible to return home. 
Speaking in Bucharest  at the ninth edition of the RePatriot ‘Top 100 Romanians Everywhere’ Gala, Romania’s President Nicușor Dan, urged fellow citizens in the Diaspora to ‘give Romania a try’, noting that despite its lingering shortcomings and dysfunctions, the country has made progress over the last two decades. “I have traveled within the Diaspora and heard sentiments like: ‘I would come home for retirement, but I’m afraid of the healthcare system,’ or ‘I would return, but I don’t know what kind of schooling my children would get.’ 
The choice remains up to each individual, we live in a free world, but my urging to those in the Diaspora is to put Romania to the test,” Nicușor Dan emphasized.  “My urging to those in the Diaspora is to try out Romania’s healthcare system, because, despite all the shortcomings and dysfunctions, Romania has made progress over the last 20 years. Medical equipment in Romania is no longer what it was two decades ago. We have doctors trained at major clinics abroad; some stayed, while others returned. We have good schools, and we also have very poor ones, at both the pre-university and university levels.” 
Bucharest
PHOTO Unsplash
Furthermore, in the Romanian President’s view, the relationship between the public and private sectors is another area where shortcomings exist, a relationship that needs improvement because, as the country’s leader noted, the private sector is the engine of the economy, while entrepreneurship is the engine of that engine. Ideally, the successful entrepreneurs from the Diaspora could become part of the Romanian ecosystem, given the performance and experience they have gained in competitive environments, assets that could prove valuable to a developing country like Romania.
“I hope that by learning from one another and working together, we can do better for this country and for us all,” concluded Nicușor Dan at the RePatriot ‘Top 100 Romanians Everywhere’ Gala.
For nine editions now, this event has brought together hundreds of Romanian entrepreneurs, managers, and professionals from the Diaspora, selected based on their achievements, contributions, and impact in the countries where they live and work.

"Residential buildings, a plumbing warehouse, a garage cooperative, shops—this strike was once again directed at civilians, at families who were sleeping in their homes. There was no military purpose whatsoever in the shelling of one of the capital’s cemeteries either," the Interior Minister reported.
According to him, all our units and the necessary services continue to work at the sites of the attacks. "In Kremenchuk and Pryluky, we are deploying mobile service centers of the Ministry of Internal Affairs—citizens can restore lost documents or deregister vehicles for free. We are also deploying units from neighboring regions in order to eliminate the consequences of the attack as quickly as possible," he noted.
Police officer injured
"Unfortunately, today is also a difficult day for the personnel of the Interior Ministry system. A police officer was injured in Pryluky in the attack. Her husband, who until recently had been fighting at the front as part of the police, and her mother were killed. Eternal memory to all those who died, and condolences to their families," the minister stated.

At Least 8 Killed in Overnight Russian Strikes on Ukraine
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
08:37:40 UTC
17:37:40 KST

Russia pounded Ukraine with waves of missiles and drones in one of its most "vile strikes" on Wednesday, President Volodymyr Zelensky said, killing at least 24 people, including children, and damaging industrial facilities and energy infrastructure.
The heaviest death toll was in Pryluky in Ukraine's northern Chernihiv region, where a Russian missile obliterated a five-story residential building. At least 18 people, including four children, were killed there, local officials said.
Zelensky said the strike coincided with Russian President Vladimir Putin's birthday.
"Today, as a birthday 'gift' to Putin, the Russian army destroyed a residential building in Pryluky," Zelensky said, adding that six more people were also killed in Kyiv, Oleksandria and Kremenchuk during the massive attack.
In total, Russia fired 70 missiles at Ukraine overnight — many of them high-velocity ballistic munitions — and dozens of Shahed attack drones, he said.
"The Russians wanted to strike painfully and demonstratively. This was one of the most vile strikes."
In Pryluky, an excavator and dozens of rescuers with shovels sifted through rubble at the site where several sections of the apartment block had collapsed.
Emergency workers used ladders to get to the upper floors of what remained of the building, and brought out 15 people alive as they worked their way down through the rubble. Around 55 people were wounded in the town, regional officials said.
"There's a lot of destruction, especially in the town center," said Danylo Savenko, deputy mayor of Pryluky, who said he had run to an air raid shelter with his wife as soon as he heard the missiles flying.
Big jump in reported drone interceptions
Russia's Defense Ministry said its forces had carried out a "massive strike" on military-industrial facilities in Kyiv and other Ukrainian regions, using high-precision land-, sea- and air-launched weapons, as well as drones.
Ukraine's air force said it had downed just over 80% of the 46 jet-powered drones launched by Russia — a sharp increase from recent weeks when, on average, air defenses took down 50% to 60%.
Since the summer, Russia has used increasing numbers of the new high-velocity drones in round-the-clock attacks on Kyiv and other cities, with Ukraine's air defenses struggling to cope with their speed.
The air force did not explain the jump in the interception rate and did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
Zelensky said the Russian ballistic missiles remained the major challenge for Ukraine, adding that he and his team were "every day looking for Patriot [missile interception] systems that can and must protect people's lives."
Ukraine received a new 1.2 billion euro ($1.34 billion) tranche from the European Union on Wednesday and will channel the funds towards defense needs, Prime Minister Serhii Koretskyi said.
The U.S.-made Patriot system is the only weapon in Ukraine's arsenal capable of stopping high-velocity ballistic missiles but tight global supplies have been drained by the Iran war as well as the Ukraine conflict.
Russia's Defense Ministry said its targets included sites where Ukrainian defense company Fire Point manufactures and stores its Flamingo cruise missiles and medium- and long-range drones in Kyiv as well as regions of Kyiv, Chernihiv, Kirovohrad, Dnipropetrovsk, Poltava and Kharkiv.
Last week Zelensky said Ukraine had fired its first domestically made ballistic missile in combat, produced by Fire Point. In an interview with Reuters, he said he expected the company to have a longer-range FP-9 missile ready by the autumn. Fire Point has said that weapon will be able to reach Moscow.
People shelter overnight in Kyiv metro
Zelensky said Ukrainian troops hit four targets in Russia over the past 24 hours, including two Russian oil facilities and a training ground in the Perm, Samara and Astrakhan regions.
In the Reuters interview, Zelensky said Ukraine would hit Russia's energy assets in response to Moscow's escalating strikes on civilian infrastructure.
Ukrainian officials and military intelligence shared warnings of the upcoming attacks on Wednesday, and many Kyiv residents took shelter in the city's deep underground metro stations.
Several loud explosions reverberated through the capital during the night.
"The metro is better because we live on the ninth floor of a high-rise, and it's really scary when you're on the ninth floor and missiles are flying at you," Lesia, a 49-year-old Kyiv resident, told Reuters.
Ukrainian officials said Russian ballistic missiles as well as the drones had targeted Kyiv.
Overnight air strikes on the southeastern city of Dnipro damaged an industrial facility, transport infrastructure in Zaporizhzhia and apartment buildings in Kremenchuk, regional officials said on the Telegram messaging app.

Jaguar unveils the long-awaited Type 01 electric car — what are its power output and range
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
11:35:41 EEST
17:35:41 KST

Jaguar unveils the long-awaited Type 01 electric car — what are its power output and range
Kyiv • UNN
The new four-seat Jaguar Type 01 is equipped with three electric motors producing 1,016 hp and accelerates to 100 km/h in 3.2 seconds. The electric vehicle's range reaches 720 km, while the expected price starts at $150,000.
Jaguar has spent years creating some of the world’s most iconic sports cars, but now the British brand is reinventing itself by introducing the ambitious new Type 01 flagship, the first step toward a new era for the automaker. Motor1.com reports, writes UNN.
Details
The Type 01 is a four-seat GT-class car, the most powerful road car in Jaguar’s history, and it is electric. This makes it a very important car for the brand: a statement of intent intended to prove to fans that it offers the same enjoyment and engagement as previous Jaguar models, the publication notes.
The Type 01 is equipped with three electric motors: one on the front axle and two on the rear, making it the most powerful road car in the automaker’s history. Total output is 1,016 horsepower and 1,007 pound-feet (1,365.31 N·m) of torque.
Jaguar claims that the Type 01 accelerates from 0 to 100 km/h in 3.2 seconds and has a perfect 50:50 weight distribution.
The electric vehicle has an 850-volt architecture and a 118-kilowatt-hour battery. According to the automaker, the Type 01 has a range of 720 km under the European WLTP standard and up to 560 km at a constant highway speed.
Jaguar has equipped the electric vehicle with a double-wishbone front suspension and a rear suspension with integrated links and adaptive air suspension. Jaguar uses air springs with adjustable volume and active two-valve dampers.
The Type 01 has five driving modes: Jaguar, Dynamic, Efficient, Ice & Snow, and Curated. In Dynamic mode, up to 87 percent of the power is sent to the rear axle, the active air springs become stiffer, and the steering and accelerator pedal become sharper.
Jaguar put considerable effort into creating a dynamic and engaging car. Seventeen percent of the vehicle’s length is accounted for by the distance between the front axle and the doors. It is a large car, but its center of gravity is below the driver’s hip level, while the yaw center is located between the passengers.
Jaguar claims that this helps create the feeling that the Type 01 "embraces the driver," and all-wheel steering also contributes to this. At low speeds, the rear wheels can turn by 6.0 degrees.
The Type 01 is also equipped with active aerodynamics. At the front, active vanes open when the powertrain and brakes require cooling. The active three-stage rear spoiler can generate up to 75 kg of downforce at speeds above 150 km/h, and when deployed, the car lowers by 1.3 cm.
The Jaguar Type 01 looks very similar to the concept. It is low and long, with a height of just 137 cm, roughly equivalent to the height of a modern Ford Mustang. It has flush door handles that, according to the automaker, can extend through ice up to 0.4 cm thick.
At the front, Jaguar has HD LED projector headlights with automatic leveling. They are the thinnest headlights in history, measuring just 8.9 cm in height. Each headlight contains 20,000 LEDs. At the rear, the designers concealed the full-width taillights in the rear bumper grille.
The car is equipped with massive wheels. Other details include a laser-engraved fender trim depicting a leaping cat and hidden ADAS components behind the Jaguar lettering on the front end.
Jaguar unveiled the Type 01’s interior in August, but there are now more details. A large 24-inch OLED screen is located behind the steering wheel, while a central 7-inch vertical touchscreen controls key functions such as multimedia and climate control.
The Type 01 lacks a traditional rearview mirror. Instead, Jaguar uses a ClearSight Rear View display built into the panoramic soundbar at the base of the windshield. The automaker positioned it at the same height as the exterior mirrors.
All four seats have heating and ventilation, while the front seats offer 12-way adjustment. The rear seats fold in a 50:50 split, increasing the luggage compartment’s capacity.
Jaguar has not announced when the Type 01 will go on sale or how much it will cost. The vehicle is expected to be priced from $100,000 to $150,000.

Advocates decry detention of Kashmiri filmmaker Arfat Sheikh by ICE in US
Arfat Sheikh was arrested at Washington Dulles International Airport on September 24, advocacy group says.
Supporters of Kashmiri filmmaker Arfat Sheikh have called for his immediate release after he was arrested by United States Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents last month.
“Sheikh was unlawfully detained by US Immigration and Customs Enforcement at Washington Dulles International Airport on September 24, 2026,” the Free Arfat Sheikh campaign, an advocacy group, said in a statement on Tuesday.
The 42-year-old artist, who resides in Alexandria, Virginia, arrived in the US on a student visa in 2019 to pursue graduate studies in film at Georgia State University and sought asylum in 2020, the campaign said.
Sheikh is being held in the Caroline Detention Facility in Bowling Green, Virginia, it added.
The filmmaker was scheduled to appear before an immigration judge on Tuesday for a procedural hearing alongside a bond assessment, the press release said.
There has been no comment regarding the detention from ICE or the Department of Homeland Security.
Sheikh’s first feature film Saffron Kingdom garnered multiple honours, notably Best Feature Film at the Chicago Filmmakers Awards, LA Film and Documentary Awards, Melbourne Independent Film Festival, Wake Forest Film Festival, and Anatolian International Film Awards, the advocacy campaign noted.
In 2025, Sheikh was also recognised with the Emerging Filmmaker Activist Award at the Teaneck International Film Festival.
Sheikh’s detention comes as the number of ICE arrests across the US hit record levels this summer, with about 50,000 arrests recorded in July and August.

Quote: "Search and rescue operations are currently underway at eight locations – in [the city of] Kyiv and Kyiv, Kirovohrad, Chernihiv and Poltava oblasts. This massive terrorist strike on Ukrainian cities has killed 12 people. More than 40 civilians have been injured."

Quote: "Sadly, today is a difficult day for everyone in the Interior Ministry system. A woman serving as a police officer was injured in the strike on Pryluky. Her husband, who until recently served with the police on the front line, and her mother were killed."
Details: Rescuers and police are continuing to search for missing people who may be trapped under the rubble of a destroyed five-storey building.
Mobile Interior Ministry service centres are also operating in Pryluky and Kremenchuk in Poltava Oblast, where people can restore lost documents or deregister destroyed vehicles free of charge.
Vyhivskyi noted that units from neighbouring oblasts are also being involved in dealing with the aftermath of the attack.
Background:
- On the night of 6-7 October, Russian forces launched a massive attack on various Ukrainian regions.
- In Pryluky, the Russians hit a high-rise residential building.
- In the city of Kremenchuk in Poltava Oblast, a residential area was hit and high-rise residential buildings were damaged.
- As a result of a Russian ballistic missile attack on Kyiv, hits were recorded in the Obolonskyi, Shevchenkivskyi and Podilskyi districts. Two people have been killed in the Darnytskyi district.

More unaccompanied children are taking dangerous crossings to Europe, UN says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
08:34:08 UTC
17:34:08 KST

More unaccompanied children are taking dangerous crossings to Europe, UN says
GENEVA, Oct 7 - More than two-thirds of refugee and migrant children who reached Europe via Mediterranean and Balkan routes last year were unaccompanied, and many experienced exploitation, a report by UN agencies showed on Wednesday.
While overall child arrivals by land and sea fell 25% from 2024 levels, the proportion travelling alone rose to 67%, from 51% in 2024, the report by the International Organization for Migration, UNHCR and UNICEF found.
More than 20,000 of the 31,100 children who arrived in European countries including Bulgaria, Cyprus, Greece, Italy, Malta and Spain in 2025 were recorded as unaccompanied or separated from a parent or guardian.
More children arriving in Italy and Spain were unaccompanied - 86% - than those arriving in other countries. In Italy, there was a 12% increase in the number of children arriving - many from Egypt, Eritrea, Bangladesh and Somalia.
Poverty, conflict and environmental hazards are among the reasons people undertake perilous sea crossings, and shrinking safe migration pathways appeared to be pushing more children into dangerous journeys and the hands of smugglers, the report found.
The number of children involved in refugee resettlement procedures in Europe dropped to 3,400 in 2025 from 8,900 a year earlier, while only 199 children - none of whom were unaccompanied - were relocated between European countries under the Voluntary Solidarity Mechanism, down 67%.
The EU arrangement, launched in 2022, enables countries receiving large numbers of migrant and asylum seeker arrivals to relocate some of them to other participating European states on a voluntary basis.
"This report shows how exposed they [children] are to violence and exploitation when safe pathways are limited, and they have to rely on smugglers," IOM Director General Amy Pope said in a statement, urging closer cooperation between European states and countries along the routes to counter smuggling networks that prey on minors.
Interviews with more than 4,600 15- to 24-year-olds travelling along Mediterranean, West African Atlantic and Western Balkan routes found nearly half had experienced physical violence. Most accounts involved multiple forms of violence including torture and kidnapping in transit and at border crossings, and some others included reports of forced labour.
Libya was the country most frequently identified as the location where abuses occurred.
About a tenth of those interviewed who had used the Eastern Mediterranean Route reported having been falsely promised well-paid jobs, safe journeys, or legal travel documents. REUTERS

14 dead in Pryluky, two each in Kyiv, Kremenchuk, and Oleksandriia: Russia’s night of 70 missiles
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
08:33:09 UTC
17:33:09 KST

Russia attacked Kyiv and 12 oblasts overnight on 7 October with about 70 missiles, many of them ballistic, as well as Shahed drones, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said. The strikes killed at least 20 people, with the deadliest hit on an apartment block in Pryluky in Chernihiv Oblast. Russia also hit Kremenchuk, Oleksandriia, Dnipro, and Zaporizhzhia, while Poland scrambled its jets.
Moscow has likely begun its winter strike campaign earlier than usual, aiming to make civilian life in Ukraine unbearable, and UN figures already show civilian casualties running 55% above last year's.
Update: Pryluky death toll rises to 14, including four children
The death toll from the Russian strike on Pryluky has risen to 14, including four children, Ukraine's State Emergency Service said on the afternoon of 7 October. Fifty people were injured, seven of them children, and rescuers pulled 15 people from the rubble, including a child.
Russia attacked Pryluky with cruise missiles, and one scored a direct hit on the five-story apartment building, Chernihiv Oblast head Viacheslav Chaus said. Earlier in the day, he reported that 27 of the injured had been hospitalized, three in serious condition. The search-and-rescue operation was still under way.
Morning repoting: five dead in Pryluky
A Russian missile struck a five-story apartment building in Pryluky early in the morning, while residents were still asleep, Chernihiv Oblast head Viacheslav Chaus said. The strike completely destroyed one sectkion of the building, killing five people and injuring 26, including five children, Ukraine's National Police reported. Rescuers pulled three people from the rubble, including a child, and more people may still be trapped, Chaus said.
"Today, for Putin's birthday, the Russian army 'gave' him the destruction of an apartment building in Pryluky in Chernihiv Oblast. It was an ordinary five-story building," Zelenskyy said.
Kyiv, Kremenchuk, and Oleksandriia
In Kyiv, Russian missiles hit non-residential buildings and warehouses in the Obolonskyi and Podilskyi districts, Mayor Vitali Klitschko said. Strikes also hit the Shevchenkivskyi district, and debris burned in the Darnytskyi district, he added. In the Darnytskyi district, a missile set fire to a garage cooperative, where firefighters rescued two people and found two men dead, Klitschko wrote. Police and rescuers worked to defuse an unexploded ballistic missile that fell among apartment blocks in the same district, the National Police said.
In Kremenchuk, Russian missiles hit a densely populated residential area, killing two people and injuring seven, Poltava Oblast head Vitalii Diakivnych said. Zelenskyy later put the number of injured at eight and said four high-rises were damaged.
In Oleksandriia in Kirovohrad Oblast, Russia hit an enterprise. One person was killed, three injured, and two were out of contact, Kirovohrad Oblast head Andrii Raikovych said. Zelenskyy later put the death toll there at two.
Drones and other targets
In Dnipro, Russian strikes damaged an industrial enterprise, apartment buildings, and a sports club, Dnipropetrovsk Oblast head Oleksandr Hanzha said. In Nikopol district, the attacks injured a 65-year-old woman and a 64-year-old man. Russia also struck Lozova in Kharkiv Oblast with a missile, and a drone hit an apartment building in Zaporizhzhia, police said.
In Zaporizhzhia, Russia attacked a transport infrastructure facility, acting oblast head Mykhailo Semikin said, a day after a strike on one of the city's bridges over the Dnipro halted traffic. In Kyiv Oblast, three production and warehouse buildings were damaged in Obukhiv district, with no casualties, the Kyiv Oblast Military Administration said.
Air defense downed five ballistic missiles, 39 cruise missiles, and 117 drones, while missiles and drones hit 18 locations, the Air Force said. Polish military aircraft took off and Poland put its ground-based air defense on alert during the attack, Poland's Operational Command said.
Russian ballistic missiles remain the biggest challenge, Zelenskyy said, adding that Ukraine is searching daily for Patriot missiles.
Strikes across the front over the past day
Russian attacks killed one person and injured 11 in Kherson Oblast over the past day, the Kherson Oblast Military Administration reported. Russia injured 12 people in Donetsk Oblast on 6 October, Donetsk Oblast head Vadym Filashkin said. Two people were injured in Kharkiv Oblast, Kharkiv Oblast head Oleh Syniehubov said.
Bridges and a maternity hospital in Russia's sights
Russia has stepped up strikes on Kyiv's bridges and has now extended them to Zaporizhzhia. In September, a Russian ballistic and hypersonic missile attack on Kyiv damaged a maternity hospital.

Russia prepares information operation on situation in Oleshky – Ukraine's Security Service
The Security Service of Ukraine (SSU) has warned that Russia has stepped up preparations for a series of information and psychological operations concerning the situation in the temporarily occupied city of Oleshky in Kherson Oblast.
Source: SSU press service
Details: The SSU said it has discovered the information during its counterintelligence activities.
Russian troops from an occupation unit have been ordered to prepare a series of "compromising" interviews with residents of the temporarily occupied city, according to intelligence obtained by the agency.
The SSU says that, under the Russian plan, local residents appearing in the videos must:
- accuse Ukraine's defence forces of constantly attacking and blockading the city;
- discredit decisions made by Ukraine's military and political leadership
- express support for and gratitude towards the military of the aggressor state.
Russia plans to carry out the psyop in October and early November this year, the SSU said.
Quote: "The aggressor has had no success on the battlefield and is therefore trying by any means possible to undermine Ukrainians' psychological and emotional state and destabilise the situation within our country.
In this regard, we urge the Ukrainian press and the public to:
- treat the emergence of such 'sensational' information critically
- not trust publications by Russian or pro-Russian Telegram channels
- not disseminate unverified information
- use information exclusively from official sources."
Background:
- On 19 September, the Ukrainian Council of Churches and Religious Organisations also reported that Oleshky was on the brink of a humanitarian catastrophe.
- On the night of 3-4 October, Ukraine's National Guard carried out its second operation to deliver humanitarian aid to occupied Oleshky. Almost four tonnes of supplies were delivered to the city by drones.

Israel’s warped logic: Nothing justifies Oct 7, but Oct 7 justifies everything
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
08:32:47 UTC
17:32:47 KST

Three years after Hamas’s cross-border blitz, Israel continues to treat that moment as a watershed that divides Israel’s history into two parts.
Nothing that happened during the decades preceding that day justifies the October 7 blitz, but the events of October 7 justify everything that Israel has done to Palestinians since then.
Nasir Qadri, an international law scholar at Koc University in Istanbul, tells TRT World that October 7 does not give Israel a blank cheque to wreak all kinds of atrocities on a besieged civilian population in the name of self-defence.
That’s because the legal framework that Israel invokes to justify three years of war crimes against Gaza's civilian population was already rejected by the International Court of Justice (ICJ), he says.
In its 2004 advisory opinion on the construction of a separation wall in the Occupied Palestinian Territory, the ICJ held that Article 51 of the UN Charter does not apply to threats from territory under the invoking state’s own occupation, he says.
Noting that Gaza has been under Israeli military siege since 1967, Qadri says the war following October 7 constitutes the act of an occupying power against the population it occupies.
“The Geneva Conventions place no threshold of prior suffering above which an occupying power’s obligations suspend,” he says.
The observation stems from the fact that a legal order admitting such a threshold would “license atrocity in perpetuity”, with each cycle of violence justifying the next without any end, Qadri notes.
What Israel calls an unprovoked attack on October 7 “occurred within an occupation that the ICJ has found to violate peremptory norms of international law”.
The right of people under unlawful occupation to resist – “including through armed struggle in pursuit of self-determination” – is recognised in Additional Protocol I of 1977 and affirmed in successive UN General Assembly resolutions, he says.
According to Gaza’s health ministry, the Palestinian death toll since October 2023 was nearly 74,000 in late September, with the number of wounded reaching almost 175,000.
Most of the victims of Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza are women and children. Relentless bombing has destroyed 90 percent of civilian infrastructure. The UN estimates that the cost of reconstruction is $70 billion.
Even though a tenuous ceasefire is still in place in Gaza, Israel has not stopped its killing spree. It has killed more than 1,400 Palestinians since October 10, 2025, the day a ceasefire agreement took effect in Gaza.
Qadri insists that the UN Commission of Inquiry, the ICC prosecutor, the ICJ’s provisional measures and Amnesty International’s genocide determination have each found that “Israel’s conduct constitutes war crimes and a plausible risk of genocide”.
The UN commission found Israel responsible for genocide in Gaza and concluded that Israeli authorities committed four of the five acts defined in the 1948 Genocide Convention.
Omer Bartov, professor of Holocaust and genocide studies at Brown University in the US, tells TRT World that Israel gave itself – and is still giving itself – a moral blank cheque, or a license to break all international laws and conventions.
“(Israeli leaders) said that, in fact, there were ‘no uninvolved’ people, which implies that there was no collateral damage at all since everyone was (considered) guilty,” he says.
Ali Murat Kursun, assistant professor of international relations at Marmara University in Istanbul, tells TRT World that no single event, regardless of its severity, grants a sovereign the licence to bypass the laws of armed conflict and execute a systematic eradication of a civilian population.
“What we’re witnessing in Gaza is not a proportional security operation, but the most technologically and comprehensively documented genocide in modern history,” he says.
In fact, the political leadership in Tel Aviv “may have cynically leveraged” October 7 to operationalise a “premeditated campaign of demographic engineering”.
“To accept the premise that this attack justifies the atrocities we see today is to permanently dismantle the post-1945 international legal order,” he says.
History didn’t begin on October 7
All three experts reject the notion that October 7 marks the starting point for a legal or moral judgement of the events that unfolded in the last three years.
Qadri says the blockade of Gaza began in 2007, while its occupation has existed since 1967.
“October 7 is an event within a war of liberation waged by an occupied population against an occupying power,” he says.
Using October 7 as the origin of legal judgement excludes six decades of documented violations that constitute the “occupation’s legal character and moral weight”.
Bartov says there are two contexts to October 7.
The first is the six-decade occupation and oppression of Palestinians that has led to their “dehumanisation in the eyes of many Israelis”, and a brutalisation of Israeli society, especially towards Palestinians.
The second context is the Nakba of 1948, a mass displacement that turned Palestinians into an occupied population, he says.
Israelis have both denied the Nakba and treated it as an “incomplete action that should at some point be completed”.
“October 7 appeared to the government and many other Israelis to be the opportunity to ‘finish the job’, first in Gaza and then in the (occupied) West Bank, by way of ethnic cleansing which, as has happened in Gaza, becomes genocidal,” Bartov says.
Any political move forward must begin with recognising the wrongs of the Nakba of 1948 and of the ongoing genocide in Gaza, he adds.
Kursun says that treating October 7 in a historical vacuum is a deliberate analytical fallacy designed to obscure decades of structural violence and asymmetrical state terror.
“The foundational starting point for any rigorous assessment must be 1948,” he says, noting that the year marked the establishment of a state structure reliant on expansion, systemic dispossession of Palestinians, and perpetual demographic containment.
“October 7 was the violent rupture of an unsustainable pressure cooker, paved by decades of illegal annexations, apartheid-like restrictions, and forced expropriations,” he adds.
Western duplicity and genocide
Western capitals affirmed Israel’s right to defend itself after October 7 and chose to look away as Tel Aviv rained down countless bombs and missiles on the densely populated enclave of Gaza.
They woke up to the horrors of Israel’s genocidal war only after it had killed tens of thousands of civilians and turned the besieged territory into rubble.
But even then, many Western capitals criticised the scale of killings and destruction without cutting arms supplies to Tel Aviv.
Qadri says their legal position changed once the ICJ issued binding provisional measures in January 2024, finding a plausible risk of genocide in Gaza.
The gap between Western governments naming genocide from the UNGA podium last month and their arms export records over the preceding three years is not merely a “rhetorical inconsistency”, Qadri says.
“It is the evidentiary foundation of their legal exposure in the accountability proceedings that will follow this war,” he says.
Kursun describes the Western position as a “catastrophic failure of international obligations, good international citizenship, and an exercise in profound geopolitical hypocrisy”.
By supplying the technical and military hardware to Israel, those states transitioned from passive observers to active enablers of a humanitarian collapse, he adds.
“Issuing belated statements of concern, while refusing to diplomatically isolate Israel and render it a global pariah, is a permanent moral stain on the transatlantic alliance,” he says.

Britain pays a Putin tax of billions a year, report says
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
09:32:34 BST
17:32:34 KST

Russian hostile activity is costing the United Kingdom between £2 billion and £2.5 billion a year, a burden carried by taxpayers, businesses and public services without anybody in government totalling it up, according to a report published by Graeme Downie, the Labour MP for Dunfermline and Dollar.
The report, written with Dr Dominic Reed and titled The Putin Tax, describes itself as the first attempt to measure the economic burden of Russian hostile activity against Britain. It argues that confirmed attacks alone have already generated somewhere between £1.6 billion and £2.1 billion in losses, and that the real figure is almost certainly far higher once unreported incidents, resilience spending and wider economic damage are taken into account.
Mr Downie sets out the central argument in the executive summary: “Far from being solely a national security challenge, Russian hostile activity represents a significant and recurring economic cost that British taxpayers and businesses are already paying every year.”
The choice of phrase is deliberate, and the report explains why at some length. The burden, as it puts it, “is not listed on a payslip, and it is not collected by HM Revenue and Customs. Yet it is paid, nonetheless. It is paid when businesses are forced to spend millions recovering from cyber-attacks rather than investing in growth. It is paid when public bodies divert resources into security and resilience measures.”
Three incidents make up the floor of the estimate, chosen because meaningful public figures exist for each. The LockBit ransomware attack on Royal Mail in January 2023 cost its parent company around £10 million in remediation and resilience work, the Russian-linked arson attack on industrial units in Leyton in east London caused approximately £1 million in direct damage, and the cyber attack on Jaguar Land Rover in late 2025 produced economic losses of between £1.6 billion and £2.1 billion. The report calls that total “the basement of a floor, not a ceiling”, since it leaves out supply chain losses, infrastructure protection costs, general resilience investment and aviation disruption.
Layered on top of that are estimates drawn from industry and from the government’s own research. The cyber-risk analytics firm CyberCube identified more than 300 Russia-linked cyber attacks on British companies since 2022, a figure it believes significantly undercounts the true number because only a minority of attacks in its database carry reliable attribution and many businesses never report an incident at all. Applying the government’s own benchmark of almost £195,000 for a significant cyber incident gives a baseline of around £58.5 million, which the report notes is less than a thirtieth of what the Jaguar Land Rover attack cost on its own.
Research commissioned by the Department for Science, Innovation and Technology puts total annual cyber losses to British business at roughly £14.7 billion, about half a per cent of GDP. The report works through what different Russian shares of that would mean, finding that even a conservative tenth would come to £1.47 billion a year, with a fifth reaching £2.94 billion.
Subsea cables account for a further £250 million to £500 million of annual exposure, a figure the authors are careful to describe as an exposure range rather than a measured loss. CyberCube also assesses a five per cent chance that the United Kingdom will suffer a single attack by a hostile power costing one British company $4.4 billion, or around £3.3 billion, more than one and a half times the cost of the Jaguar Land Rover incident.
Running through the whole document is a complaint about measurement rather than about threat perception. “Nobody in Government is currently bringing this information together,” the report states. “Instead, a patchwork quilt of information was found, spread across Whitehall, regulators, security agencies, infrastructure operators, insurers and private companies. Each organisation possesses only part of the picture.”
The authors contrast that with how other national risks are handled, observing that the costs of flooding are estimated because flood defences cost money, and the costs of fraud are measured because anti-fraud work costs money, while no equivalent effort has been made for hostile-state activity. They also take issue with the vocabulary, arguing that the term sub-threshold “holds within its definition a reason not to act” and that a patient whose treatment is delayed by offline systems does not experience a sub-threshold disruption.
Four recommendations follow from that argument, and none of them asks for new money. The government should publish an annual report to Parliament estimating the economic cost of hostile foreign-state activity, with attribution to specific states wherever possible. The National Cyber Security Centre should publish annual assessments of significant hostile-state cyber activity including attribution and estimated economic impacts. The Ministry of Defence should develop and publish a methodology for costing physical hostile activity directed at British people, businesses, infrastructure and interests. The last asks for a national public awareness campaign on hostile-state threats, cyber resilience and preparedness.
To give the sums a public-service comparison, the report calculates that £2 billion a year would cover the starting salaries of around 62,000 newly qualified nurses or the same number of police constables, and that £2.5 billion would stretch to about 78,000 of either, or 73,000 teachers.
The authors are open about what the work cannot do, and the limitations section is unusually candid. It is a desk-based study carried out within a parliamentary office, undertaken principally by a single post-doctoral researcher with no access to classified intelligence, no analytical team and no research budget, relying on published material, parliamentary questions, Commons Library briefings and industry research. The figures are offered as illustrative and conservative, and the report is explicit that it does not claim to be definitive.
In GCHQ’s first annual lecture at Bletchley Park in May, the agency’s director, Anne Keast-Butler, gave the assessment the report builds on: “Russia is scaling up its daily hybrid activity against the UK and Europe, stretching from the seabed to cyberspace, relentlessly targeting critical infrastructure, democratic processes, supply chains and public trust.”
Mr Downie’s conclusion is that the argument has moved on from whether the activity exists. “The challenge now is not proving that the Putin Tax exists but ensuring Britain starts measuring it,” the report says.
