‘We’re short of resources’: France’s student protesters, in their own words
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
08:32:16 UTC
17:32:16 KST

‘We’re short of resources’: France’s student protesters, in their own words
French students and teachers protesting school conditions spoke with Al Jazeera about their demands.
Paris, France – At least 250,000 students, teachers and parents protested across France on Tuesday, supported by trade unions and rights groups.
The demonstrations have grown since students began blockading the entrances to their high schools on September 17, starting in the Paris suburb of Creteil. The movement quickly spread throughout the city’s suburbs, with high schoolers protesting against conditions, lamenting dilapidated buildings, shortages of teachers and staff and overcrowded classrooms.
The blockades were met by a muscular police response, with riot police sent to break up the student protests.
More than 6,000 protesters have been arrested, 85 percent of them aged under 18. At least 10 investigations into police misconduct have been opened by France’s police watchdog IGPN.
On October 2, France’s Education Minister Edouard Geffray met with student leaders and the government announced a five-point plan to reform the public education system – an olive branch students agreed was insufficient to address the crisis.
Some 210 teenagers – including one who lost a hand – and 715 police officers have been wounded, according to officials.
Anne Savinel-Barras, president of Amnesty International France, called on authorities to “avoid unnecessary and excessive use of force”.
“Footage and testimonies widely reported over the last week raise alarming concerns about the dangerous use of tear gas, batons and restraint techniques by police. Tear gas grenades have been discharged recklessly, and rubber bullets have been fired causing serious injuries.”
Al Jazeera spoke to several protesters about their demands:
‘Macron’s government has to stop investing only in war’
Theo, 19, student: “This is my first demonstration. I’m here in solidarity with the high schoolers, after this week of blockades and police oppression. I’m also here for other demands: for universities, for more resources for schools, and not just schools but hospitals too. We’re really short of resources.
“Macron’s government has to stop investing only in war. We’re fed up. That’s why we’re all here together in this movement of solidarity, young and old. We all have the same demands: a better future.”
‘Teachers are absent, and compared with schools in Paris we don’t have the same resources’
Olympe, 16, high school student: “We blockaded our school all week to demand our rights and to denounce what’s happening in our schools. Teachers are absent, and compared with schools in Paris we don’t have the same resources. We’re given less money, and we don’t have the same privileges.”
Rania, 15, high school student: “We don’t feel listened to at all. We feel inferior, especially considering that we’re the future. So when no one listens to us, we do all this, but in the end will it really change anything? We don’t know.”
Maissene, student: “We came to support our classmates, simply because if they’re blockading, we blockade too. It’s a general movement, and they can’t do it on their own.”
‘We came to defend our youth’
Raphael, 17, high school student: “We came to defend our youth. Because we’re young, the state doesn’t listen to us. They think we have no political awareness and don’t know what we’re defending. We’re here to show the opposite: we know exactly what we’re defending. We know our values.”
Rose, 16, high school student: “If nothing changes, we’ll keep going for much longer. On October 17, there will be a big demonstration, with high schoolers, students and farmers. So it’ll be a bit like a new revolution.”
‘More resources, more teachers, better teaching conditions’
Clemence, 30, maths teacher in Paris: “I support the high schoolers’ movement 100%. Their demands are ones we’ve been making for years. Today, we’re taking the opportunity to march alongside them. They’re asking for more resources, more teachers, better teaching conditions. We’ve been asking for this for years, because the state badly neglects it … You saw how the heatwave was handled: our classrooms were between 35 and 40°C. It’s unacceptable.”
‘You can feel a lot of anger’
Clara, 20, fashion student: “I’m here first of all in support of the high schoolers who started this strike in the 93 [Seine-Saint-Denis]. It’s where I live, and I know these schools. They have always lived and worked in unacceptable conditions. Their demands are legitimate, and they have a right to be heard and listened to.
“So far I think the atmosphere is rather good. You can see everyone is mobilised, proud and happy to be here. But you can also feel a lot of anger, because for once we want our demands to be heard, and we want people to listen to this youth that has been complaining for several years.”
‘We were peaceful, and they chose violence’
Tina, a 20-year-old student: “Yesterday we had a general assembly at our university, and the police and riot police were called in by our own administration. We said that was unacceptable. They started blocking our university, blocking our ideals of defending the high schoolers and the current cause. We don’t find that normal, so we came to demonstrate with them today to show our support. In the end there were no classes. We hadn’t finished expressing ourselves. We were peaceful, and they chose violence.”

New definition classifies fewer children as clinically obese
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
16:32:12 CST
17:32:12 KST

MELBOURNE, Oct. 7 (Xinhua) -- A new global definition of clinical obesity classifies far fewer children as obese than the widely used body mass index (BMI), a measure of weight relative to height, an international study has found.
The findings, published in eClinicalMedicine, part of The Lancet, could lead to changes to how childhood obesity is identified and managed, according to a statement released Wednesday by Australia's Murdoch Children's Research Institute (MCRI), which led the study.
The study, involving 786,557 participants from Australia, Canada, Estonia, Finland, the Netherlands, Britain and the United States, examines the prevalence of clinical obesity from early childhood through to older age.
It found that clinical obesity affected 2.1 to 4.9 percent of children and adolescents, compared with 7 to 10.8 percent classified as obese using BMI criteria.
The new Lancet Commission definition of clinical obesity goes beyond BMI, and considers whether excess body fat is accompanied by symptoms of obesity-related health problems or limitations in daily activities, according to researchers.
The study found clinical obesity became increasingly common with age, surpassing BMI-defined obesity from age 55 to 64 onwards and reaching 52 percent among adults aged 65 to 74. Clinical obesity was also higher among men during early-to-mid adulthood, while women experienced higher rates later in life.
MCRI researcher Danielle Longmore said BMI was useful for assessing obesity across populations but failed to capture individual health, potentially affecting obesity treatment, including weight-loss medication and dietary recommendations.
The researchers said identifying children already showing signs of obesity-related health complications could help inform future prevention and treatment strategies. ■

Politkovskaya 'predicted' Russia's turn under Putin, editor says on 20th anniversary of her death

Politkovskaya had reported on the war in Chechnya and Putin's rise before she was gunned down in her Moscow apartment block on October 7, 2006.
Assassinated Russian reporter Anna Politkovskaya, shot dead outside her Moscow home in 2006, had "predicted" Russia's trajectory under Putin, her editor said ahead of the 20th anniversary of her death.
Politkovskaya had reported fearlessly on the war in Chechnya and the rise of Putin, warning of his authoritarian tendencies at a time when he was being welcomed and courted in the West.
Read moreQuestions remain a decade after Russian journalist Politkovskaya's murder
She was gunned down in the lift of her central Moscow apartment block on October 7, 2006 – Putin's 54th birthday.
Her killing marked a turning point for Russian journalism.
Two decades on, Putin is still in power, Moscow's war against Ukraine – which has killed hundreds of thousands – is in its fifth year, and domestic repression has reached levels not seen since the Soviet era.
"Everything that is happening with Russia was predicted by Anna Politkovskaya in the books she published before her death," Sergei Sokolov, the legendary reporter's editor at the Novaya Gazeta newspaper where she worked, said.
Moscow has labelled her paper, Novaya Gazeta, a "foreign agent".
Read moreRussian investigative newspaper 'Novaya Gazeta' suspends publication after Kremlin warnings
"At the time, nobody believed her and they said she was exaggerating the dangers and fears," Sokolov said.
As the West embraced Putin in the early 2000s – a strongman leader cautiously welcomed after the chaos of the previous decade – Politkovskaya warned Russian journalists would have to show "total servility to Putin" or face death or prison.
Russia, she said, was "hurling back into a Soviet abyss".
The gunmen behind her murder are in prison – but the person, or people, who ordered the killing have never been named.
Read moreRussian jury convicts all defendants in journalist Politkovskaya murder
Asked about that in 2021, Putin said his agencies "did everything to uncover these crimes".
'Nothing could make her stray'
In death, Politkovskaya has become an even more totemic figure for Russian journalists – inspiring a generation of investigative reporters who she never met, and who are now forced to work in exile.
With Russia at war in Ukraine, her reporting from both sides of the front line in the Chechen wars has taken on fresh relevance.
She covered war crimes committed by both the Russian army and Chechen rebels and pushed both to evacuate civilians.
In 2002, she walked into a Moscow theatre that had been seized by Chechen rebels to try to secure the release of hostages.
"The terrorists had chosen me as a person they wanted to talk to. I couldn't refuse," she later said.
More than 130 hostages would be killed when special forces gassed the theatre and stormed the building.
"What stood out in her was her tenacity – nothing could make her stray from the topic or idea she had," Sokolov, her editor, recalled.
That school of journalism now lies in virtual tatters.
Years of pressure from the Kremlin have culminated in censorship levels unseen since the Soviet Union.
If Politkovskaya were alive, Sokolov was certain: "she would definitely not be able to stay silent".
In her latter years, Politkovskaya had become a fierce critic of Ramzan Kadyrov, then being groomed as the future head of Chechnya.
She dubbed him a "little dragon" and accused him of being given a free hand to brutally rule over the war-torn region in exchange for loyalty to the Kremlin.
Kadyrov in turn called her an "enemy of the Chechen people", vowing she would "answer" for her criticism of him.
Icon
Despite her name being virtually erased in Russia's official narrative, Politkovskaya remains an icon for independent Russian journalists – but also a constant reminder of the dangers of her profession.
"You need an example. If there was no example of courageous journalists and if everyone kept their heads down, then things will be even worse for Russian journalism," 28-year-old exiled reporter Yegor Feoktistov said.
"Her fate always reminds you of what can happen – but it also gives you courage."
Watch more'Putin's goal is to prolong his power in Russia': Journalist Roman Badanin
Another investigative journalist forced to work in exile, Olga Churakova, said she is "surprised by the stream of people who want to become journalists" in Russia despite the dangers.
Many mention Politkovskaya as their inspiration.
"People still come and say: 'Someone needs to do this job'."
(FRANCE 24 with AFP)

NANJING, Oct. 7 (Xinhua) -- One more survivor of the Nanjing Massacre passed away on Wednesday, reducing the number of registered living survivors to 20, the Memorial Hall of the Victims in Nanjing Massacre by Japanese Invaders said.
Massacre survivor Guo Xiulan died at the age of 94, according to the memorial hall in Nanjing, the capital of east China's Jiangsu Province.
Guo was born in 1932. According to survivor recollections documented by the museum, when the Nanjing Massacre took place after Japanese troops captured Nanjing on Dec. 13, 1937, Guo's parents took their three children to hide in an underground shelter along with neighbors.
"Japanese soldiers stood at the opening and strafed it with machine guns. My parents and my youngest sister perished. Only my second sister and I survived," Guo was recorded as saying.
The Nanjing Massacre unfolded over six weeks. Japanese soldiers killed approximately 300,000 Chinese civilians and unarmed soldiers in one of the most barbaric atrocities of World War II.
Over the years, the number of survivors able to share firsthand accounts of the massacre has continued to decline.
In 2014, China's top legislature designated Dec. 13 as the national memorial day for the victims of the Nanjing Massacre. The Chinese government has also preserved survivors' testimonies through written records and video recordings.
Documents related to the massacre were inscribed on UNESCO's Memory of the World Register in 2015. To date, only 20 living survivors of the Nanjing Massacre remain on the registry maintained by the Nanjing Association for Assistance to Victims of Japanese Aggression and Inheritance of Nanjing Massacre Historical Memory. ■

China's forex reserves fall 1.11 pct in September
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
16:31:52 CST
17:31:52 KST

BEIJING, Oct. 7 (Xinhua) -- China's foreign exchange reserves stood at 3.4003 trillion U.S. dollars at the end of September 2026, down 38.1 billion dollars, or 1.11 percent, from the end of August, data from the State Administration of Foreign Exchange (SAFE) showed Wednesday.
Last month, the U.S. dollar index rose while prices of major global financial assets generally declined, amid changes in the global macroeconomic environment and monetary policies in major economies, the SAFE noted in a statement.
The combined effects of exchange-rate movements and changes in asset prices led to the decline in China's foreign exchange reserves during the month, the SAFE said.
Wen Bin, chief economist at China Minsheng Bank, said the decline came against a backdrop of rising expectations for tighter U.S. monetary policy.
The U.S. Federal Reserve raised its benchmark overnight interest rate by 25 basis points in September to a range of 3.75 percent to 4 percent, its first rate increase of the year. The Fed's latest dot plot pointed to another rate hike by the end of the year, while hawkish remarks from Fed officials further strengthened market expectations for additional tightening, Wen said.
Against this backdrop, global bonds, including U.S. Treasuries, came under selling pressure, pushing yields higher and lifting the U.S. dollar index. The stronger dollar and declines in the prices of some global financial assets in turn exerted valuation pressure on China's foreign exchange reserves.
Despite the decline, the administration said China's economy has remained generally stable, with stronger new growth drivers, an improving economic structure and continued progress in high-quality development, providing support for the country's foreign exchange reserves to remain broadly stable.
Wen said China's exports are expected to remain resilient and continue to serve as a key anchor for the country's balance of payments.
Wednesday's data also showed China's gold reserves stood at 77.47 million ounces at the end of September, up 740,000 ounces from the end of August.
The increase marked the 23rd consecutive month that the People's Bank of China had added to its gold holdings. ■

Anduril Invests $3.7 Billion in Plant to Expand Virginia-Class Submarine Production
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
08:31:13 UTC
17:31:13 KST

American company Anduril will build the Arsenal-2 shipyard to manufacture components and large structural sections for Virginia-class nuclear-powered submarines.
The company announced the project on October 6.
Anduril is investing $3.7 billion in private capital in the project. At the same time, the U.S. Navy awarded the company a contract worth up to $2.9 billion, with payments tied to production results. Thus, the total announced funding amounts to up to $6.6 billion.
Arsenal-2 will supply components and large structural sections to General Dynamics Electric Boat and Newport News Shipbuilding, which carry out the final assembly of Virginia-class submarines.
The shipyard will be located within the Tradepoint Atlantic industrial facility in Sparrows Point, Baltimore County, Maryland. The production facilities will cover more than 186,000 square meters, while the entire site will span approximately 76 hectares.
The facility is scheduled to begin operations in 2030, followed by a gradual production ramp-up. According to Anduril, the project will create 3,100 jobs directly at the facility and support more than 11,000 additional jobs in related industries.
The shipyard will use a dry dock about 366 meters long, along with road and rail connections to transport large structural sections. The production buildings and manufacturing lines are being designed to allow for reconfiguration to meet evolving U.S. Navy requirements.
Production at Arsenal-2 will be managed using Anduril’s ArsenalOS software platform. It will integrate manufacturing operations, material handling, quality control, and documentation, while giving workers real-time visibility into production progress.
Meanwhile, Anduril is developing a separate facility of about 14,900 square meters in Orange County, California. Before Arsenal-2 becomes operational, this facility will be used to test and refine manufacturing processes, train workers, and produce components for Virginia-class submarines, including torpedo launchers.
According to Anduril, the new facilities will help accelerate submarine production for the U.S. Navy and support the United States’ commitments under the AUKUS partnership.
Militarnyi previously reported on Austal USA’s expansion of its facilities to support the construction of Virginia- and Columbia-class submarines. The $450 million agreement includes developing infrastructure at the company’s shipyard in Mobile, Alabama.
Virginia-class submarines are U.S. Navy nuclear-powered attack submarines designed to engage enemy surface ships and submarines, as well as strike land targets. They are equipped with four 533 mm torpedo tubes and Tomahawk cruise missiles.

Finance ministry to use artificial intelligence in its election promises analysis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
08:31:00 UTC
17:31:00 KST

Finance ministry to use artificial intelligence in its election promises analysis
Ahead of the spring Riigikogu elections, the Ministry of Finance will analyze election promises with the help of artificial intelligence.
The Ministry of Finance has analyzed election promises ahead of Riigikogu elections since 2007. Raoul Lättemäe, head of the ministry's fiscal policy department, said the analysis assesses the financial impact of election promises — how much a particular promise would cost and what impact it would have on the budget. Where possible, the analysis also comments on whether a promise is feasible, for example, whether it complies with European Union legislation or is already being implemented under an existing development plan.
For this election, artificial intelligence will be used to assist with the analysis. Lättemäe noted that preparing the analysis involves a great deal of work that could now be done by AI. "Breaking election platforms down into individual promises, sorting them by policy area and finding relevant background information," he explained.
Analysts will review the work
For example, the system will search development plans, budgets and previous analyses or responses to determine whether the issue has already been addressed elsewhere. It will do the preliminary work needed to compile the analysis. "Of course, actual analysts will review and supplement all of it," Lättemäe said.
The analysis will be prepared and published before the election. Lättemäe said the Ministry of Finance will also give a presentation before the election to introduce the findings. The assessment itself will be politically neutral. The aim is to give voters a clearer picture of how much the promises would cost, allowing them to make more informed choices and have more substantive discussions about election promises.
The ministry is currently holding a tender to find a service provider or system developer to build the AI tool. The Ministry of Justice and Digital Affairs has a funding measure for central and local government bodies to develop AI technologies. If the tender is successful, the ministry also plans to make an election-promise search tool available to the public using the same search system.
"This would allow individuals, journalists, researchers or anyone else to connect their own AI system to ours, where we have indexed development plans, state budgets, the previous five analyses of election promises and, on an ongoing basis, election platforms as well," Lättemäe said. This would allow people to improve the quality of AI-generated answers about the election or simply search for election promises through a web search.
AI will go beyond its training data in providing answers
The artificial intelligence connected to the system would therefore answer questions not only on the basis of its training data, but would also be able to provide specific references showing where the issue has been addressed in a current government development plan, election promise or platform. The tool is thus intended both to assist the ministry in carrying out its analysis and to make information more readily accessible and usable by AI, helping the public better understand what has been promised, whether it is feasible and whether it has been analyzed before.
The tool is designed for Estonian-language text, meaning it must be able to find references to relevant Estonian-language documents and identify the necessary connections even when a question is not phrased in exactly the same way as in the original documents.
The Ministry of Finance will analyze only parties that field a full list of candidates. "Otherwise, the workload would become too large or unmanageable," Lättemäe said.
Funding is provided in accordance with the procedure established by the minister of justice and digital affairs' regulation, "A model for a future-proof data economy ecosystem and infrastructure solutions for the secure management, processing and utilization of data."

Britain has about forty days of diesel, says Tugendhat
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
09:30:44 BST
17:30:44 KST

Britain is going into winter with some of the lowest gas stocks in the industrialised world and enough diesel for roughly forty days, the Shadow Foreign Secretary told the Conservative conference,
Tom Tugendhat used his speech in Birmingham on Tuesday to put fuel at the centre of an argument about national resilience, treating energy stocks as a defence question first and an economic one second.
He said: “This winter we’re already approaching a difficult time of year for many with some of the lowest gas stocks in the industrialised world and with enough diesel only for about 40 days.
“It puts our resilience second to global politics. That is Labour’s way and it is the wrong way.”
He went on: “So what are we looking at? Thin stores. A coming winter. A world one shock from trouble. That is not resilience. That is living hand to mouth.”
Fuel stocks are among the least examined parts of British preparedness and among the hardest to fix quickly, since the country has lost most of its refining capacity over two decades and holds obligations under International Energy Agency rules that are measured in days of consumption. Moving a division anywhere is a fuel problem before it is anything else, which is why NATO has returned to the subject repeatedly since 2022.
Mr Tugendhat set out what a Conservative government would do about it. “We will prepare our troops but we know that while armies go on operations, it’s only nations that go to war, and they only go to war for as long as they can sustain it,” he said. “That’s why we will rebuild our stocks and treat fuel in the tank like shells in the store. We will use the oil and gas under our own seas and break the energy fast that costs so much and delivers so little.”
The phrase about fuel in the tank and shells in the store is the sharpest formulation anybody has given of a problem the Ministry of Defence has been circling for years, which is that munitions stockpiles have received political attention while the fuel to move the force has not.
He also invoked what he called Ferguson’s Law, the proposition that a country paying more in debt interest than on defence is in a condition no state has long endured, and said the Bank of England had warned that weak points in world markets were likely to give way at once while Britain is most exposed.
The speech ranged more widely across what he described as a world run by strong men and deals in place of rules and institutions, quoting the former chief of the Secret Intelligence Service, Sir Alex Younger, to that effect. He said the Foreign Office had for too long behaved as though it were an international non-governmental organisation and that he would make it “the long arm of British strength around the world”.
Mr Tugendhat organised his approach around three words, which he gave as right, might and money, arguing that Britain has the right to protect itself and is not properly exercising it, needs the military strength to do so, and needs a growing economy to pay for both.
On alliances he named the Comprehensive and Progressive Agreement for Trans-Pacific Partnership and the Joint Expeditionary Force within NATO, and said he would build deeper partnerships with Canada, Australia and New Zealand, bringing trade and defence together.

Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
08:30:16 UTC
17:30:16 KST

Shell’s refineries are expected to make record profits on each barrel of fuel produced after shortages in the global market caused pump prices around the world to climb to all-time highs.
In a trading update on Wednesday, the energy supermajor forecast profit margins of $42 a barrel in the July to September period, far above the margins of $24 a barrel in the second quarter.
The forecast margins are also significantly higher than the previous record for petroleum products of about $28 a barrel, set in the early months of the Russia-Ukraine war.
The margins reflect the steep increase in the price of refined fuels, including diesel, relative to the cost of the crude oil. A partial recovery of Gulf oil exports has allowed crude market prices to ease back to about $100 a barrel, while war damage to refineries in the Middle East and Russia has caused fuel prices to continue to climb.
That gap should make larger profits possible for refineries, particularly those in the US and Europe. The Middle East crisis has already helped Shell to a profit of almost $10bn (£7.5bn) for the second quarter of 2026, more than double the figure for the same period last year and its second highest quarterly earnings on record.
The market value of Europe’s biggest oil and gas company, now the second largest company on the UK’s FTSE 100 index, climbed to a record high of £36.23 a share at the end of last month.
That share price was reached despite oil prices retreating from their 2026 peak of above $115 a barrel in spring to about $100. It was lifted by European gas prices, which doubled from the previous year over the summer, and record high diesel prices.
Global oil prices were slightly lower in the third quarter of the year. Brent crude averaged $85.60 a barrel, compared with $97.05 in the second quarter, but still well above the $68.14 recorded in the third quarter last year.
The diesel price premium over the global oil benchmark jumped above $100 a barrel for the first time, indicating record high profits from refining crude into fuels.
Shell operates some of Europe’s largest refineries alongside the French energy company TotalEnergies, which has the continent’s largest refining capacity.
TotalEnergies’ chief executive, Patrick Pouyanné, welcomed the opportunities created by the global energy crisis. He told an industry conference in London this week: “We’re doing really well by being integrated. Integration means your refineries in Europe, which you thought were liabilities, are suddenly becoming goldmines.”
Europe’s benchmark gas price index more than doubled to €70.50 (£60) in August. The price of gas reached an average of more than €48 a megawatt-hour in the second quarter before leaping to almost €64/MWh in the third quarter.
Shell’s gas production has been hard hit by the Middle East crisis, which led to severe damage to one of its key gas processing facilities in the Gulf, cutting its prewar gas production of 900,000 barrels of oil equivalent per day (BOED) by a third.
Shell said on Wednesday that it expected gas production to climb to about 740,000 to 780,000 barrels of oil equivalent a day after its acquisition of Canada’s ARC Resources, up sharply from its previous forecast of 570,000 to 630,000 BOED for the quarter. It produced about 631,000 BOED in the second quarter.
The deal, which is expected to add about 370,000 barrels a day to Shell’s production of oil and gas, was completed in early September to add a month’s worth of production to its estimates for the quarter.

US risks ceding AI governance leadership to China and the EU
The voluntary agreement involving US tech companies that Trump announced rests largely on self-policing, in contrast to the approach taken by Brussels and Beijing
3-MIN READ3-MIN
2
 Listen
Denis Simon is a senior research fellow in the East Asia Programme at the Quincy Institute for Responsible Statecraft in Washington, DC. 
Standing alongside prominent technology executives, US President Donald Trump announced a voluntary agreement under which major artificial intelligence (AI) companies will use internal controls and monitoring, outside audits and board oversight to manage risks. The White House calls the commitments “morally binding”, but the accord does not create a comparable system of legal enforcement.
The administration’s logic is understandable. AI is becoming a source of economic and military power, and Washington does not want regulation to slow American companies while China races ahead. But what happens when the country developing many of the world’s most powerful AI systems tells the rest of the world that the companies building them should largely police themselves?
That question cannot be confined to Washington. A model may be developed in California, trained on American computing infrastructure, incorporated into a product sold in Europe and eventually used in Asia or Africa. Its consequences do not stop at the boundary of the country where it was developed.

Your Next Great Read Might Be Certified ‘Organic’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
08:30:00 UTC
17:30:00 KST

As scandals involving the use of artificial intelligence by professional authors pile up, a British startup has established a way for publishers to certify their books as “organic”—written by real people, no machines in sight.
On Wednesday, Books by People confirmed it had received approval from the UK’s Intellectual Property Office to begin distributing a mark that indicates a published book has been authored by a human. The stamp, which looks like a thumbprint, will be displayed on the cover.
“If people are going to be writing AI books or seeking it out for their own enjoyment, that’s their prerogative,” Esme Dennys, cofounder of Books by People, tells WIRED. “But if you want to read something that’s written by a person, you should be able to find that. We’re just trying to create that choice.”
Previous book-labeling schemes, like Human Authored, have operated under an honesty system, where an author promises they haven’t used AI in the development process. To try to add more weight to its certification, Books by People asks for an authorship declaration, runs each manuscript through proprietary software, and manually examines early drafts and research materials supplied by the writer and editor for “indicators of humanity.”
The organization is "looking at all the things that give us the best sense of whether a person wrote the work—whether the work was made during a natural process of drafting and redrafting,” says Dennys.
Books by People will charge publishers a flat membership fee, plus an additional sum for every book they put forward for certification. Five publishers have signed up so far. The startup expects the new mark to feature on its first book by the end of the year.
This year, the publishing industry has been caught up in a flurry of scandals involving the suspected use of AI by authors. A literary agent canceled a book deal reportedly worth $2 million; a publisher withdrew a novel from the shelves; readers alleged that a prize-winning short story had been generated with AI.
Writers and publishers are not necessarily worried about being replaced by AI, industry insiders tell WIRED. They believe that few people will ultimately want to read machine-generated books.
“You are essentially standing at the end of a conveyor belt, watching stuff fall off the edge. Once you know that, it prevents you from getting really emotionally invested in whatever falls into your hands from the belt,” says sci-fi author Ted Chiang, whose 1998 novella Story of Your Life was adapted into the Academy Award–winning film Arrival. “The knowledge of how something was created cannot be separated from your experience.”
However, repeated scandals could shake public confidence in the unspoken rule of publishing: That every book that reaches the shelf has been authored by a real person who has not indulged in plagiarism.
“Publishing has always relied on trust between the publisher, writer, and reading public. Cases where that trust is betrayed have been rare,” says Sam Jordison, codirector at independent publisher Galley Beggar Press, which intends to adopt the Books by People mark. “There’s almost a feeling of revulsion about the idea of reading an AI text that purports to be human. It feels like a con job.”
Against that backdrop, the idea of a certification for human-authored books has received backing from various writers and editors. In a statement praising Books by People, Markus Dohle, former CEO of Penguin Random House, described human storytelling as “the lifeblood of our industry.”
But while publishers might relish the chance to signal their commitment to “organic literature,” the routinization of AI detection is a double-edged sword for authors, who risk a false positive result spoiling their reputation.
“We need to be quite careful that this doesn’t end up becoming a witch hunt,” says Tom West, CEO of the Publishers’ Licensing Services, which helps publishers to collectively license works to third parties. “Obviously, the devil is going to be in the detail.”
New York–based startup Pangram, which has emerged as the leader in the field of AI detection, claims to be able to sniff out generated text with a 99.7 percent accuracy. But authors have questioned the reliability of its approach, which itself involves AI.
In September, Jerry Falade, the debut author whose agent reportedly pulled the $2 million book deal, alleged that detection software had misconstrued his Nigerian dialect as evidence he had used AI. Pangram’s software scored the book as 97 percent AI-generated. “It takes months, even years to write a book,” Falade wrote in a recent essay. “It takes AI-detection software two minutes to ruin your life’s work.” (Pangram did not respond to a request for comment.)
Others have warned against normalizing extreme scrutiny of authors. They claim the labeling schemes have it backward; the onus should be on platforms and publishers to declare when a piece of media is AI-generated, not when it’s written by a person. “Authors are being constantly quizzed about the origins of their ideas and their work. I think that’s something we need to resist,” says West. “The default should be that a book is human-authored.”
Approved by the Intellectual Property Office alongside the mark, Books by People’s verification process is different to Pangram’s technology-first approach, placing greater weight on interrogating documents and communication trails for signs of humanity. “I wouldn’t call it AI detection,” says Dennys. “We realized pretty early on that, as AI models get better, getting into that race is never going to be sustainable.”
In cases where Books by People is uncertain whether a piece of evidence indicates AI use, it claims to err on the side of the author. “When you have a public process that has been vetted, all we can do is make sure that a book has gone through the process,” says Dennys. “The bedrock of our organization is to avoid [writers] being unjustly accused.”
Some authors say the important thing is that publishers underscore their commitment to human-authored literature as a nonnegotiable standard for the industry, in whatever way they can. Even if methods for policing the rule are flawed.
“It’s just as important for publishers to have a ‘no cheating’ policy as it is for universities, even if there’s no perfect method for enforcement,” says Chiang. “It’s a statement of values.”

Ukrainian forces combine robots with drones to strike Russians deep in the rear. Interview with the commander of "NC13"
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
11:30:00 EEST
17:30:00 KST

"Gryphon": Ukrainian forces combine robots with drones to strike Russians deep in the rear. Interview with the commander of "NC13"
In January of this year, the "NC13" strike UGV unit of the 3rd Separate Assault Brigade tested a new tactic deep behind Russian lines. Since then, the unit has successfully carried out more than 100 similar operations, turning what began as an experiment into a proven combat system.
The new tactic was named "Gryphon" in honor of a service member from the unit who went missing in action in 2023 while carrying out a combat mission near Andriivka in the Donetsk region. It was in this area, near Bakhmut, that Oscar-winning Ukrainian director Mstyslav Chernov filmed the documentary "2000 Meters to Andriivka" during a different Ukrainian counteroffensive.
The concept behind the new tactic involves deploying kamikaze UGVs, essentially ground robots, deep behind enemy lines using heavy bomber drones. After landing, the robotic systems continue moving toward their targets and can be used to strike key positions, logistics, and personnel while also creating disruption in the enemy rear.
The "NC13" unit was also behind an operation that drew significant international attention about a year ago, when Ukrainian forces captured Russian positions without deploying infantry, using only UGVs and drones.
As a result, two Russian service members surrendered to the robotic systems, after which the machines escorted them to Ukrainian positions as prisoners of war.
Today, the new tactic is part of the Third Army Corps' large-scale operation known as "Vivaldi." Since the start of the offensive, Ukrainian forces have liberated 176 square kilometers of territory (68 square miles).
According to the Office of the President of Ukraine, Russian forces suffered more than 5,000 casualties, including those killed, wounded, and captured, during the first three stages of the operation. It is currently known that Ukrainian forces have taken 250 Russian service members as prisoners of war (POWs). The Third Army Corps separately reported 2,000 Russian personnel casualties during the latest stage alone.
Approximately 80% of logistics and 90% of wounded evacuation for Ukrainian troops during all three stages of the operation were carried out by unmanned ground vehicles, or UGVs.
"NC13" commander Mykola Zinkevych, call sign "Makar," explains how the new "Gryphon" tactic works, how the idea of air-dropping ground robots emerged, what happened during the first operations, how Russian forces are reacting to the technology, and why he believes Ukraine is shaping the future of technological warfare.
He also discusses how Western partners are becoming less able to understand Ukrainian military technologies and, more broadly, the needs of modern warfare.
Can you please explain, in general, what this new tactic involves?
In general, this is a sabotage-operation tactic that was fully planned, developed, and implemented by the "NC13" strike unmanned ground systems unit of the 3rd Separate Assault Brigade.
The tactic is genuinely new and has no equivalent anywhere in the world because no one had previously deployed unmanned ground vehicles from unmanned aerial vehicles.
The concept itself is that, using heavy bombers, we drop small ground-based kamikaze systems deep into enemy territory, at a distance of 5 to 15 kilometers (3 to 9.3 miles). From there, we carry out different sabotage operations: eliminating enemy personnel, destroying logistics, and so on.
When did you begin using this tactic? Any first operation is essentially a test. How confident were you that it would work?
We carried out the first operation about eight months ago (in January 2026- UP).
We spent quite a long time developing the tactic itself and modifying the equipment because standard ground-based kamikaze systems are not designed for this kind of use.
The engineers spent a great deal of time making it work. The pilots also had to learn how to operate with these systems and deploy them correctly. The planning department, accordingly, spent a lot of time preparing the operation.
But when it worked for the first time, the excitement was incredible. Our first operation went 15 kilometers (9.3 miles) deep behind enemy lines. We deployed two ground-based kamikaze systems near the target, and from there, the systems themselves moved into the shelter.
It was an enemy staging point where personnel were brought in. They would stop there to rest before moving on to carry out their missions. We eliminated that staging point using two ground-based kamikaze systems.
What was the enemy's reaction? What did it look like from their side?
In fact, the enemy did not understand what had happened, what system had been used, what had struck them, or what tactic we were employing.
Even now, it remains a major surprise for them because we operate in different sectors within the Third Army Corps' area of responsibility.
We combine different technologies in order to change the rules on the battlefield.
We have been able to strike the enemy from the air at significant depth for quite some time. We have also been using unmanned ground vehicles to strike enemy forces for a while.
But this combination (UGV + UAV) allows us to operate at greater depth, in areas where the enemy does not expect to be reached and where they feel relatively safe. So we are going to take that freedom away from them.
How many such operations have been carried out so far?
More than one hundred. We always work systematically. If something works once, twice, or three times, we still do not consider it a fully established capability because it could be accidental.
But when something is carried out more than ten times, it becomes a systematic approach. We have SOPs, standard operating procedures, in place for this tactic: how to use it, where it can be implemented, and what its capabilities are.
It can be used for reconnaissance, mining deep behind enemy lines, striking targets, hunting moving enemy personnel, disrupting logistics, and more. We have fully developed this tactic, identified all of its capabilities, and now use it as a full-fledged tool on the battlefield.
War in general, and especially Russia's war against Ukraine, is a war of speed. Everything depends on who can come up with something new and adapt faster. Are the Russians already trying to do something similar?
I am confident that we are far ahead of the enemy. Even when it comes to the systematic use of strike unmanned ground vehicles on the battlefield, which we have been doing for about a year, the enemy is still far behind.
So when it comes to tactics like "Gryphon," which we are discussing today, there is still a very large gap between us and them.
But I would not rule out the possibility that, over time, the enemy will begin copying this approach and using similar methods.
In fact, during more than 100 successful missions, there have been many almost meme-like moments when the enemy had no idea what they were looking at and would actually approach the robots to inspect them.
There was one occasion when we managed to completely disrupt a Russian mechanized assault that had been planned for foggy weather conditions. At the time, we were actively targeting one of the enemy's logistics routes. We eliminated several personnel over the course of the day.
They started to panic because they did not understand what was happening. They thought a sabotage and reconnaissance group, or SRG, had broken through into their rear. As a result, they canceled the mechanized assault they had planned for that day.
So these small robots can create very significant disruption.
In general, there was serious panic among enemy forces at the depth where we were operating. And panic is actually very important because if we create panic within enemy ranks, they begin to have problems controlling their personnel. Soldiers start refusing to carry out missions, which then creates panic at the command level because commanders do not understand what is happening in their rear, and so on.
That creates destabilization, and all of that works in our favor.
Why exactly do they panic?
Even when you know what it is, you can become even more afraid. You do not know where it might be waiting for you, where it might drive, where it might catch up with you, and so on. So in some ways, it is even better when they know.
You know, now you have to watch not only the sky, but also the ground beneath your feet. Not just for mines, but because something might come after you.
There was one interesting intercepted communication where an enemy soldier reported to his commander that a "Baba Yaga" (russian military slang for heavy bomber drones - UP) had flown in, landed, then started driving and chasing them.
It was pretty funny to listen to.
But it did catch them in the end.
This tactic seems to have many advantages. Which one do you consider the most important?
- The absolute advantage of using any technology is that, first and foremost, we do not have to put people at risk. We preserve human lives.
For me, as the commander of a strike UGV unit and as a former infantryman, it is actually more important to preserve our own personnel, to protect Ukrainian infantrymen, assault troops, and soldiers, than it is to destroy the enemy. Destroying the enemy comes second.
And in fact, by destroying the enemy, we prevent them from advancing toward our forces and make life easier for our infantry. So above all, any technology helps us protect human life. Robots do not bleed, and human life is priceless. That is essentially our guiding principle throughout everything we do.
The next advantage, of course, is depth. The depth at which we can operate with these systems.
Yes, 10 to 15 kilometers (6.2 to 9.3 miles) is not the maximum range. Unfortunately, I cannot disclose the exact figures. But we are deployed and then continue moving very, very deep into enemy territory. The deeper we go, the more valuable, so to speak, the resources and targets we can destroy.
You touched a little on the future. Is there already a vision for how this technology could develop? I will not ask exactly how, but should we expect it to be scaled up further?
Yes. By the end of 2026, there will be many large-scale, exciting, and interesting stories, announcements, and new tactics from our unit.
We already have a number of newly implemented applications and tactics involving unmanned ground vehicles, (including the use of UGVs equipped with grenade launchers, which is also a new and unique tactic -UP).
It is simply not yet the right time to talk about them. And we have many more things planned. So we just need to wait a little longer.
Western countries have traditionally been considered leaders in military technology. You speak with foreign military officials. How well do they understand the technological breakthrough currently taking place in Ukraine?
I attended the Munich Security Conference in February and had the opportunity to speak with many foreign military officials, various partners, and government representatives.
In reality, they are very far behind. Absolutely.
They understand what we are talking about, what we are deploying, what we are using, and how it works. But they do not fully understand its importance and value on the battlefield, or just how much the battlefield itself has changed.
And I am more than certain that the rest of the world is lagging very, very far behind.
Even the technologies I see being introduced into militaries around the world are still quite far removed from what is actually being used on the battlefield between Ukraine and Russia.
Looking specifically at unmanned ground vehicles, I have seen their entire evolution on the front line, from 2024 until today.
We work, interact, and collaborate with many manufacturers. A great deal of equipment has been developed because we provided our expertise and doctrine.
I also have a certain number of systems produced by foreign manufacturers, and there is a very significant difference between them (Ukrainian and Western UGVs - UP).
We are not even talking about price, although the prices are extremely high. But in terms of actual battlefield use, Western systems still fall far short of the needs of the modern battlefield.
Are foreign partners reaching out to Ukrainian military personnel often enough for this kind of expertise? Is there interest in contributing to the development of these innovations?
I would say they do reach out, but not nearly as actively as they should. In my opinion, this is the kind of expertise people should be actively pursuing, not just occasionally asking, "So, what are you working on?"
No one knows what will happen in the world tomorrow. We live in a time when you never know what to expect.
If Ukraine can offer something to its partners, what can it receive from them in return?
Ukraine is the sword and shield of Europe. It is defending not only itself and its own future, but the future of the entire continent.
So every time other countries help us, they should understand that they are not only helping Ukrainians. They are also helping themselves.
Right now, Ukraine especially needs effective and timely weapons deliveries from its partners. First and foremost, this means air defense systems capable of protecting Ukrainian cities from attacks, as well as heavy weapons, including artillery and armored vehicles, that can help Ukraine regain the initiative on the battlefield.
Of course, this support must always be justified. Because Ukraine is doing everything possible to defend its territory, - liberate occupied land, and protect the future of the country and the nation, - that is why all of these processes and technologies have emerged.
The battlefield has effectively become a testing ground for innovation. On the one hand, that is a positive thing.
But on the other hand, it is deeply tragic, because every such achievement comes at a price. And that price is not paid in money. It is paid with the lives of Ukrainian service members and people who should have been the future of the Ukrainian nation.
History has seen many cases where a promising technology or a major breakthrough emerged, but it was overlooked, underfunded, or never scaled up...
This is not something that appeared only today. It is something that has been developed and planned over a period of time, has already been implemented for quite a while, and is constantly being modernized.
It will continue to evolve and eventually grow into something new.
Because there are technologies that work today. There are technologies that will work tomorrow. And there are technologies that worked yesterday but no longer work today.
But each of them becomes a driving force behind the next one.
Kateryna Lisunova, Ukrainska Pravda

Triumph of Common Sense: Dissecting the Carlson-Rees-Mogg Interview
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
08:28:53 UTC
17:28:53 KST

“Sir, Rees-Mogg, thank you very much for having us in your home. It’s really pretty. I’m sad to think of it being destroyed in the war you described?”
This provocative opener to the interview between Tucker Carlson and British Conservative Jacob Rees-Mogg epitomizes the spirit of the conversation that ensued.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Sir Rees-Mogg, an Etonian, businessman and former Conservative member of parliament, is sitting in a lavish hall of his home. The discussion concerns the UK’s policy toward Russia and Ukraine, but also the more fundamental question of “what is the right thing to do in life?”
Carlson approaches it through the lens of relativism, Russian apologism and selective concern for other people’s plight. Rees-Mogg delivers an extensive reality check.
Russian apologism and economic ignorance
Carlson has long been known as one of the leading American commentators holding Russia-friendly views. In 2024, he traveled to Moscow to interview Vladimir Putin, giving the Russian leader ample space to put forward his historical claims and justify his invasion.
His interview with Rees-Mogg was no exception. He started by questioning Rees-Mogg’s assertion that the UK must be prepared for war with Russia, given Russia’s extensive acts of hostility. Such a war, Carlson suggested, could destroy the “pretty home.”
“There was attempted murder in Salisbury, and there was a murder that took place in London by agents of Putin, that Putin has invaded Ukraine, and he is making threatening noises,” Rees-Mogg said, adding that Russian figures close to the state had discussed the potential for nuclear war.
How NATO Plans to Win: ‘Theory of Victory’ Against Russia to be Unveiled in Poland
Carlson’s response was a sarcastic insinuation of the kind he likes to describe as thinking clearly about cause and effect. For Carlson, the “cause” is Britain’s behavior: namely, supporting Ukraine.
Only it isn’t.
The Salisbury attack occurred in 2018, while Alexander Litvinenko was poisoned in London in 2006. Both took place long before the expansion of British military assistance following Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine. Those attacks cannot be explained as a response to that later assistance.
The other logical fallacy concerns the “cause” itself. In the chain of events surrounding the full-scale war, Russia threatening the UK over its support for Ukraine is not the starting point. The starting point is Russia’s full-scale invasion on Feb. 24, 2022 – not to mention its initial invasion in 2014. British assistance is a response to Russia’s illegal aggression against its sovereign neighbor.
Rees-Mogg, disregarding Carlson’s innuendos, suggests that Putin wishes to reassert Russian power, linking this ambition to the loss of territory and influence following the Soviet Union’s collapse.
“In most years, Russia expands, and then you get the collapse of the Soviet Union and Russia suddenly shrinks. And it seems to me that that is looked upon by some Russians as a matter of shame and against the historic destiny of Russia. Hence, of course, the reason for activity in Georgia, and more recently in Ukraine,” he says.
Carlson’s reasoning then moves from explaining away aggression to confusing different measures of economic strength. He claims that Russia has a larger economy than Britain, insisting that it has more wealth, resources and a larger manufacturing sector.
Rees-Mogg counters that Russia’s GDP is smaller, while Carlson replies that GDP is not the only measure of an economy.
“It’s a pretty important measure of an economy,” Rees-Mogg says, arguing that Russia has failed to use its resources effectively because it is deeply corrupt.
There is a distinction to make here between nominal GDP and purchasing-power comparisons. Neither speaker makes it adequately. Carlson instead moves between economic output, natural resources and national power as though they were interchangeable.
Again, they are not.
Rees-Mogg points to African countries with extensive natural resources that have nevertheless failed to turn them into prosperity. The existence of something underground does not automatically establish how successfully a country extracts, processes, sells or uses it.
Carlson remains unconvinced. But he’ll “grant you.”
Everything is relative and no one owes anything
If you make an agreement, is that agreement worth anything?
For Rees-Mogg, the answer is unequivocally yes. For Carlson, the answer becomes considerably more elusive, as their discussion of international obligations demonstrates.
Carlson admits in plain language that Russia’s annexation of Crimea was no concern of his. But his reasoning reveals something deeper: He questions the significance of commitments countries make to each other whenever honoring them might require a cost.
The central example is the 1994 Budapest Memorandum, under which Ukraine surrendered the nuclear weapons on its territory in return for security assurances from Russia, the United States and Britain. Those assurances included commitments to refrain from the threat or use of force against Ukraine’s territorial integrity.
“So you’re saying Ukraine should have kept its nuclear weapons?” Rees-Mogg asks logically.
Carlson replies that there were subsequent arrangements violated on all sides.
Which arrangements precisely?
He eventually invokes the alleged promise that NATO would not expand toward Russia’s borders. Yet Mikhail Gorbachev, the last Soviet leader, said in a 2014 interview that NATO enlargement had not been discussed during the negotiations surrounding German reunification.
Carlson does not explain how his claim cancels the assurances given to Ukraine, or how Ukraine becomes responsible for supposedly violated arrangements between other countries.
However, things become clearer as he progresses in his reasoning.
“Do you believe in territorial integrity of nation states?” Rees-Mogg asks.
“In my own, for sure,” Carlson answers. “I’m not sure that the territorial integrity of someone else’s state is worth risking my life for.”
What is a nation state? And sovereignty?
Carlson makes a distinction between sovereignty “for yourself “and sovereignty “for everyone else.”
Carlson believes in his own country’s territorial integrity “for sure.” Smaller countries, however, are expected to live with whatever their powerful neighbors consider necessary.
But if sovereignty is a principle, it cannot apply only to countries powerful enough to enforce it. Otherwise, what Carlson is defending is a hierarchy: some countries are entitled to independence; others are obliged to accept their place.
Carlson asks why Britain should concern itself with whether Russia takes Ukraine. Rees-Mogg answers that preserving the integrity of nation states serves both British and American interests.
“If all nation states are up for grabs, for whichever country wants to take it, then why shouldn’t China take Taiwan tomorrow?” he asks.
Carlson has no good answer.
And what about an ally?
Carlson challenges Rees-Mogg over Britain’s decision to enter World War I, asking whether protecting Belgium was worth “destroying all of Europe.”
Notice who becomes responsible for the deaths. Germany invaded Belgium to reach France, and Britain had guaranteed Belgian neutrality and independence. Yet in Carlson’s formulation, the catastrophe becomes something Britain, as a guarantor, chose to inflict by deciding that protecting another country mattered.
Rees-Mogg objects to the premise altogether, despite acknowledging the dreadful cost of World War I.
“What I said was that the enemy felt free to invade because we were seen to be weak. That’s not the same as saying it was the right thing to do.”
But Carlson’s underlying question remains: why bother with Belgium? Why incur a cost for France or anybody else?
When the conversation turns to World War II, Carlson’s reasoning becomes even more revealing and disturbing. He talks of nothing but Hitler’s declarations that he did not want war with Britain and argues, in effect, that the war started because of Hitler’s grievances over territory lost as a result of World War I.
Nazi aggression cannot be reduced to territorial grievances following World War I. Hitler’s ambitions admittedly involved a racial empire: conquest for German settlement, the subjugation and displacement of populations deemed inferior, and the pursuit of racial “purity.” War and occupation enabled the regime to escalate persecution into genocide, including the Holocaust.
Britain did not enter the war in 1939 with foreknowledge of every atrocity that would follow. But Carlson, assessing that war retrospectively, has no such excuse for reducing the issue to whether Hitler wanted to attack Britain, omitting the atrocities of that period.
“I’m very surprised you’re verging on defending Hitler,” Rees-Mogg eventually replies to Carlson’s persistence.
“Yeah, I guess I’m just a secret Nazi,” Carlson replies sarcastically.
The views expressed in this opinion article are the author’s and not necessarily those of Kyiv Post.

Energy shocks, AI demand pulling global economy in different directions, IMF chief warns
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
08:27:51 UTC
17:27:51 KST

The global economy faces a negative energy supply shock and a positive artificial intelligence demand shock, the head of the International Monetary Fund has warned.
Kristalina Georgieva delivered a speech in Singapore on Wednesday ahead of annual meetings in Thailand.
She said the rapid rise of AI, persistently high energy prices and record levels of public debt are three major pressure areas on the global economy.
Her comments come as France deals with student protests over budget constraints that have badly affected school conditions, and Paris struggles with a widening budget deficit.
Global public debt is on track to exceed 100 percent of GDP, reaching its highest level since the end of World War II, Georgieva said.
Advanced economies account for some of the highest public debt burdens, she added.
Georgieva said that while issues were impeding energy supply, AI data centres were hungry for more power, pulling the global economy in different directions.
Oil prices remain around 100 dollars per barrel amid transport costs and other risks, she warned. Natural gas supplies from the Gulf also remain severely disrupted as threats to shipping through the Strait of Hormuz continue.
Meanwhile, AI hardware and related products account for more than 10 percent of global goods trade, Georgieva said. AI could add up to 0.5 percentage points to annual global growth if countries manage the technology effectively.
Georgieva urged policymakers to stop delaying necessary action and implement credible plans to consolidate public finances.
She also advised central banks to maintain a prudent hawkish bias in monetary policy, warning that the AI investment boom, energy shocks and high public debt could fuel inflation.

Delhi HC asks Centre to consider mandatory body cameras for police
NEW DELHI: The Delhi High Court has asked the Centre to consider a PIL seeking mandatory use of body-worn cameras by police during protests and crowd-control operations, saying the issue should not be treated as a “grey area” requiring court intervention.The court asked the Centre to take a decision on the plea within six months.A bench headed by Acting Chief Justice Nitin Sambhre said any direction on the use of body-worn cameras would have wider implications for policing and could not be confined to the Delhi Police alone.The bench observed while hearing the plea, “Why should we direct them to legislate? It cannot be said that it is a grey area.”The court questioned the need for judicial intervention when existing laws already provide for regulation of police procedures in areas covered by the legislature.The PIL, filed by Chahat Raghav, seeks directions for the mandatory use of body-worn cameras by Delhi Police and Rapid Action Force personnel deployed during protests and crowd-control operations. It also seeks a comprehensive framework governing the storage, retention, integrity and evidentiary use of footage recorded by the cameras.The petitioner has cited the use of body-worn cameras by traffic police and a tender issued for their procurement, arguing that the technology is already available to the authorities.
Senior Advocate Akhil Sibal, appearing for the petitioner, submitted that body-worn cameras could enhance transparency and accountability during protests, especially in cases involving allegations of police excesses and counter-allegations against protesters.Sibal said the cameras were already being used by police in some situations, but only sporadically. He argued that the Delhi Police's 2022 standing order on rallies and demonstrations did not specifically provide for body-worn cameras and that a clear protocol was needed.He also disputed that the existing videography mechanism was sufficient, saying the recording under the standing order was different from footage captured by cameras worn directly by police personnel involved in crowd control.Additional Solicitor General Chetan Sharma, appearing for the respondents, submitted that the Delhi High Court's PIL rules require a petitioner to first approach the concerned authorities through a representation. He said the present petition could be treated as such a representation.Sharma also submitted that the Supreme Court, while hearing a matter concerning protests at Jantar Mantar, had directed the authorities to frame an SOP and that the existing mechanism already provides for videography of protests. The court recorded the ASG's statement and directed the respondents to communicate their decision on framing an SOP for the use of body-worn cameras within six months.
The petitioner was given liberty to approach the High Court again in case of any inaction.The move comes amid heightened security in the New Delhi, Central Delhi and North Delhi districts following a series of demonstrations against the Election Commission over the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) exercise.Police and paramilitary personnel have been deployed in large numbers, with multilayered barricades placed at several points to prevent protesters from entering restricted areas.

Health official on Russia plague case: Estonia's risk level has not risen
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
08:25:00 UTC
17:25:00 KST

Health official on Russia plague case: Estonia's risk level has not risen
All forms of plague can be treated today, and the possible plague case in Russia has not raised Estonia's risk level, said Juta Varjas, head of service in the Health Board's infectious disease epidemiology department.
A laboratory worker at a plague research institute in Irkutsk region in Siberia fell ill and died under circumstances that have not yet been disclosed, after which authorities placed dozens of people in quarantine.
The death has sparked concern on social media about public health, even though Russian authorities said Monday that the situation is under control. A source in Russia's health sector told a publication that Irkutsk doctors are openly talking about plague, even though the disease is not mentioned in official documents.
Varjas said that although Estonia cannot get verified data from Russia and it is difficult to draw conclusions from the case, it is clear that the threat level has not increased.
"Neither here, nor in our neighboring countries, nor according to the European Center for Disease Prevention and Control's risk analysis, is there any reason to think the risk level is higher than usual," Varjas said.
Speaking more broadly, Varjas said the Health Board has extensive information about plague.
"We know plague has not disappeared from the world. There are natural hotspots where the pathogen exists, and from those it occasionally reaches humans. Plague has been diagnosed in people in America, Asia and Africa. In 2025, several countries reported plague cases," Varjas said.
According to Varjas, plague is fairly easy to treat today. "Plague is treated with antibiotics. They are available in Estonia, so people can be cured. The plague pathogen is the bacterium Yersinia pestis, and its natural reservoir is maintained by various species of small rodents, with fleas playing an important role in transmission," Varjas said.
She said Estonia has no such natural areas, where the disease persists.
Varjas explained that plague has three types. "A person can get the plague bacterium from a flea bite, and in that case we talk about bubonic plague. The person develops a fever, feels very ill and the lymph nodes become swollen and painful. This form is not directly contagious from person to person. The second form is septicemic, when the bacterium enters the bloodstream, damages organs and causes bleeding. This also is not directly contagious from person to person. And the third, rarest form is pneumonic plague, where the pathogen is in the respiratory tract. The person develops a high fever, their condition worsens quickly, they develop chest pain and cough. With the droplets they cough out, they can infect others. It is the rarest but the worst variant because it can spread from one person to another," Varjas said.
Without treatment — especially without timely treatment — mortality is very high, she said.
Varjas stressed that the risk of plague infection for Estonia's residents is very low.
"Estonia's borders have epidemic response plans. If they receive a signal about such a disease, they know how to act and whom to notify," Varjas said.

During the October 7 massacre, Israelis on the ground took action, battling Hamas terrorists who infiltrated and murdered some 1,200 people and dragged 251 hostages into Gaza.
Michal Negri, a former director-general of the Ra’anana Municipality, lost her son on October 7 while battling the terrorists. She has called on Israel’s political leadership to take responsibility for the failures of that day.
“Like my son, hundreds [of civilians] that day just took responsibility [and action].”
“They were brave, they were responsible, and they were leaders. And I expect the [Israeli] leadership to act in the same way,” Negri told The Jerusalem Post in a recent interview.
Negri is now running for the Knesset in the seventh slot on the B’Yachad list led by former prime minister Naftali Bennett ahead of the October 27 elections.
IDF Maj. (res.) Roee Negri killed in Kibbutz Be’eri fighting Hamas terrorists
Negri’s son, Maj. (res.) Roee Negri, 28, was killed fighting Hamas terrorists in Kibbutz Be’eri, one of the hardest-hit communities on October 7, after spending the day rescuing civilians. He had organized and led teams of soldiers who described the kibbutz as the place where “the gates of hell opened,” Negri said.
Nobody in the IDF had called up Roee to go south to Be’eri. He had gone on his own and entered with his team, house by house, dividing up the kibbutz with his team as they fought against Hamas terrorists.
“He insisted on going first in every house,” Negri said.
After the loss of her son, Negri said that she had never thought about going into politics. However, she decided to do so after Bennett reached out to her, as she felt she could have the biggest impact by joining his party.
Bennett’s B’Yachad party is one of the leading parties in the opposition bloc seeking to replace Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu in the October elections. The party has recently been polling around 13-15 seats, putting Negri in a strong position to enter the Knesset.
Negri said that the first thing she considered most important after October 7 was for the country’s leadership to take responsibility and for a state commission of inquiry to be conducted.
Three years after the massacre, no probe has yet been established to investigate government failures, amid an ongoing dispute over what kind of investigation should be conducted and who should lead it.
“First of all, everyone that was in the government, in any position of management, has to take responsibility and be inquired, so we will be sure that it will never happen again.”
“How can you be sure that it will not happen again if you don’t inquire and ask questions?” she continued.
“I think they owe it – first of all, to the families that gave all they had. They owe it to the people that were torn out of their houses, they owe it to the people that were murdered, they owe it to the people that were raped, and they owe it to every citizen in Israel.”
Negri: Anyone in gov't on Oct. 7 'should have stepped down three years ago'
She said Netanyahu should have stepped down immediately the day after the attacks.
“All of them should have stepped down and said, ‘let’s think, let’s take the responsibility.’”
“Anyone that was there [in the government during] October 7 should have stepped down three years ago.”
Regarding Netanyahu’s attempts to pass a contentious law for a political probe into October 7, Negri said that this was another attempt to avoid responsibility and “set the fire to anyone else but them – and this is not the way that I think a leader should act.”
Negri told the Post that the upcoming elections “are crucial.”
“I think the country needs a new leadership... a leadership that sees the people.”
“What we have experienced in the last years is a leadership that sees only itself, that works for itself, and that is interested in staying and doing anything that will keep them on their chairs,” she added.
Negri said that during and immediately after the October 7 attacks, she had also seen that Israel has citizens that are “the best people in the world.”
“I think that we can all go back to where we were together, fighting together and loving together and working together and building this country together and all the communities to come together,” she said.
“We are in a country that needs to be healed, needs to have quiet, and needs to have a leadership and government that works for it and that takes care of it, and gives the people the quiet and the safety,” Negri added.

Russia Satisfied With Nature, Prospects of Deepened Partnership With Turkmenistan - Lavrov

Who is Vivek Bhagat?: What is the controversy around Delhi Police officer
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
08:24:00 UTC
17:24:00 KST

NEW DELHI: Delhi Police officer ACP Vivek Bhagat, currently posted as sub-divisional police officer (SDPO) in Connaught Place, has come under scrutiny after three women journalists alleged sexual harassment by police personnel during a protest against Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar.The complaints were transferred to the Delhi Police Crime Branch for a “fair and impartial” enquiry. Bhagat has since consented to keeping his current duty charge as additional deputy commissioner of police on hold pending the enquiry.
Who is Vivek Bhagat?
Bhagat is a Delhi Police officer currently serving as SDPO, Connaught Place. He was among 12 Selection Grade DANIPS officers assigned the current duty charge of Additional DCP in an order approved by Lieutenant Governor Taranjit Singh Sandhu.The Delhi government later modified the order after Bhagat formally requested that the charge concerning him be kept on hold, citing the pending Crime Branch enquiry.Bhagat had also been involved in police action during protests in June, when he was injured amid clashes between protesters and police.During those protests Bhagat said that he was allegedly surrounded and overpowered during the clashes and was beaten, kicked and punched.
He reported alleged head injuries, bruises and broken teeth.An ANI report from the time said Bhagat was injured by stone and bottle pelting near Tolstoy Marg. The injuries were sustained while police were dealing with protesters during the June clashes.
What are the allegations against him?
Three women journalists complained of sexual harassment following a protest against Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar at Jantar Mantar on October 3.One journalist specifically alleged that Bhagat sexually assaulted her while she was covering the protest. She said she had approached him after noticing that no women police personnel were present while protesters were being detained.According to her complaint, she asked Bhagat about the absence of women personnel, following which he allegedly sexually assaulted and pushed her.The allegations have not been established. The Delhi Police transferred the complaints to its Crime Branch, which is examining the allegations and recording statements of the complainants and other people concerned.
Why is his promotion controversial?
The allegations emerged just days before Bhagat was among 12 officers assigned the current duty charge of Additional DCP.A senior police officer said the promotions were routine and that the request for the promotions had been sent much earlier.
After the allegations and the pending enquiry came to light, Bhagat wrote to the Delhi Police Commissioner saying he consented to keeping the order concerning him on hold until the enquiry was dealt with.The Delhi government subsequently modified the administrative order, putting his Additional DCP charge on hold.The Crime Branch enquiry will determine the facts surrounding the allegations. The complaints remain allegations at this stage, and the material available does not establish that Bhagat committed sexual harassment.The Press Council of India has meanwhile expressed “shock and dismay” over the allegations and urged Delhi Police to act on the journalists’ complaints, saying journalists must be able to work without facing aggression or threats.
Prisha Patnaik is a journalist with The Times of India, writing across geopolitics, international affairs, culture, history and internet culture. With over two years of experience in social media and digital content, she is interested in how news, politics and culture are shaped for digital audiences. She holds a master’s degree in Media and Communications from Goldsmiths, University of London.
