Three years of Israel’s mass dispossession of West Bank Palestinians
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
08:22:19 UTC
17:22:19 KST

Three years of Israel’s mass dispossession of West Bank Palestinians
Bedouin families uprooted by Israeli settlers describe a state-backed project of forced transfer in the West Bank.
Al-Awsaj, occupied West Bank – On September 23, weeks before Israel’s parliamentary elections, ministers and lawmakers gathered on an occupied West Bank hilltop to inaugurate a new settlement, Metzoke Eretz, illegal under international law. Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich used the ceremony to salute the settler outpost that made the eventual settlement possible.
“The first pioneering settlers who were here on the farm… we will lift them up as our greatest joy,” Smotrich said. “It shows that the method works: establish a farm, seize the land, prepare it, turn it into a community, move to the next point. There are many, many such heroes – those who prove they are not doing real estate. They are doing Zionism.”
Metzoke Eretz was previously an outpost – the name given to the Jewish settlements illegal even under Israeli law – called Netzah Harel, established in 2023 in the middle of al-Muarrajat, a Bedouin community on private Palestinian land east of Ramallah. Alia Mleihat, 29, and others from the community remember those settlers well. “Of course, this outpost played a major role in displacing the Palestinian Bedouin communities in al-Muarrajat and the areas east of Ramallah,” said Alia, now living in a tent in al-Awsaj, a few kilometres away, after her forced displacement in July 2025. “[The Netzah Harel settlers] took part in every attack the settlers carried out on families, and confiscated sheep, under the protection of the Israeli police and army.”
Dror Etkes, founder of Israeli NGO Kerem Navot, said Smotrich’s description of his “method” was spot-on – except for one omission. “The political discourse skips the [Palestinian] expulsion chapter,” said Etkes, suggesting Smotrich and other politicians avoid doing so explicitly to avoid potential scrutiny from international criminal courts. “They want it to happen, and they know that it happens, and they let it happen.”
Haaretz reported that Metzoke Eretz is one of 19 outposts legalised by the Netanyahu government after nearby Palestinians were violently expelled.
‘Not a single moment of joy’
Jamal Mleihat, Alia’s 45-year-old uncle, sits with eight relatives nestled inside a bare concrete-block house on the ridge in al-Awsaj, with his daughter Sewar hanging off his lap.
Below the ridge, rows of young trees climb a cultivated slope towards a factory at the foot of the hills. The ridge itself is rock and dust, now home to about 25 families from al-Muarrajat, among others forcibly displaced in the past three years.
“Before October 7 [2023 Hamas attack on Israel, and Israel’s subsequent genocidal war on Gaza], we were in the pastures – no harassment, we moved around freely,” said Jamal, a father of seven. “We had healthcare. We had a school. We had water in the same encampment. Life was a million times better than this.”
Since October 7, the Israeli government has stepped up its raids on the occupied West Bank, while settlers have largely been given free rein to pursue a pogrom against Palestinians, with little pushback from within Israel.
Just below Jamal’s shelter, alone on a slope, Muhammad Ghawanmeh lives with his wife and seven children. His toilet does not work; he relies on water tanks and has almost no electricity. The rocky track to the Mleihats’ area is too steep to drive. He built a fence around the house after recent settler attacks, and now faces constant drone surveillance from Israeli settlers.
Ghawanmeh is from Ras Ein al-Auja, which had been the largest Bedouin community in the central Jordan Valley – so robust that humanitarian coordinators told Al Jazeera in October 2023 that the village’s displacement was unlikely. Instead, its more than 600 Palestinian inhabitants experienced the largest single-community expulsion of Bedouins in the last three years, after repeated attacks by settlers from four surrounding outposts.
“From my childhood, the land was open. The water was open. We were living happily. We’d graze 10 kilometres, 15 kilometres with the sheep, and come back,” he said. “Today we can’t go 500 metres from the house.”
His flock has shrunk from about 300 to roughly 100 physically thinning sheep, which he now must buy fodder for, instead of letting them graze on the land, which he now says is largely forbidden by Israeli settlers and the army.
‘Nothing was left except this’
A few hundred metres beyond Ghawanmeh’s fence, a white trailer and a few containers mark an Israeli outpost, established about six months ago on a hill overlooking Highway 90 and the displaced families along the ridge. Two months ago, Ghawanmeh said, soldiers came to his house and told him he could no longer pass to the highway. The settlers, he said, “are with the army”.
“You leave this place, go to another one, and it follows you – the same problem, unsolved,” Ghawanmeh said. “Every three months, there’s a displacement operation.”
Al-Awsaj barely existed as an inhabited place before, but Bedouin from different depopulated communities have now converged on this barren ridge, overlooking land largely declared – again – off-limits to grazing.
Allegra Pacheco, head of the West Bank Protection Consortium, calls al-Awsaj “basically a refugee camp, an internally displaced camp, that we see in other countries. But here, there’s no safe space. Wherever people like in al-Awsaj go, they’re chased by settlers or their tents are demolished by the Israelis.”
“It’s been very painful to get the authorities, the Palestinian authorities, the international leaders, to recognise that this is a mass displacement happening in front of us, and people have nowhere to go,” she said.
Project of forced transfer
In the West Bank, the United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) counts at least 130 Palestinian communities fully or partly displaced by settler attacks and related restrictions since January 2023, and more than 6,400 people uprooted. According to the Palestinian Colonization and Wall Resistance Commission, since October 7, 2023 there have been almost 15,000 attacks by settlers, with 66 Palestinians killed by settlers. OCHA says the rate of settler attacks increased from about three a day before October 7, 2023, to almost seven per day this year.
The increase in displacement after October 2023 can also be seen in the numbers for that year. Nearly 80 percent of all Palestinians displaced by settler violence in 2023 were uprooted after October 7.
A report by Peace Now and Kerem Navot found that Israeli farm outposts had seized roughly 18 percent of the West Bank by the end of 2025. “We’re talking about a land area bigger than the size of the Gaza Strip altogether,” Pacheco said.
“What we’re seeing is a continuous, sustained project of forced transfer and mass destruction,” she said. “Israeli authority demolitions and destructions by the Israeli army, and Israeli civilians – armed groups – carrying out destructions and sowing fear to push people out.”
Israeli NGO B’Tselem’s September report, “The Elimination Project”, links this to Smotrich’s 2017 “Decisive Plan”, which offers Palestinians three choices: live under Jewish supremacy, leave, or face violent repression.
“The Smotrich Plan has been implemented,” Pacheco said. “He laid out exactly what is going on now, and he’s very proud of his success. He now wants to transfer that success to [other areas of the West Bank], and also in the Galilee [an area in Israel with a large population of Palestinian citizens of Israel]. Wherever there are Palestinians living, he wants to make life so difficult that they will leave.”
With Smotrich exercising broad powers over the West Bank through the Settlement Administration within the Ministry of Defence, and leaders in the Israeli West Bank military command increasingly coming from far-right, settler backgrounds themselves, Palestinians across the West Bank describe a deepening symbiosis of military, police, administration and settlers in exacting Palestinian dispossession. “They all work together, like a cell, one completing the other,” said Jamal Mleihat. “The army, the police, the settlers – they’re the ones who displace, they’re the ones who establish the settlement, they’re the ones who take part in the thefts, in everything. And the army covers for them.”
Al Jazeera has reached out to the Israeli authorities for comment on this piece, but has yet to receive a response.
Worse future
Smotrich has withheld part or all of the tax revenues Israel collects for the Palestinian Authority – roughly 60 percent of its income – for much of the past three years. The PA now struggles to provide the most basic of services. In al-Awsaj and elsewhere, that means classrooms that do not open. “The government school is shut down today, no salaries,” Ghawanmeh said.
There is no school bus; families pay for private transport, and “one day they study, one day they don’t, depending on the mood of the driver,” Jamal said. It has left the displaced alone on an inhospitable patch of rock.
“Palestinians have no protection in the West Bank,” said Pacheco. “They are completely vulnerable to assault, attempted murder, arson, invasion of their homes. The Israeli army is supposed to protect them and doesn’t. The Palestinian Authority can’t come in, and the international community is not protecting them.”
“We started to feel there’s no safety anywhere,” Ghawanmeh said. “Fear. Terror. Persecution. Ethnic cleansing. That’s what we feel.”
Amid the dispossession, Ghawanmeh looks out at the unwelcoming land he knows will not be his family’s refuge – only another transient stop. He sees his own brother now only once every month and a half or two. “The threats to Bedouin life have almost become extinction,” he said. “We now live in enclaves, separated.”
“For three years now, the day that’s passing is better than the one that’s coming,” Ghawanmeh said. “Yesterday is better than today. Today is better than tomorrow.”

Houthis claim new attacks on Saudi Arabia, Yemen's Aden airport

Breadcrumb
Iran-backed Houthis claim new attacks on Saudi Arabia, Yemen's Aden airport
Iran-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen on Wednesday claimed attacks on military facilities and airports in neighboring Saudi Arabia as the fighting deepened the latest front in the Iran war and threatened a crucial shipping alternative to the Strait of Hormuz.
The Houthis’ military spokesperson, Brig. Gen. Yahya Saree, said on social media that the rebels launched ballistic missiles and drones in the attacks targeting King Khalid International Airport in the capital, Riyadh, but didn’t provide evidence.
Flights to and from the airport were briefly disrupted, according to Flightradar24, a tracking platform.
Saree said Abha airport, a frequent target of Houthi drones and missiles, was targeted. The rebels also claimed to have hit an air base in the city of Khamis Mushait and two military bases Najran and Asir. All are in southwestern Saudi Arabia and near the border with Yemen.
The spokesperson for the Saudi-led coalition fighting the Houthis, Maj. Gen. Turki al-Malki, said they intercepted and destroyed a ballistic missile north of Riyadh.
Saudi Arabia and allied Yemeni forces in recent days have launched a major ground and air offensive against the Houthis in an attempt to retake territory that the rebels seized about a month ago along Yemen’s western Red Sea coast and on the Bab al-Mandeb Strait. Those positions gave the rebels better surveillance of shipping as they pursue a blockade of Saudi vessels.
On Monday, officials said forces of the Saudi-led coalition fighting in Yemen recaptured several key areas around the strait.
The fighting has since then centered in and around the crucial town of Dhubab, some 54 kilometers (33.5 miles) south of the port city of Mokha, according to both the Houthis and the Yemeni government.
Clashes were also reported in the district of Waziayah in southwestern Taiz province, which links Yemen’s mountainous highlands to the Red Sea, and overlooks roads to the Bab al-Mandeb Strait.
Houthis target the airport in Aden  
The Houthis also said they launched a missile strike early Wednesday against Yemen’s port city of Aden, the seat of the internationally recognized government. An Associated Press journalist heard explosions around 2 a.m.
The rebels hit a military camp close to the Aden airport with ballistic missiles, Saree said.
Security authorities in Aden said the Houthis targeted the airport with two missiles, with no casualties. The airport is close to the seat of government.
“The targeting of this vital civilian facility represents a direct threat to the safety of civilians, passengers, employees and flight crews,” the Aden police said in a statement.
The attack on the Aden airport threatened “a humanitarian disaster,” as one missile hit close to the runway just before the scheduled landing of a flight from Cairo, the Human Rights Ministry said.
Flight 603, operated by Yemen’s flagship airline, landed safely in Aden at 3:30 a.m., according to flight tracking platform FlightAware.
The ministry said the missile hit as other passengers were waiting to board their flight to the Saudi coastal city of Jeddah.
“The Houthis believe that they can maximize Saudi economic costs and compel Saudi Arabia to surrender to Houthi demands by striking civilian infrastructure, such as oil facilities and airports,” the Institute for the Study of War, a Washington-based think tank, wrote in an analysis.

France Protests Draw 250,000 as Police Clash With Students
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
08:22:00 UTC
17:22:00 KST

More than 250,000 pupils, teachers and parents demonstrated across France on Tuesday, according to the Interior Ministry, as police used teargas during clashes and Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu said 215 teenagers and 85 school staff had been injured since the protests began more than two weeks ago.
The Interior Ministry said 200,000 people joined mostly peaceful marches in cities including Marseille, Nantes and Lyon, while another 56,000 demonstrated in Paris. Organizers estimated the nationwide turnout at 450,000.
Most demonstrations ended without major incidents, but some, including in Paris, saw sporadic vandalism and confrontations with riot police, who used teargas and baton charges to disperse protesters.
Nearly 500 people were arrested on Tuesday, according to Interior Ministry figures reported by Liberation. The ministry also reported that 43 police officers had been injured.
Lecornu described the injuries to students and school staff as “the heaviest toll in decades paid by the school system.” His office said 715 police officers had also been wounded in clashes since the movement began.
Trade unions and rights groups have accused police of using unnecessary force against young protesters. Amnesty International called on French authorities to “put an end to the disproportionate police repression.”
Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez said the police response had been proportionate in “almost all cases” and argued that some demonstrations had turned into riots requiring police intervention.
President Emmanuel Macron summoned key ministers to the Élysée Palace for talks on Tuesday night, French media reported.
The protests began in the northern suburbs of Paris more than two weeks ago before spreading across the country. Students have blocked school entrances and demonstrated over shortages of teachers, demanding better study conditions, improved school buildings and changes to school schedules.
At a demonstration in Paris, students carried smoke flares and signs bearing slogans including “under our text books, anger,” a reference to the famous “under the paving stones, the beach” slogan associated with the May 1968 student riots. Other placards read “schools with no money = country with no future.”
Anna, a student who spoke to reporters at Place de la Nation, said students were asking for better conditions, sufficient teaching staff and decent school buildings, while criticizing the authorities' response.
"Our demands are simple: better study conditions, enough teachers, decent school buildings. The authorities’ response has been catastrophic. There’s enough violence already," she said.
The education ministry said more than 900 of France's 3,700 high schools were blockaded or closed for the day on Tuesday, while student groups put the number at 1,800. Some local education authorities shifted classes online.
Océanne, 18, was among protesters in Marseille and said she wanted to protect the education system. She said she had experienced teachers being absent and replaced either by what she called “pointless substitutes” or not replaced at all.
Teachers also joined the demonstrations. In Rennes, Romain Dubourg said he and “about 30 colleagues” had discussed police violence they had witnessed and decided to support their students if needed.
Trade union members took part as well. CGT leader Sophie Binet called on members to “protect high school students,” while Green party leader Marine Tondelier urged local officials and parents to wear white and “go and protect our children during demonstrations.”
Anne Savinel-Barras, president of Amnesty France, said, “The images and testimonies widely circulated over the past week raise alarming concerns about the dangerous use of teargas, batons and policing techniques by the police.” Nuñez said police had opened 10 internal investigations into allegations of brutality since the protests started.
Twenty-four schools have been burned or ransacked since mid-September, while more than 6,100 people have been arrested, almost all of them minors, according to the Justice Ministry. More than 1,800 people are being prosecuted, including nearly 1,500 under the age of 18.
Protesters have burned trash bins outside schools, damaged bus shelters and thrown projectiles at riot police, who have responded with batons, teargas and riot-control rounds.
On Monday, a 15-year-old lost his hand when protesters clashed with riot police in northern France. A 16-year-old in Tours lost the use of his right eye after suffering a serious head injury during a high school blockade on Wednesday.
Local prosecutor Catherine Sorita-Minard said the injuries sustained by the 16-year-old were “compatible with the impact of a defensive bullet of the blast ball type.”
In another incident, a 14-year-old lost most of his teeth on Monday after a police officer appeared to fire a grenade at him from close range during a protest northwest of Paris. His mother said he could no longer speak and had to eat through a straw because his jaw had been immobilized.
France 24 reported that the 15-year-old in the northern town of Lens lost his hand up to the elbow after being struck by a sting-ball grenade, while the 16-year-old in Tours suffered the loss of use of his right eye from what the local prosecutor said was probably a projectile fired by riot police.
The government last week instructed police to use the non-lethal weapons available to them to reopen schools after accusing the protest movement of descending into “urban violence.”
Lecornu has instructed ministers to address students' main demands, including replacing absent teachers, reconsidering the school day running from 8 a.m. to 6 p.m. and repairing aging buildings.
He rejected claims that police routinely used excessive force and said officers had generally acted proportionately. Addressing MPs on Tuesday, he said “extreme violence” had come “knocking on high-school doors, and must be condemned.” He added, “Setting fire to a school will not help repair it. Attacking a teacher will not help replace missing staff.”
The protests come seven months before presidential elections to choose Macron's successor and have increased pressure on a government attempting to reduce a growing budget deficit as investors raise concerns over France's debt and weak economic growth.
The government has accused the radical-left La France Insoumise party of encouraging and even organizing the movement after several of its MPs attended school blockades. Party leader and presidential candidate Jean-Luc Mélenchon has strongly backed the protests while calling for non-violence.
In Paris, students barricaded the Lycée Sophie Germain in the Marais district using overturned bins, steel railings and chain-link fences. Bachir, 17, said organizers had reached an understanding with authorities over the demonstration.
"The police said that as long as there aren’t any problems with fires, or firework-launchers or anything like that, as long as it’s peaceful, they won’t do anything," he said.
Bachir said he wanted the protests to draw attention to the widening socioeconomic gap between Paris and its outer suburbs. He said conditions were particularly poor there, with too few teachers, insufficient resources and overcrowded classrooms.
"Conditions are terrible in the suburbs," Bachir said. “There aren’t enough resources, there aren’t enough teachers, and the class sizes are too large. Most high school buildings date back to the 1970s, but only 14 percent have been renovated or rebuilt” in the past 10 years, he said.
He added that students were fighting over the state of education and their future.
"We’re talking about young people’s education, about the future - we just can’t leave education in this state," Bachir said.
Léa, a student at Lycée Lamartine in Paris's ninth arrondissement, said she hoped the growing protests would pressure the government to reconsider how it allocates funding.
"That they put more money into education rather than funding military operations or Bastille Day parades that no one gives a stuff about," she said. She added that some classes had one teacher for 40 students, which she said was unacceptable, particularly when temperatures reached 40 degrees Celsius (104°F).
Léa also criticized the police response, saying she found it unacceptable that protesters had lost a hand, an eye and their teeth without anyone being held accountable.
Bachir said he was not surprised by the police response, which he described as heavy-handed.
"The police, they’re happy, they’re just there to have a bit of a scrap," he said. “I know the police very well, they lose their tempers quickly. My old high school was in the suburbs, and the police, they were really just looking for a fight.”
At the Lycée Hélène Boucher, police broke up a human chain formed by CGT members and cleared a barricade from the school's entrance before pushing remaining protesters toward the middle of the avenue.
The protesters then marched toward Place de la République, with students from other barricades joining the procession. Along the route, some demonstrators overturned trash bins and one teenager briefly set fire to a piece of plywood before another person extinguished it.
Police later formed lines behind the march and searched people's bags. Officers also confiscated plastic vials of saline solution that protesters used to rinse teargas from their eyes.
At Place de la République, the demonstration brought together high school and university students, teachers, parents and trade unionists.
Gilles, a secondary school teacher from Saint-Denis, said funding shortages affected other parts of the education system as well.
"There's an overall lack of staff, of education assistants, of medical and social services staff in secondary schools," he said. "Some of the buildings are run-down – and it's the same across all levels, from primary school onward."
Gilles said he was pleased that students had joined teachers in raising the issue, recalling demonstrations in 2023 and 2024 connected to the 93 Emergency Plan over staff shortages.
"It's great. We went on a lot of demonstrations in 2023, 2024, for the 93 Emergency Plan, which highlighted the staff shortage," he said. "And it’s great that the demands of teachers and educational staff are now being echoed by high school students. It’s fantastic that they’re taking up the cause."
Thibault, a secondary school teacher working in Versailles west of Paris, said he had gone on strike to support the student movement.
"We're fed up, everyone is tired, the students can't take it anymore," he said. "High schoolers are at school from eight in the morning to six o'clock at night with just half an hour for a break - you can't even do that under French labour law."
Thibault said he was proud of the students' demonstrations but did not expect the movement to produce the changes he wanted.
"To be honest? I don't expect anything anymore, because the government will never listen to us," he said. "Instead, they take advantage of the fact that there are two or three people breaking things to say, 'See? This movement isn't legitimate.'"

Dutch government told to rule on 140,000 Ukrainian asylum claims
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
08:21:04 UTC
17:21:04 KST

Dutch government told to rule on 140,000 Ukrainian asylum claims
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
The European Court of Justice has ordered the Dutch government to process the asylum applications of 140,000 Ukrainian refugees, adding to the pressure on an overstretched system.
Ukrainians who fled the country in the wake of the full-scale Russian invasion in February 2022 are covered by the European Union’s temporary protection rules, which give them the right to live, work and receive medical care in the Netherlands.
Under Dutch rules they are also required to apply for asylum, but until now the immigration service IND has shelved their applications because the European regulations give them more rights.
The European Court of Justice (ECJ) in Luxembourg said in a judgment last week that the rules requiring the Netherlands to process all asylum claims within 21 months also applied to people who fled Ukraine.
The case was brought by a man from the Chinese Uighur minority who was married to a Ukrainian woman and lived in Ukraine with his wife and child before the invasion.
He won a ruling at the district court in The Hague forcing the asylum minister to rule on his claim by January 2024. The court also imposed a conditional penalty on the government of €100 foe every day that a decision is overdue, up to a maximum of €7,500.
Extra pressure
The government appealed, and the case was referred to the ECJ, which said the man had the right to claim asylum as a third country national through the regular procedure even though he was already protected by the EU rules for Ukrainians.
Asylum minister Bart van den Brink admitted that the decision would put “extra pressure” on the system, but the court also recognised that the Netherlands needed time to process all 140,000 claims.
“For a long time we chose not to process claims from Ukrainians because of the fact that they were already protected,” he told NOS. “It’s also because it was a very large number. Now the court has clearly said we have to do it.”
The Netherlands is one of the few countries in the EU that require Ukrainian refugees to apply for asylum through the regular channels in addition to the EU’s temporary protection rules, which are currently valid until March 2028 but are reviewed every year.
“In hindsight it wasn’t such a good idea to link temporary protection to the submission of a claim for asylum,” asylum lawyer Wil Eikelboom said.
Waiting list
Vluchtelingenwerk, the Dutch refugee council, said the need to have asylum claims processed would cause “more worry and uncertainty” for Ukrainians.
“Returning to Ukraine is not a realistic option at the moment, given that there is no sign of the war ending.” a spokesman told Dutch News.
“Vluchtelingenwerk hopes there will be a clear and above all sustainable plan for Ukrainians in the Netherlands, so that these people, who have already been through so much, know where they stand.”
Van den Brink said the government planned to deal with the Ukrainian applications in reverse order, beginning with people who have just arrived in the Netherlands and then working through the 5,000 who are currently on the waiting list for a first response from the government.
Ricky van Oers, lecturer in migration law at Radboud University in Nijmegen, said European rules allowed the government to take more time to process applications when there was a large number from a single country at once.
“They can also decide to prioritise certain groups, such as families,” he said.

‘We saw devastation’: IDF fighters return to haunting Kfar Aza photo that became an Oct. 7 symbol
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
08:20:36 UTC
17:20:36 KST

In uniform, standing beside the ruined holiday table in Rachel Cohen’s home in Kfar Aza, Yair rests his head against Netanel and bursts into tears. “We are human beings before we put on uniforms. We saw devastation,” the two said as they looked again at the photograph taken just two days after the Oct. 7 massacre.
Now, three years later, they have returned to the same house, the same table and the same memory.
A day before the war broke out, Lt. Col. Netanel Makayes, then head of Lotar, the IDF Counterterrorism School, landed in Israel after returning from a military delegation to the United States. On the morning of Saturday, Oct. 7, he woke to a phone call from a friend who lived near the unit’s base.
“Bro, I need you to help me with a force,” the friend told him. “Something crazy is happening in the south.”
After speaking with a team commander in the unit and receiving information through his wife, Adi, a Magen David Adom paramedic, Makayes decided to leave his home in Zikhron Ya’akov, saying goodbye to her and their daughter Tamar.
Sgt. 1st Class (res.) Yair Ansbacher also immediately understood what was happening. He said goodbye to his wife, Naama, and their five children and headed south, where he joined a force from the Counterterrorism School.
“We knew war was coming,” Ansbacher, who had worked in security research, said. “The moment I woke to the sirens in Jerusalem and saw the image of the pickup truck in Sderot, I knew a full-scale war had begun. It’s in our DNA to get up and move, going from zero to 100 in an instant.”
At the entrance to the Urim base, Makayes assembled a team from fighters already in the area. During the fighting, Ansbacher and another soldier joined him. The battle continued until Makayes received an order over the radio to head to Kibbutz Nir Yitzhak, where troops had gathered residents and were defending them.
That night, the two learned that the unit’s former commander, Lt. Col. Eli Ginsberg, had been killed. “To this day, I still can’t believe Eli was killed,” Makayes said. “He was an incredible fighter, someone you felt could not be hurt.”
On Oct. 7, the Lotar unit lost four of its fighters and commanders: Staff Sgt. Ben Rubinshtain, Master Sgt. (res.) Omri Belkin, Maj. (res.) Roee Negri and Maj. (res.) Sagi Golan.
The photograph taken on Oct. 9, 2023, came during a mission led by Lotar and marked the first time photographer Ziv Koren joined them. “No one was dealing with the media at the time, but the unit understood how important it was,” Ansbacher said of the decision to bring a photojournalist along. “They cleared the destruction very quickly. People did not see what we saw.”
With Koren accompanying them, the troops entered Kfar Aza. “It was still a combat zone. There were encounters, bodies scattered around, everything destroyed,” Ansbacher recalled. “You could clearly see where the fire had burned everything, where everything was scorched and riddled with holes, and where ordinary life had been.”
While documenting the devastation, they entered Rachel Cohen’s home. “At the entrance, there was still a sukkah with family photographs inside,” Makayes recalled. “There were two challahs on the table, and all around them were shrapnel, blood and destruction.”
It was there that Koren’s camera captured an unguarded moment between the two fighters. Standing beside the holiday table, Ansbacher could no longer hold back his tears. “That moment shook me to my core. Netanel was beside me and supported me. I didn’t even know Ziv had taken the picture,” Ansbacher said.
“Yair is like my brother,” Makayes added. “The melting pot of the military and the intensity of combat connect and unite people.” 
“We all cried there. It was a breaking point. There wasn’t a dry eye left,” Koren said. He said the image became a symbol in Israel and abroad because of the powerful emotion it conveys. “That moment, fighters standing in front of a holiday table with challah and wine on it, breaking down after days of fighting,” he said. “All the elements came together in that photograph. Someone looking at it can undergo a profound emotional experience and identify with that sense of rupture.”
Three years later, the three men returned to the entrance of the same home. “Each of us remembers a different detail,” Koren said. “The home blessing hanging by the entrance, the cabinet with the dishes, the bullet holes in the walls.”
“Since Oct. 7, I’ve been back to the kibbutzim dozens of times. I know every house here and the story of every person who was wounded, kidnapped or murdered,” Koren said. “Now I’m here with them, as they return for the first time since then. It’s deeply moving to come back together to the place where that moment, which became a symbol, was captured.”

The lieutenant general, the most senior US military figure on Okinawa, also announced a 30-day "period of reflection" beginning on Friday.
"During this period, we will implement a curfew in which liberty will expire at 2400 for all hands, meaning you must be back on base in your assigned quarters or at your off-base domicile from midnight to 0500".

The United States has around 54,000 military personnel stationed in Japan, mostly on Okinawa.
Crimes committed by US personnel have been a thorn in relations between the close security allies.

Palestine: The Lost Team
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
08:17:02 UTC
17:17:02 KST

Al Jazeera World
Palestine: The Lost Team
A forgotten battle over football, identity and recognition – how a Jewish team competed as Palestine in the 1930s and beyond.
In 1934, a team called Palestine entered the qualifying rounds of the football World Cup in Mussolini’s fascist Italy. But it did not include any Palestinian players. It was drawn largely from the Jewish sporting movement under the British Mandate, at a time when football reflected the changing face of Palestine.
This documentary uncovers the forgotten history of Mandate-era football – how British rule, Zionist organisation and Palestinian exclusion shaped the makeup of the first team to compete internationally as Palestine. Through archives, interviews with specialist historians and the story of the 1934 qualifiers against Egypt, the film traces how the established football association became Israel’s, while Palestinian football was plagued by revolt, war and the 1948 Nakba. Decades later, Palestinians fought to reclaim their place in world football, finally securing FIFA recognition in 1998.

Experts warn of ‘social contagion’ risk after school attacks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
08:16:21 UTC
17:16:21 KST

This photo shows Şeyh Şamil Imam Hatip Middle School, where the Oct. 6 school attack happened.
A series of school attacks in Türkiye has raised concerns over a potential “social contagion” effect, with experts warning that extensive media coverage and social media exposure could encourage copycat violence, particularly among vulnerable young people.
The latest incident occurred on Oct. 6 at Şeyh Şamil Imam Hatip Middle School in Istanbul’s Başakşehir district, where a 15-year-old student from another school stabbed students. Eight students were injured, one of whom later died. The incident followed attacks or shootings reported in Şanlıurfa, Kahramanmaraş, Manisa and Osmaniye in recent months.
Ayhan Erbay, founding director of Istanbul Kültür University’s Justice and Crime Lab, said research based on U.S. data suggests that a school attack remains “contagious” for about 13 days and is associated with an average of at least 0.22 subsequent incidents.
Another study found that intensive news coverage of school attacks increased the likelihood of subsequent attacks, with the effect lasting between four and 10 days, Erbay said.
Erbay also cited research from Finland showing that people interested in school attacks can form global online subcultures. While some seek to imitate attackers, others contribute to glorifying perpetrators or circulating their motives. “Heroization works in two directions,” Erbay said. “It is a reward given to the attacker afterward, but also a promise to the next person: Becoming someone everyone talks about instead of remaining invisible can be attractive.”
Barış Erdoğan, head of the Sociology Department at Üsküdar University, said violence that once remained largely within schools can now continue online, where images of incidents are recorded and widely circulated. “This can turn violence, for some young people, from an expression of anger into a display of power, visibility and status,” he said, while cautioning against attributing the problem solely to social media. Peer bullying, family problems, exclusion, anxiety about the future, lack of belonging and access to weapons or knives can also contribute.
Erbay urged media outlets to avoid making perpetrators identifiable, particularly when they are minors, and to refrain from publishing details that could facilitate imitation. He also advised against rankings or comparisons such as “deadliest attack,” which could create a perceived benchmark for future attackers. Instead, coverage should focus on victims, those who intervened and what families and institutions can do to prevent further violence, he said.
Parents described shock and fear following the Oct. 6 attack. One parent whose daughter attends the school called for stronger security measures, including controlled entry systems. “The children are not psychologically well. They saw very disturbing things,” the parent said. “This cannot continue like this.”
The Education Ministry said classes at the school were suspended on Oct. 6 and 7 and that psychosocial support had been launched for affected students, teachers and parents. It also said judicial and administrative investigations were underway and assigned two education inspectors to the case. The Radio and Television Supreme Council (RTÜK) said a court had imposed a broadcasting ban covering reports, interviews and commentary on the incident until the investigation is completed.

Plague Fears Rise After Russian Lab Worker Dies
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
08:16:00 UTC
17:16:00 KST

A 28-year-old laboratory worker at a plague research institute in Siberia died after falling ill on October 2, leading Russian authorities to quarantine about 200 people while officials said there was no evidence linking her death to her work or to plague.
Russian media identified the woman as Darya Shipilova, who worked at the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Research Institute of Siberia and the Far East. Authorities said she died from an unknown form of pneumonia and imposed quarantine as a precaution on people who had been in contact with her.
Several unverified accounts of how Shipilova became ill have appeared on social media.
One claim said she had dropped a test tube containing live bacteria at the institute, but Russia's health watchdog rejected that version. Another report said she became sick after a trip to Thailand, while a third said she fell ill after visiting an area near the Mongolian border.
No evidence supporting any of those accounts has been made public.
Did she die of plague?
There has been no confirmation that Shipilova died from plague, although one regional governor said she "may" have died from the disease. Health watchdog Rospotrebnadzor said the cause was an unknown type of pneumonia and reported that no relevant pathogens had been detected among people who had contact with her.
Elena Sofina, a local official in Siberia, said 60% of the people placed under quarantine had been released. Local media reported that about 200 people were initially quarantined.
Sofina said "a dangerous diagnosis" had not been confirmed.
What is plague and can it be treated?
Plague is primarily found among small animals and fleas and is caused by the bacterium Yersinia pestis, which can also infect humans. One of its major historical outbreaks was the "Black Death," which killed more than 50 million people in Europe during the 1300s.
People can contract plague through bites from infected fleas, by inhaling infected respiratory particles and, in rare cases, by consuming infectious material. Without treatment, the disease has a mortality rate of 30%-100%, while antibiotics can treat it when it is detected quickly.
How common is plague?
The disease is endemic in parts of Africa, the former Soviet Union, the Americas and Asia, with most human cases recorded over the past six years occurring in the Democratic Republic of Congo and Madagascar, according to the World Health Organization.
Plague is also endemic in Siberia, where Yersinia pestis occurs among small wild mammals and their fleas and where the first known prehistoric human outbreak was recorded. Human plague cases are rare in Russia.
What has been the international reaction?
US President Donald Trump described the laboratory worker's death as a "big problem for Russia" and offered Washington's assistance to Moscow in dealing with it. US Secretary of State Marco Rubio called on Russia to provide more information about the death.
The World Health Organization in Geneva said Russia had informed it that there were no plague cases in the city of Irkutsk. Reuters could not determine whether that statement excluded plague as a possible cause of the laboratory worker's death.
Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan and Uzbekistan said they were increasing precautionary measures at their borders to prevent the possible spread of infectious diseases.
What is the plague institute in Siberia?
The Irkutsk Anti-Plague Research Institute of Siberia and the Far East was established in 1934 to combat plague outbreaks. According to its website, the scientist who founded it helped contain outbreaks in Siberia, Mongolia and China.
The institute later expanded its work to other dangerous diseases, including cholera and anthrax.
What are the types of plague?
Plague has three forms that affect different parts of the body. Pneumonic plague is the rarest and most virulent form and affects the lungs, causing infected patients to cough up airborne droplets.
Bubonic plague is the most common form and generally results from an infected flea biting a person, producing swollen lymph nodes known as "buboes." Septicemic plague occurs when plague bacteria multiply in the bloodstream and does not spread from person to person.
One form of the disease can develop into another.
Symptoms generally begin one to seven days after infection, with flu-like signs including fever, chills, headaches, body aches, weakness, vomiting and nausea.
Why has the death attracted attention?
The COVID-19 pandemic increased fears about the emergence of new deadly diseases, while reports involving unexplained illnesses or laboratory accidents can now quickly trigger alarm online.
Most scientists believe the coronavirus responsible for COVID-19 originated in animals, although some have argued that a laboratory leak was responsible.
Public health experts have urged caution over the Siberian case, noting that only one case has been reported and that Russian authorities say there is no evidence that the laboratory worker had plague.

IMF chief signals austerity is back as global public debt heads for 100% of GDP
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
08:14:53 UTC
17:14:53 KST

IMF chief Kristalina Georgieva has urged heavily indebted governments to tighten their belts and central banks to take a hawkish stance, signalling a return to austerity as the energy shock from the Iran war, record public debt and a credit-fuelled AI investment boom weigh on the global economy.
The days when governments could lean on cheap money and fast growth to keep their debts in check are over, according to the head of the International Monetary Fund (IMF), who called for spending discipline and tighter monetary policy around the world.
Speaking in Singapore on Wednesday, ahead of the IMF and World Bank annual meetings in Bangkok next week, Kristalina Georgieva said policymakers "can no longer rely on higher growth rates alone to solve fiscal problems".
Worldwide public debt is close to levels last seen after World War II and could top 100% of GDP before 2030, the IMF chief warned, singling out developed economies as the "worst offenders".
"Yet, we don't see decisive action in the high-debt advanced economies where the need of the hour is for credible medium-term fiscal consolidation plans," Georgieva said, adding that "fiscal space is crying out for replenishment".
Borrowing costs are already climbing, she noted, with 10-year government bond yields in the US, Germany and Japan at their highest levels since 2007, 2009 and 1996 respectively.
On monetary policy, Georgieva described recent rate hikes by the US Federal Reserve, the European Central Bank and the Bank of Japan as "highly appropriate".
"Now may be a good time for a prudently hawkish bias in many countries' monetary policy," she said.
The IMF chief also warned that the global economy is being pulled in opposite directions by a negative energy supply shock from the Iran war and a positive demand shock from artificial intelligence, adding that "the combined impact of these two forces is highly uneven across the world".
Oil prices remain at about $100 a barrel, she said, well above the $89 the IMF assumed for this year in its July forecasts, which put global growth at 3% in 2026 and 3.4% in 2027.
"Even if the war in the Gulf were to end soon, the problem of high energy prices will likely persist for some time," Georgieva said.
An AI boom with risks attached
"Love it, hate it, or fear it, AI is here," the IMF chief said, describing the technology as "rapidly becoming a key driver of countries' relative fortunes in the world economy".
If done right, AI could lift global growth by as much as half a percentage point a year, according to IMF estimates.
Over a decade, that would be like adding "an economy the size of ASEAN to the world economy", Georgieva said, referring to the Southeast Asian bloc.
But she cautioned that "the AI building boom is inflationary", with spending on the technology, relative to the size of the economy, likely to outstrip past investment waves in railways, power grids and telecoms.
A letdown for investors could become "a far-reaching shock," she warned.
Georgieva also flagged dangers ranging from job losses and cyberattacks to cutting-edge models that could "escape human control and run amok".
The IMF is due to publish updated global growth forecasts during next week's meetings in Bangkok.

Nikolov said 12 crew members were believed to have been on board the ship which sank, all of them from Syria. The rescue operation will not resume, he added.
"There are no traces of the sailors from the first ship, and there will be none. There is also no information about drone remains," he told reporters.
"A boat, three life rafts and parts of the ship's equipment have been found."
It was not immediately clear who carried out the attack involving air and sea drones in waters off the coastal town of Byala in eastern Bulgaria, but there are growing concerns about hybrid attacks by Russia as it wages war in Ukraine.
"If we look at the nature of the cargo and the direction in which the ships were moving, then logically speaking, the result argues in favour of Russia," Prime Minister Rumen Radev said after a meeting of Bulgaria's National Security Council on Wednesday.
"But that does not mean that we can claim that the strike was carried out by Russia without having evidence."
In an emailed statement to Reuters, the Russian embassy in Sofia said the merchant ship was not among the targets hit by Russian drones on Tuesday.
Nikolov said the incident occurred in a so-called "responsible search and rescue zone" and not in Bulgaria's territorial waters, which extend to 12 nautical miles off the coast.
In a separate incident, Romanian authorities said on Monday that two people had died in a fire on a ship in the Black Sea outside the country's territorial waters.
SOFIA SEEKS CONSULTATIONS WITH BLACK SEA NEIGHBOURS
President Iliana Iotova said Bulgaria would invite its Black Sea neighbours Turkey and Romania for consultations on how to ensure safety for merchant shipping in the region.
Bulgaria may also ask its NATO allies to deploy "additional air and maritime surveillance capabilities and counter-drone systems to strengthen coastal and defence systems", she said.
Bulgaria does not border Russia or Ukraine, but as a NATO member it holds a strategic position on the Black Sea, where both countries have major ports.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy, speaking in a nightly video address, said an investigation jointly with Bulgaria's navy had shown that Russia was behind the attack.
Radev denied on Wednesday any joint investigation with Ukraine.
He added that, following the attack, his government would approve the purchase of five more surface-to-air missile systems. REUTERS

Russia, Ukraine trade accusations over overnight airstrikes, killing 11
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
08:12:55 UTC
17:12:55 KST

Burç Eruygur
07 October 2026•Update: 07 October 2026
Moscow and Kyiv on Wednesday traded accusations concerning overnight airstrikes that killed at least 11 people in Ukraine. 
The Kyiv City Military Administration said in a statement on Telegram that the Ukrainian capital was attacked by Russia with ballistic missiles overnight, with damage from the strikes recorded in two districts of the city. 
“Tragically, two men were killed in the enemy shelling. … In the Podilskyi district, a missile struck a non-residential building, causing a fire,” the statement said. 
It further said that a missile strike ignited a fire at a garage cooperative in Kyiv’s Darnytskyi district, noting that the blaze had been extinguished, though damage occurred. 
“Debris also fell in an open area at a separate location,” it added. 
In the Dnipropetrovsk region, Governor Oleksandr Hanzha said two people were injured in strikes that damaged an industrial enterprise, apartment buildings, and a sports club in the regional capital. 
Chernihiv Governor Vyacheslav Chaus said at least five people were killed and 25 others injured after a missile strike on an apartment building in the city of Pryluky, while Poltava Governor Vitaliy Dyakivnych said two people were killed and seven others injured in his region. 
“One of the key targets was our energy infrastructure. The Russians wanted to strike painfully and demonstratively. This was one of the most vile strikes: 70 missiles in total, many of them ballistic, as well as ‘shaheds.’ Unfortunately, only some of them were shot down,” Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on US social media company X.
Describing the overnight strikes as a “birthday gift” to Russian President Vladimir Putin, Zelenskyy said ballistic missiles remain the greatest challenge for Ukraine and that air defense packages for Kyiv are a “vital necessity.” He added that two more people were killed in the city of Oleksandriya in the Kirovohrad region. 
The Russian Defense Ministry claimed it launched a “massive strike” against Ukrainian military-industrial complex facilities in Kyiv and the Kyiv region, as well as in the Chernihiv, Kirovohrad, Dnipropetrovsk, Poltava, Kharkiv, and Odesa regions. 
The ministry also claimed that Russian air defenses downed 311 Ukrainian drones over 16 regions, as well as over the Black Sea, the Sea of Azov and Crimea, which Russia annexed in 2014. 
In Russia’s border region of Belgorod, Governor Alexander Shuvaev said seven people were injured over the past 24 hours in three districts due to Ukrainian strikes. 
In the Russian-controlled part of Ukraine’s eastern Donetsk region, Russian-installed Horlivka Mayor Ivan Prikhodko said three people were injured in a Ukrainian drone attack. 
Voronezh Governor Aleksandr Gusev said a power line was damaged in the southern part of his region due to falling debris, adding that several villages were temporarily without electricity and emergency services were working at the site. 
Ukraine’s Air Force claimed that its air defenses shot down 117 of 130 strike drones, as well as 44 ballistic and cruise missiles launched by Russia overnight. 
Separately, Zelenskyy claimed that Ukraine struck four targets that help Moscow "finance and wage its brutal war" over the past day, including two oil facilities and a training ground in Russia's Perm, Samara, and Astrakhan regions. 
Independent verification of the claims is difficult due to the ongoing war. 
Moscow and Kyiv have ramped up strikes in recent months, targeting each other’s logistics centers, ports, and energy infrastructure. 
They deny deliberately targeting civilian infrastructure, maintaining that the strikes are directed at military targets or facilities linked to military activities.

The Song of Stork and Dromedary: Nobel worthy
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
08:12:07 UTC
17:12:07 KST

The Song of Stork and Dromedary: Nobel worthy
Molly Quell
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
Novelist Anjet Daanje has been tipped as a serious contender for the Nobel prize in literature and, from her 2022 work The Song of Stork and Dromedary, for very good reason.
Published in Dutch as Het lied van ooievaar en dromedaris, the book is loosely based on the life of Emily Brontë, the author of Wuthering Heights. The work opens in 1847, with a villager laying out the body of Eliza May Drayden, who, like Brontë, has written a book widely derided at the time it was published but would go on to become a classic.
The opening scene is tinged with the Gothic horror of Wuthering Heights, Drayden’s eyes refuse to close for her burial.
The next 650 pages follow 11 interconnect stories that orbit around Drayden, and her sister Millicent, the fictionalised Charlotte Brontë who authored of Jane Eyre. Similar again to Wuthering Heights, all are largely set on the moors in England, though the final story takes the reader to the Daanje’s hometown of Groningen.
Rather than a traditional narrative, the book is written like an expansive biography, incorporating news articles, excerpts from diaries, letters, citations from fictional biographies and even parts of Drayden’s novel.
Each of the tales could be novellas in their own right, vivid and sometimes nail-biting, sending the reader off on tangents such as the mistreatment of two half-German sisters during the Second World War, or a pair of French half-sisters whose shared father creates a wedge between them.
The nature of sisterhood and the relationship between various female characters is one of the central themes of The Song of Stork and Dromedary. The work also reflects on the status of women at different times across the novel’s 200-year span.
Death is another important theme. Drayden’s death, with which the book opens, is an event that brings characters together but also tears them apart.
Anjet Daanje published eight novels before The Remembered Soldier (De herinnerde soldaat) became a hit in 2019. It was longlisted for the Libris Literature Prize, took home the F. Bordewijk Prize and the English-translation, which was published in 2025, was longlisted for International Booker Prize and included on The New York Times Book Review’s 100 Notable Books of 2025.
The Song of Stork and Dromedary took home both the Boekenbon Literature Prize and the Libris Literature Prize, the first book to ever net both awards. It was named the Best Book of the Century by the NRC newspaper. The English translation was published this year.
In 2023, Daanje was awarded the Constantijn Huygens Prize for her oeuvre.
The book was translated by David McKay, who also translated War and Turpentine by Stefan Hertmans and Multatuli’s Max Havelaar. He renders the complicated work thoughtfully, retaining Daanje’s character.
The Song of Stork and Dromedary is compelling and brilliant, and the author is worthy of the highest honour in literature.
The Nobel prize for literature winner will be announced on Thursday by the 18 members of the Swedish Academy.
You can get your copy at the American Book Center.

Israel continues demolishing buildings in Gaza a year after ceasefire
With almost the entire population homeless, displaced Palestinians face an unrecognisable landscape
It’s perhaps the most dramatic wound inflicted on the Gaza Strip by Israel’s military campaign over the past three years: the city of Rafah, once home to a quarter million people, has been erased.
Satellite imagery shows the Israeli military has systematically razed the southern city and other towns and districts to the ground and in some places ploughed away the rubble. Demolition, using bulldozers and explosives, has continued unabated since the Israel-Hamas ceasefire deal reached a year ago, as the military solidifies its hold over the around 60 per cent of the territory that it still controls.
Gaza’s mangled landscape is just one of the wounds on top of wounds that the enclave’s 2 million Palestinians have endured since Israel launched its campaign to destroy Hamas after the militants’ October 7, 2023, attack on southern Israel.
More than one out of every 10 people from Gaza’s pre-war population has been killed or wounded by Israeli fire. While nearly every family mourns dead or cares for wounded, most also had to move multiple times to escape fighting and Israeli evacuation orders.

08:11:02 UTC
17:11:02 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) – A student who hacked into the high-speed rail system causing delays should serve two years in prison, prosecutors said Wednesday.
The student named Chen (陳), 20, provided a friend named Lin (林), 22, with a Motorola MTP3150 two-way digital radio, per UDN. He also gave his friend the Tetra codes necessary to access the communication system used by high-speed rail operators.
At Taoyuan High Speed Rail Station on April 5 at 10:27 p.m., Lin hacked into the system. When boarding a bus near Taichung at 11:23 p.m., he hit a button for 3 seconds triggering a general alarm inside the high-speed rail system.
As a result, the control center automatically transmitted the alarm signal to trains in the vicinity. UDN reported. The conductors on four trains immediately halted their journey because they received the signal, causing 48-minute delays.
On April 28, police searched Lin’s homes in Taoyuan and Taichung and his office. They found communications equipment and took both Lin and Chen in for questioning.
Prosecutors said Wednesday they were charging both suspects.
Lin knew the importance of public safety, but he still hacked into the network, merely to satisfy his own curiosity about communication systems, according to prosecutors. He severely affected the rights of travelers and disrupted transportation, so he should serve two years in prison, the prosecutors said. Chen was charged as an accomplice.

Antwerp police to arrest known troublemakers even when they are not committing any offence
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
08:10:23 UTC
17:10:23 KST

Antwerp local police are to arrest known troublemakers more quickly, even if they are not doing anything wrong at the time. Those arrested will also immediately be detained for up to 12 hours, the maximum allowed. The new approach is set out in an internal memo seen by daily Gazet van Antwerpen. The police have also confirmed the switch to VRT NEWS. In this way, the police and the city aim to protect quality of life and encourage people to accept help. According to the Human Rights League, this approach is not lawful.
Antwerp police to arrest known troublemakers even when they are not committing any offence
Antwerp police are compiling a list of troublemakers, whom they also refer to as ‘claimers, a word used to refer to a known repeat offender or structural nuisance maker.’. “You aren’t simply registered as a claimer. These individuals are known for systematically causing a nuisance,” say the police.
Under the new guidelines, these claimers must be immediately placed under administrative detention for up to 12 hours if they are found anywhere, for example during a check. It is no longer necessary for them to be committing a criminal offence or actually causing a disturbance at that moment.
“This approach aims to protect the quality of life in Antwerp, to report people without lawful residence to the Immigration Service, and to refer people with addiction problems to support services.”
The police have discussed the approach with the office of Mayor Els van Doesburg (Flemish nationalist N-VA). According to the mayor’s office, there are as yet no administrative means to compel people to seek help.
“As long as we cannot compel these individuals to seek support services, we will, in the meantime, use this approach to strongly encourage them to accept help,” says spokesperson David Cleiren.
The measure applies throughout the city of Antwerp, but in practice is mainly enforced in Antwerp’s North District. This is a neighbourhood that the city itself has designated as a ‘neighbourhood requiring special attention’. Systematic identity checks had already been introduced there previously. Regular checks are also carried out to tackle public nuisance behaviour.
“Unlawful”
According to the Human Rights League, the approach is unlawful. “Making someone feel unsafe is not sufficient grounds for administrative detention,” says chair Kati Verstrepen.
“The Police Act permits administrative detention, but only if someone is actually disturbing the peace. You cannot simply detain people preventively just because you think they are going to disturb public order.”

In Afyonkarahisar, hot air balloons drift over 3,000-year-old Phrygian rock carvings, mineral-rich thermal springs have drawn visitors since 1200 BC, and poppy seeds define a UNESCO-recognised culinary tradition.

Unknown

17:09:23 KST

Riyaz ul Khaliq
07 October 2026•Update: 07 October 2026
China has called bilateral trade ties with the 27-member EU “highly integrated and mutually dependent,” stressing a need for dialogue over trade “concerns.”
The statement came after France and Germany called Monday for new EU trade instruments, arguing that the bloc’s existing measures are no longer sufficient to address challenges facing its trade system.
“Between China and the EU, the industrial and supply chains are highly integrated and mutually dependent, and our economic and trade relations are mutually beneficial in nature,” China’s Foreign Ministry spokesman Guo Jiakun said in a written statement late Tuesday.
“It is hoped that the EU will work with China in the same direction and resolve each other’s concerns through dialogue and consultation, so that the two parties can jointly keep the global industrial and supply chains stable and unimpeded and promote the sound and steady development of China-EU economic and trade relations,” he said.
In a joint letter to European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen, French President Emmanuel Macron and German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said the EU was facing “unprecedented challenges,” and proposed to reduce European dependencies, resolve existing supply-chain concentration and prevent emerging concentration risks.
Their letter came ahead of a visit by EU Trade Commissioner Maros Sefcovic to Beijing, where he will be hosted by China’s Commerce Minister Wang Wentao.
Wang and Sefcovic will meet Thursday and Friday, their first meeting in three months after they last met in Brussels.
Sefcovic earlier said that Brussels was seeking progress particularly in automobiles, medical devices, and agri-food products and could resort to defensive trade instruments if negotiations failed.
The EU imported €559.4 billion ($634 billion) in goods from China in 2025 while exporting €199.6 billion, leaving a goods trade deficit of €359.8 billion.

All companies receiving state money have signed non‑disclosure agreements with the Estonian Center for Defense Investments (RKIK), Veskimägi said on an ERR webcast.
"But I definitely think this should be public. I don't see any reason why it shouldn't or couldn't be public," he said.
"There is a clear effect here: Estonian products go to Ukraine using Estonian taxpayers' money. By sending these products to Ukraine, we actually finish them there, because every defense industry product is ultimately completed on the battlefield. And if one day we need them here in Estonia, we won't be dealing with prototypes. We will get products from Estonian companies that have been tested in Ukraine and have earned their combat credentials there," Veskimägi said.
"And when our own boys and girls have to use them, we know it's something reliable, something we can trust. So the more Estonian companies benefit from this measure, the more Estonia benefits, the more our defense capability benefits, and the more Estonian companies benefit," he added.
In September, the Ministry of Defense said it would not disclose which Estonian companies received financial support to help Ukraine, citing security concerns. In 2025 and 2026, Estonia purchased €200 million worth of Estonian defense industry products for Ukraine.
Veskimägi said all interested parties, including Russia, will find out who these companies are anyway.
"The only ones who don't know today are the general public, and because of that we lack an understanding of what capabilities we have sent to Ukraine for €100 million. Are these capabilities and technologies also needed for Estonia's defense? Does one company receive most of the funding, or is it distributed among many companies, which would be in the interest of Estonia's defense industry sector? Then we could have a public discussion about it, as well as a professional discussion between the Estonian Defense Industry Association and the Ministry of Defense about what kind of defense industry we actually want to develop in Estonia and whether this Ukraine measure supports that development," Veskimägi said.
Veskimägi said dozens of Estonian defense industry products have proven themselves on the battlefield in Ukraine.
The state should help ensure the security of defense companies
Veskimägi said Estonia has 260 defense companies. "Estonian defense industry companies today offer many technologies for many capabilities," he said.
Speaking about the arson attack on Milrem's production building, Veskimägi said defense companies have been aware of such risks for years and have made their own risk plans. "But the Milrem incident once again highlighted that this is something that cannot be ignored, must be addressed and must be invested in," he said.
"As a result, we agreed with security agencies to increase security briefings for companies and make them more frequent. I believe companies themselves will invest even more in their security systems, especially perimeter security. It was bad, but in some ways a necessary wake‑up call for our companies that this is something that must be dealt with," Veskimägi said.
Since most defense companies cannot ensure high‑level security on their own, Veskimägi said the state should step in.
"If the state sees — and the current coalition has said that defense industry and its development are priorities, which is a prominent part of the coalition agreement — then the state must provide support and guidance. Security agencies must support these companies by giving them a clear picture of the threats around us, because companies are simply not capable of doing this themselves in most cases, and they also lack the money to do it," Veskimägi said.
Defense minister: Naming firms funded for Ukraine would put them at risk
Defense Minister Martin Herem says he would not disclose which Estonian defense companies receive government funding to support Ukraine, arguing that doing so would endanger those firms. He added that disclosure could be considered if the companies themselves request it.
"In my view, there is no need to make them public, because they could become targets for the Russian Federation's special services, just as Foreign Minister [Sergei] Lavrov has threatened and as has already happened in Estonia and elsewhere," Herem told ERR.
Herem said disclosure could be reconsidered if the companies agree to it.
"Right now, my understanding is that we have an agreement with them not to disclose. If the contract says we do not disclose, then we will not. If the companies say they want it or agree to it, then of course we can do it. It's somewhat a matter of agreement, and the Defense and Aerospace Industry Association has been involved in the process. If they have proposals, they should come to the Ministry of Defense and we will review them," Herem said.
He added that he does not shape his positions based on media commentary.
"In the media we can say all sorts of things. I have no intention of making any changes because of this. There is a commission that deals with reviewing Ukraine aid — the principles on which we provide it and how. This topic will likely come up in that work. But if you ask whether opinions expressed in the press influence me much, honestly, I cannot even keep track of them," Herem said.
This article has been updated on 7 October with a comment from Defense Minister Martin Herem.

jaguar type 01 launches electric era with four-door grand tourer

jaguar type 01 launches electric era with four-door grand tourer
the first production model on jaguar’s dedicated electric architecture combines a low-slung gt profile with more than 1,000ps, 400 miles of EPA range, and an explicitly british design lineage.
Jaguar Type 01 brings its electric design language to production
After revealing the Type 01’s interior back in August, including its distinctive full-length central ‘spine,’ Jaguar now unveils the finished electric GT in New York, marking the first production model in a new generation for the British marque. Designed, engineered, and built in the UK, the Type 01 is an all-electric four-door grand tourer developed on Jaguar’s dedicated Electric Architecture (JEA). Its arrival introduces a new approach to the proportions, performance, and occupant experience of Jaguar’s next generation of electric vehicles.
The Type 01 is defined by a long bonnet, low roofline, and stretched silhouette, with proportions that recall the E-type and XJS while establishing a new visual language for the electric era. Jaguar says the design began with a single line and a blank sheet of paper, allowing its aerodynamic requirements to shape the clean, elongated surfaces of the car.
Turning heritage into a new identity
Underneath the bodywork is JEA, an 850-volt electrical architecture developed specifically for Jaguar’s next generation of electric vehicles. The Type 01 produces more than 1,000PS and is claimed to offer a 400-mile EPA range. The British vehicle brand says the vehicle can add 200 miles of range in 13 minutes when connected to a 350kW charger. The technical specifications position the Type 01 as a vehicle around which Jaguar is rebuilding its approach to performance and design.
The Type 01’s name also establishes the logic for the new generation. ‘Type’ refers to Jaguar’s history of naming significant vehicles, ‘0’ refers to zero tailpipe emissions, and ‘1’ identifies it as the first model in the new product series.
From E-type references to a new identity
Jaguar’s challenge is to use recognizable elements of its past without allowing heritage to become the entire design language. The Type 01’s long bonnet, low proportions, and emphasis on a dramatic silhouette make that connection explicit, while its electric platform allows the company to reconsider the relationship between exterior form and mechanical architecture.
Its New York launch occupied parts of Times Square, DUMBO, and the Lower East Side before moving to STORIED in West Chelsea, where visitors encountered objects representing different stages of the Type 01’s development. One of these was an aluminum version of the original line drawn by Jaguar’s designers at the beginning of the program. Another, described as the ‘Impossible Panel,’ represented the engineering effort required to translate the vehicle’s complex body shape into a production form. Jaguar also presented tire marks taken from its test track, pointing to the hundreds of thousands of kilometers of development and validation behind the car’s stated combination of composed and dynamic driving characteristics.

How Casino Gaming Is Regulated In The UK And Europe
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
08:04:49 UTC
17:04:49 KST

Casino gaming is one of the most closely supervised leisure industries around, yet there is no single rulebook that governs it. Each country sets its own terms, which means that the protections you enjoy as a player will heavily depend on where you live and which licence the gaming operator holds.
How The UK Regulates Casino Gaming
In Great Britain, the Gambling Commission licenses and polices every operator under the Gambling Act 2005. So, any operator wishing to see their platform feature a one of the top UK online casino must verify customer identities, guard against money laundering and give players practical tools they can use, such as deposit limits, reality checks and self-exclusion. Advertising and bonus terms face strict scrutiny, and operators that fall short risk not only incurring heavy fines but losing their licence.
This enforcement-first approach is expensive for businesses, but it gives customers clear routes for complaints and independent dispute resolution. Since 2014, operators servicing British players have needed a UK licence, wherever they’re based.
No Single Licence Across Europe
The European Union has never created one gambling licence that’s valid for every member state. Governments continue to retain control over which games are allowed, who may operate them and how much tax they pay. Brussels still shapes the wider picture through data protection, anti-money laundering and consumer rules. Hence, identity checks and safeguarding of payment details look broadly similar from one market to the next.
Malta, Germany And France Compared
Malta has built its reputation as an outward-looking licensing hub, and its authority remains respected across the industry as a whole. Germany takes a tighter line: its treaty-based regime introduced a joint state regulator and a central system monitoring player activity across licensed sites, a feature that supporters praise for boosting protection and critics blame for pushing some players towards unlicensed alternatives.
France stands apart. Online sports betting, betting on horse racing and poker are all licensed, but online slots and table games remain prohibited. Regulators there warn that banning a product doesn’t erase demand; it can simply move players towards unlicensed sites where there’s no recourse should anything go wrong.
Sweden and the Netherlands opened their markets in 2019 and 2021 respectively. Both introduced licensing, advertising limits and safer gambling requirements, and both now wrestle with channelisation, meaning the share of players who stay with licensed operators rather than drifting elsewhere.
Player Protection Is The Common Thread
Despite the differences, one theme unites nearly every jurisdiction: protecting players. Age checks are now standard, and most regulators expect operators to spot warning signs, such as sudden jumps in spending or extended sessions, and to step in before problems escalate. Self-exclusion schemes let individuals block themselves from licensed sites, and several markets now cap deposits or restrict certain promotional offers. The UK is often cited as a benchmark for how actively these rules are policed, although operators and campaigners still argue over affordability checks and advertising limits.
Conclusion
Before signing up to an online casino, players should always check that the operator holds a valid licence for their region. Doing so means players can trust that the platform is properly regulated by entities such as the UK Gambling Commission, with player protection at the forefront of everything.
