Taming the Curse of Dimensionality
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
08:04:09 UTC
17:04:09 KST

Many problems in computing boil down to a deceptively simple question: given one thing, how do you find the thing most similar to it? Imagine, for example, that you want to find the person who is physically closest to you. The answer seems obvious when there are only a few people around. But what happens when we have to search through increasingly complex spaces?
When you're standing in a straight line and want to find the person closest to you, the job is simple: you look left and then right, comparing your distance to the people around you. If you're in a room, however, you need to find the closest person in two-dimensional space. Again, it's not much of a problem since you can turn around and check the distances in different directions.
What if people could float in 3D space? In this case, things become complicated because you have to search in height, depth, and width. By adding a temporal dimension, things start to get frustrating. As the number of dimensions keeps growing, the task quickly becomes impractical.
Here's the shocking truth: much real-world data is represented in far higher dimensions, sometimes 100 dimensions or even more! Hence, the apt adjective “cursed” is used to describe this data.
An innovative solution for quick search among similar data in large datasets was proposed by Dr. Vahab Mirrokni, an Iranian researcher and graduate of Sharif University of Technology and the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT). His "Locality-Sensitive Hashing" (LSH) algorithm is now considered one of the popular hashing techniques in big data processing and artificial intelligence. Mirrokni, who is now a senior researcher at Google, was awarded the Mustafa(pbuh) Prize in 2025 in recognition of this achievement.
For a better grasp of this technique, we must first address one of the fundamental challenges of the age of data, a challenge which has made finding a piece of valuable information among a vast amount of data like searching for a needle in an ever-growing haystack.
Cursed Data
With the advancement of technology and the emergence of diverse forms of data into the world of computing and processing, we have encountered cursed data with remarkably high dimensionality. A color image of 1000 x 1000 pixels (where each pixel is one dimension) is considered a three-million-dimensional data on a computer! This is because each pixel is represented by the triple combination of red, green, and blue values, which is one of the standard methods of storing color images. Even after applying dimensionality reduction methods, we still deal with hundreds or thousands of dimensions in image processing.
When processing text files, we enter the realm of natural language processing, where words are converted into numerical vectors using certain methods. Each word is assigned an n-dimensional numerical vector (100-300 dimensions) so that similar words have similar vectors. Then, to process a text, key words are identified, extracted, and examined. With these methods, a text, which consists of several words, becomes highly dimensional. Thus, a paragraph can have tens of thousands of dimensions!
Another class of data that has received a lot of attention in the last decade is genetic data. Each cell of every living being contains a molecule called DNA, which is made up of four types of simpler molecules called bases. Given that the length of DNA in humans reaches about 3 billion base pairs, when represented and analyzed computationally, this enormous sequence can give rise to extremely high-dimensional data. Parts of DNA, called genes, are largely conserved over generations, determining the function of an organism's body. The preservation of each human's DNA information can be done in two ways: either the entire molecular sequence is preserved, or only parts of the gene, of which there are approximately 25,000 parts with different lengths, are preserved. In either case, we face a vast amount of information.
Close, Yet So Far Away: The Challenge of Searching in High-Dimensional Data
In such a high-dimensional space, the “curse of dimensionality” occurs. The data is uncommonly sparse, so that almost everything is equally spaced apart. In other words, the concept of “similarity” disappears as all data looks almost identical, and searching for the nearest neighbor becomes an impossible mission and computation becomes impractical.
Searching for the closest neighbor is one of the central issues in data science, machine learning, and information retrieval. The main objective of this process is to find the nearest point (or points) to a given point, which can be determined based on a similarity criterion. There are various metrics for measuring data distance, two of the simplest of which are Euclidean distance and Manhattan distance. In the former, the length of the line segment that directly connects two points in space is measured, while in the latter, the distance is calculated as if moving from one point to another step by step, that is, the sum of the differences in the data across different dimensions.
On the surface, it seems a straightforward job to find the image that most closely resembles our target image from an image database, or to find the most genetically similar organisms to create an evolutionary family tree, but these tasks present highly complex challenges. Sometimes there may be requirements for detecting textual similarity and plagiarism, or analyzing the emotions expressed in the texts. The advertising market and recommendation systems are not exempt from these challenges if they want to recommend a product based on individuals’ tastes and those of similar users. In fact, in all these cases, we are only looking for the most similar data to a specific data point. If the data were low-dimensional, the answer would be ready within a fairly reasonable time using traditional methods and fast algorithms. However, what makes it difficult to meet the demands is their high dimensionality.

Israel pauses in moment of silence to remember those killed on 7 October
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
08:00:41 UTC
17:00:41 KST

A group representing the bereaved families organised tributes, including a silence at 6:29am - the minute the attack began - and a ceremony that will follow tonight in Tel Aviv.
Israelis gathered in a moment of silence on Wednesday to mark three years since the Hamas-led attack of 7 October 2023, which a UN inquiry confirmed killed 1,200 people and saw 252 taken hostage.
In southern Israel, families mourned at road junctions, bomb shelters and the site of the Nova music festival, all places overrun by militants in the deadliest attack against Israel.
It is the first anniversary on which all the hostages that survived have returned home, bringing a new phase of mourning.
Among those marking the day was Elkana Bohbot, 37, who was abducted from the Nova festival and is spending the anniversary in Israel for the first time. He was freed last year after 738 days in captivity, most of it in a tunnel 50 metres underground. He said his daughter's birth in August this year was a message to his captors that "we [Israelis] were here, and we will always be here forever".
At the site of the Nova music festival, where Hamas militants in trucks and paragliders opened fire around dawn on October 7, family members bowed their heads in silence, although AFP reported at least one put on techno music in tribute to the fallen.
European Commission president Ursula von der Leyen paid her respects to the victims and their families in a post on X.
"The unspeakable savagery and terror of 7 October must never happen again," she wrote.
"The EU remains ready to help turn today's fragile ceasefire into a durable peace, based on a two-state solution."
The ceasefire von der Leyen referred to took effect last October, two years into the war Israel launched against Hamas in response to the attack.
Up to 75,000 Palestinians have been killed in the retaliatory campaign, according to the UN.
The UN said this summer that about 1.7 million Palestinians, roughly 80% of the population, were living in tents and temporary accommodation while Israeli maps show more than half of the Gaza strip is now controlled by its troops.
On Wednesday, AFP reporters in Israel heard loud bangs from across the border in Gaza during the commemorations as Israel carried out new strikes, despite the ceasefire agreement.
Gaza officials said at least two people were killed in overnight strikes in the region, most of which has been reduced to rubble.
Wednesday's gatherings were separate from the government's official memorial services, held on 5 October to fall closer to the anniversary in the Hebrew calendar.
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu vowed there would be "no forgiveness for the murderers" and promised never to allow Hamas to rule in Gaza.
More than 200 former hostages and relatives wrote to Netanyahu last year demanding an inquiry into the 7 October attacks or his resignation but Israel's leader opted to publish redacted government documents instead of launching an investigation and described the attacks as "a serious intelligence failure".
An election follows at the end of the month.

Police routinely failing to investigate ‘revenge porn’, research reveals
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
08:00:38 UTC
17:00:38 KST

Police forces are routinely failing to investigate complaints about the circulation of image-based abuse, previously known as “revenge pornography”, according to research that has triggered a super-complaint over the way such crimes are handled.
Lawyers have gathered evidence from 100 people who reported intimate images being shared online without their consent. Their research suggests that image-based abuse is still frequently dismissed or not recognised as criminal offending, despite being described by the former prime minister Keir Starmer as a national emergency.
Referrals to the Revenge Porn helpline, the charity that helps victims get non-consensual images removed from the internet, increased by more than 4,000% between 2015 and 2025, but data from 39 police forces in England and Wales shows that charges were lodged against perpetrators in an average of just 4.5% of cases last year. In some forces the figure was lower than 1%.
Some police officers responded inappropriately when women tried to register complaints, researchers found. One reported that the officer “almost giggled on the phone to me”, while another said the officer responded: “Boys will be boys.” Another said: “I bet you’ve learned your lesson.”
Image-based abuse overwhelmingly affects women and girls, who make up 98.9% of reported images.
Lawyers from Leigh Day and the charity the Centre for Women’s Justice are working with the charity #NotYourPorn to highlight systemic police failings in responding to image-based abuse, defined as “the taking, sharing or creating of intimate content without the survivor’s consent, or threatening to do so”.
They note that rapid innovations in AI are helping abusers find new ways to create and disseminate synthetic explicit material, sometimes known as deepfake content.
Their research classifies the policing response as “fragmented, inconsistent and incapable of meeting the scale of the threat posed by image-based abuse”. “Despite the increased public awareness, and the creation of new criminal offences designed to address this conduct, there has been no corresponding increase in charging rates, prosecutions or convictions,” the complaint says.
“The unavoidable conclusion is that the overwhelming majority of this offending goes unaddressed.”
Home Office data shows that there were only 569 charges issued for image-based abuse in 2025/2026. The Revenge Porn Helpline received almost 25,000 reports in 2025.
Researchers found that the vast majority of survivors of image-based abuse did not report it to the police, noting that “embarrassment, shame and fear” contributed to their reluctance. Police outsourced the evidence-gathering process to survivors in many cases, the report notes, leaving them to work out how to collate proof that the images were being disseminated widely and how to get the content removed from the internet.
“It felt like to them it wasn’t a priority, it wasn’t even a crime,” one woman told researchers. Another said: “Police involvement has not alleviated the harm caused by this offence. Instead, it has intensified my distress and left me feeling powerless and completely unsupported as a victim.”
A police super-complaint is a mechanism introduced in 2018 to allow concerns to be raised about ways in which the police operate that may significantly harm the interests of the public generally, rather than focusing on an individual force of officer.
The complaint will be jointly considered by the College of Policing and the Independent Office for Police Conduct, which will decide whether to respond by opening a wider investigation.
Harriet Bland, a lawyer with the Centre for Women’s Justice, said: “Without an urgent overhaul of police guidance and training on image-based abuse – which must be regularly updated – and a clear national strategy rolled out across forces, survivors will continue to be let down.”

‘The nurse used the torch on her phone to do the op’: hospitals stripped of resources in Ukraine’s occupied territories
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
08:00:38 UTC
17:00:38 KST

Earlier this summer, the once bustling corridors of the district hospital in Hola Prystan, a city in the Russian-occupied Kherson region of Ukraine, were ominously quiet. At times, it was plunged into darkness during power cuts lasting hours.
Much of the hospital’s medical equipment and supplies had been stolen and redirected to the military, and many experienced staff had gone.
“They [the Russian forces] even took some of the furniture,” says Natalia Sergeevna, who spent more than two decades working as a nurse in the hospital before escaping to Ukrainian-held territory in July.
In some ways, her hospital had been lucky, she says, with others in Russian-occupied territories repurposed for military use – as has been happening in regions bordering Ukraine – or simply closed down.
Despite its bare-bones infrastructure and dark corridors, people still came to the hospital, says Sergeevna, often making difficult journeys across the mine-infested landscape of occupied Kherson.
“They came with injuries and wounds; they came looking for oncologists or endocrinologists or palliative care. Women still came with pregnancies,” she says, “but every day it was getting harder to help them.”
In recent months, the situation has deteriorated further, with blockades and supply shortages leaving some Russian-occupied territories with limited medical support.
In June, the UN Human Rights Monitoring Mission in Ukraine said conditions in Oleshky and Hola Prystan, where Sergeevna worked, were becoming desperate, with thousands of people left without food, water and medicines.
It said ambulances had stopped coming to people’s homes, with medical assistance only available for the most urgent cases and patients dying during attempted evacuations.
Sergeevna says she had stayed in the hope of liberation, but by the summer things had become unbearable. “There is almost no available support to do any kind of surgeries; even basic procedures like removing polyps aren’t possible.
“In one case this year, we were performing a C-section, and the woman developed uterine bleeding, but there was no blood available for transfusion, because all of the supplies had been sent to the [Russian] soldiers,” she says.
Another obstacle is the forced “passportisation” of the population in occupied territories, with medical services refused to people who do not have a Russian compulsory health insurance policy, which can only be obtained through a Russian passport.
“They treat you very badly if you are Ukrainian. We have no rights, they tell us to our face, ‘you’re a nobody’,” says Marina*, who lives in a town occupied by Russian forces. She says she had to be taken to hospital in 2023 after she developed complications during her pregnancy and went into early labour.
“The baby was coming with the backside down, and I needed an emergency C-section. I was in a lot of pain,” she says. “But it was 11.30pm, and the curfew was in place. We tried getting out, but they shot at us.”
Marina says she spent an excruciating night cared for by her husband and a neighbour, before rushing to the clinic as soon as the curfew lifted. “When we got there, there was no obstetrician, no qualified staff for pregnancy, no one to help. I eventually had a C-section with the help of my neighbour, who was a nurse, and thankfully my baby and I survived.
“In a normal circumstance, we would have known about this complication, but because there were no tests or medical professionals left in our town, not even an ultrasound machine, I had no way of diagnosing this,” she says.
In another case, from earlier this year, Sergeevna says her colleagues were forced to treat a patient with endometriosis without anaesthesia.
“She was bleeding when she came to the hospital. So there was no anaesthesia, not even power. And the nurse at the time used the torch on her phone to do the procedure because there was no other option.”
Accurate figures are not available; but organisations monitoring the situation in the region detect an anecdotal rise in maternal and child mortalities, as well as long-term health problems. There are also reports of difficulties in accessing contraceptives and abortion.
Sergeevna says the situation is particularly acute for women, and that she had been dealing with women facing a range of mental health issues because of the lack of medical care and trauma they had suffered, including rape and sex slavery.
She says one 18-year-old had come with the letter “Z” cut into her torso with a blade. While inspecting her wound, Sergeevna discovered the girl had been raped. “But that was not why she came to us; she was too ashamed to admit that. She came only because she couldn’t tolerate the wound any more because of swelling and inflammation.”
With few doctors left in her district and depleting resources, Sergeevna and her team did their best to stitch her up. “But there was nothing else we could do for her. There were no resources to check her for STDs or provide her with contraceptives. We did not even have any way to provide psychological support.”
* Name has been changed

Oil prices rose amid the threat of a storm in the United States and Houthi attacks
Kyiv • UNN
Brent and WTI prices rose due to the threat of a storm to U.S. oil facilities and Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia.
Oil prices rose on October 7 due to the threat of disruptions to production and refining in the United States as a result of the storm, as well as attacks by Yemen’s Houthis on Saudi Arabia. Reuters reports this, UNN writes.
Details
Brent futures rose by $1.05, or 1.04%, to $101.63 per barrel. U.S. WTI rose by 80 cents, or 0.89%, to $90.24.
According to a forecast by U.S. meteorologists on October 6, the storm in the Gulf of Mexico could turn into a hurricane within two days and strike oil and gas facilities. Offshore areas along its path account for 15% of U.S. oil production.
Six oil refineries were also under threat. Overall, states along the Gulf of Mexico account for about half of the country’s refining capacity.
Another factor was the decline in U.S. oil inventories. According to the American Petroleum Institute, cited by the publication’s sources, they fell by 2.09 million barrels in the week ending October 2.
At the same time, increased supplies from the Middle East are restraining the price rise. However, the risks of further disruptions remain due to Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia and strikes on vessels in the region.

Wearable drone detector unveiled for individual soldiers
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
09:00:22 BST
17:00:22 KST

A drone detector light enough to be worn by a single soldier, and able to analyse the radio spectrum for threats that are not yet in any threat library, has been launched by the Swindon-based company MyDefence, the firm stated.
The device, called Wingman Edge, weighs under a kilogram, which the company puts at 17 per cent lighter than the generation it replaces. It combines signature-based detection, meaning it recognises signals already catalogued, with continuous artificial intelligence analysis of the spectrum running on the device at the same time.
That second capability is the part of the device the company is selling hardest. Rather than only matching against a stored library, the system is designed to identify and classify a wider range of activity including drone signals, controllers, communications links, Wi-Fi, analogue video and signals it has never seen before.
Dan Hermansen, chief executive of MyDefence, said: “The evolving drone threat does not wait for a database to be updated. For more than a decade, we have put wearable drone detection into the hands of soldiers. Wingman Edge builds on that foundation by giving the individual soldier a much deeper understanding of what is happening in the spectrum around them, including activity that does not match an existing signature.”
Processing on the device rather than in a remote system matters in the places this equipment is meant to work, since a soldier in a jammed or disconnected environment cannot wait for a server somewhere else to tell him what he is listening to. The system is passive, monitoring the electromagnetic environment without radiating anything itself, which keeps the wearer from becoming a target for the sort of equipment that homes on emissions.
Individual units can share detections with other soldiers, vehicles and connected systems, so that what one man picks up feeds a wider picture. Underlying all of it is what the company calls MyDefence Spectrum Intelligence, its software layer combining radio frequency data, threat knowledge and machine learning.
MyDefence says the United States Army has bought its wearable drone detection systems to a cumulative value of 77 million dollars over the past eighteen months, which is a considerable sum for equipment carried on a soldier’s body armour.
Wingman Edge is the first of what the company is calling its Edge Generation, a family of products intended to push sensing and processing out to deployed platforms rather than back to headquarters. The direction of travel matches what has been learned in Ukraine, where small drones have made the ability to detect an approaching threat in the last few seconds a matter of individual survival rather than a staff function.

Loyalty vs. Competence: Pete Hegseth’s policies have become the Pentagon&#039;s greatest threat
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
08:00:18 UTC
17:00:18 KST

Despite the “strange war” Donald Trump is waging against Iran, the purges at the Pentagon have continued unabated in recent months. Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth has fired some generals without warning and blocked others from promotion, all while using the Pentagon’s civilian leadership to impose Donald Trump’s political and cultural agenda on the military. Meanwhile, the world’s most powerful fighting force is running short of ammunition, its personnel are exhausted, and its staffing levels have been depleted. Experts say Hegseth has created (or, at the very least, exacerbated) many of these problems himself — focusing more on political issues and the loyalty of his generals than on supplying the military and ensuring the competence of his subordinates.
The blitzkrieg drags on
Criticism of Pete Hegseth had been building for months before some Republicans in Congress finally began challenging the Trump administration’s agenda when it comes to military affairs. Finally, it was Republican Congressman Thomas Massie of Kentucky who, on Sept. 15, introduced eight articles of impeachment against the defense secretary in the House of Representatives. Three accuse Hegseth of launching the war ing Iran without congressional authorization, while the others concern alleged abuses against civilians, the legality of military operations against drug traffickers and Yemeni Houthis, and the reprisals against Senator Mark Kelly after the Arizona Democrat called on service members to refuse to obey unlawful orders.
Other Republicans, however, secured enough votes to postpone consideration of Massie’s motion until November — after the midterm elections. Congress is likely to take the matter up in the future provided that Democrats gain control of the chamber (as polls currently suggest that they will).
There are ample grounds for criticism of Hegseth. The war launched by the United States and Israel in February was initially intended to swiftly decapitate the leadership in Tehran, resulting in a pro-Western shift. The allies achieved the first objective but not the second: after the old leadership was eliminated, power in Iran consolidated in the hands of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, which has not been afraid to escalate the conflict.
In September, the war shifted toward oil exports and maritime routes, with the U.S. beginning to strike Iranian oil tankers and Tehran responding with attacks on commercial vessels. Iranian missiles also began striking ever closer to American ships, and shortly after Saudi Arabia asked the United States for military assistance, Iranian attacks damaged a critical overland pipeline that had become an alternative to the waterborne route. Iran-backed Houthis also recently seized footholds in another part of the region’s maritime corridor, the Bab el-Mandeb Strait.
The U.S. administration is now being forced to plan for a long war. Vice President JD Vance and Secretary of State Marco Rubio reportedly even warned Trump that Iran could continue resisting until the end of his term — meaning early 2029 — a message that is consistent with what Hegseth is hearing from his own generals. According to the Washington Post, as early as August the military’s top commanders told the Pentagon chief that the war could not continue indefinitely at its current pace given that U.S. Central Command, which oversees the Middle East, has kept more than 50,000 troops on heightened combat readiness for months.
As early as August, the military’s top commanders told Hegseth that the war in Iran could not continue indefinitely at its current pace
Generals are concerned that the operational tempo is increasing, service members are growing exhausted without relief, and rotations may not come until early 2027 (or even later). Meanwhile, stocks of precision-guided weapons are not being replenished.
When the aircraft carrier USS Abraham Lincoln recently pulled into port in Thailand after a 286-day deployment – one of the longest in the U.S. Navy's modern history – sailors complained about poor living conditions, a lack of variety in their food, and their deteriorating psychological state. Trump, however, responded that the carrier had been at sea for “not long enough.”
Chief of Naval Operations Daryl Caudle said outright that the Navy could not sustain the current level of operations against Iran with no end date in sight and sailors already stretched to their limits. Even U.S. convoys helping tankers pass through the Strait of Hormuz are now operating on a limited schedule and no longer providing 24-hour air-defense coverage. The United States is, of course, still capable of waging war against Iran, but its problems are mounting — and not only in the Middle East. As forces have been pulled in from other regions, deterrence of other potential U.S. adversaries, above all China and Russia, has weakened, generals warn.
Generals vs. the secretary
The resource shortage is compounded by strained relations between the secretary and the military leadership. For the past year and a half, Hegseth has systematically purged the top brass, removing officers he considers disloyal to his political agenda.
Although the U.S. military is subordinate to civilian political leaders, the armed forces have traditionally enjoyed considerable professional autonomy. The assessments of the Joint Chiefs of Staff have often differed from what politicians wanted to hear, and military leaders themselves handled operational planning and execution, assessed military risks, developed doctrine and standards, and made promotion recommendations.
Trump and Hegseth began “purging” the military leadership almost immediately after the current administration came into office. The president fired Joint Chiefs Chairman Charles Brown, while Hegseth ousted then-Chief of Naval Operations Lisa Franchetti and several other senior commanders — without making any allegations of misconduct against them. Brown later indirectly criticized the administration for politicizing military appointments.
More recently, Hegseth has shifted from firing officers to controlling who gets promoted. He has personally intervened in promotion lists drawn up by the military, removing many officers he considers unacceptable. According to media reports, participation in programs connecting with Diversity, Equity, and Inclusion (DEI) was among the reasons some officers fell out of favor. In one instance, Hegseth removed all three women and two African American officers from a list of candidates for rear admiral. During the war with Iran, Hegseth also forced Army Chief of Staff Randy George to retire.
For the officers who remain, this inevitably raises the question of where the line now lies between professional assessments of their service and political loyalty. The upheaval in the Army continued when Army Secretary Dan Driscoll left his post in late August. The civilian head of the Army and one of its leading advocates for accelerated modernization, Driscoll was also Hegseth’s biggest rival for influence — and a potential successor as SecDef.
However, the personnel shakeups have not eliminated professional disagreements within the military leadership. As reported by U.S. media, in August the commanders of European Command, Indo-Pacific Command, and Southern Command, along with the Chief of Naval Operations, formally objected to extending the deployments of some forces stationed in their regions.
This was not a refusal to follow orders — which the generals and admirals were still required to carry them out. However, they still made clear that they considered the decision risky. Hegseth has yet to respond, and the dissenting commanders remain in their posts for now.
Where are the weapons, Hegseth?!
Personnel conflicts are only part of the problem. Even setting aside Hegseth’s relationship with the generals and its impact on military readiness, the armed forces simply lack sufficient ammunition and equipment. The U.S. is burning through its expensive weapons far faster than the American defense industry can replenish them. Meanwhile, cheap Iranian drones are creating a stark cost imbalance between offense and defense: Tehran can force the United States and its allies to spend many times more to intercept a drone than it costs to launch one.
According to The Washington Post, the U.S. has already expended 850 Tomahawk cruise missiles used against fortified targets, along with more than 1,000 missiles for Patriot air-defense systems and THAAD interceptors. In addition, CNN has reported that by August the United States had used about half of its prewar stockpile of Patriot missiles and roughly 80% of its THAAD interceptors. The U.S. also lost at least 45 MQ-9 Reaper heavy drones – about a quarter of its prewar fleet — as the slow, expensive UAVs proved relatively easy targets for Iran and its allies.
The United States has not only reduced its ability to strike, but also left its regional allies without adequate air defenses. They were willing to spend their oil revenues on American systems, but there are no longer enough of the systems to go around. It is hardly surprising that the Gulf monarchies are now turning to Ukraine for technology and expertise in countering cheap drones – the very experience Kyiv has gained through years of war with Russia.
The United States is learning the same lesson. The global drone market was already valued at $20 billion in 2025 and is expected to exceed $50 billion by 2034. The U.S. intends to take a leading position, albeit belatedly, with the Pentagon investing about $1 billion in the Drone Dominance initiative to produce up to 200,000 attack drones by 2027. Young people who until recently competed in drone racing are now winning half-billion-dollar Pentagon contracts to produce “killer drones” costing $5,000 apiece, and a whole new crop of companies is vying for billions of dollars being distributed by the Pentagon.
By 2034, the global drone market is expected to exceed $50 billion, and the United States wants to take a leading position
But once again, the key issue is Hegseth's arbitrary personnel shakeups, which could undermine combat readiness. After Randy George was forced out, the Army’s new leadership disbanded a 600-member experimental battalion that had spent nearly a year specializing in drone warfare — in part by absorbing lessons from Ukraine.
The Pentagon says a dedicated unit is no longer necessary and that drone skills should be spread throughout the Army. But lawmakers from both parties are demanding an explanation for why the experiment is being ended now, during a war in which cheap Iranian drones have become one of the main threats to U.S. forces.
Hegseth did not create the shortage, but he did arrive in the Pentagon promising to revive the defense industry, overhaul the procurement system, and speed up the adoption of new technologies. Instead, innovation is moving slowly — with any actual progress occurring almost in spite of a leadership that is disbanding specialized units. The military’s inability to replenish its losses is increasingly becoming a problem for which Hegseth bears primary responsibility.
Preparing for the last war
It is still too early to say that the personnel policies implemented by Hegseth and Trump have significantly weakened the U.S. armed forces. But warning signs are coming from all directions. The missile shortage, slow production, and strain on the Navy did not begin under Hegseth. As the old saying goes, U.S. generals prepared for the last war.
They were unprepared for a war of attrition against a major adversary like Iran. Hegseth, however, came to the Pentagon promising to “restore combat readiness” but is making the situation worse through personnel that appears to prioritize ideology over effectiveness. The U.S. military, for which Trump has requested a staggering $1.5 trillion defense budget for 2027, is working to address these shortcomings, with the Pentagon drawing up emergency plans to replenish its arsenal. Nevertheless, the political agenda pushed by Hegseth has already cost the military substantial resources and effort, and possibly lives as well.
The Secretary's politics are likely to remain the main obstacle to modernization programs and decisions. In other words, the Pentagon chief himself could become the U.S. military's biggest problem.

Far-right activists attempt to enter, disrupt October 7 memorial ceremony
Far-right activist Mordechai David and about 15 others affiliated with the Otzma Yehudit party attempted to enter and disrupt a civilian-led memorial ceremony at Tel Aviv's Yarkon Park on Wednesday.
Some of the activists were prevented from entering the venue, while David appeared to be detained by a police detective.
In a statement, police said David was questioned by officers and would not be allowed to enter the venue.
Oct. 7 memorial highlights trauma and failures as survivors, families call for accountability
The civilian-led ceremony marking the October 7 massacre on Wednesday highlighted the psychological toll on Israelis who responded to the attack, including a volunteer who suffered a mental breakdown and a bus driver who later died by suicide after evacuating traumatized children.
The ceremony, organized by the Kumu movement and families of October 7 victims, also focused on the failures that allowed the Hamas-led attack to take place and the need to investigate them.
Omri Shifroni, one of Kumu's founders, spoke about relatives who were killed at Kibbutz Be'eri. His niece and nephew, Liel and Yanai, and his aunt and uncle, Avia and Ayala Hetzroni, were among those killed.
He said the attack shattered Israelis' trust in the state and its ability to protect them, but that soldiers and civilians who responded demonstrated the country's sense of mutual responsibility.
"That morning, the systems collapsed and the state failed to function," he said. "In the long hours in the safe room, the trust we had as an anchor shattered into pieces."
Shifroni said rebuilding that trust would require an investigation into what happened.
"Without investigating the truth, we cannot fix things, and we cannot make sure it never happens again," he said.
Trump says Palestinians are paying 'big price for October 7'
U.S. President Donald Trump said he spoke Wednesday with Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu on the anniversary of the October 7, 2023 attacks.
"I wished him well, and I wished the people of Israel well," Trump said. "That was a horrible day, a horrible tragedy – and the other side is paying a very big price for what they did on October 7th, believe me."
U.S. Vice President JD Vance described the attacks as "the worst Islamic terrorist attacks of our lives."
In a post on X marking the anniversary, Vance highlighted the 49 Americans killed in the attacks. "May their memory be a blessing," he said.
‘I miss the brother you were’: Sister remembers October 7 victim
Aviva Chana, whose brother Israel Chana was killed by militants in Ofakim on October 7, 2023, spoke at Wednesday's memorial ceremony about his final hours. Israel was killed while fighting militants who had entered the city, on his 30th birthday.
"On your last night, we celebrated your 30th birthday together. We danced, rejoiced and laughed," she said. "Just hours later, you were facing terrorists, you, alone with a pistol, a single magazine and fifteen bullets."
Chana said she wanted to remember her brother not only for how he died but for how he lived.
"Your big smile. Your zest for life. The wonderful brother and son you were," she said. "Israel, my brother, everyone talks about the hero you were that morning. But I miss, above all, the brother you were during all the days before that."
She ended by referring to his grave at the Ofakim cemetery: "And since then, just as it says on your headstone, you have a place within us, and we have a place where you are, Block 1, Plot 16, Row 17."
'We will bear witness': October 7 memorial ceremony draws bereaved families, survivors
Hundreds of bereaved families, former hostages and representatives of communities affected by the October 7 attack gathered Wednesday evening at Yarkon Park in Tel Aviv for a civilian-led memorial ceremony marking the massacre's anniversary.
The ceremony is hosted by former hostage Eli Sharabi and actress Shani Cohen, and opened with a minute of silence.
"In the name of the murdered and the fallen, and for the sake of future generations, we will bear witness and tell the story of the day the sky fell upon us," Sharabi said. "We will remember them all, and we will never forget."

Likud defends Netanyahu's October 7 record as Lapid accuses him of ignoring warnings
On the anniversary of the October 7 attack, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's Likud party reiterated his claim that he received no advance warning of Hamas' assault and attacked Channel 12 News over its coverage.
Likud called the network's broadcasts "false political propaganda designed to bring down the right-wing government in elections," citing intelligence assessments in the days before the attack that Hamas was deterred and seeking an arrangement to maintain calm.
The party said Netanyahu was first briefed at 6:29 A.M. on October 7, 2023, and blamed field and intelligence personnel for identifying warning signs during the night but failing to alert the political leadership or forces in the field.

He also cited a July 24 warning from the Shin Bet chief, who he said told Netanyahu, "I am giving you a warning of war," and a September 13 briefing to a Knesset intelligence subcommittee on a "perfect storm" warning of a potential multi-front escalation.
Yarden Bibas' sister: Lack of state inquiry means 'no recognition' of Oct. 7
Ofri Bibas-Levy, the sister of freed Israeli hostage Yarden Bibas, said Wednesday that three years after the October 7 massacre, the absence of a state commission of inquiry means there is "no recognition – only denial and minimization."
Bibas-Levy's sister-in-law, Shiri, and her two nephews, Ariel and Kfir, were also taken hostage and murdered in Gaza.
Speaking at a Foreign Ministry ceremony for foreign ambassadors, Bibas-Levy said, "We shouldn't have to fight all the time for recognition, whether at home or abroad. What really happened really happened. These are not political slogans, but human lives."

Trump’s Lithuania base remark sparks excitement – and questions – in Vilnius
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
08:00:00 UTC
17:00:00 KST

A few words from US President Donald Trump were enough to set off a wave of excitement in Lithuania: The United States, he said, would consider establishing a permanent military base in the Baltic country.
Asked by LRT correspondent Augustinas Šemelis whether he would consider Lithuania’s invitation to establish a permanent American base, Trump offered an enthusiastic, if noncommittal, response.
“They’re friends of mine. They are wonderful people. So we will certainly look at it,” Trump said. “I know so many people in Lithuania. They are great people”
In Vilnius, the remarks were quickly welcomed as a sign that Lithuania’s push for a permanent US military presence could be gaining traction.
President Gitanas Nausėda called Trump’s statement “very good news” and said it showed that the United States trusted Lithuania.
“The most important thing now is to act consistently and wait for the rotation of US troops,” Nausėda said.
But even among those welcoming Trump’s words, there was caution about what they actually mean.
Conservative MPLaurynas Kasčiūnas, deputy chairman of the Seimas Committee on National Security and Defence, called the US president’s statement “wonderful news” but said it was too early to speak of a concrete plan.
“It’s wonderful news when the US president says such words, but, on the other hand, whether there is a real plan to establish a permanent military presence or permanent military base here, it is probably too early to talk about,” Kasčiūnas said.
Lithuania’s defence minister, Robertas Kaunas, said the idea had already been formally put to Washington. He submitted the proposal to the Pentagon about two weeks ago.
“There have been no decisions as of today. Discussions are underway. As you can see, the signals are positive,” Kaunas said.
Prime Minister Mindaugas Sinkevičius said Lithuania had also raised the issue with John Coale, the US special envoy for Belarus, about a month ago.
For Lithuania, the timing is particularly significant. After a six-month pause, about 1,000 US troops are expected to return to the country beginning in late October, but only for a rotational deployment.
“The fact is that only a couple of weeks ago it was announced that, after a six-month break, the US rotation is returning, 1,000 troops,” Sinkevičius said. “They will begin deploying at the end of October, but for now only for nine months.”
A permanent base, Lithuanian officials argue, could provide greater continuity.
“Even if a permanent base is not established, those rotations would run more smoothly and there would not be such large gaps,” said Remigijus Motuzas, chairman of the Seimas Foreign Affairs Committee.
Kaunas said Lithuania was ready to contribute financially.
“Lithuania already covers the costs of the presence of US troops. We have good infrastructure in Pabradė, which we can continue to expand,” he said. “We are not far from being able to have a permanent presence.”
The defence minister said the Pabradė area could accommodate about 1,500 troops.
But experts warned that Lithuania’s existing infrastructure would not by itself amount to a permanent American base.
“This is not infrastructure where Americans could settle with all their families and civilian personnel,” said Tomas Jermalavičius, research director at the International Centre for Defence and Security in Tallinn.
There is another missing piece: an actual US decision.
Former US Ambassador to Russia Michael McFaul has noted that Trump’s formulation – “we will look at it” – can often mean that the president has not previously considered the issue in detail.
Jermalavičius said that makes diplomacy particularly important now.
“This is an impulsive reaction that now simply needs to be taken advantage of – strike while the iron is hot,” he said.
That effort could be especially important in persuading sceptics inside the Pentagon, where the discussion has increasingly focused on reducing US troop levels in Europe rather than establishing new permanent bases.
And Lithuania is not the only country seeking a deeper US military commitment.
Trump has also signalled support for Poland’s long-running campaign for a permanent American base. Warsaw has pursued such a base for nearly a decade and at one point proposed naming it “Fort Trump”.
“They want it. And I like their president,” Trump said when asked about Poland.
That raises a question for Lithuania: Would Washington establish two permanent bases so close to each other on NATO’s eastern flank?
“It’s very close to Poland, and it is unlikely that such a decision would be made,” Motuzas said.
Jermalavičius said Washington had historically been reluctant to commit large permanent forces to the Suwałki corridor, the strategically sensitive area linking Poland and Lithuania.
“Enthusiasm for keeping large forces on this side of Suwałki has been very limited. They always wanted to maintain as much flexibility as possible,” he said.
He also pointed to another potential complication: the Trump administration could seek to link its security commitments to other issues in the region, including the transit of Belarusian fertilisers.
Lithuanian politicians have repeatedly denied that Washington is linking the two issues.
But Jermalavičius said the possibility should not be dismissed.
“This administration is very businesslike in its international relations. It is obvious that it will use such promises as a pressure tool or compensation for reopening transit,” he said.

Second death reported in Siberia as Russia denies plague outbreak
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
07:58:36 UTC
16:58:36 KST

A second person has reportedly died in Russia’s Irkutsk region amid growing concern over a possible pneumonic plague incident, Russian media reported, as international health authorities pressed Moscow for more information about the unexplained death of a researcher at a Siberian anti-plague institute.
The reported second death has not been independently confirmed, and Russian authorities have not acknowledged that plague caused either death.
The alarm began after Darya Shipilova, 28, an employee of the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Research Institute of Siberia and the Far East, was hospitalized on Sept. 29 with severe pneumonia and died on Oct. 2.
Russian and independent media reported that Shipilova may have been exposed to Yersinia pestis, the bacterium that causes plague, while working at the institute. Some reports claimed she had accidentally broken a test tube containing live bacteria, though Russian authorities have not confirmed that account.
Russia’s health watchdog, Rospotrebnadzor, said Shipilova died from pneumonia of an unspecified origin and insisted that no plague cases had been detected in the region. Authorities said people who had been in contact with her were placed under medical observation and tested.
Russian media later reported that a second unidentified person had died at a hospital in the Irkutsk region after allegedly contracting plague. No laboratory results or other official evidence have been released linking the reported death to the disease.
The uncertainty has drawn scrutiny from international health authorities. The World Health Organization has sought additional information from Russia about Shipilova’s death, the pathogen suspected by authorities, the public health measures imposed in the region and reports that another employee developed pneumonia of unknown origin.
Nearly 200 people who had contact with Shipilova were reportedly placed under monitoring, while dozens of employees at the institute were isolated. Hospitals in the Irkutsk area also imposed restrictions, and residents reported seeing health workers wearing protective equipment.
Several Russian media reports concerning the suspected outbreak have meanwhile disappeared from news websites. Independent Russian outlets said reports from major broadcasters and newspapers were deleted, while a local government warning urging residents to avoid travel to the Shelekhov area was also removed shortly after publication.
Russian authorities continue to deny that a plague outbreak is underway. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov urged the public to rely on official information from Rospotrebnadzor rather than “rumors and speculation.”
The United States has also said it is monitoring developments. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said the situation was not considered a cause for alarm but warranted close attention, while President Donald Trump said Washington was prepared to assist Russia if necessary.
Pneumonic plague is the most severe form of plague and can spread between people through respiratory droplets during close contact. It can progress rapidly if untreated, but antibiotics are effective when administered early.

- According to preliminary information, no one has been reported hurt.

- The available forces and means are sufficient to deal with the aftermath, the ministry emphasized.
- Authorities in Sochi temporarily restricted access to promenades and beaches amid the Black Sea tanker fire, Mayor Andrey Proshunin said.

WHO releases first global guidelines on child obesity as cases surge
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
07:56:51 UTC
16:56:51 KST

WHO releases first global guidelines on child obesity as cases surge
Child and adolescent obesity has quadrupled since 1990, rising from two per cent to around eight per cent of youngsters in the five-to-19 age group, according to the UN World Health Organization (WHO).
In 2024, there were around 170 million children and adolescents living with obesity – including 70 million children aged five to nine and some 100 million adolescents up to 19.
The UN health agency defines obesity as a “chronic, relapsing disease” triggered by excessive fat deposits which can nonetheless be managed through effective care.
What’s at stake
Children and adolescents with the disease can face both medical and social repercussions from very early on in life, WHO warns.
Obesity increases the risk of noncommunicable diseases, including type 2 diabetes and cardiovascular disease.
It also increases their likelihood of experiencing stigma, discrimination and bullying, which can strongly negatively affect mental health.
In its new set of guidelines, WHO strongly recommends dietary changes, physical activity and other behaviour-changing interventions.
Weight loss drugs: a last resort
It does not recommend pharmacological treatment, bariatric surgery (surgery that changes the digestive system to induce weight loss) or weight-loss devices for children aged 0-9 years.
For adolescents aged 10-19 years, treatment with approved medicines – such as GLP-1 therapies – should only be considered when a supervised lifestyle programme has failed to make improvements.
Similarly, bariatric surgery may be considered under strict conditions for those with severe obesity.
“The foundation of obesity care for children and adolescents is not medicine or surgery, but access to comprehensive support that enables healthy eating, physical activity and sustainable behaviour change,” said Dr. Luz María De Regil, Director of the Department of Nutrition and Food Safety at WHO.
Keeping spirits up
The new recommendations also emphasise the importance of addressing mental health alongside obesity, because it is both a cause and a consequence of the disease.
Anxiety, depression, low self-esteem and emotional dysregulation can contribute to unhealthy eating behaviours, physical inactivity and social withdrawal, while children and adolescents living with obesity may also experience stigma and bullying that harm their emotional well-being.
The guidelines stress that obesity care should go beyond weight loss and aim to improve health, functioning and well-being, notably by being tailored to the specific needs of each child and by ensuring long-term follow-up.
Political action
At the same time, WHO acknowledged that treatment cannot reverse the rise in obesity by itself: systemic changes are needed.
The agency called for policies and measures that make healthy diets and physical activity more accessible and affordable, including regulatory and fiscal measures and action across education, urban planning, transport and social protection.
“Our priority must be to ensure that every child and adolescent can access quality care and supportive environments from an early age, helping them achieve and maintain a healthy weight and laying the foundation for lifelong health and well-being,” said Dr. De Regil.

Russia’s military has suffered approximately 1.55 million personnel losses since the start of its full-scale invasion of Ukraine, according to an interim tally published by Ukraine’s General Staff on Wednesday, Oct. 7, as Russian President Vladimir Putin turned 74.
The General Staff said Russian forces lost approximately 1,690 personnel over the past day, bringing estimated total personnel losses to 1,545,950.

Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Ukraine’s tally also includes 12,396 tanks, 25,498 armored combat vehicles, 50,836 artillery systems, 2,192 multiple-launch rocket systems, and 1,690 air defense systems.
Russian forces have also lost an estimated 443 aircraft, 356 helicopters, 35 ships and boats, and two submarines, according to the Ukrainian military.
The General Staff reported particularly high losses in unmanned systems, estimating that Russia has lost 551,876 operational-tactical unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs), including 1,890 over the past day.
Other reported losses include 159,128 vehicles and fuel tankers, 4,800 pieces of special equipment, 5,126 cruise missiles, and 2,878 ground-based robotic systems.
The Ukrainian military did not provide a breakdown of how many of the estimated personnel losses were killed or wounded. The figures are Ukraine’s estimates and have not been independently verified.
The General Staff released the tally on Putin’s 74th birthday, framing the figures as a message to the Russian president.
ISW Russian Offensive Campaign Assessment, November 6, 2026
“On the occasion of V. Putin’s 74th birthday, the General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine presents an interim tally of Russian army losses,” the statement said.
“Having unleashed the largest war on the continent since World War II, the Russian dictator drives his country closer to the abyss – and himself toward the dustbin of history – with each passing year.”
The General Staff added Ukraine would continue fighting Russian forces to secure a just and lasting peace.
Ukraine’s Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha also used Putin’s birthday to highlight Russia’s military losses and call for greater international pressure on Moscow.
“On Putin’s birthday, Russian generals brought him his favorite present: war crimes,” Sybiha wrote on X, referring to Russia’s latest massive missile and drone attack on Ukraine.
Sybiha said the attack hit residential buildings and critical infrastructure in Kyiv, Dnipro, Zaporizhzhia, Kremenchuk, and Pryluky, killing over 10 people across the country.
“What Russian generals fail to tell Putin is that he is not winning this war and never will,” Sybiha wrote, adding that Russia had lost 1.6 million troops killed and injured without achieving a single strategic goal of its invasion.
He also argued that Russia’s advances had stalled and that Ukraine had begun liberating more territory than Russian forces were managing to occupy.
According to Sybiha, Russia’s economy is declining and its global influence is waning because Putin “refuses to end this war.”
Acknowledging the heavy cost of the war for Ukraine, Sybiha said Ukrainians would continue fighting because the conflict concerns “Ukraine’s survival as a nation and as a state.”
“Russia’s terror must not go unanswered,” he added, urging Ukraine’s international partners to give Putin “real presents” that could push him toward diplomacy.
Sybiha called for stronger sanctions against Russia’s military-industrial complex, including facilities producing ballistic missiles and the Rassvet satellite system. He also urged partners to increase support for Ukraine, particularly air-defense systems and energy assistance ahead of winter.
He said the “ultimate present” for Putin would be a dock in The Hague, referring to Ukraine’s plans to establish the Special Tribunal for the Crime of Aggression Against Ukraine.
“We are preparing the Special Tribunal for the Crime of Aggression Against Ukraine for practical launch already next year,” Sybiha wrote. “Putin and his friends should know that accountability is inevitable.”
Meanwhile, North Korean leader Kim Jong Un congratulated Putin on his birthday, pledging Pyongyang’s “invariable support” for Russia and calling Moscow’s war against Ukraine a “sacred war of justice.”
The message comes as North Korea has evolved from a political supporter of Russia’s invasion into a direct military partner.
Pyongyang has supplied Moscow with weapons and deployed thousands of troops to Russia, including forces that fought alongside Russian units in the Kursk region.
The two countries significantly deepened their military ties after Putin’s June 2024 visit to Pyongyang, when they signed a comprehensive strategic partnership agreement containing a mutual defense clause. Western and South Korean officials have said Russia has provided North Korea with economic assistance, military technology, and battlefield experience in return for its support.

UK house prices flatline as rising mortgage costs weigh on market
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
07:56:02 UTC
16:56:02 KST

UK house prices flatlined in September, according to a leading index, as rising mortgage costs started to weigh on the market.
The average cost of a home was £298,441, roughly the same as it was a year earlier and in the previous month, according to the tracker from Lloyds previously known as the Halifax HPI.
Economists polled by Reuters had predicted a 0.1% monthly rise in prices, according to the median forecast, as well as a 0.2% annual increase.
It came after house prices fell by 0.3% in August, the first decline in three years, as prospective buyers were hit by geopolitical uncertainty, combined with higher mortgage rates and stretched affordability.
In recent weeks most big banks and building societies have put prices up as a result of turmoil in the global bond markets, even though there has not been a change in the Bank of England base rate since December last year.
Andrew Asaam, the mortgages director at Lloyds, said: “While the market overall has been fairly subdued, property prices have so far proved resilient during a period of higher mortgage rates, which has been driven by changing expectations around the future path of base rate.”
On Monday the average cost of a five-year fixed-rate mortgage reached 6% for the first time in three years. Rising mortgage rates are bad news for borrowers whose fixed-rate deals are ending, as well as prospective buyers who are hoping to take out a mortgage to buy a home and the sellers who want the best price from them.
It also adds to the squeeze facing consumers as a result of higher energy bills, linked to the Iran war, while rising prices elsewhere are raising concerns of a new cost of living crisis.
Asaam said: “While higher mortgage rates and wider economic uncertainty are encouraging some people to take a more measured approach, new inquiries from prospective buyers are now at their highest since February.”
He added that any movement in house prices was likely to remain modest.
Tom Bill, the head of UK residential research at the estate agent Knight Frank, said: “This year has been a story of rising energy prices and stalling house prices, as the unpredictable Middle East conflict unfolds and drives borrowing costs higher. This month’s budget adds to the uncertainty as buyers and sellers wonder which of the recurring tax rumours proves to be true.”
The number of people applying for a mortgage to buy a property fell between July and September, as higher borrowing costs continued to affect prospective housebuyers’ budgets, according to quarterly figures from Stonebridge, one of the UK’s largest independent mortgage and protection networks.
Mortgage applications for home purchases fell by 18.2% in the third quarter compared with a year earlier, Stonebridge found, while applications from first-time buyers slumped 18.6% over the same period.
However, rising numbers of applications for remortgaging helped to slow the decline in overall mortgage activity.

Over 20,000 students killed in Gaza, West Bank in 3 years of Israeli genocide: Palestinian ministry

Mohammad Sio
07 October 2026•Update: 07 October 2026
A total of 20,748 Palestinian students and 1,058 educational and administrative staff have been killed in the Gaza Strip and occupied West Bank during three years of Israeli genocide, the Palestinian Education Ministry said Wednesday.
In a statistical report on Israeli violations against the education sector, the ministry said the figures cover students and staff at schools and universities, alongside thousands of injuries and arrests and the destruction or targeting of dozens of educational institutions. 
Gaza
In the Gaza Strip, 19,189 school students and 1,386 university students have been killed, according to the ministry.
Another 28,586 school students and 3,082 university students were injured.
The ministry said 805 educational and administrative staff at schools and 246 university personnel were killed.
Another 3,298 school staff members and 1,493 university staff were injured.
West Bank
In the occupied West Bank, 134 school students and 39 university students were killed, while 871 school students and 283 university students were injured, according to the report.
Israeli forces also detained 416 school students and 481 university students.
Seven educational and administrative staff at schools were killed and 26 others injured, while Israeli forces detained more than 176 teachers and school employees and 21 university staff members.
Since October 2023, more than 74,000 Palestinians have been killed and over 175,000 injured in Gaza by Israel’s genocide, while around 90% of the enclave’s infrastructure has been damaged or destroyed.
Over the same period, Israeli forces and occupiers have intensified attacks across the occupied West Bank, killing 1,210 Palestinians, injuring around 13,350 others and detaining more than 24,600.

Yemen's Houthi rebels targeted Aden International Airport with ballistic missiles and explosive drones early Wednesday, the Transport Ministry said, amid intensifying combat between the Iran-aligned group and Saudi-backed forces.
The Saudi-led coalition, pushing to retake strategic territory seized by the Houthis, said it had intercepted and destroyed a Houthi ballistic missile north of the Saudi capital Riyadh.
The escalation came after Yemeni government forces, with Saudi-led coalition air support, launched a lightning counteroffensive this week to capture the Red Sea coast around the strategic Bab el-Mandeb Strait shipping route and the city of Mokha.
Yemen's government said that forced the Houthis out of areas they had captured last month, reviving a complex 12-year war, which led to one of the world's worst humanitarian crises and fragmented the Arab world's most impoverished country.
One missile landed near the runway at Aden International Airport minutes before a flight from Cairo was due to land, the ministry said. Authorities cancelled the landing and diverted the aircraft to Jeddah, while two planes on the runway were moved away from the area over fears of further strikes, it added. There was no immediate comment from the Houthis.
Aden International Airport is the main international gateway for parts of Yemen outside of Houthi control.
The Saudi-led coalition backing Yemen's internationally recognized government said it had intercepted and destroyed a Houthi ballistic missile north of Riyadh.
It said it was tracking the launch platform over Houthi-controlled Sanaa and would destroy it, but gave no details of casualties or damage.
Houthi military spokesperson Yahya Saree said in a statement that the group had targeted King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh with several drones. There was no immediate Saudi confirmation of an attack on the airport.
The Houthis, which control much of Yemen's north, seized the capital Sanaa in 2014, prompting a military coalition led by Saudi Arabia, fearful of rival Iran's influence in Yemen and chaos on its borders, to intervene. A U.N.-brokered truce in 2022 largely halted heavy fighting, but it did not lead to a lasting settlement, with a spillover from the Iran conflict triggering the latest fighting.
The Saudi-led coalition accuses Iran of arming, training and funding the Houthis. The group, mountain fighters who have emerged as a force of tens of thousands with missiles and drones that threatens the region, denies being part of Iran's Middle East proxy network and says it develops its own weapons. Tehran also rejects the allegations.
Earlier Wednesday, the Saudi-led coalition said it had intercepted and destroyed a Houthi ballistic missile launched towards the southwestern Saudi city of Khamis Mushait, Saudi state television reported.
In a separate statement, Saree said the Houthis had attacked Abha International Airport and an airbase in Khamis Mushait with ballistic missiles and drones. It was not immediately clear whether this was linked to the missile the coalition said it had intercepted near Khamis Mushait. Saudi authorities did not immediately confirm an attack on Abha airport.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky reported that two civilian vessels in Bulgaria’s exclusive economic zone in the Black Sea had been attacked by Russian naval and aerial drones.
The President of Ukraine stated this in his evening address.
According to Zelensky, the Ukrainian Defense Forces had not carried out any operations in that part of the Black Sea.
After clarifying the details with Bulgaria and following consultations between the Ukrainian and Bulgarian navies, Ukraine concluded that the incident was part of a combined Russian attack.
Zelensky also said the incident was part of Russia’s ongoing attempts to make the western Black Sea unsafe for civilian shipping. He instructed the Armed Forces, the Defense Ministry and intelligence agencies to strengthen cooperation with partners to protect maritime routes.
In the early hours of October 6, at around 3:00 a.m., two merchant vessels – the ALFA WATAN, sailing under the Togo flag, and the ABLE, sailing under the Palau flag – were attacked approximately 80 nautical miles east of the Bulgarian city of Byala. It was the first known attack on merchant vessels in Bulgaria’s exclusive economic zone.
The ALFA WATAN suffered critical damage and sank. A fire broke out aboard the ABLE following the strike, and all 18 crew members abandoned the vessel. The Bulgarian ferry DIOSCURIA evacuated them.
The ABLE crew later told the Bulgarian publication Maritime.bg that they received no warning before the strike. They said one of the drones attacked the vessel from below, suggesting a maritime drone was used.
Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev confirmed that the attack involved both a maritime and an aerial drone. At the same time, he stressed that the Bulgarian side has not yet been able to reliably determine where the drones were launched from.
According to Radev, one vessel was heading north and sank, while the other was sailing south carrying wheat. He described the incident as serious and said Bulgaria would continue investigating the circumstances of the attack.
The Bulgarian government confirmed that the rescue operation is underway in the country’s exclusive economic zone.
The incident occurred a day after Russian drones sank the bulk carrier Royad Mammadov, which had departed from the Ukrainian port of Izmail carrying grain to Italy.

“I ask residents and visitors to Sochi not to put themselves at risk and to wait for an official decision on reopening,” Proshunin wrote on Telegram.
Sirius officials also closed all beaches and urged residents to limit their time outdoors and keep windows shut where possible.
“We are continuously monitoring water and air quality together with Roshydromet,” Sirius administration head Dmitry Plishkin said, referring to Russia’s weather and environmental monitoring agency.
The fire broke out around 6 p.m. Tuesday, sending thick black smoke over Sochi. Preliminary reports identified the vessel as the Aframax Rio, which may have been carrying between 95,000 and 100,000 metric tons of oil, according to open-source information cited by the independent news outlet Astra.
Transportation Minister Andrei Nikitin said the oil-laden tanker had been attacked by unmanned boats. He added that all 23 crew members, who are Indian nationals, were rescued.

Representatives of public institutions, local authorities, businesses and the recycling industry from Türkiye and Czechia gathered in Istanbul for the Türkiye-Czechia Sustainable Recycling Forum to explore new opportunities for cooperation.
Organized jointly by the Czech Consulate General in Istanbul, the Our World Foundation and the Climate and Sustainability Sciences Research Foundation (ISBAV), the forum took place at the Social Facilities Conference Hall on Istanbul Technical University's Macka Campus.
The event focused on opportunities for cooperation between Türkiye and Czechia in recycling and sustainable waste management.
Participants included Istanbul Deputy Governor Cengiz Karabulut, Czech Consul General in Istanbul Olga Hajflerova, the Istanbul Metropolitan Municipality's Head of Foreign Relations, Barbaros Buyuksagnak, and its Head of Environmental Protection and Control, Aysen Erdincler.
Representatives of Türkiye's Environment, Urbanization and Climate Change Ministry and the Turkish Environment Agency also attended.
Alongside public institutions and local authorities from both countries, the forum brought together representatives of companies, industry organizations and civil society groups operating in recycling, plastics, waste management and environmental technologies.
Discussions covered sustainable waste management, recycling technologies and industry cooperation and investment opportunities as well as potential commercial and technological partnerships between Turkish and Czech companies.
Our World Foundation President Kahraman Haliscelik delivered the first opening address.
Haliscelik said the forum brought together representatives of public institutions, local authorities, industry and the private sector from Türkiye and Czechia on a common platform.
Its main objective, he said, was to move beyond exchanging views and pave the way for concrete cooperation.
He said relations between the two countries could be further strengthened through new partnerships in recycling and sustainable waste management.
"Our aim is to turn dialogue into cooperation, and cooperation into concrete projects and commercial partnerships," he said.
Haliscelik stressed that recycling and sustainable waste management could no longer be viewed solely as environmental issues, saying they were becoming increasingly strategic in terms of technology, investment, competitiveness and economic opportunities.
Strong cooperation among public institutions, local authorities and the private sector would play an important role in implementing sustainable solutions, he said, expressing hope that contacts established during the forum would mark the beginning of new projects and long-term partnerships.
Haliscelik thanked Hajflerova for her support in organizing the forum as well as ISBAV, TUDAM and the Turkish and Czech institutions, organizations and companies that contributed to the program.
Speaking after Haliscelik, Hajflerova highlighted the importance of developing cooperation between Türkiye and Czechia in sustainability and recycling.
She said bringing public and private sector representatives from both countries together on the same platform was important for establishing new business connections.
Hajflerova said the forum provided an important platform both for sharing knowledge and experience and for establishing concrete, long-term partnerships between Turkish and Czech institutions and companies.
She said the two countries had significant potential to complement each other in this field.
She added that bringing together different stakeholders from Türkiye and Czechia would strengthen the exchange of experience.
Contacts in sustainability, recycling and waste management could also create new opportunities for the two countries' economic and commercial relations, she said.
Following the opening remarks, representatives of Czech public institutions and businesses delivered presentations.
Vlastislav Kotrc from Czechia's Environment Ministry, Jan Trnobransky from the Czech Environmental Information Agency (CENIA), Matyas Kousek from Czechia's Industry and Trade Ministry and Eva Langerova from the Czech Chamber of Commerce's International Relations Department discussed their institutions' work and opportunities for cooperation between Türkiye and Czechia.
Their presentations covered Czechia's activities in recycling, environmental protection and waste management, environmental information and data management, industrial policies, and potential cooperation between the private sectors of the two countries.
Representatives of Czech companies attending the forum also gave short presentations outlining their areas of activity and the solutions they had developed.
The presentations highlighted potential partnerships that Czech companies could establish with institutions and businesses in Türkiye.
The forum also featured a panel titled "The Future of Recycling in Türkiye: Sustainable Waste Management, Industry Cooperation and New Opportunities."
Speakers included Istanbul Metropolitan Municipality's Head of Environmental Protection and Control, Aysen Erdincler, TUDAM board member Kayhan Ural, and Salih Kanbak, representing the Turkish Plastics Industry Foundation (PAGEV).
Panelists discussed the current state and future of Türkiye's recycling industry, addressing sustainable waste management, the role of local authorities, industrial transformation and cooperation across sectors.
Alongside recycling's environmental benefits, the panel examined its potential to create economic value.
Participants exchanged views on improving coordination among public institutions, local authorities and the private sector, adopting new technologies, and expanding sustainable recycling models.
The panel also addressed challenges facing the recycling industry, more efficient use of resources, improvements to recovery processes, and new investment and cooperation opportunities that could emerge in the coming period.
During the afternoon session, company representatives from Türkiye and Czechia held business-to-business meetings.
Participants exchanged information about their activities, technologies and projects while discussing potential commercial partnerships, technology cooperation and investment opportunities in recycling and sustainable waste management.
The B2B meetings aimed to ensure that the forum would serve as more than a platform for public institutions and industry representatives to share knowledge and experience.
They also sought to establish direct connections between Turkish and Czech companies and lay the groundwork for developing concrete projects.
On the second day of the two-day program, the Czech delegation is scheduled to make technical visits to facilities operating in recycling and waste management in Kocaeli.
The visits are expected to allow delegates to examine practices and facilities in Türkiye firsthand, establish direct contact with industry representatives, and continue discussions initiated in Istanbul through on-site meetings.
They aim to help turn opportunities for cooperation between Türkiye and Czechia in recycling and sustainable waste management into concrete projects while developing contacts among public institutions, industry organizations and companies into long-term partnerships.
