Has Russia’s fuel crisis given Iranian oil an opening in Central Asia?
Iran’s oil exports have struggled amid a US blockade. A Russian energy crisis because of Ukrainian attacks could help.
Countries in Central Asia have begun buying oil from Iran as the Russian fuel supplies they have long depended on run dry amid Ukraine’s mounting attacks on Russian energy infrastructure to degrade Moscow’s war effort.
In August, Tajikistan announced it was receiving oil and petroleum products from Iran as Dushanbe faces uncertainty over its fuel supply from Russia. Tehran also agreed to establish a joint refinery in Kyrgyzstan in August, and supply the country with crude oil.
Moscow has been facing fuel shortages due to Ukrainian drone strikes on its refineries as Russia’s war on its neighbour continues to rage.
Can the Russian fuel crisis give Iran a new oil opening in Central Asia?
Here’s what we know:
Which Central Asian countries have been affected by Russia’s fuel crisis?
Ukraine’s offensive against Russian energy infrastructure has caused panic across Central Asian countries like Tajikistan and Kyrgyzstan, which are dependent on Moscow for oil and petroleum products.
Tajikistan has traditionally sourced up to 80 percent of its petroleum products from Russia. Kyrgyzstan also relies on petroleum product imports, sourcing more than 90 percent of its petrol from Russia.
“They’ve been hurt the most,” Galiya Ibragimova, a Moldova-based expert on Central Asia with Carnegie Politika, which has its headquarters in Berlin, told Al Jazeera in an interview in August.
Kyrgyzstan is a member of the Eurasian Economic Union, the free trade bloc of five former Soviet nations dominated by Russia and the Kremlin’s political decisions.
Tajikistan is not a member of the group, but it bought discounted Russian fuel as “payment for political loyalty, not because [Russian President Vladimir] Putin is so kind”, Ibragimova added.
Kazakhstan, meanwhile, boasts three giant, Soviet-era oil refineries. Still, fuel prices in the country have increased by 15.6 percent this year, the UlusMedia website reported on July 10.
Uzbekistan, on the other hand, is less dependent on Russian energy, with domestic production capable of reaching 100,000 tonnes of petroleum products per month, satisfying most of the country’s needs. But due to the increase in oil demand from its regional neighbours, Uzbekistan has also been forced to diversify its imports and has begun striking deals with countries like Georgia and Iraq.
Why is there a fuel crisis in Russia?
Russia has been facing a severe fuel deficit as Kyiv’s drone strikes – launched in an effort to degrade Moscow’s ability to maintain its ongoing invasion of Ukraine – have knocked out an estimated quarter to half of its total oil refining capacity.
To tackle the problem, Russia has imposed fuel rationing. Sales are often limited to about 20-30 litres (about 5-8 US gallons) per vehicle, and drivers must pump fuel strictly into vehicle tanks. Filling jerry cans is largely prohibited.
Earlier, the government banned petrol and jet fuel exports. Officials are now weighing a ban on diesel exports, too. Authorities have loosened fuel-quality regulations, temporarily allowing lower-grade fuel for the domestic market.
A state of emergency has also been declared in Russian-occupied Crimea, which Moscow annexed from Ukraine in 2014. A Russian-owned oil firm in India, Nayara Energy, has reportedly sold petroleum to Russia.
While Russian President Putin acknowledges the crisis, he appears reluctant to end the war on Ukraine and insists the situation is under control.
“These attacks on our facilities certainly create problems – that is obvious. We are currently seeing a certain shortage, though I would say it is not critical,” he said earlier this year.
“First and foremost, we have to rapidly and significantly increase production of air defence systems that are most in demand. We must also continue to improve them… Repairs at refineries must be completed more quickly.”
So, how is Iran helping Central Asia?
Amid Russian fuel shortages, Central Asian countries like Tajikistan have begun striking deals with Iran.
In August, Tajikistan’s Energy and Water Resources Ministry told the Asia-Plus news agency that the country is receiving oil and petroleum products from Iran. The ministry has not disclosed the route used to transport the products, but Tajikistan expects to receive 2.55 million tonnes of oil and petroleum products from Iran.
Besides Tajikistan, Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian welcomed a proposal from Kyrgyzstan in August to establish a joint refinery in the Central Asian country, according to a report by Iran’s Tasnim news agency,
Under the agreement, Pezeshkian said, “The crude oil needed by the refinery can be supplied by Iran, and the products can be divided between the two sides.”
Will exporting oil to Central Asian countries help Iran?
The United States and Israel’s war on Iran has affected Tehran’s oil revenues. Data released by the government-administered Statistical Center of Iran in September showed that gross domestic product (GDP) shrank by 10.1 percent year-on-year between March 21 and June 20, the first quarter of the Persian calendar.
Tehran’s ability to sell crude has also been dramatically curtailed by the US naval blockade of Iran’s ports, imposed for most of the war, which began in late February.
Iranian crude and condensate loadings collapsed from about two million barrels per day (bpd) in March to roughly 740,000bpd in July and just 220,000-255,000bpd in August, according to estimates from Kpler and Vortexa.
TankerTrackers.com told the Reuters news agency in September that 29 tankers, carrying 36.11 million barrels of crude, were trapped in the Strait of Hormuz. Meanwhile, Vortexa estimated that total Iranian crude afloat had fallen from 135 million barrels at the end of July to 107 million barrels by late August.
Amid these challenges, Iran has been scrambling to find new countries to trade oil with. Russian fuel shortages have opened up new opportunities for Iran in Central Asia, at least in the short term, according to analysts.
How does Iranian oil reach Tajikistan and Kyrgyzstan?
Iran does not share a border with either country.
To get to Tajikistan, Iranian “oil and refined products have to cross Turkmenistan and Uzbekistan by rail”, said Frederic Schneider, a nonresident senior fellow at the Middle East Council on Global Affairs.
To get to Kyrgyzstan, Iranian oil would also need to pass through Turkmenistan and Uzbekistan.
Is trading oil with Iran logistically sustainable for Central Asia?
It is unlikely, Schneider said.
“This opportunity [for Iran] depends on Ukraine continuing to hit Russian refineries, which seems unlikely, both given the waning of Ukraine’s strike capability and the US government’s demand to stop the attacks as they put too much strain on global oil markets,” he told Al Jazeera.
He noted that US President Donald Trump has pressed his Ukrainian counterpart, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, repeatedly in September for an “energy truce” with Russia, since diesel prices have become a political problem for Trump ahead of the November midterm elections in the US.
“Those truces have so far collapsed within hours, but the direction is clear. Once the strikes stop, or once Russia repairs its plants, Russian fuel will come back to Central Asia duty-free under Eurasian Economic Union arrangements, and Iran will struggle to compete on price,” he said.
Logistics also favour Russia with respect to importing oil to countries like Tajikistan and Kyrgyzstan, he said.
Unlike Iran, Russia shares a border with both.
“Tajikistan’s own request [for oil] would need around 51,000 rail tank cars, and its main refinery at Dangara has never operated commercially at scale. Russia, by contrast, has decades’ worth of logistics infrastructure, pipelines, rail links, and supply contracts into the region,” Schneider said.
Is Central Asia a big enough market to compensate for Iran’s Hormuz losses?
No, according to Schneider.
Tajikistan’s total demand, Schneider said, was about 50,000bpd.
That is a drop in the ocean compared with the 1.7 million bpd Iran exported by sea a year ago. China reported $9.96bn in two-way trade with Iran in 2025, a figure that does not include some $31.2bn in Iranian oil shipments, according to the US-China Economic and Security Review Commission.
“This suggests that Central Asia can be a useful outlet for Iranian diesel and gasoline, but it cannot replace the Chinese market,” Schneider said.
For Tehran, Central Asia’s importance depends on how the US-Israel war on Iran develops, he said, adding that Tehran also needs to stay on good terms with Russia, with which it has a deep strategic partnership.
“Iran cannot afford to be seen as poaching Russian customers too aggressively, so it will present itself as a stopgap supplier, which, again, limits how much it can earn there,” he said.
What other risks does Central Asia face in buying Iranian oil?
Schneider warned that Central Asian nations could be hit with Washington’s secondary sanctions on Iran.
“Legally, US secondary sanctions apply to any foreign company or bank that conducts a significant transaction in Iranian petroleum, wherever it is based, and the Treasury expanded the list of sanctionable conduct in August. A Treasury official has already warned publicly that anyone in this trade ‘incurs that risk themselves’,” he noted.
But Schneider said that, politically, the US sanctioning Central Asian governments is unlikely.
“Central Asia is the arena of a new ‘Great Game’ between Russia, China and the United States, and Washington is courting the region harder than at any point since the 1990s, chiefly for its critical minerals. Kazakhstan alone holds about half of the minerals the US classifies as critical, including uranium and tungsten,” he said.
“Sanctioning a Central Asian government for buying fuel from Iran would push them straight back into closer ties to Russia and China,” he noted.
“What I would expect instead are targeted designations of individual traders, rail and logistics operators and smaller banks, combined with quiet pressure on the region’s correspondent banks. That alone is enough to raise the cost and slow the trade, but will come at the price of these countries redoubling their efforts to decouple economically and financially from the US.”

Good morning. It’s Wednesday. On today’s docket: Israel’s Ambassador to France Joshua Zarka responds to mounting controversy over the removal of the Israeli flag at an exhibition in the European Parliament, and the latest on the suspected pneumonic plague outbreak.

Tensions high: On the third anniversary of the October 7 attacks on Israel – in which Hamas killed around 1200 people and took 251 hostage, triggering an Israeli offensive in Gaza which has killed over 70,000 Palestinians – the European Parliament has become the scene of a fresh political clash.
Israeli flag removed: On Monday evening, Rima Hassan, a Member of the European Parliament (MEP) from the far-left France Unbowed party, reportedly knocked over an Israeli flag displayed at an exhibition dedicated to victims of the attack. Photos on social media show both the Israeli and EU flags lying on the floor.
‘Intimidation’: The Parliament’s President, Roberta Metsola, told the chamber yesterday that she took the incident “extremely seriously” and that all appropriate measures were being taken against Hassan, without naming her. “We cannot have actions that could make people fearful of speaking. Hassan has acknowledged removing the Israeli flag but denied intentionally toppling the EU flag, with her office noting in a statement that neither flag was “stepped on or damaged”.
She has also framed her actions as a response to the Israeli state’s support for the exhibition, and claimed that speeches made during the event denied the existence of Palestine.
Outrage: The incident has sparked widespread outrage, with centre-right MEP François-Xavier Bellamy describing the act as a “form of complicity with those who want to reintroduce antisemitic hatred” in Europe. ‘Disrespectful’: “I cannot understand how a person that aims to be a politician, that aims to represent the public, can be so violent and disrespectful of the death of thousands of people that has been caused by the same cause that she's trying to help,” the Israeli ambassador to France, Joshua Zarka, told our chief editor Maria Tadeo in an interview.

But he added that there is “one party that is openly antisemitic in France, and that’s LFI (France Unbowed)”. Watch.
D-Day: Meanwhile, Europe’s eastern flank continues to be rattled by hybrid warfare. But a fatal drone incursion off Romania’s coast on Monday, which killed two and injured scores more, begs the question whether these incidents continue to be “hybrid” – and who is to blame, Angela Skujins writes.

KSA launches air safety probe into flydubai incident
Saudi Arabia has launched an air accident probe following last week's cockpit stabbing on a flydubai jet, as experts examine any fallout for aviation safety alongside a separate UAE-led criminal investigation, Reuters reported- citing three people close to the matter.
Safety probes designed to keep flights safe are normal after accidents but are not mandatory when a deliberate act is involved, such as the suspected attempt by a co-pilot to bring down the Israel-bound flydubai jet on September 30.
Until now, it has remained unclear whether Saudi Arabia would go ahead with such a probe, which experts say could test a system of international co-operation designed to make recommendations for safety without attempting to assign blame.
The people close to the matter said Saudi Arabia had notified specialist aviation agencies abroad that it would carry out a safety investigation under international rules into flight FZ1073, which was in Saudi airspace when the co-pilot attacked the captain with an axe.
Saudi Arabia's National Transport Safety Center, which has responsibility for accident investigations, did not immediately comment following the Reuters report.
The Saudi government and the country's regulator also did not answer requests for comment.
The US National Transportation Safety Board, which would be closely involved in any probe because the Boeing 737 MAX jet that survived a steep plunge was designed and built in the United States, could not immediately be reached for comment.

"These actions continue to demonstrate Iran’s intent to assert presence along key transit lanes and maintain pressure on transiting vessels," the JMIC said.

Drone boats fight each other at sea for the first time
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
07:30:13 BST
15:30:13 KST

A Ukrainian uncrewed surface vessel armed with a mounted gun destroyed a Russian one-way attack boat in the Black Sea last month, in what is assessed as the first direct engagement between drone boats from the two sides, according to British Defence Intelligence.
In its daily update on Tuesday, Defence Intelligence said: “On 12 September 2026 Ukraine successfully interdicted a Russian one-way attack uncrewed surface vehicle (USV) in the Black Sea. Ukrainian forces employed a Sargan-3000 USV with a mounted gun to destroy the Russian craft before it could pose a threat to Ukrainian sea lines of communication. It is highly unlikely the Russian USV was armed with any counter-drone capability. This event almost certainly marks the first time a Russian and Ukrainian USV have engaged each other directly.”
The update went on: “Ukraine has innovatively combined weaponry in its USV fleet. In early 2024, Ukraine began to equip some of its Magura USV’s with air to air missiles, which it used to successfully shoot down a Su-30 Russian fighter and a Russian military helicopter in 2025. Ukraine’s latest iteration, displayed on Ukrainian Independence Day in Kyiv on 24 August 2026 is a Magura MV11 designed to intercept Russian uncrewed aerial systems.”
Those qualifiers are not loose language, and carry defined meanings in British intelligence reporting. Under the probability yardstick Defence Intelligence publishes alongside its updates, highly unlikely means a five to twenty per cent chance, while almost certainly, the term applied to this being the first such engagement, means ninety-five per cent or more.
The Magura began as a means of attacking Russian warships at Sevastopol and Novorossiysk, and did so effectively enough to push much of the Black Sea Fleet out of Crimea. It then became a launcher for air-to-air missiles, achieving shootdowns that had no precedent anywhere. It is now being built to intercept drones, which is three roles in under three years.
Russia has meanwhile been fielding one-way attack boats of its own, and the September engagement is where the two developments met. A drone boat that can find and destroy another drone boat is a different proposition from one built to ram a frigate, and it means the Black Sea now has an uncrewed fight going on inside the crewed one.

Marlon Blackwell Architects’ U.S. Pavilion for the 2025 Venice Architecture Biennale to Be Reconstructed at Crystal Bridges, Arkansas
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
06:30:00 UTC
15:30:00 KST

The timber-framed structure designed by Marlon Blackwell Architects for the U.S. Pavilion at the 2025 Venice Architecture Biennale will be reconstructed at Crystal Bridges Museum of American Art in Bentonville, Arkansas, in late 2027. Originally installed in the Giardini as part of PORCH: An Architecture of Generosity, the structure will return in a new setting as a freestanding pavilion on the museum's 134-acre campus. Following the close of the Biennale in November 2025, it was dismantled and transported from Venice to Arkansas, where it has remained in storage ahead of its planned reconstruction.
PORCH explored the porch as an architectural space for gathering, exchange, and civic life, considering its continued relevance across different social and cultural contexts in the United States. The exhibition was commissioned by the Fay Jones School of Architecture and Design at the University of Arkansas, DesignConnects, and Crystal Bridges, with Peter MacKeith, Susan Chin, and Rod Bigelow serving as co-commissioners. Alongside the structure, the U.S. Pavilion presented approximately 50 projects selected through an open call, while performances, workshops, readings, and discussions expanded the program beyond the exhibition itself.
The pavilion structure was developed by Marlon Blackwell Architects in collaboration with designers Stephen Burks, Julie Bargmann, and Maura Rockcastle, bringing together architectural, design, and landscape perspectives around the exhibition's central theme. Rather than functioning solely as an architectural object, the porch provided an outdoor setting for the Biennale's public program and was used for gatherings throughout the exhibition. Its reconstruction in Arkansas will allow the structure to continue serving a public function beyond its original presentation in Venice.
At Crystal Bridges, the pavilion will be installed within a 134-acre campus that combines museum buildings with native Ozark forest, streams, ponds, and more than five miles of walking trails. The museum has described its grounds as an integral part of the visitor experience, with architecture and landscape connected through paths, outdoor spaces, and works of art.
The reconstruction comes as Crystal Bridges continues to expand and adapt its campus. Earlier this year, the museum completed a 114,000-square-foot addition designed by Safdie Architects, extending the original 2011 building with new galleries, educational facilities, public gathering spaces, and connections to the surrounding landscape. Coen+Partners led the landscape design, incorporating native planting, limestone, restored stream edges, and new outdoor areas. The planned reconstruction of PORCH will add another freestanding structure to this evolving architectural and landscape setting.
In other recent news, several national pavilions have begun announcing their curators and exhibition proposals for the 2027 Venice Architecture Biennale. Luxembourg will present Excess! On the Overconsumption of Living Space, curated by Céline Zimmer, Bùi Quý Sơn, and Paul-Antoine Lucas of Exutoire, exploring the unequal distribution and overconsumption of living space. Germany will present CONVIVERE — A Repertoire of Living Together, curated by Kawahara Krause Architects, Andres Lepik, and Olga Cobuscean, focusing on shared spaces within housing as sites of everyday coexistence. Türkiye will present Spolia Futures, curated by ba-be commons, which examines spolia, the reuse of architectural elements, as an evolving architectural practice.

Israel’s Central Elections Committee has ordered Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, for a second time, to remove a video from his personal social media accounts and pay legal costs after ruling it amounted to election propaganda.
Israel’s Channel 7 reported on Tuesday that committee chairman Supreme Court Justice Noam Sohlberg ordered Netanyahu to delete footage filmed at Tel Nof Air Base and pay 2,500 shekels (about $821) in costs.
Sohlberg ruled that publishing the video on Netanyahu’s personal accounts violated election law by using public resources, including a military base and an Israeli Air Force aircraft.
Netanyahu posted the footage on September 29, with an Israeli Air Force aircraft visible in the background.
He warned that Israel could face attacks before the election, saying there were “indications that our enemies will try to attack us before the elections”, according to Israeli Channel 15.
The latest decision followed Sohlberg’s ruling on Sunday on five petitions concerning Netanyahu’s use of official speeches and the military for election propaganda on his personal accounts.
The petitions included a video showing Netanyahu during a visit to an Israeli military position in southern Lebanon.
Sohlberg ruled that the edited clip focused on the achievements of the government and prime minister, while parts relating to boosting soldiers’ morale and honouring them had been removed.
“This is, of course, election propaganda,” Sohlberg said. He ordered Netanyahu to remove the posts and pay 29,000 shekels (about $9,000) in costs.
Israel is scheduled to hold a Knesset election on October 27. Parties in Netanyahu’s governing coalition, led by his Likud party, are competing against opposition parties.
Recent polls suggest neither bloc would independently secure the 61 seats needed to form a government. A poll by public broadcaster KAN on Sunday projected 52 seats for opposition parties and 51 for Netanyahu’s coalition.
Netanyahu has led the government since late December 2022. He is standing trial on corruption charges, which he denies, and the International Criminal Court has issued an arrest warrant for him over alleged war crimes and crimes against humanity in Gaza.

Estonia hold on for 0-0 Nations League home draw against Iceland
Estonia played out a hard-fought 0-0 draw at home against Iceland in the Nations League on Tuesday, leaving them second in Group C4 after four games.
The same teams opened the cycle on September 26 in Reykjavik, drawing 1-1, with Andri Guðjohnsen (Blackburn Rovers), son of former Chelsea legend Eiður Guðjohnsen, scoring in the 45th minute and defender Maksim Paskotši (KAA Ghent) later equalizing.
Estonia came into the game knowing a win would put them top of the group with two rounds left, and having beaten Luxembourg at the weekend.
Estonia sat second on five points before the match, two behind Iceland, and were without captain Karol Mets (VfL Bochum) through suspension — Paskotši wore the armband in his absence.
Elron put its last train to Keila 25 minutes back in the timetable Tuesday night to accommodate fans, and President Alar Karis, who leaves office on Monday, was present at the match, as was Estonian FA (EJK) President Aivar Pohlak.
On the night, Iceland created two dangerous situations from set pieces early on, with both requiring referee decisions on penalty appeals. The most threatening came in the 12th minute, when a corner struck Levadia midfielder Rasmus Peetson at the near post and Estonian goalkeeper Matvei Igonen (Degerfors) cleared the ball off the goal line.
Peetson has so far emerged as Estonia's most dangerous attacking player in this Nations League window, and he proved it in the first half: early on, Iceland's 'keeper Hákon Valdimarsson (Brentford) dealt with his effort toward the far corner, and in the closing minutes of the half Peetson sent a strong shot into Valdimarsson's body after a good pass from Patrik Kristal.
An hour in, striker Patrik Kristal turned brilliantly on the right and delivered an accurate cross for Estonia into the Icelandic box, but substitute Mattias Käit and Kristal's teammate at FC Thun failed to connect with his head, and the ball fell to forward Robi Saarma (K Pardubice), who was completely unmarked but not ready in time.
Estonia had 13 shots over the match and continued searching for a winner, with manager Jürgen Henn handing a debut to young Levadia midfielder Maksimilian Skvortsov. Iceland were more dangerous in the final quarter-hour, however, but Paskotši, Erko Jonne Tõugjas (Halmstads BK) and Märten Kuusk (Polonia Warsaw) all defended well.
"Very positive result, although we came to win," captain-for-a-night Paskotši told ERR post-match. "Against this team, two draws is quite a good result. Hard fight, lots of running and duels. It maybe wasn't the most beautiful game, but for me as a defender: I really enjoyed it!"
"I knew what group we're actually in. Maybe our previous results haven't been the best, but in this window we showed that these are the games we have to do properly," he said. "I want to really praise all the players. Both those who started and those who came on: they did so much and I hope our fans see that too," he went on.
The UEFA Nations League is a biennial competition in which Europe's national teams are divided into four tiers, with promotion and relegation between them and a path to the European Championship playoffs.
After Tuesday, Iceland lead Group C4 on eight points, Estonia are second with six, while Bulgaria have four points and Luxembourg three.
The next and final fixtures are on November 13 (away to Luxembourg) and November 16 (at home against Bulgaria).

Black Sea Shipping Faces Rising Risks as War Hits Ports and Supply Chains
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
06:24:00 UTC
15:24:00 KST

The Black Sea is becoming the most dangerous area for commercial shipping as Russian attacks increasingly target ports, vessels, railways and energy infrastructure, according to a Financial Times analysis.
For decades, the Black Sea served as a crucial gateway connecting Ukraine’s economy with global markets. The latest Russian air campaign is now threatening not only Ukraine’s ability to export grain and other agricultural products but also the resilience of the logistics system supporting global food markets.
The Financial Times analysis describes the Black Sea as more than a naval theater in the Russia-Ukraine war, with the maritime zone becoming an important part of the conflict’s economic front. Attacks on ports and commercial ships form part of a wider campaign that also strikes railway networks, warehouses, power infrastructure and urban systems.
According to Lloyd’s List data cited by the Financial Times, July 2026 was the most dangerous month for commercial shipping in the Black Sea since the full-scale war began.
The growing danger is no longer limited to conventional naval confrontation. Russia is striking Ukrainian ports and vessels, while Ukraine is attacking Russian ships, including vessels associated with the so-called "shadow fleet."
This has created conditions in which shipowners face increasingly difficult risk management and insurance coverage that is becoming more complicated and expensive. Data cited by the British publication shows that the Black Sea has become a deadlier area for commercial shipping during this period than even the waters around the Strait of Hormuz.
The consequences go beyond the immediate danger to ships and their crews. When maritime transport becomes excessively risky, disruption spreads through the supply chain from producers to international markets.
Odesa and its network of ports are central to this picture. Before Russia’s full-scale invasion in February 2022, more than 90% of Ukraine’s grain exports moved through Black Sea ports, representing tens of millions of tons of agricultural products each year.
That system is now under sustained pressure.
Russian strikes are hitting ports, warehouses and the infrastructure needed to handle and move cargo. Some facilities have been damaged, leaving operators to repair them while continuing work during periods between attacks.
A port’s physical survival therefore does not guarantee that it can function normally. A damaged crane, destroyed silo, power shortage or lack of locomotives can interrupt the supply chain even when the maritime route itself remains technically open.
The Financial Times analysis points to a broader feature of modern attacks on the Ukrainian economy: stopping every ship is unnecessary if the surrounding system can be made unreliable, expensive and dangerous.
Ukrainian agriculture continues to produce substantial volumes, but an increasingly difficult logistical barrier separates that production from global buyers.
As warehouses reach capacity, farmers are storing grain outdoors, while others are being forced to sell their crops at sharply reduced prices.
This has produced a contradiction in which harvests can remain strong and productivity can increase even as farmers’ revenues decline.
Ukrainian Agriculture Minister Taras Vysotskyi estimates that a prolonged closure of the ports could cost Ukraine at least billion from June 2026 to June 2027. That figure would represent about one-fifth of the country’s total export revenue in the previous year.
Ukraine had been expected to export about 64 million tons of agricultural products, but continued restrictions could reduce that amount to roughly half.
The impact would not be limited to farmers, extending to export earnings, the balance of payments and the financial stability of the Ukrainian state.
The Black Sea’s importance also reaches beyond Ukraine’s economy.
Before the war, Russia and Ukraine together supplied about one-third of global wheat exports and around one-fifth of global corn exports. Disruption to Ukrainian exports therefore carries the potential to affect international markets.
With less Ukrainian produce reaching global buyers, transport expenses increase and risks for shipowners and insurers rise.
For countries reliant on grain imports, that can create additional pressure on food prices and food security.
The conflict around Odesa therefore has consequences far beyond the local area. The Black Sea conflict now differs substantially from the situation in 2022.
At the beginning of the full-scale war, the principal threats to shipping came from Russia’s naval blockade and sea mines. The subsequent decline in the Russian Navy’s position and the Black Sea Grain Initiative allowed a significant share of commercial traffic to recover temporarily.
The character of the threat has since changed.
The widespread deployment of uncrewed aerial vehicles, or UAVs, has enabled attacks against both port facilities and ships, changing the risk calculations for commercial operators.
Routes through Danube ports, which can provide alternatives to major Black Sea terminals, also cannot guarantee complete safety.
The central issue is therefore no longer simply whether a physical maritime corridor remains available, but whether it can be used at a risk and cost level that is acceptable.
A major point in the Financial Times analysis is that maritime exports start well before a ship reaches a port.
Ukrainian agricultural products must first travel from inland areas to the terminals, making attacks on railway infrastructure directly relevant to Black Sea exports.
Damage to tracks and the destruction of locomotives reduce the amount of cargo that can reach the ports. Representatives of the port industry say locomotives have already been lost, while Ukrainian authorities are seeking replacement units from European countries that operate on the same railway gauge.
The resulting logistics chain is tightly interconnected: field, warehouse, railway, port, ship and international market.
Damage to any one part of that chain could stop the wider system from functioning.
Chornomorsk offers a particularly clear example.
Accounts cited by the Financial Times say the Risoil terminal has suffered serious damage, including damage to cranes, silos and sunflower oil storage tanks.
Russian attack tactics are also changing, shifting from isolated drone strikes toward large-scale assaults involving heavier weapons.
Even an immediate halt to the attacks would not automatically allow the port to return to its former capacity.
Infrastructure can remain technically present while operating only at a fraction of its previous level, adding another dimension to the war’s economic impact.
Energy represents another front.
Ports depend on electricity, and Russia is striking electrical substations and transformers, including facilities in the Odesa region. Some major substations have been attacked repeatedly, while dozens of transformers have been destroyed.
Such infrastructure cannot be rebuilt within a few days.
Constructing a major substation takes considerable time, while repeated attacks can turn repairs into a continuing cycle of rebuilding followed by another strike.
For ports, this creates another major vulnerability. Without reliable electricity, cranes, warehouses, pumps and other facilities cannot function normally.
The war is also acquiring a new aerial dimension.
In Odesa, the conflict is increasingly experienced as a constant threat rather than a distant front. Ukrainian forces are employing relatively inexpensive interceptor drones against Russian Shaheds, with a unit commander cited by the Financial Times saying their effectiveness against the slower drones is about 95%.
Jet-powered drones, however, present a more serious threat.
The situation demonstrates one of the basic imbalances of modern air warfare: an inexpensive attacking drone can require a much more costly defensive response.
Ukraine must distribute its limited air defense resources among different threats, from swarms of inexpensive drones to faster aircraft and missiles.
The coming winter presents another challenge.
Odesa will need to keep electricity, heating, water supplies, transportation, industry and port operations running at the same time.
Generators and temporary measures can provide assistance but cannot completely substitute for the national energy system.
As a result, attacks on the power grid and ports reinforce one another.
A less stable power system makes port operations more difficult, while weaker port activity increases economic pressure.
Ukraine is seeking ways to revive maritime exports and remains in contact with key countries and buyers.
The fundamental issue, however, is the safety of ships.
A corridor that is technically open has little economic value if shipowners cannot obtain insurance at acceptable rates or if the risk of attack remains excessive.
Black Sea security has therefore become an international issue involving not only Ukraine and Russia but also shipowners, insurers, trading companies and countries that rely on Ukrainian exports.
Kyiv is also seeking alternative ways to store and transport the harvest.
One measure involves special polymer sleeves that allow grain to be stored directly in fields, while international institutions are providing financial assistance to farmers.
These measures, however, have limited impact.
They can protect agricultural products from being physically destroyed or lost, but they do not resolve the central problem of transporting those products to international markets.
The Financial Times analysis describes a conflict in which the separation between military and economic infrastructure is increasingly disappearing.
Ports serve as civilian facilities while also functioning as strategic assets. Railway locomotives transport goods while also forming part of the export system. Electrical substations provide power while also enabling port operations.
Ships, meanwhile, are no longer simply cargo carriers.
They are becoming potential targets.
The Black Sea is consequently emerging as the most dangerous region for commercial shipping in the current conflict. The risk is reflected not only in attacks on vessels but also in higher costs for insurance, logistics, alternative routes, repairs and delays, as well as lost revenue.
The Black Sea is therefore becoming more than the geographic area between Russia, Ukraine, Turkey, Romania and Bulgaria.
It is developing into an economic front with potential consequences for food markets, European security and international trade.
The fundamental question remains whether the Black Sea can again become a reliable trade corridor rather than a zone of military risk.

The cemetery at Nir Oz contains two lines of fresh headstones, marking lives that all ended on 7 October 2023. A shared plot for a family of five – a mother, father and their three young children – has been made into a garden with space left for their still-living grandparents.
Caretaker Shlomo Margalit, who will soon turn 89, points to the graves of three of his oldest friends, founding members of the kibbutz who came to Nir Oz from Haifa with him in the 1950s.
“This is my life project, as well as my home,” Margalit said, explaining why he has come back to a place of such loss. He is waiting for a new house but, for now, staying in the former home of Gadi Moses, 82, who survived 482 days as a hostage.
The graves he tends are a silent testament to the brutality of the attacks and the scale of the state’s failure, which in Nir Oz was staggering, even on a day of terrible failures.
A five-person volunteer defence force held Hamas at bay for at least two hours, Margalit said. When they had all been shot, the kibbutz was taken over and sacked, homes burned, families slaughtered and kidnapped.
Then, before the first Israeli soldier arrived, the Hamas forces, other Palestinian gunmen and civilian looters all left. Nir Oz had been forgotten by the army and ripped apart without the military firing a single shot to defend it.
In total, 47 people were killed and 76 taken to Gaza, including Shiri Bibas, her 10-month-old baby Kfir and four-year-old Ariel, who were killed in Gaza. The dead and hostages represented more than a quarter of the small community.
Revisiting that terrible day, and the trauma that followed, is painful and exhausting for Margalit, but he still accepts interviews for a simple reason. “I want people to know what really happened here,” the 89-year-old said.

Palestinians recall life before war that 'destroyed everything we loved'
In Gaza, Palestinians recalled life before Israel launched a devastating war that transformed the Strip beyond recognition and displaced nearly its entire population.
Hamas’s 7 October attack on southern Israel ignited a war that would kill more than 74,000 Palestinians in Gaza and reduce the territory to rubble. A ceasefire declared last October has brought little relief for Palestinians, who continue to face humanitarian and economic challenges as they struggle to rebuild their lives.
The ceasefire deal has left the Israeli military in control of about two-thirds of Gaza, where it has carried out sporadic strikes and razed large areas to the ground. In its latest assault, the Israeli military carried out airstrikes in Beit Lahia in northern Gaza and in Khan Younis in the south, killing at least two Palestinians and wounding others, the Gaza health ministry said. The Israel Defense Forces (IDF) claimed it had struck a militant target in Beit Lahia, without providing details. It did not immediately comment on the strike in Khan Younis.
Umm Mohammad, a mother of five displaced from Gaza City in the north, lives with her husband and children in a makeshift camp in the central city of Deir Al-Balah. She said they were “one happy family” before the war had ripped them apart.
“The war displaced us. My son left Gaza, the other went to a separate tent, my daughters left with their husbands to other parts of the Strip and we rarely meet,” she told Reuters.
On this day, she said, “we recall how happy, despite all problems, we were before the war broke out, destroying everything we loved”.
Israel held state events on Monday, the national memorial day for the attacks. The date for official remembrance is set according to the lunisolar Hebrew calendar, one of two official calendars of the State of Israel, rather than the Gregorian calendar.
The attack was launched on the Jewish holiday of Simchat Torah. Memorial day was set for two days later, because memorial events can’t be held on the holiday.
Flags were lowered at government buildings, military bases, police stations and the communities attacked by Hamas, and Israel’s leaders gathered at Mount Herzl cemetery in Jerusalem for two events. One remembered security forces killed on 7 October, and the other the civilian victims.
A bereaved father interrupted the speech by prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu at the second event to accuse him of negligence. “You did not protect my son on 7 October, you did not protect 1,200 people murdered in one day, Shame!” Yaakov Godo shouted, before being ushered away.
Many survivors and bereaved families accuse Netanyahu of putting his political survival ahead of the lives of Israeli citizens. Top US and Israeli officials have said the prime minister rejected ceasefire deals that could have halted the war in Gaza and brought hostages home sooner.

Lithuania could restrict transit from Russia if plague threat confirmed – minister
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
06:23:00 UTC
15:23:00 KST

Lithuania could restrict the transit of Russian citizens through the country if reports of pneumonic plague in Russia are confirmed and the disease poses a threat to Lithuania, Health Minister Linas Kukuraitis said Wednesday.
Kukuraitis told LRT RADIO that any such measures would be coordinated with the European Union, which has established procedures for restricting movement during public health emergencies since the Covid-19 pandemic.
“If we saw even the slightest threat, this issue would be raised by us, and decisions would then be made jointly,” Kukuraitis said.
He said he met Tuesday with the country’s main institutions responsible for managing such an outbreak. Lithuania has established response procedures and sufficient reserves of medication, he said.
Kukuraitis stressed that reports of a pneumonic plague case in Russia have not been independently confirmed.
“It is both a worrying situation, and we would like to reassure the public,” he said, adding that information coming from Russia is being treated cautiously because it is a “warring, hostile country”.
Lithuania, other European countries and the United States are closely monitoring the situation, he said.
Lithuania’s National Public Health Centre said there is currently no increased risk of plague infection for people in Lithuania. It said available information is limited and there is no way to independently confirm that the reported case involved pneumonic plague.
Reports emerged Friday that 28-year-old Darya Shipilova, who worked at a plague research institute in Russia’s Irkutsk region, had died of pneumonic plague. Some reports said special restrictions had subsequently been imposed.
The Russian news outlet Lyudi Baikala, citing unnamed sources close to regional security services, reported that Shipilova may have contracted the disease after a test tube broke. Other media reports linked her death to a possible laboratory incident. Lyudi Baikala also reported that about 200 people who may have had contact with her were under quarantine.
Russian officials, however, have said tests conducted after her death did not detect the disease. US President Donald Trump said Monday that his administration was closely monitoring the situation.
Pneumonic plague is a rare infection caused by the bacterium Yersinia pestis. It can spread through respiratory droplets, generally requiring close and prolonged contact with a person showing symptoms. The incubation period is one to four days.
The disease can cause fever, headache, weakness, cough, chest pain and rapidly worsening breathing difficulties. When diagnosed promptly, it can be successfully treated with antibiotics, which are readily available in Europe and Lithuania.

Three years after the October 7 massacre, former hostage Omri Miran and his wife, Lishay Miran-Lavi, shared their account of the assault, his 738 days in captivity and the family’s struggle for his release at the first “Salon Otef” gathering held at the President’s Residence.
The event, organized by 255, the Hostages and Families Organization, in partnership with KKL-JNF, opened a week of hundreds of similar gatherings planned in homes, communities and public spaces across Israel.
Miran and Miran-Lavi recounted the morning of October 7, his abduction and captivity in Gaza, and her nearly two-year campaign for his return. They also spoke about life since his release and the challenges facing former hostages and their families.
President Isaac Herzog opened Monday's gathering, which was moderated by Ben Shani. KKL-JNF World Chairman Eyal Ostrinsky delivered closing remarks.
Herzog said the event reflected the broader challenge of national recovery after October 7.
“This gathering is deeply meaningful for all of us as a society. We must continue to listen, remember and ensure that the stories of those who paid the heaviest price are heard,” he said. “Recovering from the trauma of October 7 is a long process for Israeli society, just as recovery and rehabilitation are for any individual.”
Addressing Miran directly, Herzog added: “Seeing all of you here today, and seeing you here with us, Omri, is an important part of our recovery as a nation.”
First Lady Michal Herzog said the anniversary underscored the need to preserve testimony from those who experienced the attack.
“Today marks three years since October 7. The pain does not ease with time, and we carry it with us every day,” she said. “Gatherings like ‘Salon Otef,’ which bring people together to share their stories and experiences, are incredibly important for Israeli society.”
Miran said firsthand testimony was essential to understanding what hostages and their families had endured.
“To understand what happened to us on October 7 and what the hostages and their families have been through since then, we need to hear the stories firsthand, from those who lived through them,” he said.
“The hundreds of ‘Salon Otef’ gatherings taking place across the country allow these stories to pass from person to person and from home to home. I see passing these stories on to the public as a whole and to the younger generation as an immensely important national mission — a life mission.”
Organizers said the initiative is intended to bring the personal accounts of people affected by October 7, as well as members of security and rescue forces, directly to the public. The gatherings are also meant to give participants an opportunity to ask questions and preserve testimonies for future generations.
Ostrinsky said the project was aimed not only at remembrance, but at understanding the long-term consequences of the attack.
“Three years after October 7, our responsibility is not only to remember what happened that day, but also to listen to the people who carry with them what they experienced on that terrible day and what they have been going through ever since,” he said.
Mor Peretz, CEO of 255, said the events were intended to ensure that the history of October 7 is told by those who experienced it.
“The story of October 7 should first and foremost be told by those who were there and experienced it firsthand,” Peretz said. “The more these testimonies are heard and resonate in more homes and among more people, the better we can preserve the story as it was experienced by those who were there.”
The initiative is being led by 255 in partnership with KKL-JNF and the Konrad Adenauer Foundation, with cooperation from Atid LaOtef, ZAKA, Kumu, the Nova Tribe Community, the Kibbutz Movement and other organizations.

Taipei 101’s A Joy debuts autumn menu

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Perched on the 86th floor of Taipei 101, Taiwan’s highest and most expensive buffet, A Joy, is redefining luxury dining with a newly unveiled autumn menu created in partnership with celebrity chef Andre Chiang (江振誠).
The seasonal lineup, running through Nov. 30, marks the autumn chapter of the restaurant’s yearlong "Four Seasons Symphony" series. Built around the concept of "0rigin," the menu shifts the buffet narrative from abundance to culinary precision and nostalgic storytelling.
"Diners visiting a high-altitude buffet are no longer looking for endless variety," Chiang said. "It is about the quality and refinement of every single dish."
Chiang has introduced a "limited dining" philosophy, prioritizing small-batch craftsmanship over mass production. He has also created "flavor pathways," encouraging guests to pair distinct culinary components to unlock personalized flavor profiles instead of eating standalone items.
At the center of the autumn lineup is a focus on restorative, soul-warming fare suited for cooler weather. Chiang’s flagship dish is a green Sichuan pepper and peeled chili black-feathered chicken soup, blending 30 years of French culinary technique with memories of his mother’s cooking.
The dish features a slow-simmered hen broth infused with tender chicken thigh, sweet peeled chilis, and green peppercorns that impart a mild numbing warmth believed in traditional food culture to promote circulation.
Presented inside a vessel styled like the ancient medical text “Compendium of Materia Medica,” the menu opens with the word "welcome" — a gesture intended to feel like a comforting home-cooked meal served high above the clouds.
The autumn offerings also highlight what Chiang calls “Taiwanese flavors after seeing the world.” Notable dishes include a elevated take on a Shilin Night Market street snack: crispy kuruma prawn wrapped in Hong Kong-style shrimp roe noodles, encased in a seared Mexican tortilla, and seasoned with Japanese sweet sauce and truffle mayonnaise.
Another creation pairs classic French bouillabaisse with Japanese wheat gluten wafers, wild sea bass, king crab, and kelp-infused sushi rice, bridging Eastern and Western traditions in a single bowl.

The EU agrees on new Return Order, longer detention and return hubs
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
06:20:22 UTC
15:20:22 KST

EU ministers agreed on new rules allowing sanctions for migrants who refuse to cooperate with return procedures, detention up to 24 months or longer for security risks, and return hubs outside the EU. Watch the video!
EU interior ministers met in Luxembourg on October 1, and agreed on stricter rules for returning migrants, shifting the bloc’s migration policy focus from paperwork to enforcement.
During the Home Affairs Council, ministers decided that people without the right to stay must leave and cooperate with authorities. If they do not, they could face sanctions such as reduced benefits, fines, or criminal charges.
A new European Return Order would let countries choose to recognise each other’s return decisions, with a review planned after three years. For security risks, countries could impose indefinite entry bans and detention longer than 24 months. Return hubs outside the EU are also allowed. These rules exclude unaccompanied minors and will take effect in the coming weeks.
The push follows a Munich meeting on 26 September where Migration Commissioner Magnus Brunner said irregular arrivals dropped by 55% over two years. However, the number of people actually returned remains low. In 2025, the EU ordered nearly 492,000 people to leave, but only 135,000 did.
Greece’s migration minister, Thanos Plevris, said the first return hub could open in the second half of 2027 in an unspecified African country. The UN human rights office warned that the law lacks clear rules for monitoring, appeals, or conditions in host countries.

Bystanders stand near the runway of Yemen southern city of Aden’s airport shortly after an explosion hit as a government plane landed, Dec. 30, 2020. (AP file photo)
The Houthis claimed a flurry of attacks on Saudi targets on Oct. 7 including firing a ballistic missile at Riyadh airport, as the group battles for territory in Yemen against government forces supported by the kingdom.
The Houthis, who control most of northwest Yemen, captured swaths of coastal land from Yemen’s pro-government forces last month after the country’s civil war reignited in July.
The internationally recognized government this week declared a counter-offensive and claims to have uprooted Houthi fighters from strategic areas on the Red Sea and the port city of Mocha.
But the Iran-backed Houthis say they are holding their territory, and military sources from both sides contacted by AFP have not reported any major changes on the ground.
“Our armed forces have just targeted King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh with a ballistic missile. The strike was accurate, by God’s grace, and led to a disruption of air traffic,” Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree said on Oct. 7 in a post on X.
The Saudi-led military coalition that backs Yemen’s government said the missile was intercepted.
In a separate post the Houthis also said they targeted military supplies at a camp area near the airport in the Yemeni city of Aden, the interim capital for the government.
The Yemeni government’s Saba news agency reported missiles and drones targeting that airport.
Saree earlier said drones and missiles also targeted Saudi Arabia’s Abha airport and King Khalid Air Base in Khamis Mushait and had “hit their targets accurately.”
It is the second time this week that the Houthis claimed to have attacked the main airport in the Saudi capital.
Saudi Arabia leads an international coalition that has been fighting the Houthis since 2015, and is now trying to roll back the group’s latest advance.
On Oct. 6, the coalition said it was providing air support for the counter-offensive launched by the Yemeni government forces.
After a four-year ceasefire, Yemen’s civil war re-erupted in July. Last month the Houthis seized the entire western coastline along the Red Sea in the country’s deadliest fighting in years.
The renewed violence has also deepened the wider Middle East war, which has roiled world energy markets and snarled shipping routes in the region.
Yemen’s government has announced a goal of retaking all Houthi territory, home to most of the country’s population, and much of it held for more than a decade.

At least 20 killed as Russia launches ‘massive’ attack on Ukraine
Ukraine’s air force says Russia launched 130 drones, 48 cruise missiles and ballistic missiles in overnight attack.
At least 20 people, including children, have been killed as Russia launched a barrage of drones and missiles across Ukraine, according to Ukrainian authorities.
Ukraine’s air force said on Wednesday that Russia launched 130 drones, 48 cruise missiles, and an unspecified number of ballistic missiles in the overnight attack. It added air defence units downed 161 targets.
Ukraine’s capital, Kyiv, and Poltava in central Ukraine, the southeastern region of Dnipropetrovsk, and Kharkiv in the northeast were the focus of the Russian attacks, authorities said.
President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said in a social media post that Russia had fired 70 missiles and also drones in one of its biggest attacks since Moscow launched the war in 2022.
“One of the key targets was our energy infrastructure. The Russians wanted to strike painfully and demonstratively,” Zelenskyy said.
The attacks also damaged residential buildings, industrial facilities, and infrastructure, according to Ukrainian officials.
In Pryluki, in the northern Chernihiv region, a Russian missile slammed into a five-storey residential building, regional authorities said. At least 14 people, including four children, were killed and 50 others wounded, emergency services said.
Kyiv’s Mayor Vitali Klitschko said two people were killed in the densely populated Darnytskyi neighbourhood in a fire caused by an air attack.
Two people were killed when missiles hit high-rise buildings in Dnipro and Kremenchuk in central Ukraine, while two others died in Oleksandriya, Zelenskyy said.
‘Massive’ attack
Russia’s Ministry of Defence said its forces carried out a “massive strike” on military-industrial facilities in Kyiv and other Ukrainian regions, using high-precision land-, sea-, and air-launched weapons, as well as drones.
Targets included sites where the company Fire Point makes and stores Flamingo cruise missiles and medium- and long-range drones in Kyiv, as well as in the regions of Kyiv, Chernihiv, Kirovohrad, Dnipropetrovsk, Poltava, and Kharkiv, it said.
The attacks also targeted port and ship-repair infrastructure in the Odesa region, as well as vessels it said were being used in the interests of Ukraine’s armed forces, the ministry added.
“Ukraine has once again been hit by Russian missiles throughout the night,” Dmytro Lubinets, Ukraine’s parliamentary commissioner for human rights, said on Telegram.
“Another sleepless night, another act of terror, after which people still have to plan their working day despite everything,” he added.
Kyiv has come under relentless bombardment in recent weeks, with Russian air attacks on energy infrastructure, rail and road transport, including the bridges that connect the city over the Dnipro River.
Air raid sirens have sounded almost constantly, urging residents to take cover in basements, shelters and subway stations.
In a separate post, Zelenskyy said Ukrainian forces hit four Russian targets over the last 24 hours, including two oil facilities and a training ground in the Perm, Samara, and Astrakhan regions, as well as carrying out a response in the Black Sea.
He called the attacks a “just” response to Moscow’s strikes, and added that the facilities hit helped “Russia finance and wage its brutal war”.
Concerns over Black Sea navigation
As the war intensifies and expands, Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan has pressed Russian President Putin to ensure safe navigation in the Black Sea.
A statement by the Turkish presidency said Erdogan reiterated his offer to help facilitate direct talks between Russia and Ukraine, saying that safe Black Sea access was important to Ankara.
The conversation between the Turkish and Russian leaders came after drones hit two commercial vessels early on Tuesday as attacks on Black Sea shipping increase amid an intensifying Russia-Ukraine war. One vessel caught fire, while the other sank.
Bulgarian authorities say they have ended search operations after confirming that no survivors were found from the ship that sank off the country’s coast.

Isamaa, Center Party and EKRE struggle to agree on no‑confidence text
Isamaa, the Estonian Center Party and EKRE want to file a no‑confidence motion against the prime minister Kristen Michal in the coming days, but after several weeks they still have not agreed on the text. The Social Democratic Party does not plan to join the effort.
Leaders of the opposition factions will meet again next Monday to draft the text. Each faction is currently preparing its own version.
"We agreed that each faction will present its ideas on what should be included in the no‑confidence motion, and that work is still ongoing. Based on that, we cannot say that we already have a unified text," said Center Party deputy chair Lauri Laats.
Isamaa board member Priit Sibul said there is broad agreement on the main points.
"I think the issue is in different nuances. There is no doubt that the opposition includes parties that believe Michal should face a no‑confidence vote, and that agreement will be reached. Whether someone in the opposition thinks Michal's government should continue and will not support the motion will be clear in the vote," Sibul said.
"This is comedy at this point. They have been drafting this text for a month and discussing it for months. They have not managed to produce a single motion. The Social Democrats will support it if Isamaa or the Center Party can show what the new functioning government would look like. That proposal has not been presented to the Social Democrats, and until then we cannot join," said Social Democratic Party chair Lauri Läänemets.
If the Social Democrats or the independents do not join the motion, it will fail. EKRE chair Martin Helme noted that the last successful no‑confidence vote was ten years ago.
"No‑confidence motions are not filed primarily to remove a minister or bring down a government, but because political rules have been violated in a way that cannot be ignored. We must respond," Helme said.
Reform Party faction chair Õnne Pillak said the no‑confidence effort has been discussed for a long time.
"For weeks it has been called an interim government, different names are found. But there is no result. And I think there is no expectation either. People expect the country to be firmly led. They want to see things improve," Pillak said.
Helme said the opposition will file the motion next week. Laats and Sibul are not as certain about that timeline. Sibul said the opposition will definitely file it sometime in October.

Arriving in Paris, Steinmeier says Europe needs right mix of 'reason and heart'
German President Frank-Walter Steinmeier has begun a three-day state visit to neighboring France. He landed at Paris' Orly airport on a damp evening and made his way to the German Embassy.
He said Europe needed to face its various security and political challenges with a mixture of the head's reason and the heart's emotion.
"Reason and heart, that's what Europe needs again today, in a time of wars and crises, in which our democracies are under attack to an extent not seen since the second World War," Steinmeier said.
He said it was a mixture of reason, or head, and heart that had made the Franco-German reconciliation after the war possible.
Steinmeier was playing on a quote from French writer Victor Hugo, who in the 19th century said that in Europe, Germany was the heart and France was the head or the reason. Steinmeier said he would leave it open to debate whether the modern-day French or Germans might agree with this particular division of anatomical labor.
What mattered, he said, was that there could be only one response to the current circumstances: "Europe must, now above all, stand up confidently and in unison for the values that made us what we are: respect for human dignity, peace, freedom, democracy."
On Thursday, Steinmeier will visit the Pantheon monument in Paris with President Emmanuel Macron, to honor the Jewish historian and resistance fighter Marc Bloch, who was murdered by Nazi Germany.
Steinmeier also intimated that a new deal on Franco-German youth cooperation might be signed amid the visit, speaking of a "promise for a new generation of German and French youth, who want to learn to understand, value and love each other."
The visit coincides with considerable political unrest among French young people in the form of ongoing school funding protests.
Steinmeier also said prior to leaving Berlin that his state visit would be "something of a farewell tour with a truly committed European and a good friend."
Both he and French President Macron took office in 2017, and both will be leaving their posts early in 2027.
Steinmeier's post, however, is far more ceremonial and removed from daily politics than that of the French president.
Saxony-Anhalt AfD and BSW lawmakers call for end to Ukraine aid, sanctions on Russia
Immediately following its initial parliamentary session on Tuesday, Saxony-Anhalt state legislators from the far-right AfD and far-left BSW called for the federal government in Berlin to drop sanctions on Russia over its invasion of Ukraine, as well as demanding an end to all arms deliveries and financial aid for Ukraine as Kyiv defends itself from a nearly five-year Russian invasion.
Both parties are known for their Russia "friendly" stances and their ties to the Kremlin.
They have also latched onto Moscow's claim that Berlin and other EU and NATO governments are the true "war mongers" in Ukraine, baselessly claiming that Russia is a peace-loving nation forced to defend itself against hostile neighbors.
BSW founder Sahra Wagenknecht echoed AfD co-chair Alice Weidel in labeling the initiative "a signal for peace."
"Economic sanctions against Russia must end immediately," a statement said.
Germany's federal leadership, under two chancellors, has shown steadfast — if at times cautious — support for Ukraine and demanded Russia end its killing of civilians before entering into further dialogue.
Beyond dropping sanctions, the AfD and BSW insist Germany must normalize relations with Moscow, and stop "financing the war," arguing instead that money spent helping Ukraine defend its democracy would be better spent in Germany.
State governments in Germany have no say in federal foreign and energy policy, but the parties say they launched their effort in an attempt to force change in Berlin.
Merz rails against extremism, AfD sympathizers in own ranks
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz on Wednesday addressed the threat of political extremism to the existing social order, accusing the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) and far-left BSW parties of wanting to wipe out "the DNA of our democracy."
"Extremism," said Merz, "is forcing its way into our state legislatures with a vengeance."
Merz, speaking in Berlin, called this week’s election of an AfD politician as speaker of Saxony-Anhalt's state parliament — the first time a far-right politician has been tapped to lead a statehouse since 1945 — a "historic break."
Moreover, Merz slammed politicians — potentially from his own conservative CDU party — for casting ballots in favor of Tobias Rausch in the Saxony-Anhalt vote, saying he was "deeply concerned and somewhat appalled" when the AfD's candidate was elected to the speaker position.
Rausch received 48 votes but the AfD and BSW only have 44 between them. It is unclear from whom Rausch picked up four extra votes — he was elected in a secret ballot.
Observers assume these came from within the CDU, but Merz said "false flag" attacks also occur in politics, implying the Social Democrats, the Left party and the Greens, all of which are also represented in the state's parliament, could be attempting to weaken or sow division in the CDU.
"Anyone who casts their vote for the AfD is playing the extremists' game and undermining credibility," said Merz. "In any case, this is incompatible with the values of my party, the CDU."
IN DEPTH: German spy scandal threatens national security
The arrest of August Hanning, former president of Germany's foreign intelligence service, the Bundesnachrichtendienst (BND), and his former chief-of-staff, Manfred D., is threatening to cause a major rupture in Germany's intelligence relationships, according to analysts, as the full scale of the scandal begins to be understood abroad.

"According to initial expert assessments," a spokesperson for the local government said, "it could be a puma."

New Hannover-Hamburg rail line set to be built by 2050
As mentioned at the start of this blog, railroad woes are one major theme in our Germany coverage.
But here is some very positive news for once: The parliamentary transport committee has finally endorsed a plan by railway operator Deutsche Bahn (DB) to build a new line linking Hannover and Hamburg by 2050.
The project for what is one of Germany's most important transport routes is planned to cost at least €9 billion ($10 billion) and had prompted years of wrangling.
It still requires backing by the full Bundestag, or lower house of parliament, on Thursday, but that is likely to be a formality.
High-speed train line
The new two-track line will be designed for speeds of up to 250 kilometers per hour (155 miles per hour), cutting journey times between the two cities by 18 minutes.
However, it will be some time before construction begins: The preliminary planning report that forsees submitting approval documents in 2034, with construction to start in 2036.
Renovation of the existing line between the two cities is also planned for 2029 under the agreement.
According to DB, that route is already heavily congested, carrying up to 147% of intended capacity.
The agreement was reached despite opposition from lawmakers representing constituencies affected by the new construction, including Vice Chancellor Lars Klingbeil of the Social Democrats (SPD).

Majority finds Merz a failure as chancellor — survey
Most people in Germany consider that Chancellor Friedrich Merz is not up to the job, a new survey has shown.
In all, 67% of respondents in the survey by the Ipsos institute were either wholly or fairly in agreement with the statement "The chancellorship of Friedrich Merz has failed."
A whole 48% completely agreed on Merz's insufficiency as leader, according to the survey published in the Spiegel news magazine.
There were regional differences in assessment's of Merz's performance, with 80% of people in eastern states completely or somewhat dissatisfied compared with 64% in the west.
However, there was much less agreement on which conservative politician could replace him if he were to step down or be ousted.
The survey gave a choice between the leader of the Bavarian Christian Social Union (CSU), Markus Söder, his party colleague Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt or the premier of the state of North Rhine-Westphalia, Hendrik Wüst.
Altogether 43% of those surveyed said none of those named came into question, while some 14% responded with "Don't know."
Söder was, however, the favorite with 20% support, followed by Wüst on 16%.
Dobrindt lagged far behind on just 5%.
SPD questions CDU, BSW role in election of far-right speaker
The co-leader of the Social Democrats (SPD), Lars Klingbeil, says coalition partner the Christian Democrats (CDU) has questions to answer after the election of Tobias Rausch, a politician from the Alternative for Germany (AfD), as parliamentary speaker in Saxony-Anhalt.
"The fact that the candidate of the AfD in Saxony-Anhalt, which is classified as 'confirmed right-wing extremist,' was elected as state parliament speaker with considerably more than just AfD votes raises very urgent questions," said Klingbeil, who is also deputy chancellor and finance minister.
"Electing right-wing extremists to such positions breaks with a taboo," he said.
"Not just the BSW, but also the CDU must urgently explain how this could happen."
The SPD federal parliamentary party staged a march through Berlin's Brandenburg Gate on Tuesday to protest at the election result.
The state chapter of the AfD, which won a landslide victory at September elections, is classified as "confirmed right-wing extremist" by domestic intelligence.
Mysterious extra votes for Rausch
Rausch was elected speaker with 48-29 votes, though just 44 votes for him would have resulted if only his party (39 seats) and the populist BSW (five seats), which had pledged to back him, had voted in his favor.
The CDU parliamentary leader, Sven Schulze, had recommended that the 15 parliamentarians in his party abstain from voting, but there were only five abstentions altogether in the secret ballot. One CDU member was absent.
The other three parties represented in the legislature — the SPD, the Left Party and the Greens — had all declared their opposition to Rausch.
Schulze said he could not believe that the four extra votes for Rausch came from the ranks of the CDU, although there has been widespread speculation that this was the case.
All mainstream parties in Germany have so far officially stated that they reject any form of cooperation with the AfD in keeping with the so-called "firewall."
Ex-spy chief August Hanning to face court for allegedly selling state secrets

The Palestinian militant group Hamas led attacks in southern Israel on October 7, 2023 in which some 1,200 people were killed and more than 250 others abducted.
The attacks triggered the ongoing war on Hamas in Gaza, which left some 74,000 Palestinians dead, most of them civilians.

salagón stone and floating timber reshape historic rock-cut complex in la rioja, spain

salagón stone and floating timber reshape historic rock-cut complex in la rioja, spain
sergio rojo’s rehabilitation retains the existing rock-cut structure carved directly into salagón, a clay-rich stone found in the cliffs.
Salagón stone shapes two-level rock-cut complex in La Rioja
Located in Albelda de Iregua, La Rioja, Spain, the Peña de las Bodegas rock-cut complex forms part of a historic group of excavated spaces between Peña Salagona and Peña de las Bodegas. Architect Sergio Rojo takes over the rehabilitation of the space. Over time, the spaces have been used as columbaria, livestock shelters, and eremitic and monastic dwellings, with the latter associated with the nearby Monastery of San Martín. The site is locally known as the Scriptorium, referencing the Codex Vigilanus, or Codex Albeldensis, written in the monastery’s surroundings.
The complex is carved directly into salagón, a clay-rich stone characteristic of the cliffs. Its architecture is shaped by the removal of material rather than the addition of new construction. A large exterior access area overlooks the valley and the natural gateway to the Cameros region, while the interior extends across two levels connected by stairs. Two long ventilation shafts, known locally as zarceras or tuferas, are also characteristic of La Rioja’s excavated winery architecture.
Reversible timber elements preserve rock-cut interiors
Architect Sergio Rojo’s rehabilitation introduces a small number of new elements while retaining the existing rock-cut structure. An exterior area with benches provides a gathering space, while cleaned stone surfaces make the excavated spaces more legible. Inside, a backlit floating timber floor guides visitors through the complex, and the openings in the western rock face have been redefined to increase natural light.
The intervention uses dry construction systems and avoids concrete and cement to keep the new work reversible and minimize changes to the excavated architecture. Timber and the existing stone form the primary material palette, combining new elements with the material already present in the site.
project info:
name: Peña De Las Bodegas Rock-cut Space Rehabilitation
architect: Sergio Rojo | @sergiosrojo
location: Albelda de Iregua, La Rioja, Spain

Yemen’s displaced children dream of returning to school
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
