Yemen’s displaced children dream of returning to school
More than 137,000 students in conflict zones lose access to education, deepening Yemen’s already dire schooling crisis.
Taiz, Yemen – At sunrise, 12-year-old Ahmed wakes up under the roof of a tent in a displacement camp in the Wadi Bani Khawlan area of Taiz governorate’s Jabal Habashi district. He spends his days playing with other children or retreating to lie down inside the tent. This has been his routine for the past two weeks, ever since he had to flee his village of al-Ashroh, west of the city of Taiz.
Life in the camp is “boring”, he says. He misses everything about his home and his village, particularly his school bag and his walk to school every morning.
“I left my school bag in the house as we fled the clashes, and I do not know if I will carry it again and go back to my classroom and meet my teachers and classmates,” Ahmed told Al Jazeera.
There’s no school at the displacement camp for Ahmed to attend, and even if he were back home in his village, his school there is also closed. Across conflict-affected parts of Yemen, hundreds of schools have suspended classes, disrupting education for more than 137,000 students, according to UNICEF.
The United Nations body added that more than 57,000 children had been displaced as a result of the fighting in Yemen in the first two weeks of September, a number that will likely have increased as fighting continues.
After four years of relative calm, armed clashes between pro-government forces and the Houthis intensified sharply in August and September, dealing a new blow to Yemeni schools and students and further deepening the country’s education crisis.
Survival over education
After arriving at the displacement camp, Ahmed’s family had immediate priorities: securing shelter and meeting their basic needs.
“Before the war reached my house and school, my family would care if I completed my school homework,” Ahmed said. “Today, no one cares about education in the camp. Families’ focus shifted to tents, food and water.”
Meeting those needs is a difficult task for the humanitarian groups attempting to help the displaced. The UN said on October 2 that more than 150,000 people had been displaced by the renewed conflict, a number that is expected to rise. That is on top of the more than five million Yemenis who had previously been displaced as a result of the war, which began with the Houthi takeover of Sanaa in 2014.
Mohammed Radman, a displacement coordinator with the Executive Unit for IDP Camp Management in Jabal Habashi district, told Al Jazeera that thousands of students are displaced, and that many of them have been forced to put their education aside amid what he described as “horrific circumstances”.
“These students do not have options,” Radman said. “All schools near the front lines are closed. And even if these students wanted to travel several kilometres every day to reach functioning schools, those schools are already crowded. So, the displaced students cannot be accommodated.”
He divided schools in conflict-affected areas into three groups: schools being used to shelter the displaced, overcrowded schools and schools on or near the front lines.
“This creates a real challenge for society, the Yemeni government and international organisations,” he said.
‘Homelessness and begging await them’
Before the latest escalation, 3.2 million children were already out of school in Yemen, according to UNICEF.
And now, with the new and ongoing wave of displacement, the ordeal facing Yemeni children is set to worsen, said Tawfiq al-Humaidi, the president of SAM Organization for Rights and Liberties.
“This war leaves them vulnerable to homelessness, begging, and potentially forced recruitment,” al-Humaidi said. “So, alternatives available to children outside the classroom are not safe.”
While families hope that their stay in the displacement camps will be temporary, al-Humaidi said that the disruption to education caused by displacement may last for a long time.
He said that prolonged stays in displacement camps can pull children into a different daily routine and make their eventual return to school more difficult.
“The repercussions extend beyond deprivation and the loss of educational lessons to the loss of the social and psychological protection provided by schools,” al-Humaidi said. “When schools close, children become more vulnerable to violence, exploitation, recruitment and child labour.”
Finding a way back to school
Abdulkarim, a teacher in Taiz who did not wish to give his full name, told Al Jazeera that providing education in a “war zone” is challenging.
“When students hear explosions, fear bullets and stay in shaky tents, education cannot happen. I saw how little children cry when they hear the sounds of heavy gunfire,” he said.
Providing students with a safe environment is the priority, Abdulkarim said.
“Once that is achieved, we can try to accommodate students in functioning schools or create alternative centres so that students can continue to receive education,” he added.
Afrah al-Humaiqani, a sociologist in Aden, said the recent hostilities in different parts of Yemen risk denying thousands of students access to education, which she warned could contribute to creating a “new illiterate generation” in the country.
However, reducing the impact of this crisis is possible, and the Yemeni government and international organisations can cooperate and coordinate to address it, al-Humaiqani told Al Jazeera.
“There is a need for safe camps where students can feel secure,” she said. “This can be followed by the provision of teachers and textbooks, programmes to address learning loss, and provide psychosocial support for children.”

Housing crisis – Modern methods of construction can be the driver of affordable housing
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
06:15:37 UTC
15:15:37 KST

In an opinion adopted at its September plenary, the European Economic and Social Committee (EESC) stresses that modern construction methods can help lower housing costs and boost supply, but only if there is a convergence of innovation, quality and respect for workers’ rights and the interests of the public.
The days of the EU’s housing crisis could be numbered, with a potential solution on the horizon. This solution is modern construction methods. By drawing on their potential, the EU could lower building costs, shorten construction times and reduce carbon footprints, championing the circular economy in the construction sector. This is the strong conviction that the EESC outlines in its opinion on Making Housing Affordable – Increasing Modern Methods of Construction and Lowering Costs, adopted at its September plenary session.
Drawn up by John Comer and Thomas Kattnig, the opinion had been requested by the Irish Presidency of the Council of the European Union and tackles the issue of housing shortages. More specifically, the opinion deals with the framework conditions needed to increase the supply of repurposed, renovated and new housing, and provides guidance to relevant actors on implementing modern construction methods.
‘Modern methods of construction can become a key pillar of affordable housing, but only if innovation, quality, workers’ rights and public interest objectives advance together,’ said Mr Comer. ‘Modern methods of construction must not be seen as merely a technological or market-driven issue, but must be part of a broader social, labour market, affordability and industrial policy strategy,’ echoed Mr Kattnig.
Boosting industrial capacity for modern methods of construction
The construction sector remains characterised by relatively low productivity growth and fragmented supply chains. Modern methods of construction can counter these issues because they are based on innovative off-site manufacturing and on-site techniques designed to build higher-quality structures faster and more efficiently than traditional building approaches. Examples include scaling up industrialised approaches such as modular, prefabricated and off-site building.
Modern methods of construction therefore have the potential to lower overall construction costs and times and to increase structural precision, quality control, industry capacity and productivity. In addition, by being more environmentally friendly, they also contribute to the achievement of the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals (SDG). This is of the utmost importance, as it is essential that buildings built with modern methods of construction maintain the same long-term quality and value as traditionally built houses.
To achieve these objectives, modern methods of construction need a developed industrial capacity. This is why the EESC argues that the EU needs to drive forward targeted investment to increase industrial capacity to manufacture systems for prefabrication and offsite construction.
All actors must team up to fight fragmentation
The Committee also underlines that the Member States, the Commission, the Housing Alliance and all stakeholders have a role to play in promoting standardisation, eliminating fragmented regulations and ensuring that the systems for modern methods of construction are certified and monitored.
While acknowledging that each Member State has primary competence in housing, the EESC believes that the Commission should contribute to national housing plans and promote cross-border cooperation.
To allow the construction industry to make progress in innovation, the EU must launch a central funding mechanism to encourage and enable SMEs to invest in digitalisation, which should not be limited to construction projects, but also be leveraged to ensure labour rights, quality jobs, working conditions and consumer interests.
Solving the housing crisis must be a top priority
The EU’s housing emergency is not new. House prices in the EU have risen by more than 60.5% since 2013, while rents increased by 28.8% between 2010 and 2025. In 2024, the housing cost overburden rate was 8.2% on average in the EU.
Across Europe, the dramatic mix of high inflation and insufficient wage and pension increases has lowered the disposable incomes of households. This disproportionately affects vulnerable groups, women and young people. On top of this, the decrease in new housing triggers pressure on both purchase and rental markets, leading to price and rent inflation.
A number of additional factors has further exacerbated the housing crisis. The COVID-19 pandemic, Russia’s war of aggression against Ukraine, surging energy prices and increased material costs have made the situation even worse. Against this backdrop, mortgage interest rates have doubled, and the number of building permits issued in the EU between 2021 and 2024 has fallen by 25%.
The Committee continues to push the EU institutions
The EESC has been constantly pressing the EU institutions to find a solution to the housing emergency, adopting a number of key opinions in recent months. In its September 2025 opinion For a European Affordable Housing Plan – the contribution of civil society, the EESC urged the Commission to develop an action plan to enforce the fundamental right to housing.
In March 2026, following on from a Commission presentation on the European Affordable Housing Plan in December 2025, the Committee adopted an opinion on Tackling housing scarcity through affordable, sustainable and family-oriented housing policies, calling for more ambitious measures to address the structural housing crisis.
In its July 2026 opinion on the EU Strategy for Housing Construction, the EESC urged the Commission to swiftly present the initiatives that had been announced in the framework of the strategy, including the necessary framework conditions for construction to serve as a catalyst for affordable, sustainable and high-quality housing.
Currently, the EESC is assessing the Affordable Housing Act, which the European Commission unveiled on 9 September 2026, and is expected to adopt an opinion on the EU Affordable Housing Act in December 2026.

Ireland presented the resolution on behalf of the European Union, calling it “a lifeline for Russian society”.
“Extrajudicial killings of government critics, erosion of political pluralism, systematic crackdowns on civil society, independent media, journalists, indigenous peoples and minorities in Russia are met with impunity,” Dublin’s ambassador Laurence Simms said.

Bulgarian human rights expert Mariana Katzarova is the first UN-backed monitor of the rights situation in any of the UN Security Council’s five permanent member states.

'Exposed for the sham it is': Celebrations as High Court blocks major coal mine expansion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
06:14:38 UTC
15:14:38 KST

IN BRIEF:
- The High Court has ruled against a major coal mine expansion in NSW.
- Campaigners have welcomed the first case to consider broad environmental impacts.
Australia's highest court has upheld a first-of-its-kind environmental challenge to overturn a major coal mine expansion, after a years-long community campaign in east-central NSW.
In a landmark decision on Wednesday, the High Court ruled against the proposed expansion of the Mount Pleasant coal mine near Muswellbrook, in the Upper Hunter region of NSW.
It is the first time a court has upheld that project approvals must account for the broad environmental impacts of burning fossil fuels.
Environmental campaigners have termed the decision a victory for all Australians and called on the government to move away from fossil fuels.
Australian resource company MACH Energy sought to extend the life of Mount Pleasant coal mine in NSW by 22 years — to 2048 — and nearly double its yearly output to 22 million tonnes of carbon dioxide per year.
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
The state planning commission approved the proposal in 2022 before local Hunter Valley residents launched a legal challenge.
While the first bid to block the expansion was dismissed, in 2025, the NSW Court of Appeal unanimously ruled the approval unlawful, after it found planning authorities are legally required to consider the climate impact of Scope 3 emissions on local communities.
Scope 3 emissions are classified as indirect emissions tied to a company's broader business activities by the Greenhouse Gas Protocol, the top international standard for measuring greenhouse gas emissions.
MACH Energy took the finding to the High Court, which struck down the appeal on Wednesday morning.
The company said while it was "disappointed" with the outcome, it accepts the court's decision and "will carefully review the judgment to understand its implications for future project assessments and environmental approvals."
Mining approvals for the coal mine were due to end in November, before an August approval offered a lifeline from the state government, allowing for a continuation of operations to the end of 2032, as well as an increase in the approved extraction rate from 10.5 to 12.5 million tonnes of coal per year.
A years-long fight
The original case was brought by Wendy Wales, a retired science teacher and the president of the Denman Aberdeen Muswellbrook Scone Healthy Environment Group (DAMSHEG).
On Wednesday, she said the ruling acknowledged the risks to Australians posed by climate-influencing activities.
"This ruling acknowledges that many Australian communities have already suffered extreme weather devastation," she said.
"Now the true and complete long-term costs of export coal on Australians, via the climate impact from burning that coal, must be considered."
DAMSHEG said the proposed coal mine extension would generate 870 million tonnes of carbon dioxide, 98 per cent of it from coal burned overseas.
Greens spokesperson for climate change and planning Sue Higginson said the court had "exposed the New South Wales coal approval process for the sham it is, and declared that new coal cannot be approved when 98 per cent of the climate pollution are ignored".
"The High Court have sided with the climate science and declared that the NSW Independent Planning Commission was wrong to ignore downstream emissions when approving a massive new coal project."
A legal precedent in NSW
The High Court upheld the refusal of the planning commission's Mount Pleasant plan approval because the scope 3 emissions were not properly assessed.
"By majority, the High Court held the (planning) commission had failed to consider imposing conditions to minimise to the greatest extent practicable all greenhouse gas emissions, specifically 'scope three' emissions as required (by law)," the court said in a summary.
Head of climate and energy at Greenpeace Australia Pacific, Joe Rafalowicz, called on the Australian government, as well as leaders at COP31, to find the "courage, leadership and grit" to move away from fossil fuels, adding that the ruling clearly set a binding precedent for environmental challenges in the state.
"It is legally imperative that all of the pollution from fossil fuel projects be considered before approving a new project."
Rafalowicz said it was a victory for Australians "bearing the brunt" of extreme weather fuelled by fossil fuel corporations.
"Coal and gas companies have claimed they are not responsible for their pollution because it happens overseas, but today Australia’s highest court sided with common sense and scientific evidence to find that every new coal and gas approval in this country could put us at risk, no matter where it is sold or burnt."
The Minerals Council of Australia said the decision was a "further blow" to Australia's prospects of meeting continued demand from global customers for our "high-quality coal".
"Developing a coal mine in Australia is already difficult enough because of long approval times, lawfare by activists and high royalties and other taxes," Minerals Council of Australia chief executive officer Tania Constable said in a statement.
"The decision sends a very negative signal to Australia’s trade and investment partners about sovereign risk in this market."
The council said resource companies should not be "forced into a situation where well-funded legal attacks over a number of years require a High Court appeal", adding that legal challenges "seek to game the legal system by creating uncertainty and delay without ever having to pay costs".
"Investors in Australia’s resource sector will carefully review the outcome from today’s High Court judgement."
— With additional reporting from the Australian Associated Press.

‘You hear someone's final moments’: the engineers decoding the IDF’s battlefield ‘black boxes’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
06:11:24 UTC
15:11:24 KST

At first glance, the base in central Israel hardly looks like a classified facility where consequential decisions are made. 
But inside its modest portable buildings sit the people without whom much of the battlefield picture would remain obscured: soldiers, officers and civilian Defense Ministry employees whose algorithmic and engineering skills could command enormous salaries in the private sector, but who instead chose to serve as the brains behind the Defense Ministry’s Merkava and Armored Vehicles Directorate.
Until now, they have largely remained out of sight. Now they are speaking about the dramatic role they have played since Oct. 7: extracting, analyzing and decoding the “black boxes” of Merkava tanks, Namer armored personnel carriers and Eitan armored vehicles damaged in combat. They are among the first to hear the final seconds of soldiers’ lives, listen to desperate radio calls and reconstruct the angles from which enemy fire struck.
Engineers under fire
In routine times, the directorate is Israel’s national body responsible for developing, producing and restoring armored fighting vehicles. When the war erupted, however, it was assigned an extraordinary mission on an unprecedented scale.
“The footage from the armored vehicles that fought during the initial defensive battles, the footage you later saw in the media, came from the painstaking work our people carried out in the first days of the war,” recalled Lt. Col. M., head of the directorate’s software and cyber branch. “But behind the data we downloaded was a complex, dangerous operation under fire in the heart of the combat zone near Gaza. We received an urgent mission to physically reach Namers and tanks in the field and extract video, audio and telemetry files from their critical systems. The goal was to find any possible lead about hostages and reconstruct what happened in the battle.”
Lt. Col. M. assembled a dedicated team. Together with Maj. Michael, head of the electrical systems section, software and cyber officers put on body armor and helmets, armed themselves and headed south carrying laptops, communications harnesses and hard drives.
“This is definitely not something software engineers train for in routine service,” Lt. Col. M. said.
Because of the danger, unusually high-level authorization was required to send senior technology officers directly into the combat zone. Once in the south, the engineers climbed onto vehicles that had been fighting and connected to their computer systems. The following day, reports arrived of additional Namers damaged in intense fighting. Two Shin Bet personnel and a squad of combat troops were assigned to protect the engineers as they worked in exposed areas.
Inside dark, damaged crew compartments, the team carried out what members describe as “technological surgery,” extracting the full contents of the vehicles’ black boxes and sending the data directly to the Southern Command chief and personnel involved in locating missing people.
The information not only produced critical indications about missing people and hostages, according to the directorate, but also helped establish that crews inside the vehicles had fought intensely, countering rumors circulating in the confusion of the first days that some positions had simply been abandoned.
How a battle is reconstructed
After the first days of fighting, the investigative process became more organized and a dedicated operations center was established.
Lt. Col. T., head of the directorate’s control branch, said teams sent into the field were divided into two groups. “One team of software and electrical engineers extracts the raw information, navigation data and recordings, while a second team of mechanical and materials engineers conducts a physical ballistic analysis of the angle of impact, the type of weapon used by the enemy and the firing distance.”
Those findings led to immediate technological changes. When the unit identified Hamas’ growing use of drones dropping explosives during the early stages of the war, the directorate developed the “pergola” protective structure installed above armored vehicles, which it says eliminated the threat posed to those vehicles by such drones.
Behind the scenes, engineers also developed advanced artificial intelligence software capable of combining audio, video and telemetry into a single investigative environment.
“In the first days, about 40 black boxes a day were arriving here,” said A., a civilian computer engineer in the directorate. “At first we transcribed everything manually, hour after hour. The software we developed creates a timeline simulation and tells the full story of the battle.”
For the families of fallen soldiers, the technological reconstruction can carry profound significance. Maj. T., head of the fire-control systems section, said the engineers do not communicate directly with bereaved families but see how deeply they need to understand what happened in their loved ones’ final moments.
“They ask for every piece of information,” he said. “It is an entire puzzle they spend months putting together, and suddenly they find the missing piece with us.”
The daily exposure to digital forensic material also carries a significant psychological cost.
“In the end, you hear a person in the final seconds of his life,” said Maj. M. “He is speaking over the radio and nobody answers him. There is only static. That is a very difficult moment that stays with me. He calls out the names of his friends, who are already dead.”
Hoping not to recognize a voice
Because of the sensitivity of the material, the engineers are generally not given the soldiers’ names. Instead, recordings identify them only by their operational positions, such as commander, driver or loader.
But in Israel’s tightly connected society, painful encounters are sometimes unavoidable. A. said there is always a fear that someone on the team will recognize a familiar voice, and on one occasion that fear became reality.
“A relative of one of our team leaders was inside a tank that was hit,” he said. “The moment we understood that, the team leader was immediately removed from any work involving that vehicle.”
Beyond reconstructing battles and developing new protection systems, the directorate’s findings have also become important in international and legal investigations. Its analysis of firing angles and ballistics has provided evidence in sensitive inquiries, including the investigation into the tank shell fired at Pessi’s house in Kibbutz Be’eri, and has been used in formulating official IDF responses to allegations against Israel abroad.
The engineers have also examined some of the war’s deadliest incidents. In one case, 11 soldiers from the IDF’s Givati Brigade were killed when a Namer armored personnel carrier was struck. The detailed engineering investigation helped determine what had happened.
“It is a devastating event that I cannot get out of my head,” said Maj. M., head of a software section. “For days afterward, I thought about what happened there and whether the systems we developed had not been good enough. Eventually we understood that there had been a very specific firing angle. It is a case I carry with me constantly as I work to improve protection for the soldiers.”
“There are engineers and developers here who could earn a great deal of money in civilian life,” she said. “But as one of them put it, ‘We would never find the kind of meaning we have here anywhere outside’”

Finland orders halt to work on Google data centre sites

Unknown Publisher

Finland orders halt to work on Google data centre sites
Finnish opposition has called for measures to prevent power shortages, soaring energy prices caused by data centres.
A Finnish government authority has ordered work on two Google data centre sites to stop until compulsory environmental impact assessments have been completed.
The United States tech giant announced in September a 13 billion euro ($14.6bn) investment in digital infrastructure in Finland over the next two years to power its artificial intelligence (AI) ambitions.
Google has called the data centre projects in the municipalities of Muhos, Vaala, Kajaani and Hamina its single biggest investment in Europe.
But the Finnish Supervisory Agency (LVV), which is responsible for environmental issues, said it had demanded that Tuike Finland, the company representing Google, “immediately suspend, and no later than 23 October 2026, all preparatory measures that would significantly alter the environment in connection with the planned data centre projects in Muhos and Kajaani”.
The agency has been investigating whether Tuike Finland cleared hundreds of hectares of forest in Muhos and Kajaani without a mandatory environmental impact assessment.
The head of LVV’s environment department, Tommi Muilu, said trees have been removed, topsoil stripped, site roads and storage areas constructed and ditches altered.
Hanna Halmeenpaa, chair of the Finnish Association for Nature Conservation, told the AFP news agency that “nature sites which should be preserved” had been logged in a deforested area of more than 300 hectares (741 acres).
Tuike Finland must provide an explanation and detail how it intends to proceed by October 14.
It could face “enforcement proceedings” if it fails to comply, LVV said.
Google spokesman Sondre Ronander acknowledged in a statement to AFP the company’s shortcomings and said it would “study the LVV’s findings and follow their guidance”.
Ronander said Google was “advancing” its landscaping and biodiversity plans, which included tree planting across 130 hectares (53 acres) at Muhos.
The Nordic region has for years been a magnet for data centres due to its cool climate, abundant low-carbon electricity and reliable power grids, but AI builders are now facing greater scrutiny from consumers and politicians.
Opposition parties last month called for a national permit system to prevent power shortages and soaring energy prices.
While data centres are welcome in Finland, the country must make sure there is enough electricity and transmission capacity to power them, Centre Party leader Antti Kaikkonen told the Reuters news agency at the time.
The Social Democratic Party said that while it welcomed data centre investments, it too remains concerned about the implications for power demand.
Google’s deal included a 22-year purchase agreement for up to 50 percent of the energy output from Finland’s Loviisa nuclear plant, helping to extend the expected life of the plant until 2050, from a previous shutdown date in 2030.

How NATO Plans to Win: ‘Theory of Victory’ Against Russia to be Unveiled in Poland
Unknown

NATO’s top military commander in Europe is set to unveil his “Theory of Victory” in Poland, a strategy that reportedly sets out how the alliance could repel and ultimately defeat a Russian attack on its eastern flank.

Bloomberg reported on Monday that the plan draws heavily on lessons from the war in Ukraine, where relatively cheap drones and rapidly evolving technologies have reshaped the battlefield and exposed the limits of forces built around more expensive conventional weapons.
The news outlet, which saw an unclassified version of the document, said NATO would seek to stop a Russian incursion by using ground forces backed by low-cost drones, minimally crewed systems and AI-enabled targeting.
Once the alliance had gained freedom of maneuver, its forces would seek to rapidly destroy Russian command-and-control systems and inflict a quick and overwhelming defeat.
Grynkewich is due to present the plan at the Warsaw Security Forum, an annual conference bringing together senior political, military and security officials, that will be held in the Polish capital on October 12-13.

Organizers said the strategy had until now been discussed only at the highest level of NATO’s military leadership. Kosiniak-Kamysz told PAP that he had seen Grynkewich’s proposals and rated the US general’s preparations “very highly.”

‘Maintain NATO’s advantage’
Grynkewich’s spokesman, Col. Martin O’Donnell, told Bloomberg: “The Supreme Allied Commander Europe’s theory of victory is simple: maintain NATO’s advantage.”
“Given the unsettled and complex global security environment, we need to set conditions now to deter aggression and, if necessary, win if attacked,” he said.
According to Bloomberg, the strategy also covers hybrid attacks that fall below the threshold of open warfare, with NATO seeking to demonstrate sufficient readiness to convince a potential adversary that aggression would fail.
Poland is a significant setting for the unveiling. The NATO eastern-flank state borders Ukraine and Belarus and shares a 210-kilometer land frontier with Russia’s heavily militarized Kaliningrad exclave, leaving it exposed in the event of any aggression by Moscow.
Tensions on eastern flank
The plan comes amid heightened tensions between Moscow and the NATO alliance more than four years into Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
NATO says hostile Russian activity against its members and partners, including airspace violations, cyberattacks and acts of sabotage, has increased in frequency.
But NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte said last week there was “no imminent threat” to alliance territory, adding that NATO would detect and respond to any Russian military buildup.
The alliance has nevertheless steadily reinforced its eastern defenses since Russia invaded Ukraine, with Poland among nine countries now hosting multinational battlegroups.
NATO has also adopted what it describes as its most comprehensive and detailed defense plans since the Cold War.

The RBI's rate hike was its first in more than three years. (AFP Photo)
India's central bank hiked interest rates for the first time in more than three years on Oct. 7, as the Middle East conflict stokes inflation in Asia's third-largest economy and batters a weakened rupee.
The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) said the benchmark repurchase rate, the level at which it lends to commercial banks, would be raised by 25 basis points to 5.5 percent after a unanimous vote by a six-member panel.
In doing so, the RBI shifted gears to join several central banks around the world who have raised rates to curb price rises or boost their currencies.
Since the outbreak of the Iran war in February, the RBI has stood pat as it waited to assess the impact of volatile oil prices on the world's fastest-growing major economy.
But resilient GDP growth last quarter has allowed it to focus on higher costs in a country that imports most of its energy and has been hit by a weak monsoon that could result in a spike in food prices.
Retail inflation rose to 4.82 percent in August — the third straight month that headline inflation breached the RBI's medium term target of four percent — with data signalling that inflationary pressures had spread beyond food and transport.
Adding to the central bank's calculations is pressure on the Indian rupee, which has been at near record lows over the past week.
To stem the fall, the RBI has rolled out an array of moves to woo dollar inflows, including a deposit scheme for the Indian diaspora that raked in around $127 billion.
While the steps helped stop the rupee's losses, the currency has faced fresh challenges as foreign investors continue to dump Indian equities and crude hovers around $100 a barrel.
India, the world's third-largest buyer of oil, normally sources about half of its crude through the Strait of Hormuz, which has been effectively closed since the beginning of the Middle East war.
Analysts say this makes India among the most vulnerable economies to a global energy shock, as higher crude and fertiliser prices drive up the import bill.

Christa Pike, 50, was given two doses of the drug pentobarbital at a Tennessee prison on 30 September. She is believed to be the only person to survive after lethal injection drugs were administered.
"Against all odds, Christa Pike is conscious, speaking, and continues to receive critical medical care," her attorneys said on Tuesday.
"Despite the severe damage she endured to her arms, she is still handcuffed and shackled to the bed," they said. "Her prognosis remains unclear but, at a minimum, we expect a long recovery."

The Tennessee attorney general's office said the order was unnecessary because the prison system is "obliged to maintain this evidence in other cases and must assure it is preserved".
Experts have focused on whether a problem with the IV line caused the drug to pool in her tissue instead of entering her bloodstream. A court filing said both Pike's arms were "swollen, burned, and blistered" when she arrived at hospital.
Governor Bill Lee called what happened "deeply disturbing" and ordered a "comprehensive, third-party review". He has suspended executions in the state pending the investigation, and the prison chief has resigned.
Pike's lawyers have again called on Lee to commute her sentence to life imprisonment without the possibility of parole.

Estonian wildlife park bear prefers people over a winter nap

Unknown Publisher

15:06:00 KST

Estonian wildlife park bear prefers people over a winter nap
Half an hour north of Tartu, a bear at Elistvere Animal Park skipped hibernation last winter and may do so again, preferring regular meals and human attention to a long sleep.
Mõmmu-Ursula the brown bear enjoys Estonia's fall foliage and is preparing for winter, but when the abandoned cub first arrived at the park last year, staff were curious whether she would hibernate. She did not, said animal caretaker Kairi Hermits.
"She'd nap in her den during the day, but still came out to eat every morning and evening," Hermits recalled. Since her meals are provided, she may simply have decided there was no need to sleep through the winter.
"Compared with wildlife, our animals have the advantage of us providing them food each day," she said.
Ursula also really enjoys human interaction, and is even known to climb a tree to look for people whenever the park is closed, including on Mondays.
"She's very eager to interact with people; she loves the attention," Hermits said.
Alert your presence, keep your distance
Nonetheless, Hermits urged people to keep their distance from wildlife out in nature.
Wild animals generally avoid contact with people anyway, but she said talking, humming or singing can help alert them to people's presence in the woods and avoid close encounters.
"When you visit friends, you usually ring the doorbell or knock," Hermits explained. "When we visit the forest, we should be polite there too, because we're visiting wildlife."
While urban bear sightings do happen, encounters with brown bears in Estonia are more likely while hiking or foraging. A few simple tips shared by the Estonian Hunters' Society (EJS) can help keep you safe if you run into a brown bear in the wild.

Across China: Multispectral imaging system tracks condition of millennia-old wooden slips
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
14:04:32 CST
15:04:32 KST

LANZHOU, Oct. 7 (Xinhua) -- Under visual observation, virtually no writing is visible on Jiandu, bamboo or wooden slips that ancient Chinese people wrote on before the invention of paper, but in near-infrared images, the outlines of the ink marks faintly emerge.
When switched to the ultraviolet band, subtle cracks and salt efflorescence on the surface of the slips, invisible to the naked eye, become clearly visible. This "magic" is performed by Dorje Rinchen, an office staff member of Gansu Jiandu Museum's science and technology conservation department.
The bamboo and wooden slips collected by Gansu Jiandu Museum were mostly unearthed from frontier fortress sites in northwest China dating back to the Han Dynasty. Made primarily of poplar, rose willow and pine, they are about 2,000 years old.
Buried for millennia in the extremely arid Gobi environment, the slips commonly suffer from such deterioration as salt efflorescence, insect damage, mildew stains and transverse cracks on their surfaces.
All these diseases directly hinder the advancement of text interpretation and research of the slips.
"To solve this problem, the museum introduced infrared imaging technology, which uses the characteristic of infrared wavelengths being strongly absorbed by ink but weakly absorbed by bamboo and wooden substrates, to restore and identify faded and hidden writing on the slips," said Dorje Rinchen.
"However, imaging and scanning in a single wavelength band can only restore parts of textual information and can hardly capture the comprehensive conditions of the slips."
To this end, starting in 2025, the museum introduced a multispectral imaging system. Equipped with high-sensitivity sensors, the system captures images across 32 channels, ranging from near-ultraviolet to near-infrared light, unfolding the slips along the spectral dimension and enabling their "panoramic" documentation.
"Light of different wavelengths differs in its ability to penetrate and reflect off ink, stains and deterioration," said Du Peng, deputy general manager of Tianjin Hengda Wenbo Technology Co., Ltd, the developer of the multispectral imaging system.
The multispectral technology can not only make faded writing on the slips "visible" but also, by comparing different wavelength bands, accurately distinguish original ink from later contamination and pinpoint the location and extent of deterioration, such as salt efflorescence and insect damage, said Du.
The system has carried out all-round image capture of more than 500 bamboo and wooden slips at the museum, generating 33 images for each slip, including the original.
"Jiandu are non-renewable organic cultural relics that slowly decompose under natural conditions," said Dorje Rinchen. Through this multispectral imaging technology, they have established comprehensive "medical records" for the slips, documenting their current condition and the deterioration they suffer.
"By collecting and comparing images again after a period of time, we can monitor the conditions of the slips," he said.
In addition to protecting bamboo and wooden slips, the multispectral imaging system can also be applied to cultural relics such as calligraphy, paintings and artifacts, as well as grotto murals and tomb murals, said Du.
The system developer expects to provide key information support for the multispectral archiving of cultural relics, extraction of hidden information and virtual restoration. ■

SEOUL, Oct. 7 (Xinhua) -- South Korea's homegrown space rocket, Nuri, successfully blasted off on Wednesday and deployed all 15 onboard satellites into their designated orbits, achieving the most complicated and critical mission in its development history.
The three-stage liquid-fueled rocket, officially known as Korea Space Launch Vehicle (KSLV)-II, lifted off at 12:25 p.m. local time (0325 GMT) from the Naro Space Center in Goheung, about 400 km southwest of the capital Seoul.
The sequence proceeded flawlessly, with the first stage, payload fairing, and second stage separating as planned.
Around 12 minutes and 30 seconds after liftoff, Nuri's third-stage engine shut down to initiate a highly sophisticated sequential satellite deployment at its target altitude of 575 km.
The main mission of Nuri's fifth launch was to safely deliver five New-space Earth Observation Satellite Constellation for National Safety (NEONSAT) microsatellites, which were released one by one at 35-to-40-second intervals.
It represented a major advancement in complexity from the fourth launch, which carried a single primary payload.
Following the primary payloads, 10 smaller academic and commercial CubeSats were released in pairs at 10-second intervals.
Nuri will perform a series of post-mission maneuvers to prevent collisions, before re-entering the Earth's atmosphere and burning up. ■

====================================================================================================

Invasive plant spreads across Portugal and lengthens allergy season
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
06:03:55 UTC
15:03:55 KST

Known for its showy plumes and used as an ornamental for decades, pampas grass, also known as Cortaderia selloana, is spreading, threatening biodiversity and raising vegetation management costs. Experts call for urgent action to halt its advance and reduce pollen exposure.
For decades, pampas grass, also known as Cortaderia selloana, was seen mainly as an ornamental plant. Its large feathery plumes made it a familiar sight in gardens and, more recently, in decorative arrangements indoors. But what many still regard as a showy plant is, in Portugal, an invasive alien species that can spread rapidly and has potential consequences for health.
This invasive plant has already been identified in at least 208 municipalities in mainland Portugal, according to a study published in 2025 (source in Portuguese). The real number may, however, be higher, as existing maps depend on records submitted by people on the ground.
The species’ spread is particularly visible along the coast. Areas where there used to be isolated specimens have been turning into zones densely occupied by the species, according to biologist Hélia Marchante, a lecturer at the School of Agriculture of the Polytechnic University of Coimbra and a specialist in invasive plants.
"It is a very, very fast-spreading species", she told Euronews. Unlike other invasive plants that can benefit from specific triggers such as wildfires, the plant also known as cortaderia has an especially effective advantage for spreading: "It only needs the wind."
A plant that has learnt to escape the garden
The history of the invasion helps explain how serious the problem has now become. Native to South America, cortaderia was introduced in different parts of the world as an ornamental plant. For decades, the fact that only female plants were present in gardens is thought to have limited its ability to reproduce.
According to Marchante, that changed at the end of the last century, when hermaphrodite plants were introduced, 'almost certainly by accident', as "pollen donors". Fertilisation of the female plants then allowed the production of large quantities of seed.
"From then on it only needs the wind," the researcher said.
The process repeats itself every year. During flowering, the plants that produce pollen release it into the atmosphere. In female plants, once fertilisation has taken place, each flower can give rise to a seed. The plumes end up acting as a kind of transport system: thousands of tiny seeds can be carried by the wind and colonise new sites.
Spread does not depend solely on natural phenomena, however. People who move the plumes to use them as decoration, as well as vehicles, clothing or equipment, can also inadvertently help to carry seeds to other places.
"It is the movement of the plant itself that has the potential to spread it", warns Marchante, also pointing to cases where plumes are taken indoors.
Pampas grass is no longer just an ornamental feature of the landscape. It is also an invasive species capable of altering the ecosystems where it becomes established. Once the species moves from isolated specimens to large stands, it becomes dense enough to exclude other plants, which can no longer survive in those areas.
The impact extends to fauna as well, since the plant’s sharp leaves and the high density of the stands can make it harder for animals to move through.
There are also less visible effects. According to Marchante, some studies show that the species can also alter nutrient cycles and modify the soil and the microorganisms that live in it.
The problem goes beyond the environment
The environmental dimension of the invasion is only part of the story. Cortaderia also has consequences for human health.
Mário Morais de Almeida, an immunoallergology specialist and president of the World Allergy Organisation, explains that pampas grass belongs to the grass family and therefore releases pollen that can trigger symptoms in sensitised people.
"As this is a grass species, it will indeed release its pollen into the atmosphere, again carried by the wind, and it can cause significant allergic symptoms."
The problem is particularly serious because of the time of year when cortaderia flowers. The grasses most familiar to Portuguese people are prominent in spring and early summer. Cortaderia can extend that exposure into late summer and autumn.
For people with allergic rhinitis or conjunctivitis, exposure can lead to sneezing, itching, runny nose, congestion, red and watery eyes. In those with asthma, exposure can contribute to respiratory symptoms and more severe attacks.
"This grass, which can indeed release very, very large amounts of pollen, manages to do so throughout the summer, and even into autumn," says Morais de Almeida.
However, the doctor stresses that there is currently no specific epidemiological evidence that would allow a given number of allergy cases in Portugal to be attributed to pampas grass. What exists is knowledge about grass allergies, clinical experience and evidence of the allergenic capacity of this species’ pollen.
"At the moment we do not have evidence that is directly linked to pampas grass," he notes, adding that there is nonetheless a perception that allergic complaints are lasting longer. According to the specialist, the combination of climate change, different types of pollen and other agents present in the atmosphere makes the picture more complex.
Because the seeds are carried by the wind, the impact is not necessarily confined to the immediate vicinity of the plant. Marchante explains that the seeds can travel several kilometres, especially in conditions of strong wind, while the pollen can also be transported over long distances.
There is another issue: people can unwittingly help to move the pollen around.
"People pick the plumes because they are very beautiful, they paint them, they take them home," the biologist explains. In addition to contributing to the spread of seeds, that behaviour can bring potentially allergenic material into homes.
Morais de Almeida therefore offers an important piece of advice: do not take the plumes home and avoid handling the plant. On top of its allergenic potential, the leaves themselves are sharp enough to cause injuries.
"The pleasant appearance the plant may have" should not make people forget the risks associated with exposure to it, the doctor warns.
The danger of letting another year pass
For Marchante, one of the main challenges is precisely time. The more a plant grows and produces seed, the greater the likelihood that new individuals will emerge nearby and that the invaded area will expand.
"Each one that is left on its own in a more isolated area is another that will produce thousands of seeds, which will germinate and give rise to new plants next year," she explains, stressing that "if we fail to act now, next year it will be much, much more difficult, much more expensive and much worse to intervene".
The strategy does not necessarily have to focus on trying to eliminate all the large stands that are already established in one go. The biologist argues for the identification and priority removal of isolated specimens and small clusters on the edges of the areas currently occupied. The aim is to prevent these hotspots from acting as new starting points for invasion of fresh territory.
In some of the areas where the species has been established for longer, complete eradication will be much more difficult, if not practically impossible, the specialist believes. The alternative is control and ongoing intervention.
"What I think is that we still have a huge amount of work we can do, because there are so many places with small nuclei of individual plants," she says.
The timing of intervention is equally important. Removing only the plumes after the seeds have already been shed can mean working without preventing the spread that has already occurred.
"To be sure of eliminating this plant, there has to be a window of time before May; it is during that period that it should be pulled out," she explains.
And she has a clear message: "In fact, I say pull it up, pull it up by the roots, pull everything up, always pull it up; that is what we want."
However, during the period when the seeds are being released, any intervention must be carried out in such a way as to avoid the control measures themselves contributing to their dispersal.
Prohibited species still widespread
Cortaderia has been on the Portuguese national list of invasive species (source in Portuguese) since 2019. The legislation bans, among other actions, its possession, planting, sale and introduction into the wild.
In practice, however, it can still be found in private gardens, municipal spaces, industrial areas, roadsides and other locations.
Marchante points to a lack of awareness of the law and a lack of enforcement as some of the obstacles to controlling the species.
There is also a coordination problem. A municipality may remove plants from a garden under its management, only to find specimens in private plots or in infrastructure managed by other bodies.
The invasion also has a socioeconomic dimension, as the presence of large cortaderia plants makes vegetation management more difficult and more expensive, particularly in areas where vegetation has to be cleared for wildfire prevention.
There are already projects such as LIFE COOP Cortaderia (source in Portuguese), which brings together institutions in Portugal, Spain and France to fight this invasive species, and municipalities involved in control measures, but the researcher calls for a coordinated strategy.
The Institute for Nature Conservation and Forests (ICNF) has drawn up a proposal for a National Action Plan for the Control of Cortaderia under Decree-Law No. 92/2019 (source in Portuguese), although its official publication and implementation have been delayed.
The biologist hopes that the forthcoming National Action Plan against invasive alien species will set out priorities, responsibilities and ways of intervening.
To make those measures effective, she argues that the plan should be accompanied by funding mechanisms enabling municipalities, non-governmental organisations, parish councils, road management bodies and even private citizens to cover the costs of removal.
"To remove one of the big cortaderia plants, you often need a mini excavator," she notes, stressing that the size of some specimens makes control operations costly, and not everyone can afford them.
What can you do if you come across cortaderia?
For citizens, the first recommendation is not to plant or move the species. Anyone who has cortaderia in their garden should seek to remove it, ideally with technical support if it is a large specimen.
People who spot specimens in public spaces can also help to build knowledge about the species’ distribution. Hélia Marchante recommends using the iNaturalist (source in Portuguese) platform, where it is possible to photograph a plant and record its location. These data help build maps that can then be used to set priorities for action.
"That is very important when strategies are being drawn up to eliminate it," she stresses.
While the plant has not yet been removed, cutting the plumes before the seeds are released can help to curb dispersal. But that is only a temporary measure. "Removing the plumes does not solve the problem," the biologist stresses. "The aim must always be to remove the whole plant."
For people with respiratory allergies, Morais de Almeida also advises reducing exposure during periods of higher pollen concentration. In certain circumstances, wearing a mask and eye protection may be useful, along with sticking to medication prescribed for diagnosed allergic disease.
"We know that early in the morning and later in the afternoon are the times when pollen levels are highest, so at those times we should avoid airing or ventilating our homes; otherwise we may be contaminating the indoor environment. If we are travelling by car, we should probably keep the windows closed; if we are on a motorbike, we should opt for a full-face helmet and wear goggles," the immunoallergology specialist recommends.
The doctor also draws attention to specific weather conditions. During storms, humidity can contribute to the fragmentation of pollen grains, making them easier to inhale, which can worsen respiratory symptoms in sensitised individuals.

PHNOM PENH, Oct. 7 (Xinhua) -- Cambodian Prime Minister Hun Manet said on Wednesday that the government has injected nearly 500 million U.S. dollars in subsidies to cushion the domestic impact of soaring global fuel prices driven by ongoing conflicts in the Middle East.
"To date, we have subsidized almost 500 million dollars to curb rising fuel costs and stabilize electricity prices for our citizens," he said during a ceremony celebrating the 80th anniversary of the University of Health Sciences in Phnom Penh.
The prime minister emphasized that these subsidy programs will continue as long as global fuel markets remain elevated.
He said the financial relief has been delivered through direct subsidies on electricity tariffs alongside targeted tax relief. Thong Mengdavid, deputy director of the China-ASEAN Studies Center at the Cambodia University of Technology and Science, said that surging energy costs directly inflate local transportation and production expenses.
"This trend drives domestic inflation and erodes consumer purchasing power, particularly impacting food and agricultural products," he told Xinhua.
He added that these government subsidies act as a crucial fiscal cushion, ensuring long-term economic resilience and national growth.
The Southeast Asian nation relies entirely on imported petroleum and diesel, as its offshore oil reserves remain unexploited. ■

Economic Watch: Russian tourism industry eyes attracting more Chinese visitors
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
14:03:35 CST
15:03:35 KST

MOSCOW, Oct. 7 (Xinhua) -- During China's week-long National Day holiday this year, Chinese tourists are frequently seen on the streets of Moscow. "Russia is a unique country and a must-visit," said Wang Xinzuo, who visited several Russian cities and described his trip as smooth and enjoyable.
In the first half of 2026, Chinese tourists accounted for over 50 percent of all inbound tourist trips to Russia.
"We are witnessing a substantial rise in travel volumes. In 2025, the number of mutual tourist visits exceeded 3 million. According to our data, 154,200 Chinese tourists visited Russia in the first quarter alone this year, marking a 44 percent increase year on year," Chinese Ambassador to Russia Zhang Hanhui said before the holiday.
Russia is preparing for further growth. In early September, Russian Deputy Prime Minister Dmitry Chernyshenko said the country aims to accommodate more than 5.5 million Chinese tourists by 2030.
Behind the figures lies an industry adapting to a new generation of Chinese travelers.
MOSCOW: FROM GROUP TO INDEPENDENT TRAVEL
Moscow remains the main gateway for Chinese tourists. According to the Border Service of the Russian Federation, 240,000 Chinese tourists visited Moscow in the first half of 2026, up 7 percent year on year.
But the profile of visitors is changing. Guided group tours are becoming less dominant as younger and more independent Chinese travelers arrive.
More than 80 percent of travelers from China come to Moscow independently, including for business, according to Bulat Nurmukhanov, deputy chairman of the Moscow Tourism Committee.
In response, a China Friendly certification program is expanding in Moscow, covering services such as Chinese-language information, adapted menus and trained staff.
The Cosmos Hotel Group told Xinhua that two of its four- and five-star hotels in Moscow have received the certification, with more properties planned to join the program.
Moscow has also strengthened its promotion in China through Chinese-language tourism services, social media and cooperation with Chinese travel platforms, while highlighting its cultural heritage and modern attractions.
REGIONS SEEK NEW OPPORTUNITIES
Beyond Moscow, Russian regions are increasingly competing for Chinese tourists.
In St. Petersburg, the number of Chinese tourists has risen by nearly 60 percent since 2021, according to Nana Gvichiya, deputy chair of the city's Tourism Development Committee. Chinese visitors are showing a growing interest not only in historical sites but also in local cuisine and creative spaces.
In the Altai region, the number of Chinese tourists increased 1.5 times in 2025 from the previous year, exceeding 6,000 for the first time, said Alexander Baryshnikov, head of the regional Department for Tourism and Resort Development.
Although the region receives fewer Chinese visitors than Moscow and St. Petersburg partly because of a lack of direct flights, local businesses are improving services and developing China-friendly tourism products. Several hotels and resorts have received China Friendly certification, while tour operators have developed specialized routes and promoted them through international exhibitions and Chinese social media.
In Russia's Far East, the Amur region has recorded a 60 percent increase in Chinese tourists since the introduction of the visa-free policy between China and Russia in 2025, Governor Vasily Orlov said. The region plans more than 200 joint events with China in 2026.
A planned cross-border cable car linking Blagoveshchensk and Heihe is also expected to boost tourism. Once completed, the journey between the two countries will take just over two minutes, with an annual capacity of 2.5 million passengers.
ADAPTING SERVICES
The rapid growth has also exposed gaps in Russia's tourism infrastructure. Experts and tourists cite language barriers, difficulties with digital payments and a shortage of qualified staff, particularly outside major tourist destinations.
"Special attention should be paid to the training of professional guides for Chinese groups in Russia," said Anastasia Pavlova, an expert on cultural and tourism cooperation at the Russian State University for the Humanities.
Ilya Umansky, president of the Russian Union of Tourism Industry, stressed the need for closer cooperation between the two sides in the tourism sector.
"Today we find ourselves in a unique state of revival of our mutual tourist exchanges," Umansky said. "I am confident that we have a great future." ■

How Verifactu will affect Spanish SMEs and self-employed after its delay
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
06:03:25 UTC
15:03:25 KST

The Government's delay in bringing the Verifactu e-invoicing system into force gives firms and the self-employed more time, but fuels uncertainty over its rollout.
The Spanish government has postponed until 2027 (source in Spanish), and later to 2028, the entry into force of Verifactu, the electronic invoicing system designed to strengthen tax control over companies and self-employed workers. The move pushes back by one year the original timetable, which had set its implementation for 2026 (source in Spanish).
Under the new calendar, companies subject to Corporation Tax will have to adapt from 2028, while the self-employed and SMEs will have until 1 July of that same year.
The system requires invoices to be issued using certified software that guarantees the authenticity, integrity and traceability of records, as part of the fight against tax fraud.
More time, but also uncertainty
The postponement gives more time to adapt IT programmes and internal processes, reducing the immediate pressure on millions of small businesses.
However, different voices in the sector point out that the delay has also created confusion because of the lack of clarity about technical requirements and the final implementation deadlines.
These doubts are compounded by warnings from organisations representing the self-employed and from the business community itself. The National Federation of Associations of Self-Employed Workers (ATA) had for weeks been calling for an extension (source in Spanish), citing adaptation difficulties and a lack of clear information.
Even so, the union representing technicians at the Ministry of Finance, Gestha (source in Spanish), believes the extension is a "key tool" that could be "useful" for millions of taxpayers.
A structural change still to come
Despite the extension, Verifactu remains a structural change in Spain's tax system that will affect most of the business sector. The rules, promoted by the Tax Agency, form part of measures to digitise the economy and strengthen fiscal transparency, with possible sanctions for non-compliance once they come into force.
According to Eurostat data, only 58% of small and medium-sized enterprises in the EU have reached a basic level of digital services, well below the 90% target set for 2030. The gap is even wider compared with large companies, where the level of digitalisation reaches 91%, highlighting the specific difficulties SMEs face in adapting to technological and regulatory change.
In the case of Spain, the figures show progress but also limits to business digitalisation. According to a survey (source in Spanish) by the National Statistics Institute (INE), 44.3% of companies use cloud computing services and 21.1% use artificial intelligence, while 84.5% have a website.
However, the level of adoption of more advanced technologies remains uneven, especially among small companies.
Moreover, various official indicators place Spanish SMEs in an intermediate position within the EU: around 60% reach a basic level of digitalisation, in line with the European average, but still far from the goals set by Brussels for this decade.

Europe out to support chemicals industry, but at a price
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
06:02:06 UTC
15:02:06 KST

This photo shows an environmental protest held in front of the BASF pesticide factory in Saint-Aubin-lès-Elbeuf, France, Nov. 17, 2025. (AFP Photo)
Europe, spurred on by France, wants to provide support for its crucial chemical industry, which is struggling with high energy costs and global competition.
Yet a slew of stakeholders fear that bolstering the sector will harm the environment, public health and even consumers.
France Chimie, the sector lobby in France, along with its Dutch, Hungarian, Italian and Spanish counterparts, said in a joint press release at the start of the month that the European chemicals industry, which produces fertilisers, plastics, medicine and industrial gases, is facing a "systemic crisis."
The European Commission, the European Union's executive arm, has set up a "Critical Chemicals Alliance" (CCA) with industry groups, and holds its general assembly on Oct. 8 in France's eastern Moselle region.
"Over the past two years we have witnessed the announcement of closures of more than 20 major production sites in the EU, with associated job losses and the erosion of our market position," Siobhan McGarry, an EU spokesperson for industrial policy, told AFP.
"The Alliance is focused on maintaining our chemicals industry during its clean transition," McGarry said.
Between 2008 and 2024, Europe's share of the global chemicals market slid from 23 percent to 13 percent, while China's share rose from 19 percent to 46 percent, according to European industry association Cefic.
Over the same period, the global market expanded in value from $2 trillion to $5 trillion.
The European chemical sector, which is a major consumer of gas and processes petroleum-based products, is also grappling with rising fossil fuel prices owing to the war in the Middle East, which comes on top of 2022's price surge following Russia's invasion of Ukraine.
Cefic told AFP that "competitive pressures, declining investment and production challenges in certain value chains" were now so high that it "currently acts as a disincentive to large-scale investments."
The association, which brings together industry giants such as Arkema, TotalEnergies, BASF, Dow, Syensqo and Ineos — as well as public bodies and several NGOs — is hoping to reach a consensus on what chemical production is most critical to Europe's economy.
The group calls for a "level playing field" with China, arguing that it subsidises its companies, enabling them to undercut prices.
Some others fear rising customer prices if the right balance on protectionism is not struck.
France plays a key role in pushing the EU to support the chemical industry.
In mid-September, the French Minister Delegate for Industry, Sebastien Martin, urged Europe to "take concrete and swift measures" to "protect and strengthen our chemical production."
But the push has sparked concern among environmental protection groups.
On Oct. 1, the European Environmental Bureau (EEB) announced it was walking away from the alliance, which it believed would "preserve current chemical production — including hazardous substances, high emitters, and those reliant on fossil fuels — rather than initiating the transformation Europe needs."
The EEB's Tatiana Santos said the alliance comprises "around 300 industrial groups and four or five NGOs. So we know the outcome and we just don't want to be linked to any of these proposals that are so threatening for protecting human health, the environment and climate."
In July, the EEB published a report with another NGO, Corporate Europe Observatory, expressing concern that "several problematic and hazardous substances," specifically PFAS, or "forever chemicals", might be classified as "critical."
Vicky Cann of Corporate Europe Observatory says she fears that the alliance's conclusions will serve "established players in the chemical industry," making the "transition to a cleaner, safer, and more sustainable industry even more difficult."

Two months after disappearing while traveling abroad and setting off a search that drew national attention in Israel, Mali and Liel Yahalomi returned home Wednesday, people close to the mother and daughter said.
The two landed in Israel on a flight from Athens in the afternoon. “They returned to Israel to recover,” people close to them said. Police did not detain them upon their arrival.
The first images of the pair back in Israel showed the mother and daughter wearing matching outfits as they made their way through the airport without speaking to reporters.
Their attorney said the women wanted to return home and rest after their two-month ordeal. “They are not enemies of the people,” she said. “They want to get home and rest after everything they have been through.”
Mali’s brother, Moshe, also welcomed their return. “We’re happy they’re home,” he said. “For now, we’re asking for privacy.”
Their return came hours after an erroneous report that the pair had been arrested in Namibia, in southwestern Africa, on suspicion of possessing forged passports. Israeli police later clarified that the women detained there were not the Yahalomis but two Iranian nationals, a mother and daughter, who had allegedly posed as Israelis and presented forged passports.
Chabad Rabbi Yosef Rahimi, who is active in Africa, said he discovered the mistaken identification when he went to visit the detainees.
“We received a report from the police. I went to see them with breakfast, and it wasn’t them,” Rahimi said. “They are Iranian, a mother and daughter. During questioning, they claimed they were from Israel.”
The mix-up added another twist to a case that began in August, when Mali and Liel disappeared while traveling in Europe, prompting fears in Israel that they may have been caught up in a serious security incident.
About a week after their disappearance, the mother and daughter were found aboard a bus in Buenos Aires, Argentina, after Israeli authorities had expressed grave concern for their safety. An Israeli police representative in South America questioned them and found no indication of criminal wrongdoing, after which they were allowed to continue their travels. Authorities later assessed that financial difficulties may have been behind their disappearance.
Investigators determined that their journey had not begun in Vienna, as initially believed, but in the Czech Republic, where mobile phones can be purchased without presenting a passport. They were believed to have traveled from there to Vienna, where they recorded videos intended for relatives.
The videos, however, were apparently sent only after the two had already left Austria and traveled to another country, believed to be Germany. A senior Israeli police official said at the time that investigators believed the delay was intended to create the false impression that the pair were still in Vienna.
From Germany, the two flew to Argentina, where they were eventually located and questioned by the Israeli police representative. Officials believed at the time that Buenos Aires was not intended to be the end of their journey and that they planned to continue to another destination, which authorities did not disclose.
Their arrival in Israel on Wednesday brought that journey to an end, two months after their disappearance.
The two women mistakenly identified as the Yahalomis remain a separate case. Israeli police said they were Iranian nationals who allegedly falsely identified themselves as Israelis and presented forged travel documents in Namibia.
Namibia, a sparsely populated country on Africa’s southwestern Atlantic coast, borders Angola and Zambia to the north, Botswana to the east and South Africa to the south. It gained independence in 1990 and has maintained diplomatic relations with Israel since 2013, though the countries do not maintain embassies in each other’s territory. Relations have faced tensions in recent years over the war in Gaza.

HMS Queen Elizabeth trials all-day dining at sea
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
07:00:19 BST
15:00:19 KST

Sailors aboard HMS Queen Elizabeth are being fed around the clock rather than at fixed meal times, under a trial the Royal Navy has chosen the carrier to run on behalf of the whole fleet, according to the service.
The ship, currently training around the United Kingdom, is the testbed for what the Navy calls its Generational Change to Feeding programme. Fleet Caterer Warrant Officer 1 Wes Cain and Chief Petty Officer Chris Roberts of the Flag Officer Sea Training organisation have been working with nutritionists and scientists from the Institute of Naval Medicine on how the service feeds people at sea, and on what today’s sailors actually want to eat.
The carrier has two main galleys, and the forward one has been turned into what the ship’s company have taken to calling the grazing galley, serving food without a break from nine in the morning until six in the evening. Salmon bagels, fruit salad and toasted paninis are among the options, batch cooked to keep up with demand, while the aft galley carries on providing three traditional meals a day.
Warrant Officer 2 Barney Barnes, the ship’s catering warrant officer, said: “Everyone onboard is busy, so giving people a chance to eat at a time that suits them and their working pattern should be a big help to a lot of people.
“For example, we were finding many of our watchkeepers would skip breakfast to prioritise rest after a busy watch. This new way of feeding allows them to still be able to have something to eat, which in turn increases both their morale and operational effectiveness.”
He added: “Our golden rule is that we’re not taking anything away. There will still be meals served at set times; all-day feeding gives our sailors options to eat something else instead.”
Part of the purpose is easing the load on the catering department itself, which numbers 50 and faces a punishing schedule when the carrier has her squadrons embarked and around 1,600 people aboard. Spreading demand across the day rather than concentrating it into three rushes is intended to even out the shifts.
The ship’s logistics officer, Adam Cook, said: “A huge part of why we introduced this was to balance our caterers’ workload against the demands they’re facing.
“Our goal is to make catering easier in the long run. Spreading demand throughout the day will ease some of the pressure on those working regular galley shifts.”

Putin, meanwhile, is pressing ahead with the invasion in the belief that Ukrainians will buckle under the pressure and Kyiv’s Western supporters won’t stay the course, Western analysts say.
“Russia is pursuing a deliberate strategy of terror,” European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said on X. “Trying to make daily life impossible for Ukrainians who want to live in peace.”
A Russian strike destroyed an apartment block in Pryluky, in Ukraine’s northern Chernihiv region, killing 15 people, including four children, and wounding about 50, authorities said.
Deaths were also reported in three other Ukrainian cities, including the capital Kyiv, according to Zelensky.
“The Russians wanted to strike painfully and demonstratively,” the Ukrainian leader said on social media.
Ukraine is looking worldwide for available Patriot missiles, which are in short supply due to the Iran war.
“Russian ballistic missiles remain the greatest challenge. And air defence packages for us right now are a vital necessity,” Zelensky said.
In Kremenchuk, in the Poltava region, two people were killed and seven injured, said Vitalii Diakivnych, head of the regional military administration, and a rescue operation was continuing.
“That is exactly what the enemy is counting on. For us to be afraid to fall asleep. To let our children out of our sight. To plan anything. So that everyone thinks: next time it could be my address,” he said.
Russia’s Defence Ministry said the military carried out a massive strike overnight targeting industrial facilities involved in the production and storage of missiles and drones across Ukraine. The ministry said that port and ship repair facilities in the southern Odesa region and ships carrying cargo for the Ukrainian military were also hit.
Ukraine has hit back at Russia by launching long-range drones and missiles at oil refineries and storage depots.
Zelensky said Wednesday that Ukraine targeted two oil facilities and a training ground in the Perm, Samara, and Astrakhan regions of Russia.
Russian officials made no immediate comment.
Zelensky also indicated that Ukraine had struck in the Black Sea. He posted images of a fire said to show an oil tanker burning in the water near the Russian city of Sochi.
It was not possible to independently verify the images.
Some Russian online media late Tuesday also posted the images. Unconfirmed media reports said it was carrying oil from Novorossiysk to India and was attacked by Ukrainian sea drones.
