How Netanyahu survived the political fallout from the October 7 attacks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
05:24:03 UTC
14:24:03 KST

How Netanyahu survived the political fallout from the October 7 attacks
Three years after the deadly Hamas-led October 7 attacks in southern Israel, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu is fighting for political survival ahead of legislative elections later this month. Reports that Arab leaders warned him of the assault in advance have undercut his claims that Israel's security chiefs are to blame, but his political base appears to be holding.
Three years ago, thousands of Hamas-led militants breached the border between Gaza and Israel in a surprise attack, killing 1,205 people and taking 251 as hostages back to the Gaza Strip. Israel responded with a heavy hand and launched a military campaign in Gaza during which at least 74,347 people have been killed, according to the enclave’s Hamas-run health ministry.
The events have left deep scars in Israel, where voters will elect a new parliament on October 27, and have become a central issue in the campaign.
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu is running for another term, but the question of what he knew before the deadly attacks three years ago is hanging over Israel’s longest-serving leader. As Israel heads to the polls, reports that Arab leaders warned him of a looming Hamas offensive have not let up.
What Netanyahu knew
Israeli journalists Shlomi Eldar and Ruth Yuval revealed that President Mohammed bin Zayed al-Nahyan of the United Arab Emirates (UAE) had warned Netanyahu by phone about 10 days before the October 7 attacks in 2023 that a major confrontation with Hamas was coming.
In extracts of their book that were first published on September 8 by Israeli newspaper Haaretz, the journalists cited “three foreign senior sources” and a Palestinian adviser to bin Zayed who all confirmed that the UAE's president telephoned the Israeli leader. During their 45-minute conversation, bin Zayed allegedly told Netanyahu that a former Hamas leader in Gaza, Yahya Sinwar, was planning a major operation that could lead to “bloodshed” and even “destabilise the region”. To bin Zayed’s surprise, the journalists reported, “Netanyahu reacted calmly” and said “Israel was prepared for any scenario”.
The report went on to say that bin Zayed told former CIA director William J. Burns about the conversation. But for his part, Netanyahu did not brief state security agency Shin Bet, the Mossad intelligence agency or his army chief of staff about the call.
To display this content from YouTube, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.
The prime minister’s office denied the accusations, saying no warning was given and that the report was a “wicked fabrication with clear political timing” by left-wing Israeli officials.
Netanyahu has since sued Haaretz for defamation. But the newspaper is standing its ground and has been backed by The New York Times, which confirmed and added details to the report.
The debate over whether Netanyahu knew about the October 7 attacks has now reached a boiling point. Reports of Egyptian intelligence chief Abbas Kamel also warning Netanyahu days before Hamas breached the border, published by The Atlantic and the Wall Street Journal, have also flooded the scene.
The UAE has not directly addressed the reports but has acknowledged that “when necessary, all relevant intelligence has been and continues to be communicated” since Abu Dhabi reestablished relations with Israel in 2020.
Netanyahu made a secret trip to Abu Dhabi on September 27 and met with bin Zayed for about an hour, which Israel’s Channel 12 first reported. One source said the discussion centred on the Haaretz report and that Netanyahu asked the Emirati leader to deny that he had warned the Israeli leader of a looming attack.
Netanyahu’s office rejected the claim, dismissing it as “fake news”, while the official Emirates News Agency said the two sides met to discuss “bilateral relations”.
Deflect and deny
Netanyahu’s response to the reports has been mainly to shift the blame onto others, in stark contrast to several of Israel’s senior security officials.
Former military chief of staff Herzi Halevi took responsibility for letting the October 7 attacks happen and stepped down in January 2025. Following his resignation, an internal investigation carried out by the Israeli Defence Forces acknowledged the attacks as one of its “greatest failures”.
A few months later, the Israeli government sacked the head of its Shin Bet intelligence agency, Ronen Bar. The decision was in part fallout from an internal report on the October 7 attack, but Netanyahu also cited an ongoing “lack of trust” as a reason to dismiss Bar.
Bar responded with a letter saying the Israeli prime minister’s arguments were “unsubstantiated accusations” and that his real motive was to “prevent investigations into the events leading up to October 7”.
Just hours after Netanyahu renewed his accusations against Bar, on September 28 the former intelligence chief threatened to sue for defamation. He said the Israeli leader was “attempting to deflect blame away from himself by levelling accusations at those who warned him in real time,” according to an article published by The Times of Israel.
Read moreNetanyahu gave a ‘victory to Hamas’ by rejecting US-backed Gaza peace plan
“Faced with these allegations, Netanyahu has counter-attacked by pointing his finger to a ‘deep state’ composed of security services and left-wing bureaucratic elites. What he is actually saying is that generals, leaders, security agencies and judges have sought his downfall by allowing the October 7 attacks to take place,” said Nicolas Rouger, a journalist based in Israel and author of the book “Netanyahu – Agent of Chaos”.
The Israeli leader has even claimed his security chiefs intentionally let him sleep for hours after Hamas launched its assault on October 7 for fear he would trigger an aggressive response and immediately put the entire military on alert. “If they would have woken me up, everything would have looked different,” he said in a campaign video posted on X in August.
A schedule published by Netanyahu's office contradicts the claim, however, saying he was informed at 6:29am of an attack from the Gaza Strip.
“Whether it’s his ongoing corruption trial or the allegations of ignored warnings, scandals seem to roll off him like water off a duck’s back,” said Sylvaine Bulle, an expert on Israeli society and professor of sociology at Paris’s EHESS university. “He is very nimble and politically astute. The more Netanyahu absolves himself of all responsibility, the more points he scores.”
Read moreRaising the Altalena: Netanyahu digs up sunken 1948 arms ship in ‘pre-election stunt’
Netanyahu has repeatedly rejected calls to set up a state inquiry into the October 7 attacks – even as the army and intelligence services have investigated their own conduct – saying an investigation can only be launched once the war is over.
Despite much of the Israeli public being in favour of an independent investigation, Netanyahu claimed in November last year that most Israelis didn’t believe in such a commission and proposed a separate committee established by the prime minister himself.
Neck and neck
Gadi Eisenkot, a former military chief who has become Netanyahu's main challenger ahead of the October 27 elections, accused the veteran prime minister of dodging accountability for security failures. He dismissed Netanyahu's explanations, including the claim that he wasn't woken early enough on the morning of the attack, as feeble excuses.
In a post on X, Eisenkot said Netanyahu had “ignored” dozens of warnings before October 7 and declared him “unfit” to lead.
Netanyahu’s rivals, including Eisenkot, have promised to establish an independent commission of inquiry if elected.
Read moreIsraeli ex-army chief emerges as main rival to Netanyahu ahead of general election

But some believe Israeli voters are unlikely to be swayed by a centrist bloc led by Eisenkot amid the increasingly rightward shift of the electorate – notably among the youth.
“The opposition carries little weight. Their campaign doesn’t have much substance, even if [Eisenkot] has a clear path ahead. By neglecting issues like domestic policy, social justice, housing and the fight against regional inequalities, it has allowed religious parties to take control of social issues among the religious working classes,” said Bulle.
Though Netanyahu may be slightly weakened by the reports about him, he still has a loyal base.
“In Netanyahu's view, Jewish people drift from one catastrophe to the next, and Netanyahu embodies a captain who can steer the ship through the storm,” said Rouger. “October 7 confirmed that, making force the only acceptable response. That rhetoric is very well-honed in Israel and has been internalised by the population.”
“The trauma of October 7 has not weakened Netanyahu’s traditional support base, it has strengthened it,” added Bulle.
“He is the only person who can turn an entire nation’s fear of existential threat into votes. He has been doing it for three years and it’s working.”

Nevertheless, the latest polls show Eisenkot slightly ahead of Netanyahu in the upcoming elections, with 54 Knesset seats against 49 for the current prime minister's coalition.
“Even among Israelis who oppose Netanyahu, acknowledge he is corrupt and that his leadership is chaotic, international criticism always comes up against a brick wall. When the International Criminal Court put out an arrest warrant against him for crimes committed in the Gaza Strip, the argument of anti-Semitism took precedence above all else,” Rouger noted.
“Israelis only trust the Israeli media,” he said. “The rest – who are reporting on the destruction of Gaza, for example – are virtually invisible.”

Widely used, rarely disclosed: The extent of AI inside government, revealed​‌
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
05:18:06 UTC
14:18:06 KST

In Brief
- Some agencies are trialling AI agents that can analyse information and coordinate tasks.
- Experts warn AI can shape decisions even when humans retain final approval.
Hundreds of artificial intelligence (AI) use cases across 20 federal government departments have detailed experimental agents and tools being used to draft, summarise and analyse documents or workflows.
But it's the lack of transparency and apparent absence of an enforcement agency to monitor or police unapproved or 'shadow' AI use that concerns experts most.
Freedom of Information (FOI) releases over the past four weeks reveal AI is being used widely in government departments including the health department, ASIC, the Australian Competition and Consumer Commission, the agiculture department, the Department of Industry, Science and Resources and the Commonwealth Obudsman.
The Department of Industry, Science and Resources is one department experimenting with AI agents to perform tasks.
It said its trials of "agentic task automation and orchestration" are tested and evaluated, with humans checking outputs to identify and manage risks such as bias, omission or mischaracterisation of information. Among the 19 use cases, pre-built and custom AI agents conduct analysis, generate content, interact with authorised systems and "orchestrate activities across one or more data sources, tools and services".
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
"Tools remain subject to departmental governance, defined controls, human oversight and approval by departmental staff," a spokesperson told SBS News.
But Murdoch University computer science professor David Parry argues government assurances don't cater for the possibility the decision may be based on information summarised, modelled or extracted by AI tools.
"The self-declaration approach [by government departments] is unlikely to detect 'shadow' [unapproved] uses, or global issues across the government," he said.
"There doesn’t seem to be much in the way of explicit auditing or independent evaluation.
"The benefit of using these tools — that complex analysis can be performed with fewer or less-expert humans — leads to the difficulty of reliably assessing the outputs and detecting errors."
Health Department's risky AI use
In September, auditors found unapproved or 'shadow' AI use in the federal health department, which had "not yet systematically identified, assessed and established treatments for AI risks".
There were 46 novel (new) AI use cases across the health portfolio. One pilot project helped staff query and summarise Primary Health Network activity work plans. It gave links to source documents and had human oversight.
But Australian Catholic University computational intelligence professor Niusha Shafiabady said attaching source links to an AI summary is a "band-aid solution" to oversight.
"Health (appears to be) using generative models that paraphrase and hallucinate [make up information], and then hoping tired, overworked staff will click every link to catch the mistakes," Shafiabady said.
"If the goal is pulling facts from work plans, a real AI expert would engineer a purely extractive pipeline, one that retrieves verbatim information without the mathematical ability to invent anything and hallucinate. The key question is whether the system has been rigorously tested for this specific task: What is its error rate?"
A health department spokesperson said the department takes a "risk-based approach" to AI, considering transparency, explainability, human oversight, privacy, risk mitigation, and accountability.
"Any use cases that do proceed to implementation must comply with the safeguards the department has in place to support the responsible use of AI and to ensure staff remain accountable for decisions made when using AI-assisted tools," they said.
"This includes checking outputs against source material, reviewing and collaborating with subject matter experts as required, and ensuring any use of content generated by AI remains subject to human judgement, governance controls and departmental quality standards."
'Shadow AI' use by government employees
University of Sydney law professor and chief investigator at the ARC Centre of Excellence on Automated Decision-Making and Society, Kimberlee Weatherall, said her recent research across Victorian government departments didn't just find shadow AI use; it was actively being surveilled by IT teams to see if it could learn how people wanted to use AI or which tools were missing.
"The worry about shadow use is that things are going into [a public AI chatbot], and the extent of tracking and visibility that is occurring is terrifying," Weatherall said.
This shadow AI use by government employees on personal AI accounts presents many risks, said Professor Toby Walsh, chief scientist of the AI Institute and scientia professor of AI at UNSW.
"I could imagine the reason that we've had all these hacking incidents into government departments is that those departments have actually been putting information into ChatGPT, which then went into the training data, which then told the agent that there's interesting information found in these government departments, and then it's gone to the government to try and find that information in more detail," he said.
"I'd like to know, and I don't know. Which is troubling because I'm not just a citizen, I'm actually reasonably AI qualified."
Weatherall agreed, saying despite the government issuing "really quite helpful guidance and information about how to do AI well", it's guidance; it's not enforceable.
"There's no significant reporting on it, the agencies effectively govern themselves and decide what they want to tell us about AI," she said
The Digital Transformation Agency (DTA) has "never had significant enforcement power" it's purely advisory, and its main remit is to facilitate AI use, Weatherall said.
"(And) this is one of the most one of the interesting things about this trove of documents. The departments have to issue these AI transparency statements and then internally they create these much more detailed use case registers that they don't have to publish or tell us about."
DTA Deputy CEO Ramsey Beydoun told SBS News that 120 agencies have published AI transparency statements, detailing a high-level overview of where and how AI is used, without requiring them to publish individual use cases or use-case-level detail.
New rules started in December 2025 requiring agencies to assign an accountable use case owner, mandatory training for all staff, and mechanisms to monitor and evaluate AI systems.
An internal register of all AI use cases is due by 15 December 2026, but the policy does not mandate that agencies publish these.
"The AI Review Committee helps agencies adopt AI safely and consistently by providing expert advice on AI use cases with a residual high-risk rating and use cases that agencies determine to be highly sensitive, novel, or complex, Beydoun said.
Where does AI assistance end and influence begin?
At the workplace regulator, the Fair Work Ombudsman (FWO), Microsoft Copilot is used to "support first-pass review and summarisation" as well as "checking apparent continuity or gaps in pay period information".
FWO staff are trained to use the technology with mandatory guardrails. All outputs are "considered strictly advisory" with "human-in-command rules" and record-keeping requirements if AI "materially informs a decision, recommendation or other action".
University of Sydney Business School senior lecturer Raffaele Fabio Ciriello told SBS News that having a "human in the loop" is not a "complete safeguard".
"If AI has already decided what to highlight, summarise or flag, it has already shaped the human decision," Ciriello said. "Human oversight only works when staff have enough time, expertise and information to genuinely challenge the system, otherwise the human gets reduced to a rubber stamper."
The Australian government’s Microsoft Copilot evaluation didn’t assess whole-of-government cost-benefit or technically benchmark output accuracy, he said.
"Saving a public servant 20 minutes is evidence of task efficiency, not evidence that the public service, as a system, is better," Ciriello said.
Associate investigator at the Centre for Automated Decision-Making and lecturer at QUT Law School, Henry Fraser, said using this technology for brainstorming, drafting, analysis and editing, even when it's not directly making decisions, may influence how issues are framed, what's considered, and what's left out.
"The extent of AI use, often undisclosed, highlights the need for binding regulation of the use of automated decision-making and machine learning technologies in government," Fraser said.
"We are still awaiting draft legislation on automated decision-making in government, more than three years after the royal commission report on robodebt recommended its introduction."
Southern Cross University associate law professor Brendan Walker-Munro said the claims that AI will lead to cost savings and efficiency dividends omit the cost to check and verify that the models are performing properly, safely and securely.
"I think a big part of the problem is that we seem to be looking at ways to use AI to automate decisions which really need to be performed by humans," Walker-Munro said.
The Assistant Minister for Science, Technology and the Digital Economy, Dr Andrew Charlton, referred questions about which agency is responsible for policing and monitoring shadow AI use in government to Public Service Minister Katy Gallagher, who then directed the questions to the Department of Home Affairs.
A Home Affairs spokesperson said the department is responsible for the framework that sets security rules for federal government agencies, but did not directly answer a question relating to the surveillance of shadow AI use.
It said the framework "mandates that all technology systems including AI require authorisation to operate or be used by a Commonwealth entity, ensuring that an appropriate level of security is being applied to any technology system".

PHOTO facebook.com/sofia.baroque.arts.festival
Font size
The international Art of the Baroque festival opens its 20th edition tonight at Sofia’s Central Military Club with Love After the Storm, a performance by the British ensemble Saraband.
The anniversary edition brings together early music performers from Britain, Italy, Poland, Israel, the Netherlands, New Zealand, Canada and Bulgaria, with a programme tracing the development of music from the Middle Ages to the late Baroque period. For the first time, the festival – the only one in Bulgaria devoted to historically informed performances of early music – will hold a chamber music competition open to young and professional ensembles from Bulgaria and abroad.
Alongside concerts by leading musicians, the programme includes free Baroque dance sessions, a Baroque singing workshop, educational concerts and special performances for older people.
The main concert programme will close on 20 November with Giovanni Battista Pergolesi’s Stabat Mater, performed by the Italian ensemble Il Pomo d’Oro, led by concertmaster Zefira Valova, with soprano Madison Nonoa and countertenor Cameron Shahbazi as soloists.

US city council opens with ‘Hail Satan’ prayer (VIDEO)
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
00:37:26 UTC
09:37:26 KST

US city council opens with ‘Hail Satan’ prayer (VIDEO)
An Iowa city council meeting erupted into controversy after opening with a Satanic invocation that ended with the words “Hail Satan,” prompting a local pastor to demand that officials “reverse this curse.”
Matt Dalbey, an Ottumwa resident and former city council member, delivered the invocation at Tuesday’s meeting under a policy allowing residents of different religions and belief systems to open council proceedings with a prayer or reflection.
Dalbey began by addressing a “dark father” and invoking what he called the “Luciferian impulse” before concluding: “It is done. Hail Satan.”
The invocation immediately drew objections from New Life Center pastor Rick Bick, who interrupted the proceedings.
“That was a curse put on the city,” he said. “Most of you know that, and we need to just stop and reverse it… ‘Hail Satan’ is not welcome here.”
Mayor Benjamin Foote then called for a 30-second moment of silence “to reflect on whatever it is we need to reflect on at this time.”
Dalbey’s invocation was permitted under a policy adopted by the council in January. The measure states that Ottumwa, a city of some 25,500 people, seeks to respect “the diversity of both organized and unorganized religious denominations, as well as other faiths, belief systems, or the lack thereof.”
Council member Cara Galloway had specifically warned that a Satanic invocation could happen when she cast the only vote against the policy in January. “Opening with an invocation means allowing viewpoints that may not reflect our own,” she said, warning that selectively objecting to one now could expose taxpayers to legal liability.
The city said Wednesday that it had been flooded with calls over the prayer, many of them “rude and full of profanities,” but stressed that officials cannot discriminate between denominations or belief systems.
The recording of the meeting had drawn more than 12,000 views on the city’s YouTube channel by Wednesday afternoon, making it the most-watched video ever posted there.
Dalbey is scheduled to deliver another invocation at the council’s November 3 meeting. He told the Ottumwa Courier that the prayer is used by the Satanic Temple of Iowa, of which he is a member, but “has nothing to do with the belief in a satanic deity.” The organization describes itself as non-theistic.

Feature: Through a Serbian lens, a different China unfolds in Hainan
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
13:16:02 CST
14:16:02 KST

by Xinhua writers Zhang Xuan, Nemanja Cabric
BELGRADE, Oct. 7 (Xinhua) -- On brightly lit Qilou Old Street, vendors slice open pink wax apples, their juice sparkling under the lights. A drone captures traffic weaving across Haikou's cross-sea bridge, while elsewhere, women in ethnic attire craft traditional goods amid lush rainforests, and rockets launch into space from the vast coastline.
These vivid scenes unfolded at a documentary screening held in September at the China Cultural Center in Belgrade, where audiences followed Serbian producer Bosko Kozarski and his crew on their journey through Hainan, a tropical island province in southern China.
For Kozarski, the trip marked his second visit to China after filming a documentary in Beijing last year. As his China documentary series expands, his own connection with the country is also entering a new chapter.
"In Hainan, I experienced a completely different China," Kozarski told Xinhua.
While Beijing showcased a grand blend of historical heritage and modern technology, he said Hainan offered him a unique mix of natural scenery, traditional folk customs and modern resort facilities.
He described the island in three words: lush, futuristic and hospitable. He attributed "lush" to its tropical landscapes and vibrant vegetation, "futuristic" to its modern architecture and high-quality infrastructure, and "hospitable" to the sincere smiles of locals who make visitors feel at home.
Over more than 10 days, the crew traveled across Hainan, including Wenchang, Qionghai, Lingshui, Wuzhishan, Baoting and Changjiang before returning to Haikou. Local guide Huang Zhimin accompanied them. He appeared on camera multiple times under the name "Mason."
A native of Wuzhishan in southern Hainan whose ancestors were longtime laborers in Hainan's agricultural development, Huang guided the crew through historical sites, local cuisine and natural landscapes, and even accompanied them on test rides in autonomous vehicles.
Huang noted Kozarski and his team's deep fascination with the culture of the Li ethnic group.
"They were very interested in Li brocade and traditional dwellings, so I introduced them to the history, customs and intangible heritage in English, and took them to taste Li snacks and sweet wine," Huang said.
Kozarski found a strong sense of familiarity in the 3,000-year-old Li textile traditions. Drawing parallels with Serbia's own long-standing weaving heritage, he said this shared "cultural gene" created a cross-regional resonance. Despite the thousands of miles between them, "the cultural language conveyed by the looms is interconnected," he said.
But the cultural connections Kozarski discovered were only one part of what Hainan has to offer. His trip also gave him a firsthand look at the island's growing openness to the outside world.
As the Hainan Free Trade Port launched its island-wide special customs operations in late 2025, the province has increasingly welcomed international tourists with direct flights, diverse payment methods and advanced transport.
Kozarski described his trip as exceptionally smooth, thanks to China's visa-free entry policy, transport networks and digital payments linked to international credit cards.
He observed that Hainan is becoming an open global hub for trade and international tourism, facilitating the flow of people, goods and capital and serving as a "smart gateway" to the world.
For Serbian audiences, the documentary offered another perspective on China and left a lasting impression on Serbian Marina Milicevic. "China has almost everything a country can possess -- breathtaking natural scenery, well-planned cities, a clean environment, a safe society, and rich, diverse cultures and traditions," she said.
Comparing old photographs of Chinese cities with their present-day urban landscapes, she said she was amazed by the transformation.
The story of cultural exchanges between China and Serbia is far from over. While guide Huang hopes Hainan's expanded openness will bring more visitors and prosperity, Kozarski is already planning his next trip to China.
For Milicevic, the documentary has opened a window onto a China she hopes to explore in person. "Traveling all over China" is now part of her future plans. ■

Hungary expected to approve progress on Ukraine's EU accession clusters 2 and 3
The EU Council's Working Party on Enlargement and Countries Negotiating Accession to the EU (COELA) will once again consider the documents relating to clusters 2 and 3 of Ukraine's EU accession negotiations on 7 October, with Hungary not expected to block their approval.
Source: an EU source familiar with preparations for the meeting, in a comment to European Pravda
Details: The EU expects Budapest to agree today to further progress for Ukraine on cluster 2, Internal Market, and cluster 3, Competitiveness and Inclusive Growth.
"The COELA meeting will take place on the morning of 7 October. The screening results for clusters 2 and 3 for Ukraine are expected to be approved," the source told European Pravda.
The meeting is due to begin at 11:00 Kyiv time. Ukraine and Moldova's progress on clusters 2 and 3 is third and fourth on the agenda, after matters relating to Albania and Montenegro are considered.
"Later that day, Coreper is expected to approve the screening reports and authorise letters to be sent to Ukraine and Moldova inviting them to submit their negotiating positions on these two clusters," the European Pravda source added. [Coreper is the committee of the permanent representatives of the governments of the member states to the European Union – ed.]
When asked whether this meant that Hungary had already sent a clear signal that it would agree to the opening of the clusters, the source replied that "it seems there will be no surprises".
Inviting Ukraine and Moldova to submit their negotiating positions is a necessary step before the negotiations can progress further. The ultimate goal is to schedule an Intergovernmental Conference for Tuesday 13 October at which the clusters would be opened.
Background:
- On 1 October, a bill on education in the languages of national minorities was registered in the Verkhovna Rada (Ukraine's parliament). Its adoption is expected to help lift Hungary's veto and clear the way for two of the negotiating clusters.
- On 6 October, the European Commission adopted a package of proposals to revise EU policies ahead of future enlargements (pre-enlargement policy reviews), which would enable the European Union to admit new members, including Ukraine.
- Marta Kos, the European Commissioner for Enlargement, outlined five steps proposed by the European Commission for future EU members.

S. Korea's household surplus funds shrink in Q2 amid falling income, rising home purchases
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
13:15:46 CST
14:15:46 KST

SEOUL, Oct. 7 (Xinhua) -- South Korea's household surplus funds shrank in the second quarter of 2026 amid falling income and rising home purchases, central bank data showed Wednesday.
The net surplus funds held by households and non-profit organizations, which are calculated as total financial assets acquired minus total debts incurred, reached 60.7 trillion won (about 45.3 billion U.S. dollars) in the second quarter, down 18.5 trillion won from the previous quarter, according to the Bank of Korea (BOK).
Household disposable income dipped 3.8 percent in the April-June quarter compared to the previous quarter, while net property acquisitions by individuals rose to 7,000 units nationwide in the second quarter from 6,500 in the prior quarter.
Total financial asset investment, or fund management, declined to 88.5 trillion won in the second quarter from 96.3 trillion won in the first quarter.
Households shifted their cash into equities and investment funds, while withdrawing from bank deposits.
Equity and fund investments jumped from 61.4 trillion won in the first quarter to 101.6 trillion won in the second quarter, but financial institution deposits dropped into negative territory at 23.3 trillion won in the second quarter.
Total fundraising expanded to 27.8 trillion won in the second quarter from 17.1 trillion won in the previous quarter. ■

Israel marks 3 years since Oct. 7 with mourning, protests and demands for answers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
05:15:05 UTC
14:15:05 KST

Israel awoke Wednesday to memorial ceremonies, roadside demonstrations and protest installations marking three years since the Oct. 7 massacre, with events beginning at 6:29 a.m., the exact time the Hamas-led assault began. 
Families of those killed and abducted, survivors and protesters gathered across the country, combining remembrance with renewed demands for accountability and an investigation into the failures that preceded the attack.
At the President’s Residence in Jerusalem, President Isaac Herzog and his wife, Michal, lit a memorial candle at exactly 6:29. The presidency said the ceremony reflected the country’s shared grief for civilians and soldiers killed in the massacre and the war, while honoring the wounded, returned hostages and their families. 
At the same hour, families of victims and hostages gathered outside the Knesset alongside burned-out vehicles from the Nova music festival, observing a minute of silence and displaying signs accusing the government of abandoning those attacked.
In Tel Aviv, protesters briefly blocked the Ayalon Highway at 6:29 and unfurled a banner reading, ‘The people will remember their sons and daughters.’ Organizers said they were demanding a state commission of inquiry into the failures surrounding Oct. 7. Dizengoff Square was also transformed by a protest installation, while at Trumpeldor Beach rows of human figures laid across the sand represented those murdered and abducted. 
Eyal Eshel, whose daughter Roni, an IDF surveillance soldier, was killed at the Nahal Oz base, stood at the installation and said: ‘Three years have passed, and I continue to raise you.’
In Kfar Aza, one of the communities devastated in the attack, residents gathered at 6:29 near the armory from which members of the kibbutz security team went out to fight Hamas terrorists. The Israeli flag was lowered to half-staff as widows of seven members of the security team who were killed stood alongside survivors of the fighting. At the Nova festival site near Re’im, bereaved families and survivors returned to the place where hundreds were murdered, embracing beside photographs of those killed.
Protests and memorial events also spread to intersections and bridges around the country. Ceremonies were held outside the homes of government ministers who were serving on Oct. 7, with the names of hostages murdered in captivity read outside Justice Minister Yariv Levin’s home. Demonstrators outside Education Minister Yoav Kisch’s home carried signs reading, ‘7/10, no forgiveness,’ while a banner outside Transportation Minister Miri Regev’s home declared, ‘Until they go, we are all hostages.’
A convoy of dozens of vehicles also set out from Caesarea toward Tel Aviv. Ayala Metzger, whose father-in-law Yoram Metzger was abducted and later murdered in Hamas captivity, said the participants had come ‘to remember, to remind and to demand’ that the failures be investigated and that those who led the government at the time take responsibility.
The day’s events are set to continue nationwide, with memorials and demonstrations planned at some 400 locations. At noon, the October Council plans a nationwide minute of silence at hundreds of sites. At the same time, an exhibition titled ‘The Space Left Behind’ is scheduled to open at the Peres Center for Peace and Innovation in Jaffa, displaying personal belongings of dozens of people murdered on Oct. 7, accompanied by a ceremony with bereaved families.
Demonstrations involving protest groups and October Council families are planned throughout the afternoon and evening in Haifa, Afula, Tzemach Junction, Rosh Pina Junction, Sde Boker and other locations. At 6:29 p.m., exactly 12 hours after the morning commemorations began, bereaved families and members of the Nova Tribe association are scheduled to hold a ceremony at the Nova site near Re’im. A public testimony stage will open at 7:30 p.m. at the Arches Junction in the Sha’ar HaNegev region.
The day is expected to culminate at 9:15 p.m. with a national memorial ceremony at Tel Aviv’s Yarkon Park organized by the Kumu movement and Oct. 7 families. The ceremony, which will also be screened at locations across Israel, is to be hosted by former hostage Eli Sharabi and actress Shani Cohen.

Libya’s parliament removes Speaker Saleh after 12 years as discontent grows

Libya’s parliament removes Speaker Saleh after 12 years as discontent grows
Eastern-based parliament votes to replace longtime speaker with Al-Salhin Abdelnabi al-Obeidi.
Libya’s eastern-based House of Representatives has elected a new speaker, ending Aguila Saleh’s 12-year tenure amid growing discontent among lawmakers over his leadership.
Legislators in the 170-member House voted on Tuesday to replace Saleh with Al-Salhin Abdelnabi al-Obeidi, the parliament’s spokesperson announced on X.
The vote came a day after 98 members of the House approved a new system limiting the speaker and deputy speakers to a single 12-month term.
The change ended an arrangement that had been in place since the chamber’s first leadership was elected in 2014.
“There was significant discontent among MPs with the previous leadership over numerous errors,” lawmaker Jebree Oheida told the Reuters news agency. “We tried to engage with the leadership to address these issues, but to no avail. Among these errors were decisions made without consulting MPs.”
The vote was overseen by Second Deputy Speaker Misbah Douma, according to the Libya Observer.
Saleh has previously rejected the proceedings, saying the initial vote to limit the speaker’s term was “not official and had no legal effect”, according to the outlet. He had also announced that he had cancelled the session he had called for Tuesday.
The developments come as Libya remains divided politically and militarily between the United Nations-recognised government in Tripoli led by Prime Minister Abdul Hamid Dbeibah, and a rival administration in the east backed by renegade military commander Khalifa Haftar.
Haftar’s camp relies in particular on the parliament, which sits in the eastern city of Benghazi under their control.
Saleh has long been considered a staunch ally of the Haftar clan, but analysts said he appeared to be weakened as Haftar’s sons, in particular Saddam Haftar, consolidated their positions.
“Agila Saleh appears to be the latest casualty of Saddam Haftar’s drive to centralise decision-making in eastern Libya and bulldoze his way into a political role,” said Emadeddin Badi, an analyst at the London-based Chatham House.
Al-Obeidi, who comes from the same tribe as Saleh, represents the eastern city of Tobruk and has chaired parliament’s Libyan-Turkish friendship committee.
The House on Tuesday also elected Tarek al-Ashtar and Mesbah Douma as first and second deputy speakers, respectively.
Their election follows the signing of a landmark agreement by representatives of Libya’s rival political camps in Tripoli in August that could see presidential and legislative elections held within two years.
Mediated by the United Nations Support Mission in Libya (UNSMIL), the “4+4 committee” agreement attempts to resolve recurring legal and institutional disputes that have crippled the nation since the overthrow of Colonel Muammar Gaddafi in 2011.
The United States is pursuing a separate reunification plan for the oil and gas-rich North African country, led by Massad Boulos, President Donald Trump’s senior adviser for Arab and African affairs.

MOSCOW, October 7. /TASS/. Kiev’s attempts to flood the European market with agricultural products will become an obstacle to negotiations on Ukraine’s accession to the European Union, Russian Foreign Ministry Ambassador-at-Large Rodion Miroshnik told TASS, commenting on Ukrainian Agriculture Minister Taras Vysotsky’s statement that his country does not need partial EU membership if it does not receive full access to the European market to sell its grain.
"Kiev’s attempts to flood the European Union market with agricultural products will become a major obstacle for Ukraine in negotiations on EU accession. Such neighboring countries as Poland, Romania, Hungary and Slovakia will most likely fight tooth and nail against Ukrainian agricultural products entering the European market and effectively suffocating farms, for example, in Poland itself. Polish Prime Minister [Donald Tusk], most likely under pressure from farmers’ protests, will categorically oppose products grown in Ukraine entering the European market. Ukraine was told to go to Africa, so let it go to Africa. The lucrative European market is for European farmers. Ukrainian farmers are in no way regarded as European in this sense," the diplomat said.
Earlier. the European Commission presented proposals for reforming EU enlargement, including phased and reversible membership, abandoning member states' veto rights, and cutting agricultural support spending, which currently accounts for over one-third of the bloc's budget. The Commission offered Ukraine help "restoring access to traditional grain markets" while keeping quota restrictions on grain supplies. Ukraine's agriculture minister rejected the approach, citing a "fundamental difference between a temporary transition period and permanent restrictions" that "runs counter to the very logic of full EU membership."

'One of the greats' signs off after fourth Roosters premiership

Winger Daniel Tupou has retired from the NRL just days after winning his fourth NRL grand final with the Sydney Roosters.
Tupou won premierships in 2013, 2018, 2019 and 2026, and played 10 State of Origin games for New South Wales.
Roosters coach Trent Robinson said Tupou "will stand as one of the greats".
Sydney Roosters coach Trent Robinson has hailed Daniel Tupou as one of the NRL club's all-time greats after the four-time premiership-winning winger announced his retirement.
The 35-year-old, who had been coy about his future all season, became just the sixth player in Roosters history to win four premierships with the club.
Across a 307-game, one-club career, the winger scored 198 tries, the third most of any player in premiership history behind Ken Irvine and Alex Johnston.
"When you look at what Daniel Tupou has achieved over 15 seasons, he will stand as one of the greats," Robinson said in a statement.
"But those numbers only tell part of the story of Toops and what he means to this club.
"Since he made his debut, he has represented what we want a Rooster to be.
"He has been incredibly consistent, selfless and dependable, and whenever there has been a big moment or a tough moment, he has been present.
"Toops revolutionised the aerial game at the Sydney Roosters and became the greatest high-ball specialist of all time."
Tupou's exit comes as the Roosters prepare for a big off-season exodus over the coming weeks.
Fellow winger Mark Nawaqanitawase and second rower Angus Crichton are moving to rugby union, playmaker Daly Cherry-Evans is heading to Super League side Hull FC, and Connor Watson is joining St George Illawarra.
But none of them gets close to having the impact the towering winger has had on the Roosters since his NRL debut in 2012.
As well as four premierships (2013, 2018, 2019, 2026), Tupou has won three World Club Challenges and played Test matches for both Tonga and Australia.
He was part of the Tongan side that defeated the Kangaroos in 2019 in one of the biggest upsets in international rugby league history.
Tupou played 10 times for NSW at State of Origin level between 2014 and 2022.
"We love Toops, we're incredibly proud of him, and his name will always hold a very special place in the history of the Sydney Roosters," Robinson said.
Tupou retires as the greatest try-scorer in Roosters history after surpassing Anthony Minichiello in 2023.

Israelis mark three years since Hamas attack that set off Gaza assault
- Israelis marked three years since the Oct 7, 2023 Hamas attack, which killed 1,200 people and led to Israel’s assault on Gaza.
- Memorials were held at the Nova festival site and in Tel Aviv, as the anniversary came with no hostages left in Gaza and an election 20 days away.
- A US-backed ceasefire has not ended violence or resolved disarmament talks, while Gaza remains split and more than 1,400 Palestinians have been killed since October 2025.
AI generated
JERUSALEM – Israelis will on Oct 7 mark three years since Hamas attacked Israel on Oct 7, 2023, triggering a military assault that destroyed much of Gaza, where conditions remain dire despite a year-old ceasefire that is meant to halt the war for good.
The attacks, during which militants killed 1,200 people and took 251 hostages to Gaza, marked the deadliest day in Israel's history. Israel's subsequent bombardment and ground operations have killed more than 74,000 people in Gaza, health authorities there say.
On Oct 7, Israelis will hold a vigil at the site of the Nova music festival near the Gaza border, where 348 young people were killed by militants during the attack.
They will also hold an event commemorating the anniversary at Hostage Square in Tel Aviv.
Israeli election 20 days away
The anniversary is the first for Israelis without any hostages still held in Gaza, with those dead and alive exchanged in swaps with Hamas for Palestinians held in Israeli jails. The remains of the last Israeli hostage were recovered in January.
It also comes just 20 days ahead of Israel’s first election since the attack, a vote that is viewed as a referendum on Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s long tenure in power.
Netanyahu has rejected blame for the security breach and resisted calls for an independent investigation. That has frustrated many in Israel, including families of those killed in the attacks, some of whom have joined the election race.
A poll by the Israel Democracy Institute showed that 68% of Jewish Israelis said that the events of Oct 7 were a very central or fairly central element in their decision of which party to vote for.
Election polls show neither Netanyahu nor his main competitors would muster enough seats in parliament to form a coalition if a vote were held today.
US-backed ceasefire fails to halt Israeli attacks, disarm Hamas
The anniversary is also the first since an Oct 10, 2025, US-brokered ceasefire deal that halted major fighting but has failed to stop Israeli attacks in Gaza or secure the disarmament of Hamas and other militant groups.
The deal left Israel in control of some 53% of Gaza, since expanded by Israeli forces to nearly two-thirds. Hamas controls the remaining third, where the 2 million population mostly live in makeshift tents and bombed out buildings.
US President Donald Trump’s so-called “Board of Peace” has proposed several plans that would see Gaza rebuilt. But those plans, which fail to account for the property rights of Palestinians whose homes were destroyed, have failed to gain the buy-in of Israel or Hamas, which are still deadlocked in ceasefire talks.
The two have yet to agree on the terms of a deal that would see Hamas lay down its weapons in exchange for Israeli troop withdrawals. Israel says it will not pull back until Hamas fully disarms; Hamas says it has agreed to a phased process but will not disarm so long as Israeli attacks continue.
Israel has kept up a bombing campaign in Gaza that has killed a number of Hamas militants in recent months but has also killed many civilians, say Gaza health authorities, whose death figures do not distinguish between civilians and combatants.
More than 1,400 Palestinians in Gaza have been killed since the October 2025 ceasefire, the health authorities say. During the same time, five Israeli soldiers have been killed by militants or in combat, the military says. REUTERS

India's central bank raises policy rate to counter inflation
The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) raised the the key benchmark policy rate, for the first time in over three years, as it looked to control rising inflation amid the US-led war on Iran.
The repo rate, which guides the short-term lending rate for commercial banks, was raised by 25 basis points to 5.5%. The rate hike will make home loans, vehicle loans and corporate loans more expensive for borrowers. Even equated monthly installments would go up for existing borrowers.
With this, the RBI has shifted gears to join several central banks around the world looking to curb rising prices or boost their currencies. It has changed its stance to a "calibrated tightening," the report said.
"Driven by escalating energy costs and rising food prices, global inflation is projected to increase sharply prompting monetary policy tightening by major central Banks," RBI Governor Sanjay Malhotra said in his opening remarks while announcing the rake hike.
He attributed the inflationary pressures to the "reescalation of the West Asia conflict in September and consequent hardening and volatility in global crude prices."
"Further tightening of global financial conditions, uncertainty about fair valuation of AI stocks, and an elusive resolution of the West Asia conflict pose significant downside risks to the global economic outlook," Malhotra said.
Nonetheless, the RBI governor said he expects India's "strong" economy to "remain resilient."
Apart from rising prices, the RBI's calculations likely involve the state of the Indian rupee which has been near record lows over the past week.

The Caspian Sea has been shrinking for decades. Now, a new island has emerged
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
05:02:49 UTC
14:02:49 KST

Scientists warn that parts of the northern Caspian could face an Aral Sea-like scenario, while climate change and human water use are adding pressure on the region.
The Caspian Sea is the largest inland body of water on Earth, but for years it has been shrinking.
The northern and north-eastern parts along Kazakhstan's coast form the shallowest sector of the Caspian Sea, typically ranging between just three and six metres. But as water levels continue to fall, following decades of climate change and human activity, environmentalists are discovering clusters of under-water islands.
The latest was spotted days ago near Kulaly Island during a recent aerial survey.
Volunteer and environmental activist Daniyar Akimzhanov was part of the group that reported the discovery. He says that the newly emerged island is relatively small, but it is far from an isolated case.
In fact, over the past four to five years, Akimzhanov says he has documented several new islands in this part of the Caspian Sea.
“The one in the photo I sent you is the smallest. There are much bigger new islands,” he explains.
The Caspian Sea's secret islands
Some stretch around one kilometre in length and 200 to 300 metres in width and wildlife has already begun reaching the newly exposed land.
Akimzhanov says he personally spotted a wild boar on one of the islands, while wolves also make their way there across the ice. The newly emerged islands usually do not get names, he says.
The Kazakh Research Institute of the Caspian Sea, which began work in September 2025 after being established on the instructions of President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev, says more areas of land are likely to emerge. However, not all of them will become permanent islands.
“The future of each newly exposed area depends on the seabed topography, waves, wind-driven changes in water levels and the subsequent dynamics of the Caspian Sea level,” the institute says.
The emergence of new islands is one of the most visible signs of a much broader transformation: the Caspian Sea is retreating.
The Caspian Sea is retreating
The Caspian Sea is the world's largest landlocked body of water. It is bordered by five countries: Kazakhstan, Russia, Azerbaijan, Iran and Turkmenistan. More than 80 per cent of its river inflow comes from Russia’s Volga River.
Dr. Sifan Koriche, a hydroclimate scientist at the University of Alabama who has published several studies on the Caspian Sea, explains its water balance in simple terms.
“It's like a simple water balance. The incoming water is from river inflow and precipitation, while the outgoing water is only through evaporation,” he says.
According to instrumental observations, the Caspian Sea level in the Kazakh sector fell from -26.82 metres in 1996 to -29.27 metres in 2025. This represents a decline of 2.45 metres over the past three decades, or an average of around 8–9 centimetres per year.
The decline has continued. According to the Kazakh Research Institute of the Caspian Sea, the average sea level at the Kulaly Island monitoring station stood at -29.42 metres as of July 2026, the lowest level recorded during the entire study period.
The north-eastern Caspian, including the coast of Kazakhstan's Atyrau region, is particularly vulnerable to falling water levels. With an average depth of around six metres and a very gentle seabed slope, even a relatively small drop in water level can cause the shoreline to retreat over long distances.
The scale of the retreat is already visible. According to the Kazakh Research Institute of the Caspian Sea, between 2000 and 2025, the area covered by water in the studied part of the north-eastern Caspian decreased by around 16,384 square kilometres.
Satellite images analysed by the institute also show how the coastline has changed in recent years. Between 2021 and 2026, falling water levels gradually exposed new areas of seabed near Kulaly Island and the Tyuleniy Archipelago.
The Caspian has historically experienced periods of both falling and rising water levels. From the 1930s to 1977, its level dropped by around three metres. Over the following two decades, it rose again by about 2.5 metres, before beginning another period of decline.
But while fluctuations in the Caspian Sea level are not new, scientists say climate change and human activity are now affecting its water balance.
Previous research has linked the decline in recent decades mainly to increased evaporation from the Caspian Sea as regional temperatures have risen. A decrease in precipitation has also contributed, but to a smaller degree.
Human activity also affects how much water reaches the Caspian. Dams regulate the rivers flowing into the sea, while water is extracted across the basin for irrigation and other uses. The way reservoirs are managed can also affect river flows reaching the sea.
Why Caspian seals are declining
The Caspian seal, found nowhere else in the world, has already undergone a dramatic population decline. Over the past 100 years, its population has fallen from around one million to about 100,000.
The retreating sea is adding pressure on the species by transforming the isolated islands it uses as seasonal haul-out sites.
According to seal researcher Assel Baimukanova, the area of island haul-out sites has decreased more than 15-fold since 1995.
In 2021, Baimukanova and other researchers from the Institute of Hydrobiology and Ecology stayed on a small newly formed island they called New Durnev, where thousands of seals gathered. When they returned in 2023, the island had expanded significantly and could at times be reached by car. It later connected to the mainland.
“For seals, it became inaccessible. No isolated island means no seals,” Baimukanova said.
As the sea retreats, seals are also being pushed westwards. The north-eastern Caspian had long served as a natural refuge for the animals because it was difficult for people to access. Further west, seals face more human activity, including fishing, shipping, tourism and oil and gas operations.
Warming temperatures pose another threat to the seals: the loss of stable winter ice. Caspian seals give birth on ice, but Baimukanova says warmer winters are making it thinner and less stable.
The effects of the retreating sea go beyond wildlife. The Kazakh Research Institute of the Caspian Sea says shrinking shallow waters are also affecting wetlands and could pose growing challenges for fisheries, ports, shipping and other coastal infrastructure.
What happens next?
Most climate scenarios suggest that the Caspian Sea will continue to decline during the 21st century, although scientists stress that the exact scale remains uncertain.
Koriche's research projects a decline of up to eight metres by the end of the century under an intermediate climate scenario, although results vary significantly between models.
To illustrate what even a smaller decline could mean, Koriche says a five-metre drop could expose around 77,000 square kilometres of seabed in the northern Caspian.
Koriche says the entire Caspian is not facing an Aral Sea-like scenario because its central and southern basins are much deeper. But parts of the shallow northern Caspian could face significant desiccation.
“The northern part covers a quarter to one third of the water body. There is a chance that this northern region could face a scenario similar to the Aral Sea,” he says.
But the scale of the future decline is not predetermined. Koriche's research suggests that human water extraction could add up to seven metres to the decline under some scenarios.
He says measures should focus both on slowing the decline and adapting to it. This includes better management of water use across the Caspian basin, particularly the Volga, as well as stronger monitoring and data sharing between countries.
The Kazakh Research Institute of the Caspian Sea also says adaptation is becoming increasingly important. Measures include protecting vulnerable ecosystems, monitoring newly exposed seabed and adapting ports and other coastal infrastructure.
Some regional initiatives are already underway. Kazakhstan has proposed an interstate programme to conserve the Caspian Sea's water resources, while the five Caspian states are also working on a 2026–2036 action plan under the Tehran Convention to improve monitoring, assess the impacts of sea-level changes and develop adaptation measures.
“Effective solutions are only possible through coordinated action by all five Caspian states,” the institute says.

Three years of Israel’s genocide in Gaza: In numbers

Three years of Israel’s genocide in Gaza: In numbers
Three years of attacks has devastated Gaza, killing tens of thousands, destroying homes, and collapsing essential services.
Three years have passed since Israel launched its genocide against Palestinians in Gaza.
Israel’s assault began on October 7, 2023, after Hamas’s armed wing, the Qassam Brigades, and other Palestinian groups attacked southern Israel, killing 1,139 people and taking about 240 captive.
Israel responded with relentless bombardment and turned its 16-year blockade into a total stranglehold.
A “ceasefire” took effect on October 10, 2025, but attacks and killings have continued.
Here is where things stand, in numbers:
1 out of 30 people in Gaza killed
Three years of Israeli attacks have killed at least 74,000 Palestinians, including at least 21,000 children. That is about one in every 30 people, or 3 percent of the pre-war population.
The Palestinian Ministry of Health counts only deaths recorded at hospitals or officially registered. The true toll is likely much higher, as it excludes the thousands still buried under rubble or missing.
1 out of 13 people in Gaza wounded
The human toll extends beyond the killed.
More than 175,000 people have been wounded, about one in every 13 people in Gaza.
A conservative WHO estimate suggests roughly 24 percent of the wounded have life-changing injuries requiring long-term rehabilitation, a quarter of them children.
Gaza’s few remaining health facilities are overwhelmed and running on dwindling supplies.
A ‘ceasefire’ in name only
Since the “ceasefire” took effect on October 10, 2025, Israel has violated it with near-daily attacks, killing more than 1,000 people.
An Al Jazeera analysis found Israel attacked Gaza on 325 of the past 361 days, leaving only 36 days with no reported attacks, deaths or injuries.
Despite continuing attacks, the US insists that the “ceasefire” is still holding.
Israel still killing Palestinians
Since the “ceasefire” took effect at noon on October 10, Israel has killed at least 1,460 Palestinians and injured 5,116, according to the latest figures from the Palestinian Ministry of Health.
94 percent of all hospitals and clinics damaged
Israel has attacked nearly all of Gaza’s hospitals and healthcare facilities.
After three years, 94 percent are fully or partially out of service, leaving patients without essential care, according to the UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA). Only 42 of 666 facilities are still functioning.
Under the Fourth Geneva Convention, hospitals must not be attacked, and international humanitarian law gives medical units and personnel special protection. Under the Rome Statute of the International Criminal Court, intentionally attacking a hospital is a war crime.
91 percent of Gaza’s households face water insecurity
Since October 2023, Israel has systematically targeted Gaza’s already fragile water infrastructure, striking wells, pipelines, desalination plants and sewage systems.
UN experts say most of the water and sanitation network has been damaged or destroyed. Local authorities report shattered pipes and wells either contaminated by sewage or cut off by fighting and displacement.
Nearly half of Gaza’s population now survives on less than six litres (1.6 gallons) of water a day for drinking and cooking. The emergency minimum for “short-term survival” is 20 litres (5.3 gallons).
Nearly all homes destroyed or damaged
The destruction across Gaza is near total, with 82 percent of all structures destroyed.
According to OCHA, entire neighbourhoods have been wiped out, leaving 1.98 million Palestinians displaced. That is 90 percent of the population.
Newly updated Google Maps satellite imagery shows the scale of destruction across the besieged Gaza Strip nearly three years into Israel’s genocidal war.
93 percent of schools need rebuilding
Gaza’s education system has collapsed. About 93 percent of schools need complete reconstruction, according to OCHA, leaving more than 700,000 students without access to formal education.
At least 63 university buildings have been destroyed, and those still standing are being used as shelters for displaced people.
Deadliest place to be a journalist
Nearly 300 journalists and media workers have been killed in Gaza since October 7, including 12 from Al Jazeera, according to the Shireen Abu Akleh Observatory.

Štajerska, praised for its authenticity and centuries of wine culture, beat out more than 90 leading territories for the title.
A new ranking has just revealed the best wine regions in Europe, and oenophiles should take note, because number one went to a spot in Slovenia.
Crowned by European Best Destinations, Štajerska beat out more than 90 leading wine territories across countries including France, Italy, Spain, Portugal, Germany, Austria, Hungary, Greece and Georgia.
Regions were evaluated on things like the diversity of grape varieties and wine styles, the number of cellars, tasting rooms and wine rooms, the beauty of the landscape, sustainability and accessibility, among others.
Štajerska – which covers Maribor, Ptuj, Jeruzalem Slovenija, Haloze, Slovenske gorice, Ravno polje and Pohorje – topped the list thanks to its “remarkable wine stories”.
“Štajerska represents exactly what today’s travellers in Europe are increasingly looking for: authenticity, exceptional landscapes, centuries of wine culture, outstanding expertise and, above all, a very strong regional identity,” Maximilien Lejeune, director of European Best Destinations, said.
“From the World’s Oldest Vine in Maribor to the historic wine cellars of Ptuj, from wine roads and vineyards to the people who keep these traditions alive, wine here is much more than a product.”
Other wine regions in Europe making the cut
Italy’s Langhe-Roero-Monferrato took second place, with European Best Destinations highlighting its Nebbiolo red wine grape variety and its truffles as reasons to visit, particularly in autumn.
Third place went to Ribeira Sacra in Spain, praised as being “one of Europe’s most dramatic wine landscapes” with terraces carved into the canyon walls of the Sil and Miño rivers.
For fans of Riesling and Grüner Veltliner, Kamptal in Austria, which came out fourth overall, is the place to be.
Rounding out the top five is Chianti Rufina in Tuscany, the “quieter, more intimate sibling of Chianti Classico”.

I see what’s happening here in Paris: reasonable student demands met with awful violence | Helen Massy-Beresford
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
05:00:36 UTC
14:00:36 KST

It would be tough to argue that the demands of France’s protesting high school students are not reasonable ones, worth taking to the streets for: investment in crumbling schools, replacing absent teachers, reducing class sizes and overstuffed timetables, and bridging the inequality gap between schools in different areas.
The protests across the country on Tuesday, which demonstrators dubbed l’acte III (Act 3), or la grande mobilisation, were billed as the most dramatic day of action yet, with more school blockades and a march through central Paris in the afternoon. More than 400 schools closed preventively, including my elder daughter’s, a combined collège (for 11- to 15-year-olds) and lycée.
At 11 she’s too young to be involved, and after her reports of fireworks, burning bins and smoke as she and her friends ran in through the gates one day last week, I must say I’m relieved – no matter how worthwhile the cause. It was business as usual on Friday (a few more parents picking up their children than would normally, though), while on Tuesday morning, with school closed, the gates were blocked with bins and about 50 lycéens (one dressed as Batman) were there, wielding their banners. The atmosphere was calm, with attention shifting to the big protest march through the city due later in the day.
While there have been some cases of violence from protesters, heavy-handed police methods have been severely criticised. In one incident, in Tours, a 16-year-old boy lost sight in his right eye, an injury the city’s prosecutor said was consistent with a rubber bullet. In a particularly dark turn on Monday, and in circumstances that are not yet entirely clear, a lycée student lost his hand at a demonstration in Lens, northern France. A police investigation is under way.
As the protests have grown in scope, the French prime minister, Sébastien Lecornu, has promised the government will listen and try to meet the main demands – but that’s unlikely to mean suddenly freeing up billions to invest in schools that have gone underfunded for years, as the videos posted online of rat-infested, flooded or crumbling classrooms testify.
The political debate surrounding the escalating social movement is angry and polarised: a foretaste of the how the country’s April 2027 presidential election is likely to play out. The high school movement comes at an already tense time, with France’s government once again trying to push through a budget full of spending cuts without a parliamentary majority.
Last year, to get the budget over the line, the government had to use special constitutional powers to bypass the need for a parliamentary vote. This year’s budget, due for a vote in November, includes pension and healthcare cuts aimed at helping to plug the seemingly bottomless budget deficit – and is likely to be just as problematic for the government.
The intensity of the protests has prompted a mudslinging match between two of the favourites for the first round of the presidential elections. Jean-Luc Mélenchon, the leader of France Unbowed, is vocally on the side of the protesters (many of whom will vote for his party when old enough) but rejects the narrative that his party stirred up the unrest. Meanwhile, Marine Le Pen, leader of the far-right National Rally, is using the protests to call for an anti-riot law. She’s clearly not following the advice of the Socialist party leader, Olivier Faure, who during a presidential primary debate among leftwing candidates urged people not to fall into the classic rightwing trap of focusing on the violence while ignoring the cause of the protests.
Faure made reference to the proverb of the wise man pointing at the moon and the fool looking at his finger: “look at the moon, not the finger,” he said – and it’s a sensible message for all the wannabe presidents. Many of the lycéens protesting today will be voting for the first time next April.
Even if Le Pen is now looking at the finger, she certainly shouldn’t be written off for next year’s election; her message seems to be resonating with a large number of French citizens and she is the clear favourite for the first round of the presidential elections. We’ve been here before: if the polls are correct, it will be Le Pen’s third second-round run-off. The difference is that in 2022 and 2017 she was up against Emmanuel Macron – a centrist candidate who voters from across the spectrum could get behind to block her, even if many reported holding their nose at the ballot box.
As things stand, that may be harder for many in 2027. Le Pen’s opposition is fragmented, with several potential candidates still in the running on the left and centre right – and because of that, Le Pen’s second-round adversary may prove easier for her to beat, to the benefit of absolutely no one.
Everything stayed quiet yesterday in my north-east Paris neighbourhood. But in the centre of the city, organisers say some 100,000 people turned out (the interior ministry estimated 56,000). Under a blazing early October sun, huge – and mainly calm – crowds gathered in Place de la République and marched to Place de la Nation to chant and wave placards. As the main crowd dispersed, some small groups clashed with police as the sun was setting.
For now, the movement’s momentum seems to be building, not receding. Some politicians are realising that, six months away from a fraught election, they should listen to their future voters.
- Helen Massy-Beresford is a British journalist and editor who lives in Paris

Roast chicken, congee and cookies: Ravinder Bhogal’s autumn squash recipes
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
05:00:36 UTC
14:00:36 KST

The shops are heaving with pumpkins and squash, and though there are so many different varieties to choose from, most of them are interchangeable. My favourites are kabocha, crown prince and delicata, for their deeply nutty flavour and creamy texture, plus they hold their shape well when roasted or braised. And if you’re carving a pumpkin for Halloween over the coming weeks, don’t waste the flesh: chop it up and throw into a risotto. It’s hard to imagine that such deliciousness could come from such a ghoulish grimace.
Pumpkin and miso congee with chilli oil (pictured above)
Congee is a favourite comfort food that is eaten across Asia, often for breakfast. This version isn’t particularly traditional, but it makes the most of pumpkin season. I love this with a drizzle of chilli oil as a contrast to the delicata’s natural sweetness.
Prep 15 min
Cook 50 min
Serves 6
600g delicata pumpkin, peeled and chopped into bite-size chunks, plus 6 wedges 
3 tbsp avocado oil, or neutral oil
Sea salt and black pepper 
1 heaped tbsp white miso
2 garlic cloves, peeled and finely chopped
1 tbsp crushed ginger
200g short-grain white rice
1 piece kombu
1 bunch spring onions, trimmed and sliced on the diagonal
For the garnish
3 tbsp toasted pumpkin seeds
A few drops of sesame oil
Chilli oil
Heat the oven to 200C (180C fan)/390F/gas 6. Lay out the pumpkin on a baking sheet, drizzle over one tablespoon of oil and season. Roast for 30-40 minutes, until very soft and caramelised, then remove and leave to cool. Set aside the squash wedges, then puree the remaining chunks in a food processor with a splash of water.
In a large saucepan, heat the remaining oil on a medium heat, add the miso and cook, stirring, until lightly caramelised. Add the garlic and ginger, and stir until fragrant.
Add the rice, kombu and 1.8 litres of water and bring to a boil on medium-high heat. Partially cover, turn down the heat to a low simmer and cook, stirring occasionally, for 25-30 minutes, until the liquid has reduced and the rice is plump and has turned into a porridge. Stir in the pumpkin puree and half the sliced spring onions.
Divide the congee between six bowls and top each portion with a wedge of roast squash. Garnish with the remaining spring onions, then finish with toasted pumpkin seeds, a drizzle of sesame oil and your favourite chilli oil.
Chicken with kabocha squash and sage
This makes for a wonderful alternative autumnal Sunday roast, with minimal washing-up because it’s all cooked in one pan.
Prep 10 min
Cook 1 hr 20 min
Serves 4
Sea salt and black pepper
1 whole chicken (about 1½kg) 
1 whole garlic bulb, cut in half horizontally
1 unwaxed lemon, halved
1 bunch sage
2 bay leaves
2 tbsp olive oil
½ tsp dried chilli flakes 
1 tsp ground cinnamon
1 small kabocha squash (about 750g), unpeeled and cut into wedges
150ml dry white wine
800ml chicken stock
50ml double cream
Season the chicken generously inside and out, then stuff the cavity with one of the garlic halves, both lemon halves, half the sage and the bay leaves.
Put the oil in a large, deep casserole over a medium heat and, once it’s hot, brown the chicken all over – take your time to do this properly, because it really makes a difference to the overall taste. Once browned, set aside the chicken for the time being.
In the oil left over from browning the chicken, fry the remaining garlic and sage with the chilli and cinnamon, then, once the mix is smelling fragrant, stir in the squash wedges to coat them in the aromatic oil. Cook for two minutes, then pour in the wine and leave to bubble away until reduced by half.
Push the squash to the sides of the pan, then nestle the chicken in the middle. Pour in the stock, cover and leave to cook on a gentle heat for 50 minutes to an hour. Once cooked, stir in the cream, season if need be, and serve.
Fudgy pumpkin pie cookies
No tricks, just treats. These are perfect for a little Halloween indulgence.
Prep 10 min
Chill 40 min
Cook 1 hr, plus cooling
Makes About 20
For the pumpkin puree
200g red kuri or kabocha squash, halved, deseeded, peeled and cut into 2cm cubes
50g granulated sugar
1 tsp ground cinnamon
½ tsp ground ginger
A pinch of ground cloves
A good grating of nutmeg
For the cookies
225g plain flour
1 tsp cinnamon
½ tsp ground ginger
A pinch of cloves
A good grating of nutmeg
½ tsp baking powder
½ tsp bicarbonate of soda
Salt
225g light brown sugar
175g unsalted butter
2 egg yolks
1 tsp vanilla extract
Start by making the pumpkin puree. Put the pumpkin in a microwave-safe container and microwave on high for five minutes. Remove, toss, then microwave on high again for another five minutes. Keep repeating this process until the pumpkin is soft and mashable – the timing will depend on your microwave, but mine took 15 minutes. Once soft, puree in a food processor (or mash well with a fork) until smooth, then leave to cool.
In a small bowl, mix the sugar and spices. In medium bowl, mix the flour, spices, baking powder, bicarb and half a teaspoon of salt. In a stand mixer, cream the brown sugar and butter until light and fluffy. Add the egg yolks and vanilla, whisk again until pale and fluffy, then stir in the pumpkin puree until well combined. Fold in the dry ingredients, then chill in the fridge for 40 minutes, until firm.
Heat the oven to 180C (160C fan)/350F/gas 4 and line two baking sheets with greaseproof paper. Scoop out two tablespoons of the cookie mixture and roll them into loose balls. Roll these in the spiced sugar mix and place on the baking sheets spaced well apart. Repeat with the remaining cookie mix, then bake for 12 minutes, until golden brown.
Remove and leave to cool on the baking sheet for five minutes, then transfer to a rack to cool completely.
