Tories delight as satirical tapestry pokes fun at ‘turncoat’ Robert Jenrick
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
05:00:35 UTC
14:00:35 KST

As Kemi Badenoch basked in the applause of the Tory faithful at the close of her pivotal speech at Conservative party conference last year, one member of her shadow cabinet looked less than enthused.
Robert Jenrick, bested by Badenoch in the leadership contest a year earlier, looked on, and – as one shadow cabinet member now recalls – had to be prodded by Lord Ashcroft to applaud. “If you’re plotting against someone, then you at least pretend to like them,” they say. “The thing about Robert is he’s not even a good machiavellian.”
Jenrick left the party a matter of months later, swiftly – and publicly – ejected by an ice-cold Badenoch after she got wind that he was planning to defect to Reform. This week, as the Conservative ranks enjoy their annual knees-up in Birmingham, the now Reform UK economy spokesperson has been swiping from the sidelines, accusing his old party of “once again copying our policies”.
But while Jenrick’s physical presence may be absent from the migraine-inducing interior of the International Convention Centre in the West Midlands, members could be forgiven for sighing that everywhere they looked, something reminded them of him.
At the heart of the conference, members queue to chortle at depictions of Jenrick in the Conservatives’ own “Birmingham tapestry”, a 27-metre (88ft) woven graphical retelling of the past two years in British politics, as seen through Conservative eyes.
Featuring Badenoch as a glorious 11th-century conquering warrior, the “tapestry” also depicts a tiny Jenrick wailing as he loses the leadership contest, as he watches a crowd cheering on his victor. A little later, under the heading “Expelleth the Turncoat”, an outsized Badenoch is seen banishing her tiny, sobbing former colleague – as she stands next to a photocopier where, legend has it, Jenrick’s resignation letter was found.
“I think it’s great fun; every story needs a villain and he’s ours,” says one party member who’d travelled from Scotland for the event. “He’s not a big figure here any more, he’s just a figure of fun.”
Another member says they voted for Jenrick in the leadership election and had felt let down by his plots to remove the leader after failing to get the top job. “The way he did what he did was spiteful, petty and childish. I was a massive fan, but now I couldn’t care less what he does,” he says. Referring to Jenrick’s hyperactive social media output, which regularly show the Reform economy spokesperson confronting fare-dodgers and shoplifters, he rolls his eyes. “It’s just attention-seeking, isn’t it?” he says. “I do wonder now, though, as Reform falter, if he regrets what he did. I hope so.”
The schadenfreude at Jenrick’s fading star is palpable at this conference. Unprompted, shadow cabinet ministers bring him up with unbridled delight. “I miss him like I would miss an abscess in my molar,” remarks one senior Tory, before wondering aloud about whether Jenrick was likely to be punched in the face during one of his vigilante operations.
Others are surprised at their own strength of feeling towards a former colleague. “Nobody knew how much we hated Robert until he left the party,” says one senior member. Repeating the mantra that they are more united behind Badenoch than any other leader in years, some credit Jenrick for bringing them closer together, because he had “briefed against everybody”. Another adds: “Rob leaving was like pulling out a splinter.”
The commentary is not limited to gossip around the bars of Birmingham’s Hyatt hotel. Mentions of Jenrick are met with groans in the audience at a packed fringe event of shadow cabinet ministers hosted by More in Common. Asked if he would consider taking Jenrick or any of the other three Tory MPs who defected back, the response of Alex Burghart, the party’s deputy leader, is unequivocal. “No, no, no and no,” he says. Was he relieved they were gone? “Yes, yes, yes and yes.”
Badenoch has made clear that neither Jenrick nor his fellow defectors (variously described by her team as “venal”, “mad” and “hopeless”) would ever be welcome back, going as far as thanking Nigel Farage for doing the “spring cleaning” of her party for her.
Others suggest Reform were welcome to one of their former star players. “Good luck to his new friends in Reform,” one says. “It’s all about Rob and his own ambitions and he’d elbow them into the path of an oncoming express train if it meant he got ahead.”
Appreciating the Birmingham tapestry in between panel sessions, the shadow undersecretary for environment, food and rural affairs, Aphra Brandreth, insists the party is completely over Jenrick, although his shadow here suggests there may still be some healing left to do. “Honestly I don’t spend any time thinking about Robert Jenrick,” she says, with a benevolent smile. “He’s gone, and we’ve all moved on.”

The generation raised on sugar rations – and what their health reveals 70 years later
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
05:00:35 UTC
14:00:35 KST

They were born into a Britain still recovering from the hardships of war. Though the air-raid sirens had fallen silent, many everyday foods remained rationed, including sugar. Adults were restricted to about 3 tablespoons (40g) a day to stretch between cups of tea, baking and desserts; children were limited to less than a tablespoon. Babies and very young children were expected to have little or no added sugar.
Then, in 1953, the brakes came off. Separate restrictions on sweets and chocolate were lifted in February, followed by sugar in September. By the second half of 1954, average sugar consumption had almost doubled.
The lifting of postwar sugar rationing inadvertently created a natural experiment, whose consequences scientists are only beginning to unpick. A flurry of recent studies suggests that spending the first 1,000 days of life under sugar rationing may have left traces on people’s health more than seven decades later.
“What makes the end of sugar rationing particularly interesting is the nature of the exposure,” said Dr Jiazhen Zheng at Hong Kong University of Science and Technology in Guangzhou, China, who worked on several of the recent studies. “In September 1953, sugar availability changed quite abruptly at the population level, largely because of policy rather than individual choice. In a sense, history created an experiment that we could never deliberately run over a human lifetime.”
The first of this recent wave of sugar rationing studies was published in the journal Science two years ago. Dr Tadeja Gračner at the University of Southern California and her colleagues used data from the UK Biobank to compare the health of people born shortly before and after sugar rationing ended in the UK. Some had been exposed to this low sugar environment only during their time in the womb; others remained exposed for months or years, while those conceived once rationing ended were not exposed at all.
Gračner found that the longer people had spent under rationing, the lower their risk of developing type 2 diabetes and high blood pressure in mid- to later life: those exposed throughout their first 1,000 days had a 35% lower risk of type 2 diabetes and a 20% lower risk of high blood pressure than those who had never experienced rationing.
The findings prompted Zheng and others to wonder whether these effects might extend to other organ systems. Over the past few months, further studies drawing on UK Biobank data by his group and others have linked reduced sugar exposure to lower risks of a growing list of health conditions.
“I have been more struck by the consistency across different organ systems than by any single effect estimate,” Zheng said. “In our work, we have seen associations with cardiovascular disease, liver disease, respiratory health, dementia and, more recently, broader measures of ageing. Our ageing study, for example, found a lower overall incidence of diseases linked to the hallmarks of ageing and modestly younger biological and organ ages among people exposed to rationing early in life.”
Gračner is not entirely surprised. “Many of these outcomes are connected,” she said. “Diabetes, hypertension and obesity are major risk factors for cardiovascular disease, cognitive decline and several other conditions, so if early-life sugar restriction affects those upstream risks, associations across a broad set of related outcomes are what one would expect.”
Perhaps more surprising is the suggestion that the effects could extend beyond physical health. In August, Prof Nophar Geifman at the University of Surrey and her colleagues reported that people who had spent the full first 1,000 days of life under sugar rationing had a 33% lower risk of being diagnosed with anxiety than those born after rationing ended.
They were also less likely to report a preference for sweet foods decades later. “Despite increased sugar consumption after rationing, early nutritional environments appear to have lasting relevance for mental health,” Geifman said.
How such a relatively brief difference in sugar exposure might leave traces detectable many decades later remains uncertain. Gračner said: “We can show that growing up with less sugar was protective decades later, but not how: whether through sugar itself, through taste preferences formed early, or through a metabolic response set in early life.”
Her team’s latest research, now under peer review, suggests that growing up under rationing may weaken the influence of genes that predispose people to a higher body weight.
“Importantly, while we observe that people exposed to rationing do consume less free sugar in adulthood, we find that dietary difference is similar across genetic-risk groups,” Gračner said. “That points to a response that is not purely behavioural: early nutrition may act on physiological pathways such as metabolic programming, insulin sensitivity, appetite and satiety regulation, or adipose-tissue [fat tissue] development.”
Explaining the anxiety finding is slightly trickier. Geifman says the brain undergoes rapid development in the womb and during the first few years of life, which could make it particularly sensitive to its nutritional environment. High-sugar diets have also been linked to inflammation and an altered gut microbiome – both possible routes through which sugar could affect brain function.
Zheng’s ageing study offers another potential clue. It found that people exposed to rationing scored about a year younger on several measures of biological age. The researchers also detected differences in proteins involved in pathways that help cells respond to nutrients and have been implicated in ageing. “I therefore see biological ageing as a possible shared upstream pathway, rather than necessarily a completely separate phenomenon,” Zheng said.
The idea that early-life nutrition can have lasting effects is not new. Since the 1970s, researchers have used famines as natural experiments to investigate the consequences of severe nutritional deprivation early in life.
Much of this research has focused on the Dutch “hunger winter” of 1944-45, when German restrictions on food transport left millions in the western Netherlands facing severe shortages. Because this famine began and ended abruptly in a previously well-nourished population, and because food rations were recorded and detailed birth records survived, researchers have been able to compare those exposed during different stages of pregnancy with those born before the famine or conceived after it ended.
“The most reliable findings are an increased risk of overweight, obesity and type 2 diabetes,” said Prof LH Lumey, an emeritus professor of epidemiology at Columbia Mailman School of Public Health in New York. “People are likely to be more overweight starting from when they are 20 or 30, and they are more likely to have diabetes at age 50 or 60.”
Although the British rationing studies might appear to point in the opposite direction, the conditions were very different. “British sugar rationing was not famine, and it did not involve severe overall caloric deprivation. Rather, it selectively constrained sugar intake while the broader diet remained relatively adequate,” Zheng said.
The lesson, then, is not simply that less nutrition is better. “It suggests that the quality and timing of nutrition during early development can have consequences that extend across the life course,” Zheng said.
So where does this leave us? Fascinating as the findings are, they don’t prove that differences in early-life sugar consumption caused the later health differences. “There’s no causality implied,” Geifman said. “It is an association.”
Many of the recent studies also draw on overlapping groups of UK Biobank participants, meaning they cannot be regarded as independent replications. “The strongest evidence will ultimately come from triangulation across independent datasets and research designs,” Gračner said.
Lumey said the findings represented “a great first step, not the final word. They should be further examined, not to answer the question: is there an association or not? But is the risk really 30% higher or 50% higher, and does it relate to the first 1,000 days, or only the period in gestation?”
Even if the associations eventually prove causal, these current studies cannot tell parents exactly how much sugar is too much. Nor can they pinpoint a single critical window. The evidence so far suggests that exposure during pregnancy matters, but some associations become stronger when rationing continued beyond about six months of age – around the time babies begin eating solid foods.
“The emerging picture is that the whole first 1,000 days may matter, with pregnancy and the transition to solid foods representing potentially important windows,” Zheng said. “While these findings support existing recommendations to limit unnecessary free or added sugars, they should not be interpreted as evidence that severe dietary restriction is beneficial.”
Yet, this postwar experiment may be less divorced from modern life than it first seems. Sugar consumption under rationing was broadly comparable to levels recommended by current UK guidelines, which state that free sugars – those added to foods and drinks, or naturally present in honey, syrups, smoothies and fruit juices – should not exceed 30g a day for adults and children aged 11 and over, with lower amounts for younger children. “Sugars should not be added to food or drinks given to babies,” NHS guidance says.
In practice, average UK consumption is roughly twice the recommended level.
The question raised by these studies is not, therefore, whether today’s infants should experience wartime deprivation, but whether keeping sugar intake closer to already recommended levels may have benefits that extend much further into later life than previously recognised.

I was tortured because I’m a Somali woman who dared to speak out | Sadia Moalim Ali
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
05:00:35 UTC
14:00:35 KST

‘Why don’t you just drive your tuk-tuk and do your work?” the judge asked me after videos from my social media accounts were shown during my court hearing. I had spoken on TikTok and Facebook about issues in Somalia that concerned me: forced evictions in the capital, Mogadishu, high fuel prices and nepotism in government.
I had described how, when I applied for work in hospitals and government departments, I was told on three occasions that I’d have to give a sexual favour in return.
In Somalia, women have no right to be part of society or to express themselves. They are not respected. Those who do dare to speak out are subjected to violence – or even disappeared.
Two days earlier, I had been abducted by two police officers and forced into a vehicle. At the police station, I was slapped and my head was hit against a wall. I had no access to a lawyer and no formal charges were made.
In court, the judge said I would be held in custody pending investigation. I was taken to Mogadishu Central prison. The female wing of the prison held about 120 women, and there were about 30 in my cell. The prison was built in colonial times and has never been renovated. There were no windows or lights, and there was a terrible smell. The only toilet had no door and there was no privacy.
The first night was horrible. I was imprisoned with members of [jihadist militant group] al-Shabaab and they were talking about killings, explosions and targeting well-known individuals. I was too afraid to sleep.
Every day we’d get tea and one slice of stale bread for breakfast, and then half a plate of rice about three hours later. To go outside for sunshine, you had to bribe the guards.
A lot of the women were depressed and had health issues. I developed skin problems, lost a lot of weight and my period stopped.
As time went on, I started hearing other women’s stories. One woman had been imprisoned while pregnant. Her ex-husband was thought to be a member of al-Shabaab and their joint bank account was found to have some irregular payments.
She gave birth to her now 18-month-old daughter inside her cell with the help of the other women. I found that heartbreaking – the baby hadn’t committed any crime and deserved a better life.
Every time I saw her, I was reminded of my own daughter who I was breastfeeding when I was taken. I was incarcerated alongside two girls aged 13 and 17. Women were imprisoned for debt or for non-payment of fines. Many had no access to a lawyer and had been sentenced to years in prison without understanding what crime they had committed.
I noticed that many of the imprisoned women had never received an education and had been exploited. I started teaching some of them how to read and write.
I managed to get a phone in prison and decided to speak to a local radio station. I did the interview for my safety and protection, and to let people know about my situation.
An hour after it was released, a group of men came to my cell and took me to a room used for torture and punishment. The prison commander started stripping me, removing my headscarf and dress, and beating me. My hands were tied behind my back, and they told me to crawl on my chest while they threw water on me. There were CCTV cameras in the room.
After that, I spoke to the media again – this time to the Guardian. I wanted to show that I was not going to back down and that this punishment would not stop me from speaking out. Even if you torture me, I will continue to rise up and speak.
After that interview was published, I was threatened with rape. The prison authorities said they would record it and release the video.
Three men forced me to the floor and removed my headscarf. They sexually assaulted me. All this was recorded on a mobile phone.
I eventually got access to a lawyer and, after a month in jail, I had the first of three court hearings. At court, the prosecution produced the Guardian article about me being tortured, alleging that I was spreading anti-government propaganda. I knew then that the story had hit a nerve.
On 25 June, I was convicted of insulting government institutions and sentenced to three years in prison. It was like a shot to the head. I was shaking and my vision went blurry.
My lawyer filed an appeal. That, along with the knowledge that people were campaigning for my freedom, gave me hope. On 12 August, the Banadir [region] court of appeal overturned my conviction and three-year prison sentence, leading to my release on the same day.
When I reunited with my daughter, she did not recognise me. Her punishment was much worse than what I had been subjected to.
I kept receiving threats and was being pressured to stop talking. Members of al-Shabaab had seen how my case had played out and wanted me to join them. I became scared for my safety, so I left the country.
Now, I am recovering from my ordeal. I want to get mental health support because I still have flashbacks to my time in prison. I am writing a book about my experiences.
And I am using my social media channels to advocate for some of the women I came across in prison. They are invisible – I want to help them get their freedom.
As told to Sarah Johnson

O2 has struck a record deal thought to be in the region of £200m to retain the naming rights to the London venue the O2 in the largest renewal of its kind in UK history.
The 10-year agreement will extend O2’s relationship until at least 2038. It cements the sponsorship as the second longest-running UK stadium naming rights deal after Arsenal’s partnership for the football club’s London ground,
Under the deal with Anschutz Entertainment Group (AEG), which bought the site of the ill-fated Millennium Dome five years after it was shut following the millennium celebrations, O2 is thought to be paying about £20m a year in the wide-ranging partnership.
This is an almost 50% increase on the annual amount under the existing deal which was due to expire at the end of next year. It is more than triple the £6m a year O2 paid in its initial 10-year deal when the future success of the O2 and surrounding site was far from certain.
“Everyone thought it would never work, that it was crazy building on the site of the Millennium Dome, it was considered the biggest white elephant,” said Paul Samuels, president of global partnerships at AEG International, talking to the Guardian.
“In the first deal we were talking about whether to put in clauses if the O2 couldn’t hit 100 shows a year – last year we did 239. We opened in June 2007 with Bon Jovi and the rest is history.”
Newly published accounts show that the O2 enjoyed the best year in its 19-year history in 2025. Pre-tax profits surged 18% to £76.5m, while revenues climbed 14% to £148.6m, as music fans put aside cost-of-living concerns to see acts including Lady Gaga, Katy Perry, Radiohead and Usher.
The record year resulted in a healthy £27.5m dividend being paid to its US parent company.
“People will opt to save money on other things but still want to go out and spend money on live entertainment,” said Samuels. “And when it comes to technological change like AI, it can change the world but it won’t change the desire for a live experience, like music and sport.”
Samuels said that each time the sponsorship deal nears renewal he receives a lot of interest from brands hoping to take over the naming rights.
However, Gareth Griffiths, director of partnerships and sponsorships at themobile operator’s parent company Virgin Media O2, said the deal had worked so well that it was agreed within an exclusivity period.
A key component of the deal is a 50% increase in the number of priority tickets made available to O2 customers, granting access to tickets to events 48 hours before they go on general sale.
O2 sells more than 1.7m tickets each year through its Priority Tickets programme across the 20 music venues it sponsors in the UK.
“The O2 has been an amazing brand asset for us,” said Griffiths. “Two-and-a-half million people come to the [main] arena each year, and 7.5 million come to everything else that is on offer.
“Music is right in the core DNA of our brand. Customer retention is absolutely crucial and driving loyalty through entertainment is a sweet spot for the business.”
Last year, O2 lost more than 100,000 customers after a backlash following the introduction of hefty price rises.
Last month, it was reported that VMO2’s joint owners – Liberty Global and Telefonica – want to cut £600m in costs to calm investor fears over a £22bn debt pile.
“Every pound we spend we do so very carefully,” said Griffiths. “This has been such a big success for the brand.
“Churn is still one of the most important metrics in the business, it is about keeping hold of valuable customers. Both of our shareholders are absolutely fully committed to this.
“This is a 10-year investment in the UK … a huge sign of intent. It has long been proven that growth comes from investment in your brand.”

Wanted: children to rear harvest mice at home for wild release in Devon
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
05:00:34 UTC
14:00:34 KST

Children in Devon are being invited to become “citizen captive breeders”, rearing harvest mice at home for release into the wild to help revive endangered nature.
Wild Pets, a new conservation project launched by two 14-year-old friends, is seeking 20 Devon-based children to rear hundreds of mice after the duo’s own successful restoration efforts.
Eva Wishart and Emily Smith bred several hundred harvest mice in tanks in their garages and released them on a nature reserve in Devon, south-west England, where the mice have begun breeding in the wild again.
The tiny harvest mouse, the UK’s smallest native rodent, is the only British mammal to have a prehensile tail, which can grasp or hold objects. It uses its tail to clamber up grass stems, which were once commonplace in fields, meadows and scrubland but have become far more scarce because of agricultural intensification.
Eva founded Wild Pets after feeling sorry for traditional pets such as hamsters and goldfish that are confined to cages and small spaces, while also worrying about the extinction crisis and ecological collapse. She began breeding harvest mice aged 10.
“I took them to school once to do a talk when I was 10,” she said. “It was the most popular I’ve ever been and everyone voted that we should keep them. So then we kept them in school in a big tank in the corner for six weeks. It was great. They had loads of babies.”
In 2025 her Wild Pets project was a runner-up in Prince William’s junior Earthshot competition, with crowdfunding supporting the first harvest mouse release.
Advised by the ecologist and rewilder Derek Gow, who has managed long-running captive-breeding programmes for water voles, beavers, storks and other mammals and birds, Eva and Emily last year released hundreds of captive-bred mice into a nature reserve.
The new population survived and maternal nests – distinctive grass balls expertly woven and suspended in tussocky grassland or scrub by the females – were found on the reserve this year. Chris Packham called the Wild Pets concept “truly sensational” on BBC’s Springwatch.
The expanded project, supported by Gow, the Devon Environment Foundation, Mid Devon district council and the Naturesave Trust, is seeking applications from children aged eight to 13, who can apply via the Wild Pets website.
Eva said young wild breeders would require a certain sense of “responsibility but most of all, really, enthusiasm, because if you’re really enthusiastic and passionate about something, with a bit of help, you’ll probably do it. Mainly we’re just looking for passionate kids.”
Wild Pets will provide a pair of harvest mice and all the equipment after a training day next spring at Gow’s Rewilding Coombeshead centre in Devon. The children will breed the mice, which can have multiple litters over the summer, with the aim of releasing 250 next September.
Emily said taking even modest action to help wildlife alleviated feelings of anxiety about environmental destruction. “It definitely makes you feel a lot better in the long run. It just makes you feel like you’re actually doing something rather than just watching it all happen,” she said.
Eva added: “Everything’s really scary at the moment for our future, on the news and at school. Everything’s very dark. So doing something, even if it’s only a tiny thing in a tiny corner of Devon, helps us feel a bit better.”
Packham said: “It’s so inspirational when young people think of an idea and then make it happen. It’s so, so important. What I like about young people doing things is that they think clearly, speak clearly and they get things done. Top work Eva and Emily. This is a really brilliant, brilliant project.”
The founders of Wild Pets hope to expand the wild breeding programmes to other small native species that should be more commonplace in Britain such as common lizards, stag beetles, mole crickets and glowworms.
Eva said: “In the first year we’re just inspiring 20 kids, but then, next year, we’re going to inspire the whole country to become conservationists and care about the natural world.”

Beautiful butterflies get more attention from the public – and from scientists
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
05:00:34 UTC
14:00:34 KST

Large and beautiful butterflies attract far more attention than species that are smaller and dull. Now a new study has shown that this bias towards beauty results in the boring butterflies being overlooked in conservation programmes.
To understand the link between beauty and conservation, researchers surveyed more than 21,000 people from more than 100 countries, asking them to look at photos of European butterflies and rate their beauty on a scale of 1 to 10 based on their first impression. The results, which are published in Current Biology, reveal that larger more colourful and patterned butterflies, like the yellow swallowtail, were consistently rated more attractive than the smaller, less conspicuous brownish species, such as the alpine grayling. That bias also extended into scientific research, with more studies on attractive species, and more funding and resource going into conservation of showier species.
By contrast, national and European red lists, which are based on fixed measurement criteria, do not exhibit the beauty bias. In fact, the most recent lists show that many of the small, brown, less attractive species are facing the greatest threat from climate breakdown.
The authors argue that nature conservation programmes need to recognise the beauty bias and give greater consideration to inconspicuous butterflies, which, while not as showy, play equally important functions within ecosystems.

Restrictions on hiring foreign workers could cost Lithuania growth, business reps say
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
05:00:00 UTC
14:00:00 KST

Restrictions on hiring foreign workers could hamper Lithuania’s economic growth and cost the country hundreds of millions of euros, business reps say, estimating that unfilled jobs could reduce gross domestic product (GDP) by up to €150 million this year and a further €550 million in 2027.
A business press conference titled How Much Will Unjustified Restrictions on Labour Migration Cost Lithuania? was held in Vilnius on Tuesday.
The conference was attended by Živilė Simonaitytė-Vasiliauskienė, an economist at the Lithuanian Confederation of Industrialists; Andrius Romanovskis, president of the Lithuanian Business Confederation; Povilas Drižas, secretary general of the International Transport and Logistics Alliance; and Mantas Gudas, chairman and director of Metalistas Group.
Economist Simonaitytė-Vasiliauskienė said the issue of migration was often subject to different interpretations.
“Most of us probably encounter migrants in one way or another, so we look at this issue through the lens of personal experience and perception,” she said.
There are currently around 227,000 foreign nationals with residence permits in Lithuania. Of these, about 108,000 have temporary residence permits allowing them to live and work in the country.
However, the real number is higher, with around 175,000 foreign nationals working in Lithuania at the beginning of the year, according to Simonaitytė-Vasiliauskienė.
“When we discuss migration, we very often focus on the quota, thinking that all migration is about the migrant quota, which is almost 25,000,” she said.
Lithuania currently operates a quota system for workers arriving from countries outside the European Union.
“However, if we count only foreign nationals who have residence permits in Lithuania on various grounds, the quota accounts for about 10%. It is certainly a small part of overall migration, just one way of having legal migration to Lithuania, but certainly not the main one,” Simonaitytė-Vasiliauskienė said.
Citing calculations by the Bank of Lithuania, she said foreign nationals working in Lithuania had generated 45% of GDP growth between 2019 and 2024.
According to the Confederation of Industrialists economist, if the quota remained in place, the state would lose out on GDP that could otherwise be generated, as well as tax revenue.
“This year, as we all know, the quota was exhausted in September. So this year alone, we estimate that the quota running out before the end of the year could potentially mean about €100 million in GDP not being generated in Lithuania.
“Obviously, these are economic calculations, and they can be debated, but under the worst-case scenario, that figure could reach as much as €150 million,” Simonaitytė-Vasiliauskienė said.
She estimated that restrictions imposed by the quota could also result in between €20 million and €25 million in lost tax revenue this year.
The impact could be even greater in 2027 if the current restrictions remained in place. According to Simonaitytė-Vasiliauskienė, Lithuania could potentially fail to generate around €500 million in GDP and lose about €90 million in tax revenue.
Most foreign workers are in transport
Drižas, secretary general of the International Transport and Logistics Alliance, said citizens of non-EU countries currently made up a significant proportion of the transport sector workforce.
Around 80,000 drivers work in the sector, he said, which employs about 150,000 Lithuanian and foreign nationals in total.
“This means that the added value created by these people is not limited to the taxes they pay and the profits earned by companies, which are also taxed. Those 80,000 drivers effectively create jobs for another 60,000 of our fellow citizens. These are well-paid, high-value-added jobs,” he said.
Drižas rejected the suggestion that these workers were “cheap labour”. He said those coming to Lithuania under the quota system were skilled workers.
“Politicians often say: ‘Pay more and Lithuanians will come.’ It is worth mentioning that wages in the transport sector grew by almost 12% in 2025, compared with almost 9% nationally.
“So wages here are growing faster than the national average, but there are still no Lithuanians willing to work as drivers. Not because we do not want to employ them, but simply because they do not exist,” Drižas said.
According to the transport sector representative, these workers spend only about 10% of their time in Lithuania and 90% abroad.
“These people who come here are only statistical, paper migrants – they are not physically here,” he said.
Gudas, chairman and director of Metalistas Group, said the company employed around 100 people, roughly a quarter of whom were from Ukraine, Belarus, the Philippines, and Uzbekistan.
“Today, we would gladly employ another 15 people and could launch an additional shift, but we are facing the aforementioned problem of a shortage of workers and specialists.
“We cannot put together a team of welders and assemblers. We also cannot employ two painters or a forklift driver, and we cannot employ a technologist – nor would it make sense to do so. It is just like in a restaurant: if the chef is not working, the waiter is not needed either,” he said.
Romanovskis, head of the Business Confederation lobby, said Lithuania was fundamentally facing a labour shortage.
“If you ask employers what the number one problem is, the number one problem is the shortage of labour, whether it is a small company, industry or transport,” he said.
However, Romanovskis agreed that migration needed to be controlled.
“Everything is understandable – national security priorities are just as important to us as citizens,” Romanovskis said.

Celebrating the October 7 massacre is inhumanity, not solidarity
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
04:58:06 UTC
13:58:06 KST

On the anniversary of the Hamas terrorist attack on Israel on 7 October 2023, in which 1,200 people were murdered and 250 were abducted, Sacha Roytman Dratwa, of the ‘Combat Antisemitism Movement’, recalls in an opinion piece for Euronews what had already begun in many countries on 8 October 2023.
My grandfather had survived the Holocaust. On October 7, 2023, I was with him in Belgium when the images from Israel began to arrive.
For our family, genocide was not an abstract word. It was part of the history that had shaped his life and made my own possible. Now, alongside him, I was watching the first images of another massacre of Jews.
I felt horror, fear and helplessness. Nevertheless, there was something particularly painful about experiencing that moment with my grandfather. After everything he had survived, he had lived long enough to witness this.
The attack by Hamas and other armed terrorist groups would leave approximately 1,200 people dead and 251 abducted. But as the first images appeared, we did not yet know the full scale of what was happening. We were trying to comprehend what we could see.
When I remember October 7, I do not begin with a political argument. I begin with that moment in Belgium, with my grandfather, and the terrible distance between wanting to protect the people we were watching and being unable to reach them.
On October 8 anti-israel demonstrations startet
Then came October 8.
I began seeing images of demonstrations, hearing “Glory to the Martyrs”, “Free Palestine” and “From the River to the Sea” and seeing accusations of genocide. What struck me was the speed and repetition. I had scarcely begun to process the images from Israel, and already I was trying to understand the public response to them.
Moreover, the timeline of accusations matters.
On October 8, Israeli forces were still fighting Hamas gunmen inside southern Israel. The Israeli ground offensive in Gaza would not begin until October 27. These anti-Israel demonstrations were taking place while the fighting against the infiltrating terrorist attackers was still underway, not after months of ground warfare.
In New York’s Times Square on October 8, demonstrators carried signs declaring “Zionism is genocide.” Reporting from the rally described some participants mocking Israeli counterdemonstrators and chanting the then reported Israeli death toll. In Sydney outside the Opera House, they chanted “Where’s the Jews?”
These were not expressions of concern for Palestinian civilians.
For me, the shock was deeply personal. I was with a Holocaust survivor, struggling to absorb the news of people being murdered, raped and abducted, while seeing images of others treating that same event as something to celebrate.
I wanted recognition of the victims before their deaths became another argument. I wanted someone looking at those images to see the people in them.
October 8 changed the questions I asked when I heard “Free Palestine.” What did the person saying it mean? Were they advocating freedom and safety for Palestinians? Were they also able to recognize the murder of Israeli civilians as a crime? Or were they describing that murder itself as liberation?
Those questions cannot be answered by a slogan alone. They require attention to what a speaker actually says and does.
The word ‘genocide’ was already used on 8 October
The same care is necessary with the word “genocide.” The appearance of that accusation on October 8 cannot establish or disprove allegations about actions taken later in Gaza. However, later events cannot change the chronology of those first demonstrations. What was said then belongs to the record of that moment.
For someone whose grandfather survived the Holocaust, the word carries an enormous weight. That family history does not settle every subsequent allegation. It makes me insist that the word be treated seriously, with evidence and attention to what is actually being alleged.
As we commmorate the third anniversary of the massacre, I find myself returning to those first two days because of the anniversary materials my colleagues at the Combat Antisemitism Movement’s Antisemitism Research Center are collecting.
In the monitoring material, National Students for Justice in Palestine pairs “3 years of genocide” with “3 years of resistance” and “for our martyrs.” Other flyers present October 7 as a date for mourning Palestinians without naming the Israelis murdered or the people abducted that day.
Choosing October 7 as the anniversary raises a specific question: what does the organizer say happened on October 7? I think it is a way to deny the violence against Jews and focus on delegitimizing Israel, its right to defend itself and its right to exist.
Other announcements refer directly to Hamas’s operation. Across university campuses around the world there are events celebrating or commemorating the “Al Aqsa Flood”, which was Hamas’s name for the attack.
This matters when assessing an event, a slogan and a charge. Mourning Palestinian civilians and commemorating an operation that included the murder, rape and abduction of civilians are different activities. Calling both “solidarity” does not tell an audience which one an organizer intends.
Those distinctions are essential. A Jewish student is not the Israeli government. A synagogue congregation is not a military command center. An allegation against a state does not make those religiously, nationally ethnically associated with it everywhere its defendants. No other people on earth are held responsible for the supposed actions of a state it has ties too.
What I wanted on October 8 was not agreement with every Israeli policy. It was recognition that the people murdered the previous day were human beings, and that their murder did not become less terrible because someone could place it inside a political argument or ideological tirade.
Anniversary events: What exactly do they want to commemorate?
Three years later, that remains the question I bring to these anniversary events. Can they acknowledge the civilians murdered and abducted on the date they have chosen? Can they distinguish concern for Palestinian lives from approval of attacks on Israeli lives? What, precisely, are they asking people to remember?
My grandfather is no longer alive, but I still carry the memory of being with him in Belgium as those first images arrived.
I remember the horror of October 7. I remember the isolation I felt on October 8, and I remember why the people in those images must remain people, with names, families and lives, rather than becoming abstractions in someone else’s argument.
An anniversary can hold more than one community’s grief. It should not require anyone’s victims to disappear.
Sacha Roytman Dratwa is CEO of the Combat Antisemitism Movement (CAM), a global coalition engaging more than 1,000 partner organisations and seven million people from a diverse array of religious, political, and cultural backgrounds in the common mission of fighting the world's oldest hatred.

Woolworths freight fuel levy surcharge almost triples since Iran war
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
04:56:09 UTC
13:56:09 KST

Check-out pain fears as Woolworths increases freight fuel levy surcharge
Woolworths has increased the fuel levy charged through its logistics network to food and grocery suppliers to almost triple its pre-Iran war level as diesel costs continue to climb.
The fuel levy surcharges have increased for metro and regional areas, affecting some of the country's largest food and grocery manufacturers.
This includes Primary Connect, Woolworths' logistics arm, which transports goods from suppliers to distribution centres and stores across the country.
The business manages freight for more than 1,000 grocery producers, including brands such as Sanitarium, PepsiCo, Ingham's and Arnott's.
The fuel levy for metro areas recently rose from 17.47 per cent to 19.88 per cent.
In regional Australia, the levy increased from 44.20 per cent to 50.30 per cent.
University of Sydney supply chain management professor Rico Merkert said the increases were not unusual when diesel prices rose sharply.
"Fuel levies are commonly used in freight markets to manage fuel-price volatility," Professor Merkert said.
"Many transport operators use surcharges that can be adjusted periodically rather than renegotiating contracts every time fuel costs move.
"If diesel costs rise sharply, it is economically reasonable for freight providers and retailers to increase fuel surcharges to recover those additional operating costs."
Prior to the Iran war, the fuel levy Woolworths charged in metro areas was 7.28 per cent.
Within weeks of the war, it had risen to 12.47 per cent.
The regional fuel levy has jumped by more than 172 per cent since March, when it was 18.44 per cent.
"We operate a large distribution network that includes independently owned and operated transport providers, and we are committed to supporting our transport partners, just as other industry players are doing," a Woolworths spokesperson said.
"To ensure they can keep their trucks on the road and get products on shelves in stores, we increased our review of the fuel levy to twice monthly in March to reflect the challenges they still face."
Consumers likely to feel impact
Experts believe the increase in freight costs are likely to be shared across the supply chain.
"My prediction is that consumers and suppliers will get the worst end of the deal of the fuel surcharge increase," said Medo Pournader, senior lecturer of supply chain management at the University of Melbourne.
University of Sydney professor Ben Fahimnia, who is also a specialist on the issue, said continually pushing rising logistics costs back onto suppliers is not a sustainable solution.
"They have absorbed some of the costs initially and have tried to find savings elsewhere, but there is a limit to what businesses can absorb," Professor Fahimnia said.
"Someone ultimately has to pay, and, at these fuel levy rates, that will be Australian consumers at the check-out."
While Professor Merkert agrees, he believes the effect is unlikely to be one-for-one.
"Higher fuel levies can eventually contribute to higher retail prices and hence inflation, but freight is only one element of the final shelf price, so consumers would not necessarily see a direct or proportional increase at the check-out," he said.
Rising fuel prices have played a significant part in Australia's inflation rate, which recently jumped to 4 per cent in August.
Transport was the second-largest contributor to the annual inflation figure as a result of higher automotive fuel prices.
On a monthly basis, automotive fuel prices rose 14.8 per cent in August, compared with a rise of 7.5 per cent in July.
In a press conference after last week's monetary policy decision, Reserve Bank governor Michele Bullock warned businesses were preparing to pass on higher fuel costs if necessary.
"The longer it [the war] lasts, if businesses were thinking, "Oh, look, it'll come off, I won't pass on costs," the longer it goes, the more likely it is that businesses will just try to pass through the cost increases," Ms Bullock said.

- Ex-bishop of Broome Christopher Alan Saunders has been sentenced for sexually abusing two Aboriginal boys.

This article contains references to sexual assault.
A former high-ranking Catholic known for hosting boozy parties will spend at least four and a half years behind bars for sexually abusing two young Aboriginal men.
Ex-bishop of Broome Christopher Alan Saunders, 76, was found guilty of 13 sex offences following a jury trial in the West Australian District Court.
The offending between 2008 and 2019 included one count of sexual penetration without consent and a dozen unlawful and indecent assault charges.
Saunders was sentenced on Wednesday to six years and six months' imprisonment.

Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
He will be eligible for parole after serving four years and six months.
Unless acquitted on appeal, the long-serving bishop would be the highest-ranking Catholic in Australia convicted of sexual abuse over his time as a member of the clergy.
The late Cardinal George Pell was found guilty in 2018 but later acquitted by the High Court of raping one choirboy and molesting another in 1996.
Saunders was acquitted by the jury of six other charges, including two counts of indecently dealing with a child over 16 under his authority and four counts of unlawful and indecent assault.
He was acquitted of a further seven similar charges during the trial due to the lack of evidence.
The sentence was backdated to 12 August, when Saunders was convicted and taken into custody.
Saunders, who was known as "Brother B" by his victims, put on alcohol-fuelled parties at Catholic Church-owned properties to get access to Aboriginal boys and men so he could sexually assault them.
The offending included unwanted touching of genitals and kissing, often after Saunders had supplied the men with large amounts of alcohol.
Saunders was ordained as the second Broome bishop in 1996 and presided over 13 schools and nine parishes before stepping aside in 2020 when the sex abuse claims became public.
Pope Francis accepted his resignation a year later.
Church probe into Saunders' activities set to restart
A church probe into the retired clergyman's activities was suspended when the West Australian police started investigating him.
It is set to restart now that the trial has finished.
"Its findings will inform decisions in Rome about Christopher Saunders' position in the church," Archbishop Timothy Costelloe said in August.
Following the sentencing, Archbishop Costelloe said the sentence recognises "the gravity and serious nature of the offences, as well as the profound impact on the victims and survivors of these crimes."
"The bishops of Australia together, and in the name of the Catholic Church in Australia, reaffirm and renew our commitment to the work of healing, reconciliation and renewal; to listening, to learning, and to redoubling our efforts to ensure that safeguarding, accountability and transparency remain at the very heart of the Church's life and mission," he said in a statement.

Record bets against the euro: how low could it fall amid France's fiscal crisis and Europe's energy shock?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
04:49:29 UTC
13:49:29 KST

The euro hit a 17-month low as French debt fears and Europe's energy shock weigh on the currency. Bond market stress could limit further ECB rate hikes, while analysts see scope for the euro to fall to $1.10 if the pressure intensifies.
At the start of this year, the euro was one of the most popular trades in global markets. Investors expected the European Central Bank to keep raising interest rates while the dollar lost its shine, and in late January the single currency climbed above $1.20.
Nine months later, that confidence has drained away.
The single currency recorded four straight weekly losses and earlier this week fell to as low as $1.116, its weakest level against the dollar since May 2025.
Behind the fall are two crises arriving at the same time: an energy shock Europe cannot control and a French budget nobody seems able to pass.
Together they have changed how investors see the euro, and they are now betting against it on a scale never seen before.
So why is the euro falling, and how much further could it go?
A gas bill that keeps rising
The first problem is energy, and it starts at the Strait of Hormuz.
Shipments of liquefied natural gas through the strait have been largely blocked since the war with Iran began in late February.
Europe imports most of the gas it burns, so it has had to compete for the remaining cargoes.
The benchmark Dutch TTF gas price was around €73 per megawatt-hour this week. That is roughly 120% higher than a year ago.
Storage gives little comfort.
European gas reserves were 71.5% full on 2 October, against 82.6% a year earlier, with winter only weeks away.
Brent crude, the global oil benchmark, traded near $100 a barrel on Tuesday. Since the start of the year, it has risen by more than 60%
Higher energy prices are now feeding into consumer prices.
Eurozone inflation jumped to 3.8% in September from 3.2% in August, its highest level since September 2023, according to Eurostat. Energy prices alone rose 18.8% from a year earlier.
When higher inflation stops helping a currency
In normal times, that would have helped the euro.
Higher inflation pushes a central bank to raise interest rates, and higher rates attract investors looking for a better return on their cash.
This time the logic broke.
At the end of September, markets priced in roughly three and a half more ECB rate rises. They now price in about two and a half.
Last week, ECB President Christine Lagarde poured cold water on those bets.
She indicated that rising borrowing costs were already slowing the economy, and that there was still no sign of energy prices feeding into wages.
She called for a measured ECB response.
Enrique Díaz-Alvarez, chief economist at Ebury, said the September inflation surprise "did nothing to help the common currency," especially after Lagarde's remarks, "which have made clear that the bar for an October rate increase from the Governing Council is now very high indeed."
That left the euro with the cost of high inflation, but without the reward of higher interest rates.
For European households and businesses, the consequences extend beyond currency trading. A weaker euro increases the cost of dollar-priced imports, potentially amplifying the energy shock already squeezing purchasing power.
How France's budget reaches the currency
The second blow came from Paris.
Investors now want much more to lend to France than to Germany.
Last Friday, the gap between the two countries' 10-year borrowing costs closed above 1.4 percentage points, the widest since the eurozone debt crisis of 2011-2012.
Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu's 2027 budget, which includes €43 billion in savings, still lacks majority support in parliament.
Banque de France governor Emmanuel Moulin warned on Tuesday that the country risks being “strangled by interest rates” unless it addresses its public finances.
Francesco Pesole, FX strategist at ING, describes two ways in which this hurts the euro.
The first is direct.
When a large eurozone country looks riskier, investors ask for a little extra return to hold anything priced in euros, and some simply choose to hold less of it.
"With fiscal uncertainty elevated, political rhetoric becoming more challenging, and policy scenarios that would normally sit at the margins now being discussed more openly, the market has more room to demand a higher yield," said Ken Egan, KBRA’s head of European sovereign credit.
The second is indirect.
The more stress there is in government bond markets, the less likely the ECB is to keep raising interest rates and add to that stress.
Ana Munera, director of global markets strategy at BBVA, described the ECB's choice as a "clear dichotomy" between tightening policy further after the inflation surprise and the need to pause to calm risks on the eurozone's periphery.
"An ECB pause would weigh on the EUR from a rates-spread perspective, although the stabilisation of debt markets would return flows into the currency," she said.
Spain added a second layer of political risk this week, when Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez called a snap general election for 29 November.
A record bet against the euro
The clearest sign of how far sentiment has turned comes from US futures data.
Every week, the US Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC) publishes how investors are positioned on the euro. A short position is a bet that the currency will fall.
In the week to 29 September, speculative traders held 301,439 short contracts on the euro, the highest number on record in CFTC data.
Each contract is worth €125,000, so the bets add up to about €38 billion.
Their net position, bets on a fall minus bets on a rise, was 63,256 contracts short. That's the weakest positioning since April 2025.
How low could it go?
Banks are divided between those who see more pain ahead and those who think the selling has gone too far.
ING's Pesole sees room for further losses if the French bond market deteriorates again.
"The fiscal risk premium is still relatively limited, leaving scope for EUR/USD to test 1.110 or even 1.100 if bond market stress intensifies," he said.
Danske Bank expects the decline to last.
"EUR/USD hit our 12M target of 1.12 ahead of schedule, but we think the downward trend will persist towards 2027," the bank said.
It argues that Europe's struggle with high energy prices leaves the ECB caught between protecting public finances and fighting inflation.
BBVA's Munera is less pessimistic in the short term.
"The EUR punishment has been too severe, in our view, and levels are starting to look stretched," she said. Even so, she expects the euro to trade well below its recent highs, because investors' view of the currency "has clearly worsened."
Heavy short positioning can also fuel a rebound. Better news may prompt traders betting against the euro to buy it back, accelerating any recovery.
A credible French budget agreement, calmer bond markets or falling energy prices could therefore interrupt the slide.
A lasting recovery would require more than short sellers taking profits: investors would need to see Europe’s fiscal and economic outlook improve.

Argentina waves football great Lionel Messi off after 3-0 win over Benin in final international appearance
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
04:46:37 UTC
13:46:37 KST

All-time footballing icon Lionel Messi bids an emotional farewell to international duty after guiding Argentina to a 3-0 win over visitors Benin in Buenos Aires. The little magician produced a final breathtaking performance for his white and blue stripes, scoring one goal and assisting two others.
Argentina is confronting a once-unimaginable reality; a national team without football great Lionel Messi.
On Tuesday, 39-year-old Messi bid farewell to international football after 21 years, 126 goals, two Copa Américas and a World Cup title, scoring a penalty and setting up Argentina’s other two goals for a 3-0 victory over visitors Benin.
What was otherwise an unremarkable friendly against the West African nation became a moment that this football-crazed country had long dreaded.
“It feels like an era is ending, knowing he won’t play for the national team anymore,” said Valentino Ruso, 17, who was heading to a friend’s house in Buenos Aires to watch the game. “I’m sad. I think everyone is upset today. He will be missed.”
Argentines had an intense, often unforgiving relationship with the shy boy who left his hometown of Rosario at 13 for the youth academy of Spanish club Barcelona.
As he grew into a global icon of near-mythical stature, his compatriots adored and abused him, sometimes questioning his commitment to his home country and accusing him of indifference to it.
But by the time he ended his dazzling international career, his devotion to Argentina was no longer in question. Nor was Argentina’s devotion to its most famous export, whose triumphs reminded the country of its capacity for greatness through years of political and economic instability.
“Argentines often say, ‘Thank God I was born at a time when I could experience the miracle of watching Messi play,’” said Andrés Rabinovich, a University of Chicago scholar who has researched football’s role in Argentine culture.
“It’s hard living in Argentina. football is often one of the few things that offers you some respite, some joy.”
For years, Argentines had debated when and how Messi should leave the world stage. His 31 August announcement that he’d be retiring from the national team, weeks after Argentina’s loss to Spain in the World Cup final, prompted an outpouring of gratitude and grief — even as Messi will continue to light up Major League Soccer with Inter Miami.
“I don’t know if there has ever been a love story between a player and a nation as great as the one you built,” his teammate Rodrigo De Paul wrote on Instagram.
The Argentine football federation turned Tuesday’s game — Messi’s 208th — into a national farewell billed as “the last tango.”
More than 85,000 tickets to Buenos Aires’ largest stadium sold out in 90 minutes, seats that were originally priced around $60-$300 (€53-267) later fetching over $2,500 (€2,226) on resale sites.
Players from Argentina’s 1978, 1986 and 2022 World Cup-winning squads returned to see him off.
After the final whistle, Messi’s eyes glistened as his teammates gathered around him, applauding. A rumbling chorus of “Olé, olé, olé, olé, Messi, Messi” rose from the stands as tens of thousands of fans jumped, sang and bowed toward him as if in worship.
A banner at midfield proclaimed him the "Eternal Captain.”
“The truth is, I'm talking more than I ever have. I don't want to leave here, I don't want to leave this field,” Messi told the crowd, which roared as if he had scored. “I just want to tell you that I love you, I'm going to miss you, and I'm grateful to God to be Argentine."
During the 2000s and 2010s, Messi amassed trophies with his club and won diehard fans from Barcelona to Bangladesh. Yet a major championship for his own country eluded him. After Argentina lost a third consecutive final in 2016, Messi briefly quit the national team.
The turning point came in 2021, when Argentina beat Brazil to win the Copa América, South America’s championship, for the first time in 28 years. Messi collapsed to the turf as his teammates, delirious, ran to hug him. The player long accused of feeling too little could not stop sobbing.
The World Cup victory the following year in Qatar sealed his place as a national hero. Messi had delivered the one prize that had eluded him, and millions of Argentines poured into the streets in collective ecstasy, his name in their chants and his No. 10 on their backs.
When Tuesday’s match finally ended, the crowd remained, their ovation roaring through the stadium. Messi took a final lap, a tiny figure beneath the lights, soaking it in. At the tunnel, he paused to lift his arms toward his fans one last time. Then he was gone.
His contract with Inter Miami runs through the 2028 season, but the ritual of watching him carry Argentina’s hopes and anxieties into every match is over.

Hamam al-Hamami, the Omani pilot suspected of attempting to crash a Flydubai passenger flight at Ben Gurion Airport, trained at one of Britain’s largest flight schools, The Telegraph reported Tuesday.
According to the report, al-Hamami underwent professional training with the prestigious L3 Airline Academy between 2018 and 2019 as he worked toward becoming a commercial pilot. The company operated training centers in England and has since become part of Acron Aviation. Investigators believe the Omani first officer trained at one or more of the company’s British facilities. The company said it would cooperate with authorities investigating the case.
His training also took him to New Zealand, where he received a six-month student visa for additional flight instruction between November 2018 and May 2019. At the time, L3 Airline Academy operated a program connecting its British centers with a flight school in Hamilton, New Zealand.
The Telegraph also reported that al-Hamami’s now-deleted X account, @PilotHamam, appeared to document his training and his life in Britain. Earlier reporting said the account included posts expressing support for violence against women.
In a 2022 post, al-Hamami wrote that he had “studied in Australia, Britain and New Zealand for five years” and described his years abroad as “the golden years of my religious commitment.” He said he became less religiously observant after returning to Oman. In other posts, he described encounters with women in Britain and expressed support for strict Islamic expectations regarding marriage and clothing.
The account also appeared to show that he lived in London for about five months, although it is unclear whether that period overlapped with his pilot training. The British academy had business ties with Oman Air, where al-Hamami later worked as a pilot until the airline allegedly found “extremist materials” in his possession and removed him from flying duties. He continued working in an administrative position at the airline until 2025.
The Telegraph noted that Oman Air had previously listed the academy as one of five internationally recognized institutions whose graduates would be considered for its pilot recruitment program. Acron Aviation declined to say whether al-Hamami had trained with the company, saying it does not publicly disclose whether specific individuals are current or former students.
Israeli Shin Bet security officials who traveled to the United Arab Emirates are taking part in the investigation of al-Hamami. During questioning, he said he had been motivated by a desire to take revenge on Israel for its actions in the Gaza Strip, according to Israeli officials.
Israeli officials said the investigation indicates that al-Hamami intended to crash the aircraft at Ben Gurion Airport. According to the findings so far, he waited until the flight was over Jordan before attempting to seize control because he wanted the aircraft to appear to be approaching Ben Gurion for a normal landing before crashing it into the airport and causing mass casualties.
Investigators say that if he had been unable to reach Ben Gurion, al-Hamami planned to crash the aircraft into a U.S. military base in Jordan. They also say he had originally intended to carry out the attack in July but postponed it because of a personal connection to one of the crew members, whom he said he had “spared.”
The investigation has also found that al-Hamami landed in Israel in June and had prepared himself to become a “martyr,” according to Israeli officials.
His alleged plan to crash Flydubai Flight FZ1023 was thwarted in part by the actions of Indian captain Smith Machar, as well as the other pilots and Israeli passengers aboard the aircraft.
Investigators say al-Hamami planned to strike Machar repeatedly with an emergency axe until he lost consciousness, then take control of the aircraft and crash it. After al-Hamami was subdued and the plane stabilized, replacement pilots requested permission to land in Jordan. Jordanian authorities refused once they understood that the aircraft was suspected of having been hijacked.
Channel 13 reported that the Omani pilot told investigators: “I searched and checked which airline flies to Tel Aviv, and that’s why I chose Flydubai. I tried to get accepted by all the airlines. I planned the operation before I was accepted by the company.”
According to an investigation by Italian newspaper Corriere della Sera, al-Hamami disconnected the autopilot, seized the controls, shut down the engines in flight and pushed the control column forward with full force.

Taiwan flu vaccinations top 1 million
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
04:45:59 UTC
13:45:59 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — More than 1.06 million people received publicly funded flu vaccines in the first five days of the program, according to a Centers for Disease Control press release.
At a regularly scheduled press conference on Tuesday, the CDC said the flu remains in the epidemic stage, with 139,060 outpatient and emergency room visits over the past week. Health authorities define a flu epidemic as over 100,000 weekly visits.
CDC data showed influenza A remains the dominant strain, with H1N1 accounting for 90.7% of detected influenza cases. There were 219 new cases of severe flu complications and 44 deaths (41 involved H1N1, one involved H3N2, and two involved influenza A not further classified).
COVID infections are also declining but remain at the epidemic stage. The CDC said there were 7,836 outpatient and emergency room visits from Sept. 27 to Saturday, down 26.7% from the previous seven-day period.
The first phase of Taiwan's publicly funded flu and COVID vaccination program began on Thursday, with people aged 65 and older among the eligible groups. Other eligible groups include health care workers, young children, pregnant women, and people with certain chronic or high-risk conditions, per the press release.
A second phase for adults aged 50 to 64 without high-risk chronic conditions will begin Nov. 2. An interactive map offers detailed information about clinics and hospitals participating in the government vaccination program.
Health authorities are promoting simultaneous vaccination under the slogan "left flu, right COVID," referring to receiving the flu vaccine in the left arm and an updated COVID vaccine in the right arm. The CDC recommends the two vaccines be administered together when appropriate.
The government's Health Token program also began on Thursday. Adults aged 18 and older can earn 450 Health Tokens for a flu vaccination and 900 for a COVID vaccination, with the tokens available for redemption beginning Dec. 1.

Three years after Oct. 7, IDF changes as Hamas, Hezbollah endure and manpower strain mounts
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
04:39:11 UTC
13:39:11 KST

Three years after the start of the longest war in Israel’s history, today’s IDF is no longer the same military. That is the picture emerging from a series of conclusions and changes across the armed forces, including Military Intelligence and the Israeli Air Force, released by the IDF Spokesperson’s Unit. 
The three years of war have produced dramatic military achievements, but ultimately no terrorist organization has been decisively defeated. Hamas in the south and Hezbollah in the north remain standing and are still capable of posing threats to Israel.
Of all the IDF’s branches, Military Intelligence, the body responsible for providing strategic warning, suffered the most devastating failure on the morning of Oct. 7. Over the past three years, the directorate has undergone a series of structural and cultural changes intended to prevent the next major conceptual blind spot. The IDF says Military Intelligence has adopted a culture of built-in self-doubt and daily scrutiny, aimed at identifying what it calls “signals from reality,” fragments of information that depart from prevailing expectations, while giving greater prominence to minority assessments.
The weight given to “reassuring indicators” has also been reduced, with greater reliance placed on objective “warning indicators” regarding enemy preparations and intentions. The goal is to create a common language among intelligence collection units, analysts and operational commanders. A new multi-front intelligence warning operations center, known by the Hebrew acronym TMUNA, has also been established to produce a unified intelligence picture connected directly to developments on the ground. Ultimately, Military Intelligence, where a culture of overconfidence had taken root and was exploited by Hamas on the morning of the massacre, will be judged by the next warning it is required to provide and by how that warning is delivered.
To ensure the changes take root throughout the organization, Military Intelligence has established several new institutional anchors, including a basic intelligence department and a centralized training department. It has also expanded its intelligence academy as a training center for officers from major through colonel and broadened its study and research of Islam and Arab culture. At the same time, Military Intelligence is in the midst of a strategic relocation to southern Israel and has established a new technological unit dedicated to collecting and processing unstructured information using artificial intelligence and advanced data technologies.
In the south: a new barrier above and below ground
For the IDF Southern Command, the lessons of Oct. 7 were translated into engineering, operational and tactical changes on the ground. During the fighting, four Hamas branch chiefs, 17 brigade commanders, about 60 battalion commanders and roughly 300 company commanders were killed, according to the IDF. As part of the overhaul of the defensive concept for communities along the Gaza border, security infrastructure was upgraded and new fences, lighting systems, surveillance equipment and radars were deployed. Civilian rapid-response teams were also equipped with weapons, protective vests, drones and the Netz application for encrypted information sharing.
Armored ambulances were positioned at readiness points, while the training program known as Shield 46 was expanded to eight complex exercises each year. Additional command posts were established to increase the military’s presence in the area. To create a continuous defensive and offensive posture, the IDF also established about 40 new posts overlooking key terrain and deployed a new physical and technologically advanced barrier, both above and below ground, to reduce the enemy’s ability to infiltrate.
The operational effort has included the clearing and destruction of hundreds of terrorist sites, launch pits and weapons depots. Since the October 2025 ceasefire, more than 4,000 systematic drilling operations have been conducted in an effort to locate underground infrastructure.
Despite this, Hamas remains on its feet. With money it collects from aid trucks it takes control of, the organization is still able to maintain a degree of governance. Israeli assessments say Hamas, which still possesses weapons, is using the current period to rebuild manpower and stockpile arms, including by transferring weapons into civilian areas. Israel believes the terrorist group is operating on the assumption that until elections in Israel and the United States, Israel’s freedom of action will be constrained and it will not receive a green light for a broad operation in Gaza.
In the Air Force: adapting to a multi-front threat and cutting response times
The Israeli Air Force, which faced fierce criticism over its absence during the first hours of the Oct. 7 attack, has also undergone extensive changes. The Air Force has adapted its operational model to a multi-front threat environment, delegating significant authority to commanders in the field while increasing the number of forces held at immediate readiness by up to fourfold overall and by up to sixfold in some units.
To strengthen coordination with ground forces, a new framework for border and joint operations was established, alongside the creation of target banks and additional joint exercises. As part of the new deployment, the 190th Attack Helicopter Squadron, known as the Magic Touch Squadron, was transferred to Ramat David Air Base in northern Israel to shorten response times on the northern front.
In response to the threat from unmanned aerial vehicles and drones, hundreds of new detection systems and radars have been deployed, while dedicated security units have been created within the regional commands. Dedicated defense battalions have also been established at Air Force bases, alongside the Arad unit, part of Wing 7, a combat unit designed to intervene rapidly against ground and aerial threats to Air Force assets. To ensure that the lessons are incorporated into future work plans, the Air Force established a dedicated directorate led by a reserve brigadier general who had served on the command investigation team.
The multi-front threat was reflected in the unprecedented volume of fire directed at Israel during the war. According to the IDF, about 10,200 launches came from the Gaza Strip, roughly 20,000 from Lebanon, about 1,200 from Iran, some 50 from Syria and another 90 from Yemen. The reserve system also paid a heavy price during the fighting: About 70% of the fallen were killed in operational circumstances, while about 65,000 injured reservists required treatment, of whom roughly 28,000 have already returned to active service.
In the West Bank, more than 3,800 weapons have been located and confiscated since the start of the war, according to the IDF. About 45,000 wanted individuals have been arrested, including arms dealers and weapons holders, terrorists allegedly preparing imminent attacks, operatives and others. More than 46 million shekels intended for terrorism were also seized.
Reserve system could face collapse
The IDF’s decision to defend Israel’s borders from deep inside enemy territory rather than along the physical frontier has come at a steep cost and has pushed the reserve system toward the edge. Despite repeated warnings from senior defense officials, political leaders and the government continue to avoid advancing a recruitment law that would meaningfully expand the pool of combat troops.
It is a leadership failure that is pushing the reserve system toward physical and psychological collapse, raising serious doubts over whether it can continue carrying the burden in its current form. Senior IDF officials have warned that if additional segments of the population are not recruited and the burden is not shared more broadly, the reserve system could reach its breaking point, potentially triggering a crisis of confidence with the military. The IDF could soon be forced to thin its forces along several borders to an unusual degree because of the shortage of combat personnel.
The scale of the problem can be seen in the increasingly limited manpower pool the military is trying to stretch across multiple fronts. Over the past three years, the IDF has been forced to improvise repeatedly, expanding the reserve system by an unprecedented 36%. Alongside the creation of new brigades, divisions and defense battalions, the military has pushed its existing manpower to the limit.
In August 2024, a special order returned about 22,000 reservists from exemption status. A series of concentrated recruitment and screening days in 2025 and 2026 brought in thousands more, including 14,016 people during the first interview day in 2025 and another 1,655 later, followed by 5,757 during the first interview day in 2026 and another 484 later. Another recruitment drive is planned for December 2026.
Overall, the number of personnel assigned to reserve duty has risen by 38%. But this is not a sustainable manpower plan. It amounts to life support for a relatively small segment of the population. The average number of reserve-duty days per combat soldier has risen to between 80 and 100 days a year, nearly double the routine planning assumption of about 55 days.
The IDF and the government have expanded financial, psychological and academic assistance through programs that provide grants, vouchers, tuition subsidies and housing discounts. But no financial grant or assistance program can replace the combat soldiers required at the front. As long as the political system prioritizes coalition considerations over a more equal distribution of the burden, money will not solve the exhaustion consuming the reserve force.
Decision-makers must recognize that without a genuine recruitment law that brings new combat personnel into the system, the reserve force could effectively declare bankruptcy, and the security price would be unbearable.
