An oil tanker off Russia’s Black Sea coast was struck by a naval drone, triggering a huge fire and black smoke cloud that blanketed parts of the resort city of Sochi, Russia’s transport ministry has said.
The transport ministry said a Liberian-flagged tanker had been attacked and that “crude oil is burning openly in the waters of the Black Sea”.
“Firefighting efforts will begin once the fire’s intensity has subsided and rescue vessels can safely approach the tanker,” the ministry said.
A crew of 23 – all Indian citizens – had been rescued, it added.
Russia and Ukraine have targeted commercial shipping around the Black Sea since the conflict began, and Russia has recently attacked grain vessels carrying Ukrainian goods near the coast of Romania.
There was no comment from Kyiv on the attack.
Videos and photos circulated on social media from Sochi – a popular Black Sea resort city of almost 500,000 people – showed bright orange flames out at sea and a thick column of black smoke billowing into the sky.
Local officials restricted access to the coast and beaches.
Elsewhere on Tuesday, Bulgaria’s prime minister said that two commercial vessels had been struck by drones in the first attack on shipping in the Nato member’s exclusive economic zone in the Black Sea.
Bulgarian authorities said that the origin of the drones was under investigation, but Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelenskyy blamed Russia for the drone strikes. Bulgarian prime minister Rumen Radev condemned the attack.
After an emergency government meeting, Radev said: “This is an unacceptable attack in Bulgaria’s exclusive economic zone. It is a blatant violation of international law and maritime law.”
Sea and aerial drones attacked the ships about 80 miles (128km) off Bulgaria’s coast, he said.
Zelenskyy warned in his nightly address on Tuesday that a “massive strike” from Russia was likely to come, and in the early hours of Wednesday Kyiv was attacked.
Russian strikes damaged buildings and warehouses across the Ukrainian capital, Kyiv’s mayor Vitali Klitschko said on Telegram.
Agence France-Presse reported multiple explosions in Kyiv, and Reuters reported two people were killed by Russian strikes.
A separate Russian strike on Ukraine’s south-eastern city of Dnipro damaged an industrial facility, officials said, without giving details.
Kyiv has been under increased attack as winter approaches, with Russian airstrikes targeting energy infrastructure, rail and road transport, including bridges that connect the city over the Dnipro river. Air raid sirens have sounded almost constantly day and night, urging residents to take cover in basements, shelters and subway stations.

Ukraine finds US-made navigation sensor inside Russia’s new jet-powered drone

Ukraine has found the US component in a Russian jet-powered drone targeting civilians, supermarkets, medical warehouses, and bridges. According to its Defense Intelligence, the new weapon contains a PNI5GA magneto-inductive sensor made by the US company PNI Sensor.
The US-made navigation component adds to evidence that Western technology continues to appear in Russia's strike drones. HUR had already identified US-made chips in the Geran-4 in May, but the newly reported PNI5GA is a navigation sensor in a modified version of the drone that Institute for the Study of War (ISW) says Russia may seek to field ahead of winter.
A Russian engine replaces the Chinese one
Russia has also replaced the drone's Chinese-made Telefly turbojet engine with a Russian-made equivalent produced in Alabuga. Russia is using the Alabuga zone to bring more of its drone production home rather than importing Iranian or Chinese parts, according to the ISW.
"The remaining electronic units and components are unchanged and identical to those used in previous Geran UAVs," HUR said.
What the warhead is built to cut
The modified drone also carries a specialized KRSN warhead designed to cut through bridge structures and power-line supports. Presidential adviser Serhii Beskrestnov described the warhead on 30 September, saying it consists of a 40-kilogram main charge and four strike modules. Its warhead is meant to destroy hardened targets made of steel and concrete and to damage cable-stayed bridges.
Russia has stepped up strikes on Kyiv's Northern and Southern bridges across the Dnipro in recent days with such drones.
However, Russia may try to field more resilient and more dangerous versions of its strike drones before Ukraine has effective countermeasures in place. Russia could use them to degrade Ukraine's energy infrastructure and logistics ahead of a winter strike campaign that it said will very likely be brutal.

Where is Spain headed after the snap election announcement?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
04:33:00 UTC
13:33:00 KST

Spain's snap election: Housing, migration set to shape vote
October 7, 2026
Spain's economic data has been positive recently, but politically, the country has been mired in a prolonged crisis for months.
On Monday, the social democratic Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez responded with a surprise move to break the deadlock: He is calling an early election for November 29.
Why is Sanchez calling an election now?
The sudden announcement followed a dramatic political defeat for the government. On Friday, October 2, Sanchez's emergency measures to tackle the housing crisis failed in parliament. Seven lawmakers from the conservative Catalan separatist party Junts, whose support the government has relied on since 2023, brought the measures down. Sanchez says he is now calling for a "much broader progressive majority."
The defeat came after months of growing instability in the government's parliamentary base. Spain's parliament has not passed a regular budget since 2023.
The recent crisis over mass migration to Ceuta and several corruption scandals involving allegations against the Spanish Socialist Workers' Party (PSOE) and people close to Sanchez have piled pressure onto the government.
And then came Maricarmen. The forced eviction of 87-year-old Maria del Carmen Abascal last month suddenly turned the housing shortage into the headline political issue.
The fact that his emergency measures were rejected in parliament allows Sanchez to position himself as a defender of tenants. However, it remains to be seen whether that strategy will pay off.
What role is pressure from the street protests playing?
The housing shortage has been at the top of Spaniards' list of concerns for around three years. According to estimates by the Bank of Spain, the country is currently short of around 750,000 homes, and the figure could exceed one million by 2028.
More than half of 18- to 34-year-olds live with their parents or depend on them financially. Property prices have recently been rising three times as fast as wages. In Spain, social housing accounts for just around 1.7 percent of the country's housing stock, putting it at the lower end of the EU scale in comparison with other member states.
It is hardly surprising, then, that protest camps sprang up in Madrid and elsewhere in response to the plight of Maricarmen Abascal, and tens of thousands took to the streets across the country. After the government's measures were rejected, the trade unions CCOO and UGT even announced a 24-hour general strike.
These dividing lines, however, do not simply split the government and the opposition. The tenants' movement also views Sanchez's plans as insufficient. The conservative opposition People's Party (PP) and parts of the business community, meanwhile, warn that tighter rent controls could make the problem worse.
Is Sanchez's model of governance coming to an end?
Since the 2023 election, Pedro Sanchez has governed without a majority in parliament. His social democratic PSOE formed a coalition with the left-wing Sumar alliance, but also depended on the support of smaller parties. These included Basque and Catalan regional parties, but above all the Catalan separatists of Junts.
That meant its seven lawmakers were repeatedly able to determine whether government legislation secured a majority or not. Over the course of the parliamentary term, this arrangement became increasingly unstable. In the first half of 2026 alone, the government lost almost one in four votes.
Evidence of the extent of this political deadlock is the state budget: Spain continues to work with the 2023 budget because the prime minister has been unable to get a new budget through parliament in his entire term. Junts ultimately refused to support Sanchez on housing policy, leaving him without backing on an issue that has been at the top of the political agenda following nationwide protests.
What was the political fallout of the Ceuta crisis?
At the end of July, more than 70,000 people crossed the border from Morocco into Ceuta within a short period of time. Although the government declared the crisis over soon afterward, at least 10,000 migrants were still in the exclave two months later, which has a population of only around 80,000. It was not until last Sunday that police cleared an improvised camp where around 3,000 people had been living.
The crisis altered Sanchez's previously relatively liberal migration policy. A new draft seen by Reuters proposes accelerated asylum procedures and deportations, as well as tighter rules. Human rights organizations have voiced sharp criticism.
How strong is the opposition?
At first glance, Spain's conservative PP is entering the snap parliamentary election at the end of November as the frontrunner to become the largest parliamentary group.
The real winner of recent months, however, is the right-wing populist Vox party. It is now polling at just over 18%, around six percentage points more than in the 2023 election. A strong Vox turnout could increase PP leader Alberto Nunez Feijoo's chances of gathering enough seats for a governing majority from parties right of center.
Vox leader Santiago Abascal is now confidently setting conditions for cooperation. Priority for Spanish citizens, economic deregulation and a significantly tougher migration policy, including the far-right concept of deporting foreign nationals to their countries of origin.
For his part, Feijoo faces a difficult balancing act. To replace Sanchez, he also needs to win voters from the political center. At the same time, he may need a partner for a governing majority who is steering the campaign significantly further to the right.
Will Spain also be voting on Trump and Europe's political direction?
In international media coverage, Sanchez is repeatedly portrayed as Europe's most prominent critic of Donald Trump. The prime minister rejected the US president's demand for defense spending to rise to 5% of GDP, refused to allow US bases in Spain to be used for the war against Iran and criticized US-Israeli attacks.
As a result, Trump even threatened at one point to cut off trade relations. At the same time, Sanchez explicitly contrasts his more liberal migration policy with Trump's deportation policies and attacks what he calls the "tech oligarchs" from the United States.
Sanchez is also one of the most prominent social democratic leaders of a major EU country. If the left were to lose the upcoming Spanish election, the European Council would lose one of its most outspoken voices against Donald Trump . It would also lose a prime minister who has opposed climbing defense spending, defended a more liberal approach to migration and criticized Israel more sharply over the war in Gaza than most of his European counterparts.
This article originally appeared in German.

Authorities: CPR numbers can no longer be used alone to identify people
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
04:30:39 UTC
13:30:39 KST

Danish companies and organizations should use other methods to verify people’s identities after unauthorized parties accessed information on 8.8 million people in the CPR register, authorities said Tuesday.
“One must expect that one can no longer identify oneself with CPR,” said Laila Reenberg, director of Samsik, the Agency for Public Security.
“You can no longer count on that if you receive a CPR number, you have identified a specific citizen. That is the consequence of this leak.”
Unauthorized parties collected information over 10 days in September through a small Danish company that had access to the CPR system. Authorities discovered the activity when the company was invoiced for the large number of searches.
The CPR system contains information on people living in Denmark as well as people who have died or moved abroad.
CPR numbers are sometimes used to identify people when they call their doctor or collect prescription medicine from a pharmacy.
Samsik recommends using other forms of identification, including MitID, two-factor authentication or one-time codes sent by text message or email.
“You cannot use it to authorize buying something or receiving sensitive personal data,” Reenberg said about CPR numbers.
Mikkel Leihardt, a department head at the Ministry of Research, Education and Digitalization, said an overall security review of the CPR system is being launched.
“It is important to emphasize that the information accessed is name and address. There is also other information that has not been accessed,” Leihardt said.
“As a system, CPR is intact.”
Reenberg said authorities have also introduced measures covering critical state IT systems.
Serum Institute expects high flu levels this winter
Influenza infections are expected to reach a high level in Denmark this winter, according to Statens Serum Institut (SSI).
“We expect a winter where influenza will once again be prominent, while COVID-19 appears to remain at a lower level,” Bolette Søborg, chief physician and head of section at SSI, said in an update published by the institute.
SSI expects both influenza A and B to circulate during the coming season.
“Both the number of influenza cases and influenza-related hospitalizations are assessed to potentially reach a high level,” the institute said.
Influenza A has dominated recent seasons, while influenza B has circulated at relatively low levels. SSI said this may mean that the population has less naturally acquired immunity to influenza B, which could make it account for a larger share of infections this season.
COVID-19-related hospitalizations, meanwhile, are expected to remain at a low to medium level.
People aged 65 and over are being offered free vaccinations against both influenza and COVID-19. SSI said the vaccines are expected to provide good protection against the two respiratory infections.
The institute also expects vaccination against respiratory syncytial virus, or RSV, to reduce serious illness among infants.
Since October last year, the Danish Health Authority has offered RSV vaccination to pregnant women. SSI said hospitalizations among infants fell by about 70% during the latest transmission season compared with previous years.
“We therefore also expect that the vaccination will significantly reduce the burden of disease among the youngest infants this winter,” Søborg said.
RSV is still expected to circulate among older children and adults, although for most people the infection causes symptoms similar to a common cold, including coughing.
False alarm prompts heavy police response at school
Police evacuated HF & VUC on Ejlskovsgade in Odense on Wednesday afternoon after a panic alarm was triggered by mistake.
Fyn Police initially said officers had responded with “many patrols” after an assault alarm was activated at the school.
Students were evacuated from the building, while members of the public, including parents, were asked to stay away from the area and respect police cordons.
At 15:42, police said the incident had turned out to be a false alarm.
“It turned out that it was a false alarm. The alarm was triggered by accident,” police said on Politi Update.
“There is no danger, but we are investigating the area just to be safe and will be present with a reassurance effort over the coming hours,” police added.
Police said they expected to lift the cordons “within the foreseeable future.”
Earlier, a student told Fyens Stiftstidende that his class was watching a documentary when a “Red alert” suddenly came over the school loudspeakers.
“Our teacher barricaded the door with a stopper, and then we waited for the police to arrive. I am okay, but it was an intense way to be kicked out,” he said.
No injuries were reported.
Danish prison service to review training after two Kosovar officers charged with assault
Danmarks Fængsler, Denmark’s prison service, will review its training of Kosovar prison officers after two were charged with assaulting an inmate at Vestre Prison in Copenhagen.
“It is clear that when something like this happens, we are going to look at whether our training of them is good enough. Is our practical training with them good enough?” said the service’s director, Ina Eliasen.
The officers are training in Denmark ahead of the opening of Danish prison places in Kosovo, now expected in late 2027 or early 2028.
Eliasen said the service had otherwise had good experiences with the Kosovar officers.
“We expect that this is an isolated incident, because it is so different from what we have otherwise seen,” she said.
According to the police charge, the two officers jointly punched an inmate several times while on duty in Vestre Prison’s South Department on Monday. Both pleaded not guilty during a preliminary hearing on Wednesday.
The officers had completed their practical training, but Eliasen said Kosovar officers must still be accompanied by Danish colleagues.
“They are always with Danish officers. And when they are in training, they are in on-the-job training. They do not walk alone,” she said.
She declined to comment on specific details of the case. The two officers were arrested on Tuesday and appeared before Copenhagen City Court at Vestre Prison on Wednesday.
Denmark signed the agreement to rent prison places in Kosovo in 2021. The plan is for foreign nationals sentenced to deportation from Denmark to serve their prison sentences there.
The opening has been delayed repeatedly, with another delay announced in mid-September. The prison places are now expected to be ready in late 2027 or early 2028.
A leak involving nearly nine million people’s CPR numbers could increase administrative costs for Danish businesses if it leads to restrictions on access to the register, according to the Confederation of Danish Industry, known as DI.
The CPR register is Denmark’s civil registration system. Banks, insurance companies and unemployment insurance funds use it to identify customers, employees and members.
“If companies’ access were closed or severely limited, a lot of information would instead have to be collected and checked manually,” Jeppe Engell, a cybersecurity expert at DI, said in a press release.
“That would both increase companies’ administrative costs and the risk of errors, outdated customer data, and mistaken identity.”
On Monday, the Ministry of Research, Education and Digitalization announced on its website that unauthorized people had unlawfully accessed the CPR numbers of nearly nine million people in Denmark.
Denmark proposes up to four years in prison for mediation councils that seek to prevent prosecution
The Danish government has introduced a bill that would make it a criminal offense to participate in a mediation council with the aim of preventing public prosecution of a crime.
The proposed penalty is a fine or up to four years in prison. The bill targets councils that attempt to settle criminal matters outside the Danish justice system.
Justice Minister Nicolai Wammen, a Social Democrat, introduced the proposal on Wednesday, arguing that such councils undermine the rule of law.
“It must come to an end that, for example, imams or prominent criminal families can exploit their position to act as judges of law and order and attempt to override the Danish rule of law,” he said.
The proposal revives a bill from the previous government that was not passed before a general election was called in February.
Police have encountered councils in Aarhus
Wammen said several police districts were aware of mediation councils, although he could not give a figure for how many exist.
In 2024, Jyllands-Posten reported that East Jutland Police had encountered such councils in western Aarhus for several years. The newspaper described them as widespread among groups with other ethnic backgrounds.
One anonymized police interview report described a case from 2020 in which a group of “important men” visited the parents of a man who had reported a violent assault.
The visitors wanted to avoid police involvement and suggested compensation for the assault, according to Jyllands-Posten.
Under current rules, a victim and perpetrator can agree to settle a conflict without police involvement, provided there is no criminal conduct such as coercion or witness intimidation. This has made it difficult for police to act against the councils.
The proposed law would also criminalize participation in a council when the purpose is to evade prosecution.
“What we are doing with this bill is that we are taking targeted action against those who sit at the head of the table,” Wammen said.
He cited wiretapping as a tool police could use to establish whether an illegal council was taking place.
“That is because this is something that takes place behind closed curtains and in environments that do not want to talk to the police. That is why we need better tools to combat it,” he said.
The government still needs a majority in the Folketing, Denmark’s parliament, to pass the bill. It is intended to take effect on January 1, 2027.
Danish cinemas pause screenings of “Naza” on anniversary of Hamas attack
Several Danish cinemas removed the documentary “Naza” from their Wednesday schedules on the third anniversary of Hamas’ attack in Israel, following a request from the film’s directors.
A review of listings on platforms including Kino and Nordisk Film Biografer showed that several cinemas had paused screenings for the day. Some are scheduled to resume showing the film on Thursday.
According to DR, the film’s Danish importer, Angel Films, passed on a request from directors Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor that the documentary not be shown on the anniversary.
The 80-minute film examines civilian casualties caused by Israel’s military operations in the Gaza Strip and the systems behind targeted killings of Palestinians.
It draws on anonymous testimony from Israeli military and intelligence personnel. The Israeli military has strongly criticized that method, and Israel has denied deliberately targeting civilians.
The documentary won the Special Jury Prize at the Venice International Film Festival in September.
It has also drawn anger from Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s government. Both directors have been threatened with losing their Israeli citizenship for violating the honor of Israeli soldiers.
The directors’ request to pause screenings on the anniversary was circulated across Europe through film distributors, according to the Greek newspaper Greek City Times. The newspaper reported that several cinemas in Greece and the Netherlands had agreed to the request.
“Naza” premiered in Denmark on October 1.
Autumn holiday traffic could cause motorway delays across Denmark
Drivers should expect heavier traffic and possible delays on Denmark’s motorways at the start and end of the autumn holiday, the Danish Road Directorate has warned.
The busiest periods are expected to be Friday from 2 to 6 p.m. and Saturday from 11 a.m. to 2 p.m. Traffic may also be heavier than usual during the final two days of the holiday.
The directorate, Denmark’s national road authority, recommends traveling outside the busiest hours.
Routes expected to see increased traffic include the E20 motorways across western Zealand and Funen, the E45 motorway in southern Jutland and motorways around Kolding.
Drivers crossing the Vejle Fjord Bridge on the E45 should allow extra time. Maintenance work has reduced the speed limit, and queues may form during busy periods.
Those heading to the ferry terminal in Aarhus should also allow more time to drive through the city. Roadwork on Marselis Boulevard means only one eastbound lane is open.
Drivers can check traffic conditions through the directorate’s Trafikinfo service or listen to P4 Trafik, the radio traffic service.
Meny tops Danish grocery customer survey for second year as 365discount finishes last
Meny has ranked first in an annual survey of Danish grocery customers for the second year in a row, while 365discount again finished at the bottom of customers’ overall ratings.
The survey, conducted by analysis firm Loyalty Group, gathered responses from 4,255 Danish grocery customers.
Dagrofa, the company behind Meny, said in a press release that the chain had Denmark’s most satisfied and loyal grocery customers. Meny scored 71 points on the survey’s loyalty index, ahead of Rema 1000 with 69 points.
Meny also led in six of the nine areas assessed, including customer trust, organic products, service and product quality, according to Dagrofa.
“Quality pays off in the end. We invest in skilled staff and quality on the shelves. We are enormously proud of this,” Meny chain director Richo Boss said in the release.
Loyalty Group produces annual industry indexes across several sectors, offering companies insight into customer preferences.
Dagrofa highlighted service as a particular reason for Meny’s ranking. Loyalty Group research director Lars Jepsen said customers recognized a “high level of professionalism and service.”
“For the chain, it is probably worth noting that the customers’ responses show that they trust the chain, and that the experience is stable from time to time,” he said in the release.
At the other end of the survey, Coop-owned 365discount received the lowest overall customer rating for the second consecutive year, according to TV 2.
“We are of course not satisfied with the ranking, and every day we work in a targeted manner to improve the customer experience,” 365discount chain director Michael Tilsted said in a written response to TV 2.
Danish companies and organizations should use other methods to verify people’s identities after unauthorized parties accessed information on 8.8 million people in the CPR register, authorities said Tuesday.
“One must expect that one can no longer identify oneself with CPR,” said Laila Reenberg, director of Samsik, the Agency for Public Security.
“You can no longer count on that if you receive a CPR number, you have identified a specific citizen. That is the consequence of this leak.”
Unauthorized parties collected information over 10 days in September through a small Danish company that had access to the CPR system. Authorities discovered the activity when the company was invoiced for the large number of searches.
The CPR system contains information on people living in Denmark as well as people who have died or moved abroad.
CPR numbers are sometimes used to identify people when they call their doctor or collect prescription medicine from a pharmacy.
Samsik recommends using other forms of identification, including MitID, two-factor authentication or one-time codes sent by text message or email.
“You cannot use it to authorize buying something or receiving sensitive personal data,” Reenberg said about CPR numbers.
Mikkel Leihardt, a department head at the Ministry of Research, Education and Digitalization, said an overall security review of the CPR system is being launched.
“It is important to emphasize that the information accessed is name and address. There is also other information that has not been accessed,” Leihardt said.
“As a system, CPR is intact.”
Reenberg said authorities have also introduced measures covering critical state IT systems.
A 31-year-old man charged with assaulting a Swedish man at a World Cup screening at Islands Brygge will appear before Copenhagen City Court on Wednesday.
The incident happened June 30 during a screening of a match between Norway and Ivory Coast. The Swedish man was punched and suffered a ruptured artery. He died July 3.
The defendant is charged with assault under a section of the Danish penal code covering less serious violence. Prosecutors are also seeking an increased sentence because of his previous convictions.
Special prosecutor Maria Cingari said in July that he could face eight to 10 months in prison.
The man has previously been convicted of rape and attempted murder. He was also convicted in another assault case last week.
Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen of Socialdemokratiet, the Social Democrats, criticized the possible sentence in August, saying she believed it should be harsher. The defendant is a Danish citizen who came to Denmark from Congo as an infant.
Foreign Minister Lars Løkke Rasmussen of Moderaterne, the Moderates, also commented after the Swedish man’s death, writing: “May the guilty party be judged harshly and fairly.”
The government has since announced plans to increase penalties in assault cases where the victim dies and the offender has previous convictions.
Prosecutors are also seeking a nightlife ban for the defendant. He has pleaded not guilty and is protected by a court-ordered name ban.
Two other people face separate assault charges in connection with the incident. One is accused of trampling on the Swedish man while he was lying down and assaulting another Swedish man. The other is accused of kicking the second man.
People collecting prescription medicine in Denmark may be asked to show identification as pharmacies respond to unauthorized access to information on 8.8 million people in the CPR register.
Danmarks Apotekerforening, the Danish Pharmacists’ Association, which represents the country’s pharmacies, said pharmacies are increasing checks when dispensing medicine and health information, particularly medicine with a risk of abuse.
“In practice, this means that it will normally not be sufficient to state one’s CPR number when picking up medicine,” the association said.
Customers may instead be asked to show a physical or digital health card or answer verification questions.
Additional checks may also apply when collecting medicine for another person. The association said bringing that person’s health card or other identification would be the easiest option. Otherwise, pharmacies may ask verification questions.
The changes follow recommendations from Samsik, the Danish Agency for Public Security.
“One must expect that one can no longer identify oneself with CPR,” Samsik director Laila Reenberg said Tuesday.
PLO, the Danish Association of General Practitioners, which represents and advises general practitioners, has also asked its members to follow Samsik’s recommendations.
Samsik said authorities, organizations and companies should pay closer attention when CPR numbers, names or addresses are used to confirm someone’s identity and should generally use other information for identity checks.
Unauthorized people collected information on 8.8 million living, deceased and emigrated people over 10 days in September by abusing a private Danish company’s legal access to the CPR system.
The incident has been reported to Datatilsynet, the Danish Data Protection Agency. The National Special Crime Unit is investigating the case.
Around 687,000 people in Denmark currently owe money to the public sector, down from more than 1.1 million in 2023, according to the Danish Debt Collection Agency.
That represents a decline of 454,000 people. The debt can include money owed to the police, municipalities or tax authorities.
Søren Bork Hansen, deputy director at the agency, said several factors have contributed to the decline.
“It is due to a combination of people being able to log in to ‘Mit gældsoverblik’ and pay the debt, but also that we can write off the debt if we have attempted to get the debt paid, and it is for a low amount,” he told Ritzau.
The agency can also recover debt through tax refunds or deductions from a person’s salary.
Debts can be written off when the amount is small, generally below a few thousand DKK, and collection has been attempted for at least a year. In such cases, the cost of collecting the money can be too high.
People living in Denmark owed the public sector around 108 billion DKK in total as of June 2025. Including businesses, deceased and missing people and people living abroad, the figure was 164 billion DKK in June 2026.
Since 2023, around 690,000 people have become debt-free, while others have accumulated new public-sector debt, resulting in the net decline of 454,000.
In the second quarter of 2026 alone, 110,000 people became debt-free while 62,000 took on public-sector debt, the agency said.
Danish government proposes prison unit at Kærshovedgård departure center for convicted residents
Denmark’s government wants to build a prison unit at Kærshovedgård for departure center residents who receive prison sentences.
Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen announced the proposal Tuesday during her speech opening the Folketing, Denmark’s parliament.
The unit could hold residents convicted of repeatedly violating requirements to report to authorities.
“Those residents who are sentenced to prison must be able to serve their sentence behind lock and key in a prison unit located in connection with Kærshovedgård,” Frederiksen of the Social Democrats said.
Kærshovedgård houses foreign nationals who have been ordered to leave Denmark or whose asylum applications were rejected but who cannot or will not return to their countries of origin.
Some say they would face persecution or torture. In other cases, their home countries will not cooperate with Danish authorities on returns.
Frederiksen said residents had caused problems for people living near the center, including theft, drug dealing and dangerous driving.
Authorities have previously introduced stricter reporting duties, removed some residents’ driving licenses and established electronic ankle monitoring.
The Danish People’s Party and others have called for all residents to be confined at the center.
The government rejected that proposal because residents who are not serving criminal sentences cannot legally be detained under international agreements.
The planned locked unit would apply only to residents convicted of crimes and sentenced to prison.

Large search bill alerted Danish authorities to breach of 8.8 million CPR records
An unusually large invoice led Danish authorities to discover that unauthorized people had accessed personal records on 8.8 million people, an official said Tuesday.
A small Danish company had legal access to search the national CPR register. Each search carries a fee, and extensive activity produced a large bill.
“There is a very large amount being invoiced, which makes one aware that there has been a lot of activity,” said Mikkel Leihardt, a department head at the Ministry of Research, Education and Digitalization.
Unauthorized users abused the company’s access for about 10 days in September.
Authorities have not identified the company.
The accessed information consisted mainly of names and addresses, Leihardt said. The CPR system is Denmark’s national register of personal information.
Authorities do not yet know who was responsible or how the company’s access was compromised.
“It is too early to say at this point who is behind it and what method has been used,” said Henriette Erbs of NSK, Denmark’s National Special Crime Unit.
She said cases of this type often involve cross-border crime.
Laila Reenberg, director of Denmark’s Agency for Public Security, said digital fraud was an obvious possible motive.
However, she said authorities did not yet know who collected the data or how they intended to use it.

Søndergaard publishes content on Twitch, YouTube and TikTok.
Danish law prohibits marketing energy drinks to consumers under 18 because the products are considered unsuitable for children and teenagers.

The organization said Red Bull products appeared frequently in his videos and argued that many viewers were younger than 18.

Søndergaard and Red Bull began a formal partnership in 2023.
The complaints also cover DayZeroAgency, which represents Søndergaard, and Ultra, which manages marketing and events for Red Bull.
MobilePay will change its name to Vipps in Denmark from January 12, 2027, the company behind the payment app announced Tuesday.
Some of the app’s nearly 4.7 million Danish users will begin seeing a redesigned logo during the transition.
The app’s functions will not change. Contacts, payment agreements, transaction history and other features will remain available.
MobilePay’s services in Denmark and Finland merged with Norwegian payment app Vipps in 2022, creating a shared Nordic platform.
Vipps MobilePay described the name change as one of the final steps toward operating under a common Nordic identity.
“We know that the new name will require a bit of getting used to,” said Jeanette Hertzum, the company’s Danish country manager.
The company wants users in Denmark, Greenland, Norway, Sweden and Finland to use the same name and logo.
The longer transition period is intended to give Danish users time to adjust before the new name takes effect.
The app will retain MobilePay’s blue color in Denmark and Finland. The logo will change to include the smiling symbol already used by Vipps in Norway and Sweden.
Hertzum said some users would adapt quickly, while others might need more time. The company said assistance would be available to people who need help with the change.

The Region of Southern Denmark has delayed approval of a handbook designed to help healthcare workers provide respectful care to LGBTQ+ patients, Danish public broadcaster DR reported.

Venstre, Denmark’s Liberal Party, proposed revisions with support from the Danish People’s Party, Denmark Democrats, Liberal Alliance and Conservative People’s Party.
“We think that the starting point is that there are two genders, and that we should not have a woke-ideological use of language,” regional council chair Bo Libergren of Venstre told DR.
He said the guide should avoid terms including “hen,” a gender-neutral pronoun used by some people instead of “he” or “she.”
The proposed changes will be considered by the full regional council.
The handbook is part of a regional policy on LGBTQ+ patients’ experiences with healthcare, adopted in December.
Sygeplejersken, a Danish nursing publication, reported that the guide was intended to provide practical tools for treating patients with safety and respect.
It would not create new rules but provide shared knowledge and examples of situations healthcare workers may encounter.
The plan was to distribute it across regional workplaces after approval.
About eight percent of Denmark’s population identifies as LGBTQ+, according to figures cited by the Danish Institute for Human Rights.

Denmark says it is too early to decide whether breach victims need new CPR numbers
Denmark has not decided whether people affected by unauthorized access to 8.8 million personal records will need new CPR numbers, Digitalization Minister Christina Egelund said.
Egelund spoke after briefing two Folketing committees about the breach of Denmark’s national personal information register.
“I have requested a security review of the entire CPR system,” Egelund of the Moderates said.
She said the findings would determine what changes were needed to restore trust and security. No deadline has been set for the review.
Unauthorized people misused a private Danish company’s legal access to obtain names, addresses, CPR numbers and other information.
The affected records cover living and deceased people, as well as those who have moved abroad.
The CPR register can also contain details about marital status, births, family relationships, citizenship, Church of Denmark membership and guardianship.
Egelund said authorities were focused on preventing the stolen information from being used for identity theft, phishing and other digital fraud.
A website and telephone hotline have been established to advise residents about protecting themselves.
The breach has been reported to Datatilsynet, Denmark’s data protection authority.
NSK, Denmark’s National Special Crime Unit, is investigating.
Authorities have not identified who was responsible. Egelund said investigators had not ruled out any possibilities, including international involvement.
Copenhagen apartment listings exceed 2,000 as housing market begins to slow
More than 2,000 owner-occupied apartments are for sale in Copenhagen for the first time since early 2024, according to housing website Boligsiden.
At the beginning of October, 2,057 apartments were listed in Copenhagen Municipality.
That was more than five percent higher than one month earlier and almost twice the number available one year ago.
The increase gives buyers more choice and could reduce competition for individual apartments, said Birgit Daetz, communications director and housing economist at Boligsiden.
Sellers must now compete with more properties for buyers’ attention, she added.
Daetz said the changing balance had also led to larger price reductions on Copenhagen apartments.
Every district recorded an increase in listings over the past year.
Copenhagen S, which includes parts of Amager, had 530 apartments for sale at the beginning of October. That was an increase of more than 150 percent from one year earlier.
Brian Friis Helmer, a personal finance economist at Danish bank AL Sydbank, said the figures showed that Copenhagen’s housing market was losing speed.
He pointed to slowing sales activity and smaller monthly price increases.
Across Denmark, the number of apartments for sale increased 6.3 percent over the past year.
However, listings of detached homes and terraced houses moved in the opposite direction, falling 11.9 percent nationwide.
German spy chief warns Russia is waging a ‘shadow war’
The head of Germany’s foreign intelligence service has warned that Russia is intensifying what he described as a “shadow war” against the country, saying Germany risks being drawn into a violent conflict.
“No other country poses such a direct, comprehensive and concrete threat to Germany,” Martin Jäger said during a public hearing in the Bundestag, Germany’s parliament, according to AFP.
The hearing took place before the parliamentary committee responsible for overseeing Germany’s intelligence services.
Jäger pointed to a case in August in which a drone carrying an explosive charge was found near a Ukrainian cargo plane in Leipzig. Agents with Russian connections are suspected of being behind the incident.
Germany has repeatedly accused Russia of conducting hybrid operations involving sabotage, espionage and other attempts to disrupt public order. Moscow has rejected such accusations.
Jäger said Russian intelligence services were acting “highly professionally and ruthlessly.”
“Russia is waging a shadow war against us. This undeclared war does not fit into traditional military and legal categories,” he said, according to German broadcaster Tagesschau.
“We must prepare ourselves for further attempts to intimidate us and more interference,” he added.
Germany is one of Ukraine’s largest supporters in its war against Russia.
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz visited Kyiv on Sunday alongside senior executives from several German defense companies.
Merz, who last week also warned about continued Russian hybrid warfare, announced an additional 1 billion euros, around 7.5 billion DKK, in military support for Ukraine during the visit.
More than seven in 10 Danish cancer patients survive at least five years
Just over seven in 10 cancer patients in Denmark are alive five years after diagnosis, according to the Danish Health Data Authority.
The latest figures cover patients diagnosed from 2023 through 2025 and five-year survival was slightly above six in 10 during 2011 to 2013.
“Survival is still increasing, even though it is not happening at the same pace as previously,” authority deputy director Jesper Juel-Helwig said.
Lung cancer showed the largest improvement for both sexes.
Among women, five-year lung cancer survival increased from 21 percent in 2011 to 2013 to 39 percent in the latest period. For men, it rose from 14 percent to 29 percent.
Survival also improved for some of the deadliest cancers. Five-year survival among men with liver cancer doubled from 10 percent to 20 percent.
Among women with pancreatic cancer, it increased from nine percent to 16 percent.
Kræftens Bekæmpelse, the Danish Cancer Society and the country’s main cancer organization, welcomed the progress but said further improvement was needed.
“We have gone from being at the bottom in Europe to being up near the top,” managing director Jesper Fisker said.
Fisker linked the improvement to national cancer care programs introduced almost 20 years ago and a stronger focus on research and coordinated patient treatment.
Dementia patients wait five times longer than legal limit for assessment
Nearly 25,000 people have waited more than the statutory 30 days for a dementia assessment over the past four years, according to a new report from Denmark’s National Audit Office.
The Public Accounts Committee has now issued sharp criticism of the country’s regions over the delays, using the second-highest level of criticism on its scale.
Under Danish law, patients should be assessed within 30 days. In practice, however, the average waiting time nationwide was 165 days last year, more than five times the legal limit.
“The Public Accounts Committee sharply criticizes that 84 percent of patients are not assessed for dementia within the 30 days prescribed by law,” the committee said.
The criticism follows a report by the National Audit Office, which found significant differences in both waiting times and the quality of assessments across Denmark.
In the Region of Southern Denmark, the average waiting time was 133 days. In Region Zealand, it was 244 days.
“The report shows that we are very far from the target of patients being assessed for dementia within 30 days, and that waiting times are growing,” the Public Accounts Committee said.
“There are far too large differences between our regions and between citizens with a strong and a weak social background when it comes to the quality of the specialized assessment and access to necessary examinations. We sharply criticize this.”
The report also found that social background can influence how quickly patients receive an assessment.
On average, the assessment process was 24 days shorter for patients with what the National Audit Office defines as a strong social background.
This includes people with greater wealth and medium- or long-cycle higher education, as well as those who have a partner and adult children with a similar level of education.
Patients with a weak social background are defined as people with debt, no vocational qualifications and no partner or adult children.
The Public Accounts Committee said the reasons behind these differences should be investigated.
“The Public Accounts Committee agrees with the National Audit Office’s recommendation that the causes of differences in the quality of assessment and the differences in assessment waiting times and quality for patients depending on their social background should be investigated,” it said.
Mads Duedahl of the Liberal Party, chairman of Danish Regions, which represents Denmark’s five regional authorities, said the criticism was justified.
“Waiting time is often very burdensome for both patients and relatives, and therefore the regions will make every effort to get more people assessed,” he told Danish Regions’ website.
Duedahl said the system needs to be “rethought” to increase assessment capacity. One option under consideration is to allow general practitioners to carry out more dementia assessments.
The 2026 Christmas seal features 46 children holding hands to represent friendship
This year’s Danish Christmas seal features 46 children holding hands in a design focused on friendship and community.
Christmas Seal Foundation board chair Anne Glad Wagner and artist Martin Jørgensen unveiled the seal Monday at Copenhagen City Hall.
The design is titled “The best gifts cannot be wrapped.”
Jørgensen said the children represent the supportive community that young people experience during stays at Denmark’s Christmas seal homes.
“It is about helping children, and therefore I have made them the main characters,” he said. “The Christmas seal homes help children form bonds and believe in themselves.”
Jørgensen has a background in advertising. The foundation selected him because of a graphic style that combines warmth, humor and small visual surprises.
Christmas seals are special decorative stamps sold before Christmas to raise money for the five Christmas seal homes in Denmark.
The homes support as many as 1,000 children annually who experience problems including bullying, loneliness, low self-esteem and poor well-being.
Seal sales cover about five percent of the homes’ operating expenses. Private individuals, companies and foundations provide almost all other funding.
The Christmas Seal Foundation, a Danish charity that operates the homes, has had Queen Mary as its patron since 2004.
Denmark’s Christmas seals were first issued in 1904. This year’s design is the 123rd edition. Copenhagen postmaster Einar Holbøll originally proposed the idea.
Denmark faces mild start to week before cooler and wetter autumn weather arrives
Denmark will begin the week with mild temperatures before rain, showers and cooler conditions arrive from Wednesday, according to the Danish Meteorological Institute, the national weather service.
“We will have a mild start to the week with many clouds and locally a little rain from time to time,” meteorologist Anne Borrits said.
A low-pressure system approaching from the southwest will bring more typical autumn weather during the second half of the week.
Monday will begin with some sunshine in eastern Denmark, while most other areas will remain cloudy.
Light rain is possible in Jutland, and temperatures will reach between 15 and 19 degrees Celsius. The highest temperatures are expected locally on Funen or Zealand.
Winds will be moderate to strong from the southwest. Coastal areas near the Skagerrak could experience gales Monday afternoon.
Skies will clear overnight into Tuesday, bringing dry conditions. Temperatures could fall to eight degrees in some areas, though most places will remain between 12 and 15 degrees.
Tuesday will be dry with periods of sunshine.
A low-pressure system will approach from the North Sea during Tuesday evening and Wednesday, bringing rain and later showers.
Conditions remain uncertain through Friday. Temperatures are expected to fall gradually, reaching between 10 and 15 degrees Thursday and Friday.
Strong winds are also possible along some coastal areas.
Stolen CPR data could make phishing attacks more convincing, cybersecurity expert warns
Personal information obtained through unauthorized access to Denmark’s CPR register could help criminals create more convincing phishing attacks, a cybersecurity expert said.
Names, addresses, identification numbers and birth dates can be used to make fraudulent emails and text messages appear to come from authorities, Aarhus University professor Jens Myrup Pedersen said.
“The more data you have about people, the more realistic attacks you can also create,” he said.
Phishing is digital fraud in which criminals pretend to represent a company, public authority or police force to obtain sensitive information.
Denmark’s Digitalization Ministry said Monday that unauthorized people had accessed names, addresses and CPR numbers belonging to about 8.8 million people.
CPR numbers are Denmark’s personal identification numbers. The register includes living and deceased people, as well as former residents.
Pedersen said the information should not be sufficient by itself to obtain loans in another person’s name. Service providers cannot assume that someone knows a person’s identity simply because they possess a CPR number, he said.
However, the information could support other forms of identity misuse and might be sold or combined with publicly available data and photographs.
Pedersen described the breach as unusually extensive.
Unlike a 2015 incident in which records on more than five million Danes were mistakenly delivered to a visa company, the new unauthorized access appears deliberate, he said.
Danish minister says security was inadequate after access to 8.8 million personal records
Security surrounding a private company’s access to Denmark’s national personal information register was inadequate, Digitalization Minister Christina Egelund said Monday.
Unauthorized parties used the small Danish company’s legal access to obtain records on 8.8 million people over about 10 days in September.
“It is clear to me that the security measures surrounding this company’s access to CPR have not been good enough,” Egelund of the Moderates told the Danish news agency Ritzau.
The accessed information includes names, addresses and CPR numbers, Denmark’s personal identification numbers.
The total exceeds Denmark’s population of about six million because the records also cover deceased people, emigrants and others registered in the system.
An employee in the CPR administration detected unusual activity Friday, October 2. Authorities had established by Saturday that a security incident had occurred.
The company had permission to search the CPR register, but unauthorized people abused its access. That access has since been closed.
Egelund acknowledged that warnings should have been triggered sooner because the activity continued for several days.
“It is a serious incident. It should not be able to happen,” she said.
The minister declined to identify the company or say whether authorities believe those responsible had criminal intentions, citing the ongoing investigation.
Authorities have not disclosed who accessed the records or how the company’s credentials were compromised.

The EU estimates that young Europeans spend four to six hours daily using screens.

Professor: Old IT makes universities hacking targets
Danish universities hold vast amounts of personal data while some continue to rely on ageing IT systems that may not meet modern security standards, a cybersecurity professor warns following the major attack on DTU.
Old IT systems combined with large amounts of sensitive personal data make Danish universities particularly vulnerable to cyberattacks, according to Jens Myrup Pedersen, professor of cybersecurity at Aarhus University.
His warning comes after the Technical University of Denmark (DTU) revealed Friday that hackers had gained access to its user database and extracted a large amount of data.
“Universities possess a very large amount of personal data,” Pedersen told Ritzau.
“And then it is my impression that several universities have quite a few older systems that probably do not have the security level one can expect in 2026.”
Pedersen stressed that he cannot comment specifically on the quality of DTU’s IT security.
But he said the attack raises important questions about how universities protect access to sensitive information.
“The question is which accounts have had access to all this personal data, and how well they are protected,” he said.
Another key question, according to Pedersen, is whether university IT systems can detect when unusually large amounts of data are being extracted and trigger an alarm before the damage becomes more extensive.
Universities face a ‘very high’ cyber threat
The problem extends beyond DTU.
Danish universities have been targeted by hackers several times in recent years, while a 2025 assessment from the Danish Agency for Societal Security (Styrelsen for Samfundssikkerhed) rated the cybercrime threat against Danish universities as “very high”.
Universities can be attractive targets because they combine extensive personal databases with large and complex IT environments used by thousands of students, researchers and employees.
The latest attack has brought renewed attention to whether security measures have kept pace with that complexity.
More than 200,000 potentially affected at DTU
As previously reported by The Copenhagen Post, more than 200,000 people could be affected by the DTU attack.
Unauthorised parties compromised several DTU user profiles and used them to access the university’s user database. DTU says a large amount of data was extracted and that the information involved could include CPR numbers, home addresses and telephone numbers.
The university has not yet determined exactly what information was taken or how many people are affected.
The incident has been reported to the Danish Data Protection Agency (Datatilsynet), while the National Special Crime Unit (NSK) is in contact with DTU about the case.
It has not been disclosed who is suspected of carrying out the attack.

G7 releases oil reserves – could it bring down Denmark’s record-high diesel prices?
Diesel prices in Denmark have climbed to record levels. Now the G7 countries are releasing up to 100 million barrels of diesel and crude oil from emergency reserves in an attempt to ease pressure on global energy markets.
Danish motorists could see some relief from record-high diesel prices after the G7 countries agreed to release emergency fuel reserves.
The move was announced Friday following a meeting of G7 leaders and will see up to 100 million barrels of diesel and crude oil released over the next four months.
The release will be coordinated through the International Energy Agency and is intended to increase supply and help stabilise energy prices.
For Denmark, the move could take some of the pressure off diesel prices, according to Jens Nærvig Pedersen, senior commodities analyst at Danske Bank.
But motorists should not expect prices to return to normal immediately.
“It is not the grand solution that can cause prices to fall again,” Pedersen told Ritzau.
“It does not solve the supply crisis in the oil market, which is primarily due to the conflict in the Middle East.”
Diesel has hit a Danish record
The price of diesel at Danish filling stations reached a record DKK 19.19 per litre in September.
The additional supplies from G7 reserves could help cushion the market, Pedersen said, but they cannot fully replace the supplies currently missing from the Middle East.
“For us to get lower and more normal prices again, a solution must be found to the current supply crisis,” he said.
The G7 announcement has already had an impact on international energy markets, with oil prices beginning to fall following the decision.
Why is the G7 releasing its reserves?
The decision follows mounting concern about global fuel supplies and sharply rising prices linked to the conflict in the Middle East.
It also comes after US President Donald Trump raised the possibility of stopping US diesel exports to Europe.
Europe is heavily dependent on imported diesel, making any restriction on US exports potentially significant for European supplies and prices.
Following the G7 agreement, Trump said Friday that he would not impose a diesel export ban.
The G7 countries have also agreed not to introduce restrictions on energy exports between member countries.
What happens to Danish fuel prices now?
The release of emergency reserves increases the amount of oil and diesel available on the market and could therefore put downward pressure on prices.
But the underlying problem remains the shortage of supply caused by the conflict in the Middle East.
That means Danish motorists could see some relief at the pump without necessarily seeing a return to the prices that prevailed before the current energy crisis.
The G7 consists of Canada, France, Germany, Italy, Japan, the United Kingdom and the United States.

EU Commission proposes 15-year monitoring period for new member states
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
04:30:34 UTC
13:30:34 KST

The European Commission wants stronger safeguards to ensure countries continue to follow EU rules and values after joining the bloc as it prepares for possible expansion beyond its current 27 members.
Under the proposal, new members would face increased monitoring for their first 15 years in the EU. Countries could ultimately have their voting rights in the Council restricted if they fail to meet requirements.
“The enlargement of the EU is a geopolitical necessity. Today, we are laying the cornerstone to ensure that a larger union also becomes a stronger union,” European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said.
EU Commissioner for Enlargement Marta Kos said the measures are intended to prevent countries from reversing reforms after joining.
“Here we propose stronger possibilities to prevent backsliding. Including cuts to funding or restriction of voting rights,” Kos said.
Candidate countries could also gain earlier access to EU programs such as Erasmus+ as they make progress toward membership.
The Commission is also proposing greater use of qualified majority voting to make it harder for individual countries to block decisions. This could apply to sanctions, tax fraud, some energy tax measures and parts of membership negotiations.
The Commission says the changes can be made under existing EU treaties and would require approval from EU countries and the European Parliament.
It hopes to secure approval during the autumn, allowing the rules to potentially apply to Montenegro.
Montenegro could conclude accession negotiations this year and seek final approval in 2027, with the goal of becoming the EU’s 28th member in 2028. The Commission considers that timetable realistic.

Country diary: A gleaming beetle that could be bad news for my garden favourites | Susie White
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
04:30:33 UTC
13:30:33 KST

This year there have been several firsts in my garden: old lady, vestal and blood-vein moths attracted to the light trap; hummingbird hawk-moths, normally occasional, feeding summer-long from verbena and buddleia; and it’s a painted lady year – a once-a-decade event, these high-flying insects migrating from Africa through successive generations. Southerly winds and heatwaves have added to the species visiting my North Pennine garden.
Now, in a herb bed, I spot something less welcome. Among the resinous leaves of rosemary is a gleaming beetle, its elytra striped in purple and green, scintillating like lustreware. It’s not something I’ve seen before, but I immediately know what it means. Rosemary beetle, Chrysolina americana, is a Mediterranean species with no natural predators in the UK. It is shimmering and beautiful – but can reduce plants of the Lamiaceae family to bare sticks and cause them to die back. This includes my favourites: lavender, sage, thyme – and rosemary.
Rosemary beetles were first discovered living outdoors in the UK in 1994 and have increased rapidly since then in our warming climate. The Royal Horticultural Society is monitoring their spread and has asked for sightings, which I submit. The advice is to hand-pick this non-native invasive species and tolerate “where possible”, seeing them as “as a colourful addition to the garden”. I wonder how rosemary beetles made it to my borders, as they have quite short wings and can’t fly far, preferring to walk, and I’ve propagated all my own herbs.
On a hot autumn day the gleaming beetles are out in force, mating at the top of branches – they particularly like lavender seedheads rather than flowers. Just touching a stem causes them to drop, a defence mechanism common to other beetles, making them hard to spot against the soil. The grubs are dull grey with longitudinal darker stripes, and both larvae and adults feed on the leaves.
Studying the bushes makes me notice other things: cinnamon bugs in their smart finery, seven-spot ladybirds, a garden snail sheltering in a sage leaf, a dramatically patterned cabbage bug, a tiny froghopper. Red admirals flicker over calendulas in this unusual autumn warmth, but there are colder days to come. Rosemary beetles are only likely to survive in my frost hollow if it’s a mild winter.

Serum Institute expects high flu levels this winter
Influenza infections are expected to reach a high level in Denmark this winter, according to Statens Serum Institut (SSI).
“We expect a winter where influenza will once again be prominent, while COVID-19 appears to remain at a lower level,” Bolette Søborg, chief physician and head of section at SSI, said in an update published by the institute.
SSI expects both influenza A and B to circulate during the coming season.
“Both the number of influenza cases and influenza-related hospitalizations are assessed to potentially reach a high level,” the institute said.
Influenza A has dominated recent seasons, while influenza B has circulated at relatively low levels. SSI said this may mean that the population has less naturally acquired immunity to influenza B, which could make it account for a larger share of infections this season.
COVID-19-related hospitalizations, meanwhile, are expected to remain at a low to medium level.
People aged 65 and over are being offered free vaccinations against both influenza and COVID-19. SSI said the vaccines are expected to provide good protection against the two respiratory infections.
The institute also expects vaccination against respiratory syncytial virus, or RSV, to reduce serious illness among infants.
Since October last year, the Danish Health Authority has offered RSV vaccination to pregnant women. SSI said hospitalizations among infants fell by about 70% during the latest transmission season compared with previous years.
“We therefore also expect that the vaccination will significantly reduce the burden of disease among the youngest infants this winter,” Søborg said.
RSV is still expected to circulate among older children and adults, although for most people the infection causes symptoms similar to a common cold, including coughing.

A leak involving nearly nine million people’s CPR numbers could increase administrative costs for Danish businesses if it leads to restrictions on access to the register, according to the Confederation of Danish Industry, known as DI.

Denmark proposes up to four years in prison for mediation councils that seek to prevent prosecution
The Danish government has introduced a bill that would make it a criminal offense to participate in a mediation council with the aim of preventing public prosecution of a crime.
The proposed penalty is a fine or up to four years in prison. The bill targets councils that attempt to settle criminal matters outside the Danish justice system.
Justice Minister Nicolai Wammen, a Social Democrat, introduced the proposal on Wednesday, arguing that such councils undermine the rule of law.
“It must come to an end that, for example, imams or prominent criminal families can exploit their position to act as judges of law and order and attempt to override the Danish rule of law,” he said.
The proposal revives a bill from the previous government that was not passed before a general election was called in February.
Police have encountered councils in Aarhus
Wammen said several police districts were aware of mediation councils, although he could not give a figure for how many exist.
In 2024, Jyllands-Posten reported that East Jutland Police had encountered such councils in western Aarhus for several years. The newspaper described them as widespread among groups with other ethnic backgrounds.
One anonymized police interview report described a case from 2020 in which a group of “important men” visited the parents of a man who had reported a violent assault.
The visitors wanted to avoid police involvement and suggested compensation for the assault, according to Jyllands-Posten.
Under current rules, a victim and perpetrator can agree to settle a conflict without police involvement, provided there is no criminal conduct such as coercion or witness intimidation. This has made it difficult for police to act against the councils.
The proposed law would also criminalize participation in a council when the purpose is to evade prosecution.
“What we are doing with this bill is that we are taking targeted action against those who sit at the head of the table,” Wammen said.
He cited wiretapping as a tool police could use to establish whether an illegal council was taking place.
“That is because this is something that takes place behind closed curtains and in environments that do not want to talk to the police. That is why we need better tools to combat it,” he said.
The government still needs a majority in the Folketing, Denmark’s parliament, to pass the bill. It is intended to take effect on January 1, 2027.

Danish companies and organizations should use other methods to verify people’s identities after unauthorized parties accessed information on 8.8 million people in the CPR register, authorities said Tuesday.
“One must expect that one can no longer identify oneself with CPR,” said Laila Reenberg, director of Samsik, the Agency for Public Security.
“You can no longer count on that if you receive a CPR number, you have identified a specific citizen. That is the consequence of this leak.”
Unauthorized parties collected information over 10 days in September through a small Danish company that had access to the CPR system. Authorities discovered the activity when the company was invoiced for the large number of searches.
The CPR system contains information on people living in Denmark as well as people who have died or moved abroad.
CPR numbers are sometimes used to identify people when they call their doctor or collect prescription medicine from a pharmacy.
Samsik recommends using other forms of identification, including MitID, two-factor authentication or one-time codes sent by text message or email.
“You cannot use it to authorize buying something or receiving sensitive personal data,” Reenberg said about CPR numbers.
Mikkel Leihardt, a department head at the Ministry of Research, Education and Digitalization, said an overall security review of the CPR system is being launched.
“It is important to emphasize that the information accessed is name and address. There is also other information that has not been accessed,” Leihardt said.
“As a system, CPR is intact.”
Reenberg said authorities have also introduced measures covering critical state IT systems.

People collecting prescription medicine in Denmark may be asked to show identification as pharmacies respond to unauthorized access to information on 8.8 million people in the CPR register.
Danmarks Apotekerforening, the Danish Pharmacists’ Association, which represents the country’s pharmacies, said pharmacies are increasing checks when dispensing medicine and health information, particularly medicine with a risk of abuse.

Around 687,000 people in Denmark currently owe money to the public sector, down from more than 1.1 million in 2023, according to the Danish Debt Collection Agency.
That represents a decline of 454,000 people. The debt can include money owed to the police, municipalities or tax authorities.
Søren Bork Hansen, deputy director at the agency, said several factors have contributed to the decline.
“It is due to a combination of people being able to log in to ‘Mit gældsoverblik’ and pay the debt, but also that we can write off the debt if we have attempted to get the debt paid, and it is for a low amount,” he told Ritzau.
The agency can also recover debt through tax refunds or deductions from a person’s salary.
Debts can be written off when the amount is small, generally below a few thousand DKK, and collection has been attempted for at least a year. In such cases, the cost of collecting the money can be too high.
People living in Denmark owed the public sector around 108 billion DKK in total as of June 2025. Including businesses, deceased and missing people and people living abroad, the figure was 164 billion DKK in June 2026.
Since 2023, around 690,000 people have become debt-free, while others have accumulated new public-sector debt, resulting in the net decline of 454,000.
In the second quarter of 2026 alone, 110,000 people became debt-free while 62,000 took on public-sector debt, the agency said.

Denmark’s government wants to build a prison unit at Kærshovedgård for departure center residents who receive prison sentences.
Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen announced the proposal Tuesday during her speech opening the Folketing, Denmark’s parliament.
The unit could hold residents convicted of repeatedly violating requirements to report to authorities.
“Those residents who are sentenced to prison must be able to serve their sentence behind lock and key in a prison unit located in connection with Kærshovedgård,” Frederiksen of the Social Democrats said.
Kærshovedgård houses foreign nationals who have been ordered to leave Denmark or whose asylum applications were rejected but who cannot or will not return to their countries of origin.
Some say they would face persecution or torture. In other cases, their home countries will not cooperate with Danish authorities on returns.
Frederiksen said residents had caused problems for people living near the center, including theft, drug dealing and dangerous driving.
Authorities have previously introduced stricter reporting duties, removed some residents’ driving licenses and established electronic ankle monitoring.
The Danish People’s Party and others have called for all residents to be confined at the center.
The government rejected that proposal because residents who are not serving criminal sentences cannot legally be detained under international agreements.
The planned locked unit would apply only to residents convicted of crimes and sentenced to prison.
