After the Cornell Case, Should Colleges Ban Fraternities?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
04:00:03 UTC
13:00:03 KST

A lawsuit alleging the drugging and gang rape of a student by seven members of Cornell University's Chi Phi fraternity in 2024 has led to calls for greater scrutiny of fraternities on campus, and even banning them.
The case has drawn national attention in recent weeks after it was revealed that only two of the seven men alleged to have been involved were expelled. Both the university and local authorities have come under criticism for their handling of the case.
Cornell President Michael Kotlikoff said in a video message to the university community on Saturday that the school would take “a serious look at the role of fraternities and sororities in campus life” among other steps aimed at creating a safer campus environment. At a protest on the university campus on Monday, people chanted “Ban the frats!”
TIME spoke to Nick Syrett, author of The Company He Keeps: A History of White College Fraternities and chair and professor of gender and women’s studies at the University of Wisconsin-Madison, about the case, what makes fraternities different, and why they have proved so hard to rein in.
This interview has been edited for length and clarity.
TIME: You've written a book about white college fraternities. What about this case shocked or surprised you, if anything?
There's a long history of events like this happening in fraternities. Since at least the 1970s and 1980s, there have been incidents of gang rape of intoxicated, incapacitated women in fraternity houses. So it is not surprising that it has happened once again.
TIME: Is there something unique about fraternities that encourages this kind of behavior?
I do think there is something particular about fraternities. One of the things is the single-sex nature of the organization. Aside from sports teams on college campuses, these are the only single-sex organizations, and the men who join them have decided that they want to be in a single-sex organization that allows them to live out their masculinity in particular kinds of ways. They know that these organizations already have a reputation for partying, for drinking, for sometimes hazing, for being places where you can meet women, and so some men join them and other men don't. But when they get in the organizations, the pressure ratchets up because there is an emphasis upon sex and dating and hooking up. That is some fraternities' mandate that like people report who they've hooked up with, who they've had sex with, they talk about these things. It's a way to enhance masculinity.
The other thing is fraternities just have lots of power on campus. Most of them own their own houses, which means they don't have lots of oversight from university officials.
TIME: In the wake of the Cornell case, there have been calls for greater regulation and even bans on fraternities. What do you think those regulations would look like, or should look like?
It's hard to say. I think one of the things to know is that all fraternities and sororities are regulated at least to a certain degree. That is, they're recognized student organizations. They have to abide by certain rules that often have to do with things like rushing and pledging—that is how people become members of the organizations in the first place. Social events where fraternities and sororities mix with one another and with unaffiliated members are usually at least registered with university officials.
The difficulty here is that when a university does the ultimate thing, which is to ban an organization from campus altogether, it loses any ability to regulate because now they're not an official organization. But by and large, the fraternities own their own houses, and so young men who are students at any university can still choose to become members of that fraternity and live in that house if they want to, if that chapter remains recognized by its national organization. So we see that happen with some regularity. There's a fraternity right here at my school, the University of Wisconsin, that two weeks ago the police busted for illegal hazing. That fraternity hasn't been recognized by the university for 10 years, but it's still admitting members, having them pledge, hazing them, and breaking the law.
TIME: How widespread are these issues that you’re talking about among fraternities? Is it limited to a few bad fraternities, or is this kind of just a part of the life?
It's a hard question to answer, in part because we don't always know how people are behaving behind closed doors. There are a few things we know. One, we know that men in fraternities are more likely to sexually assault and participate in hazing than men who choose not to join fraternities. Of course, not all men who are in fraternities do either of those things. It's just that they are more likely to do so than non-affiliated men. So, to my mind, those are the major problems: that is, sexual assault, hazing, and also binge drinking. And most evidence suggests that people in fraternities do drink more than those who are unaffiliated, but it also gets to this question, sort of a chicken and egg question: like, are people who are more interested in those activities more likely to join fraternities in the first place? I think the answer is probably yes, but then those behaviors are simply reinforced in fraternities by older members as well, who make environments that are conducive to those behaviors.
There are, in fact, chapters that have gone to great lengths to limit binge drinking. Some have eliminated hazing altogether. Hazing is in fact illegal in most states, and all the national fraternities forbid it. But some people do it anyway.
TIME: Why do fraternity members so rarely report on each other when these things happen? Where does that loyalty come from?
Part of it is historical in that when fraternities were first founded, they were secret organizations and they were illegal on college campuses for about the first 25 years of their existence, from 1825 through the 1850s. So joining at all was breaking the rules and keeping a secret. And now there are secrets that are imparted during the rituals, like the secret of what the meaning of the motto is, and that sort of thing. They're not unique or interesting in any way, but definitely fraternity pledges learn loyalty during the period of pledging because they're often asked to do things that are demeaning. If it's hazing, it's illegal in most states, and they're bonded to one another through the process of pledging and having to be humiliated and sometimes physically harmed in some way. So that creates a bond between the members of that pledge class and then the fraternity to which they are demonstrating their loyalty by being hazed and pledged in the first place, so all of it is pretty classic anthropological ritual, and it does in the end create loyalty.
TIME: If all fraternities went away tomorrow, these issues probably wouldn't disappear entirely, right? Is it the case that they exacerbate these issues rather than create them?
I think that's right. I don't think sexual assault would go away, but I think that fraternities are organizations that exacerbate and encourage both sexual assault and binge drinking and hazing. I also think, importantly, we would see less organized versions of sexual assault and binge drinking, especially, fewer occasions when a group of men together planned out a sexual assault, which in some sense is what happened at Cornell. I think we would see less of it because there would be less pressure placed upon the men in these organizations to carry out these sorts of things. And granted, it's pressure from within, but it's generally pressure from older brothers upon younger ones.
TIME: Fraternity membership has proved remarkably resilient despite decades of scandal. Why?
When universities have attempted to regulate and/or ban fraternities, they get big pushback. There's evidence to show that alumni who were in fraternities are more active in their schools and give more, and so that is a base of alumni that universities don't want to upset because they're generous and they're powerful.
There is a subset of incoming college first year students, men and women, who find these organizations really appealing, and some of it is entirely understandable. That is, at a big school, what fraternities and sororities promise you is an instant group of friends, which is very comforting on a college campus where you know no one. Especially if you're going to a school that's farther away from home, when others from your high school are not going there, so you don't know anyone at all. So fraternities promise that kind of friendship and loyalty, and also for young people, 18-year-olds, many of whom are unsure of themselves, fraternities and sororities say this is the way to be popular. This is the way to make friends, have a good time, and you'll get to go to the good parties and you'll be part of an in-group.

Building and Unbuilding: An Approach to Circular Timber Construction Addressing Material Waste

In the face of the climate crisis and within the framework of the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals, the reuse of materials has become prominent in the fields of construction and architecture in recent years. From "urban mining" to life cycle assessments (LCAs), professionals, organizations, and researchers are exploring different solutions and strategies to address the same overarching challenge. Project (Un)Build is a research initiative developing reversible timber construction methods that use straps and friction pads to facilitate material reuse. It contributes to the ongoing debate and reflection on the act of building itself.
Today, construction waste is one of the major challenges facing many architecture professionals. The act of building and unbuilding—where materials are joined, assembled, and disassembled—calls for an exploration that goes beyond joints, intersections, and connections. It creates opportunities to discover or rethink how these processes can be transformed by considering everything from material weight and strength to the broader consequences of our actions.

A new way to fight gum disease without wiping out good bacteria
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
03:55:00 UTC
12:55:00 KST

A new way to fight gum disease without wiping out good bacteria
- Date:
- October 6, 2026
- Source:
- University of Minnesota, Twin Cities
- Summary:
- Scientists discovered that disrupting the chemical messages bacteria use to communicate can push dental plaque toward a healthier microbial balance. The approach could lead to new treatments for gum disease that control harmful bacteria without destroying beneficial species.
- Share:
Bacteria are remarkably good at adapting. That ability helps them survive changing conditions, but it can also create problems when harmful species become resistant to antibiotics and disinfectants.
At the same time, bacteria are not simply enemies to eliminate. Many species play important roles in human health, including the hundreds of different microbes that live in the mouth. That raises an intriguing possibility: instead of trying to kill bacteria, could scientists influence how they behave and encourage healthier microbial communities?
Research published in 2025 in npj Biofilms and Microbiomes suggests that may be possible. Scientists studying dental plaque found that interfering with the chemical signals bacteria use to communicate can change which species thrive, potentially shifting the community toward bacteria associated with better oral health.
How Bacteria Communicate in the Mouth
The human mouth is home to roughly 700 species of bacteria. These microbes do not simply grow alongside one another. Many exchange chemical signals through a process called quorum sensing.
Quorum sensing allows bacteria to detect how many neighboring cells are present and coordinate group behaviors. Some oral bacteria communicate using molecules known as N-acyl homoserine lactones (AHLs).
Researchers from the College of Biological Sciences and the School of Dentistry examined how these signals shape dental plaque. Their goal was to determine whether bacterial communication could be manipulated to help maintain a healthier oral microbiome.
The oral microbiome refers to the community of microorganisms living in the mouth. When that community becomes unbalanced, potentially harmful bacteria can become more dominant and contribute to conditions such as periodontal disease.
Chemical Signals Can Cross the Gumline
The researchers found that bacteria within dental plaque produced AHL signals in aerobic environments (such as above the gumline), where oxygen is available.
Those chemical messages could also be detected by bacteria living in anaerobic environments (beneath the gumline), where oxygen levels are much lower.
This connection was important because conditions below the gumline can favor bacteria associated with periodontal disease.
The team also used specialized enzymes called lactonases to remove AHL signals. Lactonases break down these communication molecules, effectively interfering with the bacterial conversation.
When researchers disrupted AHL signaling, the dental plaque community shifted toward species more strongly associated with oral health.
Their findings suggest that carefully chosen enzymes might someday be used to alter the makeup of dental plaque and help maintain a healthier balance of microorganisms.
Dental Plaque Behaves Like an Ecosystem
"Dental plaque develops in a sequence, much like a forest ecosystem," said Mikael Elias, associate professor in the College of Biological Sciences and senior author of the study. "Pioneer species like Streptococcus and Actinomyces are the initial settlers in simple communities -- they're generally harmless and associated with good oral health. Increasingly diverse late colonizers include the 'red complex' bacteria like Porphyromonas gingivalis, which are strongly linked to periodontal disease. By disrupting the chemical signals bacteria use to communicate, one could manipulate the plaque community to remain or return to its health-associated stage."
In other words, dental plaque changes over time rather than appearing all at once. Early communities may contain relatively harmless bacteria, while more complex communities can eventually include species strongly associated with gum disease.
The researchers hope that interfering with bacterial communication could make it possible to guide plaque toward an earlier, healthier state rather than attempting to eliminate the entire microbial population.
Oxygen Changes How Bacterial Signals Behave
One of the most important findings was that the effects of bacterial communication depended heavily on oxygen levels.
"What's particularly striking is how oxygen availability changes everything," said lead author Rakesh Sikdar. "When we blocked AHL signaling in aerobic conditions, we saw more health-associated bacteria. But when we added AHLs under anaerobic conditions, we promoted the growth of disease-associated late colonizers. Quorum sensing may play very different roles above and below the gumline, which has major implications for how we approach treatment of periodontal diseases."
That difference suggests that the same chemical signals can influence microbial communities in very different ways depending on where they occur in the mouth.
Above the gumline, where oxygen is more plentiful, disrupting AHL signaling favored bacteria linked with better oral health. Beneath the gumline, adding those signals encouraged later colonizing species associated with disease.
A Different Strategy for Preventing Gum Disease
The researchers now want to investigate how bacterial communication varies throughout the mouth and among people at different stages of periodontal disease.
Rather than broadly attacking oral bacteria with antimicrobial treatments, the long term goal is to find ways to influence the balance of the microbial community itself.
"Understanding how bacterial communities communicate and organize themselves may ultimately give us new tools to prevent periodontal disease -- not by waging war on all oral bacteria, but by strategically maintaining a healthy microbial balance," said Elias.
The approach could eventually have implications beyond dentistry. Similar microbial imbalances, often called microbiome dysbiosis, occur elsewhere in the body and have been associated with a range of health problems, including certain types of cancer.
Researchers hope that learning how to manipulate bacterial communication could eventually provide a foundation for therapies designed to steer microbial communities toward healthier states rather than simply destroying them.
The research was funded by the National Institutes of Health.
Story Source:
Materials provided by University of Minnesota, Twin Cities. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- Rakesh Sikdar, Mai V. Beauclaire, Mark C. Herzberg, Bruno P. Lima, Mikael H. Elias. N-acyl homoserine lactone signaling modulates bacterial community associated with human dental plaque. npj Biofilms and Microbiomes, 2025; 11 (1) DOI: 10.1038/s41522-025-00846-z

The Oct. 7 battle for Sderot still rages in the minds of its survivors
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
03:52:07 UTC
12:52:07 KST

Shalom Aida was at home when the first air raid siren sounded at 6:29 a.m. on October 7, 2023, but he wasn’t initially fazed.
Rocket sirens were a common occurrence in his city of Sderot, which is less than a mile from Gaza at its closest point.
It wasn’t until he heard gunshots that Aida, a retired police officer, realized that dozens of heavily armed Hamas terrorists had infiltrated Sderot and were gunning down any civilian, soldier, or police officer they came across.
By the time he arrived at the police station, “it was a battlefield,” he said. The sight almost paralyzed him.
“The entire street in front of the station was full of bloodied people. Police, civilians, dead or dying. Hamas kept firing.”
One of the police officers killed that day was Aida’s cousin. Many others were his friends.
Three years later, he is still haunted by the memories.
“Sderot seems quiet now, but it’s not quiet or peaceful inside our heads,” he said as he watched groups of visitors walk around the Sderot Memorial and Heroes Park. It sits on the site of the police station, which was destroyed that day and rebuilt elsewhere.
Wouldn't dream of moving elsewhere, Aida says
Despite the ongoing trauma of Oct. 7 and its aftermath, Aida said he wouldn’t dream of moving elsewhere.
“I never once thought about leaving,” he said, shocked by the question. “The best people in the world live in Sderot.”
Not all residents of the “Gaza Envelope” who experienced the horrors of Oct. 7 returned home when the government gave the all-clear, after ordering them to evacuate for their own safety. But the vast majority of Sderot’s residents — set at over 37,000 by the Central Bureau of Statistics in 2024 — who had already lived through two decades of rocket barrages from Gaza, returned to the city within months.
Once it was a struggling development town where successive governments sent immigrants who had just arrived from the Middle East and the former Soviet Union.
It generated domestic and international headlines over the last two decades, as it became the first city hit by Hamas rockets as early as 2001, and remained one of the places the Gaza-based terror group has most frequently targeted.
International dignitaries, including UN Secretary-General Ban Ki-moon in 2009 and then Sen. Barack Obama during his 2008 presidential campaign, visited Sderot.
Initially a city without adequate protective shelter for its residents, it became the only place in Israel where every single apartment and bus stop has its own bomb shelter.
City has prospered despite challenges
Despite it all, the city has prospered: gleaming new apartment buildings, parks and a sprawling mall greet visitors as they enter.
“If you were to input all the data about Sderot into OpenAI, the 25 years of rockets and Oct. 7 and the bomb shelters, it would say this must be a ghost town. But that’s not the reality here,” said Ilan Abecassis, a retired educator and now tour guide who has lived in the city all his life.
Rather than shrinking, he said, the city’s population has grown by about 5,000 people since the Oct. 7 attack.
“I know it’s counterintuitive, but the more they try to destroy us, the stronger we become,” Abecassis said. “In the Torah, a new pharaoh sees the Israelite population growing and enslaves them. But the Torah tells us ‘the more they afflicted them, the more they multiplied and grew.’ We are like those Israelites.”
Arie Yagudaev, 30, from Sderot, and his cousin Eitan Izayev, 28, who lives in nearby Kibbutz Nir Am, said they are also committed to staying, even after they encountered terrorists in the street on Oct. 7.
Drinking strong coffee outside his family’s grocery store in Sderot, Izayev recounted how he had begged his cousin to pick him up from the kibbutz, which terrorists were trying to infiltrate, so he could help defend loved ones in Sderot. Along the way, they picked up two teenage girls, survivors of the Nova music festival.
“As we approached the roundabout into Sderot, we saw some pickup trucks ahead of us,” Izayev recalled. “We thought the men in the bed of the truck were IDF soldiers. But when the terrorists saw us, they shot at us nonstop.”
“One of the bullets shattered my car’s back window. It’s a miracle we survived,” Yagudaev said. Even though he suffered from PTSD every night as an evacuee in an Eilat hotel room, he said, “I wanted to go home.”
“It wasn’t just because the hotel room was cramped,” he said. “Leaving Sderot and Israel is exactly what the terrorists want. We’re not going anywhere.”
One Sderot restaurant owner, who was born and raised in Sderot but moved to Kibbutz Nir Am several years ago, feels the same way.
“Not to return would be rewarding Hamas for its terrorism,” said the restaurant owner who requested anonymity because of his ongoing stints in the IDF reserves.
As it was, he and his wife and baby spent almost a year in a small Tel Aviv hotel room before returning to their kibbutz two years ago. It wasn’t an easy homecoming, he said. For one thing, IDF soldiers had lived in their empty house, and it needed major repairs. Returning to the area also triggered traumatic memories from the Hamas attack.
“For 22 hours I stood outside our house to protect my wife and newborn baby,” he recalled, sitting at a table in his restaurant. “Eventually we decided to flee in our car with just the clothes we could throw into a trash bag. We placed the baby under the seat of the car, hoping to protect him.”
Once the owner of three restaurants, he now owns only one. He needed to sell the two popular restaurants he owned at another kibbutz because he couldn’t operate them from Tel Aviv, and, back then, the Gaza border was an active war zone.
Although the Gaza border is much more secure due to the buffer zone the IDF maintains in Gaza, “it’s not quiet on the border,” he said. “We live one kilometer from Gaza. Every day we hear the choppers and the shooting.”
Still, he and his wife have no plans to leave.
“My parents live here, my grandparents live here,” he said. “On Oct. 7 I saw an apocalypse, bodies on the ground. I knew 100 people who were killed or kidnapped. The ground beneath us is soaked with their blood. I can’t leave.”

Report finds over 70% eSIMs connect to networks in countries outside advertised destinations
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
03:49:49 UTC
12:49:49 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — More than 70% of eSIMs tested by Taiwan’s Consumers’ Foundation used internet networks outside countries where the services were advertised to work, according to a recent report by the foundation.
The foundation tested 172 eSIMs sold to travelers traveling to popular destinations and found only 27.9% used networks registered to operators in the countries listed on the products. Most connected through roaming services in third countries or regions, or through networks registered elsewhere.
The top travel destinations for Taiwanese travelers include Japan, China, South Korea, Hong Kong, Vietnam, and Thailand, according to the National Immigration Agency.
The foundation found 40% of the tested eSIMs used networks operated by Chinese state-owned telecom groups, including China Mobile, and 70% of the networks were located in Hong Kong.
The foundation said it is often difficult for consumers to tell what network an eSIM will use until they arrive at their destination and activate the service. Only then can they find out whether the eSIM connects directly to a local telecom operator or routes their traffic through a roaming service in a third region.
The Ministry of Digital Affairs said in July that eSIMs may route users’ internet traffic to servers in third countries before forwarding it to local networks.
The foundation advised travelers using eSIMs to avoid logging into online banking, entering credit card information, or handling other sensitive data unless they have confirmed the security of the network. It also recommended using HTTPS-encrypted websites or a VPN when possible.
The foundation called on authorities to consider requiring eSIM providers to clearly disclose the telecom operator providing the service, the data transmission architecture, and if traffic is routed through a roaming service in a third region.

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Taiwan’s memory module makers have reported strong revenue growth so far this year as rising AI demand has tightened memory supplies and pushed up prices, CTEE reported Wednesday.
For September, Adata Technology Co., Innodisk Corp., Transcend Information Inc., and Apacer Technology Inc. all posted substantial year-on-year revenue gains, ranging from 157.71% to 535.71%. For the third quarter, year-on-year growth ranged from 166.14% to 579.93%.
Adata reported consolidated revenue of NT$15.7 billion (US$492.4 million) for September, up 199.95% from the same month a year earlier. Its third-quarter revenue exceeded NT$50 billion for the first time, reaching NT$53 billion to set a new quarterly record, according to Anue.
Innodisk reported September revenue of NT$8.7 billion, up 535.71% year-on-year. Third-quarter revenue reached NT$25.9 billion, up 579.93% from a year earlier.
Transcend reported September revenue of NT$6 billion, up 290.42% from a year earlier. Its third-quarter revenue totaled NT$16.1 billion, representing a 291.08% year-on-year increase.
Apacer posted September revenue of NT$3 billion, up 157.71% year-on-year. Third-quarter revenue totaled NT$8.6 billion, an increase of 166.14%.
Memory module makers operate downstream in the memory supply chain. They purchase memory chips from manufacturers and assemble them into finished products such as DRAM modules, solid-state drives, and memory cards, which are sold under their own brands or through original equipment manufacturing arrangements.
Inventory management is important to module makers. They can benefit from inventory gains when memory prices rise, but may face write-downs when prices fall, according to Sinotrade.
Adata said the rapid expansion of AI applications has increased memory demand from AI servers and data centers, tightening supplies of DRAM and NAND flash chips for traditional computers and smartphones. Higher chip prices and tight supply supported higher product prices and sales in the third quarter.
Innodisk attributed the growth to higher shipment volumes and selling prices. The company plans to begin construction of its third factory in Yilan by the end of this year, with production scheduled to start in 2028.

Taiwan indicts 10 over alleged resale of US chips to China
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
03:49:41 UTC
12:49:41 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — The New Taipei District Prosecutors' Office indicted 10 people for allegedly using forged documents to purchase restricted chips from US companies Texas Instruments and Analog Devices and resell them to buyers in Hong Kong for onward delivery to China.
Prosecutors said the chips could be used in military applications, including radar receivers, electronic reconnaissance equipment, communications systems, antenna arrays, and uncrewed military aircraft, per UDN.
The suspects allegedly falsely identified the National Chung-Shan Institute of Science and Technology as the end user to obtain the chips. After importing them into Taiwan, they allegedly changed the packaging and labeled the products "Made in Taiwan" before exporting them to Hong Kong, prosecutors said.
The investigation found that the chips were subject to restrictions on their sale and export based on their end users and intended uses. Buyers are required to provide end-user documentation identifying the recipient and intended use of controlled products.
The US Bureau of Industry and Security maintains restrictions on exports and reexports of certain controlled items to China and military end users. Under US export rules, Hong Kong transactions are generally treated as involving China unless otherwise specified.
Chen Chien-hsiung (陳建雄), who headed several technology companies, allegedly began the scheme in 2017 after previously working as a salesperson for a chip distributor. Prosecutors said he learned that NCSIST was an approved end user for products from Analog Devices and Texas Instruments and falsely claimed that the chips would be used by the institute, per CNA.
Chen and his associates allegedly used forged NCSIST documents and seals to pass the manufacturers' and distributors' screening procedures. The chips were then allegedly repackaged and exported to Hong Kong.
Prosecutors said Chen Chien-hsiung, his brother Chen Chien-hui (陳建輝), and former associate Chen Chien-wei (陳健偉) generated about NT$120 million in illicit profits through the scheme.
A second group, allegedly led by Hygge Investment head Lai Chin-lan (賴金蘭) and Huawei Technology head Chiang Kun-cheng (蔣昆成), used similar methods beginning in 2019 and generated about NT$130 million, prosecutors said.
A third group, allegedly led by ZhanKai Technology head Yuan Tung-tai (袁同台), also submitted false end-user declarations and disguised the origin of the chips before exporting them to Hong Kong. Prosecutors said the group generated more than NT$100 million in illicit profits.
The indictment alleges that the three groups generated a combined profit of more than NT$360 million, per UDN.
Prosecutors charged the 10 defendants with aggravated fraud, forgery, and violations of the Money Laundering Control Act. They are seeking a 10-year prison sentence for Chen Chien-hsiung, while prosecutors are seeking sentences ranging from one to eight years for the other defendants.
Prosecutors said the alleged scheme could affect Taiwan's national security and damage its international reputation by creating the impression that Taiwan was knowingly assisting China in obtaining restricted technology.

Turkey, Australia’s joint COP31 leadership raises doubts
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
03:40:00 UTC
12:40:00 KST

Turkey, Australia’s joint COP31 leadership raises doubts
PARIS – Australia and Turkey are co-hosting the COP31 in November, but the highly unusual decision to share leadership has raised questions about how the climate summit will unfold – and who holds the power.
Both countries had fought to host the high-profile event, forcing a compromise under which Turkey would stage COP31 but Australia would run the formal negotiations.
The two delegations insist they are working closely together and have pledged steady and predictable leadership at the summit, which starts on Nov 9 in the Turkish city of Antalya.
But the dual-presidency model “has no precedent” at United Nations climate summits and its success is not guaranteed, said Anna Perez Catala from the Paris-based policy think-tank IDDRI.
It “aims to showcase countries can work together, even in difficult times, but could bring disagreements”, Catala said.
Rivals to partners
The climate summits rotate between regional blocs, with the host normally selected by consensus after consultation among members of the relevant group.
Australia and Turkey arrived at COP 2025 in Brazil as rival bidders for the 2026 summit and a diplomatic stalemate ensued when neither would withdraw from the race.
Australia’s bid enjoyed wider support, but Turkey did not relent, arguing it could bridge industrialised and developing nations, and highlighting ample, affordable hotel capacity in Antalya.
After extensive closed-door talks, a compromise was reached: Turkey would be COP31 president, host the summit and world leaders in Antalya, and design the “action agenda” that runs alongside the formal talks.
Australia’s Climate Minister Chris Bowen was named “president of negotiations” and granted “exclusive authority” over the negotiations.
Additionally, pre-COP meetings are being held in Fiji and Tuvalu this week in a nod to Australia’s original desire for the summit to have a Pacific focus.
Who decides?
The compromise resolved the hosting deadlock – but questions over specifics soon emerged.
In April, when asked by AFP if he would have a role in the negotiations, incoming COP31 president Murat Kurum said Turkey would “play a role anywhere, everywhere, because Turkey is the COP31 president”.
“At the end of the day, the decisions will be taken by the COP31 presidency,” said Kurum, who is also Turkey’s Environment Minister.
In June, Bowen acknowledged that there was some nervousness over the unique arrangement but said concerns were misplaced.
“I do understand because it’s a new thing. But what we’re doing actually has a lot of benefits and potential,” he told AFP in Bonn, Germany, during the mid-year UN climate sessions.
When asked who would bring down the final gavel at COP31, Bowen replied: “Kurum and I... together.
“We are working very closely together.”
Yet, in September, when asked again to clarify this situation, Kurum stressed: “Turkey is not co-chairing COP31 with Australia.
“In conducting those negotiations, Australia will work in consultation with the COP31 presidency, and ultimately, the final decision rests with the COP31 presidency.”
Call for clarity
Kurum and Bowen insist the arrangement is working smoothly, calling each other good friends and joshing about football when their national sides competed in the 2026 World Cup.
“We are genuinely working in harmony with Australia and our friends there... We have not experienced any problems so far, and we do not expect to encounter any in the future,” Kurum said in September.
But it remains to be seen whether the novel arrangement works out.
Germany’s former climate envoy Jennifer Morgan told AFP: “Historically, when there has been a lack of clarity of process or roles of presidencies at the COPs, it has diverted attention from the work at hand.”
The summit comes at a fragile moment for climate diplomacy: Energy security concerns are high on the political agenda, trust in multilateral institutions is under pressure, and nations remain divided over tougher action on planet-heating fossil fuels.
A French government official said there was a “clear division of roles” between the two countries: “It’s a new approach, so we’ll see how it works in practice.” AFP

One media giant now owns Top Gun, Harry Potter and CNN. What does that mean?

Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07

What does Paramount's Warner Bros takeover mean for what we watch?
Paramount has completed its $US113 billion ($162 billion) takeover of Warner Bros Discovery, creating one of the world's biggest entertainment and media companies.
The new company will be led by David Ellison, the son of billionaire Oracle co-founder Larry Ellison, whose family has close ties with US President Donald Trump.
The mega-merger brings some of Hollywood's biggest film, television and news brands under one roof, from The Godfather, Top Gun and Star Trek to Harry Potter, Friends, Game of Thrones and the DC universe.
For audiences, it means an enormous catalogue of movies and television shows is controlled by one company.
It also brings together two businesses already serving Australian audiences, with Paramount's Network 10 and Paramount+ joining Warner Bros Discovery's HBO Max.
But for Hollywood and the wider media industry, there are concerns about what happens when fewer companies control more of the entertainment and news we consume.
Just how big is the new company?
Paramount Skydance is now a huge player in movies, television, streaming and news.
Its stable includes Mission: Impossible, Top Gun, Star Trek, SpongeBob SquarePants, South Park and The Godfather.
Warner Bros Discovery brings Harry Potter, Friends, Game of Thrones, The Last of Us, The Big Bang Theory, Succession, The White Lotus and the DC universe.
Then there's HBO, Warner Bros Television, CNN and CBS, alongside Australia's Network 10.
The deal also reshapes Hollywood's traditional studio landscape, combining two of the five major legacy studios, Paramount and Warner Bros, leaving Disney, Universal Pictures and Sony Pictures as the other three.
David Folkenflik is a media correspondent with NPR and author of Murdoch's World: The Last of the Old Media Empires.
"It's an extraordinary moment for Hollywood and for the media writ large, and it's a moment for corporates and conglomeration as well," Mr Folkenflik said.
"You have these two proud Hollywood titles, Paramount Pictures, Warner Brothers Studios under the same roof, you now have CBS News and CNN under the same roof, you have Star Trek and DC Comics under the same roof."
Loading...
Why are people in Hollywood worried?
The merger comes at a difficult time for the entertainment industry.
Traditional studios are competing with global streaming services, while production costs are rising and audiences are increasingly watching content online.
The new company is also carrying significant debt and has committed to major cost savings.
Hollywood journalist Kim Masters, a former editor-at-large at The Hollywood Reporter, said the company was under significant financial pressure.
"This company is absolutely strapped with debt and needs to, according to the agreement with their lenders, they need to do some things very quickly to get things in shape," Ms Masters said.
"And so therefore, Hollywood is cringing in terms of those lay-offs."
She also said the merger left filmmakers with fewer major studios to approach for funding.
"So we're pretty much down to … Universal, Sony, Apple, but we don't know to what extent Apple is really interested in doing movies," she said.
"You know, it's just a loss of potentially two studio buyers for that kind of product."
And she said that could make it harder for directors working on films without an obvious commercial appeal to find backing.
"I think it's going to be more difficult for our auteur directors to find that kind of backing," she said.
Does a bigger library mean more choice?
The merger brings together a huge amount of existing content.
But the issue for Hollywood isn't simply how many movies and shows are available. It's how many companies are left deciding what gets made, funded, promoted and distributed.
Professor Matthew Ricketson from Deakin University said the bigger issue was the concentration of media ownership itself.
"Diversity of views, plurality of views and stories … if there is a lack of diversity of them … that is absolutely not a good thing," he said.
What could it mean for streaming prices?
The merger also brings together Paramount+ and HBO Max under the same corporate ownership.
David Folkenflik said consumers would bear some of the cost of the new company's debt.
"It's hard to believe those prices won't go up. I think the consumers are going to be hit," he said.
The company is targeting about $US6 billion a year in savings, and Folkenflik said those savings were likely to come from both staffing and content.
He said that could affect what audiences were ultimately offered.
"And that means that, you know, prices could potentially ramp up and you could see a diminishment of the combined amount of things offered," he said.
And then there's the news
The merger is significant because Paramount Skydance isn't only an entertainment company.
It also has major news interests, including CBS News and CNN, while its Australian operations include Network 10.
US President Donald Trump said on Tuesday local time he was a strong supporter of the merger.
"That's great. It's gonna be a great company. They're terrific people and it's going to be a great company," Mr Trump said.
The new owner, David Ellison, is the son of Oracle co-founder and billionaire Larry Ellison, whose family has developed close ties with Mr Trump.
Mr Folkenflik said that relationship was one of the key questions surrounding the takeover.
"I think that's the real question for journalists, and I think it probably is a question for a lot of their audiences at CBS and CNN," he said.
Professor Ricketson said the significance of the merger extended beyond the entertainment industry.
"Skydance will now control two of the five news outlets that currently constitute the pool at the White House, that is CBS News and CNN," he said.
CNN has been in a dispute with the Trump administration over access to the White House, with the network challenging restrictions in court.
Professor Ricketson said the relationship between the new ownership and the Trump administration raised serious questions about editorial independence.
"We've already seen those efforts by the Trump administration trying to kick out of the White House, the access to the White House of CNN, and two other news organisations. And saying they're doing that on the grounds that those outlets are lying or spreading fake news," he said.
He said the issue went to the heart of the relationship between political power and news organisations.
"We've already seen that Donald Trump's idea of favourable coverage is that you say wonderful things about me, terrible things about my opponents. And if you say anything other than that, you are either fake news or you are a hoax or you are lying when in fact, that's absolutely not been the case," he said.
Mr Ellison has said CNN would remain an independent newsroom, with Mark Thompson continuing as its editor-in-chief.
Professor Ricketson said the fundamental question was who got to decide what constituted legitimate reporting.
"Who is determining what are the lies here and who is determining what is the fake news?"
What does it mean for Australians?
For most Australians, there probably won't be an immediate dramatic change.
But two streaming services Australians already use, Paramount+ and HBO Max, are now owned by the same company and are expected to eventually be combined.
It has not yet been announced what the new service will look like, what content it will include or how much it will cost.
Network 10 also gives Skydance a significant presence in the Australian media market, with the company now behind programs including MasterChef Australia, Australian Survivor and 10 News.

Faisal Mahmud
07 October 2026•Update: 07 October 2026
South Korea is seeking to formally declare North Korea’s recent activities along their heavily fortified border as violations of the Armistice Agreement, local media reported Wednesday.
The move follows a joint investigation with the UN Command (UNC) into North Korean activities around the Military Demarcation Line (MDL), according to Seoul-based Yonhap News Agency, citing the South Korean Defense Ministry.
Seoul concluded that land mines deliberately planted by North Korea on the South Korean side of the MDL caused a Sept. 21 explosion that wounded three South Korean soldiers, two seriously.
“Following a joint investigation with the UNC into North Korea's MDL incursions, we plan to formalize its armistice violations,” the ministry said in a document submitted to lawmakers.
Seoul also plans to seek inter-Korean military talks aimed at preventing accidental clashes, reopening communication hotlines and addressing discrepancies over the location of the MDL.
The border dispute intensified after last month’s explosion, with Seoul accusing Pyongyang of deliberately planting two mines inside the Demilitarized Zone.
North Korea on Tuesday rejected the accusation, calling it “blame shifting” and accusing Seoul of attempting to portray its fortification of the border as a “military invasion.”
Pyongyang said, as the country’s state owned news agency KCNA reported, the incident was an attempt by South Korea to shift responsibility for “its own accident,” after Seoul demanded an apology and the removal of mines it said violated the armistice agreement.

Australian High Court rules authorities must consider climate impacts of fossil fuel projects
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
11:30:46 CST
12:30:46 KST

CANBERRA, Oct. 7 (Xinhua) -- Australia's highest court on Wednesday upheld a landmark ruling that planning authorities must consider the climate impacts of proposed fossil fuel projects.
The High Court on Wednesday voted to dismiss an appeal brought by coal miner MACH Energy against an earlier decision by the Court of Appeal in the state of New South Wales (NSW).
The appeal court in 2025 ruled unanimously that the NSW Independent Planning Commission (IPC) failed to properly consider local climate effects when it approved Mach Energy's bid to expand and extend the operating life of its Mount Pleasant coal mine north of Sydney in 2022.
The appeal against the IPC decision was brought by an environmental group led by local residents.
Anita O'Hart, a lead lawyer for the environmental group, said that the decision was historic.
"The implications extend well beyond Mount Pleasant," she said.
"This ruling will be applied by courts and planning authorities across Australia, and it will be studied internationally as one of the most significant domestic climate law decisions in the world," she added.
The Australian Broadcasting Corporation reported that Wednesday's ruling by the High Court is expected to have nationwide implications for how the approvals process for fossil fuel projects accounts for greenhouse gas emissions and local climate change impacts.
A spokesperson for MACH Energy said the company was disappointed, but accepted the decision and would pursue all available options to ensure the long-term continuity of the Mount Pleasant mine.
The NSW Planning Department in August granted a six-year extension to the operating life of the mine through 2032. ■

CJI Surya Kant administered oath to Justices Agarwal, Upadhyaya and Singh
NEW DELHI: Three new Supreme Court Judges – Justices Sunita Agarwal, Devendra Kumar Upadhyaya and Aparesh Kumar Singh – on Tuesday took oath of office in the name of God taking the working strength of SC to 37 judges, just one short of the sanctioned strength.CJI Surya Kant administered oath to Justices Agarwal, Upadhyaya and Singh, who were chief justices of Gujarat, Delhi and Telangana HCs respectively, in the presence of SC judges, attorney general R Venkataramani, solicitor general Tushar Mehta and other senior advocates and lawyers.With the elevation of Justice Agarwal, who is the 13th women judge of SC, the strength of women judges in the apex court at present became three. The other two being Justices B V Nagarathna, who is scheduled to become the first woman CJI on Sep 24 next year, and Justice V Mohana.During the tenure of Justice N V Ramana as CJI, the Supreme Court had the highest number of sitting SC judges at four – Justices India Banerjee, Nagarathna, Hima Kohli and Bela M Trivedi, last three of whom had taken oath on Aug 31, 2021. While the Collegium led by Justice Ramana had recommended appointment of three women judges, the present collegium led by CJI Kant has so far appointed two women judges.
SC got its first woman judge in M Fathima Beevi on Oct 6, 1989, 39 years after SC was established. Justice Beevi had retired from Kerala HC on Apr 29, 1989, but was elevated to the SC five months after retirement. Other women judges in SC were – Justices Sujata V Manohar, Ruma Pal, Gyan Sudha Misra, Ranjana P Desai, R Bhanumathi and Indu Malhotra.SC judge strength was increased from 34 to 38, including the CJI, initially through an Ordinance on May 16. The corresponding Amendment Act was passed by Parliament which received the President's assent on Aug 11. In Aug 2019, during the tenure of CJI Ranjan Gogoi, the sanctioned strength of SC judges was increased from 31 to 34, including CJI.The SC had started in 1950 with a sanctioned strength of 8 Judges, which was increased to 11 in 1956, 14 in 1960, 18 in 1978, 26 in 1986, and 31 in 2009. SC as of Tuesday has a pendency of 95, 481 cases.

US stock market hits all-time high as investors bet big on AI

US stock market hits all-time high as investors continue to bet on AI
The benchmark S&P 500 is up 14 percent this year despite elevated oil prices and US government debt sell-off.
The United States stock market has hit an all-time high as excitement around artificial intelligence continues to fuel a buying frenzy on Wall Street.
The S&P 500, the benchmark stock index, closed 0.58 percent higher on Tuesday, topping the previous peak reached in mid-August.
The Nasdaq Composite, which is more heavily weighted towards tech stocks, also hit a record high, finishing up 0.45 percent.
Tech stocks were among the top performers, with each of the “Magnificent Seven” apart from Meta closing higher.
Amazon led the pack with a 1.95 percent gain, followed by Microsoft and Tesla, which rose 0.78 percent and 0.51 percent, respectively.
Apple and Alphabet both rose 0.22 percent, while Nvidia gained 0.14 percent.
Meta, which has risen more than 20 percent since the launch last month of its new AI assistant, Muse, fell 0.41 percent.
Other big movers in tech included Marvell Technology, which rose 5.81 percent, and Cisco, which gained 4.54 percent.
Technology, AI
Keith Lerner, chief investment officer and chief market strategist at Truist Advisory Services in Atlanta, Georgia, said the market rally should be seen as a “technology and AI surge”.
“Every bull market has a dominant theme, and technology and AI remain this market’s dominant theme,” Lerner told Al Jazeera.
“Technology and communication services were the only two S&P 500 sectors to rise last month, while the other nine declined.”
Wall Street has shrugged off a host of challenges facing the US economy amid hyperscalers’ multibillion-dollar investments in AI.
Despite the energy crunch caused by the US-Israel war on Iran and a sell-off of US government bonds partly driven by ballooning government debt, the market is well on track to record its fourth consecutive year of double-digit returns.
The S&P 500 has risen 14 percent so far in 2026, while the Nasdaq Composite is up 18.78 percent.
“Investors remain bullish on the prospects for AI,” Lochlan Halloway, a senior equity strategist at Morningstar Australia, told Al Jazeera.
“They are betting that the money pouring into data centres will earn a good return, and so far, that belief has outweighed rising interest rates, more expensive oil and a 10-year bond yield above 5 percent,” Halloway said.
“We are positive on AI too,” Halloway added. “But the range of outcomes is wide, and the market is concentrated in a handful of companies, so the outlook for US shares, and by extension global shares, relies on the AI story continuing to deliver.”
Lerner at Truist Advisory said the market rally had the potential to continue through the end of 2026 given historical trends and expectations for strong corporate earnings.
“We do not expect a straight line higher for markets,” Lerner said.
“Still, the fourth quarter of [US] midterm-election years has produced an average gain of 7 percent and has been positive 84 percent of the time since 1950.”
Lerner said that rising interest rates posed the biggest risk to the upward trend.
“Still, on balance, the weight of the evidence suggests this bull market still has more upside potential,” he said.
Despite the rally on Wall Street, Asian stock markets fell on Wednesday, with key indexes in Japan, South Korea, and Hong Kong racking up losses.
The Kospi in Seoul led the sell-off, falling 1.98 percent, while Tokyo’s Nikkei 225 dropped 0.92 percent.
In Hong Kong, the Hang Seng Index was down 0.57 percent shortly before the market’s close.
Oil prices, which have been elevated since the start of the war on Iran, rose on Wednesday as traders weighed the fallout of fighting in Yemen between forces aligned with Yemen’s internationally recognised government and the Iran-aligned Houthis.
Brent crude futures for December delivery stood at $101.16 a barrel as of 07:30 GMT, up 0.58 percent.

Epstein whistleblower’s suicide triggers calls for probe

Epstein whistleblower’s suicide triggers calls for probe
The sudden death of a British whistleblower who helped expose previously undisclosed links between Jeffrey Epstein and US Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick has triggered calls for an independent investigation into how he was treated by UK regulators.
Simon Andriesz, a 57-year-old former managing director at the brokerage BGC Partners, spent years fighting his former employer and Britain’s Financial Conduct Authority (FCA) over allegations of financial misconduct and retaliation against whistleblowers. His family said there is no suggestion of foul play after he died by suspected suicide in Thailand on September 23.
Andriesz had begun raising concerns about alleged accounting irregularities at BGC as early as 2016. He later accused the FCA of failing to properly investigate his disclosures and protect him after his identity became known to the company. The regulator subsequently acknowledged that it had wrongly advised him that he was not entitled to whistleblower protections and apologized.
ANOTHER EPSTEIN WHISTLEBLOWER IS DEAD. WHAT HAPPENED TO SIMON ANDRIESZ? Simon Andriesz, a British banker and whistleblower linked to the Jeffrey Epstein story, has died. He brought information to the FBI and later to Congress involving BGC, Cantor Fitzgerald, and Howard Lutnick, now one of the most powerful officials in the Trump administration. This was not someone making claims online without evidence. Federal regulators acted on information he provided. Andriesz later reviewed Epstein records and found 2018 emails between Lutnick and Epstein discussing a company called ADFIN, in which both men had investment ties. He took his findings to the House Oversight Committee. Congressional investigators later questioned Lutnick behind closed doors about his contact with Epstein. Lutnick denies wrongdoing and denies having the ongoing relationship with Epstein that reports allege. Andriesz is not the first person at the center of the Epstein story to die before the case’s major questions were resolved. Jeffrey Epstein himself died in jail in 2019 while awaiting federal trial; his death was ruled a suicide. Model Ruslana Korshunova, later reported to have visited Epstein’s island, died in 2008; her death was ruled a suicide. Jean-Luc Brunel, an Epstein associate awaiting trial in France, died in jail in 2022; his death was ruled a suicide. Steven Hoffenberg, Epstein’s former business associate, was found dead at home in 2022. Carolyn Andriano, an Epstein victim and Maxwell trial witness, died in 2023; her death was ruled an accidental overdose. Virginia Giuffre, one of Epstein’s most prominent accusers, died in 2025. Her family said she died by suicide; police said the death was not suspicious, though no final public coronial ruling has been issued. Investigative journalist and Andriesz associate John Robertson joins to discuss his legacy, his whistleblowing, and the questions his death leaves behind.
— Ben Swann (@BenSwann_) October 6, 2026
His allegations led to action elsewhere. US regulators, including the Commodity Futures Trading Commission and Securities and Exchange Commission, pursued enforcement cases connected to BGC, while Britain’s tax authority imposed penalties on the firm. Andriesz received a $420,000 whistleblower award from US authorities, although he said his legal, medical and other costs had far exceeded the payout.
More recently, Andriesz emerged as a source of information about Lutnick’s previously undisclosed dealings with Epstein.
He said he uncovered 2018 emails in the released Epstein files showing Lutnick and the convicted sex offender discussing a digital advertising company called Adfin, in which both had invested. Andriesz provided the material to the US House Oversight Committee before Lutnick testified to lawmakers in May. Lutnick told the panel he had not known until 2026 that Epstein was a fellow investor in the venture.
The revelations intensified scrutiny of Lutnick’s previous characterization of his relationship with Epstein. The Commerce Department has rejected accusations that Lutnick misled lawmakers, dismissing them as partisan attacks.
Andriesz’s death has now prompted British lawmakers and whistleblower campaigners to demand an independent examination of the FCA’s conduct.
Labour MP John McDonnell and other members of a cross-party parliamentary group have argued that the regulator should not be allowed to investigate itself. The FCA has instead appointed board member Lea Paterson to review its handling of Andriesz’s case.
The FCA claimed it took information supplied by Andriesz seriously but acknowledged errors in its dealings with him. Before his death, Andriesz had described its response to the alleged wrongdoing he exposed as little more than a regulatory “slap on the wrist.”

Background: An air-raid warning was issued in Kyiv and most of Ukraine's oblasts at 03:09 due to the threat of ballistic missile strikes. A series of explosions rang out in Kyiv almost immediately after a warning was issued about missiles heading towards the city.

Humans may not be as hardwired for violence as we thought
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
03:22:55 UTC
12:22:55 KST

Humans may not be as hardwired for violence as we thought
- Date:
- October 6, 2026
- Source:
- University of Lincoln
- Summary:
- A study comparing 100 primate species, including humans, suggests that everyday aggression and lethal violence did not evolve as part of the same simple behavioral spectrum. Species that frequently fight or show mild aggression are not necessarily more likely to kill rivals, while extreme acts such as infanticide and lethal attacks appear to follow their own evolutionary patterns.
- Share:
New research from the University of Lincoln, UK, is questioning a long standing idea about the evolutionary roots of human violence. The findings suggest that everyday aggression does not necessarily build toward deadly conflict.
Published in the international journal Evolution Letters, the study indicates that mild aggression and lethal violence may have developed through different evolutionary processes. That distinction adds a new layer to the long-running debate over whether violence is an inherent part of human nature.
The work was led by Professor Bonaventura Majolo of the University of Lincoln, alongside Dr. Samantha Wakes and Professor Marcello Ruta.
Aggression May Not Be a Single Trait
Many theories about the origins of violence treat aggression as one broad behavioral characteristic. Under that view, species that frequently engage in everyday fights or disputes might also be expected to show higher levels of lethal violence.
The new research suggests that this assumption may be too simple.
The team examined patterns of aggression across 100 primate species, including humans. Their analysis showed that species with high levels of mild aggression were not necessarily more likely to kill competitors.
Instead, deadly behaviors such as killing adult rivals or infanticide appeared to follow their own evolutionary patterns, largely separate from routine conflict.
Mild Conflict and Lethal Violence Follow Different Paths
The results challenge the idea that violence can be explained as a straightforward evolutionary inheritance.
Rather than forming a single scale that runs from minor disputes to lethal attacks, different types of aggression may arise under different social and evolutionary pressures.
That suggests the link between everyday aggression and extreme violence could be much weaker than some previous theories have proposed.
Bonaventura Majolo, Professor of Social Evolution, said: "Understanding the evolutionary roots of violence is important not only for biology but also for how we think about human behavior.
"Our study shows that the evolution of aggression follows more complex patterns than what earlier models proposed, that it is biologically inaccurate to rank species on the basis of their general propensity for aggression and that we need a more nuanced approach when discussing whether humans are inherently violent."
What 100 Primate Species Reveal
The researchers compared five different forms of aggression, ranging from ordinary conflicts to lethal attacks, using a large dataset spanning many primate species.
They found that different types of lethal aggression were moderately associated with one another. However, those forms of deadly violence showed little connection with mild aggression.
That pattern suggests that the biological and evolutionary mechanisms behind lethal violence are distinct from those that drive everyday conflict.
The findings add new evidence to a longstanding debate in anthropology and evolutionary biology over what shapes human violence. Researchers have long questioned whether violent behavior is rooted mainly in deep evolutionary history or is more strongly influenced by social and cultural forces.
Story Source:
Materials provided by University of Lincoln. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- Bonaventura Majolo, Samantha J Wakes, Marcello Ruta. Origins of violence: evolutionary decoupling between mild and lethal conspecific aggression in primates. Evolution Letters, 2026; 10 (2): 207 DOI: 10.1093/evlett/qrag002

Philadelphia teacher passing as Palestinian raised alarms for Jewish groups before she rose to fame
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
03:18:22 UTC
12:18:22 KST

The first time most of the world heard Hannah Gann’s name was in late September, when the 34-year-old Philadelphia high school teacher and activist confessed to having fabricated a Palestinian and Black identity — with media reports revealing she was Jewish in real life.
But Jason Holtzman, director of Philadelphia’s Jewish Community Relations Council, first heard Gann’s name long before that: in December 2023.
At that time, he recalled to the Jewish Telegraphic Agency, she “made some pretty strident remarks” at a local rally called “Flood Philly For Palestine,” an apparent reference to the “Al-Aqsa Flood,” Hamas’s name for its Oct. 7, 2023, attacks.
In a video from the event shared with JTA, Gann said in reference to children in Gaza, “We owe them to take it to the streets and f–k the police until Palestine is free.”
Gann would appear on the JCRC’s radar several more times before her name hit the news for being “the Palestinian Rachel Dolezal,” when her story — accompanied by Philadelphia Inquirer reporting that she has Jewish family living in Israel — ricocheted across the internet to gain her instant notoriety. (The real-life Dolezal, a white woman who posed as Black for years and held a NAACP leadership role while teaching Africana Education at a Pacific Northwest college, has meanwhile expressed interest in meeting Gann.)
Gann’s revelations have led to the dissolution of the local pro-Palestinian educators group she had helped to lead since 2024. After leaving her Instagram confessions public for more than a week, Gann’s account was deactivated in the last few days.
Yet now that Gann’s background has grabbed headlines, Jewish groups alarmed by her behavior said the real story is being missed.
“It’s just being reported as if she simply is guilty of fraud, that she’s the new Rachel Dolezal,” Holtzman told JTA. “It’s missing part of the story, which is that she’s also an extremist who has spread antisemitic tropes and has brought inflammatory content into the classroom.”
A general view of the School District of Philadelphia offices on December 31, 2015 in Philadelphia City. (Paul Marotta/Getty Images)
A catalog of troubling incidents
In the JCRC’s monitoring of the School District of Philadelphia, Gann’s name pops up often. In 2024 she helped organize a pro-Palestinian “teach-in” project, an unofficial event staged for teachers in the district that the JCRC says “directed educators to materials that erased Israel from maps” and “characterized October 7 as ‘resistance.’”
That year she also posted an Instagram image of a fist rising from the ground holding a firearm, with paragliders — a symbol of the Hamas attacks on Oct. 7, 2023 — visible in the background, one of many social media posts of hers that employed extreme language or imagery around Israel.
A key part of Jewish critics’ charges, that Gann brought her activism into the classroom or into her lesson plans, is harder to pinpoint. But in one screenshot of her whiteboard that she posted to social media, Gann appeared to have planned a lesson on “Black Power & Palestine.” In addition, district personnel who had visited her class in 2024 found that it “contained a ‘Palestine will be free’ poster, a Palestinian flag, a keffiyeh, and a map of Israel filled with a keffiyeh design,” Holtzman claimed.
Gann did not respond to multiple JTA requests for comment.
JCRC officials and a local Jewish activist group had pushed the district to discipline Gann over her conduct before the scandal over her identity broke — including, they said, presenting the superintendent with a full record of Jewish parent concerns this March. But such efforts, they say, fell largely on deaf ears.
“We’ve pointed this out to the school district many times over the years,” Holtzman told JTA. He added that, in the JCRC’s view, Gann’s rally appearances and social media activity were in violation of district codes of conduct governing staff activity that could damage the district’s reputation — with her recent admission of falsifying her ethnic identity potentially violating an ethics code requiring employees to avoid falsification in their personal records.
“And they’ve basically done nothing about it,” he said.
It wasn’t only Holtzman and the JCRC urging the School District of Philadelphia to take some kind of action against Gann. Local Jewish activists filed a federal civil rights complaint against her and fellow activists in the district with whom she had formed a coalition, even entering into mediation with the district in an effort to establish new guidelines around personnel behavior.
The complaint argued, among other points, that Gann’s social media — where she has posted many controversial messages about Israel — should be considered an extension of her classroom.
Yet Gann continued to teach 10th grade at The Workshop School, a public high school in West Philadelphia with a focus on project-based learning. Under pressure from her fellow activists, she recently came clean about her identity.
A surprising confession
“I lied about my family and have been lying for years,” she wrote on Instagram on Yom Kippur. “I have no Palestinian or Tunisian heritage. I am a white woman of significant privilege and wealth. Anyone who supported me was manipulated.”
Gann’s confession took even the Philadelphia Jewish groups who had been tracking her behavior by surprise. They told JTA they had not realized she had been identifying herself as Palestinian, nor that she was actually Jewish. Some of her fellow activists, in their own social media posts, said she had confided to them in the past that she was Jewish — while also continuing to insist she was Palestinian.
While the Philadelphia Inquirer has quoted activists accusing her of having “Israeli settler family,” it was unclear to the Jews who spoke to JTA whether Gann’s Israeli family actually lived in settlements in the occupied West Bank or whether the activists simply refer to all Israelis as settlers. Giving public comment at prior school board meetings, Gann had proclaimed, “I can’t visit my family in Palestine,” and “I have pushed myself to teach through the agony of my family living in a warzone, and only taken one day off this entire school year.”
To some Jews, such parsing is almost beside the point; they see the entire conversation around Gann’s identity as a distraction.
The bigger story, they said, is that she was using her position as a public school educator to push anti-Israel advocacy that included falsehoods about Israel without fear of punishment: a microcosm of what they see as a larger trend of growing pro-Palestinian sentiment among K-12 educators in many school districts and teachers’ unions that has raised alarm among Jewish groups.
A spokesperson for an ad hoc group of Jewish educators and families in the Philadelphia area, who asked to remain anonymous owing to what they viewed as death threats from a member of Gann’s former coalition, told JTA in a statement that the district failed to express interest in Gann until the scandal.
“Harm to the Jewish community is never addressed or rectified” by the district, the representative for the School District of Philadelphia Jewish Family Association (SDP JFA) said in an email.
A spokesperson for the School District of Philadelphia declined to comment on whether the district would be disciplining Gann or if it had communicated with Jewish groups about her behavior prior to last week.
“The District is making support available to the Workshop School staff and students, as needed,” the spokesperson wrote in an email to JTA.
Meanwhile, one of the pro-Palestinian activist groups formerly associated with Gann, Philly Educators for Palestine, announced last week that “after much reflection,” it would dissolve, though “The work continues.” Its parent group, the Racial Justice Organizing Committee, said it would be going on hiatus.
Prior to its announcement, Philly Educators for Palestine had publicly disassociated from Gann and had called for the district to discipline her.
“It’s one of the first times where I think that I really have common ground with the Philadelphia Educators for Palestine,” Holtzman quipped.
Pro-Palestinian demonstrators block roads as they rally in front of Philadelphia City Hall in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania, on September 10, 2024, ahead of the presidential debate between US Vice President and Democratic presidential candidate Kamala Harris and Republican presidential candidate Donald Trump. (Andrew Thomas / AFP via Getty Images)
Civil rights complaint filed
In 2024, SDP JFA filed a Title VI civil rights investigation with the U.S. Department of Education against a group of pro-Palestinian teachers in the district, alleging, among other things, that students had been targeted on the basis of their Jewish identity. Joining the complaint were the JCRC, the Anti-Defamation League and StandWithUs, a pro-Israel advocacy group.
The groups eventually proceeded to mediation with the district, which agreed to institute changes such as drafting a district-wide anti-harassment statement; undergoing an anti-discrimination policy review; and instituting new training for staff, according to a copy of the resolution agreement viewed by JTA. Jewish groups, however, charge that the recommendations were never fully implemented.
The names of the teachers in the federal investigation were redacted in official filings. But according to emails shared with JTA, Gann was one of the named parties in the ADL’s amended complaint.
“Evidence suggests that Ms. Gann is utilizing her actual classroom and social media platforms as a digital extension of her classroom to disseminate antisemitic rhetoric, engage in prohibited political campaigning, and promote extremist ideologies to her students,” a letter sent by SDP JFA this May reads.
Following that email, Gann on Instagram made oblique references to the allegations, calling her unnamed critics “genocide enthusiasts who love to call the School District about what I’m teaching.” She also posted a fake lesson plan from her classroom whiteboard with scheduled “lessons” including “Jesus Was Palestinian.”
The Jewish parents and teachers in SDP JFA say their frustrations with Gann are also informed by an even more antagonistic encounter with Keziah Ridgeway, a fellow teacher and former ally of Gann’s who at one point had joined Gann in holding signs reading “From the river to the sea, Palestine will be free” at a school board meeting.
In 2024, following a controversy around one of Ridgeway’s lesson plans and an SDP JFA campaign against her, Ridgeway, believing herself targeted by Jewish online harassers, posted several of the group members’ names to Instagram.
In posts viewed by JTA, she accompanied this list with another post referencing the phrase, “Ain’t no fun when the rabbit got the gun,” which refers to a sudden reversal in power dynamics. In a third post, Ridgeway asked followers for recommendations for “Black owned [gun emoji] shops in or near Philly.”
The Jewish parents interpreted the series of posts as a threat directed at them, and reported Ridgeway to the district, ultimately leading to her suspension for a year; she has sued the district, alleging anti-Islamic bias. Gann forcefully advocated for Ridgeway’s reinstatement at board meetings.
Following Gann’s recent revelations, Ridgeway, too, disowned her in an Instagram video. “I can no longer be in community with someone who caused so much harm,” Ridgeway wrote on social media.
Ridgeway declined to comment to JTA, citing ongoing litigation.
Even if they feel it’s for the wrong reasons, the members of SDP JFA still want to see action taken against Gann. They are seeking to capitalize on her newfound infamy by renewing their calls to district officials to discipline her and “ameliorate the damage done to the Jewish community.”
Such demands echo communications Jewish parents have sent to the district for the better part of two years. In an email to administrators last year, they sought to sum up their complaints: “Allowing Ms. Gann to remain in a teaching position sends the message that Jewish students’ safety and dignity are not valued — that their teacher can publicly call for their eradication without consequence.”

Three years later, October 7 is still not in the past for Israelis - editorial
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
03:17:30 UTC
12:17:30 KST

Three years ago this morning, Israel woke up to the unimaginable.
Hamas terrorists had breached the Gaza border, overrun communities and army bases, attacked a music festival, murdered some 1,200 people, and dragged 251 hostages into Gaza – all within hours, as the country suffered its deadliest day since its founding.
Three years later, it can be tempting to think of October 7 as a dark moment that belongs to the past. But Israel has never really had the chance to put it there.
The war that began that morning has yet to be fully resolved. Hamas has not been fully disarmed, its future in Gaza remains unsettled, and the questions of who will govern Gaza and what will prevent another October 7 remain unanswered.
Beyond Gaza, Iran and its proxies remain a threat, and Israel continues to confront a region in which the possibility of another war is never far away.
Life after October 7 is more about learning to live with what happened
For much of the country, then, the past three years have been less about moving on from October 7 than about living with its consequences – and with the questions it left behind.
But for many Israelis, October 7 is not simply something they have been living with. They are still living it.
For former hostages, freedom itself remains a daily reminder of what was taken from them. Emily Damari, abducted and wounded from her home in Kfar Aza, has spoken about how captivity changed her relationship with the most ordinary parts of life.
“Today, I open the fridge, and I say thank you,” Damari said. “I drink cold water, and I say thank you.”
Eli Sharabi spent 491 days in captivity after being taken from Kibbutz Be’eri. His wife, Lianne, and their daughters, Noiya and Yahel, were murdered on October 7. His brother Yossi was taken hostage and died in Gaza. After his release, Sharabi said he had learned in captivity “how precious every moment and every choice can be.”
“I choose life,” he said. “I choose to keep living fully, while carrying Lianne, Noiya, Yahel and Yossi with me in everything I do.”
For Hagar Brodutch, who was abducted with her three children and a neighbor’s daughter, returning to life has been a more complicated process than the word “freedom” might suggest. She has described the immense daily struggle, particularly for children, and recently began taking pastry-baking classes as a way to build something new.
“This is about much more than learning how to bake,” she said. “It is about finding a new path, creating something with my own hands, and slowly building a future.”
Then there are those for whom there can be no return to the life they had before October 7.
Michal Negri’s son, Maj. (res.) Roee Negri, 28, was killed fighting Hamas terrorists in Kibbutz Be’eri after spending the day rescuing civilians.
How can Israelis hold their government accountable after October 7?
In an interview with The Jerusalem Post, Negri said that three years had done little to diminish the questions raised that morning. Above all, she wants those responsible for the failures leading up to October 7 to be held accountable through a state commission of inquiry.
“Everyone that was in the government, in any position of management, has to take responsibility and be inquired into, so we will be sure that it will never happen again,” she said.
“How can you be sure that it will not happen again if you don’t inquire and ask questions?”
That question is larger than one bereaved mother.
Israel has changed dramatically since October 7, with the country’s political and defense establishments learning painful lessons about its enemies, its defenses and its own institutions. But lessons must be implemented, failures examined, decisions questioned – and responsibility determined.
Three years later, Israel still has no state commission of inquiry into the worst national disaster in its history.
That means October 7 remains unfinished business. For many Israelis, October 7 is not three years ago – it is both the past and the present.
Ahead of Israel’s national elections, Israelis must remember that our enemies aren’t within, but those seeking to destroy us. May the memory of those killed on October 7, 2023, and since, be blessed.
