Three years later, I still think about the stories we did not tell on October 7- comment
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
03:17:25 UTC
12:17:25 KST

There are families who wrote to me after October 7 and never received an answer. Others heard back too late. They sent photographs, names, and stories of people they loved, hoping we would write about them in The Jerusalem Post. Some of those stories never appeared.
To those families, I am sorry.
I understood what they were asking. After a terrorist attack, part of our job is to call the families and write about the people who were killed. An article can stay with a family for years. Somebody searches a name and finds something about the person: what they did, who loved them, what their friends remember.
After October 7, the numbers kept going up. Hundreds, then more than a thousand. We did not even know who had been killed, who was missing, and who had been kidnapped. Meanwhile, we were covering a war and trying to explain to readers abroad what had happened.
I remember looking through casualty lists and wanting an article about each person. Families were sending messages, press releases were arriving, and we used what we could get to. Sometimes a relative reached a reporter who had time to make the calls. Sometimes a message was buried under hundreds of others.
More accounts of heroism, faith, and horror than we could handle
I don’t know how many more reporters we would have needed just to write those stories. We had more than we could handle, every day. That still bothers me, especially when I think about how much harder it may be to find those families’ stories years from now.
Take Tamar and Yonatan Kedem-Siman Tov and their children Arbel, Shahar and Omer, who were murdered in Nir Oz. Yonatan’s mother, Carol, was murdered there too. The kibbutz’s memorial page recalls that Yonatan, known as Johnny, made sure the field was watered before its kite festival to keep the dust down. I wish we had published more of those details about more people.
When we looked through testimonies for our October 7 cover, there were accounts of heroism, faith, and Hamas’s antisemitism. Others described Arab and Jewish Israelis helping each other. There were so many powerful stories. Naama’s hit us in the stomach. She was 17, from Kfar Aza, and she thought she was going to die. On her grandfather’s prescription, she wrote:
“Naama of a few hours from now, if you are reading this, you are alive.” 0710JDN01
She couldn’t find a pen, so she used eyeliner. We kept coming back to that: her grandfather’s prescription, whatever she had available to write with, and the thought that she might survive to read it. At 17, she had left a message for herself on the small chance that she would get through those hours.
It was also very visual. A prescription is familiar to readers almost anywhere. They can imagine that piece of paper in their own home, belonging to a parent or grandparent. These ordinary details helped explain what we wanted the cover to convey about the everyday people caught in the attack.
Testimonies, hope for a future
There was hope in her sentence, too. She allowed for a future, even one only a few hours away, and lived to describe what she had written. The illustration on our cover is based on that account, recorded by Edut 710.
We chose one testimony for the cover knowing how many others deserved that space. I hope readers who look up Naama’s account will stay with the archive and listen to someone else as well.
Edut 710 began as a volunteer initiative after the attack. Witnesses can tell their accounts at their own pace, including life before October 7 and what followed. Their consent governs publication and use. A detail that a reporter might have left out to meet a deadline can remain available to someone studying the account decades later.
Its Smart Archive, developed with the Hebrew University of Jerusalem, makes the testimonies searchable in Hebrew and English. That gives readers overseas a way to find accounts that never reached an international newspaper.
Organizations doing this work need money to continue. Volunteers need equipment, recordings need editing and translation, and somebody has to look after the material for years. Those considering a donation should think about supporting that work beyond the anniversary, when it will still need doing.
We know from the Holocaust how much depends on what is collected while witnesses are still able to speak. Letters, photographs and recorded accounts allow people born decades later to examine what happened. October 7 is already being denied and distorted. The material we preserve has to be accurate, properly attributed and available for others to examine, with uncertainty acknowledged and errors corrected.
Families have a part in this as well. A relative may be the only person who can identify someone in a photograph or explain why an object mattered. That knowledge can be recorded now, with their consent, rather than left for somebody to guess at later.
Our cover gives space to a teenager who wrote something she thought she might never read. Because her account was recorded, readers can hear her tell it herself. There are many more people we should be listening to.
I keep thinking about the families who wanted us to know who their loved ones had been. I want us to keep making room for those stories in the Post, and to help readers find the accounts being collected elsewhere.
We could not tell every story then. We still have a responsibility to try now.

Oman evacuates injured crew from attacked tanker in Strait of Hormuz
India’s Foreign Ministry says 11 out of 12 injured crew members on board the On Peace are Indian nationals.
Oman’s air force has evacuated 10 crew members of a Panamanian-flagged oil tanker following an attack in the Strait of Hormuz.
The On Peace tanker was struck 9 nautical miles (about 17km) off the Omani port city of Limah on Tuesday, according to the Omani Ministry of Defence. The attack set off a fire on board the vessel.
“The crew members were transported to the Khasab hospital in Musandam governorate and received medical treatment,” the ministry said in a statement on X.
No group has claimed the attack so far.
It comes as security in the Strait of Hormuz continues to deteriorate amid the United States and Israel’s war on Iran.
India’s foreign ministry, the Ministry of External Affairs, said at least 12 of the ship’s 19 crew members were injured when a projectile hit the vessel as it transited the strait. Seventeen of the 19 crew members were Indian nationals, it said, as were 11 of the injured.
“The continuing incidents of attacks on shipping in the region remain a cause of deep concern for India,” the ministry said. “We reiterate our call for an immediate cessation of such attacks in the interests of peace and stability in the region.”
India is one of the largest contributors of sailors to merchant shipping worldwide. The Indian government said in July that at least 10 Indian seafarers had been killed since the US-Israel war on Iran began in late February. Another attack on a cargo ship in the Strait of Hormuz in September also killed an Indian sailor.
Iran effectively closed the waterway after the US-Israel war began on February 28. It has frequently attacked commercial vessels that do not use its designated route in the waterway, and has said it wants to charge ships for passage.
At least seven other incidents involving tankers have been reported in the past week, according to Marisks, a shipping intelligence service.
Despite the attacks, oil exports from the Middle East have risen to pre-war levels in recent weeks.
The seven-day moving average of Middle East crude exports reached 18.3 million barrels per day (bpd) on September 30, compared with about 18 million bpd on average in the 12 months before the war, according to provisional data from Kpler, a data firm.
Still, prices remain high, with Brent crude futures rising to $101.51 a barrel on Tuesday, compared with $72.48 the day before the war began.

'I chose life': Survivors and supporters mark third anniversary of October 7 attacks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

IN BRIEF
- On 7 October 2023, the Hamas-led attack on southern Israel left 1,200 people dead and 251 taken captive.
- Despite rising antisemitism, Australian Jewish figures say their communities continue to "live proudly and openly".
WARNING: This article contains distressing content.
Taken with their children or alone. Held for weeks, months or years. Confined in captors' homes or Hamas tunnels as war raged above them. Israeli former hostages seized on October 7 say they now cherish even the smallest moments of freedom.
Hamas' 7 October 2023 attack was Israel's single deadliest day since the nation was founded in 1948. The militants rampaged through villages, a music festival and army bases, killing 1,200 people and dragging 251 hostages back to Gaza.
They included civilians, soldiers, men, women, children and elderly people, Israelis and foreign nationals. Most were freed in return for Palestinian prisoners during ceasefires between Israel and Hamas, but dozens did not survive.
"Freedom has completely changed the way I see life," said Emily Damari, 30, who was abducted wounded from her home in Kibbutz Kfar Aza — a community roughly 5km east of Gaza — and released in January 2025.
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
Her ordeal taught her not to take anything for granted, she said.
"One day in captivity feels like one week. You want to give up at every moment, but I did not," said Damari, who has recently married and launched a clothing line in Israel.
"Today, I open the fridge and I say thank you. I drink cold water and I say thank you. I am thankful for everything, big things and little things. Gratitude has become central to who I am.
"Being free, at home, surrounded by my family and my people is something I will never take for granted again."
Eli Sharabi, 54, was seized from nearby Kibbutz Be'eri. His British-born wife Lianne and their two daughters Noiya, 16, and Yahel, 13, were slain by the attackers. His brother Yossi was taken hostage and killed in Gaza.
In February 2025, Sharabi was released, appearing emaciated and skeletally thin after 491 days of captivity, which he says included being held in a tunnel, hungry, shackled and beaten.
"I learned in captivity how precious every moment and every choice can be, and I carry that understanding with me now. I choose to look ahead, to keep going and to use the life I have in a meaningful way," said Sharabi.
Since his release, he has helped establish the Shalva Sharabi Family Centre with the disability charity Shalva, to treat families coping with trauma and disabilities — in commemoration of his own family lost.
"I choose life. I choose to keep living fully, while carrying Lianne, Noiya, Yahel and Yossi with me in everything I do."
His wife and daughters believed deeply in caring for others, he said.
"Their kindness and care for others will continue. Families will walk through these doors and receive help, care and hope in a place that carries their name. That gives me strength and makes me very proud."
'The daily struggle is immense'
Hagar Brodutch was seized from Kfar Aza with her three children and her neighbour's daughter, who fled to their house after her parents were killed. They were freed in a brief truce in November 2023.
Life after captivity, she said, can be far more complicated than the way it is sometimes portrayed.
"The daily struggle is immense, especially for children. I believe it will take many more years before captivity becomes just a shadow that walks alongside us, rather than something that defines who we are," said Brodutch.
Recently, Brodutch, 43, started taking pastry-baking classes, a passion she has long had.
"This is about much more than learning how to bake. It is about finding a new path, creating something with my own hands, and slowly building a future," she said.
"During my time in Hamas captivity, I began to understand that if I were released, returning to my previous life and working in management might no longer be possible.
"I chose pastry as a form of therapy, but also as a way to create something new for myself, with the hope that one day it could become my profession."
Kfar Aza was one of the hardest-hit communities in Hamas' attack.
Aviva Siegel, 65, was kidnapped with her husband Keith. She was released in November 2023, but Keith was held until February 2025.
Aviva joined the hostage release campaign movement in Israel while her husband was still being held.
Their reunion and her children and grandchildren, and even strangers she meets, give her strength every day, she says.
"I feel that I'm not alone and that there's so much love in this world and we need to keep it with both our hands," she said. "I feel very, very lucky to be alive."
Crowds mark October 7 anniversary at Bondi Beach
At home, hundreds of people have gathered at Bondi Beach to mark the third anniversary of the October 7 attacks.
Following prayers at a service at the Bondi Pavilion, Israel's ambassador to Australia, Hillel Newman, remembered the moment he learned of the attack.
He said his brother-in-law told him: "Everything is changing ... we're in a war".
"Young Israelis went out to dance at the Nova Music Festival and never came home.
"Israelis who believed in peace ... they were all murdered just for being Jews and Israelis."
The attack has since taken on a more visceral and immediate fear after the carnage on Bondi Beach.
He said he believes there was a "direct line" between the attack on October 7 and the Bondi Beach attack — where 15 people were gunned down, including a 10-year-old girl and an elderly Holocaust survivor.
The massacre took place on the north side of Bondi Beach, during a celebration marking the first day of Hanukkah on 14 December 2025.
NSW Opposition leader Kelly Sloane said the "evil and hate of October 7" had come "closer to home".
"Our community has woken up again and again to graffiti, vandalism, firebombings," she said.
Sloane said she would "never leave the side" of the Jewish community and the community of Bondi following last year's attack.
"As terrible as it was, I am glad to be there ... with our Bondi community, our Jewish community."
Zionist Federation of Australia president Jeremy Leibler said the brutal violence in Israel had an immense impact on Australian Jews that was solidified after the Bondi massacre.
"October 7 is a day of mourning for the more than 1,200 innocent people murdered when Hamas-led terrorists invaded Israel, massacring families in their homes, hunting down young people at a music festival ... and dragging men, women, children and the elderly into Gaza as hostages," he said.
"Terror and antisemitism will not define Jewish life in Australia. We will continue to live proudly and openly as Jews, and nothing these groups do will weaken the bond between Australian Jewry, Australia and Israel."
Some pro-Palestinian supporters have drawn attention to the ensuing escalation of Israel's war on Gaza, which has killed more than 74,000 people and wounded 175,000, according to the local health ministry.
One of the groups organising a vigil at Sydney's Town Hall is Jews against Occupation, representing dissident Jewish voices, with the event entitled "Don't let Israel steal the date."
It has been widely condemned as highly inflammatory and insensitive by political leaders, including NSW Premier Chris Minns.

Why comparing strikes on bridges in Kyiv with the Crimean Bridge is misleading: an explanation by the Center for Countering Disinformation
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
06:15:20 EEST
12:15:20 KST

Why comparing strikes on bridges in Kyiv with the Crimean Bridge is misleading: an explanation by the Center for Countering Disinformation
Kyiv • UNN
The Center for Countering Disinformation called the comparison of strikes on the Crimean Bridge and Kyiv’s bridges manipulative. The Crimean Bridge is a military logistics target, while Kyiv’s bridges are civilian infrastructure.
Manipulative posts are being recorded in the international and Ukrainian information spaces, in which Russian strikes on bridges in Kyiv are contrasted with Ukrainian strikes on the Crimean Bridge and other Russian infrastructure facilities. This is reported by the Center for Countering Disinformation of the National Security and Defense Council of Ukraine (CCD), UNN reports.
Details
It is noted that the narrative of "double standards" is being promoted: Ukraine and the West allegedly approved attacks on "Russian civilian infrastructure," while condemnation of Russian strikes is portrayed as hypocrisy.
Such comparisons are a classic manipulation based on distorting the norms of international humanitarian law and ignoring the military-operational context
Crimea under attack: what the 2026 holiday season was like for Russians04.09.26, 14:01 • 84191 view
It is noted that the Crimean Bridge is not merely a structure, but an illegally constructed facility in the occupied territory of Ukraine, which russia uses as a key transport artery for transferring weapons, ammunition, and occupation forces to the front. Thus, under Article 52 of Additional Protocol I to the Geneva Conventions, an object is considered a military objective if it makes an effective contribution to military action and its neutralization offers a definite military advantage. At the same time, disabling the enemy's military logistics routes as part of self-defense (Article 51 of the UN Charter) is an entirely legitimate military tactic.
By contrast, the bridges in Kyiv are civilian infrastructure in a rear-area city hundreds of kilometers from the line of contact. They ensure the functioning of a city with a population of several million, the movement of emergency services, and civilian transport. Strikes on the capital's bridges have no direct impact on the situation on the battlefield, but are aimed at intimidating the city's civilian population and creating a humanitarian collapse. This directly violates the principle of proportionality stipulated by international law concerning the laws of war
The agency emphasizes that the Russian army itself systematically destroys bridge crossings in combat zones (Sievierodonetsk, Kupiansk, Donetsk region) to impede the actions of the Ukrainian Defense Forces, recognizing them as military objectives.
"The Kremlin's attempts to portray itself as a "victim" over the Kerch Bridge are manipulation intended to justify its own war crimes. ... It is important to distinguish between legitimate actions to neutralize the occupiers' logistics and deliberate terror against Ukraine's civilian infrastructure," the CCD concludes.
Reminder
In July, Commander of the Unmanned Systems Forces of the Armed Forces of Ukraine Robert "Madyar" Brovdi stated that the Crimean Bridge was not being targeted so that collaborators and Russians could leave the peninsula.

Pakistan’s Solar Revolution is Reshaping its Power Sector
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
03:14:00 UTC
12:14:00 KST

Pakistan’s solar power generation has surpassed 20 percent of the country’s total electricity production. While this transition toward clean energy is a positive development, it is the outcome of an unplanned shift in the country’s energy landscape.
According to the World Nuclear Industry Status Report (WNISR) 2026, solar generation in Pakistan reached an estimated 36.3 terawatt-hours (TWh) in 2025. This accounts for roughly 21.6 percent of Pakistan’s total electricity generation after growing about 85 percent in a single year.
The WNISR report offers important background on this transformation. In Pakistan, solar-led power generation has not only expanded rapidly in recent years but has also overtaken nuclear power generation for the first time. The report further notes that Pakistan installed roughly twice as much solar capacity in five years as France managed in a decade.
Moreover, Pakistan imported more than 58 gigawatts (GW) of solar panels from China between the beginning of 2017 and mid-2026. Of this, around 40 GW arrived in just two and a half years, from 2024 to mid-2026. These imports over such a short period illustrate how quickly Chinese solar manufacturing found a major market in Pakistan amid falling panel prices and surging domestic electricity costs.
The surge has made Pakistan the second-largest single-country import market for Chinese solar panels, just behind the Netherlands. This data underscores the scale and speed of the change underway in the country.
Besides, the solar generation figures coming out of Pakistan are likely underestimations for several reasons.
A substantial amount of privately installed solar capacity across the country remains unregistered and does not pass through the state-controlled grid. In many cases, much of this capacity is installed on rooftops and industrial sites, where households and businesses generate and store power for their own use without becoming part of the national grid. This trend has largely been driven by high electricity tariffs, frequent load-shedding and the falling cost of Chinese solar panels. All of this has created a strong incentive for consumers to bypass the national grid system altogether.
While this shift is likely reducing the demand for grid-supplied electricity, it is impacting Pakistan’s power sector challenges and the country’s mounting capacity-related debt significantly.
For instance, as high-usage households, businesses, and industrial consumers leave the national grid, power distribution companies and remaining customers are left to shoulder a heavier burden of fixed costs. This essentially means that capacity payments for underutilized power plants continue in Pakistan. At the same time, overall electricity consumption recorded by distribution companies has declined across the country.
This situation has put coal-based power agreements reached by Pakistan previously with local and international firms under intense scrutiny. While solar adoption is surging across the country, Pakistan remains committed to long-term contracts that require heavy fixed payments to coal plant operators even if their plants remain idle or operate well below capacity. As a result, long-standing power purchase commitments have become a major financial burden for Pakistanis, even as they grapple with pressures due to the current economic strains facing the country.
It is important to note that Pakistan’s 23 loss-making state-owned enterprises accumulated roughly $1.24 billion in losses in the first half of Financial Year 2026. This is roughly equivalent to around $10 million per working day. At the same time, total state-owned enterprises’ debt, excluding sovereign guarantees, rose 14 percent to approximately $36.5 billion.
In this context, the rapid growth of solar power generation is not only a story of clean energy access and cost savings for those who can afford panels, but it is also accelerating financial stress within the formal power sector and complicating efforts to manage circular debt and capacity obligations of the Pakistani state.
For example, for ordinary consumers who remain fully dependent on the national grid, costs will likely continue to rise as the customer base continues to shrink. Meanwhile, for the energy market as a whole, the transition raises fundamental questions about planning, tariff design and the future role of large-scale coal and nuclear power in a system increasingly shaped by solar power generation.
That said, Pakistan’s energy future will depend on better planning and reform by the state. Policymakers should reorganize and renegotiate power-sector contracts and grid management to fit the new reality shaped by widespread solar power generation.
Without proactive reforms, the gap between solar power consumers and the struggling national grid will only continue to widen and strain the economy.

Trump orders firing squad for gunman who killed 13 people at Fort Hood, Texas
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
03:01:01 UTC
12:01:01 KST

US President Donald Trump has ordered the use of a firing squad to execute the former US Army psychiatrist who killed 13 people at Fort Hood, Texas, in a 2009 shooting spree the gunman later described as retaliation for US wars in the Muslim world, the Pentagon said.
Putting former US Army Major Nidal Hasan to death by Army firing squad was approved by Trump at the recommendation of Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, Pentagon spokesperson Sean Parnell said on X/Twitter on Monday.
Parnell noted that Hasan shouted "Allahu Akbar" — God is greatest in Arabic — during the attack, which killed 12 unarmed active-duty soldiers and a retired serviceman, and wounded 32 others.
Acting US Army Secretary Adam Telle said on X on Tuesday that the execution by firing squad will take place on December 3 at Fort Hood, Texas.
Death by firing squad was one of several forms of capital punishment the Trump administration recently added to permissible forms of execution for the gravest of federal crimes, along with electrocution and gas asphyxiation.
The number of federal execution options was expanded in part because of increasing difficulties in obtaining drugs for lethal injections, which have also proved challenging to carry out for other reasons at times.
Plans by the state of Tennessee to execute a woman for the first time in more than 200 years went awry last week when prison personnel botched an attempt to administer a lethal injection, leaving the death-row inmate, Christa Pike, alive but hospitalized.
Her lawyers said on Tuesday she regained consciousness. "Her prognosis remains unclear, but at a minimum we expect a long recovery," the lawyers said on Tuesday.
Pike's lawyers had previously urged the Tennessee Department of Correction to consider an alternative to lethal injection, such as hanging or firing squad, in anticipation of the trouble executioners faced in establishing a sound intravenous line.
Hasan found guilty of 45 counts of premeditated murder, attempted premeditated murder
A military jury sentenced Hasan to death in August 2013, after finding him guilty of 45 counts of premeditated murder and attempted premeditated murder for opening fire with a laser-sighted handgun in a medical facility at the sprawling central Texas military base.
The shooting came weeks before Hasan, now 56, was scheduled to be deployed to Afghanistan. He was left partially paralyzed and confined to a wheelchair after being shot by police during his arrest.
In a statement responding to Trump's decision, the group Death Penalty Action, which opposes capital punishment, said: "There is nothing Donald Trump loves more than the power to kill."
Military executions are rare, and under the Uniform Code of Military Justice, a death sentence imposed by court-martial may not be carried out "until approved by the president."
If Hasan is put to death, it would mark the first military execution since 1961, the group said. According to the Death Penalty Information Center, the 1961 execution was carried out by hanging. The apparent last known execution by a US military firing squad was one carried out "by musketry" in November 1945, the center reported.
At least five states have firing squads on the books, according to the Death Penalty Information Center. In 2025, South Carolina carried out the first such execution in the United States in 15 years.

Mali troops re-enter strategic northern town in years-long fight against insurgents

A separatist movement in northern Mali announced on Tuesday it was carrying out "a controlled withdrawal" from a strategic town in the north, a symbolic boost to Mali's army and its Russian backers in their years-long fight against insurgents including al Qaeda-linked jihadists.
Malian troops were "reinforcing their presence" in the town by Tuesday night, a government statement said, adding that this would allow for "the gradual return of public administration and basic social services."
The Azawad Liberation Front (FLA) took control of Kidal town six months ago in nationwide attacks that also killed Mali's defense minister. It had joined forces in those attacks with the regional al Qaeda affiliate, Jama'at Nusrat al-Islam wal-Muslimin, known as JNIM, posing the biggest test yet to Mali's military leaders who seized power in coups in 2020 and 2021.
The FLA's decision to leave Kidal came in response to airstrikes by Mali's military backed by Russian fighters, the FLA said in a statement.
"The FLA specifies that this is a temporary operational measure, also intended to preserve its human and logistical capabilities intact. This methodical withdrawal from the area took place without any direct combat having yet pitted its forces against the enemy," the statement said.
Mali has leaned on Russian security support for years, first from the Wagner mercenary group and then from the paramilitary group Africa Corps, which is made up of many former Wagner fighters.
'Symbolic' but not decisive victory, analyst says
Earlier on Tuesday, Mali's military said it had launched large-scale air and ground operations in the region of Kidal.
The goals of the operations included tracking down and neutralizing armed groups operating in the area, destroying their supply networks and restoring "lasting security" and free movement for people and goods, a Malian military statement said.
Pro-government fighters, including Russian fighters, re-entered Kidal on Tuesday afternoon, a security source said.
Malian forces and Wagner fighters retook Kidal from insurgents in November 2023, the most concrete gain from their partnership — only to lose it during the attacks in April.
"A successful recapture... affirms the military-led government's authority and boosts the army's morale, particularly after several high-profile setbacks both in the north and the central regions in recent weeks," said Beverly Ochieng, associate director of Control Risks.
"This is also an opportunity for Africa Corps to reprise its role as the Malian government's security guarantor after appearing to lose significant ground, including in Kidal, since April."
But the change of control in Kidal is still largely "symbolic" and not "decisive" in Mali's campaign against insurgent groups, Ochieng added.
A source close to the FLA leadership told Reuters that the aerial operations by Malian and Russian forces began three days ago.
The source played down the significance of the FLA's withdrawal, saying it was a measure to protect lives and equipment.
"For us, war is not a race against the clock," the source said.

'Looking at Australia': Sidney Nolan in six definitive paintings
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
03:00:00 UTC
12:00:00 KST

Six Sidney Nolan artworks to see at Nolan: Origins at the Art Gallery of New South Wales
Australian artist Sidney Nolan was interested in the stories and myths we tell about ourselves, from the life of bushranger Ned Kelly to the trials of saints.
"Sidney Nolan has to be one of our most creative and inventive painters that emerged out of the period of war and the decades following," says Denise Mimmocchi, senior curator of Australian art at the Art Gallery of New South Wales (AGNSW).
"He posed questions about place, our identity, and our individual search for meaning within the continent and landscapes of Australia."
Born in 1917, the modernist artist would prove to be one of Australia's most influential and prolific, initially as part of the infamous Heide Circle alongside Albert Tucker, Arthur Boyd and Joy Hester. He would go on to be acquired by the likes of the Museum of Modern Art in New York and the Tate Modern in London.
Curated by Mimmocchi, AGNSW's new exhibition Nolan: Origins charts the artist's career from 1939 until he moved to London in 1953. It features places like St Kilda and central Australia — environments that would continue to spark his imagination throughout his life.
"I wanted to look at what inspired him," Mimmocchi says. "And what we're looking at really is Australia."
Kiata
In 1943, during WWII, Nolan — who had been conscripted in 1942 — was stationed at Nhill, guarding Australia's food reserves.
The job left him with a lot of time to paint. One work he made during this period is this landscape of the nearby town Kiata, in western Victoria.
"Kiata is really a breakthrough moment," Mimmocchi says. "This is when the abstract artist also becomes a landscape painter."
As he figured out how to capture the vastness he encountered, Nolan came to appreciate an earlier generation of Australian artists, the Impressionists, like Arthur Streeton, Tom Roberts and Charles Conder, who would often paint outdoors.
"He looks to and echoes in his own way the idea of painting the Australian light and landscape, but he does it through his own modern sensibility," Mimmocchi says.
A year later, in 1944, when he found out he was going to be sent to fight in Papua New Guinea, Nolan deserted the army.
In 1948, he received an amnesty for deserters and was formally discharged.
Fire, Palais de Danse, St Kilda
When Nolan was nine and growing up in Melbourne's St Kilda, the Palais de Danse burned down. It was an event that became etched in the artist's memory.
He painted the scene 20 years later, in 1945, while living between his studio in Parkville, Melbourne, and Heide on the city's outskirts, in the home of philanthropists Sunday and John Reed.
There, Nolan had an affair with Sunday, before marrying John's sister, Cynthia, a writer, in 1948.
"When he's living in hiding, he starts to paint with greater intensity these memories of his childhood in St Kilda," Mimmocchi says.
"He goes up in scale as well. In that expansion comes this incredible impact of the energy contained within them."
She describes that energy as "frenetic", with the human figures in the painting appearing almost like ants.
"You get this sense of palpitating movement," Mimmocchi explains. "It's wonderful and vibrant but at the same time, for me, a little tense. There's something deeply anxious about them."
Mimmocchi boils that anxiety down to Nolan viewing these moments from his childhood through the lens of the "wartime present".
Ned Kelly
While living at Heide, Nolan spent a year, starting in 1946, creating a series of 27 paintings of bushranger Ned Kelly.
One inspiration for the series came from the stories Nolan's grandfather told him when he was a child, of being part of the search for the Kelly gang. But it also stemmed from his own desertion from the army.
"He's a bit of an outlaw in his mind himself," Mimmocchi says.
"He saw the Kelly figure as a rebel poet. He saw him and his family as the victims of great injustice.
"At the same time, coming out of that experience of war, where he was trained to use the 'utmost violence', the idea of brutality was at the forefront of his mind."
To create the series, Nolan pored over newspaper clippings and the 1881 Royal Commission report into the Victorian police, and visited Glenrowan, the site of Kelly's final shoot-out with police in 1880.
"He's interested in painting the landscape and the stories within it; how history becomes legend becomes mythology," Mimmocchi says.
That's perhaps exemplified by the view through the letterbox-style slit in Kelly's helmet.
"We view the landscape through the Kelly helmet," Mimmocchi says. "It's almost as if Nolan is saying our experiences of place are shaped or framed by these stories, by these figures."
The Ned Kelly series and the now-iconic blocky shape of Kelly's helmet also marked a turning point in Nolan's practice.
"He said he was an abstract painter and then he became a painter of the landscape, and this brought the two together," Mimmocchi says.
Quilting the armour
This 1947 painting from the Ned Kelly series depicts a moment of tenderness between the bushranger and his sister Margaret, where she stitched padding into his helmet.
"It's quite a beautiful and powerful image of this woman creating padding for Kelly in this foreboding landscape, perhaps in anticipation of the violence which is to come," Mimmocchi says.
"It sits so distinctly from a lot of the other paintings, which are about the guns, the violence, the bloodshed.
"It says something about a female notion of creativity or the importance of women in the Ned Kelly story."
Also hidden in the painting is a reference to Nolan's desertion from the army, living under the alias Robin Murray. On a fencepost sits a red robin.
The Ned Kelly series fell flat when it was first exhibited in Melbourne in 1948, but the Reeds were determined the paintings would find an audience, sending them to Paris and Rome.
In Paris in 1949, museum director Jean Cassou described them as "the work of a true poet and true painter".
"It wasn't until they'd had this life overseas that they came back to Australia and started to gain the recognition they deserve," Mimmocchi says.
Central Australia
In 1949, Nolan spent months travelling through central Australia, Arnhem Land and the Kimberley in Western Australia, with his wife, Cynthia, and adopted daughter Jinx.
The artist would join aviator Eddie Connellan as he delivered mail to remote communities. The view from these flights inspired this 1950 painting.
"He was deeply inspired by this vision of a country, which was so vast, so seemingly infinite, but had this vital energy in the movement and passages of the landscape," Mimmocchi says.
"It was painted at a time when city Australians commonly referred to the centre of Australia as its dead heart. Nolan encounters and paints a country that couldn't be more different to that."
The vivid red of the work comes from Nolan's use of Ripolin, a quick-drying enamel paint he first used in the early 40s.
"That gave him a saturated colour and the ability to paint the intense, clarified light of the desert," Mimmocchi says.
In 1950, in a letter to fellow artist Albert Tucker, Nolan wrote that Indigenous peoples "show you that the country is a gentle, dreaming one; the barrenness and harshness is all in our European eyes".
Mimmocchi explains: "First Nations connection to Country shaped his vision."
Temptation of St Anthony
In 1950, Nolan travelled to Europe for the first time, to Italy, Spain, Greece and the UK, where he was inspired by Christian paintings.
When he returned to Sydney, he started taking biblical scenes and imposing them onto the unforgiving Australian landscape.
In Temptation of St Anthony, from 1952, he depicted the story of early Christian monk Anthony the Great's pilgrimage through the Egyptian desert, where he was tormented by demons and faced a series of temptations.
In Nolan's telling, those demons and temptations included a goanna, a giant dragonfly and an angel with horns.
"He was deeply interested in the stories that shape us," Mimmocchi says. "It was the idea of myth. He saw the stories of the Bible as another myth that could be painted in relation to the landscape.
"In these biblical works, he's marrying this sense of the ancientness of the stories of Europe with the ancientness and the vital presence of the Australian landscape."
For the curator, Temptation of St Anthony is "pure Nolan".
"He's able to bring the action of this biblical story into the Australian desert so evocatively," she says.
Nolan: Origins is at Art Gallery of New South Wales, Sydney, until February 7.

'Congress loses even on ballot papers': Himanta hails NDA's Silchar civic polls victory
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
02:58:34 UTC
11:58:34 KST

BJP-led NDA sweeps first Silchar civic polls with 34 seats
NEW DELHI: The ruling BJP-led NDA won the first elections to the Silchar Municipal Corporation on Tuesday, securing 34 of the 42 seats.Reacting to the result, Assam Chief Minister Himanta Biswa Sarma said Congress performs poorly even when elections are held through paper ballots.“See, Congress loses even on paper ballots. In fact, Congress loses even more on paper ballots. That’s why in EVMs, sometimes people go and press NOTA or get panicked seeing the machine and vote in the wrong place. But people are well-practiced in voting on paper ballots. So whenever voting happens on paper ballots, Congress loses even more,” Sarma said.
Polling for the 40 wards was held on October 3, while BJP candidates Bijendra Prasad Singh and Bhakti Sen Talukdar were elected unopposed from wards 9 and 20, respectively. Counting of votes began at 8 am, with ballot papers used in the elections.Sarma said the verdict reflected the people's faith in Prime Minister Narendra Modi's leadership and his vision for urban governance under the Viksit Bharat initiative."Another day, another win for @BJP4Assam! The people of Silchar have given us a thumping majority in the Silchar Municipal Corporation elections, held through BALLOT PAPER," Sarma said in a post on X.
He thanked the people of Silchar for the “resounding mandate” and reiterated his government's commitment to making the city “one of Assam's foremost cities”.Assam BJP president Dilip Saikia said the results showed that Congress had failed to win public support even in an election conducted through ballot papers."The Congress always complains about EVM tampering, but this election was held through ballot papers, and they are nowhere," he told reporters.The BJP won 32 seats, while its ally Asom Gana Parishad (AGP) secured two. The Congress won two seats and Independents six, officials said. The BJP has sought recounting in two wards, 29 and 30, where an Independent candidate and a Congress candidate, respectively, emerged victorious. A decision on the demand is yet to be taken, they said.
A total of 133 candidates contested the elections. The BJP fielded candidates in 38 wards, the AGP in four and the Congress in 38, while 52 Independents and one CPI(M) candidate were also in the fray.The Silchar Municipal Board was upgraded to a 42-ward municipal corporation in 2022 and became operational in June 2025. Silchar, the principal city of the Barak Valley, had remained without an elected civic body for six years.Poor road conditions, inadequate drainage, waterlogging, erratic power supply and irregular drinking water supply were among the key issues raised during the campaign.

One last masterclass as Messi bids Argentina adieu in tears after dazzling final display
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
02:54:38 UTC
11:54:38 KST

Lionel Messi has delivered one last masterclass in blue and white as Argentina's captain brought the curtain down on his extraordinary 21-year international career by scoring one goal and setting up two others in a 3-0 friendly win over Benin.
The 39-year-old's final bow before more than 85,000 fans at a packed Monumental Stadium on Tuesday was less about football and more a national celebration of Messi's service to the national team.
Landmarks across the capital glowed in the team's iconic sky blue and white colours, while fireworks lit up the skies above the heaving stadium as fans poured their hearts into a rendition of Argentina's national anthem.
Messi's family watched proudly from the stands alongside some of Argentina's World Cup winners of 1978, 1986 and 2022.
Hours earlier, a massive No. 10 shirt emblazoned with "Gracias" was unfurled at the National Flag Memorial in Rosario, Messi's hometown.
As the team bus travelled from the training centre bearing his name, Messi wiped away tears as thousands lined the route.
When the teams took the pitch, Benin's captain looked lost for words as he handed Messi a gift and letter during the pre-match handshake.
"Messi, Messi" chants
After a goalless first half, Messi supplied the assist for Nicolas Otamendi to tap home Argentina's opener.
Otamendi shared 17 years with Messi in the national team, including four World Cups, and was also ending his international career.
Messi then set up Nico Paz, one of the players seen as a potential successor for Argentina's No. 10 shirt, to score the second goal.
In a fairy-tale ending, Messi converted a penalty for 3-0, his 126th international goal, prompting another round of "Messi, Messi" chants from the crowd.
At the final whistle, teammates, opponents and the referee gathered around Messi for embraces before a drone show lit up the sky to mark the end of his magnificent Argentina career.
Messi leaves as the country's most-capped player (208) and record scorer, having transformed years of frustration on the international stage into a story of World Cup and Copa America triumphs.
For years, Argentina asked Messi to deliver. On Tuesday, it simply came to say 'Thank You'.

EU toughens China stance ahead of Šefčovič’s Beijing visit
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
02:51:22 UTC
11:51:22 KST

Maroš Šefčovič speaks with reporters during the second day of the G20 Trade Ministerial in Wisconsin, U.S. on Oct. 1, 2026. | Kamil Krzaczynski/AFP via Getty Images
STRASBOURG — Policymakers across the political spectrum are coalescing around a stronger approach to the European Union's relationship with China — one that goes beyond trade measures.
A report from the Committee on Foreign Affairs on the EU-China political relationship paints China not just as an economic foe but also a geopolitical one that is undercutting European security.
The European Parliament will vote on the report on Wednesday, just in time for Trade Commissioner Maroš Šefčovič's trip to Beijing on Thursday, where he will meet with Chinese Commerce Minister Wang Wentao.
Advertisement
"I want him to go there with the strongest possible mandate from this house," Hilde Vautmans, the report's author, said in a debate on Tuesday evening. "Europe has economic power. It’s time to use it."
The remarks echo those made by German Chancellor Friedrich Merz and French President Emmanuel Macron in a joint letter earlier this week, advocating that the European Commission be handed more powers to restrict or even cut off imports from countries that create "severe and systematic distortions" in the EU.
While some MEPs hailed the French-German joint approach as proof of a unified position, Polish MEP Mariusz Kamiński from the European Conservatives and Reformists said creating "pragmatic economic ties is not only cynical, but irresponsible or outright stupid."
China is a "communist dictatorship that poses a threat to the free world," he continued.
He's not alone in that sentiment, as for many lawmakers, simply tackling Chinese overcapacity isn't enough. The Commission needs to address China's growing human rights abuses, escalations in the Taiwan Strait, and its role in the war in Ukraine, they said.
"We have to recognize that China is behaving in a way that is endangering our interests. Not just on trade but on security and defense," said Spanish MEP Nicolás Pascual de la Parte from the center-right European People's Party. "The human rights situation has not improved, but it has disappeared from our agenda in recent years."
Advertisement
The lawmakers called out Beijing's treatment of the Uyghur minority group in Xinjiang, which China has systemically placed in camps and prisons and persecuted. The Parliament stopped just short of calling the action a genocide in a 2024 resolution, saying it amounts "to crimes against humanity."
Others like the EPP's Michael Gahler called out Beijing's encroachment on the island of Taiwan, which China claims as its own territory. China's role in propping up the Russian economy while it fights Ukraine also received plenty of airtime.
The issues diverged, but the MEPs used Tuesday's debate to call out the EU's unequal relationship with China — a sign that Vautmans says is proof the bloc is coming to a unified stance toward the country.
"This is no longer just the position of the European Parliament or of one political group," Vautmans said after the debate. "There is a growing recognition that Europe needs a more coherent China policy: open to dialogue and cooperation, but much more willing to defend its interests when necessary."

Iran should reduce uranium enrichment capacity to end war with US — vice president
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
02:50:11 UTC
11:50:11 KST

WASHINGTON, October 7. /TASS/. Iranian authorities should significantly reduce their uranium enrichment capacity in order to end the war with the United States, US Vice President JD Vance said in an interview with Reuters.
"If you don’t want a nuclear weapon, then why do you need 60% enriched fuel? And if you want to show commitment to not building a nuclear weapon, don’t build highly enriched fuel. That’s a very basic threshold issue [when ending the conflict]," Vance said. "I think if they want to show a commitment to not building a nuclear weapon, they would do something meaningful on their enrichment capacity."
He said the United States remained open to reaching an agreement but would demand concrete concessions from Iran in the nuclear sphere. "We’re not going to trade words for actions," the vice president said. In his view, the situation is complicated by the fact that Washington is unsure who makes decisions in Tehran. Vance said the United States was holding talks with Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian and Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi. However, he claimed, it was unclear how much influence they wield within Iran’s power structure. "One of the things we picked up on is it’s not totally clear how their country makes decisions," Vance said.
The United States and Israel launched a war against Iran on February 28. In June, Washington and Tehran signed a memorandum of understanding envisaging an immediate ceasefire on all fronts, including in Lebanon. However, the United States resumed large-scale attacks on Iran overnight to July 8, having accused it of breaching the existing agreements in what concerned the Strait of Hormuz, a global chokepoint for approximately 25% of oil and some 20% of LNG supplies.
The Donald Trump administration recently signaled an end to any large-scale use of force against Iran and a transition to putting economic pressure on the Islamic Republic through sanctions instead.

French FM denounces 'poison' of anti-Semitism as Israel marks October 7 attacks anniversary
Israelis on Wednesday took part in commemorations for the victims of Hamas's October 7, 2023 attacks, which killed 1,200 people and saw 251 hostages taken. French Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot denounced the "poison of anti-Semitism" as he attended a memorial ceremony at the site of the Nova music festival massacre. Read about the day’s events as they unfolded on our liveblog.
(This live page is no longer being updated.)
UN peacekeeping force says shots fired at post on Israel-Lebanon border
The United Nations Interim Force in Lebanon says one of its posts was targeted earlier today near the border with Israel by small-arms fire, but there were no casualties.
"This morning, several rounds of small arms fire impacted a UNIFIL position near Kfar Shouba along the Blue Line in Sector East," the UN force said in a statement, referring to the de facto border between Israel and Lebanon.
The blue helmets described the shooting as "unacceptable".
"Such deliberate attacks gravely endanger the lives of peacekeepers," it said, adding that it was investigating the incident.
Death toll in Gaza strikes rises to five
The death toll from today's strikes in Gaza has risen to five, according to hospital sources.
Al-Shifa Hospital, located in Gaza City, reported two deaths at dawn following an Israeli strike in Jabalia, in the north of the territory.
The Gaza Civil Defence, a first-aid organisation, identified one of the victims as one of its volunteers, aged 23.
In Khan Younis, in the south of the territory, Nasser Hospital reported three further deaths in Israeli strikes carried out in several parts of the city.
How is Israel's economy faring after three years of war?
Israel’s tech sector – specifically its defence startups – has played a big part in spurring economic growth in the country after a small dip in the wake of the October 7 attacks three years ago.
But challenges, notably demographic ones, are on the horizon.
France rejects 'poison' of anti-Semitism, says French FM at Nova site
Speaking at the site of Nova music festival massacre, French Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot said France rejects "anti-Semitism and hatred of others".
"At a time when our societies are facing the resurgence of unchecked anti-Semitism, we will not allow this poison to spread within the Republic. For everything in the very soul of France rejects anti-Semitism and hatred of others," the minister said in Re’im, in southern Israel.
He described the October 7 attack as an "abominable assault", which "wounded the Israeli people and all Jews to the core" and caused "a trauma that must not be downplayed".
Yemen's Iran-backed Houthis claim new attacks on Saudi Arabia
Earlier today, Iran-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen claimed new attacks on airports and military facilities in neighbouring Saudi Arabia, pulling the kingdom deeper into the latest front in the Iran war,.
As the Saudi capital is targeted again, new cage-like fences have been erected this week around fuel tanks and other equipment of the Saudi state-run Aramco oil company near the Riyadh airport, AP reports.
The Houthis’ military spokesperson, Brig. Gen. Yahya Saree, said on social media that the rebels launched ballistic missiles and drones against King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh.
Flights were briefly disrupted, according to Flightradar24.
Tears, silence and techno music at Nova festival site
At the site of the Nova music festival, where Hamas militants in trucks and paragliders opened fire around dawn on October 7, 2023, family members bowed their heads quietly -- although at least one instead put on techno music in tribute to the fallen.
Katia Zohar, whose daughter Bar Zohar was killed at age 23, called the start of the attack at 6:29 am (0329 GMT) "the minute that changed our lives forever".
"Sadly I remember everything," Zohar said. "The moment she called for me to come and pick her up because there were missiles in the air. Then the second time when she called from the road, screaming that they were shooting at her."
Anna Davitashvili, 53, paid tribute to her eldest son Shaun, who was killed at 25 at Nova alongside friends, by playing the last track of techno music that the partygoers were dancing to when the attack began.
"I feel him here. I'm terribly sorry that I couldn't save him, I couldn't help him get out of this massacre," she said, tears filling her eyes.
Lebanon's Hezbollah gets $200 million from Iran to help displaced, sources say
Hezbollah has received $200 million from Iran to help Lebanese displaced by this year’s war with Israel, two people with direct knowledge of the transfer have told Reuters.
Hezbollah received the cash last month despite a tightening US economic chokehold on Iran and increasing difficulties in getting funds to Tehran's Lebanese ally, the sources said.
Intermediaries who moved the money charged a 20% fee, reflecting the risks of dealing with the group, they said. One said this was four times the normal fee.
Asked for comment, a Hezbollah official said an amount had been secured and a plan for distributing it would be announced in the coming days, without elaborating on the source of the funds.
Questions remain over what Netanyahu knew ahead of Hamas attacks
After a string of resignations by top security officials, Israeli PM Benjamin Netanyahu is the only senior figure from October 7 still in office, making the country's upcoming election in many ways a referendum on his leadership, AP reports.
His opponents — from across the political spectrum — call his outgoing coalition "the massacre government". Netanyahu says he has led a "war of redemption".
Netanyahu has repeatedly rejected calls for a commission of inquiry while trying to shift the blame to security officials. He recently accused the then-head of the Shin Bet security service, Ronen Bar, of withholding information ahead of the attack — prompting Bar to threaten a defamation lawsuit.
Netanyahu has meanwhile denied reports in American media outlets that the United Arab Emirates and Egypt warned him ahead of October 7.

French MEP Rima Hassan removes Israeli flag in European Parliament protest
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
02:45:28 UTC
11:45:28 KST

French Member of the European Parliament Rima Hassan has removed an Israeli flag inside the European Parliament in Strasbourg, confirming that her action was a direct protest against the ongoing genocide in Gaza, breaches of international law, and institutional "double standards".
The incident occurred on Monday during an unofficial event organised alongside the diplomatic representation of Israel and the American Jewish Committee (AJC).
Hassan noted that jewellery displayed at the gathering featured maps depicting Israel encompassing the entirety of Gaza and the occupied West Bank, defying the European Union's established diplomatic framework.
Hassan explained that she acted after Israeli artist Yaron Bob denied the existence of the Palestinian people during an in-person exchange, asserting: "Palestine does not exist. It is a chimera, like unicorns... there are no Palestinian refugees, nor Palestinians".
Parliamentary dispute
"As I was leaving, I removed the Israeli flag from its stand," Hassan wrote on X.
"My gesture is part of the denunciation of the ongoing genocide, of violations of international law, and of this incessant and unbearable double standard."
Hassan argued that whilst a Russian flag would never be permitted within European Parliament premises, Israel continues to enjoy "total impunity" despite diplomatic representation on site.
European Parliament President Roberta Metsola addressed lawmakers during a plenary sitting on Tuesday, accusing Hassan of damaging the exhibition and stating the matter is being treated "extremely seriously" under official disciplinary procedures.
Hassan rejected accusations of vandalism or assault, explaining that the adjacent EU flag fell purely due to base imbalance when the Israeli flag was detached.
"No flag was trampled, damaged, or thrown away," she stated.
Hassan added that she has written directly to Metsola, urging the release of security video recordings to reporters to counter misinformation.

Mali: Junta forces retake strategic town of Kidal from separatists
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
02:45:00 UTC
11:45:00 KST

Mali: Junta forces retake strategic town of Kidal
October 7, 2026
Mali's army, supported by Russian paramilitary forces, has re-entered the northern town of Kidal, forcing the Tuareg separatists to withdraw from the strategic hold, in a symbolic boost for the country's military government and its Russian allies.
The Tuareg separatist Azawad Liberation Front (FLA) said in a statement it had "decided to carry out a strategic and controlled withdrawal of its forces from the town of Kidal." It said the withdrawal took place without direct fighting.
This followed the "disproportionate use of aerial assets by Russian mercenaries from the Africa Corps," according to an FLA spokesperson.
How did Kidal fall earlier this year?
The FLA and al-Qaeda-linked Jama'at Nusrat al-Islam wal-Muslimin (JNIM) seized Kidal during a series of attacks earlier this year in April that also killed Mali's defense minister.
Tuareg separatists from the Azawad Liberation Front have been fighting for years to create an independent state in northern Mali.
Mali's junta, which came to power in back-to-back coups in 2020 and 2021, has increasingly relied on Russian paramilitary support against fighters linked to al-Qaeda and the Islamic State.
What does Kidal's recapture mean for Mali's junta?
Analysts say the latest advance is largely a symbolic victory for Mali's junta.
"A successful recapture... affirms the military-led government's authority and boosts the army's morale, particularly after several high-profile setbacks both in the north and the central regions in recent weeks," Beverly Ochieng, associate director of Control Risks, told Reuters.
Ochieng, however, added the retaking of Kidal is largely "symbolic" and not "decisive" in Mali's campaign against jihadist and separatist groups.
Human rights organizations have often accused the Malian army and Russian paramilitaries of killing civilians during military operations, with all sides also accused of committing war crimes.

U.S. Pennsylvania measles cases surpass 1,000
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
10:43:08 CST
11:43:08 KST

LOS ANGELES, Oct. 6 (Xinhua) -- More than 1,000 confirmed measles cases have been reported in the U.S. state of Pennsylvania in 2026, with five deaths and 198 hospitalizations, making it the largest state measles outbreak in more than three decades, according to state health officials.
The Pennsylvania Department of Health said Monday that 1,004 measles cases had been confirmed across 39 counties. A total of 27 new cases had been reported since Oct. 2.
Only four of the confirmed cases were among people who had received the measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccine, accounting for less than 1 percent of the total. The outbreak began in late April.
Health care providers have also seen a surge in MMR vaccinations. In a typical month, Pennsylvania health care providers administer approximately 25,000 doses of the MMR vaccine. More than 49,000 doses were administered in August and more than 53,000 in September, according to the state health department.
Full vaccination offers the best protection against measles. Two doses of the MMR vaccine provide 97 percent lifetime protection, according to the Pennsylvania Department of Health.
In response to the growing outbreak, New York State Governor Kathy Hochul on Monday declared a state disaster emergency. As of Oct. 3, New York had reported 108 measles cases this year, including 92 cases reported since July 15 in 18 rural counties with under-immunized communities, according to the state government.
The New York state government said measles cases reported this year had increased markedly beyond the typical number in the state, particularly since July 15, constituting a significant public health concern.
As of Oct. 1, the United States had reported 3,887 confirmed measles cases in 2026, according to the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, making 2026 the worst year for measles in the country since 1991. ■

RIYADH, Oct. 7 (Xinhua) -- The Saudi-led coalition intercepted and destroyed a ballistic missile launched by Yemen's Houthi group toward the southwestern Saudi city of Khamis Mushait, the Saudi Press Agency (SPA) reported early Wednesday.

Russia has not shared an official cause of the death of 28-year-old Darya Shipilova, who worked as a lab technician at the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Institute of Siberia.
Russia's official public health watchdog, Rospotrebnadzor, stated that Shipilova died on Friday of "pneumonia of unknown etiology."
However, early local reports and statements from local officials said that Shipilova had died of the pneumonic plague.
Rubio warns against speculation, says US operating with limited information
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio warned that the US was operating with limited information.
"Maybe there's nothing there, maybe it's bigger than we thought, we don't know," he said.
"It would be reckless at this moment, given the limited information we still have, to speculate about what this might or might not be or what this is or what this isn't," he added.
Rubio also called upon Russia to share additional details.
"It's incumbent upon Russia to obviously share more information with the world," he said.
The US has also warned Russia that it may be violating its international health obligations by failing to disclose additional details of the case, the Wall Street Journal cited US officials as saying on Tuesday.
A State Department spokesperson told WSJ that the department has requested additional information from the Russian government and is in official communication with other countries to share information, according to the report.
Russia is a part of a 2005 global health pact called the International Health Regulations, which requires countries to notify the World Health Organization (WHO) of an event that could become an international public health emergency.
Countries that identify such an event are required to provide the WHO with detailed updates on tests, lab results, and anti-epidemic measures.
Rospotrebnadzor stated that no microorganisms linked to Shipilova's work were found during analyses of her body and that of almost 200 individuals tested; the only infections they found were two cases of COVID-19 and two of rhinovirus.
However, Moscow has not shared which tests were conducted, according to the WSJ's report.

The scam warning Australians have heard for years is now out of date
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
02:35:03 UTC
11:35:03 KST

IN BRIEF
- ANZ has warned businesses about sophisticated scams in upcoming busy commerce periods.
- Cybersecurity experts say AI improves every stage of a scam.
Australians are being warned that some of the most common advice for spotting scams is becoming less effective, as criminals use artificial intelligence to create convincing emails, phone calls and video deepfakes.
Banks and cybersecurity experts say artificial intelligence (AI) is helping fraudsters impersonate trusted colleagues, businesses and even family members with a level of sophistication that can be almost impossible to detect.
The warning comes ahead of the Black Friday sales period and summer holidays, when scammers typically exploit heightened spending and pressure to target victims.
More than 84,000 cybercrime reports were made in 2025, while the average self-reported cost of cybercrime to businesses rose sharply, according to the Australian Signals Directorate.
How AI is changing the scam landscape
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
AI is transforming every stage of a scam, from impersonation to execution, according to Sanjay Jha, a professor at UNSW's School of Computer Science and Engineering.
"What’s genuinely new is three things: the impersonation of real, trusted people, real-time deepfakes, and the scale and personalisation that the technology brings to financial crime," he said.
AI technology allows criminals to produce deepfake videos of trusted people, including doctors, celebrities and business leaders, to promote fake products or investments. It can clone voices of family members, colleagues or executives asking for money.
The volume and quality of scam techniques are a concern, as large language models can write fluent, personalised messages in any language, with fewer spelling mistakes, and can run thousands of conversations at once.
"We used to tell people to look for spelling mistakes," Jha said, adding that advances in AI mean scammers can produce fluent, convincing messages with few obvious errors.
Scammers can appear on a live call impersonating someone else, Jha said, pointing to a 2024 case in Hong Kong, when United Kingdom engineering firm Arup transferred about HK$200m ($36.5 million) to criminals after a deepfaked multi-person conference.
"AI has turned scamming from a craft into a factory. A few seconds of your voice is now enough for a criminal to become you," he said.
Professor in CyberCrime and Cyberwar at UNSW, Richard Buckland, said any information available on the internet is accessible to criminals using AI, and that experts were "just scratching the surface" of its abilities.
"If I wanted to scam you, you might have published all sorts of stuff in your youth, your dad might have said things, your friends may have, but it's in a thousand locations, and before AI, no one would ever find it," he said
"But that's actually all inside the AI now. So AIs can access a vast amount of information about us and know about us."
AI lets criminals enact existing scams faster, at scale and more convincingly, he said, and the technology was easily accessible.
"It's really a world of outsourcing now; you could pay someone to do it, you could buy a model that does it."
The most common scams targeting businesses
The most common scams affecting businesses include the impersonation of legitimate business email accounts, known as Business Email Compromise (BEC), payment redirection scams, impersonation scams, mule accounts, identity fraud, investment scams and goods and services scams.
BEC and payment redirection scams involve criminals gaining access to or impersonating legitimate business email accounts. Victims often believe they are paying a genuine supplier or business partner, when the funds are being transferred to a fraudulent account.
Jha said scammers use AI to study a company’s public information, past emails where accounts have been compromised, and the writing style of its executives and suppliers. They then send a "perfectly worded email, in the right tone, at the right moment in a real transaction", asking to update banking details.
AI can also generate realistic fake invoices and receipts that match a supplier’s branding. "Instead of just an email, the 'CEO' now follows up with a phone call in their cloned voice, or joins a video call."
Similarly, scammers can pretend to be trusted organisations or individuals, including banks, suppliers or government agencies.
Impersonation scams generally rely on urgency and social conditioning to pressure victims to share information, click malicious links or approve payments or transfer funds.
One of the most significant emerging threats identified by ANZ is the use of stolen or falsified identities to open accounts that can receive scam proceeds. Known as "mule" accounts, these are used to facilitate financial crime, including money laundering.
Identity fraud was the most common scam reported in 2025, and ANZ said it has identified a "growing misuse" of mule accounts across the financial system.
Investment scams trick individuals and businesses into investing in fake or non-existent opportunities by promising attractive returns or exclusive offers. They rank consistently among the highest-loss scam categories reported to ANZ.
"AI easily produces deepfake videos of well-known business figures, journalists or politicians endorsing a trading platform, fake news articles, fake dashboards showing ‘profits’, and chatbots that keep victims engaged for weeks," Jha said.
"In short, AI removes the tell-tale signs we taught people to look for: bad grammar, a stranger’s voice, a generic greeting. The scam now looks and sounds like business as usual."
Individuals and businesses are also urged to look out for goods and services scams — advertised goods and services that are fake, misrepresented or never delivered after payment is made, commonly occurring through online marketplaces, social media platforms and fraudulent websites. While often lower in value, goods and services scams remain among the highest-volume scam types reported by ANZ.
ANZ general manager specialist sales, Cosi De Angelis, said that as AI evolved, financial crime was becoming harder to detect because it is "often hidden within legitimate businesses, trusted relationships, and everyday transactions".
"In many cases, criminals are exploiting trust as effectively as they are technology," De Angelis said.
How to defend against 'routine' scams
Jha said that scams would only become more sophisticated.
"We'll see real-time deepfake video calls become routine, AI agents that run entire scam conversations end to end, and scams that combine stolen data, cloned voices and fake documents in one coordinated attack," he said.
"It is an arms race, and criminals adapt quickly to every new defence."
Between October 2025 and June 2026, ANZ customer scam losses fell by 24 per cent compared with the same period the previous year. During that time, the bank said it also prevented and recovered more than $100 million in scam and fraud-related funds.
ANZ said it is encouraging businesses to review their cyber security practices and ensure staff understand the warning signs of cyber-enabled scams and fraud.
"Technology will continue to evolve, but human judgement remains one of the strongest defences," De Angelis said.
Jha said there was real progress being made by banks, telcos and digital platforms using AI to detect and prevent cybercrime.
"Reported losses have come down from their peak in recent years. Banks are also intercepting and recovering more stolen money than before. That shows coordinated action works," he said.
But Buckland said in the meantime, large financial institutions needed to stop contacting customers by phone and email.
"If you get an email, there's actually no way you can absolutely be sure it's the right email. And if we get a call, there's no way we can be sure we're speaking to who we think we are, even if the correct number shows on the screen.
"So companies have to stop doing it," he said.
While banks were "lucky" to have physical branches, Buxton anticipated acting against these threats would be a problem for many organisations, in a future where the only trustworthy communications would be "in-person".
"If you can only contact your customers electronically, you can no longer be distinguished from a scammer," he said.
"So how's it going to work?"

Football: Lionel Messi plays final game for Argentina
October 7, 2026
Lionel Messi made his 208th and final appearance for Argentina on Tuesday night, scoring his 126th and final international goal as the Albiceleste beat Benin 3-0 in a friendly in Buenos Aires.
In emotional scenes at a packed El Monumental stadium, Messi stepped up to convert a penalty in the 71st minute, prompting wild celebrations from teammates and fans alike.
Earlier, the 39-year-old superstar had already set up goals for teammates Nicolas Otamendi – who was also making his final appearance for the national team – and Nico Paz – the youngster who is widely tipped to inherit Messi's iconic number 10 jersey.
"It was a source of great pride for me to wear this jersey," Messi told fans in an address after the final whistle. "I can only express my gratitude... not coming back anymore will be deeply painful."
"Gracias, Leo!" read an intricate drone show in the sky above the stadium at full-time, which concluded with the drones forming a profile of Messi's face.
Messi: 'Proud to be Argentinian'
Widely considered the best player of all time, Messi announced his retirement from international football on August 31 – barely a month after Argentina lost 1-0 to Spain in the World Cup final.
"It was a decision which hurts and still hurts but I know it's the right time," he wrote in a statement composed just two days after the defeat in East Rutherford, USA.
"I swear that I have always given everything and that I have always fought for this shirt to make you happy and make you proud to be Argentinian through football," he said.
"Thank you, God for making me Argentinian."
Messi: following in the footsteps of Maradona
Argentina may have lost the 2026 World Cup final, but Messi's crowning moment came four years earlier when he led his nation to glory in Qatar, beating France on penalties after a spectacular final had ended 3-3.
The triumph crowned an international career which hadn't always been easy as Messi, so prolific in club football for Barcelona, struggled to live up to expectations in his home country, where fans worshipped him as the successor to the great Diego Maradona.
He announced his international retirement once before in 2016 after losing three consecutive finals with Argentina – the 2014 World Cup final vs. Germany in Brazil and the 2015 and 2016 Copa America finals, both to Chile.
But he reversed his decision and led his country to the Copa America title in 2021, ending Argentina's 28-year wait for a trophy, before finally winning the World Cup in 2022.
Messi may have retired from international football, but he still has a contract with his current club, Major League Soccer (MLS) side Inter Miami, until 2028.
