"Gryphon": Ukrainian forces combine robots with drones to strike Russians deep in the rear. Interview with the commander of "NC13"
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
05:30:00 EEST
11:30:00 KST

"Gryphon": Ukrainian forces combine robots with drones to strike Russians deep in the rear. Interview with the commander of "NC13"
In January of this year, the "NC13" strike UGV unit of the 3rd Separate Assault Brigade tested a new tactic deep behind Russian lines. Since then, the unit has successfully carried out more than 100 similar operations, turning what began as an experiment into a proven combat system.
The new tactic was named "Gryphon" in honor of a service member from the unit who went missing in action in 2023 while carrying out a combat mission near Andriivka in the Donetsk region. It was in this area, near Bakhmut, that Oscar-winning Ukrainian director Mstyslav Chernov filmed the documentary "2000 Meters to Andriivka" during a different Ukrainian counteroffensive.
The concept behind the new tactic involves deploying kamikaze UGVs, essentially ground robots, deep behind enemy lines using heavy bomber drones. After landing, the robotic systems continue moving toward their targets and can be used to strike key positions, logistics, and personnel while also creating disruption in the enemy rear.
The "NC13" unit was also behind an operation that drew significant international attention about a year ago, when Ukrainian forces captured Russian positions without deploying infantry, using only UGVs and drones.
As a result, two Russian service members surrendered to the robotic systems, after which the machines escorted them to Ukrainian positions as prisoners of war.
Today, the new tactic is part of the Third Army Corps' large-scale operation known as "Vivaldi." Since the start of the offensive, Ukrainian forces have liberated 176 square kilometers of territory (68 square miles).
According to the Office of the President of Ukraine, Russian forces suffered more than 5,000 casualties, including those killed, wounded, and captured, during the first three stages of the operation. It is currently known that Ukrainian forces have taken 250 Russian service members as prisoners of war (POWs). The Third Army Corps separately reported 2,000 Russian personnel casualties during the latest stage alone.
Approximately 80% of logistics and 90% of wounded evacuation for Ukrainian troops during all three stages of the operation were carried out by unmanned ground vehicles, or UGVs.
"NC13" commander Mykola Zinkevych, call sign "Makar," explains how the new "Gryphon" tactic works, how the idea of air-dropping ground robots emerged, what happened during the first operations, how Russian forces are reacting to the technology, and why he believes Ukraine is shaping the future of technological warfare.
He also discusses how Western partners are becoming less able to understand Ukrainian military technologies and, more broadly, the needs of modern warfare.
Can you please explain, in general, what this new tactic involves?
In general, this is a sabotage-operation tactic that was fully planned, developed, and implemented by the "NC13" strike unmanned ground systems unit of the 3rd Separate Assault Brigade.
The tactic is genuinely new and has no equivalent anywhere in the world because no one had previously deployed unmanned ground vehicles from unmanned aerial vehicles.
The concept itself is that, using heavy bombers, we drop small ground-based kamikaze systems deep into enemy territory, at a distance of 5 to 15 kilometers (3 to 9.3 miles). From there, we carry out different sabotage operations: eliminating enemy personnel, destroying logistics, and so on.
When did you begin using this tactic? Any first operation is essentially a test. How confident were you that it would work?
We carried out the first operation about eight months ago (in January 2026- UP).
We spent quite a long time developing the tactic itself and modifying the equipment because standard ground-based kamikaze systems are not designed for this kind of use.
The engineers spent a great deal of time making it work. The pilots also had to learn how to operate with these systems and deploy them correctly. The planning department, accordingly, spent a lot of time preparing the operation.
But when it worked for the first time, the excitement was incredible. Our first operation went 15 kilometers (9.3 miles) deep behind enemy lines. We deployed two ground-based kamikaze systems near the target, and from there, the systems themselves moved into the shelter.
It was an enemy staging point where personnel were brought in. They would stop there to rest before moving on to carry out their missions. We eliminated that staging point using two ground-based kamikaze systems.
What was the enemy's reaction? What did it look like from their side?
In fact, the enemy did not understand what had happened, what system had been used, what had struck them, or what tactic we were employing.
Even now, it remains a major surprise for them because we operate in different sectors within the Third Army Corps' area of responsibility.
We combine different technologies in order to change the rules on the battlefield.
We have been able to strike the enemy from the air at significant depth for quite some time. We have also been using unmanned ground vehicles to strike enemy forces for a while.
But this combination (UGV + UAV) allows us to operate at greater depth, in areas where the enemy does not expect to be reached and where they feel relatively safe. So we are going to take that freedom away from them.
How many such operations have been carried out so far?
More than one hundred. We always work systematically. If something works once, twice, or three times, we still do not consider it a fully established capability because it could be accidental.
But when something is carried out more than ten times, it becomes a systematic approach. We have SOPs, standard operating procedures, in place for this tactic: how to use it, where it can be implemented, and what its capabilities are.
It can be used for reconnaissance, mining deep behind enemy lines, striking targets, hunting moving enemy personnel, disrupting logistics, and more. We have fully developed this tactic, identified all of its capabilities, and now use it as a full-fledged tool on the battlefield.
War in general, and especially Russia's war against Ukraine, is a war of speed. Everything depends on who can come up with something new and adapt faster. Are the Russians already trying to do something similar?
I am confident that we are far ahead of the enemy. Even when it comes to the systematic use of strike unmanned ground vehicles on the battlefield, which we have been doing for about a year, the enemy is still far behind.
So when it comes to tactics like "Gryphon," which we are discussing today, there is still a very large gap between us and them.
But I would not rule out the possibility that, over time, the enemy will begin copying this approach and using similar methods.
In fact, during more than 100 successful missions, there have been many almost meme-like moments when the enemy had no idea what they were looking at and would actually approach the robots to inspect them.
There was one occasion when we managed to completely disrupt a Russian mechanized assault that had been planned for foggy weather conditions. At the time, we were actively targeting one of the enemy's logistics routes. We eliminated several personnel over the course of the day.
They started to panic because they did not understand what was happening. They thought a sabotage and reconnaissance group, or SRG, had broken through into their rear. As a result, they canceled the mechanized assault they had planned for that day.
So these small robots can create very significant disruption.
In general, there was serious panic among enemy forces at the depth where we were operating. And panic is actually very important because if we create panic within enemy ranks, they begin to have problems controlling their personnel. Soldiers start refusing to carry out missions, which then creates panic at the command level because commanders do not understand what is happening in their rear, and so on.
That creates destabilization, and all of that works in our favor.
Why exactly do they panic?
Even when you know what it is, you can become even more afraid. You do not know where it might be waiting for you, where it might drive, where it might catch up with you, and so on. So in some ways, it is even better when they know.
You know, now you have to watch not only the sky, but also the ground beneath your feet. Not just for mines, but because something might come after you.
There was one interesting intercepted communication where an enemy soldier reported to his commander that a "Baba Yaga" (russian military slang for heavy bomber drones - UP) had flown in, landed, then started driving and chasing them.
It was pretty funny to listen to.
But it did catch them in the end.
This tactic seems to have many advantages. Which one do you consider the most important?
- The absolute advantage of using any technology is that, first and foremost, we do not have to put people at risk. We preserve human lives.
For me, as the commander of a strike UGV unit and as a former infantryman, it is actually more important to preserve our own personnel, to protect Ukrainian infantrymen, assault troops, and soldiers, than it is to destroy the enemy. Destroying the enemy comes second.
And in fact, by destroying the enemy, we prevent them from advancing toward our forces and make life easier for our infantry. So above all, any technology helps us protect human life. Robots do not bleed, and human life is priceless. That is essentially our guiding principle throughout everything we do.
The next advantage, of course, is depth. The depth at which we can operate with these systems.
Yes, 10 to 15 kilometers (6.2 to 9.3 miles) is not the maximum range. Unfortunately, I cannot disclose the exact figures. But we are deployed and then continue moving very, very deep into enemy territory. The deeper we go, the more valuable, so to speak, the resources and targets we can destroy.
You touched a little on the future. Is there already a vision for how this technology could develop? I will not ask exactly how, but should we expect it to be scaled up further?
Yes. By the end of 2026, there will be many large-scale, exciting, and interesting stories, announcements, and new tactics from our unit.
We already have a number of newly implemented applications and tactics involving unmanned ground vehicles, (including the use of UGVs equipped with grenade launchers, which is also a new and unique tactic -UP).
It is simply not yet the right time to talk about them. And we have many more things planned. So we just need to wait a little longer.
Western countries have traditionally been considered leaders in military technology. You speak with foreign military officials. How well do they understand the technological breakthrough currently taking place in Ukraine?
I attended the Munich Security Conference in February and had the opportunity to speak with many foreign military officials, various partners, and government representatives.
In reality, they are very far behind. Absolutely.
They understand what we are talking about, what we are deploying, what we are using, and how it works. But they do not fully understand its importance and value on the battlefield, or just how much the battlefield itself has changed.
And I am more than certain that the rest of the world is lagging very, very far behind.
Even the technologies I see being introduced into militaries around the world are still quite far removed from what is actually being used on the battlefield between Ukraine and Russia.
Looking specifically at unmanned ground vehicles, I have seen their entire evolution on the front line, from 2024 until today.
We work, interact, and collaborate with many manufacturers. A great deal of equipment has been developed because we provided our expertise and doctrine.
I also have a certain number of systems produced by foreign manufacturers, and there is a very significant difference between them (Ukrainian and Western UGVs - UP).
We are not even talking about price, although the prices are extremely high. But in terms of actual battlefield use, Western systems still fall far short of the needs of the modern battlefield.
Are foreign partners reaching out to Ukrainian military personnel often enough for this kind of expertise? Is there interest in contributing to the development of these innovations?
I would say they do reach out, but not nearly as actively as they should. In my opinion, this is the kind of expertise people should be actively pursuing, not just occasionally asking, "So, what are you working on?"
No one knows what will happen in the world tomorrow. We live in a time when you never know what to expect.
If Ukraine can offer something to its partners, what can it receive from them in return?
Ukraine is the sword and shield of Europe. It is defending not only itself and its own future, but the future of the entire continent.
So every time other countries help us, they should understand that they are not only helping Ukrainians. They are also helping themselves.
Right now, Ukraine especially needs effective and timely weapons deliveries from its partners. First and foremost, this means air defense systems capable of protecting Ukrainian cities from attacks, as well as heavy weapons, including artillery and armored vehicles, that can help Ukraine regain the initiative on the battlefield.
Of course, this support must always be justified. Because Ukraine is doing everything possible to defend its territory, - liberate occupied land, and protect the future of the country and the nation, - that is why all of these processes and technologies have emerged.
The battlefield has effectively become a testing ground for innovation. On the one hand, that is a positive thing.
But on the other hand, it is deeply tragic, because every such achievement comes at a price. And that price is not paid in money. It is paid with the lives of Ukrainian service members and people who should have been the future of the Ukrainian nation.
History has seen many cases where a promising technology or a major breakthrough emerged, but it was overlooked, underfunded, or never scaled up...
This is not something that appeared only today. It is something that has been developed and planned over a period of time, has already been implemented for quite a while, and is constantly being modernized.
It will continue to evolve and eventually grow into something new.
Because there are technologies that work today. There are technologies that will work tomorrow. And there are technologies that worked yesterday but no longer work today.
But each of them becomes a driving force behind the next one.
Kateryna Lisunova, Ukrainska Pravda

Animals may have evolved 200 million years earlier than we thought
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
02:29:56 UTC
11:29:56 KST

Animals may have evolved 200 million years earlier than we thought
- Date:
- October 6, 2026
- Source:
- University of Oxford
- Summary:
- New research suggests animals could have evolved as early as 800 to 700 million years ago, roughly 200 million years earlier than some previous estimates. If so, the first animals may have lived before or during Snowball Earth, leaving behind little trace because their soft bodies were rarely preserved.
- Share:
New research suggests animals may have evolved up to 200 million years before they first appear clearly in the fossil record, challenging a key assumption scientists have used to estimate when animal life began.
A study led by the University of Oxford suggests the earliest animals may have existed hundreds of millions of years before the first unmistakable animal fossils appear. The findings, published Oct. 2 in Science Advances, indicate that animals could have originated deep in the Neoproterozoic Era, possibly before some of the most severe ice ages in Earth's history.
The research could reshape scientists' understanding of a major evolutionary puzzle. Animals seem to appear relatively abruptly in the fossil record shortly before the Cambrian Period (539 to 487 million years ago), even though other lines of evidence have long suggested their evolutionary story began much earlier.
At the center of the new study is a question about how researchers have used ancient fossil deposits to place a maximum age on the origin of animals.
Rethinking a key fossil assumption
One important site is the Weng'an Biota in China, a roughly 590 million year old fossil deposit preserved in rocks of Ediacaran age. The site contains microscopic organisms preserved in exceptional detail, but none can be definitively identified as animals.
Because of this absence, scientists have previously argued that animals likely evolved after the Weng'an Biota formed. The reasoning was that if animals had already existed at the time, such an unusually well-preserved fossil deposit should have captured evidence of them.
The new research calls that assumption into question.
Mongolia fossils offer a crucial test
The international team, which included scientists from the University of California Berkeley, ETH Zürich, and Yale University, conducted an extensive study of exceptionally preserved microfossils from the Kheseen Biota in Mongolia.
The Kheseen Biota is more than 40 million years younger than Weng'an, although the two fossil assemblages share some species. Importantly, animals are already known from other locations around the world by the time the Kheseen Biota formed, including sites in Namibia and South China.
Researchers examined more than 140 samples, including material collected from previously undocumented locations, using scanning electron microscopy. Their analysis revealed exquisitely preserved new microfossil species, including acritarchs (tiny spherical organisms with spines and branching projections), along with embryo-like fossils containing internal cells.
Despite the remarkable preservation, none of the fossils can confidently be identified as an animal.
Senior author Associate Professor Ross Anderson (Museum of Natural History, Oxford University) said: "The Kheseen Biota breaks the argument that the exceptional microfossils of Weng'an mean we would have seen animal fossils in the assemblage had they existed at the time. The Kheseen microfossils are just as well-preserved, yet animals continue to be absent - despite the fact we know at that point they existed."
This suggests animals may have occupied environments different from those represented in the Kheseen deposits, or that the chemical conditions responsible for fossilization there were not suitable for preserving animal remains.
A potentially hidden history of animal life
Because animals were already present when the Kheseen Biota formed but still do not appear in its fossil record, the researchers argue that the absence of animals from Weng'an cannot automatically be taken as proof that animals had not yet evolved 590 million years ago.
Instead, the team examined much older fossil deposits dating from about 850 to 730 million years ago. These included the Svanbergfjellet Formation (Norway), Bitter Springs Group (Australia) and Chuar Group (Arizona, USA) -- all fossil rich deposits considered capable of preserving animals, although no confirmed animal fossils have yet been found in them.
These sites have previously been used to define maximum possible ages for the origin of animal life.
Using those older geological constraints, the researchers carried out molecular clock analysis. This technique compares genetic differences among living species and combines them with fossil dates and estimated rates of evolutionary change to calculate when common ancestors may have lived.
When the researchers used these older deposits rather than the younger Ediacaran Weng'an site as constraints, the estimated origin of animals moved backward by about 200 million years. The new range places the possible emergence of animals between 800 and 700 million years ago.
Clues from ancient chemical fossils
Other evidence already hints that animals could have a much deeper evolutionary history than their body fossils indicate.
Chemical fossils, also known as biomarkers, preserved in ancient rocks contain evidence consistent with sponges living at least 650 million years ago. That would place them tens of millions of years before the oldest definitive macroscopic animal fossils.
The earliest animals would likely have been small and soft-bodied. Without shells, bones or other hard structures, they would have been far less likely to survive the fossilization process than many later animals.
Their chances of being preserved would also have depended heavily on where they lived and on a rare combination of chemical conditions after death.
Did animals exist before Snowball Earth?
If animals originated between 800 and 700 million years ago, the timing raises an extraordinary possibility. Animal life may already have existed before Earth entered some of the most extreme ice ages in its history, or animals may even have emerged during that harsh period.
The Cryogenian Period began around 720 million years ago, when massive glaciers expanded across the planet during episodes commonly called Snowball Earth.
The new findings reopen questions about whether the environmental conditions associated with Snowball Earth influenced the origin and early evolution of animal life.
First author, PhD student Orin Lole Durbin (University of Oxford undergraduate at the time of the study, now at Virginia Tech) said: "Pre-Ediacaran animal body fossils still elude us, and this analysis does not prove that animals existed 800 million years ago. However, our new fossil evidence from Mongolia undermines one of the main arguments for restricting animal origins to the Ediacaran interval. Meanwhile, our molecular-clock analyses show how much further back their evolutionary history could extend."
Searching for the earliest animals
The researchers say future studies should examine fossil deposits from a wider range of locations, environments, and preservation conditions in the search for evidence of early animals.
That search should also combine every available line of evidence, including animal body fossils, traces of animal activity, and chemical biomarkers.
Professor Anderson added: "Until that evidence becomes available, the precise birth date of the animal kingdom remains uncertain."
Story Source:
Materials provided by University of Oxford. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- Orin M. Lole Durbin, Eliel S.C. Anttila, Derek E.G. Briggs, Francis A. Macdonald, Ross P. Anderson. Re-evaluating molecular clock maximum age calibrations revives pre-Ediacaran divergence estimates for animals. Science Advances, 2026; 12 (40) DOI: 10.1126/sciadv.aeg6289

Are Test cricket batters getting worse? The stats say yes
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
02:22:30 UTC
11:22:30 KST

Australia's men's head cricket selector, George Bailey, pointed out some home truths recently when questioned on the woes of Test number three Marnus Labuschagne.
"Our batting group in its entirety, not just Marn, probably hasn't been functioning as successfully as we would like," Bailey said, and he's not wrong.
With the first of three Tests against South Africa beginning on Friday ahead of a mammoth run of matches against New Zealand, India and England, Australia's batting line-up will be scrutinised like never before.
Since the beginning of the Border–Gavaskar Trophy at home in 2024, Australia has played 18 Tests with only three batters averaging more than 40: Steve Smith (49.4), Travis Head (46.25), and Alex Carey (40.3).
Beau Webster (33.5) and Cameron Green (30.16) are the only other batters averaging over 30 during the period.
Australia's bowlers have repeatedly dug the batters out of a hole, with the team winning 13 of those 18 matches.
But Australia's batters aren't alone: Across all 12 Test-playing nations, the game has undergone a huge transition with batters fading and bowlers dominating.
The rise of T20 cricket, better balls and seaming wickets have all played a part.
ABC Sport has done an analysis of all Test batters over the past 40 years with the help of ABC radio cricket statistician, Ric Finlay.
We've looked at batters from one to seven and found the same patterns across all positions.
We could list a table of 40 years but to make things easy, we've broken it down to five-year periods that include every test played from the beginning of 1987 to the most recent Test between England and Pakistan.
To see the patterns, we're narrowing the numbers down to batting averages, run rates and average balls per wicket.
Looking at these figures, you can see that the average of all batters in positions one to seven peaked in the period between 2002 and 2016 before dropping back to the low 30s.
It's easier to visualise with a chart that shows the year-by-year average as well as a rolling five-year average to even out the yearly variations.
The period between roughly 2003 and 2014 is when averages were highest.
This coincides with a golden period for world-class test batsmen when the likes of Sri Lanka's Kumar Sangakkara, Australia's Ricky Ponting, South Africa's Jacques Kallis, England's Kevin Pietersen, India's Virender Sehwag and the West Indies' Shivnarine Chanderpaul, to name just a few, were at their peak.
The rolling five-year average is now at a 40-year low, but that only tells part of the story.
To understand more about the decline of Test cricket batting, two other charts fill in the picture.
The first is strike rate: how many runs batters score per 100 balls.
Batters' strike rates have increased across the board from 41.34 to 58.13: that's almost 17 runs per 100 balls, which is the equivalent of an extra run per over.
But while batters are scoring much faster, they're also getting far out more quickly.
Bowlers are now taking wickets faster than at any time in the past 40 years.
In 1989, top-order batters were lasting more than 85 balls between wickets in the rolling five-year average, while as of this year, wickets are falling every 58 balls — an all-time low.
From the peak to the current trough that's a fall of more than 32 per cent.
It's no accident that we're seeing so many shortened Test matches, like the two-day match in McKay against Bangladesh in August.
The overall figures are mirrored in virtually every individual batting position with averages on the whole going down.
In other words, we have seen a fundamental shift in the battle between the bat and ball playing out over the past four decades and right now, while batters are scoring more quickly, the bowlers are on top.
The same is true for Australia's one to seven batters.
Again we see the early 2000s peak in averages when Ricky Ponting, Matthew Hayden, Justin Langer, Damien Martyn and Adam Gilchrist were in their pomp.
The combined batting rolling average for positions one to seven is now at a 40-year low.
The strike rate rolling average is at an all-time high, although only marginally ahead of that early 2000s era.
But the balls per wicket figure rolling five-year average has dropped alarmingly from its starting high of 98.33 to its current all-time low of 54.26
That's a fall of almost 45 per cent.
To put it another way, opposition bowlers are taking Australian wickets almost twice as quickly as they were 40 years ago.
So, why is this happening?
Former Australia coach and batter, Darren Lehmann, who's currently coaching English country side Northamptonshire, highlights four major changes in cricket that are all linked.
The first is the rise and rise of T20 cricket.
"Now they [batters] just don't leave balls," he told ABC sport.
"They have to score off more, so they play more shots to more risky balls in Test cricket,"
"Hence they go at balls they shouldn't go at, which they normally wouldn't have 20 years ago."
The second reason, Lehmann said, was the state of Test wickets around the globe, which he said were spinning and seaming more and earlier.
"They've got more in them and that is a by-product of making sure you get results," he said.
Lehmann said the balls used in Test Cricket, the Kookaburra and Duke, had added an extra layer of lacquer, which meant they stayed harder and the seam stayed prouder for longer, creating more movement.
"Blokes are playing shots to balls they shouldn't because they're trying to score before they get one that gets them out," Lehmann said.
The fourth reason bowlers are on top of batters is the one that ties it all together: data analytics.
"You're honing in on the weakness of players better than you did in the past and you're relentless with that.
"So, if a bloke can't cover drive or doesn't play well off the front foot, you now target that area with more balls, and you don't go away from that."
"If a bloke gets out to a left-armer all the time, well you get Mitchell Starc straight on."
Sooner or later, the batter's lack of patience, the moving ball and seaming wicket combined with the bowler's knowledge of their opponent's weakness will result in a wicket.
Cricket's delicate balance between bat and ball has fundamentally shifted and the cost is two-day test matches like the Boxing Day Ashes test, which cost Cricket Australia millions.
Lehmann said wickets needed to get flatter or lacquer taken off balls in order to shift the balance back towards batters.
"There are consequences: two-day games in Test cricket can cost people their jobs."
Failing Test batters can also lose one of the most coveted jobs in Australian sport.

Australia top court rules against coal mine expansion, citing climate harm
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
02:17:07 UTC
11:17:07 KST

Australia top court rules against coal mine expansion, citing climate harm
Campaigners say ruling sets a ‘binding national precedent’ requiring climate damage be weighed when fossil fuel projects are considered.
Australia’s highest court has ruled against the expansion of a major coal mine, finding that planning authorities had failed to ensure that emissions of planet-warming greenhouse gases would be “minimised to the greatest extent practicable”.
Environmental campaigners called Wednesday’s court decision the first ruling on climate change. They said it set a “binding national precedent” requiring climate damage be weighed when fossil fuel projects are considered.
In the ruling, three of the High Court’s five judges found that the expansion of the Mount Pleasant mine in New South Wales must be halted. Planning authorities, they said, were obliged to consider granting consent only with conditions ensuring that all greenhouse gas emissions were minimised, and had not done so in this case.
The case was brought by retired science teachers Wendy Wales and Tony Lonergan, who had fought for years to halt the planned mine expansion in Australia’s rural coal-digging heartland.
“Today the High Court has said what we have always known,” Wales said in a statement. “We cannot dig up coal, ship it overseas, watch it drive climate change, and then pretend the consequences have nothing to do with us and won’t be felt by us.”
The mine’s operator, Mach Energy, had sought to extend the life of the open-cut mine in the Hunter Valley by more than 20 years, to 2048, and to nearly double its annual output. Mach is owned by Droxford International, a subsidiary of Indonesia’s Salim Group.
Mach argued that coal exported and burned overseas could not be clearly linked to environmental effects felt near the mine.
The company’s proposal was initially approved by the New South Wales Independent Planning Commission. But environmental campaigners disagreed, saying every ounce of greenhouse gas released into the atmosphere made bushfires, floods and drought more likely.
“Today, the highest court in the country agreed that those decisions have to account for the damage they cause,” said Lonergan. “This isn’t the end of coal overnight. But it is the end of coal mine approvals that look the other way on climate.”
Australia is one of the world’s largest fossil fuel exporters, ranking among the top sellers of both coal and liquefied natural gas.
Anita O’Hart, a lawyer for Wales and Lonergan’s community group, said the “historic” ruling was expected to affect how future fossil fuel projects are handled.
“The High Court has confirmed that planning authorities cannot ignore the chain of causation from a project’s emissions through to real, local climate harm,” she said.
“This ruling will be applied by courts and planning authorities across Australia, and it will be studied internationally as one of the most significant domestic climate law decisions in the world.”
Mach Energy said it was “disappointed with the outcome” but accepted the court’s decision.
“We will continue to actively pursue all available options to ensure the long-term continuity of the Mount Pleasant operation,” the company said in a statement.

Empty nets in Latin America as fish flee El Nino
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
02:15:00 UTC
11:15:00 KST

Empty nets in Latin America as fish flee El Nino
ECUADOR – Fishermen along Latin America’s Pacific Coast are reeling in half-empty nets as ocean warming aggravated by El Nino causes tuna, anchovies and other top catches to migrate to cooler waters.
From Ecuador and Peru in South America, to Panama and Guatemala in Central America, some skippers have stopped going out all together as fish stocks dwindle close to shore in seas running at up to 6 deg C above normal.
“The water is warm,” Juan Ollague, 56, told AFP in the south-western Ecuadoran port of Santa Rosa, where hundreds of idle fishing boats are crammed into a small port.
After a night on the water, Ollague returned with just six small tuna.
“We came away empty-handed,” he lamented.
“Fishing used to be good, now it’s terrible,” fellow skipper Darwin Zambrano, 53, complained as he untangled a net that has not scooped up big tuna like albacore or bonito in weeks.
El Nino is the warming phase of a natural cycle in the tropical Pacific that causes hotter and drier conditions in some places, and cooler and wetter in others.
The 2026 “super” El Nino, which is expected to peak later in 2026, is already wreaking havoc in Central America, where drought is endangering animals and stunting crops.
The average sea surface temperature, excluding polar regions, reached 21.07 deg C in August, tying with March 2024 as the hottest on record, according to the European Union’s Copernicus climate change observatory.
The average sea temperatures off Ecuador’s coast rose by 2.5 deg C to 3 deg C at the surface and up to 6 deg C at a depth of 40m in the past 10 weeks, said oceanographer Jonathan Cedeno, who led a mission from Guayaquil’s Polytechnic University to measure the temperatures.
‘Losing money’
On Panama’s Pacific coast, Rigoberto Gonzalez said he has to sail farther and farther from shore to earn a living.
This means spending more on fuel, food and ice to preserve the fish on the small boat he uses to catch snapper, kingfish and barracuda.
“We go out with US$100 (S$128) worth of petrol, and when we come back, we earn US$150 from selling the fish, which has to be divided among four workers”, Gonzalez, 59, told AFP, on Veracruz beach.
In nearby Panama City, some fishermen have thrown in the towel and decided to remain in port.
“We can’t keep losing money,” Jesus Morales, leader of the artisanal fishermen’s union of Panama, said.
Farther north, in Iztapa, Guatemala, 50-year-old Eliseo Ovando said it now takes three days to catch what he used to pull from the water in a day, and complains that only commercial fisheries receive government assistance to ride out the shortages.
“The big fish eat the little ones,” he said, referring to the struggles of small-scale operators like himself.
In Peru, the world’s biggest catcher of anchovies, fishermen are turning to construction to feed their families as their tiny prey slips out of reach.
Economic ripple effect
In Panama City, the poor catches are visible at a wholesale fish market next to the dock that supplies the city’s supermarkets.
“Less is arriving” off the boats, said Carlos Nieto, a 46-year-old vendor. And sometimes the catch is “damaged by the heat”, he said.
Nieto now spends about US$600 a month on ice, “practically a whole salary”.
For now, vendors in Panama have not passed on their higher costs and reduced income to consumers in the form of significantly higher prices.
But in Ecuador, the world’s second-largest tuna producer after Thailand, the prices of mahi-mahi (also known as dorado) and swordfish have doubled due to the shortage, according to the industry.
In Santa Rosa, the sea’s dwindling bounty has a knock-on effect, leading to the temporary closure of food stalls along the port.
Francisco Orlando, who earns a living filleting fish, is worried that he could soon be out of a job.
“We’re hoping they (fishermen) catch fish,” the 37-year-old said as he sharpened his filleting knives.
“If they do, we work. If they don’t, we don’t.” AFP

In response to Hamas's unprecedented assault, Israel launched a massive military offensive that has left most of Gaza in ruins and killed more than 74,200 people, according to Gaza's health ministry, which is under Hamas authority and whose figures are considered reliable by the United Nations.
In the three years since, Israel has also expanded its military reach across the Middle East – fighting on several fronts spanning from a conflict with Lebanese militant group Hezbollah to Iran.
In Gaza, the humanitarian situation remains dire despite a fragile US-brokered ceasefire declared last October, with hundreds of thousands still forced to live in tents and temporary structures.

The political future and reconstruction of the war-shattered territory also remains largely stalled in practice.
Israel says it controls more than 60 percent of the Gaza Strip and has continued its airstrikes, vowing to eliminate threats from Hamas and target those involved in the October 7 attack.
Since the ceasefire, Israeli forces have killed more than 1,430 people in Gaza, according to the territory's health ministry.

concrete letterforms become sculptural skatepark by XPOME in bulgaria
SKATEABLE, the mini skatepark by XPOME connects graffiti, typography, and skateboarding through concrete and steel.
concrete mini skatepark brings XPOME’s graffiti into Gabrovo
SKATEABLE is a project by Bulgarian graffiti artist XPOME, created for an ongoing exhibition on the history of skateboarding in Bulgaria at the Christo and Jeanne-Claude Center in Gabrovo. Invited to create a sculpture for the exhibition, XPOME developed a concrete mini skatepark in front of the center’s old building.
Five concrete and steel letters become skatepark elements
The sculpture spells out ‘XPOME,’ the artist’s name, through five concrete and steel letters, each functioning as a different element for skateboarding or resting. The X forms a double quarter pipe, while the P incorporates a classic rail around a concrete island. The O becomes the first volcano ever built in Bulgaria, and the M functions as a large bench for sliding and grinding. The E forms a small triple jumping platform.

Chinese woman snaps up nearly 200 parking spaces to flip to neighbours for profit
Residents argue that parking is a vital community asset that should not be monopolised by anyone seeking financial gain from resale
A woman in central China invested 14 million yuan (US$2 million) to acquire 196 parking spaces in a residential community, later selling them at a significant mark-up, which led to furious residents suing her.
The lawsuit centred around a residential block, the name of which was not disclosed, located in Changsha, Hunan province.
The property project was completed and put on the market in 2018. At the time, many were sceptical about the community’s prospects due to a lack of essential public facilities such as shops, schools, and public transport options. Consequently, there was little interest in both the flats and the parking spaces, according to Hunan TV.
Despite this pessimism, a woman surnamed Wu snapped up 196 parking spots in a single transaction, representing 40 per cent of the project’s total parking inventory, for a sum of 14 million yuan. The developer, facing severe cash constraints, agreed to her purchase.

‘Nobody wants a new Greece’: Calls grow for crisis election in Romania
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
02:00:00 UTC
11:00:00 KST

‘Nobody wants a new Greece’: Calls grow for crisis election in Romania
Far-right leader George Simion tells POLITICO Romanian president Nicușor Dan will face a campaign to oust him if he keeps refusing a snap poll to end months of deadlock in Bucharest.
Romanian President Nicușor Dan faces demands from allies and adversaries alike to call a snap election, the first in the country’s modern history, if his latest attempt to end five months of political paralysis fails.
The key NATO and EU member has lacked a fully functioning government since the coalition collapsed in May, and lawmakers have rejected a succession of Dan’s prime ministerial nominees.
Political parties are now weighing up whether to support Dan’s latest prime ministerial candidate, the diplomat Luca Niculescu, who must win a confidence vote in parliament within the next nine days to be confirmed in the role.
Advertisement
In an interview, Dan’s arch-rival on Romania’s hard right, George Simion, warned that no stable government can form without an election and accused the president of mounting a “blockade” against democracy because he is “afraid of us coming to power.”
Speaking separately to POLITICO, Dan’s most recently defeated candidate for prime minister, Member of the European Parliament Siegfried Mureșan, warned the country was already paying an economic price, with investment decisions being delayed. “Postponing early elections and staying in this stalemate situation would, at some point, also have economic negative consequences,” he said.
Bordering Ukraine, Romania has the sixth-largest population in the EU and plays a critical role in NATO’s defense of the region as home to a major military base and a U.S. missile shield site. The country has been plagued by political instability, corruption and a ballooning budget deficit in recent years, conditions that have fueled a surge in support for hard-right nationalist politics.
Since the coalition fell apart amid infighting over budget cuts in the spring, Romania’s deadlocked parliament has been unable to agree on a new government.
Alliance for the Union of Romanians (AUR) leader Simion, a staunch euroskeptic who has called for a halt to aid for Ukraine, told POLITICO the president must face his duty and give voters a chance to end the stalemate with a fresh election, or face being ousted. His party has been leading Romania’s opinion polls for almost two years.
Simion has been building support in parliament to censure the president, which he believes will gain momentum if Niculescu fails and Dan again refuses to call fresh elections.
Advertisement
“Everybody says, ‘OK, if this won’t pass, we will go to snap elections,’ but they do not know Nicușor Dan as I do,” Simion said. The president is “very stubborn” and could defy calls for elections even if all parties want them, he said. “In that case we will have the numbers of signatures and votes to suspend him at least, if not sack him.”
Dan has refused to contemplate handing AUR a role in government. He defeated Simion for the presidency last year and regards his rival’s politics as a threat to Romania’s pro-Western, pro-European direction. The president says he opposes a snap election because the campaign period would delay budget reforms and healthcare funding.
‘A new Greece’
The Romanian leu has weakened against the euro in the months since the crisis blew up. Simion urged international investors to remain patient and sought to reassure them that AUR would be fiscally responsible if it won power. “Nobody wants a new Greece,” he said. “We will do everything it takes to respect our commitments to our international partners and for them to recover the debts.”
The call for an early election is gaining traction in Bucharest.
So far, the leader of Dan’s former party, the Save Romania Union, has joined politicians from the National Liberal Party, and the leader of the Social Democratic Party and AUR, in suggesting an unprecedented emergency election could be required.
George Simion has been building support in parliament to censure the president. | Robert Ghement/EPA
Dan’s latest plan still has time to work, but political feuding between parties remains a problem. The Liberals say they could support Niculescu as prime minister if the Social Democrats do not get too much influence, while the Social Democrats say they want the PM-designate to take the country in a new direction — away from the austerity policies of the outgoing Liberal premier, Ilie Bolojan.
Advertisement
Mureșan, a pro-EU Liberal and European People’s Party vice-president, said the economic risks of prolonging the crisis were real. He told POLITICO a snap election could be inevitable, though this is not his “preferred” option. “The political uncertainty which exists now in the country can easily transform into economic uncertainty,” Mureșan warned. “We are already now seeing investors holding back on their investments, waiting with major investment decisions before they have more certainty.”
While Mureșan said he wants Dan to succeed, he criticized the delays in resolving the longest-running crisis since the fall of communism in 1989. “Had the president moved fast in appointing a prime minister in May and not delayed the nominations, we might even have had early elections [by] now, and we would be in a situation with a new parliament, and with a stable government with the four-year agenda,” he said.
“So, clearly, the options are narrowing down and are not getting better, following the prolongation of the political crisis.”

====================================================================================================

Can ‘Berlin’s Mamdani’ convince Jewish Berliners to trust the Left?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
02:00:00 UTC
11:00:00 KST

Getting into Gideon Joffe’s office takes some doing. Above the historic building in the heart of Berlin rises the golden dome of the New Synagogue, built in the 19th century. Out front, police officers ask who you are and where you’re headed. Past the first security door, your bag goes through a scanner. Then come more doors, all of them extra thick.
It’s not paranoia. Since the Oct. 7, 2023, attack on Israel by Hamas and the outbreak of the war in Gaza, antisemitism has surged across the Western world, according to a study by Tel Aviv University. Berlin — where senior Nazi officials gathered at a lakeside villa in 1942 to coordinate the murder of Europe’s Jews — is no exception.
Joffe, 54, who chairs the Jewish Community of Berlin, one of Germany’s largest, has grown used to a life under protection. For decades, such security has been a fact of Jewish life across Europe, with synagogues and schools fortified and, in many cities, guarded by armed police. But the situation has rarely been as bad as it is now, he tells me.
Advertisement
The Tel Aviv-born former businessman does not come across as a timid man: a firm handshake, a shirt straining at every seam and a deep and penetrating voice. Yet the mood at his conference table, where the community’s secretary general and its spokesperson also sit, is one of great concern.
The subject of that concern: The result of the recent Berlin election, in which the Left Party — a successor to the communist party that ruled East Germany until 1989 — came in first with 26% of the vote. It’s a record for the party in the capital, and more than double its previous result. Germany has been arguing about the consequences ever since.
Among the trio sitting at the table, the Left Party’s Berlin branch is seen as not just radically left-wing but also a hotbed of antisemitism. The party made opposition to Israel’s war in Gaza a central plank of its election campaign. While some Jews have declared their support for the Left, leading Jewish institutions have criticized it.
Elif Eralp takes a selfie while campaigning in the Marzahn district ahead of Berlin state elections on Sept. 15, 2026. | Sean Gallup/Getty Images
At the center of the debate is Elif Eralp, the Left’s lead candidate in the Berlin election who has become the face of the party’s transformation. Under Eralp and a younger generation of activists, many with immigrant backgrounds in the Muslim world, the party has expanded well beyond its East German roots and built a new urban coalition around housing, inequality and opposition to the war in Gaza.
Eralp and other prominent Left officials concede there have been troubling incidents among their supporters, and have condemned them. At a party conference shortly after the election, Eralp pledged to “strengthen the diverse Jewish life in Berlin and combat antisemitism.”
It was an acknowledgment of an issue that has been central to her effort to become mayor. In Germany, a single party is rarely strong enough to rule alone; forming a government means weeks of haggling among parties that dislike each other to varying degrees. If Eralp is to govern, she will need to form a coalition with the center-left Social Democrats and the Greens. Among their demands: “combating antisemitism and protecting Jewish life,” according to a joint statement by the two parties.
Advertisement
“There needs to be a binding agreement that not only condemns antisemitism and affirms Israel’s right to exist, but also stipulates clear consequences for antisemitic incidents,” SPD state chair Steffen Krach told the German press agency dpa.
The Left’s new face
“Elif! Elif! Elif!” As the petite woman in the black bomber jacket enters the hall, her comrades rise from their chairs and chant her name in rhythm. “Elif for Berlin,” read the banners in big, bright red letters. Her first major appearance since the Sept. 20 election is in a small hall at the headquarters of Neues Deutschland, a newspaper that once served as the official mouthpiece of East Germany’s communist dictatorship.
Eralp — a 45-year-old lawyer, mother of two and the daughter of Turkish socialists who fled to Germany in 1980, the year of a military coup in Turkey — is the new star of Germany’s hard left. She has thrilled young women and Muslim voters in droves. Her plea for economic justice, especially on Berlin’s crowded housing market, is what won the election, say her supporters. Critics say her success mainly depended on mobilizing pro-Palestinian activists, including some sharply hostile to Israel.
Eralp speaks to the media in Berlin on Sept. 21, 2026. | Sean Gallup/Getty Images
Eralp has been dubbed “Berlin’s Mamdani” by the press, and the comparison is more than cosmetic. Berlin’s Left borrowed from New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani’s playbook, right down to the political strategist who helped engineer his success: Morris Katz, a 27-year-old consultant who helped steer Mamdani to victory and flew to Berlin to coach Eralp this spring.
“If a leftist can win in New York, then one can just as well win in Berlin,” Eralp said after Mamdani’s 2025 election.
Where Mamdani, New York’s first Muslim mayor, promised city-owned grocery stores, Eralp promises neighborhood canteens with meals from €3. She wants a rent cap for the Berlin’s publicly owned housing and the “socialization” of big corporate landlords, taking public control of more than 200,000 apartments — which a majority of Berliners backed in a 2021 referendum. Mamdani had his potholes; Eralp has Berlin’s “garbage chaos.” Both have proven that rent bills and trash cans can win big-city elections. And both have had to rebut the same accusation of antisemitism, either personally or within their ranks.
Advertisement
Mamdani — a fierce critic of Israel who has called for the country’s Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu to be arrested — spent his campaign declining to condemn the slogan “globalize the intifada,” while saying he doesn’t use it himself and that it pains him to be called an antisemite. He eventually said he would discourage use of the phrase.
Since taking office, Mamdani has also sought to address the concerns of Jewish New Yorkers. In late September, he announced his city’s first municipal strategy to combat antisemitism, vowing that Jews in the city would be “safe and celebrated.”
Eralp, who like Mamdani calls herself a “democratic socialist,” faces similar skepticism from much of her city’s Jewish community. While international debate about antisemitism in the country has focused on the rise of the far-right Alternative for Germany party, since the election in Berlin, the controversy has centered on the Left.
Zohran Mamdani waves onstage in New York City on Oct. 3, 2026. | John Nacion/Getty Images
The party’s Berlin platform explicitly opposes antisemitism, but Eralp’s critics are not interested in what’s on paper. Instead, they point to an unofficial picture assembled from numerous examples: a campaign poster demanding “Freedom for Palestine”; the Berlin youth wing of the party that attributes a “colonial and racist character” to the “Israeli state project”; a rapper who shouted “Yalla yalla intifada” and “Death, death to the IDF” — Israel’s army — at a campaign event; and the appearance of a leading supporter of the Popular Front for the Liberation of Palestine, an EU- and U.S.-designated terrorist organization, at a Left victory party in Berlin.
Opposition to Israel’s policies in Gaza is not the same as antisemitism, and Eralp has condemned the appearances of the rapper and the PFLP supporter, blaming local party officials. But that hasn’t convinced her critics. Josef Schuster, president of the Central Council of Jews in Germany, has dismissed her expressions of concern about antisemitism as “lip service.”
Balancing act
Nowhere in Berlin has the Left changed more than in Friedrichshain-Kreuzberg, a borough of about 267,000 people. For decades, it was a stronghold of the Green Party. This time the Left won 44% there, more than double its previous result. The local party used to be run by old-school socialists, many of them veterans of the Socialist Unity Party, or SED, which ruled East Germany as a one-party dictatorship until the Berlin Wall fell in 1989.
Advertisement
Today, it is driven by young activists who have expanded the party’s base into immigrant communities, above all among young Muslims. For many of them, the principles that have guided German politics since the Holocaust — the duty to protect Jewish life and solidarity with Israel — carry little weight, and some reject them outright.
That leaves Eralp with a delicate balancing act: reassuring Jewish Berliners concerned about elements of her party while holding together the coalition that helped propel it to victory. In her first major speech after the election, she tried to do both.
The Left’s vision of an affordable and good life, she said to applause, had been stronger “than all attacks and stronger than the hatred.” She would not be showered with insults by the “most unpopular chancellor of all time” — a swipe at Merz — and other politicians in the federal government.
Israel supporters hold flags as people march to commemorate the anniversary of the Nakba, in Berlin on May 16, 2026. | Michele Tantussi/Getty Images
These centrist politicians, Eralp continued, were dividing the country, cutting labor rights and pensions and adopting the anti-migrant positions of the Alternative for Germany (AfD), the far-right party on track to secure its first state government after a breakthrough election last month. “While a fascist party in Saxony-Anhalt is on its way to power, these people seriously think they can stop a democratic party that stands for social justice, diversity and democracy with this smear campaign,” she said.
Next, Eralp presented an offer of reconciliation: The point was to “build bridges and bring people back together.” Then she offered a kind of self-criticism, but without getting specific. The Left, too, she said, must be clear “that there must never be calls for violence, and that statements that frighten Jewish people can never come from our platforms.”
Here, too, there was applause. But quite a few listeners had their arms folded. Some wore Palestinian scarves, known as keffiyehs, around their necks.
Advertisement
Eralp was not available after the party meeting, and her party’s co-chair, Ines Schwerdtner, declined an interview.
“Leave this country”
Michael Wolffsohn has grim advice for Jewish Berliners. The prominent historian and conservative commentator was born in Tel Aviv to a family of Jewish merchants from Berlin, who fled the Nazis for Palestine in 1939. As a boy, he came back with his parents to West Berlin.
In the magazine Cicero, Wolffsohn, 79, said what he would tell a young Jewish Berliner who asks whether to stay: with a heavy heart, “Leave this city and this country.” He himself, he added, was too old to uproot. Were he younger, he, too, would leave.
It is not hard to see why Berlin’s estimated 20,000 to 40,000 Jews are on edge. In the five years before the 2023 Hamas attack in Israel and the resulting war in Gaza, RIAS Berlin, a watchdog that tracks antisemitic incidents in the city whether or not they are crimes, logged just under 1,000 a year. Last year it counted 2,197. The police recorded an even steeper increase in crimes classified as antisemitic: from 381 in 2022 to 2,268 in 2025.
RIAS follows the definition of antisemitism laid out by the International Holocaust Remembrance Alliance, counting conduct ranging from insults and graffiti to statements at demonstrations. It says it did not simply count criticism of Israel’s conduct in Gaza or of the Israeli military as antisemitic, but did so when the situation in Gaza was used to disparage Jews collectively, justify violence against them or trivialize the Holocaust.
Some incidents were violent. RIAS recorded 39 physical attacks in Berlin last year, 16 of them in Friedrichshain-Kreuzberg. RIAS says multiple people who reported antisemitic incidents described becoming more cautious in daily life, including no longer openly wearing Jewish symbols after repeated harassment.
Advertisement
Speaking to POLITICO on the phone, Wolffsohn details his concerns: “Elif Eralp is the party’s star. But there is a broad base, and that’s what matters.”
Is the Left fit to govern the capital? His answer is categorical: “Is such a party capable of fulfilling the elementary task of a state — protecting its citizens, and not only the Jewish ones, at home and abroad? My answer is: No, absolutely not. The Left does not disqualify itself through opinions but through its demonstrable activities.”
A volunteer attaches portraits of Israelis killed since the Oct. 7, 2023 attack by Hamas at a commemorative installation in front of the Brandenburg Gate in Berlin on October 7, 2025. | Sean Gallup/Getty Images
Wolffsohn says he wouldn’t take a coalition contract at its word. Or a potential agreement that would commit all partners to fight antisemitism. “Paper is patient,” he says, using a German proverb: Paper will accept anything written on it.
At the moment, there isn’t even paper. Berlin’s leaders of the Left, the Social Democrats and the Greens have been meeting over the past week in “constructive” preliminary talks. They are gathering for a third round Wednesday, but have not yet agreed on a common line on antisemitism.
The trust test
Joffe, the chair of Berlin’s Jewish Community, extends the blame for rising antisemitism to Germany’s mainstream parties, which he says failed to tackle the problem. “I don’t know a single Jewish community member who is sure that his children or grandchildren will still be living in Germany.” A 2024 survey of more than 2,500 Jews across Germany found that more than half considered it unsafe to live visibly as a Jew in their city, while three-quarters said they felt less safe since Oct. 7, 2023.
In his heavily secured office, Joffe says he understands why many people find Eralp likeable. “She’s nobody’s fool, and she knows how to express herself,” he tells me. “But the antisemitic spirits in her party — she probably won’t be able to get them back into the bottle.”
Advertisement
Joffe often pauses to choose his words carefully. “There have been many statements from the Left Party that have unsettled the Jewish community,” he says. “But I don’t want the issue of antisemitism alone to decide whether a coalition comes together in Berlin or not. Then conspiracy theories will just resurface that we Jews are so powerful we can even help decide who governs this city.”
His test for Eralp’s party is less about what the Left promises than about what happens in the capital in the coming years, especially in schools and kindergartens.
The Left’s Berlin platform promises to fight antisemitism “effectively,” but also warns against the “instrumentalization” of antisemitism allegations. Joffe worries that its broader law-and-order agenda — including proposals to reduce police staffing, curb police resources and loosen restrictions on masked protesters — would make it harder to contain antisemitic intimidation and violence.
RIAS recorded antisemitic incidents at a record 239 rallies and marches last year. That’s four or five a week. On Sept. 27, 2025, the Left was among the groups that called for a Gaza march that drew up to 100,000 people. RIAS documented antisemitic incidents at the march and rally that followed, including placards equating Israel’s war with the Holocaust and chants of “child murderers” — language the watchdog says either trivializes the Nazis’ industrial-scale murder of six million Jews or draws on the centuries-old antisemitic blood-libel trope.
To leave Joffe’s office, you walk back through the three security doors and past the police officers at the entrance.
“Our Jewish institutions are physically protected, but not defended against antisemitism,” he told me at the end of our conversation. “What do I mean by that? A cocoon was built around our kindergartens, schools and synagogues. But socially, nothing was defended.”
Advertisement
Eralp has promised to make Jewish life safer. Whether she can persuade people like Joffe that she means it — and can deliver — is another question.

====================================================================================================

EU quietly braces for nightmare scenario of multiple-casualty hybrid attack
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
02:00:00 UTC
11:00:00 KST

EU capitals are quietly preparing for how the bloc should respond to a major hybrid attack that leaves several citizens dead — an outcome that looks increasingly likely, according to five EU diplomats and officials.
But the efforts to prepare are exposing splits on how much of a role the EU should play on security matters, and whether the bloc’s efforts are redundant with NATO.
The talks about a nightmare attack scenario have taken place in recent weeks among EU ambassadors from all 27 countries gathering in “restricted format,” meaning without phones or assistants. Discussions have ramped up since the discovery of an explosives-laden drone at Leipzig airport in August, said the diplomats and officials, who were granted anonymity to discuss the confidential exchanges.
While the EU has discussed such scenarios for years — unveiling a “hybrid toolbox” geared at coordinating responses to cyberattacks, election interference, and sabotage — the latest talks zeroed in on the risk of more serious attacks that cause large-scale casualties. Two diplomats said a meeting among EU ambassadors last Wednesday focused specifically on such examples.
Since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, the EU says Moscow has intensified a campaign of cyberattacks, sabotage and other covert operations across the bloc.
“Europe’s democracies are facing a growing number of threats,” European justice Commissioner Michael McGrath told POLITICO. “We are strengthening our capacity to anticipate and detect threats, improve early warning and ensure that Europe can respond quickly and collectively when our democratic resilience is tested.”
The talks among EU diplomats and ministers have focused on deploying emergency response teams, freeing up pockets of EU money to help the affected state, and how EU institution leaders should communicate, one EU official said.
“We have to be prepared for something serious,” a senior EU diplomat said. “Unfortunately, Leipzig showed us that a very serious incident, something that causes multiple casualties, is not out of the question.”
A second EU official added: “Given the scope and scale of Russia’s action there are bound to be casualties sooner than later. It’s sheer luck there haven’t been any yet.”
‘Very confusing’
The bloc is reeling from near-daily reports of so-called hybrid attacks — a label used by the EU and NATO to describe subversive activity that falls below the threshold of a direct act of war. On Tuesday, several sailors were declared missing after their ship was sunk by drones in the Black Sea, according to Bulgarian officials.
This followed the Leipzig airport incident, a suspicious fire at a Polish ground-link station handling Starlink communications, and a plot to plant incendiary devices in commercial transport hubs around the EU and U.K., alongside regular airspace violations.
“It is quite obvious that when Russia is using more and more lethal tools to test our preparedness and willingness to take counter measures, at some point there will be casualties,” said Teija Tiilikainen, director of the European Centre of Excellence for Countering Hybrid Threats. “At some point, intentionally or unintentionally, this is what happens.”
If several EU or NATO-member citizens are killed in what appears to be an attack, the pressure to act will be overwhelming on both institutions. “We’re very afraid that at some point an allied life” will be taken, said one NATO diplomat, which will make the “pressure very high” to act.
Yet EU-level discussions are prompting criticism from some capitals that the EU is overstepping its security role and potentially duplicating NATO’s core functions, the transatlantic alliance that has underpinned European security for 80 years.
“It risks being very confusing for decision-makers at all levels,” said Oana Lungescu, a distinguished fellow at RUSI and former spokesperson for NATO. “If there is confusion or duplication, that risks slowing down the decision-making, which has implications because time is always of the essence.”
Another problem is the EU’s lack of secure communications and suspicion that sensitive information shared during ambassador gatherings can be leaked, several diplomats said. Reports that Hungary’s ex-foreign minister shared the contents of leader-level talks with his Russian counterpart only deepened these concerns, leading capitals to restrict truly sensitive information to NATO formats.
“My government is very suspicious of sharing sensitive intelligence in Coreper or even in the leaders’ room,” said a diplomat from an eastern flank state. “It either shows up in the media or goes straight to Moscow.”
Overlapping protocols
The pushback coincides with European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen’s efforts to bolster the bloc’s security credentials.
In her latest State of the European Union speech in Strasbourg, the former German defense minister pitched an “emergency security protocol” to help EU states coordinate in exactly the kind of scenario being discussed. The protocol, along with von der Leyen’s pitch to create a “European Security Council,” is expected to feature in a landmark “European Security Strategy” due out in early November, according to two diplomats.
But several diplomats pushed back, arguing these efforts would take months to set up and potentially duplicate functions that already exist inside the EU.
Instead of creating new formats that add complexity, one senior national diplomat said the EU should double down on the crisis-response tools it already has.
“We’re very uncomfortable about [the] emergency security protocol,” the diplomat said. “We already have mechanisms in place. If there is a crisis, we have the Integrated Political Response (IPCR) that worked very well during the pandemic and other crises.”
Putin doesn’t care
Established under the scope of the Lisbon Treaty, the IPCR allows the holder of the EU’s rotating presidency, at the request of an affected country, to call emergency meetings involving experts from NATO, the U.N., or other international bodies.
In the event of a major hybrid attack, the onus remains on the affected country to decide on the best way forward. France triggered the EU’s Article 42.7 following the 2015 Bataclan attacks, marking the only time the mutual assistance clause has been invoked. However, Lungescu noted this was a “political decision” by Paris that did not lead to major displays of mutual assistance beyond coordinating terror investigations between France and Belgium.
To avoid confusion over who does what during a mass-casualty event, Lungescu said both parties should divide labor: NATO handling intelligence-sharing and military deterrence, and the EU focusing on civilian response.
For Tiilikainen, EU efforts to coordinate responses to hybrid attacks are useful — within limits. However, she noted they are “not comparable with resilience measures at a national level,” such as Finland’s “comprehensive security” approach.
Lungescu also stressed that Moscow makes no distinction between the two organizations. “Frankly, [Russian President Vladimir] Putin doesn’t care whether decisions are taken by Coreper 2 or the NAC,” she added, referring to the meetings of EU ambassadors or NATO’s decision-making body. “This is not how Moscow thinks.”
Victor Jack contributed reporting.

What is celebrated on October 7 in Ukraine and around the world
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
04:49:12 EEST
10:49:12 KST

What is celebrated on October 7 in Ukraine and around the world
Kyiv • UNN
October 7 marks the International Days of Cotton, Decent Work, Safe Way to School, and Trigeminal Neuralgia Awareness. Religious commemorative dates are also observed.
On October 7, the world marks International Walk and Bike to School Day and Trigeminal Neuralgia Awareness Day. What other holidays and commemorative days are observed on October 7 — read in the UNN article.
World Cotton Day
An official international UN observance proclaimed by the General Assembly in 2021 at the initiative of the “Cotton Four” countries and with the support of the FAO and the World Trade Organization.
The event highlights the importance of cotton as a critically important agricultural crop and global commodity that provides income for more than 100 million families in over 75 countries worldwide, stimulates the development of the textile industry, and contributes to poverty reduction in developing countries.
World Day for Decent Work
Established in 2008 by the International Trade Union Confederation. The event unites labor organizations around the world to protect workers’ fundamental rights, ensure fair wages, safe working conditions, social protection, the elimination of discrimination and forced labor, and the development of quality jobs.
International Walk and Bike to School Day
A global initiative launched in 1997 that brings together millions of schoolchildren, parents, and educators in more than 40 countries worldwide.
The event aims to promote an active and healthy lifestyle among children, reduce traffic congestion and harmful emissions around educational institutions, and draw attention to the creation of safe pedestrian and cycling infrastructure, the development of safe school routes, and the reduction of the risk of child injuries on the roads.
Trigeminal Neuralgia Awareness Day
A worldwide medical observance dedicated to a rare and extremely severe chronic neurological disease — trigeminal neuralgia, which, due to the intensity of its painful attacks, is often called the “suicide disease.”
The purpose of the day is to disseminate information about the symptoms and diagnostic methods for this condition, support patients and their families, encourage scientific research in neurosurgery and pharmacology to find effective treatment, and increase physicians’ awareness to ensure timely diagnosis.
Feast of Our Lady of the Rosary
A Catholic liturgical feast established by Pope Pius V in 1571 to commemorate the Holy League’s victory over the fleet of the Ottoman Empire in the naval Battle of Lepanto on October 7, 1571, which averted the threat of an Ottoman invasion of Europe.
The feast is dedicated to the prayer of the Rosary as a symbol of spiritual protection and the unity of the faithful.
Day of Remembrance of the Holy Martyrs Sergius and Bacchus
According to the new calendar, Orthodox and Greek Catholic faithful commemorate the Holy Martyrs Sergius and Bacchus — prominent Roman military commanders of the 3rd century during the reign of Emperor Maximian.
As secret Christians holding high positions at the imperial court, they refused to participate in pagan sacrifices, for which they were stripped of their military insignia, subjected to humiliating torture in Syria, and suffered martyrdom for their faith.
According to the old calendar, the faithful commemorate Saint Thecla of Iconium, the First Martyr and Equal-to-the-Apostles — a disciple of the Apostle Paul in the 1st century. Inspired by his preaching, she took a vow of virginity and refused to marry a wealthy pagan, enduring severe trials and torture for her faith.

Indian police have detained opposition leader Rahul Gandhi during a protest march demanding the resignation of the country's election chief over the large-scale deletion of millions of names from national voter lists.
Police intercepted Gandhi, a senior leader of the main opposition Congress Party, along with fellow lawmakers as they marched from parliament to the Election Commission of India headquarters.
Officers took Gandhi into custody after he climbed atop a police barricade waving the national flag, releasing him shortly afterwards.
Gandhi and his lawmaker sister, Priyanka Gandhi Vadra, then barricaded themselves inside the adjacent offices of the state broadcaster.

The street demonstrations follow explosive revelations published last month by The Indian Express, which reported that two of the election commission's three panel members formally objected at least 14 times to key decisions regarding the roll revision.
The report disclosed that authorities have struck roughly 130 million citizens off electoral registries since the purge began in 2025.
Opposition figures argue the exercise disproportionately disenfranchises marginalised and minority communities, particularly Muslims, accusing the commission of doing the bidding of Prime Minister Narendra Modi's Hindu nationalist Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP).
The Election Commission maintains the revision seeks solely to remove fraudulent registrations and eliminate "foreign illegal immigrants", though commission chief Gyanesh Kumar has declined to comment publicly.
Meanwhile, youth movements and left-wing student groups have called for mass mobilisations on Saturday, as India's Supreme Court ordered the government and the election authority to formally justify the revision decisions ahead of hearings next week.

MADRID, Oct. 6 (Xinhua) -- Mikel Merino scored twice in the second half as world champion Spain fought back from a goal down to beat Croatia 2-1 in Split on Tuesday.
The win extended Spain's unbeaten run to 42 matches and secured its place in the UEFA Nations League quarterfinals with four wins from four group games.
Merino provided the goals, while goalkeeper Unai Simon made several crucial saves to keep Spain in the contest.
Croatia coach Slaven Bilic, responding to his team's humiliating 7-0 defeat to England on Saturday, said he wanted a "game for men" and got the physical response he sought in a robust first half.
Although Spain, with Lamine Yamal, Pedri and Rodri in the starting lineup, enjoyed more possession in the opening period, the team was frequently uncomfortable.
Simon made an acrobatic stop to deny Josip Stanisic and later blocked Igor Matanovic after a counterattack, only for Ivan Perisic to follow up and score from the rebound in the 20th minute.
Simon made another point-blank save to deny Matanovic shortly afterward before getting down quickly to smother an effort from Josko Gvardiol.
Mikel Oyarzabal wasted Spain's best first-half opportunity with a tame header from Aymeric Laporte's cross, while Yamal dragged a shot into the side netting.

Simon produced another fine stop in the 78th minute after an error by Martin Zubimendi, who had replaced Rodri, presented Perisic with a chance. Perisic was sent off a minute later after receiving a second yellow card for a reckless challenge from behind on Marc Cucurella.
