====================================================================================================

Eva Marie Saint, last star of Hollywood's Golden Age, has died at 102
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
01:42:46 UTC
10:42:46 KST

Eva Marie Saint, the last star of Hollywood's Golden Age, dies at 102
Eva Marie Saint, who has died aged 102, was showered in awards across her long career. Her performances spanned from her first stage appearances in 1942 to her final film appearance in 2019.
But while she was the last star of Hollywood's Golden Age, it was television's Golden Age where she began her long career. And it was television and then even newer formats like podcasting that sustained it.
Saint was celebrated as a film star, particularly for her landmark performances working with Hollywood's best directors, including Elia Kazan, Alfred Hitchcock, Otto Preminger and John Frankenheimer.
While her film acting led to awards and nominations from the BAFTAs to the Oscars, films are only one part of a diverse career.
She received an Oscar in 1955 for On the Waterfront and an Emmy in 1990 for the miniseries People Like Us. There was a Drama Critics Award in 1953 for The Trip to Bountiful on Broadway. In 2012, she received a Behind the Voice Actors Voice Acting Award for her work on the animated series The Legend of Korra (2012–14).
Her many awards, and even more nominations, reveal her astonishing capacity to reinvent herself not just in the roles she played but the media she appeared on.
Saint showed rare versatility by changing image and style and medium and format across eight decades.
The golden age of television
Born in 1924, before the development of television and even the talkies, Saint made her television debut in 1947 in Charles Dickens's A Christmas Carol.
Saint was fortunate to be in the right place at the right time for the first Golden Age of American television.
This Golden Age gave Saint and other actors not just employment but a national audience for serious drama.
Commercial sponsorship also meant actors like Saint were infamously obliged to advertise products as well as act.
Saint had an ongoing role in the successful TV drama Martin Kane Private Eye (1949–54). But sponsorship from the United States Tobacco Company meant the cast had to, not too subtly, advertise pipes and cigarettes by talking about smoking in each episode.
Television kept her fully occupied until her big screen debut in 1954's On the Waterfront.
A move to the big screen
Today, Saint's fame rests on two entirely different films: the intense black-and-white drama about dockside corruption in On the Waterfront (1954), and spy thriller film North by Northwest (1959).
From director Elia Kazan, On the Waterfront was Saint's breakout film role in a heavy hitting movie set among men who worked on the docks. Also starring Marlon Brando, the film received eight Oscars, including Best Supporting Actress for Saint.
At least one person wasn't a fan — Alfred Hitchcock wanted to use Saint in a more glamorous role and setting.
"It's drab in that tenement house. Women go to the movies, and they've just left the sink at home. They don't want to see you at the sink," Hitchcock told her.
Normally, one break out role would be enough for any actor. But Saint had two. Showing the cycles of invention and reinvention that propelled her career, Saint moved from black-and-white intensity to colour adventure.
The "Hitchcock Blonde" is a fixture of the director's films — Grace Kelly, Tippi Hedron and Kim Novak are among them — and in North by Northwest Hitchcock added Saint to their ranks.
Playing a femme fatale (or is she?) pitched against good guy Cary Grant, Saint stepped far away from the drabness of On the Waterfront in an adventure sweeping across the United States to the final exciting chase across Mount Rushmore.
North by Northwest remade Saint's image as a glamorous blonde but her film career afterwards lacked consistency: Exodus (1960) was a hit; All Fall Down (1962) lost money at the box office.
Back to television — and to podcasts
Saint began on television, and it was television that sustained her career.
After her big screen career declined in the 1970s, Saint returned to television with award-winning success.
She received Emmy nominations for How the West Was Won (1976–79) and Taxi!!! (1978), and appeared on TV in works as diverse as Frasier (1992–2004) and Moonlighting (1985–89).
Other changes involved a shift to the superhero film in 2006's Superman Returns, and children's animation in Nickelodeon's The Legend of Korra (2012–14). Finally, she was podcasting in scripted comedy The Pack Podcast, aged 98.
Other golden age legends like Olivia de Havilland lived long lives, but few remained so active across so many mediums as Eva Marie Saint.
Fewer still showed the same ability to change in ways that found new audiences and new media over a career of 80 years.
Marcus Harmes is a professor in pathways education at the University of Southern Queensland. This piece first appeared on The Conversation.

All suffering is a kind of loss. I want to escape from suffering, so I try to control my attention…
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

All suffering is a kind of loss. I want to escape from suffering, so I try to control my attention and actions towards that goal. But in doing so, I lose the opportunity to reach the more joyful life that I could be living. That this loss occurs only because I’m attached to my own intentions is a tragedy.
I don’t need to suffer, but I do because I’m not well-accustomed to existing as the kind of being that I am. I reflect on my experiences and I automatically judge them to be good or bad, which means I form intentions about the world around me. This entirely ordinary human capability causes me to be sucked into attachment. And the result of attachment is always suffering and the loss of joy. This loss is not valuable. I do not gain anything by suffering more. I’ve already suffered enough to understand suffering, provided I’m willing to examine it.

Hong Kong’s AI city brain must understand how people really speak

3-MIN READ3-MIN

Dr Zhisheng (Edward) Wen is an associate division head and senior lecturer in the College of Professional and Continuing Education at Hong Kong Polytechnic University, where he researches and teaches second language acquisition, translanguaging and cognitive science. 
Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu’s vision of an “AI city brain” is bold and timely. An integrated system linking data across transport, public works, environmental monitoring and emergency response could help Hong Kong manage risks more proactively and coordinate services more effectively.

IN BRIEF
- Richard Morecroft has died aged 70, after sharing his cancer diagnosis in July 2026.
- Morecroft spent almost twenty years leading the ABC's 7pm NSW news bulletin.
Former ABC News presenter and SBS host Richard Morecroft has been remembered as a generational talent.
Morecroft died "at a time of his choosing" on NSW's south coast on Tuesday, aged 70, following his cancer diagnosis earlier in 2026, his family said.
"We are devastated to lose such a warm, generous and caring human and hope that all those who knew him, if only through their TV screens, will remember him fondly," they wrote in a statement shared via Morecroft's Instagram page.
Morecroft moved from England to Australia aged 10, studying at the University of Adelaide before taking a post at the ABC via the university's radio station.
He presented ABC's South Australian news bulletin before moving to Sydney, where he went on to host the network's 7pm NSW news bulletin from 1983 to 2002.
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
Morecroft also hosted the quiz show Letters and Numbers on SBS and ABC's popular children's current affairs program Behind the News.
'A beloved part of Australian life'
Prime Minister Anthony Albanese described the former presenter as a consummate professional with heart.
"I was very sorry to hear of the passing of Richard Morecroft," he said on Wednesday.
"As the face and the voice of the news of the ABC, Richard became a beloved part of Australian life."
He reflected on revelations Morecroft, a passionate environmentalist, sometimes kept a baby flying fox under his desk while presenting the news.
"Richard was a great Australian and we were lucky to have him as part of our lives," Albanese said.
SBS Managing Director Jane Palfreyman said the broadcaster was "deeply saddened" by the passing of "one of Australia's most respected and familiar broadcasters".
"We extend our heartfelt condolences to Richard's family, friends and former colleagues, and pay tribute to his wide and varied contribution to Australian television," she said.
Morecroft hosted the SBS quiz show Letters and Numbers from 2010 to 2012, alongside Lily Serna.
"Richard brought warmth, intelligence and a dry wit to SBS's Letters and Numbers," Palfreyman said.
He introduced a "generation of viewers to the joy of words and numbers across a remarkable 450 episodes".
"These episodes continue to be repeated today, reflecting Richard's enduring appeal."
'Universally admired and respected'
Fellow ABC veteran and Australian Story presenter Leigh Sales said Morecroft took pains to welcome her to the Sydney newsroom as a junior reporter.
"Richard Morecroft was not only a consummate presenter, he was a true gentleman — generous and courteous to a fault," she said.
"He was universally admired and respected."
Hugh Marks, ABC's managing director, said Morecroft was among the "great broadcasters of his generation".
Morecroft shared an update about his cancer diagnosis to social media in July after returning home to the south coast from a long stint in hospital.
"Soaking up the last rays of the winter sun on a chilly Jervis Bay afternoon," he wrote alongside a beachside selfie.
"It's heaven to come home after nearly six weeks in hospital at the Chris O'Brien Lifehouse in Sydney."

In an exclusive interview with Reuters, Vance said any agreement would require Iran to reduce its nuclear enrichment capacity, rather than offer assurances of future nuclear drawdowns.
"If you don't want a nuclear weapon, then why do you need 60% enriched fuel? And if you want to show commitment to not building a nuclear weapon, don't build highly enriched fuel.
That's a very basic threshold issue," Vance said.
"I think if they want to show a commitment to not building a nuclear weapon, they would do something meaningful on their enrichment capacity."
Vance said the US remained open to an agreement but would require concrete Iranian nuclear concessions.
"We're not going to trade words for actions," Vance said.

Vance said Washington is uncertain who makes decisions in Tehran.
The US vice president said that White House was in talks with Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian and Foreign Minister Abbas Araqchi. But it was unclear how much authority they wield within Iran's power structure, he said, after joint US-Israeli strikes at the start of the war killed Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei.
"One of the things we picked up on is it's not totally clear how their country makes decisions," Vance said. Separately, Trump said on Tuesday his "biggest problem" is no one knows who is running Iran.
Iran's Foreign Ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baghaei said on Sunday that US officials are well aware of who their Iranian counterparts are and how Iran's decision-making system works.
Vance told Reuters he has held personal conversations with field commanders to gauge battlefield conditions.
He dismissed concerns over critical munitions shortages and added that while Iranian troops are periodically able to strike commercial ships in the Strait of Hormuz, they are largely unable to prevent energy exports through the waterway.
The war — and its $3 billion monthly price tag — has become a key issue on the campaign trail. Higher energy prices have put Trump and Republicans on the defensive in competitive states that will decide control of Congress.
Vance is seen as a leading Republican contender to succeed Trump in the White House.
Vance told Reuters afterwards that he had not decided whether to seek the presidency in 2028.
"I'm inherently a procrastinator," he said. "I really haven't thought about it much."

What happens in the brain when cannabis makes you anxious?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
01:26:07 UTC
10:26:07 KST

What happens in the brain when cannabis makes you anxious?
Scientists have pinpointed brain cells that may explain why cannabis can suddenly turn a calm experience into intense anxiety.
- Date:
- October 6, 2026
- Source:
- Northwestern University
- Summary:
- Cannabinoids may intensify anxiety by removing a natural brake on specific neurons in the brain’s fear center, particularly during stressful situations. In mice, shutting down those neurons sharply reduced cannabinoid-related anxious behavior.
- Share:
Northwestern scientists have identified, for the first time, a specific group of neurons -- cells in the brain -- that appear to contribute to anxiety caused by cannabinoid drugs, particularly when those drugs are combined with stressful conditions. Cannabinoids are a category of substances that includes THC, the main psychoactive ingredient in cannabis.
To investigate how cannabinoids influence fear and anxiety, researchers exposed mice to a threatening smell derived from fox urine. Before encountering the odor, the animals were given either a placebo or a synthetic cannabinoid drug.
Mice that received the cannabinoid froze more frequently and spent less time exploring the predator scent. Researchers traced these anxiety related behaviors to increased activity in a small population of brain cells known as somatostatin neurons. These neurons are located in the central amygdala, an area of the brain involved in processing fear and stress.
When the researchers genetically silenced the somatostatin neurons, the mice that received the cannabinoid became less likely to avoid the predator odor. The result suggested that these cells play an important role in producing the anxious response.
"The results of this study could explain why a good trip can turn bad pretty quickly if people consume too much cannabis or the situation they are in turns stressful or scary," said study senior author Dr. Sachin Patel, chair of psychiatry and behavioral sciences at Northwestern University Feinberg School of Medicine.
The study was published on Oct. 2 in Nature Communications.
Tracking the Brain During a Threat
Patel and his colleagues gave mice several different doses of the synthetic cannabinoid and measured their reactions to the predator odor. The researchers recorded how much time the animals spent near the scent and whether they responded by freezing or fleeing.
At the same time, the team monitored activity inside the brain by implanting a small microscope into the mice's brain.
Researchers also studied brain tissue to determine how cannabinoids changed communication between neurons. Their experiments showed that the drug weakened a natural brain mechanism that normally acts as a "brake" on somatostatin neurons. With that restraint reduced, the neurons became more active.
"Higher doses of cannabinoids and environmental stress worked together to synergistically release the 'brake' on the central amygdala, which in turn drove excessive anxiety," Patel explained.
Why Cannabis and Anxiety Matter
Cannabis use in the U.S. has steadily increased in recent years. At the same time, emergency department visits involving adverse effects from the drug have also risen.
Previous studies have found an association between cannabis use and a higher long term risk of anxiety. Anxiety and mood disorders are also on the rise globally.
"Understanding how cannabis affects brain function to generate its psychoactive effects could ultimately reveal new ways to counteract negative consequences should they arise in some people," Patel said.
The researchers believe the findings may also have relevance beyond cannabis related side effects. Patel said the same neurons could potentially represent a broader target for understanding or reducing anxiety.
"Suppressing the activity of somatostatin neurons in the central amygdala could represent a final pathway for reducing anxiety symptoms, not just in the context of cannabis side effects," he explained.
Other Northwestern co-authors are Farhana Yasmin, Saptarnab Naskar, Danyal Zaidi, Isaac Kandil, Michelle Kwon and Dr. Luis Rosas-Vidal.
The study is titled, "Cannabinoid Modulation of Central Amygdala Population Dynamics During Threat Investigation." It was supported by the National Institutes of Health (grants MH100785 and K08 MH126166) and the Brain & Behavior Research Foundation's Young Investigator Awards.
Story Source:
Materials provided by Northwestern University. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- Farhana Yasmin, Saptarnab Naskar, Danyal Zaidi, Isaac Kandil, Michelle Kwon, Luis E. Rosas-Vidal, Sachin Patel. Cannabinoid modulation of central amygdala population dynamics during threat investigation. Nature Communications, 2026; 17 (1) DOI: 10.1038/s41467-026-77957-4

Houthis launch missiles at Yemen's Aden airport as fighting intensifies

Houthis attack Aden airport as fighting intensifies in Yemen
SANAA – Yemen’s Houthis attacked Aden’s international airport with ballistic missiles and explosive-laden drones on Oct 7, said the country’s Transport Ministry, as fighting between the Iran-aligned group and Saudi-backed government forces intensified.
Fighting has been focused in recent days on areas around the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, a shipping route that has become more crucial for energy exports since the conflict between the US and Iran restricted trade through the Strait of Hormuz.
This week, Yemeni government forces with Saudi-led coalition air support launched a counter-offensive to recapture strategic territory near the strait and around the town of Mokha that the Houthis had captured in September, but it is unclear if their advance will hold.
The fighting, a spillover from the wider US-Iran conflict, has revived a complex 12-year war in Yemen that led to one of the worst humanitarian crises globally and fragmented the Arab world’s most impoverished country.
The Houthis have repeatedly targeted infrastructure including airports, oil refineries and pipelines in Saudi Arabia, an American ally.
On Oct 7, the Saudi-led coalition said it had intercepted and destroyed a Houthi ballistic missile north of the Saudi capital Riyadh. It said it was tracking the launch platform over the Yemeni capital Sanaa and would destroy it, but gave no details of casualties or damage.
Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree said in a statement that the group had targeted King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh with several drones. There was no immediate Saudi confirmation of an attack on the airport.
Battles over the strait
Fighting on the western front remains concentrated in the Dhubab district overlooking Bab el-Mandeb, with pro-government forces attempting an advance in the strategic hills to the east of that coastal plain, Yemeni military and government sources said.
Fierce clashes have taken place, with the Houthis claiming they have repelled attacks.
On Oct 5, the Yemeni government said it had reached Mokha, which sits at a junction with a supply route to the critical battleground of Taiz, but the claim was premature, according to Yemeni military officials and analysts.
Hussam Radman, a researcher at the Sanaa Center, a Yemen-focused think-tank, said pro-government forces including the Giants Brigade, a conservative Sunni Salafi group that has led the counter-offensive, are trying to take control of Dhubab and to advance in the mountains to its east.
Control of those highlands would allow government forces to more easily advance up the rest of the coast, he said.
Airport struck
Along Yemen’s coast to the east, one missile landed near the runway at Aden International Airport minutes before a flight from Cairo was due to land, the Transport Ministry said.
The authorities cancelled the landing and diverted the aircraft to Jeddah, while two planes on the runway were moved away from the area over fears of further strikes, it added. There was no immediate comment from the Houthis.
Aden International Airport is the main international gateway for parts of Yemen outside Houthi control.
The Houthis, who control much of Yemen’s north, seized Sanaa in 2014, prompting a military coalition led by Saudi Arabia, fearful of rival Iran’s influence in Yemen and chaos on its borders, to intervene.
A UN-brokered truce in 2022 largely halted heavy fighting, but it did not lead to a lasting settlement.
The Saudi-led coalition accuses Iran of arming, training and funding the Houthis.
The group, mountain fighters who have emerged as a force of tens of thousands with missiles and drones that threatens the region, denies being part of Iran’s Middle East proxy network, and says it develops its own weapons.
Tehran also rejects the allegations.
Earlier on Oct 7, the Saudi-led coalition said it had intercepted and destroyed a Houthi ballistic missile launched towards the south-western Saudi city of Khamis Mushait, Saudi state television reported.
In a separate statement, Saree said the Houthis had attacked Saudi Arabia’s Abha International Airport and an airbase in Khamis Mushait with ballistic missiles and drones.
The Saudi authorities did not immediately confirm an attack on Abha airport. REUTERS

Awad Rjoob and Rania Abushamala

Israel has refused to allow representatives of the Palestinian Central Elections Commission to enter Gaza and occupied East Jerusalem ahead of legislative elections scheduled for late November, a Palestinian source said Tuesday.
The Palestinian news agency Wafa quoted an unnamed official source as saying the Israeli government had denied the commission entry to oversee the electoral process. No further details were provided.
On July 9, Palestinian President Mahmoud Abbas issued a decree setting Nov. 28 as the date for legislative elections in East Jerusalem, the occupied West Bank and Gaza. If held, they would be the first such elections since 2006.
The commission began accepting applications to register electoral lists on Sept. 26, receiving eight applications during the first four days. Registration remains open until Oct. 13.
Palestinian Vice President Hussein al-Sheikh told journalists on Aug. 2 that an alternative arrangement would be pursued if elections could not take place because they were prevented or obstructed in Gaza or any other part of the Palestinian territories.
“The alternative plan is to form the Palestinian National Council by consensus, as the Palestine Liberation Organization is the sole legitimate representative of the Palestinian people,” he said.
About 2.97 million Palestinians are eligible to vote, including approximately 1.59 million in the West Bank, 1.24 million in Gaza and 140,000 holders of Jerusalem identity cards.
The last Palestinian legislative elections were held in 2006, when Hamas won a majority of seats.
A political split followed between Hamas and Fatah. Hamas took control of Gaza about a year later, while the Fatah-led Palestinian Authority remained in the West Bank.
The Palestinian Legislative Council has been inactive since 2007. The Supreme Constitutional Court ordered its dissolution in 2018.

UN should clarify criteria for neutral state status — Russian Federation Council speaker

10:09:41 KST

TURKMENBASY, Turkmenistan, October 7. /TASS/. The United Nations should clarify the criteria for the status of a neutral state and update the concept in line with modern realities so that it is not "blurred," Russian Federation Council Speaker Valentina Matviyenko told reporters.
According to Matviyenko, Switzerland, which has traditionally been considered a neutral state, is moving away from this status because it follows the European Union’s directives and supports what she described as illegal sanctions, resulting in the "erosion" of the concept. Switzerland is not the only country behaving this way in today’s turbulent world, Matviyenko noted.
"I think the time has come for the United Nations to once again analyze its documents and provisions and ensure that if a state has permanent neutrality status, it strictly complies with all international rules established by the UN Charter and adheres to them. Perhaps the status of a neutral state should be clarified, perhaps updated in light of what is happening, so that the concept is not blurred and does not become merely decorative," she said.
At the same time, Turkmenistan, as the Federation Council speaker noted, is a genuinely sovereign state pursuing an independent and balanced foreign policy in the interests of its country and people. It is a state that does not succumb to any pressure, is not beholden to anyone and does not support illegal sanctions, she said. "This is exactly how countries with neutral state status should behave. And I want to say that Russia highly values Turkmenistan’s consistent position in maintaining permanent neutrality," she said.

Trump says Iran could ‘take’ San Diego, Los Angeles; draws cross-party ire
Both Democrats and Republicans have expressed outrage at Trump’s remarks, as the White House disputed their interpretation.
Members of the Republican Party have joined Democrats in questioning remarks made by United States President Donald Trump about the California cities of Los Angeles and San Diego.
Much of the backlash came on Tuesday, a day after Trump told a midterm rally in Nebraska that Americans should be willing to make sacrifices to deny Iran a nuclear weapon — even though Tehran has long rejected accusations that it is seeking atomic bombs.
“It’s a small price to pay for keeping the world safe, keeping our country safe,” Trump said, seemingly in reference to the knock-on effects of the war, including rising fuel and fertiliser prices.
Then, he said: “They can take out a city. Let them take out Los Angeles. Let them take out San Diego. This is a very small price to pay, and it’s going to be over with very soon.”
The White House said Trump was arguing that if Iran were allowed to secure a nuclear weapon, it could strike US cities.
But Democrats and some Republicans accused the president of suggesting that some of the country’s cities were expendable.
Gavin Newsom, the Democratic governor of California and outspoken critic of Trump, said the president was “deranged”.
“This is not only madness. This is dangerous,” Newsom said in a video on the social media platform X, in which he called for Congress to rein in Trump’s behaviour.
Trump has downplayed the impact of the US-Israel war on Iran – now in its eighth month – despite polling that shows the conflict is widely unpopular in the country. He has also repeatedly promised the war would end soon, though no lasting ceasefire has been reached so far.
Newsom, a possible contender in the 2028 presidential race, has clashed repeatedly with Trump.
Last year, the two faced off over Trump’s decision to deploy federal troops to California, as part of an effort to support a crackdown on undocumented immigration in the Los Angeles area.
In December, a federal judge ruled that the deployment had been illegal and ordered its end. Newsom, who opposed the deployment, cited that conflict in his remarks about Trump’s Nebraska rally.
“The president of the United States – the same one who sent in the National Guard into Los Angeles, sent 700 active duty Marines to the second-largest city in the United States of America – just invited Iran to take out Los Angeles and San Diego,” Newsom said.
He added that Trump’s remarks should convince those who “didn’t think the November election mattered” to vote in the upcoming midterms.
Some from Trump’s party have also expressed shock at his remarks.
Jim Desmond, a Republican running for California’s 48th congressional district, was among those who distanced themselves from Trump’s statement.
“I vehemently disagree with President Trump’s comments. America must stand up to Iran and defend our interests, but the first responsibility of our Commander in Chief is to protect the American people and our homeland,” Desmond wrote on X.
“No American city is expendable, and no American family should ever be treated as collateral damage.”
US Representative Kevin Kiley, an independent who caucuses with Republicans and is running for re-election in northern California, also called Trump’s comments “unhelpful”.
But the White House has dismissed criticism of the remarks, calling it part of a “media freakout” that “is not rooted in reality”.
“He was clearly stating U.S. cities would have been threatened if a nuclear Iran hadn’t been stopped,” Steven Cheung, White House director of communications, wrote on social media.
“America is safer because of the President. Iran has no nuclear, no navy, no air force, and no money.”
California has the largest population and economy of any state in the US. Because of its population, it also has the most seats in the House – 52.
All 435 seats in the House are up for grabs in November’s midterms, along with a third of the Senate. Also on the ballot are key state and local races.
With Republicans’ control of Congress on the line, the results of the midterms are expected to weigh heavily on the final two years of Trump’s second term.

MPs want 130,000 trained civilians ready for national crises

Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07

MPs want 130,000 trained civilians ready for national crises
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
MPs want 130,000 civilians trained to support the police, army and emergency services during major crises, and have asked the cabinet to open up defence ministry facilities to help make it happen.
A majority in parliament backed a motion by the centrist Christian Democrat CDA on Tuesday calling for that number of so-called civilian reservists within 4 years, public broadcaster NOS reported.
The volunteers would not join the armed forces, but would be a support force around them. Their specific role would be to stop chaos breaking out in the first three days of a disaster, when the emergency and security services are not expected to cope alone.
According to NOS, they would be trained in 3 areas – technical, logistics and security – drawing on people such as mechanics, drivers and security guards.
MPs want the cabinet to help in kind rather than with money, by making defence ministry training grounds and classrooms available free of charge. The cabinet has said it shares the aim.
From 1,000 to 130,000
The 130,000 figure matches the long-term target of De BurgerReserve, a privately run organisation that began training volunteers last year. Its two-day course at the national training centre in Vught ends with a simulated disaster and is paid for by employers and private individuals.
The organisation has trained around 1,000 people so far this year, NOS said. Reaching 130,000 within 4 years would mean training more than 30,000 people a year, while the courses listed on its website take up to 64 people each.
Fears over cyberattacks and strikes on infrastructure through AI have spread rapidly this year, with intelligence service AIVD warning the Netherlands has not been at such a high level of risk since the second world war.
Catching up
The vote follows a government campaign urging households to prepare for the first 72 hours of a crisis. Every home received an emergency booklet over the winter, and in February half of households said they now stock emergency provisions accordingly.
Karen van Oudenhoven-van der Zee, director of the social and cultural planning bureau SCP, told current affairs programme Nieuwsuur that investment in the armed forces was out of proportion to the attention paid to people and society.
She said the 2027 budget sets aside €40 million for neighbourhoods and communities, falling to €20 million in the two years after that.
“When it comes to resilience, we have catching up to do,” she said.

Haiti postpones elections indefinitely amid gang violence
Haiti has indefinitely postponed elections scheduled for December and February, the electoral council said Tuesday, citing technical and operational requirements as gang violence continues to disrupt preparations. The delay leaves Haitians without a democratic process as authorities struggle to register voters and secure areas needed for the poll.
Haiti, which has been engulfed by years of gang violence and political chaos, has indefinitely postponed elections due to be held later this year, officials said Tuesday.
Haiti has not held elections since 2016, and its last president, assassinated in 2021, has not been replaced.
The first round of presidential and legislative elections was set for December 13, and the second round for February 21, 2027.
"The period originally scheduled for the electoral campaign has been postponed," the Provisional Electoral Council's statement said, omitting any mention of a new election date and adding that the timetable "will be made public as soon as possible".
The council says the schedule will be updated to take into account the "technical and operational requirements of the process, as well as the conditions necessary for the proper conduct of the various stages".

It adds, however, that voter registration is continuing.
A member of the electoral council, speaking to AFP on the condition of anonymity, confirmed that "the December 13 date no longer stands", adding that "we are working on a new timetable".
As of Tuesday, only 769,000 voters had been registered since the process began on July 20.
Holding elections has been seen as a crucial step to stabilising the Haitian government and tackling rampant gang crime.
"I didn't have high hopes about going to vote this year," Davidson Jean Baptiste, a taxi driver in the capital Port-au-Prince, told AFP.
"Who can claim to hold elections in a country where the citizens are more concerned about insecurity and the abuses by armed groups?"
Some Haitians hope their country can get back on the path to democracy as soon as possible.
"The people have been long kept out of the political debate," said Claudette Piard at a voter registration centre in Delmas.
"We finally want to vote for a government that will bring solutions to the masses," she added.

Engulfed by violence
The Caribbean country, the poorest in the Americas, has long faced a political, economic and security crisis, but the situation has deteriorated in recent years as gangs step up killings, kidnappings, rape and child recruitment.
Of its approximately 11 million inhabitants, nearly 1.5 million are internally displaced by violence, according to the International Organization for Migration, which stressed that attacks were not confined to the capital.

The security crisis has also presented challenges to organisers hoping to coordinate a vote across the country.
Several municipalities under gang control did not have registration centres, and the closure of roads from gang threats have prevented the delivery of electoral materials to several parts of the island nation.
The country's gang violence crisis has left at least 5,700 people dead or wounded this year while more than 1,000 women and girls have been raped, UN human rights chief Volker Turk said last week.

OpenAI came to Australia to apologise. It will leave without answering these key questions | Toby Walsh
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
01:00:37 UTC
10:00:37 KST

OpenAI’s CEO Sam Altman was asked to appear before the Joint Select Committee on Artificial Intelligence in Australia and explain how and why their agents have been hacking into multiple government websites. Altman didn’t turn up but sent Jason Kwon, his chief strategy officer, instead to answer the committee’s many tricky questions on its first day of public hearings on Tuesday.
The committee is conducting a comprehensive inquiry into the economic, societal, regulatory, and national security implications of AI for Australia. It will report back to parliament at the end of November. This is an unusually fast pace, but then it’s an unusually fast paced technology.
Kwon spent much of the inquiry apologising for the company’s failings. A chief strategy officer would know there really was no other strategy than to eat a lot of humble pie and promise none of this would happen again.
Humanity was lucky that it was just the incompetence of OpenAI’s employees that resulted in these hacking incidents, rather than the competence of their AI agents. The hacks were relatively modest. For instance, as far as we know, no personal data was compromised.
But we now get a chance to prepare for much worse. Because you can expect AI agents to become much more competent, and AI hacks to be much more harmful. It won’t just be human hackers that understand cybersecurity that will be trying to hack into your website. And those AI hackers will be coming at you at machine speed.
Given OpenAI’s carelessness, it was disappointing that the committee didn’t lob a few harder questions at Kwon.
Someone should have asked him why OpenAI had no oversight for months over the swarm of agents hacking websites around the world? How many millions of dollars were spent on these experiments with no insight on what the agents were doing?
Someone should have asked him why OpenAI thinks it is safe to release Dots, their latest agent framework which puts similar technology into the hands of the public? OpenAI failed completely to monitor and prevent their agents doing harm. How do they expect random members of the public to do better?
Someone should have asked him why we should accept “bad things” in return for the benefits of AI (as Altman said in an interview on Monday)? We don’t accept drugs killing a few patients because they cure most patients. Or a few planes crashing because most land safely.
And someone should have asked him whether OpenAI is burning money so fast it’s cutting corners to get its products into the hands of paying customers quicker? For every dollar of income OpenAI currently takes, it spends about three dollars.
None of this needed to have happened. The problem is that companies like OpenAI and Anthropic are rushing to IPO to raise billions of dollars for their founders.
At the start of the aviation industry, planes regularly fell out of the skies. But we quickly realised that we needed to move more slowly, with strong regulatory oversight, to realise the potential of air travel. And flying now is the safest form of transport and the aviation industry is worth more than $1tn annually.
We could roll out AI in a similar, slower and more responsible way.

Gaza journalists pay heavy price after 3 years of Israeli war, with 263 killed
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
01:00:04 UTC
10:00:04 KST

Three years of Israel’s genocidal war in Gaza have exacted a devastating toll on Palestinian journalists, with 263 media workers killed and hundreds more wounded, detained or displaced, according to Palestinian authorities and journalism organizations.
Journalists have lost homes, workplaces and family members, with many moving between bombing sites, displacement camps and hospitals to continue reporting.
They remain the main source of on-the-ground coverage as Israel continues to bar foreign journalists from entering the territory.
263 media workers killed
Ismail al-Thawabta, director of the Gaza Government Media Office, told Anadolu that Israel had killed 263 journalists and media workers during the war.
He said 50 journalists had been detained in Israeli prisons, with 23 still in custody.
“Three journalists remain missing: Nidal Suheil al-Wahidi, Haitham Jamal Abdul Wahid and Ahmad Issam al-Agha,” he added.
Israeli attacks have damaged or destroyed 16 satellite television offices, 11 radio institutions, 12 newspaper and magazine offices, 23 digital media organizations, 27 printing houses and five union and rights organizations involved in media work, he said.
Al-Thawabta estimated losses to the media sector at about $1 billion, including premises, equipment, broadcast vehicles and technical devices.
On Sept. 7, the International Federation of Journalists said the journalist death toll in Gaza was the highest in modern journalism history, noting that it reviews and updates its lists as new information emerges.
More than a fifth of journalists killed
The Palestinian Journalists Syndicate said in earlier statements that 27 women journalists were among those killed, while nearly 500 journalists had been wounded.
The syndicate estimates that Gaza had about 1,200 journalists, meaning more than a fifth have been killed during the genocide.
It said between 60% and 75% of surviving journalists had lost their homes or been forcibly displaced, estimating the number affected at between 700 and 900.
More than 80% of media offices and institutions have been completely or partially destroyed, according to the syndicate.
The destruction has forced journalists to report from tents, displacement sites and areas surrounding hospitals amid shortages of electricity, internet access, protective equipment and cameras.
Deadly attacks in 2023
Anadolu’s monitoring documented a series of killings of journalists while they were working or present at reporting and displacement sites.
Bilal Jadallah, director general of Press House-Palestine, a nonprofit that supports the development of independent Palestinian media, was killed in November 2023 when an Israeli strike hit his vehicle in Gaza City.
Jadallah also helped establish the Sawa news agency and worked to train journalists and provide them with safety equipment.
In early December, Anadolu freelance cameraman Montaser al-Sawwaf was killed alongside his brother Marwan in Israeli airstrikes in the Gaza Strip.
Montaser, who had worked with Anadolu since 2014, had survived an attack on his family home two weeks earlier that killed his parents and several siblings. Despite injuries to his eye and nose, he continued reporting.
Born in 1990, he was married with two children and had studied journalism and media at Al-Aqsa University. His brother worked in documentary production.
Al Jazeera cameraman Samer Abu Daqqa died after a Dec. 15, 2023 drone strike at the Farhana school in Khan Younis, Gaza because emergency rescue crews were blocked from reaching him for over five hours
Although his family lived in Belgium, Abu Daqqa had chosen to remain in Gaza to continue his journalism.
Losses continued in 2024
Journalists Hamza al-Dahdouh and Mustafa Thuraya were killed in January 2024 when an Israeli strike hit their vehicle west of Khan Younis.
Hamza, the son of Al Jazeera’s Gaza bureau chief Wael al-Dahdouh, had lost his mother and siblings in an Israeli strike on a house sheltering the family in the Nuseirat refugee camp in October 2023.
Photojournalist Hassan Hamad, who worked with several media outlets, was killed in an Israeli strike in northern Gaza in October 2024.
His remains were taken to Kamal Adwan Hospital, where his brother identified him by his hair and press vest.
Journalists killed in tents and hospitals in 2025
Anadolu freelance journalist Saed Abu Nabhan was killed by an Israeli sniper on Jan. 10, 2025 while carrying out journalistic and humanitarian work in the Nuseirat refugee camp in central Gaza.
In June that year, an Israeli attack killed Palestine Today correspondent Suleiman Hajjaj, the channel’s cameraman Ismail Badah and Shams News editor Samir al-Rifai.
Journalist Youssef al-Nakhala of Al-Watania Media Agency died of wounds sustained in an Israeli strike on May 31.
On Aug. 10, an Israeli airstrike on a tent near Al-Shifa Hospital in western Gaza City killed six journalists, including Al Jazeera correspondents Anas al-Sharif and Mohammed Qreiqeh.
Al-Sharif became widely known for reporting on bombardment, starvation and displacement in northern Gaza, which faced intensive Israeli air and ground attacks early in the war.
Qreiqeh worked with local media before joining Al Jazeera. His mother was killed during the Israeli military’s assault on Al-Shifa Hospital in March 2024.
On Aug. 25, an Israeli strike on Nasser Hospital in Khan Younis killed five journalists while they were working: Mariam Abu Daqqa, Hossam al-Masri, Mohammed Salama, Moaz Abu Taha and Ahmad Abu Aziz.
Deaths after ceasefire
Government Media Office figures show that the death toll among Palestinian journalists rose from 254 to 263 after the ceasefire announced on Oct. 10, 2025.
On Oct. 12, the office documented the first journalist killing during the truce: Saleh al-Jaafarawi, who it said was shot by armed gangs linked to Israel while reporting in the Sabra neighborhood of southern Gaza City.
Journalists killed by the Israeli military in 2026 included Al Jazeera correspondent Mohammed Wishah in April and his brother Ahmad, a cameraman for the channel, on June 20.
Others included Amal al-Shamali, Anas Ghoneim, Abdul Raouf Shaat and Mohammed Qishta.
‘Journalism without walls’
Beyond the human toll, the genocide has fundamentally reshaped journalism in Gaza.
With homes, offices and equipment destroyed, many reporters and photographers have worked from displacement tents and hospital courtyards, moving with their families while carrying whatever equipment they could salvage.
The Palestinian Journalists’ Syndicate has described this reality as “journalism without walls,” reflecting the loss of hundreds of journalists’ homes and offices as they continue reporting from displacement sites.
Since October 2023, Israeli attacks have killed more than 74,000 Palestinians and wounded over 175,000 in Gaza. About 90% of the territory’s infrastructure has been destroyed.
Despite an October 2025 ceasefire agreement between Israel and the Palestinian group Hamas, Israeli attacks have since killed 1,454 Palestinians and wounded another 5,090, according to Gaza’s Health Ministry.

When Acoustic Control Needs to Move
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
01:00:00 UTC
10:00:00 KST

Acoustic design is often associated with permanent building elements, such as walls, roofs, ceilings, and insulation systems, which help control how sound travels through a space. However, not all noise sources or environments are permanent. A construction site changes as work progresses; machinery is replaced or relocated from one area to another; an industrial space may incorporate new equipment; and a temporary work area may emerge in a space that was never designed to accommodate it. Acoustic conditions are not static—they change over time and require solutions that can respond to these transformations. So, what happens when acoustic control becomes a flexible strategy?
Controlling sound does not always mean eliminating it. In many cases, the goal is to reduce sound transmission, contain it within a specific area, or minimize its impact on people working or living in the surrounding spaces. The challenge, however, arises when the source of the noise also moves. For example, introducing new machinery or modifying production lines in industrial environments can alter existing acoustic conditions without making it feasible to reconstruct the space each time a change occurs.
In these situations, portable solutions introduce a different approach by bringing acoustic control to where the sound is produced rather than permanently modifying the building envelope. Temporary barriers, acoustic blankets, curtains, and portable enclosures, such as those offered by Acoustical Surfaces, can act as a second layer that is installed, repositioned, or removed according to the needs of each space. These solutions can complement permanent acoustic strategies, transforming sound control into an adaptable element that can respond to changing conditions.
How to Design Spaces Intended to Change
When designing mobile acoustic systems, it is possible to recognize that certain needs are temporary. An intervention lasting only a few weeks does not necessarily require a permanent modification to the building. Similarly, a factory that regularly reorganizes its operations can work with elements that accommodate these changes without becoming obstacles to future configurations.
Acoustical Surfaces offers a range of solutions—including barriers, blankets, curtains, and enclosure systems—that can be used to create acoustic control zones around specific noise sources or temporarily separate areas within larger spaces. Beyond their acoustic properties, dimensions, or material composition, these systems make it possible to introduce layers of sound control according to the specific conditions of each situation. An acoustic curtain can establish a temporary separation; a barrier can define a work area; a blanket can help contain or reduce sound transmission around a specific source; and a portable enclosure can transform the conditions of a particular area without altering the space that contains it. Understood as temporary envelopes, these elements can act as lightweight infrastructure, modifying the acoustic performance of a space without architecturally redefining it.
For example, Acoustical Surfaces' Indoor Soundproof Quilted Acoustic Curtains combine sound absorption and sound blocking through flexible, modular designs. Custom-made to suit specific applications, they feature a dense mass-loaded vinyl core, available in 1- or 2-pound-per-square-foot densities, enclosed on both sides by a durable, quilted, sound-absorbing material. Suitable for industrial, commercial, and even residential applications, the curtains are often used to isolate machinery, separate noisy work areas, or create movable acoustic barriers. Designed for demanding environments, they are resistant to water and chemicals and can be easily installed, removed, and reconfigured as needs change.
How to Design Acoustics Without Compromising Flexibility
From acting studios to workplaces, portable solutions can transform not only the experience of a space but also the routines of its users. At Open Shop Studio, Acoustical Surfaces' STOP-25 fiberglass quilted curtain panels were installed to provide acoustic separation. The panels had a Sound Transmission Coefficient (STC) rating of 26 and absorbed sound on both sides. A track system was combined with interconnected panels joined by vertical Velcro seams, allowing the room to be transformed into a larger open space, divided into several smaller rooms, or configured to combine both conditions.
But this is not the only example of how design flexibility can intersect with acoustic design. In office environments, creating acoustic barriers between workers can sometimes be necessary to optimize workflows while achieving the desired levels of comfort and well-being. At Zamboni's office, however, the acoustic barrier could not be a permanent addition; it needed to be easily removable. The use of BSC-25 quilted acoustic curtains, featuring a 1-inch (2.5-centimeter) black steel tube frame that rests on the floor and a 1/8-inch (3-millimeter) thick high-density vinyl core, provided sound blocking comparable to that of a conventional 2-by-4-inch wood-stud wall with drywall panels on both sides. The screens were fabricated with the curtain material extending beyond the frame, allowing one panel to overlap and connect with the next.
Expanding the way acoustic design is understood means recognizing that not every challenge in contemporary spaces is permanent. While walls, ceilings, and insulation materials remain fundamental to establishing a building's overall acoustic conditions, mobile solutions such as those offered by Acoustical Surfaces can also address situations that cannot be fully anticipated during the design process. In response to this reality, architecture can rely not only on elements that remain in place, but also on systems that know when to arrive, where to be positioned, and when to be removed. Acoustic control thus becomes more than simply constructing barriers against sound; it becomes a strategy that can accompany the movement, transformation, and temporality of spaces.

‘I’m getting fed up’: Early US midterm voters line up before dawn in Ohio
- - Early voting began in Ohio before dawn, and Democrats outnumbered Republicans on day one in Medina County, suggesting stronger motivation ahead of the 2026 midterms.
- - Voters voiced anger over high prices, political ads, and the US war with Iran, with many blaming Donald Trump for worsening economy and endless conflict.
- - Ohio’s Senate and two House races are tight toss-ups, and independents may decide control of Congress as both parties fight for votes.
AI generated
MEDINA, Ohio – Voters started lining up while it was still dark on the morning of Oct 6 at the Medina County Board of Elections as early voting began in Ohio, a state that looms large in the nationwide campaigns between Republicans and Democrats battling for control of the US Congress.
By the time polling in the north-east Ohio county closed for the day, the Democrats’ turnout eclipsed that of Republicans in a possible early sign that they are more motivated to vote in 2026.
Though turnout is typically higher in presidential elections, which are run every four years, the 2026 midterm voters in Ohio have a say in one key US Senate race and two for the US House of Representatives that are seen as “toss-ups”, according to the Cook Political Report.
Registered Republicans, Democrats and independents interviewed by Reuters all shared similar frustrations: They are exhausted by political ads they see as deceptive and mean, they hate the US war with Iran, and they really hate the inflation that they believe has become chronic.
Nobody said they expected things to improve any time soon.
The third person in line waiting for polling to open at 8am local time was Eddie St John, 83, a retiree from the town of Wadsworth. Asked what he most wanted to see fixed as a result of the election, which ends on Nov 3, St John said: “Mostly it’s our economy. It sucks.”
“You can’t afford nothing any more. Everything’s so high. Gas is getting worse all the time,” he said, adding, “This guy in office now, he promises this, he promises that... (but) nothing’s coming down.”
“This guy,” St John said, is US President Donald Trump, who is not on the ballot but whom St John blames more than political parties.
Inflation, war on ballot
The party in power usually suffers in midterm elections. With Republicans holding the White House and both chambers of Congress at a time when Trump’s approval rating is at a record low of 32%, Democrats are feeling increasingly competitive.
Political analysts will be watching closely what unfolds in Ohio, as Trump has been a dominant force, especially among blue-collar workers who used to align with the Democratic Party.
But with inflation running at around 3.4%, there is deep discontent over rising food, energy and housing costs. The US war with Iran, launched by Trump on Feb 28 for reasons that critics say he has not clearly articulated, also has voters worried that it will become yet another “forever war”.
Troy Flohr, 59, a retired policeman with the Medina County Sheriff, complained about the array of campaign ads that he said were riddled with “half-truths”.
Standing just feet away from a voting booth, Flohr said he usually backs Republicans but was still undecided whether to vote to re-elect Republican Representative Max Miller for a third term. “I tend to like the rest of them” running as Republicans on the 2026 ballot, Flohr added.
He said his nephew is serving in the US Army and stationed in the Middle East.
Without mentioning Trump by name, he said: “I’m tired of him saying the war’s going to end in two weeks, the war’s going to end next month... I’m getting fed up with that.”
Yet, Flohr said he would “probably” vote for Trump again, given the chance. “I don’t like where the Democrat Party has gone. I’m going to leave the rest of that comment alone,” he said when asked to elaborate.
Independents
Trump won Ohio and the state’s 17 electoral votes handily in 2016, 2020 and 2024 despite losing the 2020 presidential race to Democrat Joe Biden.
This election could depend on whether disaffected Democrats return to their party and whether many independents turn their backs on Trump’s Republicans.
Medina County, seen as a swing district, has 132,345 registered voters, of whom 29,466 are Republicans and 15,872 are Democrats. Election officials say there are 86,762 independents who could determine whether Republicans continue their success there.
Despite Republicans’ advantage in registered voters in the county, 499 Democrats cast ballots on Oct 6, compared with 374 Republicans, along with 291 independents.
That is a significant reversal from the first day of voting in 2024, when 369 Democrats voted, compared with 702 Republicans and 433 independents, according to county data.
Even more telling is data from the 2022 midterm election, when 198 Republicans cast a vote on the first day of early voting, compared with 139 Democrats and 68 independents.
Senate seat in play
Former senator Sherrod Brown, a Democrat from Ohio, is trying to return to the Senate, where he served for 18 years before being defeated two years ago by Republican Senator Bernie Moreno.
This time around, Brown, a populist Democrat who has long railed against US trade deals with foreign competitors, is attempting to unseat Republican Jon Husted in a special election, with the winner holding the seat through 2028.
Political analysts see the race between Husted and Brown as a toss-up.
With Republicans currently holding a 53-47 majority in the Senate, Democrats are hoping for a net gain of at least four seats, including in Ohio, in order to control the Chamber.
Close House races
Meanwhile, two neck-and-neck US House races could help determine the 2026 majority in that Chamber, which Republicans currently hold with a 218-214 margin. One independent is aligned with Republicans and there are two vacancies that will be filled in the midterm elections.
In the seventh congressional district, which includes Medina, just south of Cleveland, incumbent Miller is seen facing a tough challenge from Democrat Brian Poindexter.
While Miller has raised far more funds than his Democratic opponent and has Trump’s endorsement in a Republican-leaning district, his campaign has been hit by allegations of domestic violence, which he denies.
Poindexter is a labour union ironworker and member of a suburban city council.
Meanwhile, in Ohio’s ninth congressional district that covers most of north-west Ohio and hugs the shores of Lake Erie, Democratic Representative Marcy Kaptur, a moderate who was first elected in 1982, is battling in another toss-up race against Republican challenger Derek Merrin, who nearly defeated her in 2024.
Annie Wild, 64, a retired public schoolteacher, said she will vote for all Democrats on the ballot.
She also said that since the early days of Trump’s second term, she has begun to see some of the President’s supporters saying they are abandoning him. But that is not coming from the voters she calls “MAGA (Make America Great Again)”.
“I’ve lost friends that I’ve had for 50 years,” she said of some Trump supporters, because of the gulf between them. REUTERS

October 7: Hamas’s profit-and-loss statement - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
01:00:00 UTC
10:00:00 KST

On August 3, Ghazi Hamad, a member of Hamas’s political bureau, sat across from Piers Morgan for a half-hour interview. Most viewers remember the denial. Hamad said he was “100%” confident that Hamas never committed crimes against civilians, and that whatever happened at the Nova music festival, in the kibbutzim, and in the homes set on fire was, at most, a “mistake” by individuals.
The denial was shocking, and rightly so. It was also the predictable part of the interview. The important part came some 15 minutes later, when Morgan asked whether October 7 had been a strategic failure, given what it brought down on Gaza.
Hamad conceded that “we paid a big price” and moved straight to the profit column. Israel is isolated. Its prime minister is wanted by the International Criminal Court. And, in his words, “All the world now, they put the Palestinian cause on the table.”
Before October 7, he said, there were only Security Council meetings and Arab statements that changed nothing on the ground. Now there are “strategic achievements.” He closed the answer by saying Hamas had not changed.
This was a profit-and-loss statement, delivered by one of the people who signed off on the investment.
The massacre dividend
For Hamas, the massacre was an investment. The killing, the rape, and the abductions were meant to provoke a harsh Israeli response, the images from Gaza that followed, and the international pressure those images would generate. Call it the massacre dividend: the political return a terrorist organization extracts from its own atrocity once the world translates it into urgency to “solve the issue.”
Gazans paid the price. Hamad himself left the Gaza Strip before October 7 and never went back, as he acknowledged in the same interview. The dividend is being collected in European capitals, and Washington may be next.
Whoever rewards a massacre with statehood is inviting the next one, and not only in Israel. Paris and London are within range as well.
The Israeli wall
On the Israeli side, the picture is the reverse. The Jerusalem Center for Security and Foreign Affairs has measured public opinion seven consecutive times over 30 months. Opposition to a Palestinian state has held steady at 64% to 68% of the public, and at 75% among Jewish respondents in the latest wave. Total support, including conditional support tied to recognition and demilitarization, has not exceeded 25% in any survey.
One figure is rising sharply. Concern about an October 7-style attack from Judea and Samaria climbed from 62% in February 2025 to 77% in September 2026. Even among left-wing respondents, a majority now shares that concern.
A poll captures attitudes at a given moment and cannot predict how the public will respond to sustained pressure. But three years on, this is no longer post-traumatic shock. Israelis understood Hamad’s sentence better than most of the West: a state established now would be credited to the massacre.
Pressure from outside
Europe reads the same map and draws the opposite conclusion. In September 2025, the European Commission proposed suspending part of Israel’s trade preferences under the EU-Israel Association Agreement. The proposal stalled, and Spain’s attempt to revive it in spring 2026 ran into broad opposition. Yet the economic lever is now legitimate in Brussels, and it has advanced alongside a wave of European recognitions of a Palestinian state. All this on a continent where the Islamist voice, in the street and at the ballot box, grows louder every year.
In Washington, the process is slower, but it cuts across party lines. If Democrats retake Congress in November’s midterms, the wing that wants to condition aid to Israel and impose sanctions will gain committees, budgets, and a platform.
And on the same Morgan episode, Joe Kent, former director of the National Counterterrorism Center, called for ending American funding of Israel and spoke of a new political movement on the Right. By 2028, the issue will be on every candidate’s desk.
Hamad was right about one thing: the issue is back on the table. The question is who will pay for it, the slaughtered or the slaughterers.
What is required
For anyone who still believes a Palestinian state would end the conflict, Hamad supplied the answer in the same interview. When Morgan told him he supports a two-state solution and a full Palestinian state, Hamad shot back: “So why should Israel exist?”
At the end of the interview, when asked three times for a yes or no on whether he still believes Israel should be annihilated, he would not say no. Instead, he called Israel “a big burden on the shoulder of the world” and said the world “should reconsider the existence of Israel.”
For Hamas, a Palestinian state is a stage. The destination has not moved.
Jerusalem must stop treating recognitions of a Palestinian state as symbolic gestures, and should put Hamad’s words before every international forum: Hamas itself is declaring that recognition is a reward for October 7. European capitals must understand that every economic measure against Israel tied to the demand for statehood is recorded in Gaza as a return on the investment.
In Washington, in both camps, anyone who talks about sanctions should answer one question: How much is he willing to pay an organization that has openly admitted the massacre was worth it?
The writer is the communication director of the Jerusalem Center for Security and Foreign Affairs (JCFA) and a former senior editor in Israeli and international media.

When Acoustic Control Needs to Move
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
01:00:00 UTC
10:00:00 KST

Acoustic design is often associated with permanent building elements, such as walls, roofs, ceilings, and insulation systems, which help control how sound travels through a space. However, not all noise sources or environments are permanent. A construction site changes as work progresses; machinery is replaced or relocated from one area to another; an industrial space may incorporate new equipment; and a temporary work area may emerge in a space that was never designed to accommodate it. Acoustic conditions are not static—they change over time and require solutions that can respond to these transformations. So, what happens when acoustic control becomes a flexible strategy?
Controlling sound does not always mean eliminating it. In many cases, the goal is to reduce sound transmission, contain it within a specific area, or minimize its impact on people working or living in the surrounding spaces. The challenge, however, arises when the source of the noise also moves. For example, introducing new machinery or modifying production lines in industrial environments can alter existing acoustic conditions without making it feasible to reconstruct the space each time a change occurs.
In these situations, portable solutions introduce a different approach by bringing acoustic control to where the sound is produced rather than permanently modifying the building envelope. Temporary barriers, acoustic blankets, curtains, and portable enclosures, such as those offered by Acoustical Surfaces, can act as a second layer that is installed, repositioned, or removed according to the needs of each space. These solutions can complement permanent acoustic strategies, transforming sound control into an adaptable element that can respond to changing conditions.
How to Design Spaces Intended to Change
When designing mobile acoustic systems, it is possible to recognize that certain needs are temporary. An intervention lasting only a few weeks does not necessarily require a permanent modification to the building. Similarly, a factory that regularly reorganizes its operations can work with elements that accommodate these changes without becoming obstacles to future configurations.
Acoustical Surfaces offers a range of solutions—including barriers, blankets, curtains, and enclosure systems—that can be used to create acoustic control zones around specific noise sources or temporarily separate areas within larger spaces. Beyond their acoustic properties, dimensions, or material composition, these systems make it possible to introduce layers of sound control according to the specific conditions of each situation. An acoustic curtain can establish a temporary separation; a barrier can define a work area; a blanket can help contain or reduce sound transmission around a specific source; and a portable enclosure can transform the conditions of a particular area without altering the space that contains it. Understood as temporary envelopes, these elements can act as lightweight infrastructure, modifying the acoustic performance of a space without architecturally redefining it.
For example, Acoustical Surfaces' Indoor Soundproof Quilted Acoustic Curtains combine sound absorption and sound blocking through flexible, modular designs. Custom-made to suit specific applications, they feature a dense mass-loaded vinyl core, available in 1- or 2-pound-per-square-foot densities, enclosed on both sides by a durable, quilted, sound-absorbing material. Suitable for industrial, commercial, and even residential applications, the curtains are often used to isolate machinery, separate noisy work areas, or create movable acoustic barriers. Designed for demanding environments, they are resistant to water and chemicals and can be easily installed, removed, and reconfigured as needs change.
How to Design Acoustics Without Compromising Flexibility
From acting studios to workplaces, portable solutions can transform not only the experience of a space but also the routines of its users. At Open Shop Studio, Acoustical Surfaces' STOP-25 fiberglass quilted curtain panels were installed to provide acoustic separation. The panels had a Sound Transmission Coefficient (STC) rating of 26 and absorbed sound on both sides. A track system was combined with interconnected panels joined by vertical Velcro seams, allowing the room to be transformed into a larger open space, divided into several smaller rooms, or configured to combine both conditions.
But this is not the only example of how design flexibility can intersect with acoustic design. In office environments, creating acoustic barriers between workers can sometimes be necessary to optimize workflows while achieving the desired levels of comfort and well-being. At Zamboni's office, however, the acoustic barrier could not be a permanent addition; it needed to be easily removable. The use of BSC-25 quilted acoustic curtains, featuring a 1-inch (2.5-centimeter) black steel tube frame that rests on the floor and a 1/8-inch (3-millimeter) thick high-density vinyl core, provided sound blocking comparable to that of a conventional 2-by-4-inch wood-stud wall with drywall panels on both sides. The screens were fabricated with the curtain material extending beyond the frame, allowing one panel to overlap and connect with the next.
Expanding the way acoustic design is understood means recognizing that not every challenge in contemporary spaces is permanent. While walls, ceilings, and insulation materials remain fundamental to establishing a building's overall acoustic conditions, mobile solutions such as those offered by Acoustical Surfaces can also address situations that cannot be fully anticipated during the design process. In response to this reality, architecture can rely not only on elements that remain in place, but also on systems that know when to arrive, where to be positioned, and when to be removed. Acoustic control thus becomes more than simply constructing barriers against sound; it becomes a strategy that can accompany the movement, transformation, and temporality of spaces.

Cornell names former acting US attorney-general to lead review on rape allegations

Cornell names former acting US attorney-general to lead review on rape allegations
Debra Kamin
- Cornell University has appointed Sally Yates to lead an independent review of a former student’s rape claim and the school’s sexual assault policies.
- The case has caused anger after Jane Doe sued Cornell, saying it mishandled her report and failed to investigate properly after an alleged 2024 fraternity assault.
- Yates will review support and investigation rules, while state and campus probes continue; the case has renewed national debate on campus sexual assault.
AI generated
Cornell University named Sally Yates, the former acting US attorney-general, on Oct 6 to lead an independent internal review of a former student’s rape claim amid growing outrage about how it was first handled.
Yates, 62, will also examine the school’s policies related to sexual assault allegations, including how they are investigated and what support is given to students, the university said in a statement.
Anne Smalling, the head of the committee that hired Yates, told The New York Times that the university was obligated to the woman who had filed the rape complaint.
“We owe it to her and to our community to take a hard look at what happened so that we can determine what we can do better around both prevention and response,” she said.
Yates and the white-collar law firm King and Spalding, where she is a partner, will “have independence in conducting the review”, Cornell said in a statement on Oct 6.
Students and politicians have demanded answers from Cornell after the former student sued the university, seven men, a fraternity and her sorority in September, claiming she was sexually assaulted in October 2024 at a fraternity party. She claimed the university allowed a culture to flourish that led to the assault, and then did not conduct a thorough and proper investigation after she alerted campus police.
Her claims have set off a wave of shock and anger across the country and renewed national conversations over sexual assault on college campuses.
Three weeks after the incident in 2024, the woman, identified as Jane Doe in court papers, filed a report with campus police, which was then passed to the Tompkins County district attorney, who declined to file charges.
All of the men have denied any wrongdoing. None of the men have been charged with a crime. Their fraternity, Chi Phi, has been banned from campus.
The university, though, conducted its own months-long investigation, which includes more than 1,000 pages of transcripts, text messages, hours of interviews with a dozen people and the woman’s statement to police, which she signed.
A three-member panel at the school met on Zoom over 12 days in May 2025 and expelled two men, barred one who had graduated from campus, suspended two and gave lighter punishments to the rest, according to the documents.
The panel did not conclude that Jane Doe was sexually assaulted by all the men she had accused, according to discipline summaries reviewed by the Times.
The district attorney, Matthew Van Houten, has said that the Cornell University Police Department forwarded only a six-page summary to him. But, according to the records, the police did offer Van Houten more evidence to review, but he declined to do so.
Governor Kathy Hochul rebuked Van Houten on Oct 1 and appointed the state’s attorney-general, Letitia James, to review the evidence and determine whether criminal charges should be filed.
It is a common practice for universities to turn to outside law firms when faced with a significant public scandal, and the reactions to those inquiries have typically been mixed.
In 2011, Penn State hired former Federal Bureau of Investigation director Louis Freeh of the firm Freeh, Sporkin & Sullivan to identify what the university might have known about the allegations of child abuse against Jerry Sandusky, a former assistant football coach.
Freeh delivered a damning indictment that declared several leaders had known about the abuse and concealed it from law enforcement. Critics said he had overstepped his mandate.
Columbia University also commissioned Joan Loughnane, a partner at Sidley Austin, to conduct an external investigation into the school’s handling of sexual abuse allegations made against former Columbia gynaecologist Robert Hadden in 2012. In her findings, released in 2026, Loughnane documented systematic failures by administrators to address his abuse, but the university was criticised for the slow process of the report.
Yates is a high-profile choice for a role that will inevitably be deeply scrutinised. She previously led the US Soccer Federation’s investigation into allegations of abuse and misconduct in women’s professional soccer, and currently leads King and Spalding’s crisis management practice.
She has spent nearly four decades with the Department of Justice. She became assistant US attorney for the northern district of Georgia, her home state, in 1989 and rose through the ranks to become the first woman to lead that office in 2010.
She became deputy US attorney-general in 2015 under then President Barack Obama.
In that role, she wrote a policy memo, known as the Yates memo, redefining how the country prosecutes white-collar criminals.
In 2017, just days after accepting the role of acting attorney-general under then President Donald Trump, she was fired for refusing to enforce the president’s immigration ban. NYTIMES
- This article originally appeared in The New York Times.

NATO membership for Ukraine ‘not on the table’ – Rubio
NATO membership for Ukraine is not currently under consideration, as Washington is focused on ending the conflict between Kiev and Moscow, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio has said.
Asked about Washington’s stance on Ukraine's bid to join the US-led military bloc during a joint press conference with Icelandic Foreign Minister Thorgerdur Katrin Gunnarsdottir in Reykjavik on Tuesday, Rubio said “there’s no yes-or-no answer to that.”

Ukraine has made NATO membership a key foreign policy objective since the Western-backed Maidan coup in Kiev in 2014, eventually enshrining the goal in its constitution. In September 2022, Vladimir Zelensky formally applied for “accelerated accession” to the bloc.
NATO has never set a timetable for Ukraine’s admission, however, and several member states have opposed the move.
US President Donald Trump has repeatedly ruled out Ukraine joining NATO as part of a potential peace settlement. Ahead of his February 2025 White House meeting with Zelensky, which descended into a heated exchange, Trump told reporters: “NATO – you can forget about.”
The Trump administration has recently intensified its diplomatic push to resolve the Ukraine conflict, with the president’s envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner visiting Moscow and Kiev last month for talks with both sides.
Russia has cited Kiev’s NATO ambitions among the key reasons for the Ukraine conflict, describing the bloc’s eastward expansion as a major threat to its national security.

French European Parliament member Rima Hassan said Tuesday that she removed an Israeli flag at a European Parliament event in France to protest the genocide in the Gaza Strip, violations of international law and "unbearable double standards."
